en: The forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Seizing of the King's Horse. ||49||
The fifty-fifth chapter.
Śeṣa said:
Then Rāmānuja, having arrived with speed, [addressed] his own servants.
He asked, "Where is that most beautiful sacrificial horse? ||1||
Then those of great strength spoke these words to Śatrughna:
"We do not know which soldiers have come to the city leading the horse. (2)
We have all been treated with contempt by the powerful royal servants;
in this matter regarding what ought to be done, the Blessed One is our authority. (3)
Having heard those words of theirs, Śatrughna became exceedingly enraged;
out of fury, he gnashed his teeth and repeatedly licked them with his tongue.
The hero said: "Having seized my horse, where will you go?
Now I shall strike down this city along with its people with my arrows. (5)
Having said this, he spoke to Sumati: "Whose city is this?
Who is its ruler whom I have carried off? (6)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of the king, which were filled with anger, the minister spoke with a fine voice and distinct syllables. (7)
Know this most enchanting city by the name of Kuṇḍala;
in it dwells the righteous and powerful Kṣatriya Suratha. (8)
Constantly devoted to dharma, he was a servant of the two feet of Rāma;
like Hanumān, he was a servant with his mind, his actions, and his speech. ||9||
Hundreds of practitioners of dharma follow his conduct;
Suratha possesses a great force of followers and is most excellent in every way. (10)
If this best of steeds were taken away, a great battle would ensue here;
many heroes skilled in the forest would fall. (11)
Having heard what was thus spoken, Śatrughna,
the best among speakers, addressed his minister once more with these words.
Śatrughna said:
"What should be done here if Rāma’s horse has been seized by him? He does not come to fight our powerful army, which is inhabited by heroes. (13)
Sumati said:
"O great king, let an eloquent messenger be dispatched to the king, so that by his words the best among the powerful may come with his army. (14)
Otherwise, if he has been seized by some arrogant person either through ignorance or intentionally, he will surely restore to us the auspicious horse, the best of sacrifices. (15)
Having heard those words, the wise and powerful Śatrughna replied with these humble words to Aṅgada: 16.
Śatrughna said:
"Go to the great city of Suratha, which is nearby,
and having gone there as a messenger, speak thus to the king."
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, you have seized Rāma’s vehicle;
let it be returned to him, or else come forth for battle accompanied by your heroes. (18)
Just as Rāma performed the mission to Laṅkā against Rāvaṇa, so too did he [Buddha], endowed with wisdom, act toward the one accompanied by a force consisting mostly of Kurus. (19)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this, O hero, Gada addressed the lord of the earth with the word "Om" and departed into the midst of the assembly, which was filled with ranks of warriors.
He beheld King Asuratha, wearing a garland of tulasī,
as Rāmabhadra spoke with his tongue to his own servants.
The king, too, having seen the monkey who possessed a captivating form,
and considering him to be the messenger of Śatrughna, spoke to the son of Vālī.
Suratha said:
"O Lord of Monkeys, why have you come here? How are you?
Tell me the entire reason, so that having understood it, I may act accordingly. (23)
Śeṣa said:
As he was speaking thus, the lord of monkeys replied to that king who had performed service to Rāma, his mind filled with great wonder. (24)
O best of kings, know me to be the son of Vālin and lord of monkeys;
I have been sent into your presence by Śatrughna for the purpose of a messenger.
"O King, some of my servants have now come and seized my horse; acting out of ignorance, they have suddenly committed a great injustice. (26)
Filled with joy, [he gave] that horse along with the kingdom and his sons; [then] having prostrated at the feet of Śatrughna, he quickly said: "Please depart. (27)
With your body wounded by the iron arrows discharged by Chaturghna,
you shall lie adorning the surface of the earth with your head severed.
Where will you go after having stolen the sacrificial horse of him by whom the Lord of Laṅkā was brought to ruin in an instant as if in play? (29)
Śeṣa said:
To him who was speaking these words and others, the Lord of the Earth replied:
"Everything you say is true; nothing false has been spoken by you. (30)
But listen further to my words, O servant at the feet of Śatrughna:
I have been seized by the great thief Rāmacandra, the wise one. (31)
"I shall not flee at all from the fear of Śatrughna and the others, provided that Rāma himself comes and grants me his sight. (32)
Then, because my feet have become swollen, I shall go accompanied by my son, along with my entire kingdom, family, wealth, grain, and great army. (33)
This is the duty of Kṣatriyas; it is not even contradicted by their master, for even there, Rāma desired a battle fought according to righteousness.
"Now, having defeated those great heroes, Śatrughna and the others, in even a moment, I shall bind them in my house—provided that Rāma does not return. (35)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this, the wise Gada then spoke these great words, endowed with supreme fortitude, to King Ajahāsa. (36)
Aṅgada said:
"Devoid of wisdom, you speak thus because of your old age and your arrival;
that you, though powerful, should reproach King Śatrughna with such a mind. (37)
He who effortlessly slew the Daitya Lavaṇa, the enemy of Dhātṛ, and by whom many powerful and arrogant foes were conquered in battle. (38)
O Lord of Heroes, struck by Vidyunmālin’s weapon, this Rākṣasa, mounted upon his wish-fulfilling chariot, appears to me as one devoid of intelligence, for you have bound him. (39)
His brother’s son was the exceedingly powerful Puṣkala, a master of supreme weapons,
by whom Vīrabhadra— the leader of Rudra’s host— was thoroughly gratified in battle.
Shall I describe his valor and mighty strength, by which he has no equal on earth in power, fame, or splendor? (41)
Hanumān, whose mind was fixed upon the lotus feet of the Lord of the Raghus in his presence—he whose many heroic deeds have been heard by you. (42)
By him, the city of the Rākṣasas on Laṅkā was forcibly burnt in an instant;
by him, Akṣa, the son of the evil-minded lord of the Rākṣasas, was slain. (43)
The mountain named Droṇa, by the tip of whose tail he has repeatedly brought deities for the sake of sustaining the lives of his soldiers. 44.
Rāma alone knows his conduct; no other of deluded intellect knows it—this lord of monkeys, your servant, whom you do not forget even for a moment from your heart. (45)
All those lords of monkeys, headed by Sugrīva, who could swallow the entire earth,
now served King Śatrughna, eager for his very sight.
Kuśadhvaja, Nīlaratna, Riputāpa, who was skilled in great weapons, Pratāpāgrya, Subāhu, Vimala, and likewise Sumada. (47)
King Vīramaṇi, endowed with truthfulness and a servant of Rāma—these and other kings, lords of the earth, wait upon him. 48.
In that matter, O hero, you are like a mere gnat compared to the ocean; who indeed are you?
Having understood that, go, accompanied by your sons, to the compassionate Śatrughna. (49)
Having entrusted me to the lotus-eyed Rāma, you have made your own body fruitful;
indeed, you have been born with purpose.
Śeṣa said:
The king spoke to that messenger who was speaking in many ways:
"Show these [beings] to me quickly; let them all come within my range of vision. (51)
O messenger, such is my strength as that of Hanumān;
he who, placing Rāma behind him, went forth for the protection of the sacrifice.
If I worship Him with my mind, speech, and actions, filled with longing, He will quickly reveal His own form within my heart. (53)
Otherwise, the heroes headed by Hanumān would have forcibly bound you, or they would have seized you along with the essence of the Vāhana, being filled with devotion. 54.
"Go, O enemy-slayer of kings, and tell my words to him:
'Let the great warriors prepare; I am eager for battle.'"
Having reflected, he will act as is appropriate on the field of battle;
I shall release the great steed and take the nine [arrows] from you. ||56||
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this and smiling, the hero went to where the king was;
having arrived, he reported exactly what Suratha had said.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Suratha and the Messenger," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
(51) The fifty-first chapter.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard those words spoken by Suratha from the mouth of Aṅgada,
all those skilled in battle, stationed upon their chariots, prepared themselves for the fight.
The sound of kettledrums arose, as did the roar of drums;
the shouts of the warriors resounded throughout the field of battle. ||2||
The entire world was pervaded by the sound of the rattling of chariots and the trumpeting of elephants; that great roar reached unto heaven. ||3||
Endowed with enthusiasm for battle, heroes skilled in combat utter various cries that strike terror into the cowardly. ||4||
When such a clamor had arisen, the king named Suratha, surrounded by his sons and soldiers, then advanced onto the field of battle. (5)
He was seen by the soldiers making the earth full with elephants, chariots, horses, and throngs of foot-soldiers, as if flooding it like the ocean.
Seeing him prepared for battle, resounding with the blast of conchs and likewise with shouts of victory, the king spoke to Sumati.
Śatrughna said:
"This king has arrived, surrounded by a vast army.
O high-minded one, tell us what our duty is in this matter. (8)
Sumati said:
"In this matter, one must fight against many heroes who are skilled with the bow, such as Puṣkala and others, who are exceedingly fierce and proficient in all weapons and missiles. (9)
Let Subala, the son of Samīra, who possesses supreme valor and is skilled in the warfare of others, engage in battle with the king. (10)
Śeṣa said:
Even as the great minister was speaking thus, the sons of the king,
arrogant in spirit, drew their bows straight upon the field of battle.
Seeing them, the very powerful warriors headed by Puṣkala, who were fierce in battle, advanced in their own chariots with bows and arrows in hand. ||12||
The great hero Campaka, Puṣkala, who was highly skilled in supreme weapons,
fought in single combat with that illustrious great hero.
The son of Janaka, together with Kuśadhvaja, fought against Mohaka;
while Subāhu fought against the invincible Vimala, who was difficult to restrain.
Aṅgada was [conquered] by Pratāpin, Bala by Apratāpāgrya, Nīlaratna by Haryakṣa, and Satyavān by Sahadeva. (15)
The powerful King Vīramaṇi fought with Bhūrideva;
and Ugrāśva, accompanied by his army, fought with Asutāpa.
Those experts in combat engaged in a great duel on chariots;
all were skilled in weapons and missiles, and all were proficient in the art of war. ||17||
O best of sages, as the battle thus proceeded with the sons of Suratha, a great slaughter took place there at that time.
Puṣkala said to Campaka: "O prince, what is your name?
You are fortunate indeed, that you have come into the midst of battle with me. (19)
Stay now! Why do you flee? How could your life continue?
Come and fight with me, O you who are skilled in all weapons and missiles! (20)
Having heard these words spoken by him, the powerful and heroic prince spoke to Puṣkala with a voice as deep as a thundercloud. (21)
Campaka said:
"This battle here shall not take place between two who are nameless;
nevertheless, I shall tell you my own name, preceded by its power. (22)
My mother is remembered as Rāghaveśī, and my father is remembered as Rāghava;
my brother-in-law is Rāmacandra, and my kinsman is Rāghava. 23.
Mannāma, Rāmadāsa, and Sadārāma, the servant of Rāma—may Rāma, who bestows grace upon his devotees, deliver me from battle. ||24||
Adopting the common view of the world, I shall now speak:
I am the son of Suratha, and my mother is Vīravatī.
Indeed, that which is called "man" prepares all things beautifully during the spring;
yet those deluded by honey abandon the dwelling of nectar, the drink of honey. (26)
O Hero, know that my enchanting form, which bears the body of a linga in its center and is like gold in color, is designated by that very name. 27.
Fight with arrows in the battle; for indeed, no one is capable of conquering me.
Now I shall display my own wonderful prowess. 28.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these great words, Puṣkala was delighted in his heart;
considering him difficult to conquer, he remained in the battle discharging arrows. (29)
As Puṣkala advanced, discharging a multitude of arrows by the millions, Campaka, filled with rage, then strung his bow. (30)
He released sharp arrows capable of rending the hosts of enemies,
marked with his own name and equipped with gold-tufted shafts.
The great hero Puṣkala cut them down on the field of battle,
discharging everywhere a darkness of arrows with shafts whetted on stone.
Seeing his own arrow severed by the hero Campaka, Puṣkala, filled with rage, challenged that powerful warrior. (33)
Saying again in the midst of the battle, "Do not flee,
abandoning the fray," he swiftly pierced Puṣkala in the heart with ten arrows.
Indeed, those arrows of Puṣkala, possessing fierce velocity, having arrived and struck deep into his heart, drank his abundant blood. (35)
Pained by those arrows, the hero, out of great wrath, took up five shafts with very sharp points, as if to ward off mountains.
Then those powerful arrows of his and the other's,
having been drawn in the sky, were severed by the son of the King into a hundred streams.
Having severed those extremely sharp-pointed arrows,
the powerful son of the Earth (Balarāma) took up a hundred excellent arrows to strike him in the heart.
Those arrows, severed in a hundred ways by the high-souled Puṣkala,
fell upon the edge of the battlefield, tormented by the force of his shafts.
Then, seeing that great feat of the king's son,
the powerful [Ghaṭotkaca] struck him clearly in the chest with a thousand arrows.
Puṣkala, an expert in supreme weapons, swiftly cut those down as well; then once more, he quickly fixed ten thousand arrows upon his own bow.
Puṣkala, the knower of supreme missiles, swiftly cut those down as well;
then, becoming exceedingly enraged, he unleashed a rain of arrows.
Perceiving that downpour of arrows as it arrived, Campaka-vīra-han struck Puṣkala, who was exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! ||43||
Seeing the Campaka tree endowed with great power, Puṣkala,
who was skilled in all weapons, fixed Brahmā’s missile upon his own bow.
That great weapon, discharged by him, blazed forth through the ten directions;
pervading the sky and the two worlds, heaven and earth, it was intent upon bringing about the dissolution of the universe.
Seeing that Campaka had released his weapon, he who was skilled in all weapons discharged that very same weapon to counteract his adversary who was intent on attack. (46)
People considered the fire of one or the other to be the cause of destruction;
then that supreme weapon, having become unified with the other's weapon, withdrew.
Seeing that miraculous feat of his, Puṣkala cried out, "Stay!
Stay!", and while discharging unerring arrows, he struck Campaka in anger.
The high-minded Campaka, disregarding those arrows released by Tāṭakā,
then discharged the exceedingly fierce Rāmāstra at Puṣkala.
As soon as the high-souled Campaka beheld that released weapon and formed the intention to cut it down, he was swallowed up by that very arrow.
Bound by Campakavīra and placed once again upon his chariot,
the high-minded king then set his mind on sending him back to the city.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when Puṣkala was bound;
the warriors, intent on flight, fled toward Śatrughna. (52)
Seeing them broken, Śatrughna said to Hanumān: "By which hero has this army, adorned with warriors, been shattered? (53)
Then the slayer of enemy heroes said: "The hero Campaka, who is firm in his own station, has bound this Puṣkala, the lord of the Ahīnas, and is bringing him here. (54)
Having heard these words of his, Śatrughna, filled with anger, said to the son of the Wind-god: "Release [him] quickly from the prince! (55)
His son Mahābala, having bound the excellent warrior Puṣkala with iron chains, said, "O foremost of heroes, release him from there; why do you stand thus in the battle? (56)
Having heard these words and saying "So be it," Hanumān went to liberate Puṣkala from the warrior Campaka.
Then, beholding Hanūmān who had arrived to liberate them,
that exceedingly enraged one struck him with hundreds and thousands of arrows.
The high-souled one shattered those arrows discharged by Jāśu;
yet he [Jāśu] again began discharging even more inauspicious arrows at him. (59)
He pulverized all those iron arrows released by the enemy;
then, taking up the Śālaṅkāyana weapon, he struck the prince.
The powerful Lashas released the *śāla* tree; it was hurled by Gaja and Hanumān and released upon the head of the prince. (61)
Struck by Campaka, he too fell dead upon the ground;
then Hanumān, the knower of supreme weapons, shattered the rocks.
O Brahmin, Campaka violently reduced all those rocks to powder in an instant by means of his three arrows; this was a great marvel.
Seeing all those rocks shattered by his own release, Māruti became exceedingly angry in his heart, remembering that one of great prowess.
Having arrived, seized it, and placed it upon his back, the monkey leapt into the sky;
then, with great speed, he passed out of the range of vision above.
Campaka, stationed in the sky, fought with Hanumān;
that bull among monkeys was struck by him in a great hand-to-hand struggle.
The one who served pride, as fierce as a mountain of arrogance, became enraged;
seizing Campaka by the foot, he dashed him against the ground.
Struck by the lord of monkeys, that powerful one rose up in an instant and,
seizing Hanumān to weigh him in the balance, whirled him about in every direction.
Seeing that force, the Lord of Monkeys laughed and seized him again by the foot;
having whirled him around a hundred times, he threw him down upon the back of the elephant.
The prince Subāhu, along with Campaka, fell to the ground;
fainting, they adorned the battlefield, which was richly decorated with the ornaments of heroes.
Then the people of the three worlds, following Campaka, cried out, "Ah!
Alas! as they released Puṣkala, who had been bound by Campaka's noose.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation of Puṣkala," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||51||
The fifty-second chapter. Śeṣa said:
Seeing Campaka fallen, the powerful Kṣatriya Suratha [acted].
Overwhelmed by grief for his son, he went [to him] seated upon a chariot.
Then Suratha, filled with rage and endowed with great strength, hissing with the force of his breath, summoned the lord of monkeys. ||2||
Seeing the king challenging him, the heroic lord of monkeys, endowed with great speed, went toward that great hero. ||3||
To Hanumān, who had arrived treating even the most formidable warriors as mere blades of grass,
King Suratha spoke in a voice as deep and resonant as a thundercloud.
Suratha said: "O best of monkeys, you are blessed, possessing great strength and prowess,
by whom this difficult task for Rāma was accomplished in the city of the Rākṣasa."
"You are a devoted servant at the feet of Rāma;
by you, O hero, my powerful son Campaka has been struck down."
Now, O Lord of the monkeys, you must stay with effort in this city of mine, which is connected to you; O Lord, what I have spoken is the truth, as I recall.
Having heard these words spoken by Suratha,
the Lord of Monkeys spoke with a steady voice to Rāṇu, who was uniquely adorned as a hero.
Hanumān said:
You are one who remembers the feet of Rāma, while we are the servants of Rāma;
if you bind me by force, my Lord will set me free. (9)
Remembering Rāma, who abides within the hearts of the Kuru heroes, one reaches the end of suffering through that truth which was promised; thus the Vedas declare this.
Śeṣa said:
Having praised the son of the Wind-god who was speaking thus,
Suratha pierced him with many sharp arrows, whetted on a grindstone and fierce.
Then, disregarding those blood-drinking arrows that had been discharged,
he took up his bow in his hand and strung it, equipped with an arrow.
Seizing his bow with both hands, the enraged monkey broke it,
letting out a roar that terrified the heroes while rending the soldiers with his claws.
Seeing his own bow, which was strung with a cord, thus broken, he took up another bow adorned with a great string. (14)
The monkey seized that bow as well out of anger and broke it; he took up another bow, but the one of great strength broke that too. (15)
When his bow was broken, he took up another bow;
but he too, endowed with great speed and power, shattered that bow as well. (16)
Thus, in every moment, out of great rage and uttering various cries, he shattered eighty bows belonging to the king of the Tushitas.
Then, becoming exceedingly enraged, he took up a fierce spear;
struck by that spear, the hero fell instantly, though full of vigor. ||18||
Rising up in great wrath, he seized the king’s chariot;
having taken hold of it, he flew with extreme speed toward the ocean.
Observing him flying up, Suratha, the slayer of enemy heroes,
struck the advancing Māruti in the chest with iron clubs.
Released by him, the chariot was instantly pulverized at a distance;
he mounted another chariot and proceeded with speed like the wind.
Hanumān, having encircled that chariot with his tail in the midst of the battle,
shattered it along with its horses, charioteer, and banners.
Mounting another chariot, the king of great strength departed;
meanwhile, the enraged son of the Wind-god violently shattered that broken chariot with his speed.
Seeing that chariot shattered, Suratha took refuge in another;
yet he too was suddenly broken, along with his horses and charioteer, by the power of Satena.
In this way, forty-nine chariots were destroyed by Hanumān;
beholding that feat, the king, along with his army, was filled with amazement.
Enraged, he said to the lord of monkeys: "O son of the Wind, you are fortunate!
No one else would have performed this deed, nor will anyone do it. (26)
Wait for a single moment, O bee at the lotus-feet of Rāma stirred by the wind, until I have strung my bow.
Having spoken thus and having strung his bow, he, overflowing with rage,
fixed the weapon named Pāśupata upon his arrow of fierce power.
Then, spirits, vetālas, and piśācas led by yoginīs suddenly appeared, terrifying the son of the Wind-god.
While the monkey was bound by the Pāśupata weapons and watched by the people crying out "Alas!
Alas!", even as they were speaking thus, the son of the Wind [Hanumān] appeared.
Remembering the grove in his mind, he tore it down at that very moment;
with his body thus liberated, he suddenly fought against King Suratha.
Seeing his body thus released, Suratha, an expert in supreme weapons,
considering him to be possessed of great strength, took up the Brahma-weapon.
The powerful son of the Wind-god swallowed that Brahma-weapon while laughing;
seeing it swallowed, the king, the lord of the earth, remembered Rāma.
"O bull among monkeys, having remembered Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, and having fixed the Rāma-weapon upon your own bow, speak these words. (34)
Having heard that, just as he was setting out,
the heroic Hanumān, the servant of Rāma, appeared on the arena grounds with a shower of arrows from the king's garden.
Hanumān said to the king:
"O lord of the earth, this man has been bound by my master's weapon; he cannot be released by any other ordinary means."
Therefore, O King, I honor you; please lead me back to my own city.
My lord, that ocean of compassion, will come and set me free.
Enraged at Baddhesama, Puṣkala went toward the king;
he struck the approaching Puṣkala with arrows as numerous as Vasus. (38)
The powerful one struck the king with many thousands of arrows;
in that arena of battle, his numerous elephants were cut down by the king.
When Samara and Puṣkala were thus enraged,
the entire world— both the stationary and the moving— was pervaded by their arrows.
Beholding their exertion for battle, the soldiers of the gods were bewildered; meanwhile, the humans, having fallen into a state of terror at that very moment, fled in all directions. 41.
Through the discharge of missiles and counter-missiles, and the chanting of great mantras, there arose a tumultuous battle among the heroes that caused the hair to stand on end. ||42||
Then the king, provoked to anger, took up an iron arrow;
but it was cut down by the Vatsadanta arrows discharged in fury by the Bharatas. ||43||
When these arrows were severed, the king, out of anger, took up another; he cut it down as soon as it was released, yet [the previous one] remained stuck and wounded his heart. (44)
Having engaged in a great and most wonderful battle with the king, the highly intelligent Puṣkala, possessed of great splendor, fell into a swoon. 45.
King Śatrughna, the scorcher of enemies, the lord of Puṣkalāvatī, mounted upon his chariot, advanced in great rage against Suratha. ||46||
The brother of Rāma, possessed of great strength, spoke to King Suratha:
"A great deed has been performed by you, in that the son of the Wind-god has been bound. (47)
Puṣkala, the great hero, as well as my other soldiers, possessed of immense strength and prowess, have been struck down in this terrible battle. (48)
Now stay, O lord of the earth! Having struck down my heroes on the field of battle, where will you go? Endure my arrows. 49.
Having thus heard the speech of the hero, the powerful Suratha spoke, holding the beautiful lotus-feet of Rāma in his heart. (50)
By me those heroes were struck down in battle while facing the son of the Wind;
now I shall strike you down as well upon the field of combat.
"Remember Rāma, that hero who will come himself and protect you;
otherwise, there is no life for you in my presence, O scorcher of enemies! (52)
Having spoken thus, the lord of the earth struck him with thousands of arrows and placed Śatrughna within a cage of a multitude of shafts.
Śatrughna discharged the weapon presided over by Agni,
which released a multitude of arrows, for the purpose of burning those straight-jointed shafts.
Beholding that weapon released, the great King Suratha neutralized it with the Vāruṇa weapon and pierced [the enemy] with ten million arrows. ||55||
Then he fixed upon his bow that wondrous weapon bestowed by her yoginī, which bewilders all heroes and induces sleep. (56)
Seeing that great weapon which causes delusion, the king, remembering Hari, said to Śatrughna: "He is skilled in all weapons and missiles. (57)
For me, who am thus deluded, by the remembrance of the glorious Rāma, no other delusion appears, even one that brings fear and torment. (58)
When the hero had spoken thus, he released that great weapon;
severed by that arrow, it fell upon the field of battle. (59)
Seeing that great weapon, which was intended to bewilder him, rendered fruitless by the king,
Bāṇa was struck with extreme amazement and fixed an arrow upon his bow.
He fixed upon his bow that terrible arrow, which had slain Lavaṇa— the crusher of great asuras— and which blazed with a splendor like fire.
Seeing him, the king said: "This arrow strikes the heart of the wicked;
even when facing one devoted to Rāma, it does not appear [to have effect]."
As he was speaking thus, the slayer of enemies swiftly pierced him in the heart with this arrow, which possessed a brilliance equal to the flames of fire.
Afflicted by that arrow and possessed of great pain,
the scorcher of enemies fell into a swoon for a moment on the seat of his chariot.
Having instantly overcome that pain, he spoke to his enemy standing before him:
"Endure this one blow from me; where will you go past me? (65)
Having spoken thus in that great battle, he fixed an arrow upon his bowstring—
an arrow whose body was encircled by garlands of flames and which was equipped with a golden shaft.
That arrow, released from the bow by Śatrughna while he stood on the path, was severed by the tip of [another] fruit, yet it quickly struck him in the heart. (67)
Stricken by that arrow, he fell unconscious upon his chariot;
then the army raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! and, utterly broken, fled in all directions.
Suratha, the servant of Rāma, achieved victory in battle;
ten heroes and ten sons were rendered unconscious and fell somewhere. (69)
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Victory of Suratha," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
(53) The fifty-third chapter. Śeṣa said:
Seeing that army broken on the field of battle and his master even rendered unconscious, Sugrīva went forth to fight against the king. ||1||
O you who have arisen from nowhere, having stupefied all the kings, come quickly and give me battle, O you who are skilled in war! ||2||
Having spoken thus, filled with strength, he uprooted a certain large tree provided with branches and struck it upon his head.
Then, having observed Sugrīva with that blow, the king of great strength fixed [an arrow] upon his own bow.
Fixing sharp arrows with great fury, that exceedingly courageous and powerful one struck him in the chest. ||4||
Laughing loudly, the exceedingly powerful Sugrīva suddenly shattered all those arrows and struck Suratha in the heart.
With mountains, peaks, and trees as large as the bodies of elephants,
he violently struck him, tearing at Suratha with his claws.
Bound by that extremely terrible weapon known as the Rāma-śakti, which was discharged with great speed,
the monkey leader Sugrīva seized Suratha, the servant of Rāma.
Just as an elephant, having encountered a trap made of iron set for its feet,
is unable to do anything at all, so indeed did he become.
Victory has been won by that great king Asuratha, who possesses excellent sons; having placed all the heroes upon his chariot, he departed toward his own city. 9.
Having gone to the assembly, that great being spoke to the son of the Wind-god:
"Remember the glorious Raghunātha, who is compassionate and the protector of his devotees. (10)
Just as the wise man will immediately release you from bondage,
so shall I release Nanda from bondage after twelve years.
Having heard these words, Samīraja then observed himself to be well-bound and beheld the heroes.
Remember [the Lord] for the sake of liberation from bondage, for those who have fainted and are afflicted by the pain of being struck by the arrows of their enemies. 12.

With all his senses free from sorrow, he meditated upon Śrī Rāmacandra, born of the Raghu dynasty, the husband of Sītā, whose eyes are like lotus petals, the compassionate one who has liberated him from bondage. 13.
Hanumān said: "Alas, O Lord! Alas, O most excellent of monkeys, O you of great compassion!
O you whose face is beautified by the lovely locks of hair belonging to the husband of Sītā!"
O you who burn away the suffering of devotees and possess a captivating form, release me from this bondage immediately and without delay! 14.
By you, Gajapumgava and others were liberated,
as well as the gods who were being consumed by the fire of the Dānava race.
The hair-binding situated upon the head of that beautiful woman has been loosened; remember me, O abode of compassion! 15.
O Lord of the great sages, you are devoted to the performance of sacrificial rites;
O King whose feet are worthy of praise, you investigate the Dharma.
"O Great Being, O Pure God! Here today I am bound by the tightly fastened noose of Suratha; release me! (16)
Salutations to you, whose name alone, when remembered, transcends all else— O you whose lotus feet are worshipped by the best of all gods!
The world would have laughed at you for this;
therefore, I vomit it up—release me quickly from this! ||17||
Having heard this, Raghuvīra, the Lord of the World and ocean of mercy, set out in the Puṣpaka chariot with great speed to liberate his devotee. 18.
Then the monkey beheld him, beautifully adorned by his followers Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata, and accompanied by throngs of sages headed by Vyāsa.
Seeing her own lord, the king, who had arrived, she said to him:
"O King, behold Hari, who has come out of compassion to liberate his own. (20)
"Many of my own servants were previously liberated by him through his remembrance;
likewise, he has come to liberate me who am bound by the noose. (21)
Seeing Śrī Rāmabhadra approaching, Suratha, overwhelmed by a flood of devotion,
immediately performed hundreds of prostrations.
The four-armed Śrī Rāma embraced him with his own arms, repeatedly sprinkling his own devotee on the head with tears of joy. 23.
He said, "O you of blessed body, a great deed has been performed by you;
Hanumān, the lord of monkeys and possessor of all-encompassing strength, has been bound by you. (24)
Śrī Rāma released that best of monkeys from his bonds;
seeing all those soldiers unconscious, he restored them to life with his glance.
Having regained consciousness, they were abandoned by Rāma, who was served by the gods;
as they rose, they beheld the glorious and enchanting Rāmacandra.
Having bowed down to the Lord of the Raghus, those kings asked after his welfare; being reassured of his well-being, they told the king that all was well with themselves.
Seeing that Rāma had come for the sake of his charioteer,
Suratha joyfully offered him his entire kingdom along with his horse.
She gratified Śrī Rāma with manifold acts of service, saying,
"O Raghava, you have committed an injustice against me."
Then Śrī Rāma said to him: "The protection of your cows has been accomplished. (29)
This is the duty of Kṣatriyas: to fight alongside their master.
You have performed this deed well; by your actions, the heroes have been fully gratified.
While Nṛhari was speaking thus, his son honored him and remained there;
Śrī Rāma, having stayed for three days, departed after taking leave of him.
Accompanied by sages, the Great One traveled in a celestial chariot that moves at will;
seeing him, they were filled with wonder and recounted enchanting stories about him.
Having installed Campaka in his own city, the powerful Kṣatriya Suratha, possessed of great strength, set his mind on going together with Śatrughna. (33)
Having recovered his own horse, Śatrughna caused kettledrums to be sounded and had various kinds of conch shells blown everywhere. ||34||
The hero released the sacrificial horse along with Suratha;
it wandered through other lands, and no one seized that powerful steed. (35)
Wherever Vāha went, there Śatrughna followed, wandering about with a great army along with Suratha.
Once, at dawn, he went to the excellent hermitage of Vālmīki on the banks of the Ganges, which was frequented by the best of sages and marked by smoke.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Meeting with Raghunātha," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||53||
The fifty-fourth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having gone out in the morning to perform his rites, he took sacrificial fuel wood suitable for those rituals.
Lava, the son of Jānakī, was chosen by the sons of the sages to bring him back. ||1||
There he beheld the sacrificial horse, marked with a golden leaf and perfumed with the divine fragrance of saffron, agallochum, and musk.
Seeing the sons of the sage, he, whose mental speed was unsurpassed, spoke with curiosity:
"By chance, one who possesses the speed of thought has arrived at my hermitage."
"Come with me and behold her; do not be afraid," he said, and having spoken thus, Salava quickly went near Vāhasya. ||4||
Standing near the king of the lake, the descendant of Raghu, bearing a bow and arrows upon his shoulder, was difficult even for you to conquer. ||5||
Having gone together with the sons of the sage, he read the excellent letter,
which was situated upon his forehead and adorned with rows of clear syllables.
The great lineage of Vivasvat is renowned throughout all the worlds;
in it, there was no one who oppressed others or was greedy for the wealth of others. (7)
The archer who is the banner of the Solar dynasty, the preceptor of the initiation into archery—the Guru whom all the gods, together with the immortals, bow down to with their jeweled crowns. (8)
His son was the illustrious Rāmacandra, the upholder of the Raghu lineage, who stripped away the pride of Vīrabala, and who is the crest-jewel of all heroes. ||9||
His mother was the daughter of the King of Kośala, born from a jewel;
Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, was the jewel born from her womb. (10)
Well-instructed by the Brāhmaṇa, Karoti performed a horse sacrifice for the removal of the sin arising from the slaughter of the eminent lord of sages named Rāvaṇa.
That chief sacrificial horse was released by him;
it was well-guarded by a great force of attendants and surrounded by moats. ||12||
His protector is my illustrious brother Śatrughna, the slayer of Lavana, accompanied by a host of troops consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. (13)
O King, he whose mind becomes inflated with pride, thinking, "We are the bravest," "We are the best of archers," or "We are the most powerful here"—[he is lost]. (14)
Then he took that horse, adorned with a garland of jewels,
possessing the speed of thought and the swiftness of desire, which was radiant as it moved in every direction.
Then his brother Śatrughna, having effortlessly and by force liberated [the sage], made him like a calf released from its tethering post by means of a bow. ||16||
Those Kṣatriyas born of a Kṣatriya maiden,
who are born into families that are excellent fields of merit.
But she, whose body was the opposite of that, having offered her kingdom to Raghava, bowed down. 17.
Thus addressed, the enraged Lava, bearing sword and bow, spoke to those sons of the sages with words faltering from rage. (18)
Behold quickly the audacity of that kṣatriya;
the king has inscribed his own valor and strength upon the leaf of his forehead. (19)
Who is this Rāma? Who is Śatrughna? They are mere insects relying on their meager strength.
We alone are superior, born as we are in the lineage of Kṣatriyas. (20)
And his mother was Jānakī, the mother of heroes, who gave birth to Kuśa;
she bore that jewel named Kuśa just as the fire-drill produces fire.
Now I shall demonstrate his kṣatriya status and other qualities in every respect;
for if he becomes a kṣatriya, he will be a slayer of enemies.
I shall seize the horse bound for the sacrificial rite;
otherwise, having abandoned my status as a Kshatriya, I shall become a worshiper at the feet of Kuśa.
Now he shall fall asleep by the arrows released from my bow, as well as those other great heroes who are the ornaments of the circle of the forest. (24)

Having uttered these and other such words, that supreme wielder of bow and arrow seized the horse, which was protected by the tip of a blade of grass, treating all the kings as if they were mere blades of straw.
Then the sons of the sage spoke to Lava, who desired to seize the horse:
"Rāma, the king of Ayodhyā, possesses great strength and prowess. (26)
Even Śakra, arrogant in his own power, could not seize his mount;
therefore, do not seize it, but listen to these words of mine, which are full of benefit.
Having spoken thus, he, possessing great learning, addressed the sons of the twice-born: "O best of the twice-born, you do not know the strength of the kṣatriyas. (28)
"O Kṣatriyas, you who possess heroism, majesty, and the excellence of providing food for the twice-born;
therefore, go home and eat what has been brought by your mothers. (29)
Having been addressed thus, they became silent and watched his prowess;
those sons of the sages stood at a distance outside while Lava performed his feat.
While this event was thus unfolding, the servants of that king arrived; seeing the horse tied up, they then spoke to the cowherd.
Alas, the King of Dharma is enraged at someone who has taken a pledge;
standing in the midst of a multitude of arrows, he will attain supreme liberation.
Then that excellent horse said quickly:
"The great Kuśa, my brother, is swift and will release me; he is the one who shall set me free. (33)
"What will Yama do even though he has come here in person as the Lord?
He will not depart quickly until he is satisfied by a shower of arrows. (34)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, they said, "This is but a boy," as they arrived here to release the horse of Hari that had been bound. (35)
Having arrived to liberate those servants of Śatrughna,
he took his bow in his hands and discharged razor-sharp arrows.
With their arms bound by grief, they approached Śatrughna;
when questioned, they all told him how Lava had lopped off their arms.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Binding of Lava's Horse," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||54||
Fifty-fifth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Having heard this delightful account of the powerful Lava, the sage—
Full of doubt, he questioned the thousand-faced Nāga.
Śrī Vātsyāyana said: You have stated that the Lord of Tripura, being lustful for women, abandoned Sītā while she was alone in the forest due to the harsh words of a washerman. (2)
How did the two sons born of Jānakī attain such prowess and mastery over the bow? And how was it that Rāma acquired the sciences he had not previously learned? (3)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the sage, the high-minded serpent Śeṣa praised the brāhmaṇa and the wonderful life-story of Rāma, the Lord of the World.
Śeṣa said:
Rāma, together with his brothers, ruled the kingdom in Ayodhyā, protecting the entire realm righteously along with his wife. (5)
Then, for five months, the earth bore that embryo which was the essence of Sītā;
the goddess Earth shone exceedingly while carrying the personification of the Three Vedas.
Once at a certain time, Rāma asked the daughter of Videha: "O virtuous lady, what longing do you have?
I shall surely fulfill it for you."
Being thus questioned in private by her husband,
that virtuous woman, her voice faltering with bashfulness, spoke these nectar-like words.
Sītā said:
"By your grace, I have enjoyed and shall enjoy everything auspicious;
there is nothing whatsoever that exceeds my heart's desire. (9)
For her who has such a master as you, whose virtuous foot is praised by the gods, everything abounds in excellence;
nothing whatsoever remains lacking. (10)
"O charming Lord of the Tantuvasu, you ask me this longing that dwells in my heart out of persistence; I shall speak it before you in truth. (11)
"O Lord, it has been a long time since I have seen Lopāmudrā and other women;
my mind is eager to behold those beautiful ladies. (12)
Having obtained the kingdom, I have enjoyed manifold pleasures together with you;
yet I am ungrateful, for I have never before come here to pay my respects. (13)
Having gone there, I shall honor the treasuries of asceticism with garments and other offerings; I shall also present radiant jewels and ornaments. (14)
Just as those truthful, ocean-like, and heart-stealing blessings were bestowed upon me, so too is this longing of mine, which fills my mind with desire for my beloved. (15)
Having thus heard these most charming words of Sītā, Rāmacandra, filled with supreme joy, spoke to his beloved.
"Blessed are you, O ascetics; you shall go forth this morning. Let Janaki be seen by you, and having accomplished your purpose, you shall come back into my presence. (17)
Having heard these words of Rāma, she attained supreme joy, thinking:
"Truly, tomorrow morning will be the time for me to behold the female ascetics. (18)
Then, at the end of that night, the scouts sent by Mena to observe his own fame, having heard it, arrived slowly at midnight.
Every day they listened to the most enchanting stories of Rāma; on that particular day, they went to the great house of a wealthy man.
Seeing that lamp blazing and observing those human beings,
the spies stood there for a moment and heard another very great sound.
There, delighted by the child with eyes as beautiful as molten gold, she spoke these most charming words to the infant who was still nursing at her breast.
"Drink my heart-stealing breast milk as much as you desire;
later, O my son, it will become very difficult for you to obtain. (23)
Rāma, the lord of this city, possesses the luster of a blue lotus petal;
indeed, for the people dwelling in that city, there shall be no further rebirth.
Since there is no birth, how can there be the drinking of breast-milk for one who is born on earth?
Therefore, drink repeatedly; the milk is difficult to obtain, and another [reality] dwells in the heart. (25)
Those who remember Śrī Rāma, meditate upon him, and speak of him—for them, too, there shall never again be the drinking of milk [in the form of rebirth]. 26.
Having heard these and other such words, which were like the nectar of Śrī Rāma’s glory,
they departed for the great home of another fortunate man, filled with joy.
Meanwhile, another spy remained there in that charming house,
considering it his duty to serve Rāma for even a moment’s fame.
There, a certain beautiful woman, chewing the betel-leaf affectionately offered by her husband, sat comfortably upon his lap.
Richly adorned with the beauty of tinkling sounds and perfumed with camphor and agallochum incense, she, her eyes flickering as she gazed upon her beloved of god-like form, spoke: (30)
Such lordship appears to me as that of the Lord of the Raghus,
who bears an exceedingly beautiful and very delicate body.
With a pair of eyes like the edges of a lotus, a broad chest that enchants the mind,
and arms adorned with armlets, he appeared before me as if Rāma himself.
Having heard these most enchanting words of Kāntā, he,
who was as beautiful as the god of love, spoke while making the corners of his eyes dance.
Listen, O virtuous lady, to that which you have spoken, which is most pleasing to the mind;
for Rāma alone is indeed worthy of devoted wives like yourself. (34)
But where am I, unfortunate as I am, and where is Rāma, the greatly fortunate? Where am I, as insignificant as an insect, and where is he, who is worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā? (35)
Where is the glowworm and where the jewel of the sky? Where is the moth and where the celestial nymph? Where is the lion, the enemy of elephants, and where this dull-witted rabbit? (36)
Where is the goddess Jāhnavī, and where is the water of a street leading astray?
Where is Meru, the abode of the gods, and where is the insignificant guñjā flower? (37)
Likewise, where indeed could he have gone, by the dust of whose feet this woman, who had assumed a form that deludes even Brahmā, became like a stone in an instant? (38)
Thus speaking these words,
she, her desire awakened and her love aroused, embraced her own husband, her bow-like eyebrows dancing with emotion.
Having heard these and other such words, he went to another dwelling;
meanwhile, he heard the voice of another person, accompanied by fame.
Having prepared a bed of flowers, sandalwood paste with moon-patterns, and everything else worthy of Kāma, one woman spoke these words to her husband: ||41||
Spread out a bed fit for enjoyment upon a flower-strewn couch; likewise, apply ointments such as sandalwood and provide the means for pleasure. (42)
Only those like you are worthy of enjoyments, and not those who turn their backs on Rāma; enjoy everything obtained through the grace of Rāma exactly as it is. 43.
A beloved woman like me, sandalwood that removes the heat, and a couch fashioned of flowers—all this has arisen from the grace of Rāma. 44.
They will not worship Yerrāma; therefore, they themselves will not be able to support the king's treasury, being utterly deprived of clothing, enjoyments, and other such things. 45.
Speaking thus, her husband, filled with joy, said to that woman:
"Everything you say is true; it has arisen from my grace toward Rāma. (46)
Having thus heard the fame of Rāmabhadra, the spy departed;
meanwhile, another spy staying in his house heard these words.
One woman, intent on playing the lute with her husband,
sang to her lord while singing of the excellent fame of Rāma.
O Master, we are most blessed, for the Lord of this city is the sovereign Śrī Rāma, who protects his subjects exceedingly, like his own sons. 49.
He performed that great deed which was difficult to accomplish and not easily attained;
he bridged the ocean, which had the serpent as its womb, and there he bound the causeway.
Having slain Rāvaṇa, the enemy of the gods, and having seized Laṅkā with the monkeys,
he brought back Jānaki and performed a great deed.
Having heard these words spoken in such sweet syllables, her husband smiled and then spoke this sentence to her again: ||52||
O beautiful lady, this great deed of Rāmacandra—beginning with the slaying of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa and ending with the subduing of the ocean—was performed by one who was [then] still innocent. 53.
That Great One, who was entreated by Brahmā and others, has descended to the earth through his divine play;
he performs noble deeds that destroy even the greatest sins.
Do not fail to recognize Rāma, the one who bestows joy upon Kausalyā;
he creates and sustains this universe, having assumed a human form through his divine play.
Blessed are we, who behold the lotus-face of Rāma, which is difficult even for the gods beginning with Brahmā to see; we are doers of great merit.
Standing in the water at the entrance, he repeatedly heard these and other words, such as "He heard the life-story of Rāmacandra, which grants joy to the ears. (57)
One person, having gone to another's house, stood there to hear the glory of Hari;
even there, he heard the beautiful fame of Rāmabhadra.
While playing dice with Tīsvāmī,
the charming woman spoke these sweet words, dancing and whispering them into his ear.
Everything has been conquered by me with the speed of my beloved; what will you do now, O one whose mind is carried away?
Having uttered such words preceded by laughter, she joyfully embraced her own beloved. (60)
The beloved spoke in a charming and melodious voice:
"O beautiful one, Rāma is constantly under my spell; there is no defeat for me anywhere. Now, however, I shall conquer you by remembering the enchanting Rāma."
Just as in the past, the gods, remembering [the defeat], conquered the sons of Aditi in an instant.
Having spoken thus, he performed the exchange of the dice;
then, having attained victory, he spoke these words with joy: ||63||
My word has proven true: you have conquered yourself and possess fresh youth;
yet, O Rāma-smārī, it may still happen that you become afraid of your enemies.
Thus, both of them, eager for one another,
embraced each other firmly out of love and then returned home by way of the sky.
Thus, having heard the account of the five great wandering kings,
they praised one another and returned to their respective homes with joy.
A certain sixth wandering mendicant, having observed the houses of artisans there,
went forth desiring to hear the fame of King Yaśorāja, O Lord of the Earth.
Touched by anger, the washerman, his eyes bloodshot and uttering words of reproach, struck his wife— who was staying in another's house— with his foot.
"Go from my house to that home where you stayed for a day;
I will not accept you, for you are wicked and contemptible in your speech. (69)
Then her mother said: "Do not abandon her, who has come to your home—she is free from offense and devoid of wicked deeds."
Then the washerman, filled with anger, replied to his mother:
"O Rāma’s mother, I will not take one who has dwelt in another's house, even if she were most beloved. (71)
The king indeed performs all this himself, and it becomes consistent with policy:
"I shall take my wife who is staying in another's house. (72)
Again and again he said this: "I am not Rāma, the lord of the earth, who [rescued] Jānakī while she was staying in the house of another, the enemy of the Rākṣasas."
Having heard these words, Acāra, overwhelmed with anger,
took a sword in his hand and set his mind upon killing him.
"Remembering what was said by Sarāma, 'This son of mine is invulnerable,' the high-minded one, realizing this, withdrew [his weapon] with great anger. (75)
Having heard that, afflicted by great sorrow and standing with his five senses withdrawn,
he then departed, enraged, sighing and panting repeatedly.
Having gathered there together, they spoke to one another about the life of Rāma, which is uniquely honored by all the world, as each had heard it.
Having heard this speech and consulting with one another, they said, "This which has been uttered by wicked people must not be told to the Lord of the Raghus. (78)
Having thus deliberated, they went home and slept, full of eagerness; at dawn, they returned to the king with their minds resolved upon his praise.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Observation of the Spies," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||55||
The fifty-sixth chapter.
Śeṣa said:
Having performed his daily morning rites, he [honored] those Brāhmaṇas who were most proficient in the Vedas.
Having gratified [the assembly] with gifts of gold according to the prescribed rites, he went to the council.
All the worlds went to the assembly hall to pay homage to Raghunātha, the lord of the earth, who was protecting all his subjects like his own children. ||2||
Then Lakṣmaṇa held the royal parasol over the head of the king,
while Bharata and Śatrughna held a pair of chowries.
There, the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha waited upon him;
there also were the ministers headed by Sumantra, who carried out their duties with justice.
Thus, at the time of departure, those six well-adorned spies went together to pay homage to the king as he sat in the assembly hall. (5)
Seeing those spies desirous of speaking, the best of kings,
filled with eagerness, entered the private inner chamber within the assembly hall.
In private, King Sumati questioned all those spies:
"O subduers of enemies, tell me truly as you have learned it. (7)
People ask me: "What is my wife like? What is [my son] like? What is the conduct of my ministers like? And how do people speak of my deeds? (8)
Having heard these words, Cārurāma then spoke; with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, he questioned that leader of the Raghus.
The spies said:
"O Lord, Nāthakīrti now purifies all people on this earth;
we have heard her praised in every house by both men and women. (10)
The great lineage of Vivasvat was further elevated by you, O Supreme Lord;
having descended to earth to adorn it, your vast fame has been spread abroad.
Many others, such as Sagara and the rest, were renowned and possessed great strength;
yet their fame was not like yours. (12)
By you, who have no other protector, all subjects have been made successful;
for them there is no untimely death, nor any affliction such as passion and the like. (13)
Just as the moon appears, and just as the river Jāhnavī flows,
so does your excellent fame illuminate the surface of the earth.
Hearing of your fame, which reached even as far as Brahmā and the other gods, your father was deeply moved;
O Lord, your fame now purifies people everywhere. 15.
O King, we are all most fortunate, for moment by moment we behold your enchanting face. (16)
Having observed these and other words of the five spies, Rāghava questioned that sixth spy, whose facial expression was marked by a look of embarrassment. (17)
Rāma said:
O one of great intelligence, you speak the truth regarding what was heard concerning the confusion of the worlds;
all that praise is exactly like that of one who has committed sins and the like. (18)
Rāma questioned him again and again in great detail; nevertheless, he did not speak a single word of worldly discourse to Rāma. (19)
Then Ārāma replied to Cāra, whose face was marked with embarrassment:
"I swear to you by the truth; tell me everything exactly as it happened. (20)
Then he spoke these words slowly to the park attendant—words that should not have been told, yet were uttered like a father, as they had been spoken by the artisans. (21)
The spy said: "O Master, your fame regarding the slaying of the Ten-faced one and other deeds resounds everywhere;
yet, oh, how it concerns the wife of another who was staying in the house of a Rākṣasa!"
A certain weaver, seeing his own wife at midnight staying in another man's house, rebuked her and beat her. (23)
His mother replied to her: "How can you strike this innocent woman? Take me instead; do not cause harm to a devoted wife. Follow my word. (24)
Then Sarajaka said: "I am Rāma, the lord of the earth;
for you have abducted Sītā, who was dwelling in the house of a Rākṣasa. (25)
O Lord, every action performed by the king becomes wise policy,
whereas even the deeds of other merit-makers may be unwise.
Again and again he said, "I am not King Rāma. O King, at that moment I became enraged, and I forgot your words.
Then, having severed his head, we cast it down upon the surface of the earth; yet again, I reflected: "Where indeed is that washerman Kvarāma? (28)
"This wicked man speaks a falsehood; this which he says is not the truth. If you command me, O Rāma, I shall kill him right now. (29)
Although this was not even to be spoken, it has been told to you due to your persistence;
let the King now consider which of these two is appropriate as the authoritative standard in this matter. (30)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, whose syllables were like a great thunderbolt, he sighed repeatedly, drew deep breaths, and fell down unconscious. (31)
Seeing the king thus unconscious, they were filled with grief;
for the sake of removing his suffering, they fanned him with the edges of their garments.
Regaining consciousness after a moment, the king said to them:
"Go quickly to Bharata and send him here to me."
Distressed by that sorrow, those messengers went quickly to his house and delivered Āma’s message.
Having heard Rama’s message, the wise Bharata went to the assembly hall;
hearing that Rama was staying in private, he was filled with great haste. (35)
Having arrived, the high-minded one said to that doorkeeper:
"Where is my brother Rāmabhadra, that treasure-house of compassion? (36)
The hero went to that house pointed out, which was enchanting with its jewels;
seeing Rāma distressed, fear entered his mind.
"Is Rāma angry, or is this some sorrow of the Lord?
Thus he spoke to the king, who was sighing again and again. (38)
O Master, how is it that your face, so easy to please, is now bowed down? It is perceived by its tears, like the moon whose body has been seized by Rāhu. (39)
"Tell me everything truthfully and without cause; what may I do for you?
O Great King, cast off this sorrow; why are you a vessel for grief? (40)
Thus addressed by his brother in a voice faltering with emotion,
the heroic and righteous Rāmacandra spoke to his brother.
"Listen, brother, to my words regarding the cause of my sorrow;
O high-minded brother, perform its cleansing this very morning. (42)
O King, no one in the lineage of Vaivasvata has ever been wounded by infamy; today my fame, once clouded, has arrived like the Gaṅgā joined with the Yamunā. (43)
The lives of those men whose fame exists upon this earth are truly well-lived;
but for those wounded by infamy, life is equal to that of the dead. (44)
For those whose fame exists upon the earth, their worlds shall be eternal;
but for those bitten by the serpent of ill-repute, may there be a downward descent.
Today, the celestial river, renowned throughout the world for its singular impurity and ill-repute, has been addressed by a washerman;
listen now to the words he spoke. (46)
"O brother, today in this city there is something that must be said regarding the birth of Jānakī from the washerman; therefore, what shall I do on this earth? (47)
"Should I abandon myself today, or this woman, Jānakī?
What ought I to do regarding both of them? May you tell me that. (48)
Having spoken thus, the crest-jewel of the righteous, his voice agitated by trembling and flowing tears, fell upon the dustless ground.
Seeing his brother fallen, Bharata was overcome with grief; looking at Rāma, he slowly restored him to consciousness. (50)
Seeing Rāmacandra deeply distressed and having regained consciousness,
he spoke these most enchanting words for the destruction of his sorrow.
"Who is this Vairaja? What is this speech he utters?
I shall cut out the tongue of this speaker of what should not be said regarding Jānakī. (52)
Then Tadarāma spoke these words that had issued from the mouth of the washerman;
and all of that was heard by the high-souled Bharata through his spy.
Having heard that, Bharata spoke to his brother who was grieving in sorrow:
"Jānaki was purified by fire in Laṅkā; she is honored by heroes. (54)
Brahmā said: "This [Kaikeyī] is pure; she was given to you by Daśaratha.
How can she, who is honored by the world, be abandoned on account of the words of a low-born woman?"
Indeed, your fame, praised by Brahmā and others, purifies the worlds;
how could it ever become defiled by the words of a washerman? (56)
Therefore, abandon this great suffering arising from the reproaches regarding Sītā,
and rule the Kuru kingdom together with that fortunate woman who is carrying a child in her womb.
Why do you wish to abandon your own beautiful body?
We are all ruined today, deprived of you, the destroyer of our suffering. (58)
For a moment, O Sītā, this great festival of life would have been meaningless without you;
therefore, let that devoted wife enjoy abundant prosperity along with me.
Having heard these words of Bharata, that righteous one, the best among those skilled in speech, spoke this sentence to him once again. (60)
"O brother, all that you have said is consistent with the Dharma; however, perform this one word which I speak by my command. (61)
I know her to be purified by fire, pure, and honored by the world; yet, fearing public scandal, I am abandoning this Jānakī, though she is my own sister-in-law.
Therefore, having grasped this most terrible sword in your hand,
either cut off the head of the Lord of the Sages, or else release his wife Jānakī in the forest.
Having heard these words of Rāma, Bharata fell down,
fainting upon the ground, his body overcome with tears.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Speech of Bharata," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||56||
(57) The fifty-seventh chapter.
Vātsyāyana said:
O you of noble vows, tell me how the Lord performed the recitation of the *Vācyavācana* together with Jānakī, whose pure fame purifies the world. (1)
O Śeṣa, act today so that there may be beautiful happiness for my mind,
through the nectar issuing from your mouth.
For one who drinks [it], there shall be satisfaction itself, by which the stream of rebirth is severed. ||2||
Śeṣa said:
In the great city of Mithilā, there was a king named Janaka;
he ruled that kingdom righteously, honoring his subjects with dharma. (3)
As he was plowing the earth with his long-tailed plowshare,
a most beautiful maiden emerged from the furrow of Sīradhvaja.
Then King Sīraketu, having attained supreme joy,
gave the name Sītā to that Mohinī, who was the very fortune of the world.
Once, while playing in the grove of a garden,
she beheld a pair of parrots, most enchanting to the eye, conversing with her own beloved in her mind.
Extremely filled with joy and exceedingly greedy for sensual pleasures,
they spoke to one another with affectionate and auspicious words.
Then, as that pair was sporting with great speed in the sky, it suddenly leapt up and,
remaining upon the peak of a mountain, let out a sound.
A captivating lord of the earth named Rāma will appear on this land; he shall have a noble lady as his wife, known by the name Sītā. (9)
The wise and powerful one will exercise sovereignty for ten thousand years— ten times a thousand years of Satayugas— attracting other lords of the earth to himself.
Blessed is the lady Sītā, daughter of Janaka, and blessed is he named Rāma, who, having come together with one another, rejoice on earth. (11)
But the daughter of Mithilā, perceiving that the pair of parrots being addressed was actually a pair of deities, and observing their speech, [spoke]. (12)
"My pair of parrots, however, composes delightful stories;
taking this [book], I shall ask them for the entire meaning of every statement. (13)
Having reflected thus, she spoke to her own female companions:
"Gently catch this charming pair of birds. (14)
Having gone to that mountain, those friends, desiring to do what was pleasing for their friend, presented this excellent pair of birds while they were seizing them. (15)
Seeing it producing many various and charming sounds, he then comforted it and spoke these words: (16)
Sītā said:
"Do not fear; you two are beautiful. Where have you met? Who is Rāma, and who is Sītā? From where has this knowledge been remembered? (17)
"Tell me all of that quickly, so that the fear you have from me may pass away.
Thus questioned by her, the pair of birds told her everything. (18)
The pair of birds said:
"The great sage Vālmīki, the most excellent knower of dharma, resides there; his hermitage is always situated in that place which is exceedingly beautiful. (19)
The sage, devoted to the welfare of all beings, caused his disciples to sing the forthcoming Rāmāyaṇa every day while recollecting its verses.
Then we heard the entire great Bhāvirāmāyaṇa, which had arrived through oral transmission and was being sung again and again. (21)
Listen, for we two shall tell you of Rāma and Janakī,
and of whatever will happen to them as they sport with Rāma, whose soul is at ease.
Through the sacrifice performed by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Hari will attain a fourfold state; the glorious one, whose noble deeds are sung by the wives of the gods, shall manifest. (23)
Accompanied by his brother and with bow in hand, he will reach Mithilā along with his skill; then, seeing that [bow] which is difficult for other kings to grasp, he will prevail. (24)
"Having bent the bow, you shall obtain the most enchanting daughter of Janaka;
it has been heard by you, O best of men, that he will rule a great kingdom together with her."
This and other things were heard by us as we stood there and listened;
O beautiful one, you have told it to us, and now we both desire to go. (26)
Having placed these most enchanting words into their ears, he spoke this speech once again to the pair of birds: ||27||
Where does Sarāma reside? Whose son is he? How will she choose him? And what kind of form will that man, the bridegroom, possess? (28)
"Tell me all this that I have asked exactly as it is;
afterwards, I shall do everything that is pleasing and agreeable to you. (29)
Having heard that and seeing her afflicted by the god of love, Sītā quickly recognized Jānakī in her heart and then recited it before her.
The wise and powerful King Paṅktiratha will be the banner of the solar dynasty;
relying upon him, the gods shall utterly conquer all their enemies.
He will have three wives who will assume forms enchanting like those of Śakra; by him there will be four sons of great strength.
Among them all, Rāma was the eldest; Bharata was remembered as the next;
after him was the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa; and Śatrughna was the strongest of all.
O friend, that high-minded and powerful Rāma will attain the infinite names of those [devotees], and he shall become renowned as Raghunātha.
Her face is as beautiful as a lotus bud,
and her very long eyes resemble lotuses.
Her nose was elevated, broad, and beautiful;
her eyebrows were well-proportioned, arching, and lovely.
His arms, reaching down to his knees, were enchanting; his neck was exceedingly short, yet graced by a beautiful throat.
This stainless chest, marked with auspicious signs, possesses the beauty spread across the surface of its six well-formed sides.
Endowed with the splendor of beautiful thighs and hips,
his pair of stainless knees was well-served by them.
[I bow to] the Lord of the Raghus, who is most beautiful and whose lotus feet are always served by all his own [attendants]. ||37||
How can I possibly compare Rāma, who bears such a form, to anyone? Even the hundred-faced Indra does not approach him; how much less so those like me, who are merely birds? 38.
Beholding her form, Lakṣmī, who possesses a body so graceful and enchanting, was infatuated; for what woman on earth does not become deluded? (39)
Possessing great strength, great heroism, and assuming forms that cause great delusion—how can I describe Śrī Rāma, who is endowed with all sovereign powers and virtues? ||40||
Blessed is that Lord who assumed a form of great enchantment for the sake of the goddess Sītā, and with whom she rejoiced joyfully for ten thousand years. (41)
O beautiful Kāśikī, you who are so charming, why do you ask me with such cleverness and devotion about the fame of Rāma? 42.
Having heard these words, the pair consisting of Janaki and the bird spoke, describing their own enchanting and beautiful birth. 43.
"I am that very Janaki who was described by you; I am the daughter of Janaka.
When the exceedingly charming Rama comes to me, he shall obtain me. (44)
Therefore, I shall truly liberate us both from the snakes, who have enticed us with their words;
let us remain here in my house, sweet-voiced as we are, cherished in happiness.
Having heard what was thus said, they both trembled and were overcome by fear;
their strength shaken, they spoke to one another regarding Jānakī.
We are forest-dwellers who live among the trees; we wander everywhere as our opponents, for there is neither happiness nor even a home for us. (47)
"Having gone to my own place while pregnant and having given birth to sons, I shall return to your place; this word spoken by me is the truth. (48)
When she had spoken thus, the husband himself released Śukī from her bonds;
then, free from anxiety, he spoke to her with humility.
"O Śīta, release my wife; how can you protect this Manoharā?
Let us both go and wander happily together in the forest. (50)
"My beautiful wife is pregnant;
O lovely one, I shall return after bringing her child to birth."
Having been addressed thus, he said to him: "Go in peace, O high-minded one;
I shall protect this happy woman, who does what is pleasing to me, by my side. (52)
Having been addressed thus, the bird, filled with compassion, spoke to her in distress:
"That which is indeed proclaimed by the yogis is certainly the truth. (53)
"One should not speak, one should not speak; let one remain established in silence.
Otherwise, like a rutting elephant, one will come to be tethered by the fault of one's own speech. (54)
If we had not spoken these words against the bull, how could we have been bound? Therefore, one should observe silence.
Having said this, he replied to her: "O beautiful one, I do not live with this wife, Sītā; therefore, release me, O charming lady! (56)
Though she was then exhorted with many kinds of words,
the angry and sorrowful wife cursed the daughter of Janaka.
"Just as you have separated me from my husband here, so too shall you be separated from Rāma while pregnant. (58)
When she had spoken thus, being repeatedly tormented by grief and filled with sorrow for her husband,
her life-breaths departed from her due to that anguish.
Remembering Rāma again and again, they cried out "Rāma! Rāma! repeatedly;
then, having gone to heaven, the bird-like celestial chariot appeared beautifully.
When she had died, her husband, afflicted by grief, together with the king of birds,
fell into a state of supreme rage and, overcome with sorrow, plunged into the Ganges.
Likewise, in the city of Bhavāmirāma, which was filled with people,
she became agitated by my words and deeply distressed by separation.
Having spoken thus, O father, he fell into the waters of the Ganges, which were beautified by clouds,
distressed, enraged, and terrified by the separation from her.
Due to his anger, his misery, and the insult to Sītā,
the washerman named Krodhana attained the supreme state of being born as an outcaste.
O best of the twice-born, he who, out of anger, performs a wicked act toward great beings and thereby gives up his own life, becomes upon death an Antyajaja.
Born from that [union], she was separated from her husband due to the washerman’s words;
and by the washerman’s curse, she was separated and went to the forest.
This has been told to you, O Brahmin, as was asked by the daughter of Videha;
now hear again from me this further account that is being related.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Washerman’s Previous Birth," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||57||
The fifty-eighth chapter.
Śeṣa said:
Seeing Bharata unconscious, Raghunātha was deeply distressed.
He spoke thus to the doorkeeper: "Quickly bring Śatrughna here. ||1||
Having heard those words spoken, he brought Śatrughna in an instant to where his own brother Rāma was staying together with Bharata. ||2||
Seeing Bharata unconscious and Raghunātha distressed, he bowed down and, filled with grief, said: "What is this great and terrible calamity? (3)
Then Rāma spoke these words, which were censured by the world, to Śatrughna, his foot-servant, who had abandoned that which was proclaimed by Atyaja.
With face cast down, voice faltering and weak, and trembling in every limb, listen, O brother, to my words today; perform them with immediate diligence.
"May your stainless fame spread across the earth like the Ganges;
having heard the incomparable reproach regarding Sītā in the world, abandon what has been spoken. (6)
"I wish to abandon this body, as well as this very Sītā," having heard these words of Rāma, the slayer of enemies indeed [replied]. (7)
Saṃpātipatha, the destroyer of enemies, fell distressed upon the earth;
regaining consciousness after a moment, he spoke to the Lord of the Raghus.
Śatrughna said:
"O Master, why do you speak such harsh words regarding Jānakī—words uttered by heretics of wicked mind who are excluded from all dharma? (9)
Even if censured, the Veda is not to be rejected by those of noble birth;
it is like the Ganges for all people—destroying sin and removing misfortune. (10)
Touched by men who are free from sin, yet unworthy of contact by the wicked—oh, how the sun rises in this world for the illumination of the universe! 11.
There would be no desire for this on the part of owls;
therefore, you yourself should take this irreproachable woman born of ministers. (12)
"By the grace of Śrī Rāmabhadra, carry out my word.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Śatrughna, [he replied: ||13||
Having heard those words spoken by his brother again and again regarding Bharata, he was overwhelmed by a flood of grief.
He fell unconscious upon the ground like a tree whose roots have been severed;
seeing his brother fallen, Śatrughna was deeply afflicted with grief. (15)
He spoke these words to the doorkeeper: "Bring Lakṣmaṇa here at once. Having gone to Lakṣmaṇa’s house, he delivered this message.
The doorkeeper said:
"O Master, Rāma is summoning you with great haste.
Having heard that summons from Rāmacandra, [he went] with speed. ||17||
He went swiftly to that place where the sinless one was with his brothers;
having seen Bharata unconscious, he saw Śatrughna also unconscious.
Afflicted with grief himself, he spoke these words to the sorrow-stricken Śrī Rāmacandra:
"O King, what is this terrible state that is seen, such as fainting and the like? (19)
Then, O sinless one, the king told him the entire account from the beginning, explaining the primary cause for everything he had desired.
He quickly spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who was overwhelmed by a flood of sorrow;
and Lakṣmaṇa, having heard those words concerning the abandonment of Sītā, [was deeply moved]. (21)
Sighing repeatedly with labored breaths,
his limbs became rigid as he looked again and again at his brother whose body was paralyzed with fear.
Seeing him saying nothing at all, Śoka, afflicted with grief, said: "What shall I do, standing upon this earth, marked by infamy? (23)
"O brother, out of fear of the world of the glorious Malla kings, I am sorrowful and shall abandon this body;
you have always been eager to carry out my word. (24)
Now even they act with words contrary to fate; where shall I go? To whom shall I go? Kings upon this earth will mock me. (25)
O men, you who possess beautiful forms, do not speak ill of me, who am of ill-repute;
for in the lineage of Manu, there have been kings born in the past who were superior in their virtues. (26)
"Now that I have been born, that has become the opposite.
Observing Rāmabhadra speaking thus, he—
Having restrained his abundant tears, he spoke with a faltering voice:
"O Lord, do not despair; how has your mind been so stolen away? (28)
Who would abandon the blameless Sītā, especially one such as you who are learned? I shall summon the washerman and question him regarding this matter.
How is it that you, by whom the blameless Sītā—the best among women—was taken away, have now forcibly oppressed even a lowly person in your own domain? (30)
Therefore, act in such a way that he may have confidence in you;
why is this timid woman, devoted to her husband, being tormented? (31)
In thought and in word, the daughter of Janaka knows no other;
therefore, accept her, do not abandon this Janaki.
"Having shown compassion toward me, quickly take refuge in what I have said.
To him who was speaking thus, the monkeys, emaciated by grief, replied:
I awakened Lakṣmaṇa with words of dharma as I prepared to abandon my efforts.
Rāma said:
"How can you speak thus to me? Do not abandon this blameless woman; though I know her to be sinful, I shall abandon her only because of public censure. (35)
For the sake of my own fame, I shall abandon this wretched body;
and you too, O brother, I shall abandon, for you are censured by the talk of the world. (36)
How much more so his other houses, sons, friends, wealth, and splendor?
For the sake of his own fame, he abandoned everything, including the daughter of Mithilā.
Neither my brother, nor my wife, nor my kinsmen are as dear to me as this stainless fame, renowned throughout the world, which is so beloved. (38)
Now, it is certain that the washerman need not even be questioned;
in time, the entire world will become colored by his dye. (39)
Just as a disease on earth that is incurable by medical treatment perishes only through the ripening of time, so too [does this]. (40)
Likewise, since this is impossible at present, do not delay;
abandon this virtuous woman in the forest and strike me with your sword. (41)
Having heard these words spoken, the great Lakṣmaṇa then became sorrowful; and, emaciated by grief, he thought of his own self.
Commanded by his father, the son of Jamadagni even put his own mother to death;
for the command of a guru is always to be honored, whether it be appropriate or inappropriate in every respect. (43)
