"Therefore, desiring to do what is pleasing to Rāma, I shall indeed abandon her.
Having thus reflected in his mind, he spoke to his brother. (44)
Lakṣmaṇa said: "Even an improper act must be performed at the command of a superior; one should never disregard it. Therefore, O you of noble vows, I shall carry out your word, whatever you say. (45)
To Lakṣmaṇa, who was speaking thus, he replied: "Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Your mind has been well-restrained. (46)
"Tonight itself, Janaki has a longing to see an ascetic woman;
under that pretext, place her in the chariot and release her into the great forest."
Having heard what was thus spoken, his face withered on all sides; weeping and shedding a stream of tears, he went to his own dwelling.
Then, having summoned Sumantra, he spoke these words to him:
"Prepare my chariot, O Vaideha, and equip it with the finest horses. (49)
Having heard those words, he then brought the chariot;
seeing that chariot brought, Lakṣmaṇa was overcome with grief. (50)
Having mounted his excellent chariot, he who had fallen into supreme misery set out for Jānaki’s abode, sighing deeply and accompanied by his brother and servants.
Having gone to the inner apartments, the brother [Lakṣmaṇa] addressed these words to Rāma’s daughter of Mithilā, sighing deeply and overwhelmed by a flood of grief: 52.
O Mother, Janaki has been sent by Rama to your abode; please deliver her to the female ascetics so that she may obtain the fulfillment of her pregnancy longings.
Having heard these words of Lakṣmaṇa,
the daughter of Videha was filled with supreme joy and replied to Lakṣmaṇa.
Jānakī said:
"Blessed am I, the queen of Mithilā, who remembers the feet of Rāma;
for the sake of fulfilling his longing, he sent Lakṣmaṇa to me. (55)
Today, for my part, I shall pay homage to those ascetic women who regard their husbands as deities, and I shall honor those enchanting ladies with garments. (56)
Having said this, [he gave her] beautiful garments, highly precious ornaments,
jewels, pure pearls, and fragrant substances such as camphor.
Desiring to do what was pleasing to her husband, the wife of Raghunātha took up thousands of various articles, such as sandalwood and other things. 58.
Taking all the items from the hands of her maidservants again and again,
she then went toward Lakṣmaṇa and stumbled over the threshold.
Without reflecting on that eagerness, he spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who was intent on doing what was pleasing to him: "Where will you take me with this chariot?"
Sighing deeply, he entered the golden chariot with Jānaki;
then, he spoke to Sumantra, "Drive the horses that are as swift as thought."
At Lakṣmaṇa’s word, he summoned the chariot already yoked,
while looking again and again at Lakṣmaṇa, whose face was filled with tears.
Struck by him, the horses carrying the chariot fell upon the path;
when the horses did not move, he then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
Sumantra said:
"O Master, the draft animals do not move even when urged with effort;
I do not know the cause for this failure of the beasts of burden."
To him who was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa replied with a faltering voice:
"O charioteer, summoning your courage, strike them with whips and the like."
Having heard this which was spoken by him, she somehow moved away;
then Jānakī’s right eye throbbed, foreboding sorrow.
At that very moment, grief arose in his heart, foreboding misery;
at that very moment, the auspicious birds began to wheel about.
Having observed this, Vaidehī then replied to her brother-in-law:
"O descendant of Raghu, why do you wish me to go for the sake of penance?"
May there be great prosperity for Rāma, and likewise for his younger brother Bharata;
may all their subjects everywhere be well, and may no adversities arise.
Having spoken thus and beholding Jānakī, Lakṣmaṇa said nothing; his throat was choked and he was overwhelmed with tears.
As he was approaching those lovely deer who cause one to turn back, he saw them creating a mass of suffering and spoke to them. (71)
That they should now turn their attention to the forest is desired;
yet that they should depart, leaving the feet of Śrī Rāma, is indeed improper.
For women, the supreme duty is the worship of their husband's feet;
having abandoned that, it would indeed be appropriate for her to go wherever she wishes. (73)
Thus, they perform their contemplation on the earth, though not from the perspective of ultimate reality—[the earth] which is like the river Ganges, a goddess served by the multitude of sages. (74)
In which the waves of the water appear like milk,
and where the ripples bear the form of stairs leading to heaven.
At the mere touch of whose feet, the accumulation of great sins flees away, seeking no place to remain anywhere near him. (76)
Having reached the Gaṅgā, the son of Sumitrā, with tears streaming forth, spoke to Jānakī as she sat in the chariot: "Come, descend from the chariot to the ground."
Having heard those words of Sītā, she descended in an instant;
held by Lakṣmaṇa by the arms, she stumbled upon the thorns of the path. (78)

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Jānakī’s Vision of the Gaṅgā," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The fifty-ninth chapter.
Śeṣa said:
Then, having crossed the Ganges by boat, Lakṣmaṇa [proceeded] at that time.
Taking Jānakī by the hand, he went to the forest from the opposite shore. ||1||
With her face parched from the heat of the path,
she was seen with her noble feet wounded by thorns, stumbling at every step.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, carrying out the command of Rāghava, caused her to enter that most terrible forest which brings such sorrow.
There, the trees— extremely terrible *arbūla*, *khadira*, *agha* [trees],
*śleṣmātaka*, and *ciñciṇīkā*— are dried up by the fire of the desert.
Great serpents dwelling in hollows hiss, being greatly provoked to anger;
there, owls shriek, causing fear in the minds of people. (5)
Where tigers, lions, jackals, leopards, and other extremely terrifying creatures are seen—straight-fanged, man-eaters, and exceedingly wrathful. (6)
Buffaloes, boars, and wicked men, distinguished by their two tusks,
cause suffering to living beings, being arrogant with the intoxication of pride.
Beholding such a forest, her fever of fear departed;
though her feet were pricked by thorns, she spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
Jānakī said:
"I have not seen the hermitages frequented by heroic sages and seers, which grant delight to the eyes, nor have I seen their wives who are rich in asceticism. (9)
We see only terrible birds and withered trees;
this entire forest is being consumed by a forest fire. (10)
And I see you afflicted by grief, your eyes clouded and filled with tears;
at every step, a thousand misfortunes would befall me. (11)
Tell me that, O foremost of heroes: how was the evil-hearted one quickly released by the high-souled Rāma? Tell me this, for it is my desire.
Having heard these words, Lakṣmaṇa, emaciated by grief, with his face choked with tears, said nothing at that time. (13)
As she was traveling through that very same formidable forest accompanied by Tīla and Lakṣmaṇa,
she, afflicted with grief, beheld the face of the hero struck down once again.
Then, eager to see something, he spoke to her with humility;
then, questioning her, he made a persistent effort to obtain that [information]. (15)
When Lakṣmaṇa was questioned persistently by Sītā,
his throat choked and he, grieving repeatedly, spoke of the cause of her abandonment.
O best of sages, having heard those words which were like a thunderbolt,
she became devoid of all pride, like a fine tree whose roots have been severed.
At that very moment, she took hold of this daughter of the earth, thinking with hope:
"May Rāma not abandon the sinless Sītā."
Seeing Vaidehī fallen there, the son of Sumitrā, filled with longing, revived her with the breeze from the tips of the young leaves. 19.
Regaining consciousness, she spoke these words: "O Lord of the gods, do not act with such cruelty!
Why does the descendant of the Sun abandon me, who am free from sin? (20)
Having lamented thus at great length, she beheld Lakṣmaṇa, who was overwhelmed by grief; then, deeply afflicted, she fell to the ground in a swoon.
Having regained consciousness after but a moment, she, overwhelmed by suffering and pierced by the grief of separation from Rati, spoke to the feet of Rāma.
How could the great Raghunātha, possessed of supreme intelligence, abandon me—he who, for my sake, crossed the ocean together with his monkeys? (23)
"How will that Great Hero abandon me, who am free from sin, on account of the washerman's words? Surely my own destiny here must be adverse. (24)
Speaking thus, the daughter of Videha fell into a swoon once more;
seeing her thus unconscious, he then wept with a piteous voice. (25)
Regaining consciousness once more, she, deeply distressed, spoke thus to the son of Sumitrā as she gazed upon him, who was afflicted by grief and choked with sobs.
O son of Sumitrā, go to Rāma, who is the embodiment of dharma and a treasury of glory;
in the presence of that storehouse of asceticism, you must speak these very words of mine.
O Bhavānī, even though you know her to be a sinner, why do you not abandon her?
Is this truly consistent with your lineage, or is it the fruit of your knowledge of the scriptures? ||28||
"O Lord, you have abandoned me—who am eternally devoted to your feet, who subsist on your leftovers, and who am pure—but my own destiny is surely the cause of this. (29)
"O best among the foremost of heroes, may all be well with you everywhere! As for me, I shall go to the forest, remembering you as my sustainer of life. (30)
O descendant of Raghu’s lineage, through thought, deed, and word, you alone have become the supreme non-existent; all others have been rendered insignificant by your mind.
In birth after birth, may Bhava alone be my husband, O Lord of the Earth;
and may I, having my many sins destroyed by the remembrance of your feet, become the mistress of virtuous women. 32.
O best of the Raghus, tell all my message to your mother-in-law:
"The sinless Sītā has been abandoned by Rāma on this most terrible earth. (33)
I remember your feet in the forest filled with herds of deer,
which were abandoned by the great-souled Rāma because he thought it was pregnant.
O son of Sumitrā, listen to my words; may it be well with the best of the Raghus.
Now he shall give up his life, while Rāma’s prowess remains well-protected.
Since you act in accordance with Rāma’s truthful words, this auspicious task must be performed by you, who are devoted to the lotus feet of Rāma. (36)
Go to the presence of Rāma; may your paths be auspicious.
You should remember me from time to time as one for whom I have shown compassion. (37)
Having spoken thus, she then fell unconscious upon the ground before him;
seeing Jānakī fallen in a swoon, Lakṣmaṇa was overcome with grief.
Having regained consciousness by her very nature, she was fanned with excellent garments;
and the son of Sumitrā repeatedly revived her with sweet words.
Lakṣmaṇa said:
"I am going to Rāma; having gone there, I shall report everything in its entirety.
Not far from here lies the great hermitage of the sage Vālmīki."
Having spoken thus and circumambulated her, he, distressed and filled with tears, shedding a stream of tears out of grief,
went toward King Rāma.
Seeing her brother-in-law, the husband of Jānakī, departing, she, with eyes wide with wonder, said:
"O highly fortunate Lakṣmaṇa, this man here is my brother-in-law. (42)
"How has Rāghava abandoned me, his most beloved, sinless as I am, even while I am still alive?
Thinking thus, she gazed at him with unblinking eyes.
Knowing for certain that she had completely crossed the Gaṅgā and that her life was truly at stake,
he then fell into a swoon, his very life-breaths becoming uncertain.
Then, having brought water from all sides with their two wings, they sprinkled me;
meanwhile, a sweet-scented breeze blew, carrying the fragrance of flowers. (45)
Then, having arrived, the elephants washed their bodies, which were covered with dust, using their own trunks filled with water. ||46||
The deer, having found him, stood with eyes wide in wonder;
even the trees, though laden with flowers, remained at that moment as if devoid of spring.
At that moment, having regained consciousness, that virtuous woman, afflicted by intense sorrow, lamented, crying out, "O Rāma! O Rāma! (48)
O Lord of the helpless, O ocean of compassion, O presence of grace, why do you abandon me in the forest, except for my transgressions? (49)
Thus speaking such words, lamenting repeatedly again and again, looking here and there, and fainting over and over. (50)
Then the Blessed Vālmīki, having entered the forest together with his disciples, heard there a sound of weeping uttered in a piteous tone. (51)
Then he spoke to his disciples: "Behold, in the midst of the forest, in this most terrible wilderness, a crow cries out with a piteous sound. (52)
Directed by the sage, they went to where Jānakī was, who was crying out "Rāma, Rāma! and was overwhelmed by a torrent of intense tears.
Seeing that woman, they approached the sage Vālmīki out of curiosity;
having heard the words spoken by her, the sage then departed from there.
Having seen that mass of asceticism, Janaki, whose deity was her husband, [prostrated], saying: "Obeisance to the sage, who is the very embodiment of the Vedas and whose wealth is his vow! (55)
Having spoken thus, he greeted Sītā with blessings:
"O daughter, may you live long with your husband; may you obtain two auspicious sons. (56)
"Who are you, and why have you come to this terrible forest? Why are you such as this?
Tell me everything; tell me the cause of this suffering. (57)
Then Rāma’s wife, sighing piteously with her voice trembling, replied to the sage: 58.
Listen to my words, which speak the truth that is the cause of all suffering;
know me to be a servant of Aghunātha, the lord of the earth. (59)
I do not know the reason why they were abandoned without fault;
Lakṣmaṇa has gone there from here by the command of Rāghava, leaving me behind. (60)
Having spoken thus, Vālmīki, consoling the lotus-eyed Jānakī, who bore a face-lotus filled with tears, said to her: (61)
"Know me to be Vālmīki, the sage and preceptor of your father;
do not grieve, O Vaidehī, come to my hermitage."
"O you for whom your husband is a god, know that my father’s house is now divided;
such is my wrath toward the king for this deed. (63)
Having heard these words, she whose deity was Janaka’s daughter,
her face filled with tears of sorrow, attained a measure of comfort.
Śeṣa said:
Vālmīki then led her, whose eyes were agitated by a flood of sorrow,
to his own holy hermitage, which was filled with throngs of female ascetics.
I followed behind that Valmiki, a treasure-house of asceticism;
his arm shone behind him like the enchanting Vaitarini river.
Having reached his own hermitage, which was filled with sages, Vālmīki announced to the female ascetics that Jānakī had gone to his hermitage.
The high-minded one paid homage to all the female ascetics of Vaidehī;
delighted with one another, they engaged in mutual embraces.
The storehouse of asceticism, Vālmīki, spoke to his own disciples:
"Indeed, let a beautiful leaf-hut be constructed for Sītā."
Having heard these most delightful words spoken by Vālmīki,
he constructed a very beautiful hall out of wood and leaves.
There, devoted to her husband and dedicated to her vows, Vaidehī lived;
subsisting on fruits, she performed service for Vālmīki.
There, with Jānaki as her deity, she herself spent her days performing the recitation of the *Tīrāmarāma* mantra both mentally and verbally.
At that time, two sons were born to her, possessing enchanting bodies and appearing like the twin Aśvins, the very representatives of Rāmacandra, to Jānakī. (73)
Having heard that news of Jānakī’s birth of a son, the sage, the best among those who know mantras, was filled with joy and performed the birth rites and other purificatory ceremonies.
The sage Vālmīki performed his ritual acts with *kuśa* grass and *lava* grass;
thus, the names of his two sons became clearly known as Kuśa and Lava. (75)
Where Vālmīki was, she went to that Virajā-maṅgala;
with her lotus-like eyes, she became exceedingly joyful in heart. (76)
On that very day, having slain Lavaṇa with a small force of soldiers, Śatrughna arrived at the hermitage of Vālmīki during the beautiful night.
Then Vālmīki instructed Śatrughna regarding the leader of the Raghus:
"I shall describe the two sons of Janakī before him. (78)
There, the two sons of Janaki grew up, delightful to the mind; nourished by roots and fruits, the two excellent youths became spirited.
On the first day of the bright fortnight, two sons as charming as the moon were born;
in due time they were consecrated and initiated, becoming truly enchanting. (80)

Having initiated his two sons, the sage taught them the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches; he also instructed Rāma in the science of archery together with its secret doctrines and taught him the Rāmāyaṇa.
Vālmīki then gave him two bows, beautifully adorned with gold, unbreakable, strung with excellent strings,
and capable of tearing asunder hosts of enemies.
Then he gave to the two sons of Janaka quivers filled with arrows, inexhaustible swords, and impenetrable shields.
Those two archers, masters of the science of archery (dhanurveda), wandered joyfully in that hermitage; they shone there like the two beautiful Aśvins.
Beholding her two excellent sons, who bore swords and shields,
Janaki was filled with supreme joy and cast off the sorrow born of separation.
O Brahmin, the birth of Jānaki’s son has thus been told to you;
now hear what occurred regarding the mangled arms of Vīra.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Birth of Kuśa and Lava," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||59||
The sixtieth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Śatrughna, beholding the severed arms of his own warriors, [spoke].
With his lips bitten in a fierce rage, he spoke to them, greatly agitated by anger. ||1||
"By which hero was this arm of mine severed? O, tell me who made it so!
I shall give that person my own arm; indeed, he is my protector. [2]
This great fool does not know the immense power of Rāma and Candra;
now I shall demonstrate my own strength through valor. (3)
Where does that Vīra exist, and where is the charming Hayagrīva? Or what fool, knowing his prowess, would seize sleeping serpents? (4)
Having spoken thus, the heroes were filled with wonder and profound sorrow;
they praised the boy as a true representative of Rāmacandra. ||5||
Having heard this, Bālaka, his eyes copper-red with rage and eager for battle, commanded Vaikartanajit, the commander-in-chief of the horse-seizing force.
"O General, array the entire army according to my command;
the enemy, possessing great strength and prowess, must now be confronted. (7)
"Surely this horse-holder is not the boy Hari;
or perhaps it is Tripurāri, since my horse has been carried away."
A great slaughter of the powerful army was inevitable;
yet the child, sporting with his own pure deeds, remained fearless in mind. (9)
"Therefore, we must go there, fully prepared and invincible against our enemies. Having heard these words of Śatrughna, the lord of the army [replied].
He readied that army, poorly arrayed yet consisting of four divisions;
and Śatrughna, seeing it prepared, excellent, and joined by the four [divisions], [proceeded].
He then commanded that army where the one who bears the horse Bālāha was; then that army, equipped with fourfold divisions, set forth.
Then the commander of the army saw that boy, who possessed the form of Rāma, terrifying the enemy forces by his strength as he traversed a certain portion of the earth.
Having reflected, he spoke these beneficial words, resembling those of Rāma himself:
"Release the excellent horse of the mighty Rāma. (14)
The commander-in-chief of that king, named Kālajit, who was exceedingly haughty, felt compassion arise in his heart upon seeing you, who resemble Rāma. (15)
"Otherwise, due to my wickedness toward you, my life shall not continue.
Having heard these words of the soldier Śatrughna, indeed—
Out of some slight anger, he spoke these extraordinary words:
"Go and tell Rāma, who has been released, that I have seized the horse. (17)
I do not fear you, O hero, for your words are full of policy;
for me, there is no reckoning here even if there were tens of millions of such as you.
By the grace of your mother’s feet, you have undoubtedly become like cotton;
you conquer time, O Kālajit, by means of your pleasing mind which acts according to your mere name. 19.
Like a ripe bimba fruit in color but not in potency, display now your power, marked by the strength of your own name! (20)
"Defeating me in battle, you shall become one whose name is true.
Śeṣa said:
"Pierced by those words, which were like thunderbolts, that crest-jewel of great warriors—"
He became extremely agitated in his heart and spoke these words again:
"In what family were you born, and what is your name, O boy?"
I recognize your name, your lineage, your conduct, and likewise your age. ||22||
"How can I, standing in my chariot, defeat him who is on foot through unrighteousness?
Then, becoming exceedingly enraged, he spoke these words again: ||23||
"What does it matter about lineage, conduct, or even a name that pleases the heart?
I am Lava; by my own power, I shall conquer all the enemy soldiers. (24)
"Now I shall make even you a foot-soldier," having spoken thus, the powerful one, full of haste, strung his bow.
Then Lava, keeping the heroic Anaka in his heart,
first remembered Vālmīki and his mother Jānakī.
Filled with rage, Kālajit fixed his bow with a string and immediately released sharp arrows that snatch away life.
Skilled in battle, the younger brother of Kuśa instantly and with great speed cut that javelin into a hundred pieces. ||28||
With his own excellent arrows, Vasu deprived the commander of his chariot;
being without a chariot, he mounted an elephant brought by his own soldiers.
Seeing him mounted upon an elephant that was intoxicated with rut, possessed of great speed, and provided with seven flowing streams of ichor, he struck him with ten arrows released from his bow.
Laughing, the victorious Kālajit pierced all the hosts of his enemies with arrows;
seeing his prowess, Kālajit’s mind was filled with wonder.
He released a massive mace, fashioned with great glory;
that mace, weighing ten thousand bhāras, came rushing down with great speed. ||32||
Together with his younger brother Kuśa, he swiftly cut that sharp, terrible iron club— which was said to take the lives of enemies— into three pieces with his arrows.
But he, endowed with great speed, swiftly cut that [missile] apart as it was released;
having severed that terrible iron club, his eyes became bloodshot with rage.
Thinking that he was mounted upon the back of an elephant, he became enraged;
at that very moment, he severed the trunk of that tusker with his sword.
Having seized the feet of those two, he ascended the head of the elephant;
having shattered his crown into a hundred pieces and his armor into a thousand.
Having seized the commander-in-chief by the hair, he threw him to the ground;
once thrown from the back of his elephant, the commander-in-chief became enraged once more.
I struck him in the heart with my vajra-fist;
being thus struck by my fists, he [discharged] sharp arrows like razor-edged blades.
He whose bow was drawn into a circle quickly released [the arrow] at the heart;
he shone with his bow circled, like a king amidst the sounds of battle.
Wearing a helmet and armor impenetrable by millions of arrows,
though pierced by sharp shafts, he took up his sword to slay him.
Hissing and sighing repeatedly from the rage of his teeth against his own teeth, Lava [beheld] the heroic general approaching with sword in hand. (41)
The sword, however, cut through the middle of his arm, and the hand fell;
seeing his hand severed while still holding the sword, the army commander was filled with rage. (42)
With his left arm holding a mace, I struck him;
his arm, along with its armlet, was also severed by my sharp arrows.
Then the enraged hero struck Lava with his two feet;
yet, though struck by those feet, Lava did not waver on the field of battle.
He inflicted a severing of the feet like an elephant struck by a garland;
then, with his crown, he began to strike him back.
Then, considering the lord of the army to be possessed of superior prowess,
he took up a sword in his hand that resembled the fire of universal destruction.
The head of that [general], adorned with a great crown, was severed; a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when the commander of the army was struck down. (47)
The soldiers, filled with great rage, came together to slay Lava;
Lava, however, rendered them intent on flight by the blows of his own arrows. 48.
Some Gakas, their limbs severed yet unbroken, departed from the field of battle; others, having warded off all opposing warriors, joyfully plunged into the army. (49)
Like a boar, having sighed at the great ocean during the dissolution of the world,
the earth was split in two by elephants and filled with pearls.
The path became impassable for the foremost of warriors, as if it were occupied by mountains;
the horses, beautiful with golden saddles and glistening with jewels, [followed]. (51)

The chariot-warriors, splendidly adorned by their strength as they lay drenched in blood upon the ground where they had fallen, shone brilliantly with the staffs of their bows held firmly in the middle of their hands.
Falling from their positions on the floorboards of the chariots, the gods appeared as if they were ascending to heaven;
their faces, with lips bitten and trembling beauty, were marked by embarrassment.
There were seen fallen heroes, skilled in the forest of battle; a river of blood flowed there, with elephant heads for its turtles. 54.
Causing fear to her enemies who sported in the great current, the arms of some were severed and the feet of others were cut off. (55)
The ears, noses, and nostrils of some were severed, and the armor and earrings of others; thus did that slaughter occur when the commander of the army fell in battle.
All the heroes fell there, and some were deprived of life;
then Lava, having attained victory in battle and having conquered the host of his enemies, [remained].
Focusing his mind on the hope of another's arrival, he was indeed not harmed;
some who had survived the battle were killed by fate while fleeing. (58)
They went into the presence of Śatrughna to report the wonderful event;
having arrived, they related exactly what had occurred on the field of battle.
Hearing that the death of Kālajin was brought about by a child through a marvelous feat of archery, Śatrughna was filled with wonder and spoke to them.
Biting his teeth in anger and remembering those who seize children as if they were horses, he said:
"O sons of Revā, are you intoxicated with pride, or are you practitioners of deception? (61)
What deficiency has come upon him, or how can there be death at this time for one whose victory over hosts of enemies in battle was so terrible? (62)
Hearing those words of Śatrughna—which were difficult even for him to overcome—those heroes, drenched in blood, spoke as follows: ||63||
"O King, know from Lava that there is no deception on our part such as being intoxicated with pride, nor is there any gambling; the death of Kālajit is the truth. (64)
The entire army has been crushed by that boy of incomparable prowess;
therefore, O best of noble men, whatever task remains to be done, let those messengers be dispatched.
"Knowing him to be a child, you should not commit an act of forceful violence here.
Having heard these words of those heroes, the slayer of enemies then [acted].
And he spoke to Sumati, the best of the wise, regarding the cause of the battle.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Death of the General Kālajit and the Defeat of the Army during the Battle between Kuśa and Lava" in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||60||
The sixty-first chapter.
Śatrughna said:
"O great minister, do you know who this boy was that brought the horse?"
By whom this entire army, resembling the ocean, was utterly destroyed. ||1||
Sumati said:
"O Lord, this is the great hermitage of Valmiki, the best of sages;
O scorcher of foes, there is no dwelling here for Kshatriyas."
Indra will become a supreme ṛṣi;
he shall bring this horse, just as Purandara brought the steed for you. ||3||
By which Kālajit, most terrible, met his destruction;
toward him, Puṣkala, having heard from others, set out for the illustrious Mahārājagarta. ||4||
And you, surrounded by all your heroic warriors and kings,
go there with your great army, O destroyer of enemies.
"Having gone and bound that heroic Jīvita for the sake of curiosity, I shall show him to Rāma; let this plan of mine be respected. (6)
Having heard these words, he commanded all the heroes:
"Come with a great army; you shall follow behind me. (7)
At the hero's command, they went to where the powerful Lava was;
there he stood, stretching his very firm bow, which was fully drawn with a string.
Having seen that great army, filled with heroes, approaching, even Lava, though possessed of strength,
was not afraid in his mind.
Lava, like a lion, sprang up, perceiving all the warriors to be deer;
stretching his bow in rage, he discharged arrows by the thousands.
Being tormented by those arrows and filled with great rage, they then rushed toward him, regarding the hero as a mere child. ||11||
Seeing thousands of heroes surrounded by whirlpools, he,
filled with rage, fixed arrows to his bowstring with the speed of Lava.
The first [circumambulation] is with a thousand [revolutions], the second with a number of ten thousand;
the third with two times ten thousand, and the fourth with five times ten thousand. ||13||
The fifth [circle] is surrounded by one million warriors; the sixth by more than ten thousand warriors;
and the seventh is encircled by two million warriors and seven *bhramis*.
Then, pervading the whirlpool in its center and moving like fire, it indeed began to burn all the soldiers who had created that whirlpool. 15.
One was struck by swords, another by arrows, one by spears and lances, and another by sharp-edged spears and iron clubs; all were shattered by that great-souled one.
Released from the seven whirlpools, Rāma,
along with Lakṣmaṇa, was like the moon at the onset of autumn when it has emerged from a mass of clouds.
He struck down all the warriors in every way, as well as many elephants with trunks like elephant tusks; he severed the heads of the brave heroes and even the great discus-bearing Bhrūṇis.
Afflicted by the arrows of Lava, many heroic warriors fell;
some fainted in the battle, while others, being utterly cowardly, perished.
Seeing the army intent on flight and oppressed by Lava’s arrows,
the hero named Puṣkala advanced to fight in the battle.
Saying "Stop! Stop! with eyes filled with rage, the powerful one, standing upon his chariot richly adorned with excellent horses, advanced against Lava.
Then Puṣkala, an expert in supreme missiles, replied to Śalava:
"Stay here, O enemy, on this chariot of mine, adorned with excellent horses, for battle!"
"How can I fight in battle with you while you are on foot?
Therefore, stay behind in the chariot; I shall fight with you from there."
Having heard these words, Asulava spoke to Puṣkala.
If I were to engage in battle on the field while standing upon a vehicle provided by you, then that would indeed be a sin for me;
for victory would certainly be uncertain.
"We are not Brahmins devoted to the acceptance of gifts;
we are Kṣatriyas who are constantly intent on the performance of acts of giving. (25)
"Now, out of anger, I shall smash your chariot every single day;
you shall indeed have to travel on foot until afterwards you engage in battle. (26)
Having heard Puṣkala’s speech, which was endowed with righteousness and fortitude, he was amazed in his heart for a long time; then he strung his bow. ||27||
Seeing him with his bow drawn, Lava, filled with rage,
cut off the bow held in his hand while he was in the act of aiming an arrow.
To whatever extent he drew his bow with its string,
to that same extent the powerful one, laughing in the battle, rendered his chariot shattered.
Seeing his own chariot shattered and his bow cut by the high-souled one,
he, considering himself a great hero, fled on foot from the battle.
Both were heroic archers, both were bristling with arrows;
both were drenched in splashes of blood, and both had their armor shattered.
Their bodies marked by wounds from each other's arrows,
they both desired to slay one another and exerted themselves with the hope of victory.
Just as the enemy of Tripura, the destroyer of cities, [conquered] Jayanta and Kārttikeya,
so too did they engage in mutual combat upon the field of battle.
Then Puṣkala replied to the boy:
"O crest-jewel of heroes, I have never before seen anyone like you, a true ornament among the brave. (34)
Today I shall strike down your head with my sharp, well-jointed arrows;
do not flee from the battle, but protect your life with self-restraint.
Having spoken thus, he covered the heroic Alava with a shower of arrows; Puṣkala’s arrows remained filling the entire expanse of the sky.
Śarapaṃja, standing in the midst of the army, spoke to Puṣkala:
"O hero, you have performed a great deed; you have afflicted me with your arrows. (37)
Having spoken thus and severed the multitude of arrows, the hero, skilled in the fitting of shafts, addressed Puṣkala once more.
Protect yourself while standing in battle; afflicted by the strike of my arrows, you shall fall upon the surface of the earth drenched in blood. (39)
Having heard this spoken, Puṣkala, filled with wrath, engaged in battle the heroic and mighty Lava. (40)
Lava, provoked to anger, seized from his quiver a sharp arrow capable of rending enemies,
as if it were a venomous serpent, out of rage.
Blazing as it was released from Lava’s bow along with the arrow,
it was swiftly severed by Bharata just as it was intent on piercing his heart.
When his bow, standard, and countless life-taking arrows were destroyed,
he, becoming extremely enraged, took up another terrible arrow.
A sharp arrow, released from a bow drawn back to the ear, pierced the heart of that Puṣkala in the great battle. 44.
Struck in the chest by a swift-moving arrow from the hero Bhinna,
that crest-jewel of great heroes fell upon the surface of the earth.
Beholding Puṣkala fallen, the son of the Wind-god took him up and,
though he was overcome by a swoon, gave him to Rāghava’s brother.
Beholding him unconscious, his mind overwhelmed with grief and filled with rage, he commanded Hanumān and Lava to slay him.
Hanumān, consumed with rage, went forth with speed to conquer the immensely powerful Lava in battle, uprooting a śālmali tree.
The powerful Hanuman struck Lava on the head with a tree; as he was rushing forward, the heroic [Lava] cut that [tree] into a hundred pieces. 49.
Having severed them, the one of great strength did not again uproot the trees from their very foundations; instead, he struck them on the chest and the head out of anger. (50)
Whichever trees the son of the Wind gathered and struck with them,
the powerful one swiftly cut each of those down with his straight-jointed arrows.
Then the monkey Māruti, having uprooted boulders resembling great crags,
hurled them with swift force upon his head.
Struck by the masses of rocks, he raised his single bow and pulverized them with his arrows,
just as a pestle grinds grains into dust.
Then the son of the Wind-god, highly enraged and skilled in battle, performed a tail-encirclement upon that exceedingly powerful Tail-less One.
Seeing his own tail lashed by his own arm and remembering it in his heart,
the powerful son of the Wind struck that arm with his fist.
Pained by the blow of his fist, Māruti released him;
once released, he became powerful in battle, discharging arrows from his tail.
His body tormented by the strike of the irresistible arrow,
the monkey perceived the heavy rain of shafts in battle as unbearable.
"What should be done by us from here? If we flee toward whatever direction, then shame will strike me; my young master would beat me here. (58)
"Because of the boon granted by Brahmā, there is neither fainting nor death for me;
yet, what should I do now regarding this unbearable pain from the arrow? (59)
"Let Śatrughna go to battle and obtain victory from Bālaka; meanwhile, I shall lie down on the ground, feigning death through a deceptive faint. (60)
Having thus resolved in his mind,
he fell into the circle of the battlefield while all the heroes were looking on, feigning unconsciousness.
Perceiving that Hanumān of great strength had fainted,
he who was skilled in the discharge of arrows struck all the kings.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Fall of Hanumān," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||61||
The sixty-second chapter. Śeṣa said:
Hearing that Māruti had fainted, Śatrughna was overcome with grief.
"What should I do with this child, O Sage? He possesses great strength. ||1||
Standing himself upon his golden chariot, accompanied by the best of heroes,
he went to fight where Lava, skilled in diverse modes of combat, was located.
He saw Lava, who had attained childhood while still perceiving [the world] as a lotus, appearing like Rāma on earth,
with bow and arrow in hand, casting down heroes at the forefront of the battle.
He then reflected: "Who is this who has assumed the form of Rāma, bearing a captivating body dark as the petal of a blue lotus?"
Indeed, this son born of her body will not remain as he is;
having defeated us in battle, he will depart like the king of beasts. ||5||
For us, whose souls are devoid of power, there is nothing to be cultivated through battle;
being powerless, what shall we do, even though we are skilled in the art of war? (6)
Having reflected thus, he then spoke to the boy,
who delighted in the excitement of battle and brought down millions of heroes.
"Who are you that, in this battle of children, you strike down our heroes to the earth? You do not know the power of King Rāma, the destroyer of the Danujas. (8)
"O you of great strength, whose mother and father are they? You have attained such good fortune; what is your world-renowned name that I might know it? (9)
"How was Muṣcavāha bound? Because of his childhood, I forgive that.
Come, see Rāma; he will give you much. (10)
Having been addressed thus, the heroic boy spoke these words to Śatrughna:
"What is the use of that age which is so distressed by being fatherless? (11)
"O hero, fight in battle if you possess strength;
having bowed at the feet of the heroic Kuśa, go there as you please. (12)
"O hero, brother of Rāma, you are the foremost among the strong;
release my horse by force if you possess the power. (13)
Having fixed an arrow to his bow, the formidable one struck him in the heart, on the head, in the two arms, and in the region of the navel. (14)
Then the king, provoked to anger, strung his bow, making it sound as deep as a thundercloud, as if to terrify the boy. (15)
The best among the strong released countless arrows;
Bāla, by his own strength, cut down all those volleys of shafts. ||16||
The surface of the earth was covered by the many arrows discharged by Lava;
they became inexhaustible, like gifts bestowed during the *vyatīpāta* conjunction. (17)
Those arrows, having reached the entire sky and joined together in a moment,
reached the solar disc and then proceeded forth simultaneously from there.
The wind entered where the arrow fell within the range of old age,
amidst men whose lives were measured by moments and who were like fleeting birds.
Seeing those arrows spread out, Śatrughna was filled with wonder;
skilled in the discharge of shafts, he cut down hundreds of thousands of them.
Seeing all those arrows of his cut down, the younger brother of Kuśa swiftly severed the bow of King Śatrughna.
As he was taking up another bow and discharging arrows,
[the other] shattered his chariot with sharp-jointed shafts.
He severed with his hand the very firm bow, which was fully strung;
the heroes standing in the circle of the battlefield honored that feat.
With his bow broken, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
he mounted another chariot and went forth by force to fight Lava.
Pierced by many arrows, his body streaming with blood, did he not shine in the midst of the battle like a flowering *kiṃśuka* tree? (25)
Struck by Śatrughna’s arrow, he fell into a state of supreme rage;
quickly fixing an arrow to his bow, he drew the curved weapon into a circle.
He rendered Śatrughna’s body with its armor shattered, its head deprived of its crown, and drenched and soaked in flowing blood.
Then Rāmānuja, becoming exceedingly enraged, angrily discharged ten sharp-pointed arrows that were capable of destroying life.
Having reduced Satāṃstāṃ to pieces as small as sesame seeds with his sharp-jointed arrows,
he struck Śatrughna in the heart with eight shafts.
Remembering the powerful Lava, who was then intensely afflicted by the pain of the arrows,
and considering him difficult to withstand, he [Rāma] did not discharge his shafts at that time.
Then, his broad chest was pierced by that sharp arrow,
which resembled a crescent moon and was beautiful with its keen joints.
Having suffered most terrible agony from an arrow piercing his heart,
he fell from the seat of his chariot, his hand still beautifully grasping the bow.
Seeing Śatrughna unconscious, King Suratha and the others then fled from the battle, intent on securing victory over Lava.
Suratha, Vimala, the hero Rāja, as well as Vīramaṇi,
Sumada, Riputāpa, and others surrounded him in the battle.
Some kings struck from all sides with razor-edged arrows and clubs, some with most dreadful shafts, and others with spears and axes. (35)
Seeing them eager for battle but acting contrary to dharma, that crest-jewel of heroes struck each of them with ten arrows in the encounter.
In the midst of that forest shattered by the rain of his arrows, some became exceedingly enraged, while others fled or were bewildered on the field of battle. (37)
Then King Aśvatthāman, having cast off his fainting in the battle, set out with his forces to fight the great hero Lava. ||38||
Having arrived, he said to Lava: "You are blessed, appearing like a child;
yet you are not a mere child, but some god who has come here to deceive me. (39)
"O hero, I have been struck down by someone within the circle of the archway; I have been rendered unconscious right before my very eyes as I looked on. (40)
Now behold my prowess; I shall strike you down in battle. Endure even a single arrow from me; do not flee, O boy! (41)
Having spoken thus, he took up a single arrow in battle,
as terrible as the mouth of Yama, by which Lavaṇa was struck down.
Aiming a blazing arrow at Lava, who was like fire that eternally consumes thousands of heroes, he fixed his mind on piercing his heart. (43)
Seeing that blazing arrow illuminating the ten directions,
he remembered the powerful Kuśa, the slayer of enemies.
If at that time my heroic brother were powerful, then there would be no intense fear under the control of Śatrughna. (45)
Thus, a great and terrible arrow, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, struck the heart of that high-souled Lava from his body. 46.
Struck by the arrows of King Āvīra, he fell into a swoon on the battlefield,
which was adorned with the heads of all the warriors.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Fainting of Lava," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||62||
The sixty-third chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having seen Lava, the destroyer of Bali’s enemies, rendered unconscious, [he spoke].
The mighty Śatrughna attained victory at the forefront of the battle. ||1||
Having placed the young Lava upon the chariot, adorned with a helmet and other ornaments as a physical representative of Rāma, he then desired to depart.
Overwhelmed with intense sorrow because their own friend had been seized by the enemy,
they quickly informed Sītā, who was no more than a child.
The children said:
"O Mother Janaki, our son has forcibly carried off the horse of some proud and powerful king. (4)
Then a terrible battle took place between him and the army of the son of Janaka;
at that time, everything was struck down by your heroic son.
Afterwards, your charming son also attained victory,
having rendered that king unconscious on the field of battle.
Then, regaining consciousness from his fainting spell, that most formidable king became enraged and struck down your son upon the field of battle.
Previously we forbade you, saying, "Do not seize this best of horses," yet you have disregarded all of us Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas. (8)
Having heard this most cruel speech of the children, she fell upon the surface of the earth and, filled with grief, wept aloud.
Sītā said:
"How can a king, devoid of noble lineage and acting unrighteously with a wicked mind, fight against a child—he who struck down my son? (10)
"Where does that exceedingly powerful Lava-vīra reside?
How did you, O merciless one, seize the excellent horse from the king? (11)
You are but a child, while they have been well-trained and are experts in all weapons;
you are without a chariot while they stand upon theirs—how can the battle be equal? (12)
"O father, together with you I abandoned the misery of being separated from Rāma;
now, deprived of my lord, how shall I live in this forest? (13)
"Release this horse for the sacrifice; let this lord of the earth depart.
You do not recognize my suffering, you who are supposed to be the one who wipes away my grief. (14)
If Kuśa, that crest-jewel of heroes, had been present here, he would have liberated you from the king's side this very moment. (15)
"Even he is not near me due to my own fate; what can I do now?
Thus, it is fate alone that is the cause for the arising of my suffering. (16)
Thus she lamented with many such words of grief, scratching the ground with her big toe and shedding tears from both her eyes. (17)
That young prince, together with the king, spoke to the children:
"How could my son fall in battle? Where will he go? (18)
While this lady, whose deity is the husband of Jānakī, was speaking these words,
Kuśa arrived in Ujjayinī accompanied by great sages.
Having worshipped Mahākāla on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha and obtained many boons from him, he returned to the presence of his mother.
Seeing Jānakī overwhelmed, her eyes clouded with rising tears,
distressed and wretched with grief, he, full of longing, spoke these words.
Then his own arm, throbbing with the omen of battle, spoke;
for the heart of that great car-warrior was filled with the enthusiasm for combat.
He spoke to his mother, who was speaking with a piteous and faltering voice:
"O Mother, your sorrow has vanished now that I, your son, am present."
While I was still alive, tears did not fall from their eyes upon the ground;
[the son] spoke to his mother, who was distressed by tears and speaking piteously with a faltering voice. (24)
"My brother Lava, the crusher of enemies, who is patient of mind and who endures suffering here for the sake of virtue—where is he now, though he is currently afflicted by immediate pain? (25)
Knowing that Śambara had arrived, he went into his presence with great joy, [thinking]: "How is it that the hero is not seen? Where has the powerful one gone to play? (26)
"Out of childishness, who has gone away not to look for me? Why do you weep, O mother? Where does Lava dwell? (27)
"Tell me all that which is the cause of your sorrow.
Having heard those words of her son, she, being distressed, spoke to Kuśa.
There, a certain horse-guardian named Lavodhṛta, acting on the king's command, bound this boy to the sacrificial horse suitable for the ritual.
The powerful king alone conquered many of his protectors and numerous enemies; having rendered him unconscious, he bound him on the field of battle.
The children said to me, "The moon has indeed risen together with the stars. Then, having heard this, I became distressed, thinking that the nectar had been stolen. (31)
"Release her from that best of kings now that the time has come. Hearing the words of his afflicted mother, Kuśa was filled with wrath.
As they cried out, he bit their lips with his teeth, crushing them with those very teeth.
Kuśa said:
"O Mother, know that Lava has been released from the bond of the noose;
now I shall slay him with my arrows, along with his entire army and vehicles. (33)
Even if it were a god or an immortal, or even if Śarva himself had arrived,
he would still release him from this [bond] with his sharp-jointed arrows.
I did not weep for my mother, who had fainted on the battlefield of heroes;
for in this world, fame belongs to the one who stands firm, while flight leads only to infamy.
"O Mother, give me a divine single-piece armor, a bow equipped with a string, a helmet, and likewise a sharp sword. (36)
Now I shall strike down that great force in battle;
I shall release my own brother, who has fainted in the midst of the fray.
"O Mother, today I shall deliver your son from the great battle;
at that time, let your feet, which have become enraged, rest upon the earth. (38)
Śeṣa said:
Satisfied by these words, Jānakī, who possesses auspicious marks, bestowed the entire collection of weapons upon him, enjoining him with blessings for victory. (39)
"Go to the battle, my son, and release the unconscious Lava!
Thus commanded, the powerful Kuśa, clad in armor and wearing earrings, entered the fray.
Wearing a crown, a sword, and a shield, and holding a bow,
he placed two inexhaustible quivers upon the shoulders of those two who possessed the prowess of lions.
The leader of the chariot-force went swiftly to the feet of his mother; as he proceeded with speed toward the battle, he quickly arrived at the field of combat.
Just then, those great warriors beheld the hero Kuśa approaching, the destroyer of enemy hosts, who had slain his own kinsmen. 43.
Seeing his brother Kuśa arrived with great force, Lava perceived him as if the Destroyer himself had appeared to annihilate the entire universe. ||44||
Shining intensely like fire fanned by the wind,
he dismounted from his chariot and went forth to battle.
Kuśa cast all the warriors stationed in the east toward the western direction;
out of anger, Lava drove them all back toward the eastern direction. (46)
Just as those afflicted by the arrows of Kusa and Bana were overwhelmed, so too all the people in the army experienced turbulent delusions of mind. 47.
Then, tormented by showers of arrows from Kuśa and Lava,
the entire army, though filled with heroes, found no refuge.
That army, broken here and there and terrified again and again, did not remain anywhere in the battle; even though possessed of strength, they no longer desired to fight.
At that time, King Śatrughna, the scorcher of enemies,
went forth to fight the heroic Kuśa, who was like Lava himself.
Seeing Kuśa overcome by Bala and possessing a splendor equal to the form of Rāma,
the slayer of enemy heroes, standing in his golden chariot, spoke.
Śatrughna said:
"Who are you, appearing so similar to my brother Lava, who possesses such great strength? What is your name, O great hero, and where is your father and your mother? (52)
"O bull among men, how is it that you remain here in this forest frequented by birds?
O one of great strength, tell me everything so that I may fight with you."
Having heard these words, Kuśa spoke to the king, filling the battlefield with his voice as deep as a thundercloud. (54)
Only Sītā, devoted to her vow of fidelity to her husband, gave birth;
those two remained in the forest, intent on worshipping the feet of Vālmīki.
O sinless king, those two, devoted to the service of their mother and proficient in all branches of knowledge, became renowned as Kuśa and Lava.
"Who are you, O hero, who boasts of your prowess in battle? For what purpose has this most excellent horse been released? Why do you wish to conquer it today, accompanied by an army? (57)
"Fight with me, O king, if you are indeed a hero;
now I shall strike you down at the forefront of the battle. (58)
Śatrughna, realizing that the son was born from the grove of Sītā, was struck with wonder;
yet, out of anger, he himself took up his bow.
Seeing him with his bow taken up, Kuśa, filled with anger,
drew his own very firm and excellent bow.
Śatrughna, who was skilled in all weapons, released sharpened arrows;
Kuśa, laughing in the battle, effortlessly cut them all down with ease.
O Sage, hundreds of thousands of arrows from both Kuśa and the king [Kuśadhvaja] pervaded the entire world; that was truly marvelous.
With the fire-weapon (agny-astra), the powerful Kuśa swiftly burned them all;
then the heroic king, with the rain-weapon (parjanya-astra), extinguished that [fire] within a month.
The king, possessing extreme prowess, then subdued the wind with the Vāyavya weapon;
at that time, a fierce wind arose throughout the entire circle of the archways,
but he enveloped that agitating wind with the Parvata weapon.
With the Vajrāstra, the king cut down the mountains and boulders in their thousands.
Then the formidable Kuśa discharged the Nārāyaṇāstra;
yet that [weapon] was unable to afflict King Nārāyaṇa.
Then Kuśa, extremely provoked and overcome with anger,
spoke to King Śatrughna, who possessed great strength and prowess.
I know you, O great hero, as one who is victorious in battle;
for even the terrifying Nārāyaṇa weapon could not distress you.
"Now, O King, I shall strike you down to the earth with my arrows today; hear my solemn vow: if I do not accomplish this, let there be a change in my destiny. (68)
He who, having obtained a human body—which is difficult to attain even through millions of merits—should disregard it out of delusion; for him, O Lord, let there be the sin of killing a cow. 69.
"Be attentive here; I shall immediately cast the spear of the Lord of the Gaṇas at your chest. Having said this, [he fixed it] upon his own bow.
He discharged a terrible arrow, radiant as the fire of cosmic destruction,
aiming it at the enemy's broad, vast, and firm chest.
Seeing that arrow aimed, Śatrughna, overwhelmed with rage,
released sharpened arrows capable of piercing even the skin of a kuśa grass blade.
Accompanied by his arrows, he indeed set out to pierce his heart—
[the arrow] which was terrible in form, like fire, and hissing like a venomous serpent.
Recognized immediately by that best of kings as Rāma, he [the opponent], remembering Rāma,
cut down the sharp-jointed arrow released by Kuśa along with its shaft.
Then, enraged by the destruction of Kuśa’s arrow,
he fixed another sharp-jointed shaft upon his bow.
Just as he, impetuous with power, was about to break through his chest,
[the other] cut off that arrow of his, which shone like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Then, remembering the feet of his mother Akūśā, filled with rage,
he fixed a third arrow, most wonderful, upon his bow.
Śatrughna took up an arrow to swiftly cut that one as well;
at that moment, he himself was pierced by an arrow and fell to the surface of the earth.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when Śatrughna was struck down;
there, Kuśa, proud of the strength of his own arms, achieved victory. (79)

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Fainting of Śatrughna and the Arrival of Kuśa and Lava," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||63||
The sixty-fourth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Seeing Śatrughna fallen, Suratha, the preeminent king, [acted].
Then, we proceeded toward that most wonderful creation fashioned from jewels, where he was standing. ||1||
Having first struck down Puṣkala with his horse while reflecting deeply, he then went to fight Lava, who was exalted by the strength of a great hero. ||2||
Suratha, that crest-jewel among great heroes, having approached Kuśa and discharging arrows in many ways, caused him pain in the battle. ||3||
With ten blazing arrows, he rendered Suratha chariotless;
he then swiftly severed his very firm bow, which was fully strung with a cord.
Through the discharge and withdrawal of missiles and counter-missiles, and through hurling and parrying,
there occurred a tumultuous battle among the heroes that caused the hair to stand on end.
When King Durjaya was thus intensely engaged in battle, Kuśa reflected: "What must be done by me in this conflict?"
Having reflected, he, endowed with great strength, took up a sharp and terrible arrow for the purpose of slaying this king. ||7||
Seeing that approaching arrow, which possessed a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction,
he quickly resolved to cut it down with his own great arrow, which was fixed to the bowstring.
Then, in that battle, the charioteer of the great hero Balarama fainted;
he fell upon the seat of the chariot, and the driver carried him away.
Seeing Kuśa endowed with victory as he had fallen from his chariot,
the son of the Wind-god approached, terrifying the hosts of heroes.
Seeing the powerful monkey, the son of the Wind, approaching, he laughed,
baring his fangs as if to provoke him with anger.
And he said to Hanumān: "Come here before me;
I shall pierce you with a thousand arrows, and you shall go to the night of death."
Having been addressed thus, Hanumān, recognizing the son of Rāma to be possessed of great strength, ran forward, thinking, "The master's task must be accomplished. (13)
Having swiftly uprooted the vast śāla tree with its hundred branches,
the one of great strength, seeing Kuśa before him, went forth to fight.
As the mighty Hanumān approached with a *śāla* tree in his hand, the powerful [Rāvaṇa] pierced him in the chest with three crescent-headed arrows that resembled moons. 15.
Pierced by all those arrows, the powerful Māruti, crushing them with his speed, struck them in the chest with the *śāla* tree he held like a goad. ||16||
Struck by the arrow, the boy did not even blink with his eyes;
then the heroes praised him for his composure despite such childhood. (17)
Struck by Śālana,
the hero Kuśa, an expert in supreme weapons, took up the Saṃhāra missile in anger to destroy his enemy.
Beholding that invincible weapon of destruction discharged by Kuśa,
Rāma reflected in his mind upon himself as the destroyer of obstacles for his devotees.
Then that weapon, which had been mastered by Kuśa, struck the heart of Māruti;
having pierced him deeply, it caused him to fall unconscious once again.
Seeing that Plavaṅga had fallen into a swoon, Bala, joined by his forces,
struck that entire great army with sharp arrows.
His entire army, consisting of the fourfold forces, was shattered on the field of battle by ten thousand arrows and became intent on flight.
Then Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys and great protector of the Rākṣasas, rushed out in anger toward the formidable Kuśa,
uprooting many trees.
Laughing, the powerful Kuśa effortlessly cut down all the trees; when they grew back again, he swiftly felled them once more.
Afflicted by many arrows in the midst of the battle-host, Sugrīva seized a formidable mountain from the middle of its grassy peak.
Seeing Kuśastha approaching the mountain, he crushed him in many ways with arrows and rendered him worthy of being slain by the Great Rudra.
Seeing that great feat performed by the youth, Sugrīva’s hope for victory in the midst of the battle was completely extinguished.
Seeing Kuśa, who was difficult to assail in the midst of battle and who struck with his lāṅgūla-tāḍaka weapon, he, overcome by extreme indignation and rage, seized a mountain to strike him. (28)
Seeing Sugrīva intent on killing him, he respectfully struck him with many sharp-jointed arrows. (29)
Struck by many kinds of arrows and overcome with pain, he set out to kill Kuśa; he went forth and took up a *śāla* tree. ||30||
Then the heroic Añjaka took up the Vāruṇa weapon;
and that son of the Wind bound him with a firm noose.
Bound with smooth nooses by the powerful Kuśa,
he fell into the midst of the battle, which was adorned by great heroes.
Seeing Sugrīva fallen, the heroes fled in all directions;
only the brother of Jāmbavat, the crest-jewel of great heroes, attained victory. ||33||
Meanwhile, having conquered Lava, Bhaṭa, Puṣkala, Aṅgada,
as well as Pratāpāgrya and Vīramaṇi, those kings [were subdued].
Having attained victory in battle, the heroic Lava approached his brother,
who had achieved triumph in the conflict and struck down millions of enemies.
Exultant and embracing one another,
those two intoxicated warriors, having achieved victory, then related their news to the sage.
Lava said:
"O brother, by your grace we have crossed the ocean of battle;
now let us clear the beautiful field of heroes."
Having spoken thus, those two heroes, Kuśa and Lava, departed in haste;
he took the king’s wonderful crest-jewel, set with gold. (38)
The heroic Lava took Puṣkala’s auspicious crown,
as well as the two highly precious armlets belonging to Śatrughna and his other brother.
Seizing a multitude of weapons, they approached Hanumān, the lord of monkeys,
and Sugrīva, and bound them both.
Then the younger brother of Kuśa, having seized this son of Vāyu by the tail, replied to his brother: "I shall take him to my own home. (41)
Out of affection for our mother, I took hold of his tail for the sake of play with the sons of the sages, and likewise out of curiosity for my own sake. (42)
Having heard these words, Cakshu then spoke to Lavana:
"I myself shall seize this monkey, who is firm in his strength. (43)
Speaking thus, those two best among the powerful,
seizing the two tails of the mighty [serpent], went toward their own hermitage.
As those two best of monkeys were departing for their own hermitage, they saw them and spoke to one another in voices trembling with fear: ||45||
Hanumān, his mind moistened with fear, replied to the king of the monkeys:
"These two sons of Rāma will lead us back toward their own hermitage."
Formerly, when I was returning toward Janakī due to karma previously committed, there the enchanting Manoharā appeared before me in the presence of Queen Janakī. (47)
He will see me, O Vaidehī, bound by a noose of sin;
then he will reproach you, and there will be great distress here.
"What must I do here? My life will be lost;
great suffering has befallen me. What will Rāma do? (49)
Having heard those words, Sugrīva said, "O great monkey, it would be the same for me; if he carries her off in this manner, it will lead to my own destruction. (50)
While they were thus conversing with one another, both filled with fear,
Kuśa and Lava reached their mother’s dwelling with great speed.
Upon seeing them both arrive, the mothers of the two rejoiced;
out of supreme affection for one another, they embraced their own sons. (52)
Seeing those two monkeys holding him by the tail,
Jānakī beheld Hanumān and Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys and a hero among all.
Seeing those two bound by the noose of the hunter, the female deer spoke these excellent words for the sake of their liberation: ||54||
"O monkey, let go of my two sons, those great heroes of immense strength; if you do not release them upon seeing me, they will give up their lives. (55)
This is the heroic Vihānuman, who burnt the city of Danu;
this too is the king of the bears, the sovereign of all the monkeys. 56.
For what purpose were you two restrained, where, or what was done out of disregard?
I ask you both about this restraint; I am filled with great wonder.
Having observed these gentle words of their mother, those two sons,
endowed with great strength and preeminent in discipline, then spoke.
"O Mother, there is a certain powerful king, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha;
by him was released this horse, beautifully adorned with a golden leaf upon its forehead. (59)
"Let those Kṣatriyas who worship my mother Mātarekavīrā, as she is depicted there, take it; otherwise, let those who worship the soles of her feet take it. (60)
Then, O lady devoted to your husband, this agitation of mine was indeed improper;
for are you not a Kṣatriya woman? Could it be that you have not given birth to a hero? (61)
Seeing that audacity of the king, the horse was seized by me by force;
the army was defeated by the heroic Kuśa and struck down in battle.
O goddess who regards her husband as a deity, know that this crown belongs to the lord of the earth;
and this one also belongs to the other hero, the high-souled Puṣkala.
"Know this other crown, resplendent with jewels and pearls, to be that of King Kāma; this horse is his, which captivates my mind. (64)
"Know these two excellent monkeys, the brothers of Añjanā, to be powerful;
these two best among the strong have been brought by me for the purpose of sport. (65)
"Only for your sake were these two made to engage in battle in this conflict.
Having heard these words, she whose deity is Janaki [Sita]— ||66||
She spoke again and again to her two heroic sons, "Release him!
Sītā said, "By both of you, a great injustice has been committed; the horse of Rāma has been seized. (67)
This lord of monkeys, who has slain many enemies and wears a crown of matted locks,
has by this means liberated your father’s heroic horse for the sake of the sacrifice.
"O monkeys, why have you carried off even him, or why have you stolen the Jina at the best of sacrifices?
Release these two monkeys; release the best of horses! (69)
"Forgive the king's brother Śatrughna, who is prone to great anger.
Hearing those words from their mother, the two powerful ones spoke to her.
"By the code of the warrior (kṣātradharma), we have conquered that king who was endowed with strength;
there shall be no future [conflict] for us with these two as they fight according to the warrior code. (71)
It was spoken by Vālmīki in the past; let it be recited before us as we read. ||72||
Having been raised in Kaṇva’s hermitage, I have adopted the conduct appropriate for the performance of sacrifice;
therefore, even a son may fight with his own father, and a younger brother with his elder brother. (73)
Since even a disciple has not been bestowed by the Guru, there can be no possibility of [attaining] the Upāya;
therefore, by your command, we two shall now offer this supreme horse.
"We shall release these two monkeys and fulfill your word," having spoken thus to their mother, those two lords of monkeys, the foremost among heroes, departed for the field of battle.
They also released the horse suitable for the horse-sacrifice rites;
meanwhile, Queen Sītā, having heard that her army had been struck down by her two sons, [was overcome with grief].
Having meditated upon Śrī Rāma with his mind, he gazed at the Sun as the witness, [thinking]:
"If I [have offended] the Leader of the Raghus by thought, word, or deed... (77)
I worship no other with my mind; for otherwise, this king would still live, as would this entire great army which was forcibly destroyed. (78)
"O Lord of the worlds, may you both live by virtue of my truth," thus spoke Janaki, whose deity was her husband. (79)
And all that force was [routed] at the front of the battle. ||80||

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Sustenance of the Army," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
[65] The sixty-fifth chapter. Śeṣa said:
In that assembly of warriors, the heroic Śatrughna abandoned his fainting spell in an instant;
other weak heroes who had fallen unconscious also regained their lives. ||1||
Śatrughna saw before him the best of horses standing there,
as well as himself, his life-force within the army, deprived of his helmet.
Beholding this wonderful sight, he spoke to his own minister Sumati, the best among counselors, who had then recovered from his swoon.
Having shown compassion, the boy gave him a horse for the completion of the sacrifice, saying, "Go to Amarāvatī; the time for my arrival there has been shortened."
Having spoken thus and mounting his chariot,
he took his horse and departed swiftly from that hermitage to a great distance, without the sound of kettledrums or conchs.
Behind him followed a great army equipped with the four divisions of troops,
which moved along, causing the lord of serpents to bend under its own weight.
Having swiftly crossed the Gaṅgā, which abounds in surging waves,
he went to his own domain, adorned by his own people.
Endowed with Puṣkala and accompanied by Suratha,
the king stood upon a chariot made of jewels, wielding a great bow.
Placing that horse, adorned with a garland of jewels, before him,
he held a white parasol over its head, decorated with chowries.
Surrounded on all sides by many thousands of kings, who were powerful, adorned with the beauty of raised bows, and embellished by the shouts of heroes; ||10||
In due course, he reached the city adorned by the Solar dynasty,
graced with many excellent banners and shining with its formidable fortifications.
Having heard that the horse had arrived with Śatrughna, this sage, and the heroic Puṣkala, Rāma experienced manifold joy.
He pointed out the swift and mighty Kaṭaka and dispatched his brother Lakṣmaṇa, the best among the strong. 13.
Lakṣmaṇa, accompanied by his army, went forth and, overcome with joy, embraced his brother who had arrived with limbs adorned by wounds. (14)
Having been asked about his welfare everywhere, he in turn offered greetings; Śatrughna, filled with supreme joy, was delighted by their company.
The high-minded and heroic son of Sumitrā, remaining on his own chariot together with his brother,
set out toward his own city accompanied by a great army.
The Sarayū, whose holy waters sanctify the three worlds, is purified by the dust of Rāma’s feet and possesses a luster equal to the autumnal moon. 17.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by *cakravāka* birds, and resounded intensely with the cries of birds of most diverse colors. (18)
There, many pavilions were caused to be built by Rāmacandra, resounding with the distinct sounds of recitation from Brahmins learned in the Vedas. (19)
There were many Kṣatriyas there, their hands beautifully adorned with bows,
making the earth resound with the great twanging of bowstrings.
Where the Brahmins were feasting on various delightful foods, they looked at one another and engaged in charming conversation. ||21||
The milk-rice dishes were pure white, equal in luster to the moon,
abundant in milk and ghee, and mixed with sugar.
There were many cakes there, equal in splendor to the orb of the moon, scented with the fine fragrance of camphor and other perfumes, and most enchanting. ||23||
There were smooth oil-cakes, ghee-pots, and vessels with a hundred holes that dripped for a long time;
there were fried cakes, pancakes, and various seasoned sweet foods. ||24||
The cooked rice, resembling white water-lilies and mixed with split mung beans, was endowed with a fragrant aroma and was exceedingly pleasing. ||25||
Accompanied by Bhīmasena, he was joined by an ocean of rice,
prepared by those skilled in sweet cooking and served from vessels by the attendants.
There, some twice-born men, seeing the milk-rice placed in the vessel, said to one another: "What is this wonder that is seen? (27)
Is it the orb of the moon fallen from the sky out of fear of darkness?
It has become nectar here, wonderful in that it destroys death. (28)
Having heard that, another best of the twice-born, his eyes copper-red with rage, said:
"The orb of the moon is not at all flooded with nectar. (29)
How is it that this single roll of cloth appears identical when placed in each individual vessel of a thousand Brahmins? (30)
Therefore, know that this must be either a night-lotus or camphor;
do not mistake it for the deer-mark on the moon, which is endowed with white splendor. (31)
Meanwhile, another was overcome by hunger and shook his head;
yet those foolish brahmins, lacking the discernment to perceive the delicious taste, did not notice him. 32.
But this honeyed [preparation], cooked with the juice of the *dasyu* plant—know that its flowers are sweet lotuses (*śatapatra*). (33)
Thus, O Sage, those brahmins, subsisting on roots and fruits, lived together while speculating about one another, being devoted to asceticism yet intensely greedy for the knowledge of flavors.
Then another twice-born man said: "The birth of Kṣatriyas is superior;
you shall enjoy such food as that, prepared through great merits. (35)
Then the brahmin spoke to him: "Such is the fruit of that [act]:
whatever one gives to the twice-born, they obtain that which they desire. (36)
For those by whom Hari has not been repeatedly worshipped with various kinds of food offerings (naivedya),
such food as this would never even come within the range of their vision.
Those men by whom the twice-born have been fed with various flavors, enjoy [the fruit] of those who have attained a delicious taste, yet are abandoned by the eye. (38)
Thus, having been fed with such sweet foods, those best of the twice-born,
who were experts in the Veda as the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), recited [the scriptures] in the pavilion.
Some were dancing, some were laughing, and some, filled with joy, were singing;
a great festival was manifest there when Śatrughna arrived.
Then Rāma, beholding Śatrughna approaching together with Puṣkala, was unable to restrain the joy that arose within him. 41.
By the time Rāma rose to address his brother, the horse-keeper,
Śatrughna, who was devoted to his brother, had already taken hold of Rāma's feet.
Seeing his brother fallen at his feet, full of humility, he embraced him firmly with joy, his body adorned by wounds. 43.
Shedding many tears out of joy, Rāghava touched his head [to the ground] and attained an extreme,
supreme delight that transcended words.
Bewildered by his own humility, he pressed Puṣkala— who was bowing at his feet—
firmly between his arms and squeezed him very tightly.
[He saw] that hero Hanūmat, as well as Sugrīva, Aṅgada, Lakṣmīnidhi, Janakaja (Sītā), Pratāpāgrya, and Ripuñjaya. ||46||
Subāhu, Sumada, Vīra, Vimala, Nīlaratnaka, Satyavanta, Vīramaṇi, Suratha, and Rāmasevaka. ||47||
Then Raghunātha himself firmly embraced those other illustrious kings, who were affectionate toward him and prostrated at his feet. 48.
Sumati, filled with joy, firmly embraced the illustrious Lord of the Raghus, who bestows grace upon his devotees, and stood before him with uplifted head. 49.
Then, seeing his own minister who had arrived in his presence,
that best of speakers, who delighted in him, spoke to the minister with supreme affection.
"O best of wise ministers, O foremost of those who know the sacred fires!
Who are all these rulers of the earth, and how have they gathered here? (51)
Where was the horse found? By whom was it led away?
And how was it liberated by his brother, who was endowed with great strength and majesty? (52)
Śeṣa said:
Thus addressed by the best of ministers,
the highly intelligent Sumati, laughing with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, spoke to the descendant of Raghu.
Sumati said:
"How can I speak today before you, the omniscient one?
You ask according to worldly custom, yet you are all-seeing and know everything. (54)
Nevertheless, always placing your command upon my head, I shall speak;
listen now, O crest-jewel of all kings. (55)
"O Master, by your grace, oh, I have as it were wandered everywhere upon the surface of the earth, adorned with the leaf of the forehead [as my banner]. (56)
No one, proud of the strength of his own name, could subdue his mind;
then, having surrendered their respective kingdoms, they bowed at his lotus feet.
Who else, free from old age and death, desiring victory, would seize this best of steeds that slew the Daitya lord Rāvaṇa? (58)
Meanwhile, O Lord, your delightful horse reached Ahicchatrā;
hearing that your horse had arrived, King Sumada came forth. (59)
Accompanied by his son and surrounded by a powerful army of all his forces,
he surrendered the entire kingdom, now free of all thorns.
Having propitiated the Mother of the universe, the leader of the worlds and the destroyer of worldly existence,
King Yauvanāśva obtained long life and a kingdom free from all thorns.
This Sumada bows down to you, who are served by lords;
accept him with a glance of compassion, for he has long been desirous of seeing you. (62)
Then, in the city of King Subāhu, which was filled with troops,
his son Damana seized that excellent horse.
A great battle took place between him and Damana;
Puṣkala achieved victory, having rendered the son of Subhūja unconscious.
Then Subāhu, filled with rage in the battle, forcibly fought against the son of the Wind-god,
the best among the strong, who was a servant of his own lotus feet.
Having obtained the knowledge [of the Vedas] that had been struck down by his foot and eclipsed by a curse,
he offered it all to you and became the protector of the horse.
"O King of noble arms, this mountain-peak bows down before you;
please look upon Subāhu, who is skilled in statesmanship, with a compassionate eye and grant him your blessing. (67)
Then, on that very day, while the two horses were still free,
the powerful Śatrughna arrived there with the weapon of delusion (mohanāstra).
Then he went to the city of the gods, adorned by the dwelling of Śiva;
there you indeed know him, since you have arrived there.
O high-minded one, you know that after the Daitya Vidyunmālin was slain, Satyavat then engaged in battle with Suratha.
Then, freed from the headstall, the horse galloped everywhere;
no one, arrogant in his own prowess and strength, could restrain him.
O best of men, listen to what occurred there when that beautiful horse arrived at the lovely hermitage of Vālmīki. (72)
There, assuming the likeness of a young bull and appearing sixteen years of age,
that most powerful one seized a horse with its ears pricked up upon seeing it.
O best of men, a great battle then took place there with Kālajit; he was slain by that hero with a sharp-edged weapon. (74)
Many mighty warriors, such as Saṃkhya and Puṣkala, were slain;
furthermore, that crest-jewel among heroes rendered Śatrughna unconscious.
Then the king, reflecting upon that great suffering in his heart during the battle,
the hero— the best among the strong— became overwhelmed with rage.
While you were unconscious, another arrived;
by him, having restored [the army] to life, your entire camp was destroyed. (77)
Having seized the weapons and ornaments of all those who had fainted,
the two monkeys, bound together, departed toward their own hermitage.
Out of compassion, he once again gave him a great sacrificial horse;
thus, the entire army, which had lost its lives, was restored to life.
"Having taken that vehicle, we have arrived in your presence;
thus was that speech which you spoke previously understood by me. (80)
