Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Submission by Sumati," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||65||
The sixty-sixth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Thus were the two children described by Sumati in the hermitage of Vālmīki.
Knowing that they were his own two sons, he spoke to Vālmīki.
Śrī Rāma said: O Kauśika, why do these two, who possess a form similar to mine, who are the best among the strong,
and who are experts in the science of archery, remain there?
Having heard what was said by the minister, amazement arises within me, for those two bound Śatrughna and Hanumān with ease as if in play. (3)
Therefore, let all this be well for the Sage and for the two children;
may it be as desired, so that my supreme joy may come to pass.
Having heard that which was spoken by the wise king of kings,
he spoke these supreme words, composed of clear syllables.
Vālmīki said: How could there be knowledge of you, the inner controller of men?
Nevertheless, I shall speak so that the virtuous may find satisfaction.
The two princes, the best among the strong, were in my hermitage;
they bore a resemblance to you and possessed enchanting forms. (7)
When Jānakī, though innocent, was abandoned by you in the forest, she was pregnant and lamented again and again in that dreadful wilderness. (8)
Seeing your beloved, the daughter of Janaka, afflicted with grief like a female osprey, I then brought that virtuous lady to my hermitage.
In that [hermitage], a leaf-hut had been beautifully constructed by the sons of sages;
in it, she gave birth to two sons who illuminated the ten directions.
I made their names clearly known as Akara and Vaikuṇṭha;
there they grew incessantly, like the moon during the bright fortnight.
In due time, O King, I performed for him all the rites beginning with the initiation (upanayana), and I caused him to master all the Vedas together with their auxiliary limbs (sāṅga).
Listen from my own mouth to all these along with their secret doctrines:
Āyurveda, the science of archery, and likewise the science of weapons. (13)
Having mastered the Vidyā-jāla-dharī and become skilled in music,
they sang along the banks of the Gaṅgā and in the groves of jasmine creepers.
O best of the Raghus, when those two, whose minds were both restless and unsteady yet proficient in all branches of knowledge, arrived, I then attained the highest satisfaction.
Having bestowed all the weapons and placed his hand upon [his] head,
he who was exceedingly skilled in singing caused the people to marvel upon seeing him.
They were experts in the distinctions between the notes ṣaḍja, madhyama, gāndhāra, and dhaivata. ||16||
Having observed such a sign, I caused this enchanting and auspicious Rāmāyaṇa to be sung, through the application of my knowledge of the future. ||17||
Expert in playing clay drums, hand-drums, and other instruments, as well as in the lute, those two wandered from forest to forest, singing and enchanting the deer and birds. ||18||
The wonderful sweetness of the song of you two, Rāma and Kumāra,
was such that Varuṇa brought those two boys there for the night to hear it.
There, at the command of Lokeśa, the two Kumāras, who had crossed the ocean of the arts of youth, beauty, song, and knowledge, spoke melodiously.
Varuṇa, together with his family and singers, heard your supreme, sweet, delightful, and purifying life-story. (21)
O descendant of Raghu, even Varuṇa, together with Mitra, did not reach satiety while listening to his conduct,
which was sweeter than nectar itself.
With the functions of his life-force and senses stolen by the great greed for the bliss of singing,
he commanded Kumāra and Anahita to return.
Although the two boys were tempted by delightful and great enjoyments,
they did not waver from the recollection of the lotus feet of their spiritual preceptor and their own mother.
And I too went afterwards to the supreme abode of Varuṇa;
there, O Lord, Varuṇa, filled with affection, performed worship for me.
To Varuṇa, who was questioning me about the births, deeds, and everything else concerning both myself and Bāli, I related my entire account, beginning with my birth and my acquisition of knowledge.
Having heard this, the Lord [Rāma], out of respect for my words, accepted the two sons of Sītā along with the discus and excellent ornaments, saying, "Let them be known as Devadatta. (27)
That which was given by Varuṇa, who was pleased with the two princes on account of their musical skill, singing, knowledge, age, and virtues, was brought [by them].
Then the virtuous Varuṇa spoke to me with reference to Sītā.
Sītā, preeminent among women devoted to their husbands, endowed with beauty, character, and youth, possessing heroic sons and great fortune, ought never to be abandoned. (29)
O descendant of Raghu, there is great loss in abandoning this;
for this is your supreme accomplishment among all accomplishments, and it is indeed imperishable. (30)
If this greatness of his is not understood by the base who are defiled by sin, what loss is there for him whose name is meritorious to hear and chant? 31.
With us as witnesses, her conduct has always been pure;
those who meditate upon the feet of Sītā shall attain perfection immediately. (32)
By whose mere volition these lords—the perpetual functions of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds—come to be. (33)
Sītā is death and she is nectar; she both scorches and rains down. Jānakī is heaven, liberation, austerity, yoga, and charity. (34)
This Sītā, your beloved, creates Brahmā, Śiva, and other world-protectors such as myself; she alone does this, no other woman can.
"You are the father of all the worlds, and Sītā is the mother; therefore, this wicked view is never at all conducive to your welfare. (36)
The Blessed One himself knows Sītā to be eternally pure;
you too know your daughter, O Lord of the Earth, to be dearer to you than life itself.
Therefore, O Lord, you must hold Janaki dear as one who is pure;
there is no curse nor any defeat for Sita, nor for you.
O Vālmīki, best of sages, you must speak these words of mine directly to Rāma, the Lord of the worlds. (39)
Thus was I addressed by Varuṇa regarding the matter of seizing Sītā;
for it is exactly the same with all the world-protectors as well, O Lord.
The singing of the Rāmāyaṇa was heard by your two sons, as well as by the gods, the asuras, and all the gandharvas, whose minds were filled with curiosity. (41)
All of them, being delighted, praised those two sons, saying: "The three worlds have been enchanted by their beauty, song, youth, and virtues. (42)
That which was given by the world-protectors was accepted for the benefit of their two sons; likewise, boons were granted to them by the sages, and fame was bestowed upon them over all others.
Formerly, the entire world was seen by the sage as having only one Rāma; now, at its end, it has been seen by you and your two sons as having three Rāmas. 44.
Previously, he was seen in the worlds as one whose form was overcome by a single desire;
now, however, he is born here and there, increasing through four desires.
Wherever the son of Rāma and Kuśīlava are present among the lords of kings, there the song is sung without hesitation; why then have you, a learned man, acted with such timidity? 46.
When all these deeds were accomplished, a great hymn of praise was heard regarding the renunciation of Sītā by you, O crest-jewel of those of meritorious fame. (47)
O Lord of the three worlds, by you who are emulating the life of a householder, two sons endowed with learning, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities must be accepted. (48)
Having abandoned their own mother, they will remain nearby; therefore, you must summon those two sons together with their mother. 49.
Now, by reviving the army, Datta has once again become the purifier for all people, even for those who have fallen from grace. 50.
O subduer of pride, neither he nor we, nor the gods, know that which has been lost;
it is certain that it has perished here from the worlds of that pure one.
Śeṣa said:
Thus addressed by Vālmīki, Rāma, though omniscient, praised and bowed to Vālmīki and spoke to him along with Lakṣmaṇa. (52)
"Go now, my friend, and having mounted the chariot with Sumantra, bring back our companion in dharma together with her son. (53)
Having caused these words of mine and of the sage to be heard,
and having awakened this city, quickly bring back Sītā.
Lakṣmaṇa said:
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, at your command I shall go for the sake of us all;
if the Queen comes to this divine procession, then it will become fruitful."
It was only out of malice toward me, due to the influence of former faults, that she acted thus; since she has not yet arrived, please forgive whatever offense I have committed.
Having spoken thus, Lakṣmaṇa, mounting the chariot by the king's command,
went with Sumitrā and his two disciples to the hermitage of the daughter of the earth (Sītā).
"How might the venerable Sītā be made to feel confidence toward me, who always recognizes my former fault and remains under the control of Rāma? (58)
Reflecting thus, with his heart caught between joy and trepidation, Lakṣmaṇa reached Sītā’s hermitage, which dispels all weariness. (59)
Then, descending quickly from the chariot with eyes choked by tears, he spoke repeatedly, saying, "O Noble One! O Venerable One! O Blessed One! O Auspicious One! (60)
Trembling all over, he fell at her feet;
and he was raised up by that goddess, who was overwhelmed with affection.
For what purpose have you come, O gentle one, to this forest dear to the sages?
Is that Lord—the pearl from the oyster-shell of Kausalyā—well? (62)
Free from the nature of anger, honored by his singular fame,
he is celebrated by all the worlds as an ocean of auspicious qualities.
Overcome by the fear of ill repute, he appointed you to abandon me;
because of this, his stainless fame has spread throughout the worlds. (64)
Even after death, O Lord, they maintain their husband’s good reputation and remain steadfast;
therefore, let her surely attain proximity to her husband. (65)
Even though I have abandoned it, he has not been abandoned by me in the slightest;
for the fruit depends upon the means, but the cause does not depend upon the fruit.
O Mother, she who is empty of the thorn of Kausalyā, filled with compassion, and always free from disease—she whose son is the protector of the three worlds—is well. (67)
Are all my kinsmen, Bharata and the others, well?
And is the highly fortunate Sumitrā well, for whom I am dearer than her own life? (68)
Why then have you also been abandoned by me? Proclaim this throughout all the worlds!
What is difficult for that king to renounce, when even his own self is not dear to him? (69)
Thus questioned in many ways by her, the younger brother of Rāma spoke to that virtuous woman:
"The Lord is well; he inquires after your welfare."
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and the other wives of the king asked after your welfare, O Queen, with affection and blessings.
"O auspicious lady, preceded by inquiries after your welfare, I offer my salutations at your feet for your benefit; I announce that Śatrughna and Bharata have arrived. (72)
O auspicious Jānakī, all the gurus and their wives have bestowed blessings upon you and inquired after your welfare. (73)
The self-possessed god, free from guile, has taken you as his consort;
O beautiful lady, he finds no pleasure in anyone other than you anywhere else.
"O daughter of Janaka, all these directions are truly empty without you!
Seeing this, the Lord wept, causing even others to weep. (75)
O Goddess, wherever you were stationed, Rāghava constantly remembered you;
he considered that very place to be not empty, even though it was devoid of the daughter of Videha.
"Blessed is this hermitage where Janaki was born, wherein Valmiki dwells speaking of my news as he passes the time"—thus [he spoke]. (77)
"O Lord, listen to that which you have said while weeping;
whatever is in the heart of a speaker becomes manifest without a doubt. (78)
The world says of me alone that I am the Lord of all lords;
yet I declare that their independence, which you have not seen, is the cause [of their state]. (79)
Even if one were invisible, everyone would still follow after him;
why then would those who are subject to his power not follow him in matters of pleasure and pain? (80)
The breaking of the bow, the confusion of the mind, the death of his father in the single combat, the departure for the forest, and there, the abduction by you from the ocean. (81)
Even in the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, in that battle free from fear,
the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas became my allies.
O beautiful lady, when the promise you made has been fulfilled and truth established, and when you have regained your own kinsmen and the kingdom, [then... 83.
Furthermore, that very cause for our separation from our beloved, which was previously irresistible, has today become favorable once again for our union. (84)
I am indeed the first cause, by whom the Veda was fashioned according to its form, from which the origin and dissolution of the worlds proceed, and who follows after the worlds. 85.
People who possess true understanding follow what has been unseen;
that unseen merit is worn away by experience, and each of those things has been experienced by you, O Earth. (86)
O Sītā, this causeless affection of mine for you, which increases daily, has disregarded what is seen by the world; therefore, he calls out to you with earnestness.
Even by a suspected fault, there occurs an immersion in the impurity of affection;
therefore, that which is entirely pure should always be tasted by the wise. (88)
O noble lady, this purification through affection has been performed upon you;
yet it must be understood that even though this world is protected by one who follows the conduct of the virtuous, [it remains as it is]. (89)
O Goddess, let there be no enmity between us for the sake of our purity in all circumstances; otherwise, this world would perish, being utterly deluded by the conduct of these great ones. (90)
Our fame is radiant; our aesthetic flavor is radiant;
our lineages are radiant; and our deeds are radiant. (91)
May our fame be sung by radiant singers throughout the earth;
and those who possess devotion to us, may you, O wise one, protect them. (92)
Having been addressed thus by him, who was pleased by her virtues, she made her mind compassionate so as to behold the lotus-feet of her husband. (93)
Delightful garments, great ornaments, as well as saffron, perfumes, and other pleasing things have been bestowed upon you. (94)
Chariots, elephants, and horses, sent by Rāma for the festival, shone brilliantly along with beautiful umbrellas and fly-whisks. 95.
He was being praised by the best of the twice-born, by bards, panegyrists, and heralds;
he was being saluted by the women of the city and attended upon by his warriors.
The goddess was being covered with flowers by the gods, Gandharvas, and others,
as she was bestowing wealth upon those twice-born ones according to their desires.
Placing Kumāra, mounted upon an elephant, at her head, Jānakī,
followed by me, went to her own city, Ayodhyā.
When you had gone there and were united with your beloved, all those royal women who had arrived from every direction likewise [were united] with their lovers. 99.
Let there be a great festival today for all the wives of the sages as well as those of the Kosalas, with auspicious instrumental music, songs, and other festivities. (100)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this report, the goddess Sītā said to him:
"O King, I am not one who brings fame; indeed, I myself am infamy. (101)
What could be accomplished for him by me, who am devoid of virtue, pleasure, and wealth?
Since this is so, O King, why do you place such boundless trust in me, who am as unsubstantial as a blade of *niraṅkuśa* grass?
Whether manifest or unmanifest, the faults residing in the mind of the husband cannot be spoken of by one born of an ignoble family who resembles a woman of evil lineage. (103)
In whatever form he stood in her heart at the time of taking his hand in marriage,
in that very form he never departs from her heart.
O Lakṣmaṇa, these two are delicate yet born from a portion of my own splendor;
they are scions of the Ikṣvāku lineage, great heroes, and experts in the science of archery. (105)
"Having led my father near the scales and having weighed him with great effort,
I shall remain here and propitiate Rāma through austerity according to my desire."
"O noble one, you must convey my salutations at the feet of the venerable ones, and inquire after the welfare of everyone on my behalf. (107)
He commanded his two daughters: "Go to the presence of your father;
he, who has bestowed his own position upon you, must indeed be served by you both. (108)
Although they were reluctant, those two, Kuśa and Lava,
at the command of Vālmīki, went there together with Lakṣmaṇa as soon as they were commanded.
The two sons went to the vicinity of Vālmīki’s own lotus-feet;
Lakṣmaṇa also, accompanied by the boy, went there and paid his respects to him. (110)
Valmiki and Lakshmana praised the two princes;
having learned that Rama was seated in the assembly hall, these men who had gathered there departed in eager anticipation. 111.
Then the wise Lakṣmaṇa, bowing down, related everything to Rāma—including Sītā’s words—filled with both joy and sorrow. (112)
From the words of Sītā’s message, Rāma experienced a faint;
having regained consciousness, he spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who was skilled in statesmanship. (113)
"Go again, O friend, and with great effort bring him here quickly; may it be well with you, having reported these words of mine. (114)
"O Jānakī, why do you perform austerities in the forest? Has some other arrival been contemplated, or has something heard or seen by you? Why, O water-born one, do you not come? (115)
By your own will, you yourself went to the forest beloved by sages;
there you were honored by the wives of sages and the hosts of sages were seen by you. (116)
"O beautiful lady, your desires are fulfilled today; why do you not come? You see no fault in me, having observed my own inner inclination. (117)
Wherever a woman goes, her destination is the broad banks of the Thavāmō river;
for even one devoid of merit attains virtues there, so what need be said of one who is desired by the mind? 118.
Whatever action women of noble family perform for the satisfaction of their husbands, I was already pleased by it before; now, however, I am even more so with you. (119)
Sacrifice, recitation, austerity, charity, vows, pilgrimage, compassion, and so forth—the gods and all this are undoubtedly satisfied when I am satisfied. (120)
Śeṣa said:
Having received this message from the Lord of the World regarding Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, bowing with affection, spoke to Hari, the Lord of his own soul. (121)
Regarding that which you spoke with a gracious mind concerning the bringing back of Sītā, I shall relate those words endowed with humility. 122.
Having spoken thus and bowed at the feet of Raghunātha, Lakṣmaṇa went quickly toward Sītā, standing in a chariot of great speed.
Vālmīki, beholding the two illustrious sons of Rāma endowed with great majesty, spoke while putting on a smile and making his face charming. 124.
"O you two, sing forth the wonderful life-story of Rāma’s son;
play the lute, beautified by your sweet and melodious singing. (125)
Thus, O highly fortunate one, those two sages sang the life-story of Rāma, which bestows great merit and is adorned with excellent words and phrases. 126.
In this [family], the dharma-code is manifest, and therein resides the virtue of wifely devotion;
there is great brotherly affection, and likewise reverence for elders. (127)
Where indeed the policy of master and servant exists as if personified, and where the punishment for unrighteousness is meted out directly by the scion of Raghu; 128.
The world was pervaded by his singing; even the gods in heaven remained there, and even the kinnaras, upon hearing his song, fell into a swoon in an instant. (129)
Hearing the resonance of the lute, beautified by rhythmic timing and measure,
the entire assembly there became like a painted figure in a temple mural.
Shedding tears of joy, King Rāma and the other rulers were likewise enchanted by the sound of his singing in the *pañcama* scale; they stood motionless, as if painted in a picture. (131)
There, Rāma, having seen those two sons who were enchanting with their great singing,
gave to each of them one hundred thousand pieces of gold separately.
Then, seeing Vālmīki, the best of sages, intent on taking it up, those two, with slightly arched eyebrows, spoke while laughing. (133)
Indeed, that sage, the great leader and lord of the earth, acts thus when he desires to give us gold, tempting us with it. (134)
The acceptance of gifts is praised for Brahmins, but certainly not for others;
a king who is devoted to accepting gifts leads only to hell.
"O Lord of the Earth, having enjoyed the kingdom granted by our grace, how can you, whose mind is intent on the highest good, wish to give away gold coins? (136)
Having spoken thus and seeing those two, Vālmīki was filled with compassion and declared:
"Know him to be your father, O you two most skilled in ethics. (137)
Having heard these words of Mūrkha, the two boys, endowed with humility and exceedingly pure through devotion to their mother, fell at the feet of King Bālaka. (138)
Embracing the two boys firmly against his own body, Rāma was filled with joy;
he then considered those two to have arrived as Dharma and Mūrti incarnate.
O Lord of Sages, having beheld the charming faces of both Sabhāpīra and Amasuta, they truly considered Janakī’s devotion to her husband to be genuine.
Having heard what was thus spoken by Śeṣamukha, Vātsyāyana, desiring to hear the Rāmāyaṇa which is endowed with all virtues, spoke. (141)
Vātsyāyana said: O Lord, at what time was this great Rāmāyaṇa composed? For what reason did he compose it, and what is described therein? Please tell me that. (142)
Śeṣa said:—
Once, the brahmin Vālmīki came to a great forest where there were palm trees,
tamāla trees, and flowering kiṃśuka trees. (143)
Where the ketakī flowers, perfuming the forest with their pollen,
appear like great moons, bearing white ears of light.
The campaka, the bakula, the kovidāra, and the kuraṇṭaka [are also mentioned]. ||144||
In that beautiful forest, many trees were in bloom,
resounding with the cries of cuckoos and the humming of bees.
Resounding on all sides, delightful, and endowed with captivating youth, there was a charming pair of *krauñca* birds, tormented by the arrows of love. (146)
Delighted with one another, they remained there in affectionate union;
then a hunter approached and [slew] one of those two, who was captivating.
"A certain merciless man, greedy for the taste of it, killed me;
then, seeing her husband slain by the hunter, she was filled with grief. (148)
He lamented intensely out of grief, crying out loudly from the bank;
then the sage became enraged at the Niṣāda who had killed the krauñca bird.
Having touched the auspicious and purifying waters of the river, he cursed him: "O Niṣāda, may you remain in this place for eternal years! (150)
O twice-born ones, because you killed one of the two krauñca birds while it was deluded by passion, this continuous stream of verses has arisen from that very act. 151.
Those virtuous ones, being greatly delighted, said to the sage, "Excellent! Excellent!
O Lord, by their words, as if impelled by a desire, Sarasvatī composed this verse.
O best of sages, O bull among brahmins, this verse was exceedingly enchanting;
thereupon the sage became delighted in his heart.
At that time, Brahmā arrived there accompanied by his sons. ||153||
Speech addressed Vālmīki: "O Lord of Sages, you are blessed;
having resided in your mouth, the Goddess of Speech has attained the state of being a verse. (154)
Therefore, compose the delightful Rāmāyaṇa in sweet syllables, by which your stainless fame shall endure until the end of the kalpa. (155)
Blessed indeed is this speech, endowed with the name of Rāma;
any other talk of desire produces nothing but sin for men. 156.
Therefore, relate the world-renowned life of Rāma, by which there may be the destruction of the sins of sinners at every step. (157)
Having spoken thus, the Creator, accompanied by all the gods, vanished;
thereafter, he reflected: "How might the Rāmāyaṇa come to be? (158)
Then, intent on meditation, he was born upon a delightful riverbank; and there, a charming grove appeared for him. (159)
Having beheld Rāma, who was dark as the petal of a blue lotus and possessed of lotus-like eyes,
[he observed] his past conduct and the entirety of what was yet to come.
Then, having attained that ultimate joy, he composed the Rāmāyaṇa, endowed with beautiful words and diverse poetic meters. (161)
O sinless one, in that Rāmāyaṇa there are six charming sections:
the Bāla, the Āraṇyaka, and likewise the Kiṣkindhā and Sundara. (162)
O Great-minded One, any man who hears these six other [sections], including the Uttara-yuddha, shall be liberated from all sins through that merit. 163.
There, being content with that [child], Paṅktiratha obtained four sons through the Putreṣṭi sacrifice, including Hari himself, the eternal Brahman. (164)
Having gone to the sacrifice of Kauśika and married the daughter of Bhārgava, Sītā,
he returned to the city and was appointed to the exalted position of heir apparent.
Following his mother's words, he went to the forest; having crossed the Gaṅgā, he reached Mount Citrakūṭa accompanied by his wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having heard that [his brother] was in the forest, the wise Bharata went to his brother;
not finding him there, he himself took up residence in Nandigrāma.
Listen, O child, to this other account arising from the forest—a description of the dwellings of sages as they resided here and there in their hermitages. 168.
The cutting off of Śūrpaṇakhā’s nose, the destruction of Khara and Dūṣaṇa, the slaying of Mārīca through his illusory power, and the abduction of Sītā by the demon Rāvaṇa. ||169||
The wandering in the forest by one separated from his beloved, filled with human-like behavior;
there, the sight of the headless trunk (kabandha), and likewise the journey to Pampā. ||170||
This section concerning Hanumān’s meeting [with Sītā] is known as the "Forest" (Vanaparvan);
listen to another part as well, O Sage, which I shall relate to you in brief.
The division of the seven palm trees, the wondrous slaying of Vālin, the granting of the kingdom to Sugrīva, and likewise the description of the mountain; 172.
From Lakṣmaṇa comes the commission of the task; the exile of Sugrīva;
likewise, the mobilization of the army and also the search for Sītā. (173)
Therein are the sighting of Sampāti, the crossing of the vast ocean, the arrival at the opposite shore, and the wondrous *Kaiṣkindha* section. 174.
Listen indeed to the beautiful Sundarakāṇḍa, wherein lies the wondrous story of Rāma;
it contains the monkey’s wandering from house to house and his seeing of Citrā.
Therein is the sight of Sītā and likewise her conversation with Jānakī;
the destruction of the grove by the enraged [demons], and the binding of the monkey. (176)
Then follows the burning of Laṅkā, the meeting with the monkeys,
the granting of Rāma’s token of recognition, and the departure of the army.
The building of the bridge across the ocean, the alliance with Śuka and Sāraṇa—thus has been narrated the beautiful account of the reunion with Sītā in battle. ||178||
The dialogue with the sages in the northern region and the commencement of the sacrifice are told there;
the many stories of the hermitages destroy the sins of those who hear them. 179.
Thus has been declared this six-sectioned [work], which removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
it has been narrated by me to you in brief, being most enchanting. (180)
That Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses and marked by six sections, is proclaimed as the destroyer of great sins. ||181||
Having heard that, Rāghava was delighted; he seated his two sons on a throne, embraced them firmly, and then remembered his beloved Sītā.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Singing of the Rāmāyaṇa," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||66||
The sixty-seventh chapter. Śeṣa said:
Then Saumitri, having arrived, bowed repeatedly to Jānakī.
With a voice faltering with love, he uttered the words prompted by Rāma. ||1||
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa reunited with Sītā and full of humility,
she heard Rāma’s message from his mouth and spoke, overcome with bashfulness.
"O son of Sumitrā, how could you have come here without having abandoned Rāma in the great forest?
Stay here in the hermitage of Vālmīki, remembering Rāma. (3)
Having heard those words uttered from her mouth, the son of Sumitrā said:
"O Mother, Rāma, devoted to his wife, is repeatedly summoning you."
A devoted wife does not take to her heart any fault committed by her husband;
therefore, come with me, staying upon this excellent chariot.
Having heard these and other such words, Janaki, whose deity is her husband,
abandoned her mental anger and remained seated in the chariot with the son of Sumitra.
Having bowed down to all the female ascetics and the sages who were radiant with Vedic knowledge,
and remembering Rāma in her mind, she boarded the chariot and went to the city.
Gradually reaching the city and adorned with costly ornaments, she arrived at the river Sarayū where Rāma himself was staying. ||8||
Descending from the chariot accompanied by Lailitā and Lakṣmaṇa,
she who was devoted to her husband clung to the feet of Rāma.
Seeing Jānakī arrive, overwhelmed with love, Rāma said: "Excellent! Now, together with you, I shall perform the completion of the sacrifice."
Having offered salutations to Vālmīki as well as to those other most excellent brahmins, she went forth,
eager to perform a prostration at her mother's feet.
Then, having bestowed blessings upon Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and his beloved Janakī, the mother of heroes,
he experienced manifold joy.
Seeing the daughter of Videha bowing at Kaikeyī’s feet, she bestowed this blessing upon her:
"Live long with your husband and your son. (13)
Beholding the daughter of the King of Videha, who was as radiant as the moon,
Sumitrā offered her a blessing that would grant her sons and grandsons.
Sītā, the beloved and virtuous wife of Rāmacandra, who was bowed down on all sides by heat, attained supreme joy, it is said, like the submarine fire (Vāḍava) [upon receiving its fuel]. 15.
Seeing that Rāmacandra’s wife had arrived,
the pot-born sage (Agastya) censured his golden wife and bestowed that [status] upon the woman who walks in righteousness.
Then Rāma shone together with Sītā in the midst of the sacrifice, like the autumnal moon of radiant luster accompanied by Tārā. ||17||
At that delightful time, he performed a ritual there for the removal of all sins of Vaidehī, who was a practitioner of dharma.
Beholding Rāma together with Sītā, deeply engaged in the sacrificial rites,
those present there rejoiced, filled with curiosity.
There, at that excellent sacrifice, Rāma said to Vasiṣṭha and Sumati:
"O masters, what must I do next that is most essential? (20)
Having heard Rāma’s words, the high-minded preceptor said:
"The honoring of Brahmins must be performed so as to bring about their satisfaction. (21)
Formerly, Marutta had performed a sacrifice for which all the necessary materials had been gathered;
at that time, the Brahmins there were gratified with wealth and other offerings. (22)
The brahmins were indeed unable to carry away such an immense accumulation of wealth;
unable to bear the burden of that wealth, the twice-born cast it into the region of the Himalayas.
Therefore, O best of kings, you too, possessing the preeminent fortune of royalty,
should give gifts and other offerings to the Brahmins so that there may be supreme satisfaction.
Having heard this, that foremost of kings, regarding the pitcher-born one as worthy of worship,
first honored the son of Brahmā, whose wealth is his asceticism.
With many collections of jewels and various loads of gold, surrounded by countries and people who bestowed extreme joy. ||26||
They honored the charming Agastya together with his wife,
likewise with jewels, gold, and various regions as well.
He likewise honored Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī;
and he honored Cyavana together with his wife with excellent jewels.
He also honored all the other sages, those repositories of asceticism who served as officiating priests,
with heaps of jewels and numerous loads of gold in manifold ways.
Then Rāma gave a profuse sacrificial fee to the Brahmins;
he bestowed a hundred thousand pieces of gold upon each member of the twice-born.
He bestowed gifts in many ways upon the poor and the wretched, with riches and captivating jewels acquired through righteous means. (31)
There he bestowed, according to the scriptures, variegated garments and soft foods that brought joy to everyone. (32)
The city, crowded with joyful and well-nourished people, thronged by all living beings, and filled with men and women, became exceedingly delighted.
Seeing that best of sacrifices, which bestows joy upon all, the twice-born sage born from the womb of a jar attained the highest and most intense delight. (34)
Then, for the purpose of the consecration bath, he summoned sixty-four kings along with their wives to bring water that was like nectar. (35)
Rāma, together with Sītā, went to fetch water,
carrying a golden-colored pitcher that was adorned with every kind of ornament.
The son of Sumitrā [Lavaṇa] married Ūrmilā; King Bharata married Māṇḍavī; Śatrughna married Śrutakīrti; and Puṣkala married Kāntimatī. (37)
Subāhu was born from Satyavatī, Satyavān from Vīrabhūṣaṇā, Sumada from Satkīrti, and King Vimala from Rājñī. 38.
There, King Vīramaṇi was with Śrutavatī, Lakṣmīnidhi with Manojñā, and Ariputāpa with Aṅgasenā. (39)
Vibhīṣaṇa was mounted on a horse of great stature, preeminent in majesty and renowned; Ugrāśva was on one that moved at will and was exceedingly beautiful with its dark-blue jewels.
The brahmin sage Vasiṣṭha dispatched Suratha with Sumanohārī, and likewise Kapī with Mohanā, and other such kings.
Vasiṣṭha, the knower of mantras, went to the Sarayū river, which was flooded with auspicious and holy waters,
and consecrated the water with a Vedic mantra.
O Payasvinī, purify this horse with water drawn by mind, for the sake of the sacrifice of Rāmacandra, the sole protector of all the worlds. (43)
All the kings, headed by Rāma, brought that water touched by the sage to the floor of the pavilion,
which was being praised by the foremost of brahmins.
Having bathed the horse, who was white as milk, with pure waters,
the son of the pitcher (Agastya) consecrated it with a mantra using the hand of Rāma.
Purify me, O great steed, in this assembly crowded with Brahmins;
by your sacrificial offering, may all the gods be gratified and fully satisfied. (46)
Having spoken thus, Rāma, together with the king and Sītā, touched him;
then all the twice-born ones, out of wonder and curiosity, considered it a marvel.
"We said to one another: 'By the mere remembrance of the name of the thief, men are liberated from great sin; what indeed does Rāma say? (48)
When the lord of the earth had spoken thus,
the sage who had arisen from the earth took up a sword, consecrated it with mantras, and placed it in Rāma’s hand.
When the sword was grasped by Rāma at the sacrifice, his companion,
having abandoned his state as a sacrificial animal, immediately assumed a divine form.
Then, having ascended an excellent celestial chariot together with the apsarases,
he was fanned with yak-tail whisks and adorned with Vaijayantī garlands.
Then, seeing that excellent one who had abandoned his horse-like form and assumed a divine appearance,
all the people at the sacrifice were filled with wonder.
Then Tadarāma, himself knowing [the answer], informed all the people and questioned that most righteous celestial being of divine form.
Who are you, possessing a celestial form? Why have you attained the state of a horse? How is it that you are accompanied by a divine woman? Tell us, what do you wish to do? (54)
Having heard Rāma’s words, the god spoke to the lord of the earth; laughing, he uttered a most charming voice with the sound of thunderclouds.
"Though you know everything everywhere, moving both externally and internally, nevertheless, since you ask, I shall tell you the truth as it is. (56)
Formerly, O dispeller of the enemy's fear, I was a most righteous brahmin named Rāma; yet I acted in opposition to the Vedas. (57)
Once in the past, I went to the bank of the Dhūtapāpā river,
which was delightful in every way and graced by many trees.
Having bathed there, gratified the ancestors, and given gifts according to the prescribed rule,
O mighty-armed one, he performed meditation in accordance with the Vedas.
O King, many people gathered there at that time;
for the purpose of deceiving them, I performed this miracle. (60)
The supreme courtyard was filled with the materials for numerous sacrifices;
it was beautiful, vast, covered with cloths, and equipped with sacrificial posts and other implements.
The smoke arising from the Agnihotra sacrifice, assuming a wondrous form, made the entire expanse of the sky incomparably beautiful.
Adorned with the splendor of many auspicious marks, he was honored by great gōs;
was he perhaps the Lord himself, resplendent with *darbha* grass, holding sacrificial fuel in his hand, assuming a physical form? 63.
There, Durvāsas, wandering over the surface of the earth with his pure vision,
reached that place on the bank of the river Dhūtapāpā, O one of great splendor.
I saw him before me, the maker of the moon, observing silence,
his hands of priceless value, appearing like one intoxicated, and offering no word of welcome.
Seeing this, the great-minded sage, overcome by intense anger like the ocean during the change of the moon, cursed him: "May you be split asunder by me, who am fierce. (66)
"O evil-minded one, O lowest of ascetics, since you have broken this bridge, you shall therefore attain the state of a beast, which is beyond reproach. (67)
Having heard the curse that was bestowed, I then became distressed;
indeed, I seized the feet of that sage Durvāsas.
Then the twice-born Rāma bestowed a supreme favor upon him, saying:
"O ascetic, may you attain the state of a horse for the king of kings, Makha. (69)
Thereafter, through contact with his hand, she assumed a divine form that captivated the mind, possessed of the supreme state and free from rebirth.
Thus, even the curse he pronounced has turned into a favor for me, since I have obtained the delightful touch of his hand. (71)
That which is difficult to attain even for gods such as Indra over many lifetimes—this very touch of your hand, so rare in this world—I have now obtained. (72)
"Command me, O Great King! By your grace, I shall go to that great, eternal abode which is free from suffering and all such evils. (73)
O Lord of Men, by your grace, may I go to that place where there is no sorrow, no old age, no death, and no confusion of time. (74)
Having spoken thus and circumambulated him, he ascended that excellent celestial chariot,
which was inlaid with many jewels and honored by all the gods.
By the grace of Rāma’s feet, he has gone to that eternal abode, which is free from rebirth and devoid of sorrow and delusion. (76)
Having heard what he said and recognizing Rāma,
all the other people were filled with wonder and became mutually overjoyed.
Listen, O twice-born one of great intelligence: even if Hari is remembered by chance, he grants liberation; how much more so from the complete abandonment of worldly existence! (78)
In whatever way possible, one should perform the supreme remembrance of Rāma, by which one attains the highest state that is difficult even for the gods to reach. 79.
O sages, they considered themselves blessed upon beholding that wondrous sight,
which had been purified by the touch of the hand of one who gazed upon the feet of Rāma.
When that Lord, who had previously assumed the form of a horse, had departed for heaven,
Rāma spoke to those foremost among the knowers of the Vedas, who were treasures of asceticism.
"O Brahmin, what must I do so that this horse, having perished, may attain happiness?
How shall the future oblation be performed, which satisfies all the deities? (82)
"O sages, act in such a way that there may be great satisfaction for the gods, that this may become my supreme sacrifice, and that it may be performed according to the prescribed rites. (83)
Having heard these words,
Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages and an expert in discerning the thoughts of all the gods, spoke.
"Bring the camphor quickly, so that the gods themselves, impelled by my word, may now receive the oblation upon arriving in person. (85)
Having heard these words, Rāma quickly brought forth camphor, broken into many pieces for the pleasure of the many gods. (86)
Then the sage, his soul filled with joy, summoned the wondrous gods;
they all arrived at that very moment, accompanied by their own retinues.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Sacrifice," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||67||
The sixty-eighth chapter. Śeṣa said:
There, Indra saw the sacrificial offering prepared by Rāmacandra.
Even when joined by the gods, he did not attain satisfaction from eating his fill. ||1||
The great god Nārāyaṇa, the four-faced Brahmā, Varuṇa, Kubera, and likewise the other world-protectors were present there. ||2||
There, the sacrificial oblation was savory, unctuous, and prepared by Vasiṣṭha;
yet there, O best of Brahmins, they were like those afflicted by hunger longing for food.
Having gratified all the gods with the sacrificial oblation, that treasury of compassion, urged by Vasiṣṭha, performed everything that was to be done. ||4||
The Brahmins were satisfied with their gifts, and the excellent gods were pleased;
all of them, having taken their respective portions, went to their own abodes.
He bestowed the kingdom of the four quarters upon the sages, headed by the Hotṛ priests;
satisfied, those twice-born ones granted him auspicious blessings.
Then, having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), Vasiṣṭha, along with his excellent wives,
congratulated the lord of the earth for having perfectly completed the supreme sacrifice.
Having heard those words, the women joyfully showered him with parched grain—him who surpassed Kandarpa in beauty and was adorned with great jewels. (8)
Then, having urged the king to perform the avabhṛtha bath, Rāma went with his own followers to the excellent bank of the Sarayū. ||9||
Surrounded by many tens of millions of kings traveling on foot, he went to that most excellent river, which was crowded with flocks of birds.
Just as the lord of the stars shines with his own wives, so too did Rāma, possessed of great splendor, shine forth surrounded by hosts of kings.
Having learned of that festival, people arrived with great haste,
their eyes rendered motionless by the sight of the face of Sītā’s husband.
As the lord of kings proceeded toward that river together with Sītā,
the people, their eyes filled with joy and longing for a long time to behold him, gazed upon him.
Many actors and gandharvas, singing of his glorious fame, followed the Lord of the Earth, who is honored by all the worlds. (14)
There, dancing girls were dancing, agitating the mind of their lord; they went to serve Śrī Rāma, sprinkling him with water from their jars. 15.
They smeared the great king with turmeric, saffron, and other substances; they anointed one another and attained a state of supreme joy. 16.
They were beautifully adorned with pearl necklaces resting upon their pairs of breasts, and were distinguished by golden earrings shimmering on their two ears. (17)
Traversing a path crowded with many men and women,
he reached Vatsarita, which was flooded with the holy waters of the Śiva.
Having gone there with Vaidehī and accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and the others, the lotus-eyed one entered the sacred water along with Rāma.
All the kings and the people likewise entered that water,
which was purified by the dust of his feet and honored as the sole refuge of the world.
Sprinkling one another with delightful water-sports,
they all, with their beautiful red eyes, attained an exceeding joy of mind.
Together with Sītā, he sported for a long time in that flood of meritorious waters amidst the waves; then, endowed with righteousness, he emerged. ||22||

Clad in fine linen, adorned with a crown and earrings, graced by armlets and a radiant necklace, and possessing the splendor of ten million gods of love, the king shone while being praised by the most excellent of sovereigns. (23)

Having erected a sacrificial pillar at the excellent bank of the river, adorned with supreme beauty, that high-minded king—by means of his own arms—seized the wondrous glory of the worlds of the three realms, which is difficult for others to attain. (24)
Thus, performing three horse-sacrifices with the daughter of Janaka as the sacrificial fee,
he attained incomparable fame throughout the three worlds, which is very difficult even for the gods to achieve.
Thus, O dear one, the virtuous story of Rāma, which you asked for, has been narrated by me at length;
O twice-born one, what more do you wish to ask?
Whoever hears with devotion the excellent sacrifice of Rāmacandra, the moon of the Raghus, shall instantly cross over the sin of killing a Brahmin and attain the eternal Brahman. ||27||
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth shall obtain wealth;
one afflicted by disease is released from disease; and one who is bound is released from bondage. 28.
By hearing whose story even a wicked outcaste attains the supreme state; how much more so a preeminent Brahmin who is devoted to the worship of Rāma? (29)
By remembering the highly fortunate Rāma, even sinners shall attain the supreme state and the highest heaven, which is difficult even for Śakra and the gods to reach. ||30||
Blessed are those men who behold and remember the best of the Raghus;
having quickly crossed over the cycle of worldly existence, they attain imperishable bliss. ||31||
Each individual syllable is a forest fire for the destruction of the sin of killing a Brahmin;
the wise man who causes that [text] to be heard should fully honor that teacher. (32)
Having heard the narrative, one should cause a pair of cows to be given to the reciter,
after honoring him along with his wife with garments, ornaments, and food.
They shone with two earrings, adorned with finger-rings;
they were beautiful, excellent, and resembled golden images of Rāma and Sītā.
Having performed [the rite], he said: "O best of the twice-born, if this body is given away, then the gods and the ancestors shall attain Vaikuṇṭha. (35)
O Brahmin, the story of Rāma, which you did not ask about, has already been told to you by me; what else may be told before you, O wise one? (36)
Those who hear this narrative, which destroys the flood of sins arising from the killing of a Brahmin, shall attain that supreme abode which is very difficult even for the gods to reach. (37)
Even a killer of a cow, a killer of a son, a drinker of liquor, or one who violates the teacher’s bed becomes purified in an instant; there is no room for doubt in this matter. (38)
Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa,
within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana concerning the Horse Sacrifice of Rāma,
this is the section titled "The Description of the Merit of Hearing and Reciting."
The sixty-eighth chapter. ||68||
Thus ends the section on Rāma’s Horse Sacrifice.
The Greatness of Vṛndāvana (69):
The Sixty-ninth Chapter.
The sages said:
O highly fortunate one, you have duly related from us the account of Rāma’s horse-sacrifice;
now, please describe the majesty of the great-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Sūta said:
O tigers among sages, listen to the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deeds;
I shall relate to you that which Pārvatī asked of the Lord of Beings.
Once, the goddess Pārvatī, her heart full of affection for Śiva, bowed with love and spoke these words: ||3||
Pārvatī said:
For Viṣṇu, who abides within and without the infinite millions of universes, there is a supreme abode that is the foremost, the best, and the most excellent among them. (4)
I wish to hear all about that most delightful place dear to Kṛṣṇa, which has no superior; please tell me, O Great Lord. (5)
Īśvara said: This secret, more secret than the secret, which produces supreme bliss,
is most wonderful— a private place, the highest and ultimate bliss.
O Goddess, it is the most difficult among the difficult to attain, supremely enchanting, composed of all powers, and hidden in all places. (7)
The eternal place named Vṛndāvana, situated above the universe, is the foremost abode of the Sātvatas and is extremely difficult even for Viṣṇu to attain. ||8||

The complete Brahman’s bliss, sovereignty, eternal, and imperishable joy—of which Vaikuṇṭha and other realms are but partial portions—a fraction of that very essence is Vṛndāvana itself upon this earth. (9)
Whatever sovereignty belongs to Goloka is established in Gokula;
whatever majesty belongs to Vaikuṇṭha is indeed established in Dvārakā. ||10||
That Brahman which is supreme sovereignty, eternal, and centered in Vṛndāvana—the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa—is especially present within that forest. ||11||
Therefore, within the three worlds, the earth is renowned as blessed, because it contains the place named Mathurā, which is the singular favorite of Viṣṇu. 12.
The region of Mathurā is its own preeminent name;
it is a manifold, hidden place situated within the city. 13.
The district of Mathurā has the form of a thousand-petaled lotus;
through the revolution of Viṣṇu’s discus, it is indeed a wondrous Vaiṣṇava abode. (14)
The extent of the petals of the pericarp is said to be the Secret Tree;
the greatness of the primary Twelve Forests has been described in sequence. (15)
Bhadra, Śrī, Lohabhāṇḍīra, Mahātāla, and Khadīraka; Bakula, Kumuda, Kāmya, Madhu, and likewise Vṛndāvana. ||16||
This number, twelve, extends as far as the western side of the Kālindī; to the east, Pañcavana is proclaimed, where that supreme secret resides. (17)
The great forest named Gokula, as well as Madhuvana and Vṛndāvana, and other groves are declared to be the sites for the aesthetic flavor of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes. (18)
The Kadambakhaṇḍana, Nandavana, Nandīśvara, as well as the Nandanandanakhaṇḍa, and the Palāśa, Aśoka, and Ketakī groves. (19)
Sugandhamānasa, Kailāsa, Amṛta, Bhojanasthala, Sukhaprasādhana, Vatsaharaṇa, and Śeṣaśāyika. ||20||
Śyāmapūrvadadhigrāma, likewise Cakrabhānupura, Saṃketa, Dvipada, and Bālakrīḍanadhūsara. (21)
The lovely wish-fulfilling tree and the grove filled with longing;
various sports of diverse flavors and a place for manifold playful delights. ||22||
The great station called Gokula is described as the secret tree, supported by the expansion of the Nāgas, and possessing a thousand-petaled lotus. 23.
That pericarp is the great abode, the supreme station of Govinda;
there, upon a golden throne, it is adorned with a pavilion of jewels. (24)
In the pericarp, the petals are said to be arranged in order in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
that petal which is declared to be in the south is the supreme, most secret, and most excellent. (25)
Upon that petal is the great seat (mahā-pīṭha), difficult to access even through the Vedas and Āgamas, hard for even the lords of yogīs to attain—that Gokula which is the soul of all. 26.
The second petal is in the southeast; likewise, it is the petal of the secret.
There is the convention of the two-footed, and the two huts situated within that family. (27)
The eastern petal and the third, the preeminent and supreme station, are remembered as being a hundred times more meritorious than the touch of all sacred fords (tīrthas) such as the Gaṅgā. ||28||
On the fourth petal in the northeast, at the Siddha-pīṭha, is that very station;
there, by practicing yoga, a young cowherd girl shall obtain Kṛṣṇa as her husband. (29)
The seizing of garments and ornaments is declared to be its petal;
in the north, the fifth petal is proclaimed, which is the best of all petals. (30)
Right here is the twelve-sun lotus, its petals equal in size to the pericarp;
in the north-western direction is the sixth petal, where the Kālī-lake is said to be located. ||31||
The supreme among the supreme is indeed called the primary station;
the most excellent petal is remembered as the seventh in the west. ||32||
It bestows the desired boons upon the hosts of the wives of the sacrificers;
even an asura attained here that nirvāṇa which is difficult for the gods to reach. (33)
Right here is the petal that deludes Brahmā, which brings about the lake of Brahmā;
in the southwest is declared the eighth petal, the destroyer of the void.
The slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, which is a place for the essence of various pastimes, is said to be the eighth petal situated within the Vṛndāvana forest. (35)
The beautiful and glorious Vṛndāvana, situated to the right of the Yamunā, was seen;
there he beheld the abode of the auspicious Liṅga known as Gopīśvara. (36)
Outside of that is a sixteen-petaled [lotus] filled with Śrī; one should worship that Lord in all directions, as prescribed, proceeding clockwise in due order. (37)
The great state, the great abode, known as the refuge of one's own nature;
it is the foremost single petal, the most excellent, and its majesty is like the pericarp. ||38||
There, on the beautiful Govardhana mountain, which is the eternal abode of rasa, in the pericarp lies the Great Pastime (mahā-līlā), a deep cavern of the nectar of that pastime. ||39||
Where Kṛṣṇa, the eternal lord of the Vṛndā forest, resides—Kṛṣṇa who has attained the state of Govinda—what is the use of further words? (40)
The third petal has been described as the most excellent and supreme of all;
the fourth petal is described as the locus of the most wonderful aesthetic flavor (rasa). ||41||
The delightful Nandīśvara forest is there, where the abode of Nanda is remembered;
the greatness of the pericarp-petal is described as the fifth petal. ||42||
The presiding deity here is Gopāla, who is devoted to the protection of the cows;
that which is called the sixth petal is known as Nandavana. (43)
The seventh petal is proclaimed as the beautiful Bakulāraṇya;
there is the eighth, Tālavana, where the slaughter of the cow is recorded to have occurred. ||44||
The ninth petal is proclaimed as the delightful Kumuḍāraṇya;
and the tenth is Kāmāraṇya, the foremost cause of all. (45)
The adornment of Brahmā, the manifestation of Viṣṇu’s disguise, and the locus of the aesthetic flavor of Kṛṣṇa’s play—this is called the primary petal. ||46||
In the eleventh [chapter], it is declared that the cause for bestowing grace upon devotees is the construction of the Setubandha, a place consisting of various groves of trees. (47)
The delightful and enchanting Bhāṇḍīra forest has twelve groves;
there Kṛṣṇa, intent on play, is surrounded by Śrīdāmā and others. 48.
The thirteenth petal is most excellent; therein is remembered the supreme Bhadra.
The fourteenth petal is declared to be the place that bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). ||49||
There is a beautiful forest, the cause of all sovereignty, consisting of the leaves from Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, which increases splendor, beauty, and fame. (50)
The fifteenth petal is the most excellent; there, the Iron Forest (Lohavana) is remembered.
The sixteenth petal is said to be equal in majesty to the pericarp (karṇikā). ||51||
The Great Forest is sung of there; therein lies the supreme secret.
There He is engaged in childhood play, surrounded by cowherd boys. (52)
Therein occurred the slaying of Pūtanā and others, as well as the breaking of the twin Arjuna trees;
there the presiding deity was Bālagopāla, five years of age. ||53||
He is called by the name Dāmodara, an ocean of the nectar of the bliss of love;
this petal is renowned and declared to be the most excellent of all petals. (54)
The play of Kṛṣṇa is the pericarp, and the vihāra is said to be the petal;
it is also declared that the principal perfected ones constitute the pericarp and the petals. ||55||
Pārvatī said:
"O Great Lord, what is the greatness or the wonderful secret of Vṛndāvana? I desire to hear that; please tell me. (56)
Īśvara said:
O most beloved one, I have told you that which is the secret of secrets, the highest of the high, the mystery of mysteries, and the most difficult to attain among all things difficult to attain. (57)
O Goddess, this place is protected by the three worlds, highly honored by the Lord of Gods, desired by Brahmā and others, and frequented by the gods, siddhas, and so forth. ||58||
For the lords of yogis are always devoted to him with faith, intent solely upon his meditation;
and by the Apsarases and Gandharvas, there is constant dancing and singing. (59)
The glorious Vṛndāvana is enchanting, the abode of the nectar of perfect bliss;
its waters are like a multitude of cintāmaṇi jewels, filled with the nectar of immortality. 60.
There, one should visualize a tree as the Guru-tree, frequented by hosts of fragrant deities;
the woman as Lakṣmī and the man as Viṣṇu, arising from a tenth part of that [tree]. (61)
Therein, he is eternally of youthful age, an embodiment of bliss, with movement and dance, and with a face constantly adorned with sweet speech and smiles. (62)
That forest was inhabited by pure-hearted Vaiṣṇavas full of love;
it was immersed in the bliss of the perfect Brahman, vibrating with His form and identical with Him.
It was enchanting with the sweet warbling of intoxicated cuckoos, bees, and others;
it possessed the concert of parrots on its temples and thousands of frenzied bees. 64.
Abounding in the dance of the enemy of serpents (the peacock), possessing the playful charm of every fragrance, and filled with the pollen of various colored flowers. ||65||
It is like the full moon, ever-rising; it is served by the gentle rays of the sun;
it is free from suffering and brings an end to suffering; it is devoid of old age and death. (66)
Free from anger and devoid of envy, undivided and without egoism;
it is the essence of the nectar of perfect bliss, an ocean of the happiness of full love. ||67||
The great abode transcends all qualities; its very nature is perfect love, where even trees and other beings experience horripilation and shed tears of the bliss of divine love. 68.
How much more so, then, for those devotees of Viṣṇu who are endowed with conscious intent—what can be said of them?
For by the touch of the dust of Govinda’s feet, Vṛndāvana is eternally present upon this earth.
Vṛndāvana is the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus;
by the mere touch of it, the earth becomes blessed throughout the three worlds. (70)
More secret than the secret, delightful, situated in the midst of Vṛndāvana on earth, it is the imperishable, supreme bliss, the eternal abode of Govinda. (71)
The liberated state is the complete Brahman, the abode of bliss, non-different from the body of Govinda; what more can be said of its majesty, since even the touch of its dust brings liberation? (72)
Therefore, O Goddess, with your whole being, make that forest reside within your heart—Kṛṣṇa, whose form is that of a youth, during his pastimes in Vṛndāvana. (73)
And the Yamunā performed a circumambulation around its pericarp—water that was profound with playful liberation and enchanting with fragrance. (74)
It is a dense abode of the nectar of bliss mixed with that [nectar], resplendent with various colors through flowers such as lotuses and water-lilies. ||75||
The water, graced by *cakravāka* ducks and other birds with various sweet songs, was beautiful within and delightful to the mind. (76)

Beautiful on both its banks and fashioned from pure gold, that place is said to possess ten million times the merit of the Gaṅgā, where even a single cowrie shell touched there [is of such value]. (77)
In the pericarp [of that lotus] is Kālindī, where Lord Hari, who is of one indivisible form with Kṛṣṇa, delights in play ten million times more intensely than elsewhere. (78)
Pārvatī said:
O Govinda, whose form is fashioned from beauty itself, what is so wonderful about you?
O ocean of compassion, I wish to hear that; please tell me. (79)

Īśvara said: In the midst of beautiful Vṛndāvana, which is adorned with the splendor of tinkling bells, and decorated with the branches and sprouts of excellent trees extending for many yojanas; ||80||
In the center of that, within the abode of Mañjuśrī, is a brilliantly shining yoga-seat; its construction consists of eight corners, enchanting with various splendors. (81)
And above that is an auspicious lion-throne made of rubies;
upon it is a lotus with its petals vanished, providing a comfortable refuge within the pericarp. 82.
What can be said of the supreme abode of Govinda? It is praised for its greatness, being served by the multitude of cowherd maidens who abide in the mantra of the glorious Govinda. (83)
Kṛṣṇa, the divine Lord of Vṛndāvana, who possesses the age and form of a cowherd boy, the sovereign of Vraja, whose opulence is eternal, and the sole beloved of the children of Vraja. ||84||
His childhood was bursting forth with youth, his form was wondrous by virtue of his age;
he is the beginningless origin of all, the beloved son of Nanda Gopa. (85)
Sought after by the Vedas, unborn and eternal, the captivator of the hearts of the gopīs, the supreme abode, the supreme form, two-armed Lord of Gokula. (86)
One should meditate upon the son of the cowherd women, the sole cause of the attributeless [Brahman], who is most glorious, ever-new, pure, the beautiful abode of dark splendor, and enchanting. (87)
Glistening like a row of fresh rain-clouds, with beautiful earrings, possessing the lovely luster and pleasant touch of a blooming blue lotus, it brings happiness. ||88||
Śyāmamohana, who is as smooth as a mass of crushed blue lotuses, with hair that is exceedingly glossy, dark blue, curly, and entirely fragrant; 89.
Above that, in the southern direction, [is a forest] enchanting with dark crests, radiant with various colors, and adorned with the plumage of royal peacocks. (90)
In some places, his crest was adorned with *mandāra* flowers, *mañju* grass, and cow-tails, beautifully decorated;
in other places, it was graced by a crown consisting of rows of large petals. 91.
In some places, he was adorned with crowns and ornaments of many gems and rubies; in others, his face was surrounded by trembling locks of hair and resembled ten million moons in its splendor. ||92||
His forehead was adorned with a musk tilaka, shimmering with black pigment and yellow orpiment;
his eyes were long and exceedingly lustrous like the petals of a blue lotus. (93)
With smiles accompanied by the embrace of dancing creeper-like eyebrows and sidelong glances, it was exceedingly captivating with the beauty of her well-formed, elevated nose-tip. 94.
The three worlds were enchanted by the rays of the pearls from the tip of her nose, and she was most captivating with her lower lip, beautifully glossy and reddened by vermilion. 95.
[He wore] earrings in the shape of golden makaras, shimmering with various colors;
their radiance shone like the surface of a mirror upon his excellent cheeks, which were adorned by clusters of rays. 96.
Adorned with ear-lotuses, jasmine, and *mandāra* flowers as makara-shaped crest-jewels, his chest bears the *śrīvatsa* mark and the *kaustubha* gem, and his neck is radiant with a pearl necklace. 97.
Adorned with shimmering divine rubies mixed with fine gold,
he wears bracelets and armlets on his arms, and is beautified by small bells at his waist.
It is resplendent with feet possessing the glorious beauty of smooth and soft soles, and it is adorned with camphor, agallochum, musk, shining sandalwood, and other such substances. (99)
Adorned with divine body-unguents mixed with gorocanā and other substances, she shone with a smooth yellow garment reaching down to her forefeet, as she swayed to and fro before the people. (100)
With a lotus-like navel deep and beautiful, a line of body hair like a curved garland, a pair of well-rounded knees, and feet as charming as lotuses; ||101||
Adorned with a banner, a vajra, a goad, and a lotus upon his hands and the soles of his feet, he is the singular cause of Brahman, filled by the rows of rays from his moon-like nails. 102
Some say that a portion of Him is Brahman, the non-dual form of consciousness;
the wise declare Mahā-Viṣṇu to be one-tenth of that portion. ||103||
That very form, with its three-fold bend (*tribhaṅga*), fashioned from the essence of all graceful emanations, is meditated upon in the heart by the lords of yogis such as Sanaka and others. (104)
Beautiful as infinite millions of Kandarpas with necks turned sideways, and with a golden earring shimmering on his noble cheek resting upon his left shoulder. 105.
Smiling with sidelong glances, as beautiful as ten million gods of love, he plays the sweet and melodious notes of the flute placed upon his slightly pursed lips. ||106||
To Him who deludes the three worlds and is immersed in the nectar-ocean of divine love, Śrī Pārvatī said:
"Kṛṣṇa, known as Govinda, is the supreme cause and the great abode. (107)
The Lord of Vṛndāvana is eternally the sole cause of the Nirguṇa;
what wonderful and beautiful mystery of His greatness could there possibly be? 108.
"Tell me that, O Lord of the gods; I wish to hear it, O Master.
Īśvara said:
"The limit of the majesty of the moonbeams from the nails of whose feet cannot be reached. (109)
O Goddess, listen with joy as I describe how great that majesty is:
within infinite millions of universes, and within the infinite expanse of the three qualities (guṇas). ||110||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are but a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of that [reality];
endowed with the functions of creation, maintenance, and so forth, they remain as its manifestations. (111)
Portions consisting of millions upon millions of parts of that form, possessing bodies like those of Kandarpa, residing within that cosmic egg, cause delusion for the world. (112)
The All-pervading Lord is but a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth fraction of the splendor shining from His body;
the rays of His light, which are but a ten-millionth part of that [splendor], take the form of the suns. ||113||

By means of the rays of his own body— which consist of the nectar of the essence of supreme bliss, which are the form of consciousness characterized by supreme fragrance, and which are the sole cause of the attributeless [Brahman]— ||114||

The rays of light, consisting of the splendor from the moon-like jewels of the nails of His pair of lotus feet, sustain [the world] as a mere infinitesimal fraction of a fraction of that [light]. (115)
They say that even the perfect Brahman has as its cause that which is difficult for the Vedas to fathom;
an infinite croreth part of a fraction of its fragrance is what deludes the universe. (116)
The source of various fragrances, such as the scent of flowers touched by Him, is His beloved primordial nature, Rādhikā, the consort of Kṛṣṇa. 117.
Durgā and the others, who consist of the three qualities (guṇas), are but a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth fraction of that [energy];
from the touch of the dust of her feet, ten million Viṣṇus are produced. (118)
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Life of Kṛṣṇa," within the "Glorification of Vṛndāvana" in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
— o)0(o— (70) The Seventieth Chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord, I desire to hear about those who listen to this [narrative] and who are the attendants of the Master; tell me, O ocean of mercy! (1)
Īśvara said:
[He saw] Govinda seated upon a golden throne together with Rādhā, possessing the previously described form and beauty, and adorned with divine ornaments, garments, and garlands. 2.
The pupils of the eyes of the cowherd girls are beautifully smooth with the three-fold arching curve;
outside of that, on the Yoga-seat surrounded by a golden lion-throne. ||3||

The principal consorts of Kṛṣṇa, such as Lalitā and others, are possessed by an intense absorption in each of His limbs; they are portions of Prakṛti, while Rādhikā is the primordial Prakṛti herself. ||4||
Goddess Lalitā is in the center, Śyāmalā in the northwest;
Śrīmatī Dhanyā is in the north, and Śrī-Haripriyā in the northeast. (5)
Viśākhā is likewise in the east, Śaibyā in the southeast thereafter;
Padmā is in the south, and subsequently they are stationed in order in the southwest.
On the seat of yoga, at the tip of the filaments, is her dear consort Candrāvatī;
there are eight meritorious primary energies, the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa. (7)
But the primary primordial nature (pradhāna-prakṛti) is the first Rādhā, who is equal to Candrāvatī;
[she is also] Candrāvalī, Citrarekhā, Candrā, and Madanasundarī. (8)
Priyā, Śrīmadhumatī, Candrarekhā, and Haripriyā—the sixteen primary Prakṛtis are the chief beloveds of Kṛṣṇa. ||9||
Rādhā, the Queen of Vṛndāvana, and her beloved Candrāvalī possess identical virtues, grace, and beauty; they are both possessed of lovely eyes. ||10||
Manoharā, charmingly dressed and radiant with the youth of adolescence,
was at the forefront, along with thousands of other cowherd girls.
With complexions like pure gold, they were serene and possessed beautiful eyes;
with their forms ascended upon his heart, they longed for his embrace. (12)

Immersed in the nectar of Śyāmā’s sweetness, their minds overflowing with that very emotion, they have offered their hearts to Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, which are honored by the blue lotuses of their eyes. ||13||
Then, tens of thousands of daughters of Śruti were born to Dakṣa;
their forms enchanted the world, and they longed for Kṛṣṇa who dwelt within their hearts. (14)
There, enchanting the three worlds with the various sounds and conversations of diverse beings, they sing of secret mysteries, overwhelmed with love. (15)
Then, on the left side, there were celestial maidens in divine attire, radiant with passion, skilled in various Vedic sciences, and endowed with an abundance of divine emotion. ||16||
Abounding in extraordinary beauty and enchanting with their sidelong glances, they were shameless there toward Govinda, intent on touching his limbs. (17)
With their minds immersed in that state, casting smiling and sidelong glances,
they then went outside the temple, which was clearly covered by their beloved.
They were equal in dress and age, equal in strength and prowess, equal in qualities and actions, and equally fond of ornaments. ||19||
They were intent on playing flutes and singing songs in unison;
Śrīdāmā was at the western gate, and likewise Vasudāmā was at the northern gate.
Sudāmā is likewise in the east, and Kiṅkiṇī in the south;
outside of that, on a golden pedestal surrounded by golden pavilions.

But [He who was] situated within a golden altar, adorned with golden ornaments, accompanied by Subhadra and others, and by tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of cowherds, some of whom were slightly dark-complexioned; ||22||
Even by those who were overwhelmed as they sang—possessing the forms, dress, and voices of deer, lutes, flutes, reeds, birds, and bees, and joined with meditation on His qualities. ||23||
With forms depicted in various colors, shedding tears of constant bliss, and with all their limbs bristling with horripilation, they were like the lords of yogis filled with wonder. ||24||
It is surrounded by innumerable iron Govinda-fences;
outside of that is a golden wall, blazing with the brilliance of ten million suns.
In the four directions is a great garden, enchanted by its exquisite fragrance; to the west, directly in front, is the shelter of the glorious Pārijāta tree. ||26||
Below that, however, upon a golden throne adorned with golden ornaments, and in its center, resplendent with a divine lion-throne of jewels and rubies; (27)
Therein, above, is Vāsudeva, the Lord of the universe, supreme bliss, whose form is consciousness transcending the three qualities (guṇas), and the cause of all causes. ||28||
Dark blue like a sapphire or a rain cloud, with dark, curly locks of hair, large eyes like lotus petals, and earrings shaped like sea-monsters. ||29||
Four-armed, bearing as weapons the discus, sword, mace, conch, and lotus; devoid of beginning and end, eternal, the primordial source, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||30||
The ancient, great abode in the form of light, wearing a forest garland, clad in yellow garments, gentle, and adorned with divine ornaments. ||31||
With divine unguents, their limbs were adorned with royal ornaments, making them enchanting;
there were Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Nāgnajitī, and Sulakṣaṇā. (32)
Then there were the eight wives dear to Vāsudeva: Mitravindā, Anuvindā, Sunandā, Jāmbavatī, Priyā, and Suśīlā. ||33||
The attendants, radiant and devoted to their duties,
surrounded the two [princes] in the great northern garden, which was filled with *hari-candana* trees.
There, below, upon a golden pedestal adorned with a pavilion of jewels, in its center, on a brilliant lion-throne with petals fashioned of gold; (35)
In that very place, together with Revatī, he beheld Saṅkarṣaṇa, whose weapon is the plow—the beloved of the Lord, who is non-different from Him in qualities and form. (36)
Resembling pure crystal, with eyes like the petals of a red lotus, wearing a blue silk cloth, he is radiant and adorned with divine ornaments, garlands, and garments. (37)
Always addicted to drinking honey-wine, with eyes rolling from intoxication, he was situated within Mañju, on the right side of the Great Hero. (38)
At the foot of the tree of the lineage, adorned with a palace of jewels;
in its center, radiant with a divine lion-throne of gems and rubies. (39)
Thus Pradyumna moves there, situated above in bliss, whose very essence is the aesthetic flavor of the series of the quintessence of beauty that deludes the world. 40.
She was dark-complexioned, with eyes like the petals of a lotus blooming at dawn, adorned with divine ornaments and anointed with celestial perfumes. ||41||
His form was a marvel of beauty that enchanted the entire world;
he was in the great forest of the eastern garden, taking refuge among the celestial trees.
There, upon a golden pedestal below, adorned with a golden pavilion,
in its center shone a firm and resplendent divine throne.
The glorious Aniruddha, Lord of the universe, who is like celestial nectar, a dense mass of blissful dark-blue, and possesses very glossy, dark locks of hair. 44.
With eyebrows like the curve of a bow, beautiful cheeks, a fine nose, and lovely ears, he was handsome, with a chest that was both enchanting and captivating. (45)
Wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with ornaments upon his neck, his form was exceedingly beautiful due to the exquisite sweetness of his soft, smooth voice. 46.
Therein dwells He who is to be propitiated by His beloved hosts of servants, who delights in music, who is the full Brahman, eternally blissful, and whose essential nature is pure sattva. ||47||
Above him, in the intermediate space, they all beheld Viṣṇu, the Lord of lords,
who is without beginning, the primordial form of consciousness, supreme bliss, and the all-pervading sovereign.
Beyond the three qualities, unmanifest, eternal, imperishable, and immutable; his dark form possesses the sweetness and beauty of a cluster of blossoming clouds. 49.
Extremely beautiful with a mass of dark, curly, and glossy hair;
possessing long, lovely eyes as smooth as lotus petals. (50)
It was surrounded by those whose very selves were pure beings with uplifted cheeks adorned by crowns and earrings—
those who delight in the Self, whose nature is consciousness, and who were intent on meditating upon His form.
With that meditation ascended in the heart and eyes fixed on the tip of the nose,
causeless devotion is performed through bodily actions, mental states, and speech.
To its left were yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others, along with groups of beautiful apsarases intent upon dance and song. (53)
Then, that womb-born person, along with those who were devoted to the Lord and eager for the black fruit (kṛṣṇala),
was indeed placed upon a comfortable seat in the intermediate space by all those Vaiṣṇavas standing before him.

By Prahlāda, Nārada, and others; by Kumāra, Śuka, and the Vaiṣṇavas; and by Janaka and others, who were radiant with devotion and intent upon the manifestation [of the Divine] within and without the heart. ||55||
With all their limbs bristling with horripilation, overwhelmed by throbbing love,
and drenched in the nectar of the secret, they [uttered] the mantra consisting of two syllables.
It is proclaimed as the crest-jewel of mantras, the sole cause of all mantras;
it is the youthful essence of the mantras of all the gods, having mantra as its source. (57)
The Cūḍāmaṇi mantra is the cause of all the mantras of youth;
those who take refuge in the bliss of perfect love perform its recitation mentally. (58)
They desire that unwavering devotion as the means to attain His lotus feet;
[they seek it] outside [the temple], within beautiful, lofty pavilions made of crystal and other precious materials. (59)
With saffron and white, red, and other colors arranged in the four directions,
one should [visualize] Viṣṇu, who is white and four-armed, as the guardian of the western gate.
Adorned with a conch, discus, mace, lotus, crown, and other ornaments,
he is red in color, four-armed, and holds the weapons of a lotus, conch, discus, and mace.
In the north, one should place Viṣṇu, fair-complexioned, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, and mace as weapons, with his gatekeepers illuminated by his crown and earrings. 62.
Adorned with a crown, earrings, and other ornaments, and wearing a forest garland—this fair-complexioned Viṣṇu is proclaimed as the doorkeeper at the eastern gate. (63)
One should meditate on Śrī Viṣṇu, who is dark-complexioned, four-armed, adorned with conch shells, discs, and other ornaments, and who stands as the guardian of the southern gate. (64)
Indeed, he who, being self-restrained and pure, recites this account of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, or even he who hears it with devotion, attains love for Govinda. (65)
Thus ends the seventieth chapter in the Kṛṣṇa-carita of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||70||
(71) The seventy-first chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, Soul of all, Source of all; O Great God, Lord of gods, Omniscient One, Mine of Compassion! (1)
"O Lord, you have indeed shown me compassion;
furthermore, O Master, you have spoken to me alone the mantras that enchant the three worlds."
Therefore, tell me by what various special means did he, the god who assumes forms of great enchantment, sport with the cowherd women? (3)
Mahādeva said: Once, the eminent sage Nārada, playing his lute and having learned of the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, went to the cowherd settlement of Nanda.
