Having gone there to the house of Nanda, he beheld the Lord, the imperishable Master who consists of great yoga, who assumes the dance of a child, and whose appearance is divine. (5)
He was reclining upon a golden couch covered with very soft cloth,
being gazed upon by cowherd girls, and ever filled with joy.
She was exceedingly delicate, charming, with a lovely gaze,
and her mass of dark, curly hair hung down over the circle of her shoulders.
It was slightly reminiscent of a single elephant’s temple-bud made of stone,
illuminating that interior of the palace equally with its own splendors.
Beholding him who was clothed in the directions (naked), he attained great joy;
and having conversed with the Lord of Cows (Śiva), he, who is dear to all lords, spoke to Nanda.
Indeed, the life of those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa is exceedingly difficult to attain;
no one here knows his incomparable power.
Even Brahmā and the other gods desire eternal delight in him;
and the conduct of this child brings joy to everyone.
Those whose minds are affectionate toward you, O son, who possess inconceivable power, sing with joy, listen, and rejoice in such a manner. (12)
There are men for whom there shall be no obstruction to their prosperity; O best of cowherds, abandon all desires for this world and the next.
"Show your affection toward this child with single-minded devotion and with undivided intent.
Having spoken thus, the bull among sages departed from Nanda’s house. (14)
Honored by him with the thought that he was Viṣṇu, and having been saluted and dismissed,
that sage, a great devotee of the Lord, then reflected.
Then the blessed Lakṣmī,
having assumed the form of a cowherd girl for the sake of sporting with Nārāyaṇa Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, [entered] his mouth.
She must certainly have descended; of this there is no doubt.
Today I shall search for her house by house among the inhabitants of Vraja. (17)
Having reflected thus, the best of sages entered the houses of the residents of Vraja as a guest; being honored with the thought that he was Viṣṇu himself, he was well-received. ||18||
Seeing the supreme devotion of all the cowherds and others toward the son of Nanda,
the best of sages mentally prostrated himself before them all.
In the house of the cowherds, he saw a young girl of white complexion;
having seen her, he reflected: "Without a doubt, this is indeed Ramā. (20)
Then the wise one entered the great house of a certain eminent cowherd named Bhānu, who was a friend of the high-souled Nanda.
Having been honored by him according to the prescribed rites, that high-minded one also asked:
"O virtuous one, you are renowned on earth for your steadfast devotion to dharma."
I perceive your abundance of wealth, grain, and other riches;
do you have a worthy son or a daughter endowed with auspicious marks? (23)
"Since your fame shall pervade the entire world," having been addressed thus by the best of sages, Bhānu brought his son.
Seeing him, who possessed great splendor and was proud, and who was peerless on earth in beauty, the best of sages saluted Nārada.
With eyes as broad as lotus petals, a handsome neck, beautiful eyebrows, lovely teeth, and charming ears—he was beautiful in every limb. (26)
Embracing him with both arms and shedding tears of affection,
the great sage then spoke with love in a faltering voice.
Nārada said:
This child shall become your friend and the companion of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa; he will sport with them day and night, unwearied. (28)
Then the bull among sages addressed that preeminent cowherd, just as the sun spoke to him when he had set his mind on going there. (29)
"O God of gods, I have one daughter who is like the wife of a god;
she is younger than this child, yet her form is like that of one who is dull-witted, blind, and deaf. (30)
Out of enthusiasm for my growth, O Most Blessed One, I beg a boon from you:
by the mere glance of your gracious eye, make the girl firmly established. 31.
Having heard these words, Nārada, his mind drawn by curiosity,
then entered the palace and saw his daughter rolling upon the ground.
Having raised her up and placed her on his lap, his mind overwhelmed with excessive affection, even the Sun-god approached the presence of the excellent sage, bowing low in devotion. (33)
Then the sage, the best of the devotees and most dear to Kṛṣṇa,
beheld her supreme form— wonderful, unseen, and unheard of before.
The great sage Śrī Haridāsa, who had previously been deluded, became enchanted by love for Hari as he plunged into the ocean of supreme bliss, that singular elixir. (35)
For two muhūrtas there, the Sage remained like a pillar;
but the Lord of Munis, having awakened, slowly opened his eyes. (36)
Overcome with great wonder, he remained silent;
with his great intellect, he reflected thus within his heart: ||37||
I have wandered through all the worlds, moving according to my own will;
yet, despite seeing many forms, I have never seen anywhere one equal to her. (38)
My destination is the world of Brahmā, the world of Rudra, and the world of Indra;
yet not even a ten-millionth part of her splendor has been seen anywhere. (39)
The Blessed Lady Mahāmāyā, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, has been seen—by whose form the entire world, with its moving and unmoving beings, is infatuated. (40)
Even Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Kānti, Vidyā, and other such excellent women never attain the splendor of her delicate limbs. (41)
Even her shadow is never seen when it touches [the world], by which form of Viṣṇu as Mohinī Hara was utterly deluded. (42)
And even that which was seen by me—how could it be her equal?
Therefore, I have no power whatsoever to know her true nature.
Moreover, others generally do not know this beloved of Hari;
yet, simply by the sight of her, [one attains] Govinda’s lotus feet. 44.
That power of love which once existed has never before been mine;
I bow to you in solitude, having displayed such great majesty. (45)
"Kṛṣṇa’s form will appear for her supreme satisfaction.
Having reflected thus, the sage sent away the foremost of the cowherds somewhere else. 46.
In private, he praised the girl of divine form:
"O Goddess, sovereign mistress of great yoga and illusion, O you of great splendor! (47)"
O you of divine limbs who utterly enchant, O showerer of great sweetness, O you whose mind is softened by the bliss of the most wonderful rasa! 48.
By some great fortune you have come within the range of my vision;
O Goddess, your gaze is perceived as being eternally turned inward. 49.
O Mahānanda, you appear as if inwardly satisfied; this face of yours is serene, sweet, and gentle. (50)
The power of the bud associated with rajas manifests some supreme wonder arising from internal bliss; that indeed is exceedingly beautiful. (51)
You are established as the embodiment of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal;
you are the supreme Vidyā, whose essence is pure being and whose power is swift. 52.
Who [is she] who bestows the supreme Vaiṣṇava mass of ultimate bliss, O you of wondrous power, who is difficult to reach even for Brahmā, Rudra, and the others? (53)
You never touch the path of meditation of the lords of yogis;
rather, you are the will-power, the knowledge-power, and the action-power of the Lord.
"Only a mere portion of you"—such is the thought that arises in my mind;
for the manifestations of Māyā are inconceivable, belonging to that Magician who is the Child of Māyā. (55)
All those are but parts of the parts of the Supreme Lord Mahāviṣṇu;
you, O Sovereign Lady, are the power whose form is bliss—of this there is no doubt. (56)
And Kṛṣṇa surely plays with you in the forest of Vṛndāvana;
with your youthful form, you are the enchantress of the entire universe. 57.
Touched by the bloom of youth, what kind of wondrous form is yours?
What is the nature of your loveliness, accompanied by playful smiles and glances? (58)
O beloved of Hari, out of a longing for that divine human form adorned with wonders, I desire to behold that body of yours.
O Maheśvarī, out of compassion for me now, reveal Your own form, by which Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, will fall into a state of delusion. (60)
"You ought to reveal [this] to one who is bowed down and has sought refuge," thus was he addressed by that best of sages, whose mind was devoted to him. (61)
Having bowed to the supreme Mahāmāheśvarī, who consists of great bliss,
whose auspicious eyes are agitated by the intense longing of great love— (62)
While gazing at Govinda, he stood thus describing him:
"Victory, O Kṛṣṇa, captivator of the mind! Victory, O beloved of Vṛndāvana! (63)

Victory to You, charming with the knitting of Your eyebrows! Victory to You, filled with the sound of Your flute! Victory to You, who wear a peacock feather as a crest! Victory to You, the enchanter of the gopīs! 64
Victory to you whose limbs are smeared with saffron! Victory to you adorned with jewels!
When, by your grace, shall I [be united] with this one of divine form? (65)
O Lord of the World, I shall behold you in your youth, endowed with the beauty of a body that captivates the mind through its fresh adolescence, enchanting even in your childhood.
As he was thus proclaiming this, at that very moment she once again assumed a divine form, exceedingly enchanting.
At that very time, there were other girls from Vraja who were of equal age, charming and exceedingly beautiful, appearing as if they were fourteen years old.
Arriving, they surrounded him, adorned with celestial ornaments, garments, and garlands;
yet that lord of sages remained motionless, stupefied by wonder.
Then those young female friends, having sprinkled the sage with drops of water from their feet,
awakened him and spoke, filled with compassion.
O most excellent sage, O highly fortunate one, O Lord of the great masters of yoga!
By your supreme devotion alone, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, [was pleased]. (71)
Surely the God who fulfills the desires of his devotees has been propitiated, since he [has appeared] even before gods such as Brahmā and Rudra, and the lords of perfected sages. (72)
She is difficult to behold and hard to attain even for other great devotees;
she is the beloved of Hari, enchanting with her most wonderful age and form. (73)
By some inconceivable fortune, she has come within the range of your vision.
Arise, arise quickly, O brahmin-sage, summoning your fortitude! (74)
Having circumambulated her, pay homage to her again and again;
do you not see this lady of beautiful limbs, who appears as if utterly distressed? (75)
At this very moment, she will surely vanish;
you will not have any conversation with her whatsoever. (76)
Furthermore, O best of the knowers of Brahman, you shall not obtain a vision of her;
however, in Vṛndāvana, a certain auspicious Aśoka creeper shines forth. (77)
Abounding in flowers at all times and possessing a fragrance that pervades all directions, [it is located] on the bank of the lake named Kusuma, not far from Govardhana. (78)
"For at its base, at midnight, you shall see us all without exception.
Having heard these words of theirs, whose hearts were overwhelmed with affection, [he went]. (79)
Having circumambulated her, the sage prostrated himself like a staff before the young woman for two muhūrtas, as she shone with various emanations. (80)
Having summoned Bhānu, Nārada said to her, "O daughter of Bali, this girl possesses such power that she cannot be overcome even by the gods. (81)
However, in that house which is adorned with her footprints,
the god Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava himself, dwells.
And Lakṣmī dwells here eternally with all her various supernatural powers;
today, let this woman of beautiful limbs, adorned with every ornament, [be honored]. (83)
"O best of men, protect her in your home with great effort, as if she were a supreme goddess.
Having spoken thus, that most excellent of great devotees [dismissed her] with his mind alone. (84)
Recalling that very form, the best of sages entered the dense forest and reached the foot of an *aśoka* creeper. (85)
Expecting the arrival of that queen there at night, he remained here, overwhelmed with love, thinking of the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. (86)
Then, at the hour of midnight, young women of supreme wonder appeared;
first those previously seen, and others as well, adorned with various ornaments and garlands. (87)
Seeing this, she was bewildered in her mind and fell prostrate on the ground like a staff;
then all those auspicious women, having surrounded the sage, entered [the hermitage]. 88.
Although that sage desired to ask something agreeable that was to his own liking, he was unable to do so, being overwhelmed by her love, her beauty, and her charming speech. (89)
Then they approached the best of sages, who stood with palms joined in reverence, his neck bowed by the weight of devotion, filled with wonder and agitation. (90)
Thereupon, the deity of the Aśoka grove, named Aśokamālinī, filled with compassion, spoke to him who was most perfectly disciplined: 91.
Aśokamālinī said: "O great sage, I dwell within this bud of the aśoka tree;
I am always clothed in red garments, wearing red garlands, and anointed with red unguents. (92)
Her bud-like crest is vermilion-red, and she wears a red lotus as an ear-ornament;
she is adorned with ruby armlets, a crown, and other finery. ||93||
Once, while sporting with their beloveds during the spring festival,
the cowherd girls, dressed in variegated garments, gathered together in that very place.
And I, with garlands of *aśoka* flowers, properly worshipped Hari, who was wearing the guise of a cowherd, along with all those women who were the very forms of Ramā, out of devotion. (95)
From that time onwards, I have always remained among them, pleasing the Lord of Ramā with various ornaments. (96)
I know everything here from every perspective, even that which is beyond the beyond; I also know the secret of the cows, the cowherds, the gopīs, and all others.
Everything you desired to know has been answered within your heart;
[I have described] that goddess of wondrous form, who bestows marvelous bliss. (98)
How shall I behold Hari’s beloved, who has a golden luster and rings blazing with diamonds; or how shall I behold her tremulous eyes, or her lotus-feet? (99)
"O Brahmin, you have reflected that [the Lord] is propitiated by supreme devotion;
regarding that, I shall relate to you the history of those great-souled ones. (100)
Staying at Lake Mānasa, they engaged in intense austerity, chanting perfected mantras and meditating upon Hari, the Lord. ||101||
Of those sages of great luster, numbering seventy-one thousand, who constantly long for that very lotus-foot of hers. 102.
Therefore, I shall tell you today that supreme secret in this forest.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa," in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(72) The seventy-second chapter.
The Lord said:
Therefore, O lady of beautiful countenance, listen with a one-pointed mind:
there was once a sage of firm vows named Ugratapas. (1)
Maintaining the sacred fires and subsisting on fire alone, he performed most wonderful asceticism;
he recited the supreme mantra to be recited, consisting of fifteen syllables.
Enveloped by the Kāma-mantra, the word "Kāma" which bestows the boon of desire, followed by the term "to Kṛṣṇa" together with Svāhā, is the supreme bestower of success. (3)
And she meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, who was dark-complexioned, adorned with ornaments, intoxicated by the rāsa dance, and eager for the best of women;
he wore yellow silk garments and held a flute to his lips with his hand.
Thus absorbed in meditation for hundreds of kalpas, he released his body while [still] holding that beloved woman— who was endowed with fresh youth— by the hand.
The daughter of the cowherd named Sunanda was that great sage,
known as Sunandā, who held a lute in her hand.
Another sage, renowned as Satyatapas, was a great observer of vows; he subsisted on withered leaves and was devoted to the constant recitation of the supreme mantra.
The best of sages meditated upon Hari, who wears diverse garments, while reciting the ten-syllable mantra encased at both ends with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja). 8.
Holding the two creeper-like arms of Māyā, which were radiant with bracelets,
he danced wildly, repeatedly embracing her.
Laughing loudly within the space of his belly with waves of bliss,
he held a flute reaching down to his knees and was resplendent with the Vaijayantī garland.
With his face and forehead drenched by drops of perspiration,
the great sage repeatedly cast off his body through ascetic penance.
Indeed, born within the interval of ten kalpas, he [was born] from the daughter of the cowherd named Subhadra, who was renowned by the name Bhadrā, in the Nandavana forest and other such places. 12.
On whose back a divine fan was seen, there was once a certain great sage named Haridhāman. (13)
He too performed severe penance, subsisting constantly on a single leaf;
he recited the twenty-syllable mantra, which brings swift accomplishment. (14)
Immediately thereafter, that very seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) ascends;
from the city of Māyā, it is the syllable Haṃ in the sky, possessing the luster of blood and the moon. (15)
Then he meditated upon the Lord, beginning with the ten-syllable mantra joined with "namas" and preceded by the seed-syllable of Smara, within a beautiful mādhavī bower in Vṛndāvana. 16.
And by a certain female attendant, whose eyes were reddened with excessive passion, [he was seen] lying on his back upon a beautiful bed of sprouts.
Repeatedly covering her pair of breasts with her expansive chest, her cheeks being kissed and her lips being satiated. (18)
Embracing his beloved with both arms, laughing and filled with wonder,
the sage abandoned many bodies over the course of three kalpas.
From Sāraṅga, the cowherd, there was born a daughter endowed with auspicious marks,
renowned as Raṅgaveṇī, who was highly skilled in the art of painting.
In those [spots], there appeared what seemed to be vermilion drops;
there was a certain sage who discoursed on Brahman, renowned as Jābāli. (21)
A yogi of great asceticism and beautiful conduct, wandering this earth, came upon a certain great forest extending for ten thousand yojanas. ||22||
Having arrived by chance, he beheld a single, most beautiful pond,
with banks bound on all sides by crystal and filled with sweet water.
In the western direction of her [abode], at the base of a banyan tree, there was a spot frequented by breezes fragrant with the scent of blooming lotuses. ||24||
He saw a certain female ascetic performing severe penance, endowed with the bloom of youth and exceedingly captivating in her beauty. (25)
Having fashioned [the image] with a luster resembling the moon's rays, beautiful in all its limbs, with the left hand placed at the hip and the right hand likewise; 26.
She bore the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā) and had unblinking eyes;
she had abandoned food and movement, remaining perfectly motionless. ||27||
Desiring to know her, that best of sages remained there for a hundred years;
then, having raised her up from her seat, the sage moved on with humility.
He asked: "O lady of wondrous form, who are you, and what will you do?
If it be fitting, you should please tell me. (29)
Then, emaciated by the morning sun, the maiden spoke softly:
"I am Brahmavidyā, who is sought after by the incomparable lords of yogis. (30)
Desiring the lotus feet of Hari, I have performed austerities for a very long time in this formidable forest, meditating upon Puruṣottama. (31)
I am filled with the bliss of Brahman, and my intellect is satisfied by that bliss;
nevertheless, without the delight in Kṛṣṇa, I consider myself empty. 32.
Now, being utterly weary of this body, I desire to cast it off right here in this auspicious pond. (33)
Having heard those words of hers, the sage was utterly amazed;
falling at her feet, he [inquired] about the auspicious method of worshiping Kṛṣṇa.
Having abandoned the inner illumination (adhyātma-virocana), he, supremely delighted, asked about the mantra spoken by her; having received her instruction, he departed for Lake Mānasa.
Then he performed an extremely difficult penance that caused wonder, standing on one foot and gazing at the sun without blinking. ||36||
He recited the supreme mantra consisting of twenty-five syllables; with a state of supreme devotion, he meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, whose form is bliss.
He was walking through the streets of Vraja with a playful and variegated gait,
making his anklets tinkle with graceful steps.
By means of her glances from the corners of her smiling eyes and her various gestures, she captivated him with her artful,
reddish-brown, and variegated gaze known as "the Enchanting."
With sweet, playful words that kiss the bimba-fruit of her lips, O mind, sprinkle that Hara— who is the very embodiment of the hearts of the women of Vraja.
He was suddenly embraced upon arrival by women whose waist-knots had loosened;
he wore divine garlands and garments, and was anointed with divine perfumes and unguents. ||41||
Filling the three worlds with the flood of his dark-complexioned splendor, he thus deluded them;
and so Bahudeva worshipped that Lord of the World.
Born within nine kalpas, she possessed a divine form in Gokula as the daughter of the highly illustrious cowherd named Pracaṇḍa.
Renowned as Citragandhā, the maiden of auspicious countenance gladdens the ten directions with the various fragrances of her own limbs. (44)
Behold this beautiful woman here, drinking honey in groups, her limbs overwhelmed by the intensity of passion as she holds her own husband close. 45.
The embrace of her breasts is obstructed by all the household burdens,
which fall from her chest, scattering their various fragrant scents and perfumes.
Other excellent sages, whose minds were perpetually pure, performed austerities while subsisting on air alone, chanting the supreme mantra. 47.
Smara [should worship] Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the functions of desire, austerity, suffering, and art, having joined the fifteen-syllable mantra together with Āgneyī. 48.
The best of sages beheld the form of Kṛṣṇa, adorned with divine ornaments,
his full and fleshy waist encircled by a divine, variegated silk garment.
Her crest was fashioned from peacock feathers, and she wore brilliant earrings;
with her left hand she held [the skull-bowl], while her right lotus-foot was raised.
Having joined his two beautiful lotus-hands in the *sampuṭa* mudrā,
he held a flute placed against his side, its ends slightly quivering.
Bringing joy to the eyes and minds of those cowherd women,
he entered the circular pavilion in a form of supreme wonder.
Then, in another kalpa, they were born here now, having abandoned their former bodies, while being filled on all sides by the cowherd girls with showers of flowers.
In whose ears were seen earrings illuminated by rays of light;
on whose necks were jeweled garlands, and on whose braids were jewel-flowers.
Muni, named Śuciśravas, and another named Suvarṇa—
these two were the sons of the brahmin-sage Kuśadhvaja, both of whom had mastered the Vedas.
With their feet raised upwards,
those two, with restrained minds, performed a terrible penance while repeatedly chanting the three-syllabled mantra *hrīṃ haṃ saḥ*.
He meditated upon Kṛṣṇa in the cowherd settlement as a ten-year-old boy,
possessing a form equal to Kandarpa and graced with the charm of youth.
Beholding the beautiful lips of the cowherd women and incessantly enchanting them,
he cast off those two bodies belonging to that kalpa and attained birth in Vraja.
O most beautiful daughter of the cowherd named Suvīra, in whose hands these two parrots, so full of sweet sounds, are seen! (59)

The matted-hair ascetic, the one purified by smoke, the one who subsists on clarified butter, and the speckled one— these four sages are blessed, for they are free from longing for this world or the next.
Having surrendered with exclusive and single-minded devotion to the Lord of the Cowherdesses,
they remained submerged in the water, chanting the mantra alone.
Enveloped by the three *ramās*, that eight-syllable mantra beginning with *smara* was meditated upon with intense devotion by the cowherd women in forest after forest.
Honoring him as he wandered about, charming with dancing, singing, and other arts, his entire body smeared with sandalwood paste and adorned with a crest of *japā* flowers; 63.
Adorned with garlands of white water-lilies and draped in blue and yellow garments, those born from the three *kalpas* possessed auspicious marks and were the lords of Gokula. (64)
These are those lovely women seated before me with their brows slightly bent,
whose forearms bear bracelets made solely for the sake of dharma.
In a previous kalpa, the sage Vyāsa, known as Dīrghatapas, was adorned with various jewels and divine pearls.
His son was Śuka, thus known as the excellent and wise sage;
even as a child, that highly intelligent one was always mindful of the supreme state.
Having abandoned his father, mother, and others, he went to the forest after meditating upon Kṛṣṇa;
there, day and night, with divine mental offerings, [he worshipped Him].
Taking no food, he worshipped the Lord Viṣṇu in the form of a cowherd,
while muttering the eighteen-syllable mantra encircled by the name of Ramā.
With a state of supreme devotion, he [saw] Hari beneath a golden tree,
within a golden pavilion, and upon a golden throne.
Seated there, he held a golden flute with the tips of his golden hands,
while with his right hand he whirled a golden lotus.
He beheld his own hermitage, adorned with various paintings by his beloved wife of golden complexion, and seeing it, he laughed with exceeding joy.
His body covered in horripilation and his eyes filled with tears of joy, he cried out loudly, "Be gracious, O Lord!
and then fell prostrate upon the ground in a full-length salutation before the Creator of the three worlds, trembling all over.
To him who had fallen upon the ground desiring devotion, saying loudly,
"I am weary," [the Lord] took his two arms as he prostrated like a staff and touched him with eyes brimming with the joy of affection.
Hari said to Śuka, who had attained a form dear to him:
"O auspicious one, you are most beloved to me; therefore, remain ever near me. (75)
Thinking of my form, she has become the object of intense love;
O auspicious ones, she is two principal gopīs, equal in age to me. (76)
Devoted to a single vow and focused on a single goal, she whose name was that of a constellation shone there like another flash of lightning, resembling molten gold.
One had eyes that were half-closed in sleep, while the other had gentle, long eyes;
he worshipped those two on the left and right sides of Hari with supreme devotion.
Having abandoned that body at will, she was born in Gokula as the daughter of the high-souled Upananda, possessing the luster of the petals of a blue lotus.
This very woman is clothed in the garments of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s wife;
her breasts are golden jars filled with a red bodice.
Wearing vermilion red as her forehead mark and a veil over her entire body,
she was most beautiful, with the regions of her cheeks radiant with golden earrings.
Her beautiful breasts were smeared with saffron and adorned with garlands of golden lotuses;
in her hand was seen that which was to be tasted, offered by Hari. 82.
She was exceedingly skilled in playing the flute and was an attendant of Keśava; once, when Kṛṣṇa was well-pleased during a performance of song— (83)
With her auspicious necklace placed upon her neck, she shone intensely;
though out of Kṛṣṇa’s sight, she was tormented by love with his glances and splendors.
Having dressed this bride in the attire of her beloved, he should have her dance while she is accompanied by friends who play instruments and sing most melodiously. (85)
Again and again she embraces and kisses Govinda with deep devotion;
she is the most beloved of all the gopīs, and Kṛṣṇa is likewise exceedingly fond of her. 86.
A certain son of Śvetaketu, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary branches, renounced everything entirely and devoted himself to fierce asceticism. ||87||
She whose feet are served by Murāri, who resounds with a sweetness like nectar,
the beloved power of Govinda, difficult to be reached even by Brahmā, Rudra, and others.
Worshipping me alone with single-minded devotion, he meditated upon my enchanting splendor and constantly chanted the eleven-syllable mantra. (89)
Making their laughter full of blemish by joining it with deceitful arts, they cause the world to dwell around them while laughing with women such as Kāntā and others. 90.
Constantly reflecting on the meaning of the mantra, "Dwelling in the spring," he too attained perfection within two kalpas and obtained birth here.
This daughter of yours acts like a young girl, though she is slender, with breasts like flower-buds, her neck adorned with a string of pearls, and dressed in pure silk. (92)
She wore jasmine seeds sprinkled with pearls as collyrium, and carried a seal-ring engraved with the Kaṇā-gada;
she bore two divine, auspicious earrings that dripped with nectar.
Like a dot of vermilion in the midst of a braid of musk, she wore a tilaka on her forehead, half of which was decorated with sandalwood paste. (94)
That supreme state which is seen by those who possess such vision belonged to a royal sage named Candraprabha, who was pleasing to behold. 95.
By the grace of Kṛṣṇa, he had a son of sweet appearance,
renowned as Citradhvaja, who remained a Vaiṣṇava from his childhood until death.
He commanded the twice-born to recite the supreme eighteen-syllable mantra for twelve years, beginning auspiciously with the king, his sons, and himself, remaining steadfast throughout.
Being consecrated with the nectar-like waters of the mantras,
the infant immediately bowed with love to the king, his eyes filled with tears.
On that day, the boy, pure and wearing clean garments, was adorned with necklaces, anklets, sacred threads, and other ornaments such as neck-chains, bracelets, and earrings.
Having touched upon devotion to Hari while adorned [with it], his heart became pure;
having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu and standing there alone, he reflected.
How shall I worship that devotee, the deluder of the cowherd women, who sports eternally with them on the banks and in the forests of the Yamunā? (101)
While the boy was thus reflecting with a deeply agitated mind, he then attained a supreme knowledge and experienced a dream. (102)
In front of him was a beautiful image of Kṛṣṇa made of stone, seated upon a golden pedestal and endowed with all auspicious marks. (103)
She became dark as a blue lotus, endowed with smooth and radiant beauty, her form graced by the three-fold bend and adorned with peacock feathers. ||104||
She was joyfully playing her flute, which was placed against her golden lower lip,
and she was attended by two beautiful women, one on her right and one on her left.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa thus sporting in such attire, Citradhvaja observed how he was increasing their passion with kisses, embraces, and other endearments.
Bowing his head before them with a heart filled with shame,
Hari then spoke, smiling, to his beloved who was seated at Dakṣa’s side.
Having fashioned for herself a divine and wonderful youthful form, marvelous and equal to her own, she approached him with great modesty as he sat upon his seat. 108.
O fawn-eyed one, contemplate the non-difference between [him] and your own body;
then, when he has departed, touched by your splendors, he will attain your form. (109)
Then she, whose eyes were like lotus petals, went to the temple of Citradhvaja and stood there,
meditating on the non-difference between her own limbs and those of the deity.
Then, as she moved, you filled her white teeth with radiance, and by means of your light, you made her breasts full and beautiful.
The hips were born from the light of the *nitaṃba*, the heart-stealing buttocks;
from the light of the *kuntala* [hair-ends], the mass of hair arose; and from the hands, the two palms were formed. (112)
Thus everything— ornaments, clothing, garlands, and so forth— is perfectly accomplished,
because the inner self possesses a fragrance born from being highly skilled in the arts.
Like one lamp from another, he beheld that beautiful maiden on earth, Citradhvajā—charming with the splendor of a bashful smile and captivating to the mind. (114)
Having affectionately taken her by both hands and joyfully removing her fatigue,
he embraced his beloved who was standing at the left side of Govinda.
He said: "Give her this name, and perform for her service that is pleasing and appropriate to her, according to her desire. (116)
Then,
for the sake of service, she assumed the name Citrakalā by means of that [disguise], and she even took up a bow and arrows.
Always remain nearby and sing with various melodies;
O Soul of Virtue, this is the duty ordained for you, the Lord of Life.
Then, having acquired knowledge of the art of painting, he painted that Mādhava;
and having grasped the foot of his beloved, he [painted] the dust from her feet.
They sang a sweet song that was a cause of joy for both;
then she was embraced with affection by Kṛṣṇa, who is the embodiment of bliss.
Just as long as the wise one remained full of bliss, for that long Citradhvaja remained likewise unaware, overwhelmed by great love and intent upon his remembrance. 121.
Then, having spoken thus to Hariviracāraka, she wept aloud with her throat and chest unbound, lamenting that very Supreme Bliss from that time forward.
Though addressed by his father and others, he did not utter a single word;
having stayed in the house for only a month, at midnight he took refuge in Kṛṣṇa.
Having departed, he practiced in the forest a penance difficult even for sages; at the end of a kalpa, that great sage cast off his body through that very austerity.
The daughter of the cowherd named Vīragupta was the auspicious Citrakalā, whose shoulders were truly enchanting. (125)
The lute, adorned with the seven musical notes, is seen constantly;
it stands before the fire like a wonderful vessel of jewels.
Holding in his right hand a water-vessel made of precious gems, he was formerly saluted by all the ascetics. (127)
The sage named Puṇyaśravas, a descendant of Kaśyapa and a knower of all dharmas, was his father; he was a devotee of Śiva and would recite the Śatarudrīya every day. (128)
Praising the Lord of the gods of gods, the Lord of the universe who is affectionate toward his devotees, the Blessed One Śaṅkara became pleased with him along with Pārvatī. 129.
On the fourteenth day, at midnight, he appeared in person and granted a boon:
"O Kṛṣṇa, even as a child, your son shall indeed be devoted. (130)
"Having initiated him in the eighth year, you must instruct him in this perfected mantra; it is said that by means of that iron [weapon], he shall live for twenty-one years. (131)
This mantra, named Gopālavidyā, bestows the perfection of speech;
its wondrous play resides upon the tip of the tongue of its practitioner. (132)
The one of infinite forms comes of his own accord as the bestower of boons;
Kāma, Māyā, Ramā, Kaṇṭha, Indra, and others are radiant within Dāmodara. 133.
Having recited the ten-syllable mantra in the middle, one should again point to those same [mantras].
I shall now declare the seers (ṛṣis) and other attributes, as well as the visualization (dhyāna), for this ten-syllable mantra as previously described. ||134||
One should meditate on an island composed of light in the midst of the full ocean of nectar;
there, one should contemplate the forest of Vṛndāvana, encircled by the Kālindī river.
It was covered with coral creepers dripping with flowers of every season,
resounding with the cries of dancing, intoxicated peacocks, and the songs of cuckoos and bees.
In its center dwells a single great Pārijāta tree,
rising a hundred yojanas high with the expansion of its branches and sub-branches.
Then, on its pure surface, he envisioned a circle of cows all around;
within that was the inner circle of cowherd boys playing flutes and carrying horns. 138.
Within that [space], the beautiful circle of the fair-browed women of Vraja gathered,
their hands bearing various offerings and their minds unsteady with intoxication.
With their hands joined in the gesture of reverence, they were clad in white garments,
adorned with white ornaments, and their souls were overwhelmed with love for the maṇḍala.
One should contemplate the daughters of the Vedas as they utter pleasing words;
thereafter, one should meditate upon Hari, clad in silk garments, at the jeweled altar.
Lying on his thigh upon the trunk of a plantain tree, he gazed at Rādhā’s enchanting face, which was beautifully smiling like the moon. (142)
With his left foot slightly tucked up, he embraces his beloved with his left hand—upon which a flute rests—while touching her chin with his right hand. (143)
Having the luster of great emeralds and the brilliance of pearls, with large eyes like white lotuses, he is clad in pure yellow garments. ||144||
His head was radiant with a mass of peacock feathers, he was charming with a necklace of pearls, and beautiful makara-shaped earrings gleamed upon the edges of his cheeks. (145)
Adorned with a tulasī garland upon his feet, decorated with bracelets and armlets, and embellished with anklets, rings, and a waistband.

One should meditate upon Him as exceedingly delicate and endowed with youthful age; the worship is exactly as described for the ten-syllable mantra, and the preparatory rite consists of one hundred thousand recitations of the Veda. 147.
Having spoken thus, the God and the goddess, the virtuous daughter of the mountain, vanished;
and the sage, having returned, instructed his son in that very same manner.
But Puṇyaśravas, by the mere reception of that mantra, himself surpassed all the sages and described Keśava in various ways. (149)
Then, his mind filled with joy at the sight of her wonderful marks of physical form, grace, eloquence, and beauty, the boy departed from his own home. (150)
Subsisting on air, he performed austerities for thirty thousand kalpas;
at the end of that period, he himself was born in Gokula in the house of Nanda’s brother.
"Lavaṅgā" was her name; she watched for Kṛṣṇa’s gestures, and in her hand could be seen a face-cleansing brush. (152)
Thus, some of the principal beloveds of Kṛṣṇa have been described to you. ||153||

The person who here reads with devotion, or causes others to read, this chapter joined with Hari, various sentiments, and so forth, along with the beautiful glances of the excellent daughters of Vraja;
He goes to the abode of the Blessed Lord Śrī Vāsudeva. ||154||
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter in the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Māhātmya of the Pātāla-Khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(73) The Seventy-third Chapter: [The Greatness of Mathurā]
Īśvara said:
That wonder which was asked by you has been related by me in due order;
wherein even Brahmā and the others are bewildered—who indeed would not be bewildered? (1)
Nevertheless, I shall relate to you what was spoken by the supreme seer concerning the great king Ambarīṣa, who was a devotee of Viṣṇu and endowed with devotion to Śiva.
Having reached the hermitage of Badarī, the king bowed down to the self-controlled sage who was seated there, and praised him with a desire to learn the dharma of Viṣṇu. ||3||
O highly fortunate one, you are the arranger of the Vedas, the omniscient Supreme Person;
you ought to protect me here in this ocean of worldly existence so difficult to cross. ||4||
I am detached from sense objects; salutations to them all.
That state which is free from agitation, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss—salutations to that entire whole.
The supreme Brahman, the ultimate space, which is spaceless and free from affliction—having directly realized which, the sages indeed cross over the ocean of existence. (6)
"In that regard, how may I always attain the state of the mind?
Vyāsa said:
"What you have asked is extremely secret, which I have not [revealed] even to Śuka."
I have spoken thus to my own son; but what shall I say to you, who are dear to Hari?
This entire supreme universe was that very form in which it is established. (8)
Listen to that which is unmanifest, undisturbed, and composed of the Lord:
formerly, I performed austerities for many thousands of years. (9)
Then, as I was subsisting on fruits, roots, leaves, water, and air,
the Blessed Lord Hari spoke to me while I was absorbed in my own meditation.
"O high-minded one, for what purpose do you have this desire to act or this wish to know? I am pleased; choose a boon from me, the best of givers of boons. (11)
"I tell you the truth: saṃsāra ends with the vision of me.
Then, my body bristling with horripilation, I spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
O Madhusūdana, I desire to behold with my own eyes You who are that which is the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the source of the universe, and the Lord of the universe. (13)
They speak of the wondrous Lord Cākṣuṣa as the head of the Vedas.
The Blessed One said: "In the past, I was thus questioned and entreated by Brahmā, just as [you have asked] before. (14)
What I have said to him is now being told to you as well:
some call me Prakṛti, and likewise Puruṣa and Īśvara. (15)
Some [worship] Dharma, some wealth, and some liberation which is free from fear on all sides;
some [worship] the Void, some Being, some Śiva, and some Sadāśiva. (16)
Others [saw] the one eternal reality situated at the head of the Vedas, the true being devoid of transformation, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss. ||17||
"Behold, today I shall show you my true form, which has been hidden by the Vedas.
Then, O King, I beheld a boy with the luster of a dark rain cloud. (18)
He was surrounded by cowherd girls and laughing with cowherd boys;
he sat at the foot of a Kadamba tree, wearing yellow garments, a wonderful sight. (19)
There is a forest named Vṛndāvana, adorned with fresh sprouts, filled with the warbling of cuckoos and bees, and enchanting to the god of love. 20.
I saw the Kālindī river, possessing the luster of the petals of a blue lotus;
then I saw Govardhana, lifted up by the hands of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
Seeing Gopāla— the destroyer of Mahendra’s pride, the bringer of happiness to the cows and cowherds, who rejoices in the company of the young women and plays the flute,
and who is adorned by all ornaments— I became exceedingly joyful.
Then the Blessed One himself, who wanders in Vṛndāvana, spoke to me.
This divine and eternal form of mine which has been seen by you is partless, beyond price, peaceful, and the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss. (24)
"Full [is He], with eyes like lotus petals; there is nothing higher than this for me.
These Vedas themselves declare Him to be the cause of all causes. (25)
Know my Mathurā to be eternal truth, perpetual bliss, a mass of consciousness, everlasting, and auspicious; and likewise, know Vṛndāvana forest to be eternal. (26)
The Yamunā, the cowherd maidens, and likewise the cowherd boys—this is my eternal incarnation; do not entertain any doubt in this matter. (27)
For I am the beloved of the virtuous, the omniscient one, higher than the highest;
I am the fulfiller of all desires, the all-pervading lord, the embodiment of all bliss, higher than the highest. (28)
"All this universe shines within me as the unfolding of Māyā.
Then I spoke to the Lord, the cause of the cause of the world. (29)
Who are the cowherd women, and who are the cowherds? What kind of tree is this considered to be?
What is the forest, and what are the cuckoos and other birds? What is this river, and what is the mountain? (30)
"Who is this illustrious Veṇu, the sole vessel for the joy of the worlds?
The Blessed One, his lotus-face serene, spoke to me with affection. (31)
The gopīs should be known as the Śrutis; indeed, the cowherd girls are the Ṛgvedic verses.
And the daughters of the gods, O King of kings, are those who are endowed with austerity and desire liberation. (32)
All the cowherd sages are embodiments of the bliss of Vaikuṇṭha;
this kadamba tree is a wish-fulfilling tree, the sole vessel of supreme bliss. (33)
Indeed, the forest named Ānandaka destroys even the greatest sins; there, Siddhas, Sādhyas, Gandharvas, Kokilas, and others dwell—of this there is no doubt. (34)
Some say his heart is bliss itself, while others say his body is the Yamunā;
this mountain is the beginningless servant of Hari—of this there is no doubt. (35)
Listen, O Vipra, for this matter is known even to you:
there was once a twice-born man who was tranquil in mind and devoted to the peace of austerity. (36)
By name Devavrata, he was self-controlled and proficient in the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa) of the Vedas;
dwelling in the midst of a multitude of Vaiṣṇava devotees, he was devoted to religious rites.
O King, having heard that there was a lord of sacrifices who performed them only once, a brahmin, his resolve firmly fixed, then went to his house. (38)
Somewhere, being full of devotion, he performed worship with *tulasī* leaves and water; in that house, he offered some fruit and roots. (39)
The wise man gave some of the water from his bath to him;
and he too, having displayed a smile out of lack of faith, accepted it from the twice-born.
By that evil deed, he was born as a bamboo stalk of most dreadful nature;
by that merit, he then attained the state of being dear to me.
By this [knowledge], that lord of kings also shines like Ketumān; at the end of the age, having become devoted to Viṣṇu, he shall attain union with Brahman.
Alas, those whose hearts are like those of men do not know my supreme, eternal city,
which is praised by the lords of gods, the lords of serpents, and the lords of sages.
That ancient city of Mathurā, so enchanting to the mind. ||43||
Although cities such as Kāśī exist,
among them Mathurā alone is blessed; for it is there that [the Lord’s] birth, the investiture with the sacred thread, the vow, death, and cremation occurred.
It bestows liberation upon men in four ways. ||44||
When people, possessing pure intentions through austerity and other means, are continuously rich in meditation,
at that very time they behold my supreme city.
And not otherwise, O best of the twice-born, even in hundreds of kalpas. ||45||
The inhabitants of Mathurā are blessed and worthy of honor even by the gods;
they all possess four arms and their greatness is beyond counting. (46)
But those men who perceive faults in the residents of Mathurā do not perceive the fault arising from thousands of births and deaths within themselves. 47.
Even now, those who remember Mathurā are blessed, for there dwells the Lord of Beings, the deity who grants liberation even to sinners. (48)
My supreme beloved is always the Lord of Beings, the highest deity, who never abandons that city for the sake of my pleasure. (49)
That man of evil conduct who does not bow to Bhūteśvara, nor worship him, nor even remember him,
shall not behold this Mathurā of mine.
[She who is] self-luminous and known as the Supreme Deity. ||50||
How could that sinful man obtain devotion toward me, who does not indeed worship Śiva, my supreme devotee? (51)
Those lowest of men, whose intellects are generally deluded by my māyā, neither bow down to the Lord of Beings, nor remember him, nor praise him. (52)
Even as a child, Dhruva, intent upon his worship, attained that supreme, pure state which even his grandfathers could reach only with great effort. (53)
Upon reaching that city of mine, Mathurā, which is difficult even for the gods to attain,
Khaṣja or Andhaka shall surely lose his life.
O highly fortunate Vedavyāsa, do not entertain any doubt whatsoever regarding this secret of the Upaniṣads which has been revealed by me to you. 55.
Whoever, being pure, shall recite this chapter spoken by the Blessed One, or whoever shall listen to it with devotion, for them too there is eternal liberation. (56)
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Vṛndāvana and Other Places in Mathurā," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(74) The seventy-fourth chapter.
Īśvara said:
Once, in private, the glorious Uddhava, a dear associate of the Lord,
questioned Sanat-kumāra in seclusion, O Master.
Where Govinda eternally sports with the cowherd maidens in that eternal abode of the gods—where is that supreme place, and what is it like? ||2||
Whatever other wonderful accounts of those various pastimes you may have known—if there is any affection remaining in you, they should be told. (3)
Sanat-kumāra said: Once, on the bank of the Yamunā, beneath a certain tree,
there sat a well-behaved attendant of the Blessed Lord.
Whatever was his private experience, and whatever was seen and done by the high-souled Pārtha— each of those has been related to me in the course of conversation.
I shall tell this to you; listen with focused attention to this supreme [teaching].
However, this must never be disclosed anywhere at any time.
Arjuna said:
O Lord, out of compassion, please tell me all of this by your grace—that which has never been seen nor heard even by Śiva, Brahmā, and the other gods. (7)
What did you say previously regarding the Ābhīrīs who are dear to you?
O Lord, how many kinds are they, and what is their number again? (8)
How many are their names, or what are they, and where are they situated? O Lord, how many are their activities, and what are their ages and appearances? (9)
O Lord, with whom will you sport in secret, and in which forest—forests that are eternal, characterized by eternal bliss and eternal splendor? (10)
Of what nature is that place, where is it, and how is it eternal, supreme, and great?
If you have such compassion, you ought to tell me all of this here. (11)
O illustrious one, destroyer of the suffering of the afflicted, you will tell me all that which I have not asked, that which I do not know, and whatever is your secret.
The Blessed Lord said:
That place, those beloved ones, and such pastimes of Mine are truly beyond the reach of even those men who are as dear to Me as My own life-breath. (13)
"O child, when this has been told, you will feel a longing to see that which is invisible even to Brahmā and the other gods; how much more so for any other person? (14)
"Therefore, my child, desist from this; for what indeed is it to you without him?
Having thus heard these most dreadful words of the Blessed One, [he was overcome]. ||15||
The distressed Arjuna fell like a staff at the pair of the Lord’s lotus feet;
thereupon the all-pervading Blessed One, smiling, raised him up with His two arms.
He, who is affectionate toward His devotees, spoke with supreme love to the devotee:
"What is that which you have not yet seen here, which I shall now describe? (17)
I bow to that Goddess Śrīmat Tripurasundarī, from whom everything has arisen, in whom it still abides even today, and into whom it shall go to its dissolution. 18.
Having propitiated her with supreme devotion, offer yourself to her;
without her, I am never able to grant this station. (19)
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, Pārtha, his eyes overflowing with joy,
went to the base of the sacred sandals of the illustrious Goddess Tripurā.
Having gone there, he beheld that Śrī-Cintāmaṇi altar, which was exceedingly beautiful with stairs fashioned from various jewels. (21)
There, the wish-fulfilling tree was bent down by various flowers and fruits,
with tender leaves of every season dripping with sprays of honey.
It was made radiant by sprouts trembling in the wind as they rained down, and by parrots, flocks of cuckoos, sārikās, and pigeons. (23)
It resounded with the songs of other birds, including the playful cakora birds,
and was filled with the tumultuous humming of swarms of bees.
At its base was a divine and most wonderful palace of precious gems, radiant with jewels and as enchanting as a blazing forest fire. 25.
There, a jeweled lion-throne made of great gold, enchanting, was present;
upon it [he saw her] resembling the rising sun and adorned with various ornaments. (26)

This beautiful Vṛndāvana is My own exclusive abode, wherein even the animals, trees, insects, humans, and demigods are directly Me. (8)
These women who dwell with me will abandon me when I am dead;
even the wives of the cowherds live in my house. (9)
O gods, those very yoginīs are thus devoted to Him; for this forest, which is five yojanas in extent, is indeed His divine form.
This Yamunā is called Suṣumnā, carrying the supreme nectar;
here the gods and all beings return in a subtle form.
I am all-pervading and shall never abandon the forest;
my manifestation and disappearance shall occur in every age.
This place is composed of splendor and is invisible to those with physical eyes;
behold my secret power and Vṛndāvana in this age.
"That [state] is not visible in any way whatsoever to the deities beginning with Brahmā. The Lord said:
Having heard that, Nārada approached both Kṛṣṇa and Brahmā.
He came to the world of mortals to the mixed Naimiṣa forest;
there he was honored by the lords of sages, headed by Śaunaka and others.
"O Brahmin, you have arrived; tell me now, from where have you come?
Having heard that, Nārada said, "I have come from Goloka. (16)
Having heard from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa the secret of Vṛndāvana from the descendant of Bhoja, Nārada said:
"There, various questions were asked again and again. (17)
I have heard all the lineages and the yogas therein;
I shall explain them exactly as you have asked, according to their true nature.
Śaunaka and the others said:
"O you who have been spoken to by Brahmā regarding the secret of the Vṛndā forest, please explain that to us, for we have your compassion. (19)
Nārada said: Once, on the banks of the Sarayū, we beheld Gautama,
who was high-minded yet deeply distressed, his mind overwhelmed with anxiety.
Upon seeing me, the god Gautama fell to the surface of the earth;
"Arise, O dear child! I said to him. 21.
"If it pleases you, please tell me how you are considered wise.
Gautama said:
"From your own mouth, I have heard such a reality regarding Kṛṣṇa."
The secret concerning Dvārakā and the secret concerning Mathurā have been heard by me many times;
however, the secret of Vṛndāvana has not yet been heard from the lotus of your mouth. (23)
"O True Guru, by this my mind shall attain steadfastness.
Nārada said:
"This, however, is the supreme secret, more secret than the most secret. (24)
"O Lord of Gods, as previously told to me by Brahmā, speak that same secret concerning the origin of Vṛndāvana, for which I have been sent by Vṛndāraṇya."
Having heard this which he desired to know, he remained silent for a moment;
then I said to him, "O child, go to my lord, Mahā-Viṣṇu."
"I must also go there with you; of this there is no doubt.
Having said this, he took me by the hand and went quickly to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever was spoken by me was indeed declared by Mahā-Viṣṇu;
having heard that, Mahā-Viṣṇu himself then commanded Svayambhū.
"By my command, take the sage Nārada yourself and cause him to bathe in the lake named Amṛta."
Commanded by Mahā-Viṣṇu himself, Bhūmi acted accordingly;
there, having entered the lake of nectar, I performed my ablutions. (30)
At that very moment, I became a woman endowed with all auspicious marks beside those women at the edge of that lake, and I was utterly amazed by my beautiful form.
Seeing me on that assembly, they questioned me again and again.
The women said: "Who are you? From where have you come? Tell us of your own activities. (32)
Having heard their pleasant words, I said: "Listen to that;
from where have I come, who am I, or how did I come to have the form of a woman? (33)
"Everything is seen like a dream; or am I deluded on this earth?
Hearing these words of mine, the Goddess spoke in sweet-toned voices: (34)
This city named Vṛndā is eternally dear to Kṛṣṇacandra;
I am the goddess Lalitā, beyond the fourth state (turyātītā) and partless (niṣkalā). 35.
Having spoken thus, the Great Goddess, her mind overflowing with compassion, replied to me once more: "O Goddess, come together with me. (36)
All other women are devoted to the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
they speak of me in this way: "Come together with her. (37)
Then, out of compassion, the fourteen-syllable mantra of Kṛṣṇacandra and that of the high-souled Goddess were also told to her. 38.
At that very moment, I attained equality with them through various similes;
together with them, I went to that place where the eternal Kṛṣṇa resides. (39)
The Lord himself, who is pure existence, consciousness, and bliss, having become a woman and whose heart was filled with the joy of womanhood, looked at me and spoke repeatedly: (40)
O best of the twice-born, he united with me, his beloved and devoted wife, and embraced me; there he took delight for a period measured by a year.
Regarding that, it was said by Ramaṇeśa concerning the goddess Rādhikā:
"This is my Prakṛti; and there, assuming the form of Nārada, I was present. (42)
"Having led her to the delightful Amṛtasara lake, engage her in bathing.
To him, she spoke these affectionate words. (43)
I am sung of as the goddess Calalitā and Rādhikā; and I am known as Vāsudeva, eternally consisting of the essence of the arts of love. 44.
It is true that I am the very nature of woman, and I am the eternal woman;
I am the goddess Lalitā, whose form is the body of Kṛṣṇa in the guise of a man.
"There is no difference between us; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Nārada.
He who understands this reality, as well as the convention and the law-code (Manu), [attains the highest state]. (46)
This Vṛndāvana, which possesses its own conventional conduct and is as dear to me as Lalitā herself, is my secret abode. 47.
It must never be spoken of anywhere or at any time to anyone who is not an initiate, nor ever to a beast;
therefore, having led this Goddess Anurādhikā to that lake, [he should place her there].
Having remained there, they returned once more to the feet of Śaśāṅka;
then, from that very immersion, I, Nārada, arrived.
Another, with a lute in hand, repeatedly sang its secret with joy;
having personally bowed to Svayambhū, I went there to the assembly of Viṣṇu’s attendants.
"Furthermore, although Svayambhū saw [it] in that manner, he did not say anything at all then.
Thus, O child, I have told you this which is very secret even from me."
You too must strive to conceal the pure, conscious splendor of Kṛṣṇacandra, just as a lover conceals his beloved from his mother. 52.
Just as it was taught by me to my disciple Gautama without any secret, so has it been told to you in its entirety, though it is extremely well-guarded. 53.
O Brahmins, whenever and wherever this [work] is revealed by the bull among sages, the fulfillment of the desires of Kṛṣṇacandra will certainly come to pass. 54.
Whoever reads or even hears this supreme chapter, endowed with the divine sports of Kṛṣṇa, attains the highest state. (55)
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Conciliation by Nārada," in the *Vṛndāvana-māhātmya* of the *Pātāla-khaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
(76) The seventy-sixth chapter.
Īśvara said:
Having heard here that Śiśupāla had been slain, Dantavakra came to Mathurā to fight with Kṛṣṇa. ||1||
But Kṛṣṇa, having heard that, mounted his chariot and went with him to Mathurā. ||2||

Then, having slain him and crossed the Yamunā, he went to Nanda’s cowherd settlement; there, having saluted his parents and comforted them, he was embraced by them, and after embracing all the elder cowherds and consoling them, he gratified everyone residing there with many garments, ornaments, and other gifts. ||3||
On the beautiful bank of the Kālindī, which was filled with sacred trees, he dwelt there for three nights, enjoying the pleasure of play day and night with the cowherd women. ||4||

There, on that spot, all the people such as Nanda and the cowherds, together with their sons and wives—even the beasts, birds, and wild animals—by the grace of Vāsudeva, assumed divine forms, ascended celestial chariots, and attained the supreme realm of Vaikuṇṭha. ||5||

Śrī Kṛṣṇa, however, having granted His own abode free from all suffering to Nanda Gopa and all the inhabitants of Vraja, entered the glorious city of Dvārāvatī while being praised by hosts of demigods. ||6||

There, Vasudeva, daily honored by Ugrasena, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Akrūra, and others, as well as by his sixteen thousand and eight queens, assumed his universal form (viśvarūpa) and took delight within bowers of divine jeweled creepers, upon very soft couches strewn with flowers from the celestial trees. ||7||

Thus, for the welfare of all the gods and for the destruction of the entire burden of the earth, Vāsudeva descended into the Yadu dynasty; having brought about the destruction of all the *rākṣasas* and eliminated the great burden of the world, and having liberated the inhabitants of Nanda’s cowherd settlement and Dvārakā—both mobile and immobile beings—from the bonds of worldly existence, he established them in his own supreme, eternal, and beautiful abode, which is meditated upon by yogis; there, being eternally served by his divine queens and others, Vāsudeva spoke to all of them. (8)
The Brahman remained indeterminate, like water and clarified butter;
established in his original nature, he was freed from the qualities (guṇas), and having become fluid, he ascended to heaven. ||9||
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vṛndāvana," in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiva within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||76||
(77) The seventy-seventh chapter.
Pārvatī said:
Explain in detail the gravity of the names, meanings, and words,
as well as the true nature of the Lord, his abodes, and his manifestations.
O Lord of the Gods, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, as well as the various manifestations of Hari, and even the reality known as Nirvāṇa—all this belongs to me. (2)
Īśvara said:
In the essence of Vṛndāvana is Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by millions of gopīs;
there the Gaṅgā is the supreme power (parā śakti), and situated therein is the Forest of Bliss (Ānanda-kānana). ||3||
Made fragrant by breezes carrying the scent of various beautiful flowers, and cooled by the divine, colored waves of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā). ||4||
It was frequented by the foremost of sages, the devotees headed by Sanaka,
and adorned by herds of cows with their delightful and sweet lowing.
It was surrounded by dancing boys adorned with beautiful garlands and ornaments;
there stood the glorious Kalpa tree, its foliage like that of a hibiscus flower.
Abounding with various jewels and corals, radiant with various mani-gems as its fruit, at its base was a jeweled altar illuminated by the luster of gems. (7)
There, a supreme lion-throne composed of the three Vedas was present;
upon it sat the Lord of the World, who transcends the three qualities and is imperishable.
Resembling ten million moons, radiant as ten million suns,
and possessing the beauty of ten million gods of love, he illuminates the ten directions.
Three-eyed, with two arms, fair-complexioned, and possessing the luster of molten gold;
he is embraced on all sides by the goddesses who are his own manifestations.
It is to be meditated upon by Brahmā and others, as well as by Sanaka and the rest, who have been brought under control through devotion;
it is always being danced to by those with rolling eyes during great festivals.
With millions upon millions of Vedic scriptures that have assumed the forms of gopīs, he was kissed by those laughing intensely, and embraced again and again by those clinging to him. (12)
Surrounded on all sides by those whose minds were intoxicated by the honey of his lotus feet,
there was among them a goddess with the luster of refined gold.
Illuminating all directions and making them blaze with lightning,
she is the primordial Prakṛti, by whom this entire universe is pervaded.

She is the supreme triad of ignorance and knowledge, which serves as the means for creation, maintenance, and dissolution; she is the power of her own nature, appearing in the form of Māyā, consisting of consciousness, and yet unmanifested.
He is the cause of the causes of the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others;
the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is embraced by His Māyā. 16.
Embracing that Lord of Vṛndāvana, who dwells there with joy for the sake of imitating Rādhā, the mistress of Vṛndāvana, he remained there. 17.
One should meditate upon Lord Kṛṣṇa thus—as reeling with the intoxication of mutual kissing and embracing—and one shall attain all spiritual perfections. 18.
That knower of mantras who should recite or even listen to this secret king of mantras and its mantra is a great-souled one, exceedingly rare to find. (19)
Rāī, Dhakā, Citrarekhā, Candrā, Madanasundarī, Śrīpriyā, Śrīmatī, Umā, Rekhā, and Haripriyā. (20)
Deluded by the splendor of his golden complexion, her hair stood on end with love; overcome by paleness and perspiration, she was attached to him and spoke what was dear to her. (21)
She who wears a golden garland, who delights in the company of gods and celestial nymphs,
who is compassionate toward the suffering of all women, and whose heart is pure.
She is celebrated as the receptacle for the essence of the nectar of names that have been drunk;
she possesses the luster of molten gold combined with a very long smile. 23.
O people, behold Rādhā, whose eyes are veiled by a surging river of love, and whose life is the sovereignty of giving, joined with neither illusion nor envy. 24.
Renowned for her wonderful artistic lines in the battle-festivals of love, she is fair-complexioned, possesses a very long neck, and is ever intent upon playing musical instruments. (25)
She who is characterized by wretchedness, passion, dancing, fainting, horripilation, and agitation;
she who stands at the right side of Hari; and likewise she who is dear to all mantras. 26.
She was celebrated as Anangalobhamadhuri, with a graceful and trembling gait, her eyes sealed shut by passion.
She was radiant and strewn with a stream of love, beautiful to all people,
a connoisseur of the essence of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, and eager for the sound of His flute.
I am one whose face eclipses the moon, who is possessed of the conceit of "I," and who am the crest-jewel of those with senses conquered by proficiency in sweet speech. (29)
She is endowed with a beautiful smile, more lovely than Madana himself; she delights in secluded amorous play, and though dark-complexioned, she is enchanting in her deep blackness. 30.
She who deludes the mind of Hari with her love and loving sidelong glances,
who has conquered her senses and subdued her anger— she is celebrated as his beloved.
She is fair as molten gold, beautiful with her graceful and playful gait,
her hair standing on end from the love born of passion, and her form is wonderfully sweet.
His face, endowed with a beautiful smile, puts the moon to shame; he is a jewel among those who have conquered their senses, being adept in sweet conversation. ||33||
She is celebrated as being intent on the practice of love for Madhumatī; she is endowed with the fever of infatuation, horripilation, and a continuous stream of affection. (34)
She who sports in the dust of charity, the great actress of the path of nectar, and who is known as the crescent moon—she is always the beloved of Gopāla. 35.
Her soul is Kṛṣṇa; she is most excellent, dark-complexioned, with eyes as tawny as honey;
through the delusion of love for His feet, she is sometimes kissed by horripilation. 36.
Śivānandā is at Śivakuṇḍa, Nandinī on the bank of the Dehikā, Rukmiṇī at Dvāravatī, and Rādhā in the forest of Vṛndāvana. (37)
Devakī, my supreme goddess, was born in Mathurā;
likewise, Sītā is at Candra-kūṭa, and Vindhya-nivāsinī is on the Vindhya mountains. (38)
Viśālākṣī was given to Vārāṇasī and Vimalā to Puruṣottama; and sovereignty over Vṛndāvana was granted to her by the gracious Lord. (39)
But the Goddess Rādhā is not elsewhere than in Kṛṣṇa within the forest of Vṛndāvana;
Śauri, whose body is eternal bliss, is said to be bodiless.
The presiding deities of wind, fire, the celestial vault, and the earth are established in the letter *a*;
likewise, the form of Govinda is established even in the letter *brahmā*. (41)
Just as the sun, though possessed of senses, cannot be perceived by its own brilliance, so too Kṛṣṇa, endowed with splendor, certainly deludes Time itself. 42.
His form is not composed of flesh, fat, or bone like that of ordinary beings;
he is a yogi and indeed a Lord, distinct from others, the soul of all, possessing an eternal body. 43.
Through divine power, hardness arose [in the foot] like that of hailstones or ghee;
yet the sole of the foot of Kṛṣṇa, whose reality is immeasurable, is not a mere deity. 44.
In that mass of dust from Vṛndāvana, there may be ten million Viṣṇus;
yet, in the multitude of blissful rays, He alone is the treasury of all arts who pervades the universe as Vṛnda. ||45||
Just as individual souls are the very essence of the qualities within the Self, so too are they its rays;
Kṛṣṇa is sometimes depicted with two arms and sometimes with four.
There, Govinda himself, as the Supreme Person, always sports while surrounded by a single gopī; Brahmā and the other gods are likewise [present], yet they are all female. 47.
Therefore, this very nature is the Lord who is the essence of primordial matter;
Puruṣa and Prakṛti are the two primordial Lords, Rādhā and Vṛndāvanīśvara.
Everything that is a modification of primordial nature is devoid of the Lord of Vṛndāvana.
This world arises through its very origination, yet it undergoes differentiation through its destruction;
for there is no destruction of gold, and likewise, even upon the destruction of the fish and other forms, there is no departure from Kṛṣṇa.
This phenomenal world of the three gunas and so forth belongs to the one who sports in Vṛndāvana;
just as the ocean is not produced from its waves, nor the waves from the ocean. 51.
A woman equal to the most excellent of men, a man resembling Kṛ�ṣṇa; an age beyond mere youth, and a nature transcending material nature. (52)
The youthful form is to be meditated upon; the forest of Vṛndāvana is to be meditated upon as the forest.
The dark-complexioned Supreme Form, the primordial God, is the highest essence. (53)

Childhood (bālya) lasts until the end of the fifth year; the stage of youth (paugaṇḍa) extends up to the tenth year; adolescence (kaishora) lasts for eight years [from the eleventh to the eighteenth], with its limit being the fifteenth year.
That age in which childhood has been shed by youth is called "fresh youth";
that very age is his all-in-all, while any other age is merely a vision.
He whose youth in childhood, boyhood, and adolescence is enchanting;
he who is the protector of the cowherd boys, yet himself a cowherd boy; he who possesses the form of Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd who captivates the mind. ||56||
Vaṃ! [I bow to] that wonderful form of the cowherd boy of Gokula, who is called the enchanting Śrī-Madana-mohana, whose beauty has blossomed with the onset of youth. 57.
Victorious is the secret form of the Lord of Śrī, manifesting in the shape of a youth—an immeasurable great ocean of bliss from the nectar-essence that is unbroken and peerless. 58.
Though He was previously but one, immutable, and situated in the midst of the cowherd women,
those of diverse intellects perceive Him differently according to their varying inclinations, even as He is accessible through meditation.
I bow to that Lord of Devṛndāvana, who is as beautiful as the moon on his forehead, who is worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, and who transcends the three qualities (guṇas). 60.
Govinda’s abandonment of Vṛndāvana does not exist; wherever his form appears otherwise, it is undoubtedly artificial. 61.
It is easily attained by the women of Vraja, yet difficult for those seeking liberation;
I worship that Son of Nanda, the splendor of whose toenails is the supreme Manu.
Pārvatī said:
As long as the demoness of longing for worldly enjoyment and liberation dwells within the heart, how can there be the arising of the bliss of divine love here? (63)
Īśvara said:
"O blessed lady, you have asked well regarding that which dwells in my mind;
I shall tell you all of that, so listen attentively. (64)
Remembering his qualities, chanting his name, and singing of the Dwarf Incarnation,
one awakens the self by means of the self and constantly merges into divine love.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiva.
(78) The seventy-eighth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
Tell me truly all that is the dharma of the Vaiṣṇavas, by performing which all human beings indeed cross over the ocean of worldly existence. (1)
Īśvara said:
Now, the twelvefold purification of the Vaiṣṇavas is described here:
the smearing of the house with cow-dung and likewise the going to the temple of Hari. (2)

Furthermore, circumambulation with devotion and the cleansing of the feet, as well as the gathering of leaves and flowers for the sake of worship, should be performed with devotion alone toward Hari. (3)
Among all purifications of the hands, this purification is preeminent:
namely, the chanting of His name and the celebration of His virtues. (4)
Through devotion to the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa, purity of speech is desired, as well as listening to His narrations and witnessing His festivals. (5)
The proper purification of the ears and the eyes is now correctly described here:
[it consists of] water for the feet, the remains of offerings (nirmālya), and also the wearing of garlands.
It is said, O beloved, that the purification of the head consists of bowing before Hari,
as well as smelling the flowers and other offerings from His garland (nirmālya).
Purification is prescribed even for the internal sense of smell, as well as for whatever flowers and such are offered at the pair of Kṛṣṇa’s feet. (8)
That alone is the purifier in the world, for it shall indeed cleanse everything.
Worship is said to be fivefold; hear from me their distinctions. (9)
Approaching, receiving, union, and likewise private recitation;
I shall describe to you in sequence this fivefold worship consisting of sacrifice. (10)
Approaching the reality (tattva) consists of cleansing the deity’s place and removing the five types of floral offerings from the stone slab. ||11||
"Upādāna" means the gathering of perfumes, flowers, and so forth; likewise, "yoga" means the contemplation of one's own deity as being identical with one's own self. (12)

Svādhyāya consists of the recitation preceded by an investigation into the meaning of the mantras, as well as the reading of hymns, praises, and the like, and likewise the congregational chanting of the names of Hari. (13)
The practice of the scriptures concerning reality and so forth is proclaimed as *svādhyāya* (self-study);
and *ijyā* (sacrifice) is the worship of one's own deity according to the true principle. (14)
Thus, O lady of virtuous vows, the fivefold worship has been described to you;
it bestows, in sequence, the states of being of equal power (sārṣṭi), proximity (sāmīpya), residence in the same world (sālokya), union (sāyujya), and similarity of form (sārūpya).
In this context, I shall describe the worship of the Śālagrāma stone,
beginning with Keśava, according to the sequence of the four arms starting from the upper right hand.
The one named Keśava holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; Gadādhara likewise; and Nārāyaṇa is characterized by the sequence of the lotus, mace, discus, and conch as his weapons. (17)
Mādhava is characterized by the discus, the conch, the lotus, and the mace;
and he who holds the mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus is the one named Govinda, the wielder of the mace. ||18||
Salutations to you in the form of Viṣṇu, who holds the lotus, conch, discus, and mace; salutations to the form of Madhusūdana, who possesses the conch, lotus, mace, and discus. ||19||
Salutations to Trivikrama, who is endowed with the mace, discus, conch, and lotus; and to Vāmana, whose forms hold the śārṅga bow, the kaumodakī mace, the lotus, and the conch.
Salutations to the form of Śrīdhara, who holds the discus, lotus, conch, and mace;
salutations be to you, Hṛṣīkeśa, who possesses the sword, mace, conch, and lotus.
Salutations to You, whose own form possesses the lotus, conch, mace, and discus, and whose navel is a lotus; O Dāmodara, who hold the conch, mace, and discus, let there be obeisance to You.
Salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa, who holds the conch, lotus, discus, and mace;
salutations be to you, Vāsudeva, who possesses the sword, conch, mace, and lotus. 23.
Salutations to Aniruddha, who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, who bears the form of Pradyumna, and who wields the mace, conch, lotus, and the enemy (the sword). 24.
Salutation to the form of Puruṣottama, who holds the lotus, conch, mace, and discus;
salutation to the form of Adhokṣaja, who possesses the mace, conch, enemy (of the demons), and lotus.
Salutations be to the form of Acyuta, who possesses the form of Nṛsiṃha, who holds the lotus, mace, conch, and discus, and who wields the lotus, discus, conch, and mace. ||26||
Salutations to the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who holds a mace, a lotus, a discus, and a conch, and who bears two wheels firmly fixed at the entrance of the Śālagrāma stone. 27.
That Lord Gadādhara has white-hued lines and is rich in splendor;
his two wheels are fixed, he is red-hued, and his front portion is abundant. 28.
Then Saṅkarṣaṇa is [the letter] *a*, Pradyumna is *u*, Sūkṣmacakra is *ū* which is yellow, and Aniruddha is *m*, which is circular and possesses a very long, hollow opening. ||29||
At the opening it is blue and has three lines; then Nārāyaṇa is black.
In the middle there are lines in the shape of a mace, and the navel-lotus is very prominent. (30)
He who is Pṛthucakra, Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, or Tribinduka—
or rather, for the celibate student (brahmacārin), the worship is that of Pañcabindu.
That which has three marks is Varāha; it has two uneven discs, is blue, has three lines, is thick, and furthermore, that which has the form of a tortoise has a dot. 32.
Kṛṣṇa has circular whorls and is pale on the back;
Śrīdhara has five lines and wears a forest garland marked with a mace. ||33||
The middle wheel is named Vartula, which is dwarfish and blue;
Anantaka, however, has the coils of a serpent of manifold colors in a single form. ||34||
Sthūla, Dāmodara, and Nīla; in the middle is Cakra with Nīlaka;
then Saṅkarṣaṇa and Dvārako; and then Brahmā, who is deep red.

One with very long lines, one with a single cavity, one with a single lotus, one that is broad, one with broad spokes, one with a thick hole, one that is black, and one possessing a dot (bindumān). ||36||
Hayagrīva has the shape of a goad and five lines, and is accompanied by the Kaustubha gem;
Vaikuṇṭha shines like a wrestler, possessing a single wheel and being well-settled in iron. (37)
The Matsya is shaped like a long lotus, pale white, and marked with long lines;
the Rāmacakra has lines on the right side; and that which is dark blue is the Trivikrama. (38)
Salutations to the wielder of the mace who resides at Śālagrāma and Dvārakā;
may that Sudarśana, the bearer of the mace, who is marked by the single [disc], protect us. (39)
