Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is formed by two [syllables], Trivikrama by three, Catur-vyūha by four, and Vāsudeva by five. ||40||
May Pradyumna protect with six [mantras], and Saṅkarṣaṇa with seven;
may Puruṣottama be present with eight, and the ninefold manifestation (Navavyūha) as the ninth for our welfare. 41.
May Aniruddha protect us with his ten incarnations;
then may the twelvefold one protect us with his twelve forms, and beyond that, the infinite one. ||42||
Brahmā has four faces, carries a staff, and is elevated with a water-pot and a garland;
Maheśvara has five faces, ten arms, and the bull as his emblem. 43.
As is Yudha, so too are Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, the Mothers, Padmahasta, and Divākara. (44)
Gajāsya, Gajaskandha, and the six-faced one—these various Gaṇas should be stationed, installed, or worshipped in a temple. ||45||
For indeed, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are attained by a person. ||46||
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Śālagrāma," in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(79) The seventy-ninth chapter.
The Lord said:
The worship of Śrī Hari should be performed daily at the Śālagrāma stone, on a gem, on a yantra, on a maṇḍala, and on images; however, it may also be performed in the temple alone. ||1||
In a certain region of the Gaṇḍakī river, there is a great site known as Śālagrāma;
the stone originating from that place is established as being called Śālagrāma. ||2||
By the mere touch of a Śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million lifetimes are destroyed;
how much more so, then, the worship of Hari there, which is the cause of His direct presence! (3)
By worshipping a single Śālagrāma stone, one obtains the fruit of worshipping a hundred liṅgas;
provided that, through the merits of many births, one has obtained the Kṛṣṇa stone. ||4||
And by the mark of a cow’s footprint, one's lineage is determined;
first, one should examine the stone—smooth, excellent, and dark-blue.
The middle [nature] is said to be blackish, yielding mixed and unmixed fruits;
fire always resides within wood and is made manifest by friction.
In whatever manner Hari is all-pervading, he is perceived in the Śālagrāma;
whoever worships twelve Śālagrāma stones every day [attains the fruit]. (7)
One who possesses a stone from Dvāravatī is honored in Vaikuṇṭha;
moreover, a man perceives a cavity in a Śālagrāma stone. (8)
His ancestors remain satisfied in heaven until the end of the kalpa;
there, where the stone of Dvārāvatī is, lies the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
One who dies there goes to the city of Viṣṇu; for three yojanas around that sacred site, chanting, worship, and fire-offerings—all become ten million times more efficacious. (10)
There is no doubt that within the distance of a single krośa, one attains the most desired of all mental wishes;
for even a mere insect meets its death there and goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha. 11.
The man who sets a price upon a Śālagrāma stone, the seller, the one who approves of it, and the one who examines and consents to it—[all these share in the sin]. (12)
All go to hell for as long as the sun and moon endure;
therefore, O Goddess, one should avoid the buying and selling of the wheel. 13.
The deity born from Śālagrāma and the deity born from Dvārakā—wherever there is a union of these two, liberation occurs; of this there is no doubt. (14)
Born from Dvārakā, enriched with the discus, and marked by many discs, the eternal person is the very nature of consciousness, having the form of a stone seat for the discus. 15.
Salutations to you whose form is the syllable Om, whose nature is eternal bliss;
O highly fortunate Śālagrāma, grant your grace to this devotee. 16.
O Lord, for me who desires your grace and am bound by debt to you,
I shall hereafter joyfully proclaim the ritual procedure for the *tilaka*.
Having heard which, all the immortals attained the same form as Viṣṇu;
one should know Keśava on the forehead and Śrī-Puruṣottama on the throat.
Likewise, one should meditate on the Lord Nābhonārāyaṇa in the heart, Vaikuṇṭha on the left side, and Trivikrama on the right side. (19)
One should place Hṛṣīkeśa on the head and Padmanābha on the back;
likewise, one should place Yamunā and Gaṅgā on the two ears, and Kṛṣṇa and Hari on the two arms.
Just as the deities remembered as the twelve [Dvādaśa] are pleased when [worshipped] in their respective places, one should recite these twelve names in the Tilaka. 21.
He whose vertical mark with upward lines is seen upon his forehead goes to the world of Viṣṇu, his soul purified of all sins. ||22||
Even a Cāṇḍāla whose soul is pure is indeed worthy of worship, there is no doubt;
for that man upon whose forehead the vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) is seen. ||23||
One should not look upon such a person; having seen him, one should gaze at the sun.
For that Brahmin upon whom the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is visible, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is not seen. 24.
Upon seeing or touching that [impurity], one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
the *puṇḍra* mark, shaped like the foot of Hari, should be applied with space between its parts.

If that lowest of the twice-born should draw an upward sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on his forehead without leaving any space between the lines, the foot of a dog will constantly rest upon him; of this there is no doubt. (26)
One should know that the beautiful vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), extending from the tip of the nose up to the hairline and provided with a central aperture, is the abode of Hari. (27)
Brahmā is situated on the left side, while Sadāśiva is always on the right;
one should know Viṣṇu to be in the middle; therefore, one should not apply [the paste] to the center.
O highly fortunate one, he who, having observed [the mark], diligently applies the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* even upon water in a mirror, attains the supreme goal. (29)
Fire, water, the Vedas, the moon, the sun, and likewise the wind—these always abide eternally on the right ear of the Brahmins. (30)
The Gaṅgā is in the right ear and Hutāśana (Fire) is in the nose;
by the contact of both, one is purified at that very moment.
Having performed the water libation for the high-souled Vaiṣṇavas with a conch shell,
one should offer water mixed with Tulasī, drink it, and place it upon one's head.
One should consume it and sprinkle the body, as well as one's son, friends, and dependents;
the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, when drunk, destroys the sins of ten million births. (33)
By letting a drop fall upon the ground, that very same sin is multiplied eightfold;
for one who holds a conch with water in the hand, yet fails to offer praise, prostration, or circumambulation.
The fruit of birth is truly attained by one who constantly maintains [the conch] and does not obstruct it, in whose house there is a conch accompanied by a bell and the image of Garuḍa. (35)
In the Kali age, he who travels by means of vehicles or sandals to the house of the Lord is not a devotee of the Blessed One. (36)

Not attending the festivals of the deity, not bowing before him, and performing the salutation of the Blessed One while one is still impure from eating leftovers or is in a state of ritual impurity. (37)
Prostrating with one hand before him, circumambulating him, stretching out one's feet in his presence, and likewise sitting cross-legged; 38.
Sleeping, eating, speaking falsely, speaking loudly, idle chatter, mutual quarreling, weeping, and physical conflict; ||39||
Inflicting punishment and bestowing favor, speaking harsh words to women, excessive concealment, censuring others, and praising others [inappropriately]. (40)
Speaking vulgar words, the emission of downward wind, the use of secondary designations for the sexual organs, and eating without having first offered [the food]. ||41||

The failure to offer fruits and other items that arise at their respective times; the giving away of what remains after it has been assigned [for ritual use]; and the serving of food that is unpalatable. (42)
Making one's meal public, disparaging others, praising oneself, remaining silent toward the guru, praising oneself, and likewise reviling the deity. (43)
Likewise, thirty-two offenses of Viṣṇu have been proclaimed. ||44||
O Madhusūdana, thousands of offenses have been committed by me against you day and night; considering me as "mine," please forgive me. 45.
Having recited this mantra, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground;
Hari always forgives thousands of offenses.
Eating in the evening and in the morning according to the injunctions of the Vedas for the twice-born,
as well as eating what remains after devotion to Viṣṇu, one is liberated from the sins of the day.
"Brahmā is the food, Viṣṇu is the juice; reciting this, one should eat me.
Knowing this, he who eats is not defiled by the defects of food. 48.
A Vaiṣṇava man should not eat a round gourd, lentils, the bark of the *cavalkala* tree, white palm fruit, or *vṛntāka*. (49)

A man who is a devotee of Viṣṇu should not eat from the leaves of the banyan, the holy fig tree, or the sun plant; nor from a water-pot, a skull, or the leaves of the *duka* and *kadamba* trees; nor from the *kovidāra*, the *kadaṃba*, or the *vacana*. (50)
One should avoid leafy vegetables in the month of Śrāvaṇa, curd in Bhādrapada,
milk in the month of Āśvina, and meat in Kārttika.
Food that has been burnt, food that is bitter, and whatever has not been offered to Viṣṇu;
likewise, the citron fruit, leafy vegetables, and salt that is visibly present [in the dish]. (52)
Whatever food one has eaten by chance, one should then recollect its name:
winter rice, white rice, steamed rice, grain, mung beans, sesame, and barley. (53)
Kalāpaka, gunīvāra, śāka, cahila, mocikā, kālaśāka, vāstūka, mūlaka, and red and other varieties of keta; ||54||
Salt, rock salt, sea salt, cow's milk, curd, and ghee;
milk from which the essence has been extracted, as well as jackfruit, mango, and harītakī. (55)
Long pepper, cumin, ginger, garlic, and tamarind;
plantain, lavalī fruit, and āmalakī fruit, along with jaggery and sugarcane juice. (56)
Sages declare that food fit for sacrifice is that which has not been cooked with oil;
and the man who wears a garland made of tulasī leaves, flowers, and the like, [is likewise purified].
One should know that even he is Viṣṇu; this is the truth, the absolute truth, there is no doubt.
By planting a Dhātrī tree, a man becomes equal to Viṣṇu. (58)
One should know that Kurukṣetra extends for one hundred and fifty hastas;
[therein, one should worship] with rosaries fashioned from tulasī wood or made in the form of rudrākṣas.
Having placed the fashioned garland around one's neck, one should begin the worship;
likewise, [one should place] the *malaka* garland and the *puṣkara* garland correctly.
A worshiper of Viṣṇu should diligently wear a garland around his neck,
and he should also place the sacred remains (nirmālya) and a Tulasī garland upon his head.
One should mark the body with the remains of flower offerings and sandalwood paste while reciting his names;
and on the forehead, one should bear the mace, as well as the bow and arrow upon the head.
If a Brahmin, bearing the Nandaka sword in the center of his heart and the conch and discus on his two arms—thus endowed with the conch and discus—should die in a cremation ground; 63.
For him who, devoted solely to Viṣṇu, wears a tulasī leaf upon his head, no rebirth is declared; his non-return [to saṃsāra] is certain. (64)
Performing all his duties while adorned with garlands of Tulasī wood, he attains imperishable fruit.

An offering of a garland made from *tulasī* wood presented to Keśava shall result in merit for the ancestors and the deities that is ten million times greater than what was performed [otherwise]. (66)
The sin of that man who carries [the image] with devotion perishes;
then, having honored it with water for the feet and other offerings, one should recite this mantra: ||67||
She who, when seen, pacifies the entire multitude of sins; who, when touched, purifies the body;
who, when saluted, utterly dispels diseases; and who, when sprinkled, puts an end to the fear of Death.
Salutations to that Tulasī, who, when planted by the Lord Kṛṣṇa as a means of establishing proximity to Him, bestows the fruit of liberation when placed at His feet. 68.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Tilaka and Other Rites," in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Devīśvara and [the Goddess].
(80) The Eightieth Chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord, now that the terrible Kali age has arrived, which is teeming with the crocodiles of sensual objects,
how can that [dharma] be maintained by those afflicted by sons, wives, wealth, and the like?
"O Great God, O treasure-house of compassion, tell me the means for that.
Īśvara said:
"The name of Hari, the name of Hari, the name of Hari alone is everything. (2)
"O Hare, O Rāma, O Hare, O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa!"—
those who constantly utter this mantra are not afflicted by the Kali age.
Having performed the intermediate rites and remembered their names, he says again and again, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! ||4||
By joining his own name with yours, even he shall be liberated from sin through that transgression, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton. (5)
Whether this [name] beginning with "Jaya" was obtained by you, or else preceded by the word "Śrī," one who chants this name of mine is liberated from sin. (6)
One should remember [the Lord] at all times—by day, by night, and during the twilight;
by remembering Rāma day and night, one beholds Kṛṣṇa with one's own eyes.
Whether impure or pure, at all times and on every occasion, by the mere recollection of the Name, one is liberated from saṃsāra in an instant. ||8||
Even the mere mention of his name removes the sin of one burdened with various offenses;
indeed, in the Kali age, sacrifice, vows, austerity, and charity are not complete in all their constituent parts.
Bathing in the Ganges and the name of Hari—this pair is free from all danger.
Ten thousand murders, a thousand fierce sins,
the violation of ten million teachers' wives,
thefts, and whatever other [sins] there may be— [all these are destroyed] by that which is dear to Hari.
And there are none, O blessed lady, who bear the name Govinda. ||11||
Whether impure or pure, or even if one has reached any state whatsoever, whoever remembers the lotus-eyed Lord is pure both externally and internally. (12)
Merely by recollecting its name and likewise by reflecting upon its meaning,
one should fashion a form shaped like a garland, either of gold, silver, or even made of flour.
Having marked the two feet [with the signs], one should begin the worship;
he who bears the discus at the base of the big toe of the right foot. (14)
There, for the sake of cutting through the cycle of existence even for humble people, Acyuta holds a lotus at the base of his middle finger. (15)
To attract the bees that are the meditating minds,
he holds beneath the lotus a most beautiful banner, which is a victory-banner over all misfortunes.
From the base of the little finger is the vajra, which shatters the flood of committed sins;
in the middle of the side is the goad, which causes the mind to be drawn toward the offering. (17)
On the thumb-joint, she bears the form of the perfection of enjoyments;
and at the base, she holds a mace that shatters the mountain of sins for all embodied beings.
The unborn Lord, for the sake of illuminating all branches of knowledge, assumed these [symbols]; furthermore, he placed the lotus and other emblems there by means of his skill.
With his left foot resting upon him, this ocean of compassion bears Govinda;
therefore, the majesty of Govinda is beautiful with the essence of bliss. 20.
One who constantly hears or recites this shall undoubtedly be liberated;
I shall now proclaim the monthly rites that are supremely pleasing to Viṣṇu.
Being pure, one should diligently perform the ritual bathing of Śrī Viṣṇu during the month of Jyeṣṭha; this removes daily sins as well as those born of the fortnights, months, seasons, and years.
Thousands of killings of Brahmins, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally, as well as tens of thousands of thefts of gold, drinking of liquor, and violations of the Guru’s bed; ||23||
Indeed, thousands of millions upon millions of minor sins—
all of them perish on the day of the full moon.
If this water from the jar were upon my head, then—by means of the Puruṣasūkta mantra and the Pāvamānī verses—[I would be purified]. (25)
Then, with coconut water, as well as with the juice of palmyra fruit, with water containing jewels, with scents, and likewise with water containing flowers; ||26||
Having propitiated [the deity] with the fivefold offerings according to the extent of one's resources,
one should cause the sounding of the bell, beginning with the syllable "Ghaṃ," to be performed.
For me, who have fallen into a heap of sins cast upon the great path, protect me, a sinner sinking into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. (28)
The learned Brāhmaṇa, a master of the Vedas, who is pure and acts in this manner, shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu. ||29||
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the great festival of the Lord’s sleep;
in Āṣāḍha, one should prepare the chariot, and in Śrāvaṇa, the ritual of the Śravaṇā constellation.
In the month of Bhādrapada, on his birthday, he should be intent upon fasting;
in the month of Āśvina, he should perform the ritual turning over of the one who has fallen asleep.
One should perform the awakening of Śrī Hari; otherwise, one becomes an offender against Viṣṇu. Furthermore, in the auspicious month of Āśvina, one should worship Mahāmāyā. (32)

One who worships Viṣṇu but is unrighteous should not perform the *hiṃsā* (injurious) rites accompanied by hatred; nor should he offer a sacrifice consisting of a golden or silver image of Viṣṇu without the *bali* offering. ||33||
In the months of Kārttika and Puṣya, one should perform meritorious acts according to one's desire;
one should offer a lamp to Dāmodara in a place facing the east.
The lamp should be four finger-breadths in height and seven wicks in measure; furthermore, a beautiful row of lamps should be fashioned in the shape of a crescent moon. (35)
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Lord of the World with white garments, and especially Brahmā.
In the month of Pauṣa, one should avoid the flower-abhiseka and soft sandalwood paste;
and in the month of Māgha, during the solar transit (saṃkrānti), [one should perform the rite] from consecrated rice grains.
One should offer the food oblation (naivedya) to Viṣṇu while reciting this mantra, and one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas standing before the God of gods. 38.
Having honored the devotees of the Lord and the twice-born with the thought that they are the Lord himself, when one devotee is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed. (39)
Merely by feeding a Brahmin, one will certainly attain the eternal state along with its constituent parts.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, having bathed Keśava, [one should worship Him]. 40.
Having performed worship according to the prescribed rite with mango sprouts, various powdered fruits, and perfumes prepared on cloth. ||41||
The forest was delightful and brilliantly illuminated by lamps;
it abounded in grapes, sugarcane, dates, ginger, and cardamom.
[He saw] coconut trees, *dhātrī* trees, jackfruit trees, and *harītakī* trees, as well as other clusters of trees endowed with flowers of every season. ||43||
And with various other [ornaments] provided with fruits and flowers, with canopies profuse with blossoms, and likewise with jars filled with water. ||44||
Adorned with the branches and twigs of mango trees and with parasols and chowries, one should remember, "Victory to Kṛṣṇa! while performing a circumambulation.
Especially in the Kali age, the festival of the swing is ordained to be held on the fourteenth day of the month of Phālguna, which is known as the eighth lunar mansion (Aśleṣā).
Alternatively, on the full moon day, at the junction known as the *tupratipat*,
one should worship according to the rules with devotion using the four kinds of *phalgu* powders.
With white and red, pale and yellow pigments mixed with camphor and other substances, and with beautiful fragrant powders produced by the application of turmeric dye. 48.
Or one may propitiate the Supreme Lord with other materials and forms;
beginning on the eleventh day, one should complete the rite by the fifth day.
A swing festival is prescribed for five or three days;
men behold Kṛṣṇa swinging toward the south just once. (50)
Seeing that he was undoubtedly liberated from his great wealth by thieves,
he placed the sword named Mādhava into a water-vessel.
Whether in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay,
he who worships the deity originating from Śālagrāma while it is situated in water— (52)
Or, O highly fortunate one, the merit of making an image of Him cannot be calculated;
having performed the planting of *damanaka* flowers, one should offer them to Śrī Viṣṇu. (53)
Or that offering should be performed in Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādra;
however, in rites such as the *damanaka* offering, it should be done in each preceding month when the wind is situated in the east.
It should be performed according to the prescribed rite so that it does not become fruitless, especially on the third lunar day of Vaiśākha while in the midst of water. ||55||
Alternatively, one should perform it in a mandala, a pavilion, or in a large forest;
and day by day, one's body should be well-nourished with fragrant sandalwood.
Just as one would diligently apply that which provides nourishment to one with a wasted body, [so too should one apply] sandalwood, agallochum, hrībera, black saffron, and gorocana. 57
They know that jaṭāmāṃsī and murā constitute the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu;
with these various scented substances, one should anoint the limbs of Viṣṇu. (58)
Boldly, the wood of *tulasī* combined with camphor and agallochum, or else joined with saffron, is called *haricandana*. (59)
And those men who behold Kṛṣṇa with devotion at the time of his departure shall not return again, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Those who bathe the God of gods with waters mixed with fragrant scents, or else place the Lord of the World amidst flowers; ||61||
Having gone there to Vṛndāvana and having prepared fruits,
he should feed them all without exception to a worthy devotee of Viṣṇu.
One should offer a coconut fruit after removing its seed-vessel;
one should also offer a *ghoṇṭā* fruit after removing the core of the jackfruit. ||63||
One should cause food mixed with curd to be given after sprinkling it with ghee;
likewise, cooked flour-cakes and *pūpa* pastries should be offered with eighteen-fold ghee (*aṣṭādaśaghṛta*).
One should cause ripe fruit mixed with sesame oil to be offered;
whatever is pleasing to oneself, that very thing one should offer to the Lord.
Having offered it with food, clothing, and other gifts, one should by no means take it back;
rather, having dedicated what has been relinquished to Viṣṇu, one should give it especially to His devotees.
Thus, O Maheśvarī, a little has been told in brief;
it should be guarded with effort like one's own private parts, O Pārvatī.
If one is satisfied with the study of the various sections of scripture that describe the beauty and qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, what need is there for other recitations?
And if the mind is truly intent upon the great festivals of the play of devotion—the essence of the sentiment of love for Him—then what use are women? (68)
May that Lord of the World, the foremost of the boys of Vraja,
his earthly abode in Vṛndāvana, and the waters of the Yamunā—
mixed with the dust from the lotus feet of that Lord— be shared by you with your hearts.
Indeed, the body is smeared in vain with agallochum, sandalwood, and other such substances. ||69||
Thus ends the eightieth chapter in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya, within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||80||
(81) Chapter Eighty-One.
The Sages said:
O Sūta, may you live long, O virtuous one! You have revealed the entire nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, which delivers all devotees from worldly existence. ||1||
O Lord, please describe the entirety of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s daily pastimes, by hearing which devotion to Kṛṣṇa increases in those who are not yet perfected. 2.
O highly fortunate one, you who are our supreme friend, tell us the separate rules and characteristics of the mantra for the disciple of the guru. (3)
Sūta said:
Once, having prostrated before Sadāśiva, the teacher of the world and god of gods, who was seated on the bank of the Yamunā, Nārada spoke. 4.
Nārada said: O God of gods, Great God, omniscient Lord of the universe, best among those who know the truth of the Lord's dharma and the mantras of Kṛṣṇa! (5)
The Kṛṣṇa-mantras obtained from you, as well as those from my father and others beyond him—
all those, beginning with the King of Mantras, have been mastered by me according to reality.
For many thousands of years, he subsisted on vegetables, roots, and fruits; he ate dried leaves, water, air, and so forth, or even remained without food.
By avoiding looking at or conversing with women, by sleeping on the ground,
and by conquering the six qualities beginning with desire, one achieves restraint of the external senses.
Even when this has been done, O Śaṅkara, my soul is still not satisfied; therefore, tell me that by which it may be perfected, O Lord, even without the purificatory rites and the like. (9)
O Lord of Gods, if I am worthy, then please tell me out of your grace that which bestows the supreme fruit from a single utterance alone. (10)
Śiva said:
"O highly fortunate one, you who desire the welfare of the world have asked well. Though it is very secret, I shall tell you this *mantra-cintāmaṇi*."
That which is the secret of secrets, the supreme mystery of mysteries, was not previously told by me to the gods or to my elder brothers. Now it has been told by me to the Goddess. 12.
I shall declare to you the supreme pair of Kṛṣṇa mantras;
this pair is indeed the "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel" (Mantracintāmaṇi) of the two. (13)
The synonyms for this mantra are likewise "the five-worded" (pañcapadī) and "the beloved of the Gopījanapada" (gopījanavallabha), ending with the words "to his feet" (taccaraṇābhyām). 14.
One should take refuge in this mantra consisting of five words;
it is proclaimed as the Great Mantra of sixteen syllables, a wish-fulfilling gem of mantras. ||15||
Having uttered "namo gopījana," one should then say "vallabhābhyām";
this mantra, consisting of two words, is indeed said to have ten syllables.
Having recited these five words even once, whether with faith or without faith, one certainly attains the presence of those dear to Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.
There is no wearing of anklets, no rule for the sequence of placing perfumes on the face, no restriction regarding place or time, and no purification of enemies, friends, and so forth. (18)
O Lord of Sages, all are qualified for this, including even Caṇḍālas, women, Śūdras and others, as well as those who are dull-witted, mute, and so forth. (19)
The Anyas, the Hūṇas, the Kirātas, the Cūliṅdas, the Puṣkasas, as well as the Ābhīras, Yavanas, Kaṅkas, Khasas, and other such beings of sinful birth. ||20||
These wicked ones, devoted to violence and intent on backbiting, were slayers of cows and Brahmins; they were possessed of great heinous sins. (21)
Those devoid of knowledge and dispassion, as well as those lacking in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—all these and others shall be eligible for the Manōratha [rite]. ||22||
O best of sages, if they all possessed devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of lords, then all would be qualified; it is not otherwise.

One who is devoted to performing sacrifices and giving gifts, who serves all the sacred traditions, who speaks the truth, or even an ascetic who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; ||24||
One who is devoted to Brahman, of noble birth, an ascetic, or intent upon vows—even such a person would not be qualified for this [practice] if they are devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa. ||25||
Therefore, this should not be told to one who is not a devotee of the Black One, nor to an ungrateful person,
nor to one who is conceited, nor to one devoid of faith, nor to an atheist.
This should not be spoken to one who does not wish to hear it, nor to one who has not served for a year;
rather, it should be told to one who possesses exclusive devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and is free from greed and delusion. (27)
This should be given with great effort only to one who is free from desire and anger;
I myself am its seer (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chandas). 28.
The mantra of the goddess Ballavīkā has been fully proclaimed;
its application is declared to be service to her beloved, Hari. (29)
Likewise, one should perform the placement of the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) with the mantras beginning with *āḥ cakrāya*;
or else, one should perform the hand-placement (*karanyāsa*) using the seed-syllable *piḥ*.
The first letter of the mantra, adorned with a bindu upon its head, thus becomes the seed-syllable *gaṃ*; here, *namaḥ* is declared to be the power (*śakti*).
Worship should be performed with incense, lamps, and likewise with offerings such as perfumes and flowers, or even with water alone if these are unavailable. (32)
It should be performed according to the preliminary rules of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the pleasure of Hari;
for this very reason, others speak of various other [preliminaries] such as *nyāsa* for this mantra. (33)

Although [this mantra] grants the fulfillment of all duties through a single utterance alone, nevertheless, one should always perform its placement in ten ways for the purpose of recitation and so forth. (34)
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the meditation upon this mantra:
[He is] clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, two-armed, and wearing a forest garland. (35)
With a crest made of peacock feathers, a face resembling ten million moons, eyes rolling in intoxication, and adorned with an ear-ornament of *karṇikāra* flowers. ||36||
He bore upon his forehead a circular tilaka-mark, fashioned with sandalwood paste on the outer edges and a drop of saffron in the center.
Resembling the rising sun, he was radiant with two earrings;
his cheeks shone like mirrors upon which droplets of perspiration glistened. (38)
With eyes fixed upon the face of his beloved, with playful side-glances and raised eyebrows, and with a prominent nose shimmering with pearls set at its tip. (39)
His lower lip, like a ripe bimba fruit, shone with the moonlight of his teeth;
his hands gleamed with armlets, bracelets, and rings set with excellent gems. 40.
Bearing a flute in his left hand and likewise a lotus, with his waist shimmering with a girdle-string and his feet resplendent with anklets. 41.
Fickle-eyed and agitated by the intensity of the savor of amorous play,
he was laughing with his beloved and repeatedly making her laugh.
Thus, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa seated with his beloved at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru) upon a jeweled lion-throne in the forest of Vṛndāvana. 43.
Then one should remember Rādhikā standing at his left side, clothed in a blue bodice and possessing a luster like molten gold. 44.
Her lotus-face, half-covered by a silken cloth, was beautifully smiling;
her eyes, as flickering as those of a female cakora bird, were fixed upon the face of her beloved. ||45||
And with her thumb and forefinger, she was offering a betel nut together with leaf and lime into the lotus-face of her own beloved. 46.
Her beautiful, full, and elevated breasts were radiant with a pearl necklace;
she had a slender waist and broad hips, adorned with a network of tinkling bells. ||47||
Wearing jeweled earrings, armlets, signet rings, and bracelets;
with tinkling anklets and jeweled toe-rings on her feet. 48.
Her limbs are charming with the essence of loveliness, and she is beautiful in every part; she is immersed in the flavor of bliss, serene, and in the bloom of fresh youth. ||49||
And her friends, O best of Brahmins, were equal to her in age and qualities;
they were intent on serving her with fly-whisks and other such attendants. (50)
Now I shall explain this meaning of the mantra to you; listen, O Nārada!
Through external and internal manifestations, as well as through His own powers such as Māyā and the rest, He unfolds the universe.
Because she was protected from the intermediate space by those eternal manifestations, beginning with Cidādi, she is called Gopī; Rādhikā is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
The Goddess is declared to be composed of Kṛṣṇa; Rādhikā is the Supreme Deity. ||52||
Since she is the embodiment of all fortune and the nature of Kṛṣṇa’s bliss, O Brahmin, she is therefore called Hlādinī by the wise. (53)
Within a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth of that [time], there are the threefold goddesses beginning with Durgā;
she herself is Mahālakṣmī, and Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
O best of sages, not even the slightest difference exists between these two;
this Durgā is Harī-Rudra, and Kṛṣṇa is Śakra, while this Śacī is [Durgā]. (55)
Sāvitrī is this Hari-Brahmā, and Umā-Hari is that Dhūmorṇā;
O best of sages, what need is there for much? Without these two, nothing exists at all.
The entire world, characterized by both the conscious and the unconscious, is composed of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa;
know thus, O Nārada, that everything is but the manifestation of those two alone. (57)
It is not possible for me to describe, even in hundreds of millions of years, how this Jambūdvīpa, honored by the earth in the three worlds, is superior to that [other island]. (58)
Therein lies Bhārata-varṣa; therein, moreover, is the city of Mathurā;
there is the place named Vṛndāvana; and there is the assembly of gopīs. 59.
Among them is the circle of Rādhā’s friends, and among them, the most excellent is Rādhikā;
due to her superior proximity [to Him], there is a progressive increase in excellence.
But nothing else has been mentioned here regarding the Earth and the other [elements];
she is indeed the serpent-king’s consort, and the cowherd women are her circle of friends. (61)
May the feet of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa—the beloved life-partners of that assembly of friends—be my refuge here in this shelter. 62.
"I have come for refuge, a living being deeply afflicted by suffering; I am that very one who has sought shelter, and whatever belongs to me is yours. (63)
"Everything belongs to those two; that is their purpose, their benefit, and what is to be enjoyed by them; 'I' and 'mine' do not exist.
Thus, O Brahmin, the meaning of this mantra has been explained in brief. (64)

The meaning of the couple, as well as the ritual placement (nyāsa), surrender (prapatti), seeking refuge (śaraṇāgati), and self-surrender (ātmārpaṇa)—these five synonyms have been declared by me. (65)
This alone should be contemplated day and night by those who are free from pride. ||66||
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vṛndāvana," in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||81||
(82) The eighty-second chapter.
Śiva said:
Now I shall describe the procedure for initiation; listen, O Nārada, according to the truth.
By merely hearing it, one may be liberated even without performing its ritual application. (1)

Having realized that the entire world is perishable until the final dissolution, and having experienced the threefold suffering—namely, that which is internal and so forth—the wise one [proceeds]. (2)
And because all pleasures are impermanent, O best of sages, having relegated them to the side of suffering, he has turned away from them. (3)

Having become dispassionate toward cyclic existence, one should contemplate the means for its abandonment; and, being profoundly at peace, one should contemplate the means for the attainment of unsurpassed bliss as well. (4)
Having realized the difficulty of this for men, O Brahmin, the one of great intelligence, being deeply distressed, would then go for refuge to me, his teacher. (5)
Peaceful, free from envy, devoted to Kṛṣṇa with no other purpose, having no other means, glorious, and devoid of lust and greed. ||6||
He is a knower of the essential truth of the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the best among those who know the Kṛṣṇa-mantras;
he eternally takes refuge in the Kṛṣṇa-mantras, is always devoted to the mantras, and is ever pure. (7)
One who constantly teaches the true Dharma, enjoins others to right conduct, transmits the tradition, is full of compassion, and is free from passion is called a Guru. (8)
One who possesses such qualities as these, who is generally desirous of serving at the feet of the guru, and who is intensely devoted to the guru, is called a disciple seeking liberation. ||9||
That direct service toward Him which arises from love is called liberation by the wise who have realized the Vedas and the Vedāngas. ||10||
Having taken refuge at the feet of one's own guru, one should report one's own conduct;
he, having removed doubts and having instructed [the disciple] again and again, [should do so]. (11)
With a deeply delighted mind, he should teach the supreme mantra to that disciple who bows at his own feet, who is tranquil, and who is desirous of serving his own feet. 12.
O Brahmin, one should also scratch the bases of the left and right arms with soft sandalwood paste,
drawing a conch and a discus respectively.
Then one should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead and other parts according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should impart the two mantras into his right ear.
And one should explain the meaning of the mantra to him properly and in due order;
his name should be diligently maintained as being joined with the word "dāsa. (15)
Then, with great devotion and affection, the wise person should feed the Vaiṣṇavas;
he should also worship the venerable guru with garments, ornaments, and other offerings. (16)
O great sage, one should give all one's possessions to the guru, or at least half of them;
having surrendered even one's own body to the guru, one should remain without any worldly attachments.
One who is learned and becomes purified by these five purificatory rites shall partake in the service of Kṛṣṇa; it cannot be otherwise even in tens of millions of kalpas. (18)

Marking with a sign, the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the mantra, the assumption of the [divine] name, and the fifth, sacrifice—these are declared by the ancient sages to be the purificatory rites (saṃskāras). ||19||
Marking with the conch, discus, and other symbols, along with the *puṇḍra* marked with a central hole, is prescribed;
the name joined with the word "servant" (*dāsa*) is called the mantra known as the *yugala*. ||20||
The worship of the Guru and the Vaiṣṇavas is designated as *yāga*.
These supreme purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) have been proclaimed by me to you. ||21||
Now, O Nārada, I shall declare to you the duties for those who have sought refuge,
by following which men in the Kali age will go to the abode of Hari.
Thus, having received the mantra from the guru and being devoted to the guru, the wise disciple, constantly serving the guru, should cultivate his grace. (23)
Therefore, one should learn the dharmas of the virtuous, especially those who have taken refuge;
one should always satisfy the Vaiṣṇavas with the thought that they are one's own chosen deity. (24)
Just as women accept beating and scolding as objects of enjoyment for their lovers, so too should the wise accept whatever is offered by Vaiṣṇavas. 25.
One should never entertain concerns regarding this world or the next;
rather, one's worldly condition at any time is always determined by the karma performed in the past. (26)
Likewise, Kṛṣṇa himself will provide for the next world;
therefore, men should by all means abandon effort on its account. (27)
Abandoning all other means, she worships him as if he were Kṛṣṇa himself,
just like a woman devoted to her husband when he has been away on a long journey.
Loving her beloved, distressed, and longing solely for union with him, she constantly contemplates his virtues; she sings of them and listens to them as well. (29)
One should likewise practice the remembrance of the qualities, pastimes, and other attributes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
however, one should never perform them as a means to an end. 30.

Just as a woman, upon meeting her beloved who has returned after a long absence, kisses him, embraces him with the thought that he is her lover, and even drinks him in with the corners of her eyes; so too [does she regard the Buddha]. (31)
Or, having attained the bliss of Brahman, one may quickly serve with supreme joy;
likewise, one should worship Hari through the glorious arcāvatāra (the incarnate form). 32.
He is eternally one who has no other refuge, and likewise one whose means of accomplishment is none other; because his purpose is accomplished by no other means, he has no other motive. ||33||
One should never worship another deity, nor bow to them, nor remember them; one should not look upon them, nor sing their praises, nor ever disparage them. (34)
One should not eat the remnants of another's meal, nor should one keep what remains from another;
one should avoid conversation, salutation, and other such interactions with those who are not Vaiṣṇavas. (35)
One should never listen to the censure of Īśvara or Vaiṣṇava;
having covered one's ears, one should depart, and if capable, one should inflict punishment. (36)
O twice-born one, relying upon the way of life of the *cātaka* bird until the fall of the body, one should remain having cultivated the purpose of the two; such is my conviction. (37)
Just as a cātaka bird, having abandoned lakes, oceans, rivers, and the like, either dies of thirst or begs from a rain-cloud; ||38||
In this very way, one should contemplate the means of accomplishment with diligence;
one's chosen deity should always be entreated: "May you become my refuge. (39)
One should always abide in favorability toward one's chosen deity, his followers, and especially toward the guru; one should avoid all hostility. (40)
I shall describe the auspicious qualities and the limits of these two;
having reflected upon them, one should place trust in them, for these two will deliver me. (41)
O Lord, from this ocean of saṃsāra, crowded with friends, sons, and home, you two alone are my protectors, the destroyers of the fear of those who have sought refuge. 42.
Whatever I am, and whatever belongs to me, in this world and in the next—all that is today offered at the feet of you both. (43)
I am an abode of offenses, having abandoned all means of spiritual practice; since I have no other resort, O Lord, may you alone be my refuge. (44)
I am yours, O beloved of the most enchanting deeds, through my mind and my speech;
I belong to you alone, O lover of Kṛṣṇa; you two indeed are my only refuge.
I have taken refuge in you both, who are mines of a multitude of compassion;
show favor toward me, a wicked servant who has committed offenses. (46)
O best of sages, those who desire that state of servitude should remain constantly reciting these five verses; before long, they shall attain it. 47.
Thus, these external dharmas have been briefly described; now, the supreme internal dharma for those who have taken refuge is being declared. (48)
Resorting diligently to the state of being a friend of Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds, one should perform service to the two of them day and night with unwavering devotion. 49.
O Nārada, the mantra has been described, as well as its constituent parts, its qualified practitioners, their respective duties, and the fruit resulting from those mantras.
If you practice this as well, you will attain the state of servitude to those two;
O Brahmin, there is no doubt whatsoever regarding the exhaustion of your own authority.
To one who supplicates, saying "I have sought refuge in You even once," Hari grants His own service; there is no doubt about this. (52)
In this regard, I shall describe to you this most wonderful secret,
which was previously heard by me directly from the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa.
O best of sages, this internal dharma has been declared to you;
it is more secret than the secret, and must be guarded with great effort. (54)
Formerly, chanting this jewel of a mantra on the summit of Kailāsa, I dwelt in the dense forest while meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa. (55)
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, appeared before me; when he said, "Choose a boon," I opened my eyes.
The Lord was seen seated upon Garuḍa together with his beloved;
having prostrated before the granter of boons, the Lord of Kamalā, I spoke.
That form of yours, which is a sword of compassion bestowing supreme bliss, is the eternal refuge of all joy, embodied and superior in every respect. (58)
O Supreme Lord, I desire to behold with my own eyes that Brahman which the wise know as devoid of qualities, beyond all transaction, and tranquil. (59)
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of Kamalā, said to me as I approached him:
"Therefore, today you shall behold that form which has been desired by your mind."
"Go to my Vṛndāvana on the western bank of the Yamunā.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the Master of the World, vanished along with his beloved. (61)
Then I too arrived at the auspicious bank of the Yamunā,
and there I beheld Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of all gods.
The beloved one, wearing the dress of a cowherd, endowed with youthful vigor, and enchanting, has his left hand gracefully placed upon the shoulder of his beloved. (63)
Laughing and causing them to laugh in the midst of the assembly of gopīs,
he possesses a luster like a gentle rain-cloud and is the abode of all auspicious qualities.
Then, laughing, Kṛṣṇa, whose speech is nectar, said to me:
"O Rudra, having known your desire, I have come into your sight. (65)
This extraordinary form of mine which you have seen today is a physical manifestation of condensed, stainless love, being, consciousness, and bliss.
The collection of Upaniṣads describe this very one of mine as formless, devoid of qualities, all-pervading, free from action, and higher than the highest; it is stainless.

Because the qualities arising from primordial nature (prakṛti) are absent, because [the Lord] is infinite, and likewise because my qualities are not established [in others], they indeed call me "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa). ||68||
"O Maheśvara, because this form of mine is invisible to the physical eye, all these Vedas declare me to be formless. (69)
Because of its pervasiveness through the aspect of consciousness, the wise know me as Brahman;
and because the phenomenal world is devoid of an agent, they indeed call me "Priceless" (Niṣkriya). //70//
Since it is through the qualities of Māyā that my portions perform creation and so forth,
I myself, O Śiva, do nothing at all regarding creation and the rest.
O Great God, I am overwhelmed by love for these gopīs;
I know no other activity, nor even myself, O Nārada. (72)
I dwell with her constantly, held under the sway of my love for her;
know this Rādhikā, the supreme deity, to be my beloved. 73.
And look all around her, O friends, by the hundreds of thousands;
all these are eternal, just as I, O Rudra, am of eternal form. (74)
The cowherds, the cows, and the cowherd girls—Vṛndāvana is always mine;
all this is eternally of the nature of the essence of consciousness and bliss. 75.
Know this Vṛndāvana of mine, O Ānanda, to be called the "Root-Bulb" (Ānanda-kanda);
by merely entering it, one shall not enter into worldly existence again. 76.
That fool who, having reached my forest, goes elsewhere again, is indeed a destroyer of his own self; this is the truth, the truth that I have spoken.
Leaving Vṛndāvana, I shall never go anywhere else;
I dwell here forever together with her.
Thus everything that was in your heart, O Rudra, has been told to you.
Tell me now: what else do you wish to hear? (79)
Then, O best of sages, I said to that god:
"How can you be obtained in such a form? Tell me the means for that."
Then the Blessed One said to me: "Excellent, Rudra, what you have spoken!
For this is indeed the most secret of secrets; it must be guarded with great effort. (81)
O Lord of Gods, he who has approached us even once and worships having abandoned all other means, doing so with the sentiment of a cowherd girl—he alone comes to me, and no other. (82)
Whether one has approached me even once, or else serves my sole beloved with undivided devotion, he comes to me; of this there is no doubt. ||83||
O Maheśvara, he who has taken refuge in me alone and not in my beloved [Goddess] shall never attain me; thus have I spoken to you. (84)
Even one who has taken refuge but once and says, "I am yours," attains me even without [further] practice; of this there is no doubt. (85)
Therefore, with every effort, one should go for refuge to my beloved;
O Rudra, by taking shelter in my beloved, you shall be able to bring me under your control. (86)
This supreme secret has been proclaimed by me to you;
O Mahādeva, this too must be guarded with great effort by you. ||87||
You too, taking refuge in this Rādhikā, my beloved, remain always in my abode while chanting my couple-mantra. 88.
Śiva said:
Having spoken thus into my right ear, Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion,
instructed me with the supreme mantra and indeed performed the purificatory rites.
O Brahmin, he vanished right there along with his retinue even as I was looking on;
and from that moment until now, I have remained here continuously.
All of this has been proclaimed by me to you in its entirety;
now speak, O best of Brahmins, what more do you wish to hear? (91)
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter in the Vṛndāvana-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(83) The Eighty-third Chapter.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, O Teacher, everything that was asked by me has been explained;
now I wish to hear about the unsurpassed path of realization (bhāvamārga). ||1||
Śiva said: "Excellent, O Brahmin! You have asked this out of a desire for the welfare of all the worlds.
I shall speak even the secret; listen to it as I declare it. (2)
O best of sages, here all the maidservants, friends, parents, and beloved consorts of Hari reside eternally, endowed with virtuous qualities. (3)
Just as they are celebrated in the Purāṇas within the manifest pastimes, so do they exist in the eternal pastimes on the earth in Vṛndāvana. ||4||
He constantly traveled back and forth between the forest and the cow-pen;
he tended the cattle with his companions, except for the slaying of the Asuras.
Likewise, his beloved women, conceiving the pride of being his handmaidens, delight their own lover with a truly secret affection. (6)
There, in their midst, one should contemplate oneself as a charming young woman, endowed with beauty and youth, possessing the form of a maiden. (7)
She was skilled in various arts and crafts, suited for the enjoyments of Kṛṣṇa; though solicited by Kṛṣṛṇa, she remained averse to worldly enjoyment.
There, she was a follower of Rādhikā, devoted to her service, and manifesting a love for Rādhikā even greater than that for Kṛṣṇa. ||9||
Through love, she was made to bring about their daily union with great effort;
she was exceedingly contented by the state of blissful joy derived from serving them.
Having thus reflected upon oneself, one should perform service there, beginning from the Brāhma-muhūrta until the time of the great night (mahā-niśā). ||11||
Nārada said:
I wish to hear, in accordance with reality, the daily pastimes of Hari;
for how can Hari be served in the mind by one who does not know His pastimes? (12)
Śiva said:
"O Nārada, I do not know that pastime of Hari in its true essence.
Go from here to Vṛndādevī; she will describe that pastime to you. (13)
Not far from this place, near the Keśī-tīrtha, she dwells surrounded by a multitude of her companions as an attendant of Govinda. (14)
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus, Nārada, the best of sages, circumambulated him with joy and, bidding him farewell again and again, then departed for Vṛndāvana. 15.
Vṛndā, seeing Nārada, bowed down again and again and said: "O best of sages, how have you come here? (16)
Nārada said:
O beautiful one, I wish to know from you the eternal life-story of Hari;
tell it to me from the beginning, if I am worthy, O auspicious lady. (17)
Vṛndā said: O Nārada, you are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa; therefore, I shall speak even this secret.
This great mystery, more secret than the secret, must not be disclosed by you. 18.
In the midst of beautiful Vṛndāvana, adorned with fifty ponds, within a house made of divine jewels and surrounded by groves of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa). ||19||
Though they were sleeping on the couch, embracing each other tightly,
they were awakened later by the birds who carry out my commands.
Fearing the interruption of the bliss born from their deep embrace,
they do not move even slightly from the bed to rise.
Then, repeatedly awakened from all sides by flocks of sarika birds, parrots,
and others with various words, the two rose from their own couches.
Then, seeing the two of them seated joyfully upon the couch, their friends entered and performed the services appropriate for them at that time.
And again, at the words of the sārikā, they both rose from their beds and went to their respective dwellings, agitated by fear and longing. (24)
And in the morning, having been awakened by his mother, he rose quickly from his bed;
having performed his ablutions and taken up a wooden ladle, he set out accompanied by Baladeva.
Permitted by his mother, he went to Goshala surrounded by his friends;
meanwhile, Radha was awakened from her bed by her Brahmana companions. ||26||
Having risen and prepared this paste of clay, wood, and other ingredients, one should perform anointing;
then, having gone to the bathing altar, she is bathed by her own female companions.
She should go there to the dressing room, where her companions adorn her with various divine ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments. (28)
Then, after her friends had diligently entreated her mother-in-law, Yaśodā,
accompanied by her companions, was invited to prepare the food.
Nārada said:
O Goddess, how was she summoned by Yaśodā for the purpose of cooking, even though there were other cooks present, headed by Rohiṇī? (30)
Vṛndā said:
"O great sage, I previously heard from the mouth of Kātyāyanī that a boon was formerly granted to her by Durvāsas. (31)
O Goddess, whatever food is cooked by you shall, through my grace,
be as sweet as nectar, rivaling ambrosia, and likewise bestow long life upon the eater.
Thus Yaśodā, who was deeply affectionate toward her son, constantly called out to her;
and being so, she [the child] became long-lived through that greed for sweets.
Having heard this, delighted and thrilled, she too would go to Nanda’s abode;
having gone there with her circle of friends, she would prepare the food.
Kṛṣṇa too, having milked some cows himself and having others milked by people,
returned to his own home surrounded by his friends, in accordance with his father’s command.
Having had an oil massage performed and being joyfully bathed by his servants,
he put on clean garments, wore garlands, and anointed his body with sandalwood paste.
With his hair tied in two tufts on either side of his head, and with a shimmering tilaka-mark on his forehead shaped like the moon shining above his neck, he has conquered [the world]. ||37||
His hands are radiant with bracelets, armlets, and jeweled seals; his chest gleams with a pearl necklace, and he wears earrings shaped like sea-monsters. ||38||
Repeatedly summoned by his mother, he would enter the dining hall,
supporting his friend’s arm and remaining devoted to Baladeva.
Surrounded by his brothers and friends, he ate various foods;
making them laugh with diverse jokes, he himself laughed along with those companions. (40)
Having thus eaten and sipped water, he rested for a moment upon a divine couch;
then, while chewing the betel-leaf offered by his attendants, he distributed it among them.
Wearing the dress of a cowherd and preceded by a herd of cows, Kṛṣṇa was followed affectionately along the path by all the inhabitants of Vraja.
Having bowed to his father and mother, and having dismissed the group of attendants led by Anetrā,
as well as others as was appropriate, he should depart for the forest.
Having entered the forest and played with his friends for a moment,
he then sported joyfully there in the forest with various diversions.
Having dismissed everyone else, he should then proceed to the rendezvous point, surrounded by two or three dear friends, out of joy and eager for the sight of his beloved. (45)
She too, having seen that Kṛṣṇa had gone to the forest,
returned to her own home under the pretext of worshipping the Sun and other deities, likewise for the purpose of gathering flowers.
Having abandoned their elders out of a desire for the company of those they dearly loved, and having thus met with great effort in that forest, [they remained there]. 47.
There, they sported joyfully throughout the day in various ways; at times, having mounted a swing, they were rocked back and forth by their friends.
Once, Hari, searching for his flute which had slipped from his hand and was hidden by his beloved, was reproached by the groups of his beloveds who were themselves deceived. (49)
Laughed at by many kinds of laughter, he remains there;
somewhere, a forest grove is graced with joy by the spring breeze.
Having entered, they sprinkled one another with water from camphor, saffron, and other fragrant substances, as well as with water released from their conch shells. 51.
Their friends likewise forbade them, yet they continued to sprinkle [him] from all sides in the forest groves fanned by the breezes of spring. (52)
O best of sages, O twice-born one, having rested at times under the root of a tree somewhere with your attendants through various pastimes suited to each occasion, [you spoke]. (53)
Having sat down upon a divine seat, they partook of the honey-wine;
then, intoxicated by the wine, their eyes grew heavy with sleep.
Having come under the sway of the arrows of desire, they clasped each other’s hands and,
with their speech and minds faltering on their path, entered the cave desiring to sport.
Then, as they were playing there like a female elephant and the leader of a herd,
even their friends became intoxicated by the honey, their eyes overcome by sleep.
In all the thickets of *mañju* and *kuñja* trees, he appeared everywhere;
though Kṛṣṇa is but one, the omnipresent Lord manifested simultaneously with many distinct bodies.
Urged repeatedly by his beloved, he should go into the presence of all of them and, like a lordly elephant with female elephants, take delight with all of them. (58)
Then, for the sake of sport, he should go to a lake with his beloved and those women;
there, he and his retinue should play with one another by splashing water. 59.
Adorned with divine garments, garlands, sandalwood paste, and ornaments,
they were as if in a house made of divine jewels upon the bank of that very lake.
O Sage, long ago I prepared fruits and roots;
however, Hari first ate them while surrounded by his beloved. (61)
Served by two or three attendants, he should go to a bed fashioned of flowers;
there, with fans made of bird feathers, massages of the feet, and other such services, [he should rest]. (62)
Being served by them, he rejoices while remembering his beloved;
and Rādhikā too, while Hara was asleep, was joyful within herself along with her attendants.
Moreover, he eats the leftovers of that [food] even from one whose life has departed;
having eaten just a little of that, he would go to his bed-chamber. (64)
To see the Bhoja king, who was like the moon to the cakorī bird longing for her beloved’s face,
she reported to you there that he had chewed betel leaf.
While they were chewing betel and distributing it among their beloved friends,
Kṛṣṇa also attended to them, listening to their clear and private conversations.
Though he was wide awake, he appeared as if asleep, covered by his garment;
having observed them with a sidelong glance, he inferred from some sign that they had come from somewhere.
Tasting their tongues with their teeth and gazing at one another’s faces,
they were submerged in an ocean of shame and for a moment said nothing at all.
In an instant, they removed his garment and departed;
laughing and mocking him, they said, "O holy man, you have fallen fast asleep! (69)
Thus, O best of sages, having experienced the pleasure of sleep for a moment while being amused by those various groups of jesters, he [awoke]. (70)
Having joyfully sat down upon two expansive, divine seats,
the two hosts staked against one another necklaces, kisses, embraces, and garments.
While playing with dice, preceded by affectionate and playful conversation, even though he was defeated, he would say to his beloved, "I have won! (72)
When she began to seize her necklace and other ornaments, she was struck by him; thus struck by him, Kṛṣṇa seized her lotus-like hand with his own. (73)
Becoming despondent in mind, he made up his mind to depart:
"O Goddess, if I have been defeated by you, let that which was staked be taken. (74)
Saying, "It was given by [him] through kissing and so forth," she should act accordingly;
she should watch for a crookedness of his eyebrows and listen for his words of reproach. (75)
Then, having heard the mutual vocal contest of the female and male parrots,
they departed from that place, desiring to go toward the house.
Having taken leave of whom would Kṛṣṇa go toward the cows?
She, however, accompanied by her circle of friends, would go to the house of the Sun. (77)
Having gone some distance from there, Hari turned back again;
assuming the guise of a brahmin, he proceeded toward the house of Sūrya.
There, entreated by her circle of female friends, she should worship the Sun with Vedic hymns composed on that very occasion, infused with playful jests. (79)
Then, having recognized that beloved command, those who were discerning plunged into an ocean of bliss; they knew neither themselves nor anything else.
Having thus spent two and a half watches of the night with the Sage through various pastimes, they should go to their homes; he, however, should go together with Kṛṣṇa to the cow-pen.
O Sage, having met his friends and taken them with him, Kṛṣṇa then went along; he was returning to Vraja with joy, making the flute resound.
Then Nanda and all the others, having heard the sound of Hari’s flute and seeing the sky covered by a mass of dust from the cows, [were amazed]. (83)
Having abandoned all their duties, even women, children, and others,
they went toward Kṛṣṇa, eager for the sight of him.
At the entrance to the royal road where all the inhabitants of Vraja were gathered,
Kṛṣṇa also approached them and spoke to each one in due order.
Through seeing and touching, through speech and glances preceded by smiles, and through prostrations to the elder cowherds—both physical and verbal. (86)
O Nārada, with eight steps, Pitṛ ascended Rohiṇī,
and likewise his beloved wife with a modesty indicated by the mere corners of her eyes.
Thus, having been duly honored by those cowherds according to their fitness,
he then entered the cow-pen together with the cows.
Requested by his parents, he went to his own home with his brothers;
having bathed, drunk, and eaten something there, he was encouraged by his mother. (89)
Then, desiring the milk of the cows, he goes again to the cow-pen;
having milked them, or having caused them to be milked, or having caused some of them to drink [water]. (90)
He goes home together with his father, following hundreds of dispositions there;
there, [he is surrounded] by his father, paternal uncles, their sons, and kinsmen.
He enjoys various kinds of food, including those to be chewed and sucked;
yet his mind is fixed on Rādhikā alone even before he makes such a request. 92.
Then Hari should send cooked foods to her house through a female friend;
and having eaten them along with his father and others, Hari should praise those [foods]. 93.
One should go to the assembly hall frequented by those twice-born men and others;
there, her female friends, having taken cooked foods, arrived beforehand. (94)
Moreover, many of those were given by Yaśodā;
there, her friends also brought what had been left over from Kṛṣṇa’s meal.
Everything was brought by them and offered to Rādhikā;
she too, accompanied by her circle of friends, ate it in that same order.
Adorned by her friends, she stands ready to go out to meet him;
therefore, I shall dispatch a certain friend from right here.
Then, led by her [the messenger] to the vicinity of the Yamunā, she [Rādhā] entered this divine jewel-adorned house within a grove of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpa-vṛkṣa). ||98||
Clad in attire suitable for the night—white and black—and surrounded by her close friends, Kṛṣṇa too then beheld various wonders there. 99.
Having heard the delightful musical performances of Kātyāyanī, he also gratified them according to the prescribed rites with wealth, grain, and other gifts. (100)
Having been worshipped by the people, he went to the house of his very dear friend; and when his mother had departed, he then took her to his own home after having fed her.
He should meet his beloved at the rendezvous unobserved;
having met there, the two of them shall sport together in the forest groves. (102)
Having spent two and a half watches of the night in various pastimes preceded by rāsa, lāsya, and laughter, thus engaged in diversion; ||103||
Desirous of sleep, the two entered the cave unobserved by the female birds,
where a charming bed for dalliance had been prepared with flowers in a secluded spot.
They remained there asleep, attended by their own handmaidens;
thus has the entire daily conduct of Hari been narrated to you.
"O Nārada, even sinners are liberated by hearing this.
Nārada said:
"I am blessed, O Goddess; I have been graced by you, there is no doubt. (106)
"Since the daily pastimes of Hari have been revealed to me today.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, he circumambulated her and was honored by her in return. (107)
O Brahmin, the supreme sage Nārada vanished from sight;
and thus, I have also related all of this to you in its proper sequence. 108.
One should daily recite with effort this supreme pair of mantras, which was formerly obtained effortlessly by Rudra from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa. (109)
He said to Nārada: "This was not approved by me even for Nārada; having performed the purificatory rites (saṃskāra), this has been told by me to you as well. (110)
"You too must keep this most wonderful secret concealed.
Śaunaka said:
"O Guru, by your grace I have truly become one who has accomplished his purpose."
"That which is the secret of secrets has been revealed by you to me.
Sūta said:
"Observe these duties and recite this mantra day and night. (112)
"Before long, O Brahmin, you will undoubtedly attain that state of servitude; I too shall go, O Lord, to the eternal abode of the All-pervading One. (113)
On the bank of the Yamunā, at the shrine of Gopīśvara, which is the teacher of teachers. ||114||
This supreme and most purifying conduct, possessed of great majesty, was proclaimed by Maheśa;
those men who listen to it with devotion—
They go eternally to the station of the Unfallen One. ||115||
It brings fortune, fame, and long life; it bestows the attainment of health and desired goals; it is the cause of the wealth of heaven and liberation, and it destroys all evil. ||116||
Those men who, devoted to Viṣṇu, constantly recite this with devotion, shall never again return from the world of Viṣṇu by any means whatsoever. (117)
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vṛndāvana," in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The *Vṛndāvanamāhātmya* is completed.
The Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha (84):
The Eighty-Fourth Chapter.
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate son of Romaharṣaṇa! A delightful narrative, which bestows joy upon the world, has been recounted by you. (1)
The great and most wonderful life-story of the illustrious Kṛṣṇa has been heard by you in its entirety as it was told; therefore, you have attained complete satisfaction. 2.
Oh, how great is the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who grants the ultimate goal to His devotees! For what fortunate person would not attain liberation through Him? (3)
Therefore, once again, we desire to hear the great life-story of the illustrious Kṛṣṇa, as well as other matters such as vows, gifts, and worship. (4)
O highly fortunate one, tell us in detail everything regarding the ritual bathing as it was performed by each person in the past, so that we may attain complete satisfaction.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, you have asked well concerning that supreme means of liberation for the worlds;
by your devotion to Kṛṣṇa, you have achieved your life's purpose and your hearts are fulfilled.
O best of the twice-born, I shall narrate the meritorious and supreme account of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, which brings great joy to the virtuous and is a most excellent, great narrative.
Once, while wandering through the worlds, Nārada, who is dear to the Blessed One,
reached Mathurā, where Ambarīṣa was entirely devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
The best of sages beheld that illustrious one, devoted to his vows;
having greeted the excellent sage who had arrived with a respectful salutation, that best of sages [honored him]. (9)
You yourself, with a joyful mind and full of faith, have asked this very question.
Ambarīṣa said:
"O sage, that which is called the Supreme Brahman by those who discourse upon the Vedas—" (10)
He is the divine one, the lotus-eyed, Nārāyaṇa himself, the Supreme;
he who is formless yet possesses form, the Lord, unmanifest yet manifest, the eternal. (11)
How is that Hari to be meditated upon—he who consists of all beings, who is inconceivable, and in whom this entire universe is woven like warp and woof and is established? (12)
The Unmanifest, the One, the Supreme, renowned as the Supreme Self—from which the birth and so forth of the world proceed, it is the source of the self-existent Māya. (13)
He bestowed upon them the Vedas, which are established in the Self alone;
how then is He, the bestower of all human goals, to be propitiated? (14)
This is difficult even for yogis to comprehend; therefore, please speak of it out of compassion.
Those who have not propitiated Govinda do not know this source of welfare.
He who has not tasted the nectar of the lotus feet of Govinda obtains the supreme fruit of austerities, sacrifices, and gifts. 16.
One should not disregard the abundant fruit that transcends the path of mere wishes, by neglecting the propitiation of Hari, which wards off the flood of misfortunes. (17)
O Sage, I see no other supreme expiation for living beings than this, wherein all supernatural powers are heard to abide, dancing upon the eyebrows. (18)
How is this Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, propitiated?
How is that Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa, worshipped by men? (19)
And being pleased, tell all this for my benefit and for the world:
by what kind of devotion is that Blessed One, who is fond of devotion, propitiated? (20)
How may devotion toward him arise? How is he propitiated by all?
You are a Vaiṣṇava, you are dear to Hari, and you are a knower of the supreme truth.
Therefore, O Brahmin, supreme knower of Brahman, I ask you alone about that person of Hari who is both the listener and the speaker, as well as the questioner. (22)
A question concerning Kṛṣṇa purifies just like the water from His feet;
yet for embodied beings, a human body is difficult to obtain and is as fragile as a moment. (23)

Even there, I consider the sight of those dear to Vaikuṇṭha to be difficult to attain; in this cycle of birth and death, even half a moment of association with the virtuous is a treasure for human beings. 24.
Since all four aims of human life are obtained from you, O Blessed One, your journey is for the welfare of all embodied beings. (25)
But for children who follow the path of the Illustrious One, O God, the conduct of living beings leads both to suffering and to happiness. (26)
For indeed, for the virtuous like you whose souls are fixed on the Imperishable, [the gods] act solely for their happiness;
just as people worship the gods, so too do the gods [reciprocate] toward them. (27)
Virtuous people, who are compassionate toward the distressed, follow their actions like a shadow;
therefore, O Blessed One, instruct me in the Vaiṣṇava dharma.
"By giving instruction to whom one obtains the fruit born of the Vedas.
Nārada said:
"O protector of the earth, you who possess devotion to Viṣṇu have asked well. (29)
Knowing the supreme dharma to be the singular service of Mādhava, by which, when Viṣṇu is propitiated, the entire universe becomes propitiated. (30)
When Hari, who embodies all the gods, is pleased, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pleased;
by the mere remembrance of him, the multitude of great sins is destroyed. (31)
At that very moment, it goes to destruction; therefore, Hari alone is to be served. O King, who that possesses senses would not [serve] the lotus feet of Mukunda? 32.
Death, which is worshipped by sages and deities on all sides, has been heard, recited, meditated upon, honored, and approved. (33)
Indeed, this True Dharma, the Hero, instantly purifies even those who are hostile toward all;
it is that which is the cause even of the cause of causes and effects. (34)
The sole cause of nothing else, the life-force of the world, consisting of the world;
minute, vast, slender, and gross; devoid of qualities yet the bearer of qualities; the Great One. (35)
That Hari, who is beyond birth and dissolution, should always be meditated upon.
O bull among men, you have understood this perfectly. (36)
Since you inquire about the bhāgavata-dharmas that nurture the universe—those which, through association with the virtuous, serve as an elixir for the self, the mind, and the ears. (37)
The pure stories of Kṛṣṇa, who is worthy of being glorified, come forth; for this Lord is to be realized through devotion—indeed, you yourself know that. (38)
Nevertheless, out of respect for you, I shall speak for the benefit of the world;
for they say that the Supreme Brahman is beyond Pradhāna and Puruṣa. (39)
That Acyuta, by whose māyā all this is pervaded, bestows everything—
sons, a wife, long life, sovereignty, heaven, and liberation.
O men, when the Unconquered One is worshipped with devotion by those intent upon him through action, mind, and speech, he grants all that is desired here and now.
O best of kings, for their sake and out of affection, I shall declare their vows:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from desire. (42)
These mental vows are said to lead to the satisfaction of Hari:
eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, and remaining free from desire. (43)
Thus, O Lord of Men, the physical vow for men has been described:
the study of the Veda, the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names, and the speaking of truth. (44)
O King, this absence of backbiting is the supreme vocal vow;
one should always proclaim the names of the wielder of the discus everywhere. (45)
There is no impurity for one who recites it, because his hands are held with the *pavitra* grass;
for by a man who follows the conduct of his caste and stage of life, the Supreme Person [is attained]. (46)
Viṣṇu is worshipped in five ways by virtuous women who seek his favor:
through devotion to the welfare and pleasure of their husbands, and through restraint of mind, speech, and body. (47)
Vāsudeva, the ocean of compassion, is propitiated by women through vows;
even women and Śūdras may perform worship according to the path taught in the Āgamas. 48.
Service must be rendered to Kṛṣṇacandra, who has assumed the form of the best of the twice-born;
for the other three castes are solely intent upon following the path prescribed by the Vedas. (49)
Only women, Śūdras, and others may be solely intent upon worship by means of the Name;
Mādhava is not [attained] through ritual honors, nor through sacrifices, nor even through vows. (50)
He is pleased by devotion alone; thus he is proclaimed as one who is dear to devotion.
For chaste wives, indeed, the husband alone is their deity. 51.
He, however, should be honored with devotion to Viṣṇu through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
having meditated upon Viṣṇu as her husband within her heart, she should perform [her duties] with faith. (52)
And for the Śūdras, the worship of the deities shall indeed be performed by name;
all of them should act according to the path of the Āgamas, which imitates the Vedas. (53)
Women also have the right to perform the worship of Viṣṇu and other such rites, provided they are devoted to the pleasure of their husbands; this is the eternal Vedic injunction. (54)
Whatever vow has been prescribed for each person according to the dharma appropriate to his own family, he should perform that very one; by that, Keśava is pleased.
The wise worship Hari constantly with oblations in the fire, with flowers in the water, with meditation in the heart, with chanting in the assembly of men, and with the recitation of mantras. 56.
Non-violence is the first flower; the second is the restraint of the organs of action; the third is compassion for living beings; and the fourth is indeed patience. (57)
Tranquility is the fifth flower, self-restraint is the sixth, and the seventh is meditation; truth is the eighth, for by these Keśava is pleased. (58)
Hari is indeed pleased when worshipped with these very eight flowers;
there are certainly other external flowers as well, O best of men. (59)
Viṣṇu is thoroughly pleased by those who worship Him with devotion using water from Varuṇa, flowers from Soma, ghee, milk, and curd. (60)
Likewise, food and such belong to Prajāpati; incense and lamps belong to Agni;
and fruits, flowers, and so forth belong to Vanaspati as the fifth.

That which originates from the roots of *kuśa* grass and the like is called *pārthiva*; that which consists of fragrant sandalwood is *vāyavya*; that which is known as faith (*śraddhā*) is the *viṣṇupuṣpa*; and that which begins with the five [elements] is remembered as *viṣṇupada*.
Even when worshipped with these flowers, Viṣṇu is pleased;
so too are the sun, fire, a brāhmaṇa, cows, a Vaiṣṇava, the sky, the wind, and water. (63)
The earth, the self, and all beings are the objects of worship for Viṣṇu;
thereafter, one should worship him with the recitation of mantras before the sun and with oblations in the fire.
One should worship the foremost of Brahmins with hospitality; cows by providing mouthfuls of grass and water;
Vaiṣṇavas by honoring them as kinsmen; and the heart by steadfastness in meditation.
With the thought that the wind is the primary element, one should worship within the self by means of substances preceded by water,
using the heart-mantras upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and with offerings.
One should worship the all-pervading Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) with equanimity within all beings;
