in these abodes, one should meditate upon His form with conch, discus, mace, and lotus.

One should worship Him with a concentrated mind, meditating upon Him as four-armed, peaceful, and disciplined; by worshipping the Brāhmaṇas who have been honored, He Himself is undoubtedly worshipped. (68)
When the Lord, having been reproached by those four who were themselves reproaching the king, established the Veda and the Dharmaśāstra, he set them into motion. (69)
Those brahmins are indeed the form of Viṣṇu, considered the supreme purifier. ||70||
Everything auspicious in the world is obtained through dharma alone; O King, the path of dharma is known from the Vedas and the treatises on dharma.
Indeed, the path of those two [the Vedas and the Dharmaśāstras] is the gods upon this earth; when they are honored here, the Lord of the World is honored.
Neither by sacrifices nor by other austerities, nor by the application of yoga, nor by worship,
does the God of gods, the All-pervading Lord, become so pleased.
Just as the earth [is satisfied] by the propitiation of the deity. ||72||
Devoted to Brahman, a knower of Brahman, a Brahmā, and the promulgator of the Veda of Brahman—he should be pleased by the Brāhmaṇas alone; when he is satisfied, the deity Brahman is satisfied. ||73||
Even those ancestors submerged for a long time in hell within both families go to heaven at that very moment when a son worships Hari.
Of what use is the life of those who act like beasts in this world, whose minds are not inclined toward Vāsudeva, who pervades the universe? (75)
I shall explain his meditation, which has not been seen by anyone;
listen, O King, to this absolute liberation that is solitary and free from all impurity. (76)
Just as a lamp standing in a windless place, motionless and free from air, O Great-Minded One, when burning, would destroy all darkness; ||77||
In the same way, the self, freed from defects, becomes truly free from affliction;
it is without desire, immovable, and for the hero, there is neither friend nor enemy. //78//
One is liberated from fear, joy, dejection, greed, envy, delusion, agitation, idle chatter, infatuation, and from pleasure and pain. (79)
When one is completely liberated from all objects of the senses, then absolute knowledge arises and the state of liberation (kaivalya) is attained. ||80||
O King of kings, through the application of the rite of the flame, the lamp-dwelling oil is dried up by means of the wick-support; it is free from duality and devoid of wind. 81.
O Great-minded One, it vomits soot after [the oil], and even of the oil;
O Great-minded One, a black line is seen before the lamp. 82.
Just as that oil, when drawn out by itself, becomes stainless through its own brilliance,
so too does the karma-oil situated within the body dry up.
Having turned the objects of the senses into collyrium, one should display them directly;
having become as pure as a flame, one should manifest oneself. 84.
Completely freed from the winds known as anger, greed, and the like,
and having become free from desire and motionless, one's own inner light shall blaze forth.
Remaining in his own place, he beholds the entire three worlds by his own splendor;
this one, whose nature is absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna), has been described to you by me. ||86||
I shall now describe the two-fold meditation (dhyāna) of that Wielder of the Wheel (Cakrin), which is perceived by the eye of others in the form of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna). ||87||
The great-souled ones, disciplined in yoga and devoted to the supreme truth,
do not perceive him who is the omniscient and all-seeing one, though he is perceived by the deluded.
Though devoid of hands and feet, he moves everywhere;
furthermore, he grasps the entire three worlds, both the stationary and the moving. (89)
O King, though devoid of nose and mouth, he smells and eats;
though earless, he hears everything—the Lord of the World, the witness of all. (90)
Though formless, he is connected with form; though subject to the power of the fivefold group, he who is the life-breath of the entire world is worshipped by all that is moving and unmoving. (91)
Though tongueless, he speaks everything in accordance with the Vedas and the Shastras; though skinless, he perceives the touch of all things. 92.
He is eternal bliss, with senses withdrawn, uniform, and without support;
devoid of qualities, free from the sense of "mine," all-pervading, possessed of [transcendent] qualities, stainless, and sinless.
He is the self-subduer of all that must be subdued, the giver of all, the supreme knower of all;
he has no mother, nor indeed does he have a father; he is the all-pervading one, consisting of everything. (94)
Thus, he who, with undistracted mind, perceives this meditation which consists of all things, goes to the supreme abode, which is formless and like unto immortality. 95.
But I shall now proclaim the second; listen to it, O high-minded one!
It has a manifested form, yet it is with form, formless, and free from all affliction. (96)
O prince, because the entire incomparable universe is perfumed by his latent impression (*vāsanā*), he is therefore truly called Vāsudeva. 97.
Through the splendor of that raining cloud, he became like the brilliance of the sun; he was the Lord of the Gods, possessing four arms. (98)
On his right shines the lordly conch, adorned with gold and jewels;
his mace, Kaumodakī, is the destroyer of great asuras. 99.
In the left hand of that great-souled hero shines a sword,
while in his right hand is a great lotus, rich with exquisite fragrance.
He always remains resplendent, bearing weapons, possessing the beauty of a lotus, with a beautiful neck, a well-rounded face, and eyes like lotus petals. (101)
Hṛṣīkeśa, who shines with teeth resembling ivory, whose lower lip, belonging to Guḍākeśa, has the appearance of coral; 102.
The lotus-eyed Keśava shines with his radiant crown, and he, the broad-chested one, shines with his vast and beautiful form. 103.
Janārdana shines brilliantly with the Kaustubha gem as his mark,
and he also radiates splendor from his two earrings which resemble the brilliance of the sun.
By what merit does Hari always shine with the Śrīvatsa mark, with armlets, and with necklaces of pearls resembling stars? (105)
Resplendent in his form, Vijaya, the best among victors, shone;
that Govinda also shone with his golden-colored garment.
Hari shines with well-fitted finger-rings upon his fingers,
and is adorned with all divine weapons and perfectly complete celestial ornaments.
The creator of the worlds and lord of the universe, mounted upon Vainateya—thus a man who meditates constantly with a one-pointed mind. (108)
One is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. Thus, O Lord of the World, I have explained to you all these various forms of meditation upon the Lord. 109.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa,
within the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa concerning the majesty of the month of Vaiśākha, this is the section titled "The Description of Meditation upon the Blessed Lord."
The eighty-fourth chapter. ||84||
(85) The eighty-fifth chapter.
Ambarīṣa said:
Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, you who act for the benefit of the world!
You have described the meditation upon Viṣṇu, both with attributes and without attributes. ||1||
Now, O you who bestow grace upon the virtuous, please describe the characteristics of devotion—of what kind it is, by whom it is performed, how, where, and when. (2)
Sūta said:
Having heard what was spoken by the best of kings,
the sage was delighted and spoke to the monarch.
Listen, O King, I shall properly declare to you that devotion to Hari which removes every sin. 3.
Now I shall proclaim the various forms of devotion that destroy sin;
devotion is declared to be of many kinds, arising from mind, speech, and body. (4)
It may be worldly, Vedic, or likewise spiritual;
for it is the recollection of the Vedas through the intellect by means of meditation and concentration. (5)
The mental devotion that brings pleasure to Viṣṇu is said to consist of the uninterrupted recitation of mantras and Vedas and of constant contemplation. (6)
Devotion through speech is said to consist of the recitation of mantras and the study of the forest scriptures (āraṇyakas),
as well as vows, fasts, observances, and the restraint of the five senses.
That very devotion, which accomplishes all goals, is described as being twofold:
physical, through ornaments marked with gold and jewels, and verbal, through diverse words. (8)
With garments, protective amulets, and threads, with the raising of fire and fans, with dances, instrumental music, songs, and all manner of offerings for the bali ritual; ||9||
Whatever worship is performed by men with various kinds of food, edibles, and drinks, dedicated to Nārāyaṇa, that is considered worldly devotion. (10)
That very devotion, which accomplishes all goals, is described as being physical;
it consists of the recitations of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the study of the Saṃhitās. (11)
Action performed with devotion directed toward Viṣṇu is called Vaidiki (Vedic);
action performed with Vedic mantras, oblations, and sacrifices is considered Vaidaki.

The New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices must be performed, as well as the Agnihotra; likewise, the partaking of the oblation, the giving of the sacrificial fee, the offering of the *puroḍāśa*, and the preparation of the *caru*. (13)
Sacrifice, fortitude, the drinking of soma, and all sacrificial rites;
fire, earth, wind, space, light, the moon, and the sun. (14)
O King, whatever action is performed with reference to him has Viṣṇu as its deity; it consists of various forms of spiritual devotion established in the worship of Brahman. (15)
Listen now to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, born from Yoga, as it has been proclaimed:
the twenty-four principles, beginning with Pradhāna, according to their enumeration. (16)
The twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, is conscious; he is declared to be the non-agent and the non-enjoyer of actions, while [the other principles] are insentient and objects of enjoyment.
The Self is both impermanent and eternal, the presiding controller and the instigator;
the Puruṣa is unmanifest and eternal, and Maheśvara is the cause. ||18||

The creation of the principles, the creation of non-existence, and the creation of the elements according to reality; enumeration, detailed analysis, and primordial matter consisting of the qualities. (19)
Having understood both similarity and dissimilarity, as well as the primary principle (pradhāna) and its various properties, this desire for the state of being Brahman is said to be the cause. ||20||
This is stated as the point of dissimilarity with the Pradhāna:
that while Brahman is the agent in all cases, the Puruṣa is non-agent. (21)
This equality with the insentient *pradhāna* is what is being stated;
it is indeed the cause and effect of the principles (*tattva*), yet it is itself a distinct principle among those principles. (22)
Having understood the purpose and the state of being employed through the discernment of reality, it is called "discerned" by the wise who contemplate for the sake of victory. (23)
Considering its existence, its reality, and its enumeration according to truth,
the wise know the principle of the elements (bhūtatattva) to be even superior to the principle of Brahman.
This devotion performed by the followers of Sāṃkhya is remembered as spiritual (ādhyātmikī) devotion;
O King, listen also to the devotion born of yoga which I shall now describe.

Constantly devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), possessed of meditation, with senses restrained, subsisting on alms-food according to his vow, and having withdrawn all his senses [from external objects]. ||26||
Holding Maheśvara in his heart while meditating upon Him—seated upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, clad in yellow garments, and possessing beautiful eyes—[he attained success]. 27.
He beheld him with a radiant face, the sacred thread reaching down to his hips,
white in complexion, four-armed, and with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The perfection of the mental faculty born of yoga is remembered as supreme devotion to Viṣṇu;
he who possesses such devotion is called a devotee of Viṣṇu. (29)
Thus, O King Nanda, devotion has been described as being of various kinds; these are distinguished by their qualities as sāttvikī, rājasī, and tāmasī.
The various kinds of insentient objects belonging to Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor are like a fire with well-kindled flames, which reduces fuel to ashes. (31)
In that same instant, devotion to the Blessed One likewise burns away all evils. ||32||
As long as people on earth do not hear of devotion to Viṣṇu—
which is manifest nectar, the singular essence of all flavors—
so long will they suffer the blows of hundreds of births, deaths, and old age.
He experiences those many sufferings born of numerous bodies. ||33||
The Lord Ananta, whose fame is celebrated and contemplated within, and whose majesty is heard,
destroys all evil on every side like a cloud.
Just as the wind [dispels] darkness, like the sun. ||34||

The inner self does not attain such purity through acts of charity, worship of the gods, sacrifices, bathing at sacred fords, scriptural learning, right conduct, or austerities, as it does when the infinite Lord resides within the heart. //35//
The discourses of the Lord of Men, which are pure and true, are indeed wholesome and true when they concern the Lord of the Green One (Hari);
where the holy form is glorified, there the virtuous fame of the One who has heard [the truth] is heard. (36)
O fortunate one, you are blessed—steadfast bearer of the earth, leader of the Dharma, whose heart is single-mindedly absorbed in meditation upon the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
For this resolute devotion of yours, the glorious beauty of good fortune, has been brought to your ears by the merit of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 37.
O King, for a man who considers himself his own master, how could there be any spiritual welfare if he fails to propitiate with devotion the imperishable Viṣṇu, the bestower of boons? (38)
O King, this Māyājālinī is free from illusion; she is won over by devotion, not by deceit, by virtuous men—you yourself know that well. (39)

"O King, this reality of Dharma was not known by me; yet, out of respect for Vaiṣṇavas, you have asked me about this stainless truth regarding the Lord of Tīrthas, even as we were engaged in the essence of conversation. (40)
Beyond this, I see no other merit that so appropriately nourishes a supreme and particular satisfaction for one another,
wherein the virtuous, by their very nature, manifest infinite qualities to the infinite.
Those who enjoy an exalted state of being worship the treasures of the highest good. ||41||
The Brahmins are the fragrant waters of truth and faith that have arrived; they are the limbs of Hari, consisting of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, compassion, initiation, and tranquility. 42.
The Sun, the Moon, Vāyu, Earth, Water, Fire, the Quarters, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—the all-pervading Lord who consists of all beings. ||43||
The Universal Form itself created this world of moving and non-moving beings;
having entered the Brahmin himself, he always partakes of the food.

Then they worshipped the dust from the feet of that Supreme Soul—the very abode of sacred fords—who is the mountain, the self, and the earth-gods; who is the auspicious Fortune of merit, the essence of all things, and the soul of all beings. (45)
He who perceives a brahmin as Viṣṇu, being learned and well-composed, is indeed a Vaiṣṇava; so too is he who is solely devoted to his own respective duties.
I have spoken this little secret to you, which is my sacred pledge;
there is no further time for conversation, as I must go to bathe in the Gaṅgā. 47.
This meritorious month of Mādhava, beloved of Mādhava, has arrived;
even more difficult to attain than that is the seventh day of its bright fortnight at the Gaṅgā.
In ancient times, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the Gaṅgā was drunk out of anger by Jahnu, yet she was released again from his right ear. 49.
In that [place], a fortunate and meritorious man, having bathed according to the proper rite, should worship the goddess Gaṅgā, the girdle of the sky.
Any mortal who, according to the prescribed rite, gratifies the gods and the ancestors there,
directly beholds that person who has bathed in the Gaṅgā as one whose sins have been destroyed.
There is no month equal to Mādhava, and no river like the Gaṅgā;
indeed, this rare conjunction is obtained only through devotion to Hari. 52.
Born from the water of Viṣṇu’s feet and having come from the world of Brahmā,
she tirelessly purifies the three worlds with her three streams.
It is a ladder for ascending to heaven, a constant source of bliss,
a remover of the outpouring of manifold evils, and a deliverer from misfortune.

She who dwells in the matted locks of the illustrious Maheśa, she who destroys the suffering [of beings], and she who puts an end to the amorous play within the hearts of those who worship her. ||55||
She who brings about the liberation of the lineage of the ocean, the upholder of the Dharma, the goddess who moves along the three paths, and she who acts as the ornament of the world. ||56||
By means of being seen, touched, bathed in, glorified, meditated upon, and served,
they purify thousands of men, both virtuous and non-virtuous.
If "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" is uttered three times at the three junctions of the day by those standing even at a great distance, it destroys the sins accumulated over three lifetimes. (58)
The man who remembers the Gaṅgā even at a distance of thousands of yojanas, even if he be a doer of evil deeds, attains the supreme goal. (59)

O protector of the earth, this [occasion] is especially difficult to obtain even on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha; it is attained only through the grace of Hari and the brāhmaṇas. (60)
There is no month equal to Mādhava, nor is there any Lord equal to Mādhava, for he is the one who has gone [to rescue] people sinking in the ocean of evil. (61)
O King, whatever is given, recited, offered in sacrifice, or used for bathing with devotion during the month of Mādhava,
that merit shall become inexhaustible, exceeding a hundred millionfold.
Just as among the gods, Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari is the soul of all, so too is Gāyatrī among prayers, and the Jāhnavī among rivers. (63)
Just as Umā is among all women, just as the sun is among those that shine, and just as the brahmin is among bipeds, so is the attainment of health the best of all gains. (64)
Benefiting others is as [essential] to merits as the Veda is to branches of knowledge;
just as the *praṇava* is to mantras, so is contemplation of the Self to meditations. (65)
Truth is the best among one's own duties, and austerity is the best among ascetic practices; purity of wealth is the best among purities, and the gift of fearlessness is the best among gifts.
Just as the destruction of greed is considered the primary virtue among all virtues, so too is this month of Mādhava regarded as the most excellent among months. (67)
Whatever śrāddha, sacrifice, gift, fasting, austerity, study, worship, and so forth is performed there, that is remembered as having inexhaustible fruit. ||68||
Sins end with Vaiśākha; darknesses end with the sun;
and good deeds end with the injury of others and slander. ||69||
O King, whatever bathing, giving of gifts, and other such acts are performed in the month of Kārttika when the sun is situated in Libra, they shall yield a merit a hundred billion times greater.
Therefore, [the merit] in the month of Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn is a thousandfold;
even greater than that, in the month of Vaiśākha when the sun is in Aries, it is said to be a hundredfold.
Blessed are those men, truly virtuous, who in the month of Vaiśākha bathe at dawn according to the prescribed rite and worship the Enemy of Madhu.
Bathing at dawn in Vaiśākha, performing sacrifices, giving gifts, fasting, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and practicing celibacy destroy even the most heinous sins. ||73||
Furthermore, O King, in the Kali age this shall become something to be hidden:
namely, the greatness of Mādhava which consists of the horse sacrifice and other such rites. (74)
The meritorious horse sacrifice does not take place at all in the Kali age;
this ritual of the month of Mādhava is equal to that horse sacrifice. (75)
In the Kali age, sinful people of wicked intellect will not recognize the merit of the horse sacrifice, which bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation. ||76||
In that [world], sinful men must go to the ocean of hell;
therefore, its practice is rare among those who have not been [properly] fashioned.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||85||
(86) The eighty-sixth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada, the royal sage Ambarīṣa, filled with wonder, spoke these words. ||1||
Ambarīṣa said: O great sage, setting aside the meritorious months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa,
why do you praise the month of Vaiśākha, which is superior to all others?
Why is Mādhava, the beloved of Mādhava, superior even to all others?
What is the ritual injunction there, what is the gift, what is the austerity, and who is the deity? (3)
O Sage, my feet have been touched by the dust of the feet of that Bhoja;
it behoves you to show me favor through the grace of your instruction.
O Great Sage, you are the upholder of the Dharma and the paths of the Dharma;
you alone are the knower of the meaning of all truths and the teacher of the Dharma. (5)
The doer, the instructor, the consenter, and the instigator—these are declared by the best of sages, who know the scriptures, to be equal sharers in the result. (6)
Whatever fruit is obtained through vows, sacrifices, austerities, and gifts—all that is attained simply by teaching the Dharma. (7)
O Sage, whoever may be the one who initiates [the practice], he too shall partake in the fruit of whatever bathing at sacred fords, austerity, sacrifice, or ritual action one performs. (8)
Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows it. (9)
Therefore, it is fitting for you to teach the Dharma; that is truly wonderful.
For the awakening of a teacher is difficult to attain, as are the favorable circumstances of place and time. (10)
No other states whatsoever cool our hearts as much as this meeting with you, even more so than the acquisition of a kingdom and such things. (11)
Sūta said:
Then, following the radiance of his teeth which were shining with a gentle smile, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke to Ambarīṣa. 12.
Nārada said:
Listen, O King, I shall declare for your benefit and for the benefit of the world that ordinance of the month of Mādhava which was heard by me from Brahmā in the past. 13.
Birth in the land of Bhārata is difficult to obtain; more difficult than that is human status.
Within the human state, it is rare in this world to engage in one's own specific duty (sva-dharma). 14.
Even more difficult than that, O King, is devotion to Vāsudeva;
even among those, the month of Mādhava, which is dear to Mādhava, is most rare. (15)
Having attained that [opportunity], those fortunate and accomplished men who then perform bathing, giving, recitation, and so forth according to the prescribed rule, are truly blessed. (16)
Merely by the sight of them, even sinners become free from defilement;
permeated by the state of the Blessed One, they become seekers of the Dharma. (17)
Those who bathe in the month of Mādhava at dawn, endowed with self-restraint, sport in the Nandana grove for a period of ten million years. (18)
Just as there is no body of water in the world equal to the ocean, so too there is no month like Vaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava. (19)
The sins of human beings remain within their bodies only so long as Mādhava has not arrived, seated at the very boundary of the destruction of impurity. 20.
Indeed, for all the remaining days of that month, starting from the eleventh day until its very conclusion— 21.
O King, those by whom the Lord Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, was worshipped in the month of Vaiśākha with various offerings have attained the fruit of their birth. ||22||
What, indeed, is not more difficult to obtain when attained through bathing and the ritual worship of the Supreme Lord in the month of Mādhava? 23.

Neither has been given as a gift, nor offered in sacrifice, nor recited as a mantra, nor has death been met at a sacred ford by those who have not meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all sins. (24)
O King, the birth of those men in this world should be known as fruitless, who remain miserly even while wealth is present. (25)
For the wealth of one who dies without having given is useless;
through ascetic practices such as bathing at sacred fords, birth in a noble family is obtained. ||26||
O King, nothing whatsoever stands forth without charity, even from the greatness of the five-day Vaiśākha bath. (27)
One obtains birth in a noble family as well as various forms of prosperity;
a virtuous son, a good lineage, kings, wealth, grain, and excellent women. (28)
There is also an auspicious birth and death, excellent enjoyments, and indeed happiness;
there is constant and superior joy in giving, as well as magnanimity and supreme fortitude. (29)
O King, through the grace of that god Viṣṇu, the high-souled Nārāyaṇa, these perfections desired by you have arisen.
In the month of Ūrja, in the month of Tapas, and in Mādhava, which is dear to Mādhava,
having bathed with devotion, one should worship Dāmodara, Mādhava, and Madhusūdana.
Having honored [the deity] with special care and having given gifts according to one's ability, one attains happiness in this world and shall go to the supreme state of the Lord of Men. ||32||
O King, the multitude of sins accumulated over many lifetimes dissolves by bathing in Mādhava, just as darkness vanishes at sunrise; thus did Svayambhū himself instruct me. 33.
Viṣṇu, whose movement is vast, made the month known as Vaiśākha;
he rendered the world of men—protected by Yama and beyond thought—into a realm of the gods.
Therefore, when this month of Mādhava has arrived, the Vaiṣṇavas, having bathed in the purifying waters of the Gaṅgā—the sacred ford that cleanses men—[should perform their rites]. (35)
O best of kings, on the banks of the Revā, the great Yamunā, or the Śaradā,
at dawn before the sun has risen, one should perform [the rite] according to the prescribed rule.
And having worshipped Mukunda, Madhusūdana, the Lord of Gods, one who desires welfare shall obtain sons, grandsons, wealth, and various pleasures. (37)
Having experienced the fruits of your asceticism, you shall attain imperishable heaven;
knowing this, O highly fortunate one, worship Madhusūdana.
Having bathed according to the proper ritual, especially during the month of Vaiśākha,
one should worship the Lord Govinda, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment.
Having paid homage to Mādhava, the God of gods and the destroyer of sins, you shall obtain happiness, a son, wealth, and the station of Hari. (40)
O King, one should undertake this vow on the full moon day of the month of Madhu, being endowed with restraints and observances, and having given something according to one's ability. (41)
Eating sacrificial food, sleeping on the ground, established in the vow of celibacy, emaciated by austerities such as the *kṛcchra* penance, he meditated upon Nārāyaṇa within his heart. (42)

Having thus reached the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should devotedly give honey, sesame seeds, and other offerings, as well as food to the foremost of the twice-born, along with a cow and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||43||
O King, one should also request the Brahmins to ensure that his bath is free from defects, so that Lakṣmī may become as dear to him as she is to Mādhava, the Lord of the universe. 44.
In this very way, the month of Mādhava is dear to Madhusūdana;
thus, a mortal who performs the prescribed rites and bathes for twelve years [attains the fruit]. (45)
One should perform the concluding rite according to one's ability for the satisfaction of Madhusūdana.
Thus has this majesty of the month of Mādhava been recounted to you. 46.
O King, that which was formerly heard by me from the mouth of Brahmā.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||86||
(87) The Eighty-Seventh Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Nārada, the lord of the assembly (the king),
bowing down in amazement, spoke while meditating upon Hari in his mind.
Ambarīṣa said:
O Sage, how is it that we are bewildered by this—that such a fruit, so exceedingly difficult to attain, is obtained merely by bathing with very little effort? (2)
Nārada said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth; by means of little effort, a great fruit is obtained therein. Have faith in that which has been declared by the Lord of Ritual. (3)
The courses of Dharma are subtle and difficult to comprehend even for the lords; even the learned are deluded herein regarding the inconceivable power of Hari’s creative acts.
O King, Viśvāmitra and others, though born of the kṣatriya caste, attained the status of Brahmins through their preponderance of dharma; therefore, the course of dharma is subtle.
Ajāmila was known as the husband of a king’s slave-girl;
he had abandoned his lawful wife and remained constantly on the path of sin. (6)
While dying, out of affection for his son, he cried out, "Nārāyaṇa!
By that meditation and the utterance of the name, he attained the station that is so difficult to reach.
Just as fire, when touched, burns even against one's will, so too does that which is uttered even under the pretext of Govinda’s name burn [away all sins]. 8.
The grandsons of the sage Kānīna, who had approached his brother’s wife,
as well as the sons of Golaka and Paṇḍu, were themselves likewise Kuṇḍas.
Then the five kings were also enamored of Draupadī;
consequently, they attained the status of those of "meritorious renown" (puṇyaśloka), and from that arose the subtle course of dharma.
Diverse are the karmas, diverse are the manifestations of the elements;
diverse are the elements themselves, and diverse are the potencies of karma. (11)
Sometimes a well-performed deed that has remained as a stable accumulation increases further through some other auspicious action, O King. (12)
Dharma, though subtle and exceedingly profound, yields a very great fruit in some birth or another; it cannot be measured in such a way.
No certainty is heard regarding the granting of its fruit—that whatever meritorious deed has been performed, even if it is concealed by other sins. (14)
Then, coming from somewhere or other, it bestows its own fruit; for there is no destruction here of what has been done, whether it be merit or demerit. (15)
Likewise, O King, a most terrible sin is removed by many merits; as you have stated, it does not arise from an excess of exertion. (16)
And there too, great merit [accrues]; hear my reason for this:
that smallness or greatness [of the result] depends on whether the exertion is slight or great. (17)
Consequently, those such as farmers and others would possess great merit; however, from that [merit], there would result an abundance of exertion, such as the labor of plowing and the like. (18)
Indeed, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are highly praised; by undertaking this vow, one becomes free from sin.
Therein lies the abundance of duties, its greatness, and its smallness [of requirement]. (19)
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of entering water, fire, and so forth, due to other vows;
for the distinction that "this is small" and "that is great" is not a restrictive rule at all. (20)
O Great King, the result that has been taught in the scripture would indeed be great;
for as the destruction of the great is from the great, so too is the destruction of the small from the small. (21)
But rather, even by a tiny spark, a heap of grass is consumed by fire. ||22||

Ten thousand killings, a thousand fierce sins, the violation of ten million teachers' wives, and sins such as theft—all those born of ignorance are utterly destroyed by the devotees of Kṛṣṇa within You. (23)
Whatever small amount of virtuous deed is performed by a hero devoted to Viṣṇu, even if it be slight, that good action performed by one who knows the truth shall yield inexhaustible fruit. (24)
No doubt should be entertained in this matter: by worshipping Mādhava with devotion during the month of Mādhava, a person shall obtain whatever they desire. (25)
Offspring, wealth, jewels, wives, mansions, horses, and elephants—happiness, heaven, and even liberation are not far from devotion to Hari. (26)
Thus, by following the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, even if it is performed to a small extent, there is no doubt that even great sin will be destroyed and merit will increase. (27)
An abundance of results arises from the predominance of the state of being a sovereign over both disposition and action;
however, the movement of subtle dharma is to be understood through various means as well. 28.
This month of Mādhava is dear to the high-souled Mādhava; even a single observance performed by people bestows all desired objects. (29)
O King, he who is devoted to bathing at the proper time and place in the meritorious waters of the Gaṅgā,
even if he has been corrupted by his disposition since birth, remains a donor.
"It does not attain purity"—this is my view. ||30||
Living beings dwelling at holy sites such as the Gaṅgā,
and flocks of birds in temples, constantly undergo destruction despite having observed fasts.
Devoid of existence, they do not attain any state of rebirth at all. ||31||
Then, having placed the being Śrī Mādhava within the lotus of the heart with devotion during the month of Mādhava,
he who is pure and intent on ritual bathing should worship Him.
We are not able to describe its merit.
Having kindled a fire at the proper time, drenched with ghee and oil, its flames curling to the right,
one who is corrupt in disposition is indeed said to enter it and be consumed.
One does not attain the fruit of heaven, nor anything else. ||33||
Therefore, O King, have faith in the fruit of Mādhava;
even a very small auspicious act destroys hundreds of both virtuous and non-virtuous deeds. (34)
O King, just as all multitudes of evils surely perish at dawn when the sun has entered Aries, so do they vanish through fear of Hari's name.
By bathing at a sacred ford and by the chanting of Hari’s praises. ||35||
Indeed, by the splendor of the Vaiśākha bath at dawn, those evils certainly flee from him like serpents. (36)
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā or the Narmadā when the sun has entered Aries,
whoever recites this hymn for the pacification of sins with a spirit of devotion, ||37||
O Lord of the Earth, whether once a day, twice a day, or even at the three junctions of the day, he who is freed from all sins goes to the supreme abode. (38)
O Ambarīṣa, perform a pilgrimage for the sake of attaining great merit;
indeed, bathe in the month of Mādhava at dawn, established in your religious observances. (39)
That which was said to be attained by those dwelling in the city of Anarta for ten million years is obtained by a single morning bath in the month of Madhava. 40.
O King, listen here to this ancient account concerning the dispute between the brahmin Devaśarman and his wife. (41)
At the very holy Revātīra on the sacred ford of Amarakaṇṭaka,
Devaśarman, the best of the twice-born, was born as the son of Kauśika.
Deprived of wealth and sons, he was beset by manifold sufferings;
tormented by the extreme misery of poverty, he was afflicted by every deity. ||43||
Day and night he pondered upon the means of obtaining both a son and wealth;
then once, his beloved wife named Sumanā, who was firm in her vows, [spoke].
She observed her husband filled with anxiety, his face cast downwards;
then, looking at him as he stood there dejected, the illustrious lady spoke to him.
O Great-Minded One, your mind has been drawn away by countless nets of suffering; being utterly deluded by confusion, abandon your anxiety. 46.
Tell me your sorrow; may you become well and attain happiness.
There is no suffering equal to anxiety, for it truly withers the body. (47)
Having abandoned that [state], he proceeds; he does not rejoice in unhappiness.
O Lord, tell me the cause of this anxiety. (48)
Nārada said: Having heard those affectionate words, the highly intelligent Devaśarman,
though sorrowful, spoke these words with joy, accompanied by his virtuous wife.
Devaśarman said:
"O blessed lady, whatever cause of sorrow you have contemplated, I shall explain it all to you; having heard it, let it be well understood. (50)
O lady of excellent vows, I do not know by what sin I have been deprived of wealth;
likewise, I am bereft of sons—this is the cause of my suffering. (51)
Sumanā said:
Listen, for I shall declare that which destroys all doubt—the true nature of instruction, which reveals all knowledge. (52)
The Lord Hari has said that the company of the virtuous is the supreme merit and the cause of happiness and other blessings, whereas the company of the wicked is the supreme sin. (53)
Greed is the seed of this evil, and delusion is indeed its root; falsehood is its trunk, and great deceit spreads extensively from its large branches. (54)
Always blooming with the petals of intoxication and crookedness due to its evil intellect, its fragrance is falsehood and its fruit is indeed ignorance. //55//
Walls, stones, floods, thieves, cruel men, deceivers, and sinners—these are like the great branches of the tree of delusion upon which birds take their perch. (56)
Ignorance is its excellent fruit; for the juice of that fruit is indeed the Dharma.
Its growth is nourished by the water of devotion, and it is fond of faith and ritual offerings. //57//
For him, the essence of unrighteous acts turns sweet through its overflowing;
thus indeed does the tree of greed bear such fruits as its own.
A man who dwells in reliance upon its shade eats its fruits, which are naturally ripe, day after day. (59)
Even if nourished by the juice of fruits, a mortal who has been sustained by unrighteousness will, once fully nourished, lead to his own downfall.
Therefore, having abandoned anxiety, one should not harbor greed for a master;
one should not entertain such anxiety regarding wealth, sons, or wife.
Indeed, that wise man who does not follow the very path of the beloved fools is perpetually deluded, thinking falsely both day and night.
"Desiring the welfare of my son, how may I obtain sons?"—thus he constantly thought, deluded day and night. (63)
For a single moment one may behold great happiness amidst anxiety, yet again one is tormented by the arrival of immense suffering. (64)
Abandoning anxiety and delusion, follow him, O twice-born one; for in this cycle of existence, O great-minded one, what connection exists with anyone? (65)
Friends, kinsmen, sons, father, mother, daughters, as well as one's own relatives and likewise wives and so forth—these have all come into being [as such]. (66)
Devasharman said:
"O auspicious one, tell me in detail what kind of connection it is, by which all those—wealth, sons, and other kinsmen—are produced. (67)
Sumanā said: "O Lord, five kinds of sons are born; I shall describe them to you:
first, the one who misappropriates a deposit, and second, the one connected by debt. (68)
They consider an enemy to be obtainable and a neutral one to be desirable;
O Lord, I shall now describe their characteristics individually.
Sons, enemies, beloved wives, fathers, mothers, and kinsmen—these exist on the surface of the earth through their respective relationships with one another. (70)
By the act of restoring what was stolen from a deposit, whoever on earth has taken it from whomsoever, that owner of the deposit shall become a virtuous and handsome son upon this earth. (71)
For he who has stolen a deposit dwells in his house with constant fear;
the suffering caused by the misappropriation of a deposit is more terrible than even the act of giving it away. (72)
The son of Nyāsasvāmī became the one who seized the deposit;
he was virtuous, handsome, and endowed with all auspicious marks. ||73||
Having become his son, he should show devotion to him day after day;
being sweet-spoken and eloquent, he should display great affection. (74)
Having seized his own property and generated incomparable joy, he gave it back to him after the recovery of the deposit. (75)
O highly fortunate one, such is the terrible, life-destroying suffering that even a son of great virtue might inflict upon him. (76)
Having thus become short-lived, one meets with death;
having inflicted suffering in this way, and having struck [others] in this way again and again, one simply departs. (77)
When someone utters the lamentation "Son!
Son!", then this [self] laughs; for who is the son, and of whom? (78)
"My deposit has been stolen by this evildoer; indeed, by this theft of my property, my very life-breaths have departed. (79)
"O great sage, in former times, when [the world] was afflicted by immense and unbearable suffering, I took up that supreme wealth only after first inflicting that very suffering upon myself. (80)
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(88) The eighty-eighth chapter.
Sumanā said:
I shall now describe before you the son who is connected by debt:
he who, having taken a loan, indeed passes away. (1)
Having become a donor of wealth, or a son, or a brother, or even a dear father, he always behaves with the appearance of a friend while remaining inwardly wicked. (2)
That cruel one of harsh appearance does not perceive virtue at all;
he always utters harsh speech even toward his own kinsmen.
He constantly eats sweet after sweet, perpetually indulging in sensual enjoyments;
he is ever devoted to the practice of gambling and has a longing for the act of theft.
When forbidden, he steals property from the house and becomes angry;
day after day, he reviles both his father and his mother. (7)
"In this way my wealth is being exhausted, yet he says this:
'The house, the fields, and everything else belong to me alone; of this there is no doubt. (8)
Day after day, he indeed harms both his father and mother with terrible blows from clubs and pestles, and by the violent plucking out of their hair.
But when that father or mother has died, he becomes exceedingly cruel, devoid of affection and harsh; of this there is no doubt. (10)
He always performs the ancestral rites and acts of charity;
O Lord of the Earth, such are the beloved sons that come into being.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the enemy who dwells within one's own son;
even when he has reached the stage of childhood, he always behaves as a son. (12)
While playing, he would strike his father and mother;
having struck them, he would go away laughing in this manner again and again. (13)
He brought his father and mother there once again; full of anger, he behaved toward them constantly and reviled them day after day.
Thus he constantly engaged in the practice of enmity;
having struck his father and then his mother as well. (15)
Thus does one of wicked soul depart due to the influence of former enmity;
now, therefore, I shall explain how that which is dear may be obtained. (16)
Immediately upon birth, one should act for the pleasure [of the parents]; in childhood, by means of play and gentle striking;
and upon reaching maturity, one should act for the pleasure of the mother and father without delay.
With devotion, one should always serve them and satisfy both of them with affection, kind words, and pleasant conversation. 18.
Having received the instructions from the assembly of elders, he wept again out of affection;
[he performed] all the śrāddha rites, including the actions such as the offering of the piṇḍas.
Afflicted by great suffering, he indeed provides them with the means for their journey;
though bound by the three debts, he resolutely seeks to liberate them out of affection. (20)
Because it shall be obtained, O beloved, there is no doubt;
having become a son through this very rite, O one of great wisdom. (21)
I shall now speak to you of the indifferent one (udāsīna), who is dear to me;
he always revolves with an indifferent disposition.
O best of the twice-born, having renounced everything, he neither gives nor takes, neither becomes angry nor is pleased; he does not go forth, remaining indifferent.
Servants, as well as cattle, horses, elephants, buffaloes, female slaves, and male slaves—these are known to be connected with debt. (24)
Indeed, by means of a single illusion, we two took [the form] of Naka;
thus, the deposit of Naka was made by us both in a previous birth.
O beloved, listen even for a moment from Rādhā;
indeed, hear how she was transformed by her new love, just as in a previous birth.
"O Brahmin, from my childhood my husband has never been abandoned by me;
knowing this, be at peace and abandon this useless anxiety. (27)
"Nothing has been taken by anyone, nor have you given anything back;
how then does your wealth increase? Do not be amazed, O Lord. (28)
For even that which has already been obtained does not remain with its protector;
knowing this, attain tranquility and abandon useless anxiety. (29)
Whose are sons, whose is a beloved wife, and whose are kinsmen and relatives?
O best of the twice-born, who in this world belongs to whom? There is no enduring relationship. (30)
Deluded by the illusion of ignorance, men of sinful intent think:
"This is my house, this is my son, and this indeed is my wife. (31)
O beloved, indeed, this unreal appearance is the bondage of saṃsāra. ||32||
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||88||
(89) The Eighty-Ninth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Thus enlightened, the brahmin Devaśarman, the best of the twice-born,
spoke again to his beloved wife, who was endowed with wisdom.
"O auspicious lady, you have spoken the truth that destroys all doubt;
for indeed, virtuous men who are experts in truth desire such a thing. (2)
Just as I have anxiety for my son, so too for my beloved;
by whatever means possible, I shall procreate a son. (3)
Sumanā said:
"By a son one conquers the worlds; a son delivers his lineage. O highly fortunate one, through a virtuous son, both father and mother truly live. (4)
A single excellent son is better than many who are devoid of virtue;
for one alone can deliver [his family] from those others who cause suffering. (5)
Previously, I have stated this: others share in the bond [of kinship];
by merit a son is obtained, and by merit a noble family is obtained. (6)
A good death is attained through merits, while a bad death comes likewise from sins;
I declare this to be the truth, my beloved, regarding the accumulation of happiness. (7)
O beloved, [he is won] by celibacy, truth, austerity, constant observances, charity, restraints, forbearance, and purity.
One always practices non-violence according to one's ability, or even proceeds by means of non-stealing;
through these ten limbs, dharma is thus brought forth. (9)
Dharma becomes complete within him, just as a fetus develops in the womb through the limbs;
the righteous-souled one creates dharma by means of the threefold action.
For him whose mind is serene, Dharma bestows merit and happiness;
whatever that wise man contemplates, even if it be difficult to attain, he obtains it. (11)
Devaśarman said: "O Goddess, you have fully explained the supreme knowledge known as Dharma.
How may I obtain a son who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and endowed with virtuous qualities?"
Speak to me, O highly fortunate one, if you know it, O lady of excellent vows:
O sinless one, has the entire path of dharma been attained by you from your father in the past? (13)
"This is known to me: how you, O lady, became a speaker of Brahman through the grace of Cyavana and by the satisfaction of Viṣṇu in the past. (14)
Sumanā said:
"Go to the great sage Vasiṣṭha, who is knower of dharma;
entreat him, for from him you shall obtain that son, a knower of dharma and a lover of righteousness. (15)
When these words had been spoken by her, Devaśarman, the best of the twice-born, replied: "I shall do exactly as you, auspicious lady, have intended; of this there is no doubt. (16)
Having spoken thus, Devaśarman, the best of the twice-born, approached Vasiṣṭha—the knower of all, the radiant one, the foremost among those who practice austerity. (17)
He saw that most excellent of the twice-born seated upon his throne on the holy bank of the Gaṅgā,
enveloped in a blaze of splendor like a second sun.
Having bowed again and again with devotion to that high-souled sage Daṇḍavakra, who was shining like a lion of Brahman and the best among the twice-born, [he spoke]. ||19||
The son of Brahmā, possessed of great splendor, said to that stainless one:
"O you of great intelligence, sit comfortably upon these auspicious seats. (20)
Nārada said:
Having sat down, that practitioner of yoga spoke again to the one whose wealth is austerity:
"O child, [behave] always toward your wife and servants as you would toward a person in your own home. (21)
O highly fortunate one, may there be safety for you amidst the fires of your virtuous deeds; may you be free from ailment among your subjects, and may you always protect the Dharma. (22)
Having spoken thus, the one of great wisdom spoke again to the protector of the earth:
"O best of the twice-born, what dear wish shall I fulfill for you, your most beloved desire? (23)
Nārada said:
Having thus spoken these auspicious words to the brāhmaṇa, he became silent. Then the highly fortunate brāhmaṇa addressed Vasiṣṭha, the foremost of sages. (24)
He spoke thus to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who practice austerity:
"O Blessed One, O best of the twice-born, please listen to these words which will bring about our separation. (25)
"By what cause does poverty arise, and why is there no happiness from a son? O father, tell me this which I doubt: from what sin does this come? (26)
"O twice-born one, deluded by great ignorance, I was awakened by my beloved;
sent by her, O dear father, I have come here to your side. (27)
Tell me all of that which destroys every doubt;
may you, the giver of liberation, release me from the bonds of saṃsāra. (28)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Sons, enemies, brothers, and other kinsmen and relatives—these are the five types of relationships that exist for a man. (29)
O best of the twice-born, all those who are connected by debt have already been described before you by Tetasumana as "bad sons. (30)
I shall now proclaim before you the meritorious characteristics of a son:
he whose soul is devoted to merit and who is always delighted in truth and righteousness. (31)
Pure, endowed with knowledge, an ascetic, the best among those skilled in speech, well-restrained in all his actions, and devoted to the study of the Vedas. ||32||
He was a master of all the scriptures, a worshiper of gods and Brahmins, a performer of all sacrifices, a donor, one who practiced great renunciation, and a speaker of pleasant words. ||33||
Constantly devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, ever peaceful, self-controlled, and friendly; always intent upon his father and mother, and affectionate toward all his kinsmen. ||34||
A wise man who rescues his family and nourishes his own kin—one endowed with such qualities is a good son who bestows happiness. (35)
O sinless one, what need have you for those who are connected with others, who cause grief and torment, and who are indifferent and devoid of fruit? 36.
O best of the twice-born, they all come and go after inflicting most terrible suffering upon one in the form of sons within this cycle of existence. (37)
Whatever karma was performed by you in previous births and has now reached its fruition—all that I shall indeed declare; listen once more to this wonder. (38)
O Śūdra, you were of great wisdom in a previous birth, yet you were a farmer, devoid of knowledge and possessed by great greed. (39)
Having only one wife, always full of hatred, and having fathered many sons, you have indeed not given anything;
you do not know dharma at all, nor the truth that is firmly established.
O noble-minded one, you have given no gift whatsoever, nor have you studied the scriptures; you have not visited any sacred ford, nor have you undertaken any pilgrimage. (41)
"O best of the twice-born, you have thus repeatedly cleared the path for me; go first, as you did previously, while tending the cattle. (42)
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, you yourself previously performed the repeated tending of buffaloes and pregnant cows; such was the karma you committed in the past.
When did you ever perform an expenditure of that vast and infinite wealth accumulated through greed for the sake of merit? (44)
Indeed, no gift was given in the proper vessel, nor was it seen that the recipient was weak;
having performed agriculture, nothing was given, and thus there was indeed only poverty. 45.
Having abandoned all this cow dung and indeed the accumulation of livestock, you have sold away the vast wealth accumulated by you, O Brahmin. (46)
Buttermilk, ghee, milk, and curd were constantly sold;
he was bewildered by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu and tormented by the anxieties of a time of famine. ||47||
"O best of Brahmins, having made this wealth truly of great value, you, being merciless, did not indeed give it as a gift at that time. (48)
The worship of the gods was never performed by him with the devotion due to Brahmins; even upon reaching the auspicious festival days, no wealth was ever offered to the Brahmins. (49)
"When the time for the ancestral rites arrived, you did not perform them out of faith;
thus your virtuous wife has passed away even though the day had reached its midday. (50)
O high-minded one, it is also the time for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) for your father-in-law and your mother-in-law;
having heard those words of theirs, you have abandoned your home and fled.
Indeed, the path of Dharma has never been seen nor heard by you at any time;
greed is your mother, father, and brother; greed is your kinsmen and relatives. (52)
Having always abandoned unrighteousness, this greed alone has become my protector;
therefore, I have become miserable, born and exceedingly tormented by poverty. (53)
Day after day, great thirst arises within the heart;
whenever one acquires wealth, it always increases further. (54)
Burning with craving that takes the form of fire during the day, you lie fast asleep at night; yet even then, you dwell excessively upon greed.
Having reached the day [of death], one is indeed always pervaded by great delusions—
whether for a thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, or even a hundred million years.
"When will there be a *kharva* and a *nikharva* in my house? Likewise, a thousand, a *lakṣa*, a *koṭi*, and even an *arbuda*? (57)
From a *kharva* a *nikharva* is born, yet craving does not depart;
thus, even as time passes, it always continues to increase.
O Brahmin, you have never given, offered in sacrifice, nor ever eaten;
you have certainly cast it into the midst of the earth, O son, without anyone knowing. (59)
For the sake of obtaining wealth, you always employ such means as these;
being intelligent, you constantly consult with people of the world. (60)
Deluded by craving, he wanders alone, questioning people about digging for treasure and, beyond that, the doctrine of alchemy.
You constantly inquire about all the meditations that bestow accomplishment throughout the eons, as well as the entry into the variegated colors and the wish-fulfilling gem.
Burning with the fire of craving, you find no happiness at all;
inflamed by the fire of craving, you have become like a serpent, devoid of consciousness. (63)
"O Brahmin, you have thus become subject to the power of time;
when your wife and sons questioned you regarding that wealth, you remained silent. (64)
"That which was spoken was not given; having abandoned his life-breaths, he went to Yama.
Thus have I related to you this entire account of the past. (65)
By this karma, you have become a Brahmin who is destitute and poor;
yet in this cycle of existence, you always possess virtuous sons who are truly devoted.
Those endowed with good character and knowledge, who are always devoted to truth and righteousness,
are born in the home of him with whom Viṣṇu is pleased.
Wealth, grain, wife, and endless sons and grandsons—he who has Viṣṇu’s favor truly enjoys all these in the mortal world. (68)
Without the grace of Viṣṇu, neither wife nor sons come to be;
even a noble birth in a family, O Brahmin, is that supreme state of Viṣṇu. (69)
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Devaśarman," within the "Glorious Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha" in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa.
(90) The Ninetieth Chapter. Devaśarman said:
"O eminent Brāhmaṇa, you have indeed told me this very thing: that the sin committed in a previous birth was thus expiated by you through your status as a Śūdra while earning wealth. (1)
O best of the twice-born, how was that state of being a Brahmin attained by Himaya?
O master learned in knowledge and realization, tell me the entire cause of that.
Birth in Jambudvīpa is difficult to obtain; more so than that is human status, and within human status, the state of being a Brāhmaṇa born of a noble family is even rarer still. (3)
Even there, such a wife—omniscient, sweet-spoken, virtuous, and endowed with every excellence—is difficult to find; from where did she come? (4)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O twice-born one, I shall fully relate that which was performed by you previously as a righteous deed; listen, if you so desire. (5)
There was a certain Brāhmaṇa, a virtuous soul of excellent conduct and well-learned;
he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous in nature, and eternally devoted to Viṣṇu. (6)
Wandering alone over the earth to visit sacred fords for the purpose of bathing, that man of great intelligence arrived at your house while on his travels. (7)
By the mere sight of him, a pure intellect arose within you;
for the arrival of the virtuous occurs only in a house that has attained righteousness. (8)
O Brahmin, what indeed cannot be obtained by serving a Vaiṣṇava? Whatever in this world may be difficult to attain—even the stable state of liberation—is attained through such service. 9.
O best of beings, he requested a single dwelling place for the sake of his livelihood;
it was granted by your wife alone, along with you and your sons. (10)
"O Brahmin, by this much and by this little, you have lived happily in my house," he said again and again to that meritorious Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa.
"O observer of noble vows, remain here at your ease; this house is yours.
Today I am blessed, and today I have reached a holy place of pilgrimage. (12)
Today, through the sight of you, O Brahmin, I have obtained the fruit of visiting sacred fords;
the supreme and most meritorious abode of cows has been revealed as my place of residence. (13)
The vehicle was properly massaged at its flanks, and his feet were likewise rubbed and washed again with water; he then bathed with the water used for washing the feet.
Fresh ghee, curd, and milk—each one gave the other;
you likewise gave them to that Brāhmaṇa, impelled by the Unseen Force. ||15||
Thus, the noble and wise Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa Śitikaṇṭha, together with his wife, his sons, and his attendants, remained there. ||16||
Then, at dawn when the sky was clear, while he was going to the Gaṅgā in the month of Mādhava for the purpose of bathing, the Lord, being pleased, [spoke] out of compassion.
The greatness of the Vaiśākha bath has been taught before you;
indeed, you have performed it according to the rules, together with your wife and son. (18)
Just as in this world there is not even a single reservoir of water equal to the ocean, so too there is no month like Navavaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava. (19)
Sins remain unimpeded within the body for as long as the Slayer of Mura (Kṛṣṇa) has not yet reached the threshold of the heart.
Having heard his words, the service [of the month] of Vaiśākha was performed;
Madhusūdana, being pleased in mind, was worshipped by the brāhmaṇa. (21)
Indeed, during the remaining days of that very month,
beginning from the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), he performed his ritual bathing according to the prescribed rules.

O Brahmin, by virtue of your association with the Brāhmaṇas, you have performed the morning bath every day during the month of Vaiśākha; indeed, it is by that much alone [that merit has been gained]. ||23||
The Lord of the gods of gods, the slayer of Madhu, the Supreme Sovereign, was worshipped;
yet the entire month prior to this was not obtained by you for the purpose of bathing. ||24||
Thus, although you performed this bath for only five days, by that merit—and especially through the association with a Brahmin—[you have attained this]. (25)
By the grace of Govinda, you have indeed attained the status of a Brahmin;
through the conjunction of this month, you have obtained this great lineage.
It is rare for kings to find one endowed with truth and righteousness;
even rarer is the attainment of a virtuous wife who is chaste and possessed of every excellence. (27)
Born in the house of Cyavana, she was all-knowing and a speaker of Brahman;
O great sage, beauty alone is the supreme ornament for women. (28)
Virtue alone is the second, and truth is the third;
noble conduct is the fourth, and supreme merit is the fifth. (29)
Likewise, sweetness is the sixth, and great purity is the seventh;
among women, it is always present both externally and internally as the seventh of all ornaments. (30)
The eighth is indeed the state of contentment, the ninth is service, the tenth is forbearance, and likewise the eleventh is delight. (31)
O best of Brahmins, devotion to one's husband is remembered as the twelfth quality of women;
adorned with these, a wife is virtuous and a speaker of the truth regarding Brahman.
By means of the merit diligently obtained through the ritual bath of Vaiśākha, what indeed is not most easily attained during the month of Mādhava? 33.
Through bathing and worshipping the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rites, may this delusion, which has utterly bewildered us and is pervaded by craving, depart from us. 34.
In your previous birth, you indeed accumulated wealth as a Brahmin, yet you did not give it to the Brahmins, nor indeed to other miserable ones. (35)
Neither your circle of kinsmen nor your sons and wives were of any concern to you as you died; for you thought only of greed. (36)
Nothing was given in charity, no oblation was offered, no mantra was recited, nor was death met at a sacred ford;
indeed, the god Nārāyaṇa was not meditated upon to destroy all sins. (37)
When wealth is present, a man becomes a miser;
what indeed could be more painful than for one who dies without having given anything? (38)
Through penance such as bathing at sacred fords and the like, one may obtain birth in a noble family; yet nothing whatsoever comes to pass without the giving of gifts to a Brahmin. (39)
Due to the absence of that merit, poverty has come upon you;
you have become childless and are constantly afflicted by suffering. (40)
Even from the greatness of the Vaiśākha bath consisting of five days,
as well as from the worship of Hari at that very time and the company of a brāhmaṇa, [one attains this].
O Brahmin, birth in a noble family has been obtained, and even the status of a Brahmin is difficult to attain;
likewise, a virtuous son, a distinguished lineage, wealth, grain, and excellent women. (42)
Excellent birth and death, as well as excellent enjoyments and happiness; a mind always inclined toward giving, magnanimity, and supreme fortitude—[these are the results]. (43)
"O Brahmin, through the grace of that god Viṣṇu, the high-souled Nārāyaṇa, these perfections desired by you have been attained. (44)
In the month of Ūrja, in the month of Tapa, and in Mādhava, which is dear to Mādhava,
having bathed with devotion, one should worship Dāmodara, Mādhava, and Madhusūdana.
Having worshipped with special care and having given gifts with devotion,
people attain worldly happiness and thereafter go to Hari.
The multitude of sins accumulated over many lifetimes dissolves by bathing in Mādhava, O Brahmin, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun; thus spoke Svayambhū himself to Bhūridatta. (47)

Viṣṇu performed a pure deliberation regarding the month of Vaiśākha, the sole ordinance of Mādhava, which is hidden from Yama and cannot be reached by the worlds of men even when contemplated with the mind. 48.
Therefore, when this month of Mādhava has arrived,
having bathed now in the sacred waters of the Tīrthas before the sun has risen, one should worship the Sun.
Having worshipped Mukunda, the slayer of Madhu, according to the prescribed rite, one who desires sons, grandsons, wealth, spiritual welfare, and various pleasures [attains them]. (50)
Having experienced this, you shall attain imperishable heaven;
for all that was performed by you through your efforts in previous births [shall bear fruit]. (51)
O Brahmin, I have thus related this conduct before you;
having understood it in this way, O highly fortunate one, [one should practice it] especially during Vaiśākha.
Having bathed according to the proper rite, worship Madhusūdana;
having propitiated the god Govinda, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment.
You shall obtain happiness, a son, and inexhaustible wealth and horses. ||54||
Nārada said:
Even by the son of Brahmā, that most excellent of brāhmaṇas was indeed enlightened;
filled with joy, that noble-souled one there bowed down with devotion to Vasiṣṭha.
The great seer went to the house of the unripe (uninitiated) Tryarvī, where his wife Sumanā was;
he spoke to that wife about all the events of my former conduct, which had been brought about by that very brahmin through your grace.
O blessed lady, my delusion has been destroyed this very day by Vasiṣṭha, who brought about its dissolution;
yet, I shall propitiate Madhusūdana.
Having bathed with devotion in the month of Śrī-Mādhava (Vaiśākha), ||57||
Nārada said:

Having heard those words, which were supremely pure, most auspicious, and a cause of great welfare, she was filled with joy and spoke to her beloved: "Blessed are you, for you have been enlightened by the brāhmaṇa. (58)
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Devaśarman," within the *Māhātmya of the Month of Vaiśākha* in the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. ||90||
(91) The Ninety-First Chapter.
Nārada said:
The highly wise Devaśarman, together with Sumanas, [went] to the very famous Tīrtha of Ekanaḷa on the Gaṅgā, which is meritorious. ||1||
In the month of Vaiśākha, when the sun was situated in Aries, he performed his ritual bath according to the prescribed rules and worshipped Acyuta Madhusūdana according to the injunctions.
Endowed with the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), he should then give something according to his capacity;
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), sleeping on the ground, and remaining established in the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya). ||3||

Having performed austerities such as the *kṛcchra* penance and meditating on Nārāyaṇa within his heart, he arrived there on the full moon day of Vaiśākha and offered honey, sesame seeds, and other gifts.
Having given food to the Brahmins with devotion, along with a cow and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he requested the twice-born ones there to declare the bath to be free from defects.
That virtuous woman of beautiful hips, devoted solely to her husband,
constantly served him after bathing and worshipping Keśava.
Having crossed the river whose waters had subsided, they went to their own home, gladdened by the virtuous;
then, considering themselves to have accomplished their purpose, they rested without any doubt.
It is said that, through the power of that merit, in the course of some time,
his wealth, grain, and riches became immeasurable.
The four sons were endowed with modesty, proficient in the Vedas,
knowers of dharma, constant devotees of Viṣṇu, and devoted to their father and mother.
They possessed immeasurable wisdom, were awakened to the goals of human endeavor, were renowned as knowers of the truth of ritual, knowers of Brahman, and devoted solely to Brahman.
Fame is firmly established in those who are endowed with a complete array of virtues. ||11||
Having enjoyed for a long time the happiness of complete prosperity in their son and the rise of merit,
that couple then attained the supreme state through devotion to Him.
And in Śrī Mādhava, by means of his good deeds and the favor of the king. ||12||
Just as Mādhava is traditionally known as the manifest husband of the Goddess of Knowledge and Fortune (Vidyā-Lakṣmī), so too is the month of Mādhava beloved by Madhusūdana. 13.
O sinless hero, this greatness of Mādhava has been briefly recounted by me to you, just as it was heard by me in the past from my father. 14.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha," in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(92) The Ninety-second Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Nārada, the lord of the assembly (the king),
filled with wonder, bowed down and spoke while meditating upon Hari in his mind.
Ambarīṣa said:
O Sage, how can we be bewildered by this—that a Śūdra of sinful conduct attained the highest status of a Brāhmaṇa with so little effort? 2.
O dear one, even through various kinds of meritorious deeds, the status of a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain;
how then could a base person obtain it merely by bathing in the month of Mādhava? (3)
Neither by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by fierce austerities,
nor by other things designated as meritorious, O Lord, do kings such as ourselves become possessed of wealth.
They do not attain the status of being objects of worship on earth. ||4||

Even after performing various kinds of most formidable austerities incessantly for a long time, the son of Sagara obtained [the boon] only with great difficulty after a full hundred years, alas, through many strenuous efforts. (5)
How is it that this sinful man, though born of equal caste, has fallen away from his own duty; though possessing wealth, he is a non-giver?
Because of that small amount of merit performed without effort, depart from here to that [higher] reality. (6)
Nārada said:

"O King, you have spoken the truth; the status of a brāhmaṇa is exceedingly difficult to attain. Likewise, the subtle destinies [of beings] are hard to understand according to the principles of dharma."
Diverse are the actions, diverse are the formations of the elements, diverse are the elements themselves, and diverse are the potencies of karma. (8)
O King, sometimes a well-performed deed that has been accumulated remains stable;
it increases further through some other auspicious action. (9)
It yields a very great fruit even in that same birth;
yet this Dharma is profound and subtle, and it must be practiced exactly as it is.
No certainty regarding the timing of its yielding fruit is heard of for that meritorious deed, however small, even if it is concealed by other sins. (11)
Then, having arrived from somewhere or other, it bestows excellent fruit; for there is no destruction here of what has been done, whether it be merit or demerit.
Likewise, O King, through many merits, even a most terrible evil passes away; as you have said, it does not arise from an excess of exertion. (13)

Listen to the truth as it has been spoken by me regarding the fruit of that [action] in each respective case, whether it be effortless or involving great exertion, and whether its magnitude be small or great. (14)

Consequently, they would be constant performers of great vows, such as the Karmaka and others; furthermore, they would undergo much hardship from consuming the urine and other secretions of lions, tigers, and similar beasts. (15)
The excellence of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) constitutes this vow;
thus, while there is a great abundance of ritual procedures, its magnitude is actually small. (16)
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence that one might enter water, fire, and so forth, due to some other vow;
for the distinction that "this is small" and "that is great" is not a restrictive rule at all. (17)
The fruit described in the treatise shall thus be of great success:
just as there is the destruction of great [sins] by great [means], so too is there the destruction of small [sins] by small [means]. (18)
But how can the destruction of grass be seen by a tiny spark? Even Ajāmila was known as the husband of a king's slave-woman. (19)
Abandoning his lawful wife and constantly remaining on the path of sin, as he was dying, he called out to his son, saying, "Nārāyaṇa! (20)
Likewise, by the mere utterance of whose name one attains a state that is very difficult to reach;
he burns even against one's will, just as fire consumes whatever it touches.
Likewise, it burns even when impelled under the pretext of the name "Govinda. (22)
Ten thousand killings, a thousand fierce curses, the violation of ten million gurus' wives, and all manner of thefts—these are instantly destroyed by the name of Govinda, which is dear to Hari. (23)
Whatever small amount of virtuous deed is performed by a wise person, even if it is slight, when it consists of devotion to Viṣṇu, that shall yield inexhaustible fruit. ||24||
One should not entertain any doubt; by worshipping Mādhava with devotion during the month of Mādhava, people shall obtain whatever they desire. 25.
Offspring, wealth, wife, land, mansions, horses, and elephants—happiness, heaven, and even liberation are not far from devotion to Hari. (26)
Thus, by following the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, even for great sin, there will undoubtedly be its destruction through the correct performance of the rite. (27)
O learned one, there may be an abundance of fruit due to the predominance of intention and action;
yet these two subtle factors, in their course, are difficult to discern even by the wise. (28)
This month of Mādhava is dear to the high-souled Mādhava; even alone, it bestows all desired things throughout the three worlds. (29)

Even if a wise donor has been afflicted by evil intentions since birth, he may somehow become pure through merit, by going to a sacred place at the proper time and being intent on bathing in its waters; this is my firm conviction. (30)
Having kindled a fire at the proper time, drenched with ghee and oil, and possessing flames that curl to the right,
one who is corrupted by evil intent, though burnt upon entering it, does not attain heaven nor any other fruit.
The gods dwell eternally at sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, and hosts of yakṣas dwell in temples;
yet those who have performed fasts go to destruction.
Therefore, those who are free from conceptual existence obtain the fruit. ||32||

Therefore, having placed the glorious Mādhava, the embodiment of bliss, within the lotus of one's heart with devotion during the month of Vaiśākha, he who is purified by being intent on ritual bathing should worship Him; the merit of this act is beyond my power to describe.
In this regard as well, O Lord of the Earth, listen to an ancient account;
I shall relate a wondrous tale concerning the various fruits of actions. (34)
By the grace of that month of Mādhava and of Mādhava [Viṣṇu] himself, just as a certain unchaste Brāhmaṇa woman obtained an auspicious fruit. (35)
In former times, there was a lord of Kāntī well-known as Divodāsa;
his offspring was Mahāratnā, who was always the most excellent among women. (36)
Endowed with virtues and beauty, possessed of excellent character and a charming neck, she was renowned as the divine goddess Divyādevī, peerless in form upon the earth. (37)
Beheld by her father, she was endowed with beauty and grace;
seeing his daughter, that divine lady then became as if indifferent, like a celestial goddess.
Thinking, "To whom shall this maiden be given as a bride to that great-souled one? the best of men became absorbed in reflection while looking about. (39)
Having correctly understood the king of Rūpadeśa, the lord of the earth,
that sovereign monarch then summoned the high-souled Citrasena.
Divodāsa gave his daughter to the wise Citrasena;
O King, when the time for her marriage had arrived, at that very moment— (41)
Indeed, Citrasena died according to the law of time;
and the righteous king Divodāsa began to reflect.
King Nanda summoned the brahmins and questioned them:
"At the time of her marriage, Citrasena departed for heaven. (43)
"Tell me, what kind of karma will befall her?
The Brahmin said: "O King, the marriage of a maiden occurs according to the prescribed rites. (44)
The husband surely goes to death, or he practices renunciation;
terrified by a great mental or physical ailment, he departs after having made his renunciation. (45)
O King, it is seen in the treatises on Dharma that he becomes an outcast; furthermore, while she is in her menses, another husband is ordained for her. (46)
The father himself should perform the marriage with the primary authority; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O King, has it been ordained in the Dharmaśāstras by auspicious people. 47.
"Let her marriage be performed," said those best of the twice-born;
and the righteous Divodāsa, urged by the Brāhmaṇas, [consented]. ||48||
O King, O best of monarchs, by the non-returning of what had been given, he caused the mind of the great king to be set upon marriage with the divine goddess. 49.
To that noble-souled Puṣpasena, who was a field of merit, the king fell subject to the law of death even at the very time of his marriage. (50)
Whenever the illustrious king, the lord of the earth, became exceedingly distressed, he would exert himself toward the marriage with the divine goddess. (51)
At every moment when the auspicious hour arrived, even her husband would die;
thus, twenty-one husbands died one after another in due course of time.
Then the king, whose valor was renowned, became deeply distressed;
having summoned the minister along with his three sons, he gazed at him and remained silent.
The lord of the earth himself chose the one of great intelligence;
then, various kings and rulers were summoned by him. (54)
For the sake of choosing her in marriage,
many kings devoted to righteousness were sent by Death, agitated by her beauty.
Those deluded ones waged war against one another and perished;
thus, O lord of men, the destruction of those Kṣatriyas occurred. (56)
Then Divyādevī, afflicted by grief, wept piteously;
and beholding that young girl, the king wept for her who was so deeply distressed.
First, Dhara, endowed with humility, bowed down to the priest Jātūkarṇya, who was a knower of dharma, possessed of wisdom, and an ascetic.
Divodāsa said:
"Out of your grace, tell me what sin this daughter of mine, a divine goddess, has committed that she has performed such an act. (59)
Jātūkarṇa said:
O hero, I shall relate to you the deeds of that divine lady;
