listen as I recount everything she did in her previous birth. (60)
There exists the meritorious city of Vārāṇasī, which destroys all sins;
in it dwells a man of great wisdom named Suvīra by name. (61)
Born into the Vaiśya caste, he was well-provided with wealth and grain;
his wife, named Citrā, was highly wise and very beautiful. (62)
Abandoning the family tradition, she conducts herself with wicked behavior; she does not respect her husband and engages in cruel deeds.
Deprived of meritorious deeds, that evil-minded woman practices sin;
she constantly reviles her husband, being wanton and fond of quarreling. (64)
Constantly delighting in dwelling in the houses of others, she wanders excessively;
she always perceives the faults of others and is ever malicious toward living beings. (65)

She always censures the virtuous, torments her husband, and constantly indulges in excessive laughter; she delights in evil company, is fond of wandering, speaks ill, and is dear to those of wicked conduct. (66)
"Having recognized her as a rogue woman who causes harm through unrighteousness, who harbors hatred toward people, and who speaks falsehoods,
Suvīra should marry another woman after this."
Accompanied by that well-disciplined wife, the hero constantly enjoyed the objects of the senses, which were dear to his heart, according to his pleasure.
The meritorious soul, whose mind was always fixed on truth and virtue through his practice of dharma,
shone forth, having been propitiated by Satya, Amitā, Satyā, and Sumati.
Therefore, she was cast out—she who was variegated and yet not variegated, of excellent complexion, a wanton woman, and a hater of the dharma consisting in the cultivation of virtues. ||70||
In that [practice], one who possesses the luster of wandering through old age and is engaged in the conduct of both the bound and the liberated is a messenger (dūtī) devoted to passion;
she is one who is intent on sin and is engaged in the transgressive rite of attachment.
Driven by a crooked mind, she caused the destruction of the household and the ruin of the purity of her husband— who was skilled in all arts and crafts— and of the other women.
Having summoned a virtuous woman, he should incite her with sinful words— by means of jokes, greed, stories, and playful banter that serve as causes for the arousal of trust.
One should not cause the minds of wicked men or women to waver;
however, one should entrust virtuous women to worthy others.
She indeed practices hypocrisy by abandoning the village of Dharma;
having thus enjoyed [the fruits of her actions] for a hundred years, she later remains in the state of a prostitute.
Having met her death at the proper time, she who was constantly intent on evil was born as a daughter in your house; that son is a divine maiden, a goddess. (76)
Endowed with a most beautiful form, she was urged by one never seen before.
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of his, Divodāsa was greatly amazed.
Then the king spoke these sweet words to the sage Karṇa.
Divodāsa said:
Since she, whose conduct was so full of sin, always delighted in wicked behavior, has thus departed;
How can she be a suitable daughter for me, whose deity is Śrīpati and who am of noble lineage? (78)
O Sage, by some pure merit she obtained a most rare and blessed birth in a vast and glorious royal family.
And Citrā is the performer of manifold actions through her diverse nature. ||79||
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of the king,
the wise sage then smiled slightly and spoke these truthful words.
Jātūkarṇa said:

"Furthermore, having experienced various and manifold amorous pleasures with passionate, hidden lovers and libertines who were destitute of wealth and intellect, she became a prostitute in the great and famous city of Ākāśanagara, where she consumed the poison of [her] conduct for a long time. (81)
In the evening, a certain brahmin, afflicted by distress, arrived there; though pure in soul, he entered the city as if it were a serpent-infested place. ||82||
Seeing no other place, the fool went to the picture gallery;
he was utterly deluded by that prostitute through the contact of her gaze. (83)
Though he was gratified by massaging his feet, bathing him, betel, seats, food,
and amorous pastimes, he nevertheless became free from weariness at that time.
Then, by means of various amorous services,
that brahmin was attended upon by her throughout the entire night, as if she were acting with an invisible intellect.
He said: "Because he was greedy for a particular state of being. ||85||
At dawn, as he was about to depart,
his heart full of affection and gratified by his own conduct and deeds, he spoke these wonderful words with some difficulty:
And at that time, by means of her speech and with a single-pointed mind. ||86||
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O dear one, since I have been gratified by you, I must perform a service for you in return;
I shall tell you my own deep and innate sorrow without reservation. (87)
Listen with reverence to that auspicious ancient tale, which destroys all sins, as it was told by Brahmins on the banks of the Narmadā. 88.
If he bathes with effort for even three days when the sun has entered Aries,
or even before the sun has risen in the month of Mādhava, he is liberated from his accumulation of sins.
Whoever performs an external bath during the entire month of Vaiśākha and worships the Lord Mādhava according to the prescribed rite, he too is a destroyer of sin.
By means of bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites performed especially at sacred fords during the month of Mādhava, a human being shall be liberated from great sins. 91.

How can there remain even a trace of such a great accumulation of sin within the body of the embodied soul, as long as he joyfully bathes in the rays of the risen sun when it has reached the sign of Aries? 92.
Thus was I heard by me as those brahmins were speaking—[this teaching] which is the supreme boat for crossing the ocean of manifold misfortunes. (93)
Not far from the body of Śiva lies this excellent river;
I shall go there to bathe for the destruction of the multitude of my sins.
If it pleases you, or if your mind has become detached from desire, then come with me for the sake of the Vaiśākha bath. (95)
This life is impermanent, and this youth is exceedingly beautiful; yet it becomes an irresistible cause for dwelling in hell. (96)
I have been propitiated by you and cast down from the ocean of misfortune;
for it is the truth that even among the great, there are embodied beings who remain wicked. 97.
What is the use of much speaking here? Do not let this moment pass by; I shall deliver you as well, provided there is detachment in your heart.
Citra said:
"O Master, through the power of destiny and by virtue of our association with you, my mind has certainly become detached from this worldly existence.

Surely this is what I have heard in the scriptures: that association with the virtuous is inconceivable; therefore, let my salutation be directed toward him, who is both the unconditioned and, once again, the conditioned.
Jātūkarṇa said:
Having spoken thus, she then set out with him toward Citrā;
urged by the sage, she took whatever wealth was available. 101.

Thereafter, that twice-born man once again attained a body from the body of Śiva during the month of Vaiśākha; the compassionate Lord then immediately granted him the sun for his bath so that he might bathe.
Then this compassionate brahmin bathed Citrā,
who spoke with such wonderful eloquence, according to the prescribed ritual.
There, she heard with great joy the majesty of the Vaiśākha bath while the Brahmins were reciting various Purāṇas individually. (104)
By the mere hearing of which the heap of evil deeds is destroyed, just as the mass of darkness perishes at the very rising of the sun. (105)

Through the performance of ritual bathing once more in the waters of the Śiva-Śakti (Sāśiveśivatanūjala), which brings about rebirth, she shone forth as stainless as the splendor of the sun, her pure mind having arisen from that bath. 106.
There, in the month of Vaiśākha, various people who are devoted to the service of Hari and who desire the bliss of the worlds bathe in the Revā river. (107)
By means of this [observance], which bestows happiness here on the Narmadā, they purify even those of impure bodies;
especially in the month of Mādhava, mortals become like the playful lords of the world of mortals. (108)
By its mere remembrance, the Revā destroys the sins committed from birth; when seen, it destroys those born of ten lifetimes;
when one has somehow bathed in it, it destroys those born of a hundred wombs; and when fully served, it leads to the world of Rudra.
Throughout the entire month of Mādhava, he bathed daily in the waters of the Narmadā at Sācitrā and constantly gave gifts to the brāhmaṇas according to his capacity.
This twice-born man heard with faith the hymn that removes all sins from Hari while he was in the company of brahmins reciting it there. (111)
Having bathed in the waters of the Revā at Āsīpūrṇa during the month of Āśvina,
and having obtained the rite of *acchidra* (the seal of no defects) from the Brahmins there according to the prescribed rules, I also spent the month of Kārttika there in a wonderful manner.

Having constructed that small hut for him, the one named Sudeva, who was himself a god upon earth, dwelt there constantly out of compassion, as if submerged in the waters of the Revā due to his attachment to his friend. (113)
Then, after some time, O King, that brahmin met his end; not long thereafter, Citrā likewise passed away.
Surely, by virtue of that merit performed in the month of Mādhava on that very day,
she became your daughter, having not seen this torment of Yama.
This is the ripening of his karma: that he has obtained birth in the pure family of a king, a Vaiṣṇava lineage difficult for those of sinful deeds to attain. (116)
O best of men, in this [city] there arose a boon from the divine goddess named Divyādevī, and whatever food she bestowed, it resulted in enjoyments, comforts, and happiness. (117)
Although she was a courtesan, she associated with that very Brahmin;
and having bathed in the month of Mādhava, she gave him something there as well.
She enjoys the arising fruit of that gift and of her bathing;
likewise, she drinks cool water and eats sweet food incessantly. (119)
While enjoying divine pleasures, she dwells in the house of her lord;
yet, afflicted by suffering, grief, and the like, she consumes only what is provided by fate. (120)
That which formerly became the destruction of the houses of men and women has now, as the ripening of that karma, come upon her to some extent. (121)
By the greatness of the Mādhava-bath, Virasundarī became possessed of a son, even without undergoing the torments of Yama, though she was burdened with great sin. (122)
All this has been told to you regarding the conduct of your daughter, occurring throughout all her births and arising from both heroic deeds and evil actions. (123)
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Narrative of Citra," in the *Māhātmya of the Month of Vaiśākha* within the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
(93) The Ninety-third Chapter.
Nārada said:
Having heard these wonderful words of Jātūkarṇa, the king, having paid homage with respect to that wise sage, spoke to him. (1)
Divodāsa said:
"O sage, how may she now be released from this suffering?
Jātūkarṇa said:
We shall relate a great merit by which she may become happy. ||2||
Although it is generally not publicly known, I shall nevertheless proclaim before you this wondrous rite,
which, though small in scale, destroys hundreds of transgressions.

Just as all great sin goes to its destruction through the power of meditation on Hari, so too does terrible sin go to dissolution by bathing at dawn during the month of Mādhava while giving a gift. 4.

Just as all the multitudes of serpents perish out of fear of Hari, so indeed does the roar [of the sun] appear when it has entered Aries, through bathing at sacred fords and the chanting of Hari’s praises. (5)
By the splendor of the son of Vinatā, the snakes flee as if struck by a downfall; and by bathing at dawn during the month of Vaiśākha, they certainly do so.
Therefore, O King, even a divine queen herself should personally perform the Vaiśākha-śravaṇa rite and listen to this sin-destroying hymn.
She will become a sharer in the enjoyment of the bliss of union with her husband;
moreover, there is a powerful king named Sudeva, born of the same lineage, who is the ruler of the Pāṇḍya country. (8)
O King, by the merit of bathing on this very day of the month of Vaiśākha,
give that pure daughter to him as well, likewise purified by the bath.
O King, by hearing this hymn of praise to Mādhava once again, no doubt should be entertained here; behold its wondrous power! (10)
"The fruit of that meritorious deed is proclaimed as being [beneficial] both in this world and the next.
Nārada said:
Having heard all this thus spoken, the king then [acted accordingly].
Vīrasena, the ruler of the Pāṇḍya country, had his daughter undergo the rite prescribed by Jātūkarṇa.
Married to the divine prince, her sole friend from a previous birth, she— who had long observed her vows with virtuous conduct— enjoyed manifold sensory pleasures for a long time.
This has been related to you in brief concerning Ambarīṣa, by his friend Vīrasena, on account of what was done in a previous birth. (14)
What else do you wish to hear regarding the greatness of the Vaiśākha bath? ||15||
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Citra," in the *Māhātmya of the Month of Vaiśākha* within the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
(94) The ninety-fourth chapter.
Ambarīṣa said:
O Lord, I wish to hear that hymn which pacifies evil, by the mere hearing of which a heap of sins is dissolved. (1)
I am blessed, I am favored, and I have been made to hear this auspicious method, by the mere hearing of which even that [karma] acquired through improper action is destroyed. (2)

What wonder is there in this, O Madhusūdana, that during this month of Mādhava, which is a holy sacrifice, the destruction of heaps of sins occurs through baths performed as a mandatory duty, and even his world [is attained] by the mere recitation of his name? (3)

That alone is the supreme merit, the most holy, heart-pleasing, and the sole fruit of good deeds in this world, which is called by the name Keśava; O wise ones, consider this auspicious month of Mādhava to be such. 4.
Blessed are those who remember the names of Madhava, the slayer of Madhu, during this month of Madhava;
for even a single day’s account of His life is purifying and beneficial to the entire world.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of that best of kings, who was dear to Hari, the sage was pleased;
though he was eager for his bath at the Madhava-tirtha, he laughed due to the essence of the story of Mādhava.
Nārada said:

O protector of the earth, it is true that this pure practice of conversing with you about the nectar of Mukuṇḍa’s stories is superior even to the ritual bathing prescribed for the month of Mādhava, since your deity is Hari himself.
He whose life is for the sake of dharma, whose dharma is solely for the sake of Hari, and whose days and nights are for the sake of merit—him I consider a Vaiṣṇava on this earth. (8)
O King, I shall tell you something of the fruit arising from the Vaiśākha bath;
even my father is not able to describe it in its entirety in detail. (9)
In that supreme water of the Narmadā, those sinners attained liberation merely by immersion during the month of Mādhava.
While wandering in connection with ancient holy sites,
there was a certain Brahmin renowned as Muniśarman, who was righteous-souled, truthful, and pure.
Endowed with tranquility and self-restraint, characterized by the three qualities and joined with the six duties;
he is devoted to the rites for the ancestors and follows the ordinances of the Śruti and Smṛti.
He was skilled in sweet speech, devoted to the worship of Hari,
intent on the company of Vaiṣṇavas, and a sage possessed of knowledge of the three periods of time.
Devoted to his own duty, wise, compassionate, indifferent to the pleasant and unpleasant, merciful, exceedingly intelligent, a knower of reality, and fond of Brahmins. ||14||
While wandering along the Revā river in the month of Mādhava for the purpose of bathing, he saw five men before him who were exceedingly distressed. (15)
They were seated together, remaining motionless and relying on the shade of a banyan tree, their dark bodies not coming into contact with one another.
Seeing them in all directions with their minds agitated by misfortune, that best of the twice-born, filled with wonder, reflected upon them. ||17||
There, in that forest, these two thieves were seen with dejected movements, terrified by the single man,
their forms disfigured as they shared in the consequences of their association.
And they spoke to one another, being emaciated and possessing dark complexions; while the foremost of brahmins, firm in intellect, was reflecting in this manner. (19)
Then all those who were at a distance approached the sage with reverence;
having joined their palms in *añjali* and bowed down, they spoke these words clearly: ||20||
The five men said:
"We consider you to be a fortunate one, a supreme person, resplendent and venerable for your conduct;
we regard you as the foremost among the compassionate Brahmins, becoming friendly upon hearing your words. (21)
The virtuous are the destroyers of the suffering of those who are distressed by calamities such as loss of status, whose sins have arisen through fate; they provide relief merely by their appearance.
"I am a Kṣatriya named Vīravāhana from the Pāñcāla country;
out of delusion, I have killed a Brāhmaṇa with an arrow that hits by sound alone. (23)
Deprived of my topknot and sacred thread, and devoid of my marks and forehead-tilaka, I shall wander this earth proclaiming, "I am a slayer of a Brahmin. (24)
"Alms should be given to me, a most sinful slayer of a Brahmin.
Thus wandering through all the holy places, I have arrived here. (25)
O best of sages, even the sin of killing a Brahmin departs [from one who performs this];
thus, O Lord, a full year has passed for me while performing it. (26)
"O twice-born one, this other brahmin who is seen here, Candraśarman by name, has his mind overwhelmed with grief as he is being consumed by sin. (27)
O Brahmin, one whose mind is agitated by delusion is a killer of the guru;
because his mind is agitated by delusion, he is called a murderer of the guru. ||28||
O Sage, having been abandoned by his own kinsmen while living in the Magadha country, he too, wandering by the turn of fate, arrived here.
Devoid of the topknot and the sacred thread, and having abandoned the marks of a brahmin,
that twice-born man related the account exactly as it was asked by me, speaking only the truth.
While living in the house of his preceptor, with a mind agitated by anger and overcome by great delusion, he acted toward his guru just as Vighātin did. (31)
Burned by that evil deed, he wanders about, tormented by grief;
and this third one, O Lord, is Vedaśarman, who is composed.
"A Brāhmaṇa born from a woman of the Vaiśya caste through illicit union with a prostitute became a drinker of liquor out of delusion;
when questioned by me, he too spoke of his conduct exactly as it had occurred. (33)
Afflicted by mental anguish over all his own actions,
he was shunned by all the world, as well as by his wife and kinsmen.
Smeared with that sin and wandering about, this man has come here;
he is a Vaiśya named Vidhura, the fourth, who violated his teacher’s bed.
Out of delusion, he enjoyed his mother—who had become a courtesan—while she resided in Videha for as long as three months; however, having subsequently realized the truth, he abandoned her.
Afflicted with grief, this fifth great sinner, who associates with the wicked, has returned here once again, wandering over the earth. (37)
Day after day, out of greed for wealth, he committed sins such as theft;
thus, overcome by great crimes, the Vaiśya was abandoned by his own people.
With minds full of despondency, they were joined by Nanda and Mehasa;
thus, all five of those most wicked ones arrived at one place. (39)
O highly fortunate one, O best of the twice-born, no one established contact with anyone else through food, clothing, and so forth, except for the exchange of news. 40.
They dwell in a single dwelling and sleep upon a single mat;
thus, having departed from various heretical paths, they are not overcome by suffering. (41)
O best of sages, our terrible sin does not remain;
having seen that radiant form, our minds have become serene. (42)
O Lord, they declare that the end of evil comes from beholding the merit of the virtuous,
just as one speaks of the means by which there is no destruction of sin.
O Lord, we have come to know Karuṇa, the knower of the meaning of the Vedas and the Brāhmaṇas, who has felt remorse for us as we were distressed and searching [for him]. (44)
"You are certainly the one who shall uplift those who have incurred sin through delusion.
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the sage Muniśarman then [acted].
Having reflected upon this, that ocean of compassion, Muniśarman, spoke:
"You have incurred sin through ignorance, yet you are speakers of truth. (46)
Therefore, since you are filled with remorse, you should now be favored by me;
listen to my truthful words, for I speak with my arms raised high. (47)

That which was previously heard by me from the sage Aṅgiras in an assembly of sages, as well as what was seen in the Vedas and the Śāstras, and likewise heard from the mouth of my guru—[all of that]. (48)
This was first spoken in its true essence by Viṣṇu himself when he was propitiated:
"There is no satisfaction other than eating, and no teacher greater than one's father. (49)
There is no vessel superior to the Brahmins; there is no deity higher than Keśava; there is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; and there is no gift equal to a cow. (50)
There is no recitation equal to the *gāyatrī*, no vow equal to the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), no friend equal to a wife, and nothing equal to the arising of righteousness (*dharma*). (51)
There is no happiness equal to independence; there is no stage of life superior to that of the householder; there is no conduct higher than truth; and there is no bliss greater than contentment. (52)
The month of Mādhava, along with the month of Māsa, is the supreme destroyer of great sins;
when performed according to the prescribed rites with devotion, it is beloved by Madhusūdana. (53)
And at holy sites such as the Gaṅgā, it is especially very difficult to obtain;
so too are all the expiations, beginning with those lasting twelve years. (54)
Sins roar only so long as Mādhava has not arrived—
that is, for one who is devoted to bathing throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha.
With a mind as pure as the water arising from the feet of Hari, he alone is the destroyer of all sins; yet he is perceived as such by sinners.
The Kinnaras must speak [to him] solely for the sake of expiating the flood of his own sins. ||57||
He who bathes in this month known as Vaiśākha is indeed liberated from all sins,
especially when the sun is situated in Aries at the Narmadā, which bestows happiness and wards off all evil.
For great rivers are difficult to find everywhere during the month of Mādhava;
even more difficult than those to find are the Gaṅgā, the Revā, and likewise the Yamunā.
Among these three, he who bathes with devotion even in one of them during the month of Mādhava shall become free from sin and go to Hari. (60)
Therefore, oh! May you who have committed sins come with me this month of Vaiśākha— the very essence of all meritorious deeds— and bathe in the Revā, which is frequented by hosts of sages.
In the waters of the Revā, for the sake of removing the fear of all sins. ||61||
Having been addressed thus by the sage, they all then departed with him, joyful,
toward the river Revā, which brings welfare even to sinners and performs wondrous deeds.
Then Muniśarman, proceeding on his way followed by those men,
saw on the path eight terrifying Piśācas who were greatly agitated.
Making various sounds and wandering here and there,
they had hair standing on end, bloodshot eyes, black teeth, and emaciated bellies.
In a solitary forest overtaken by predatory beasts and devoid of trees or water, he saw a deer running directly toward him, its mind agitated by fear. (65)
"Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," he said, "protect me, protect me! (66)

Hearing the loud utterance of "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," the sole treasury of Dharma, those demons—who had been obtained through the power of their own past karma—approached him in their minds even in another birth. (67)
Seeing them, whose minds were endowed with discipline, Muniśarman, speaking sweet words, said: "Who are you, O deformed men? (68)
What deed was committed by Vaka, by which he has attained this transformation?
How is it that all of them are thus afflicted with suffering and so exceedingly terrifying? (69)
The pretas said:
"Constantly tormented by hunger and thirst, agitated by a multitude of various sufferings, cruel in heart and mind, their wisdom lost and their consciousness clouded. (70)
We did not know which direction to take, for we were bewildered slayers of innocent men;
that indeed is what is called suffering, and that alone is misery again and again. (71)
Just as the dawn appears upon seeing the rising of the sun, so it is for me upon hearing your soft voice loudly uttering "Nārāyaṇa. (72)
O Brahmin, having seen this vision, we have attained a state of pure being;
indeed, O Brahmin, it was through this very vision and by hearing the name of Hari.
When one has reached another state of existence, these compassionate ones destroy ill-repute and even clarify the intellect. (74)
For the most part, the Vaiṣṇava doctrine establishes itself among men;
I am named Paryuṣita, and this second one is Sūcaka. (75)
Another is Śīghragorodhaka; this fifth is Calekhaka.
This sixth is Vāgduṣṭa, and this seventh is Vidaivata. ||76||
"And this eighth one, who constantly causes sacrifices, brings great suffering.
Muniśarman said: "From where do you have the names of these beings born from the karma of the departed? (77)
"What is that cause on account of which you all share this same name?
The pretas replied:
"I always ate delicious food, yet I gave stale food to a brahmin. (78)
I have been anointed with clarified butter, yet by that very act I have become defiled; by nature, I am a seeker of others' faults and vital weaknesses, falsely and repeatedly. (79)
By that [act], he was revealed as a betrayer, impure, and afflicted;
indeed, when entreated by an agitated Brahmin, he perished quickly.
O best of the twice-born, for this reason you have come so swiftly:
this sinner has consumed delicious food that was set out upon his house. (81)
He was remembered as one who had conquered his senses, being alone, free from malice, and ever remaining silent;
he did not even scratch the earth with his foot.
Even for us, this most wicked man, through association with the world of scribes, hates the virtues of the virtuous and perceives a lack of virtue in those who possess discernment of merit. (83)
He is known as one whose speech is defiled by being ignorant of the yoga of wisdom;
due to his state of atheism, he constantly disregards the ancestors, the gods, and human beings. (84)
He considers virtuous deeds as evil, being one whose gods are the gods of ignorance; he is always a beggar, false in his speech, and a constant exhibitor of his own misery. (85)
This man is a beggar who causes agitation among those born into prosperity and is greedy for stolen goods;
having experienced the torments of hell due to these previously committed sins, [he now endures this]. (86)
"O hungry ghosts, by the sight of you today we have been reborn and are once again well-established.
We have related to you all this that arose from our own history. (87)
And as for the question regarding faith that you asked, I shall tell you something else.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"All living beings who exist on earth have their root in food. (88)
"I also wish to hear about your food.
The pretas said:
"Listen to our food, which is despised by all living beings. (89)
O Brahmin, having heard this, one should repeatedly and constantly revile the woman, who is filled with phlegm, urine, excrement, and filth. (90)
There they indeed eat those houses that have been abandoned by their owners, devoid of purity,
burnt by women, scattered about, and strewn with iron filings.
There, the deceased eat food that is contemptible and impure;
there they do not worship Mādhava, and their households are dominated by women. (92)
Those devoid of compassion and patience eat there as if they were hungry ghosts, where there are unpleasant words and women lacking in purity. (93)
Where there is constant quarreling, there the hungry ghosts (pretas) eat;
where the sisters-in-law are not honored in the house, by that [omission], O noble ones, women are despised. (94)
We shall eat only where there is no association with the wicked, and where there is neither service to Hari nor discourse concerning the Vaiṣṇavas. 95.
Those for whom there is no devotion to Viṣṇu do not eat at a funeral feast;
however, those in whose house He is thus pleased, they too eat with great haste. 96.
Through their own evil, they become hungry ghosts (preta) who destroy their own merit;
O Brahmin, as he speaks, his own food vanishes.
Nothing else can be said that is more sinful than this;
despondent because of my state as a ghost, I ask you, who are firm in your vows.

"Just as one who is not born does not die, and just as liberation is the freedom from the state of being a ghost," the Brāhmaṇa said: "By means of meritorious vows such as Ekādaśī, and by the chanting of the names of Acyuta. (99)
Likewise, by means of honoring the deities and guests, honoring the gurus and so forth, and through daily practices and the conduct of the virtuous as proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti; ||100||
Thus, by means of funeral rites and gifts performed according to the rules, and through compassion, generosity, self-restraint, patience, virtue, and respectful salutation to the learned; ||101||

By means of such qualities as these, they shall indeed become preta-beings within their own family; [they shall see] cows, brahmins, sacred fords, the gods, the foremost mountains, rivers, streams, and many aśvattha trees. (102)
Indeed, one who is disciplined toward his own kinsmen becomes a preta in this world;
however, a man who is diligent and gradually performs worship, especially with distinction, [attains a higher state]. ||103||
The merit of that person at holy pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā is infinite;
even I, the Lord myself, am not able to describe it fully even in thousands of years. (104)
Merely by seeing it, even one who is a preta shall be liberated from that state.
[One should offer] the month of Kārttika, which is full of vigor and dear to Dāmodara. (105)
The month of Vaiśākha is the best of months for austerity; it is dear to Mādhava, and its presiding deity is Madhusūdana. (106)
That which the sages know as the one among all things to be attained that is supreme, by that very means every task is indeed accomplished. (107)
She, the creator of the universe, who possesses the same splendor as the one known through the knowledge of Brahman, is her abode;
therefore, he is remembered as Māsa and Mādhava. 108.
Just as the god [Viṣṇu] is certainly celebrated among the gods as Mādhava, so too among all months is he celebrated as the one dear to Umā and Mādhava. 109.

By hearing with devotion even the majesty of that month of Mādhava, one is liberated from the state of being a ghost; what need is there to mention [the merit] obtained through its ritual performance? 110.
Merely by conversing with the virtuous, by resorting to sacred pilgrimage sites, by reciting the name "Nārāyaṇa," and even by hearing that name; ||111||
A person devoted to this [practice] is liberated from all sins;
I shall strive for the liberation of you who have become ghosts as well. (112)
Since merit born from helping others cannot be attained even through sacrifices,
he went to bathe in the waters of the Revā at Āmardaka for the sake of the deceased.
When the sun was situated in Aries during that month, these five men, following one another, accumulated a mass of sins through delusion once again. 114.
They come to bathe in the speech of the Compassionate One alone. ||115||
Therefore, O Lord, please remain here in this forest, free from sorrow, until we have gone to the waters of the illustrious Narmadā and performed our ritual ablutions. (116)

Bound by compassion, he thought: "I shall immerse even these illusory men, who are in reality blades of kuśa grass, in the waters of the Narmadā every day from the first of the month of Mādhava according to the prescribed ritual. (117)
Thus, by this very means, within just three days, there shall be liberation for you from the state of being a preta;
there is no doubt that it occurs merely through the ritual bathing of the darbha-baṭuka.
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus, and being honored by those who were pleased,
Muniśarman departed, followed by those five.
Having gone there, they bathed in the morning and performed the prescribed rites; then they bathed those deceased spirits by means of effigies made of darbha grass, calling them by name.

Furthermore, the deceased ancestors who were bathed at that sacred ford by the sage, as well as those who were likewise bathed by that meritorious man, immediately attained liberation and went to heaven. (121)
Those five sinners, as soon as they were submerged in the waters of the Revā by his mere word,
became pale-bodied during the month of Śrī-Mādhava.
They immediately became as radiant as pure gold. ||122||
When the hymn that pacifies evil was recited by Śramaṇaśarman in the presence of all the worlds, they became possessed of supreme splendor. (123)
There, the inhabitants of Sthāmanavā remained free from dust merely by bathing; O King, even the mention of contact with impurity did not touch them.
Then, at the request of Muniśarman and according to the authority of Dharma, a divine voice immediately spoke: "Since he is thus freed from sin... (125)
For those who have bathed in the month of Mādhava, whose hearts are fixed on Mukunda, this hymn—which pacifies all sins—is for those who listen here with reverence. (126)
What wonder is there in this that impurity arises from the accumulation of sin?
For all sins whatsoever, this is the supreme expiation. (127)
That which is the bathing with devotion at a sacred ford in the month of Mādhava in the morning—by that alone, even the deceased whose sins are great are bathed. 128.
They were remembered by the meritorious Muniśarman and liberated by him. ||129||
Having thus heard those most wonderful words from the sky, the men immediately praised the gods,
the five meritorious ones, the month of Vaiśākha, and the sage Carva.
Then the king, having heard that hymn which destroys misfortune—
a hymn by hearing which with devotion a man is liberated from heaps of sins— [acted accordingly].
By the mere hearing of which, sinners attained purification;
many others also were liberated from the sins born of ignorance. (132)
When people's minds become inclined toward adultery, the property of others, and such sinful acts, then praise [of the deity] serves as their expiation. 133.
Salutations always to Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu;
I bow to Hari, Viṣṇu, who resides in the mind and has entered the causal source. 134.
The Lord who resides in the mind, unmanifest, infinite, unconquered,
Viṣṇu, the one to be praised by all, the pervasive one without beginning or end.
That Viṣṇu who has entered my heart, and that Viṣṇu who has entered my intellect;
that Viṣṇu who is the agent "I," and that Viṣṇu who resides within me. (136)
He became the agent of the act for all that is stationary and moving; that evil comes to destruction when he is meditated upon within the heart. (137)
I bow down to that beloved Mahāviṣṇu, the Upeṃdra, by meditating upon whom even the sins seen in a dream are removed through contemplation. 138.
I praise Viṣṇu, the Madhusūdana, the infallible Acyuta, who is beyond the supreme, in whom the world finds support when it is without refuge, and whose hand is the resort for those seeking aid. 139.
O Lord of all lords, O All-pervading One, O Supreme Self, O Adhokṣaja!
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations be to You.
O Nṛsiṃha, O Govinda, O Keśava who brings beings into existence!
May whatever was ill-spoken, ill-done, or ill-thought be pacified; salutations to You. (141)
O Keśava, whatever evil, improper, and most terrible sin I have committed while under the sway of my own mind, please bring that to rest.
O Govinda, who is devoted to Brahman and the gods, whose supreme goal is the ultimate reality; O Lord of the World, Sustainer of the World, O Acyuta, pacify my sin! 143.
Whatever evil was committed through body, mind, or speech during the afternoon, the evening, midday, or likewise at night, while unaware [of its nature]. (144)
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, O Mādhava, for one who knows [this], by the utterance of these three names, there shall be the imperishable [fruit] for all. 145.
O Mādhava, may my bodily sin, O Hṛṣīkeśa, and my mental sin, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, as well as that committed by my speech, come to complete pacification. 146.
Whatever sin I have committed for the sake of wealth—while eating, drinking, standing, sleeping, waking, or remaining engaged in activity—with body, mind, or speech; (147)
Whether great or even small, such an act generally leads to a miserable birth or hell; may that sin be pacified through the chanting of the names of Vāsudeva. 148.
When Viṣṇu—the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, and that which is most pure—is thus glorified, may whatever sin exists be utterly destroyed. 149.
May that state of Viṣṇu, which the wise reach and from which there is no return, and which is devoid of touch and other sensory objects, pacify all this. 150.
The person who recites or hears this hymn that pacifies evil is liberated from sins committed through body, mind, and speech. (151)
One who is liberated from evil planets and other such afflictions attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
therefore, one should recite this hymn which destroys all sins and was composed for the purpose of removing evil. 152.
The best of men should recite this expiation for the multitude of sins;
through excellent hymns of praise and vows, transgression is destroyed. (153)

Therefore, O Lord of Men, for the sake of accomplishing these tasks and for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, [one should perform rites] for the removal of sins acquired in previous births as well as those of this life. (154)
By merely hearing this hymn, that which destroys sin instantly dissolves;
it is an axe for the tree of evil and a forest fire for the wealth of sin. 155.
O King, this light of the sun for the mass of darkness that is evil has been revealed by me to you out of compassion for the world. (156)
O lord of men, this hymn which I have obtained as a secret from my father with great reverence—this meritorious history, whoever listens to it, [attains the highest goal]. (157)
Even Hari himself is capable of describing the greatness of its merit.
May it be well with you, O Great King; now go quickly to the Gaṅgā. (158)
"I have come here to bathe; this month of Mādhava has arrived. (159)

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Sins," within the Narrative of the Pretas, in the *Vaiśākha-māhātmya*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa, in the *Pātāla-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. 94.
(95) The ninety-fifth chapter.
Sūta said:
Then, as that sage was preparing to depart, the king bowed with joy and asked him about the ritual procedures appropriate for the acts of bathing and giving gifts.
Ambarīṣa said:
O Sage, what is the ritual procedure in this month of Vaiśākha? What is the superior austerity? What is the gift, how is the bath performed, and how is the worship of Keśava conducted? (2)
O compassionate one, O foremost of Brahmin sages, you are omniscient and beloved of Hari; therefore, O Lord of the sacred ford, please explain specifically the procedure for worship.
Nārada said: O best of beings, when the sun enters Aries in the month of Mādhava,
[one should bathe] in a great river, on a riverbank, at a sacred ford, or in a mountain spring.
Or he should bathe in a natural pool or in whatever body of water is available,
such as a long pond, a well, or a large tank, with self-restraint while remembering Hari.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu, one may [perform the rite] on the fifteenth day,
or even at the time of the sun's transition into Aries.
Having obtained the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, one should perform the vow of the Vaiśākha bath,
preceded by a thorough ablution, after having worshipped Madhusūdana.
Throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha, during which the sun enters Aries, I shall bathe at dawn with self-restraint; may Madhusūdana be pleased.
By the grace of Madhuhan and through the favor of the Brahmins, may my meritorious daily Vaiśākha bath be free from obstacles. 9.
O Madhusūdana, O Murāri, during the month of Mādhava when the sun is in Aries, by this morning bath, be the bestower of the aforementioned fruit upon me. 10.
Just as this month of Madhava is dear to you, O Madhusudana, may my morning bath in it be fruitless in [granting worldly] results, yet be the destroyer of sins. 11.
Having recited this, washed his feet at that sacred ford, and restrained his speech while remembering the god Nārāyaṇa, he should perform his bath according to the prescribed rule.
The wise one should prepare a sacred bathing place while reciting this root mantra:
"Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa"—this is declared to be the root mantra. (13)
With *darbha* grass in hand, having sipped water according to the rule and bowed upon the ground, [he should prepare] a square area measuring four cubits on all sides. (14)
Having performed the visualization, a person should invoke the Gaṅgā with this mantra:
"You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu; you belong to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is your deity. (15)
"Protect us from that sin which begins at birth and ends with death," said Vāyu to the three and a half crores of heretics. (16)
O Jāhnavī, these [names] exist for you in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space:
"Nandinī" is indeed your name in the Vedas, and also "Nalinī. (17)
She is skillful, the broad earth, the bird, the song of the universe, and the beloved of Śiva;
she is the Vidyādharī, the Great Goddess, and likewise the one who gladdens the world. ||18||
Kṣemaṃkarī, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī—one should recite these auspicious names at the time of bathing. (19)
There, the Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths, shall be present when [the water] is held within the hollowed palms joined together and consecrated seven times with the mantra. (20)
Having placed water on his head four, five, or seven times, O King, and likewise having bathed with clay after addressing it according to the prescribed rite; ||21||
O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu;
O Clay, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me. (22)
You were lifted up by Viṣṇu in the form of the boar with a hundred arms;
salutations to you, O source of all worlds, O lady of excellent vows! 23.
Having bathed in this manner, and thereafter having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules,
one should rise and put on two clean, white garments.
Then, indeed, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the nourishment of the three worlds;
first, one should offer libations to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati.
The gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras;
the cruel serpents, garuḍas, trees, insects, and birds. ||26||
The Vidyādharas and the clouds, as well as those who move through the sky, those living beings who are without support, and those who are devoted to sinful deeds—[all these he saw]. (27)
For the sake of their satiation, water is offered by me;
having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (kṛtopavītī), a man should become one who wears it around the neck (nivītī) when offering to the gods. ||28||
One should satisfy human beings with devotion, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the sages—namely Sanaka, Sanandana, and the third, Sanātana. (29)
May Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha—may they all always attain satisfaction through the water offered by me. (30)
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada. ||31||
One should satisfy all the gods and the brahmin-sages with water and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, one should perform the *apasavya* rite, placing the left knee upon the ground.
Likewise, the Agniṣvātta, the Saumya, the Haviṣmat, and the Uṣmapā;
then again the Kavyānala, the Barhiṣad, and the Ājyapa. (33)
One should devoutly satisfy the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood paste, offering to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, and Antaka. (34)
To Vaivasvata Kāla, the destroyer of all beings;
to Udumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, and Parameṣṭhin. ||35||
Salutations indeed to Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta;
then, with darbha grass in hand, one should duly gratify the ancestors.
Having gratified the fathers and others by name and lineage, as well as the maternal grandfathers, according to the prescribed rule, he should recite this mantra for all of them: ||37||
May those who are my kinsmen in this life, and those who were my kinsmen in other births—whosoever from me desire water—attain complete satisfaction. (38)

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, one should properly draw a lotus in front [of oneself] with unbroken rice grains, flowers, water, and red sandalwood paste. 39.
One should offer the *argha* with diligence while reciting the names of the Sun:
"Salutations to you who have the form of Viṣṇu; salutations to you who have the form of Brahmā. (40)
Salutations to you, the thousand-rayed Sun; salutations to you, the embodiment of all splendor.
Salutations to you whose form is Rudra; salutations to you, who are affectionate toward your devotees. 41.
Salutations to you, O Padmanābha; salutations to you, adorned with the conch and the mace.
Salutations to you, the awakener of those who sleep in all the worlds. 42.
You always behold everything, both good and evil deeds;
salutations to you, the deity of truth! Be gracious to me, O Bhāskara.
"Salutations to you, O Maker of Day; salutations to you, O Maker of Light.
Having thus paid homage to the Sun and circumambulated him seven times, [he should proceed].
Having touched a twice-born man, a cow, or any water, one should then go to one's own home;
thereafter, one should worship the deities residing in the hermitage and also worship the images.
O King, a householder who has restrained his self should first worship Govinda with devotion; he should worship Him with devotion at both [times], according to the prescribed rule. 46.
Especially in the month of Vaiśākha, whoever worships Madhusūdana, by him Mādhava has been worshipped for the duration of an entire year. (47)
When the month of Mādhava has arrived, with the Sun situated in Aries as the witness of one's actions, one should perform a collection of vows dedicated to Keśava for the pleasure of Keśava. (48)
One should give various gifts, such as sesame seeds, clarified butter, and so forth, which bring an end to the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes. (49)
Gifts such as water, food, sugar, a cow, and sesame-seed cows should be given according to one's means for the attainment of desired goals. (50)
One who bathes daily throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha, with senses subdued, reciting prayers and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), is liberated from all sins. ||51||
He who, free from sloth, observes eating once a day, or eating only at night, or eating only what is unasked for during the month of Mādhava, obtains everything he desires. (52)

In the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform two ritual baths outside in a river or similar body of water according to the prescribed rules; one should also observe the consumption of sacrificial food (haviṣya), celibacy, sleeping on the ground, and adherence to the various restraints. ||53||
Vows, charity, recitation, burnt offerings, and the worship of Madhusūdana burn away even the most terrible sin accumulated over a thousand lifetimes. (54)
Just as Mādhava destroys sin when meditated upon, even so does bathing performed according to the rules during the month of Mādhava. (55)
Daily bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the libation to the ancestors with sesame seeds, the giving of gifts such as the "vessels of dharma" (dharma-ghaṭa), and the worship of Madhusūdana. ||56||
In the month of Mādhava, one should perform [this rite] which grants satisfaction to Madhusūdana, consisting of water with sesame seeds, gold, food, sugar, garments, and ornaments. (57)
One should give foot-protectors, umbrellas, and water-pots to the twice-born;
and one should worship the Lord Madhusūdana with devotion during the three junctions of the day.
With a concentrated mind, he should honor many Brahmins according to his ability with vessels of gold and sesame seeds, which are endowed with manifest, stainless prosperity.
He who offers libations with vessels of water dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
he who, being composed, bathes at dawn in a river during the month of Vaiśākha [attains the same]. (60)
Having worshipped Hari with devotion using flowers and fruits produced in their season,
one who is free from association with heretics should worship a Brāhmaṇa according to one's ability.
One should satisfy [the preceptor] with gifts of clothing, cows, jewels, and stores of wealth;
furthermore, one should offer other riches according to one's ability, little by little.
Thereafter, in the month of Mādhava,
a person who has become free from debt should worship Madhusūdana according to the ritual for the offering of flowers.
Freed from all sins, he shall deliver a hundred ancestors;
for a hundred thousand lifetimes, he shall not experience the fruit of sorrow.
He shall have no fear of disease, nor poverty, nor bondage;
that devotee of Viṣṇu shall be blessed in birth after birth. (65)
For as many thousands of yugas as there are one hundred and eight,
for that long shall he dwell in heaven, O hero, and he shall become a king once again.
Having enjoyed various pleasures at ease as a lord of the earth, he then merged into Mādhava by the grace of Mādhava. 67.
Listen, O King, I shall describe in brief the worship of Mādhava—
whether Vedic, Tāntrika, or mixed— which destroys all sins.
O King, there is no end to the worship ritual of Anantapāra;
therefore, having briefly summarized it, it shall now be described in its proper sequence.
The Vedic sacrifice for Śrī Viṣṇu is threefold, consisting of the three types of oblations; one should worship Hari according to whichever of these three methods is desired.
The Vaidika-miśraka is prescribed for the Brahmins and the other [twice-born] classes;
that same Trika is proclaimed for the Śūdra who is a devotee of Viṣṇu.

As stated in one's own scripture: "Having attained the status of the twice-born, a person, remaining a celibate student and being composed, should worship Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rules. (72)

One should worship one's own guru with devotion and material offerings upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in the fire, in the sun, in water, or in the heart, or within a twice-born (brāhmaṇa), with his permission. (73)
First, one should perform the bath with cleansed teeth for the purification of the limbs;
the bath for both [the deity and oneself] is performed with mantras, beginning with the taking up of earth.

One should properly perform the worship prescribed by the Vedas, such as the twilight rituals (sandhyopāsti) and other rites, which purify one's actions according to the ritual manual (saṃkalpa). //75//
An image is said to be of eight kinds: made of stone, wood, metal, plaster, painting, sand, mind, and gemstone. (76)
The installation of the temple of the living soul is of two kinds: mobile and immobile;
in the worship of Mādhava, the rites of dismissal and invocation are performed for the mobile, while they are omitted for the immobile.

If the image is unstable, there may be conceptualization; if it is stable, both would be the cause. However, bathing is for that which is not to be plastered, whereas wiping is for that which is [plastered]. (78)
One who is free from deceit should perform worship of the gods, images, and so forth, with well-known substances,
or with whatever is obtained, and indeed with a spirit of devotion.

O King, bathing and adorning are excellent for the worship of an image; likewise, for an altar, it is the ritual placement of mantras, and for the fire, it is the offering of oblations with clarified butter. (80)
For the Sun, the offering of water, flowers, and other substances is most excellent;
for Hara, even water offered with faith by a devotee is supreme. (81)
Having offered incense, flowers, lamps, food, and so forth—how much more so when one is pure and has gathered the necessary materials—having first prepared a seat with *darbha* grass; ||82||
Seated, facing either east or north, or facing the image,
and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), he should touch the image of Hari— which has likewise had nyāsa performed upon it— with his hand.
One should prepare the *kalaśa* and the *prokṣaṇīya* vessel according to the rules; with their waters, one should sprinkle the sacrificial ground, the ritual materials, and oneself as well. (84)
Having sprinkled the three vessels with water, one should place them with their respective substances;
one should provide three vessels for the purpose of the foot-water (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
One should consecrate the headless body with the *śikhā* and *gāyatrī* mantras;
then, once the *piṇḍa* has been perfected through the elements of air and fire, one should [invoke] the Supreme Goddess of the Lord residing within the heart-lotus.
One should meditate upon the subtle particle of the individual soul (jīvakalā), which is the resonance (nāda) cultivated for the attainment of perfection;
having become one with that Goddess who has become his very self, he should worship her and become absorbed in her essence.
Having invoked her and established her in the image and other receptacles, one should worship that cow;
one should offer the services such as water for the feet, the arghya offering, the bath, and the respectful salutation.
Having fashioned a seat for Hari with the nine [principles] beginning with Dharma,
one should place there an eight-petaled lotus, radiant with a pericarp and filaments.
For the sake of achieving both [perfections] for Hari,
he took from both of them the Sudarśana discus, the Pāñcajanya conch, the mace, the sword, the bow, and the plow.
One should worship in succession the pestle (muśala), the Kaustubha gem, the garland, and the Śrīvatsa mark;
as well as Naṃ-daṃ, Su-naṃ-daṃ, Garuḍa, Pra-caṇḍa, and Caṇḍa. (91)
Mahābala, Bala, Kumuda, Kumudekṣaṇa, Durgā, Vināyaka, Vyāsa, Viṣvaksena, the gurus, and the gods. 92.
One should worship them, facing their respective positions, with sprinkling and other rites,
using [substances] scented with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, kuṅkuma, and aguru.
One should always bathe [the image] with waters while reciting mantras, or, if that is not possible, with the *Svarṇagharma-anuvāka* and the *Mahāpuruṣavidyā*. (94)
With the *Puruṣasūkta* hymn, with *sāmans*, with the *Nīrājana* rite and others, and with garments, sacred threads, ornaments, leaf-earrings, garlands, perfumes, and ointments; ||95||
A devotee of Viṣṇu, full of love, should perform the rites as is appropriate:
offering water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), perfumes (gandha), flowers (sumanas), and unbroken grains (akṣata). (96)
The worshipper, with faith, should indeed offer incense, perfumes, and other offerings,
as well as jaggery, milk-rice, clarified butter, fried cakes, flour-cakes, and sweetmeats.

One should offer milk-rice, curd, and ghee as the sacrificial food (naivedya), along with various offerings; likewise, one should provide anointing, rubbing with cow-dung, a mirror, and an ablution. 98.
Then, every day, food, dance, and song—all these—should be provided according to the prescribed rite within a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) equipped with a girdle, a whorl, and an altar (vedi). 99.
Having established the fire, he should sprinkle water around it with his hand;
then, having strewn grass around it, sprinkled water again, and offered fuel according to the rule.
Having set out the materials for the sprinkling, the sprinkling of the clarified butter (ājya) is performed with the very water used for sprinkling.
[He should meditate on Him] who resembles molten gold and who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in His hands.
He has four arms and is peaceful; he is clothed in the filaments of a lotus, and his crown, bracelets, and girdle are shimmering, as are his excellent mace.
Meditating upon Him who has the Śrīvatsa on His chest, who is adorned with the radiant Kaustubha gem and a forest garland,
he should worship Him with offerings of wood, oblations, and clarified butter.
Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) and the two *āghāra* libations, and having honored the oblation soaked in clarified butter,
he should then pay homage and offer the sacrificial cake (*bali*) to the attendants (*pārṣada*).
O Brahmin, one should mutter the root mantra while remembering that it has Nārāyaṇa as its essence;
having offered water for sipping, one should offer the remnants to Viṣvaksena.
One should offer fragrant mouth-perfumes such as betel and the like;
and while singing and reciting the ritual acts constantly with pleasing syllables. (106)
One should listen to a virtuous discourse and remain attentive for even a moment;
one should offer praise with various hymns and laudatory verses, whether from the Purāṇas or even in the vernacular. (107)
Having praised him, saying "Be gracious, O Blessed One," and having placed his head at the [deity's] feet while holding each other's arms, he spoke thus. (108)
"O Lord, protect me who have sought refuge, for I am terrified of the ocean of the jaws of death.
Having thus spoken, the serpent Śeṣa respectfully placed his heads upon the head of Hari.
If one should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*), one should dismiss the light into the light of the Self;
wherever there is a sacred footprint (*pada*) in images and the like, the person of faith should worship there.
Seeing the Self abiding as the universal soul within all beings and in oneself,
a person thus attains the state of the Vedic through the paths of ritual action and yoga by means of the triads.
By worshipping it constantly, one shall obtain from Hari whatever desired perfection one seeks;
having installed that image, one should cause a firm temple to be built.
Delightful flower gardens, worship, processions, festivals, and so forth—these are for the sake of maintaining the continuity of worship and other rites on great festival days as well as daily. (113)

By giving fields, marketplaces, cities, and villages, one attains union (sāyujya); by means of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one becomes a sovereign of the earth; and by means of a temple, one [attains mastery] over the three worlds.
Through worship and other means, one may reach the world of Brahmā; through three [of these], one attains equality with Him.
But one realizes that very [Brahman] alone through the yoga of devotion characterized by independence from all else.
Thus, he who worships Hari attains indeed the yoga of devotion. ||116||
That body which is white with the dust from prostrating before Kṛṣṇa is auspicious;
by means of that, Hari is seen by these two in this world, which is made beautiful by the penance they have earned.
That intellect is stainless, pure, white as the sky, and pervasive like the month of Āṣāḍha;
that tongue is soft-spoken, which repeatedly praises Nārāyaṇa, the protector of kings. 117.
The worship should be performed with the root mantra; it may be performed even by women and Śūdras, as well as by other Vaiṣṇavas, with faith according to the path indicated by one's own guru.
All this purifying worship of Mādhava has been recounted to you;
O King of the Kurus, perform this especially during the month of Mādhava. 119.
Sūta said:
Having thus heard these wonderful, meritorious, and purifying words of the son of Brahmā, [the sages spoke].
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence, that curious king, the foremost among devotees of the Lord, spoke.
Ambarīṣa said:
I am the lord of the entire circle of the earth, my commands are unimpeded, and I serve the gods;
yet my mind is fixed upon the lotus-feet of Govinda, and I have satisfied the Brahmins with the contentment of my own heart. (121)

I am a famous man, possessing the jewel of a character befitting a king; I am constantly devoted to righteousness, illustrious, endowed with beauty and valor, generous by nature, possessed of excellent sons, and have conquered the host of my enemies. (122)
By what merit has my mind become purified so that I have attained such splendor endowed with these virtues?
Furthermore, from where has this one come, who is like the Goddess Śrī herself, a personification of merit, whose radiant beauty surpasses all others? (123)
"O Sage, O Abode of Compassion, Knower of All, please explain correctly all this that was previously performed by me through my actions in former births. (124)
Nārada said:
In another birth, she was an unchaste woman among beautiful women; now, due to her virtuous conduct, she has become your wife Satyabhāmā, who is exceedingly beautiful.
The noble lady should conduct herself according to the prescribed dharma of a courtesan,
performing auspicious rites at the command of the twice-born.
In a previous birth, you were a goldsmith known as Devadāsa, and the husband of this woman was a serpent. (127)
This lady, beautiful in form, again resorts to you, O Blessed One;
for the sake of her expenditure, she seeks the path of Dharma, which is the supreme wisdom established in steadfastness. ||128||
And having once heard of the dharma arising from the Vaiśākha bath,
Dharmavatī performed her ablution in the water when the sun was in Aries.
Dānanda, Dattavatī, Dakṣā, Veśyā, Rūpavatī, and Sadā—these [women] always offered salutations to the Brahmins with devotion and respect. (130)
O Devadāsa, having been awakened by Sataya and impelled by affection, you performed the ritual bath with devotion in the month of Mādhava, guided by your intellect. (131)
There, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, having reached the third [stage] which was stainless,
he spoke with reverence to that goldsmith Devadāsa.
The prostitute said:
"Having worshipped the supreme golden Acyuta Madhusūdana with barley grains, one should then satisfy the sacrificial fire with these same grains. (133)
And I shall give it to a Brāhmaṇa with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas;
this gift is declared in the Purāṇas to be inexhaustible therein. 134.
I have heard from the Brāhmaṇas that this third lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha bestows inexhaustible fruit. (135)
"In this [image], I shall fashion this golden, imperishable Madhusūdana.
Nārada said: Having heard these sweet words of his, the goldsmith... (136)
For the sake of dharma, he—avoiding theft—made a golden image of Cakreśvara and a beautiful statue of Acyuta with a sincere heart. (137)
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite, she gave that beautiful image of the moon as it had been described, endowed with all its characteristics, to the brahmin Sunda.
Having performed worship there, O King, one attains imperishability.
After some time, that prostitute became established in the dharma of immortality;
meanwhile, Devadāsa also died when his own lifespan came to an end.
O King, by that merit, that goldsmith became you, endowed with every virtue, having attained sovereignty over the earth in another birth. (141)
By that dharma, she became like a beautiful courtesan;
she was known by the name Kāntimatī and was overflowing with affection.
O Father, the origins of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*), heroic deeds, and previous existences, as well as the diverse courses of rebirth, are known even by the wise. (143)
This month of Mādhava must certainly be observed;
even Brahmā was instructed in this matter by that very god, Mādhava.

The religious duty of the month of Mādhava cannot be attained by those who associate with the wicked, those who have not acquired knowledge, those who are unrestrained, those who lack the virtues of their stage of life, those who have not visited sacred fords, and those who have not observed vows. (145)
O Govinda, Keśava, Mukunda, Hara, Murāri, Lakṣmīnivāsa, Madhusūdana, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu!
For those whose mouths dwell upon these excellent words, there shall indeed be the observance of the Vaiśākha month. (146)
Those who do not listen to the abundant words of praise for the virtuous nor to the nectar-like accounts of Hari’s deeds,
and who do not behold the banners bearing the emblem of the Lord of Kamalā, do not attain the merit of the religious observances of the month of Vaiśākha.

Those sons by whom their venerable teachers were served, who were honored with gifts of excellent maidens at the proper time, and who were instructed in the duties of discipline and so forth—such sons do not incur sin even if they fail to observe the religious observances of the month of Vaiśākha. (148)
Sūta said:
Having thus instructed the king, who was intent on his welfare, that sage—the foremost among those skilled in mantras—took leave of him;
then, O brahmins, he went with him to the Gaṅgā to bathe during the month of Mādhava.
Then the king, whose fame purifies the world, together with his wife, reflected with a mind intent on merit upon that very ritual for the month of Vaiśākha as ordained by the Sage. (150)
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Nārada and Ambarīṣa," within the "Greatness of the Month of Vaiśākha" section of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(96) The ninety-sixth chapter.
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, O one of great wisdom! May we live for a hundred lives, so that we may proclaim this meritorious time which is beneficial to the world. (1)
O Sūta, we drink your words most abundantly again and again; yet, though we drink that supreme nectar, we are not satiated. 2.
Sūta said:
In this regard, I shall also cite this ancient history,
a dialogue between the First Being and the Lord of the worlds concerning the universe.
Its height is six thousand [yojanas], and its width is likewise three;
thus, having established it at nine thousand yojanas, [he created it].
In the beginning, the Earth was lifted up by the left tusk;
for a thousand divine years, the Goddess was supported by that tusk.
In the course of explaining the Dharma, she spoke with humility to the Lord.
Pṛthivī said:
"These twelve months and sixty days that exist therein—"
O Keśava, among these, which is the most meritorious and dear to you?
The month of Kārtika is purifying when the sun is situated in Libra.
The month of Māgha, when the sun is situated in Capricorn, is remembered in the Purāṇas as purifying; the month of Phālguna, when the sun is situated in Aries, is likewise recited by the wise.
Mārgaśīrṣa is also proclaimed as the most purifying among the months;
thus these months are sacred—what [specific] days could possibly be described as such? (9)
The beginnings of the Yugas, the Yugas themselves, and likewise the beginnings of the Kalpas—tell me which month is more purifying than all of these. (10)
"O glorious one, consisting of all sacrifices, please declare this with certainty.
Varāha said:
"Those lowest of men who sacrifice according to the rules or even outside the rules," 11.
In the month of Mādhava, I am always to be worshipped with devotion by those [devotees].
O fair-faced lady, in this month of Mādhava, Madhu was slain by Hiraṇyākṣa’s enemy.
Because you have slain both these primordial Daityas, you have been uplifted;
in the Tretā Yuga, there shall be the dharma of the three Vedas and the established order of knowledge and social classes.
Because he was born in the month of Mādhava, Mādhava is dear to me;
[he appeared] on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mādhava during the Tretā Yuga.
The threefold dharma (trayī-dharma) has been set in motion; it has proceeded and flourished.
This third [night], which is imperishable and beyond grief, is called Harivallabhā in the world. 15.
Those who worship Viṣṇu with barley during bathing, giving, worship, ancestral rites (śrāddha), recitation, and the libations for ancestors, and who perform the śrāddha with diligence; ||16||
To them I give everything that is most desired by their minds; those righteous men who give even these gifts are truly blessed.
Those who constantly perform various sacrifices to Hari, and he who worships me during the month of Mādhava—the fruit for the latter is greater than that of the former. (18)
O Goddess, listen to the fruit of the merit of whatever bathing, charity, recitation, fire-offerings, austerity, sacrifice, vows, and so forth, is performed during the month of Vaiśākha. (19)
For ten, five, and seven crores of manvantaras,
they remain in my presence, free from fear.
Even if all the planets should be malefic, occupying the birth, twelfth, or eighth houses,
they all become auspicious through the morning bath in the month of Vaiśākha.
He who, being devoted to that [practice], feeds Brahmins in the month of Vaiśākha,
shall provide for the satisfaction of his ancestors for as many yugas as there are grains of rice in the mouthful.
There they offer foods exceeding sweetness,
as well as meals of wind and sesame-water;
they provide parasols and garments, and protection suitable for their feet.
They alone are truly blessed, for they bring satisfaction to Viṣṇu. ||23||
In this case, sesame seeds mixed with honey should especially be given for the sake of great merit and as a cause for the destruction of long-standing misdeeds. (24)
But when this has been done, what merit is obtained by those men—that how could it be calculated even in hundreds of millions of years? (25)
One obtains here, as desired, wealth consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as long life;
and in the next world as well, one attains Me alone. ||26||
The multitude of sins accumulated over many lifetimes dissolves by bathing in Mādhava, whether one resorts to that sacred ford at dawn according to the prescribed rite or otherwise. (27)
He who, having abandoned the Vaiśākha vow, should practice another,
is like one who, having discarded a great jewel held in his hand, begs for a clod of earth.
Sūta said: Thus did the Blessed One, the primordial God,
the all-pervading upholder of the world, formerly speak regarding the month of Mādhava on this earth.
O brāhmaṇas, what need is there for much speaking on this matter?
There is nothing that cannot be attained in the month of Mādhava through the worship of Mādhava. (30)
Listen to this most wonderful account of past events here,
concerning the conversation between a brahmin and the high-souled Yama.
In the Middle Country, there was a great village of Brahmins situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, at the foot of the Yamuna mountain.
At that time, many learned Brāhmaṇas were residing there.
Then Yama sent a certain man with dark-brown hair.
"Go to the great village of Bhauma and, having gone there, bring back a Brahmin who has red eyes, hair standing on end, and eyes and a nose like those of a crow. (34)
Born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, named Yajñadattaka,
he was a learned man established in tranquility and skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites.
And you should not bring another from his side who belongs to the same lineage, even if he were endowed with such qualities and equal to him in learning and birth. (36)
"O best of beings, bring him here by his physical form, his marks, and his entire appearance as described; for I must perform worship unto him. (37)
Having gone there, he caused that unpleasant and unrighteous command to be carried out; thus he brought him [the enemy] under his control, for this conduct of his was not forbidden.
Then Yama, the knower of dharma, having risen and performed worship for him, said: "Let this one be led away;
let another be brought here. (39)
Sūta said:
When these words had been spoken by the King of Dharma, that virtuous twice-born man,
despondent over the journey, spoke to the King of Dharma.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Lord, why have I been brought here, and why do you urge me again to go? I have no desire at all to return to that world of mortals. (41)
Yama said:
"In this place, there shall be a dwelling for those men whose lifespan has been exhausted, provided they are meritorious;
for this world belongs indeed to the King of Dharma and is proclaimed as the realm of righteousness. (42)
This is the ground of bliss; I am the sovereign king of all dharmas, bestowing happiness and suffering upon living beings according to their merit and demerit. (43)
To sinful men, I am Yama, the giver of hell;
likewise, to the meritorious, I am the embodiment of Dharma, the bestower of happiness and heaven. 44.
Go this very day to your own abode as a Brahmin, just as you arrived;
even now, ten years of your lifespan remain.
The attainment of this world will come to an end through the exhaustion of the life-span;
indeed, you must ask another question as well—ask it, and I shall explain it to you.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Tell me that by performing which great merit heaven may be attained;
for you are the authority for all in the determination of dharma and adharma. (47)
O Goddess, if it is right for me to go to my own abode, then tell me:
by what action do men fall into hell? (48)
"By what means indeed do they go to heaven? Tell me all that out of compassion.
Yama said:
"Those men who are averse to dharma in deed, thought, or speech... (49)
Those who are devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu indeed go to hell;
those who perceive Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Hari with a sense of duality [are likewise fated for that state]. (50)
Men who are indifferent toward the knowledge of Viṣṇu go to hell;
he who, having abandoned the duties appropriate to his family and country, practices something else [is likewise lost]. (51)
Whether out of desire or out of delusion, that man goes to hell; as does one who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, and one who abandons those worthy to sacrifice. (52)
One who abstains from the sciences of Viṣṇu, yet fails to give to the ancestors, the gods, the brahmins, and his mortal kinsmen, shall suffer many hells. (53)
The sinful man who dies possessed of wealth goes to many hells—he who makes distinctions in the cooking of all prepared foods. (54)

O twice-born one, he who eats without first performing the Vaiśvadeva rite goes to hell for a long time; likewise, those who acquire wealth through great cruelty toward living beings [fall into the same fate].
The wealthy, due to atheism, greed, or delusion as it arises in this Kali age, fall into hell and become partakers of the suffering of begging.

Those who, out of devotion, fail to give food at a funeral rite (śrāddha), shall be cooked in hells; likewise, the evildoer who does not give wealth being offered to the Brāhmaṇas [shall suffer]. (57)
That man who creates an obstacle shall go to hell;
having received the common sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he alone takes it out of delusion. ||58||
A man devoted to the disposition of nihilism would dwell in the abode of hell;
his intolerance toward virtues would be the cause of that. (59)
A great sin has arisen; it is the cause of hell for him who, in the course of time, abandons his blameless wife, the beloved of his friends.
Those who possess the nine-fold weapons shall fall into hell along with their sons, as shall he who, having fallen under the sway of delusion, speaks of unrighteousness as righteousness. (61)
But that person who is a rationalist nihilist has hell as his abode; he who, with a mind of another disposition, speaks otherwise than what is [right] through his speech. (62)
Those men who, having disregarded the chanting of the Lord's glories, depart with turbid hearts, shall dwell in hell. (63)
They go to a terrible hell because of that sinful deed, even while beholding the gateway of the Blessed One adorned with the scriptures of His Name. (64)
Having failed to offer him salutations and other marks of respect, those men go to dwell in hell; likewise, men who take a second wife without cause commit an offense. (65)
Those men who abandon a virtuous wife go to hell;
as does that man who does not listen to the words of his guru nor to the treatises on Dharma. (66)
One who causes affliction to the minds of others shall go to hell;
yet one who enjoys a superior delicacy while their kinsmen and children look on [shall likewise suffer]. (67)
He who fills his belly alone goes to a terrible hell;
however, one who observes the rules should perform the morning bath during the zodiac signs of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries.
And for one who shows no respect toward rivers and other [sacred sites], there shall be a dwelling in hell;
likewise, he who, upon seeing a Vaiṣṇava person, does not rise to greet them. (69)
O Brahmin, out of affection and respect, that man becomes a guest of hell,
[pierced] by wooden stakes, spikes, pikes, or even stones.
Those who obstruct the paths to Him—the Primordial Person, the Lord, the Great Sovereign of all worlds—they indeed go to hell. (71)
Those men who do not contemplate Viṣṇu surely go to hell;
likewise those who destroy a sacred field, a livelihood, or a home, and those who sever friendships. (72)
They cause the frustration of the hopes of those dwellers in hell by [ignoring] the Brahmins who have arrived, emaciated for lack of livelihood, seeking food. (73)
That foolish-souled person who would examine [with contempt] one who is without a protector, a Vaiṣṇava, the destitute, the afflicted by disease, or even the aged, shall become a guest of hell. (74)
Those fools who do not show compassion are indeed destined for hell—
those who, having undertaken religious observances, later fail to conquer their senses.
They utterly destroy those [virtues], and they indeed go to hell;
O Brahmin, hear how compassionate men go to heaven. (76)
Out of respect for you, I shall speak briefly;
those who worship the divine Hari, the victorious Viṣṇu, the eternal one—[77]
Those who meditate upon Nārāyaṇa—the unborn Kṛṣṇa, Viṣvaksena, the four-armed, the divine Puruṣa—and those who remember him as Acyuta; ||78||
They attain the imperishable state; this is the ancient Vedic revelation.
This alone is the true goal of life, and this alone is the true acquisition of wealth. (79)
