The fruit of living is this: the chanting of the praises of Dāmodara, through the chanting of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor. (80)
At the rising of the sun, those who are filled with faith daily sing the Vaiṣṇava song, whereby their great darkness is utterly dissolved. ||81||
Those men who are constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas go to heaven;
casting off all afflictions, they indeed praise Viṣṇu alone. (82)
Those men who are steadfast and devoted to their own duty go to heaven;
so too do even people who have committed sins, provided they are intent on the chanting of Vāsudeva. ||83||
O Brahmin, the terrible messengers of Yama do not approach those who have abandoned the chanting of Hari's glory; they see no other path for living beings. 84.
O best of the twice-born, this is the expiation that pacifies all sins:
those who are asked for something rejoice and speak kindly when they have given what is pleasing. (85)
Those men who have renounced the fruits of their giving go to heaven;
so too do those men who avoid sleeping during the day and are patient with all things.
On the sacred festival days, these mortals, having become a refuge [for others], go to heaven;
for they never speak of the faults even of their enemies. (87)
And those men who, upon seeing the prosperity of others, do not burn with envy, proclaim their virtues and go to heaven. (88)
And those men who go to heaven, being greatly delighted, praise both the path of worldly engagement and the path of withdrawal as they are described in the Vedas and the scriptures. (89)
People who go to heaven honor this by tradition; those born in whatever family they may be, provided they are compassionate and renowned. (90)
Those men who are compassionate, who follow virtuous conduct, and who are purified by never having committed adultery with another's wife through deed, thought, or word, go to heaven. (91)
Abiding in the state of the Nāsatyas, those men delight us and go to heaven;
they always perform their prescribed duties as enjoined by the sacred law.
And those men who, having recognized their own capacity, always maintain faith in the virtues of mind, speech, and body, go to heaven. (93)
May he who has conquered the impulse of speech, the impulse of the mind, and the impulse arising from the stomach, become one who is honored by the virtuous and a guest for the gods. (94)
The man who endures the impulse of sexual passion becomes a dweller in heaven;
those whose satisfaction lies in virtues and whose speech is directed toward sacred learning [attain the same]. (95)
Those whose minds are fixed on the ultimate truth are the most excellent and go to heaven;
those who guard their vow from anger protect their prosperity from envy.
Those who protect their learning from honor and dishonor, themselves from negligence, their intellect from greed, and their minds from desire; ||97||
Those men who protect the Dharma from bad association go to heaven;
likewise, those who are devoted to fasting according to the rules on the eleventh lunar day [attain the same]. ||98||
By accumulating white and black [karma], men go to heaven;
[right conduct] is like a mother to all children, and like medicine to the sick. (99)
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) was created for the protection of all the worlds;
there exists nothing equal to Ekādaśī for the preservation from sin. (100)
Having fasted according to the prescribed rule, O twice-born one, men go to heaven; whatever sin has been committed by the eleven senses, [it is destroyed]. (101)
Having quickly shaken that off, a person becomes joyful and attains the state of heaven;
[this is equal to] thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices. ||102||
All sacrifices taken together, and all pilgrimages and austerities, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the fast on the eleventh day. (103)
On one side are the great gifts and other forms of giving, along with the Vaiṣṇava vow;
on the other side is the merit born of the Vaiṣṇava vow, as well as the merit arising from sacrifices and the like. (104)
If these two were weighed together by the Creator, the former would be the heavier:
those who are devoted to the day of Hari and who speak of Acyuta and Ananta. (105)
O Brahmin, I am not their teacher; indeed, I have no fear of those whose sons and grandsons observe the fast on the eleventh lunar day. (106)
That great-souled one forcibly rescues a hundred men;
thereafter, he should observe a fast during both fortnights.
On the eleventh day, that person becomes the sole vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is indeed Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśinī. 108.
Trispṛśā, Aṃjulī, Pakṣasaṃvardhinī, Varā, Tiladugdhā, Aparājitā, and likewise Akhaṇḍadvādaśī. (109)
Likewise, there is the one called Manorathākhya and the formidable Bhīmadvādaśikā;
in this manner, there are numerous such varieties of Dvādaśī. 110.
Those who are capable of these vows should be known as established in Brahman; they are listeners of the Dharmaśāstras, endowed with conviction in dharma. (111)
Those men who perform the śrāddha vow on the single day of the new moon (darśa) every month, doing what is pleasing to children, go to the heavenly world. 112.
Blessed are those whose ancestors are satisfied; they go to heaven, for when meals are prepared, they offer food with reverence. (113)
Those whose facial complexion remains unchanged are disciplined and destined for heaven. ||114||
Those who possess devotion to Madhusūdana, Nārāyaṇa, the leader of all—
even if they are devoid of truth and joined with passion— go to that realm of infinite merit.
Those of virtuous conduct, devoted to bathing and giving gifts, resort to the Vitastā, the Yamunā, the Sītā, and the holy river Godāvarī. (116)
They never see that path to hell, by which they might sink into this Madā, the giver of pleasure, even by the sight of it. (117)
Having shaken off their sins, they go to the world of Maheśa and rejoice there for a long time.
Men who bathe on the bank of the Carmanvatī river for three nights, remaining self-restrained,
especially at Vyāsa’s hermitage, are remembered as being equal to those who possess no bodies (liberated souls).
Those who die in the waters of the Gaṅgā, at Prayāga, at Kedāra, at Puṣkara, at Vyāsāśrama, or at Prabhāsa, go to Viṣṇu. (120)
Those who have attained immortality through the practice of yoga at Dvāravatī or Kurukṣetra,
and whose lips utter the syllables "Hari," are not subject to rebirth.
Even those who stay for just three nights in the city of Dvāravatī and bathe on the banks of the Gomatī are blessed;
they are dear to Keśava.
Those who have taken refuge for three nights at the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, those dear to Keśava, are blessed; they shall receive a vision [of the Lord] in the world of mortals. (123)
Having dwelt for six months in the presence of the Supreme Person,
who is never-falling (Acyuta), they will surely become embodiments of the Imperishable and destroyers of sin upon seeing Him.
Those who bathe in the waters of Maṇikarṇikā, which consist of the merit accumulated over many births, and who reach Kāśī and bow to Viśveśvara—they indeed become worthy of my veneration here. 125.
Having worshipped Hari on that ground with darbha grass and sesame seeds, having scattered sesame seeds and offered iron, and having given a milch cow; 126.
O Brahmin, those men who have died according to the prescribed rites go to heaven,
having produced sons and established themselves in the station of their fathers and grandfathers.
Free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, they were as if immortal;
they constantly desisted from theft and were ever content with their own wealth.
Those kings who live by their own good fortune go to heaven;
they speak gentle words that are harmless and free from deceitful means. (129)
Those people who address others with a greeting go to heaven, [regardless] of the accumulation of the fruits of their auspicious or inauspicious deeds. (130)
Those people who possess the accumulation of the knowledge of maturation go to heaven—those who are engaged in wealth and Dharma, and who follow the path of Dharma. 131.
Those men who increase the encouragement of others, who give joy to them, who provide clothing in the winter, who give fire in the cold, and likewise who provide water in the summer; 132.
Furthermore, one who provides shelter during the rainy season rejoices in heaven for a long time, as does one who gives at all auspicious times, such as during daily and occasional rites. (133)
He who performs a śrāddha with devotion will certainly partake in the world of the gods. ||134||
Generosity in the poor, forbearance in the powerful, silence in the young, and likewise in those possessed of austerity and knowledge;
the cessation of desire in those accustomed to pleasure, and compassion toward all living beings—these lead one to heaven. (135)
The connection with karma, which arises from both demerit and merit, is of two kinds;
it is here that the determination is made by relying solely upon truth. (136)
For the wise, austerity and meditation joined together are said to lead to liberation from existence;
likewise, evil is said to lead to falling—this is the truth, without a doubt. (137)
For a man who is endowed with strength, service, and valor,
yet is devoid of merit, that very strength and so forth become powerless.
In the high mountain fastnesses there are trees that are well-nourished;
yet, by the force of the wind, they fall along with their very roots, however massive they may be. (139)
Deprived of truth and righteousness, they likewise go to the abode of Yama;
for all living beings, strength is common, but righteousness alone is unique.
By means of this, one attains splendor in both this world and the next;
I have correctly set forth all of this as the bestower of the path to heaven. (141)
This has been explained in brief; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(97) The Ninety-Seventh Chapter.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Even a fool knows this: a man who performs auspicious deeds goes to heaven, while one devoted to sinful actions goes to hell. (1)
Through various sacrifices performed with offerings, through vows, charity, recitation, and so forth, and by those skilled in truth and right conduct, the happiness of heaven is attained. (2)
Heaven is attained by ṛṣis who have mastered the Vedas and are endowed with the wealth of knowledge and conduct through the power of merit; it is not reached anywhere by means of sacrifices alone.
Even with abundant wealth, it is not possible to give much of a gift if one's mind is attached to one's family, despite possessing riches. (4)
Rites such as the Agnihotra are difficult to perform in the Kali age without distinction;
O Blessed One, even the duty of giving is considered difficult to accomplish. (5)
"A collection of merit is obtained through dharma with little effort;
therefore, O revealer of dharma and adharma, explain that to me in detail. (6)
Therefore, let that one Dharma be told—the most supreme among all Dharmas—by the performance of which alone here all evil may be destroyed. (7)
That by which wealth, grain, fame, dharma, and longevity increase; that by which friendship even in the mortal world may exist, and through which heaven becomes inexhaustible—[that is this]. (8)
By whom Nārāyaṇa himself is directly propitiated, he bestows fearlessness upon his devotees; through his grace, every desire remains as if held in the palm of one's hand. ||9||
O son of Vivasvat, tell me that by which the fruit superior to all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and pilgrimages is obtained.
O Lord, since I am indeed worthy of being favored by the instruction of the Dharma, please out of compassion tell me that one essence which is the core of all religious practices. (11)
Just as penances corresponding to various evils have been prescribed by the wise after due reflection, so too [these] have been declared. 12.
O Lord, it is impossible for men to perform those [meritorious acts] individually;
if there exists a single meritorious act that removes all sins, please tell me of it. (13)
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to Yama, who is the very embodiment of Dharma, that best of brāhmaṇas,
being self-restrained and desiring to understand the subtle nature of dharma, offered praise.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Salutations to you, the pacifier of all; salutations to you, O Lord of the worlds!
Salutations be to you, who possess a divine form and bestow the path to heaven. (15)
Obeisance to you, O Dharmarāja, whose very nature is the Dharmaśāstra;
by you the earth, the gods, the intermediate space, the sky, and the Maharloka are protected.
Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—everything is protected by you;
for there is nothing in this world, whether stationary or moving, that exists without you. (17)
If you were not held [by us], the world would surely perish this very moment;
you are the Self of all beings, the embodiment of the essence of the virtuous. (18)
You are the quality of passion (*rajas*) among those characterized by passion, and likewise the quality of darkness (*tamas*) among those characterized by darkness;
you alone are the four-footed one, possessing four horns and three eyes. (19)
Salutations to you who are seven cubits tall, bound in three places, and whose form is that of a bull;
Dharma, consisting of all sacrifices, has taken bodily form within you.
You have been seen directly in the world; O Lord Lokeśa, salutations, salutations to you!
You abide in the hearts of all beings as the witness of their merit and demerit. (21)
Therefore, he became the teacher of all beings, the giver, the divine ruler, the promulgator of the Dharma, and the wielder of divine punishment upon the earth. ||22||
"Tell me with absolute certainty that one essence which consists of all phenomena.
Yama said:
"O Brahmin, I am thoroughly pleased, especially by this hymn of praise. (23)
Nevertheless, O best of beings, you are worthy of honor according to the dharma of the scriptures;
yet that which has not been told to anyone is my supreme secret. (24)
Having extracted the essence from all [teachings], that which I have determined to be the one [path]—the supreme means for expelling [beings] from the mass of great hells—is this. (25)
O Brahmin, though it is inexpressible, I shall speak of it to you, as I am pleased by your disciplined devotion.

Those various ancient scriptures may serve to delude the world of moving and unmoving beings; indeed, let them each proclaim their respective deity as supreme within the ritual prescriptions of their own Kalpa.
But in the final conclusion (siddhānta), the Blessed Viṣṇu alone is the subject of all the scriptures.
When the activities of the discerning have been brought into contact [with one another], the truth is determined. ||27||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—these three alone are considered the Triple Veda (Trayī).
O Brahmin, just as a lamp consists of fire, the wick, and the oil, so too is Hari.
Having propitiated Hari with devotion, one shall attain the auspicious Goloka realms;
when Hari is propitiated, all desires rest within the palm of one's hand. ||29||
O twice-born one, among all meritorious acts, giving alone is supreme and most excellent;
by giving, all evil is destroyed, and by giving, everything is obtained. (30)

The daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the desire-driven (kāmya), another consisting of prosperity (abhyudaya), and yet another which is supreme (parama)—thus giving is remembered as being fivefold. ||31||
At the three times of day—morning, midday, and afternoon—one should diligently give whatever one can; this is proclaimed as the constant duty.
One who desires their own welfare should not let a day pass empty-handed;
whatever is given in a particular family remains present right there. (33)
If one who is devoid of wisdom should, out of delusion, eat this himself without having given it away, I shall produce a disease for him that prevents him from enjoying [the fruit]. (34)
In those undertakings, it is satisfied; it bestows much affliction;
it is joined with the sin of giving; and its door causes torment. ||35||
Those by whom nothing desirable was given to brahmins and gods during the three times of day, yet who themselves ate what they desired, have committed a very great sin. (36)
I shall purify them through fierce expiatory rites,
such as fasts that cause the body to wither, O gods of the earth.
Just as a leather-worker, being merciless, would clean the interior of a leather bag with whips and other tools, and would cause its impurities to burst forth; ||38||
In this way, I shall undoubtedly purify the evildoer through the excellent application of medicinal herbs and certainly through bitter decoctions. (39)
Just as those in the form of physicians [treat] with hot water and various torments, others enjoy before him other pleasures that were desired by his mind. (40)
"What can I do? Though capable, I have not given the supreme gift.
One should surround that person with a great form of disease, dark in appearance. (41)

O god among the earth-dwellers, whatever gift was not given by those sinful ones at all times—neither with faith nor according to their own capacity, including even their own selves—[that has been taken]. (42)
"Indeed, I shall burn those who have gone there by means of terrible expedients;
now, I shall declare before you the occasional time for giving. (43)
Likewise, when a great festival has arrived, upon reaching a sacred ford (tīrtha), on the anniversary of one's father's death, and with diligence during the month of Vaiśākha and others; ||44||
Giving during the auspicious months is known as occasional (naimittika) charity;
I shall now describe the times for optional (kāmya) giving, which bestows specific fruits.
Whatever desire is properly declared with reference to vows and the like, conceived as the fruit of one's longing, that is entirely connected with the mountain [Giri]. 46.
Through the power of that gift, one who is thoroughly permeated by cultivation enjoys such a fruit as that, being superhuman, due to his serene confidence. (47)

I shall now proclaim that which is remembered as leading to prosperity (ābhyudaya) in sacrifices and other rites, in ceremonies such as the birth-rite (jātakarman), and in rituals such as the investiture of the sacred girdle (mauñjī) and marriage. 48.
Through great effort, the consecration of palaces, banners, and deities—such as these constitute the gift to the Brahmins (mahīdeva) which brings about prosperity. 49.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall describe the gift that increases progeny and bestows enjoyment, fame, and the happiness of heaven. (50)
Having understood the destruction of desire and being afflicted by old age,
one should bestow gifts with diligence and should not place hope in anyone.
"And when I am dead, O sons, how will these wives, kinsmen, brothers, and my friends exist without me? (52)
Thinking, "How shall I continue to live if I am destitute of wealth? he gave away nothing at all. (53)
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope through mere good fortune,
the foolish-minded man goes toward death, and then his sons weep.
Afflicted by suffering and with minds agitated by delusion, they somehow contrive to give even a very small gift, though it be meager. (55)
When this time has arrived and great suffering has ensued, they do not forget their grasping; out of greed, they do not even give. (56)
This man has died; having learned of it, the bond of affection will cease. He who was dead—that god on earth—was bound by my snares. (57)
Overcome by thirst and hunger and tormented by manifold sufferings, he is cooked in a terrible hell for a long time; of this there is no doubt. (58)
Therefore, one should personally give gifts without any doubt;
for whose sons or grandsons are they, and whose wife or wealth are they? (59)
To whom would one who is an atheist regarding cyclic existence give anything? Therefore, drink, food, betel, water, and likewise gold are given to them. (60)
He gave garments, cows, land, umbrellas, and bowls of many kinds, as well as various fruits and gifts of land according to his own ability. (61)
O gods on earth (brahmins), gifts must be given here; there is no need for hesitation.
O brahmin, I shall now describe the characteristics of sacred fords (tīrthas) before you. 62.
This Sarasvatī, possessing excellent bathing-ghats, shines like the Gaṅgā;
as do the Revā, the Yamunā, the Tāpī, and likewise the river Carmaṇvatī.
The Sarayū and the excellent Veṇī, which are full and destroyers of sin;
the Kāverī and the Kapilā, as well as the Viśalyā and the Viśvatāriṇī. ||64||
The Godāvarī is well-known, as are the Tuṅgabhadrā and the Gaṇḍakī;
the river Bhīmarathī is remembered as the constant bringer of fear to sinners.
The Devikā, Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, and other excellent rivers—these and many other sacred fords (tīrthas) exist at auspicious times. ||66||
Whether in a village or in a forest, wherever there are rivers that purify all, there indeed one should perform such acts as ritual bathing and giving of gifts. (67)
O twice-born one, when the name of that sacred ford (tīrtha) is not known, one should utter "here" (tatra);
[then it is understood as]: "This is the great Viṣṇu-tīrtha. (68)
Viṣṇu is the deity of the sacred ford (tīrtha) everywhere; of this there is no doubt. A practitioner should remember that name "Nārāyaṇa" while at the sacred fords.
For him, the full fruit of the sacred ford arises through the name of Viṣṇu alone;
there is no doubt that this applies even to sacred fords and deities whose names are unknown.
A human being should proclaim these names by the name of Viṣṇu alone;
all meritorious accomplishments are [attained], and the ocean becomes a sacred pilgrimage site.
Lakes, rivers, streams, waterfalls, ponds, and even all small streams—by the name of Hari, they are all sacred fords (tīrtha). ||72||
The mountains take the form of sacred fords (tīrtha), and likewise the earth is a field of sacrifice;
there, learned Brahmins reside even out of mere curiosity.
That very place is known as a most great sacred ford (tīrtha), which removes all sins;
it is the ground for ancestral rites (śrāddha), the site for offerings, the hall of the gods, and the place for burnt oblations (homa).
Where the sound of the Vedas resounds correctly and where there are auspicious stories of Viṣṇu, one’s own home is endowed with merit, and even a cow-pen becomes purifying. (75)
Where there is a grove of Aśvattha trees, even a mere dwelling is purifying;
such are the sacred fords (tīrthas), as are one’s father and mother.
Where food is cooked for the sake of dharma, the Guru himself is present there;
where a virtuous wife resides, that is a sacred pilgrimage site—of this there is no doubt. (77)
Wherever a wise son constantly takes delight in the Dharma,
there for him is established that beneficial ford for the sake of crossing over.
In this manner, [he visited] the royal palace at Tīrthānī and likewise other such holy places (tīrtha), especially on the occasion of festival days. ||79||
It is certain that no one, anywhere, can obtain anything whatsoever without propitiating Hṛṣīkeśa, the giver of everything to all embodied beings. (80)
Offspring, wealth, wives, palatial mansions, horses, and elephants—happiness, heaven, and even liberation are not far from devotion to Hari. (81)
Nārāyaṇa, the supreme deity, Janārdana whose nature is truth, the Blessed Lord and Supreme Sovereign, divided himself into three forms. (82)
Endowed with rajas and tamas, yet with rajas predominating over sattva,
the Lord created Brahmā, the lotus-seated one, within the navel-lotus.
The omnipresent Lord created Rudra, who was possessed of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas);
these three—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are thus called the triad.
By means of *sattva*, one is liberated; that *sattva* has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
Through *rajas* joined with *sattva*, one becomes illustrious and preeminent in fame. (85)
That Vedic statement which one practices while aiming at dharma is celebrated among men as the distinguished "Rudra. (86)
Therefore, the king would become like the world when it is shrouded by passion and darkness;
for his dharma would be deficient in passion and consist solely of a mass of darkness. (87)
That indeed brings misfortune to men both in this world and the next;
he who is Viṣṇu is himself Brahmā, and he who is Brahmā is himself Hara.
O best of the twice-born, in this sacrifice, the three gods are eternally to be worshipped among the deities; whoever creates a distinction between these three [is at fault]. (89)
One who commits evil deeds and is of a sinful nature shall attain an undesirable state.
O twice-born one, Viṣṇu alone is the Supreme Brahman; Viṣṇu alone is the universe.
Among all his ritual activities, this month of Mādhava is his favorite;
it is proclaimed as the bestower of the fruits of great sacrifices, such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and others. ||91||
It yields a fruit superior to that of bathing at sacred fords, ascetic penance, charity, recitation, and sacrifice. ||92||

Those who, during this period when the sun is in Aries, regularly and incessantly perform their ablutions in a river at dawn, and even offer worship to the Brahmins, do not become sharers of my wrath. (93)
O Citragupta, what is the use of repeatedly killing the multitude of sins before you, or repeatedly erasing their records?
Rather, bathe again and again in the sacred ford during the month of Mādhava and deliver your ancestors here from sin.
This supreme secret, which cuts through fear, must not be revealed to those who lack devotion;
for it is the cause of expulsion from heaven, the cause of hell, and the cause of the exhaustion of my own authority. (95)
The Bhāgīrathī, Narmadā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Viśokā, and Vitastā are situated to the north of the Vindhya mountains. (96)
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Devikā, Tāpī, and Payoṣṇī are proclaimed as being to the south of the Vindhya mountains. (97)
He who performs the ritual bath in a river in the morning during the month of Vaiśākha has constantly immersed himself in these twelve great rivers. (98)
All rivers flowing to the ocean are meritorious; all excellent cities are meritorious; all sacred sites are meritorious; and all meritorious forests are places of refuge. (99)

Therefore, having plunged into it, one who is disciplined should perform the ritual bath in the month of Vaiśākha when the sun has half-risen, after having beheld, bowed to, and served many [deities].
No god on earth is able to describe his merit, even if he were to possess thousands upon thousands of mouths. (101)
O best of the twice-born, if the lifespan of Brahmā were short, then it might be possible to describe the fruit of the month of Mādhava. (102)

Like the spring month of Mādhava [extinguishing] the fire that drags one into the great hells, [this practice destroys] sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and approaching those who should not be approached. (103)

Sin committed through desire or without desire constitutes both a major transgression (pātaka) and a minor offense (upapātaka), as well as secret sins, the performance of rituals, and the highest [sins]. (104)

The loss of caste, which is terrible, as well as that which renders one unworthy of receiving gifts, that which brings impurity, and miscellaneous sins—all these arise from speech, mind, and body. (105)
The month of Mādhava, when properly observed according to the prescribed rites,
shall burn away [the sins] for thousands of crores and hundreds of crores of kalpas.
The illustrious one who worships Hari during the month of Mādhava shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||97||
(98) The Ninety-Eighth Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the King of Dharma,
the Brahmin again inquired about the auspicious ritual for the month of Mādhava.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O Dharmarāja, O highly fortunate one, you have perfectly revealed this profound secret—the supreme merit arising from the Mādhava-bath, which grants liberation to men. (2)
Having bathed in the month of Mādhava during the month of Mādhava, how should one, being composed, worship the God in the morning? Tell me that procedure and with which flowers. (3)
The King of Dharma said: "Among all species of leaves, Tulasī is dear to Keśava;
likewise, Puṣkara and other holy places, as well as the Gaṅgā and other rivers [are present there]."
The gods, beginning with Vāsudeva, dwell within the leaf of the tulasī;
at all times and on every occasion, the tulasī is the beloved of Viṣṇu. (5)
Having abandoned the *mālatī* flower and having discarded the lotus, one should worship Mādhava with devotion, taking instead the *tulasī* leaf. (6)
Even Śeṣa himself would not be able to describe the fruit of his merit for one who, without having bathed, cuts a Tulasī plant for the sake of a deity or for ancestral rites. ||7||
All that becomes fruitless; even very many sins, such as poverty, suffering, and the experience of misfortune, are purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). ||8||
Tulasī quickly removes diseases, just as the myrobalan fruit does;
she is known by the names Kṛṣṇā and Gaurā, and with her one should worship the Enemy of Madhu.
A man who is especially devoted to Hari becomes Nārāyaṇa himself,
because he diligently worships Mādhava with Tulasī throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha.
By worshipping the Slayer of Madhu at the three junctions of the day, there is no rebirth for him;
even if flowers and leaves are not available, one should worship with food and other offerings.
In the month of Mādhava, which is dear to Mādhava, one should always eat rice, mung beans, wheat, barley, or even green gram, having bathed according to the prescribed rite in the morning.
He who always satisfies the ancestors, gods, and humans, along with all things moving and unmoving, by pouring abundant water at the root of the Aśvattha tree; 13.
Then, one should perform circumambulations until the end for that which consists of all the gods;
thereafter, whoever worships the divine Aśvattha tree with water as well.
By him, ten thousand families would undoubtedly be delivered. ||14||
O dear one, misfortune, ill fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—all suffering dissolves through the propitiation of the Aśvattha tree. 15.
The ancestors are gratified by him, and Viṣṇu is duly worshipped by him;
that hero who worships the Aśvattha tree has likewise honored the planetary deities.
One should touch white horse-ears flowers, as well as the śamī tree, fire, sandalwood, the orb of the sun, and the aśvattha tree; thereafter, one should perform the duties of one's own caste.
Having relieved bodily distress, fed a cow, bathed, offered libations to the Pippala tree, and performed worship of Govinda, one shall not fall into a miserable state of existence. (18)
On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day of Vaiśākha— for these three days—
even a woman or a man who is entirely incapable [of performing all rites] should act according to the prescribed rule.
Endowed with the previously mentioned observances and having bathed in the morning according to his ability, he is liberated from all sins and attains imperishable heaven. ||20||
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, he should also feed ten Brahmins according to his capacity;
having risen for three nights, bathed, and being restrained and pure, he should do this once.
Having given twelve white sesamum seeds mixed with honey, or alternatively black ones,
to twelve Brahmins, he should have them pronounce a blessing with those very seeds.
"May my Dharmarāja be pleased; one should satisfy the ancestors and the gods.
Whatever sin has been committed throughout one's life perishes at that very moment. (23)
He shall remain in the heavenly world for ten million times ten million years, enjoying happiness as he pleases;
there, honored by all the deities, he shall behold none but me.
For the satisfaction of the ancestors and the deities, [one should offer] cooked food, water, jars, and so forth,
for three days on the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day.
Whoever should give with devotion to a Brahmin is liberated from great sins; [one should offer] vessels of gold and sesame seeds to Brahmins daily according to one's capacity. (26)
By satisfying [the ancestors] with vessels of water, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
these [rites] were ordained by the Lotus-born [Brahmā] on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
Sesame seeds should also be offered with devotion for the sake of attaining a multitude of blessings;
O observer of noble vows, listen now to an ancient account regarding this matter.
The fruit of the full moon day of the month of Mādhava is most wonderful;
the thirty lunar days beginning from the sun's entry into Aries are supreme. (29)
These are proclaimed in the Purāṇas as meritorious and superior to all sacrifices;
indeed, those three are especially pure and difficult for sinners to attain. (30)
Even more than that, the full-moon day of the month of Mādhava is meritorious and dear to Mādhava;
it is the first lunar day at the beginning of the Vārāha-kalpa and yields great fruit. (31)
In ancient times, the two primordial Daityas were deluded by Nārāyaṇa in this [form];
Hiraṇyākṣa and Madhu were slain, and the earth was uplifted, O Brahmin. (32)
On the thirteenth, fourteenth, and full moon day,
this omnipresent Lord sequentially performed these three acts during the bright fortnight of this month of Mādhava.
From that time forward, O eminent Brahmin, this full-moon day became especially distinguished;
it is known as the beginning of the Kalpa, the purifier, and the witness of the deeds of the Kalpa. (34)

O Brahmin, what is the use of the birth of one who, though observant of religious restraints, does not perform his morning bath during the month of Vaiśākha? Surely such a person is a betrayer of his own self. (35)
Especially on the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day, whether it be a woman or even a man, [one should perform this] according to the correct ritual procedure. (36)
Having bathed in the morning and observed the prescribed rules, he is liberated from all sins;
[even] those devoid of the merit of bathing, giving, worship, ancestral rites, and other such acts. ||37||
He who indeed neglects the Vaiśākhī day will surely have his abode in hell;
there is no scripture equal to the Veda, and no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā.
There is no gift equal to [the gift of] water and cows, nor is there any lunar day equal to Vaiśākhī;
he who, devoted to Viṣṇu, gives a water-cow on the day of Vaiśākhī, [attains the highest goal]. (39)
This fourth [sin] is especially distinguished among the three types of gods:
the killer of a mother, the killer of a father, the killer of an embryo, and the violator of the Guru’s bed. (40)
Upon seeing a water-cow (jaladhenu), one is said to be liberated from all sins; they rescue ten preceding and ten succeeding generations of their lineage from hell. 41.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, they bestow a water-cow according to the prescribed rite upon the descendant of Atri,
along with sugar, fruit, betel, sandals, and a knife.
Those who bestow water-jars, water-pots, cooked food, and golden sacrificial fees upon the foremost of the twice-born are proclaimed here as truly fortunate. (43)
He who bestows [a gift] on the full moon day of Vaiśākha shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history as an illustration.
O sinless one, in the great forest there was a conversation between a Brāhmaṇa and the departed spirits;
formerly, O blameless one, that Brāhmaṇa was named Dhanaśarman in the Middle Country.
Having gone to the forest for the sake of kuśa grass and other items, he then beheld this wonder;
terrified, he saw those evil pretas and most dreadful women. (46)
With hair standing on end, bloodshot eyes, black teeth, and emaciated bellies,
they ran hither and thither, uttering various cries.
Seeing them, the Brahmin, terrified with fear, fled with speed;
then they too, crying out, pursued him at once.
Being thus tormented by those hungry ghosts (pretas), Dhanaśarman spoke these sweet words:
Dhanaśarman said: Who are you, and from what state have you arisen that you are in this condition suited for hell? (49)
"You ought to protect me, who am afflicted by fear, worthy of compassion, and distressed—a Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa who has come to the forest, possessing many dependents yet being destitute. (50)
"Keśava will surely grant what is most beneficial even for you;
for the Lord Viṣṇu, who is devoted to the Brahmanas, is pleased with me out of compassion. (51)
Viṣṇu, who resembles the flax flower, is Hari wearing yellow garments;
by the mere hearing of his name, even the great darkness departs. (52)
The God who is without beginning or end, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace;
the imperishable, lotus-eyed one, the bestower of liberation upon the departed spirits. ||53||
Yama said:
"Merely by hearing Your name, Viṣṇu has satisfied these piśācas, who have attained a virtuous state and are restrained by compassion and courtesy. (54)
Pleased by his words and impelled by his instructions, the departed spirits, tormented by a flood of hunger and thirst, spoke thus to the brahmin: ||55||
The pretas said:
"O Brahmin, by the mere sight of you and by hearing the name of Hari, we have attained a different state of being and have become compassionate. (56)
Association with the devotees of Viṣṇu surely dispels evil, bestows spiritual welfare, and swiftly spreads one's fame. (57)
Who indeed would not be delighted by this moonlight of the nectar of Vaiṣṇava devotion—cool, composed of elixir, and bestowing supreme bliss? (58)
This one is named Kṛtaghna; this second one is Vidaivata;
and this third one is Avaiśākha—all three of them are evildoers. (59)
This wicked one has always practiced extreme ingratitude;
therefore, his name born of his karma is established as "Kṛtaghna" (the Ungrateful).
"O twice-born one, in a previous birth this man was a Śūdra named Sudāsa; having committed ungratefulness, that sinner has reached this present condition. (61)
Expiation exists even for a great sinner, a rogue, or one who has acted against a guru, a master, or a benefactor; but for one who harms a brahmin, there is no expiation.
"O twice-born one, having reached this state, experience now the various aggregates of hells with bodies capable of enduring torment. (63)
Because he always ate food without having performed the worship of the deities,
and without having given to his guru and the Brahmins, for that very reason he has become one whose deities are lost.
This king, the lord of ten thousand villages,
was known by the name Harivīra in his previous birth.
Out of anger, laziness, and atheism, I failed to carry out the commands of my guru; thus, without performing great sacrifices, I ate while being censured by the brahmins. (66)
Due to that evil karma, having experienced the agonies of the great hell, he was thereafter born as a preta named Vidaivata.
I am the third among the three who are devoid of the month of Vaiśākha and are evildoers;
therefore, by that karma-born name, I am established as a non-Brahmin. (68)
Born in the Middle Country, I am Gautama by name and also by lineage; in my previous birth, I was a Brahmin living in Vāsapura who maintained the sacred fires.
By me alone, following solely the path of the Śrutis, the god Mādhava was not worshipped during the month of Mādhava. (70)
Nothing was given that was not abundant, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha;
there, the slayer of Madhu was worshipped, and the wise were fully satisfied.
The ancestors and deities were gratified by the gifts of water-pots filled with jewels,
as well as offerings of sesame seeds mixed with honey presented to those learned in the Vedas.
There, the wise ones, honored with choice offerings of betel, sandalwood, and fans, were worshipped without flowers or fruits for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the deities.
Not even a single full-moon Vaiśākha day, which bestows the fruit of fulfillment, has been observed by me through the meritorious acts of bathing, giving, ritual performance, and worship. (74)
Because of that, all my Vedic rites became fruitless;
thus, due to my pride, I was born as a preta named Vaiśākha. (75)
All this has been told to you, the cause for all three;
for you are our deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence, since you are indeed a virtuous brahmin.
The holy men have made the Brahma-tīrtha liberated, because from it they deliver even those who have committed great sins, once they have taken refuge there, from the hells. (77)
Between the man who always bathes in holy pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā and he who cultivates the company of the virtuous, association with the virtuous is superior. (78)
Alternatively, O Lord, there is my son, renowned as Dhanaśarman;
go to him and awaken him, having made an effort for our sake. (79)
When the time for another's task has arrived, one who exerts effort toward it obtains abundant fruit, which is even greater than that of the performance of sacrifices and acts of charity.
Yama said:
Having heard those words of the deceased, Dhanaśarman was deeply distressed; he recognized that his own father had fallen into hell. (81)
Standing before the fire, he spoke these words to himself.
Dhanaśarman said:
"O Lord, I am the useless son of Gautama."
But that son who does not perform the funeral rites for his father is not liberated;
he cannot purify himself, even if he possesses pure wealth.
For the Dharma is to be known as profound, even by a wise person with great effort;
just as my father and you have both fallen into this miserable state.
And when you have obtained from me this continuity of happiness, it is considered that you have likewise attained the continuity of happiness in both worlds for yourself and your sons. (85)
In this world, according to the Dharma, there are two fathers for a man: his biological father and his maternal grandfather.
Of these two, the biological father is superior, as it is observed that the seed is the primary factor.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? O Father, how is your state? I do not know the true nature of dharma; I take refuge in your word. (87)
The preta said:
"Listen, my son, to these truthful words; by the power of an inevitable future event, and perhaps through some merit, a happy state will surely come to me. (88)
While performing the rites pertaining to the sacred fires, I acted out of pride;
I disregarded the words of my guru, and thus the guru was insulted by me. (89)
Through disrespect toward one's gurus, through excessive joy, anger, and pride, and through wicked conduct that harms one's reputation, meritorious deeds go to ruin.
Out of ignorance, I have performed only Vedic rites, which were not in conflict with the Śrauta rituals and were according to the ancient injunctions. (91)
Not even a single Vaiśākhī full-moon day has been observed by him according to the rules—a day that is a forest fire for the fuel of sin and an axe for the tree of evil. (92)
That man whose Vaiśākha [month] passes without vows becomes one who has missed Vaiśākha;
thereafter, he is born for ten lifetimes among the wombs of animals. ||93||
Having long experienced suffering, that preta becomes, in turn, a human being—a birth that is somehow difficult to obtain. (94)
I shall now declare to you that supreme means which brings about the desired liberation—
the very one that I heard previously in a former birth from the mouth of my own guru.
Go, my son, to your home and bathe in the Yamunā according to the prescribed rites;
from this day forward, she has arrived as the bestower of all goals until the end of the kalpa.
On the final day of Vaiśākha, the worship of the ancestors and the gods is beneficial. 96.
If one should devoutly offer water mixed with sesame seeds, along with fruits and a water-pot, to the ancestors here, that Śrāddha offered by him shall always endure for a thousand years. (97)

Whoever should feed the deities of the earth on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, for every mouthful [siktha] offered, the ancestors shall attain satisfaction for a number of ages equal to the count of those morsels. 98.

Having bathed according to the prescribed rite on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should feed ten Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice (pāyasa); one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt. ||99||
Having given white or black sesame seeds mixed with honey to ten Brahmins, one should have them pronounce a blessing with those very seeds.
One should satisfy the ancestors and the gods with the words, "May Dharmarāja be pleased!
At that very moment, the sin committed throughout one's entire life is destroyed. (101)
O twice-born one, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, sesame seeds were created by the Lotus-born One; they should be given with devotion and touched by all who have gone [to the river]. 102.
Then, to him who has bathed his entire body with sesame seeds mixed with barley, Brahmā grants here the desired boon. 103.
Whoever should offer water-pots for the pleasure of Dharmarāja, by that act seven times seven families shall be delivered; of this there is no doubt. (104)
On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day, being intent upon devotion, one should bathe, mutter prayers, offer oblations, give gifts, and worship Mādhava. (105)
"O sir, bestow upon us that fruit which arises from having a son; for until these two familiar deceased ones have departed, I shall not resort to the path of heaven. (106)
"The end of the sin of these two has now arrived.
Yama said:
"Having said 'So be it,' he departed; then the brahmin related everything to Kṛṣṇa."

Delighted by supreme devotion, one who performs bathing and giving on the full moon day of Vaiśākha—having bathed with fervent devotion upon reaching the full moon of Mādhava—[attains the highest state]. (108)
Having given many gifts to them, he bestowed merit upon each individually;
at that very moment, they all ascended celestial chariots and went to heaven.
O best of the twice-born, Dhanaśarman, that eminent brāhmaṇa who was learned in the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Purāṇas, was also delighted by the application of that gift of merit. (110)
Having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, he attained the world of Brahmā;
therefore, this Vaiśākha full-moon day is most meritorious and purifies the entire universe.
O Brahmin, it shall be told by me in brief, because of its extreme gravity.

Blessed indeed are they, the virtuous, truly born into this world, and truly men who possess the goal of human endeavor—those whose hearts are purified by the rule of bathing at dawn, who worship the Slayer of Madhu during the month of Mādhava. (113)
In the month of Jyeshtha, if a man bathes at dawn and worships Ramesha, endowed with all the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), he will surely destroy his sin, even if it be complete. 114.

By those very people has time been conquered; they alone among men are blessed and freed from sin—those who, joined with the month of Mādhava, do not enter a womb again and do not sink back into rebirth. 115.

Through the practice of yoga, the roar of meditative absorption, the application of sacrificial rites, and the performance of austerities, charity, and ritual observances, whatever small merit may have been performed in this month shall once again become equal to a kalpa in this world. (116)

In the month of Mādhava, at the break of dawn, for the sake of worshipping Mādhava, even a base man becomes pure; for even a drop of water, through contact with the moon, brings about purification. (117)
Having ascended this body, embodied beings wander about only so long as they do not call upon that Great One (Virāṭ), the beloved of Śrī Ramā’s lover, who is known by the name Samādhi. 119.
The month of Mādhava, beloved of Mādhava, when one has bathed, burns away many fierce sins that are like Mount Meru or the thunderbolt. 120.
O twice-born one, out of favor toward you, I have thus briefly declared this majesty of the Vaiśākha bath, which brings about the destruction of the sins of the listener. (121)
But whoever shall listen with devotion to this history spoken by me, he too, liberated from sin, shall behold my face. (122)
Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, though committed many times over, are certainly destroyed by the observance of the rites of Vaiśākha. 123.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite in Vaiśākha, one shall deliver thirty ancestors, thirty descendants, and thirty more beyond them— those both preceding and following— from hell.
On one side are all the sacred fords and all sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees; on the other side is the month of Mādhava observed with disciplined restraint. (125)
For this reason, among all months, the month of Mādhava is dear to that Blessed Lord Hari of exalted deeds; it is the most excellent and superior.
O Great God, do not entertain any doubt whatsoever regarding what I have declared concerning the month of Vaiśākha, whenever it arrives. 127.
In this regard, listen to that wonderful ancient account which has occurred;
although it is something that should not be told, I shall nevertheless relate this narrative to you. (128)
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(99) The Ninety-ninth Chapter.
Yama said:
In former times, there was a king renowned by the name Mahīratha,
who had attained abundant sovereignty and prosperity as the fruit of his past merits.
He remained solely devoted to the graceful charms of the goddess of sensual desire;
addicted to that one vice alone, he was not established in the pursuit of dharma or artha. ||2||
The royal glory of that king, who was averse to the affairs of state and accompanied by his beloved consort, enjoyed the objects of the senses for me. (3)
He does not recognize wealth, nor does he perceive dharma, nor purpose, nor what ought to be done;
his mental impressions are occupied solely with the amorous dalliances of women. (4)
Then, after a long time, his priest Kaśyapa spoke these words of dharma to him, as he was reflecting upon it. (5)
If a preceptor does not restrain the king from unrighteousness out of delusion, he too partakes in that sin; therefore, he must be awakened by the family priest.
If, even after being enlightened, he disregards the words of the family priest,
then the priest would be faultless and the king would be the bearer of all the faults.
Listen, O King, to the words of my preceptor, which are consistent with dharma and artha, coherent in meaning, full of significance, and free from desire, passion, and the like. (8)
This alone is another dharma: abiding by the words of the guru. By honoring the command of the guru, one's life, sovereignty, prosperity, and happiness increase. (9)
The Brahmins were not satiated by your gifts, nor was Viṣṇu propitiated by you;
neither any vow, nor any austerity, nor indeed any pilgrimage was performed by you. (10)
Alas, O timid one, under the sway of desire, you did not think of the name of Hari; instead, by associating with you, I have brought about my own association with the ignorant. 11.
Whose beloveds would not be dear when they serve as bearers of the fly-whisks of Love? Yet, they are as fickle as the leaves of a plantain tree tossed by the wind. 12.

Those of great resolve are not satiated by riches that vanish like waves, by enjoyments that are as fleeting as the flickering of a brow, or by youthful vigor that can be drunk up in a mere moment. (13)
Of what use is knowledge, or austerity, or renunciation, or statesmanship;
of what use is a mind secluded in solitude, for one whose heart has been stolen away by women? (14)
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even in death;
everything else will perish along with the body. (15)
One should gradually accumulate merit, just as termites build up an anthill;
with merit as one's companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
O King of kings, do you not know that the flickering of the lives of mortals is as unstable as the surging waves of water tossed by the wind? 17.
For those who have the Vinaya as their jewel-crown, the True Dharma as their earrings, and renunciation as their bracelets—what need have they for the ornaments of the dull-witted? (18)
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the kinsmen depart with averted faces; only Dharma follows him.
When all things are passing away, when youth is thus wasting away, and when life itself is being snatched away, why do you rise up and run about? (20)
The family, children, wife, and so forth, as well as the body and the accumulation of wealth, are alien and impermanent; what then [is truly one's own] except for one's own good and evil deeds? (21)
Since you must inevitably depart, abandoning everything, why are you attached to what is worthless and do not practice your own duty? (22)
Without rest, without provisions, without wealth as your travel-stipend, and without a guide—once dead, how will you travel alone along that long road? (23)
No one at all will follow behind you as you set forth;
only your good and evil deeds will follow after you as you go.
Diligently practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti, appropriate to one’s family and region, beneficial, and rooted in Dharma. (25)
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of dharma;
for through dharma, all happiness, including wealth and pleasure, is attained. (26)
One should practice the yoga of mastery over the senses day and night;
for one who has conquered the senses is indeed able to establish the subjects on the right path.
The fortunes of kings, though made fickle by the side-long glances of exceedingly bold women, remain steadfast for a long time through their dedication to discipline.
The prosperity of those with deluded minds—who possess the habits of desire, pride, and the like, and who act without reflection—is destroyed along with their very lives. (29)
O noble-minded ones, he dances with ashes whose vision has vanished;
his intellect is filled by rivers that have neither arrived nor departed. 30.
Between vice and death, vice is said to be the more grievous;
for the king addicted to vice sinks lower and lower, whereas the king free from vice ascends to heaven.
O Great King, abandon desire, which is especially contrary to dharma and brings about calamities that are difficult to endure. 32.
These kingdoms, which are to be enjoyed by fortune, belong even to those who are dull-witted, lacking discrimination, asuras, evil-minded, and devoid of statesmanship. (33)
These [faculties] are not stable here due to the misdeeds one has cultivated;
they dissolve just as wealth does through contact with fire. (34)
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, he whose mind is not intent on discernment is as good as dead. (35)

Since an instructor is called a "guru" by those who have not heard the scriptures, what then are instructions to those whose calamities are already at hand? They are merely like hair on the head. (36)
Having cast aside the fever of sensory objects with an intellect that is equanimous and healthy,
and by means of practical reasoning, the wise man accomplishes his own true purpose.

The mind of a living being wavers from the unwholesome and goes toward the wholesome, and from that [wholesome state] it goes to the other; therefore, one should forcefully steady it, just as one would with a child. (38)
O King, one should restrain with supreme intelligence a mind that has strayed onto a wrong path, having heeded the counsel of the elders who perceive the Dharma. (39)
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor kinsmen provide assistance;
neither the movement of hands and feet, nor travel to another land [can help]. (40)
There is no exhaustion from bodily mortification, nor reliance on the abodes of non-Buddhist sects;
that state is attained solely by one whose mind is fixed upon it through recitation. 41.
Therefore, O King, a wise person should certainly exert effort to restrain the mind when it is engaged with sense objects, just as one restrains horses that are running away. 42.
O King, you should perform those various acts by which you have been thus honored; for this very reason, listen now to what has been said by the sages regarding their respective fruits. (43)
Even by a person who is deluded, wise friends should be questioned;
and whatever they say when questioned, that should be done as is appropriate. 44.
One who seeks their own welfare must restrain desire and anger by every possible means;
for these two are ever intent on destroying that very welfare. (45)
Lust is a powerful enemy residing within the body of even the king of monkeys;
a person who desires their own welfare should not fall under its control. 46.
He who was formerly burnt by the fire from the forehead of that very Śūlin, the god of gods Kāma, has now been rendered one whose movement and stability are gone.
When we two set out to kill that woman, he, having become one with our minds, assumed a male body and revealed his true form. 48.
As he reflects again and again upon that ignoble form,
she, having taken refuge in that which is unseen, drives that man to madness.
In the same way, O King, this Smara (the god of love) undoubtedly intoxicates women;
for him, O King, [his power] arises from the mere recollection of his name. 50.
Whatever kind of cow-hide garment a hero may take as his refuge,
by the radiance of his own splendor, it shall become something to be drunk from like a stream of tears.
Having mounted upon the form of a woman, it deludes even that steadfast man; but having taken refuge in a man, it causes this woman to melt away. (52)
O King, he alone is the co-emergent (sahaja), bodiless yet dwelling within the body;
O Lord, how can sin be attributed even to such a physical frame? (53)
Upon reaching which even the most purifying five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sacrificial oblations (havis) become impure in an instant—who else could be more impure than that? (54)
Even while smelling its own foul odor and seeing its own impurity,
this world does not become dispassionate, even though it afflicts its own nose.
Having obtained delicious food, drinks, and fragrant things, this [body] quickly becomes impure; therefore, something else must be the truly impure one.
Indeed, the food that has entered one's stomach quickly loses its own form and becomes known as impure, mixed with worms. (57)
Even so, one should abandon the natural form of protecting the body;
for afterwards, it becomes like a dog, dwelling in a foul place among worms within the family.
There, indeed, wind-born worms or those dwelling in the anus arise; together with the worm, it produces a boil accompanied by a most terrible itching and burning sensation. (59)
It would cause even greater pain and shake the entire body;
when rubbed by the tips of the fingernails, it produces a burning sensation.
In that same way, O Asura, happiness surely arises for him; there is no doubt about this.
Thus the mortal enjoys savory tastes and furthermore drinks excellent foods.
There, as if by fire, the digestive heat cooks [the food], causing the waste to fall into the downward wind (apāna);
there, the essence, which has become the vital nutrient (rasa), is produced in its full abundance.
Stainless and possessing pure vigor, he proceeds to the abode of Brahmā;
drawn along by that very wind which is equalized within him.
Vital energy finds no stable place and exists in a state of constant flux;
within the skulls of living beings, there are indeed five types of worms.
O King, these two [should be placed] at the root of the ears; then again, at the location of the eyes, according to the measure of the little finger, they are red-tailed. 65.
There was no doubt that they had black tails with the color of fresh butter;
hear from me as I recite their names, beginning with Bhadra.
Piṅgalī and Śṛṅgalī are two worms located at the roots of the ears;
another, Śṛṅgalī, resides within the eyes.
There is no doubt that there are one hundred and fifty such worms;
they all reside within the forehead, each the size of a mustard seed. (68)
All those afflicted by the disease of the skull undoubtedly undergo transformation;
I shall likewise describe another, the great worm of Prajāpati. 69.
O King, listen: there is a doubt regarding its color, as it is the size of a *ḍula* fruit; moreover, two hairs are found upon its face.
When Prajāpati turns his face away, even for living beings who remain in their own places, their intellect perishes and their doubts are destroyed in that very instant.
That potency falls in the form of a liquid; there is no doubt about this.
One drinks the potency with ease, and by that, intoxication arises from it. (72)
Having pierced through the location of the palate, the breath moves with a state of vibration;
there, the channels Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā are situated.
O King, even by its own power, it brings about the destruction of the life-force of all living beings at every moment, at every breath, and at every instant. (74)
O King, the male organ is the sign of the man, and the female organ is that of the woman;
when both the man and the woman are impassioned, they then engage in union.
By rubbing body against body through sexual union, pleasure arises;
yet that pleasure lasts but a moment, while the resulting itching and irritation are of such a nature as to be constant. (76)
Indeed, such is the heroic state seen everywhere;
there is no doubt that this is the bitter ripening of that very poison. ||77||
Furthermore, Dharma alone, when practiced according to the prescribed rules, is the highest good; therefore, summoning your fortitude, practice Dharma alone. (78)
This breath is fickle; in a single moment it performs hundreds of arrivals and departures. Since the life of embodied beings depends upon it, who would practice a delay in the Dharma? (79)
O King, even today his mind does not cease from its restless longing for those forbidden objects of sense. (80)
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it increases all the more. (81)
Whom else is capable of liberating a mind seized by the female serpent, except for that Blessed Lord Mādhava, the Sovereign who delights in the Self? (82)
Therefore, everything has become fruitless due to the corruption of desire;
even your own youth has now become devoid of noble conduct, O King. (83)
I tell you what is for your benefit, the most excellent of all things; for I am your priest, sharing in both your good and evil deeds. (84)
On one side are all the merits for the destruction of the sins of sinners; on the other side is the month of Mādhava, which is always dear to Mādhava. 85.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher's wife—these alone are proclaimed by the lords of sages as the great sins (mahā-pātakas). 86.
In that regard, whatever has been committed by men through thought,
word, or deed, the month of Mādhava destroys all of it, including even the greatest darkness of sin.
Just as the sun destroys darkness in every way, O King, so does the illustrious Mādhava destroy the darkness [of ignorance] through the performance of this rite. 88.

O great king, having abandoned those terrible sins committed from birth onwards, mortals, through the merit of the power of performing the rites prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha, joyfully attain the city of Hari. (89)
If even a single person observes the month of Vaiśākha according to the prescribed rules and with devotion,
even though they be a sinner, they go to the abode of Hari.
Therefore, O King, you too should now go to this Mādhava;
having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rite, worship the Enemy of Madhu.
Just as the husk of rice or the blackness of copper is removed by action,
so too is the impurity of a heroic man destroyed.
Even for one who is living, though it be natural and hair-raising, it will surely perish—of this there is no doubt; therefore, perform the action that has been set forth.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||99||
(100) The Hundredth Chapter. The Blessed King said:
Awakened by your words—which are like the waters of the Ocean of Milk, cool and pure in their vision, truthful yet diverse—I have been enlightened. (1)

O gentle one, you have caused me to drink the nectar that does not arise from the ocean, which is no ordinary substance, the medicine for calamity, and the remover of the disease of worldly existence. (2)
Association with the virtuous, O Brahmin, is indeed a bestower of joy upon men, a destroyer of sins, a life-giving medicine, and a remover of old age and death. (3)
Whatever things on the surface of the earth are difficult to attain, those very things are obtained solely through association with the virtuous. (4)

For one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā of association with the virtuous, which removes all sin—what need has he for charities, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices? (5)
For men who are sinking and surfacing in the ocean of worldly existence,
the virtuous— who know the Dharma and are tranquil— are the supreme refuge, like a sturdy boat for those drowning in the waters.
O Lord, that state of being which I formerly possessed—eagerly longing for the sole pleasure of desire—has today become its opposite through seeing you and hearing your words. (7)
For the sake of happiness in a single birth, a wise person may destroy thousands [of future births];
yet by means of a single birth, he accumulates [merit] for thousands of births.
O twice-born one, with my mind craving the pleasure of tasting the sentiment of passion, I, being deluded, have not performed anything for my own welfare. (9)
Alas, what delusion is this of my mind, by which for the sake of women, I have been cast into a terrible calamity that results in suffering and is difficult to overcome? (10)
O Blessed One, I am thoroughly satisfied by these words concerning awakening;
you ought to uplift me here by granting this instruction. (11)
I, whose merit was accumulated in former lives, have been awakened by you;
indeed, I have been especially purified by the dust of your feet.
O best among speakers, please tell me the ritual procedure for the month of Mādhava, which you have described as that which effects the destruction of all sins. (13)
What is the gift there, what is the bath, who is the deity, and what are the observances?
O brahmin-sage, tell me this for the sake of crossing over my sins.
Yama said:
Having been addressed in this manner, the venerable Kaśyapa, a treasure-house of compassion, spoke these words that were righteous for the brahmins, beneficial to all the world, and auspicious. 15.
Kaśyapa said:
O King, that which has been asked by a wise man whose intellect is capable of reconciling the preceding and the following should not be spoken to one who is base and of sinful mind. (16)
Having thus bestowed upon that one engaged in evil conduct a virtuous mind, he shall fully obtain the fruit of the gift of knowledge; of this there is no doubt. (17)
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner;
for even though he knows, the wise man should behave among people like one who is dull-witted. 18.
Even for learned disciples, sons, or those who act like kinsmen, that which is beneficial and conducive to the welfare of those possessed of faith should be spoken, even if unasked. (19)
O Lord of the Earth, you have now become pure of heart through my words and by virtue of some merit performed in the past. (20)
That body of yours, which had been in a state of sin due to its dependence on me, became established in righteousness through the hearing of the Dharmaśāstra. ||21||
That which is in a state of evil, called unrighteousness (*adharma*), devoid of knowledge of dharma, and characterized by false vows—know that to be the "other" (inferior) righteous person. ||22||
The third internal organ is the mind (manas), which serves as the instrument for the experience of merit and demerit;
indeed, those who know the Dharma call this body threefold.
To the extent that there is the enjoyment of dharma and liberation—these three being its divisions—that body which is in a state of sin is called "consisting of sin. (24)
Now, as you practice devotion to the guru and listen to my words which are the very form of Dharma, your body shall remain established [in its true state]. (25)
By that very [means], a stainless purity arose, appropriate for the performance of dharma; for among embodied beings, both their names and their deeds are determined by destiny. (26)
Bodies flourish and undergo transformation from time to time;
surely, at present, your mind is set upon dharma. (27)
"Therefore, I shall cause you to perform this supreme Mādhava-bath.
Yama said:
"Then it was performed by him, with Kaśyapa as his domestic priest."
In the month of Mādhava, accompanied by the rite of truth, there is bathing, giving, and worship;
this is the procedure arising from the Vaiśākha-bath as it was seen in the ancient scriptures. (29)
The sage replied to the king as he had been instructed;
having been made to hear the essence of the hymn, he was made to recite it to the one whose intellect is Hari.
If one hears this [text] even without having studied it, one shall obtain the full fruit. ||31||
Then the king, his disposition purified by that deed, also performed the praiseworthy rite for Śrīmādhava according to the prescribed method, just as he had heard it with devotion. (32)

In the morning, that best of kings performed his bath, offered water for the feet, presented the respectful offering (arghya), worshipped Hari with a spirit of devotion, and offered food oblations (naivedya). ||33||
Just as one performs charity and the observance of vows with devotion according to the prescribed rites during Vaiśākha and other months,
so too should one who acts with devotion perform this every day and likewise every year.
Having performed this, the foremost of the gods on earth departs for the abode of Hari. ||34||
Then, during the other months, he becomes devoted solely to sensual enjoyment, sporting with the breasts of his beloveds, according to his desire. Thus it is indeed. (35)
Under the sway of passion, he disregarded the established rules of conduct and failed to deliberate upon matters of state, setting aside Māsa and Samādhi.
O foremost of Brahmins, even for the great, the god of love is difficult to restrain;
indeed, the succession of latent impressions (vāsanā) is innate to the body and truly beginningless.
Because the flames of fire—though beautiful with their hair-like soot and pleasing to the eye—are difficult to touch and, being ignoble, burn a man like straw. (38)
Desire, as it truly is, is a terrible enemy residing within the bodies of men;
consisting of the smoke of delusion, this evil does not leave anyone unscorched. 39.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||100||
(101) The One Hundred and First Chapter.
Yama said:
Then the king, marked by the side-glance of Kālaka, died; his body was wasted away by consumption arising from excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures.
Being led away by groups of men and being beaten again and again, he cried out with great wails, remembering his own sins. ||2||
The messengers of Viṣṇu approached and struck my followers, saying,
"This man is righteous," and then they ascended that celestial chariot.
The king, his sins destroyed by the morning bath in the month of Vaiśākha, was led to the city of Hari while being praised by hosts of apsarases. ||4||
Then, thinking "this man is devoid of dharma," those messengers of the gods, by the command of Viṣṇu, once again [seized] that lord of the earth.
From no great distance, he proceeded with focused mind along the path to hell. ||5||
As he was going along, he then heard again the various cries of living beings who were screaming while being cooked in hell.
Hearing the most terrible wailing of the sinners being boiled, the king of the Brahmins was filled with amazement and became deeply distressed. ||7||
The messengers said: "What was this dreadful wailing that was heard?
It is not heard again; you ought to tell me the reason for it. (8)
The messengers said:
"Those who have abandoned the bounds of propriety, the sinful ones devoid of right conduct, have been cast into the terrible hells, such as Tāmisra and others. (9)
Those who have committed sins, immediately after casting off their lives here, take to the path of Yama and experience terrible suffering. (10)
Dragged here and there by the terrible messengers of Yama,
they fall into blinding darkness and are devoured by those most cruel beings.
By dogs, jackals, flesh-eaters, crows, herons, vultures, and the like;
by fire-lickers, wolves, tigers, serpents, scorpions, and so forth. ||12||
Being burned by fire, being pierced by spears,
being split apart by saws, and being tormented by thirst.
Afflicted by hunger as well as by terrible hosts of diseases,
they faint at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
In some places they are boiled in oils, in other places they are beaten with pestles; in some places they are roasted on iron spikes, and in others they are cooked upon stones.
In one place they eat what has been vomited; in another, pus and blood; in another, excrement; and in another, putrid flesh—terrible indeed to the mind. (16)
And in some places they are being devoured by worms and by sparks of fire, amidst heaps of hair, blood, flesh, gore, fat, and bones. (17)
The corpses lay scattered, clearly devoured by worms and torn apart by the beaks of crows, herons, and great vultures. ||18||
In the fortress of Śiva, amidst hundreds of millions of violent collisions, and among the saws, stone-slicers, and those heated without oil; (19)
In houses made of iron, oil, fat, and heaps of thorny śālmalī trees,
it shines with razors, axes, spikes, and fierce flames.
[They were] scorched individually in [the hells] filled with the pus of the Vaitaraṇī river,
and in the Asipatravana forest where the breasts of men and women were lopped off.
Tormented repeatedly by the terrible seizing of the syllable *dhakāra*,
they cry out as they are cooked by various horrific forms of execution.
In some places they were bound by nooses at their necks and coiled around by serpents;
likewise, they were being tormented by crows and dragged along by their knees.
With their backs, heads, and necks broken, and their jaws rendered stiff, they suffer most terrible torments,
being whirled about in gabled towers with bodies capable of enduring such agony.
O King, those sinful evildoers who cry out in distress are made to wail together with the very tastes of the sensory objects they once enjoyed. (25)
All this that has been done by you, born of every vice, is now being experienced; attachment to the wives of others, though performed for pleasure, brings only suffering. (26)

The taste of the sensory objects experienced for even a moment gives rise to suffering for many years; such is the case for one who performs the morning bath in the month of Mādhava while your body is adorned with the king of hymns. 27.
Having obtained your touch according to the prescribed rite, these winds, though previously impure, have attained happiness for a moment and have been nourished by your splendor. (28)
Deprived of all cries for help by that [sin], they remain in hell;
even the name of those of virtuous conduct is proclaimed to bring happiness when heard. (29)
The touch of the wind that brushed against his body became a source of great comfort.
Yama said:
Having heard these words of the messenger, the king, who was a treasure-house of compassion, [spoke]. (30)
He replied to the messengers of Viṣṇu, the performer of wondrous deeds:
"The hearts of the virtuous are surely as tender as fresh butter. (31)
"Just as that which is heated by fire melts and bursts apart when scorched," the king said,
"I cannot bring myself to go and afflict him, even though he has caused me no harm."
Fie on that most wicked man who, though capable, does not alleviate the suffering of those in distress;
for he has been purified by the touch of the wind from my mouth, which was defiled by contact with wine and remnants of food. (33)
Since they have become happy through austerity, therefore I must lead them there;
by that very act, these men purify their mother and the earth as well.
Those who cut away the suffering of others are like sandalwood trees;
those who cause pain even while performing service for others are not considered wise men.
Those who destroy the suffering of others remain steadfast in this world;
for the sake of destroying the affliction of the distressed, their own lives are as insignificant to them as a blade of grass. (36)
This earth is sustained by those men who are intent on the welfare of others;
for that constant happiness of the mind is like heaven itself, though it may appear as hell to others. (37)
Therefore, the virtuous are always happy through the happiness of others alone; in this regard, it is better to fall into hell than to remain otherwise, and better to give up one's life. (38)
"Furthermore, for those in distress, there is no happiness except for the destruction of that distress.
The messengers said:
"Those sinners who are being cooked by you in this terrible hell—" (39)
They subsist solely on their own karma; no ground for delusion exists for those by whom nothing has been given, no oblation offered, and no bath taken at sacred fords. (40)

O King, by those who have not rendered assistance again with devotion, nor performed the highest good deed, nor offered sacrifice, nor practiced austerity, nor recited prayers, nor rejoiced with gladness—[they have failed]. (41)
In the future, they— those of evil character, wicked conduct, and censured for their dwellings, food, and habits— will be cooked in the most terrible hells.
Those who harm others, those who commit evil, those who live wickedly, and those who tear open the vital points with their speech—such sinners indeed cause distress to the hearts of others. (43)
Those who consort with the wives of others are surely cooked in hell;
come now, O protector of the earth, let us go to the abode of Hari. 44.
"Therefore, it is not fitting for one who possesses merit to remain here any longer.
The king said:
"O messengers, if I am a man of virtuous deeds, why then do you [afflict] me with this great terror?"
"Or was some supreme merit brought from hell?
For even I, though possessed of desire, did not perform such meritorious deeds. (46)
"How can I, who am lying down, avoid being taken away?
The messengers said:
"Truly, no good deed was performed by you, whose soul was under the sway of desire. (47)
It was not desired that you eat what remains from sacrifices or from the remnants of offerings;
