rather, it was intended that you should do so according to the prescribed rule for three years during the month of Mādhava.
In the past, having bathed at dawn, Viṣṇu—the Lord of the Universe, the slayer of Madhu—was worshipped by you with devotion, impelled by the words of your guru. (49)
O Lord of Men, he who is compassionate toward his devotees and destroys the flood of great sins and even greater evils, is that one alone who is the sole essence of all dharmas. 50.
Being honored by hosts of gods, he is led to the abode of merit; for even great sins are destroyed when Mādhava is worshipped. 51.
In that very manner, Mādhava and Umā, impelled by fate, were like a heap of grass being set ablaze by a single spark. 52.
By means of the morning bath in Vaiśākha, even a multitude of sins is consumed; for as long as [one does not bathe], even great sins prevail within the body. (53)
As long as a man bathes at dawn in the sacred ford during the month of Āṣāḍha,
and remains disciplined throughout the month of Vaiśākha according to the prescribed rules— (54)
"Only through devotion to Hari shall you be liberated from the flood of sins and go to the abode of Acyuta;
for whatever merit was performed by you previously since birth—" (55)
"O Lord of Men, you have thus been led onto the path to the abode of hell.
Then, by us, the hosts of Maruts, the King of the Earth was quickly [rescued]. (56)
Being praised, go by means of a celestial chariot to the abode of Govinda.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||101||
(102) The one hundred and second chapter.
Yama said:
Then, O Brāhmaṇa, that king, an ocean of compassion, afflicted by grief for them, spoke with humility to the messengers of Śrī Hari.

For those who are born into sovereignty, for those of noble lineage, for those of merit, and for those of virtuous deeds—the true fruit of these is indeed counted as the protection of those who are afraid. ||2||
If there is any merit whatsoever belonging to me, by that alone may you go to heaven;
O multitudes of liberated ones, I shall dwell in your stead.
Having thus heard the words of the king, who was intent on the welfare of Satyavat, they meditated upon his truthfulness and magnanimity and spoke these words to the monarch: (4)
The messengers said:
"O King, by this compassionate deed and these words of yours, there has been a particular increase in your accumulated merit. (5)
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, austerity, worship of the gods, and so forth—whatever is performed in the month of Mādhava, they know that to yield infinite fruit. (6)
The donor sports in heaven with the gods, amidst golden lotuses in the ponds and at the foot of the wish-fulfilling trees.
Being sung of with joy by hosts of celestial nymphs,
he attains the auspicious realm of Varuṇa through the gift of water and food.
The giver of a cow effortlessly delivers seven generations of his lineage;
by giving a horse, a man goes to the world of the Sun; and the giver of knowledge [attains the highest state]. ||9||
Likewise, by the gift of gold one goes to the world of Brahmā; and he who gives a maiden in marriage likewise goes to the abode of the supreme gods, the realm of Viṣṇu. (10)
Having bathed in the month of Mādhava, having given gifts, and having fully worshipped Mādhava, one attains all desires and proceeds to the imperishable state. ||11||
On one side are the activities such as austerity, charity, and the performance of sacrifices;
on the other side is the great month of Mādhava, which by its very nature [outweighs] them all according to the sacred injunctions.
O King, whatever meritorious deed is performed even on a single day of that month of Mādhava was formerly declared by you to be superior to all other gifts. (13)
O Lord of the Earth, O treasury of compassion, grant merit for even a single day to those suffering beings who are being cooked in hell. (14)
There is no dharma like compassion; there is no austerity like compassion; there is no gift like compassion; there is no friend like compassion. (15)
A giver of merit always obtains merit a hundred thousand times greater;
through compassion in particular, therefrom shall arise an increase of dharma.
Indeed, he who is the remover of the suffering of beings who are afflicted with pain—he alone, O son of Nārāyaṇa, is to be known as a man of merit in this world. 17.
O Hero, the bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites which were performed by you at the sacred ford on the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha have destroyed all sins. (18)
Therefore, having made Hari the Lord the witness for them according to the ritual for the body,
let him perform the threefold verbal rite so that these people may attain heaven instead of hell and other lower realms.
In former times, Śibi, a treasure-house of compassion, gave his own flesh out of pity for a pigeon;
that ocean of fame now shines in heaven.
The royal sage Dadhīci, having given his own collection of bones,
attained fame that was like moonlight to the three worlds and an imperishable heaven.
The highly illustrious royal sage Sahasrajit, having renounced his dear life-breaths for the sake of a Brahmin, went to the unsurpassed worlds. 22.

A person does not obtain that happiness even in heaven or in liberation which arises from the relief of the suffering of others; such is my conviction regarding the merit born from the gift of nirvāṇa. (23)
O Lord of the Earth, among all those born as givers, you were born first;
by this deed, O wise one, you have established yourself in steadfastness. 24.
Having seen this unwavering commitment to the gift of the Dharma out of compassion, we too, who speak of the Dharma, shall exert ourselves. (25)
O King, if you truly desire it, then bestow upon them that merit which burns away the suffering of their torments. (26)
Having been addressed thus, the compassionate Gadādhara then acted accordingly and, according to the prescribed rite, bestowed upon them the merit of his testimony three times over.
In that month of Mādhava, on a day when [the festival] occurs for even a single day, those who perform it themselves shall be freed from the torments of hell. (28)
Mounted upon excellent celestial chariots, they all went to the third heaven, bowing down, praising, and gazing at him with great joy. (29)
Having obtained that merit bestowed by the king, which arose from a single day of the month of Vaiśākha, they all went forth; liberated from hell, they reached heaven in marvelous celestial chariots.
Surely the multitude of beings on earth is diverse; the manifestation of existence is manifold and varied.
Likewise, the application of all actions is diverse, and the accumulation of the power of those actions is diverse. (31)
Being praised by the hosts of sages and gods, he— having acquired even greater merit through those specific [deeds]—
went to the supreme state unattainable even by the best of yogis, while being saluted by the attendants of the Lord of the World.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter in the Vaiśākha-māsa-māhātmya of the Pātāla-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||102||
The one hundred and third chapter.
Yama said:
This has been described briefly and in summary regarding the month of Mādhava.
O best of the twice-born, [I shall describe] the greatness of the full moon day, especially its excellence.
He who recites this history, which is dear to Madhusūdana, during the month of Vaiśākha, becomes purified and swiftly goes to the abode of Kṛṣṇa; he rejoices there for many kalpas.
This great rite of auspiciousness brings prosperity, fame, and long life; it leads to heaven, bestows fortune, grants mental well-being, is highly praised, and purifies all sins. (3)
This is the majesty of the month of Mādhava, which is dear to Mādhava;
it is the history of that king and also our own conversation.
Having heard, recited, and duly rejoiced in this which is dear to the mind, may there arise devotion to the Blessed One through which the destruction of one's sins occurs. (5)
Then, O Mahīdeva, we departed from the world of the gods as we pleased;
having cast the King of Videha down upon the earth, his kinsmen continue to weep even now.
Even as those kinsmen lamented, they did not cast my body into the fire;
thus, like one who has fallen asleep and remains unawakened, I have not yet departed from this world.
"By my grace, perform this rite exactly as you have heard it, for through this conjunction of merit;
by performing it according to the rules at the proper time, your meeting with the gods shall surely come to pass."
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the god and having bowed to the Lord of Dharma, the twice-born man then fell down again here with a deeply satisfied mind. 9.
Then, by the grace of Dharmarāja, he rose up there upon the surface of the earth as if from sleep, accompanied by his circle of kinsmen.
Every year, this twice-born man himself performed this rite on earth,
and he personally caused the people to perform the ritual bathing of Mādhava.
This dialogue between Yama and the Brahmin has been fully narrated by me in connection with the meritorious ritual bathing during the month of Mādhava.

If a wise person constantly performs ritual bathing with devotion during the month of Vaiśākha, which is dear to Hari, and likewise offers gifts, performs fire-sacrifices, and practices virtuous deeds, then for him the abode of Hari will never be difficult to attain. 13.
He who listens with a one-pointed mind to this majesty arising from the Sun in Aries, being liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (14)
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta of great wisdom, by you, whose soul is exceedingly compassionate, has been proclaimed the majesty of the month of Vaiśākha, which destroys all sins. (15)
The worship, bathing, giving of gifts, and so forth, for the slayer of Madhu during the months of Niyama and Mādhava, which were described by you according to the Śrauta and Smārta injunctions— [16]—
Just as Lord Mādhava, the destroyer of sins, is pleased, we now wish to hear the meditation (dhyāna) upon that Great-Souled One. 17.
The incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, who is dear to the multitude of his devotees, for the sake of their deliverance. ||18||
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to the [deeds] of Kṛṣṇa, the Soul of the universe, whose very life-breath is the cows, the cowherds, and the gopīs, and who wanders in Vṛndāvana. 19.
O best of the twice-born, once Nārada was questioned by Gautama;
I shall now describe to you that meditation which he taught him, which destroys all sins. (20)
Nārada said:

One of sharp intellect should constantly meditate upon the beautiful Vṛndāvana, which possesses the splendor of being bent by clusters of fresh sprouts on trees shimmering with honey-dripping blossoms of exquisite fragrance, and which is entwined by charming creepers bearing clusters of newly blossomed flowers. 21.
Its interior was made resonant by the humming of bees moving about while tasting the nectar of blossoming jasmine flowers;
it was filled with the cries of pigeons, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and other birds, and was agitated here and there by the dancing of peacocks, the natural enemies of serpents. ||22||
It was incessantly served by winds that bore the spray of the tossing waves of the Yamunā, were grey with the pollen from the bellies of blooming lotuses,
and were restless as they stirred the garments of the playful women of Vraja whose passion had been kindled.

One should meditate upon that wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) rising within it— possessing sprouts of fresh coral and emerald leaves, buds with the luster of a multitude of pearls, various fruits with the hue of lotuses, most massive, constantly served by all the seasons, and granting all desires. (24)

Then the wise man, unwearied, should again meditate upon that golden ground below the mountain of excellent golden peaks, which shines like the rising sun, which showers sprays of nectar, whose jeweled pavement is ablaze, which is radiant with a mass of flower-pollen, and from which the six waves have departed. (25)
Having meditated upon an eight-petalled red lotus situated upon a most expansive yogic seat set within that jeweled pavement,
one should then contemplate Mukunda seated comfortably in its center, possessing the splendor of the rising sun.

O King, [his head] possesses a mass of very glossy, dark-blue, thick, and curled hair, shining like a cluster of fresh blue lotuses—clouds of collyrium shattered by the wind of the Great Ancestor (Brahmā)—and is crowned with the crest of the beautiful, blue-throated Śiva’s peacock feather. 27.

It was endowed with the splendor of the son of the celestial tree (Pārijāta) cherished by the Rolamba bees; it had a fresh blue lotus as an earring that was beginning to bloom, a tilaka-mark of gorocana shining on its forehead flickered by restless bees, and it possessed a radiant bow of Cillicāpa.
His face was as beautiful as the orb of the autumnal full moon; his eyes were wide like lotus petals;
his cheeks served as mirrors illuminated by the radiance of shimmering jewel-encrusted makara-shaped earrings; and his nose was high and lovely. (29)
Her lower lip is more beautiful than vermilion; her smile, radiant as the moon, jasmine, and mandāra flowers, illuminates the quarters of space;
her conch-like neck is lovely and brilliant, adorned with a necklace fashioned from a cluster of wild sprouts and blossoms. (30)
It was adorned with a long, flowing garland resounding with the humming of intoxicated, wandering bees;
it possessed thick thighs shining like the sun-kaustubha gem upon the expanse of the sky, which was graced by a multitude of pearl necklaces.
He was beautifully marked with the auspicious Śrīvatsa sign; his arms were elevated, reaching down to his knees, thick, rounded, and well-formed;
his belly was slightly concave, possessing a noble and deep navel; and his line of body hair was dark like a swarm of female bees.

His arms were adorned with armlets fashioned from various jewels, as were his bracelets, necklaces, girdles, anklets, and waist-bands; his slender body was anointed with divine unguents, and the curves of his hips were draped in saffron-colored garments. (33)
With beautiful thighs and knees, and lovely calves that follow their natural curve, his lovely and elevated forefeet surpass the splendor of the tortoise.
His lotus-like feet are beautiful, with toenails shining like rubies and toes as lovely as crimson petals. ||34||
His palms and soles were beautiful, marked with the fish, goad, lotus-stalk, banner, barley-corn, lotus, and thunderbolt;
his limbs were fashioned from the very essence of loveliness, and the splendor of his body surpassed that of the God of Love in beauty. (35)

I bow to Him, the ocean of infinite bliss, who constantly brings about the cessation of suffering for all beings through the divine melodies produced by His fingers moving over the holes of the flute filled by His lotus-like mouth.
Then he was surrounded by cows whose eyes were fixed upon his lotus-like face, who moved slowly and languidly as they stumbled under the weight of their udders,
who held the tips of remaining blades of grass between their teeth, and whose creeper-like tails were swaying.
And with the calves, whose mouths were fixed and full of the milk flowing from their teats and ornaments, which was thick with froth as it trickled steadily;
and who had pricked up their pair of ears for the charming, slow song set to the flute; [he was surrounded] by those young ones as well. (38)

With herds of young male and female calves, whose heads were tender with fresh horns, who struck the ground with their hooves as they frolicked in playful excitement, whose dewlaps were thick and moist, and whose tails were held erect; (39)

With great bulls whose bellowing agitated the circle of the quarters, who were weary from the burden of their massive humps, and whose broad nostrils blossomed wide as they drank the nectar of the sound of the *vaṃśa* flute poured into their ears; ||40||

Accompanied by cowherds whose qualities, character, age, grace, and dress were identical to his own, who played flutes and lutes with sweet, resonant sounds, who were intent on singing in low, high, and sharp modulations, and who were skilled in performing charming dances with their swaying, vine-like arms. (41)
It was surrounded by playful children whose calves were thick at the ends and whose broad hips were bound with clusters of dangling tinkling bells that jingled as they ran;
these children wore beautiful ornaments fashioned from the claws of hyenas and spoke indistinct, sweet words. (42)

Then [he beheld] the beautiful cowherd girls, graceful and slow-moving due to their broad hips and heavy braided hair; they bore prominent lines of body hair that emerged as their triple folds of skin were pressed by the weight of their heavy breasts.

Of those whose sprout-like limbs were made to blossom by the nectar-essence of the exceedingly beautiful and charming sound of the flute, and whose creeper-like bodies were adorned with the pure and lovely buds of rising horripilation; (44)

Of those whose ocean of the waters of passion was expanded by the moonlight of that exceedingly beautiful gentle smile, [the faces] were covered with a dense mass of drops of perspiration, like a multitude of droplets from the breaking of most tremulous waves. 45.

By the rain of sharp arrows of glances discharged from the exceedingly charming bow of her slightly arched eyebrows, there arose unbearable pains of trembling spreading through limbs distressed by every vital point being pierced. ||46||

Of those whose lotus-eyes were languidly tremulous, flowing with the floodwaters of affection, and who were eager to drink the nectar-essence of the beauty of his exceedingly radiant attire and form; (47)

[The faces] of those women, whose soft voices faltered with the intoxication and madness of passion, who were repeatedly attended by swarms of bees greedy for honey dripping from the full-blown flowers falling from their loosened tresses, and who shone with dangling waistbands— ...
...the radiance of their hips, where the edges of their Chinese silk garments were loosened by their *nīvī* (waist-knots). ||48||
Of those whose faces in all directions were filled with the tinkling of jeweled anklets set in motion by the gentle impact of lotus-feet stumbling in playful gait,
and whose bud-like lower lips quivered, their eyes long-lashed like blossoming buds—
Of the two lotuses, with their shimmering earrings. ||49||

It was constantly attended on all sides by rows of women whose sprout-like lips were withered by the heat of the wind from their longest sighs, and whose lotus-hands shone as they offered various gifts.
His entire body was worshipped by them with garlands of full-blown lotuses resting upon their long, tremulous, dark-blue eyes; he was the locus of manifold amorous graces,
and she tasted the honey-like nectar trickling from the lotus-face of that charming youth.
Wearing with affection a captivating garland of bees that steals the honey from my eyes. ||51||
Outside and in front of him, one should visualize the host of gods, led by Brahmā, Śiva, and Indra, who are intent on praise and seeking wealth from the cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle.
Likewise, to his right was a multitude of sages who were devoted to the sacred tradition out of a firm desire for Dharma;
and behind him were the lords of yogis, Sanaka and the others, seeking liberation through meditative absorption.

Then he [beheld] the yakṣas, siddhas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and cāraṇas, together with their beloveds on their left, along with the kinnaras and the principal apsarases who, desiring love, were engaged in dancing, singing, and instrumental music. (54)
To him who is as white as a conch, the moon, or a kunda flower, who knows all the scriptures, whose mass of matted hair is tawny like a multitude of lightning flashes,
and to the stainless devotion directed toward his lotus feet—
Desiring [this], having utterly abandoned all other attachments. ||55||

He who, with devotion, fully delights [the senses] through the enchanting modulations (*mūrcchanās*) belonging to the three scales (*grāmas*) and the seven musical notes (*svaras*), which are endowed with the qualities of various Vedic melodies and have arisen.
He reflected upon the boundary of the sky, produced by Druhiṇa.
Having thus meditated upon himself as the son of Nanda, a person of sharp and clear intellect should worship Him again with devotion—
both through blameless offerings such as the *argha* water and so forth, by means of the intellect alone,
and with external riches within his own body.
Thus has everything been declared that was desired, O best of the gods on earth.
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vaiśākha," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Glorification of the Month of Vaiśākha is complete.
The Dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava (104):
The One Hundred and Fourth Chapter.
The sages said:
O highly fortunate one, speak further of the wondrous life of Rāma—the entire essence of Rāma’s majesty, which bestows joy upon his devotees. (1)
Sūta said:
Just as the son of Daśaratha performed the horse sacrifice, the best of rituals.
Engaged in worldly affairs and skilled in the performance of scriptural duties, he was [sent] by the high-souled Śaṅkara, who desired to go to Ayodhyā. ||3||
Having dwelt on the bank of the Sarayū with the Goddess Pārvatī, the sages approached him who was accompanied by Śaṅkara and possessed a universal form. ||4||
Kaśyapa and the other great-souled ones questioned him of immeasurable splendor:
"Welcome to you, O best of sages; from where have you come with your wife? (5)
"What is the purpose of your coming? To which country are you prepared to go?
Śaṅkara said: "I am a brahmin known as Śambhu, residing on the Himālaya mountain. (6)
"I must go to see Rāghava, for I have a great task;
lest that king, who is devoted to hearing ancient lore, summon me. (7)
"May you also come; Rāghava will be well-pleased.
Then those sages went to Śambhu, desiring to see Rāma.
Vasiṣṭha, having learned that they had arrived, informed Rāma;
thereupon, the family priest rose quickly and went out.
The subduer of enemies honored all those sages with offerings of water for the hands and feet and other rites;
then he led them all into the king of houses.
Having offered individual seats and welcomed them as they sat,
that tiger among the Raghus honored those sages one by one in due order.
Pleasing them with sweet words as they sat there, Śrī Rāma spoke this:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today the fruit of my penance has been attained. (12)
Today the time has come for the fruit of my studies and sciences;
today my ancestors are satisfied, and my kingdom is fruitful. (13)
"Today my conduct has borne fruit; today my learning has borne fruit.
To the king who was speaking thus, the brahmins, Kaśyapa and the others, [replied]. (14)
The sages spoke these most pleasing words to the lotus-eyed Rāma:
"This brahmin Śambhu has arrived; he is an expert in all the scriptures. (15)
A knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, devoted to the welfare of all beings, he dwelt constantly on Kailāsa, firmly resolved upon ascetic penance. ||16||
In sacred splendor he was equal to Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman;
in affection for Brahmins he was like Hari, and in graciousness he was comparable to Śaṅkara. ||17||
Such was Śambhu, the preeminent among brahmins, possessed of great splendor;
he was a knower of the eighteen Purāṇas and an expert in Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya. ||18||
"O Lord, it is solely due to the weight of your good fortune that this best of sages has arrived;
having been summoned by you, the excellent sage has come from Kailāsa. (19)
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, descendant of Raghu, we have come to you today desiring to hear the supreme narrative of the Purāṇa; we ask you about it.
For that man who knows the meaning of all the scriptures and the Vedas, yet has not heard the Purāṇas, there is no correct perception of the ultimate goal. (21)
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by the sages who perceive the ultimate truth, the best of the Raghus,
eager to hear the Purāṇa, experienced incomparable joy.
Śrī Rāma said:
[Tell me] the method of worshipping the liṅga and the majesty of the liṅga itself, as well as the majesty of the name of Maheśa and the majesty of the worship itself. (23)
The greatness of the prostration, as well as the greatness of the vision, the greatness of the offering of water, and the greatness of the offering of incense, O best of beings. (24)
The greatness of giving lamps, incense, and so forth, as well as the majesty of flowers, and the story that destroys sin from various legends and histories. (25)
O observer of noble vows, O most excellent of sages, I wish to hear from you all that pertains to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, as well as their respective means. (26)
Śambhu said:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed Rāghava, you are meritorious;
for one so devoted to sovereignty, a delight in hearing the Purāṇas has arisen. (27)
O Rāma, it may come about through service to the great and by frequenting sacred pilgrimage sites;
yet that alone is the true tongue which sings of Śiva, and that alone is the true mind which is dedicated to Him. 28.
Only those two hands are truly praiseworthy which perform worship of Him;
that alone is a truly noble birth and body throughout all future lives. (29)
That you shine with such horripilation from the chanting of Hara’s name—you have achieved your purpose, O Great King, for your intellect has followed after that inquiry. (30)
Immediately thereafter, messengers arrived, exhausted from their rapid journey;
taking a letter from the hand of one of them, the best of the Raghus read it. (31)
Rāma wondered in his mind, "How has this come to pass?
Then Śambhu, appearing in the guise of a brahmin, spoke to Rāma in the presence of the Goddess.
"O descendant of Kakutstha, what are you thinking, even though the sages are seated before you?
Having heard those words, Rāghava questioned the preeminent sages. (33)
Śrī Rāma said: "How was this Bibhīṣaṇa bound with chains by men?
Alas! Having seen the Śiva-liṅga Rāmeśvara installed by me! (34)
"Let that be considered by you yourselves, O crooked and wicked Dravidians!
Having reflected thus, the best of sages, the lords, became desirous of knowing it through subtle means. (35)
"We do not know," they said to Rāma; then Rāma spoke to them:
"O best of beings, having examined that ancient [account] according to the prescribed rule, tell me all of it. (36)
Immediately after that, one should investigate the cause of your ignorance: which ancient texts are worthy of examination, and likewise, which are to be avoided? (37)
What kind of verse is praised, and what would another be like? In what kinds of rites, moreover, what kind of worshiper is likewise required? (38)
"And by what kind of devotees should worship be performed according to the definitive vision?
Having heard these words of Rāma, those best of the twice-born [replied]: ||39||
They replied to that best of the Raghus, whose mind was agitated by anxiety:
"O Rāma, those who know the Purāṇas do not say that it is better for one who is looking [for a bride] to wait. (40)
Having heard that, Rāghava, filled with humility, questioned Śambhu;
and he too, having heard those words, the high-minded one, replied. (41)
Śambhu said:

One who lives according to the Purāṇas, is worthy of worship, studies his own Vedic branch, is pure, possesses knowledge of the principles of Mīmāṃsā, is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), and is a censurer of falsehood; ||42||
Maintaining an equal vision toward all the gods, he was devoted to Śiva;
he was a reciter of the Śatarudriya, a maintainer of the sacred fires, and an eloquent speaker. ||43||
A wise person should especially worship the manuscript of the Yajurveda, which is auspiciously written on palm leaves in the Devanagari script. (44)
That which simultaneously transcends the vast proliferation beginning with bondage is the syllable *praṇava*;
it is the one that joins the tip of the *praṇava* to the ends of the two lines at the top. 45.
In the absence of lines, there is a single *deva* (the letter *e*), with the letter *a* at its side;
beginning from the head portion, it hangs down from below the corner. 46.
That form should indeed be understood from the line of the beads on the rosary;
on the left, it is proclaimed as having six curves, two dots, and two openings. (47)
That which rests upon the line of its left head is called Āī;
all the lines of the heads of the letters, except for the *praṇava*, are straight. (48)
In that [line], the letter *u* is well-known as being like the two blades of a grass-cutter (*lavitra*), with its head and tail resembling the lines of a balance-scale. 49.
In this way, Bhāratī spoke all the other syllables; "Indeed, the Purāṇa written by you in this very script is praiseworthy. (50)
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Mārtaṇḍa spoken by Nārada, the Mārkaṇḍeya, the Āgneya, the Kaurma, and the Vāmana; ||51||
The Gāruḍa, Laiṅga, Skānda, Mātsya, and Nṛsiṃhaka have been proclaimed;
likewise, O Rāma, the Kāpila Purāṇa has been spoken.
The Vārāha, Brahmavaivarta, Śaiva, Bhāgavata, Daurga, and the Bhaviṣyottara are likewise praised among the Śakunas. (53)
One should avoid other future designations as well;
having set aside the book and placed it upon a jeweled throne, one should perform the consecration. //54//
Having bathed, wearing clean garments, pure, free from anger and feverish distress,
he should first worship himself and then make his formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
One should meditate upon Sarasvatī, who is white in color, with a serene countenance, and holding a goad, a rosary, a noose, and a book. (56)
Śiva has a form resembling cow's milk, possesses three eyes, and has a bull as his vehicle;
he has a smiling face, is peaceful, and wears white garments. 57.

He holds a deer and the gesture of fearlessness with his two upraised arms, wears a crown, displays the gesture of exposition (vyākhyā-mudrā) in his lower right hand, and grants boons with his left hand. 58.
Richly adorned with various jewels, seated upon a lotus half-shared with the Daughter of the Mountain, his lotus feet were being meditated upon by many eminent sages. (59)
He was being praised by the ancient Vedas in their embodied forms,
and his lotus feet were served by all other worlds.
Having meditated thus, the worshipper should properly commence the worship at the outset;
"Āpo vā idam" (Water indeed [was] this) is the consecration of the water-pot.
Having taken that water and placed it in a vessel,
one should consecrate it with the mantra "tat sad brahma" and then praise it with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Then one should invoke the Self and all the vessels; this is done with the three verses beginning with "yad vāk," and the sixteen-fold worship is performed for Bhāratī. (63)
One should perform the worship either with the Puruṣasūkta or with the Gāyatrī;
one should worship the Purāṇa with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, [Name], the Purāṇa."
Having brought dūrvā grass with the mantra "From the stalk" (kāṇḍāt), one should worship it with:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lady Dūrvā. ||65||
There may be worship of the world-protectors (lokapālas), or else the honoring of a maiden;
she is auspicious when she is more than five years old and less than ten years old. ||66||
Even if the season has not yet arrived, one should worship her with effort using perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, lamps, betel, and ornaments. (67)
The worshipper should also cause this maiden to recite this mantra. ||68||
"Speak the truth, speak what is pleasant; O Blessed Sarasvatī, homage to you, homage to you! ||69||
However, according to the sequence of the Gāyatrī, one should place a pair of dūrvā grass blades beneath the book using the verse beginning with "sahasra-paramā. (70)
The wise [preceptor] should place two or three blades of *dūrvā* grass into her hand;
she should then insert them one after another into the joints of the book. (71)
"Let it be released again; one should give [the offering] with 'Salutation to Śiva and Śivā.
For the middle verse between the two leaves is indeed indicative of the success of the undertaking. (72)
O Rāghava, if the completion of a verse occurs on the front leaf, one should recite the verse on the back leaf and explain its meaning after careful discernment. //73//
The wise man should recite slowly and explain slowly;
for speech uttered with haste becomes agitated, as there is nothing to be done in haste.
A quarter of a ghaṭikā should be allowed for the time; it should be more than that, yet one should not urge the speaker.
O twice-born one, this is to be understood regarding the pacification [of obstacles].
Having carefully analyzed the recitation of the verse and determined its meaning in one's mind, O descendant of Raghu, one should not speak against it after such deliberation. (76)
If that worshipper, being a virtuous twice-born, should set aside the book and recite another verse, whether it be appropriate or inappropriate; 77.
That should indeed be understood as such; a false report is not praised.
For a verse that has come by chance is powerful, for fate is indeed most mighty.
Just as one should not feel resentment toward a Brahmin who has overheard [one's secrets], so too one should not give way to wonder; crooked is the course of destiny.
That which is in the reversal of the syllables, on the leaf, and surrounded by water—having disregarded that, one should then recite the second [syllable]. 80.
Then the third [letter] should be recited, and thereafter the discernment must be performed:
those ending in a visarga, the first letters of the vargas, and the fifth letters other than the labials (pa-varga). (81)
A verse devoid of praise or the optative mood is commended among omens;
likewise, the beginning of a chapter, its conclusion, a blank leaf, and illegible writing [are auspicious]. (82)
Reciting what has been said, as well as both forms of *upastuta*, and likewise *atha*;
"burnt leaf," "lost writing," and "doubtful syllable" (83).

However, certain differences in purpose are described as being useful for mortals;

Then, having approached him, he asked that question; what does he remember here? He again took up that document; on that document, the question is praised. (87)
Alternatively, it may be endowed with equanimity toward that [object], or even with supreme dispassion;

Furthermore, having set aside that which is inauspicious regarding that matter, the question "Does the deceased grasp the meaning of the words? is a source of inauspiciousness. (89)
In a query regarding victory in a dispute, a malefic [planet] is desired as an indicator of victory;

When [the composition] is composed with various means and is tranquil, it becomes the Viḍvara; that which contains descriptions of cities and so forth is either middling or excellent. 91.
In the description of erotic sentiment, the apprehension of strife is auspicious;
in the deliberation on the administration of a kingdom, the signs of sovereignty are auspicious. (92)
Whatever is appropriate for whomsoever, that should be considered by the wise;
the dissolution of both praise and detachment is proclaimed as the goal. (93)
When there is little success in one's task, one fails to reach completion due to stumbling; this is the transformation of one thing into another when reflecting upon Rama’s tranquility. 94.
And there will be a reversal of the first half, ending with the visarga, just as the meditative object (bhāva) intended [by the practitioner] is completed in the meditation (adhyāya). //95//
However, upon the completion of a section (kāṇḜa) or the like, there may be the destruction of that effect; therefore, in such a case, there is a reversal of the omen. 96.

That [work] is middling in its results where the creation is described as "saṃtāna";

In marriage, in the giving of medicine, in legal transactions, and likewise in agriculture,

By means of this analogy, that effect is either accomplished very quickly, or it is not accomplished at all;

O King, even on the days specifically appointed for it, one's undertaking may fall into doubt;

Having eaten, one should rise; likewise, one should not look upon anything old.

On the following day at dawn, after the bird has eaten its food,

One should declare the specific nature of an omen based on distinctions such as its process and other characteristics;

The infliction of punishment, the reversal of the regions of curses, and the pure slaughter of living beings by the Rākṣasas, those of wicked nature. (119)
From burning arises the manifestation of a deity; from spitting, vomiting, weeping, laughing, loathsomeness, sorrow, bad dreams, delusion, and sin. (120)
There will be the filling of cloth and other items, as well as suffering, quarrels, and death;

"Be compassionate toward all; you have become my servant in every way.

Adorned with lovely groves, ponds, and climbing plants,
it summoned the god of love by means of the humming swarms of bees.
The sun proceeds as if to ascend the midday twilight;
having bathed in the waters of the shadow-pool, he puts on two fine garments.
Having smeared themselves with excellent sandalwood paste ground from musk and camphor, they were joined together by firm braided hair adorned with garlands of sallakī flowers.
There, in a beautiful fountain-house, they tasted and relished betel-leaf of abundant and excellent quality, while exhilarated and joyful.
Amidst the abundant cries of peacocks and sweet songs outside,
they remained upon their spread bed, dwelling in mutual happiness.
If my face, with its broad smile and red lips, is kissed, then the fruit of our essence will have been inhaled by us both. (9)

"Was this idle chatter out of attachment to your beloved? Or was our word disregarded? Then, from her face, which was turned away in anger, there arose a most extraordinary [sound]. 11.
Emerging from the flames, she too became one with a terrifying countenance;

Seeing Rāma, she was intent on flight and became afraid;

Rāghava departed by means of the Puṣpaka chariot itself, repeatedly speaking of liberation; yet he did not even remember to discharge Bāṇa with his bow.
Even Śambhu, having beheld extremely meritorious forests, sacred shrines, and various wonderful cities, did not remember Rāma.
In an instant, he reached the great mountain Lokāloka;
then Rāghava beheld that mountain, which was filled with paths leading to dwellings.
"O illustrious one, where has my wife gone? he asked the twice-born ones. They replied to him, "She has gone to the region of darkness belonging to Aṅgiras. (17)
Rāma, his face pale, thought, "Alas, what misery!
Then Śambhu, of great splendor, bestowed upon him incomparable light. 18.
By the power of that light, Rāma followed after the Kṛtyā;
she was a great ground consisting of darkness, devoid of all living beings. 19.
Extending for hundreds of millions of yojanas up to the shell of the Brahma-egg,
the great silver ground is situated in the midst of the waters.
There they beheld Nārāyaṇapura, radiant with the splendor of ten million suns and praised by Rāma and the best of sages; seeing it, they were filled with wonder.
Thinking, "What is this? he considered: "How could there be an entry [into the body]?

"Or rather, what will be better for you— death or life?"—

I shall tell you this wonder: by your deed, this Maya has been rendered as if it were non-existent."
This, however, is the supreme abode of Nārāyaṇa, radiant and luminous;
it is impenetrable by heat, cold, and the like, accessible through knowledge, and not visible to the eye. ||25||
Furthermore, behold those led by Brahmā as they worship that [Supreme Being], and behold the stainless sages in all directions as they offer their worship. (26)
Beholding the four Vedas and praising the supreme state,
the yogis headed by Sanaka and others diligently applied themselves to yoga.
They meditate upon that supreme splendor; behold this, O Raghava!
Behold this man with the hairy body as you perform a circumambulation to the right.
He was performing [his duties] for tens of millions upon tens of millions of Vālakhilyas, the lords of sages,
while his supreme abode was being worshipped by all women, beginning with Lakṣmī.
Brahman is proclaimed to be both with form and without form;
those lacking knowledge do not see it, but those who possess the eye of wisdom do see it. (30)
Therefore, following the words of Śambhu, they all worshipped Acyuta,
as well as girikarṇī, tulasī, mallikā, and likewise māruta.
With blue lotuses, water lilies, and even dark, unopened aquatic flowers,
the great-souled ones were worshipping the Great-Souled Janārdana.
Then they beheld Nārada in the sky, with matted hair and carrying a lute,
resounding with the sound of the word "Nārāyaṇa," and wearing a long beard and a sacred thread.
Even as he was reflecting in his mind, "Is this Nārada?",
he fell at the feet of the Lord Śambhu, overflowing with joy.
The sage mentally recited the five-syllabled Śaiva mantra:
"I am blessed; I am favored; this birth of mine is fruitful from its very beginning. (35)
Having reached the world of Brahmā and the celestial realm, I have realized that state;
then Śambhu spoke to Nārada, saying, "Do not speak thus."
Just as they do not know me, so let my conduct remain hidden;
go quickly and tell Hari of my arrival in brief. (37)
Then, having arrived with great haste, he informed Hari of everything;
then, with haste, he took the auspicious water for the arghya offering from Viṣṇu.
Accompanied by Kamalā and surrounded by millions upon millions of yogīs,
the one whose banner is Garuḍa went forth, taking Nārada by the hand.
Uttering "Salutations, salutations, salutations to this Śaṅkara," Keśava worshipped them all with water for the hands, water for the feet, and other offerings.
The immeasurable-souled one caused him to enter the auspicious city of Nārāyaṇa;
then, standing within that king of palaces, Nārāyaṇa spoke.
"How have these arrived? Who is this king of great renown?
This entrance is superhuman; it is beyond the reach even of Brahmā and the other gods. (42)
Śambhu said:
"Just as we have arrived here in the guise of sages, so too has this king;
and this powerful King Rāmacandra is likewise yours. (43)
"O Raghava, it is fitting to behold this wife of yours, who is like a digit of the moon;
saying 'So be it,' Narayana told him, 'Enter.'"
Then, having entered the palace, beheld Lakṣmī, and paid her homage, he,
bowing low with humility, spoke these words to Sucāriṇī.
"You have accomplished your purpose; of this there is no doubt. Tell me, however, what you think. Śrī Devī said:
"O Rāghava, you are young, drawn by passion, and possessed of beauty. (46)
Formerly, you were separated from Sītā, who was beautiful in every limb; at that time, you were utterly overwhelmed by the pangs of separation. (47)
Tell me all of that, or else you shall not depart;
[tell me] those words accompanied by smiles that captivate the hearts of young women. (48)
Having heard all those words, the self-controlled Rāmabhadra bowed his lotus-like face toward him and desired to depart from that place.
Having tormented the Lord whose crest is the moon with the lotus-arrow of Smara,
the Goddess Padmā, who is fond of the lotus forest, departed after following him.
Having learned of his vow of fidelity to a single wife, they approached Rāma;
meanwhile, the king’s entire body trembled and his gait faltered as he moved with stumbling steps.
Seeing Śiva and Nārāyaṇa, they were struck with supreme amazement:
"Aha! Behold the firmness of this man’s mind, even though he is a magician and lacks self-control! (52)
Behold his unwavering fortitude; because of it, Rāma possesses great renown.
May all be auspicious for him in every respect; may nothing inauspicious ever occur anywhere.
Then Rāma spoke these words: "O Blessed One, O Lord, I shall go.

Accompanied by the sages, Śambhu, and Nārāyaṇa, he went quickly to Lokāloka and from there proceeded to the Sweet Ocean (Svādūdaka). ||55||
Then, having traversed the islands and oceans, he returned once more to Jambūdvīpa and stayed at Bharadvāja’s hermitage on the bank of the Gautamī.

setting aside all other [Śrāddhas] that might have occurred during the birth-impurity or any other obstacle.
For there is no doubt that all subsequent rites—every monthly śrāddha as well as the annual śrāddha—must be performed immediately thereafter. (69)

If an obstacle should arise regarding whatever task is to be performed immediately after the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), it must be done on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight by one who desires auspiciousness. (70)
In that case, if there is an obstacle, one should perform this [rite] without deceit;
provided that it is performed on the subsequent days without hindrance. (71)
On the new moon day of the dark fortnight, the rite performed by Rāma should be observed;
this applies whenever the month of the anniversary of death cannot be ascertained in any way whatsoever.
The śrāddha is prescribed for that day in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha;
however, when there is uncertainty regarding the specific day or even the month itself, [the following applies].
If the day and month are unknown for one who has gone abroad or for one who has died, the annual śrāddha shall be performed on the very day of the new moon within that same month.
That particular day should be taken as the lunar date when knowledge arises therein;
[this applies to] the three days of the new moon in the months of Āśvina, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Māgha.
In that regard, one should adopt whichever [period] is appropriate, since neither days nor months are specifically prescribed;
this includes the monthly śrāddha for deceased relatives, extending up to the seventh month of increase.

The daily water-pot rite (*nityodakuṃbha*), the monthly ancestral rites (*māsa-śrāddha*), those performed on special occasions (*adhika*), as well as during eclipses, at the birth of a son, and in propitiatory ceremonies (*śāntika-karman*). ||77||
If everything has been mentally resolved upon, the intercalary month (adhimāsa) does not cause any fault,
provided that a sick person or a non-human being is present when the rite of śrāddha is about to take place.
One may employ one's wife, or even one's brother or disciple;
in their absence, there would be a loss of the merit of the rite known as Śrāddha.

In the daily *śrāddha*, one should engage as many eaters as possible according to one's capacity; this applies to the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the monthly rites, and any [rites] other than those performed on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*).
If one is personally incapable of performing the ritual action, one should employ a son or a Brahmin;
this applies to one who is engaged in royal service or who lives as a servant. 81.
In all types of calamities, a Brahmin should have the Śrāddha performed;
however, the best of the twice-born do not perform the Śrāddha at the time of dawn.
In the case of occasional Śrāddhas, no restriction regarding time is prescribed in the Smṛtis. ||83||
The period beginning after one has left the house and so forth is known as *kutu-pa*; or else, that which occurs before *kutu-pa* is called *āsannakutu-pa*. (84)
Just as it is prescribed that the Śrāddha ceremony should touch the afternoon month after month, so too,
when the new moon (Amāvāsyā) occurs on both days, it should be one that extends into the afternoon.
In the case of waning [of the moon], the first [Amāvāsyā] should be observed; in the case of waxing or equality, the latter is traditionally taught.
However, that Amāvāsyā which occurs entirely within the two afternoon periods (aparāhṇa) [is also significant]. 86.
In the case of waning, waxing, or even remaining constant [in size], there is no defeat [of the moon];
however, where the moon is diminished, the *śrāddha* should be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rite. ||87||

If it is argued that this [lunar day] is subtle by an eighth part of a māṣa and thus does not exist as a remainder of the eight parts of the elements, then for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, that lunar day should be the one which extends through midday. ||88||
In the case of the Pārvaṇa [śrāddha], that lunar day (tithi) which extends through the evening (sāyāhna) should be observed;
however, for the śrāddha and other rites, that which falls within even a small portion of the afternoon (aparāhṇa) is to be accepted.

On the day of death, if the lunar day (tithi) should last for three muhūrtas during the evening time, or if it lasts for three muhūrtas on the following day after the sun has set, [the rite is performed] as previously described. ||90||
In that regard, if on the following day there should be a Śrāddha for the eldest son, one should perform the Amā-Śrāddha when the anniversary of the death has arrived. (91)
"For in that case, it is ordained for one who is not twice-born that [the rite] must extend through midday.
Rāma said:
"Tell me the entire sequence of the śrāddha, as well as the sequence of mortal rites."
"You ought to state the determination of the auxiliary dharmas.
Śambhu said: "When the day of the śrāddha has arrived, one should be endowed with restraints on the preceding day. (93)
He invited the best of Brahmins, endowed with the auspicious marks of a sage,
instructing them to observe eating once a day, celibacy, and silence.

Having performed bathing, anointing, and the clipping of the nails and hair on the previous day, one should perform [the main rite] on the following day after having renounced [worldly attachments]. 95.
One should undertake the unspoken observances and abandon all this;
if there is worship at the three times of day, one should worship one's own deity in the morning.
If one performs worship at the time of dawn, sleeping on the ground and rising in the morning as one who knows his duty; 97.
Having performed even those duties pertaining to the morning preceded by bathing, he,
liberated from the three debts, shall go to that supreme Brahman.
He who performs the worship of Śiva at the time of sunrise becomes equal in splendor to the sun and is glorified in the world of Śiva. 99.
If one performs worship within an interval of one ghaṭikā after the sun has risen, possessing splendor equal to Rudra, one is glorified in the world of Śiva. ||100||
In the third ghaṭikā, however, one should perform the worship of Śiva; possessing splendor equal to that of Kubera, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. ||101||
In the third ghaṭikā, however, one should perform the worship of Śiva; possessing a splendor equal to that of Kubera, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. 102.
He who worships Śiva with devotion during the fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh ghaṭikās [of the day] becomes equal to the Maruts in the world of Śiva. (103)
The worship that was prescribed for a specific time should be performed at that very time; or else, one who has undertaken a vow should perform it according to his promise. ||104||
In the ritual services, one should observe the lack of fixed rules according to one's capacity;
for even upon the transgression of a rule, the sacrifice of the All-pervading Lord would still take place.

Śrī Rāma said: Where is the worship of the God of gods, Śaṅkara, who possesses immeasurable splendor, by the mere remembrance of whom sins are destroyed and by the mere remembrance of whom liberation is granted? (106)
To Śiva, whose form is auspicious, who knows the true meaning of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), who is adorned by the moon, whose eyes are the moon, and who is the sovereign ruler; ||107||
To that yogin who is the embodiment of the Veda yet formless, who knows the essence of the Veda,
who is the knower of the Vedas and their limbs, and for whom all that is to be known has been known.
To him whose body is like cow’s milk, who delights in bathing in cow’s milk, the protector of cows, the three-eyed one, the one whose eye is the triple Veda, and the master of illusion. ||109||
Then, in the midst of the questioning, Śiva, remaining as if motionless with his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose, imparted the knowledge of Śiva to Rāma. (110)
With the region of his cheeks touched by the flow of tears streaming from eyes overflowing with bliss,
he held the god Giriśa within the lotus of his heart.
His body is exceedingly smooth and beautiful, like cow's milk. ||111||
Then, a reflection appeared upon Rāma’s body;
having seen that reflected Śambhu with four arms and three eyes, [he was struck with wonder]. (112)
All the sages and lords of monkeys were filled with supreme wonder upon seeing Rāma of radiant and auspicious form stationed upon the chest of Śambhu. (113)
They remained silent for half the watch and then looked up at Rāma; having reflected upon their own question, they said, "Tell us everything. (114)
Śambhu said:

Worship may always be performed with a fixed [image], or it may be mobile according to one's desire. The worship of the *liṅga* is primary; in its absence, [worship is performed] with images and the like. (115)
Through the excellence of one's qualification, the worship of the Liṅga—whether performed with or without ritual attributes—is fruitful in each respective case. 116.
Worship performed toward an image and such is deficient and not fruitful;
worship is praised whether directed toward a stationary or a mobile *liṅga*. (117)
I shall describe the worship of the mobile [deity], as well as its installation and dismissal;
no one, not even a sage, understands both of these anywhere. (118)
The yogins always establish the Lord of Gods, Śaṅkara, within the lotus of the heart, protect him, worship him, and finally cause him to depart. 119.
The ritual for the *hotṛ* priests is performed in the fire for the god Tryambaka;
for the remaining worshippers, it is for Maheśvara in the form of the Śiva-linga. 120.
The installation of the *liṅga*, its worship, and likewise its dismissal;
the wearing [of it]—the *liṅga* alone is indeed Maheśvara, the source of auspiciousness. (121)
The *sajjikā* should be made of the most excellent gold, or it may be fashioned from silver leaves;
that which is made of silver or bamboo is likewise acceptable.
Furthermore, it may be fashioned from creepers and threads, or even from wood;
it may be fashioned from cloth, or it may be constructed from clay. ||123||
There, having wrapped [it] in a fragrant cloth, [place it] upon a pair of clean, washed garments provided with a soft seat. ||124||
Free from cold and heat, provided with four legs, equipped with a covering and a means of cutting [the cord], and devoid of worms and insects. ||125||
Wrap the auspicious Lord on all sides with a clean, soft cloth;
having placed him in the center of the crucible, cover the Master once again. (126)
For this *sajjikā* has been highly extolled before the Lord Rāma;
its installation and recitation [should be performed] in secret for the Great Lord. (127)
Alternatively, it may be at the base of a wall or on a divine altar;
likewise, in a well-guarded location, one should appoint a guardian. ||128||
One should establish the inseparable connection of the vital breaths and so forth with the observances;
for this is declared to be the royal method of installation of the Supreme Self.
The sattvic [form of] dhāraṇā is that which stays near oneself; the tāmasa, on the other hand, is the dhāraṇā consisting of contact with the limbs and the protection of the entire body. 130.
The wearing of the crest is primary, and it was likewise performed by Brahmā;
having placed it at the end of the crown, its wearing is said to be auspicious. (131)
Its wearing on the forehead is praised, as it was auspiciously worn by Lakṣmī;
furthermore, it was worn by Bāṇa upon his head or again upon his right breast.
Then, by the sage Karṇa, that supreme ṛṣi, having pierced his own body, he fashioned a place for the iron [spear]. (133)
Some of the most excellent Rākṣasas likewise bear the liṅga;
for those mortals who are homeless and incapable [of carrying it elsewhere], wearing it upon the head is prescribed. (134)
The wearing of the waist-knot (*nīvī*) and so forth is declared to be the lowest of the low;
however, among those [practices], when one has received the remains of food (*ucchiṣṭa*), there should be the wearing of it upon the head. (135)
Indeed, the wearing of the sectarian mark (liṅga) by those of the most base conduct is always [observed];
it is even a marvel that this is known in the world of Yama regarding sinners as well. (136)
Śrī Rāma said:
"The writing inscribed by Citragupta upon the forehead is firm;
how can one go to hell otherwise than as determined by that writing? (137)
"How does one perform the worship of Śambhu so that it destroys sin?
Śambhu said: "It destroys all sin, even that accumulated over hundreds of lifetimes. (138)
Because it repels all sins and because of the remembrance of the Great Lord, the word "ash" (bhasma) is so designated; its wearing is supreme. (139)
Just as the fire on the forehead of Brahmā, by maintaining its fiery power,
would destroy Yama’s written decree, so too does the fire consume the sin situated upon the cloth.

Sin committed above the ears is destroyed by wearing [the mark] on the face; by wearing it on the throat, the sin committed through the enjoyment of the throat [sensual pleasures] and so forth is removed. (141)
Sin committed with the arms [is purified] by the arms; sin committed with the mind [is purified] by the chest;
sin committed with the genitals is [purified] by the navel; and likewise, sin committed with the anus [is purified] by the back. 142.

O Rāma, because it is worn on the two sides, the wearing of that ash as the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) everywhere is praised for warding off the effects arising from embracing another's wife and similar acts. (143)
By him alone was performed the upholding of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the three sacrificial fires, and the preservation of the three worlds through their protection. (144)
Pure ashes, consecrated with mantras, are placed in the fifteenth position;
likewise, they are applied to the pair of stomachs, the pair of arms, and the pair above the stomach.
The wearing [of ashes] on all parts of the body is considered by the Dharma to be for the purpose of worship.
[Those who practice this] eat ashes, sleep on ashes, and have their bodies smeared with ashes. (146)
Those who perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) are always liberated from sins; of this there is no doubt.
At the beginning of the Brāhmaṇa-initiation (brāhmaṇadīkṣā), it is traditionally remembered as "triyāyuṣam. (147)
This is indeed a practice for all: a protector even against possession by spirits among humans, and for the purpose of neutralizing the venom of snakes and other creatures. (148)
Whether it be a mortal devotee of Viṣṇu or any other person, one who bathes in ashes and is joined with ashes indeed becomes qualified for ritual actions. 149.
Śrī Rāma said:
First, tell me the greatness of the sacred ash (bhasma); for whom indeed does this ash bestow long life?
How does it protect all this? Tell me all of this.
Śambhu said:
It is the cause for increasing the lifespan of all three types of embodied beings;
it destroys sin, and through its cool and warm touch, it bestows the state of Śiva. 151.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history:
there was a twice-born man of the Vasiṣṭha lineage named Dhananjaya.
He had one hundred wives endowed with beauty and charm;
O Sage, among them, one gave birth to Ākāśakarṇa. (153)
The ascetics had as many sons as they had wives;
their father divided them unequally, and thus a great bond of enmity arose among those brothers. (154)
For humans of the same species, enmity is indeed inevitable. (155)
Then, moved by compassion, he went to the bank of the Bhavanāśinī river together with various hosts of sages, desiring to behold Narasiṃha.
For the purpose of beholding Nṛsiṃha, a certain brāhmaṇa brought a hero born of excellent fruit, endowed with beauty and fragrance. (157)
As Karuṇa was smelling that excellent fruit which he had taken, the flocks of birds dwelling there afflicted him with a curse. 158.
O you whose nature is sinful due to your existence as a fly, the end of this curse shall come after a hundred years through the high-souled Dadhīci. (159)
Then, having attained the state of a fly, he spoke thus to his wife:
"O auspicious lady, I have become a fly; please protect me. (160)
Having spoken thus, he became such [a being] and wandered here and there;
then, those kinsmen of evil resolve perceived him in this state.
Having exerted effort accordingly, she caused him to fall into the midst of oil;
then, taking her deceased husband, that sorrowful woman of slender waist departed. (162)
O Goddess, for the sake of pacifying that suffering, you who bear the trident have said:
"O lady of pure smiles, I shall revive this man today by means of ash alone. (163)
Then, having offered the ash produced from the Agnihotra fire into the sacred fire, he sprinkled that ash,
which was born of immortality, upon them both with the mantra "Mṛtyuñjaya."
Then, fanning me with her hand like a chowrie, she of the pure smile rose up from that heap of ashes by its power. (165)
Then, when a hundred years had passed, Jyotiratha died. When her husband was dead, that virtuous woman of pure smiles was filled with grief.
The virtuous woman went for refuge to the eminent brahmin sage named Dadhīca, a great devotee of Maheśvara; the brahmin, whose wealth was his asceticism, spoke to her. (167)
Kaśyapa likewise restored to life the son of Atri, Jamadagni— a treasury of asceticism who had been deprived of his triple lifespan— and one such as him, reducing them both to mere ashes.
"Even the gods were once such as they are, and I too was like this in the past;
therefore, O sinless one, I have restored you to life by means of these ashes."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Dadhīca went for refuge to Maheśvara;
then, having consecrated the ashes and taken them in his hand, he restored the husband of Susādhvī to life.
Through the touch of Maheśa’s hand, Karuṇa was freed from his curse; having returned to his own true form, he went to his own hermitage. ||171||
Having brought even Dadhīca to the house of the virtuous woman for a meal, she requested the brahmin-sage; then that excellent twice-born one ate. (172)
Then, when the eminent Brahmin had finished eating, ten million disciples arrived;
thereafter, the gods arrived, their bodies smeared with ashes.
Having paid homage to Dadhīca, the gods, desiring the welfare of Śiva, questioned him.
The gods said:
"O great-minded one, our knowledge has indeed been lost. (174)
But having seen Gautama’s wife, we became afflicted with desire;
thus the goddess, who had been consecrated by the auspicious rites of marriage, was violated. (175)
As they were desiring her alone, their knowledge was lost;
thereafter, we all went to the sage Durvāsas.
"O Sāvitrī, I shall now remove all this impurity, consecrated by Śambhu himself with the Śatarudriya mantra. (177)
"By that very same [deity], this was given to me as well for the pacification of the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils.
Having spoken thus, Durvāsas gave him the excellent sacred ash.
Then, at his word, we all became transformed in mind;
our bodies were smeared with ashes by means of the Śatarudriya mantra. (179)
In that very instant, they were all indeed cleansed of their sins;
we recognize this as a marvel, such is the power of the sacred ash.
Dadhīca said:
We shall describe to you briefly the power of the ash of Śiva;
it would not be possible to describe it in detail even in hundreds of years. (181)
In this regard, I shall proclaim to you the ancient account of those two gods,
Hari and Śaṅkara, which destroys all sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Formerly, when the dissolution of Brahmā had occurred and all was a single, terrible ocean,
the blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu lay reclining upon the waters of that dissolution.
Having reached both his sides, there are two hundred cosmic eggs;
twenty are on the sides of his feet, and twenty are within the space of his head. (184)
The Lord fashioned the cosmic egg from the state of the pearl of his nose;
within its navel-center dwell certain lords of sages, such as Lomaśa and others. (185)
Performing very great austerities, they worshiped Īśvara;
then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, fell into reflection with the desire to create.
Having become intent upon the yoga of meditation, he did not perceive anything at all;
then, with great sorrow, he wept aloud again and again. (187)
Immediately thereafter, a certain radiance appeared that was unlike anything in the world;
and upon seeing it, Hari closed his eyes out of fear. (188)
Approaching with a physical form whose splendor is equal to the milk of a cow,
he holds in his two hands a pair of bracelets fashioned from millions of cosmic eggs.
Upon his chest he bore a single cosmic egg fashioned from millions of worlds,
which was falling and rising within his pair of feet.
Seeing him thus, endowed with all ornaments and imperishable, Viṣṇu was pleased and spoke for the sake of his own vision.
Viṣṇu said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, the eternal and immutable one. O Blessed One, I do not know who you are; you alone know yourself—homage, homage!"
I know his nature to be stainless, for his luster is difficult to behold;
he is adorned with ruby earrings and a network of golden chains.
Wearing a beautiful jewel-encrusted armlet as an ornament upon his forearm, his long, radiant eyes were filled with a slight redness at the corners.
[He saw] the imperishable Lord, whose eyes resemble the eye of Bāṇa, whose forehead-eye is [blazing], and whose eyebrows produce the illusion of Cupid’s bow. (195)
With glossy, prominent, and beautiful ears, and symmetrical, even cheeks; with a gentle smile and a serene countenance, the Lord appeared as a child, difficult to behold.
O Lord, I have taken refuge in you, who are clothed in the red garment of consciousness and adorned with ornaments fashioned from feeling; please grant me sight. 197.
"Be the refuge for those who are wretched, miserable, and lost through ignorance.
Then he granted him divine vision, possessing the power to behold his own Self. 198.
Then, seeing Śambhu standing before him with three eyes, Hari said, "Who are you? and, being of great renown, he did not recognize him.
"In this world, one is only able to perform prostration; it is not possible to fully know [the Lord].
Sadāśiva said: "I shall bestow knowledge upon you; perform the ritual bath in the waters of Varuṇa. (200)
"After that, there is the ash-bath; thereafter, I shall speak of knowledge.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Water fit for my bath does not exist anywhere at all."
Thus addressed, Brahmā sat down with his body touching the shell of the cosmic egg;
however, the water reaching only up to Hari’s thighs was not sufficient for him to bathe.
Śambhu laughed, saying, "Oh, this water for bathing and sacrifice is indeed excessive!
Dadhīca said:
Then the god Śiva gazed at Viṣṇu with his eye on the forehead.
He gazed with his left eye at Viṣṇu, whose subtle limbs had dissolved;
then Viṣṇu’s body became subtle and cool by Śambhu’s power.
And it was said: "Obeisance! This lake of Viṣṇu has been prepared for you to bathe in.
Then Hari went to that lake, which had been prepared by Hara, in order to bathe. 205.
Then, out of fear, he was unable to enter that lake;
Hari said, "Come near, for there is no entering this lake. (206)
Then Śambhu said to the deity Mārgome:
"In ancient times, this great water was terrifying and extended for ten million yojanas."
O Lord, when you were seated, the water reached only up to your thighs;
yet now, even as you stand, why is there no entry into the lake? (208)
"This thigh is eight finger-breadths in measure; within it is a hollow.
Behold, you shall enter it, and I shall grant you the touch of my foot. This single sentence was the staircase issued forth from my speech.
Hari said:
"In this world, no one possesses the capacity to ascend by means of sound."
"How is the grasping of form possible, or how is the grasping of sound?
Śambhu said:
It is through the power (śakti) of the Person (puṃs) in the holding and ascending of the nine substances."
"Take this great Veda," [said Brahmā]; then Hari also took it, his hand bent low as if falling from exhaustion, O Janārdana. (212)
"I am not able to hold it," Hari said to Śiva;
laughing, Śiva cast it down into a very great lake.
"O Keśava, having ascended those steps, you ought to bathe.
Dadhīca said:
"The Vedas indeed serve as the steps; knowledge is found there, reaching up to the thighs."
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and having emerged outside, he said, "I have bathed; what should be done next? Then Śambhu spoke to Hari.
"What are you meditating upon here in your heart? Speak something. Hari replied, "Nothing. Then Śambhu spoke to him: 216.
"Purified by the ash-bath, you shall know the supreme auspiciousness;
it is beneficial for one who is initiated, so I shall perform that protection for you. (217)
Dadhīca said:
Śaṅkara, having taken a portion of the ash situated upon his own chest with his fingernail,
then consecrated it with the *praṇava* and with the *gāyatrī* which has become Brahman.
Taking him up with his two fingers, Śiva indeed cast him down upon all the limbs of Hari’s head by means of the five-syllabled mantra.
Then, looking at him with a peaceful gaze, Hara said to Hari, "Live! "Meditate upon Him," he said; and he became intent on meditation upon that [Lord]. (220)
He saw a lamp in his heart, long in shape and exceedingly radiant; Hari said to Śiva, "The lamp has been seen by me. ||221||
Śiva said: "O Hara, when this knowledge has fully ripened, then the entire knowledge of consuming the ashes will arise. (222)
Hari said:
"Having previously bathed in ashes, I shall eat the auspicious [ashes];
having seen the Lord who is accessible through devotion, Acyuta ate the ashes. (223)
In that regard, there was a great marvel: Vāsudeva, who previously possessed a luster like that of a ripe bimba fruit, in an instant became the color of pure pearls. (224)
From that time forward, this Vāsudeva became pure and gracious;
once again becoming intent on meditation, he beheld the Puruṣa within the midst of the lamp.
Śiva is like pure crystal, three-eyed and two-armed;
the all-pervading Lord grants boons with his right hand and bestows fearlessness with his left.
With the body of a five-year-old child and the splendor of ten million autumn moons,
he wore ruby earrings and was adorned with a network of golden chains and necklaces.
Adorned with a beautiful jewel upon his upper arm, he was a magnificent ornament for the region of his forearm;
his lips were slightly red, and his long, wide eyes reached to his ears.
I bow to the imperishable Lord, whose eyes resemble those of Bāṇa,
whose eye is upon his forehead, and whose eyebrows produce the illusion of Cupid’s bow.
The Lord, who is difficult to behold even for the gods, has a face that is gentle, smiling, and serene; his nose is smooth, elevated, and very beautiful, and his cheeks are perfectly even.
He whose garment is consciousness, whose anklets are fashioned from feeling, and who possesses the imperishable Great Praṇava situated between the left toe and the middle [toe]. 231.
Then Viṣṇu beheld him and became one who had accomplished his purpose.
Then Śambhu said to Viṣṇu: "O Bhava, what has been seen by you in your heart?"
"Before the city, a man of tranquil form was seen," said Hari;
having spoken thus, Mahāviṣṇu fell at the feet of Śiva. (233)
Hari said:
"I do not know the power of the ashes, nor from where your authority comes.
Salutations to you, salutations to you; I have come to you alone for refuge. (234)
Sadāśiva said: "O highly fortunate one, choose a boon; this is what you desire in your mind.
Then, having heard Śiva’s words, Hari chose the most excellent of boons. (235)
Hari said:
"May there always be devotion to the pair of your feet for me, O Śambhu.
Then, having granted this boon, Śambhu spoke these words to Hari: 236.
"Endowed with the wearing of ashes, you shall become my devotee.
Dadhīca said:
"Thus has this great knowledge concerning the origin of the ashes been spoken from the beginning. (237)
Therefore, all you gods, hold that with reverence; and the gods, their eyes wide with wonder, said, "So be it. (238)
Whoever should constantly hear this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative, being liberated from all sins, goes to that state which bestows peace. (239)
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ashes," in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(106) Chapter One Hundred and Six: Śucismitā said:
O Great Sage, you have observed that the consumption of sacred ash increases longevity;
tell me of this which is capable of granting passage to the next world. (1)
Dadhīca said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history which became well known between Citragupta and Yama.
In ancient times, in Mithilā, a certain dog wandered about, tormented by hunger;
