"Salutations to you, O Eternal One! Salutations to you; be the granter of boons.
Vīrabhadra said:
"With my ashes, I shall restore to life the gods, the sages, and the monkeys."
"You must be satisfied; you should not feel grief now," having said this, Vīrabhadra restored them to life with sacred ash.
Then the sages, the gods, and the monkeys rose up;
filled with joy, they spoke these words to the one born from the water who was stationed at their head: 83.
O Father, we have been brought back to life by you; O Śaṅkara, O Source of all, may you be our eternal refuge according to the Dharma. 84.

Having observed the wicked conduct of children, you should instruct them accordingly and protect them from harms inflicted by others and from diseases, just as you would your own biological sons. (85)
O sinless one, those who committed offenses at Dakṣa’s sacrifice were disciplined by you;
now, O Lord, we are protected by you like children. (86)
Vīrabhadra said:
This is true, there is no doubt; whenever you experience any affliction, remember me quickly there, and that affliction shall come to an end.
Then, one should recite the eight hundred names beginning with "Vīrabhadra," preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with "namaḥ," accompanied by the dative case suffix. ||88||
There shall be the destruction of those afflictions caused by *rākṣasas*, as well as in cases of affliction by *brahmarākṣasas* and fears such as those caused by *piśācas*. (89)
By recollecting the name, all afflictions are destroyed. ||90||

[I bow to] the Lord, whose gaze is fierce like the radiance of lightning, who has a beautiful face, whose lips are adorned with reddish fangs, whose body is deep blue, who wears a garland made of matted locks, and who bears a white triple-tilaka mark on his forehead. ||91||
This recollection has indeed been proclaimed for the sake of liberating the Brahmarākṣasa;
all of this has been declared within the mantra of Vīrabhadra. (92)
Dadhīca said:
"O best of sages, O gods, since you have come here in this manner,
I shall thus relate this supreme majesty of the sacred ash, which bestows the three goals of life."
This [text] destroys the sins of one who recites it, hears it, or even remembers it;
it bestows devotion to Śiva, is meritorious, and increases longevity and health. (94)
Śucismitā said: "I am one who has achieved her purpose and am blessed; I am the most excellent among women. My sins have been destroyed; likewise, salutations to you, O bull among sages. (95)
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava.
(108) The One Hundred and Eighth Chapter. Śrī Rāma said:
O highly fortunate one, tell me of the origin of the ashes, as well as the majesty of the ashes,
the merit in wearing the ashes, and likewise the gift of the ashes.
Śambhu said: O King, listen as I describe the origin of the sacred ash (bhasma), which destroys all sins; by remembering it or chanting its name, one attains the state of Rāma. 2.
He who is the one eternal God, the source of Brahman, the ever-auspicious Śiva; the three-eyed one, the substratum of qualities, yet transcending qualities, imperishable and immutable. ||3||
Then, having perceived the three qualities residing within himself, the desire to create arose in him;
for this triad of qualities is indeed to be known as the three Vedas.
Having separated himself, O dear one, and divided his own station there,
he created Dakṣa as a son from his right side and Hari from his left.
From his back, the omnipresent Lord Maheshana created three sons;
as soon as they were born, these three gods were Brahma, Vishnu, and Maheshvara.
They spoke these words clearly: "Who are you, and who are we? Śiva said to those sons, "You are my sons; I am your father."
"O sons, devote yourselves to these three qualities which have karma as their cause.
The sons said:
"O Lord, which quality did whom resort to, and for how long?"
"How can there be a cessation of merit? Speak on this, O Voice. Śiva said:
"As long as your knowledge lasts, or even as long as your life endures."
The sustaining of each of its qualities is as follows:
Brahmā partakes of sattva, Viṣṇu of rajas, and Maheśvara of tamas. (10)
Thus it was said by Ātreya; then the Lord of Devas took hold of Brahmā’s being.
He was not able to move him, so how could he be capable of supporting him? (11)
Having suppressed that quality [sattva], he then seized the quality of rajas;
but being unable to move it, he then seized the quality of tamas.
Unable to move it, he fell down and wept;
and Viṣṇu held fast the quality of passion (rajas) with his left hand.
Maheśa also held the quality of Tamas with two fingers;
he placed Sattva alone with two fingers, and then he established Viṣṇu as Sattva.
And he placed Brahmā upon a footstool, and likewise Viṣṇu. ||15||

Beholding Śiva—who was dancing with intense grace, who possessed three eyes, who was radiant like the interior of cow’s milk, who bore everything [as his ornaments], and who had performed the auspicious rite—the Bestower of Boons spoke to his sons. (16)
Śiva said:
"I am pleased with you, my son; choose a boon as you desire.
Then the son said to his father, "Grant me this boon. (17)
O Śiva, worship performed with me as the object shall be worship unto yourself;
may you always abide within me, for you alone am I, the immutable one. (18)
Śiva said:
"O highly fortunate one, it shall be exactly so; there is no doubt.
These two sons of mine, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, are indeed red and fair-complexioned. (19)
The hair on the roots of his arms was of excellent quality, and likewise his two thighs;
then he said this to Brahmā: "May you resort to one single quality. (20)

Brahmā said: "O Lord, I am not able to sustain the quality (guṇa) designated by you. O God, I shall sustain the quality of passion (rajas); let Hari indeed resort to the quality of goodness (sattva). (21)
"And this Lord Śambhu shall sustain the remaining quality. Śambhu said:
"O gods, having taken up the qualities, you were unable to sustain them eternally."
He spoke again to Śiva for the sake of his ability to provide sustenance:
"They are not capable of supporting their offspring at all times. (23)
"O Blessed One, let power be granted if you, my lord, are the bestower of boons.
Then, having heard those words, Śiva spoke these words: ||24||
Śiva said:
The power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) is designated as the "power" (śakti) of all things;
ignorance (avidyā) rests upon the three qualities (guṇas), while non-ignorance (vidyā) rests upon that [knowledge].
Having indeed burnt away the three qualities (guṇas), you ought to maintain that essence;
whatever else may exist therein, let that which is beneficial be maintained by you.
Then they said: "The words of his sons are not burned without fire. Śiva replied: "Indeed, there is fire in the eye of Maheśa. (27)
These three qualities are the cow; knowledge is its auspicious dung;
the Upaniṣads are said to be its urine; thereafter, one should prepare the ashes.
One should consecrate the cow there with the mantra "āgāva" [RV 1.164.40], using its dung which has arisen from her whose calves are remembered.

One who observes the vow, having fasted on the fourteenth day of either the bright or the dark fortnight, should cause the cows to eat grass and drink water, saying, "O cows, O cows, come! (gāvo gāvo gāva iti).
Having risen early the next morning, being pure and composed,
and having performed his bath and put on washed garments, he should go to the cow for the sake of cow-dung.
Having raised her with effort, one should collect her urine in the Gāyatrī;
one should hold it in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay.
One should place cow's urine in a vessel made of lotus leaves, banyan leaves, or even the leaves of the pātrega or gośṛṅga trees; and one should place cow dung with the mantra "gandhadvārām. (33)
One should collect [the leftovers] without letting them fall on the ground, in the previously mentioned vessel, provided they are not excessive;
the wise one should purify the cow-dung with the mantra "May Śrī attend to me. (34)
One should wipe away the cow dung with the mantra "alakṣmīrmayi" and pour the cow urine into the cow dung with the mantra "saṃ tvā siñcāmi. (35)
With the mantra "pañcānām," one should prepare fourteen piṇḍas;
having dried them with the rays of the sun, one should then take them up.
Then, one should place balls of cow dung into the previously mentioned vessel; having established the fire according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, one should kindle it.
The wise one should cast the rice-balls for the respective deities of each syllable; having offered the two Āghāra oblations and the two Ājyabhāga portions, he should perform the two Homa offerings.
Then, for the dissolution of that [state], thirteen oblations beginning with Jaya should be offered to the Five Brahmans, ending with the mantra "namo hiraṇyabāhave. (39)
Having offered all the oblations with those mantras in the dative case, he then [offers] to Śarva, to Rudra, and to him whose name begins with "yasya vai kaṅkata. (40)
The wise man should offer oblations with these [mantras] in that manner for one who has not received instruction;
then, having offered the *vyāhṛtis*, he should subsequently offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation.
Then, having set aside the remainder of the fuel, one should augment the water in the full-vessel (pūrṇapātra) with other water using the *yajus* mantra ending with "pūrṇamāsa."
One should pour that water, [reciting] "The nectar is in the Brahmins," upon one's head;
with the indicative marks of the directions, such as "In the east," one should pour water in the various quarters.
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmā, they made this resolve and brought forth Lakṣmī, saying:
"I shall bring her for the protection of the ritual of all the gods."
Having brought you here with the mantra beginning with "jātavedasam," one should then cover that fire with the *pulāka* (grain-offering) using this mantra. 45.
It is taught that for three days one should remain standing in fire and cover oneself with horripilation;
one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas and eat oneself while restraining one's speech.
If one desires more ashes, one should collect more cow dung; this may be done over three days or on a single day, as much as is required.
On the third or the fourth day, having bathed in the morning, wearing white garments, with a white sacrificial thread, and adorned with white garlands and unguents; ||48||
Having uttered "tadvai tathā," the knower of mantras, whose teeth are white and who is smeared with ashes, should not abandon the truth that consists of ashes by means of this mantra. (49)
Then, the sixteen services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) should be performed;
thereafter, one should withdraw the fire by means of the offering of oblations (āhuti).
One should take up the ash that has arisen with the mantra "agnerbhasma" (the ash of Agni),
and thereafter, one should wipe it [on] with the mantra "agnirasmi" (I am Agni).
Having mixed [the powder] with the waters of the Gaṅgā or with the milk of a Kapilā cow, one should likewise add camphor, saffron, uśīra, and sandalwood.
Having ground the two types of aguru extremely finely, one should cast that powder into the ashes while reciting the Brahma-mantra "Oṃ. (53)
Then, regarding the sprinkling with milk, the Manu of Kapila declared:
"O Goddess, your milk is nectar; it is pure and has increased here. (54)
By your grace, may these men be liberated from all sins;
then, the wise man should bring the *avaṭakas* with the *praṇava*, as if with ashes. 55.
With the mantra "aṇoraṇīyān," Śambhu said to the wise one:
"Having thus prepared the ashes and taken them while they are dry, the knower of mantras [should proceed]. (56)
Then, having wiped it with the *praṇava*, one should consecrate it seven times with the *praṇava* mantra;
[one should touch] the head region with the *Īśāna* mantra and the face with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra.
One should consecrate the chest region with the Aghora mantra, the private parts with the Vāmadeva mantra, the feet with the Sadyojāta mantra, and the entire body with the Praṇava (Om). 58.
Then, having smeared his entire body from the soles of his feet to the top of his head with ashes,
he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and put on a clean, white garment.
Having sipped water again, one is fit to perform all ritual acts;
then, having taken up the ashes, one should wipe them [on the body] with the *praṇava*.
Meditating upon the three-eyed Lord, the support of the three qualities (guṇas) and the progenitor of the three [worlds],
one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead while reciting "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya."
Having said "namaḥ śivābhyām," one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on both arms; and with "aghorāya namaḥ," one should apply it on both forearms.
Then, one should offer [the oblation] to Bhīma on the back, and likewise to Śirodhi on the west;
then, with the mantra "Salutation to Nīlakaṇṭha, the Soul of All," one should cast it upon the head.
Then, having washed both hands, one should perform the ritual action.
Śiva said:
"In this manner, you yourselves, having prepared the sacred ash and rubbed it [upon yourselves]," 64.
"Only those capable of upholding the qualities shall then create progeny.
Śambhu said: "Thus addressed by Śiva, the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—" (65)
Having acted thus according to the prescribed rite with a spirit of mutual emulation,
they, being unable to awaken one another, bowed to Śiva and spoke.
What quality does he possess, or who is he other than Śiva, that he would then laugh at his sons?
For one's power of action as well as knowledge perishes through mere talkativeness. (67)
Brahmā is seen to have a short lifespan, and his life is measured by the Manus;
whereas I, who am adorned with garlands of cosmic eggs, am the protector of Brahmā.
Then, having seized the quality of rajas, you did not know the limit [of his power];
Viṣṇu possesses greater strength than Brahmā, and he is superior to Brahmā in lifespan.
May Maheśa, whose ornament is a garland of cosmic eggs, be mine alone;
for the lifespan of Viṣṇu is said to be exhausted by merely four of his breaths.
Because Brahmā possesses a preponderance of *sattva*, Hari took recourse to *sattva*;
he knows me at all times, yet he might perhaps forget me. (71)
His worship is exclusively of the *sāttvika* type; it is never *rājasa* or *tāmasa*.
He is peaceful, auspicious, and characterized by the quality of *sattva*, due to his disregard for the face of *rajas*. (72)
Likewise, Śambhu partook of that quality which is as blue as the sky;
indeed, he formerly assumed a body composed of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Therefore, various forms of worship are prescribed for this Śaṅkara;
for passion (rajas) joined with darkness (tamas) is proclaimed to be fierce.
Even from that [ignorance], worship directed toward Śaṅkara grants a favorable rebirth;
for passion (rajas) joined with darkness (tamas) is fully capable of setting the scriptures in motion. //75//
Even when interrupted, worship grants the fruit of Śaṅkara;
and [the mind] characterized by darkness joined with goodness is the "mixed" type that sets [the practice] in motion. ||76||
O Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, there is no fear that mixed worship will be fruitless;
for the Lord, whether the worship be of such a kind or that kind, it is effective when performed according to the prescribed rule.
"O Śambhu, tell me how this ash, which grants swift results even for any embodied being whatsoever, is to be used.
Śambhu said:
"O sinless one, this procedure for the ash has been declared by me in brief. (78)
And it brings about the destruction of all the sins of both the speaker and the listeners. ||79||
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Method for the Production of Sacred Ash," in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava within the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(109) The one hundred and ninth chapter. Śambhu said:
In this regard, I shall narrate a story that destroys all sins;
having heard it, the righteous-souled one attained unsurpassed devotion to Śiva. (1)
O best of brahmins, there was a man named Ikṣvāku, possessed of great learning and vast intelligence;
he was proficient in many scriptures and an expert in the science of ethics. ||2||
He was neither a sacrificer nor a giver, nor a worshiper of the gods;
he was neither a teacher of the Veda nor an expounder of what has been heard.
One who diligently studies the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Śrutis, or Āgamas, likewise becomes a consumer [of their fruits] and the sole impeller of the purification of the body. (4)
Then, as that twice-born man was thus observed, his life passed away;
specifically, in one hundred thousand years, in the fifth month of a certain year.
On the night of the third day, he heard this ancient account of how that king,
who had acquired wealth through his own efforts, performed a new act of generosity.
That which is consumed day after day will indeed become devoid of essence in due course;
for that many years, one will certainly be cooked in hell.
After that, having experienced a thousand births as worms,
one becomes poor, diseased, friendless, possessed of a wicked wife, and burdened with many children.
Day after day, my livelihood was sustained by what was obtained through begging and solicitation, never by searching for seeds that had been submerged anywhere. (9)
The livelihood of servants is by means of what they have obtained; and their livelihood is through labor.
In the midst of this, one who is devoid of ears and devoid of eyes stumbles amidst impurity.
Having thus heard the Purāṇa, that descendant of Ikṣvāku became deeply distressed;
remembering it again and again, that lowest of the twice-born reflected thus in his mind.
Durgā, who is full of buffalo-milk, is devoid of flowers of form and likewise of fruits;
similarly, the path of liberation is not seen by those whose knowledge is bereft of the Purāṇas.
Even for a man who has thoroughly mastered many treatises and the Vedas along with their extensive branches, if he has not heard the Purāṇas, there is no correct vision of the ultimate goal. 13.
Śambhu said:
While he was thinking thus, his untimely death occurred;
he then went to the world of Yama and was addressed by Yama.
Yama said:
"Though you are joined with many sins, this merit of yours is not at all great. That sin incurred from teaching the Veda is already known to you. (15)
"O twice-born one, your residence in hell shall last for ten million years;
your lifespan here is exceedingly short, so return to your former body. (16)

One should perform meritorious and beneficial acts such as giving charity, worshiping the deities, and the recitation of mantras; likewise, the teaching of the Vedas with their ancillaries, feeding Brahmins, and the wearing of sacred ash. ||17||
Worship the Lord Viśveśvara, the God of gods, the Consort of Umā;
by his mere effort, you shall go to the stainless world. 18.
O sinner, listen daily with devotion to whatever Purāṇa you may hear; then, by that very hearing, you shall no longer behold my torments. 19.
Having heard the words of Yama, the brahmin returned to his own body;
then that virtuous twice-born man applied himself with effort to the worship of the Lord.
He went to the excellent sage Tujābāli, a worshiper of Śiva, who was perfected in austerity and Vedic study, and was a discerning knower of the Śruti and Smṛti. ||21||
To the knower of the truth of the Purāṇas, surrounded by a hundred thousand disciples,
whose every limb was weakened by old age, and who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.
Desirous of seeing it, he went to Mount Mandara, which was beautiful,
delightful, filled with various birds, and covered with various flowering creepers.
It was endowed with flowers of every season, adorned with various fragrances, and its great caves were filled with the songs of pairs of kinnaras. (24)
Its trees were gratified by women endowed with manifold beauty and grace;
its trees were adorned by those various [women] hanging from them.
Awakening those who had fallen asleep from the fatigue of lovemaking,
the female cuckoos warble at will, as if to unite those who are separated.
It was crowded with various throngs of sages, frequented by peaceful deer,
filled with hosts of apsarases, and served by groups of gandharvas.
The interior of the forest was filled with songs emerging from the mouths of various Siddhas;
it was replete with diverse fruits and endowed with many temples of the gods. ||28||
It was crowded with hundreds of palaces and endowed with various houses, featuring faces like lions, faces like elephants, and faces like owls. ||29||
With faces that were distorted, severed, fierce, half-faces, or the faces of deer;
and also with the faces of ruru deer, goats, iguanas, snakes, monkeys, and bears.
[He was surrounded] by the lords of the Gaṇas, whose faces resembled those of tigers, scorpions, bears, camels, dogs, and donkeys, and whose mouths were like the faces of all living beings.
With faces like creepers, faces like trees, faces like rocks, and faces like iron. ||31||
It was adorned with faces like conch shells, pearls, and other aquatic creatures;
it was further graced by those with matted hair and those with shaven heads, all possessing abundant necklaces.
With faces like birds, with twelve faces, and even with three bodies and multiple heads;
with bell-like mouths, and even with mouths, ears, feet, and faces shaped like winnowing baskets.
Whether with mouths like bells, mouths like flutes, or even mouths like cymbals—whatever the nature of an object exists in the world, such are their faces, or even those with iron-like muzzles. (34)
By some who were disguised, yet possessed of pride, beauty, and grace, and who resembled ten million suns with a splendor like ten million moons; ||35||
With various colors, with faces everywhere, with universal forms, with four faces, with two faces, with five faces, with three faces, and even with six faces; ||36||

Endowed with peaceful forms, both singular and manifold, who are happy at all times and possess the abundance of various enjoyments, they move about even while equaling the fulfillment of desires. (37)
I behold that mountain, served by Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and others whose forms are equal to Umā and Īśa, as well as by others who assume various forms. (38)
Where the Vedas, like milch-cows, are joined with the *Camū* and *Sāvitrī*, and where Dharma and the others, possessing their full forms, [are united] with the Purāṇas through their ritual action.
The Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Āgamas have become embodied and reside within that cave, which, together with its mountain, is the destroyer of sins. 40.
In its center was a city of great merit, supremely beautiful, adorned with hundreds of ponds, lakes, groves, and palaces. ||41||
It was surrounded by seven walls and moats, endowed with jeweled watchtowers,
possessed nine gate-towers, and filled with various wonderful mansions.
And his splendor was peerless, devoid of heat, cold, and other such qualities; in the midst of that city was a holy place, and in its center was an auspicious assembly hall. (43)
In its center was a majestic throne, variegated with the four Vedas as its legs;
it possessed a most beautiful footstool fashioned from all the Upaniṣads. 44.
The Purāṇas and Āgamas [proclaim] "May there be well-being" at the feet of that Śiva;
seated there was the great yogi, whose form resembled cow's milk. 45.
The Lord, eight years of age, with a most beautiful smiling face,
wore a necklace of gems fashioned from rudrākṣa beads around his chest.
Wearing the sacred thread, possessing a luster equal to the karṇikāra flower,
the god was adorned with excellent jeweled earrings, a crown, and golden garments.
Adorned with various ornaments and anointed with various fragrant unguents, he has the daughter of the mountain resting on his left lap as he gazes upon her face. 48.
She was a charming young girl with a beautiful face, graced by fresh youth;
she was adorned with ornaments on all her lovely limbs and held a golden lotus.
Embracing the goddess with his left hand and raising her face with his right,
he touched her head with his left hand.
And the Lord, applying a tilaka with his right hand... ||50||
Devotion fans the Lord with the fan of the *praṇava*, while she, bearing a garland for the God made of flowers from the forest of worship, [wafts him]. (51)
His attendants are Jñapti, Virakti, Vanitā, Vibhūti, Yoga-cāmara, Samādhi, Kārya-kartrī, and Dhāraṇā. 52.
What are the *yamas* and *niyamas* said to be for him?
*Prāṇāyāma* is his priest (*purodhā*), and *pratyāhāra* is his bearer of gold (*suvarṇadhṛk*). (53)
Meditation is the treasurer, and truth is likewise the commander-in-chief;
those beginning with Brahmā and ending with insects are the cattle, and Śiva is their lord. (54)
Dharma is the protector of the cattle, and the thief is adharma; Kāśī is the death that releases those bound by the snares of illusion. 55.
Various kinds of celestial maidens [attend] the God of gods, the Lord of Umā;
one should constantly remember such a Lord of Umā as being born from ten million [suns]. (56)
Having obtained his desired enjoyments, he is then glorified in the world of Śiva;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the others are the gatekeepers of that city. ||57||
Because the worship of the goddesses Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī at the threshold and other locations is observed, the gods and celestial nymphs are appointed by the God of Gods. (58)
The Ikṣvāku king beheld such a great mountain, at which all the gods were servants and all the great-souled ones were slaves. (59)
Then, having prostrated before the sage Jābāli, he spoke these words: "O Sage, I desire to go to the great mountain; are you able to go there as well? (60)
In the past, Yama, who lacks wisdom, declared that my life was short.
"Since hell has been described as so vast, how will there be any well-being?
Jābāli said:
"I too have understood all this through my divine eye."
O Brahmin, though he was learned and a performer of dharma, his life lasted only ten days; for neither austerity nor yoga bears fruit without long-term practice over a short period of time.
Due to the lack of wealth, lack of capability, and likewise lack of worthiness, there is no gift; for one who lacks longevity, there is neither sacrifice, nor vow, nor meritorious work, nor merit.
Nor can it be [performed] due to conflicts with the time required for teaching, visiting sacred fords (tīrtha), and other such duties;
therefore, no expiation exists for the destruction of that sin.
"O Sage, go or stay according to that dharma which grants the [proper] state of existence.
Ikṣvāku said:
"O twice-born one, whatever vow is undertaken for as long as life lasts, that is the bull-like dharma."
"Therefore, the avoidance of evil will be certain; tell me that dharma by which my sin shall be destroyed. (67)
By what connection of merit will there be a path to heaven?
O brahmin-sage, become a refuge for me, who am terrified of hell. (68)
"They say that protecting one who has come for refuge yields the fruit of all meritorious deeds.
Jābāli said:
"It is true; such a merit as this is not obtained in so short a time by any other means."
Even in dreams, it is impossible to speak of immortality or falsehood;
yet there is a certain secret that is not told to just anyone. (70)
Ikṣvāku said:
"O sage, protect me as your refuge; my time will pass away.
Jābāli said:
O Brahmin, this secret, ordained by the Vedas, is dearer to me than my own life. (71)
The worship of the Śiva-liṅga, performed by Brahmā and the other gods, pacifies all sins and destroys all calamities. (72)
Therefore, O Sage, perform the worship of Śiva, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for one should never neglect the auspicious adoration of the Śiva-linga. 73.
Whoever should interrupt the worship of Śambhu, by him my head is severed in the snow.
Better is the thrusting of the trident; better is the dragging of the śālmali tree. (74)
It is better to give up one's life than to neglect worship;
better to throw oneself into fire, and better to have one's head cut off. (75)
It is better to eat one's own impurities than to neglect the worship of the Lord;
for that lowest of men who eats without having worshipped the Lord [incurs great sin]. (76)
It is said that his food consists of sins in the form of grains;
if he eats and chews without having first uttered the name of Śambhu, [he consumes those sins]. //77//
For whomsoever the auspicious name "Śiva" proceeds upon the tongue, millions of great sins are instantly reduced to ashes. (78)
Whatever merit a person obtains by circumambulating the earth, they shall obtain that same merit by circumambulating Śiva and bowing down to him. (79)
Having performed three circumambulations and five prostrations,
and having again performed a circumambulation and bowed down, one shall be liberated from sins.

Whoever should play all kinds of musical instruments, or cause them to be played, in the temple of Śiva, provided it is accompanied by a great sacrificial offering (bali), there the service of the Vedas is produced. 81.
He who causes the Purāṇas concerning the three-eyed God of gods to be heard shall be liberated from all sins and, being fulfilled, shall dwell in the city of Śiva. 82.
The Lord always speaks pleasant words to him with constant reverence;
thus has this supreme worship of the Lord been briefly described. 83.
O Brahmin, since your lifespan is short, perform the worship of Śiva three times a day, twice a day, or even once a day. (84)
Perform the worship of Śiva for a watch or even half a watch;
having entered the stage of life of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), take recourse in the practices prescribed for a forest-dweller. ||85||
In the morning, worship Śaṅkara with forest flowers, bilva fruits, śatapatra lilies, and fragrant lotuses. (86)
With *nīpa*, *japā*, *punnāga*, *karavīra*, and *pāṭala* trees, as well as with *tulasī*, *cāruvidala*, and *aparājitā* [plants]. ||87||
With leaves of the *apāmārga*, *rudrajaṭā*, and *damana*—all these having equal fruits—as well as with *bilva* leaves and *dhūrtaka* [leaves]. (88)
With *droṇa* flowers, *śirīṣa*, *śakta*, and even with *dūrvā* buds, as well as with *naṃdyāvarta* flowers—mixed with sesame seeds or offered alone—and with unbroken grains (*akṣata*). ||89||
One should worship Śiva with whatever other materials are available according to one's capacity;
the worship of Śiva may also be performed with *karṇikāra* flowers, gold, or even *dūrvā* grass. (90)
One should not worship the deity with buds, nor with unripe fruits— with the exception of water-born flowers— and for all water-born flowers, there is no restriction regarding their petals.
O King, just as one might prepare various other things cooked in oil using *kuśa* grass, flowers, silver, or even gold, so it is with this. (92)
It is declared that this does not become stale; it may be used for cakes and the like.
That which has been sprinkled with oil, alkali, sour substances, or cumin is said to be fit for fruit.
O King, roots, fruits, vegetables, and so forth that have been sprinkled with this water are not said to be stale; nor is the water of the Gaṅgā or the ocean considered stale. (94)
O Raghava, all the water of the great rivers as well as the water of the fields— that sacred site which exists in the form of a lake, and the sacred site of the well— [are all equal].
Whatever collection of water there may be from tanks, ponds, lakes, or wells—that entire water from those sacred sites shall never become stale. ||96||
Water for human consumption should be drawn at night; one should prepare water during the day.
Likewise, it should be kept with sand, and it is not beneficial to use water that has been left standing overnight.
"Knowing this, perform worship to the Śivaliṅga.
Śambhu said:
"Having been thus addressed by the sage, Ikṣvāku, who was dear to the Brāhmaṇas," (98)
Devoted to the worship of Śiva, he remained thus for eight days;
then, when the ninth day arrived, he performed his morning worship at the break of dawn.
When the moment of death arrived, he performed the worship of Śiva and offered his own life-breaths as a sacrifice to the Great Lord. 100.
Then, perceiving him to be dead, the messengers of Yama arrived; those who lead one to the world of Yama took their positions and stood firm. (101)
The Śaivas, as well as the messengers Agnimukha and the others who had arrived, engaged in mutual debate, each saying, "Mine, mine! (102).
Then Yama, noose in hand, struck Śiva’s messenger;
thereafter, the fire-faced one angrily assailed a hundred messengers of Yama.
Having thus become massive in body, he seized it with one hand and,
pressing it with another, cut off its head like a blade of grass.
Having killed those messengers, he then took [the head] and went to the descendant of Ikṣvāku;
he presented it to the wise Vīrabhadra.
Then Maheśvara spoke the truth to Śaṅkara:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you have performed worship for only eight days, day after day. (106)
"In the past, you were blameless, yet you called me a 'liṅga' and even 'the tip of the penis.
By that very connection with sin, you shall become one whose face is like a penis. (107)
At the tip of your penis there will be an aperture and a wheel; you will be devoid of a tongue, nose, and other such organs.
Because you previously spoke my name, you shall also become a speaker. (108)
By the word of the Lord, he too became such [a being] in an instant. Śambhu said:
"Whoever should constantly hear this supreme narrative of the Purāṇa... (109)
Freed from the bonds of sin, he shall become a devotee of Śiva;
he shall go to the abode of Śiva and likewise become a speaker [of the truth]. (110)
Whoever tells this story shall become equal to Hara;
formerly, after telling this story, a king named Adhīra [attained that state]. 111.
Then that king, though he had committed a sin, went to heaven together with his wife.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Vibhūtis," in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(110) The One Hundred and Tenth Chapter. Śrī Rāma said:
This fire named Agniśikha is indeed a follower of Śiva;
how did he become such as that? Tell me this, for salutations be unto you.
Śambhu said: "In former times, there was a certain kṣatriya who was always prone to anger;
he was deeply distressed, having lost his wife, his army, and his kingdom. (2)
Having obtained a pair of rams, he engaged in agriculture together with his sons;
yet, burdened by a great debt, he became once again exceedingly miserable.
Moreover, the king was distressed by the loss of his son to a serpent;
being thus affected, the protector of the earth even abandoned agriculture.
Having abandoned even his two sons and having renounced all food, he wept;
then the two sons, having approached, spoke thus to their father: (5)
"Father, why do you weep?
There is nothing lost here from weeping; rather, your grief today will only lead to the withering of your body."
Through grief, your two eyes are lost, as is your sense of shame;
likewise, your religious practice is lost. Why do you lament?
One should protect one's own life even at the cost of losing everything else; however, protecting many is meritorious, especially when they are those who have sought refuge. (8)
"How can you grieve for this enemy who is dependent on another?
The father said:
"How can a son be an enemy? You two are my sons, and likewise, he is mine. (9)
"How could you speak of your son, who is exceedingly happy, as an enemy?
The two sons replied:
"Upon being born, he seizes his mother's wife; as he grows, he seizes her wealth. (10)
Likewise, as one is dying, the vital breaths act as enemies; what could be more so than this?
As for that pleasure which you have described through touching, embracing, and so forth— [it is nothing but suffering]. (11)
"O King, I tell you all this because it results in suffering:
at the time of my son's birth, there arose the thought that my wife might perish. (12)

When one's wife is afflicted by a life-threatening illness, it causes the destruction of one's own happiness; furthermore, when she is born from an impure womb, union with her is not appropriate. (13)
While she was intent on embracing him closely, her breast was drenched with milk; nevertheless, the woman’s union with her beloved was interrupted by the crying of the infant. (14)
The mind becomes firmly fixed upon childhood, and from that, a sense of revulsion [for worldly objects] arises.
Then, if one has fallen into the womb, there is an upward movement toward sexual union in the midst of the earth.

In the midst of pleasure, when it is interrupted, there arises a certain suffering that resembles non-existence; for even when all time is limited, the occurrence of pleasure happens only at some rare moment. (16)
At that time, there is no food, no sleep, and no wife;
there is only the suffering of protecting children from disease, thirst, malevolent spirits, and other such afflictions. (17)

That pleasure which is manifold is considered his [the father's]—such as that produced by the embrace of his father at Mākoṣṭhaka, and likewise that produced by kissing him on the head and so forth. (18)
O Lord of Men, the pleasures derived from exceedingly sweet speech and the like do not equal even a sixteenth part of the joy found in the cessation of worldly attachment.
There are indeed thousands of other sorrows;
why are you made to suffer by this one, which brings opposition both here and in the hereafter? (20)
"Therefore, abandon this grief; we two, O son, have risen here.
Śrī Rāja said:
"I shall abandon this grief, which is difficult to restrain and obstructs all undertakings. (21)
"I must accomplish what is beneficial for myself in this world and the next;
therefore, let us go to this unprecedented great preceptor, my family priest. (22)
Having spoken thus, "O Vasiṣṭha, best of sages, always grant me your protection," he went to his preceptor, the brahmin who was residing in Vārāṇasī.
Then, having prostrated himself like a staff, he was honored by the sage;
he was embraced, his head was smelled, and he was offered a seat.
He was asked, "What is the purpose of your arrival? What service may I indeed perform for you?
The king said:
"O Brahmin, grant me a means of escape from this calamity. (25)
"Exhausted by perpetual karma, I have gone to him for refuge.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Behold the Great Liṅga, the goal known as Viśveśvara, established thus. (26)
Worship this king of kings, the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
by propitiating him in the past, the sage Śakti became the son of Arundhatī.
Though devoured by a *rakṣasa*, he did not go to the world of Yama;
after remaining there for some time, he went to heaven and from there proceeded to the world of Brahmā.
"O Great King, look at this hunter who roams the forest—my son, who sports in the world of Viṣṇu after departing from the world of Brahmā. (29)
He was worshipping the Lord of All with mere leaves gathered by himself, as well as with *śamī* tree leaves and *pūga* flowers. ||30||
Behold him worshipping Maheśāna with kadamba flowers, arka flowers, yūthikā blossoms, and these other varieties. (31)
It is a marvel that he will perish in just half a watch;
even at this final hour, the hunter has arrived for the sake of Śiva.
While seeking an offering to present, he saw a jar by his side;
it was filled with mango fruits, but defiled by a dog and thus contemptible.
Because the intended offering was indeed absent, the hunter likewise uttered these auspicious words, which indicated his devotion toward the world. (34)
In the absence of flowers, the Sun is the *guḍa* (molasses) oblation;
likewise, Jamadagni is the Ṛṣi, and Sanaka is the *liṅga-vistraṃsana*. (35)
In the division of the Liṅga and the pedestal, he pierced his own body and gave it;
other great lords have performed another supreme act of daring.
I too must act in such a way that I do not become a partaker of the fault;
meanwhile, a certain madman approached Śiva. (37)
Then, having brought the offerings made by the hunter, he consumed them instantly;
and likewise, the hunter vomited at the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Śiva.
Then Śaṅkara thought, "Shall I kill this one who has harmed Śiva? and he applied himself to the very effort of slaying his own self. (39)
This covering of the *liṅga* is indeed performed by one who is intoxicated, having offered worship to the impure as they arise;
it belongs to that embodied being for whom there is "this" and "mine. (40)
This skin of yours is now my garment; you must quickly cast it off so that I may perform the ritual dismissal and avoid the loss of the fruit [of my practice]. (41)
Having thus reflected, he then [cut] the skin with a sharp, wondrous axe;
having cut the skin of the right leg below the hip, [he proceeded].
Then, with his left foot, he placed it upon the wheel at the hip;
thrilled and as if trembling, he then cut it off from above.
The hunter, being greatly delighted, pierced the skin of his hand, his brother's heart, and his belly,
and likewise pierced the skin of his head.
From between those two, having pierced his body from within,
he cut off a circular piece of flesh along with a finger and offered it to the god as a skin-offering.
From afar, the son of Śaṅkara appeared in a divine form, with beautiful eyes and four arms, adorned with various ornaments, standing in the sky. 46.
Then hundreds of thousands of Śaiva messengers arrived, wearing various types of crowns and adorned with all kinds of ornaments. ||47||
All of them held tridents in their hands, resembled pure crystal in appearance, possessed four arms, were handsome in form, and were stationed upon excellent celestial chariots. ||48||
All are as radiant as the sun, peaceful, and united with their beloved consorts;
they are accompanied by sons, wives, strength, energy, and hundreds of graceful women. ||49||
Resembling the sun in their splendor, they showered down a rain of flowers;
though summoned by them, the hunter did not come and spoke to them thus: (50)
"Accompanied by my wife and kinsmen, I shall go there or not;
having heard those words of his, the Śaivas then spoke this sentence. (51)
"Whatever merit or evil has been committed by one, its beneficial fruit must be experienced by that same person.
The hunter said: "For all impure beings, dharma is performed by a single agent. (52)
And while the fruit of the Maheśvara teachings was being realized in many ways,
in this very interval, Vīrabhadra arrived with a hundred children.
Accompanied by a multitude of many millions and joined by his kinsmen, the hunters, he came;
and everything you said was exactly so, along with his wife and his kinsmen.
"Ascend this celestial chariot and go to auspiciousness; may it be well with you.
Then, by those words, he reached the world of Śiva, traveling in the celestial chariot.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"You have seen everything; now perform the worship of the Lord.
Freed from the bonds of sin, you shall go to the world of Śiva. (56)
O King, if sovereignty is not desired by you, then cleanse this assembly of the Gaṇas;
perform daily the smearing with cow-dung and water. 57.
By this much, the sovereignty of the earth shall certainly be yours;
as long as you live, your kingdom shall remain, and you shall attain the state of Śiva.
For these [beings], there is no attainment of sovereignty until death;
therefore, having attained another body through the power of service to Śiva, [they shall attain it]. (59)
"Your kingdom shall endure, and likewise your devotion to Śiva shall remain steadfast.
Śambhu said:
"Then, having performed worship in that manner, he died and subsequently went to heaven."
Having regained his royal birth and established his kingdom, he remained devoted to auspiciousness;
then, on one occasion, the king went to the house of the god.
Adorned with various lamps like the king of serpents with his jewels,
there was then a crushing conflict of the warriors when the sole lamp fell upon the king.
Then that king, filled with rage, quickly took up a lamp and,
possessed by anger, cast it into the beautiful city of Devālayapura.
By him a temple was burnt, and thus sin was incurred;
then he further burnt houses, dwellings, and so forth in that place. (64)
The king had [an image of] Maheśāna fashioned and then worshipped him;
thus, on the day his death was to occur, the king had propitiated Śaṅkara.
Bathing in ashes, sleeping on ashes, and chanting the Rudra-mantra, he passed away;
having gone to the world of Śiva, this was related by Vīrabhadra. (66)
O tiger among the Gaṇas, become my attendant;
by my command on behalf of Śaṅkara, bring Umā here immediately.
"You shall also be headless and have a face of flames," he said to the high-souled Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas.
The eye, the ear, as well as the tongue, the nose, the mouth, and the collection of limbs including the head—if deprived of these, how will my worldly activity be possible? (69)
"O Lord, what sin has Umā committed that her head is now missing?
Vīrabhadra replied:
"Previously, you yourself accepted the supreme cave as the Goddess."

One should always [construct] the abode of Maheśa, which brings about the four castes through its syllables (ga), as well as auspicious designs such as the svastika, the sarvatobhadra, the naṃdyāvarta, and so forth. 71.
A lotus, a blue water-lily, a swing-stand, a fan and a chowrie, a trident, a conch, a discus, a mace, and likewise a bow. (72)
The trident, the *ḍamaru* drum, the sword, the bull, the mountain, Giriṭi, Śiva,
as well as the eight-petaled lotus, and other [objects] such as the *yaṣṭi* and so forth.
Meditating thus, she worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord every day;
then once, that courtesan arrived at the temple of the god. (74)
A certain jailer of the king entered the temple of the god;
having seen her there, he spoke these words: ||75||
The jailer said:
"I am neither a courtesan nor a youth; I am an old man.
[One does not desire] an old man, one who is diseased, a eunuch, one who is impotent, or one who is destitute of wealth. (76)
A woman should abandon a man who has a short penis, who is dejected, who is beardless, covered in filth, dull-witted, and defiled by a foul odor. (77)
"One should avoid women from afar, for even a small amount [of association] leads to addiction;
therefore, O courtesan, grant me sexual union so that you may quickly restore my life. (78)
The courtesan said:
"We have indeed heard that for women of all castes, devotion to one's husband is the supreme duty, which bestows happiness both in this world and the next. (79)
When she is dependent on him and under his influence, she cannot be united with another;
therefore, she is renowned as a devoted wife (pativratā), and for that reason, he should protect her.
The jailer said:
"If death will indeed come so soon, there is no doubt;
then, having gone before the king, he spoke these words to the king. (81)
"Nor is it appropriate to say that one's wife is like a prostitute or a courtesan.
Having thus spoken to the king, he then [offered] a *maṇḍa* made from *āranāla*.
Having taken something from her, he went to his own dwelling;
then, seeing an opportunity for sleep, he released his hand.
There, the evil-minded man threw poison into the opening of the garment;
having done this, he departed and spoke thus to the king: [84]
O King, having gone out and approached that foremost of courtesans who was staying within her quarters, you ought to see the entire city after having raised up that courtesan.
Then, having effortlessly seen a garment with its fastenings loosened, he went to the house of a courtesan, which was marked by the form of a king; such were his words. (86)
He said, "This is sleep; look at this which you see.
But he replied to the king there, "O King, this is not proper for me. (87)
Or rather, direct your mother or father to see him;
upon seeing him, all of this will quickly become clear. (88)
Then, having been brought by the king, his mother prepared to look [upon him];
yet, at the very word of the monarch, she acted as if she were merely cleaning her garment. (89)
Then, perceiving that the scum remaining there had dissolved into the outer water, the King asked:
"The garment has become wet from the crushing; what is that? (90)
"Nothing, Your Majesty, nothing at all," said even the prostitute's mother;
then the king, with many words and out of suspicion, looked at the garment. (91)
"This garment is stained with semen; look at this! he said.
Then, having seen it, those standing nearby replied to the king with the words, "So it is. (92)
Then the king, having gone to his own palace, spoke to the magistrate: "Without further deliberation, have the head of the prostitute cut off this very moment. (93)
"Her head is beautiful to behold within this hour; having acted thus at the king's command, show it to her," he said, and so he did. (94)
Vīrabhadra said:
"You have done this unprecedented thing, and today you have reaped its fruit.
You hear with your mouth, you see with your ears, and you smell with your tongue. (95)
"You shall know the taste [of suffering] and become exceedingly wrathful.
Śambhu said:
"Thus was Jvālāmukha born, O King, the son of Maheśvara, who is intolerant. (96)
Therefore, one who desires happiness in this world and the next should cultivate patience;
whoever should constantly hear this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative. (97)
And, being liberated from the bonds of evil, he shall dwell in the world of Śiva. ||98||
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Śiva-worship," in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(111) The one hundred and eleventh chapter. Śrī Rāma said:
The greatness of the name of Maheśa, as well as the greatness of worship, the greatness of prostration, and likewise the greatness of the [divine] glance. ||1||
O best of teachers, please tell me the greatness of the gift of water, the greatness of the gift of incense, and the greatness of the gifts of lamps, perfumes, and so forth. (2)
Śambhu said:
"It is not possible to describe the greatness of each individual name in detail; therefore, I shall speak of them in brief. Listen with respect, O Rāghava."
In ancient times, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a powerful king named Vidhṛta.
When his father died, he, being a child, was consecrated to the sovereignty of the earth.
He brought all those who were of his own age into his presence;
yet even those who were elderly and learned were not esteemed by him.
They were young men, esteemed for their wickedness and their performance of improper deeds; they were skilled at abducting beautiful women and experts in the arts of thieves.
Those skilled in the appraisal of goods, in music, and in dance were esteemed by him;
likewise, those who knew the mantras for subjugation and were experts in garments and medicinal herbs.
That king abandoned those who were fond of singing and dancing, rogues, gamblers,
and those who disregarded their fathers' wishes.
Having deliberated with wicked and untruthful men, he caused evil deeds to be performed;
likewise, he associated with such people and other wicked ones.
Relying on this teaching, he did not abandon his disciplined friend;
those who would clench their fists against his chest and utter cries of "phe-ket" were dear to him. (10)

At that time, the kingdom became devoid of royal policy, even though it was filled with those who were experts in the science of statecraft and proficient in the principles of the characteristics of fortune. 11.
Whatever elephants, horses, chariots, camels, goats, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth there were—all that perished through being plundered here and there. (12)
Then, treasures and wealth were no longer seen in that city;
subsequently, he was defeated by another king and fled.
Then, having gone down into the great forest, he established himself in a mountain stronghold;
there, with a small retinue, he adopted the livelihood of a bandit.
Having pointed out gold, garments, grain, jewels, perfumes,
and so forth in various places, he caused the thieves to bring them.
When he could not find any food for the purpose of procuring the materials required for the binding and other rites, he then prepared a meal [for himself].
When the food consisting of the flesh of cows, buffaloes, and other animals was no longer available,
he prepared for the army's meal the flesh of horses and men.
Such was his conduct, devoid of the twilight prayers and other religious rites;
he had a single minister, a Rākṣasa named Surāpa.
He constantly commanded him, "Bring them here" and "Strike them down.
Thus, remaining with a mind fixed on destroying the Rākṣasas, he [sent for] men who had come from various countries. (19)
Surrounded by a thousand men, that abode of cruelty would seize whatever women he desired, taking them away after having fully considered them.
Having eaten them for some time, she then devoured me as well;
thus, having slain men and women, she ruled a kingdom that was exceedingly difficult to endure.
Thus, having ruled the kingdom for a thousand years,
that lowest of men became frail with old age, his entire body relaxed and marred by wrinkles and grey hair.
That place, extending for many yojanas, became lifeless and level;
then, the day of death arrived for that great-souled king.
When the time of death had arrived, the king was bathed and laid upon the ground;
all his attendants stood around him, surrounding him.
The liquor-drinking minister said, "Command me, what must I do?
Then the king, thus afflicted and his life-force having departed, spoke accordingly.
With his life-breath exhausted below the navel, he somehow uttered these words:
"O Lord of Daityas, strike, strike, and kill me at all times! (26)
Having spoken thus, the messengers of Yama, the enemies of the gods, arrived;
intent on inflicting blows, they made every effort to bind him with various fetters. (27)
The nooses of their bonds were pulverized, and their weapons and staffs were crushed; by the mere touch of his body, it was as if a miracle had occurred. (28)
Then Death himself arrived and bound him with his noose;
but seeing that even the noose of Death had been severed, Death reflected: ||29||
"There is no death anywhere that is as terrible as this one seen here, whether visible or invisible"—
while Mṛtyu was thus absorbed in thought, the powerful Jvālāmukha appeared.
Suddenly commanded by Vīrabhadra, the wielder of the trident arrived;
then, beholding Jvālāvaktra, Death fled in haste.
Seeing him fleeing, Vahnimukha then cried out:
"O thief! O thief! You are a thief! Stop, stop! Where will you go? (32)
"A thief is released from sin merely by being impaled on a stake.
Having addressed Death in this manner, he caused him to be transfixed upon a stake. (33)
Having placed the stake upon his shoulder and bound the messengers with a rope,
he took them, their feet fettered in chains, into the midst of the king.
Having placed him upon a magnificent celestial chariot, beautifully adorned with songs and instrumental music,
he descended to Vīrāntika and reported everything to him.
Vīrabhadra offered all this to Śaṅkara, the immeasurable Self, together with hosts of various sages and gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu. ||36||
Having prostrated before the God who is being served, together with Pārvatī, and having then announced that Mṛtyu himself was fixed upon the stake; ||37||
The all-pervading soul, the powerful Vīrabhadra, became silent.
Seeing Agnyānana, Śiva censured him, saying: "How have you committed this act of audacity against my attendants?
Do you not fear death, which is even more formidable than Yama? Tell me everything according to the ultimate truth."
Vahnimukha, seeing Mṛtyu filled with extreme rage, danced with joy and said:
"A theft has been committed by Mṛtyu; therefore, he has been impaled upon the stake by me. (40)
Śiva liberated them from death and made all the messengers free from disease.
Beholding Death, Śiva spoke: "Death does not reside in these. (41)
"Whether for those of focused mind or those of distracted intellect, there is no name that lacks a syllable or possesses extra letters;
I truly bestow my own world [upon them]. For it has been said: 'By this very name, one shall strike away [suffering]. (42)
They say that one should utter the word "vai" as an addition to the mere sound "pra," and they call it the "pada-less pada.
You should recite this mantra from afar while chanting "namas-tvam," and you too should speak my words. 43.

When Dilīpa had previously questioned Vasiṣṭha, he spoke this;
listen to that, O best of sages, and all ignorance will vanish. 24.
Then, at those words, the brahmins, who were devoted to hearing the Purāṇas, said to the sage: "How should it be heard now, and what must be done? (25)
He too related everything: "Listen to the eternal Dharma;
having first paid homage to the knower of the Purāṇas, one should then offer him water for the feet and a seat. (26)
Having said, "Sit there," one should worship her with perfumes and flowers; and one should offer her the practice of self-yoga (ātma-yoga) along with betel-leaf and additional garments. ||27||
"O Brahmin, please tell us the ancient discourse on merit," he should say;
and he should not sit upon a bedstead, nor even upon a high seat. (28)
One should listen while seated on a low seat for the sake of attaining success in dharma, kāma, and artha.
Having been told "Listen," one who knows the Purāṇas should recite this mantra: [29]
Having first paid homage to Hari, Hara, Gaṇeśa, and Bhāratī, as well as his chosen deity, he ought to speak the Purāṇa. (30)
It may last for half a watch every day, or it may be according to one's desire;
having thus heard the completion of the recitation, one should perform the concluding rite.
The listener’s silent reflection or even silent hearing [is required];
otherwise, Bhāratī would become angry, and from her anger, muteness would ensue. (32)
Therefore, the listener of the Purāṇa should offer betel and other gifts to the reciter, providing for his livelihood according to one's own capacity. (33)
According to the procedure of the Purāṇas, she should give this along with a garment for emerging from the bath; then she should offer either a fine cloth or a pair of garments.
One should likewise give a seat that is vast, variegated, beautiful, powerful, and soft; or else one may give gold, as well as cows, land, houses, and so forth. (35)
O best of Brahmins, all of this was spoken in the past by Śaṅkara, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, to the sages and the inhabitants of heaven.
Then all those sages, having bowed down to him as he sat upon his seat and having offered their individual salutations, stood waiting with a desire to hear [his teaching]. ||37||
The best of the twice-born heard everything he narrated—the entire Purāṇa with all its traditions, beginning from the Upodghāta and ending with the Adhyāya. (38)
Dilīpa said:
"By means of this celestial chariot that moves at will, which is enriched with every prosperity and endowed with happiness in every respect, you have arrived at this holy place. (39)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, you have not asked enough; there are even further distinctions beyond this.
For it is said that by means of this merit, they shall sport [in heaven].
Then, having whitened it with lime so that it resembled the abode of Śiva, [he brought] women rich in the charms of their forms and adorned with every ornament. (41)
There were four, eight, or six women skilled in various beautiful songs and proficient in various dances, who produced the sound of mṛdaṅga drums.
Vaśinī, Audvegā, Avarjikī, Koṇikā, and Dhamanī—these two; Lāsikī makes four; then Saṃtuṣṭā and Gāyikā. (43)

When the two, namely the singer and the musician, have been proclaimed as having become silent—having ceased their vocalizing and the playing of cymbals—the six or eight [musicians] remain in silence. 44.
All were women of every form and grace, all with breasts that had not yet fallen [to the ground], skilled in the arts of love, and for that very reason free from hesitation.
Clad in extremely fine garments, with glances as flickering as lightning—by such women was this dance indeed performed. (46)
And on a certain day, O King, that youth, traveling in his celestial chariot for many years, his face gazed upon by hundreds of women and honored by many, [fell from the sky]. ||47||
Filled with the nourishment of bliss, free from anger, envy, and the like, his face is like a blooming lotus petal, and he is smeared with the five fragrances. 48.
Resembling the sun, all those women were endowed with teeth,
and they wore garlands made of *pārijātaka* flowers that were freshly blossomed and fragrant.
Wearing garlands made of all fully blossomed, climbing, and red sandhi-flowers, they bear their braided hair upon their chests, with lips curved in gentle smiles.
He wanders about, delighted by such dances and songs;
having thus become a lord of celestial chariots, he dwells there for an inexhaustible period of time.
Having acted thus once more, he shall subsequently be born as a king;
and after enjoying a kingdom that yields the fruit of heaven, he will become a devotee of Śiva.
Śambhu said: Dilīpa spoke the words of the sages as told by Vasiṣṭha;
and they performed those threefold musical offerings for the Lord of Umā accordingly.
Having heard the Padma Purāṇa in its entirety, they became happy;
these very Brahmins have now ascended to an excellent celestial chariot.
They are seen as dwellers in the sky, happy and with minds ever-joyful;
all this has been declared to you, as determined in the Purāṇas.
O Rāghava, what more do you wish to hear beyond this? 56.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava. ||113||
The one hundred and fourteenth chapter.
Rāma said:
"Who is this seen in the sky, adorned with all ornaments?"
He stood in his celestial chariot like another sun blazing at midday. ||1||
O Brahman, in that [city] there were five beautiful women who smiled sweetly; they were difficult for all mortals to behold, like another Śrī herself. ||2||
They sing sweet songs with the glances of their beautiful brows,
and likewise with smiles, the clapping of palms, and the sound of hand-slaps.
In some places, with songs produced by [voices from] the throat, with mutual clapping of hands, and with mutual glances at each other's faces preceded by singing, [they were enticed]. ||4||
The great yogi sits playing, resembling the filaments of a lotus;
tell me, by what merit of conduct did he attain this? (5)
Śambhu said: "O Rāma, this brāhmaṇa was formerly endowed with all prosperity,
possessed of various kinds of happiness, and devoted to supporting his wife."
He was childless, devoid of generosity, and abandoned the worship of the deities; he neglected the five great sacrifices and completely renounced the private recitation of the Vedas. ||7||
Devoted to eating at dawn, midday, and evening, and being impure,
he once went to the home of the high-souled Gautama.
By the merit of Tryambaka’s speech, [he reached] that place resorted to by hosts of sages;
there too was a splendid house constructed of crystal.
His wall was anointed with aloe-wood, liquid musk, camphor, and saffron,
and it possessed the excellence of the fragrance of jasmine flowers.
Its floor was sprinkled with musk and the juice of flowers,
and it was adorned with various fine, white canopies.
The grove was adorned with magnificent plantain and areca trees,
and it resounded with the humming of bees born from the nearby lotus ponds.

The quarters of the sky were filled with the fragrance arising from the *pāṭīra* tree, and the quarters of the sky were filled with songs that brought delight through the singing of the precepts. ||13||
It was fashioned by the Creator to destroy the heat produced by the summer season;
it was covered with plantain leaves and provided a roof fashioned from fire.
Its doors were made of the smooth, liquid resin of the *pāṭīra* tree,
and its inner walls were fashioned from the great fragrance of *saugandhika* flowers.
In the northeastern quarter, there was an altar fashioned from beautiful gems,
its base constructed of gold and adorned with variegated altars.
It was situated at the foot of a banyan tree providing very lush and dense shade, its perimeter beautified by groves of flowering plantains and lakes. ||17||
With its clouds made white by frost clinging to the tops of great banyan trees, it was adorned with various groves as magnificent as those in the pleasure gardens of the celestial realm. ||18||
Adorned with many groves, including ponds, wells, and tanks, a gentle and pleasant breeze blew there in that house, bestowing happiness. (19)
And the excellent women, skilled in all beautiful gestures and possessing the wealth of the god of love,
played upon the vīṇā, the flute, and the triple-flute.

Women who perform the triple arts (song, dance, and instrumental music) from the four directions as well as from above, and auspicious balls of ash in vessels made of gold and other materials, [are favorable]. (21)
They were perfumed with all kinds of fragrances and incensed with excellent incense; there were also millions of rosaries made from strung kuśa grass. ||22||
Thousands of black antelope skins were spread out on the outer veranda;
in such a magnificent house as this, O Lord of Sages, the god Indra himself dwells.
Having placed camphor and other substances in the four directions, the lord of sages fashioned a lion-throne of camphor upon a seat of sandalwood.
Having bathed Śaṅkara with fragrant scented waters and milk—[the image] being fine, white, very smooth, and covered with camphor—[one should worship]. 25.

Having bathed Sadāśiva with other Vedic mantras, and having placed a wooden pedestal upon the seat of cloth, one should place a vessel in front; then, having established these [deities] upon the petals: 26.
And in which vessel are the flowers, in which are the sesame seeds and unbroken grains;
in one is the five-fold fragrance, and in which is the vanished fragrance? (27)
Having placed saffron from Kaśmīra, musk, camphor, and likewise sandalwood in other vessels, one should arrange them at the place of worship.
Worship is performed there by means of various paths;
the five-faced Lord Sadāśiva resides within the liṅga. (29)
His covering is the Liṅga, and Śakti is ordained as his [covering];
Viṣṇu is the covering of Śakti, and Brahmā is the covering of Viṣṇu. ||30||
Brahmā is the covering, and Indra is his [covering]; from him comes the Sun, and from that the Śruti.
The protection of those [deities] is by the deities of the directions, and the covering of them is the directions themselves. (31)
Śambhu is the covering of the directions, and his covering is the qualities (guṇas);
this worship of the Śiva-liṅga is indeed the auspicious tenfold covering. 32.
Some may hold this view: "Now, another covering is declared;
it is called the covering of knowledge (vidyāvaraṇa), and that is remembered as the covering of Umā (umāvaraṇa). (33)
Viṣṇu is the covering for him; Vidhi is the covering for Viṣṇu;
Candra is the upper covering for Brahmā; and Bhānu is the covering for him. (34)
If there is an obscuration of the sun, it is known as the sixfold veil (ṣoḍhāvṛti).
Without the ritual procedure, the excellent fivefold veil (pañcāvaraṇa) is proclaimed.
This triad of coverings belongs to Śaśin, Kavi, and Viṣṇu;
it is declared to be the covering of Ambikā, the single, supreme covering. (36)
Alternatively, the world-protectors (Lokapālas) may serve as the enclosure during the worship of Soma;
or rather, worship without an enclosure is praised for Śiva.
One should worship Śiva with substances placed upon the eight petals of the leaf-diagram (patrikā).
I shall now describe the characteristics of the leaf-diagram, which is useful for all ritual acts. (38)
One should fashion an auspicious eight-petaled lotus leaf, resembling a pearl oyster shell, made of gold, silver, or copper. (39)
One should fashion it with eight corners resembling lotus petals;
then, a foot-measure (pāda) in weight is recommended, being well-finished and broad. 40.
It should be neither thick nor thin, with the shape of a lotus above and eight petals;
or else, one should fashion it with five petals according to the path of the power (śakti). ||41||
Alternatively, one may make it with three petals according to one's capacity and inclination; the wise practitioner should fashion the vessel in such a way that it is beautiful.
An auspicious sacred thread (upavīta) is fashioned from eight hundred Rudrākṣas separated by beads of Śakti; it may also be prepared with thirty-eight [beads]. ||43||
Then, one [bone] was bound on each of the two forearms, two on the two wrists, one was placed on the head, and another supreme Ṛṣi held one on his shoulder. 44.
Having fashioned a rosary from rudrākṣa beads, crystals, and gems,
and having prepared a seat of tiger skin, the sage sat in the lotus posture.
Having performed the invocation, the offering of a seat, the arghya, the pādya, and the water for sipping (ācamanīya),
he bathed Śaṅkara with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
With Bakula and Pāṭala flowers endowed with the eight fragrances, placed in golden vessels, purified with a cloth, and strongly perfumed; 47.
At the door there is a copper cauldron; it is an ill omen if there is a continuous flow from a *droṇī* [water-vessel], or if there is a cow's horn, a [deer] antler, or a buffalo horn somewhere. 48.
Or else, with right-spiraling conch shells, or with vessels made of jewels,
or even with those made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal.
One should bathe [the deity] according to one's desire with golden or small earthen jars, or else with lotus leaves. ||50||
One should bathe the Lord with vessels made of palāśa, cūta, and other materials;
among all types of baths, the continuous stream-bath (dhārā-snāna) is preeminent.
One should worship Īśvara with the mantra beginning with "namaste," known as the Śatarudriya,
and with the Anuvāka beginning with "śaṃ ca," which consists of propitiatory formulas (śānti).

Having performed the circumambulation according to one's ability, one should subsequently place the incense and other offerings; then, one should worship with beautiful flowers, leaves, and bilva fruits.

With the leaves of *tulasī*, with white water-lilies (*kalhāra*), great blue lotuses (*mahotpala*), blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*), red lotuses (*utpala*), and all other remaining *karavīra* flowers; ||54||
With *karṇikāra* flowers, white *bhoja* flowers, and likewise with *aparājitā*, with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains, and with *śrī* leaves mixed with sesame; ||55||
In this manner, Gautama worshipped Maheśa, the Lord,
with camphor, agallochum, musk, sarja, agaruka, and sandalwood.
Then he offered sixteen incense burners, and he lit lamps placed upon them,
provided with wicks made of camphor.
Then the supreme food offering was presented to Maheśa:
well-cooked rice-flour cakes, along with foods to be chewed, licked, and sucked. (58)
It was endowed with sweet flavors and the like, provided with the five kinds of edible foods, rich in many varieties of cooked vegetables, and mixed with many different cooked dishes. ||59||
The beverage was prepared with twenty ingredients, including grapes, mangoes, and other fruits, combined with eight kinds of soups and various roots and fruits. (60)
The sage presented an offering of food (naivedya) prepared with other suitable ingredients as they were available, accompanied by the finest flowers.
Having offered a thousand lamps for the lustration ceremony placed in golden vessels,
along with ritual offerings, to the God, he bowed down to him.
Then, pieces of betel nut were ground, and the leaves were washed;
their stems and tips were removed, and they were covered with a very white cloth. (63)
This auspicious betel leaf, with its three layers of leaves and camphor powder,
placed upon a golden vessel, [is offered] to the Lord.
Then, after performing a circumambulation and offering salutations immediately thereafter, eight women arrived, carrying the triple-braided hair and other items. (65)
Accompanied by women playing various musical instruments, she arrived in the presence of the sage;
then, taking up a pair of small cymbals, she herself began to sing.
When Gautama was about to depart, the women then made sounds of lamentation; others likewise played musical instruments such as the *maṃ-daṃ* and *ca-va*.
Likewise, the Sage, assuming a physical form, sang sweetly with a divine voice;
as he danced before the Great Lord, it was like a marvel.
In the meantime, the venerable sage Nārada arrived;
Gautama, for his part, having honored him upon his arrival, prostrated before him. (69)
And he said to him: "In this matter, no one has achieved his goal equal to mine.
What is the purpose of your coming, and from where have you come? (70)
Śrī Nārada said:
"I have come here from Pātāla after eating at the palace of Bāṇa.
The high-souled ones, Bāṇa, Śukra, and others, will come to my house."
Then, in an instant, Bāṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities, arrived;
that asura mounted his elephant, accompanied by twenty akṣauhiṇīs.
Furthermore, Śukra [took] the elephant of Prahlāda, Vṛṣaparvan [took] an excellent chariot, and Bali [took] a supreme steed. (73)
Having learned that all those in distress had arrived, Gautama,
together with his disciples, then went forth in haste, taking with him the water for guest-offering and other necessities.
And seeing Gautama, the Daityas descended from their elephants and other mounts; having paid homage to him, they bowed down to that descendant of Bhṛgu.
Having embraced all the Rākṣasas and honored them according to the prescribed rites,
that bull among sages arranged the encampment of the army.
Having washed Śukra’s feet and likewise held the water upon his head,
the sage offered him an honoring gift accompanied by various fruits.
Having performed their rites preceded by bathing in ponds, lakes, and pools,
they remained at the auspicious hermitage of Gautama situated at the confluence.
Then, having entered that house, all the Rākṣasas along with their priest performed the worship of the gods and acts of devotion within the abode of the twice-born.
On an altar prepared immediately, Śukra sacrificed to Śiva;
on his left side, Prahlāda sacrificed to Acyuta.
Soma, Bali, and likewise other preeminent Asuras worshipped him;
then Bāṇa sacrificed to the one God alone, Triyambaka.
Śukra also worshipped that Blessed One, the Lord of Umā;
and then Gautama, at midday, worshipped Śaṅkara.
All [the practitioners] wore white garments, their bodies smeared with ashes;
having applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) in every place with white ash, they remained. ||83||
Having bowed to the descendant of Bhṛgu, they all proceeded with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi):
within the hollow center of the heart-lotus, there [is] the pentad of elements.

In the midst of those [elements], within the great space, one should meditate upon the pure fire by means of space; and in the center of that, one should meditate upon Maheśāna, radiant and auspicious. 85.
One should burn that body—which is joined with ignorance, composed of impurity, and attached to all things—with the fire of knowledge, as one would burn a lamp in the sky. 86.
Having burned away the obstruction of space, one should then cause space itself to burn;
having burned space, one should then burn the iron-like wind that has become fire.
Having burned that which is extraordinary and having reduced it to the very earth,
and having burned the qualities dependent upon it, one should then cause the body itself to be consumed by fire.
Having thus burned away all unrealities with the fire of that knowledge, one should contemplate Viṣṇu, who resides in the center of the crest-lock and is filled with supreme bliss. 89.
The perfected [deity] possesses rays resembling the light of the moon, which are auspicious;
and the auspicious [consort] is endowed with rays produced from her own body, joined with the liquid of nectar. ||90||
Then, from that state of intense cold, the flames were extinguished like moonbeams;
and through the spreading rays of nectar, the entire flood became solidified.
One should then contemplate the supreme [state], in which the entire collection of beings has been gradually inundated. 92.

Having thus performed the purification of the elements (*abhūtaśuddhi*), the mortal becomes truly pure through the rite of action (*kriyāhoma*). Only then may he perform worship and the practice of recitation (*jāpyakarma*); subsequently, through meditation on the Deity, there occurs the destruction of even such sins as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). ||93||
Having thus meditated upon this intensely radiant light and, through meditation, having projected it onto the swift liṅga of Śiva,
one should contemplate Sadāśiva in the midst of the lamp and perform the imperishable worship with the five-syllabled mantra.
Having likewise performed the ritual services beginning with the invocation, the bathing of Śaṅkara is done as before;
here, every pedestal—whether made of udumbara wood, silver, or gold—is covered with cloth and so forth. (95)
Having formed the syllable *aṃ* and a rain of bubbles, one should place a single serpent upon each pedestal in front;
and with an upward-pointing [syllable], one should place a pair of serpents on the pedestal to the right and left of the deity.

Having placed a hibiscus flower in the center of the serpent, and a very white cloth upon that in the middle of the twelvefold [circle], one should worship Maheśa there in the form of a *liṅga* together with its pedestal.

Having done this, and having offered or not offered the five fragrances and the eight fragrances to the Lord of the Gods, beginning with Bāṇamukhya, one should worship him thoroughly with flowers, leaves, auspicious sesame seeds, unbroken rice grains mixed with sesame, or even by themselves alone. ||98||
Having offered incense prepared according to the ritual rules, having offered lamps and the aforementioned offerings,
and having completed the remainder of the worship, they all performed singing and dancing here and there.
Then, in the meantime, a disciple of Gautama named Śaṅkarātman arrived. ||100||
Wearing the garb of a madman and clad in various rags, he sometimes appeared as the most excellent of the twice-born and at other times resembled a caṇḍāla. (101)
In some places there was an ascetic associated with Śūdras, and in others he roared, leaped up, danced, praised, and sang. (102)
He weeps, hears clearly, falls down, and sometimes stands up;
he is uniquely endowed with the knowledge of Śiva and is overflowing with supreme bliss. (103)
Having arrived at the time for the meal, he went to Gautama’s hermitage;
there he ate together with his teacher, and in some instances, even the leftovers.
In some places he went silently with his bowl filled with food;
in other places, taking the hand of his teacher himself, he ate.
Seeing urine in one part of the house and mud plaster in another, the Guru always took hold of my hand and [led me] inside. (106)
