Having led him in and seated him upon his own throne, he fed him;
the sage Gautama himself ate from that same vessel.
Then, in order to test his mind, that inauspicious woman once summoned a disciple of Ahalyā and said to him, "Eat this. (108)
Having placed food in a golden vessel and drinks and so forth in a goblet, he then again [placed] fire in one [of them]. (109)
Having deposited a heap of firewood and a pile of axes elsewhere, the sage ate his meal, saying, "Eat, eat!
even as he himself was eating.
Just as he had drunk water, so too did the twice-born one drink fire;
and having eaten the thorns, he remained just as he was before. (111)
In former times, invited by the daughters of sages for a meal, he was given day after day clods of earth, cow dung, and wood chips. (112)
Having joyfully and with delight eaten the clay and the wooden staff, this sage, though appearing like a caṇḍāla, is truly such a one. (113)
Taking a well-worn sandal in one hand and likewise [another] in his other hand,
he approached Vṛṣaparvan with words appropriate for the occasion.
The one clothed in the directions (the Wind-god) stood between Vṛṣaparvan and Īśa;
not recognizing him as the son of Vṛṣaparvan, he pressed him down and cut off his head. 115.
When that best of the twice-born was slain, this world of mobile and immobile beings became exceedingly turbid,
as did the sages dwelling there.
Great sorrow arose within the high-souled Gautama;
tears flowed from his eyes as if manifesting his grief. (117)
Gautama spoke these words in the presence of all the Daityas:
"What sin has been committed by this man, such that his head has been severed? (118)
For this yogin of Śiva, who is always dearer to me than my own life, even my death is certain, since the Guru has appeared in the form of this disciple. (119)
Wherever death is seen for those who follow Śiva, who are endowed with righteousness, and who always abide in Śiva, there certainly is no non-death. 120.
Śukra said:
"I shall restore this one to life—he who is without lineage and dear to Śiva. Why does he die, O Brāhmaṇa? Behold the power of his asceticism!"
When the sage Itivādini had thus spoken, Gautama also died; and when he was dead, Śukra likewise gave up his life through the practice of yoga.
Having learned that he too had been slain, all the lords of the Dānavas died in an instant; it was like a marvel.
Then the army of that wise Bāṇa was dead;
tormented by grief for Ahalyā, she wept aloud again and again.
The all-pervading Lord Vīrabhadra, the great yogi, having been worshipped by Gautama through the worship of Maheśa, became enraged upon seeing everything.
"Alas, what a tragedy! Alas, what a great tragedy! O Maheśas, many have died.
I shall inform Śiva; I will do whatever he commands. (126)
Having thus resolved, he went to the imperishable mountain Mandara;
having paid homage to the three-eyed Lord, he then spoke all this. ||127||

Seeing Brahmā and Hari standing there, Śiva, the bestower of boons, spoke these words upon witnessing the daring deed performed by his devotees: 128. "Having seen this bold act performed by my devotees..."
"Having gone, we shall see Viṣṇu; you two shall also come.
Then Īśa, having mounted his bull, with chowries fanned by the wind, [departed].
O Lord, it was beautiful that the umbrella was held by Dikena in a fine disguise, with its very white golden handle, and not by anyone else. (130)
Having obtained the permission of Maheśa, Hari stood at the end of the serpent;
he shone, adorned with a visible kaustubha gem and two canopies, one reddish and one blue.
Then, with Śiva’s permission, Brahmā also ascended the swan;
the Creator shone with two umbrellas having the luster of indragopa insects.
Then Indra and all the other gods, accompanied by their respective mounts and cheered by various musical instruments, set forth together. (133)
Crowded by hosts numbering in the tens of millions, they went to the hermitage of Gautama;
having seen Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, they were struck by that supreme wonder.
He restored his own devotee to life by glancing at him from the left corner of his eye;
then Śaṅkara said to Gautama, "I am pleased with you; choose a boon."
Gautama said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, O Maheśvara, may I always possess the capacity to worship your liṅga. (136)
"O God, O Three-eyed One, hear this which has been chosen by me: my disciple is highly fortunate, free from what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. (137)
One does not perceive with the eye that which is to be seen as "mine," nor that which is to be smelled with the nose, nor that which is to be given, nor anything else. (138)
Having understood this and acting accordingly, that yogi of great renown, with his appearance made strange and like a madman, became celebrated as Śaṅkara. ||139||
"May no one hate another's mind, and may no one harm another;
O Lord, let this be granted to me, as well as immortality for these beings. (140)
The Blessed Lord said:
"These shall remain as living beings until the end of the kalpa, and thereafter they shall attain liberation.
This abode constructed by you is vast, wonderful, and auspicious."
"Let us stay for just a moment; then we shall go to that other region.
Gautama said:
"O Lord, one who is seeking wealth does not perceive the fault in requesting what is improper."
"If it pleases you, O Lord of Gods, let that which is unattainable even by Brahmā and others be granted.
Then the Lord, looking at Viṣṇu, took hold of Hari’s hand.
Laughing, Sadāśiva spoke thus to the lotus-eyed one:
"O Govinda, you appear dejected; what food shall I give to you? (144)
Either enter yourself and enjoy it as if it were your own home,
or go to the house of Pārvatī, which shall fill the womb of Yāku.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, leaning upon him, went to a secluded place; and having instructed the gatekeeper for that day as previously directed, the god departed.
He spoke this reply to Gautama at the command of Viṣṇu.
Sadāśiva said: "O Sage, prepare food for all of us, for we desire to eat. (147)
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara went to a secluded place with Vāsudeva; having ascended a soft bed, those two supreme deities lay down.
Having conversed with one another, both of them rose up;
having gone to the deep lake, those two best of gods intended to bathe. (149)
Having separated their hands and drinking water from one another at both ends, the sages and the rākṣasas engaged in water-sports. ||150||
Then Viṣṇu and Maheśa, with great speed, caused the falling of water; Śaṅkara seized the lotus-stalk of Hari with his hand.
They showered streams of filaments from their eyes, which were like blooming lotuses, into his face;
yet Keśava closed his eyes.
In the meantime, Maheśvara mounted Hari’s shoulder;
seizing Hari by his two arms, he submerged him in the highest ocean.
Having caused him to emerge again and again, and repeatedly pressing him down, that Hari caused Śaṅkara to fall into a state of extreme exhaustion.
Then, seizing Hari by the feet, he dragged him and whirled him around;
he struck the chest of Hari and caused Acyuta to fall.
Then Hari, having risen, took water in his joined palms and sprinkled it over Śambhu; then Śambhu likewise sprinkled it over Viṣṇu.
Thus the water-sport took place in the midst of the assembly of sages;
through the excitement of the water-play, the binding of their matted locks became disheveled. (157)
Then, out of agitation, those lords of sages became entangled with one another’s matted locks; their matted locks were bound together with each other’s.
Those possessing power forcibly drag away those lacking power, casting them down while they cry out and wail in distress. (159)
When the water-activity had thus begun and become tumultuous, Nārada,
seeing it from the sky, danced and sang aloud.
Making the *vipaṃcī* lute resound, he sang a charming song;
with that beautiful singing, he sang ten verses in a graceful manner.
Śaṅkara, the creator of the worlds, heard a sweet song; he himself began to sing it playfully: "Maṃ daṃ maṃ daṃ. (162)
O Lord of Gods, she herself sings the mixed Maṅgalakaiśikī;
while Nārada performs the dance, she sings in a modulation of notes.
Having firmly grasped the tone, which is endowed with all the characteristics and joined with the nectar of its own stream, he conquered Māra by means of song alone. 164.
Vāsudeva struck this mṛdaṅga drum with his two hands;
meanwhile, the four-faced one, having plunged into the water, shone loudly from within the depths. 165.
Tānaka, Gautama, and the others remained silent, unable to sing;
only Hanumān, the lord of monkeys, sang a sweet song. (166)
Then that which was withered became fresh, and those who were emaciated became nourished;
thereafter, all of them, having surpassed their respective songs, became thus enraptured. (167)
All the hosts of gods, sages, and dānavas became silent;
he alone, along with Hanumān, was the speaker, while all of them were the listeners.
At the time of midday, when the occasion for a meal had spread out,
Maheśvara, hearing a song, put on a pair of fine linen garments.
Viṣṇu [wore] two yellow garments, and the four-faced one [Brahmā] wore reddish ones;
then all of them, having performed their respective appropriate duties for the Kali age, [proceeded].
Having mounted their respective vehicles, all the deities departed; Maheśa, who is fond of song, then spoke to the Lord of the Monkeys.
"Having been commanded by me to leap, mount the bull without hesitation;
then, facing toward me, sing the song of all songs. (172)
Then the tiger among monkeys said to the Blessed Maheśvara:
"Since you possess the capacity for mounting the bull... (173)
"O Lord, having mounted your vehicle, I would become a sinner;
O Lord of Gods, let Śiva’s vehicle, the celestial bird, carry me instead. (174)
"Behold me; I shall sing facing toward you.
Then the Lord mounted Hanumān, as one mounts a bull. 175.
When Lord Śaṅkara had mounted [the mountain], Hanumān,
having severed the head of the earth and turned back its skin, sang with his face directed forward as before.
Listening to the nectar of the song, Śambhu went to the house of Gautama;
all the hosts of celestial sages and dānavas also arrived there. (177)
Then, when the time for the meal had arrived, Gautama honored whatever household utensils and such were made from dry wood. (178)
Everything became fully developed while Hanūmat was singing; as he sang, the minds of all were fixed upon that wondrous vision. (179)

With two arms, bowing at the feet of the Lord, endowed with ornaments upon all his limbs, he has a gracious form and is youthful; with slender waists, he stands with his head bowed and is praised by the gods with joined palms. (180)
Grasping Hanumān’s head with both hands, Śaṅkara made his eastern face;
then, while Hanumān sat in the lotus posture, he placed one foot upon [his lap] and the other upon his mouth.

The Lord affectionately grasped his feet with his toes, his nose with his nose, his mouth with his mouth, his forehead with his forehead, his chest with his chest, and his heart with the space between his breasts. ||182||
Then, having pressed that second [hand] against his navel-circle within the womb,
Śaṅkara took hold of the head, bent it down, and touched the back with his chin, making a sound.
Śiva placed around Hanumān’s neck a necklace fashioned from pearls;
then Viṣṇu spoke these words to Maheśāna: ||184||
In the entire circle of the universe, there is none equal to Hanumān;
indeed, that state of yours which is inaccessible even to the Vedas and the gods remains established within him. 185.

O Monkey, Your state is unmanifested by all the Upaniṣads, yet it is joined with everything; Your state is not attained even for a moment through yogas consisting of the means such as restraint (yama) and the rest. ||186||
The pure heart of the great yogi Hanumān, possessing the strength of Bhoja, attained this after performing difficult austerities for thousands of millions of years. (187)
The lords of sages do not recognize your form; how then could they know a single foot?
Oh, what extraordinary fortune it is that even a fickle monkey has become a deer! 188.
Even if I were to place my pair of feet upon your head for a thousand years, or even for a thousand ages, day after day, it would still not be enough to satisfy your heart.
O Lord, although you were worshipped with devotion and even shown the space under your feet by me, there is a great rumor in the world that you are a mere mortal who is fond of Nārāyaṇa. 190.
"Lord Hari is dear to Śambhu; such good fortune as yours does not exist for me.
Sadāśiva said: "O Blessed Lord Hari, there is no one as dear to me as you. (191)
"O Pārvatī, there is no other equal to you; there is none other who exists for me.
Then the great Gautama, having prostrated himself before the Goddess, [spoke].
O immeasurable soul, O ocean of compassion for the world, he informed him:
"Midday has passed, and it is now the time for everyone to eat. (193)
Then, having sipped water for purification, the omnipresent Great God, accompanied by Viṣṇu,
entered the house of Gautama and proceeded to take his meal.
With jeweled bracelets, anklets, and a silk sash as bright as lightning, with many necklaces, armlets, a golden breastplate, a sacred thread, and an upper garment. (195)

The Lord was adorned with dangling jeweled earrings, with his excellent hair-knot beautifully blossomed, with the application of fragrant sandalwood paste, with armlets upon his arms, and with golden finger-rings.

Thus adorned, Śiva sat upon an excellent seat, and likewise seated Hari upon a superior throne facing him. As the two best of gods, Hari and Īśa, sat facing one another, Gautama then presented golden vessels to them.

There were thirty varieties of solid foods and four kinds of excellent milk-rice, prepared from well-cooked grains in two hundred ways; furthermore, one hundred varieties were prepared as uncooked, cooked, and mixed, and likewise, the Sage prepared one hundred, one hundred, ten, and ten more. (198)
He gave twenty-five [pots] filled with vegetables and clarified butter, as well as excellent sugar and the like, along with fine cloves, pomegranates, and so forth;
the fruit of the plantain tree (*mocāphala*), *tugākṣīrī*, fine *kharjūra* dates, ginger, the fruit of the rose-apple (*jambūphala*), *priyāluka*, *vikaṅkata*, and likewise the fruit of the *kata*.
Having offered these and other such articles according to the prescribed rule, and having given the *āpośana* water, the Brahmin said, "Eat. (200)
Taking a fan made of fine cloth himself,
Gautama fanned Śiva and Viṣṇu while they were all seated for their meal.
The Supreme Lord desired to make a jest:
"Behold, O Viṣṇu! How can that monkey Hanumān eat [this]? (202)
While the assembly of sages looked on, Maheśvara saw a monkey and threw that monkey, who was like a piece of meat for Viṣṇu, into the vessel of Viṣṇu.
He gave Hanumān his own leavings, such as milk-rice and other foods;
yet, O Lord, by your very word, those leavings of yours are not to be eaten.
If my offering is unworthy—whether it be a leaf, a flower, or likewise a fruit—one should cast all that has been offered to me into a well. (205)
"Surely this was because you had not yet eaten, or perhaps it was due to your compassion even after you had eaten.
Sadāśiva said:
"For you were stationed there at the self-manifested Bāṇaliṅga Caṇḍakāṇḍa."
The consumption of Śambhu’s food offering (naivedya) should be known as equal to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
this is the time for eating now, whereas its lack of relish arises from other talk. (207)
"Having eaten, I shall speak to the Lord without hesitation.
Then the sage Gautama performed the water-consecration rite.

With those waters from the pond— purified by being rubbed with seeds and thoroughly cleansed— he filled the pitchers, which were reddish, very smooth, and of very fine texture, having been washed and dried many times.
Having covered a fresh sand altar by the river with pure, very white, and fine cloths, one should then place jars filled with water upon it.

Having placed a cluster of lotus stalks and a covered vessel, one should put into the interior of the vessel the powder of nutmeg and musk, along with a garland as bright as the rays of white sandalwood.

Furthermore, having purified it with water and cloth, one should cast a *yāma* [measure]; then, having placed a *caṇḍagraha* [seizure] and a *bakula* flower, one should likewise cast a *pāṭala* flower. (211)

Then, having first placed a cluster of *śephālī* flowers and water there to perform the purification of the water, one should wrap the mouth of the *sṛṇikā* with a very soft, fine piece of cloth and [place] a fine cotton [filter]. (212)
Then, having placed the water-jars in a shaded place, one should fan them with a fine fan while a gentle breeze is present. ||213||
Then, O King, having consecrated even a blade of grass with water from the ocean, men or women there, being well-prepared and self-restrained, [should perform the rite]. 214.
They wore garments washed by the water of that maiden's voice; they were clad in freshly laundered clothes and anointed with the resin of madhūka flowers, honey, and liquid aloe-wood.
One should apply the *sāndrama* ointment at the base of the arms and the *jāpyaka* ointment on the head; for such a person, there is the anointing with the five fragrances (*pañcagandha*). ||216||
With beautiful hair adorned with flowers, praised, fair-faced, and perfectly pure; likewise, O Noble One, they possess bodies as fragrant as saffron. (217)
Young women, beautiful in every limb and adorned with ornaments, or even such monkeys, should cause water to be brought by these ladies. (218)
At the time of giving, look for one whose water-pot is wrapped in a fine cloth or a small piece of clothing, or who holds the pot in the left hand. (219)
Then, having removed the water placed in the water-pot, he should cause it to be offered;
in this manner, the venerable sage Gautama performed the hospitable reception.
When all those great-souled ones, beginning with Maheśa, had finished eating,
their feet and hands were washed and their hands were rubbed with fragrant unguents.
Then, while Maheśvara, the God of gods, was seated upon that throne,
the gods along with the hosts of sages likewise sat down upon lower seats.
Having wrapped pieces of betel nut in jeweled vessels, well-perfumed, neither angular nor circular, neither too large, nor too small, nor too thin; 223.
Having purified white leaves and cast them in, along with pieces of camphor and powder,
Gautama then offered them to Śaṅkara.
When the sage had spoken these words, "Accept the betel for the deity," [he said], "O monkey, accept that betel;
give me unbroken [areca nuts]. (225)
The monkey said: "O Maheśvara, there is no impurity for me;
since I have eaten many fruits, how can a monkey be impure? (226)
Sadāśiva said: By my word everything shall be purified; by my word poison becomes nectar;
by my word all the Vedas are realized; and by my word the deities and others [are established]. 227.
Knowledge of Dharma comes from my word; liberation is said to come from my word.
The Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Smṛtis likewise arise from my word.
"Take this betel; give me pieces of sugar-candy.
Hari took the betel and the pieces of areca nut with his left hand. (229)
Then, having gathered the leaves, he offered the pieces;
Śiva took the camphor placed before him and ate it.
Having heard from the mountain that this was the work of the gods,
Pārvatī took Jayā and Vijayā by the hand and went to the hermitage of the sage.
Then, having bowed at the feet of the Lord, she stood with her face downcast;
raising her face, the Three-eyed One spoke this to her: ||232||
O Lord of the gods, for your sake I have committed an offense;
namely, that I ate while leaving you aside—listen to this, O Śaṃdari. (233)
Then he established his own self in the supreme state, devoid of the god of gods,
liberated from all bonds, and having performed a great act of merit.
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to forgive me; look upon me with anger abandoned.
Having spoken thus, she departed, leaving Aruṇa behind.
Perceiving that she was departing, the sage prostrated himself like a staff;
from that time forth, he offered praises to Maheśa accompanied by such prostrations.
Śiva said, "O Gautama, what do you desire?
Gautama replied:
"O Lord of Gods, I have accomplished my purpose; if there is a boon to be granted to me... (237)
"O highly fortunate one, please accept this food from me.
The Goddess said:
"O sage, with the permission of Śaṅkara, I shall eat here in your house. (238)
Having gone to the Lord and received his permission, the brahmin Gautama returned;
he then caused the beautiful goddess Girijā, who was bearing [the child], to be fed.
Then, having eaten everything, Pārvatī— adorned with perfumes, flowers, and ornaments—
went to Hara accompanied by her thousand attendant maidens.
Then Śaṅkara said to the goddess: "Go to the hermitage of Gautama;
having performed my twilight devotions, I shall return home again. (241)
Having been addressed thus, the goddess departed from the hermitage of Gautama; and all those desiring to perform the evening twilight worship likewise went forth.
Having performed the twilight rites at the lake, Maheśa and the others did so in their entirety;
then Śambhu, facing north, performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and recited the mantra.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, spoke this to Maheśa:
"He who is saluted by all and who alone is worshipped by all. (244)
You are invoked in all sacrifices; what else will you chant?
All the rivers flow toward you alone as their sole object of worship. (245)
O Lord of the gods of gods, I offer my joined palms in salutation to you;
O Maheśvara, you are the bestower of the fruits of meritorious acts such as prostrations. 246.
"Who else but You is the giver of fruits in this world? Who indeed is greater than You?
Śaṅkara said:
"O Govinda, meditate on nothing else; do not bow down to anyone else here. (247)
"I shall not worship anything, nor shall I recite any mantra; however, this was spoken by me for the sake of engaging those who are nihilists. (248)
Just as those who commit evil deeds would take away what is beautiful to behold, therefore all this has been done by me for the sake of benefiting the world. ||249||
Having said "Om," Hari then bowed to him and stood there;
then those hosts of gods and sages arrived at the house of Gautama.
Then they all performed worship to the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
meanwhile, the Lord, the best of the Raghus, remained seated with Hanumān, singing.
All of them recited that great five-syllabled vidyā;
then Hara, taking Hanumat by the hand, went into the presence of the Goddess.
Both these lords of the gods were seated together on a single bed;
the powerful Nārada remained there singing, while Tumburu likewise offered hymns of praise.
The Supreme Lord performed various kinds of playful sports;
having summoned Pārvatī, the Lord spoke these words.
Śrī Sadāśiva said: "O auspicious one, I shall arrange the braid of the Goddess in front of Himavat;
for it is not fitting that a woman should perform service for her husband. (255)
If one were to perform the grooming of hair, one would incur no different kind of harm;
for by the mere grooming of hair, the entire reality of the deity is not attained. (256)
Then, after the binding has been performed, there follows the wiping of the corners of the mouth;
thereafter, the final cleansing of the body, including the hair, flowers, and so forth, that were attached to it. ||257||
When those great-souled ones arrived while he was still in that state, what answer could you possibly have given to the gods and others? (258)
"If you do not come, O Lord, then my fear will surely perish.
As she was speaking thus, Śaṅkara drew her toward him by the hand. (259)
Having placed her upon his thighs and loosened the binding of her hair,
he parted it with both hands, even using his fingernails.
Having taken the Pārijāta garland given by Viṣṇu even though it was upon her hair,
she fashioned it into a braid and placed the garland that had come into her hand around her neck.
Taking a garland of *mallikā* flowers, Maheśvara bound it upon his hair; he also took the garland of celestial blossoms given by Brahmā.
The Lord then performed the cleansing of the back and the sides, which were rich with fragrance and concealed within Pārvatī’s garment. 263.
Having descended below the lower garment of the Goddess, which had become loose, the Lord said, "What is this? and then tied up her waist-knot.
"Look at this nose-ornament of yours; I shall take it from you," saying this, the virtuous woman herself took away the lusterless pearl.
A pearl becomes radiant through contact with turmeric;
let this pearl, which is dear to me, be worn by you. (266)
Pārvatī said:
"O Śambhu, how wonderful is this palace of yours, so richly endowed with all things!
Previously, I knew all these objects only through their ornaments. (267)
The abundance of his wealth during the day is discerned by his ornaments;
his head is adorned with a garland from the crest of Brahmā, the Lord. (268)
Likewise, he had a garland from hell as an ornament for his chest,
and Śeṣa and Vāsuki, both full of poison, as earrings on his ears.
His direction was the north; his matted hair and locks were white like ash;
his vehicle was a great bull; and his lineage and family were indeed unknown. (270)
"You two may know your fathers, but not Virūpākṣa, whose body is thus [deformed].
As the daughter of the mountain was speaking thus, Viṣṇu, becoming exceedingly enraged, said to her: ||271||
"For what reason would I bite the god of gods, the Lord of the Universe?
O auspicious one, I shall surely give up my dear life-breaths, for there is no doubt that you are unrighteous. (272)
"O auspicious one, where there is the granting of wealth by the Lord, there let our vow not be in vain.
Having said this, Hari then approached with his two claws to sever [the head]. 273.
Maheśa, taking his hand, said: "Do not commit such a rash act;
all of Pārvatī’s words are dear to me, even if they are unpleasant to you. (274)
"Whatever is desired to be done that is unpleasant to me, O Hṛṣīkeśa," [he said];
then the Blessed Lord Hari, having replied "Om," became silent.
Then Hanumān informed Lord Atha of these words:
"I request that my vow of worship be likewise fulfilled without any desire for reward. (276)
"I wish to go for the sake of worship; you should grant me permission.
Śaṅkara said:
"Whose worship? Where is the worship? What is the flower? What is the leaf? Tell me! (277)
"Who is the preceptor? What is the mantra? And what is the manner of worship?
Thus spoke Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, to the Lord of Gods. (278)
With his entire body trembling, Hanumān began to offer praise.
Hanumān said:
"Obeisance to the great god Śaṅkara, the immeasurable Self. (279)
Salutation to the yogi, the sustainer of yoga, the teacher of yogis;
salutation to the God accessible to yogis, the Lord of the knowers of Brahman. ||280||
Salutation to you, the Lord of the Vedas; salutation to the Lord of the gods.
Salutation to the one who is meditation itself, who is attainable through meditation, and who is the preceptor of the sustainers of the world. ||281||
Salutation to the one who is the teacher, who is accessible to both the learned and the unlearned, and who is the lord of the earth and other realms;
salutation to the treasury of Vedic utterances beginning with "namaste" and so forth. (282)
Salutation to Him who is propounded by such words as "Spread yourself out" (ātanuṣva);
salutation to You, the eight-formed one; salutation to the Lord of creatures (Paśupati). ||283||
O you who have the form of Tryambaka, the three-eyed one, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire; you who take pleasure in bhr̥ṅgarāja, dhattūra, and droṇa flowers! 284.
O you who are beloved by the multitude of Bṛhatīs, by Puṃnāgas, Caṃpakas, and others;
salutations to you, salutations to you, again and again salutations, salutations! ||285||
Śiva then said to Hari, "Do not fear; tell me everything. Hanumān said:
"The worship of Śiva’s liṅga must be performed by one whose body is smeared with holy ashes. (286)
With waters gathered during the day and likewise with flowers and other offerings, I shall inform the Lord of the auspicious ritual for the worship of Śiva. (287)
When evening has arrived, one should perform a bath without washing the head;
having put on clean, dry clothes and sipped water (ācamana), one of clear intellect should perform the rite twice.
Then, having taken up the ashes, one should perform the fire-related bath (āgneyasnāna),
having consecrated them with the *praṇava* either eight times or even more.
With the five-syllable mantra, or by name, or by whatever [mantra] it may be, one whose hand holds darbha grass should collect ashes consecrated seven times. (290)
Having uttered "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," one should cause [the water] to fall upon the head; having uttered "Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe," one should sprinkle the ashes upon the face. (291)
One should place [the ashes] on the chest with "To the non-terrible ones and to the terrible ones";
one should place them in the secret place with "Salutation to Vāmadeva. || 292 ||
One should recite "I take refuge in Sadyojāta" and then place [the ashes] on the feet;
the wise one should then dust the entire body with the Praṇava.
The supreme procedure for bathing and other rites has been declared for those of the three higher castes;
now I shall explain that which was taught by the Guru regarding Śūdras and others. (294)
The wise one should consecrate the ashes while reciting the word "Śiva" seven times; then, taking it up, he should apply it to his head with the words "To Śiva. (295)
One should place [the mantra] spoken by Śaṅkarāya in the heart of Sarvajñāya;
having said "namas sthāṇave," one should also [place it] in the secret part of Svayambhū. ||298||
Having uttered [the mantra] and cast it upon the feet, thereafter, having uttered "Namaḥ Śivāya," the entire body should be smeared with ashes; this is known as *uddhūlana*. (297)
Having washed his hands and sipped water, with darbha grass in hand and composed in mind;
in the absence of darbha grass, gold may be used, and in its absence, cow-hair.
In its absence, dūrvā grass should be used; in its absence, silver.
Having performed the twilight worship and the recitation for the Goddess, one should proceed to the temple.
Alternatively, one may prepare a divine altar, or a consecrated earthen mound that is pure and adorned with designs such as lotuses. ||300||
By means of four colors, or again by white alone,
one should likewise draw various lotuses, svastikas, and other such figures.
Likewise, the lotus and other [emblems], the mace, the conch, the trident, and the ḍamaru drum;
the five types of temples mentioned by Sarva, and furthermore, the Śiva-liṅga. (302)
The tree that grants the fruit of all desires, as well as the *kulaka* and *kolaka*, [should be drawn] as a hexagon, a triangle, or even a nonagon. (303)
A swing with twelve corners, sandals, and fans;
likewise, a pair of chowries and an umbrella, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others.
The wise one should fashion [the altar] with powders upon a sacrificial mound (vedi) or even in a temple;
wherever there is worship of the deity, the learned one should arrange it in that very place. (305)
That which is fashioned with one's own hand is the best; that which is purchased is mediocre; that which is obtained by begging is inferior; and that which is taken by force is the lowest. (306)
That which is given by force to those who are unworthy, even if they are worthy, is fruitless.
[This is illustrated] by red śāli rice, japā flowers, a stone pillar, kalama rice, and black and red [grains]. (307)
That [should be performed] with ears arising from *dul* rice and so forth, measuring only a *vrīhi* grain, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and likewise inferior [qualities]. (308)
One should properly perform this sacrifice by means of the installation of the lotus and other [mandala elements];
one should face either the northeast or the east. (309)

And I shall describe the seat as it has been seen and as it has been heard: one made of kuśa grass, one made of leather, one equal to [a garment of] cloth, one made of wood, or one made of palm leaves. (310)
One should prepare a seat from lead, tin, silver,
or even copper, or else from cow-dung or the seeds of the arka plant.
The fourfold types of skins are to be known as those of the tiger, the ruru deer, the antelope, and the deer; and likewise, the bandhūka skin.
One should arrange a seat among these according to what is available;
one may sit either in the lotus posture (padmāsana) or even in the auspicious posture (svastikāsana). ||313||
Seated upon darbha grass and ashes, having restrained the breath and controlled the speech, one should perform internal meditation for that long, visualizing the form of the deity. (314)

The Śiva who is your crest-lock, residing in the twelve fingers, subtle-bodied, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with 'ra', exists within the cave of the heart among all beings who possess universal forms. (315)
Having meditated upon him as endowed with all ornaments and possessed of qualities such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and the rest,
one should hold him in the mind and fill the body through his pervasive presence.
By that radiance, the sin residing within his body was destroyed, just as gold becomes red through contact with mercury and then turns white. ||317||
Having fashioned a pure seat consisting of twelve, eight, or five petals arranged in a circle, and having placed the *liṅga* there; ||318||
One should likewise meditate upon Maheśāna, the Lord of the Liṅga, as residing in the cave;
and [one should place] water purified in a cleansed jar, scented with fragrance.
Having cast down fragrant flowers consecrated with the *praṇava*, one performs breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the *praṇava*; however, these are not prescribed for Śūdras. (320)

Meditation on the stages of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the recitation of the mantra "Oṃ Śiva," and whatever materials for worship there may be, such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains; ||321||
Having established those [images] nearby, he will then resolve:
"I shall perform the worship of Śiva for the sake of pleasing Śiva alone. (322)
Having thus performed the mental visualization,
and having carried out the rites beginning with the invocation up to the ritual bath, one should then perform the actual bathing.
By means of the mantra beginning with "namaste" according to the ritual procedure of the Śatarudriya, that stream which flows without interruption is celebrated as the "Stream of Liberation. (324)
With that [water], one should bathe with iron for a month while muttering the Rudra-hymn in a low voice,
either once, three times, five times, seven times, or nine times.
Furthermore, this eleventh bath, accompanied by eleven [repetitions], should be known as the "Liberation Bath" (*muktisnāna*); performed for a month, it bestows liberation. ||326||
The bath is performed with the Śaiva-vidyā, as well as with the *praṇava* alone,
and likewise with earthen vessels, pieces of coconut shell, and water-waves.
One should bathe the Lord of the God of Gods with water from conch shells, pearls, or flowers, using their pollen and so forth, as prescribed according to what is available.
I shall now describe the procedure for the horn so that it becomes fit for ritual bathing:
first, one should purify the interior, and then one should purify the exterior. (329)
Having made it very smooth and light, one should then somehow cut the elephant [from the pillar],
using two well-rounded wooden troughs placed at a low spot on one side.
One should offer water for bathing to the deity using kuśa grass;
thus, the form of water from the horn of a gavaya is described. (331)
At the door, one should fashion a curved jointed staff in the shape of a serpent, made of half-iron and provided with a secret entrance. ||332||
In the place of the fruit, however, one should perform a combat with a staff;
there, one should cause water contained in a jar to fall from above. 333.
Then, having caused it to fall by means of another hand or even the left hand, a stream of liberation is thereby created; that is the purifier which destroys sin. (334)

Having thus established the Lord of Gods, one should likewise bathe him with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the three sweets (madhuratrika).
Having adorned the god Maheśvara with ornaments and having bathed him again,
one should then perform the cooling services as well as the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and so forth.
Likewise, there should be a garment, a sacred thread, and the five fragrant substances; as well as camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood. (337)
Or one should worship the liṅga of Viśava with both [substances] mixed together;
or the entire pedestal filled with fragrance, according to the extent of one's available wealth. (338)

Then, remaining silent, one should offer the ritual service and a flower from the *vākālika* species; one should offer the sacred leaf (*śrīpatra*) and the *maruci* fruit, entirely according to one's ability and as appropriate. (339)
Incense made from many ingredients, guggulu alone, or likewise mixed with the ghee of a tawny cow, is recommended for all types of incense offerings.
Having offered incense according to one's ability, along with lamps of ghee from a tawny cow,
or else having offered lamps consisting of mere clarified butter, one should present the offering.
Having spoken as is appropriate according to one's ability and having offered flowers,
one should then provide purification of the mouth and respectfully offer betel.
Thus, the worship consisting of circumambulation and prostration is completed; thereafter, I shall explain to you those five songs of the Gītā. (343)
Song, instrumental music, the Purāṇas, dance, and even humorous speech; the waving of lights (nīrājana), offerings of flowers, water-libations, and the dedication of everything. ||344||
Forgiveness, as well as banishment, are proclaimed as forms of service;
likewise, ornaments, the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the fan [are included]. (345)
The sacred thread of Śiva is service; it consists of the sixfold worship of the Lord.
He who propitiates Śiva with the thirty-two modes of service— ||346||
The destruction of all sins is certain in a single day;
indeed, worship with thirty-two services is the most excellent of the excellent. (347)
Sadāśiva said: "O best of monkeys, it is even so; I shall describe your worship. By worshipping my pair of feet, become one who performs the worship of all. (348)
"Having propitiated [the Lord] in this manner, perform this worship of my *liṅga*.
Hanumān said:
"The worship of the *liṅga* alone has been ordained as my constant duty by my preceptor."
"I shall perform that first, O Lord, and afterwards the worship of your feet.
Having spoken thus, she bowed to the Lord and became intent upon the worship of the Śiva-linga. (350)
Then, having gone down to the shore of the lake and constructed a sand altar,
one should prepare a seat fashioned from palm leaves.
Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water for purification with a concentrated mind,
he then performed the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), again sipping water and remaining silent.
Then, upon the altar of the gods, he fashioned most beautiful lotuses;
immediately thereafter, the monkey sat in the lotus posture upon a palm leaf.
Having restrained his breath and performed renunciation while endowed with pure meditation, he bowed to the Guru and the Lord, and thereafter sat down reciting [the mantra]. (354)
Then, although he had set about making an effort to perform the worship of the deity,
[he found] pure water brought in two leaf-cups made of *palāśa* leaves.

Having placed the fire, consecrated with three mantras, into the water-pot held at his head, he should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the bath (snāna). ||356||
Then, taking the deity in the hollow of his hands in order to bathe him,
the monkey performed the ritual inspection of the deity but did not see the pedestal.
Seeing only the linga in his hand, he was filled with fear and said this:
"O Great Yogin, what sin have I committed? (358)
If this pedestal-less Śivaliṅga remains in my hand, my death today is certain, even if the pedestal does not arrive. (359)
"Then I shall recite the Rudra-hymn; at that time, Maheśvara will arrive.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he recited the Śatarudriya. (360)
Then, even though Maheśa had not yet arrived, Vīrabhadra, having come forward, struck Kapīśvara down to the earth. ||361||
"O devotee, why do you weep? Tell me the reason for your weeping.
Hanumān said:
"Behold this linga, bereft of its pedestal; behold this accumulation of my sins. (362)
Vīrabhadra said:
"If the Pīṭha does not come here, O Teliga, do not act so rashly!
I shall burn the world if the Pīṭhaka does not arrive. (363)
"Behold this liṅga; see whether the pedestal has arrived or not.
Then Vīrabhadra saw that the liṅga was present, but the pedestal had not yet arrived.
Desirous of burning all the worlds, the powerful Vīrabhadra cast a fire onto the earth;
at that moment, the earth was instantly consumed by flames.
Then, having burnt the seven lower worlds (tala), it moved upward again;
it burned the five higher worlds inhabited by the residents of Janaloka.
The Lord took the fire produced from the eye in his forehead with his nail,
and having made it resemble the seed-vessel of a jambu fruit, he held it in the palm of his hand.
"If you do not come to the seat, these worlds will undoubtedly be consumed by fire.
Then, seeing that he had not arrived, the powerful Vīrabhadra [acted].
The high-souled Sanaka and others, having understood through yoga, arrived at the excellent hermitage of Gautama and approached the Lord. (369)
Although they saw that the God was present, the twice-born did not perceive him;
nevertheless, they praised him with hymns arising from all the Vedas.
Oṃ, salutations to that God of gods, whose form is pure radiance and consciousness;
salutations to him, the sovereign lord of the deities; salutations to him, the pure one who is the secret of the Vedas. 371.
Salutations to that Śiva, the primordial deity; salutations to him who wears the serpent of darkness as his sacred thread;
salutations to him who sustains the universe with drops from the three Vedas, which rain down the essence of the nectar of the gods. ||372||
Salutations eternally to that Śaṅkara, who is accessible through knowledge, whose eight forms are earth, water, wind, ether, fire, moon, sun, and the self. (373)
Then, having heard this hymn of praise, Śiva, the restorer of Bhaga’s eyes, said to Viṣṇu: "Go and bring those twice-born ones here."
They were brought by that deer and prostrated before the God;
Śaṅkara spoke these words to them: "For what purpose have you come? (375)
The sages said:
"The ashes of twelve worlds of the gods are visible;
behold this single remaining forest, the destruction of the world. (376)
Sadāśiva said:
"We have no doubt regarding the burning of the five worlds situated above;
but how is it that there is a shower of fire, and how is it that there is this great roar? (377)
The sages said:
"Fear of Vīrabhadra now besets us;
he has poured down this shower of arrows as if he were thirsty. (378)
Having summoned the hero Devotha, Bhava said to him, "O Hero! [Devotha replied:
"This was done by Vīra because of the absence of a liṅga-pīṭha for Hanūmat. (379)
This great undertaking was performed by me in order to fully understand the mind of the monkey;
then the Lord, a treasury of compassion, fashioned it just as he had done before. (380)
Then the omnipresent Lord, the soul of the universe, having fashioned all the worlds anew from the beginning in their former splendor— even though they had been consumed— spoke to Vīrabhadra.
Having embraced her and smelled her head, Hara gave her betel;
then Hanumān performed the worship of the Lord.
There, he spoke thus to a certain forest-dwelling Gandharva who was accompanied by his lute-player: "Let this great vīṇā be given to me. (383)
"The Gandharva Unmāda must not be abandoned; he is as dear to me as my very life.
My lute, too, is like my own life," so said the Lord of the Monkeys.
Then, as the Gandharva fell by the strike of his fist,
the monkey seized his great lute, which was endowed with perfect pitch and tone.
Having fashioned a gourd joined together in the shape of a *rājavṛkṣa* fruit,
he placed it upon his chest and went singing the auspicious *Śivātikā*.
He worshipped the feet of the God with pure *bṛhatī* flowers; then the God granted him a boon: life once more until the end of the kalpa.
Then he granted another boon: the power to fill the ocean with clouds.
Adorned with all ornaments, surpassing the luster of the gods with his own radiance,
possessing a gracious form, youthful, and having Śiva as his body, he honored all the gods.
Taking up his yellow garment of fine cloth, Maheśvara said:
"O Hari, accept this auspicious yellow garment, which is the mark of divinity. (390)
The giver of wealth likewise gave red garments to the Brahmins, and a pair of garments to all the gods, sages, Dānavas, and others. (391)
Having heard this, Rāma also presented to Śambhu a pair of garments that were very fine and of great value, as well as golden ornaments.
Then, having eaten and being seated comfortably on the bank of the Gautamī, together with his ministers, his domestic priest, various groups of sages, kings, and monkeys— [393]
Rāghava spoke these words to Śambhu, the knower of the ancient truth:
"You alone know everything that dwells within the secret cave of all dharmas. (394)
"O Brahman, tell me what is distinguished in each respective age.
Śambhu said:
"In the Kṛta age, meditation alone is supreme; in the Tretā age, sacrifice indeed is so."

In the Dvāpara age, they worship; in the Tretā age, they recite the Vedas; and in the Kṛta age, they celebrate [the Lord]. All these are praised everywhere, but meditation is not [praised] in the Kali age. (396)
O Lord of the People, because the minds of men are deluded when they are in a state of distress,
their intellect is not fixed upon dharma, nor is it established in the Veda or the Smṛti.
Neither in the *nakra*, *tauna*, or *svadhākāra* mantras, nor in the hearing of the Purāṇas; neither through sacrifice nor at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), nor by serving the virtuous. (398)
O King, neither in the worship of the deities nor in any similar ritual action should one fail to remember the gods, even if it be for a moment.
Therefore, since humans are unable to endure virtues that require a long period of time, they are able to practice generosity because it takes only a short time. (400)
And for this reason, there is no expiation for those corrupted by the Kali age;
yet, through various expiations, the destruction of the sins of some may indeed occur. (401)

O Raghava, he who knows the Brahman, he who performs the śrāddha at Gayā, he who goes to Kashi, he who is devoted to the Vedas, he who knows the Puranas, and he who is humble—these are the ones who hear his [teachings]. 402.
Because it discriminates the meaning in accordance with the [succession of] ages, because it produces conviction in oneself and others, and because it illuminates the supreme Brahman. ||403||
A Brahmin who recites the Purāṇas is distinguished above all others; even the sin committed by him shall not cling to him, let alone that of anyone else. 404.
For some others as well, the Purāṇa is the destroyer of sins;
he who has faith in the Purāṇas regards the speaker as his guru. (405)
To one who bestows the knowledge of Brahman, who is superior even to kinsmen and relatives, all his sins undoubtedly go to destruction. 406.
Now follows the journey of the worshiper of the Great Lord to Śrīśaila;
therefore, this Purāṇa is the destroyer of the sins of men in the Kali age. 407.
Listen to the account of what occurred in the former Kali Yuga: there was a Brahmin named Gautama who was devoid of the Vedas. (408)
His prosperity consisted of two brothers who were like cattle, being devoid of the Vedas;
he practiced agriculture together with them and attained growth therein.
Then he gave some wealth, grain, and other such things to the king, and spoke these words: "Appoint me to some office. ||410||
"I shall cause my two brothers, who are capable, to bring the wealth.
The King said:
"For the Brahmin has authority indeed in Vedic religious rites. (411)
"Therefore, for one who is appointed there, his Brahminhood perishes.
Gautama said: "This is the dharma of other ages; the dharma of the Kali age is not like that. (412)
For the protection of the earth is declared to be the duty of kings;
thus, even a Brahmin who has fallen into distress does not incur sin by performing it. (413)
"Agriculture is the duty of Śūdras, not even for the twice-born in times of distress.
Therefore, I shall live by the profession of a Kṣatriya; point out a village to me. (414)
"Furthermore, my intention is that you should live here under my protection; otherwise, it shall not be so. Having said this, he gave villages to the twice-born. (415)
But your conduct as one corrupted by authority over the village was such that you ate meat, drank wine, and spoke foul words. (416)
Likewise, he was hostile toward the wives of others, the property of others, and enemies; he repeatedly engaged in gambling and sports, and his arms were misshapen. (417)
Neither Śiva nor Viṣṇu was worshipped by the lords of the worlds. Thus, after some time, the king spoke these words to the one of evil conduct: ||418||
Having abandoned the status of a Brahmin, you have attained the state of a Śūdra; therefore, by the law of our appointment, we shall cause you to fall from that [status]. 419.
"Let me not be a Brahmin this very day; let Śūdra-hood alone be better for me.
For if those who are not Brahmins eat that [food], then let it be better for me. (420)
"O Lord of the Earth, I am not able to renounce all of this.
Śambhu said:
"While the wicked brahmins were speaking thus, the king remained silent."
Equal to a *satuva* or a *śūdra*, he ate food along with meat;
once, that man of wicked conduct was stationed in a pavilion on the city gate. (422)
Having heard this verse being recited by the twice-born, that lotus [the heart] remained fixed within his heart, uttered by the twice-born. (423)
Those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa go to that which is higher than the highest;
but those who hate Maheśvara shall not go there.
Having heard the explanation as well, he spoke according to the Purāṇas:
"What kind of being is Nārāyaṇa said to be, and what kind is Maheśvara? (425)
What is declared to be the supreme goal? How is hatred described? What is that which is known as "the beyond," and what is even further than that? (426)
The Paurāṇika said:
That supreme abode of Brahmā is characterized solely by manifest bliss;
yet beyond that is the station of Viṣṇu, which is superior even to that of Brahmā. (427)
That supreme state is proclaimed as being by virtue of its indestructibility;
within that is the Person Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord who is its very limb. 428.
Because he was born from the waters (nārāḥ), he is called Nārā by the wise;
and because the waters (nārāḥ) were his place of rest (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. ||429||
Those for whom that is the supreme goal are called *tatparāyaṇāḥ*.
He who is the Lord of those principles beginning with Mahat is [the Supreme]. (430)
He whose eyes are the sun, fire, and moon is neither Soma nor Maheśa; he is Umāpati.
Hatred and enmity are to be understood as existing only toward the Lord, the Supreme Self. 431.
Śambhu said:
Having reflected upon these words thus uttered by the Paurāṇika, I spoke once more:
"How can there be a way for one such as I? (432)
Then the Paurāṇika said to him: "Listen, I shall tell you the way [to liberation];
perform the penance with all effort according to the prescribed rule. (433)
Practice the Dharma according to your ability, at the proper time, and according to the prescribed rules;
then, freed from sin, you shall attain the supreme goal hereafter.
Listen attentively to this eternal Purāṇa;
being free from desire, worship the Great Lord, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Or else, having performed the ritual surrender (saṃnyāsa) to the lotus-eyed Lord Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, become one who is constantly devoted to the knowledge of Brahman. 436.
Alternatively, go to Kāśī and attain liberation or immortality;
or go to Gayā, where you should diligently perform the ancestral śrāddha rites.
Alternatively, one should daily recite with devotion the Rudra hymn, which is the essence of all the Vedas, the destroyer of sins, and that which is dear to Rudra. (438)
Or else go to Śrīśaila, or to Kedāra according to your desire;
or else, every year, undertake the ritual bath in the month of Māgha.
What is the use of much speaking here? Always be devoted to the Dharma;
otherwise, O lowest of the twice-born, there shall be no dwelling in hell for you.
Gautama said: "Having heard everything from your mouth, I shall act according to the Purāṇa; please tell me also the scripture that is a cause for confidence, excluding anything else. (441)
The reciter of the Purāṇas said:
One should avoid meat, liquor, women, sensual enjoyment, gambling, boastfulness, harshness, falsehood, deceit, and the reviling of the God of gods. (442)
The disparagement of gurus, the elders of the gods, and those who proclaim the ancient Smṛtis; the white-ant hill; and the application of a false gourd [as a substitute for a real one]. (443)
The citron, the kusumbha flower, vermilion, and the horn;
likewise the aralu, the coconut, and the kūṣmāṇḍa gourd. ||444||
Kovidāra fruit cooked in oil, human milk, the milk of a Vārdhrīṇasa (rhinoceros), a she-goat, and a ewe—[these are the substances for the preparation]. (445)
The milk of a camel, the milk of one-hoofed animals, the milk of a doe, a goat, or a human;
the milk of a cow whose calf has died or of a cow in heat; and salt—these are what the yogi should avoid.
One should not cause coconut juice, bronze, copper, honey,
lead, tin, brass, iron, or bell-metal to be mixed with ghee-soaked food.
A wise person seeking auspicious results in this world should not perform a fire sacrifice with an earthen vessel, nor should he offer a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in a silver one. 448.
Even the powder or paste inside the vessel, as well as the chewing of betel nut (kramuka) and indeed the powder and leaf thereof, [are forbidden]. 449.
The consumption of even ripe betel nut by one engaged in the practice of *krama* [is forbidden], as is milk-rice with salt, and anything offered solely with the hand. 450.
In Sindhu, Saurāṣṭra, Vojaka, and Magadha, milk mixed with salt will not cause any harm there. (451)
All milks and salts, when combined with other substances, may lead to defects in other regions; however, regarding their consumption here [in this land], there is no doubt. (452)
"What is the use of speaking much more on this matter? One should avoid what is censured by the virtuous. Śambhu said:
"Having thus heard the words of that high-souled brāhmaṇa..."
Having gone to his own abode, he reflected, distressed:
"Neither at night nor by day does even a great man know when death will come. (454)
Happiness in the next world is suffering, while the diversion of enjoyments here is likewise;
worms, insects, humans, and others each experience their own distinct pleasures and pains. (455)
Moreover, the distinction among the causes for each individual soul is well-established;
indeed, even for a single soul, there is no state of uniformity. (456)
At the time of birth there is great knowledge; in infancy, there is slight awakening;
in the stage of faltering steps, there is slight discernment; and likewise in childhood, it is still slight. (457)
In childhood, one delights in play; in youth, one is devoted to sensual objects and women; and when youth has passed, the desire for the acquisition of wealth arises. (458)
Moreover, in old age, the desire for enjoyment is unable even to enjoy, due to rheum, phlegm, saliva, wrinkles, gray hair, and trembling. (459)
Possessed of impaired senses cast about by breathlessness, coughing, and wind, he is unable to grasp anything at all, nor does he perceive anything whatsoever. (460)
Standing before the wives of others, he reveals his private parts;
intent on scratching his scrotum, he is cruel according to the signs of life.
Scratching his buttocks while lifting his garment and moving it about, he eats with phlegm in his mouth, yet he is unable to swallow his food. (462)
When there is space, then there is the casting forth of the vital breath and the wind accompanied by sound;
and there is also the exit of impurity as well as the discharge of phlegm.
Reflecting again and again upon the rebukes from his daughter-in-law and others, the example of the laughter of the young palm tree, and the departure of his elders and so forth. (464)
Summoned for the sake of a meal and other provisions, he rejected the food and other offerings; having been rebuked for keeping it warm for a long time, he fell once again into deep anxiety.
I am a doer of exceedingly evil deeds; how shall I eat, how shall I sleep, how shall I stand, how shall I walk, and what will become of me in the next world? ||466||
O Rāghava, constantly agitated by such thoughts and accompanied by his younger brother, he went to the house of a brahmin who was well-versed in the Purāṇas. 467.
With his face cast down in shame, he asked, "What shall I do?
But that twice-born Paurāṇika did not say anything at all then.
Realizing, "This man is a sinner," the disciple drove him away;
Gautama also, having gone out, stood right outside the gate. (469)
Having somehow or other obtained a seat, he did not honor it, even though he was seated upon the earth as an investigator of the meaning of the ancient texts and possessed of great wisdom.
Having sat down upon the ground, he spoke to the knower of the ancient lore:
"I shall perform an expiation; let that be prescribed right here. (471)
The Brāhmaṇa said: "Proclaim all the sins you have committed in every way; yet he, declaring, 'Not even a single sin has been committed by me'—" (472)
Weeping and crying out "O father! in great distress, he fell upon the ground; then the brahmin said to him, "There is no atonement."
"If a great sin has been committed even three times over,
what shall I do, O illustrious knower of the Purāṇas, having approached you? Gautama said.
"Association with the best of the twice-born who is joined with sin shall become fruitless.
The reciter of the Purāṇas said: "The scripture is the authority for all in determining expiation. (475)
If one were to prescribe a penance for that which is not beneficial for it, that would not be [a true penance].
What is prescribed for a single occurrence applies to a single occurrence; in the second instance, it shall be double.
The third is said to be threefold, while for the fourth there is no atonement;
yet you have committed all four types in many ways according to your will.
"How can I be capable of prescribing an expiation for one such as you?
Gautama spoke again: "Where must I go?
[The sage replied: "Having observed three fasts, you shall attain Śivarātri. (480)
Deeply distressed, he observed the fourth fast;
and on the new moon day, he took his breaking-fast meal with the bark of fruitless trees.
Then the virtuous twice-born man performed a circumambulation of Śrīśaila and subsequently went to his home,
sighing and exceedingly emaciated by anxiety.
How will my turning away from evil succeed while you remain silent? Is there any evil so great that it cannot be remedied by reflection? (483)
Upon hearing this, I too would say: "Let an expiation be prescribed;
however, by listening to which Purāṇa will it be understood? (484)
Having formed this thought, he then spoke to the knower of the Purāṇas:
"O Blessed One, please explain to me one Purāṇa. (485)
"Quickly perform for me the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony;
having become a twice-born, I shall today hear [the dharma] and thereafter perform penance. (486)
"The Purāṇa proclaimed to me shall be prescriptive;
therefore, having determined the meaning of the Purāṇa, I shall perform what is possible. (487)
The Paurāṇika said: I shall proclaim the Purāṇa, which destroys all sins,
according to my knowledge, according to my ability, as it is pure, and according to the prescribed rule.
"What shall I recite for you—the *Cchasi-purāṇa* or this very one?
Gautama said:
"The entire *Ruci-purāṇa* must be told; tell me what is beneficial. (489)
Upon hearing which, no distinction whatsoever arose between Viṣṇu and Śiva.
The Paurāṇika said: That Purāṇa which was spoken by Kūrma proclaims the non-difference of those two deities. 490.
Whoever hears this first, their sin is destroyed; and for the Brahmin from whose mouth it is heard, there shall be an end to all obstacles. (491)
If a wicked man thinks he should listen [to advice] when his wife is perishing, I shall say one thing that is difficult to do: it is not easy for either the listener or the speaker. (492)
The love for the teacher arises from the Dharma itself, which illuminates [the truth] and demonstrates proper conduct, skillfulness, and the path to liberation and other goals. (493)
Then Maheśa, as Viṣṇu, shall be pleased and bestow the desired fruit;
by him the ancestors are delivered, and they attain the supreme goal. 494.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava. ||114||
The one hundred and fifteenth chapter. Śrī Rāma said:
"O lowest of Brahmins, how can one overcome the multitude of accumulated sins?"
O best of the twice-born, how did the knower of the Purāṇas provide his exposition? (1)
Śambhu said:
Through teaching and through studying, a union is brought about;
by that union, O child, the sin of a great sinner perishes within a year.
O Kākutstha, knower of the Purāṇas and the meaning of all principles, even the mass of sins committed by one who has not abandoned the multitude of transgressions is destroyed. ||3||
Just as a mass of smoke is destroyed by a great fire, a moth is not capable of extinguishing the fire for the sake of its own extinction. ||4||
The knower of the Purāṇas destroys the sins committed by others;
he is the liberator from the fear of spirits and the like for mortals seized by such beings. ||5||
Just as one who possesses a mantra would remove [a disease] himself when he is not ill,
so too an expert in the Purāṇas is not liable to incur any sin.
The knower of the Purāṇas destroys the sin committed by oneself as well as that committed by others, even if it be exceedingly wicked or one's own past karma.
He was equanimous toward Bhavānī and Īśa, possessed of discernment,
a knower of the rites of the world and the Vedas, devoted to the recitation of the Rudra-mantras, and entirely free from desire.
Contented, tranquil, skilled in action, abundant in means, a practitioner of yoga, and self-controlled—
just as was the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, who was formerly a knower of the Purāṇas.
O protector of the earth, by your command he remained in Ayodhyā;
he protected the entire world while you were away when a Rākṣasa fell upon him.
Then, by the instruction of Śakra, the Rākṣasa approached you, thinking, "I shall kill him while he is addicted to sleep, just as a snake kills a rat. (11)
Or else, O Vipra, Vasiṣṭha, who desires your welfare, having learned this, will undoubtedly slay the descendant of Kakutstha while he is asleep and heedless. (12)
Thinking, "Since Brahmā has granted him a boon, this must indeed be my task to prevent it," the brahmin-sage set out, taking his army with him.
Then the sage, unable to kill him because he was free from death, himself became a rākṣasa and the great sage spoke these words. (14)
"For what purpose have you come here to this forest frequented by sages?
He replied, "I am a king, a slayer of Rākṣasas, and I have come here to kill him. (15)
The sage also said: "What is the use of that life, or even of death?
Having eaten my flesh, however, go forth to victory after engaging in battle. (16)
The Rākṣasa said:
"How will you, a Rākṣasa, become my food?
For even Vasiṣṭha has assumed a human form and stands here in the sky. (17)
Spitting upon his head, he struck him with his fist;
being thus struck by the Rishi, that Rakshasa fled from him.
As both of them were fleeing from one another, having reached the shore of the ocean,
that Rākṣasa was then seized by a crocodile dwelling there.
The sage remained in Ayodhyā as before.
Śambhu said:
"Therefore, one who knows the Purāṇas and is free from envy should act according to his own inclination. (20)

I shall now describe the auspicious procedure for listening [to the scripture]; listen attentively. It should be performed during the bright fortnight, on a pure day, in conjunction with an auspicious weekday and lunar mansion.

And when the ascendant at the time of the rite is endowed with the strength of planets and stars, and Jupiter is situated there while the planet Saturn is neither obscured, nor immature, nor old; ||22||
One should listen to the Purāṇa, endowed with the characteristics previously described, neither during the dark fortnight nor in the presence of an atheist. ||23||
In a pure house, or on a pure altar, or in a monastery; or on a riverbank, in a temple, or even in an assembly hall. ||24||
O Lord of the Gods, wander through the streets, monasteries, or beautiful and meritorious halls;
personally pay homage to the eminent Brahmins, especially those who are knowers of the Purāṇas. (25)
One should prepare a seat that is elevated and distinguished above all others;
it should be addressed as "the seat of the coming Dharma" (ehi-dharma-āsana) in a manner that is not harsh. ||26||
On the day the Purāṇa begins, one should proclaim that which is to be done;
one should honor the expounder of the Purāṇa with garments and other offerings. (27)
Having given auspicious garments that are fine, new, and beautiful, as well as a water-pot, ornaments, vessels, and even a seat. (28)
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and offer betel;
[one should meditate on] Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, and has four arms.
One should meditate upon him with a serene countenance for the pacification of all obstacles; then, having honored the members of the assembly, one should pray to Gaṇeśa. (30)
One should perform worship with the mantra beginning with "Oṃ namaḥ" and offer praise to Bhāratī; then, at the time of dawn, one should commence the recitation of the Purāṇa. ||31||
On the day of the commencement, fifteen inauspicious [periods] occur during the night;
on the second day, auspicious [periods] are double that number. (32)
On the third day, it is desired that [the recitation] be even more extensive;
likewise, the exposition and the listening should continue without interruption of the days. (33)

When the formal establishment [of the lineage] has occurred from the unborn one, then, having first offered betel and other gifts to the ancient guru, one should listen [to the teachings] on the following day.
"The Purāṇa should be heard thus every single day"—such is the sacred tradition.
Whatever man listens to the Purāṇa in the form of a religious vow, [attains the highest goal]. (35)
When this occurs, that person undoubtedly goes to that Purāṇa;
even if only a single verse of the Purāṇa is heard by one desiring to hear it. (36)
It destroys the sin committed on that day; of this there is no doubt. ||37||

Thus, whoever hears this Purāṇa is liberated from the bond of sin committed even by killing a Brahmin; likewise, the drinker of liquor, the stealer of gold, and the violator of the Guru’s bed attain liberation. (38)

Other sins committed by men, even those previously performed, all perish; likewise, those sins acquired over a hundred years both here and elsewhere perish for the listener as well as for the speaker. (39)

Omniscience does not exist in all the Brahmins of the Kali age; for even if they were endowed with [all] qualities, it would be like the act of giving the fruit of an explanation that has not been imparted. //40//
Vyāsa knows the intention of the Purāṇas, and another, Veda, knows it as well; but I know it specifically even more than Vyāsa and even more than Brahmā.
Neither Vedic study nor austerity, nor even mantras and oblations,
bear fruit in the Kali age as much as the listening to the Purāṇas does.
Merely by hearing each one, even a great sin goes to destruction without a doubt, just as by staying at Śrīśaila.
Therefore, there is no other guru superior to him—who is a knower of the Purāṇas, who delights his listeners, who destroys sins, and who bestows the supreme goal. 44.

Those who are considered gurus regarding mantras and those who are so regarded in the Vedic scriptures are not able to bestow all-encompassing knowledge; therefore, they are not true enlighteners. (45)
Piśācas are generally known by the names Rākṣasas and Brahma-rākṣasas;
they are seen as knowers of Vedic mantras, but not as knowers of the Purāṇas. (46)
One who is averse to the Purāṇas does not see anything at all;
therefore, one who knows the Purāṇas is beneficial, for such a master brings about the destruction of sin. (47)

The worship of that [deity] shall be the worship of all; likewise, causing harm to that [deity] is the injury of all. Just as among all forms of giving, the gift of knowledge is praised as supreme, [so too is this]. (48)
Likewise, for one who knows the Purāṇas, a gift given there yields great fruit.
Rāma said:
What should be given by one who knows the Purāṇas, how much, and of what kind? (49)
"What kind of Purāṇa is to be avoided? What kind of person who knows the Purāṇas is to be avoided?
Śambhu said: "Food and drinks possessing the six tastes, as well as substances containing oils... (50)

One should cause a house, complete with its furnishings, to be given to a knower of the Rāmāyaṇa Purāṇa; indeed, all things should be provided in abundance, for the fruit increases with the excellence of the gift.
One should give wealth more than that, along with soft, beautiful garments and wet clothes; one should present ornaments according to one's capacity as is appropriate.
Every day, one should offer incense and flowers; at times, only incense alone, and likewise only flowers alone, as well as fruits during the fruiting season. (53)
One should likewise offer betel-leaf and pay obeisance with devotion;
and upon the completion of the Purāṇa, one should likewise give gifts and other offerings.
O King, one should give even more than that, such as land, gold, and so forth;
for who indeed would not wish to listen when approached with such an offer? (55)

Whether the worship is performed by all the members of the assembly or by a single individual, it is desired that everyone perform the worship according to their ability, as if in the presence of the deity. (56)
Furthermore, O Raghava, one who knows the Purāṇas should perform worship according to his ability at sacred fords and in holy sanctuaries.
O King, I have previously described the characteristics of the listener;
now I shall tell you the characteristics of every kind of reciter of the Purāṇas. (58)
One who is of low birth, afflicted by great disease, a great sinner, treated with contempt, devoid of purity and proper conduct, and bereft of the Vedas and Smṛtis; ||59||

One who worships another deity, one whose speech is foul, one who is deficient in limbs, one who has surpassed his own father in wealth, the husband of a woman previously married to another, a thief, a killer of living beings, and one who is deformed— [these are excluded].
Alternatively, O best of kings, I shall relate to you that Purāṇa which was spoken by former knowers and proclaimed by the supreme sages. (61)
To those excellent sages, Vyāsa and the others, he said:
"One should proclaim that which is found in the Purāṇas; one should read the text and explain it with careful reflection. (62)
By whatever language of the world it may be, whether in the language of a particular region or composed in a local dialect,
one shall obtain the fruit [of merit] upon hearing a work written in that regional language.
Having explained the Ākāpikākutstha Purāṇa for the sake of [discerning] what is beneficial and what is harmful,
you, O Goddess, should therefore request that I explain this Purāṇa.
Śambhu said:
Having heard what was thus spoken by the knower of the Purāṇas, Gautama himself gave three garments to that high-souled Brāhmaṇa.
We have heard that he first listened to the Kūrma Purāṇa;
he gave away abundant gold as well as auspicious garments.
Then he heard the Āgneya, the Vaiṣṇava, and likewise the Vāmana;
as well as the Pādma, the Gāruḍa, the Saura, and the Brāhma.
In this manner, Gautama heard the eight Purāṇas,
as well as the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kūrma Purāṇa once again.
He constantly performed the recitation of "Śiva-Nārāyaṇa" alone;
having met his death, he attained the state of Brahman.
Having worshipped that Brahmin who was honored by Brahmā, he then went to the world of Viṣṇu;
and being worshipped by Viṣṇu, he then went to the abode of Śiva.
Thus, O Goutama, best of sages, this is the heaven for all;
and these rules have been declared by me for the purpose of listening to the Bhārata.
That which was formerly composed by the sage Vyāsa, auspicious from its very beginning,
he who has proclaimed it in its entirety for the sake of its hearing is the bearer of that burden.
One should not bow to any brahmin whatsoever, with the sole exception of the most excellent yogi; such is the glory of him who expounded the Bhārata. 73.
That brahmin who constantly explains or recites the great Mahābhārata is superior to all others,
and he shall likewise cause other men to spread it.
Whether he performs one *vyākaraṇa-parvan* or several, being liberated from all sins, he excels in offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). ||75||
One should bow down to that very Brahmin, honor him as worthy of worship, feed him constantly, and offer everything to him. (76)
O twice-born one, at the time of the exposition, the ritual for his worship has been declared;
he should be honored with garments and other offerings, and then one should worship him according to the prescribed method.
At the conclusion of the Ādi-parvan, one should give three fine garments and gold according to one's ability; likewise, two garments at the Sabhā-parvan.
O bull among kings, [this was established] during the Parvas of the Ānuśāsana, Araṇya, and Svargāroha, as well as during the worship in the Ādi-parva. 79.
During the Karṇa, Aśvamedha, Vairāṭa, Śalya, and Droṇa parvans, one should give three clean, fine garments or else two gold coins (niṣkas). ||80||
Then, one should bring together niṣkas for the other minor joints;
however, for the Harivaṃśa, there should be one niṣka and three garments.
Upon the completion of the entire Mahābhārata, one should become a donor of land;
during the hearing of the Rāmāyaṇa, one should offer worship at the conclusion of each Kāṇḍa.
One should cause a field or even gold to be given to the teacher who explains [the scripture], for his word destroys all impurities. (83)
O best of kings, wealth, virtue, pleasure, and liberation—all these, as well as excellent understandings, are accomplished through hearing the explanations. (84)
The destruction of all sins, even including the murder of a Brahmin, occurs through a single hearing of this; what has not been heard by men on earth? (85)
One should constantly worship this expounder with vehicles, wealth, gold, and other offerings, since he is the destroyer of the entire mass of evil. (86)
Other Purāṇas as well, spoken by sages, serve to destroy the sins of the listeners and especially those of the speaker. (87)
And whoever should recite or listen to all the Purāṇas, including the thirty-six supplements (Upapurāṇas), for him there shall never be a cutting off of his consciousness. 88.
The first is the ancient Brāhma Purāṇa; the second is called the Pādma;
the third is indeed the Vaiṣṇava, and the fourth is called the Śaiva. ||89||
Then the Bhāgavata is declared as the fifth; the sixth is now being spoken of;
and the seventh is proclaimed to be the Bhaviṣya and the Nāradīya. ||90||
The eighth is called Mārkaṇḍeya, and likewise the ninth;
the tenth is proclaimed as the Āgneya and the Brahmavaivarta. ||91||
The Laiṅga, the Vāmana, the Skānda, and likewise the Mātsya;
the Kaurma, the Varāha which has been proclaimed, and also the Gāruḍa which is celebrated. 92.
The wise know that the *Brahmāṇḍa* constitutes the eighteen Purāṇas;
likewise, I shall hereafter describe the Upapurāṇas. (93)
The first is named Sanatkumāra, after that the Nārasiṃha;
the third is designated as the Āṇḍa, and then likewise the Daurvāsasa.
Then there is the Nāradīya, and another, the Kāpila, as well as the Mānava;
likewise that which was proclaimed by Auśanasa, and after that, the Brahmāṇḍa.
The Vāruṇa, the one called Kālika, the Māheśa, the Sāmba, the Saura, the Pārāśara, the Mārīca, and the one named Bhārgava. ||96||
The Kaumāra and the Purāṇas are indeed proclaimed to be eight or ten;
Manu shall be the expounder of the eighteen Purāṇas. (97)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Purāṇas," in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava.
(116) Chapter One Hundred and Sixteen.
Sūta said:
"Let the twilight rituals be performed," said Rāma to the sage;
for even as the sun was setting, this flock of birds was returning to its nest.
Desiring to perform the twilight devotions himself, he abandoned his vehicle and proceeded toward the northern direction;
there, the music of the *hāhā* and *hūhū* [gandharvas] resounded, and their fame was proclaimed by the radiant-faced [beings]. ||2||
Having reached the bank of the Gautamī, Rāghava— his pair of sandals washed clean by the wind,
and having taken the hand of Jāmbavān as his support— reached the supreme river, the Gautamī.
Holding kusha grass in both hands along with Rama, he then proceeded toward the excellent northern direction;
having offered the three-fold arghya according to the ritual injunctions, his hair standing on end with joy, he then muttered the sacred syllable "Om."
Having offered prayers to Varuṇa in due order, Rāghava bowed to Śambhu and Vasiṣṭha;
having received their blessings, he reached the abode of his mind, where the lotus-like feet of Hanumān had been washed.
Then, having offered oblations into the fires, he went outside while being praised by the bards and panegyrists.
The sky, as if plastered with nectar by the rays of the laughing moon,
was like a canopy spread everywhere with the flowers of bright stars.
Then the king went to the assembly hall on the roof of the palace, which had been prepared by the elderly minister and was furnished with various seats.
Then, having seated the Sage, Rāghava himself occupied the first seat;
