the hosts of monkeys, with their massive bodies, took their positions surrounding him on all sides.
Beholding the king established in happiness, Śambhu then spoke these appropriate words to the virtuous brahmins:
"How is it that one who is honored by all while staying here is now engaged in a conversation about a cave, O best of kings? (9)

Having heard the words of the twice-born, the descendant of Raghu became desirous of hearing the story; at that moment, everyone standing there, having skillfully silenced their own speech, listened intently.

"How shall I serve [her], who is so exceedingly wonderful and whose nature is rooted in the self?"—thinking thus, the king spoke these words: "What then is this that you say regarding the warding off of the Rākṣasa? (10)
"Kumbhakarṇa was killed first, and only afterwards did Rāvaṇa meet his death"—
thus does this man speak of the Rāmāyaṇa as it has been composed.

"Who is this best of brahmins who, bringing about atheism among all the people, has approached the presence of kings and speaks? According to the established rule, is he to be punished or is he to be honored? (11)
Then he spoke to that best of the Raghus regarding the story:
"This Rāmāyaṇa, however, is composed according to your own opinion."
O Goddess, listen as I speak from the entirety of the *Mātṛ-vistara*;
this was indeed heard by me long ago from the son of Pañca-keruha.
Having informed him who was speaking thus, he spoke these words to Rāmacandra. ||13||
Śrī Rāma said:
"I am desirous of hearing the Purāṇa; out of curiosity, I wish to know by whom it was composed."
Salutations again and again to the two creators, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and likewise to Śiva and Keśava.
Now I shall relate the ancient Rāmāyaṇa. ||16||
By hearing which, the destruction of all sins accumulated throughout one's entire life occurs. ||17||

Then, with a force greater than that of Daśaratha himself—Daśaratha being the possessor of a chariot equal to his own—the illustrious [Rāma], desiring to conquer the city named Sumānasana, summoned Vasiṣṭha, the son of the son of the Lotus-born (Brahmā). Having paid homage to him and received the sage’s permission, he mounted a horse whose body was as bright as the moon, and accompanied by an army of a hundred akṣauhiṇīs, he set out on a punitive expedition, filled with intense wrath after having propitiated Viṣṭaraśravas (Viṣṇu).
Sādhya, surrounded by his own army, advanced toward Daśaratha to fight, and a battle ensued between them. ||19||
Having fought for one month, Daśaratha captured that Sādhyas.
Then Sādhyasūnu, named Bhūṣaṇa, with a small retinue, fought against Daśaratha.
Daśaratha, too, beholding his son—the ornament of the earth—desired nothing other than to fight. ||22||
"How shall I kill such a one? And once he is killed, how will his father fare? How will his mother? And how his beloved wife, who is in the prime of her youth? ||23||
Upon his body, the marks of embracing, kissing, and rolling about appear like fresh-petal lotuses or flowers. (24)

"Of similar complexion and age to him, such a fortunate son, named Paramaprītivardhana, who increased my supreme joy, has been eaten by a bear and is dead; yet even having entered the path of memory, he seems to wish to protect me, as he affects my heart in this way. Having reflected thus in her mind, she began to take up the very young child. (25)
Even though he was capable of accomplishing it himself, he became dependent on another. ||26||
And together with Prince Sacu, he dwelt in happiness, disregarding even the weariness caused by defeat. ||27||
Daśaratha, too, having stayed there for a month and beholding the joy of seeing his son, reflected thus: ||28||

Ah! This beholding of his face, called "the increase of a son," is capable of dispelling all suffering; it is a victory for the entire kingdom, yet to one who remembers the separation from a son, it becomes nothing but sorrow. (29)
Therefore, I shall pose this question to him; let it be considered how such a son is born—thus he asked, reflecting.
Sādhyo also instructed the lord of the earth in the entire path to liberation.

Having worshipped Hari, Īśāna, and Saha along with their retinues, and having fasted on all Ekādaśīs and worshipped Brāhmaṇas on the Dvādaśīs; having procured food and other offerings according to the prescribed rules, including fruits appropriate to each season, flowers, and incense; having bathed Keśava with the ghee of a tawny cow (kapilā); having smeared Him with powdered mudga beans; and having bathed Him again with sweet water; one should then personally rub the Lord’s entire body with fragrant sandalwood paste, or with musk and the essence of aguru.

Having worshipped as available with incomparable petals of *sī* flowers, and with *yūthikā*, *karavīra*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), lotus (*kamala*), red lotus (*kokanada*), *droṇa* flower, *maruvaka*, *damana*, *girikarṇikā*, and *ketakī* petals, and having propitiated the Lord on the twelfth day with either the twelve-syllable mantra, the *Puruṣasūkta*, or His name, using the sixteen-fold service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), and having prostrated and performed a dance, one should ask the God for forgiveness. ||32||
Likewise, one should perform various diverse vows for the purpose of pleasing Nārāyaṇa. ||33||
The Lord, the Sage, being pleased, granted a desired son; he said to Daśaratha, "Therefore, propitiate him."
Even though that which was to be accomplished remained there, he went to Ayodhyā and performed everything accordingly.

Then, when the *Aputrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice was completed, the embodiment of the sacrifice, bearing a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, arose from the *Āhavanīya* fire and said to the king, "Choose a boon. (36)
Sagara requested his sons, saying, "Grant me sons who are exceedingly righteous, long-lived, and benefactors of the four worlds. ||37||
And there were four queen-consorts of the king: Kauśalyā, Sumitrā, Surūpā, and Suveṣā. ||38||
They said to the king, "O Lord, there must be a son who is your equal. (39)
Then Kauśalya said: "If the Lord is pleased with me, then let this [child] be born to me. (40)
The king said:
"If that which is desired by me is to be granted, then let this Hari be entreated.

O Viṣṇu, be gracious! O Lord of gods, O Consort of Kamalā, O Wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, O Terrifying One, O Eternal Hari, whose pair of feet is worshipped by the entire creation, the world-protectors, and others—salutations to you, salutations to you! Thus praised, the Blessed One then spoke to the king.
Mādhava said:
"I shall become your son through Kauśalyā.
Then Hari entered the sacrificial oblation (caru).
Having divided that sacrificial porridge into four parts, he gave them to his wives.
Then Rāma was born to Kauśalyā, Lakṣmaṇa to Surūpā Sumitrā, Bharata to Suveṣā, and Śatrughna was born; and a rain of flowers fell from the sky. ||43||
Then the Four-faced One himself approached and performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies for him.

Having bestowed upon them the names Tribhuvanābhirāma (Delight of the Three Worlds) because they were pleasing to the three worlds, Arāma (Garden) because they possessed the splendor of beauty, valor, and other virtues, Lakṣmaṇa because he was worthy of the fortune [of Lakṣmī], Bharata because he would rescue the earth from its burden, and Śatrughna because he would slay his enemies, Brahmā returned to his own abode; and the children attained growth.

Then he saw a young boy walking on foot, appearing like a lotus stalk; his lower lip was as red as the *bimba* fruit, his nose was high and adorned with a sesame flower, and a jeweled leaf-hang ornament dangled from the topknot of his head. His ears were graced by dangling earrings that swayed to and fro, and a thick pearl necklace trembled upon his chest. He wore shimmering golden armlets and bracelets, a jeweled ring on his finger, and a girdle fashioned from gold and gems around his hips. His feet were beautified by anklets, and the spaces between his toes were adorned with toe-rings.

Her feet are marked with vajras and adorned with the beauty of kusha grass and lotuses; her broad soles are as beautiful as a canopy; her calves resemble quivers; her thighs are like the trunks of elephants; her hips are broad; her waist is slender; her navel is deep and circular; her chest is vast like a slab of sapphire; her neck is shapely; her face resembles the orb of the moon; her forehead is like a half-moon; her dark, curly hair is disheveled; she is pale with dust clinging to her breast; and her tremulous eyes are as red as the petals of a blooming lotus.

Seeing Rāma, who was like Maheśvara with his body smeared with ashes and like Kumāra, the lord of the directions, King Daśaratha, his heart overflowing with joy, embraced his son, kissed him, and pressed him firmly to his chest. ||46||
Then the prince also, having placed his arm upon her side, spoke something with his eyes half-closed in amorous play. ||47||

Looking here and there at his son who was begging for this and that, saying, "Father, go," "O Father, eat," "O Father, play," and so forth, he experienced the joys of fatherhood again and again and attained supreme bliss. ||48||

Then once, when King Nala had come to eat, Rāma—his heart intent on children's play, his lotus-like hands full of many toys—leaped up and ran about; seizing with his left hand the food placed in a gold vessel inlaid with jewels that stood before the king, he threw it at him.
The king, however, considered even this a source of pleasure.
Rāmacandra performed other such deeds as these. ||49||
Then, on one occasion while they were playing, Rāma caused Vātyārāma to fall, and Rāma himself fell down weeping.
Immediately thereafter, the Brahmarākṣasa seized Rāma, and Rāma fell into a swoon.
Then his companion, a young boy, wandering here and there while crying out, informed Rāma of the king’s condition as it was. ||52||
Then the king, taking Rāma with him, said to Vasiṣṭha and asked, "What is this regarding Rāma? ||53||
Then Vasiṣṭha, taking some ashes and consecrating them with mantras, liberated the brahmarākṣasa.

He asked, "Who are you? and he replied, "I am a Brahmin proud of his Vedic learning; having repeatedly stolen the wealth of others, I have become a Brahma-rākṣasa—consider a means of atonement for me. (55)
Vasiṣṭha said:

"Now, beyond this, you shall experience the state of a Rākṣasa—a hellish condition—to be endured for one hundred years. However, by bathing once in the Bhāgīrathī and offering a hundred bilva leaves to Śiva, and then bathing again, you will be liberated from that sin. (56)

Having heard Vasiṣṭha’s words, “Perhaps at some time I shall grant you such a state of merit that you may attain a higher destiny,” the Brahma-rākṣasa, by the power of the merit instructed by Vasiṣṭha, assumed a divine body, paid his respects, and departed for heaven. ||57||

Then, when the time had arrived, Vasiṣṭha initiated Rāma and taught him the Vedas; he also taught him the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), the two systems of Mīmāṃsā, and the treatises on ethics (nītiśāstra). ||58||
Then [he studied] the science of archery (dhanurveda), the science of medicine (āyurveda), the Bharata, the Gāndharva, architecture, augury, and various treatises on warfare. ||59||
Then, King Daśaratha, desiring to perform a marriage, dispatched messengers to the lords of various countries.
Then, someone having arrived quickly, spoke thus to the king: ||61||

"O King, there is a king named Videha, the sovereign of the Vidarbha country; his daughter is Vaidehī, who was obtained through a sacrifice. She is equal to Lakṣmī in beauty, endowed with all auspicious marks, and worthy of Rāma. That king is prepared to give her to Rāma; therefore, let us go there quickly. ||62||

Then he dispatched Vasiṣṭha and the others; they went there, and having observed her, determined the auspicious moment (lagna), and returned to Ayodhyā. They informed the King, and then, together with Rāma and the lord of the earth, they quickly set out with various elephants, horses, carts, palanquins, and swings. [The women accompanying them were] skilled in the graceful arts of love and enjoyment, well-acquainted with all manner of gestures, and highly proficient in the science of erotics; they possessed soft, firm, and full breasts reaching to their necks, and faces like lotuses with broad or slender foreheads and beautiful lips.

With their hair tied in curls at the base and long locks flowing down, adorned with golden leaf-shaped earrings; their teeth as red as *japā* flowers, made beautiful by the bristling of body hair arising from the act of bathing; their eyes like shimmering saphari fish, their ears resembling oyster shells, and the cavities of their nostrils adorned with large pearls like stars; their cheeks like mirrors, their noses like sesame blossoms, and the nipples on their sunken midsections; their lower lips, resembling indragopa insects, marked by the wounds of teeth; they stood there, displaying all their limbs in perfect symmetry.

Their armpits were rounded and not overly fleshy; their shoulders were well-filled and their upper arms were covered with hair that had grown for no very long time, appearing yellowish like the petals of the *karṇikāra* flower. The middle parts of their arms were soft, smooth, round, and slender. Their breasts were firm, thick, and round, with nipples deeply set; they stood close together as if vying to occupy each other’s space. Their chests were adorned with various necklaces made of shimmering jewels.

With their waist-regions made slender by the weight resting upon their breasts, and with a succession of youthful glances that were peerless, they possessed midsections adorned with three folds—like a waist that could be grasped in a fist—which were graced by a line of hair above the navel resembling a well; their hips were like the trunks of elephants, their knees were hairless, soft, smooth, stainless, and even, and their pair of thighs resembled the trunks of plantain trees, while their calves were slender like *kuśa* grass, rounded, and free from the protruding ankle-bones.

Women whose ankles were submerged in their garments, whose feet had slender, smooth, and very long toes, who summoned passion with the sound of their anklets, who walked with the gait of an elephant, and who were auspiciously inclined—having tucked up the edge of their lower garment at the side so that the tip of their thumb touched it, and having secured the knot of their waist-cloth; with both hands they drew up the portion of the cloth near the hips, yet left the upper part of the garment covering the breasts partially uncovered; and with the hem of that same garment on the right side, which reached down to the navel, they adorned their slender bodies as they came repeatedly for the performance of the marriage rites.

Young girls, their slender bodies purified like streaks of lightning, their chests adorned with various necklaces upon budding lotus-blossoms of breasts, speaking only a few words and moving with an exceedingly swift yet gentle gait, arrived along with elderly women.

Now, in Videha, at a distance of only one *krośa* ahead, there was a mango grove where young forest deer kept their ears pricked to listen to the warbling of various birds amidst the expanse of diverse branches; a region adorned with high and low palaces fashioned from great silver, and filled with various birds; a place where rows of trees were graced by throngs of matted-haired sages whose bodies were smeared with ashes and clad in golden bark-garments, engaged in meditation and worship; and where the wind moved restlessly, overwhelmed by the weight of the breasts of various *vidyādhara* women.

In that lake, filled with *gasara* fish, where young men were being summoned by young women gathering *sairandhra* flowers on the shore; where every region was perfumed by the fragrance of various colored blossoms; where courtesans with bodies radiant with luster displayed wide eyes like shimmering fish as they sought to please lovers here and there; and full of diverse wonders—Daśaratha dwelt happily together with his ministers, priests, and beloved sons, headed by Rāma. (65)

Then the King of Videha [entered] Mithilā, which was adorned with various banners; beautified by diverse palaces, gate-towers, gardens, and temples of the gods; crowded with young women clever in their mutual sports; featuring great water-stations made of fragrant *uśīra* grass; and whose streets were graced by people engaged in pleasant pastimes.

There, the streets were adorned with various kinds of merchandise; the monasteries (*maṭha*) were graced here and there by the sound of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*); every house was filled with the study of the *Mīmāṃsā* and other commentaries, as well as the *Sāman*, *Adhyayana*, *Supuṇya*, *Havis*, *Gandha*, *Sāman-svara*, *Padakrama*, *Śruti*, and *Brāhmaṇa* recitations. In the courtyards of the Brahmins, many masters (*parivṛḍha*) entered and exited wearing the attire of the *Ācārya*, *Hotṛ*, *Kuhū*, and *Adhvaryu* priests, clad in soft garments, while their beloved wives—possessing lips as red as *tāmbūla*—uttered both gentle and harsh words with their hands.

It was adorned with artisans bringing various implements for the preparation of wine, and beautified by women whose left sides were graced by breasts that were smooth, round, and pressed against one another, their upper garments draped over soft, white hips; it was illuminated by thousands of garland-makers with lips as red as the *japā* flower and necks adorned with various pearl necklaces; it was a city of pure streets where intoxicants were produced, featuring wonderful archways here and there.
There, he further beautified that already splendid city, which was adorned with wish-fulfilling trees established here and there and whose gates were embellished with future ornaments. ||66||

Then, for the purpose of the auspicious rite of *abhikalanā*, the king went forth accompanied by women carrying golden vessels filled with clarified butter, *guggulu* resin, fruits, and other substances of good fortune—substances fit for adorning the nose and mouth with various ornaments, their hair-knots beautified by locks of *niśā* grass, *dūrvā*, unhusked rice, and black collyrium; as well as by other splendid people. ||67||
At that time, the sounds of auspicious musical instruments—namely, the *devadundubhi*, the *bherī*, the *niḥsāṇa*, the *mardala*, the *śaṅkha*, and others—manifested. ||68||
And the singers sang auspicious songs. ||69||
The Vedic Brahmins are those who [distinguish themselves] by the recitation of the auspicious Vedic sentences.
Filling the entire sky with the sound of the drum of the family preceptors. ||70||
Then, first exchanging auspicious parched grains with one another and being praised by bards, brahmins, and others, they entered the city.
Daśaratha entered the palace constructed to the west of the city of Videha. ||72||
And the remaining ones entered their respective dwellings as was appropriate. ||73||
Then, at that very moment, Nārada arrived in Mithilā. ||74||

Videha, too, having honored the celestial sage and seeing that he had arrived, had him take food; and once the sage was seated comfortably, the king gave him camphor and betel leaf and addressed him thus.
"You ought to remain for tomorrow's wedding; you must cause the marriage ceremony to be performed."
Nārada said: ||77||
If the lunar mansion of the sun is visible on the following day, a marriage ceremony must not be performed therein. ||78||
Then, having summoned Vṛddhagārgya, who was an expert in determining auspicious moments, the king asked: "What is the auspicious moment for the wedding? (79)
Śvaitigārgya said: ||80||
The king, looking toward Nārada and Gārgya, asked this: "Is it thus? ||81||
Then Nārada spoke to Gārgya.
"How can you say, 'I will give the auspicious moment'? ||83||
Then Gārgya said, "Setting aside the hour of poison, I shall give you the auspicious moment."
Nārada also said to Gārgya, "Do you not even know the words of Brahmā? (85)
Gārgya, however, being pleased, recited those faults.
The Ulkāca, the Brahmadaṇḍa, and likewise the Moghakaṃpa were seen of old by Brahmā for the destruction of all undertakings. 87.
In the consecration of images, marriages, the tying of the sacred thread, and royal inaugurations, as well as in all other undertakings, one should avoid the poison-veins (viṣanāḍī). 88.
Henceforth, however, one does not incur fault by performing these rites;
rather, from this point on, I shall describe the faults regarding rites such as marriage and others. (89)
A meteor would consume the entire family; the rod of Brahmā would bring about destruction; and for one whose actions are sinful, even a mere trifle would lead to death.
Having heard these words spoken by Nārada, the sage Gārgya became intent upon observing silence. ||91||
"Having abandoned the *dadhyauravi* [constellation] and the lord of the planets, let the marriage be performed during the *viṣanāḍī*s. ||92||
Nārada said:
How is it that this is the word of Brahmā? 93.

Sūrya said: Since the regulations are declared to differ according to region, therefore, in this particular region, the marriage must indeed be performed after avoiding the "poison-hour" (viṣaghaṭikā). 94.
Nārada also gave his consent. ||95||
He said, "Tomorrow afternoon the Kṣatriya wedding shall take place; therefore, for the sake of the self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara), send messengers to the kings to invite them. (96)
Then, with the consent of King Daśaratha, he summoned all the kings and deliberated.
How is it that she has gone to Rāma, completely disregarding all the Vaidehīs? ||97||
Then, sighing repeatedly throughout that night, though drowsy, he did not obtain sleep. (98)

Then, in the middle of the night, the king, having purified himself, beheld the three-faced Baka-Sāmbika, who was clothed in auspicious silken garments and whose lotus feet were being served by all the gods headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra; by the foremost sages headed by Bhṛgu; by the Gandharvas headed by Hāhā; by the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas personified; by the hosts of Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Mātṛkās; and by the Gaṇas headed by Nandin. All—

His head was being massaged by the Gaṅgā, whose waters are exceedingly meritorious and which liberates from all inauspiciousness; he was receiving a betel-roll offered by the Daughter of the Mountain seated upon his left lap, while she looked at him with longing and affection; his hair was like cow’s milk and his forehead like musk; his matted locks were fashioned into a topknot that was soft, fine, and glossy; and the regions of his cheeks were adorned with earrings of pure gold.

He mentally contemplated Kāma, who appeared like ten million [flames] of pride, resembling a sixteen-year-old youth, with a complexion like that of a *kausumbha* flower and thick pearls as white as cow’s milk; his head was encircled by a halo, his chest was adorned with gold ornaments set with various jewels, his body graced by an exceedingly white sacred thread (*upavīta*), and his fragrant form was reddened by saffron applied near Ambikā, while he gazed at him, making the arrows of desire tremble. ||99||
He recited the Śatarudriya, offered oblations of clarified butter with that very same [mantra], and praised [the deity] with the Puruṣasūkta. ||100||
Then, Maheshvara himself appeared there in such a form. ||101||
Then, having paid homage to the king, he should praise him. ||102||
The King said:

O Eight-formed One, whose forms are earth, water, ether, wind, fire, sun, moon, and the sacrificial priest; O Universal Form, Form of the World, Form of the Three Worlds, Form of the Vedas and Purāṇas, Form of Sacrifice, Form of Hymns, Form of the Śāstras, Form of the Svadhā offering, Form of Nārāyaṇa, Form of All Deities, Whose essence is the three Vedas, Whose eyes are the three means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas), Who are dear to the Sāman chants, dear to the flow of wealth, dear to devotion, easily accessible to devotees, fond of the praises of those far from You, fond of incense, fond of lamps, fond of ghee and milk, fond of droṇa-flowers and karavīra-flowers, fond of śrī-patra leaves, and fond of lotuses and kahlāra lilies... [naṃ]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "naṃ".)

Salutations to you, who are fond of the *dyāvarta*, *bakula*, *priyayūthikā*, *priyaka*, and red lotuses; who are fond of dwelling in the waters during the summer; who are fond of self-restraint and religious observances; who are fond of those with controlled senses; who are fond of recitation; who are fond of the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*); who are fond of singing and fond of female singers; who are fond of the five *brahmas*; who are fond of virtuous conduct; whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; who are the giver of birth to the lotus-born [Brahmā]; who are the one requested by Hari; who are the producer of the water-born [lotus] and the exhibitor of the discus; who are the giver of memory and reasoning; who are remembered as the bestower of auspiciousness; salutations to you, the conqueror of death—salutations to you! 103.
Having heard this hymn of praise, the Lord Bhava said to the king, "I am the granter of boons; choose a boon."
The King said:

"O illustrious one, my daughter Vaidehī was intended to be offered by way of a self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) to Rāma; yet, in an assembly of all living beings—including many kings, Rākṣasas, and Brahmins—endowed with noble lineage, beauty, strength, and prowess—if someone possessed of superior strength than Rāma had taken her."
Then my word would become a lie, and I would incur sin. ||105||
On the contrary, even Daśaratha is capable of conquering all those who have arrived; and if Rāma, the slayer of kṣatriyas, should come, what will he do with my daughter?
What will he send forth, what will he cause to be done, and what will he himself do? For a king possessing such vast forces and vehicles could indeed destroy the entire three worlds.
How much less so for one of little merit? How much more so for me! You alone are my refuge; tell me the means by which there will be welfare in the marriage and Rāma shall become my son-in-law.
Śambhu also said, "I shall do so. ||107||
"Rāma alone shall be the protector of Sītā.
Having made Rāma my refuge, I shall ensure her well-being this very day; take up this bow, Ājagava."
The king said:
"What is the use of this Ājagava bow? Let Sītā herself choose Rāma. (109)
Śaṅkara said: "This bow is unstrung; he who shall string it, to him I shall give Sītā. Make such a vow. (110)
Having spoken thus, Lord Hara vanished along with his attendants;
then the king was unable to take up the bow, despite his greatest efforts.
Then, having summoned the brilliant [army] possessing the strength of a hundred thousand elephants, he said, "Take it! ||112||
Having bowed to his maternal uncle and let out a loud laugh, he leaped up and seized him with both hands as far as the knees.
Hearing this, Mārīca, his maternal uncle, assumed the guise of a Brahmin and alone requested [his release], saying:
"Know me to be an *atithi* (guest) who has arrived for your *vaiśvadeva* offering. (113)
The king said: "Welcome, O Brahmin! Here is a seat; please sit there. ||114||
The guest, having said "So be it," sat down.
Then the king, having taken water and washed his feet, worshipped Mahājana with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and having offered him [food], entreated him for a meal. ||116||
Moreover, even as he beheld that food, endowed with the six flavors and placed within a golden vessel, he gazed at it from one side to the other.

At that very moment, she appeared, wearing garments slightly reddened like the filaments of a lotus; her forehead was graced by dark, curling locks that moved as they drew the hearts of young men, as if breaking their gazes with their beauty and demonstrating that "the heart of women is thus"; her face was adorned with a bow-like brow, lotus-petal eyes reddened at the corners, a nose like a sesame flower, and cheeks soft, smooth, hairy, and radiant.

Her chin was exquisitely adorned by lips as red as coral, a seat for her teeth which resembled rubies, and a lower lip as crimson as the *dāḍima* fruit or the *japā* flower; her ears were graced by pearl-shell earrings, her neck was long and well-proportioned, her chest was full and fleshy, and she was of lovely form, adorned with many necklaces upon her swelling, budding breasts.

With arms like charming, long, and even creepers, her fingers like red lotus petals and various many-jeweled rings serving as ornaments; with a waist graspable by a fist, a line of hair, a deep navel, broad hips, thighs like the trunk of an elephant, and feet adorned with anklets and other foot-ornaments; she approached the presence of Mārīca, making her hands into blossoming *saugandhika* flowers. (118)
Having seen her, he thought, "How shall I abduct her? How shall I embrace her? How shall I do something else? Finding no opportunity for such actions, he departed in silence. ||119||

Then, as the goddesses were striving to string that bow, they vied with one another to be first; yet, while disregarding each other, not even Mahendra was able to bend that supreme bow beyond its two ends. (120)
Then Sūrya, taking up his bow, fell down while still drawing it. ||121||
Vāyu, the best among the powerful, seized the Ājagava bow with his own hand; as he raised it upward, he fell down, and the bow fell upon Vāyu, whereupon everyone then broke into laughter.
Then, having mounted his excellent horse, the thousand-armed Bāṇāsura, surrounded by Daityas with many heads and accompanied by Prahlāda, arrived at the city of Videha.
Then, illuminating the quarters with his own ornaments and eclipsing the deities with his own splendor, he listened to various kinds of songs and stopped at a distance of two *gavyūtis*. ||124||
Prahlāda and Bali both ran forward and then paused.
Then, while the Rākṣasas remained silent, the exceedingly powerful kings, unable to break the sacrificial bond, withdrew and stood aside. ||126||
Then the brahmins assembled. ||127||
Then Viśvāmitra, taking up the bow and stringing it as far as one finger-breadth, desisted.
Others have turned back from their horses.
Then, after a mere day had passed while all beings remained silent, Rāghava arrived with his younger brothers; having approached, he gazed at the bow and touched it.
Then hundreds of princes gathered together;
having seen the bow adorned with all its ornaments, they touched it but were not capable of moving it. (130)
Then the princes, headed by the son of Daśaratha, assembled together.
Alternatively, those with bamboo flutes in their hands gathered together and drove everyone away. ||132||
Then Rāma, taking Lakṣmaṇa by the hand, adorned with all his ornaments, approached the bow; having touched it, bowed to it, and circumambulated it, he took up the bow and strung it. ||133||
At the moment of seizing it, everyone there uttered a simultaneous cry: "The great chariot-warriors have been defeated here! (134)
Then, having lowered the position of the bowstring together with the arrow, and placing his knee upon the bow, he drew it up with one hand and bent it at the tip.
Then, seeing that everything was made ready, everyone placed their thumbs upon the tips of their noses. ||136||
Rāma also made his bowstring resound;
by that sound, the minds of all were agitated. ||137||
The report spread everywhere that Rāma had strung the bow. ||138||
Janaka also gave Sītā to Rāma; having fought with the kings and defeated them, he returned to his own city. ||139||

Then, on one occasion, after Daśaratha had consecrated Rāma as the heir apparent, he became happy; and because the people rejoiced, there arose a cry from all the subjects: "By the king's favor, Rāma has become the king! ||140||

Then, unable to endure King Asahamāna—who was as fond of fine garments as he was of his kingdom—the daughter of the ruler of the Kaikaya country said to him, "This is the occasion for granting a boon;
O King, what should be given? ||141||
The Goddess said:
"May Rāma enter the forest for fourteen years, and may Bharata protect the kingdom. ||142||
Out of fear of the fault of speaking untruth, the king accepted it with great difficulty. ||143||
Then Vasiṣṭha’s wife, filled with anxiety, said to Rāma as he was departing for the forest: "Consider what may happen to him—both the auspicious and the inauspicious—and tell me.
Vasiṣṭha, having reflected, spoke to the king with joy.
Having gone to the forest, he performs various kinds of worship for Śambhu, the slayer of all the Dānava heroes;
meanwhile, Rama, enraged by the separation from Sītā, crosses the ocean with his army of monkeys and slays the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
Having obtained the kingdom, the descendant of Raghu ruled for many years;
possessing illustrious fame throughout the entire world, he dwelt there for a long time with Lord Śiva. (147)
He is endowed with excellent sons, performs many sacrifices, is preeminent, and possesses all virtues in abundance. ||148||
Having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha and recollecting the virtues of Rāma, Daśaratha spoke thus: "Death would be better for me than the departure of Rāma. ||149||
Then Rāma, having paid homage to his mother, his father, his preceptor Vasiṣṭha, and the wives of his father, departed for the forest. ||150||

Then, having stayed for one day in the grove, he caused his hair to be matted, put on bark garments, and, wearing a single sacred thread (*upavīta*), bound his matted locks with that same thread. With his entire body smeared with ashes and his form made rugged by cow-dung ash, he placed upon his chest a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads interspersed with strings of pearls and gems. Adorned with few ornaments, accompanied by Sītā and followed by Lakṣmaṇa, he entered the interior of the forest.

Then, having slain numerous Rākṣasas there, he made everything regarding the abduction of Sītā and so forth exactly as it had occurred in the presence of Bhava (Śiva). Thereafter, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma went to Sugrīva’s hermitage on Mount Ṛṣyamūka; reaching a mango tree with dense shade, he prepared a shelter.

Having strung his bow upon a tree, seated Lakṣmaṇa, and placed Keśin’s head before him, Rāma lay upon a bed of tiger-skin, listening to a song, observing the fruits of the trees, and seeing a certain monkey wearing jeweled earrings and a golden necklace, clad in a firm bark-girdle and a clean sacred thread, moving very nimbly, tossing fruit at himself, scattering flowers, imitating the song, and fanning Rāma with a fan; even climbing a branch, he continued to fan him. Seeing that monkey holding only mango fruits, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"This monkey is Lakṣmaṇa. ||153||
Lakṣmaṇa also did not know him and spoke; then Rāma, having summoned him, asked, "Who are you? What is your name? (154)
Hanumān spoke thus to the truthful Sugrīva: ||155||

Having bowed to Rāma and approached Sugrīva, he who was like another divine Nārāyaṇa—a youth dark as a cloud, with matted hair and arms reaching to his knees—sat here with another man of exceeding fame who resembled the sun.
Then, seeing the two princes, who were endowed with all auspicious marks, standing beneath the shade of a tree, he said to them, "Inform Sugrīva of this," and it was thus reported by him.
Then Sugrīva, rising quickly, took materials such as flowers and water, performed the washing of the feet and other rites, offered fruits, and made his request. ||158||
Having heard Sugrīva’s words, "O princes, for what purpose have you two ascetics come here?", Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"We two, the sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, have gone to the forest for the sake of suppressing the wicked and protecting the virtuous. ||160||
Then Sugrīva said: "It appears that there is some matter for which you two must either render assistance or inflict harm. ||161||
"Lakṣmaṇa said, 'There is another matter to be attended to, as they will arrive accompanied by an army.'"
"Whose wife has been abducted is not known; we have come to search for her. That alone is our purpose; everything else is incidental."

For that purpose, we shall even cross the ocean, we shall even enter the netherworld (pātāla), we shall accomplish the impossible, we shall even topple Mount Mahendra, we shall slay the powerful one—we shall do whatever it takes. ||162||
Sugrīva said:

"I shall show you those ornaments which were dropped by a certain woman who was being carried away by Rāvaṇa after she had been abducted; they fell as she was coming along, and I collected them. Having spoken thus to Rāma, he brought him to his palace and showed them to him.
Rāma also, having observed and reflected, wept aloud and asked, "Where has that Rāvaṇa gone? and it was replied, "He has gone toward the southern direction. ||164||
Then Rāma formed a friendship with him.
He asked, "For what reason do you remain here deprived of your wife?"
Sugrīva said:

"My brother Vālin, who possesses great strength, has seized my wife and kingdom and dwells in Kiṣkindhā. I was defeated by him in battle; therefore, I am constantly anxious for his death. Just as he is being slain by you, so too, once I have bridged the ocean, I shall deliver to you Sītā—who was abducted by Rāvaṇa and resides in Laṅkā on the opposite shore. Having spoken thus and made a solemn oath, Sugrīva fought with Vālin, who was exceedingly powerful and had challenged him to combat.
Rāma, too, did not kill Vālin immediately due to his uncertainty. ||167||
Then Sugrīva, having fled, spoke this to Rāma: ||168||
"Without knowing your mind, I have set out for my own death. (169)
"O Rāma, because of my lack of specific knowledge regarding you two, I remained silent; now that I have observed your mark, I shall kill you. (170)
Then Sugrīva, having made a sign, challenged Bālin to battle and stood his ground.
Tārā spoke to Bālin.

Sugrīva appears as if he has an ally; otherwise, he would not have summoned me. I have understood it: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the sons of Daśaratha, who are portions of Nārāyaṇa, have arrived to relieve the burden of the earth, and they have become his allies.
Vālin said:

"I have heard that Rāma is possessed of policy and affection. Such a person does not abandon one who is strong to resort to one who is weak. Let Rāma come; even if he has promised [to help another], he might fear if he sees a stronger party. If the heroic Rāma himself comes for battle, then we must fight. Having spoken thus and honored Tārā, he set out for battle with Sugrīva. (174)
Then a fist-fight took place between them. ||175||
Rāma also slew Vālī. ||176||
He fell from his chariot as if struck by a weapon in battle; then, with blood flowing everywhere, he became like a mountain of gore. ||177||
Then Tārā and Gada, having arrived, became free from pain. ||178||
Then, as Rāghava arrived, the monkeys fell at his feet and wept aloud. ||179||
Then he spoke to Tārārāma: "O Rāghava, you who are skilled in the scriptures, heroic, and righteous, how could you have committed such an evil deed even in the past? (180)
You should know the dharma of the constellations, which is practiced by hosts of kings.
If two people fight one another in battle until the victory or death of either occurs,
and if one of them should kill the other, he is declared a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā).
Did you kill Vālin out of enmity, or with the hope of obtaining monkey meat?

If you consider that monkey meat is unfit to be eaten because it is unpleasant to yourself and lacks pleasure, and you think the same applies to others as well—alas, what delusion is this, that for the sake of taking her [the meat], you have undertaken this vow of being devoted to a single wife? 184.

If it is possible to bring back Sītā, who was abducted by Rāvaṇa, with the assistance of Sugrīva, then why is this great task not accomplished in this very way? For the sake of his own purpose, it could be achieved by Vālin—possessed of great strength and vast power—who was capable of bringing back Sītā from within the orbit of the sun through his true nature, and who was capable of remembering and confronting Rāvaṇa; [why not] by that king of monkeys, accompanied by an army of fifty *parārdha*s of monkeys and bears? Why must this task be accomplished by means of the ape Sugrīva, who possesses little prowess and leads an army of only seven *parārdha*s, even though he speaks so eloquently? (185)
Oh, it is known that all is well with the gods, since you have been told so. ||186||

We shall speak further: it is the duty of a lord of the earth to suppress the wicked and protect the virtuous. In this case, Vālin abducted Sugrīva’s queen Ruma and seized his kingdom; therefore, there is no fault in such killing. ||187||
Tārā said:

"Even Sugrīva, who was worthy of death, fought with Vālī while he was in the cave; Vālī remained there for a year, and in the meantime, Sugrīva abducted me and took over the kingdom. Therefore, though he was previously [my enemy], I shall kill him later. ||188||
Rāma said:
Tell me, how long ago did this happen?
Tārā said: "Sixty thousand years ago, in the eightieth year, the kingdom was seized by Sugrīva during a war with the rākṣasas."
And again, when another rainy season had arrived, Sugrīva fled from Vālī. ||191||
His wife was abducted and his kingdom was seized. ||192||
On that very same day, the consecration of your father Daśaratha took place. ||193||
Rāghava said:

"By me also, at the command of my father, the suppression of the wicked within the kingdom was carried out; for the word of a guru is not to be transgressed, and thus, at the time of his abduction, I occupied the royal throne."
Alternatively, there is the independence of the deer and the hunter; and for the deer, there is the killing of Vālin and the mutual tearing apart of other deer, which is not loathsome. ||195||
For it was like a hunt for me, or rather, a hunt for deer—whether moving, stationary, or bound; whether advancing, wandering, or fleeing.
Then, having abandoned the hunt, he released [the deer] without attachment. ||196||
This hunt was conducted by me according to the rules prescribed in the treatises on hunting, while pursuing [the deer] by alternating between sighting them and losing sight of them. (197)
Beyond the descent, the station of the sattvic beings is distinguished;
for the king, hunting is his dharma, as is the consumption of meat. (198)
Then, having heard Rāma’s words, they all bowed their heads. ||199||
Vālin, placing his joined palms upon his head, spoke to Rāma: "O Rāma, you are my master; hear my words. ||200||
"Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, clad in yellow garments, the Teacher of the World—Nārāyaṇa himself—is you in person; thus have I heard. (201)
Yogis meditate upon you, and sacrificers worship you;
you alone consume the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, assuming the forms of both the deities and the manes.
By contemplating death, liberation is not far off; you have attained the vision of reality, and the destruction of all evil has occurred. (203)
"Take up your arrow, O descendant of Kakutstha; I am greatly tormented. ||204||
Then Rāma, saying "So be it," took up the arrow and said to Vālī: "Tell me what you desire; let it be given. (205)
The monkey said:
"If the Blessed One is pleased with me, grant me a good destination."
This Sugrīva must likewise be protected; furthermore, the offense committed by Aṅgada and Tārā was sinful, and its fruit has now been experienced. ||207||
Then, while still looking at Rāma, Vālī ascended to heaven.
Then, having consecrated Sugrīva in the kingdom, he himself entered the forest.
Then, having gone near the ocean with that companion, Rāma asked Sugrīva, "Where is Kāla, where is Kāla, where is Sītā, and where is the enemy? ||210||

Then Hanumān said: "Having entered Laṅkā and searched for Sītā, and having ascertained the full truth of the matter, either war or peace must be undertaken. Therefore, may the Blessed One command someone to cross that ocean. (211)
Then we brought Sugrīva [before him], asking, "How can this be possible? ||212||
The monkey said:
"I have tens of millions of followers, headed by monkeys and bears."
Having appointed one person and having considered everything, one should act in whatever way is appropriate. ||214||
Then Jāmbavān said:
"Let Hanumān alone go; he will surely understand the matter. (215)
Then Hanumān, having searched the inaccessible Kāpura grove and found Sītā seated in the Aśoka grove, spoke with her, gained her confidence, and then destroyed the grove and its guardians.
Having bound the Rākṣasa and burned the grove, he went to the northern bank; seeing the garden, he related the events and remained silent. ||217||
Then Rāma reflected upon all this; he said, "The Lord of the Earth spoke thus to me: 'O Rāma, you will be destroyed by monkeys and bears,' as was told to me by Nārada. (218)
Therefore, one must remain resolute in the effort to cross over the ocean. ||219||
Then Rāma, having propitiated Śaṅkara and reported everything, said, "I shall do as you have instructed. Having thus addressed Śiva, he worshipped him, bowed down, and made this request: ||220||

O Great God, the Great Devourer of all beings, the Cause of the Great Dissolution, adorned with a great serpent; O Mahārudra, Śaṅkara, Parameśvara, Virūpākṣa, whose sacrificial thread is a serpent and whose garment is an elephant hide; who is adorned with a garland of skulls from the heads of Brahmā, who wears ornaments of human bones, and who is smeared with ashes; O beloved of the supreme Nārāyaṇa, whose conduct is auspicious, who is the five-faced lion among the gods beginning with the Five Brahmas, who is known through the four Vedas; who is easily accessible to devotees yet difficult for non-devotees to attain; the Supreme Bliss, the Supreme Knowledge, the Bestower of the highest nourishment, who is skilled in the destruction of the sacrifice and the decapitation of Dakṣa’s head.

O beloved of Pārvatī who took away the fifth head of Brahmā; O Śarva, whose auspicious deeds are sung by Nārada; O three-eyed one, wielder of the trident and Pināka bow in hand; O single-braided one, wearer of manifold forms, whose vehicle is the bull; O you who resemble pure crystal, four-armed Dakṣiṇāmūrti bearing various weapons; O Lord of the gods, Īśvara; O bearer of the Gaṅgā, destroyer of Tripura; O dweller on Śrīśaila, Lord of Kāśī, Kedāreśvara, Siddheśvara, Gokarṇeśvara, Kanakhaleśvara, Parvateśvara, giver of the discus, destroyer of Bāṇa and Cintāpāda, whose lotus feet are worshipped by Murāri; O you adorned with the moon and Soma; O All... [the text continues].
Salutations, salutations to you, whose nature consists of consciousness, light, and the universe.
While Rāma was thus offering praise, a form composed of radiant energy, accompanied by a central liṅga, manifested before him.

Then Rāma beheld the Lord of Kāma, who was fearless, seated upon a lotus throne, presided over by Umā, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a beautiful diadem, and whose waist was touched by the daughter of Himavat; he saw him granting the gestures of fearlessness and the boon with his two hands, while various directions were indicated by his many gestures, full of splendor, with a smiling face and a serene countenance. ||223||
Having bowed with joined palms to the Supreme Lord, he fell again like a staff.
Then the Supreme Lord said to Rāma, "Choose a boon; I am the giver of boons. ||225||
Rāma said:
"O Śambhu, tell me one means by which I may cross the ocean; where shall I go? (226)
Śambhu said: "My bow Ājagava becomes, at that time, like Time itself, free from all hesitation. Mounting it, cross the ocean and obtain your desire."
Rāma, having thus resolved, called to mind the Ājagava bow.
Then, once the bow had arrived, Rāma worshipped it.
Then, taking up his bow, he gave it to Rāma.
Rāma also cast it into the ocean.
All the monkeys, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa ascended; when those sixty parārdhas of innumerable monkeys had mounted their bows, he proceeded at his ease.
Then the monkeys went to the bank of the Dhanuṣkoṭi and looked about. ||233||
Then the Rākṣasa named Atikāya, beholding the army of monkeys, spoke to Rāvaṇa.
Rāvaṇa also said: "What is the use of these monkeys, these forest-dwellers? What is the use of those two non-humans, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa? What has come here? This is surely food sent by fate. ||235||

Then Sugrīva, accompanied by Hanumān—who resembled the sun hanging in the western sky—and other great forces led by Jāmbavān, went to the side of Laṅkā with countless, massive-bodied [monkeys]. Entering the grove, they ate various fruits and drank water; having put the Rākṣasa guards of the grove to flight, they seized the entire forest one by one and rushed toward Laṅkā. Reaching the city gate, they climbed the palace and, shattering it, some took up pillars and fought with the Rākṣasas one by one.
They destroyed some single-hall structures and pulverized others; they slaughtered everyone, including children, the elderly, women, and the rest. ||237||
Then, once one rampart had been conquered, Rāvaṇa commanded Indrajit. ||238||
Having fought in the battle against Indrajit, the monkeys fled in fear. ||239||

Then Hanumān, having learned that Rāvaṇa had departed with his entire retinue, summoned the monkeys, rebuked them, and having formed a great army, he assumed the form of the Ten-faced one and caused him joy. ||240||
Then, even while remaining in the sky, the monkeys saw him being struck by Indrajit. ||241||
Then Hanumān and Jāmbavān, leaping up with great speed, struck Indrajit with two mountain peaks. ||242||
Then he fell to the ground, and Lakṣmaṇa dispatched him to the realm of Yama.

Then, having slaughtered the vast army of monkeys many times over, having afflicted Lakṣmaṇa, and having fought with Rāma, those two—Atikāya and Mahākāya—having made Sugrīva their captive and having bound Hanumān and Jāmbavān, fought on; being defeated, those two warriors were captured, taken to the presence of Rāma, and reported to him.
Rāma spoke to Atikāya. ||245||
Tell me of Rāvaṇa’s battle with Śambara, and of the others who were filled with great fear by his ministers.
Atikāya said:

"This was certainly decided by us previously: having divided the army into sections, the immensely powerful Rākṣasa named Vidyunmālī, a warrior of diverse skills who fights both from sight and out of sight, shall fight alone against all the monkeys."
"Other powerful ones, great warriors skilled in weaponry, have arrived; we two shall fight with you both, while Rāvaṇa, having mounted the Puṣpaka, will slay you alone from another direction. ||248||
Other rākṣasas, headed by Kuṃbhakarṇa, will assume their own forms, surround and seize you, show you to Sītā, and kill you right there in her presence. ||249||
Rāma said: "Alas! What indeed is impossible for the powerful? Such is the crooked course of destiny. Seeing Rāma thus enraged, Sugrīva, who was himself exceedingly wrathful, spoke to him. ||250||
These two, who were to be executed, must be released. ||251||
Rāma said, "These two are not to be killed; they must be released. Bring garments and ornaments. As soon as this was said, Hanumān brought them, and Rāma gave them to the two.
Having bowed down to this, which is seen here at the entrance of Laṅkā as a wooden five-faced [image], it was said by Śukra that Rāvaṇa is slain when this is cut. ||253||
Then, immediately after the wood was cut, the instruction spoken by Bhārgava, "One must go to Pātāla," was written down. ||254||
Therefore, with a single effort and a single discharge of an arrow, you must split this wood into five pieces; then, having recognized your power, we shall engage in a most strenuous battle.

Then, having understood the words of Bhārgava, Rāma fixed the bowstring at the front tip by mere touch, joined an arrow to the bow, and released it while making his intent heard to the two Rākṣasas and Hanumān.

Observing that the arrow and the bow had been rendered useless and watching the path of the Rākṣasa’s arrows, [the two monkeys] saw that his own formidable arrow had been split into five pieces; they then informed Rāma, "Our two children must be protected by you," to which Rāma replied, "So be it.
The two Rākṣasas entered Laṅkā.

Then, in order to wage a battle against the rampart, the monkeys arrived and, covering the entire enclosure on all sides with their heels, feet, knees, hands, and backs, made it level with the ground; having thus reached the second rampart, Rāvaṇa then approached, drove them all away with arrows, and following after them, went toward Rāma.
Then he also pierced Rāma with five arrows.
Then, with eight arrows, Rāma made Āvaṇa wounded.
Between these two, there occurred an exceedingly fierce battle with one another. ||261||
Rāvaṇa pierced him with ten arrows. ||262||
Then, his body wounded by Rāma’s arrows, the rākṣasa became intent on flight. ||263||
The monkeys and Lakṣmaṇa slew ten million times ten million rākṣasas.
Then, on the following day, Vibhīṣaṇa, having reflected, spoke this to Rāvaṇa: ||265||
This is the time for the third method; do not deliberate upon the fourth.
The fourth is contrary and is not praised for one who seeks to accomplish the goal.
Having ascertained that the enemy's power is inferior and one's own power is superior, then war is recommended; otherwise, it leads to destruction. (267)
There shall be no battle between you, who are weak, and the powerful Rāma;
for you already know from before that he is the slayer of Vālin.
Even you fled from Mārīca with a single arrow;
the heroic Rākṣasas were slain, and your son Indrajit was killed. (269)
The three boons have been exhausted by him, and you shall have no battle with him;
instead, obtain Sītā by surrendering yourself to the state of servitude.
Furthermore, Rāma will kill you by means of that wooden five-faced arrow which he has fixed upon his bow and which he shall release while standing at the gate-tower. ||271||
For your sake, many have perished, and others will perish;
there is but one right course for the sake of happiness, and not folly, O brother. (272)
Having honored her—a human woman, devoted to her husband, unwilling [to go], and the wife of a powerful man—release her. (273)
In union with one who does not desire it, there arises supreme suffering;
association with women is loathsome, being joined with foul odors and impurities. (274)
If detachment has arisen, then engaging in improper conduct leads to suffering;
if passion should persist, then death follows, and from that, hell. (275)
My own death would be in vain upon meeting her today;
O dear one, there would likewise be either the abandonment or the death of my lawful wife.
Such and other defilements will likewise arise;
I shall tell you another word that is dear and beneficial to all.
Having gone into the presence of Rāma, having bowed, praised, and informed the descendant of Raghu:
"Forgive me, O Rāma, great hero, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge. (278)
All of us Rākṣasas are of a dark nature and exceedingly wicked;
setting aside the fault arising from the abduction of Sītā, regard us as your sons. (279)
"O Rāma, we are dependent on you; protect us or kill us as you wish.
Having spoken thus, we stood before that descendant of Raghu. (280)
"O Ten-faced One, we shall have long lives and a stable kingdom.
Then Rāvaṇa spoke these words: "Oh, you are a Rākṣasa! (281)
You are no hero, nor do you understand the eternal dharma of kings, due to your pursuit of another's wife, another's wealth, and another's kingdom. ||282||
The highest dharma belongs to the brave, not to eunuchs such as yourself, O King;
for if you wish to depart while embracing the side of the enemy, [you are no hero]. (283)
Then Bibhīṣaṇa, having gone to his palace and approached Rāma, sought refuge with him. ||284||
Then Rāvaṇa, having emerged from the city, fought with Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and the monkeys; the rākṣasas also fought. ||285||
Then Rāma, unable to slay the mighty Rāvaṇa, looked toward the face of Vibhīṣaṇa and, having identified him by the signs and marks mentioned, struck and killed him with an arrow. ||286||
Then Kumbhakarna, seizing a great mace and having accomplished everything by devouring many monkeys, struck Rāma’s head with that mace.
Then Rāma struck him with a hundred sharp arrows, and Kumbhakarṇa died. ||288||

Then, having caused Vibhīṣaṇa to perform the funeral rites (*śrāddha*) for Rāvaṇa and the others, and having had a temple of Śiva built in his name, he consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa himself in the sovereignty of Laṅkā. After causing Sītā—purified by her entry into the fire—to bow down before Umā and Maheśvara, and having been granted all nectar, strength, and long life by the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), he mounted the excellent Puṣpaka chariot, crossed the ocean, and stationed his army on the shore of the sea. Having performed the installation of Śiva there, he was honored by sages and gods and returned to Ayodhyā. ||289||
Then, accompanied by Bharata and others, and honored by the citizens, Vasiṣṭha, and the sages, he went to his own home. ||290||

Having honored the gods, Indra and the others, who had arrived in person, with seats and other offerings, and having likewise worshipped the monkeys, Rāma—having cast off his matted locks and been consecrated in the kingdom—was addressed by the gods, who were delighted by the slaying of Rāvaṇa.

"Established by you in our own kingdom, protect us always! You are the primordial Lord Nārāyaṇa, descended for the sake of subduing all the wicked; having slain Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen, you are the protector of the three worlds. Be happy together with Śrī! Having spoken thus, they departed for heaven. ||292||
Then the inhabitants of Ayodhyā, filled with great joy, spoke to Rāma.
Having slain your enemies, you have returned; having seen [the truth], you have indeed attained auspiciousness.
By good fortune you shine, O Rāma; by good fortune you protect the subjects. (294)
"You shall perform sacrifices for me; through you, dharma shall flourish.
Having heard these words of the townspeople, the lotus-eyed Rāma [replied].
Then, having honored all the citizens with garments and other gifts,
the righteous-souled one, after all the people had been worshipped, spoke to the sages.
Is your asceticism flourishing? Is your sacrifice well-performed?
Are you devoted to your own wives? And is the Lord worshipped? (297)
Are your wives blessed with good offspring? Is everything attended by supreme happiness? (298)
The sages said:
"O King, descendant of Kakutstha, everything is well for the ascetics under your rule.
We shall depart from this place; what do you think, O King? (299)
Rāma said:
"Śambhu is pleased with him with whom the Brahmins are pleased;
for him with whom Īśāna is pleased, there shall be prosperity. (300)
"Having performed that [fast], you ought to come here immediately after completing the fast.
Then, saying "So be it," the hosts of sages performed the supreme fast. (301)
Having honored him with blessings, they departed for their respective homes filled with joy;
Rāma too, exceedingly delighted, went along with his wife and his younger brother.
He who was beloved by all people performed the *akaṃṭaka* rite for his kingdom;
whoever hears this narrative, even if they be a sinner, [is purified]. (303)
Freed from all evil, he attains the supreme Brahman;
that man who remembers this shall not fall into an evil rebirth. (304)
And whoever should proclaim this—this has been declared thus for him. ||305||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Rāmāyaṇa of the Ancient Kalpa," in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava within the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||116||
The one hundred and seventeenth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having eaten at the house of Bhāradvāja, Rāmacandra was of serene mind.
The sage, accompanied by Draviṣṇu and joined by monkeys and bears, [proceeded]. ||1||
Just as when the sky is covered by clouds and a gentle breeze blows, so too was there within that forest a most excellent and divine palace. ||2||
It was adorned with eightfold chessboard patterns, fashioned with golden bands,
set with jewels and pearls, and provided with silver pitchers.
It was made fragrant with sandalwood, camphor, musk, and saffron;
it was provided with latticed windows and covered with a canopy above.

He saw the entire interior floor of the house, which was like the arrival of moonlight, impossible to behold even by the sun due to its middle wall, and sprinkled with the essence of the nectar of the moon.
Likewise, the northern direction is entirely devoid of the conception of walls;
it is fashioned by its own feet, acting as a painter for pillar after pillar.
His palace was a hundred cubits high, constructed above with crystal,
and it possessed a shade even greater than that of the Pārijāta tree.
There, the entire region was covered by a dense grove of plantain trees,
surrounded by plantain groves and encircled by groves of *ketakī* flowers.
Abounding with the cries of peacocks, filled with the humming of bees, resounding with the calls of flocks of pigeons, and adorned with various groves. ||9||
It was crowded with hundreds of palaces, resounded with the songs of intoxicated cuckoos,
and featured many trees adorned with great jewels hanging from their branches.
The quarters of the sky were filled with the sound of the songs of Kinnara women;
it was the most excellent bank of the Gautamī, beautiful with its many groves. 11.
The holy house of Bhāradvāja was adorned with those virtues;
it was delightful, filled with pride, and provided with hundreds of male and female servants. 12.
The auspicious house of Bhāradvāja was equipped with various articles of utility;
within it was a palatial mansion, and therein were inner courtyards.
In the midst of those eight was one house, most magnificent,
adorned with the palaces and temples of the Great God in the four directions.
Every house was beautifully adorned with dark-colored triple archways,
as if specially designed for the rest of the excellent women dwelling in heaven.
Having departed from the house of Bhāradvāja accompanied by his entire retinue,
Rāma went to that great dwelling situated in the middle of the forest.
Then that army, covered within and provided with separate garments and seats, entered;
likewise, one lion-throne situated in the center and many ascetic seats were entered.
After the incomparable seat of the Paurāṇika, there was the excellent lion-throne of the king;
having first seated the Paurāṇika, he then [seated] Vasiṣṭha and the other eminent sages.
Nārāyaṇa himself approached the kings, the monkeys, and those of lowly station;
the sky was shrouded by clouds, the quarters were clear, and the surface of the earth was strewn with beautiful flowers like sown seeds.

Then, beholding Śambhu—who was neither hot nor cold, whose body was adorned with flowers, and who possessed the fragrance of the *dama* flower—Rāma spoke these words: "Relate the story of Śaṅkara. (20)
No satiety was reached by that best of sages as he listened to this narrative of Maheśa, which destroys the multitude of sins.
Or rather, what did Maheśvara, the lord of the hosts of gods, not perform while surrounded by them in the hermitage of Gautama?
Śiva said:
Relying upon the great scholar, the son of Vāyu remained steadfast and questioned Śiva:
"O Lord, tell me, what kind of fruit results from worshipping the All-pervading One with wealth acquired through unjust means?"
O Lord Śambhu, tell me quickly: what is the fruit for those who offer stolen goods—that is, for those who present substances they have acquired through theft?
O Blessed One, please explain the answer to this question one by one. (23)
Then Īśvara spoke to Vānara: "I shall tell you everything; listen with concentration!
Having worshipped the unborn Sadāśiva with wealth acquired through righteous means, Gautama indeed attained this sovereignty. (24)

Formerly, from the city came a twice-born man named Ākatha, the son of Maṅkaṇa; he was a virtuous brahmin, uniquely poor, filled with compassion, eating only on the sixth day, and deprived of his father. (25)
Having observed the five-day fast, he was just beginning to eat when the ascetic arrived.
The ascetic then spoke sweetly: "How is it that you, who have been fasting for a month, have come here to eat? (26)
"I shall remain here as long as you stay, O Sage; I have no hunger to eat food from another's house.
Ākaṭha said: "O best of the twice-born, my meal was not available for five days; on the sixth day, my meal arrived. (27)
"Then I shall wash away this incurable disease of mine, which is beyond thought, by washing your feet.
Saying "Om," the yogi, having washed his pair of feet, desired to take his meal.

Having cooked this food—which was prepared with rain-clouds as its fuel and mixed with clarified butter—and having carefully combined it with forest-grown provisions, he ate it all, leaving not even a morsel remaining. (29)
Then, seeing the Sage highly pleased, the ascetic Akatha, together with his wife, was filled with joy.
Having eaten, the sage departed; then Akatha, with a contented heart, performed his recitation of prayers.
Then the sage, who lived like a pigeon and was a virtuous man whose wife had spread a canopy of cloth against the heat,
having seated that Lord of Umā, Śiva— who was accompanied by his attendants— upon a pedestal, worshipped him within the *liṅga*.
Then, having set down the *liṅga* and looking about, he saw a certain twice-born man of emaciated form;
a lord who was naked, footless, one-eyed, with a withered arm, and devoid of ears.
Then he saw him approaching his home, a master who had reached the further shore of many scriptures, uttering [the words] with joy.
Then Akatha spoke these words to his wife Suśobhanā: ||34||
For here comes this Brahmin in a strange disguise. (35)

"Half of this food should be given to him, and half of the meal should be kept for his protection; for since the sixth day has passed without food, it appears to me that your life will not endure. But tell me, what do you think? (36)
Sāśobhanā said:
"The lifespan written upon the forehead does not perish in the interim. (37)
He said:

"Just as the head of Yajña, though his life-span was bound [to last], was severed by Vīrabhadra—what need is there to mention those of sinful nature who are transient? Therefore, having avoided him, this is enjoyed by you;
however, if food is given to him by me, my duty must be performed according to your wish. (38)
"How shall I eat while you have not eaten? "I ate before; listen to this other [reason]. (39)
Food is indeed the life-force of living beings; this is evident to all embodied beings.
Therefore, he who bestows food is said to be a giver of life. (40)
From food all beings are born, and by it they flourish; indeed, they arise from it.
Therefore, there is no gift superior to food that yields such great fruit. (41)
For one who would give away their life while wealth is as unstable as a drop of water clinging to the tip of a trembling leaf of the holy fig tree, that person's birth is indeed in vain. (42)
For dharma alone is the companion in the next world; wife, sons, and kinsmen are not.
Wife, parents, and sons remain companions only as long as life lasts. (43)
O best among the upholders of dharma, you are our friend, our two-fold prosperity, and our welfare in this world and the next; what else remains for us to enjoy? (44)
Having heard these words of his wife, Ākāśa, a treasury of compassion,
gave her powerful food without any hesitation.
This is that Lord Śaṅkara, who has arrived for the purpose of making a distinction. ||45||
Having thus resolved in his mind, he went to that river which destroys all evil.
Having washed his feet up to the ankles, and then the other [feet] up to the knees,
and having washed the ankle and that which is below it, he should offer water for sipping to the twice-born guest.
Then, having loosened the joints of his feet, Akatha brought the group of householders near and,
releasing the joints of his feet, sat down upon the offered seat.
Having honored him thoroughly, they fed the sage with great care;
in the meantime, a certain madman arrived at the house.
Then, having taken hold of the joint of a leg, he brought it outside the house;
thereafter, he set that house on fire and also struck the husband and wife.
Though reviled and beaten, the Brahmin then entered the burning house in order to quickly retrieve the god Īśāna.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having taken Maheśāna whose worship had been burnt,
he went out and saw that his face was indeed scorched.
Having disregarded the burnt offering and seeing that his wife too was burnt,
the righteous-souled one spoke to her concerning the worship of the Great Lord.
"In that same way, you must perform my entire rite without hesitation.
Vyoma said:
"Even if performed later, your worship shall become fruitful. (54)
Just as such [an offering] is given by people when burning other substances, so too, for the sake of worship, let this worship be performed for Him. (55)
Ākaṭha said:
Even if one worships the Enemy [Śiva] with wealth acquired through theft, it would be beneficial;
however, O Brahmin, worship of Śambhu performed with ill-gotten gains does not bestow auspiciousness. (56)
Having spoken thus, he quickly began to burn his own body;
then, as the liṅga was being consumed, the madman seized it and vanished in an instant.
Then, having become a bull, he blocked the path and spoke:
"O Brahmin, why do you grieve? I am a granter of boons; choose a boon. (58)
Ākaṭha also chose unwavering devotion at the feet of the Lord.
Sūta said:
Having heard this story, Rāma, surrounded by the sages, was greatly delighted.
Having paid homage to Bhāradvāja, he requested permission to depart.
Then the sage Bharadvāja, being pleased, bowed down to Śambhu, Vasiṣṭha—the bull among sages—Nārāyaṇa, and the hosts of ṛṣis, and dismissed them; they too departed after bowing to him.
The sages of Naimiṣa said:
Having gone to Ayodhyā accompanied by all the sages, what did the highly effulgent Rāma do thereafter,
along with Śambhu, he of great fame?
Sūta said: On the following day, Rāghava, desiring to perform the monthly śrāddha for Kausalyā, invited the most excellent of the twice-born, who were like ṛṣis.
Then Śambhu, Samas, Tattvajña, Nārada, Romaśa, Bhṛgu, Viśvāmitra, and thereafter Rāma, who was devoted to the vow of eating only once a day. 64.
On the ground spread with a soft carpet, having slept soundly with his senses undisturbed, he then,
when the following morning had arrived, bathed according to the prescribed rules, being one who knows the ritual injunctions.
He had people prepare pure food such as vegetables,
as well as various kinds of diverse foods, including those to be sucked and so forth.
Likewise, he prepared thirty-eight kinds of eatables such as *vaṭaka* and others,
six varieties of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and two hundred kinds of cooked vegetables.
And there he prepared a mixture of raw and cooked foods,
including potherbs such as *kālaśāka* and various kinds of fruits.
Having had the roots and the bark of the single tree prepared, Rāghava went to the river together with his brother and the family priest.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarayū and offered oblations into the fire,
the king, having performed the worship of the gods, welcomed those brahmins by saying, "Welcome."
Having restrained his breath and performed the mental visualization, Rāma offered a moment of time and invited Nārada Romaharṣaṇa to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
He invited Śambhu, Bhṛgu, Kauśika, and others to the place of the Mothers;
then, having prepared a mandala with cow dung, he worshipped the Arhats.
He performed the washing of their feet with the water he had offered; having caused those brahmins to sip water for purification, he then prepared to go home.
An elderly man of deformed appearance arrived as a guest;
he was emaciated, his limbs were trembling, and likewise his feet and head were shaking.
Afflicted by the protrusion of hanging skin and by labored breathing and coughing,
his cheeks were moist with rheum and his beard was smeared with saliva.
He said to King Rāma, "I am standing here alone as a twice-born man;
food must also be given to me, for I am old and emaciated. (76)
Rāma, having heard those words, spoke this sentence to Lakṣmaṇa:
"You wash his feet; I shall honor the brahmin."
Even a guest who has arrived brings me distress;
for you, my food is desired only after your feet have been washed. (78)
"O twice-born ones, why do you disregard me, who am superior even to him?
You do not know the dharma of the śrāddha, which is practiced by the hosts of great sages. (79)
By insulting me, you insult all brahmins;
furthermore, your śrāddha offering will be frustrated, and you shall go to hell. (80)
Then Rāma himself washed the brahmin’s feet;
having offered him water for sipping, he then led the brahmin into the house.
Having sipped water himself, Rāma then offered a seat;
and when the Brahmins were seated, he restrained his vital breaths.
Then, having obtained permission to perform his own ritual duties, he should scatter water mixed with sesame seeds at the entrance while reciting the mantra "apahata. (83)
One should likewise pour water from the vessel for the ancestors while reciting "udīratām";
and one should pour consecrated water (akṣatodaka) into the place of the vessel for the gods while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
Likewise, having sprinkled that which has been cooked, one should recite this mantra: ||84||
Having meditated again and again upon Gayā, the field of the Śrāddha, and likewise upon Janārdana,
and having meditated upon the ancestors, beginning with the Vasus, one should then proceed with the Śrāddha.
One should perform the worship of the Viśvedevas with barley or rice grains;
having taken two *darbha* blades joined at their roots and tips, together with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Touching the ground with the right knee while offering water from the hand of a twice-born—one such as this is the seat for the gods, namely Purūravas, Ārdrava, and the Vaidevas. (87)
Having thus offered them a seat, the giver of the śrāddha should request their presence for the occasion.
Having then performed the *argha* offering, one should subsequently place the vessel face down upon *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing north, and then place a knot of *kuśa* grass on top of it.
Then, having turned it face upwards and sprinkled it with water from golden vessels,
one should pour water for the Lord and the Goddess into a vessel covered by a purifier (pavitra).
All ritual action pertaining to the Vaiśvadeva, as far as it is enjoined by the rules, [is performed];
one should throw barley grains into the vessel with the mantra, "Thou art barley, the king of grains. (91)
Then one should offer water mixed with honey, along with fragrant flowers and *stukarakas*.
Having said, "May there be *arghya* for the twice-born," one should then offer the *arghya* from the north.
Having asked, "Shall I invoke these deities? and having received the affirmative reply, one should say, "O Viśvedevas," and cast kuśa grass upon the heads of the Brahmins. (93)
One should mutter the mantra: "O Viśvedevas, hear this; may you come hither.
Then, once they have arrived and are seated, one should bring forward a vessel containing Darbha grass.
Then, having poured the water from the primary vessel onto his right foot,
he should place it upon the brāhmaṇa’s right hand, where a pavitra-grass ring with its tips pointing eastward has been laid.
One should pour water from the vessel while reciting the *yā divyā* mantra; having said, "O, this is the *argha*," the *argha* should then be placed to the north.
Having taken the water for the *argha* offering in that vessel, one should place that vessel somewhere;
then, having poured water into his hand, one should worship him with these barley grains.
Having asked, "Worship! Worship! from the north, he then worshipped [the deity] from the feet up to the head and offered water. 98.
Having said "So be it" with the mantra *gandhadvāram*, he should then stand to the north;
in this very manner, he should perform the worship of the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).

Having made the twice-born person wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder, and having placed broken kuśa grass mixed with sesame seeds upon his left knee which is set upon the ground, one should then offer him a seat.
Facing south, he should then utter the inquiry regarding the auspicious moment (*akṣaṇapraśna*).
Upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, he should place three vessels face-down.
Then, one should fashion [the vessel] with three knots made of kuśa grass and turn it face upwards;
thereafter, having sprinkled water over the vessels containing pavitra-grass and sesame seeds, [one should proceed].
Having sprinkled water with the mantra "śaṃ no devīr," he should scatter sesame seeds with the mantra "tilo 'si.
Then, having offered fragrance and flowers, he asks, "Svadhā-argha? (103).
Having given the response "Let there be *argha*," he should then invoke the ancestors;
standing, he should offer the prepared *argha* water with sesame seeds, flowers, and *kuśa* grass. (104)
One should offer water for the feet three times with the mantra "uśantas tvā";
however, their worship at that time is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), as was done previously.
Having washed the vessel, one should provide a golden one for the gods; for the ancestors, one should use a silver one, or whatever is available.
In the absence of that, one should use a vessel made of *tūka* wood, which is excellent when not smeared by others; in the absence of that, vessels made of *pālāśa* wood are middling.
Rambhāṇī, mango leaves, jambū, puṃnāga, parāka, campaka, madhūka, and kuṭaja as well; ||108||
The leaves of the *mātuluṅga* tree should indeed be offered by men during the *śrāddha*;
having taken the food with a ladle, and likewise the clarified butter (*ājya*) with both hands. (109)

Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), he should ask the twice-born guest, "I shall perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa)"; the latter's reply should be, "Do so. (110)
Having served the food, he should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī), sprinkle it with clarified butter, and collect [the portions];
he should then offer oblations to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, uttering "Svadhā namaḥ."

Having offered the second oblation with the mantra "To Yama, to Aṅgiras, to Pitṛmat, svadhā namaḥ," and then having sprinkled it with clarified butter, he should place the unbroken grain (akṣata). ||112||

Then, after offering with the mantra "Svadhā namaḥ agnaye kavyavāhanāya," and having performed the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should proceed to serve the food to the twice-born.
Then, one should repeatedly pour [the remnants] from the stirring-spoon into the vessel for the ancestors.
After that comes the vessel for the rice-balls (piṇḍas), then the remainder, and finally the washing of the ladle.
Then, having placed the stirring-spoon into the fire, one should arrange the vessels;
immediately thereafter, one should place the food on the southern side of the vessels.
