He gave away all kinds of food, edibles, and vegetables;
then a very old guest, looking here and there, [beheld this]. (116)
He spoke to Rāghava: "O peaceful one, pay homage to him immediately!
Hunger afflicts us; I shall eat by his command. (117)
Rāma spoke thus to him: "O Sage, wait for a moment;
the deities and the ancestors are now being saluted by me with reverence. (118)
Having spoken thus, Rāghava then gave the food placed upon the vessel;

for the rite to the gods (daiva), he laid down the kuśa grass with their tips pointing eastward and northward, and for the rite to the ancestors (pitrya), with their tips pointing westward and southward.
Then, for the ancestors and the purifiers, they offer darbha grass, barley, and sesame seeds, performing the offering of food with the mantra beginning "pṛthivī. (120)
Having touched [the water] with his thumb while reciting "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should first offer it to the gods while reciting "ye devāḥ. ||121||
One should offer this to the ancestors and then to the guest;
having uttered the names of the deities beginning with "Agnaye," one should give the *āpośana* water.

Having recited the Gāyatrī three times while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder and facing the east, he should thereafter, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, recite the three "Honey" verses.
Having said to them, "Eat," while the twice-born were eating,
he caused the recitation of mantras that destroy demons (rakṣoghna) and had foodstuffs such as hard and soft foods served.
In the meantime, a Brahmin guest performed a great marvel; I shall relate that briefly. (125)
He consumed everything remaining in the vessel with a single mouthful and said, "Let enough be given for the oblations of the vital breaths. (126)
"If you are unable to give even this much, how can you be intent on performing the Śrāddha rite? O Rāma, if you are incapable of giving to me alone, why do you exert yourself in vain? (127)
What is the use of Rāma’s effort to provide food for many?
Those who have performed actions impulsively do not reach completion. (128)
"Since you have not performed it for all [beings], the offering of my life-breaths is not sufficient. Tell me, how can there be enjoyment for me, and likewise for them? (129)
The heroic Rāma said to him, "Eat as much as you please," and having spoken thus,
he gazed at that most wonderful deed performed by his mouth.
Then, having summoned Śambhu, he said: "You serve as the waiter;
it is my conviction that you are the father and Pārvatī is the mother, the goddess Śivā. (131)
"It is my conviction that she is the goddess Annapūrṇeśvarī, the consort of Bhava. To her, Śāṃbhavī spoke these words: "I shall give you as much of that as you require. (132)
Then, having taken a vessel made of emerald and filled with wine,
and having taken a golden ladle containing fragrant and lustrous milk-rice (pāyasa), [he offered it].
Thinking, "May this of his become inexhaustible," she joyfully and respectfully placed the milk-pudding into the right hand of the twice-born man.
Shaking his head, he then cast his gaze upward;
with his hand extended, he took the milk-rice (pāyasa) into his palm.
"Let this delicious and well-cooked milk-rice be given; what else is there?
Śambhu’s wife spoke thus, and he gave it to her with his own hand. 136.
Then the Brahmin ate that which remained in his palm;
and knowing it to be inexhaustible, he then stretched out his other hand. (137)
Then, while that hand of the goddess was still offering the milk-rice,
the virtuous woman also gave inexhaustible cooked food to the other brahmins.
Then, perceiving that the inexhaustible porridge was contained within both hands, the virtuous brāhmaṇa saw another hand and extended it toward him. (139)
"Excellent food, together with soup and ghee, must be given," said Śivādevī; and so she, the beloved of Śambhu, provided inexhaustible food. 140.
Whatever that virtuous woman gave away at that time, all of it became inexhaustible;
then another hand was created, which was likewise full again and again.
Having thus performed a thousand oblations, the Brahmin ceased; he then spoke these words to the water used for rinsing his mouth: "O Dehika!"
I have been gratified by you, O auspicious one, as I was by Rāma and Sītā.
Śambhu said:
"That which was given by Rāma, by Sītā, and indeed by me—what more is there to be given? Tell me, are you not satisfied?"
The twice-born said:
"O learned one, I was satiated with this; more than this remained in my hand. Therefore, though it was within my grasp, it did not fall out by any means. (144)
Seated there, he reflected for a long time: "How is it that this entire meal has been prepared for me alone? It is not for any other purpose of mine. (145)
"Therefore, all this [claim] of being created by another will prove empty.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he became a guest with his limbs smeared [with ashes]. (146)
While all the gods were watching, that appeared like a miracle;
then Rāghava, the knower of the supreme truth, perceiving that the twice-born were satisfied, [acted]. (147)
Then, having asked according to the prescribed rite, "O Darvīkaras, are you satisfied?",
and [receiving the reply] from the lords of Brahmins, "We are satisfied," he should scatter food accompanied by mantras.
Facing the south, he should place the rice-ball (piṇḍa) near the vessel;
likewise, he should provide water for rinsing the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa) for the Brahmins there.
They rinsed their mouths using leaf-plates that had been used as leftovers; moreover, those two brahmins entered within the house without even a guest. 150.
"O Lord of the Twice-born, the guest must be sent outside by me;
O descendant of Raghu, I am not at all able to rise, for my hand is pierced. (151)
Then Rāma gave his hand, but that best of brahmins did not rise;
then Hanumān gave him a powerful hand to support him.
But the lord of monkeys, seizing the eminent twice-born with his other hand, dragged him along; then the brahmin spoke with cries of protest.
The twice-born said:
"Clearly, one [pillar] was being cut; then, from another direction, he violently raised it up along with its base, encircling it by force from head to foot. (154)
Then the twice-born ran toward the earth and did not waver;
meanwhile, the heroic monkey tore up the ground with his feet.
Placing his two feet firmly and striking the head of the twice-born man, the house fell into ruin, and all the twice-born men likewise went outside. (156)
Then Hanumān, accompanied by the elderly brahmin,
went outside and seated the aged, emaciated brāhmaṇa upon a throne.
Taking water in an earthen jar, Jāmbavān said to the twice-born one, "O Brahmin, you must take this pure water along with the vessel. (158)
Sītā shall wash his limbs, and Lakṣmaṇa shall become the cloud;
Jāmbavān shall strike Rāma, as instructed by the Brāhmaṇa in its entirety. (159)
Rāma commanded his younger brother to wash the twice-born and his beloved wife;
likewise, Saumitri took water for the washing of the brahmins' bodies.
They washed every limb [of the king], as if he were a statue;
then, by Rāma’s instruction, the two of them did exactly so.
Then the guest released his own mouthful of water into Sītā’s mouth; thereupon the virtuous lady washed away the *sālaṅkāra* [stain] that had pervaded it with those waters. (162)
The unchaste wife of the Brahmin repeatedly wiped her mouth, which was overflowing with phlegm and saliva, and while washing it, she did not even cast away the mucus from her nose. 163.
Having offered water for rinsing the mouth, the son of Sumitrā said to the twice-born, "Arise!
The twice-born replied, "It is not possible," just as Hanumān had arrived.
The guest, a brahmin, said to him: "I was tormented by Hanumān;
having seized me, that monkey first lifted me up and then cast me down. (165)
"O Brahmin, you have said that my hair is soft;
therefore, I shall bear it for you, and no pain will arise. (166)
Having spoken thus, he took the brahmin by the arms and lifted him up; then, taking the edge of the bird's wing, he set that sage down.
Then Rāma, having been granted blessings by the Vipras, circumambulated them clockwise and gave them betel-leaf in their presence.
Rāma, supporting his feet, spoke together with his brothers: "O Sītā, this guest's body has not been washed by you. (169)
Since the mouth of an atithi is impure and filled with filth, a twice-born man cannot endure that filth even if he has thoroughly washed his face. (170)
Sītā said: "Now that it has been thoroughly washed, it has emerged again.
Rāma said:
If one were to wash away the stain again, it would result in a fault just as mine.
Then Sītā, having done so, remained silent;
and the twice-born man, filled with supreme rage, seized both Sītā and Āhara.
"O King of the Immortals, let Sītā quickly take hold of my two feet;
and may you, O Bhava, grant me my seed, Bharata. (173)
May Lakṣmaṇa become the one who arranges the mass of hair;
may Śatrughna perform the removal of phlegm with his own garment. (174)
Sūta said:
Then those brahmins, monkeys, and rākṣasas performed for the guest everything that had been instructed, and likewise experienced great wonder. 175.
Śivādevī and Śambhu gazed at him with a knitting of their brows;
and in their minds they spoke, for Śambhu himself was the guest.
And the guest became pleased—the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace;
clad in yellow garments, adorned with all ornaments, and exceedingly radiant. (177)
Śambhu, the three-eyed one, who had been propitiated in the past, became pleased;
he resembled pure crystal and was adorned with all ornaments. (178)
Resembling ten million suns, wearing a crown, and a treasure-house of compassion,
Sadāśiva took hold of the hand of the Discus-bearer and stood there.
Rāma, whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma,
his body covered in horripilation and his eyes overflowing with tears, prostrated himself upon the earth like a staff.
His brothers, prostrating themselves on the ground like a staff, raised the descendant of Kakutstha; Śiva then embraced him and smelled the crown of his head.
Śiva spoke these sweet words to the lotus-eyed Rāma:
"Choose a boon; I am pleased, even though it be difficult for Brahmā and others to obtain. (182)
"There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be given by you; choose [a boon] for me without delay.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Lord of the Universe, this kingdom is not now to be requested by me. (183)
Heaven was attained through my past actions, and devotion arose from the sight of your feet; now, seeing you, I enjoy health along with Sītā, the best among women. (184)
All the kings have been brought under control and are endowed with the duty toward their subjects;
O Acyuta, we have attained such great joy because of your arrival. (185)
Likewise, O Lord, if you have even a slight and firm devotion toward me, then, O God, remain for three years in my house. (186)
O Śaṅkara, proclaiming all dharmas through this very form, Śiva said: "So be it; O Rāma, everything shall come to pass for you accordingly. (187)
Then he said to King Rāma, the lotus-eyed cakravartin:
"O highly fortunate one, I am pleased; choose whatever boon you desire. (188)
O Śrī Rāma, there is indeed nothing further for me to request;
whatever was to be obtained from Śambhu has been attained, and everything else you have spoken has already been achieved. (189)
Furthermore, choose one boon, O Viṣṇu, and be gracious to me at all times.
Then Hari said to Sītā: "I am now pleased with you. (190)
"Choose a boon; I shall grant it. To this Sītā replied: "A boon was already chosen by my husband long ago; no other boon is superior to that. (191)
If you would grant me my desire and turn away from another man, then let there be food for you;
salutations to you, O lord of the twice-born! (192)
Then all those sages bowed down to the two supreme deities.
Thereupon, he said to Rāghava: "O descendant of Raghu, eat together with your kinsmen."
In a secluded and delightful place,
Viṣṇu, possessing all his faculties, dwelt together with the daughter of the ocean.
And in which [place] did you, being greedy, remain for me?
Now, in this pure great house, rich with seats and many vessels. (195)
The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha sat at the head of those two;
behind them sat all the other sages and kings according to their seniority.
Facing them, King Rāma, together with his brothers, seated them upon a youthful and equal throne. (197)
"O Rāma, summon your servants headed by Hanumān; you all must remain behind and protect the rear of the army. (198)
Then they all offered water for the feet and respectful offerings (arghya) in due order; and all those who were Rāma’s attendants partook of food as well. 199.
Having given them betel-leaf, he then fed the monkeys, headed by Drida;
when they had all finished eating, the lotus-eyed Rāma—
Having given food to the snakes and to those who were miserable, wretched, and so forth—including beasts, birds, and deer—he began to perform his evening twilight devotions (saṃdhyā). ||201||
Then, having performed his twilight prayers and other rites, King Rāma, seated upon the lion-throne, paid homage to them along with the citizens, country-folk, and others.
Being attended by his followers as he stood in the assembly hall, Rāghava shone like the god Śacīpati (Indra) surrounded by all the deities. ||203||
Having performed all the duties of the kingdom together with his brothers,
he dismissed them all one by one by name, along with Rāghava.
He dismissed his brothers, the monkeys and others, as well as the rest;
then the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha spoke these words to Rāma.
O Rāghava, you must not forget whatever task is to be done this morning;
for the Lord Śambhu, the Master of the Universe, the Blessed One, the Lord of Ambikā, is present.
"The Blessed One is to be meditated upon and honored without effort.
Having said "So be it" to his guru, the king bowed to him and dismissed him. (207)
He himself, contemplating the God of gods, approached his wife.
The sages said:
"Rising early in the morning, that best among the wise [approached] his guru, Aṅgiras."
Tell me what he did then; we have a great curiosity to hear it.
Sūta said:
Then, having beheld Śambhu, Rāma spoke: "O best of sages, as I listen to the greatness of Maheśa, which destroys the multitude of sins, no satiety has arisen in me; tell me the story of Śaṅkara."
Śambhu said:
Now I shall proclaim to you the answer to the remainder of your question as spoken by the Lord:
those who worship the Lord with wealth acquired through unjust means do not attain the state of Viṣṇu. 210.

For example, a certain Rākṣasa named Rūpaka, having propitiated Śaṅkara with wealth acquired through unjust means, made a ghaṇṭā (bell) out of that very same wealth for the pleasure of the Lord. ||211||
His son was known as Sampāti;
he worshipped Śaṅkara with wealth acquired through theft. ||212||
On which day did both of them die and go to the world of Śiva, as told by Vīrabhadra? ||213||
Since you have performed worship with wealth acquired through the unjust means of extortion, by that disposition you shall become a bull and then a pack of thieves. 214.

From the words of Śiva’s messenger, his name was clearly heard; his hearing was destroyed by that sound, and his vision likewise vanished. By this much alone, O Goddess, the worship of the Lord has been perfectly performed.
"Therefore, devotion shall arise; as for Vīrabhadra, he has been commanded to wander somewhere with a group of attendants known as 'Anashana' (those who do not eat). ||216||
And having become thus, the two of them remained in the world of Śiva. ||217||
Śambhu said:
Now I shall relate the account of Hanūmat regarding worship with defiled substances, as spoken by Maheśa. 218.
Listen, O Raghava; I shall relate the conduct of the Pramathas and the ripening of the karma for each one of them. ||219||
When Hanumān asked, "Let an explanation of the sky be given," Śiva said: 220.
One will offer that substance, defiled by that [ignorance], as water of knowledge to the Lord; therefore, listen to what is said regarding the possessor of knowledge. ||221||

He is perspiring all over at all times; with his garments moistened by sweat, his body marked by slight trickling streams produced by perspiration, and sweat-drops falling from the tip of his nose, he is seen to be unfit for touch. ||222||
He performed the worship of the Lord with fresh flowers and warm water;
here I shall proclaim an ancient legend. ||223||
A Brahmin known as Cekitāna became a farmer;
having daily cultivated his crops, he would always bathe in the morning. ||224||
When midday had arrived, that Brāhmaṇa, while engaged in his recitation, said to his wife, "Bring food quickly. (225)
With the food brought by her, he quickly performed the worship of Śiva;
scorched by the sun's heat, he was perspiring at all times. (226)

With perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, accompanied by drops of perspiration; then, when evening has arrived during that day, having bathed, he becomes most beautiful. (227)
He worshipped the Lord of Gods with offerings appropriate for the time;
then, that one of great intelligence died and went to the world of Śiva.
And Vīrabhadra also said: "Become a sweat-born attendant (svedila-gaṇa);
in ancient times, Śambhu was worshipped with objects touched by sweat. (229)
"Since you are constantly joined with sweat, therefore become a host of sweat-beings.
Śambhu said:
"Then, commanded by Vīra, this host of Rāma's attendants arrived. (230)

Look at this man, Ghaṇṭāmukha! Formerly, there was a righteous Vaiśya named Vibhāvasu, a great performer of charity who constantly fed Brahmins. Having completed his daily observances and paid homage to Śiva in the morning, he worshipped Him with flowers, smeared a certain area with cow dung, prepared lotuses and other offerings, presented them to the God, and then struck the sound of a bell. ||231||
Rāma said:
"How is it that your sin has been destroyed?"
Śambhu said:
In ancient times, there was a certain powerful man renowned as Soma;
his son, named Manda, was ten years of age.
O King, he threw even those half-cooked grains of millet that had been cooked over fire into his mouth;
yet he ate them, and he was not harmed by them. (234)
Then, striving to seize that Vaiśya, he spoke this;
or rather, the Vaiśya himself, having determined there the purification of the substance, [spoke]. (235)
Having performed worldly deeds and having become an object of worldly convention, he became like a heap of filth through this connection with evil. (236)
Rāma said:
"How can that which is purified by the purification of material substances (dravya) be a cause of sin?
You have correctly stated that it is for the sake of purifying substances; how then could it not be a purifier of substances? (237)
Śambhu said:
"Whether in worldly affairs or otherwise, he shall become a devotee;
he shall go to the abode of Śiva, and the speaker shall likewise be so. (238)
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, he who narrates this story is equal to Satī on earth; it is the most secret of secrets and bestows the knowledge of Śiva. 239.
O brahmins, this great [account], which is most meritorious and life-prolonging, has been told to you;
whoever hears this with devotion is glorified in the world of Śiva. (240)
To the reciter of the Purāṇas, one should give clothing, cows, gold ornaments, and land endowed with crops and fruit, according to one's capacity. (241)
Whoever reads or even hears this dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava, which destroys the flood of all sins, attains the supreme state. 242.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Rāma," in the latter portion of the Śiva-Rāghava-Saṃvāda within the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||117||
The fifth section, the Pātālakhaṇḍa, is completed. ||5||
Thus ends the fifth section, the Pātālakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Śrī Padma Purāṇa
(Now begins the sixth section, the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Narrative of Jālandhara (1).
The First Chapter. Om. Salutations to Śrī Viṣṇu.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Vedavyāsa.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya. (1)
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the probe of the medicinal collyrium of knowledge. ||2||
The sages said:
O best among the learned, you have narrated the Pātālakhaṇḍa, which is endowed with various legends and bestows supreme bliss. (3)
Now we wish to hear that which increases devotion to the Blessed One;
O Guru, please tell us out of compassion what remains here from the *Pādma*.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to that knowledge which destroys sin, as it was indeed spoken by Śaṅkara to the inquiring Nārada. (5)
Once, Nārada, who is dear to the Blessed One, while wandering through the worlds,
went to Mount Mandara to ask Śambhu about a certain matter that was on his mind.
Having prostrated before the Lord of Umā seated there, he sat down upon the throne directed by Śiva’s command, facing the All-pervading Lord.
Nārada said:
O best of beings, he asked this very same thing of the Lord that you ask me:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Lord of Pārvatī, Teacher of the world! (8)
"Instruct me so that I may attain the knowledge of the true reality of the Blessed One.
Śiva said:
"Listen, O Nārada, I shall declare the Purāṇa which is equal to the Vedas. (9)
Having heard which, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
There shall be the glorification of the first and the subsequent [sections], as well as the narrative of the mountain. 10.
Likewise, the description of Jālandhara, then that called Śrīśaila, the exposition of Haridvāra, and similarly [the account] of that which originates from the foot of Viṣṇu. ||11||
I shall describe to you the sacred site of Prayāga and that of Daśāśvamedhika,
as well as the greatness of Tulasī and the significance of the conch, discus, mace, and other emblems.
Then follows the narrative of Dvārakā and the procedure for the great festival;
likewise, the merit derived from tanks, as well as from ponds, wells, and water-stations.
Next, I shall describe the Gāṇapatya and the Vaiṣṇava Āgamas,
as well as the majesty of the restoration of ruined temples and the confluence of the Mandākinī.
The majesty of the Sābhramatī, as well as the majesty of those born on her banks;
likewise, the dharma for women and Śūdras, and the wearing of what is not to be discarded. (15)
The Thousand Names were proclaimed in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśa;
they were brought from Kailāsa by Nārada, the twice-born sage. (16)
It should be recited with a concentrated mind by people of all classes—especially by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, and particularly by women and Śūdras. (17)
This supreme purifier, meritorious and increasing longevity, should be recited especially; one shall attain union with Viṣṇu. (18)
One should here recite the thousand names of Viṣṇu, renowned on earth as purifying, as well as the locations of his twenty-four forms. (19)
And I shall declare their mothers and fathers, as well as their lineages, their Vedas, and likewise their deeds in this world. (20)
I shall describe their women according to the insight and vision [of the scriptures], [namely those] of the twenty-four, the eleven, and the twelve powerful ones. (21)
The greatness of the Godāvarī, the wearing of the conch, the discus, and other marks, and especially the wearing of these by Brahmins according to the prescribed rule. ||22||
O Sage, I shall tell you the greatness of the Yamunā, as well as that of the Gaṇḍikā and the Vetravatī; of this there is no doubt.
I shall fully describe in this section known as the Uttara-khaṇḍa all that merit arising from the Gilli-tīrtha and that great Śilā-kṣetra. ||24||

The majesty of Arbudeśvara and whatever sacred bathing places (tīrtha) exist there, as well as the majesty of the Sarasvatī and whatever Siddhakṣetra and other sites exist—[all this has been told]. ||25||
The origin of Padmanābha and the wearing of Tulasī, the greatness of Gopīcandana, and likewise the worship of the sacred thread; 26.
The majesty of Nirañjana, as well as the vision of higher knowledge, [is attained there];
and therein, the offering of lamps and especially the offering of incense [are performed]. (27)
Now, the majesty of the month of Kārttika, as well as the majesty of Māgha, and the majesty of all religious observances according to the prescribed rites. (28)
Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the supreme [place] called Jagannātha, by seeing which the world is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. (29)
Where food is prepared and eaten in such a manner that it bestows rewards in the next world, there the Brāhmaṇas, who are experts in the Vedas and Shastras, partake of the meal. ||30||
O observer of noble vows, what need is there to speak of other worlds?
There are likewise twenty-five varieties of serpent-dancers and various others as well.
The killing of a Brahmin, the killing of a child, and likewise the killing of cows—all these go to dissolution by the sight of the Lord of the World. (32)
By uttering "Jagannātha," one is liberated from great sins;
I shall now describe the majesty of worshipping Viṣṇu with flowers.
Therein is the description of the mountains and likewise the description of the regions, as well as the majesty of the worship of cows and other rites, and the worship of the Siddhas. ||34||
I shall now declare all the merit that arises from the gift of cooked food;
following that is the gift of the heart of a plantain tree, and after that, the gift of trees.
The gift of horses, the gift of elephants, the supreme majesty of recitation (japa), the tradition of mantra-initiation, and the characteristics of the guru. ||36||
The characteristics of a disciple have been declared as the ancient sages know them, as well as the greatness of the water from the feet and the ancestral rites (śrāddha) for the ancestors. 37.
Then follows the gift for the anniversary of the father's death, the ritual for the release of a dark-colored bull, and whatever gifts should be given during lunar and solar eclipses. (38)
The majesty of the gift of a Śālagrāma stone, of garlands and perfumes;
the piercing of the tenth by the eleventh, and the twelfth day as the day of Hari. (39)
And likewise, their own majesty, as well as that which consists of the names of Rudra and so forth, the majesty of Mathurā, and similarly that of Kurukṣetra and other such places. ||40||
Likewise, there is the narrative of Setubandha arising from Śrī Rāmeśvara, the majesty of Tryambaka, and the fruit of Pañcavaṭī. (41)
O best of the Āḍavas, listen to the majesty of the Daṇḍaka forest;
the majesty of the Daṇḍaka forest is the cause of the manifestation of Nṛsiṃha. (42)
The greatness of the Gītā and likewise of the Bhāgavata, as well as the greatness of Kālindī and the description of Indraprastha. ||43||
O best of the Vāḍavas, listen to the story of Rukmāṅgada and the greatness of Vaiṣṇava, which occurs when one eats only once a day in honor of Viṣṇu. 44.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving away the entire earth together with its oceans,
one attains that same fruit by eating even a single meal at a Vaiṣṇava temple.
Those endowed with *sattva* are known as *sāttvika*; those characterized by passion (*kāma*) are considered *rājasa*;
and the lowest are declared to be *tāmasa*. This is the defining characteristic of Vaiṣṇavas. (46)
O Nārada, I shall describe the greatness of those Brāhmaṇas who are Vaiṣṇavas and devoted solely to the Vedic dharma, exactly as it has been told. 47.
O best of sages, O most excellent one, I shall now describe in detail the sin of those who, out of greed for wealth, delight in reviling Viṣṇu. (48)
I shall now describe the narrative of Jvālāmukhī, as well as the vision on the Snowy Mountain (Himaśaila), the origin of Brahmā, and the praise by Vaiyatra regarding that sacred region.
The origin of the Kāyasthas and the exposition of Gayā, as well as the true nature of Gadādhara and the description of Phalgutīrtha. ||50||
The greatness of these very [sages], as well as that of Pādma, has been seen and likewise heard;
so too the nature of Mahābodha and the glory of Sakalki. (51)
I shall now relate the majesty of Rāmagayā, as well as that arising from Pretaśilā,
the narrative of Brahmā, and the account of the Stone.
I shall now tell you all about the account of the Brahmayoni and the banyan tree named Akṣaya, as well as the great merit that is obtained from performing a śrāddha there.
The devotion performed for Maheśvara by the high-souled Viṣṇu is still being recited today in Kāśī; indeed, the Mahārudra is free from all affliction.
Thereafter, O Nārada, I shall describe the majesty of the ocean,
as well as the merit arising from the libation of sesame seeds and the merit arising from barley.
I shall now proclaim the greatness of the libation (tarpaṇa) offered to the gods accompanied by Tulasī leaves, exactly as it was told to me by Brahmā. 56.
The greatness and the merit of the sound of the conch shell are known to be incalculable. ||57||
The greatness of Sunday, the greatness of the yoga named Viṣṇu,
as well as the greatness of Vaidhṛti and likewise of Vyatīpāta.
I shall explain all of this exactly as it was told, O Nārada:
the gift of food, the gift of clothing, and likewise the gift of land. (59)
The gift of a bed, the gift of a cow, and likewise the gift of a bull;
the majesty of Janmāṣṭamī and the majesty of the Fish [Avatāra]. ||60||
The greatness of the tortoise has thus been declared, as well as that of the Boar;
now I shall proclaim the greatness of gifts such as cows and others.
O best of divine sages, listen as I shall now describe the greatness of those few devotees who are renowned on earth, headed by Prahlāda.

O best of divine sages, [I shall describe] the greatness of keeping vigil and the fruit of offering lamps, as well as the fruit of worship performed during each of the individual watches of the night.
The narrative of Paraśurāma, as well as the slaying of Reṇukā, and the gift of land to the Brahmins which was performed by Rāma himself. 64.
I shall describe in its entirety the merit arising from Rāma’s hermitage,
as well as the narrative of the Narmadā, and likewise the merits of bathing and worship there.
The description of charity, the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the stages of life (āśramas);
the merit of the gift of gold, and likewise the gift of the Cosmic Egg (brahmāṇḍa). ||66||
The gift of the Padma Purāṇa consists of its distinct sections (khaṇḍas):
first, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and second, the Bhūmikhaṇḍa. ||67||
The third section is Svargakhaṇḍa, the fourth is known as Pātālakhaṇḍa, and the fifth is declared to be Uttarakhanda; these are indeed the sections in their proper sequence.
This Padma Purāṇa was composed by the high-souled Vyāsa for the welfare of the world and likewise for the spiritual well-being of the Brāhmaṇas. (69)

O Nārada, having heard this— which generates merit for Śūdras, destroys intense poverty, bestows liberation and happiness, grants immediate auspiciousness, and is imperishable— one should perform the gift according to the prescribed rite.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Collection of Seed-Syllables," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Maheśa and Nārada. ||1||
(2) Second Chapter. Maheśa said:
There are one hundred and twenty-five thousand mountains;
in their midst lies the supremely meritorious and excellent Badrikāśrama. ||1||
O Nārada, lord of speech, I shall here describe the true nature and the splendor of that place where the divine Nara and Nārāyaṇa reside.
O twice-born one, because of its black appearance like the peak of the Himavat mountain,
two persons reside there— both Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
One man is white and another is black;
by that path, those who have made an effort toward the Himalayas proceed.
He is of a reddish-gold and white complexion, wearing matted locks, and is the great Lord;
he is indeed Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the primordial source of the universe and the Great Master. ||5||

O you of excellent vows, there occurs a great worship during the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa) of that eternal one who has four arms, who is possessed of great glory, and who is both manifest and unmanifest.
The offerings and ritual services continue for a period of six months and so forth; at that time, it becomes enveloped in snow until the sun reaches its southern course.
Therefore, no god such as this has ever existed, nor will there ever be;
for there dwell gods there, as well as the hermitages of the ṛṣis.
The sound of the Agnihotra sacrifices and the Vedas is always heard there;
one should visit that place, which destroys ten million killings.
One should perform a bath at the confluence of the Alakanandā and the Gaṅgā;
having performed that bath there, one is indeed liberated from great sin. ||10||
O Brahman, there is no doubt that Lord Viśveśvara resides right there; on one occasion, I performed intense penance at that very spot.
Then the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the compassionate one toward his devotees,
the imperishable Puruṣa, the manifest Īśvara whose banner bears Garuḍa,
being well-pleased, said to me: "O you of excellent vows, choose a boon."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Whatever divinity you desire, I shall grant that very thing to you.
You are the sovereign of Kailāsa, Rudra himself, the protector of the universe.
Rudra said:
"Enough! O Lord Janārdana, you are well-pleased; I shall accept [this]. Grant me these two boons, whatever it is that you wish to give. (14)
"May your devotion be eternal; I shall become the king of devotees.
Then all the worlds said, "Indeed, this one is always a devotee. (15)
"By your grace, O Lord of Gods, I shall become a bestower of liberation;
there is no doubt that I will grant those worlds to those who shall worship them. (16)
I shall indeed become renowned in the world as "Viṣṇubhakta," O Lord; by the granting of this boon to him, his liberation shall be secured.
O Gohī, I am one with matted hair and smeared with ashes; in your presence, by the grace of your feet, may I become renowned in the world. (18)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Grace of Rudra," in the *Badarī-Nārāyaṇa-Māhātmya*, within the dialogue between Nārada and Umāpati, in the *Padma Mahāpurāṇa* consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(3) The Third Chapter.
Sūta said:
Once, the brahmin Nārada went to the Kāmyaka forest to see the Pāṇḍavas, who were emaciated by grief; he was honored by them according to the prescribed rites.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to that best of sages:
"O Blessed One, by what karma have we fallen into this ocean of suffering? (2)
The sage said to him: "O son of Pāṇḍu, abandon your sorrow;
in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is a collection of pleasure and pain, what man is truly happy? (3)
Even one endowed with lordship is afflicted by the accumulation of bodies;
for no embodied being is free from suffering, since they must endure it. ||4||
Because the powerful Rāhu swallows the body of the Sun, and because the head of Rāhu was covered [by the nectar] by Śauri during the drinking of the nectar of immortality. (5)
That god Śārṅgadhara was also cast into the abyss of the ocean;
he too was slain by the hero Jālandhara, and that [Jālandhara] was slain by Śambhu.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Who was that hero Jālandhara? Whose son was he, and from where did his power come? How did the Bull-bannered Lord slay Jālandhara in battle?
"O ascetic, explain all of this in detail.
Thus addressed by the king, Nārada began to relate it.
Nārada said:
Listen to the divine story of the king, which destroys the entire multitude of sins, and the most wonderful battle between Īśāna and the son of Sindhu. 9.
Once, the subduer of Pāka set out to praise Giriśa,
accompanied by hosts of Apsarases and surrounded by many gods.
That god was surrounded by Gandharvas well-versed in the three Śikṣās,
as well as Rambhā, Tilottamā, Ārāmā, Karpūrā, and Kadalī.
Dancing girls adorned with all ornaments, as well as others who were like the very essence of the god of love, arrived at the abode of the gods.
The Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Siddhas, as well as Nārada and Tumburu,
repeatedly arrived there, along with the Kinnaras and the wives of the Kinnaras.
Vāyu and Varuṇa, Kubera the giver of wealth, Yama, Agni, Nirṛti, and whatever other hosts of deities there may be; ||14||
Indra, seated upon his celestial chariot, and the gods and goddesses stationed in their own aerial vehicles, as well as the deities mounted on their respective mounts, departed swiftly for Kailāsa.
Then the gods beheld that Kailāsa, the best of mountains,
which was like an ornament for all the mountains and for the earth itself.
It bestows happiness in every way, pure, and stands like a source of all accomplishments;
there, the trees are wish-fulfilling trees and the stones grant whatever is desired. (17)
The mountain was adorned with *punnāgas*, *nāga-campakas*, *tilakas*, and *devadārus*, as well as *aśokas*, *pāṭalas*, mango trees, and *mandāras*. (18)
The winds that carry the fragrance from the surrounding forests attain a state of lameness through their constant wandering; such is the nature of those Malaya breezes. 19.
The ponds had crystal steps and were filled with deep, pure water;
their lotuses, resembling gold, were attached to stalks made of lapis lazuli.
There, the luster of white water-lilies shines in every direction;
the ponds are beautified by white lotuses and appear as if covered with rubies.
They were set with emeralds and surrounded on all sides by gomedas;
they were constructed with rubies and variegated with various minerals.
They beheld the most beautiful Kailāsa, the best of mountains, fashioned as if by one superior even to the Creator; having seen it, they were filled with great wonder.
Having descended from their celestial chariots, those gods, led by Maghavan, approached the gatekeeper and spoke these words. ||24||
O you, best among the excellent hosts, listen to my supreme words! Command quickly that [the dancer] who has come here for the sake of dance. (25)
Having heard the words of Indra regarding the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign who is surrounded by all the deities, Nandin spoke to Giriśa.
"O Lord, here has arrived Purandara, the king of the gods, accompanied by all [the hosts].
For the sake of the dance, he said to me: 'Bring the husband of Śacī quickly. (27)
Then Nandin ushered Vāsava along with them;
having seen the god Giriśa, he praised the one who has the bull as his emblem. 28.
Then all those dancers, Rambhā and the others, performed a dance with joy before Hara, accompanied by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, and other musical instruments. (29)
Taking up other musical instruments made of bell-metal, along with lutes and cymbals, they performed a dance with great excitement; and the god Purandara himself joined in.
He performed an exceedingly beautiful dance, difficult even for the gods to behold; the Lord, having attained satisfaction, spoke these words to Vāsava: ||31||
"I am pleased, O best of gods;
choose a boon," said the Lord of Gods when he had spoken thus, [to whom] [the king], proud of the strength of his own arms, [replied]. (32)
He replied to Hara with these words: "A battle has been prepared by me;
O Lord, grant me that battle wherein there shall be a warrior such as you."
Having spoken thus and obtained a boon from Lord Śambhu, Ajiṣṇu departed;
when he had gone, Śakra then spoke these words to Giriśa.
"O Gaṇas, let the words of the exceedingly arrogant King of the Gods be heard.
Having said this, Hara then became filled with anger.
Then, anger appeared in embodied form standing before him;
resembling thick darkness, it then spoke to Mṛḍa.
"Having received this command from you, what shall I do, O Lord?
Then the Lord of Umā said: "Go, conquer Vāsava."
Having reached the celestial river and the ocean, the valiant one [plunged in];
thus addressed, he dived, and those hosts were filled with wonder. (38)
When the Īśāna-kalpa had begun at the confluence of the ocean with Kāma,
the celestial river then became intoxicated by the heat of the fullness of her own youth.
Upon seeing her, the king of rivers became possessed of surging waves;
then, O lord of kings, there occurred the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. ||40||
Having reached that great river, he crossed it by his own power;
thereafter, Subhaṭa became the guardian of the ocean's shore.
O King, from that great river, a powerful son was born from the ocean;
as soon as he was born, O monarch, he was produced by the offspring of the great ocean.
The earth became resounded by the cries of his father weeping for him, and the four-faced Brahmā abandoned his meditative posture and hand-gesture. ||43||
In the meantime, having observed that the three worlds were utterly terrified,
the Creator, at the word of the lord of the Asuras, proceeded toward the great ocean.
Thinking, "This is a marvel," I mounted [the horse] and went with speed.
Seeing that Brahmā had arrived, the Ocean performed worship for him.
Then Brahmā said to him, "O wise one, why do you roar in vain? (45)
The Ocean said:
"O Lord, I am not roaring out of pride; my son is powerful, O Master of the Gods.
Yet, even for this child, protection is difficult to find, and your vision is hard to obtain."
Let this most beautiful wife of Cātana be seen;
by her husband's command, she went into the presence of Brahmā along with her son.
Placing his son on the lap of the four-faced one, he bowed at his feet;
then [he beheld] that wonderful son of the Ocean.
Upon seeing it, the Creator was indeed filled with wonder. ||48||
When the child, holding a tuft of grass in his hand, was unable to release it from the mouth of the serpent Vṛtra,
the Ocean approached laughing, taking the grass and releasing the child’s hand.
Seeing such prowess of that boy, the Self-born (Brahmā) affectionately called him Jālandhara; thus he became known by the name Jālandhara. (50)
Then Prajāpati, out of affection for Utathya, granted him a boon:
"This Jālandhara shall be invincible even by the gods. (51)
"He shall enjoy the heavens together with the netherworld by my grace.
Having said this, I, Brahmā, quickly ascended [my vehicle] and vanished.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa,
[this is] the chapter titled "The Origin of Jālandhara and the Arrival of Brahmā."
The Third Chapter. ||3||
(4) The Fourth Chapter. Nārada said:
Growing gradually during his childhood, this boy,
having fallen into the lap of the wind, ran toward the ocean.
Intent on play, he would bring young lion cubs from their lairs and make them fight with elephants such as Siṃhādika;
thus his prowess was put to the test in combat.
Therefore, having risen into the sky, he caused the sky-dwellers to fall to the earth;
with his roars, he suddenly terrified heaven and the ocean.
O King, every living being who had entered the ocean was seized by the son of the River; out of fear of him, they all became hidden.
Seeing the water devoid of living beings, the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala), out of fear of it,
abandoned its own region and entered the Himalayas.
Having gradually abandoned his childhood,
the son of the Ocean attained youth and then, by his prowess, ascended to heaven.
Once, the son of Sindhu laughed at his father and said: "Father, grant me a very vast place suitable for my residence."
Having understood the words of his son, the great ocean spoke: "O son, I shall give you a kingdom that is difficult to obtain on earth."
Immediately thereafter, Bhārgava, the preceptor of the Daityas, went to the ocean;
seeing that he had arrived, the sea honored him according to the prescribed rites. (9)
Then, seated upon that throne which had been offered by the Lord of Men (Indra) and which was radiant with hundreds of jewels emerging from its splendor,
he slightly surpassed the beauty of the lotus-born Brahmā, who resides on a beautiful peak of Mount Sumeru, the mountain of lovely luster.
Having joined his palms in reverence, the Ocean addressed the poet:
"By good fortune you have come here; tell me, what may I do for you? (11)
Then the sage Kavi, the preceptor of the Daitya clan, said to that ocean:
"Of what use is he who has been born, having robbed his mother of her youth? (12)
Just as the banner atop a grain stalk grows upward by its own nature, so shall your son certainly enjoy the three worlds through his valor. (13)
Jambūdvīpa is a great seat (pīṭha) frequented by hosts of yoginīs;
it has now been flooded by you—release the abode of Jālandhara! 14.
"O Mahārṇava, bestow this kingdom upon him;
for while staying there, he shall be both unconquerable and unslayable. (15)
Thus addressed with affection by Bhārgava, Arṇava then sportingly drew back,
and out of love for his son, he revealed dry land within the water.
The meritorious region of Jālandhara, renowned by that very name, is one hundred yojanas in width and three hundred in length. 17.
Having summoned the best of the Daityas, the Ocean spoke to him:
"Build a city in the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara, specifically for Kurujālandhara."
Thus addressed by the Bodhisattva, Tuṣita created a city made of jewels, complete with walls, gate-towers, gates, staircases, houses, and floors. (19)
There, peacocks standing in their dancing postures upon the floors of palaces inlaid with sapphires mistook them for the gathering of clouds.
Where the rays rising from palaces of coral and rubies are to be enjoyed by birds, and where the mango trees are beautiful with their sweet songs. (21)
Wherever they were in the palaces, the timid peacocks, seeing those splendors which resembled fires, fled in all directions as if into a forest conflagration.
Where the quarters of the sky, mingled with the light emanating from the crystal pavilions, shine like the ocean with its foam tossed up by Mount Mandara.
In their own palaces, established in the light of dawn,
the women turned their faces— resembling the full moon— toward the direction of the chariot.
Where the women, delighted by the groves and gardens of indranīla-blue lotuses,
would enter their hearts with a fever of enchantment.
When people behold the amorous dalliance of others depicted in paintings,
they surely redouble their own efforts toward their own beloveds.
Where the streaks of incense smoke wafting from the windows made the sky resemble the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī. ||27||
There, the entire sky shone as if filled with rainbows, due to the light arising from many houses,
like high autumn clouds.
There, at midday, the horses of the sun, exhausted by their incessant wandering, come to rest while stationed upon the summit of the palace.
In whatever mansions they dwelt, wearing garlands of jasmine,
those excellent women shone at night like the sky filled with stars.
Where the sound produced by the friction of the swings against the golden peaks made the earth clearly manifest as the very ground of Mount Meru.
Together with the rivers and his son Uśanas, the Ocean performed an ablution there, using musical instruments in the form of his own roars.

She whom the Self-Existent Lord himself proclaimed at the great festival of his universal sovereignty after his victory over Tāraka; she who was the consort of that Lord of Śacī, whom even Bṛhaspati praised.
With those words, which are like the variegated lotus-faces of swans upon a lake, we pray that this earth may celebrate the festive occasion of her marriage at this time. 33.
The Great Ocean gave to his son Jālandhara a formidable army of a thousand great padmas, born from his own belly.
Śukra, the son of Jālandhara,
also affectionately gave him his own lore named Mṛtasañjīvanī, an illusion that deludes even Rudra.
The science of weapons and missiles, as well as other sciences, were taught according to the prescribed rites to the Son of the Ocean;
furthermore, everything else was then explained to him by the Sage.
Then, having consecrated his son Jālandhara, the Ocean departed for his own abode in a divine body, surrounded by rivers. (37)
Having beheld the divine city of Ājālandhara, adorned with gate-towers,
he wandered about together with Śukra, highly honored by throngs of twice-born brahmins.
At that time, the exceedingly powerful Daityas dwelling in Pātāla,
all led by Kālanemi, arrived at Jālandhara.
Then they appointed that heroic and mighty Daitya, whose body was as radiant as the ocean of milk, as his general.
Having brought his own power under his control and having made the waters stable upon the earth, he then ruled the kingdom bestowed by his father, Jālandhara. (41)
In the meantime, there was formerly a certain Apsaras named Svarṇā in heaven; by the grace of Krauñca, she had a daughter named Vṛndā. 42.
The various individual beauties that were created separately by Dhātṛ, joined together and united,
were fashioned into the body of Vṛndā so that they might be seen all at once.
He gave that most beautiful woman Vṛndā, who deludes all people with her song,
to Śukra when he requested her for the sake of his son Ājālandhara.
Śukra said:
"O timid one, by this wondrous form which is a weapon that blinds the eyes of the world with pride, may you become long-lived and happy. (45)
Having himself created him, his mind filled with wonder,
the Creator placed upon him the pinnacle of his own labor in the essence of beauty.
What man do women regard as pride when he is not seen, for he is the ultimate limit of all that is worthy of being beheld?
Obtain that husband, the long-eyed warrior. ||46||
O King, the son of the Ocean married Gāndharvī according to the gāndharva rite;
he became her husband, bringing joy to the people within the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Having abandoned his fickle nature, even Jālandhara,
though engaged in mature duties, did not desire another's wife.
Once, while seated in the assembly, having seen Rāhu with his head severed, he asked Bhārgava: "Why is this one left with only half a body? (49)
Satyaka related from the beginning that past event,
just as the ocean of milk had been churned by the gods for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
Having heard those words, the asura Jālandhara was struck with wonder and said: "O Rāhu, you who can assume any form at will, now be gracious and look upon me with a favorable countenance. (51)
Thus, by means of the mantra of Śukra, the powerful son of Sindhu,
remembering his paternal uncle, engaged in battle with the gods.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa,
in the dialogue between Nārada and Yudhiṣṭhira, in the narrative of Jālandhara,
[this is] the section titled "The Marriage of Vṛndā and the Coronation of Jālandhara."
The Fourth Chapter ॥4॥
(5) The Fifth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Who was the paternal uncle of the son of Sindhu, and what occurred during his conflict? How did that Daitya fight? O Nārada, tell me that.
Nārada said:
Listen, O tiger among kings; the Ocean of Milk was your paternal uncle.
That wealth was recovered by the gods after churning Jālandhara.
Previously, that [king] had been attacked by gods and asuras beginning with Śrīcandra, Amṛta, Nāga, and Aśva;
having heard of that, the asura Jālandhara waged war against the gods.
Once, the powerful one dispatched his messenger Durvāraṇa toward the abode of the Lord of the Gods, having instructed him that he must speak exactly as told.
Then, having mounted his excellent elephant, he went toward heaven;
desiring to enter the celestial abode, he was stopped at the gate by the gatekeepers.
The messenger said:
"O Śakra, I am the messenger of Jālandhara, arrived in your presence; having gone there, you ought to inform him of my arrival."
Having heard these words of his, the messenger went at that very moment to the Lord of Śacī, prostrated himself, and said: "O God, a messenger has arrived from the earth."
The gatekeeper, having been answered thus by Mahendra, said, "Bring the messenger.
Seizing that messenger by the hand, he brought him into the presence of Vāsava.
Having entered the city of Durvāraṇa,
he beheld Hari surrounded by thirty-three crores of gods.
A divine golden lion-throne, fanned by the breeze of chowries,
with a thousand lotus-eyes blossoming from the nectar of Śacī’s love.
Then Durvāraṇa, beholding the Lord of the Gods together with his preceptor,
bowed down while laughing out of self-conceit at the beauty of [the Lord's] eyes.
Having been assigned a seat, he [the messenger] should practice Jālandhara-bandha;
then Hari should say to him: "Who are you, and for what purpose have you come? (12)
"I am the messenger of Jālandhara," he said to Purandara;
"let the king, who rules over all the worlds, hear his command from my mouth. (13)
By you, the ocean of milk that nourishes my paternal uncles has been suddenly churned by means of Mount Mandara; thus, the treasury of great wealth has been seized. (14)
O Purandara, quickly abandon all that belongs to embodied beings—such as the moon, nectar, serpents, horses, their jewels, coral, and so forth—as well as heaven itself. 15.
O King, at my word, quickly perform everything as is appropriate;
beg his forgiveness if you wish to live. (16)
Then Indra, laughing, spoke to Durvāraṇa:
"Listen, O messenger, to the cause of the churning of the ocean in brief. (17)
Formerly, the son of Himavat named Maināka, the enemy of the gods,
was held within his belly by that ocean and by the dull-witted Jaḍa.
By that fire, which took the form of a horse, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings was consumed;
yet even he was held back by that evil-minded ocean.
This lord, the refuge of the Dānavas who hate the Dharma,
constantly bestows curd, ghee, and milk upon the Dānavas.
For this very reason, he was agitated by us with irresistible force,
punished, and stripped of his splendor by the ancient gods.
"Listen, messenger: this man has been withered by my brahmin [Agastya];
moreover, why is he being tormented by this very evil association? (22)
He too, surrounded by our entire army, will come for the sake of battle; indeed, he shall meet his destruction through destiny alone.

Having spoken thus, the slayer of Vṛtra ceased his loud address to the messenger of the son of the Lord of Rivers; and that messenger, having returned, reported everything exactly as it had been said by the Lord of the Gods to the son of the Ocean from the very beginning.
Nārada said:
Having heard the words of Mahendra through the mouth of his own messenger,
the son of the Ocean, filled with rage, summoned his entire army.
By Jālandhara’s command, the Daityas dwelling in the subterranean realm (rasātala) and those residing on the surface of the earth arrived there with their armies. 26.
O King, at the commencement of the son of Sindhu’s march, the heavens, the netherworld, and all the directions burst asunder with the roars of his army.
With faces like those of horses, elephants, camels, and cats, they were terrifying;
with faces like tigers, lions, and mice, their eyes resembled flashes of lightning. ||28||
Some with serpent-like hair and massive bodies have the fur of swords;
others run about, roaring with the sound of rain-clouds. (29)

O King of Kings, at that time you shattered the entire army—which was crowded with chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry; which provided the diversion of battle; which was radiant; and which was led by hundreds of thousands of millions of lotuses.
A celestial mansion a hundred yojanas in extent, joined with ten million [beings], possessing a flood of thousands of splendors, and filled with every object. ||31||
Having ascended that celestial chariot, he immediately departed for Jālandhara;
on the first day, accompanied by his forces, he reached Mount Mandara at midday.
On the second day, having been jolted by the carriers of the palanquin and crushed by many camels, he reached Mount Meru accompanied by his army.
In Ilāvṛta, however, that great mountain ridge stood firm;
meanwhile, the forest of Nandana and Khāṇḍava was destroyed by the lords of the Daityas.
The peaks of Mount Meru, shattered by the bodies of the Dānavas,
were fashioned into swings tied to the Santānaka trees.
The Siddhas, together with their hosts, drove away the malevolent Daityas with the fragrance of their breasts, camphor, betel, sandalwood, agallochum, and ornaments.
The river of Mount Meru was filled with flowers fallen from their masses of hair,
and the eastern quarter of Sumeru was struck by his elephants.
They moved through the south with their attendants, the north, and the west with their soldiers;
then the Asura Jāladhara dispatched the Daityas.
And on another day, with the sounds of their drums, they went to the peak of Mount Mahendra,
having broken through the cities of Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa.
They went to Amarāvatī from the presence of the other world-protectors;
then, portents occurred in the heavens, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
A thick dust fell and a mass of darkness spread;
then the thunderbolt of Indra, the wielder of the vajra, became lusterless.
Seeing these omens that portended fear, Mahendra spoke thus to his preceptor:
"What shall we do? To whom shall we go for refuge? Behold, the battle is at hand."
Then Vācaspati spoke these words to the lord of the gods:
"Seek refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha."
Having been addressed thus by the preceptor, Indra, together with the gods, quickly went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha for refuge to the enemy of Kaiṭabha.
Śaśin, the protector of the gateway to victory for Vāsudeva, [spoke];
all the gods, terrified by the fear of Jālandhara, had assembled there. ||45||
Śrī said:
"O Lord, your brother should not be slain; he is fighting for the sake of the gods.
Bound by my oath out of affection for me, O God, he shall not be subject to death."
Having heard these words of Śrī, Viṣṇu, the protector of the three worlds, then mounted Garuḍa, who covered the sky with the flapping of his wings. 47.
Then Hari, having quickly emerged from the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, beheld the gods who were terrified by the fear of Jālandhara and had lost their luster. 48.
All those gods beheld Hari, resembling a dense cloud, with his four arms adorned with the Śārṅga bow, the conch, the mace, and the lotus. 49.
Having recited this hymn before the Lord of Rivers, Indra said:
"The celestial realm has been shattered by my son Jālandhara."
Having heard those words of Indra and having granted fearlessness to the inhabitants of heaven,
the Destroyer of the Asuras set out with the gods to conquer the Asura.
Then, having mounted the chariot brought by Mātali, Vāsava,
holding his thunderbolt, set forth in front of Vāsudeva.
All the gods came from the left, and he approached from the right;
Agni, the beloved of Svāhā, stood on the south, mounted upon his ram.
Then the son of Śakra, having mounted the elephant Airāvata,
and Indra, having mounted Uccaiḥśravas, both stood before the Blessed One.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśa, Mitra, Varuṇa, and likewise Bhaga;
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth. ||55||
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, Urejet, Dhanya, and Jaghanyaja—these are the twelve Ādityas who stand before Indra. (56)
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly renowned Giriśa; Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita. ||57||
O Lord of the people, Bhuvanādhīśvara, Kapālī, Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhaga—these are remembered as the eleven Rudras. (58)
Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, Māruta, Prāṇa, Apāna, and Sajīva—these eight Maruts were before him. (59)
Vivasvān, his father, also went there in the midst of them with twelve forms;
and Dhanada, mounted upon a palanquin—did the lord of men go forth at that time? (60)
The Rudras, mounted upon bulls, and the Maruts, with deer as their vehicles,
went at the front of the army, armed with tridents and iron clubs.
Gandharvas, cāraṇas, yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, and guhyakas—all bearing weapons—went at the front of the entire army. ||62||
When the enemy troops had occupied the front, rear, and flanks,
Hari, the lord of the earth, assumed the form of a boar and entered that place.
Having returned from heaven with great speed, desiring to slay the army of the Daityas,
the northern region of Mount Sumeru was occupied by the host of the gods.
Causing the burden of the army to arise, he stood at Jalandhara,
quickly taking his position on the southern side of Kanakaśṛṅga.
Within this Nīlavṛta, which is traversed in a single day and night,
the field of battle is established between Mount Meru and Mount Mandara.
Thereupon, filled with joy, those Dānavas quickly went to the ground called Ātmajayā, as described by Kavi; the gods went to the place described by Guru.
Surrounded by preeminent chariot-warriors, by elephants resembling clouds with streams of flowing ichor,
by countless horses swift as Garuḍas, and by foot-soldiers, the earth shone resplendent with Sāraṇa.
Then there arose the sound of musical instruments from both armies,
along with the clamor of heroes shouting at one another.
Then a terrifying battle took place between the Dānavas and the gods,
with the crushing clash of the entire army like the destruction of the three worlds.
Overcome by fear and greatly exhausted, she lamented repeatedly with cries devoid of her usual voice and form;
at that time, [the field] was completely filled with arrows.
Shaking her garment of moving clouds, she illuminated the sky with her mass of hair;
out of terror, she cried out intensely at the fierce shrieks of the birds.
Commanded then by the Lord of the Gods, the clouds beginning with Saṃvartaka mounted upon elephants and fought the Asuras in battle.
The horse-riders among the gods became Gandharvas and Kinnaras;
the chariot-warriors became Sādhyas and Siddhas; and the elephant-riders became Yakṣas and Cāraṇas. ||74||
Are these foot-soldiers men, or are they serpents that feed on air?
O King, the lord of diseases, consumption, has become the leader of Yama himself.
There, a most terrible battle took place between the Dānavas and the diseases;
afflicted by ailments such as colic and fever, the Daityas fell and rolled upon the ground.
Struck down by the Dānavas, the diseases fell upon the front lines of the battle;
some fled toward the mountains.
Herbs such as the Vaiśalyakaraṇī, which were born together with them, rendered those in the armies free from arrows; thus, they fought without regard for Yama.
All the foot soldiers were struck down by the Dānavas with arrows, mallets,
and spears, as well as by groups of infantrymen using sharp swords and battle-axes.
By the tens of millions, they struck one another, their bodies crimson with blood;
then, mounted on swift horses, they leaped into the sky.
Embracing one another, they struck each other, their bodies crimson with blood;
a terrifying mass of charioteers covered the earth with floods of chariots.
They pierced the great chariot-warriors with sharp arrows released from their bows,
just as one might firmly bind cows with temples drained of rut-fluid by using their own horns.
Enraged rival elephants threw down other elephants upon the surface of the earth;
the furious Daitya, lifting his chariot with both arms, rose up and ascended into the sky.
He struck down the horse-riders, horses, and elephants to the ground;
then, seizing him by the shoulder, he swiftly rushed toward Jālandhara.
Seizing two by the armpits, a third by the belly,
and a fourth by the head, someone ran toward the forest.
Drawing his sword from its scabbard and brandishing that stainless,
excellent blade, the asura went forth, felling thousands of gods in battle.
A certain slender celestial woman with full breasts, wearing a fine garment,
quickly came from the sky and led the Daitya away from the midst of the battle.
Then, having bound that army of the gods— its faces bitten by dogs and pinned with sharp iron arrows— Kālanemi danced.
Then Janārdana, filled with rage, went forth against Kālanemi;
as Yama [goes] against the irresistible hero Durvāraṇa, and Svarbhānu against the Moon and the Sun.
The god Vaiśvānara went toward Ketu, Bṛhaspati toward Śukra,
and the two Aśvins went there toward the Saṃyatas and Daitya-maṅgāraparṇaka.
Śakraputra went against Saṃhrāda, Dhanada against Nirhrāda,
Niśumbha was surrounded by the Rudras, and Śumbha by the Vasus in the battle.
The Viśvedevas approached that which stood in the form of a cloud;
the winds went toward him whose hair was like thunderbolts, and then Death went toward him who was composed of illusion.
Vāsava, with a spear in hand, rushed impetuously toward Namuci;
the Daityas were likewise surrounded by other gods, each equal to himself in prowess.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Battle between the Gods and the Dānavas," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
(6) The Sixth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Thus, when many such duels had commenced,
the enraged Hari then struck Kālanemi with his mace.
Having overcome his swoon, he struck Viṣṇu with arrows after reflecting;
then, by the enraged Hari, he was struck down lifeless upon the earth.
O King, having reflected, the Moon struck Rāhu with his sword;
but Rāhu, abandoning him, then fled toward the Sun. ||3||
Having defeated the thousand-rayed sun in battle, Rāhu pursued the moon;
however, the lord of the night struck him with his sword in the conflict.
Then, because of the hardness of his arm, the sword of Saiṃhikeya turned to powder;
the tormentor struck Viṣṇu deeply with his hard fist.
In that great battle, the Moon was lifted up and held by the throat with force;
though swallowed by Rāhu, the Moon was then vomited out once again.
Placing the deer, his own emblem, upon his chest, he released it; then, seizing the jewel among horses, Uccaiḥśravas, he departed like the moon.
Having brought Jālandhara before him, he presented him with devotion;
but Durvāraṇa, enraged in battle, struck that Yama with his mace.
Pierced in battle by the son of Śakra with sharp arrows,
Saṃhrāda seized Jaya— who had fainted from the blow of the iron club— and carried him away.
Having mounted Airāvata,
he went toward Jālandhara and struck Nihrāda with his mace in the battle.
The Rudras struck Niśumbha with force using the blows of their tridents,
and Niśumbha, in turn, greatly oppressed them with a multitude of arrows.
Then, having bound Mṛtyu—who was composed of illusion—with iron nooses, he brought him under his control; meanwhile, he filled the hosts of radiant gods with his arrows. 12.
He gave it to Jālandhara, he to Pauloma, and he also to Sindhu;
let the world, cast into the mouth of the ocean, live free from fear.
Having bound Vāmana with nooses, even Vāsava led him to the netherworld (rasātala);
I, however, went to rescue the universe, and then Jālandhara advanced.
Then, O King, a most terrible battle took place between Indra and Bala;
with his power, he illuminated the ten directions like the sun with its rays. (15)
All the weapons of Śakra and Aṅgabaḷa were shattered;
the powerful Indra was struck in the heart by the mallet of Bala.
Then Indra roared a terrible roar; hearing that, the Lord with his army laughed.
As he laughed, pearls issued forth from his mouth. 17.
Then, out of a desire to seize her, he engaged in battle;
Vāsava praised that Bala, an ocean of strength, exceedingly.
"O best of gods, choose a boon," being thus addressed, he spoke to Bala:
"If you are pleased, O lord of the Daityas, you ought to give me your own body. (19)
Having heard those words of Indra, he said to Bala: "Pierce [the door] with weapons and take me! He also asked: "What is there that cannot be given by the high-souled? (20)
Like a garland of flowers upon others, the prosperity of a miser is fruitless—like speech for one deprived of ears, or like a fickle-eyed woman for one who is blind. (1)
For great-souled men do not seize even their equals, let alone their enemies;
rivers carry their rival streams to the ocean, but never to the sea.
A virtuous person, devoted to the welfare of others, does not undergo extreme transformation even at the time of destruction;
even when cut down, the sandalwood tree perfumes the blade of the axe.
O King, even as your body perishes, your splendor does not perish; it has been offered to the virtuous.
Indeed, that very same digit which rests upon the head of Śiva remains for me. 4.
"Those virtuous ones have become the crowns of the world's circle who demonstrate goodness even toward those who have done them no favor;
who, for the sake of their own purpose, have had their bodies mangled by those who previously wronged them, yet remain devoted even to their enemies.
Having said "So be it," the thousand-eyed Indra struck Bala with his mallet.
Then Indra, his body pierced by the thunderbolt, fell into deep anxiety.
Reminded by Mātali, he struck Mount Aṅga with his thunderbolt;
by that blow of the thunderbolt, Mount Aṅga was shattered to pieces. ||21||
One portion fell upon Mount Tuṣapātaka in Bālāṅga,
a second upon the Snowy Mountain (Himavat), and the third upon Mount Goṇa.
The fourth fell at Devanadī, the fifth likewise at Mandara;
the sixth, Vajrākara, and the seventh was Vijaya-gaja.
Through his perfectly pure karma, all the limbs of that one who is pure by birth have become seeds of jewels. (24)
From his adamantine bones were scattered hexagonal gems;
from his two eyes came sapphires, and from his ears, rubies.
From his blood there arose rubies, from his fat emeralds, from his tongue corals, and from his teeth pearls. (26)
Emerald (*marakata*) arose from his marrow, and the *gārutmata* gem from his nose; bronze was his excrement, silver his semen, and copper was born from his urine.
From the rubbing of the syllable *aṃ* on the head, the Brahmavītikas were born;
from the resonance (*nāda*), the exceedingly beautiful gem vaidūrya was produced. ||28||
From his nails gold was produced; from his blood, coral arose;
crystal was born from his fat; and ruby originated from his flesh.
The jewels produced from the body of Balarāma were upon the surface of the earth;
they were to be enjoyed by pure people through the attainment of an accumulation of merit.
In the meantime, having heard that the army was being struck down in battle by Maghavan,
Queen Prabhāvatī went to his side.
Seeing her husband with his limbs scattered in battle,
Prabhāvatī, her eyes filled with tears, her hair disheveled, and her breasts heaving, wailed aloud.
O Lord of Hānātha, you who possess great strength and valor, and who are dear to the world as its very body—why have you abandoned me here and departed for the state of absolute liberation? (33)
Seeing that this body is pervaded by old age, leprosy, and other ailments, embodied beings do not abandon it; yet you have abandoned this body in vain—what other [body] could there possibly be? (34)
O beloved, with your divine body eager for battle, you shall adorn my necklace, which was once woven into my braid. (35)
"O dear one, untie her yourself, for she is afflicted by the sorrow of widowhood.
Seeing Queen Bālā lamenting thus, the son of the Ocean (Vāli), being pained, spoke to Śukra: "O Bhārgava, bring Bāla back to life! (36)
Śukra said:
"How can I restore to life one who has attained death by his own will?
Nevertheless, through the power of mantras, he shall utter speech."
Jālandhara said:
"O Bhārgava, I wish to hear the words of Bala.
Having been addressed thus by Jālandhara, he became absorbed in meditation for a moment. (38)
Then there arose from her mouth a sound, enchanting to the ear, clearly manifesting toward Prabhāvatī as if it had issued from a musical instrument. (39)
"O Prabhāvatī, manifest your own body and lead me to absorption within its limbs.
Having heard these words of his, the river was born as Prabhāvatī. (40)
The river flowing to the east of Sumeru is merged within the very limbs of his body;
by its water, the supreme luster of jewels is produced.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Ascent of the Daitya Bala to Heaven," in the Jālandhara episode of the Uttara-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(7) The Seventh Chapter.
Nārada said:
Then Jāladhara, filled with rage, said to that slayer of demons:
"O lowest of the strong, having slain Bala through deceit, where will you go? (1)
Having spoken thus to that performer of a hundred sacrifices, the powerful son of Sindhu covered him—
along with his charioteer, horses, banner, and chariot— with his arrows.
Wounded by arrows, Śakra fell unconscious upon his chariot;
seeing Śakra fallen, the son of the Ocean roared.
Abandoning his faint, Indra released the thunderbolt toward Jālandhara;
then the Ocean-born [Kṛṣṇa], seizing that mountain-shattering weapon in his hand, [struck him].
Holding the vajra in his armpit, the lord of the daityas quickly descended from his chariot and rushed toward the lord of the gods in battle to seize him.
Then, abandoning his chariot while remembering Hari,
the son of the Ocean, intoxicated with pride, fled toward the chariot of Indra.
Having made Tāra his charioteer, he whose desires were fulfilled swiftly drove Indra’s chariot against the forces of Yātudhāna and Yātu.
Jālandhara, whose arms were like great pillars, himself became as formidable as a cloud;
then Puruṣottama, filled with wrath, himself raised his sword and struck Daka in battle.
Having dispatched Garuḍa, who is as swift as thought, he struck the army of the Daityas in his wrath;
by his power, he brought down chariots, horses, elephants, and throngs of foot-soldiers by the thousands.
Janārdana, surrounded by the sons of Kaśyapa, wrought a terrifying carnage in battle—
a river flowing with floods of hair, bones, marrow, and blood, frequented by Piśācas and Vetālas.
[He saw] that river filled with the weapons and missiles of the enemy, exceedingly difficult to cross, infested by tigers and lordly elephants;
it was crimson, adorned with severed heads and maces, possessing a beauty that was a festival for the rolling eyes, and clothed in garments. (11)
Seeing the army of the Dānavas struck down by Viṣṇu, all the sons of Gavākṣa,
by the command of Jālandhara, surrounded Hari on all sides.
There, the Daityas rained down floods of arrows, like clouds upon Mount Arbuda,
as bees swarm a lotus or as rain-clouds fall upon a mountain.
Just as a flock of birds leaves the mango tree, so too the mass of incense vanished from the sky;
at that moment, Viṣṇu was no longer seen amidst the tumultuous roar of Garuḍa.
Mounted upon all kinds of chariots and armed with every weapon, the great asuras struck the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha while roaring with terrifying sounds.
Then the enemy of the Daityas, enraged and assuming a terrifying form, struck them all down in battle,
just as the wind scatters a heap of leaves.
Then the Daitya Śailaroma rushed at Viṣṇu in a fit of rage;
even the arrows of Hari were shattered upon his body. (17)
Hari struck the body of the Daitya Śailaromā with arrows;
then, brandishing his sword, he severed his head.
When the head of the Daitya was severed, his headless trunk, with mountain-like hair and arms, seized Garuḍa by the two wings as he displayed his prowess in battle.
Then his head, having flown up with great speed, became firmly stuck between the two shoulders;
at that, Hṛṣīkeśa was also struck with wonder by this wrestling match.
Seeing his head attached [to the body], Garuḍa fell to the ground; then, springing up again with speed, he returned to the place where the head was. ||21||
Then the powerful Śailaroma snatched Viṣṇu from Garuḍa; Hari struck him with his palm, and he, his life-span exhausted, fell to the earth.
Then Jālandhara said to his charioteer Khaḍgaroman:
"Drive the chariot to that place where the Lord Janārdana is."
At the word of Jālandhara, Khaṅgaroman brought forth a chariot;
seeing Viṣṇu before him, the son of the Ocean spoke.
"O Niḥśaṅka, abandon this [weapon]; O Viṣṇu, I shall not kill you, O Mādhava!
Having heard those words of his, he (Viṣṇu) became enraged, his eyes bloodshot with anger.
Nārāyaṇa covered him with life-taking arrows,
and the powerful son of the Ocean, pierced by Viṣṇu, [fought back].
He incessantly filled Hari with a flood of arrows;
Nārāyaṇa, for his part, covered him with life-taking shafts.
Seeing Garuḍa fallen to the earth by the arrows of the son of Sindhu,
Janārdana called to mind his chariot situated in Vaikuṇṭha.
His charioteer arrived, accompanied by horses devoid of a driver;
seeing the chariot joined with horses, the Blessed One was struck with wonder in the battle.
Having awakened Garuḍa, he appointed him to the office of charioteer;
he placed the crown upon his head and the Kaustubha jewel as an ornament upon his heart.
Having made the goals of human endeavor his horses, Hari went to Jālandhara;
together with the asuras, he tore the earth apart with the wheel of his chariot.
Commanded by the King of the Gods in the midst of the host of battles, Vītihotra swiftly struck the army of the Dānavas with his arrows.
Accompanied by the wind, it consumed the host of Dānavas;
then that army of Daityas was struck down by the Blessed One along with the gods.
Seeing his own army reduced to a mere remnant, Jālandhara then said to Bhārgava: "O King, my army has been slaughtered by the gods. (34)
While you remain thus, you are renowned as a knower of mantras through your learning;
O Brahmin, what is the use of that learning, or of kṣatriya power, or even of strength? (35)
Hearing Jālandhara’s words, Bhārgava spoke to him regarding those who had sought refuge, who were weak, afflicted by disease, and deprived of their vehicles.
"Behold, O King, the power of this Brāhmaṇa in the midst of the host of warriors!
Having said this, they were touched with water and awakened by the sound "Huṃ."
Upropped by the floods of his arrows which destroyed the enemy and snatched away their lives,
those gods fell together with the son of Sindhu as he was being struck down.

O lord of men, O best of beings, though their bodies were shattered by arrows and they were pierced by shafts, they did not die because they retained their vital breaths and possessed immortality. (39)
Then the god Nārāyaṇa spoke to Bṛhaspati:
"Fie upon your power, O teacher of the gods, that you do not restore the asuras to life!"
Then Dhiṣaṇa spoke quickly to the Lord of the World:
"O Master, I shall restore these gods to life by means of medicinal herbs. (41)
Having spoken thus, Adhiṣaṇa also departed for Mount Droṇa situated in the Ocean of Milk;
having arrived there, he himself easily gathered the medicinal herbs.
And by means of yoga, the Guru restored those ageless ones to life;
then, having risen, the gods struck down the army of the Dānavas.
Seeing the gods risen up, the son of Sindhu spoke to the poet: "Without your science, how have these [gods] arisen through poetry? (44)
Having heard these words spoken by the Daitya, Śukra said to the son of the Ocean:
"In the midst of the Milk Ocean stands a great mountain named Droṇa. (45)
There the medicinal herbs abide, bringing life to those who are not immortal.
Having gone there, the preceptor of the asuras seized that collection of herbs.
