Having heard the words spoken by Bhārgava, the one of great strength raised from the battlefield the gods who had been struck down by means of mantras, [taking up] the burden of the army.
Then, having swiftly cast Jalandhara into the ocean,
he entered the milk-ocean and reached a divine abode of great splendor.
Entering there, he beheld the pleasure-ground of the Ocean of Milk,
where the wind was neither hot nor cold, and where no darkness was seen.
Where excellent women—endowed with the weight of full breasts, slender waists, and beautiful teeth—sing, dance, and sport. (50)
By the casting of glances with playful movements of the eyes, by the turning of her face, by her enchanting and lovely limbs, and by the swaying of her creeper-like arms; ||51||
With the sweet sounds of the placement of their feet and with hymns of speech.
With garments that bestowed fragrance and comfort, and which caused the bees of her eyes to hum; ||52||
Having gone there, the playful women performed service for the Son of the Ocean with the graceful swinging of chowries, with garlands, and with smiles and glances. (53)
Beholding that milky ocean playing there, he, eager for battle,
then prostrated himself and said to the Ocean of Milk: "O Father,
flood the mountains of Droṇa with the medicinal herbs under the pretext of waves."
The Ocean of Milk said:
"How can I drown with my waves that one who has come to me for refuge?
O lords of sages, those who abandon one who has sought their protection do not attain liberation."
Having heard his uncle's words, the king of the Daityas, out of intense anger, struck Mount Saṃkata with a blow from his palm.
Then, O King, Droṇa, being greatly afraid of Jālandhara,
approached Jālandhara in a disguised form and spoke to him.
I was once your slave; protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
O mighty-armed one, by your command I shall go to the netherworld (rasātala).
"O Lord, I shall remain as long as you rule the kingdom, [enduring] the sound of medicinal herbs and the weeping of the perfected ones (siddhas). (59)
While the son of the Ocean looked on, the mountain went to Rasātala;
then the hero Jālandhara entered the great battle.
Having mounted the chariot prepared beforehand, he went toward Keśava who was standing in the chariot;
seeing Mādhava standing in the chariot, the son of the River laughed aloud. (61)
"Stay right here, O Śakaṭa, until I have slain the enemy Marīs!
Having spoken thus, he quickly struck that divine army with his arrows.
The gods, pierced by arrows, cried out, "Save us! to Bṛhaspati;
thereupon, Bṛhaspati quickly went to the Ocean of Milk.
O King, not seeing Droṇa there, [Dharma] became lost in thought;
then Bṛhaspati, having quickly returned to the forest, spoke to the immortals.
"Fly away, all you gods! Mount Drona has met his destruction.
As his preceptor was speaking thus, the son of the Ocean [Bhīṣma] cut off his head.
Laughing at the gods with his sharp arrows, he cut off their sacrificial threads and hair;
then the Guru, afflicted by the fear for his life, fled away with great speed.
O King, having abandoned their armor, all the gods fled;
thus, having routed the gods, he indeed rushed toward Janārdana.
Hṛṣīkeśa also pursued the lord of the Daityas, eager for battle;
then a terrible combat ensued between Viṣṇu and Jālandhara.
The invincible one flooded Keśava with nets of arrows;
the great one, having cut those arrows into pieces, filled [the air] with his own shafts.
Vāsudeva afflicted the asura Jālandhara with arrows;
Jālandhara, his body tormented by the shafts, abandoned his chariot.
Then he rushed swiftly toward Viṣṇu, who was stationed on Saṃyati;
seeing him approaching in battle, Hari pierced him with arrows.
Then that son of Bāṇa reached the presence of Viṣṇu, who had the Garuḍa-banner;
with one hand he seized Garuḍa, and with the second he struck Hari.
Having whirled him around, the Lord of Birds cast him down upon Śvetadvīpa;
Garuḍa, too, who had been hurled by Jālandhara, fell there as well.
There, on Krauñcadvīpa, Acyuta took rest for a long time; then he descended from that revolving orb of a chariot as it wandered.
Having come to the battlefield, the lord of the Daityas, seeing Keśava who was fond of combat, spoke again, saying, "Stay! Stay! ||75||
Covering the earth with his arrows, the son of the ocean roared.
Hari swiftly pierced the Daitya with a dart that quivered in his heart; he then fell down.
As the charioteer was leading him away from the battle, [the Daitya] struck him, saying: "I have been rendered shameless by this one blow."
Then a great battle took place between the enemy of the Daityas (Viṣṇu) and Jālandhara, both standing upon the surface of the earth.
Out of love for Lakṣmī, Hari did not slay that Dānava himself; instead, he fell [unconscious] from his own arrows.
Then, seeing Govinda fallen upon the surface of the earth,
the Daitya took him up and ascended his own chariot, which was as swift as the waters of the ocean.
Thereupon, having reached that [chariot], Viṣṇu’s beloved wife wept aloud.
Beholding her husband, the lotus-eyed one who had been seated upon the expanse of lotuses,
now fallen into the fire, Lakṣmī spoke to the son of the Ocean.
Listen to my words, brother: Viṣṇu has been conquered by you. O one of great strength, it is not fitting for you to grant widowhood to your sister. (81)
Having heard his words, the mighty-armed Jālandhara released the Lord of the World and bowed down out of devotion to his sister. (82)
Then, out of affection for his sister, Viṣṇu touched her feet with his own hands;
pleased by her deed, Viṣṇu said to Jālandhara, "O Lord of Daityas, I am satisfied; choose a boon—what excellent boon shall I grant you? (83)
Jālandhara said:
"O Keśava, if you are pleased with this valor of mine,
you must remain in my father's abode together with Kamalā."
Having said "So be it" and called Garuḍa to mind, the upholder of the earth,
the Lord of the World, mounted [him] and went to the Ocean of Milk together with his beloved.
From that time forward, O Lord of Gods, Kṛṣṇa has resided in the palace of his father-in-law and dwells in the ocean out of a desire to do what is pleasing to Lakṣmī.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
(8) The Eighth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Nārada, tell me what was done by Jālandhara, the son of the Ocean, after he had distressed the gods in battle and established Viṣṇu in his own abode.
Nārada said:
Having given the gift born of his favor to Śumbha and the other powerful ones,
Jālandhara then went to heaven and, having arrived there, looked about.
Day after day, adorning the people with a shower of gold,
the trees constantly bear fruit— the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Elephants, garments, gold, cows, maidens, and sesame seeds;
flowers, camphor, betel nut, musk, and saffron. (4)
Those great-souled ones who desire [heaven] behold Amarāvatī by virtue of giving shelter during the rainy season and providing fire during the winter.
They play all kinds of musical instruments in the temple of Śiva,
and those who provide water-stalls here, supplied with curd and rice.
For there, the sārikās, parrots, and swans, along with wandering bees and cuckoos, themselves swing upon the swinging cradles.
While performing the duties of a messenger and granting you union with your beloved, Menakā was like Tilottamā in the city of Rāma. 8.
There, Suṣamāsundarī, Ghṛtācī, Puñjikasthalī, Sukeśī, Sumukhī, Rāmā, Mañjughoṣā, and Acamālinī [were present]. (9)

Those [teeth] which bestow the happiness arising from deer, grant wealth, possess a luster like that of a boar's tusk, and yield the fruit of the horse sacrifice and the royal consecration sacrifice; ||10||
O King, there, millions of sinless apsarases sport;
thus did the son of the Ocean establish heaven as a place of abundant happiness.
Śumbha, Niśumbha, and the great Daitya Prāṇa were in Yauvarājaka;
and the King of the Sindhus himself, having come from heaven to the Jālandhara-pīṭha,
ruled the kingdom by his own power for two hundred million years.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
That unconquered one fought against the Asuras in battle.
"Thereafter, what did the powerful king, the son of Sindhu, do?
O celestial sage, tell me that in detail, for I am desirous of hearing it."
Nārada said: Listen, O King, to the truth of what was done by the son of the Ocean;
having conquered the gods in battle, he indeed ruled a kingdom free from all thorns.
The Gandharvas, headed by Citrasena and others, served that lord of the Asuras;
moreover, the lord of the Asuras consumed the sacrificial portions belonging to all [the gods]. (16)
Whatever jewels and other treasures had been taken from the ocean of milk by the gods,
all of that, as well as other things, the powerful one seized after defeating them.
O King, while the son of the Ocean was ruling the kingdom on earth, no mortal died, and no one at all went to hell. (18)
There is no other falsehood than affection, no other exhaustion than worldly enjoyment, and no woman more unfortunate than one who is devoid of ornaments. 19.
Neither the ugly, nor the destitute, nor the wicked, nor the infamous are seen there; nor is there any woman who is a widow, nor any person who is impoverished. (20)
There are givers everywhere who do not accept anything in return;
indeed, meritorious people bestow their own wealth upon the twice-born.
In every house there were women endowed with beauty and youth; for there, the people were like the immortals, possessing cow's milk, curd, and clarified butter.
May there be auspiciousness for all; may there be no killing or imprisonment anywhere;
may there be no injury by arrows, and may no one be oppressed by anyone. 23.
O King, no debt is seen; wealthy people exist everywhere.
O Ruler of the Earth, the subjects are contented and abound with all kinds of grain in every place. (24)
The milk-sap produced from the stalks of sugarcane was exceedingly sweet in the houses of men;
and he heard the beneficial words of women and men, for he was never a remover of the burdens of those traveling on the road. (25)

From that cloth, which was like a fragment of the sky, there issued streams of ghee mixed with sugar and honey; these flowed forth from the mouths of men simply by their remembrance of the Son of the Ocean.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sovereignty of Jālandhara," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
(9) The Ninth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, what was done then by Indra and the other gods when they were defeated by Jālandhara and their sovereignty over heaven had been seized? (1)
Nārada said:
Then, having been cast out from heaven, the gods experienced a long period of misfortune;
they obtained neither the nectar nor the sacrifices, and they departed from the abode of Svayambhū.
In the world of Brahmā, they beheld Brahmā, the Supreme Lord,
who, through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), was making his own mind known within the Supreme Self.
Then all those gods, filled with reverence, praised him with truthful words.
Thereupon the Blessed One became pleased and said, "What shall I do? (4)
Then the gods again reported everything concerning Jālandhara, as well as their own defeat, to Brahmā.
Having meditated for a moment, Brahmā went to Kailāsa together with the gods;
on the side of that mountain, which was filled with various wonders,
the gods, led by Brahmā and Śakra, stood and offered hymns of praise.
Homage to Bhava and Śarva; homage to you, the blue-necked one!
Homage to the gross and the subtle; homage to you of manifold forms! ||7||
Having heard these words, Śaṅkara, becoming manifest with all his faces, spoke to him:
"Bring the gods here quickly today. (8)
Having heard the words of Śambhu, the gods were summoned; they quickly entered that city and, with eyes wide with wonder, gazed upon it.
There, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was seated upon his throne,
attended by thousands of crores of his hosts who were full of devotion.
Having prostrated before him along with his sons, the Grandfather laughed at those who were deformed, crooked, matted-haired, and grey with dust.
Just as Śakra was once afflicted by the disease of pleasure, so has he come here in vain;
O Great God, you who are compassionate toward those who have sought refuge, please show mercy! 12.
Then, hearing the loud laughter of the Lord who wields the Pināka bow, Brahmā spoke to the God of gods: "Behold the condition of the inhabitants of heaven."
Then the Supreme Lord, the Lord of All, having understood the desire in Brahmā’s mind and the shattering of Śakra’s pride for the sake of the gods, [acted].
Addressed with affection by Bhavānī, the king’s messenger spoke these words:
"How can that enemy who was not slain by Viṣṇu be killed by me? (15)
O Grandfather, that Asura Jālandhara, the son of Bali, cannot be slain by those weapons such as the thunderbolt and others created in previous creations. (16)
He was not struck down by the weapons with which he had previously come into contact;
for the gods had fashioned a firm weapon of ice that was incapable of sustaining life. ||17||
Having heard this reply from Śambhu, Brahmā then spoke to Śaṅkara:
"O Great Weapon, you yourself create; you alone know your own power. (18)
Having heard these words of his, Maheśvara replied:
"O Brahmā, release this energy charged with wrath along with the gods. (19)
Then Brahmā, the indicator of the Brahmāstra, released his splendor;
thereafter, Rudra himself discharged the splendor born from his three eyes.
All the gods released that mass of energy along with their wrath;
at this moment, Madhusūdana was remembered and arrived by means of Hara.
When he asked, "What shall I do?", Śiva said to Janārdana:
"O Viṣṇu, why was Jālandhara not slain by you in battle?"
How is it that he has abandoned the gods and gone to lie upon the Ocean of Milk? ||23||
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord of Gods, since this Śrī is my beloved, how can I kill him? Therefore, O Consort of Pārvatī, slay Jālandhara in battle."
"Release the fiery energy born of your wrath," Śarva said to Keśava as he was being urged; Keśava released the Vaiṣṇava energy, and all of that increased.
Seeing that expanded and pervasive energy, he spoke to Keśava.
Śaṅkara said:
"By means of this splendor, you ought to quickly fashion my weapon.
Having heard those words spoken by Śaṅkara, Viśvakarman and the others [acted].
Then, looking at one another, they were filled with doubt as to what they should do;
seeing them standing silent, he understood what was in their minds.
Then the Blessed Lord Brahmā said: "Indeed, these deities are unable to endure that which is not to be looked upon; by whom could its splendor be borne? (28)
Then, laughing, the Blessed Lord Śambhu leaped up above the [other] splendors and danced the *bhramarī* movement with the heel of his left foot.
Then the gods, headed by Mahendra, seeing Śaṅkara dancing with such splendor, were filled with joy and played various musical instruments.
From that time forth, this swarm of female bees has been made to whirl in dances;
furthermore, the *cakra* (wheel) was produced from the crushing of Śambhu’s dancing.
It was three hundred thousand leagues in extent and filled with tens of millions of bones;
from the friction of Śarva’s foot, sparks were emitted from his splendor.
Viśvakarman fashioned that weapon as well as the celestial chariots;
then, seeing them, he [Śiva] took up the Sudarśana discus out of fear of the gods.
"Save us! Save us! they cried to the Lord of Gods, O King;
[the gods] having taken up the hardness of the earth, as well as the metals and even the fiery elements.
That treasury which had been fashioned by Viśvakarman was reduced to ashes;
and by that very [fire] created by him, Kāla was consumed and fell to the earth. (35)
Then Śiva, together with Umā, placed that discus in the hand of Brahmā;
seeing his beard burnt by the mass of flames from the discus, the Lord of Umā [withdrew it].
Having laughed and quickly taken the discus from the hand of Brahmā, Śiva placed it in the fold of his garment, like a pauper finding a treasure.
Therefore, the wheel is not seen when it remains within the hollow of Śiva’s armpit;
it is just like the fruit of a gift given to one who is utterly foolish. (38)
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa,
within the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada, in the narrative of Jālandhara, [this is] the chapter titled "The Origin of the Discus Consisting of the Splendor of All the Gods."
The Ninth Chapter. ||9||
(10) The Tenth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Having gone there, I spoke these further words to the son of Sindhu:
"O Lord of all heroes, I have been commissioned by Śambhu to come to you.
Having heard these royal words of mine, that asura then questioned me.

Viśālā, the daughter of the King of Mountains, possessed of high and swelling breasts. (4)

Then Kīrtimukha, together with his attendants, laughed before the Lord;
having prostrated before the god Śiva, he said, "O Lord, I am exceedingly hungry. (38)
Then Śaṅkara said to him, "Alas! Eat those slain in battle.
Having reflected for a moment, he and his attendants then searched everywhere but did not see the battlefield anywhere.
He arrived intending to devour Brahmā, but was restrained by Śaṅkara;
thereafter, Kīrtimukha then devoured his own body and everything else.
Though he was hungry and forbidden from all sides, he saw that [the food] being offered with devotion by Kīrttimukha and ate it. 41.
The Lord, being pleased, said to him: "Remain here in my palace forever; and whoever shall be devoid of thought for you shall dwell in my abode."
"Indeed, he will depart quickly," it was said; having spoken thus, he vanished.
Then the gods showered the head of Śambhu with rains of flowers. (43)

Having thus witnessed such a marvel in the assembly of the Trident-bearer, Svarbhānu, filled with wonder, spoke again to the Lord of the Gods: evam atyadbhutaṃ dṛṣṭvā sabhāyāṃ tu triśūlinaḥ | svarbhānur api deveśaṃ punaḥ provāca vismitaḥ ||44||
How can they forcibly touch your state, you who are self-dependent and a yogi?
For you are to be worshipped by the senses; how could you be attained by the objects of the senses? 45.
You accept worship from all sides from the world-protectors, beginning with Brahmā;
yet you do not perceive which god you are worshipping, nor do you know whom you are honoring. 46.
O Lord, how is it that you, who subsist on alms in this world, remain established [in such a state]? O King of Yogins, give me Gaurī, who is so delightful. 47.
"Now, accompanied by your two sons Skanda and Dala,
take up an alms-bowl and wander constantly from house to house."
In this manner, Rāhu addressed the Lord of the Planets (Rāhu) in many ways;
yet the Blessed One, having heard that, did not utter any reply at all.
Then, having abandoned the silent Īśa, Arāhu spoke for a day: "O Vikaṭānanabimbadhṛk, you are the commander of the army; go forth! (50)
"You ought to instruct one who has thus fallen away from his conduct;
otherwise, Indra, struck down in battle by anger, will fall. (51)
Having heard these words of his, Nandī informed Īśvara;
and by a mere sign of his eyebrows, he then understood the intention of the wielder of the trident.
Having worshipped him, the leader of the hosts of gods sent Rāhu away;
then, having gone to Jālandhara, Svarbhānu related in detail that account of his enchanting form as Gaurī.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa,
in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada, within the narrative of Jālandhara,
[this is] the chapter titled "The Return of Rāhu from Kailāsa."
The Tenth Chapter. ||10||
(11) The Eleventh Chapter.
Nārada said:
Then, having heard the words of Jālandhara’s messenger, the powerful king summoned his entire army and set out on his expedition.
Then, from those assembled armies, a great clamor was heard. ||1||
He roused the kinnaras who were sleeping in the caves of Mount Mandaraka with their wives; he awakened the elephants in the caverns of Mount Meru, whose trumpeting echoed through the mountain;
and he dispersed the herds of lions from his path—such was the one who traveled before him.
The clamor of the great army deafened the world. ||2||
Then, O beloved of the heroes, there arose the sound of kettledrums upon the throne of King Jālandhara,
accompanied by that great and pleasing noise.
The mountains tremble, the earth shakes, and the palaces and mountains quiver;
the Daityas and Dānavas have emerged from within the womb of the seven oceans. (4)
Equipped with armor and joined by various mounts, they roar loudly;
outside the city, there is the great sound of the neighing of horses.
Then, with its surface thrilled by the rain, the earth trembled; and with her forests shaken by the moving herds of elephants, she seemed to break into a laugh.
Accompanied by ten thousand terrifying Jālandharas stationed in chariots,
two hundred thousand and twenty million horses, and also a hundred million elephants.
A hundred thousand chariot-warriors with their banners shone forth;
ninety-nine crores of principal leaders were seen.
That great army marched out, obscuring the sun with its umbrellas.
In some places, the grove of pale lotuses was like a forest of parrots with its white parasols; in other places, it became like a bed of deep blue lotuses with the peacock-feather sunshades.
In his procession, the sky was at times cloudless, yet at other times it became filled with clouds of rising dust;
it was at times full of waves due to the fluttering of the banners' cloths, as if it were a noble lake.
As the Daitya army advanced, the earth was composed of elephants and horses, the sky was filled with banners and parasols, and the circle of the quarters was made of fly-whisks.
Then the Daitya Jālandhara, eager for his departure,
placed upon Skanda’s shoulder a spear adorned with various jewels.
Mahāviṣṇu arrived to question the ocean-dweller;
having saluted Hari, Jālandhara then spoke this to him.
"Tell me, Bhāvuka, what wealth shall I bestow upon you?
Having heard these words of Nārāyaṇa, the son of Avidhaja was filled with joy. (13)
He said, "What pleasing service may I perform that is desired by the son of Sindhu?
Being thus addressed, he was delighted and then spoke quickly to Hari.
"I am going to fight in battle; you remain here happily in this ocean.
Then, having been given [the sword] Lakṣmī by Keśava, he was honored there. 15.
Having departed from Hari’s abode, he came to the ocean to inquire after him;
having prostrated before the sea, he spoke from a short distance away.
"You ought to grant permission for Nīlakaṇṭha to conquer him in battle," [said he] upon hearing the words of his son who was desirous of going toward Śaṅkara.
He was also told by Sindhurāja: "O son, abandon your distress!
Enjoy the kingdom granted by me; cast your sorrow far away. (18)
Your majesty is most wonderful; there is no king on earth equal to you.
By you, it has been raised to a state superior even to heaven, reaching as far as the surface of the earth.
In your kingdom, the earth shines like Vaikuṇṭha;
that god who is invincible by the Daityas has been brought here along with Śrī.
"Abandon this mendicant who dwells near me, who is like a calf to Vāsava and Śaṅkara.
Thus was the ocean addressed by the daughter of the mountain, who was filled with passion for him.
Disregarding his father’s words, he arrived with his own soldiers; then Vṛndā spoke to Jālandhara, who was ready for battle.
Vṛndā said: "O Lord, O Indra among kings, you should not engage in battle with that contemptible yogi.
Turn back your mind; behold how it has been set toward Pārvatī."
"Why do you desire Gaurī? Is Pārvatī superior to me?
She is a poor ascetic, without support, who is forever attached to the motionless Sthāṇu. (24)
"Like one truly enamored of her son, this artificial doll has been praised in vain by Nārada; abandon her and accept me. (25)
Having heard these words of Vṛndā, the son of the Ocean replied:
"Without beholding the form of Pārvatī, my mind does not turn back. (26)
"O Caṇḍī, may you protect this realm, its people, and the capital;
and I should always be remembered by you if Śaṅkara should slay me. (27)
Having heard these words of her husband, Vṛndā, filled with laughter, then departed for the city of Jālandhara, mounted upon a palanquin. 28.
Nārada said:
Then the mighty son of the Ocean set out for Kailāsa,
surrounded by an army of sixty thousand great padmas.
In the meantime, Śaṅkara, having abandoned Kailāsa, went to Mount Mānasa, accompanied by his beloved and his son Gaṇeśa. ||30||
Then, on the first day, he reached Jālandhara and Kailāsa;
having stationed his armies there, he was filled with curiosity to behold Kailāsa.
The winds, laden with the pollen of divine *kesara* and *mandāra* flowers, blow forth, bending down under the weight of showers of cool water droplets.
Where the breezes from the Mandāra groves blow, fragrant with the scent of the firm, swelling breasts of the Siddha women. ||33||
There, seeing the gathering of women whose feet were as lovely and tender as the Ashoka flower,
the lord of the Danavas became overwhelmed with longing.
The gods attain joy, delighted by the sight of their own reflection, where the splendor of the Kinnaras and Gandharvas is surpassed by the brilliance of their celestial pleasures. (35)
There, mandāra trees with withered foliage shine everywhere,
where various trees are crowded by the waves of the ocean and frequented by the hosts of Śambhu’s attendants.

There, swarms of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of sandalwood and musk shine as if they were the fame of King Manmatha borne aloft; they gleam like the extinguished embers of the fire of Kama’s pride once it has been consumed.

Having beheld the entire fragrance, supreme luster, and friendliness of the *yaṣṭimadhu* plants, I believe that their very blackness is the result of being embraced by musk, which delights the mind. (38)
In some places, there were lotuses shining like the finest red ochre, and bees resembling the petals of those blossoms; in other places, there were cakora birds with faces like the moon;
in some places, there were earrings shimmering like the sun upon the banks of mountain rivers; and in others, there were bees bowing low, as if in submission, beneath the swaying nicula trees.
In one place, with fresh mango trees crowded by cackling cuckoos, frequented by flocks of *kuraṅkuraṅga* birds, and possessing the roots of robust rice plants;
in another, purified by the footsteps of celestial nymphs who are most beautiful and excellent—this forest brings about a transformation even in the minds of sages like me. (40)
Thus beholding the temple of Hara, endowed with such qualities—wondrous, like Kailāsa, and the refuge of all jewels. (41)
Greatly astonished, the Daitya spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu:
"Why do those like you speak of that as 'suffering' (tāpa)? (42)
Seeing such a charming house belonging to one whose wife was like that, Śambhu looked about and said, "O poet, where has Hara gone? (43)
When asked, "How [did you escape] from my fear?", Bhārgava replied:
"The god Śambhu went to the great mountain Mānasottara, which is inaccessible. (44)
"Mahādeva went there, which cannot be reached by others. Having heard these words of Kāvya, the exceedingly powerful Daitya spoke.
Jālandhara said:
"O Bhārgava, I shall go to the Lord of Gods; you go there first.
Having said this, he departed for that place where Śaṅkara himself resides.
He beheld that best of mountains, Sindhujomānasottara;
its height was sixty thousand yojanas. ||47||
O King, surrounded by the armies of the Daityas, many Daitya kings swiftly ascended the mountain along with Mount Mānasa. 48.
With the sound of the letter *dhakāra* [uttered] by Chatrā, and with trembling caused by the roar of the primordial sound (*ādināda*), the tumult of their armies filled the heaven and earth. 49.
Nārada said: Then, seeing that great army of the Daityas thus arrived,
she stationed Gaurī, surrounded by her companions, upon a very high peak of the mountain.
And Lord Śiva, surrounded by all his hosts—armed and fierce in battle—with thirty thousand great *abja* divisions of the Pramathas, [departed]. (51)
Śambhu spoke to him, the lord of the Gaṇas: "By you..."
The great Daitya, the heroic Jālandhara, must be struck down in battle.
As long as you are surrounded by heroic warriors such as Mahākāla and others, you must fight with great prowess in that battle. (53)
"O my hero, the victory over the enemy will come about through battle.
Having heard these words of Śambhu, he spoke to his charioteer.
"O Great-minded One, bring my Kākatuṇḍa chariot here today! Having heard these words of his, he too brought that chariot. 55.
It was yoked to thirty-two horses, possessed sixteen wheels, equipped with sixty banners, and extended for thirty-two yojanas. (56)
And he obtained a chariot belonging to the village-headman, fully equipped with all weapons;
his two sons, Dama and Vināyaka, were appointed for the protection of its wheels.
Commanded by Śaṅkara, those two,
having equipped their respective mounts and being surrounded by the Gaṇas, honored the Lord with auspicious words.
Having mounted his great chariot, he set out against the Dānavas;
a parasol twelve yojanas in extent shone resplendent upon his head.
As the Danavas were emerging from their city,
they beheld the Danavas of terrible appearance who had ascended the mountain.
Struck by the sharp weapons of the Gaṇas, the Daityas fell to the ground;
being slaughtered by the Gaṇas, they abandoned the mountain from afar.
Then, descending from that mountain which was like smoke,
O King, the hosts struck down the mighty Daityas with sharp weapons.
Seeing it filled with the immortals, the demon soldiers attacked;
then a battle ensued between the hosts and the Dānavas.
Then, in that battle, the fire-faced [beings] struck all the elephants of the Dānavas and the gods with an exceedingly fierce shower of arrows.
Chariots, horses, and foot-soldiers, as well as the exceedingly powerful Cakākaṭuṇḍas—
these were the hosts of Daityas slain in the battle, all of whom were great practitioners of illusion.
The sky was filled with their heads, which were laughing and terrifying,
with disheveled hair and ruddy faces, and fearsome fangs and eyes.
It was filled with the severed heads, trunks,
and limbs of corpses, and with headless torsos drenched in blood that lay everywhere upon the ground amidst the funeral pyres.
Then a great clamor arose from the lords of the Daityas as they fled with their banners and quivers,
their soldiers struck down by Śambhu’s hosts,
like the roaring of oceans at the end of an eon.

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Defeat of the Daitya Army" within the Jālandhara episode of the dialogue between Nārada and Yudhiṣṭhira, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty thousand verses.
The eleventh chapter. ||11||
(12) The Twelfth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Seeing the army of the Daityas destroyed by the Gaṇas led by Nandin, the enraged Daityas, Śumbha and others, rushed against the Gaṇas. ||1||
Then the great Daitya Niśumbha fought against Nandin,
while Kāla fought Mahākāla, and Kāla [fought] Lokeśvara in the battle.
O King, that one of great strength reached Puṣpadaṃta, Śailaroma, Mālyavat,
Kolāhala, and Raṇera by means of his power of illusion.
The fierce and terrifying Rāhu rushed toward Skanda, as did Kūṣmāṇḍa, Sarparomā, Cagharghara, and Romada. ||4||
I went to Śubhaketurmukha, and Tuṅga to Bhavivānāyaka;
Hāsa to Sampātālaketu, and Romakaṇṭaka to Bhṛṅgīśa. ||5||
"Daityas and hosts of Rudras by the millions fought with one another;
while both lords looked on, they perished in that battle."
Then the hosts of Daityas struck Dṛḍhaprahārin with arrows;
he, however, released those shafts against them like a great elephant against mountains.
Then I filled the mouth of Śumbha with my feathered arrows,
just as the wind fills the cave of Mount Mandara with heaps of leaves.
Then, casting aside his bow, he rushed at him from the chariot;
and the Sun, having uprooted a mountain, struck him in the chest with it.
Having pierced and crushed Naṃdin’s heart and chariot in battle,
it fell to the earth like a thunderbolt striking a mountain.
Having fallen unconscious for a moment, the impetuous Niśumbha regained his senses and fled;
however, Mahākāla struck him in the heart with a mallet.
Having arrived, he struck the Daitya on the crown of his head with a mace;
disregarding that blow, the exceedingly powerful Niśumbha [remained unshaken]. ||12||
Seizing Mahākāla by the feet, the one of great strength whirled him around and hurled him from the palm of his hand with a roar.
Having drunk the wind from the mouth of the six-faced one, he became crimson with blood;
then, struck on the face by a fist as hard as a mountain of flowers, [he fell]. (14)
Having struck Śailaroman with his mace, he felled him to the ground. Seeing him fallen upon the earth, the exceedingly powerful Giriketun [rushed forward]. ||15||
He crushed that most terrifying Puṣpadaṃta with a mallet;
then, with a sword, he severed the head of Giriketu, who was known as Puṣpāṃta.
Having seized his shield and sword, he rushed toward the mountain-bannered god (Śiva);
the latter said to him, "O head, why do you flee, abandoning me who am seeking combat? (17)
"Since this body of yours is headless, why are you not ashamed while crying out in hunger?
When he had spoken thus, that headless trunk (kabandha) seized him by the feet with its head.
Held fast by Puṣpadanta and cut open with a sharp sword,
the immensely powerful Asura emerged from the belly with a hundred heads.
O King, possessed of two hundred eyes and crowded with two hundred arms,
his head wandered about and approached the vicinity of the headless trunk.
Seeing that head arrive, Puṣpadanta cut it off with his sword;
from that, a fever named Kaṃpana arose, bringing fear to the Daityas.
O King, crushed by those two teeth,
he was then afflicted by that fever, which was unbearable, extremely violent, and distressing.
Leaving the battle with his host of inauspicious beings, he went toward Mount Kampana;
he [struck] Kolāhala, Mahādhanvī, and Mālyavat with three arrows.
Then Mālyavat pierced Skandha in the forehead,
and the Asura [in turn] struck Mālyavat with various kinds of sharp weapons.
Kolāhala struck out, displaying his own agility;
he too, the leader of the Gaṇas, cast off the pain caused by the weapon. ||25||
Seizing a mountain, he then struck Kolāhala in battle with it;
from him emerged a terrifying fever named Jvalana.
Having three heads, nine arms, and nine feet,
and being exceedingly tawny, he bewildered Mālyavat with his own splendor while he was afflicted by fever.
Mālyavat, abandoning the battle, fled to another mountain;
Caṇḍi was struck in the heart by Bhayānaka with a noose made of entrails.
A horse emerged from that [ocean], and he too was cast into the sea—
he who, in the month of Kārttika, struck Rāhu in battle with sharp arrows.
Having covered him with nets of arrows, he quickly released a spear;
that great spear fell, blazing as if with fire in its splendor.
Seeing this, Rāhu rose up and quickly seized him with both hands;
having grasped the power of the virtuous, he roared loudly again and again.
Svarbhānu struck him on the head with a spear;
when he was hit by that spear in the chest, a river gushed forth from his body.
Flooded by her in the encounter, the son of Mahādeva somehow reached the mountain peak, which was like a mass of clouds obstructed by a river.
Having heard the harsh cry of the *kadaṃba* tree in the army camp, which was like the feverish roar of the ocean,
she did not even remember that lord of cuckoos, so skilled in melodious speech.
While he was scattering arrows and burning [the enemy] with his sword, Barbaraka slew him; then Kūṣmāṇḍa was struck down on the head by Sarparoman with a fist-blow.
Struck by Pātālaketu with a mallet,
an elephant emerged from his body and seized the mallet.
Struck on the trunk with a fist-blow by Pātālaketu,
Romakaṇṭaka mangled Bhṛṅgīśa with his weapons.
Even Bhṛṅgīśa, terrified by the arrow, fled swiftly toward the mountain;
suddenly, the smoke-colored [arrow] fell white upon the face of the banner.
The Daitya, possessing a massive body and a vast mouth, swallowed the host;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when the banner was swallowed in the battle.
As Jṛmbhaṇa covered him with sharp arrows, Go-vināyaka severed his trunk-staff with an axe and struck at his tusk.
Then Jṛmbhāsura struck Laṅbodara with a spear;
though pierced by arrows, the mouse entered the mouth of a cave.
Afflicted by the blow, Vināyaka lamented in distress amidst the fray:
"Alas, my mother! Alas, my father! Alas, my brother! Alas, my dear little mouse! (42)
Having heard that Gaṇeśa had been struck down by the Blessed One, Pārvatī then approached Śiva from another peak and spoke to him. (43)
"O Skanda, even you have been struck down by the Daityas;
why then, O son of Śiva, do you play with the mountains? Protect your own troops and the Gaṇas as well! ||44||
Upon seeing today the constant holding of weapons such as spears and the like,
Śiva, having heard the words of Gaurī, spoke to Vīrabhadra.
When it was said, "Let the bull be readied quickly," he did so;
he bound upon its two horns a crown with the brilliance of the sun.
Having tied a hundred bells around her neck, she held mirrors in her ears; on her shoulders was a mass of tinkling ornaments, and on her feet were large anklets.
He asked the thousand yak-tails about his eight nooses in the mouth;
at that time, the auspicious goddess was standing by the side of Śarva. 48.
There, joined with eight nooses, the goddess Bhadrakālī held a sword;
all her weapons were deployed, and she shone forth, ready for action along with her bull.
Then, adorned by Pārvatī with her own garland of bells and having had a tilaka mark applied by the Goddess, he was addressed with words of honor.
"O bull among men, you must not abandon Hara in the peril of battle;
having conquered the enemies, you must return from the conflict together with Śambhu. (51)
Having heard these words of the goddess, Hara then mounted his bull;
equipped with a thousand weapons and adorned with his own garlands and ornaments, he spoke respectfully to Pārvatī as she was departing for the battle: "I am going. (52)
Īśvara said: "O beautiful woman, though you are alone and possess a form that inspires desire, you have approached these Dānavas with evil intent."
"Therefore, O fair-faced one, you must protect yourself by yourself alone.
Having said this, Rudra, mounted upon his bull, went toward the host of the gods.
Surrounded by thirty thousand great *abja* hosts of *pramatha* attendants, Śiva, together with Vīrabhadra, quickly mounted a chariot yoked to swift lions. 55.
O King, Maṇibhadra, the slayer of enemy heroes, protects the left side of Maheśa with a chariot yoked with horses. 56.
The wielder of the bow protected the right side of Dhūrjaṭi;
having descended from that lord of mountains, he reached the battlefield together with his hosts.
Seeing Maheśāna seated upon his bull, the Daityas roared; then a great clamor arose between the armies of the Daityas and the Pramathas.
Then, O King, there occurred between those two a most terrible mutual clash;
thereafter, the exceedingly powerful Kālaskanda, the Great Time, [attacked] Nanda.
Mālyavān, Puṣpadanta, Vṛṣalī, Svarṇadantika, Caṇḍīśa, Madanāṅkuśa, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Guptalomaka. (60)
Those very Daityas of great strength who had previously been defeated in battle and had encountered this perilous conflict, now fought in front of Śiva.
A terrifying battle took place between the hosts of Dānavas and the warriors;
then those exceedingly powerful ones, having put the army of the Gaṇas to flight... [62]
In the battle, they enveloped Śiva on all sides with floods of arrows,
as well as with spears, javelins, maces, clubs, and iron bludgeons.
Just as the senses strike their own self with the fivefold objects,
so too did Aghora strike the Daityas with fivefold, most terrible arrows;
just as one destroys sins through bathing in the month of Āśvina at that very moment.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa,
in the dialogue between Nārada and Yudhiṣṭhira, in the narrative of Jālandhara, [this is] the chapter titled "The Arrival of Śrī Mahādeva for Battle."
The Twelfth Chapter. ||12||
(13) Chapter Thirteen.
Nārada said:
Then Jālandhara, hearing the clamor of the Daityas in battle,
mounted his chariot and arrived where Lord Sadāśiva was.
In anger, he quickly spoke to his charioteer Khaṅgaroman:
"Drive the chariot, yoked with a thousand horses, forth with speed! (2)
I slew him who was scorched by the heat of his own valor, adorned with matted hair, ashes, and bones, and mounted upon a bull;
for what power does one mounted on a bull have in battle against me, who am lame? (3)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus and addressed Akhaṅgaroman in that arrogant manner,
he seized a formidable bow and rushed swiftly on his chariot.
Then Vīrabhadra obstructed him with sharp arrows;
though rendered breathless, he remained covered by arrows even in his body.
Even though the consort of Bhūteśa was equal to the gods, nevertheless, do skulls ever attain equality with the moon, the storehouse of digits? (6)
Maṇibhadra also pierced the son of the Ocean with arrows;
then, having struck Maṇibhadra with his noose, he spoke these words to the Lord: ||7||
"Come to fight, O Mahādeva! If you have practiced with weapons, then strike me first; I shall strike the one with matted hair first. (8)
As he was speaking thus out of pride, the enraged Vīrabhadra then covered him with arrows,
just as the sun fills a lotus with its rays.
Then Maṇibhadra struck his army with his mace:
chariot upon chariot, and heroic horse upon horse.
Having slain an elephant upon another elephant, he cast it down to the ground;
in an instant, the earth became impassable due to the mire of blood.
The leaders of the Gaṇas struck down the Dānavas in battle from the mountain;
the heroic Dānavas fell upon the surface of the earth, their lives departed. 12.
O King, the brave Dānavas fell, filling the earth with their severed arms, trunks, heads, and hands and thighs. 13.
Nārada said: Having seen such an invincible army in battle,
he likewise beheld other auspicious signs throughout the world.
The splendor of the other gods, the stars, the moon, and the lunar mansions is one thing;
the radiance of the sun, which has opened wide the treasury of the world, is another.
O King, Jālandhara, having been defeated, thought again of you;
he did not see that Gaurī whom I had seen, and then Nārada spoke to me. (16)
"Now, at this very moment, I shall behold Umā stationed in her eternal abode;
for I am going there to see her, and afterwards I shall sport with Śambhu. (17)
Having reflected thus in his mind, the son of the Ocean spoke to the Daitya Śumbha:
"O hero Caṇḍajaya, whose valor is equal to mine! (18)
"Assuming a form similar to my own, you ought to engage in battle;
this burden of the fight belongs to you, as well as to Śibi and his army. (19)
"I shall go to see Gaurī, who has stolen my heart," he said, and then he gave him his own boat, having removed its ornaments.
Having provided armor, weapons, and the like, as well as a chariot equipped with a charioteer,
the son of the Ocean, accompanied by Durvāraṇa, left his army behind.
Then, O King, having gone unobserved to a secret cave on Mount Mānasottara, he assumed the form of Hara.
Having assumed the forms of Durvāraṇa and Nandin respectively,
the two then ascended the mountain in the guise of Śaṅkara and Nandin.
O King, on that peak where Gaurī was accompanied by her friends,
the Sun, having pierced him with his arrows, took refuge in Skanda.
Seeing his upper garment smeared with blood, Bhavānī was struck with amazement;
her friends, Jayā and the others, went toward him filled with agitation. (25)
Having gone into the presence of Śaṅkara, they, being deeply distressed, questioned him: "O Lord of Gods, what has happened? By whom have you been defeated in battle? (26)
"O Lord, how is it that you, though pierced by the arrow [of passion], weep like a worldly being?
Thus addressed, he gave those ornaments to them one by one.
Having slowly lifted him from the water, he saw Vāsuki and the others,
as well as Gaṇeśa and Skanda, with their heads severed and visible within his belly.

Having seen the Gaṅgā, they rejoiced; having bathed and performed their ablutions, and having worshipped their own bodies, they subsequently sat down on the bank of the golden river.
Then, looking at one another, Gaurī laughed at her friend Jayā and said,
"O friend, go quickly to his presence, assuming my form."
"Find out whether he is Śambhu or someone else;
for if he embraces you and performs acts such as kissing," [he will reveal his true nature].
Then, employing an illusory disguise, you should recognize that an Asura has arrived;
for he might speak to you concerning my welfare or misfortune. (12)
"Without doubt, the wielder of the Pināka bow must have come here and spoken to me. Having been thus instructed by Queen Jayā, she went into the presence of Gaṅgādhara.
Seeing her approaching, he was intensely tormented by the god of love;
meditating upon her as Gaurī, he embraced her. (14)
Then Jālandhara immediately discharged his own semen;
O descendant of Kuru, he became one with diminished virility due to that discharge. 15.
"By her [Gaurī] it was proclaimed: 'You shall become Rudra, a Daitya by nature; you will be of little prowess and base conduct. I am not Gaurī’s friend, who acts for her benefit. (16)
Having spoken thus, she resumed her own form and said to him again:
"By this sinner you have indeed been struck down by Pinākin.
Realizing this, she arrived there, went to Umā, and spoke to her.
O Goddess, Śambhu, who is fond of your praise, is here in Jālandhara. ||18||
Then, afflicted by fear on both sides, the beloved of Hara quickly entered the midst of a lotus;
O King, her friends became bumblebees within the lotuses, having attained freedom from fear through the son of Jālandhara.
In the meantime, not seeing that woman who had gone to the forest,
her guards became afraid and quickly returned to the battlefield.

Then, having been questioned by Śumbha, they bowed to him and, filled with trepidation, spoke thus to Viṣṇu, the lord of the asuras, for the sake of their own protection: [Note: The provided text contains a typographical error "śumbhenate" which has been corrected to "śumbhena te" based on the context of the verse.]
Having heard that Aṭṭahāsā had been abducted by Rudra,
Śumbha then abandoned the battle and dispatched Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa toward Jālandhara.
Having arrived at Mānasottara, those two demons, possessing a great surge of force,
spoke from within the branches of a tree to the Daitya who had assumed the form of Hara.
O tiger among kings, what is the use of that prosperity which has gone to a foreign land—prosperity which enemies do not behold and which is not enjoyed by one's kinsmen? (24)
"O Jitashumbha, your army has been destroyed in battle by Devarudra. Come, come! Engage in combat; you shall not obtain Parvati."
How does a jackal obtain the consort of the five-faced one?
O King, how does the letter *a* attain the splendor of the sun? (26)
"It is reported that the queen has been carried away from the sacred seat of Jālandhara by the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu);
therefore, wage war against him. (27)
Having conquered all in battle, he became the Lord of all auspicious lords;
or else, being shattered by the arrows of Śiva, he went to that [Śiva’s] state.
Having heard these words of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, Jālandhara,
his eyes red with anger, emerged from that mountain in a fury.
Having reassured Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa and abandoned his form,
Hara went along the path to Jālandhara and spoke to Durvāraṇa.
Behold now, O Durvāraṇa, what was done there by Viṣṇu:
resorting to his illusory power (māyā), he brought the hosts of kings to his own abode.
A wise man should never place his trust in a son-in-law who remains living at home;
indeed, a prudent man, having given him his daughter, should send him away.
A man should by all means establish his son-in-law in his own house;
he gradually takes possession of everything, including wealth, wife, and so forth. (33)
Durvāraṇa said:
"O King, whatever action is performed, that very thing is experienced [in return].
You came to abduct Gaurī; by Hari, your wife has been taken away."
Having heard his clear words, he remained silent for a moment and reflected.
Jālandhara said:
"Is it to conquer Prayāga, or rather the formidable Hari?
Since two tasks have arisen, let that which is more important be declared. (35)
Durvāraṇa said: "If you go to conquer Hari, Hara will strike you from behind;
the heroes in battle will slay you, and Rudra will not allow you to return."
Therefore, having conquered Paśupati and brought him under your own control, you may afterwards go to Govinda, if you know his abode. (37)
Now, O hero, go quickly against the exceedingly powerful Daityas;
wage a most terrible battle so that your own well-being may be secured.
Having heard those words of Durvāraṇa, which were appropriate to the time and place,
Jālandhara then went forth to fight with Rudra, the yogin.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Jālandhara’s Illusory Form," in the Jālandhara Episode of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(17) The Seventeenth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Then Jālandhara beheld the battlefield, terrifying with heaps of headless trunks, impassable due to floods of blood, flesh, marrow, fat, and bones.
There, the Daitya Jālandhara, distressed by the abduction of his beloved,
beheld the Lord of Pārvatī mounted upon his bull on the battlefield.

The son of the Ocean beheld Gaṅgā, adorned with the coils of terrible serpents, her mass of matted locks decorated with the moon, and graced by the sparks of fire from her eyes; he saw her as she was being led away. ||3||
Then, having quickly mounted his own chariot, the enraged son of the Ocean struck Śumbha and said: "The ascetic has not been slain by you!"
They said, "Jalandhara has performed a great feat;
that Hara, invincible in battle, cannot be overcome by us. ||5||
Having heard these words of Śumbha, the son of the Ocean (Kubera), overwhelmed with rage,
[approached] Hara, who was surrounded by an army of Daityas numbering a thousand padmas.
Taking up the Akālakedāra bow, Jālandhara set forth,
along with many sharp, exceedingly thick arrows and iron spears.
The invincible one released his weapons like a cloud pouring rain at the onset of the monsoon;
then the hosts of Śambhu obstructed that son of Sindhu as he advanced in battle.
Then, struck with fury by Rudra with volleys of fierce arrows,
his armor was cast down upon the earth by those shafts of Rudra.
Then, like a mountain released from a cloud, he shone forth, his armor having been pierced;
furthermore, Jālandhara’s body was pinned down by Śambhu with arrows.
Much blood flowed from the body of Jālandhara;
by that swift torrent of blood, the entire earth was inundated.
Then the gods attained fearlessness and the dānavas were struck with terror; abandoning that battlefield, those heroic Pramathas fled in all directions. ||12||
Like a river, your supreme form has spread forth everywhere;
now, O best of archers, you shall ascend Rudra born from the ocean.
"Now I shall do that by which you will go to your destruction.
Having said this, he took up his arrow and [proceeded toward] Kālakedāra.
He quickly filled Śiva with various kinds of arrows;
Śiva shone amidst those thousands of millions of arrows that had filled him. ||15||
Seeing Maheśvara covered by those sharp arrows discharged by the Daityas, he moved through the air as if through space, like a great mountain amidst trees. ||16||
Then Vīrabhadra, of immeasurable soul and great strength, rushed toward Jālandhara in a fit of rage and oppressed the son of the Ocean.
Then Jālandhara, becoming enraged, pierced him with thousands of arrows, striking his bow,
arrows, chariot, umbrella, and charioteer with his shafts.
The powerful son of Sindhu struck Vīrabhadra;
then Vīrabhadra, deprived of his chariot, slew the son of the Ocean with a mace.
In the same manner, he too struck him with his mace and felled him to the ground;
seeing him fallen from the blow of the mace and deeply unconscious, [he stood there].
Then Maṇibhadra rushed toward Jālandhara in the battle;
seeing him approaching in such great fury in that great conflict, the Daitya [fled].
With his equipment scattered by arrows, the son of the River (Bhīṣma), along with his charioteer,
then cast off his fainting spell and rose up, roaring and devouring [the enemy].
Then, out of anger, the powerful Vīrabhadra and Maṇibhadra struck the son of the River (Gaṅgā), who was stationed in the sky, with two mountains. ||23||
Then, seeing him fallen there,
Vīrabhadra roared and struck the son of the River with a blow of his fist.
Maṇibhadra, grasping the son of the Ocean by the feet, whirled him about with sandalwood paste; it was like a marvel. (25)
Although seized by Maṇibhadra, the exceedingly powerful king of the Daityas struck Maṇibhadra with a kick and cast him down.
Then Jālandhara, the mighty-armed one, struck Vīrabhadra with his fist;
thereupon the Lord of the Gods arrived, accompanied by his hosts, intent on the enemy.
Seeing Śumbha arrive, [the gods] ascended with their armies;
then the hosts and the Daityas approached one another for duels.
Then Śumbha went to battle against Śilādaja, Rāhu against Mahākāla, Niśumbha against Kolāhala, and Ketu rushed against Kāla. (29)
The mighty Mahāpārśva went to the cave within the belly of the mountain,
while Caṇḍīśa, the lord of Caṇḍa, went to the fierce Romakaṇṭaka and Bhaumāli.
Then Vikaṭāsya, Vaibhrāja, Girimūrdhan,
and Vināyaka— thus the lords of the Gaṇas set out together with the lords of the Daityas.
Then Śilādaja, struck by the arrows and weapons of Aśuṃbha,
crushed Kapituṇḍa with his massive mountain peaks.
Then, afflicted by that spear, Śumbha struck Śilāda with it;
thereafter, Mahākāla struck Rāhu at the forefront of the battle.
With a spear, he struck Śambara; with a great mountain, he struck Bala;
the powerful Niśumbha was struck by Kolāhala with a spear.
Seizing a spear, he struck down the chariot along with the charioteer;
then, the Daitya, deprived of his chariot and exceedingly enraged in the battle, [continued the fight].
Struck by the lord of the Asuras, Kolāhala, who possessed a thousand hoods,
he slew him with great speed and approached another chariot.
Struck by the discus of the hooded serpent, he recovered from his swoon in an instant; swiftly leaping down from his chariot, he took up his sword and shield.
Having severed the entire chariot, along with the horses and the charioteer, with his sword, he mounted his own chariot again and struck the Daitya with arrows. (38)
Niśumbha, though struck down by that [missile], being filled with extreme rage and amazed by his [the opponent's] prowess,
the mighty one destroyed his chariot along with its horses using a spear.
Amidst a tumultuous roar, the powerful Niśumbha fled on foot, deprived of his chariot;
[the enemy] rendered him chariotless by seizing him by the arm and dragging him along with his own chariot. 40.
Seizing the tail of the banner, he whirled it in the sky;
Kāla hurled the mountain, but he swiftly shattered that mountain as well. ||41||
Seeing that mountain pulverized, Kāla struck him with his fist; with his entire body crushed by the fist, he fled in fear.
Likewise, Śailodara struck Skanda on the chest with a mace;
however, Ṣaḍānana, having struck him with a spear, felled him to the ground.
Seeing the Dānava rendered immortal by the blow of the spear, the Six-faced One roared there with a wondrous sound,
like when Mount Krauñca was split asunder.
Then Mālyavat tormented Jaṃbha with floods of arrows in the battle;
Jaṃbha, too, having pierced him with sharp shafts, abandoned him as he lay unconscious.
Seizing Mahāpārśva’s chariot with a flood of arrows, he stripped it of its horses; having effortlessly deprived it of its steeds, he brought down Caṇḍa.
Then, seeing the chariot deprived of its horses, Caṇḍa seized an elephant;
as Mahāpārśva rushed toward him, Caṇḍa struck him with a mace.
Disregarding the falling mace, that exceedingly fierce asura struck him violently with his fist and felled him to the ground.
The great asura Romakaṇṭha, struck by the weapon of Caṇḍīśa,
seized Caṇḍīśa by the feet and threw him down from the top of his chariot.
Lambodara, whose eyes were terrifying, suddenly fell to the ground when he was struck in battle by Urunetra with arrows. ||50||
Having struck Daṃtenora with that [weapon], he caused him to fall upon the ground;
and in an instant, Ūrunetra attained peace, and in a moment his chariot was destroyed.
The Lord of the Gaṇas struck him on the head, adorned with vermilion, with a mallet; he struck the Dānava on the chest with a sharp-edged spear.
Then, O King, a great being with nine heads, no body hair, and eighteen arms emerged from his mouth and rushed toward Śaṅkara.
In the battle, Vināyaka, though his body was shattered by the nine heads and thighs of [Skanda], seized his axe in fury.
Then the Lord of the Gaṇas took up weapons for cutting with his teeth.
Seeing the Lord of the Gaṇas thus obstructed by those two in the battle, the Six-faced One [Kārttikeya] then [intervened].
The general, arriving swiftly, struck Navaśīrṣaka;
having slain Navaśīrṣa in battle, he rushed toward Urunetra.
O King, Skanda struck him down with a blow of his own spear;
meanwhile, Jālandhara, surrounded by his army, advanced toward Skanda while watching him.
Out of affection for his son, Śaṅkara, accompanied by his hosts, also set out to slay the Asuras;
then, a most terrible battle broke out between those two wondrous armies.
When the two worlds had reached the brink of destruction in the battle between Hara and Sindhuja,
Jālandhara, filled with rage, fixed a terrible arrow to his bow.
With that arrow, adorned on all sides with hundreds and thousands of feathers,
the lord of the Daityas struck Śiva on the forehead.
With its base at my marrow and its tip reaching the forehead of Śaṅkara,
that arrow of great splendor shone upon the brow of Śambhu like the moon.
Just as the sun blazes intensely at the time of twilight at the onset of the rainy season,
then the mighty-armed Rudra seized a great arrow that resembled a flaming fire.
The wind is its speed, fire and the sun are its fruit;
time is its fierce form in all its stages, and the Goddess Earth stands upon its arrow.
With that arrow, Hara quickly pierced the son of Sindhu in the heart;
by that blow from the shaft, he was drenched in a flood of blood.
Shattered by the arrows, he fell like a mountain struck by Indra’s thunderbolt;
then the Daityas cried out in alarm, and the Pramathas likewise roared.
Seeing Sindhuja unconscious, the Dānavas rushed toward Śiva;
some prepared themselves for his protection, while others stood around him.
Just as the son of the Ocean attained a swoon from the arrows of Jālandhara,
so too was Jālandhara’s army struck down by Rudra with his iron shafts.
After a long time, O King, Jālandhara abandoned his swoon;
seeing his army slain and his forces scattered in that battle, he was filled with fear.
Then, with his mind, he remembered Śukra, his supreme preceptor;
remembered by him, the sage quickly arrived at Jālandhara.
Then Bhārgava, having offered a blessing, spoke to the son of Sindhu:
"O Great King, O one of great strength, what task of yours shall I perform?"
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of Kāvya and honoring Bhārgava,
King Jālandhara then bowed to his preceptor and spoke as follows.
The King said:
"Bring these dead Daityas back to life all at once, O Śakra!
Thus addressed by the son of the Ocean, Agni surveyed the army there.

Then he saw the earth, piled up to a height of ninety-five yojanas,
as if filled with the bodies of warriors and their mounts.

having granted permission to the wielder of the trident, the sage spoke to him in private.

Having heard these words of the poet, Śaṅkara cast aside the trident,
remembering that former event in which the head of Brahmā had been attached to him.
A Brahmin must not be slain here, even if he takes away one's own dear life;
however, this one, who is reviving the Daityas, must be restrained by me in every way.
"Therefore, I shall quickly cast him into the submarine fire that devours the life of Daityas.
As Śambhu spoke thus, [a flame] issued swiftly from his third eye.
She was extremely fierce, having driven away all ritual efficacy; she had disheveled hair and a massive belly, with thick testicles, a vulva, and fangs and eyes that were terrifying to behold. (84)
Being addressed with "Command me," Śiva said to her:
"O Kṛtyā, cast this evil-minded teacher of the Dānavas into your own womb. (85)
"I shall slay this Jālandhara with my thunderbolt; once the Daitya Jālandhara is killed, you may afterwards cross over and be liberated. (86)
Having been addressed thus by Hara with a meaningful gesture, he rushed toward Bhārgava;
seeing her fallen on the ground, Kaśyapa fled, and the Daityas ran away.
O son of Sānti, you who conquer your enemies, you drew Bhārgava by his hair and shook him while he was naked, yet you embraced him with a noble disposition. 88.
Seeing the Guru cast into Bhaga's lap, the asura Jālandhara drew his arrow; meanwhile, she vanished from sight through her supernatural power.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses,
within the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada, in the narrative of Jālandhara, [this is] the section titled "The Entry into Śukra’s Womb."
The seventeenth chapter. ||17||

Then Jālandhara said: "Protect yourself from me; I shall quickly cast you down from Śiva to where Madhusūdana dwells. (1)
"Afterwards, having dragged Brahmā down, I shall cast him into the ocean;
for when you have been held in check, I am indeed the Lord of All."
Having spoken thus, he entrusted the military equipment to Śumbha, Niśumbha, and others,
and appointed Niśumbha and his like to guard the swift-moving Antaka with his soldiers.
Śumbha, Niśumbha, Bha, Pheṃ, Kāla, Karāla, Uṇḍa, Dhūmralocana, Ketu, Biḍālaja, Ghaśca, Rāhu, Durvāraṇa, and Yama. ||4||
Then Kālāsura, Lavaṇa, Bhūmiretas, Dhakāsura, Raktavīrya, and others—Caṇḍī, Cāmuṇḍī, and the Daityas and Puṃgavas. ||5||
O King, seeing all those Dānavas prepared for battle in the great conflict, the hosts led by Vīrabhadra and others hemmed them in.
Then there occurred a fierce, tumultuous, and hair-raising battle,
where even the foremost Daityas fell, afflicted by their wounds.
Then, O King, in that great battle, other hosts were struck down by the Daityas headed by Aśumba with all their weapons and fell; others fled in retreat.
Having conquered the hosts in battle, the Dānavas besieged Śiva with showers of arrows,
just as clouds shroud Mount Meru with torrents of rain.
Then, drawing his Pināka bow upon his bull,
the formidable one struck the Dānavas in the battle with multitudes of arrows;
the powerful one slew the Dānavas with volleys of sharp-pointed kṣurapra shafts.
Some fell at the front of the battle with a single blow;
having rendered the sun and others shattered by his arrows, the bull-bannered god [Śiva] acted swiftly.
He swiftly slew the remaining army with various weapons and missiles in the midst of the battle-host;
the field of battle was strewn with fallen elephants, men, and horses.
The surface of the earth became like mountains shattered by thunderbolts; then the son of the Ocean created Gaurī, who was composed of illusion. 13.
Having created Jayā, who was endowed with the quality of beauty and adorned with every ornament, yet composed of illusion, the son of the Ocean spoke to her.
"Go before Rudra and quickly delude him in the forest!
Having been addressed thus by the lord of the Daityas, Jayā assumed a form consisting of illusion (māyā).
Having gone before the inauspicious one in the battle, she, with her hair disheveled, wept.
When questioned by Hara, she said: "From the Mānasottara mountain... (16)
Having heard these words of hers, the bull-bannered god, whose beloved wife Pārvatī had been carried off by the son of Sindhu, spoke to her.
"Defeat this bull; the Dānavas will carry you away.

Having descended from his chariot, he went toward the sacrificial enclosure;

Embraced by the illusion of the Daitya, O King, he did not perceive himself;
at that very moment, he was approached by one surrounded by a vast army.
Having placed Māyāmṛḍānī upon his own chariot, the ocean-born Śiva likewise conquered Jālandhara; meanwhile, there was the sound of musical instruments.
By which the earth trembled and the mountains resounded,
the son of the Ocean showed Pārvatī to Hara.
Rudra also beheld his own beloved standing upon the enemy's chariot—
distraught by separation, miserable, slender, and with eyes full of anguish.
Seeing her repeatedly crying out, "O Hānātha! O Priyarudra!", he, like a formidable enemy, regarded her as a heretic who had strayed from the sacred scriptures.
Then Śambhu, deluded by the illusion of the Daitya, brooded upon Gaurī and lamented: "How can my beloved be obtained by me? (26)
"O beloved, how was you carried away by the demons of Moha and Mada? Seeing Śaṅkara overwhelmed by grief and delusion, the son of the Ocean [consoled him]. (27)
A certain compassionate person spoke these words with a smile:
"I am devoid of all means of valid cognition, free from memory, and bereft of passion. (28)
"Even the Lord Śiva became a wretched man without Ambikā;
do not weep, Virūpākṣa, for I shall give you your beloved."
"Having seized Pārvatī from the battle, I have protected her by means of this sword.
Having said this to Giriśa, he quickly helped Umā down from his own chariot.
He dispatched his army toward Śaṅkara;
Hara, for his part, swiftly charged at that army with his bull.
While she was crying out, "Protect me! Protect me!
Do not seize me!", as soon as the bull-bannered Lord seized Gauri by the hand, [she vanished].
Then the powerful Hara, having quickly seized Śumbhāsura by the throat, stood upon his vehicle and hurled a trident at him.
Then, completely abandoned by Bhena, she fell upon the stake, crying out piteously with all her senses, joined with the stake and deprived of song. ||34||
Having said "So be it" before Śaṅkara, he prostrated himself;
then, seeing Māyā-Gaurī as if dead, he was overwhelmed by grief and delusion. ||35||
Crying out "Alas, I am undone!", Rudra fell to the ground in a swoon;
then, regaining consciousness after a moment on the battlefield,
the Lord of Umā cursed Śumbha and the others, saying, "Gaurī shall slay you all."
Nārada said:
O King, after the Daityas Śumbha and Niśumbha had been struck down by the Goddess, they passed away due to the curse of Maheśvara. 37.
Having cursed them, Śaṅkara then wept and, having gone out, spoke, saying, "O beloved, where have you gone? while I was distressed amidst the hosts in battle.
"O beloved, having abandoned our pleasure, I, Śrīkaṇṭha, have been made to suffer the pain of separation by you;
even Vāsudeva does not know that I have been forsaken by you. (39)
O Goddess, this head was offered by you into the sacrificial fire-pit of Dakṣa;
since it has now been recovered by you, why do you abandon it once again? (40)
"Arise, arise, O beautiful one! O daughter of the mountain, awaken this Śiva here, who has been deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of the Daitya. 41.
Standing in the midst of the host of deities, the Lotus-Seated One, remaining invisible, approached him from the intermediate space as he was lamenting and spoke these words to him.
Brahmā said:
You are devoid of grief, delusion, father, and mother; there is neither suffering nor happiness, nor son, wife, or enemy.
You were not born from a progenitor, nor will you ever be born; since even the hosts of sages regard you thus, whence can there be delusion? (43)
Though you are one, you have manifested many forms through your sword, appearing like the sun reflected in the waves of the ocean;
by means of meditation, the self-restrained reach your footstool—that supreme form which is difficult to comprehend and truly ineffable.
She was not undone by her lack of affection for you; abandon this illusion fashioned by Jālandhara.
That Pārvatī, who dwells within the lotus-bud of Śambhu’s heart, has destroyed the multitude of her own enemies in battle; abandon [this foe] and protect us! 45.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Maheśvara understood;
recognizing that as the illusion of a Dānava, he hurled a massive boulder.
With her, O King, she struck three hundred crores of Daityas in battle;
then, mounting her bull with great wrath, [she pursued them].
Dhūrjaṭi took up his bow Pināka and arrows for battle;
then, seeing Śarva divested of his illusions, the son of the Ocean [Rāvaṇa]— ||48||
O King, on another occasion, he manifested a most wonderful and extremely inauspicious net of illusion, a great power of māyā that enchants even the Lord of the Gods.
Jālandhara, who possessed ten million arms, fought with Vṛṣākapi using trees as weapons;
then the son of the Ocean made the earth between the mountains level, adorned with the minerals of the hills.
The delighter of the ocean adorned the royal land with delightful shrines for the deities, crowded with various flowers;
there, enchanting apsarases such as Urvashi and Menaka danced. (51)
Forgetting Śambhu and casting aside his bow, he immediately set forth mounted upon his bull;
utterly deluded on earth by the sounds of musical instruments and songs, as well as by the illusory *tāṇḍava* dance of the lord of the Daityas.
Seeing Hara seated upon his bull, perpetually enchanted by the Tāṇḍava dance, the Ocean, assuming a form before him,
sought to delude him with song, instrumental music, and the grace of his dancing, out of a desire for diversion.
"Having cast down thousands of oceans and being constantly engaged in festivities, where have all the gods gone, and where are the hosts headed by Indra?
Even you, O Daitya, who are worthy of honor, have been deluded by his illusory power. (54)
O Śambhu, O Blessed One, why is this being overlooked today?
Having raised the discus residing within your belly,
O Maheśa, it has been prepared for his very destruction.
One withdraws Jālandhara, but not in battle. ||55||
Thus, having remembered himself as the Lord from the words of Kṛṣṇa, [he reflected].
Having swiftly mounted his bull, he arrived at the great battlefield;
seeing that Śiva had arrived, [the enemy], surrounded by his entire army, [prepared for battle]. ||57||
O King, the enraged asura Jālandhara obstructed him in battle;
for the wrathful Hara possesses the power to create and destroy the universe. ||58||
O King, having seen the form of the Blessed One consisting of fierce flames, the Dānavas were like moths in the fire of his third eye. 59.
Then those Daityas, headed by Rāhu,
seeing Rudra, were terrified and entered Pātāla out of fear.
Having seen many soldiers of the army slain in the great battle,
and having seen Śuṃbha and the others who remained after the slaughter as they fled, [they were filled with fear].
Then Ājālandhara stood alone in the battle like a mountain,
joyfully beholding the ultimate reality in the form of Rudra before his very eyes.
Then Jālandhara, laughing, said to Mahādeva:
"Withdraw this form of yours; you are burning all that is moving and unmoving."
"Engage in battle with weapons, abandoning your own power of yoga.
Having heard these words of Jālandhara, Śiva then spoke:
"Choose a boon, O Lord of Daityas! I am pleased by this deed of yours, since even upon seeing my form such as this, you remain fearless now. (65)
O Dānava, even the entire cosmic egg is not capable of beholding the splendor of this form of mine; therefore, you are fearless therein.
Nārada said:
Having thus perceived the grace of Śambhu and becoming indifferent to worldly existence,
Jālandhara chose liberation from Hara in the form of supreme *sāyujya* union.
Śrī Mahādeva said: This divine body of yours, endowed with the perfection of enjoyment as a Daitya,
enchanting Vṛndā and beautiful, remains here and consumes time.
O fool, how can you desire liberation while abandoning that single, immutable Supreme Self for even a moment without realizing it? (69)
Queen Priyā, the beloved of Vṛndāvana, was carried away by Yogamāyā;
having realized the true nature of Brahman, she attained that supreme state. (70)
Now, this [opportunity] is difficult to obtain, and that state itself is indeed difficult to attain;
therefore, between heaven and liberation, choose the better [path] within saṃsāra. (71)
Jālandhara said:
"The state of the Divine is attainable by someone who has accomplished his purpose;
now I am one who has accomplished his purpose, since I have seen you, having been struck down by you."
Śiva said:
"If you are eager to go to my supreme field, my abode, then do not provoke me;
quickly slay the Daitya with firm arrows."
"Then, O sinless one, I shall slay you; you shall go to this place.
Having heard the words of Maheśvara, Jālandhara spoke to Śiva:
Since you are worthy of worship by the entire world, I shall not strike you first. (75)
Nārada said:
Thus addressed, Śiva quickly struck the son of Sindhu with arrows;
those arrows, having struck the body of Sindhu’s son, shone brilliantly.
Just as bamboo forests on the peaks of a mountain of iron are set ablaze by fire,
so did Jālandhara fill the throat of Hara with his arrows.
With those arrows, Rudra shone like the sky filled with celestial beings;
O King, the battle between the two lords of Jālandhara proceeded in that manner.
I could not endure those [blows] from the son of the Ocean, which were borne by none other than Hara;
even with thousands of crores of mountains uprooted from the hollows of the earth, he was then unable to withstand them.
The son of the Ocean overwhelmed the Lord of Pārvatī in battle;
then the Dānava was struck in the chest with a trident by Rudra.
From his mouth issued forth a fever that caused intense fear;
he was named Vīrajvara, having the face of a lion and the form of a man.
Seeing the lion-faced fever emerging from the body of the Daitya,
he let out a terrible roar of "Huṃ," and thereupon the Śarabha emerged.
He was struck down by the Śarabha emitted from Śiva,
who saw that Śaṅkara was invincible and accompanied by the lord of bulls.
The son of the Ocean came near Vṛṣabha;
seizing the bull by the tail, he whirled him around in the sky.
The mighty-armed Jālandhara hurled it at the Himavat mountain;
then the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain discharged an exceedingly fierce trident.
Taking him by the hand, the Lord of the Daityas, mounted upon his chariot and holding his bow, brought the ocean-born Kālakedāra into the presence of Śiva.
He filled Śiva, who stood upon the surface of the earth, with arrows;
Ugra, having cut down those weapons and shafts, then pulverized the chariot with his own arrows.
Rāvaṇa, though deprived of his chariot, rushed toward Śiva in battle with a net ten yojanas wide, complete with charioteers and horses.
A terrible, wonderful, and hair-raising battle took place between the two of them;
seeing that conflict which resembled the end of an eon, the gods were struck with fear.
Those two of terrifying prowess struck each other with all their weapons;
they made the earth tremble with their feet and the sky with the sounds of their arrows.
Then, seeing the formidable power of the lord of the Dānavas, Śaṅkara swiftly withdrew his mass of weapons by means of the power of his yogic illusion (yogamāyā).
Then the Daitya with ten million arms, his eyes terrifying with bared fangs,
though deprived of weapons, rushed toward Hara across the earth.
In the battle, he bound Śiva with a vast noose for the hands;
then, with his sword, he severed that [noose] from the forest of hands.
Urged on by the arms of the Sindhu-born [Kṛṣṇa], the fierce Nīlalohita became enraged; he, the son of Sindhurāja, fought with him playfully in the battle. 94.
Even with his hand severed, Svarbhānu fought on;
likewise, the son of the River pleased Śaṅkara through wrestling.
Being thoroughly pleased, Śambhu said, "Choose a boon that is difficult to obtain.
Jālandhara was also told by him, "Give me your own position."
"You ought not to show contempt for me, who am devoid of arms and weapons;
grant me success quickly, otherwise I shall destroy you. (97)
Having spoken thus, he became a demon and struck him on the chest with his fist;
then [he seized] the Sudarśana discus, which had been fashioned of old by himself.
Vomiting it from his mouth, he seized it with his hand and, out of rage,
brandished that [weapon] which possessed the luster of ten million suns and was capable of destroying all things, both moving and unmoving.
And with that [weapon], he severed the head of Jalandhara;
then that head, having leaped up, rose into the sky to a height of one hundred yojanas.
O King, that abode of Brahmā has a face made terrifying by hundreds of fangs and eyes reaching down to the earth; it is approached with the stride of a tiger.
Again, having been struck in the heaven, Mṛḍa ran toward his head;
that blood flowed profusely, producing a terrifying sound.
Then those directions vanished and that sky went to dissolution;
there was no light from luminous bodies, and the earth trembled out of fear. (103)
As he was rushing forward, the swift Rudra struck off his head with his discus;
having been split in two, O king of kings, it then fell upon the Himalaya mountain.
Then, while all beings were looking on at Vṛṣākapi, Jālandhara’s head was indeed severed from its body as he entered it. 105.
From his throat emerged hundreds of thousands of Daityas,
and they were slain by him with his hand adorned with a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
That headless trunk of Jālandhara danced, crimson with blood;
again and again, Dānavas emerged from his throat.
Again and again, the entire earth was filled with the fat of the son of the Ocean, which had been severed by the powerful Śambhu with his discus.
O King, this mountain attained its name from the very fat of the earth,
for here the blood of this preeminent Daitya turned into stone.
To the north of Kailāsa, there was the city of Śoṇita;
then, seeing me standing there, having covered it on all sides with heaps of flesh.
Then the Lord of Gods remembered his sixty-four attendants in battle; through the power of that recollection, the goddesses arrived in the presence of Śaṅkara.
With palms joined in reverence, they said: "O Śiva, what shall we do? (112)
Mahādeva said:
"O Daityas, eat these heaps of grain which resemble mountains;
eat them quickly together, for permission has been granted to you."
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Māhendrī—all of them adorned by their own respective retinues. ||114||
