Thus, looking with a cruel eye at the multitudes of goddesses pointed out by Śaṅkara, he caused them to vanish from sight in an instant.
Then, when the body of Jālandhara was emaciated and overcome by those powers (śaktis),
his body emerged from his frame once it had been consumed by them.
Having reached Prabhāsa, she vanished in an instant along with Śaṅkara;
that splendor, resembling the sun, attained dissolution within Maheśvara. ||117||
Thus having attained dissolution before the three-eyed enemy of the three cities, all of you choose a boon; Maheśvara, being pleased, spoke.
Then all the yoginīs, who were desirous of the excellence of worldly enjoyment and liberation within the mortal worlds, questioned the Lord of the Universe.
They shall constantly worship the host of Yoginīs in their own homes;
by your grace, may all their desires be fulfilled. (120)
Mahādeva said: "Whoever, endowed with a spirit of devotion, should constantly worship your host, I shall be the bestower of boons upon him on the surface of the earth. (121)
If my devotee hates even a single group of yogis belonging to Keśava,
then I, as Bhairava, shall take away all the merit he has performed.
Thus, while the yoginīs were delighted by the boon granted by the All-pervading Lord in the battle,
at that interval Hara called to mind Bhavānī and his bull.
As soon as she was remembered, Pārvatī’s bull arrived in an instant;
and the beloved of Hara, accompanied by her circle of friends, arrived.
Having abandoned his bee-like form, he ascended the half-body of Hara;
O King, Maheśa then emerged from there accompanied by Girijā.
He said this to the Yoginīs: "O King, drink the blood residing in the headless trunk of Jālandhara. Hearing this, they rejoiced greatly. (126)
Having mixed me with fat and drunk my blood, the yoginīs danced with joy;
then Hara became pleased by witnessing their play.
Having himself assumed a terrifying form, he stood in their midst and drank;
at that time, the hosts of Yoginīs possessed large bodies and sharp fangs. (128)
"O Grahas, even now and at this very moment, drink his blood;
by that means, the Daitya Jālandhara, though struck in battle, shall not rise."
Then the hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the sages, the Maruts, and the gods, assembled there and offered praise to Maheśvara.
The quarters became serene, the wind blew fragrant, and showers of flowers fell from the sky;
and as he was being consecrated, the drums resounded with a deep, resonant sound.

With its upper regions perfumed by swarms of bees descending with sweet sounds as they bore away its fragrance, its ground was sprinkled by the steady downpour of streams of honey, while a rain of flowers released by the gods fell upon the assembly. 132.
Then, by the blows of iron arrows from Hara upon the daughter of the Sindhu, the three worlds shone forth;
showers of flowers fell, and the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Suras, Kinnaras, and others danced and sang. (133)
Śambhu, being constantly praised by hosts of gods, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas, returned to his own vast mountain of fame, which had arisen from his victory over his enemies;
and Gaurī also went quickly from the mountain to Śveta.
Shrouded by her friends, she performed the ritual service with a shower of flowers, O lady.

That Lord Śaṅkara, whose nature is compassion, established the hosts of gods each in their respective positions; having understood his own wealth, he gave even more to his consort. What more need be said? If there were anyone else who was so devoted to the grace of the Lord!
Who is this person here, or who could bring this earth and its subterranean realms entirely under his own power?
Having regained their own sovereignty, the gods shone as they did before;
having assumed the status of world-protectors, they enjoyed their shares of the sacrificial offerings. ||136||
Nārada said:
O King, thus has the most wonderful life-story of Jālandhara, the hero of the world, been related to you exactly and in due order. (137)
O King, even Viṣṇu has not yet abandoned his dependence on Kṣīrabandhu; everyone experiences the fruit of their own karma—know this for certain, without doubt. (138)
This supreme narrative has been told for the sake of dispelling suffering;
as long as the body exists, there are actions, and from action come pleasure and pain. (139)
O King, the embodied soul experiences [pleasure and pain] under the power of destiny; there is no protection other than through knowledge.
Even for Kṛṣṇa and others, while bound in a body, pleasure, pain, and so forth persist.
In that regard, what more need be said of others who are averse to detachment, having understood such a course of karma to be the most powerful of all? (141)
O steadfast one, wait for the arrival of your unwholesome karma;
having conquered your enemies, you shall regain your own kingdom at the appointed time. 142.
Having heard this history, one is not overcome by the suffering of rebirth;
and herein, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa have been proclaimed exactly as they are. (143)
Leading to heaven, removing sin, meritorious, and destroying grief and delusion—by this, a Brāhmaṇa attains knowledge, and a Kṣatriya attains sovereignty. (144)
Upon hearing of great prosperity, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra may obtain happiness;
likewise, a king who has lost his kingdom, remaining devoted, abides on the path of righteousness.
By constantly hearing this, one regains even a lost kingdom;
having heard this from the virtuous, O King, no other thing is found pleasing to hear.
Just as the call of the cuckoo is rendered harsh by the cry of a crow,
so too this sinless narrative, when heard, becomes dear to the hearts of the virtuous.
One should satisfy the reciter with gifts of gold, sesame seeds, clothing, and the like, as well as by the donation of cows and land; when he is satisfied, one obtains the fruit. 148.
The deities shall be pleased when the reciter and the teacher are honored;
one should give gifts of food and worship the Brahmins. (149)
He who hears this supreme narrative becomes eternally victorious, endowed with the prosperity of sons and grandsons, and is born in the world of Viṣṇu. 150.
O King, by this pretext, those best of men who hear the cause of the origin of Tulasī shall never have any sin anywhere. 151.
This sacred greatness of Tulasī destroys sin; having heard it, one attains incomparable liberation, and there is no doubt even in speaking of it. 152.
Tulasī, when planted in one's own home, is the destroyer of sin;
by its mere sight, even the murder of a Brahmin perishes—of this there is no doubt. (153)
One should worship Hari with Tulasī during both the months of Kārttika and Māgha;
however, worship of Hari is especially prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha.

By a single circumambulation alone, all sin is gone; those Śūdras on earth who are always devoted to giving have attained purity through time. They too shall possess bodies worthy of worshipping the gods, having moved far away from sin—those indeed who [act thus].
Indeed, in this current age of Kali, those who are devotees of Viṣṇu are even more difficult to find. 155.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Great Festival of the Slaying of Śrī Jālandhara," in the Jālandhara Episode of the Uttara-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||18||
The narrative of Jālandhara is completed.
The Nineteenth Chapter: The Episode of Śaila (19)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Nārada, where is the beautiful Śrīśaila mountain situated?
What holy site (tīrtha) is located there, and which deity is worshipped?
In which direction is he proclaimed among the worlds? Tell me now. (1)
Nārada said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe Śrīśaila, the best of mountains; by hearing of which, the world is liberated from sins such as the killing of a child. 2.
That mountain forest was delightful and frequented by sages;
it was filled with various trees and creepers and adorned with diverse flowers.
It resounded with the songs of cuckoos and the cries of peacocks, and was filled with *śrīvṛkṣa*, *kapittha*, *śirīṣa*, and *ājavṛkṣaka* trees. ||4||
That forest on the mountain was perfumed with pārijātaka flowers, excellent kadamba blossoms, and various other flowers rich in fragrance. (5)
It was well-served by all the wives of the sages along with their disciples;
some were engaged in meditation, while others were intent upon exposition.
Some stood there with their arms raised, others with the tips of their thumbs touching their foreheads; some were intent on meditating upon Śiva, while others were devoted to Viṣṇu.
Some there remained without food, some were devoted to eating only leaves;
some subsisted on water, roots, and fruits, while others remained observant of a vow of silence.
Some stood on one leg, some were seated in the lotus posture, and some, abstaining from food, performed most difficult austerities. ||9||
He saw sacred hermitages and various auspicious rivers,
as well as many natural pools and numerous tanks.
O Great King, this mountain is indeed seen on all sides;
it is here that King Mallikārjuna dwells eternally.
And that very delightful peak, frequented upon the mountain, grants liberation by the mere sight of its summit; of this there is no doubt. 12.
This best of mountains lies situated in the southern direction;
here the great and beautiful Gaṅgā has taken refuge in the netherworld (Pātāla).
There, by merely bathing, one is liberated from great sins;
and having seen the peak of Śrīśaila, one certainly [attains liberation] upon dying in Vārāṇasī. ||14||
Having drunk the water at Kedāra, rebirth no longer exists;
it is a great place for ascetics and likewise for yogis. (15)
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause him to be seen;
for he is the deity of consciousness, the destroyer of great sins. (16)
The city of Siddhapura is delightful and brings the happiness of heaven;
there, the Apsarases constantly sing and wander about. (17)
Therefore, this king of mountains brings happiness upon being seen;
men who desire liberation should behold it for that reason. (18)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Śrī-Śaila episode of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(20) The twentieth chapter.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
O best of divine sages, hear about the greatly meritorious Haridvāra, where the Gaṅgā flows; there, it is said, is the most excellent sacred ford (tīrtha).
Where the gods, the ṛṣis, and likewise the Manus reside;
where the Lord Keśava himself is eternally present in person.
Long ago, in former times, that great Vatsatīrtha came into being;
by the mere sight of it, even a great sin departs from afar.
Where the Ganges, most beautiful and born from a preeminent merit arising from the water of Viṣṇu’s feet, was produced by the touch of His feet; ||4||
O learned one, Bhagīratha brought [the Ganges] there along that path;
thus, the deliverance of his ancestors was accomplished by that great-souled one.
Nārada said: Who is this one celebrated as a god, Bhagīratha of great austerity,
by whom a sacred ford was brought down for the sake of the welfare of the worlds?
The Gaṅgātīrtha is greatly meritorious and the destroyer of all sins; all the worlds declare this to be the most excellent of all sacred fords. (7)
Even if one were to say "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" from a distance of hundreds of yojanas, one is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||8||
"How was she brought by him? O you of excellent vows, tell me what was done.
Mahādeva said:
"By whom the Gaṅgā was brought to the most beautiful Gaṅgādvāra..."
I shall relate all of that in due order;
formerly there was Hariścandra, the protector of truth in the three worlds. (10)
Rohita was his son, the one who was solely devoted to Viṣṇu;
his son was Vṛka, who was most righteous and established on the path of truth.
At that time, Subāhu was born as his son in this family;
his son was named Garga, who was exceedingly righteous.
At one time, through the turn of fate, he became afflicted by suffering here for no apparent reason; moreover, the king was threatened there on account of his adherence to dharma.
Taking his own family with him, he went to the hermitage of Bhārgava;
there, Bhārgava then protected them out of compassion.
O twice-born one, he had a son named Sagara who grew up in that holy hermitage,
protected by the descendant of Bhṛgu.
For the Kṣatriya, all [the rites] beginning with the investiture of the sacred thread (upavīta) are performed in that same manner;
likewise, there is the practice of weapons as well as of the Vedas. (16)
Then, having obtained the Āgneya weapon from Bhārgava,
King Sagara went and slew the Tālajaṅghas along with the Haihayas across the earth.
He of great ascetic power slew both the Śakas and the Pāradas.
Nārada said: Now, tell me in detail the majesty of Sagara.
Mahādeva said: There was a great king, Sūryavasu by name, renowned and possessed of great strength;
it is said that his kingdom was seized during a calamity caused by poison.
O Nārada, along with the Haihayas, Tālajaṅghas, Śakas, Yavanas, Pāradas, Kāmbojas, and Pahlavas; (20)
O Brahmin, these five groups displayed their prowess for the sake of the Haihayas;
thereupon, King Sagara, his kingdom having been seized, went to the forest.
Followed by his wife, he, being distressed, gave up his life-breaths;
his wife, however, was auspicious, pregnant, and devoted to her vows.
Previously, Bhārgava had been chosen by his co-wife for the sake of obtaining a son;
she, having prepared her husband’s funeral pyre, wept aloud upon the forest floor. (23)
Having restrained her, Aurva presented that wife of Aṅgiras to Nārada—
her virtuous, pure, and beloved son.
Then, having been informed of the death of Bāla, she returned;
subsequently, when two months had passed, [the child] grew up in the hermitage of Aurva.
And the performance of the birth-rite and other ceremonies was likewise carried out by Aurva;
there, everything including the investiture with the sacred thread (upavīta) was accomplished for that great sage. 26.
There, having studied everything beginning with the Vedas through the yoga of Aurva, he taught the Vedas and the Shastras and then imparted the Astra-mantra.
O highly fortunate one, that [weapon] was of the nature of fire, difficult even for the immortals to endure;
it was endowed with the power of truth, the power of life-force, and the power of vitality.
Enraged, he swiftly slew the Haihayas with his own army;
he brought them under his control in all the worlds and attained great fame.
Then the Śakas, along with the Yavanas, Kāmbojas,
and Pallavas, being thus slaughtered, sought refuge with Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha, of great luster, having made them enter into a covenant and granting them assurance of safety, restrained Sagara, O King.
Having heard his own promise and the words of his preceptor,
Sagara struck them with weapons and rendered them deformed.
He ordered that half of the Śakas have their heads shaved and then be released; likewise, he ordered the same for all the Yavanas and the Kāmbojas.
With beards shaven off like those of paramours, with hair like sprouts, and with their beards guarded [by others], they thus conquered all; Vaikṛta then performed the collection of the dharma.
Having conquered this earth, that king, the victor over all dharmas,
quickly prepared it for a horse sacrifice.
As he was driving it, that horse was carried away near the shore in the southeastern ocean and made to enter the earth.
Then the sons of Sata dug everywhere for that region;
however, even as they were digging in the great ocean, they did not find the horse.
There, filled with haste, they beheld a certain primordial being—
that divine primordial being Kapila, the Lord of the worlds.
As his eye was being awakened by the fire that had arisen, sixty-four thousand were consumed, and these four remained as survivors. (39)
Hṛṣīketu, Suketu, and likewise Adharmaratha; Śūra and Pañcajana were his sons, O twice-born one. (40)
The Lord Hari himself granted him five boons:
progeny, liberation, great fame, and an ocean as his son, O powerful one.
Because of that deed, he indeed attained the state of being the ocean. He recovered from the sea that horse belonging to the Aśvamedha sacrifice,
and that highly illustrious king performed a hundred Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||20||
The Greatness of Haridvāra (21): The Twenty-first Chapter
Nārada said: O Lord of Knowledge, tell me how the sixty thousand heroic and immensely powerful sons of Sagara were born, endowed with such great prowess.
The Lord of Śrī Pārvatī said:
The two wives of Sagara had their sins burnt away by ascetic penance; the most excellent sage Aurva, being gratified, granted them a boon. (2)
The lady, endowed with the power of choosing a boon, chose sixty thousand sons who were each masters of a hundred horses,
and one son who was the master of a hundred chariots, according to her desire.
There, one woman gave birth to two sons who were both brave and numerous;
they were all, in due order, nurtured by nurses.
In jars filled with ghee, those boys who increase one's joy were present;
and there was the milk of those great-souled Kapila cows.
By that very method of milking, those great-souled ones flourished;
one son named Pañcajana became a king.
After that, Pañcajana had a son named Aṃśumān, who was full of prowess;
his son was Dilīpa, and his son was Bhagīratha.
But he, firm in his vows, brought the Gaṅgā, the most excellent of rivers;
having brought her to the ocean, he ordained her as his daughter.
Nārada said:
How was the Gaṅgā brought down? What penance was performed by him? O you of excellent vows, O ocean of mercy, tell all of that to me. (9)
Mahādeva said:
For the sake of the welfare of his ancestors, he went to the Haimaka mountain;
having gone there, he then performed austerities for ten thousand years.
The primordial God, who is the stainless deity, became pleased;
by him this Gaṅgā was granted and has descended from the sky.
There, where the god Viśveśvara dwells eternally, Gaṅgā arrived; having seen her, he then received the daughter of Jahnu.
Even while remaining for ten thousand years with the Gaṅgā held within his mass of matted hair, she did not flow out at that time, solely through the power of the Lord himself.
Then he reflected: "Where has my Mātṛkā gone?
Having thus investigated through meditation, it was indeed grasped by Īśvara.
Thereupon, King Bhagīratha went to Kailāsa;
having gone there, that best of sages performed intense penance.
Then, being propitiated by him, I gave him the river;
having relinquished a single lock of hair, the triple-pathed river was then bestowed.
Having taken [the Ganges] and come to the Gaṅgā where his ancestors were in Pātāla, he gave them alms; this is remembered as the first [bestowal] of the Gaṅgā.
When the Viṣṇupādodakī arrived at Haridvāra, that very place became a preeminent holy site, difficult to attain even for the gods. (18)
Those men who, having bathed at that sacred ford and especially having beheld Hari, perform circumambulation, do not become partakers of suffering. (19)
There are many heaps of sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin;
all of them always go to dissolution by the sight of Hari. 20.
Once I went to Haridvāra, the abode of Keśava;
by the power of that sacred site (tīrtha), I was born with the form of Viṣṇu.
Those best of men who go there indeed proceed to the state free from suffering;
all the worlds, as well as men and women everywhere, become four-armed. 22.
All of them go to Vaikuṇṭha merely by the sight of me;
indeed, the most excellent and beautiful Haridvāra is a sacred ford even greater than mine.
This is the most excellent of sacred fords, bestowing the fourfold aims of life;
it establishes dharma for men in the Kali age, and likewise grants liberation and wealth.
Where the great and beautiful Gaṅgā flows eternally pure, there lies this meritorious and supreme narrative known as Haridvāra. (25)
And it is said: "For men who listen, there arises an eternal fruit, equal to that obtained when the Aśvamedha sacrifice has been performed, or likewise from a thousand cows. (26)
The wise man obtains that merit merely by the sight of Hari;
this applies even to those who have killed a cow, those who have killed a Brahmin, and others who have killed their fathers. ||27||
O twice-born one, even many such sins as these all go to destruction merely by the sight of Hari. (28)
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses,
in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada, in the *Haridvāra-māhātmya*,
[this is] the chapter titled "The Majesty of Haridvāra Preceded by the Origin of the Gaṅgā."
Chapter Twenty-One ||21||
(22) The Twenty-Second Chapter. Mahādeva said:
O best of sages, I shall describe the greatness of Gaṅgā as it has been told;
by the mere hearing of which, sin is destroyed at that very moment. (1)
Whoever should utter "Gaṅgā-gaṃ-geti," even from hundreds of yojanas away, is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||2||
O Nārada, she is renowned by the name Gaṅgā, born from the lotus-feet [of the Lord], and she is the destroyer of vast heaps of sins. (3)
The Narmadā and the Sarayū, as well as the river Vetravatī, the Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Candrabhāgā, Vipāśā, and Karmanāśinī. ||4||
Just as one obtains the certain fruit from giving a thousand bulls during the Puṣya full moon, so too does one obtain it by lighting lamps with the brilliance of the sun.
One attains that fruit in an instant simply by the sight of the Gaṅgā;
this Gaṅgā is of great merit, especially for those who have slain a Brahmin.
O sinless one, for those bound for hell, this [practice] destroys the sins of the Gaṅgā;
it yields that same fruit which is obtained during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
One attains that fruit merely by beholding the Gaṅgā;
just as, at the rising of the sun, pervasive darkness departs to a great distance. ||8||
Likewise, by the power of the Gaṅgā, even a great sin goes to destruction;
she is always to be honored in the world as pure and the destroyer of evil. 9.
Of auspicious form, she was created by Viṣṇu in ancient times; possessing a divine form, she is remembered as the mother of the wretched and the purifier of all. 10.
Just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, so is the Gaṅgā among rivers;
those men who perform their ablutions in the month of Māgha [attain] eternal liberation.
For them, there shall be no suffering for three hundred kalpas.
Wherever the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī are present, by bathing and drinking there, one becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt. 12.
Mahādeva said:
I speak of your news because it is dear to me; that which is praise for you, O Lord, is my own praise; whatever I offer is an offering unto you;
whatever I give is your service; that I am peaceful and sleep with my mind fixed on the pair of your feet—that is our prostration like a staff.
O Master, may the Lord of the Universe be pleased by whatever I have done for you. ||13||
By merely seeing, hearing, touching, or holding it, men are liberated; such indeed is this water of the Yamunā.
Human beings wander through this world, overwhelmed by the calamities of poverty, disease, and death arising from worldly existence,
only so long as they do not behold your waters— deeply blue like a great river— borne upon the head of the daughter of the Sun.
The mere remembrance of which instantly destroys a flood of misdeeds and conquers a multitude of sins even from a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas;
by good fortune, that Gaṅgā, whose name when uttered purifies the world and whose sight is the path of non-violence, shall manifest today.
For one whose mind is filled with joy and who longs for the light, once the path to this river has been traversed, he recognizes her as the first-born celestial stream;

then, bathing, twilight rites, offerings to the gods, ancestral sacrifices, the feeding of Brahmins, and so forth—all this becomes complete and grants delight to the Blessed One, which is not at all surprising. (17)
O Goddess, who has become the Supreme Brahman and bestows supreme bliss, accept this water offering; O remover of all sins, salutations to you! 18.

I bow to that [lotus] which directly flows as a torrent of Dharma, the essence of the nectar from the feet of Murāri, a boat for crossing the ocean of suffering, praised by gods and men, a path and staircase to heaven,
possessing a multitude of supreme qualities that destroy all sins, and which carries one across.
Salutations to you, O Devika, who gladden the mind of the illustrious Bhagirathi. ||19||

O Mother Gaṅgā, purifier of the world who destroys the mass of darkness with your stainless luster, you whose radiant waves are like a boat for crossing over the ocean of worldly existence for people submerged in it;
O vessel of compassion, purify me, who am terrified by the fear of evil deeds and have come to you for refuge.
It has gone to the protection of the refuge-giver, O you who are terrified! ||20||
"O Haṃsa! Are you not scorched? Why do you tremble with fear from the hell named Pasikimusa?
Do you have any fear of it? Thus addressed, the one who committed the sin became a denizen of hell.
[The messenger said: "Do not fear; hear my word, O mountain of sin! If by me...
What else could have been the cause for her falling into hell? What other wealth of dharma did she possess? 21.

Therein is described the experience of the submergence that bestows praise from the Lord of All; and it is said that upon seeing the celestial women, Indra, the lord of the gods, was filled with joy at the prospect of attaining them,
while those devoted to vows and restraints bathe in the waters of this daughter of Jahnu, the goddess Śrī.
Even one who has committed evil deeds clearly attains divinity here; in this matter, the Vedas are the authority.
May your intellect be truly wise; may there be well-being for you both, O companions of the mind. May your feet remain ever steady here, and may your vision be that of the virtuous.
O beloved of life, whose body reveals manifest virtues, may you attain the nourishment of living beings, since [this is] by all of you.
I have attained incomparable happiness through the merit of the sacred ford. ||23||

O Prayāga, the best of holy fords, the ornament of the three oceans—the daughter of Śrījāhnavī, the daughter of Ravi, and the daughter of Parameṣṭhin—grace me, the servant of the Lord of All; lead me upward and shatter the tenfold darkness with Your splendor.

Victorious is Prayāga, the king of holy fords, whose banks—dark yet not blue—are resorted to even by Vāgīśa, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Purandara, and others, who are themselves knowers of all that is to be known, for the destruction of their own sins. (25)

Victorious is Prayāga, the king of holy fords, which, having reached the confluence of the celestial river that flows westward with modesty, washes away the Kali age and the threefold internal afflictions of people.
The dark banyan tree, possessing a dark quality, covers the people with its dark shadow;
where that tree is seen, it dispels the fatigue of exhaustion—may that Prayāga, the king of holy fords, be victorious! 27.
Even Brahmā and the other gods, setting aside their own self-origination,
worship the meritorious fortune of that place where the Lord of Tīrthas, Prayāga— the bearer of the staff— triumphs by casting down his own rod of punishment.
Through service to whom the gods, celestial beings, and divine sages daily invoke heaven and sovereignty over all supreme lands—may that Prayāga, the king of sacred fords, be victorious! (29)
By the majesty of this [river], even those renowned for their mastery over the Vedas become like lions in their gaze;
for by her spreading waves, Prayāga—the king of sacred fords—conquers the three worlds. (30)

Victorious is Prayāga, the king of sacred fords, where the two preeminent rivers, white and black, bear on both sides the beautiful luster of chowries; there the primordial banyan tree shines like a royal parasol. (31)

Victorious is Prayāga, the king of sacred fords, where the confluence of the three paths—the Brāhmī, the Āpagā, and the Tripathā—unites; by merely visiting it with an unbroken resolve, it leads those who have reached it to the state of Brahman.

For some who utter fine words, ten million births pass away with the thought "I am going, I am going" toward that which is most excellent; for others who desire it, even a multitude of years passes by as their minds remain fixed upon it.
That which is attained through hundreds of thousands of fortunes becomes, for us, something beyond the reach of the speech of Indra himself.
By good fortune, you have become a guest to my eyes, distinguished by your matted locks; who else could be such a supreme pilgrimage site as Prayāga?

How can there be victory for those worlds who are incapable of performing sacrifices, who desire heaven through rituals, and who are distressed by thoughts of attaining the immortal state through words such as "May there be victory"?

Having thoroughly considered the fruits of sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and Aśvamedha, Brahmā and the other gods unanimously declared this very Prayāga, the king of holy places, to be the bestower of desired goals. (34)
Due to the faults of negligence, addiction to illness, and so forth, the ritual of the twilight prayers was not performed by me.
If one performs the twilight prayer here through grace, let that twilight prayer be as complete for me as for anyone throughout their entire life. (35)

Furthermore, even from afar, those who meditate with love upon Him whose greatness is celebrated by all, and who constantly bestows desired goals while remaining free from worldly expectations— [they too attain Him].
[One should go] to the illustrious Prayāga, the king of holy places (*tīrtharāja*), the peerless Lord of the Triveṇī, where the dust is sacred.
I bow to that very one, the supreme immortal, who is consciousness and the manifestation of the syllable *laṃ*. ||36||

Did we perform intense austerities? Did we offer sacrifices? Or did we give various kinds of gifts to worthy recipients? Did we worship the gods? Did we visit sacred pilgrimage sites? Or did we honor the community of Brahmins with offerings and service—by doing what have we attained this eternal state?
It is itself the royal capital of Śiva’s servant, Śiva. ||37||
By my good fortune, attained through many births, is this city of Śiva— filled with all wonders, the destroyer of all sins, and the boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
The fruit of a virtuous birth has been obtained, and my lineage has been fully purified.
Everything has been accomplished by my own self; what more remains? I stand above all. ||38||
"A living man sees only a hundred thousand auspicious things; therefore, such a statement is false.
For this reason, even though Kāśī has been attained by me in such a body that is as fragile as a moment, [I do not abandon it]. (39)

I bow with joined palms to those ancient, perfected *liṅgas* of the sacred sites in Kāśī—which, even for the gods, cannot be fully enumerated or worshipped in this divine land—whether they be hidden or manifest. (40)

What is the use of fear of a multitude of sins? What is the use of joy over countless merits performed? What is the use of pride from the study of sciences? What is the use of despondency due to the fault of dull-wittedness?
What is the use of arrogance born from the rise of wealth? And what, O people, is the use of the torment of poverty?
If, after bathing in the waters of the illustrious Maṇikarṇikā, one beholds Viśveśvara; ||41||
By him, who possessed a strength rich in enthusiasm, whose self-nature was clearly capable of reducing even slight prosperity, freedom from disease, and physical thinness,
and who had desire as his only companion— that [state] was attained, though it was beyond the reach of desires and outside the scope even of the activity of dreams.
The city of Pigeon-Ear (Pigadādhara) bestows immediate liberation;
I consider that this is neither the result of one's own effort, nor the power of past ancestors,
nor even the influence of one's kinsmen, since such things as sleep and fever are not constant.
The attainment of Gayā, Prayāga, Yamunā, and Kāśī—which are difficult to reach—through the arrival of this auspicious festival is where the grace of Śrī Śāradā reigns with great fruit. ||43||
I bow to Śrī Gadādhara, who, though merely remembered from afar at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, grants liberation to the ancestors; I bow to him who is present in person at Gayā. 44.
Having traversed this difficult path, which from afar appears even more remote and is crowded with petty tigers, hyenas, thorns, venomous serpents, and enemies,
a person comes here with a piteous voice and begs for alms in a begging bowl— the first expenditure [of his journey].
The illustrious Gadādhara of Vārī longs to see you every day. ||45||
O Soul of All, by beholding you in person and by performing the *śrāddha* at Gayā, the gods are indeed gratified; how then can you remain indifferent here toward the universe as if devoid of effort?
Is it that you have now become eternally merciless, or is it the sovereignty of the Kali age?
Or what is the point of long observing the non-existence of a self among men, or what is the point of his relish for service? ||46||
By your grace, the Śrāddha rite consisting of Gadādhara has been fully performed;
please grant me permission to go from here to my home.
One should constantly recite this hymn to the four deities, which bestows the fruit of heaven, at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, as well as at the time of bathing. 48.
O twice-born one, bathing at all sacred fords is equal to the merit gained from hearing, reading, or reciting the praise of Prayāga, the Gaṅgā, and the Yamunā;
by hearing this, even those defects born of past actions are destroyed. 49.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Praise of Gaṅgā, Prayāga, and Yamunā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
(23) Chapter Twenty-Three. Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall speak of the majesty arising from Tulasī;
by hearing which, one is liberated from sin committed from birth until the end of death.
Leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, branches, bark, and wood—all these originating from the Tulasī plant, as well as earth and other such things, are purifying. (2)
The bodies of those who are cremated with the fire of *tulasī* wood, or for whom *tulasī* wood has been placed upon all their limbs at the time of death, [attain liberation]. (3)
Even he who performs cremation afterwards is liberated from sin;
for one whose death has arrived, the chanting and remembrance of Hari [are the means]. 4.
There is no burning [of sins] more terrible than Tulasī, yet for one who possesses it, there is no returning again to this world;
even if a single piece of Tulasī wood is placed in the midst of a hundred other pieces of wood.
At the time of cremation, there shall be liberation even for those with tens of millions of sins;
by the sprinkling of Ganges ashes, merits attain further sanctity.
Wood mixed with Tulasī wood attains merit;
as long as the funeral pyre is kindled while mixed with Tulasī wood, [so it is].
Indeed, his sins committed over ten million eons are burned away when one sees a man being consumed by the fire of *tulasī* wood.
The messengers of Viṣṇu lead him away, and those servants of Yama do nothing;
liberated from thousands of millions of births, he goes to Janārdana.
The gods scatter handfuls of flowers upon those who, in the sight of men, burn tulasī wood as fire; they cast them into celestial chariots.
All the apsarases danced, and the singers sang songs;
Viṣṇu was beheld by them, together with Śambhu, being well-pleased.
Taking him by the hand, Śauri led him to his home and went to his own chamber;
while the inhabitants of heaven looked on, he cleansed him of all sins.
Having caused a great festival to be celebrated preceded by shouts of "Victory!", where the fire of tulasī wood blazes with clarified butter; 13.
The sin of men is not burned away even in a fire-sanctuary or a cremation ground;
however, those Brahmins who perform a *homa* with the fire of *tulasī* wood,
or even with every drop of water sprinkled [with it], shall obtain the fruit of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice.
He who offers incense produced from *tulasī* wood to Hari obtains merit equal to a hundred sacrifices and the fruit of giving a hundred cows. (15)
Whatever food offering is cooked by the fire of Tulasī wood, that food offered to Keśava becomes equal to Mount Meru. 16.
Furthermore, he who offers a lamp to Hari using a Tulasī wick obtains the merit and fruit of thousands of lakhs of lamps. (17)
No Vaiṣṇava equal to him is seen on this earth, who offers the sandalwood paste from tulasī wood to Kṛṣṇa. (18)
O best of the Vāḍavas, he becomes a vessel for the compassion of Viṣṇu. (19)
In the Kali age, by constantly and with devotion smearing Lord Hari with sandalwood paste produced from Tulasī wood, one rejoices in the presence of Hari.
He who performs the worship of Viṣṇu using Tulasī leaves obtains in a single day the fruit that is attained by a hundred days of worship or by a hundred cows.
Listen to the fruit of merit that remains as long as the sandalwood paste from tulasī wood used for the purpose of anointing Kṛṣṇa stays within the temple. ||22||
Whatever merit a man may obtain by giving eight measures of sesame seeds, that same fruit is produced for men through the grace of the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu). 23.
O Tulasī, for those ancestors who offer you a leaf from the *piṇḍa*, satisfaction arises;
for every single leaf, their gratification lasts for a hundred years.
One should especially perform a bath using the clay from the root of the Tulasī plant;
by that, a bath is considered performed at all sacred fords (tīrthas) as long as the clay remains on one's body.
He performed the worship of her vehicle with various flowers, offering such adoration as long as the moon and sun endure. (26)
In whatever house there may be a grove of Tulasī trees,
O Nārada, by the mere sight and touch of it, all sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa are dissolved simply by that sight.
Mahādeva said:
Now I shall tell you something else; listen with a one-pointed mind. O best of divine sages, listen to that which has not been told to anyone else. 28.
In whatever house, village, or forest the Tulasī plant may be found, there the Lord of the Universe, Hari, dwells with a delighted soul. (29)
In that house where Tulasī resides, there is no poverty, no lack of yoga, no absence of kinsmen, no suffering, no fear, and no disease. (30)
Everywhere, and especially in all sacred and non-sacred fields,
by planting it upon the surface of the earth in the presence of that deity, [one attains merit].
For those who perform the planting of Tulasī, Viṣṇu’s abode is eternal. When Tulasī is worshipped with devotion, Hari becomes the pacifier of severe diseases, calamities, and manifold ill omens. 32.
Wherever the wind goes after having smelled the fragrance of Tulasī,
those ten directions become purified, as does the fourfold collection of living beings.
In whichever house there is the earth from the root of the Tulasī plant belonging to the best of sages, all the deities, as well as Śiva and Hari, reside there forever. (34)
O twice-born one, wherever there is the shade of a grove of Tulasī,
whatever libation one offers for the ancestors there becomes inexhaustible.
Brahmā resides at its root, the god Janārdana in its middle, and Rudra dwells within the Mañjarī; thus Tulasī is purifying by its very presence.
If one performs the twilight purification (ārjana) without having rinsed the mouth, all of that is seized by Rākṣasas and it bestows hell. ||37||
He who carries on his head the water dripping from a *tulasī* leaf obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā and gains the merit of gifting a hundred cows.
If one plants a tulasī plant especially in a temple of Śiva,
one dwells in heaven for as many yugas as there are seeds.
O Goddess, in ancient times, for the sake of Śaṅkara, you planted a hundred Tulasī trees on the Himalayas; to them I bow. 40.
If one plants Tulasī on a festival day, on an auspicious occasion, in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
or on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), it bestows great merit.
One should worship Tulasī daily; even a poor person shall become a lord.
Her form bestows all perfections, and Kṛṣṇa grants him fame.
Lord Hari is ever-present there at the Śālagrāma stone;
bathing and giving gifts there yield a hundred times more merit than at Vārāṇasī. (43)
The merit gained from worshipping a Śālagrāma stone is ten million times greater than that of Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and the Naimiṣa forest combined. 44.
Wherever a seal made of Śālagrāma stone is situated, all the merit that exists in Vārāṇasī shall be found right there. 45.
Whatever sin a man commits, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth, he shall quickly destroy it all by worshipping the Śālagrāma stone. 46.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Tulasī and Śālagrāma," in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(24) Chapter Twenty-four. Mahādeva said:
I shall proclaim the majesty of the Prayāga tīrtha as it has been heard by me;
for there indeed dwell those devoted to great gifts and performers of meritorious deeds. (1)
Where the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī [meet], that is the preeminent divine tīrtha, difficult even for the gods to attain. ||2||
Such a being as this has never existed nor will there ever be in the three worlds, just as the sun is among the planets and the moon is among the stars. (3)
O learned one, the supreme among all sacred fords is the unsurpassed ford known as Prayāga;
you should perform your bath at Prayāga during the morning hours.
Freed from great sin, he goes to the supreme state;
one who desires the absence of poverty should give something according to his ability.
Having gone there to that Yonara at Prayāga, one should perform a ritual bath;
he becomes wealthy and long-lived—of this there is no doubt. (6)
Where a person beholds the imperishable banyan tree, by that mere sight, even the murder of a Brahmin is destroyed. (7)
It is renowned as the imperishable banyan tree (Akṣayavaṭa), which is seen even at the end of the kalpas;
on its leaf Viṣṇu reclines, and therefore it is remembered as the Imperishable (Avyaya).
There, men who are dear to Viṣṇu perform worship;
having covered it with a thread, they should indeed cause the worship to be performed. (9)
The deity named Mādhava dwells there eternally in bliss;
by beholding him, one is liberated from great sins. (10)
Wherever the gods, the ṛṣis, and humans alike reside, they always remain there, each occupying their own respective place.
Whether he be a killer of cows, an outcaste, wicked, or evil-minded;
whether he be a slayer of children or unlearned—if he dies right there at that time, [he attains this state]. (12)
Having become possessed of all four arms, he dwells for a long time in Vaikuṇṭha;
so too does the man who performs the Māgha bath at Prayāga. (13)
There is no limit to the fruit of that [act of] bowing; listen, O best of divine sages!
We have heard it proclaimed in all the worlds that "āpaḥ" (waters) are called "nārāḥ. (14)
Therefore, he is called Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation to those who have bathed;
he is like the sun among the planets and like the moon among the stars. (15)
Among all months, Māgha is the most beneficial and the best for all ritual acts;
likewise, when the sun is situated in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, at the pure time of dawn.
Even bathing in the water of a cow’s footprint bestows heaven upon sinners;
yet this yoga, O learned one, is difficult to attain within the three worlds of moving and non-moving beings. (17)
One who has undertaken this effort should bathe here for even three days, or perhaps five,
seven, or more, performing the bath that originates at Prayāga.
O best of the Vāḍavas, he too increases in his lineage like the moon;
so it is with all living beings, both moving and unmoving, as well as human beings and others. ||19||
Resorting to the sacred site of Prayāga, they go to Vaikuṇṭha without delay— those sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, and Sanaka and his companions who dwell there.
They too, repeatedly resorting to the sacred ford of Prayāga, where Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra likewise dwell; ||21||
All of them indeed reside here at Prayāga, the most excellent of sacred fords (tīrtha);
they praise giving there, as well as religious observances (niyama). ||22||
Having bathed and drunk there, one is not subject to rebirth again. ||23||

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prayāga," in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(25) Chapter Twenty-Five.
Nārada said:
Thus, by your grace, I have heard the greatness of Tulasī;
now, please describe the three-night vow of Tulasī.
Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O Brahmin of great intellect, to this ancient vow;
by hearing it, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt. (2)
In a former kalpa, there was indeed a king named Purāraibhya, who was a lord of creatures (Prajāpati).
His wife was the renowned and great chaste lady Candrarūpā.
She performed this vow which bestows the fruits of all desires;
indeed, her three-night vow grants dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. ||4||
O Nārada, the lives of those by whom the Tulasī vow has been heard are truly fruitful, specifically on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
Abiding by the rules, the observer of vows should remain with his senses conquered, sleeping on the ground;
having undertaken the three-night vow, he should be pure and self-controlled in mind.
One should sleep according to the prescribed rule in the vicinity of a grove of *tulasī* trees;
thereafter, at the time of midday, one should bathe in pure water at the beginning of the river.
Having performed his bath, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods according to the prescribed rites;
he should have an image of Janārdana made in gold, together with Lakṣmī.
One who desires his own welfare must not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
Thereafter, a pair of garments should be prepared—either two yellow ones or two white ones.
Then, the pacification (śāntika) rite for the nine planets (navagrahas), including the propitiation of their asterisms (ārāmbha), should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
Having cooked the sacrificial oblation (caru) dedicated to Viṣṇu, one should perform the fire-offering (homa) there;
having diligently worshipped the Lord of the gods on the twelfth lunar day.
One should place a flawless, pure water-pot according to the prescribed ritual,
provided with the five jewels, sprouts, and medicinal herbs.
Upon that, one should place a vessel containing Janārdana together with Lakṣmī;
one should install him at the root of the Tulasī plant with mantras from the Vedas and Purāṇas.
One should water the grove of *tulasī* with pure milk alone;
one should bathe the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).

May that God of gods, who is formless yet possesses the form of the entire universe, who sustains the world-ordinance within the waters of the cosmic egg, and who by his *māyā* is the creator of the universe—may he be gracious; may this Goddess be gracious. 14.
The prayer-mantra: O Lord of Gods, Acyuta, mass of splendor, Master of the World! Come, destroy the darkness of my constant delusion and protect me from the ocean of worldly existence. 15.

The invocation mantra: May [the Blessed One], who has been well-bathed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) as well as with scented water and the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, be pleased with this offering. 16.
The bathing mantra: "O God, together with Lakṣmī, please accept this unguent of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and the like, which has been offered by me with devotion. (17)
The mantra for anointing.
Obeisance to you, Nārāyaṇa, who delivers one from the ocean of hell;
O Lord of the three worlds, grant me well-being, O Auspicious One, the Mistress of garments. (18)
The mantra for the garment.
O Dāmodara, salutations be unto you; protect me from the ocean of worldly existence!
O Supreme Person, accept this sacred thread offered by me. (19)
The mantra for the sacred thread.
O Lord, O Ruler of Gods, please graciously accept these fragrant flowers, such as mālatī and others, which have been offered by me. (20)
The mantra for the flowers.
O Lord, please accept this food offering accompanied by various kinds of eatables and delicacies;
O Supreme Lord, accept it, which is perfectly endowed with all these essences.
The mantra for the food offering (naivedya).
O Lord of Gods, please accept this betel leaf offered by me, together with areca nut, betel nut, and camphor. (22)
The mantra for betel-leaf.
Having offered incense with devotion—namely agallochum and guggulu mixed with clarified butter—one should perform worship in this manner and offer a lamp with clarified butter. (23)
Having prepared various lamps with a concentrated mind before Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, in the vicinity of a grove of Tulasī, O tiger among sages; 24.
There, an *argha* offering should be presented to the God of gods, the wielder of the discus;
for the sake of obtaining a son, an excellent *argha* should be offered with nine coconut fruits. (25)
On the tenth [lunar day], one should offer a citron for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
on the eleventh, with a pomegranate, one shall always destroy poverty. (26)
O Nārada, it should be joined with the seven grains and placed in a vessel of bamboo,
together with seven fruits and provided with betel leaves.
Having covered it with a cloth, one should present it before the God;
listen, O best of Brahmins, with a one-pointed mind, to this mantra: ||28||
O God, accompanied by Tulasī and joined by Sadāśiva, accept this arghya offered by me; O God of gods, salutations to you. (29)
The *argha* mantra:
Having thus worshipped Janārdana together with Lakṣmī, the Lord of Gods, one should pray to the God of the gods for the successful completion of the vow. (30)
"O Lord of Gods, I have observed the fast, free from desire and anger;
O Lord of Gods, by virtue of this vow, you alone are my refuge. (31)
O Lord, whatever has been performed by me that was incomplete while this vow was being undertaken—may all that become complete through your grace, O Janārdana. (32)
Salutations to you whose eyes are like lotus petals; salutations to you who recline upon the waters. O Keśava, by your grace, this vow has been performed by me.
O Keśava, by means of this vow which destroys the darkness of ignorance, become gracious with a favorable countenance and grant us the vision of knowledge. (34)

Then, there should be a vigil during the night, accompanied by singing, the recitation of sacred texts, and auspicious, meritorious narratives performed by those skilled in music, dance, and the arts. (35)
When the night has dawned and the stainless sun has risen, he should,
with devotion, invite the Brāhmaṇas and perform the Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha.
Having fed them as desired with milk-rice and ghee, accompanied by betel, flowers, perfumes, and other gifts along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā). ||37||
An upper garment, a lower garment, a seat, a garland, sandalwood paste, a pair of sandals, three types of food, clothing, ornaments, and saffron. (38)
One should fill the vessels for the Śapas with whatever one is able, using sprouted grains, coconuts, cooked foods, various garments, and fruits. (39)
One should cause the preceptor, together with his wife, to put on garments right there;
one should honor him with divine ornaments, perfumes, and garlands. (40)
One should give a milch cow equipped with all necessary utensils, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and garments; listen as I declare this to you. (41)
Whatever merit arises for men who have bathed in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), he shall obtain that entire fruit through the grace of the God of gods. ||42||
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures and all delightful objects of desire, one attains the station of Viṣṇu at the end through the grace of Viṣṇu. ||43||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Three-Night Tulasī Vow," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada.
(26) The Twenty-sixth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Tell me, what things in this world might a person give, even while desiring to bestow gifts upon Brahmins who are superior in virtue?
Mahādeva said:
O best of divine sages, having understood the true nature of the world, listen! They praise food alone in this way; everything is established upon food.
Therefore, human beings especially desire to give food;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to that of food. (3)
By food the entire world, both the stationary and the moving, is sustained;
food provides vigor in the world, for the vital breaths are established in food. (4)
One who desires his own welfare should give edible food as alms to a high-souled Brāhmaṇa, even by causing hardship to his own family. (5)
O Nārada, he who, being the best among attendants, gives food to a distressed Brāhmaṇa who asks for it, provides for his own welfare in the world beyond.
One should seek to provide for one's own prosperity by honoring a twice-born guest who has arrived at the proper time—one who is weary from the road and has come to the house of a householder. (7)
The wise man who gives food, being well-behaved and free from envy,
having cast off arisen anger, attains that happiness which exists both here and in the divine realm.
One should neither revile a guest nor bear him ill will in any way;
one should offer food to a knower of Brahman, for that gift is preeminent.
Whoever gives food to one who is exhausted, to one who has never seen such hospitality before, or to one returning from a journey—even if it be but meager—he shall attain all dharmas. ||10||
O great sage, that man who gratifies the ancestors, the gods, the brahmins, and guests with food gains infinite merit. (11)
Even after committing a very great sin, he who gives food to one who asks—especially to a Brāhmaṇa—is liberated from those sins. (12)
A gift of food given to Brahmins yields inexhaustible merit, while food given to a Śūdra yields great fruit;
indeed, the gift of food remains [efficacious] both for the Śūdra and for the Brahmin.
One should not ask about his lineage, conduct, or even his Vedic study; for a Brahmin who arrives as a mendicant gives food and departs. (14)
For the giver of food, auspicious trees bearing the fruits of all desires arise both in this world and in heaven, where they bring him joy. (15)
"Listen, O great sage, to those worlds attained through the gift of food;
the celestial chariots of these high-souled ones shine brilliantly in heaven. (16)
Trees of various forms and structures, endowed with diverse desires, stood throughout the world, yielding the fruits of every wish.
There were auspicious golden ponds and all kinds of large lakes everywhere,
as well as thousands of resonant musical instruments that had been set free.
There were mountains consisting of various kinds of food and drink, as well as garments and ornaments;
likewise, there were rivers flowing with milk and mountains of clarified butter.
Palaces possessing a brilliant white luster and couches resplendent with gold—because people desire to give such things as food, one should therefore become a giver of food. (20)
These worlds belong to those who perform meritorious deeds; the gift of food yields great fruit.
Therefore, food in particular should be given by men on this earth.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Gift of Food," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
Chapter Twenty-Seven. Mahādeva said:
The gift of water is always the supreme among all gifts and the most excellent.
Therefore, one should cause large oblong ponds, wells, and tanks to be constructed. ||1||
Wells that constantly provide flowing water take away half the sin of a person who performs improper actions, provided they themselves are always well-conducted.
If one causes cattle, Brahmins, and virtuous men to always drink from a water reservoir that he has himself excavated, it brings him auspiciousness. (3)
O Nārada, in the summer season, water remains for him in a place that is difficult to access,
rugged, and arduous, which is never found at any other time.
And I shall describe the merits that are traditionally ascribed to constructed reservoirs;
for the owner of a reservoir is honored everywhere throughout the three worlds. (5)
Alternatively, one should recognize that a tank is the best kind of friend's abode, for it increases friendship with friends, generates renown, and is most excellent. (6)
The wise say that the fruit of dharma, artha, and kāma is a well-constructed reservoir in a suitable location, serving as a great refuge in the midst of the land. (7)
One should observe the four kinds of beings in the pond;
all ponds indeed bestow the highest welfare. (8)
Gods, humans, gandharvas, ancestors, nāgas, and rākṣasas,
as well as immobile beings, all take refuge in a reservoir of water.
In whatever pond the water remains during the rainy season, the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice is produced there; of this there is no doubt. ||10||
He in whose water remains even during the months of Hemanta and Śiśira obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt. ||11||
If water remains even during such a scorching summer,
the wise declare that its merit is equal to the fruits of the Atirātra and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Now, O great sage, hear the merits of planting these trees, which benefit both the ancestral lineage of the past and the future. (13)
The planter of trees shall deliver [beings]; therefore, one should plant trees. There is no doubt that these trees become sons and grandsons. (14)
Even having gone to the next world, he attains imperishable worlds;
with flowers he honors all the hosts of gods, and likewise with leaves, the ancestors.
The trees honor all guests with their shade—Kinnaras, Uragas, Rakṣasas, Devas, Gandharvas, and humans alike. (16)
Likewise, hosts of sages take refuge in trees that are flowering and laden with fruit, thereby satisfying those who are weary.
In this world and in the next, these are considered sons according to dharma:
those who plant tanks and trees, and those twice-born ones who perform sacrifices and rites. (18)
These do not fall from heaven, nor do others who speak the truth;
truth alone is the supreme Brahman, and truth alone is the supreme austerity. (19)
Truth alone is the supreme sacrifice; truth alone is the supreme sacred revelation.
Truth awakens among the gods, and truth is the highest state.
Austerity, sacrifice, merit, as well as the worship of gods and sages,
the primary ritual injunctions, and knowledge— all these are established in truth.
Truth is sacrifice, as well as charity; the mantras are the goddess Sarasvatī;
the practice of vows is truth, and the syllable Oṃ is indeed truth itself. (22)
By truth the wind blows; by truth the sun rises;
by truth the fire burns; and by truth heaven stands firm. ||23||
The worship of all the gods and bathing in all the sacred fords—by speaking the truth in this world, one obtains all of these without a doubt. ||24||
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
of all sacrifices whatsoever, truth alone was found to be superior. (25)
By truth the gods are pleased, as are the ancestors and the seers;
they say truth is the supreme dharma, they say truth is the supreme state.
"They say that truth is the supreme Brahman; therefore, speak the truth.
The sages, devoted to truth, performed most difficult austerities. (27)
Delighting in truth and righteousness, those perfected ones (siddhas) then went to heaven,
surrounded on all sides by celestial chariots resounded with the voices of throngs of apsaras.
And it should be said: "The unreal is not true; there is nothing higher than the real, within the heart that is a pure, deep, vast, and perfected sacred ford. (29)

Those who are disciplined in mind should bathe; that is remembered as the supreme bath. Whether for their own sake, for the sake of others, or even for the sake of their sons, those men by whom no falsehood has been spoken go to heaven. (30)
The Vedas, sacrifices, and likewise the sacred mantras abide eternally within the wise; they do not exist in those who have abandoned truth. Therefore, one should practice truth.
Nārada said: Tell me again, specifically, the singular fruit of austerities,
and the power of austerity belonging to all the castes and especially to the Brāhmaṇas.
I shall proclaim the austerity of meditation, which accomplishes all desired aims; it is extremely difficult for the twice-born to practice—listen as I speak of it. (33)
For austerity is declared to be supreme; through austerity one obtains the fruit [of one's desires].
Therefore, he who is constantly devoted to austerity rejoices together with the gods. (34)
Through austerity heaven is attained; through austerity fame is attained;
through austerity one attains liberation; and through austerity one obtains the Great.
Through austerity, one obtains everything— perfection in knowledge and discernment, good fortune, and beauty itself— whatever one desires in one's mind.
Those who have not performed intense austerity never go to the world of Brahmā;
whatever purpose a person may have in mind, they perform austerity while remaining steadfast in it. (37)
A human being attains all of that in the next world;

even a drinker of liquor, a violator of another's wife, a slayer of a Brahmin, or one who has violated the teacher’s bed—through austerity, they overcome it all and are liberated from everything. (38)
Even Sthāṇu, the Lord of All, Viṣṇu the Eternal, Brahmā, Agni, Śakra, and whoever else is endowed with ascetic power [are surpassed]. (39)
Eighty-six thousand sages of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) dwell there, performing austerities together with the deities. (40)
By means of austerity, Śakra and all the Asuras of old attained sovereignty;
through austerity they protected everyone, bestowing cessation [of suffering] day after day.
The two gods, the Sun and the Moon, who are devoted to the welfare of the entire world,
illuminate the constellations and the planets by means of their ascetic power alone.
One attains everything through austerity and enjoys all happiness;
he who practices austerity in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, [attains this]. (43)
O Sage, the merit that an excellent twice-born man obtains from teaching the Śruti is equal to the merit of all forms of austerity combined, provided he first studies the Śruti himself. (44)
By reciting that chapter, one enjoys twice the fruit;
for without the moon and the sun, the world would be without light. 45.
O great sage, one who performs penance and maintains knowledge according to the scriptures must likewise study the Purāṇas from us. (46)
Therefore, he awakens the world and is the most venerable teacher;
among all worthy recipients, the knower of the Purāṇas is the most excellent recipient. (47)
Because it protects one from falling, it is therefore called a "vessel" (pātra);
[one should give] wealth, grain, gold, or various kinds of garments. 48.
Those who bestow [gifts] upon a worthy recipient attain the supreme state;
likewise, those who give cows, female buffaloes, elephants, and beautiful horses.
Listen to the fruit of that merit for one who bestows [this] upon a preeminent person:
he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, which is inexhaustible for all worlds. (50)
He who gives to another a beautiful, fertile, and ploughed field of earth truly delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants.
And by means of a divine celestial chariot, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
the gods do not attain satisfaction through sacrifices, nor even through ritual sprinklings.
He who should cause a Dharma manuscript to be placed in a temple of Viṣṇu by means of offerings, flower-worship, and recitations from the book according to the rules, [attains great merit]. (53)
Furthermore, a human being obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices by [worshipping] the Goddess, Śambhu, Gaṇeśa, and likewise the Sun.
By reading the meritorious books of Itihāsa and Purāṇa,
one attains all desires and pierces through to the world of the Sun.
Having pierced through the world of the sun, he goes to the world of Brahmā;
staying there for hundreds of kalpas, he becomes a king upon the earth.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from a thousand horse-sacrifices, that same fruit one obtains by reciting the *Devāgneya*. (57)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the recitation of books concerning the Itihāsas and Purāṇas within a temple of Viṣṇu;
for nothing else is so pleasing to Viṣṇu, nor likewise to the other inhabitants of heaven. (58)

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Exposition of Dharma Concerning Trees, Wells, Lakes, and Austerities," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||27||
The twenty-eighth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
In this regard, I shall also cite this ancient historical narrative.
The Purāṇa is supremely meritorious, auspicious, and the remover of all sins. ||1||
Having paid homage to the Grandfather of the worlds, the Kumāra spoke this narrative of mine, O divine sage, as told by the son of Brahmā.
Sanatkumāra said: "O Indra, I went to see Dharmarāja;
having been honored with supreme devotion by the Śrutis, I was addressed by him while seated on a comfortable throne."
As I sat there, I beheld a certain great marvel:
a celestial chariot with a pedestal made of lapis lazuli.
O best of gods, a man arrived there, adorned with a network of tinkling bells and variegated with jewels and pearls, [seated] upon a throne.
Rising up in haste and seeing Adharma himself,
the Lord took him by his right hand and honored him with the offering of water (arghya).
Then the Lord of Gods, having smelled [his head] and placed him before him, and having honored that Dharma, spoke these words: ||7||
"Welcome, O seer of the Dharma! I am delighted by the sight of you.
Please sit near me and tell me whatever knowledge you possess. (8)
"Furthermore, you shall go to that place where Brahmā resides. Having been told this, another [being] then mounted an excellent celestial chariot.
The god-like man arrived where Dharmarāja was stationed;
he was honored by him, who stood in his celestial chariot, bowing down with humility.
Having spoken thus with conciliatory words, the man himself asked as before: "What deed has been performed by this man, for which you are so exceedingly pleased? (11)
In this matter, a single curiosity has arisen in me, which I have resolved for myself:
that you performed his worship with such boundless wonder. (12)
In the same way, I considered those two men of excellent character— who had performed worship for the second time— to be doers of auspicious deeds as they ascended the celestial chariot.
Since you yourself perform worship to these two for the sake of Dharma, you are yourself constantly and perpetually worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (14)
What deeds did these two perform, by which such supreme merit was acquired? Tell me, how did they obtain this divine fruit of omniscience? (15)
Having heard that, Aśvatthāman said: "Listen, O high-minded one, to the deed performed by these two; hear how, having done what was worthy, they have arrived here. (16)
Dharma said: There is a city on earth renowned by the name Vaidiśa; there lived a protector of the earth known as Dharāpāla. (17)
At what time in the past did the Goddess, out of anger, curse her own attendant, saying: "Except for me, no other woman shall be placed by you with another as her husband"? (18)
"Therefore, you shall become a jackal for twelve years.
Having been told this, he wandered as a jackal over the surface of the earth. (19)
"At the world-renowned confluence of the Vetasī and the Vetravatī,
you shall become a son through a curse," thus was it said by the Daughter of the Mountain.
Having performed a fast there in that sacred field, he then gave up his life-breaths;
having assumed a body of divine form, he went into the presence of Viṣṇu.
Having witnessed that great marvel there, King Adharapāla constructed a sanctuary for Viṣṇu and then cast off his life-breath in that sacred field.
Having assumed a body of divine form, he established that Lord there,
appointing all the men in that city to the task of gazing upon him.
That auspicious abode of Viṣṇu was always filled with people, including Brāhmaṇas and others; having honored them all, he reached Kadaṃbaka.
The high-minded one, having especially honored that best of the twice-born reciter, who was an expert in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and preeminent in learning, [proceeded]. (25)
Having worshipped the book in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
the king, filled with humility, then addressed that reciter.
This abode of Viṣṇu was constructed by you in front [of him];
and this fourfold order of society (cāturvarṇya) also desires to hear about the Kadamba tree. ||27||
"O best of the twice-born, remain here for one year reading the Kuru-pustaka, while receiving from me an unsurpassed livelihood. (28)
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, for the sake of my own welfare, I shall give another hundred gold *niṣkas* when the year is complete. (29)
O best of sages, when the recitation of the book has been thus performed there for even a single year, such merit is produced.
Then, upon the exhaustion of his lifespan, he met the law of time;
and by me, his celestial chariot was driven from heaven by Viṣṇu.
Thus ends this manifestation of karmas, known as the meritorious narrative;
the great and holy *Pādma* [Purāṇa], which is sacred and the destroyer of sins. 32.
Just as satisfaction does not arise for all the gods here through offerings of perfumes and flowers, so it is produced by listening to the Purāṇas. (33)
Indeed, satisfaction does not arise from the gift of objects such as gold and jewels, nor even entirely from garments, villages, or cities. (34)
O best of sages, just as all the inhabitants of heaven experience joy from hearing the Dharma, so too do they from hearing the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. (35)
Just as there is great joy for me when this goal, which fulfills all desires and aims, is accomplished, O best of sages, may there be great joy for me in the giving away of this maiden. (36)
And it did not please her as much as reading from the book; so, what is the use of saying more? Nothing else is pleasing to me. (37)
This secret of the Brahmins has been proclaimed without exception as a narrative of merit;
and this other best of men who has arrived here, O Brahmin— ||38||
Having followed this excellent hearing of the Dharma through association, he developed devotion toward the Supreme Self with faith. (39)
Having performed a circumambulation of that high-souled reciter,
O best of sages, this brahmin gave him a māṣaka of gold.
Never did he perform any other act of giving with a mind possessed by greed;
yet, there is no doubt that the attainment of fruit from giving to worthy recipients has arisen for him. (41)
Thus has this action been described by these two, O great sage.
Mahādeva said:
Those wise ones who hear this greatness of this merit shall never experience an evil fate in birth after birth. 43.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Exposition of the Scriptures," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||28||
The twenty-ninth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Now I shall proclaim another [matter]; listen, O best of divine sages!
The greatness of Gopīcandana, as it has been seen and heard by me.
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even a twice-born man, one who is smeared with Gopīcandana is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. ||2||
Whoever applies a tilaka mark produced from Gopīcandana is liberated from the faults of drinking liquor and other such sins; of this there is no doubt. ||3||
Anointed with Gopīcandana, a devotee of the cow and of Viṣṇu who is intent upon Viṣṇu shall be liberated from all defects, just as one is purified by the ashes of the Gaṅgā.
Whether he be a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief of gold, or likewise one who has violated the teacher’s bed—whether he be a Śūdra or even a twice-born (dvija). ||5||
One is immediately liberated from the sins accumulated over hundreds of lifetimes;
this "Twelve Tilaka" is proclaimed for all people, and especially so.
For Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas who desire prosperity,
the mark on the forehead should be in the shape of a staff, while that on the chest should be in the shape of a lotus.
Another [mark] at the base of the arm resembles a bamboo leaf, while another has the shape of a lamp;
furthermore, there are four prominent circles (cakras) at the right base of the arm.
One should hold two name-seals (nāmamudrā) below, and a single conch-shell seal beneath those two as well; furthermore, one should place two lotus seals on either side of that [conch]. (9)
From the left nipple, one should utter the name as before, followed by *śaṃ* and *khān*.
One should recite "one wheel" for these two, according to their distinction. (10)
On the forehead, one mace, and likewise a name-seal on the heart;
three each on the two middle branches, and three each on both [the other] branches. (11)
Above the heart, the sides, and the breasts are the mace and the lotus, like the arms;
there are three and four wheels respectively at the roots of the two ears below.
One should wear each [mark] upon the other *tilakas*, and one should wear the *sampradāya* mudrā according to the tradition of one's lineage. ||13||
It may be worn according to one's preference, for there are no restrictive rules in this matter; even those as low as the outcaste Cāṇḍālas are purified simply by wearing the *tilaka*.
I consider one who reviles Vaiṣṇavas to be worse than a Cāṇḍāla; he should be known as equal to Viṣṇu himself—of this there is no doubt to be made. 15.
That brāhmaṇa who is a Vaiṣṇava and is devoted to meditations upon Viṣṇu—no one else should be known as such;
he alone is truly Viṣṇu in this world. (16)
The Brahmin who bears the conch and the discus and is devoted to the study of the Vedas is indeed recited in the Veda as "He is Nārāyaṇa. (17)
O Brahmin, the bearer of the heated discus is the purifier of those who purify the world;
one who possesses devotion toward him, O Brahmin, is liberated from great sins. 18.
By wearing a garland of Tulasī leaves or one made from Tulasī wood, a Brāhmaṇa shall undoubtedly become a partaker of liberation. 19.
Since a brahmin possesses the form of Viṣṇu, he is traditionally remembered as a Vaiṣṇava;
even after his death, he bears a tilaka made from gopīcandana.
Having ascended a celestial chariot, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
O Nārada, I shall now describe the *tilaka* made of Gopīcandana for the Kali age. 21.
For those best among men who wear the conch and likewise the discus on the right and the left [arms], there is never an evil rebirth anywhere.
By holding it with haste, one is liberated without distinction from great sins—even those addicted to drinking liquor and those who are slayers of women and children. (23)
O Vāḍava, such things as approaching those who should not be approached are seen on this earth;
there is no doubt that your statement regarding devotees is exactly so. 24.
In this cycle of existence, whose essence is so trivial, where indeed could Vaiṣṇava people come from?
For I have been born as a Vaiṣṇava through the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu. (25)
Indeed, for those dwelling here in Kāśī, by the power of repeatedly chanting "Rāma, Rāma," Śiva himself will surely appear;
of this there is no doubt. (26)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gopīcandana," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||29||
The thirtieth chapter.
Nārada said:
O Brahmin, [I shall describe] the supreme procedure for the lamp known as the Year (Saṃvatsara).
Please proclaim the greatness of that which is the foremost of all vows.
By this, all vows have indeed been performed; of this there is no doubt.
There shall be the fulfillment of all desires and the destruction of all sins. ||2||
Mahādeva said: I shall declare the secret of the divine sage as you have requested, which destroys all sin;
by hearing which, even a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a betrayer of friends, or one who violates the teacher’s bed [is purified].
A cruel-souled betrayer of trust attains eternal liberation;
having uplifted a hundred generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||4||
Therefore, I shall describe this unsurpassed Dīpa-vrata,
including its procedure for a period of one year and its greatness as well.
Having reached the auspicious eleventh day (Ekādaśī) in the first month of Hemanta,
one should rise during the Brāhma-muhūrta, free from desire and anger.
One who has not disciplined his self should perform his bath at the confluences of rivers, at sacred fords, in ponds, or in streams; or he may do so at home.
I have bathed in all sacred fords; grant me this bath forever.
The mantra for bathing.
Having gratified the gods and the ancestors, performed his silent prayers, and subdued his senses,

Ten *hasta*s constitute a *daṇḍa* here; six *daṇḍa*s make a *nivartana*.

Where this Trita stands with a thousand cows and a bull, along with a cow that has recently calved, that is traditionally known as *gocarma*.
If one should give [this] to a brahmin endowed with virtues, possessed of austerity, and whose senses are subdued,

"The son who goes to Gayā shall be a savior from old age.

He who accepts land and he who bestows land—both of them are performers of meritorious deeds and are destined for heaven. (33)
Those men by whom land has been taken away through unjust means,
and those who cause it to be taken away— they shall be slain along with their lineage up to the seventh generation.
But he who steals it or causes it to be stolen, being dull-witted and shrouded in darkness, is bound by the nooses of Varuṇa and is born among the animal wombs. ||35||
The proclamation of those gifts is accompanied by falling tears;
