Indeed, when the breaking of the fast is performed on the twelfth day, the merit is multiplied a thousandfold;
[so too for fasting on] the eighth, the eleventh, the sixth, the third, and the fourteenth. (112)

One should not observe the Ekādaśī that is pierced by the previous day; one should fast on the one pierced by the following day, for the Ekādaśī must last for a full day and night, even if it consists of only a single ghaṭikā at dawn. ||113||
That lunar day (tithi) should be avoided; instead, one should observe the fast on the one joined with the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
Such is what I have declared regarding both fortnights. 114.
One should certainly observe a fast on the eleventh day; of this there is no doubt.
They go to the abode of Viṣṇu, where the one whose banner is Garuḍa resides.
Blessed are those men in the world who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu and who recite the greatness of Ekādaśī at all times. (116)
That person who listens with devotion, whether by day or by night, obtains the merit equal to the gift of a thousand cows. ||117||
They are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
O best of kings, there is nothing equal to the Viṣṇu-dharma, nor is there anything equal to the meaning of the Gītā;
there is no vow for the destruction of sin equal to Ekādaśī. (118)
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara,
[this is] the section titled "The Origin of Ekādaśī and the Slaying of Mura."
The thirty-eighth chapter. ||38||
(39) Chapter Thirty-nine.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

Oṃ! [I bow to] Lord Viṣṇu, the all-pervading one, who is manifestly the bringer of happiness to the three worlds, the Lord of the universe, the creator of the universe, the ancient one, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||1||
I ask you, O Lord of the gods of gods; I have a great doubt for the sake of the welfare of the worlds and for the purpose of destroying sins. (2)
On which day does the Ekādaśī fall during the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa? What is its name, what is the ritual procedure for it, and which deity is worshipped there?
O Lord, explain this to me in detail and exactly as it is.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, you have asked well; thus you possess pure fame.
O Indra among kings, I shall describe the most excellent day of Hari.
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is most dear to me when it arises in the month of Āśvina;
its appearance in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is the very source of my own body. ||5||
O bull among the Bharatas, O best of kings, I have related to you this account of how she was born for the purpose of slaying the gods and asuras, and how it was told to me by Agni.
O King, this Ekādaśī is foremost in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile;
it is known by the name Utpatti, occurring in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim that which occurs on the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa,
by the mere hearing of which one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
This is declared to be the supreme *Mokṣānavī*, which removes all sins;
O King, one should worship the god Dāmodara with great effort. ||9||
With Tulasī sprouts, incense, and lamps, one should worship with diligence according to the previously mentioned procedure on the tenth and eleventh lunar days.
The eleventh day known as Mokṣā destroys even the greatest sins;
on that night, a vigil should be observed for me with dance, song, and hymns of praise. (11)
Listen, O King, I shall relate a divine ancient tale, by the mere hearing of which the destruction of all sins occurs. (12)
And by the gift of merit from this [person], the ancestors who have fallen into lower wombs through his sin attain liberation; of this there is no doubt. (13)
In that very city of Campaka, adorned by Vaiṣṇavas,
a king named Vaikhānasa protected his subjects like a father protects his own children.
Many Brahmins, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary branches, resided there;
for the subjects of that King Vaikhānasa were indeed prosperous.
O King, while governing his kingdom in this manner, he saw his own ancestors in the midst of a dream at night, having fallen into lower births.
Having seen all of them thus, his mind filled with wonder,
he related the account of what had occurred in his dream to the twice-born ones.
The king said:
"I have seen my own ancestors, the twice-born, who have fallen into hell;
they said, 'O son, you must deliver us from this ocean of hell.'"
O best of the twice-born, I certainly saw her speaking thus and weeping again and again; therefore, there is no happiness for me. (19)
"O twice-born ones, this great kingdom of mine, which bestows happiness, along with all its horses, elephants, and cattle, is now yours. (20)
"O best of the twice-born, neither my husband, nor my sons, nor my mother please me.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? My heart is being constricted. (21)
O best of the twice-born, tell me that vow and that application of austerity by which my ancestors attained liberation immediately, and indeed reached a state of freedom from worldly distress.
While this powerful great soul is still alive, what fruit is there for his father in that terrible hell? (23)
The brahmins said:
"O King, there is a great hermitage near the sage Parvata;
O tiger among kings, go there, for you recognize what is auspicious. (24)
Having heard their words, the great king Vaikhānasa then went quickly to that very hermitage of the mountain.
Surrounded by brahmins and accompanied by kings,
that best of monarchs arrived at his vast hermitage.
There, he was surrounded by sages who were experts in the study of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda,
just as the second [face] of Brahmā is surrounded by them.
Having seen that tiger among sages,
King Vaikhānasa likewise prostrated himself like a staff and touched the feet of the sage.
The sage inquired after his welfare in the seven constituent parts of sovereignty,
as well as the king's freedom from thorns [enemies] and his possession of royal happiness.
The king said:
"O Lord, by your grace, all is well with my seven limbs;
for how could there be any obstacle for those who are devoted to Viṣṇu and the Brahmins? (30)
O best of the twice-born, I have seen my own ancestors situated in hell in a dream; by the power of whose merit do they attain liberation? (31)
"O Lord, this doubt of mine has brought me here to question you;
O best of sages, some means must be employed in this matter. (32)
Having heard these words, the mountain, that best of sages, became motionless with eyes fixed in meditation; he was an ascetic equal to Brahmā.
Remaining absorbed in meditation for a single moment, he replied to the lord of the earth:
"O Indra among kings, the former deeds of your ancestors have been understood."
In a previous birth, you were a kṣatriya proud of his kingdom;
when your co-wife approached her season, you acted contrary to the duties of a king. ||35||
Having gone to another village, he left his own wife for the sake of his business;
however, her father did not grant her the gift of the fertile season (ṛtudāna). ||36||
O tiger among kings, by the power of that evil deed, your father has fallen along with his ancestors into a most terrible hell. (37)
Then the king spoke again to the Vaikhānasa sage: "O Sage, by the power of what vow can their liberation be attained? (38)
The sage said:
"In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, there is one known by the name Mokṣā;
this vow should be performed by all, and let merit be offered to the ancestors. (39)
By the power of that merit, their liberation will come to pass;
this is true, O highly fortunate one, just as the word of Brahmā is.
Then, having heard the sage’s words, he returned to his own home;
indeed, the month of Mārgaśīrṣa arrived for him with great difficulty.
Having performed that vow according to the sage’s word, the king, that lord of the earth, offered the merit together with all [others] to his father. 42.
At that very moment of merit, no rain of flowers fell from the sky;
indeed, the son of the Vaikhānasa entered liberation through his ancestors.
And he spoke these auspicious words to King Cāṃtarikṣa: "May there be well-being, may there be well-being for you, my son," and having said this, he departed to heaven.
O King, for one who thus observes the auspicious Mokṣa-Ekādaśī, his sins are destroyed; upon death, he shall attain liberation. ||45||
There is no Ekādaśī superior to this which bestows liberation;
O King, I do not know the measure of its merit, for this vow is dear to me. (46)
This [work] is equal to the Cintāmaṇi jewel for men, bestowing liberation;
by reading or hearing it, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. (47)

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Liberating Ekādaśī of the Bright Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||39||
The fortieth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa?
Tell me this in detail: what is the ritual procedure for her?
O Lord, please explain this: which deity is worshipped there? (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O king of kings, out of the bonds of affection for you, I shall speak;
O King, my satisfaction is not so great from sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees as it is from this.
Just as satisfaction and prosperity indeed come through the Ekādaśī vow, therefore the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) should be observed with every possible effort. ||3||
O confident one, this is true and not false for those established in righteousness: that on the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, there is no fruit for those who do not know [the name]. (4)
On that [day], one should worship the god Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rite;
the auspicious Ekādaśī should be observed by means of this very same procedure as before.
Just as the consumer of serpents is among the snakes and all winged creatures, as Viṣṇu is among the gods, and as the twice-born is among bipeds; ||6||
And just as, O King, the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) is the best among vows, so too, O King,
the Tejanas and Bhoras are always to be honored by me.
Those who remain secluded on the day of Hari and observe the Ekādaśī vow obtain wealth in this very world and, upon death, attain liberation.
O King, when the *saphalā* tree bears fruit, one should worship Hari by His names with its fruits, as well as with coconuts, betel nuts, and citrons. (9)
With *jaṃbū* fruits, pomegranates, and likewise auspicious *āmalaka* fruits;
with *lavaṅga*, jujubes, and especially with mangoes. (10)
One should worship the Lord of the gods with incense and lamps;
indeed, one should especially perform the offering of lamps on the Saphalā day.
A vigil should indeed be observed at night together with the Vaiṣṇavas;
one remains awake through the night for as long as it takes for a single blink of an eye.
Listen indeed to the merit of one whose mind is single-pointed and who is free from the stain of kingship; there is no sacrifice equal to that, nor is there any sacred ford (tīrtha) equal to it. 13.
All other vows do not equal even a sixteenth part of this;
likewise, the fruit that is obtained through asceticism for thousands of years is not even a fraction of this.
He who performs the vigil for the Twice-born attains that fruit;
O tiger among kings, hear now the auspicious narrative of its fruitful result. (15)
And there was the city of Māhiṣmatī, renowned as Caṃpā;
that royal sage had five sons who were young princes.
Among them, the eldest was indeed always devoted to great sins;
he was an adulterer with the wives of others, addicted to prostitutes, and a drunkard. (17)
That man of sinful deeds squandered his father’s wealth; he was constantly devoted to an evil way of life and a reviler of the Brahmins. (18)
He constantly reviled the Vaiṣṇavas and the gods;
seeing his son acting in such a manner, King Māhiṣmata [was distressed]. (19)
He recited the *Atulumpaka-itihāsa* among the princes;
consequently, he was expelled from the kingdom by his father and his kinsmen.
Abandoned by his own followers and likewise opposed by others, Lumpaka then reflected upon this. (21)
"Abandoned by my kinsmen and indeed expelled from the kingdom by my father"—
thinking thus, he then formed a sinful intention.
"I must indeed dwell in this dreadful, dense forest;
therefore, I shall utterly destroy the entire city of my father. (23)
Having thus formed this resolution, the Lumpaka,
by the turn of fate, departed from that city and went into the dense forest.
Constantly devoted to the slaughter of living beings and a treasury of skills in theft and gambling,
that man of evil deeds plundered the entire city.
Having been caught by the night-stalkers in the city for committing theft, he said to them: "I am the son of King Vairāja of Mahiṣmatī. (26)
Released from them, that doer of evil deeds returned once more to the forest, constantly delighting in sensual pleasures and feeding on the fruit of the tree. ||27||
In the vicinity of that wicked Vāsudeva was his hermitage;
there stood an old, many-year-old aśvattha tree. ||28||
The great divinity of that tree resides in the forest;
and right there dwells Lumpaka, who is evil-minded. (29)
When much time had passed, due to the accumulation of merit by someone, on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, thus [it occurred]. ||30||
Having eaten the fruits of the trees and being afflicted by the cold at night, the most wicked man named Lumpaka, stripped of his clothes and with his vision failing, departed. (31)
Afflicted by the extreme cold near the harivṛkṣa tree, she could neither sleep nor find comfort; her life-breath seemed as if it had already departed.
Thus the entire night was spent with her mouth covered by her teeth;
even at sunrise, that most wicked man did not regain his senses.
When the sun had reached the middle of the sky, the thief Lumpaka likewise attained consciousness through the power of the *saphalā* and other mantras.
Then, looking back from here and there, he became distressed and, with faltering steps, moved away from that seat, striking the sky again and again.
Having entered the middle of the forest there, he became afflicted, emaciated by hunger;
yet the wicked-souled Lumpaka had no power to kill living beings.
O King, that hunter gathered those fruits;
meanwhile, by the time he had returned there, the sun had set.
"What will happen, father? he cried out in lamentation;
there, at the foot of the tree, he placed many fruits.
"By these fruits, may Hari, the Lord of Śrī, be pleased," he said;
and having spoken thus, the thief indeed obtained sleep that very night.
O sinless one, Viṣṇu considered the night-vigil of that evil-minded man to be [fruitful], whereas he considered the worship with fruits of that fruitless person to be likewise [fruitful]. 40.
"This Vaisya outcaste performed this very vow spontaneously;
by the power of that merit, he obtained a kingdom free from all thorns. (41)
Viṣṇu traveled for as long as it takes for the sun to rise; at that moment in the sky, an incorporeal voice spoke.
"You shall obtain the kingdom and [the status of] a son through the grace of Saphalā.
When these words were spoken, he assumed a divine form. (43)
Then, O King, his supreme devotion to Viṣṇu arose;
richly adorned with divine ornaments, he obtained a kingdom free from all thorns.
He ruled the kingdom for fifteen years;
by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, Manojava became his son and Dāra his wife.
Having renounced his swift sovereignty and having entrusted it to his son,
he went to the presence of Kṛṣṇa, where, having gone, one does not grieve.
O King, he who thus performs this most excellent and fruitful vow shall obtain happiness in this world and, upon death, attain liberation.
Blessed are those men in this world who are devoted to the fruitful [practice];
there is no need for deliberation here that their birth is truly fruitful. 48.
O lord of the Vaiśyas, by reading, hearing, and performing [this], a human being obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. ||49||

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Fruitful Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of Pauṣa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||40||
The forty-first chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you have described this auspicious Ekādaśī that yields all fruits."
Please tell me, by your grace, that which pertains to the bright fortnight. ||1||
What is the ritual for it, and which deity is worshipped there?
To whom are you, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Person yourself, pleased? (2)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe that which occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa;
I shall tell it, O Great King, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
O King, this [rite] should be performed with diligence according to the previously mentioned procedure;
it is known by the name Putradānā and is supreme in removing all sins.
Nārāyaṇa is its presiding deity, the granter of desires and the bestower of perfection;
there is nothing superior to this in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile. (5)
Hari makes that man possessed of knowledge and possessed of fame;
listen, O King, I shall relate the supreme story that removes all sins. (6)
In ancient times, there was a king named Suketumān in the city of Bhadrāvatī; likewise, he had a queen who was devoted to the practice of almsgiving.
Deprived of a son, the king was led away by time through his long-held desires; yet that ruler did not obtain a son who could act as a creator of prosperity.
For a long time, that king reflected upon his unrighteousness:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can the attainment of a son come to pass? (9)
King Suketumān obtained happiness for his people, his kingdom, and his city;
yet, together with that virtuous woman, he became sorrowful day after day.
Both of them, constantly devoted to anxiety and grief for their husband, [suffered thus];
for his ancestors consume only lukewarm water when it is offered. (11)
"Who will we see behind the king, who will satisfy us?"—
thus remembering this, his ancestors became sorrowful.
The ministers, friends, as well as the elephants, horses, and infantry, were pleasing to that king, even though they had no kinsmen and were not his enemies. (13)
Despair constantly dwells within the mind of that king;
for a man deprived of a son, there is indeed no fruit of birth. (14)
The house of one without a son is empty, and his heart is always sorrowful;
without a son, there is no discharge of debt to the ancestors, the gods, and men. (15)
Therefore, with every effort, a man should procreate a son; for them there is fame in this world and a fortunate rebirth in the next world. 16.
But for those performers of meritorious deeds in whose house the birth of a son occurs, longevity, health, and prosperity prevail in their home. (17)
O King, for those people who perform meritorious deeds, there is no attainment of this world where the birth of a son occurs without merit and without devotion to Viṣṇu.
"Whether sons or wealth shall be obtained—this is my firm conviction.
Thinking thus, O King, that monarch found no peace. (19)
Then, at dawn he thought one thing, and at midnight he thought another; thus, the bannered king himself brooded over his own destruction.
Then that king, having reflected upon suicide and the miserable states of existence,
and having seen his own body fallen and his sonlessness, spoke these words.
Having reflected once more with his own intellect upon the means for his own welfare,
the king then mounted his horse and entered the dense forest.
The domestic priest and all the others did not know that the king had gone to that forest frequented by deer and birds, which was filled with fear. 23.
Then the king wandered about, observing the forest trees:
banyans, holy figs, bilvas, dates, and likewise jackfruit trees.
The king saw bakula trees, saptaparṇas, aśokas, tilakas, as well as śālas, tālas, tamālas, and saralas. ||25||
And likewise, [he saw] *iṅgudī* trees, *śleṣmātaka* trees,
as well as *śallakī*s, *karamarda*s, *pāṭala*s, and *badara*s.
Aśokas, capalas, jackals, and even hares; forest cats, buffaloes, porcupines, and yaks as well. (27)
The king saw serpents half-emerged from an anthill,
as well as wild elephants in rut accompanied by their young.
Seeing those fourteen herd-leaders standing in the midst of their female elephant herds,
the king reflected upon himself along with his elephants.
Moving through their midst, the king attained great splendor;
the monarch beheld a forest endowed with a most wonderful sight.
Hearing the cries of jackals on the path as well as the hooting of owls,
and seeing those various bears and deer, he wandered through the middle of the forest.
Thus the king beheld the dense forest as the sun reached its midday course;
afflicted by hunger and thirst, the monarch ran hither and thither.
The king, his throat parched, reflected:
"What deed have I committed that such suffering as this has befallen me? (33)
Indeed, the gods were gratified by me through sacrifices and acts of worship;
likewise, they were gratified by gifts to Brahmins and by offerings of desired food.
And the subjects have always been protected by me most diligently, like my own children;
why then have I encountered such great and terrible suffering? (35)
Thinking thus, the king went forward into the forest; by the power of his merit, he beheld an unsurpassed lake.
It was graced by the touch of fish and further beautified by lotuses;
it was adorned with kāraṇḍava ducks, ruddy geese, and royal swans.
It was filled with many crocodiles, fish, and other aquatic creatures;
nearby that lake were many hermitages of sages.
The fortunate king beheld auspicious omens through the birds;
his right eye throbbed, as did his left hand. (39)
He told the king about the auspicious fruit that was throbbing;
having seen the lord of sages on its bank performing Vedic recitation (japa).
Overcome with great joy, the prince dismounted from that horse and stood before the sages. (41)
Having joined his palms in reverence, he bowed down repeatedly like a staff before those sages who were observing white-vows, addressing each one individually.
The sages replied, "O King, we too are pleased.
The king said, "Tell me who you were, and tell me what that woman named Kācā was to you as well."
"For what purpose have you gathered here? Speak the truth before me. (43)
The sages said: "O King, we are the Viśvedevas who have come here for the purpose of bathing;
we arrived near Māghona on this fifth day."
And today, O King, is the Ekādaśī known as Putradā; on this day, Viṣṇu grants a son to those men who observe the Putradā vow.
The king said:
"This indeed is my great doubt regarding the procreation of a son;
if you are truly pleased with me, then let a son be granted to me. (46)
The sage said:
"O King, today itself begins the day of the gift of sons;
let this supreme vow, renowned as Ekādaśī, be observed."
Therefore, O King of Kings, through this consecration and by the grace of Keśava,
you will certainly obtain a son.
Thus, at their word, the king performed that supreme vow according to the instruction of the sages and the prescribed ritual for the granting of a son.
Having performed the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day and having bowed repeatedly to the sages, the king returned home; thereafter, the queen conceived a child.
A son was born at the time of childbirth, radiant due to his meritorious deeds;
he brought joy to his father and became a protector of his subjects.
Therefore, O King, the supreme Putrada-vrata must be performed for the sake of the welfare of the worlds; it has been described by me before you. 52.

Those mortals who, with single-minded devotion, observe the Putrada vow, shall obtain sons in this world and, upon death, go to heaven. O King, by reading or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (53)

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Ekādaśī for Bestowing Sons in the Bright Half of Pauṣa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
Chapter Forty-Two.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O virtuous Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World, Primordial God, Sovereign of the Universe!"
Please speak out of your grace; show mercy toward me. ||1||
In the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, there occurs the Ekādaśī known as Tuṣṭi;
tell me in detail what the ritual procedure for it is.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O tiger among kings, to that which concerns Kṛṣṇa Māgha; it is renowned as the "Six Sesame Seeds" (Ṣaṭtilā), which destroys all sins. (1)
Listen, O Ṣaṭtilā, to this auspicious narrative that removes sin, which the eminent sage Pulastya once told to Dālbhya. (2)
Dālabhya said:
"O Janaka, those who have entered the world of mortals commit sin;
they are indeed joined with various sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and others. (3)
O Brahmin, tell me truly: how is it that those who steal the property of others and are deluded by the calamities of others do not go to hell? (4)
"O Blessed One, you should tell me how evil may be pacified through a small gift given without effort. (5)
Pulastya said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! This secret is very difficult to obtain, which has not been told to anyone even by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and the gods."
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, being asked by you, I shall relate it;
when the month of Māgha has arrived, one should bathe with purity and have the senses subdued.
Free from lust, anger, pride, envy, greed, and malice,
and having washed his feet with water while recollecting the God of gods.
A person should take cow dung that has not fallen on the ground,
scatter sesame seeds over it, and have small balls of cotton-wool made from it.
And indeed, one hundred and eight [recitations] should be performed; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Then, when Māgha has arrived, if the asterism Āṣāḍhā should occur, ||10||
The root of the dark fortnight is the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) and its observances; therefore, one should undertake them at the auspicious time. Listen now to the procedure for that.
Having thoroughly bathed, being self-restrained and pure, and having worshipped the God of gods,
one should chant the names of Kṛṣṇa whenever there is a stumble or other such mishaps.
One should keep a vigil at night and perform the initial fire-sacrifice;
on the second day, one should again worship Hari, the Lord of the gods.
Then, having consecrated the food offering with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, as well as the *kṛsara* dish, he should do so repeatedly while recollecting [the deity] by the name "Kṛṣṇa. (14)

O best of Brahmins, having worshipped Janārdana according to the prescribed rite, one should offer the *arghya*— filled with *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruits, coconuts, or citron fruits, or, in the absence of all these, with excellent betel nuts— according to the ritual injunctions.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, you who are compassionate, be the refuge for those who have no refuge; be gracious, O Puruṣottama, toward us who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. 16.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe! Salutations to you, O Subrahmaṇya; salutations, O first-born of the Great Being!
Accept this water offering given by me, O Lord of the world, together with Lakṣmī.
Thus ends the mantra for the arghya offering.
Then one should honor the Brahmin and cause him to receive a water-pot, along with an umbrella, sandals, and garments, saying, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased. (18)
A black cow should be given to an excellent twice-born according to one's capacity;
O best of the twice-born, one who is discerning regarding worthy recipients should give a vessel of sesame seeds. (19)

O Sage, at the time of bathing, the first feeding, and the tonsure ceremony, one should diligently offer black sesame seeds to the best of the twice-born according to one's ability. O Brahmin, as many sesame seeds as there are in the sprouts grown from those [seeds], for that many years, O Kṣatriya, [the merit lasts]. (20)
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world— he who bathes with sesame seeds, rubs himself with sesame, performs oblations with sesame, and offers water with sesame.
The giver of sesame seeds and the consumer [of them]—these six types of sesame seeds destroy sin.
Nārada said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, salutations to you, the creator of the universe! 22.
O Yādava, if you are pleased with me, tell me the story along with its narrative: what kind of fruit indeed accrues from the Ṣaṭtilaikādaśī?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, as it happened; I shall relate to you that which was seen.
Long ago in the mortal world, O Nārada, there lived a certain Brāhmaṇī.
Always delighting in the practice of vows, they were ever devoted to the worship of the gods. ||23||
She was constantly devoted to month-long fasts, always intent on my worship, and dedicated to the fast of Kṛṣṇa. ||24||
O best of the twice-born, your body has indeed been emaciated by fasts out of devotion toward the gods, the brahmins, and young maidens. (25)
O twice-born one, that great virtuous woman always gave away her house and other possessions; yet she herself always remained engaged in extreme hardships. 26.
Alms were not given to mendicants, nor were the Brahmins satisfied. ||27||
Then, after a long time, O twice-born one, I thought to myself:
"Her body is indeed purified by arduous vows; of this there is no doubt. (28)
The world of Viṣṇu is indeed attained by this bodily mortification;
for no gift of food has been given by which such supreme satisfaction might be achieved.
Knowing this, O Brahmin, I have come to the world of mortals, having assumed the form of a Kāpālika and begged for alms in a mendicant's bowl. (30)
"O Brahmin, why have you come? Why do you stand before me like a ghost?
When I had spoken thus, she replied, "O beautiful one, give alms to this embodied being. (31)
O Brahmin, out of anger she threw a large lump of clay into a copper vessel; O twice-born one, by the time this occurred, I had returned to heaven once again.
Then, after a long time,
that female ascetic of most rigorous vows attained heaven in her very body through the power of her practice of ascetic discipline.
O brahmin-sage, by the gift of a lump of clay, a charming house was obtained; yet it has come into being entirely devoid of any heap of grain. (34)
"O twice-born one, as long as he gazes at the house and sees nothing else, so long have you come from outside the house, O Mātaṅga. (35)
Overcome with great anger, he spoke these words:
"By me, through many vows, arduous penances, and fasts... (36)
The Lord, the protector of all the worlds, has been propitiated by my worship;
yet, O Janārdana, nothing at all is to be seen there in my house.
Then I said to him: "O lady of great vows, go to his house;
they will surely come, filled with intense curiosity. (38)
The wives of the gods, filled with wonder at the sight of you,
will not open the door unless the recitation of the merit of the six sesame seeds has been performed.
When she had spoken thus,
O Brāhmaṇa, the wives of the gods, overcome with grief, then arrived at that crossing.
They said to her there, "We have indeed come to see you;
open the door now so that we may behold you, O beautiful one. (41)
The human woman said:
"If my sight has a purpose, then the truth must be told, especially regarding the meritorious vow of the six sesame seeds for the sake of opening the door. (42)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: One woman there observed the vow of Ekādaśī with a single sesame seed; another told me that it should be observed with six sesame seeds. (43)
Then, having opened the door, she was seen by them; she was neither a human woman, nor a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a Pannaga woman.
O bull among the twice-born, such a woman as this has never been seen before;
by the instruction of the goddesses, she performed the Ṣaṭtilā vow.

Though she was a human woman devoted to the vow of truth, she did not obtain in an instant that which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is endowed with beauty and splendor. 46.
Wealth, grain, clothing and the like, gold, and silver, as well as a house endowed with every excellence—all this came about through the power of Ṣaṭtilā. ||47||
Endowed with the beauty of form, he did not attain a moment of rest. ||48||
One should avoid excessive greed and must abandon deceit regarding wealth; according to one's own means, one should cause sesame seeds and garments to be given.
In birth after birth, that person indeed attains health;
neither poverty, nor hardship, nor even misfortune shall befall them. (50)
O best of the twice-born, by fasting on the day of the six sesame seeds according to this rite, one becomes a giver of land and sesame seeds; of this there is no doubt. (51)
A human being is liberated from all sins without effort;
and giving a gift according to the rules to a worthy recipient destroys all transgressions.
There is no misfortune whatsoever, nor any physical exertion, O best of kings. (52)

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Ekādaśī of Six Tilas on the Dark Half of Māgha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada.
(43) Chapter Forty-three—
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Excellent, O Kṛṣṇa! You have spoken well; you, O Lord, are the primordial god.
[All beings]—whether born from sweat, born from eggs, born from sprouts, or born from a womb—" ||1||
You are their creator and destroyer, their protector and bringer of decay;
you have described the Ṣaṭtilā vow to be observed during the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
O God, tell me by your grace: what is the Śuklacakra? What is its name, what is the rite for it, and which deity is worshipped therein? (3)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King of kings, I shall describe that which occurs on the bright [fortnight] of Māgha;
it is renowned by the name Jayā, the supreme destroyer of all sins.
The *Trīcaka* bestows purity, removes sin, and grants the fulfillment of desires and liberation to men; it destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin and eradicates the state of being a *piśāca*. (5)
When this vow has been performed, the state of being a preta does not arise for men;
there is nothing superior to this, which destroys sin and bestows liberation.
For this reason, O King, it should be performed without hesitation;
listen, O tiger among kings, to this auspicious ancient narrative.
In the Pañcakajeca Purāṇa, her greatness has been described by me:
once, in the world of Nāka, she indeed ruled as the queen of Indra.
The gods dwell there in that very delightful place with ease,
devoted to drinking nectar and served by throngs of apsarases.
There, in the Nandana grove frequented by the Pārijāta tree,
the inhabitants of heaven delight Rāma with the Apsarases.
Once, O King, while sporting at his own will, that lord of the gods, the leader of fifty million [demons], caused [the demon] to dance out of great joy. (11)
The Gandharvas sing there; the Gandharva Puṣpadantaka is there, as is Citrasena and the son of Citrasena.
The wife of Citrasena was named Mālinī;
from Mālinī was born the one known by the name Puṣpadantī.
Puṣpanda was his son, known by the name Mālyavān;
he was so utterly infatuated with Puṣpandī because of her beauty that he became Mālyavān (the "Garlanded One"). ||14||
For by her, through such side-long glances, both Kaṭa and Akṣamālya were brought under her sway;
behold now her form, endowed with beauty and grace. (15)
Her arms were as if made into nooses for her throat by desire;
her eyes reached toward her ears, and she was thus rolling about in agitation.
O best of kings, her ears were beautiful with two earrings;
she was adorned with divine ornaments and possessed a neck as long as that of a swan. 17.
Her two breasts were full and elevated like golden jars;
her waist was slender, exquisite, and so fine it could be grasped by a single fist—truly unsurpassed. (18)
Her hips were broad and her loins were expansive;
her two feet shone with a luster like that of red lotuses. (19)
Mālyavān was utterly infatuated with such a woman in her season;
the two of them came together for the purpose of dancing to please Śakra.
There, frequented by hosts of Apsarases who sang and offered hymns of praise,
Mālyavān went to Mount Go-puṣpadanta, which was overwhelmed by the god of love.
Overcome by mutual passion and falling under the sway of delusion,
they sang no pure song, being possessed by the confusion of their minds.
With their gazes fixed upon one another, having fallen under the power of the arrows of love,
the bull among sages perceived there the union of their minds.
Due to the loss of rhythm, tempo, and measure, as well as the improper delivery of the song, Indra reflected upon his own humiliation.
And his father, wishing to pronounce a curse upon them for their sake, uttered this:
"Fie, fie upon you two! You fools have fallen, having committed a breach of my command. (25)
"May you two become Piśācas, maintaining the state of husband and wife;
having reached the world of mortals, you shall experience the fruit of your karma. (26)
Thus cursed by Maghavan, both of them, their minds filled with sorrow and bewildered by Indra’s curse, reached that mountain Himavat.
Both attained the state of Piśācas and experienced truly terrible suffering;
with their minds tormented there, both fell into a miserable plight caused by the cold.
Deluded and tormented by the heat of summer and the suffering born of their fallen bodies, these two did not recognize their state as Gandharvas or Apsarases.
Afflicted by their karma, they found neither happiness nor peace even at night;
they continued to argue with one another within the mountain cave. (30)
Afflicted by the cold produced by the frost, they rubbed their teeth together, their bodies covered with bristling hair. (31)
Then the Piśāca spoke to his own wife, the Piśācī:
"What great, terrible, and hair-raising sin has been committed? (32)
By which [cause] he attained the state of a piśāca through his own evil deeds, considering both hell and the state of a piśāca to be miserable. (33)
"Therefore, with every effort, one should not commit a sinful act.
Thinking thus, the two remained there, tormented by sorrow. (34)
By the turn of fate, for those two, the eleventh lunar day of the month of Māgha arrived—the most excellent of all renowned days known as Jayā. (35)
When that day arrived,
O King, they remained there deprived of food and deprived of even the drinking of water.
Having committed no killing of living beings and subsisting on leaves and fruits, those two always remained near the Aśvattha tree, joined with suffering. (37)
While the two of them remained standing there in that manner, O King, the sun set;
and then the night arrived—terrible, fierce, and life-destroying.
Trembling, they stretched out and fell asleep upon the ground,
their limbs and even their arms entwined with one another.
There, they found no pleasure and did not experience the happiness of union;
thus were they both afflicted by the curse of Indra, that tiger among kings. (40)
Thus, while the two of them were in such distress, the night passed away;
the twelfth day arrived, and the sun rose.
O tiger among kings, I have held liberation in my heart for those two;
I have observed the excellent vow of Jayā and kept a vigil throughout the night. (42)
Therefore, listen to how it happened through the power of that vow,
once the twelfth day had arrived and the Jayā-vow had been duly observed.
O King, by the power of Viṣṇu, the state of being piśācas departed from them both;
Puṣpadanta and Mālyavān returned to their former forms. (44)
Filled with their former affection and wearing their previous ornaments,
the two ascended a celestial chariot as delightful as the Nākemanorama.
Having gone before the Lord of the Gods, they joyfully prostrated themselves;
seeing them in such a state, Indra was amazed and said: ||46||
Indra said: "Tell me, by what merit did you two abandon the state of being Piśācas, and by which god were you both liberated from my curse? (47)
Mālyavat said: "O Lord, through the grace of Vāsudeva, by the vow of Jayā, and by the power of devotion to your hymn, this state of being a piśāca has been attained. (48)
Having heard this, the Lord of the Immortals replied once more in the same way:
"Both you and I have been born as purifiers and sanctifiers of the lineage of Danu. (49)
The two who observe the day of Hari are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu;
those who are absorbed in the day of Hari are likewise devoted to Kṛṣṇa. (50)
They are to be honored by us mortals as well, there is no doubt;
O Puṣpadanta, dwell at your ease in the abode of the Asuras.
Kṛṣṇa said:
For this reason, O King, the day of Hari must be observed;
it is the destroyer of the sin of killing a Brahmin, O tiger among kings, and it brings victory. (52)
By her alone were all gifts and all sacrifices performed in their entirety;
she gave and caused them to be given, and the vow of Jayā was undertaken.
O King, by reading or hearing this, one shall certainly rejoice in Vaikuṇṭha for ten million kalpas and obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (54)

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Jayā Ekādaśī in the Bright Half of Māgha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
(44) The Forty-fourth Chapter—
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of Phālguna? O Vāsudeva, please tell me out of your grace in my presence. (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: On the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, Nārada questioned Brahmā, who is seated upon a lotus, regarding that which is known by the name Vijayā.
O best of the twice-born, please tell me by your grace what the merit of that [action] is. ||2||
Brahmā said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall tell you the supreme story that removes all sins;
this vow of Vijayā has never been told to anyone by me before.
For this is an ancient vow, pure and a destroyer of sins;
it bestows victory upon kings, of this there is no doubt. (4)
Having gone to the forest of Pura-rāma for fourteen years,
he dwelt at Pañcavaṭī together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
While that Rāma, whose nature is victory, was dwelling right there,
his illustrious wife Sītā was carried off by Rāvaṇa out of greed.
Then, due to that sorrow, Rāma too was overcome by delusion; wandering about, he then beheld Jaṭāyus, whose life had departed.
After Kabandha was slain, while wandering in the midst of the forest,
he entered into a friendship with Sugrīva.
Then, after the monkey armies had assembled for the sake of Rama’s purpose,
Hanumān beheld Jānakī in the grove of Lankā.
A means of restoring consciousness was given to him, and a great service was rendered;
then, having come together again with Rāma, everything there was reported to him. ||10||
Then, having heard the words of Hanumān, Rāmacandra approved the departure with the consent of Sugrīva. 11.
"O Saumitri, this abode of Varuṇa cannot be crossed without merit;
it is exceedingly unfathomable and teeming with aquatic monsters.
I see no means whatsoever by which it might become easily traversed. (12)
Lakṣmaṇa said:
"You alone are the primordial god, the ancient Supreme Person;
and the sage Bakadālbhya dwells here in the middle of the island. (13)
O Rāghava, half a yojana from this place is his hermitage;
and there are many other Brāhmaṇas there as well, O descendant of Raghu. (14)
"Go and ask that bull among sages, the ancient king of kings.
Having heard these most excellent words of Lakṣmaṇa, [Rāma spoke]. 15.
Rāghava went to see the great sage Bakadālbhya;
Rāma bowed his head to the sage, as a god bows to Viṣṇu. (16)
Then the sage, having recognized Rāma as the ancient Puruṣottama who had entered a human body for some particular reason, [spoke]. (17)
The sage, being pleased, said: "O Rāma, from where has this speech of yours come?"
Rāma said:
"By your grace, O Lord of rivers and streams, I have arrived here with my army upon the far shore; what enemy, even including the Rākṣasas, shall I conquer here?"
"O Sage, since you are well-disposed toward me, please show me favor and tell me that means by which the ocean may be crossed by me. (20)
"For this very reason, I have come here to see you.
Having heard Rāma's words, the great sage Baka-dālbhya—
He spoke to the lotus-eyed one, whose soul was supremely serene and who delighted in the Self: "Today, the most excellent vow among the vows of Rāma must be performed. (22)
By this deed, victory shall swiftly be yours;
having conquered Laṅkā and the rākṣasas, you will attain stainless fame.
Having become single-minded, observe this vow;
on the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, there occurs Vijayā Ekādaśī. (24)
By means of that vow, victory over Rāvaṇa will be yours;
without doubt, you shall cross the ocean together with the monkeys.
O King, listen now to the procedure which bestows the fruit of this vow:
when the tenth day arrives, one should have a single water-pot fashioned. (26)
One should place a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay, which is beautiful, filled with water, and adorned with sprouts.
One should place seven kinds of grain and barley around the base of that [pedestal];
upon it, one should place the golden image of the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
When the eleventh day has arrived, one should perform the morning bath;
one should then place a steady water-pot (kumbha) adorned with garlands around its neck and with ointments.
One should worship especially with betel nuts and coconuts,
as well as with perfumes, incense, lamps, and various kinds of food offerings.

On this day at the Kumbha [festival], the wise man should spend the time in front of Him with excellent discourses and other activities, and likewise cause a vigil to be held before Him during the night.
One should light a ghee lamp for the sake of fulfilling the vow without break when the twelfth day arrives and the sun has risen. (32)
Having taken the water-pot to a body of water, a river, or a spring,
and having placed it in a pond, he should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
One should give that pitcher to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
along with the pitcher, O King of kings, one should cause the great gifts (mahādānas) to be bestowed.
By this method, having united with the leaders of the monkey hosts,
you shall diligently perform the vow of Kuru, and victory will be yours.
Having heard this, Rāma then did exactly as he was told;
once the vow was completed, that joy of the Raghus became victorious.
Having obtained Sītā and having conquered Rāvaṇa, the son of Pulastya,
men perform this vow for the sake of their sons according to this ritual procedure.
Victory is attained in this world, and likewise, the next world becomes imperishable;
for this reason, my son, the Vijayā-vow must be observed. (38)
The greatness of Vijayā destroys all sins;
by reading or even hearing it, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. (39)

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vijayā, the Dark Lunar Day of Phālguna," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.

(45) Chapter Forty-Five.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Kṛṣṇa, I have heard the greatness of Vijayā and its great fruit;
now tell me of her who bears that name during the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna. (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O fortunate son of Dharma, listen; I shall now speak to you that which was spoken by the Creator, the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, when he was questioned by me.
O King, a specific distinction regarding the month of Phālguna has been told;
it is the meritorious Āmalakī vow, which bestows the fruit of the world of Viṣṇu.
Having gone beneath an *āmalaka* tree, one should perform a vigil there;
by performing the vigil at night, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. ||4||
Māndhātṛ said to him:
"O best of the twice-born, when did this Āmalakī tree arise?
Tell me all of this, for my curiosity is great. (5)
Why is this [vow] purifying? Why is it the destroyer of sin?
And why, by performing the vigil, does one obtain the fruit of a thousand cows? ||6||
Vasiṣṭha said: O highly fortunate one, I shall relate how this great Āmalakī tree, the destroyer of all sins, came to exist upon the earth.

When the world had become a single ocean, when all moving and stationary beings had perished, when the hosts of gods and asuras had vanished, and when the serpents and rākṣasas were utterly destroyed; (8)
There, the Lord of the gods of gods, the eternal Supreme Self,
went to the supreme, imperishable state of Brahman, his own abode.
Then, from the mouth of Brahmā as he was awake, a being with the luster of the moon emerged from his spittle and fell upon the earth.
From that, the great Dhātrī tree itself arose—a tree with many branches and twigs, bent down by the weight of its fruit. ||11||
The primordial growth of all trees is proclaimed to have been by Brahmā; thereafter, these creatures were created. 12.
The Blessed Lord created the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas,
as well as the great sages who are free from impurity.
The gods came to that place where Dhātrī and Hari had gone;
seeing her, O highly fortunate one, they were filled with supreme wonder.
"We do not know this tree; let us stand around it and deliberate. While they were thus deliberating, an incorporeal voice spoke.
This excellent Vaiṣṇava tree, known as Āmalakīnagohya, is highly esteemed;
by its mere remembrance, one obtains the fruit born from the gift of a cow. 16.
The merit from touching [it] is twofold, and likewise, from wearing it, it is threefold;
therefore, one should always serve the āmalakī with every effort. 17.
She is declared to be the remover of all sins, the Vaiṣṇavī who destroys evil;
Viṣṇu resides at her base, and Pitāmaha (Brahmā) above her. 18.
The Lord Rudra, the Supreme Sovereign, is established in the trunk;
all the sages are in the branches, and the deities are in the twigs. (19)
The gods reside in the leaves, and likewise the Maruts in the flowers;
all the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) are established within the fruits.
Indeed, this Dhātrī has been described by me as consisting of all the gods;
therefore, she is most worthy of worship by those who are solely devoted to Viṣṇu. 21.
The sages said: "Who are you? We do not know; for what reason have you come here? Are you a god or someone else? Tell us the truth. (22)
Speech said:
"He who is the creator of all beings and of all worlds in every respect—who, upon seeing even the wise filled with wonder, declares 'I am that eternal Viṣṇu'. (23)
Having heard those words spoken by the God of gods, the sons of Brahmā proceeded there to praise the God who is without beginning or end.
Salutations to the one who has become the self of all beings, to the Self, the Supreme Self;
salutations to Acyuta, the eternal, the infinite; salutations, salutations!
"Salutations again and again to Dāmodara, the poet, the lord of sacrifice!
Thus praised by the sages, the Blessed Lord Hari was gratified. (26)
He replied to those great sages, "What desired thing shall I give to you?
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with us out of a desire for our welfare," (27)
Please describe some vow that bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, which grants wealth and grain, is meritorious, and brings satisfaction to the self. (28)
This vow, which yields abundant fruit from little effort, is the supreme among vows;
by performing it, O Lord of Gods, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (29)
Viṣṇu said:
"If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) falls on a Puṣya asterism during the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, it becomes highly meritorious and the destroyer of great sins. (30)
O best of the twice-born, listen to the special rite that must be performed there:
having reached the Āmalakī tree, one should observe a vigil there. (31)
One shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows and be completely liberated from all sins.
O brahmins, this supreme vow among vows has been recounted to you;
by worshipping Acyuta on that day, one is never again separated from the world of Viṣṇu.
The sages said: "Tell us the procedure for this vow; how may it become complete? Who are the protectors? What are the salutations? And which deities are proclaimed [for this rite]? (33)

How is giving practiced, how is bathing performed, and what is the prescribed procedure for worship? Please tell me, exactly as it is, the mantra for the offering of water (argha) and the act of adoration.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of the twice-born, hear the proper procedure for this vow:
having remained without food on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one should likewise do so on the following day. (35)
"I shall eat [only after], O Puṇḍarīkākṣa; be my refuge, O Acyuta"—having thus made this vow, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth, ||36||

One should not speak with those who have fallen [from their status], thieves, as well as heretical men, those of evil conduct, those who have broken the bounds of propriety, and those who violate the wives of their gurus. (37)
Then, in the afternoon, the wise man, with self-restraint, should perform his bath according to the prescribed rite in a river, a pond, a well, or at home.
First, one should perform the touching of the earth, and then have the ritual bath performed [with the mantra]:
"O Earth, trodden by the horse, trodden by the chariot, and trodden by Viṣṇu! (39)
O Earth, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me. (40)
Thus is the mantra for the earth:
"O Water, you are the life-force of all beings and the protector of their bodies; homage to the Lord of the juices of the species born from sweat and those born from sprouts. (41)
I have bathed in all sacred fords, in lakes and springs, in rivers and in pools dug by the gods; may this indeed be my true bathing. (42)
Thus is the mantra for the bath:
having caused a golden image of the sage Jāmadagnya to be made from one māṣaka of gold, or half of that, or even half of that again; ||43||
Having returned home, one should perform the worship and the fire-sacrifice (homa) for that worship;
thereafter, accompanied by all the necessary ritual implements, one should go to the Āmalakī tree.
Then, having gone to an *āmalakī* tree and gathered [the fruits], one should then thoroughly cleanse them and constantly place them in a flawless jar, preceded by the recitation of mantras. (45)
Endowed with the five jewels, perfumed with divine fragrances, provided with a parasol and a pair of sandals, and honored with white sandalwood paste. (46)
One should make it beautiful on all sides, with garlands and wreaths hanging from the necks [of the pillars], perfumed by all kinds of incense, and filled everywhere with rows of lamps.
Upon that, one should place a vessel filled with divine parched grains (lāja);
upon the vessel, one should place the deity, the son of Jamadagni, who possesses great splendor. 48.
Salutations to Viśokāya for the feet; to Viśvarūpin for the knees; to Ugra for the thighs; and to Dāmodara for the hips. (49)

Salutations to the lotus-navelled one for the belly; salutations to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa for the chest; salutations to the wielder of the discus for the left arm, and to the wielder of the mace for the right. (50)

Salutations to Vaikuṇṭha for the throat; salutations indeed to Yajñamukha for the mouth; salutations to Vāsudeva, the treasury of freedom from sorrow, for the nose; and [salutations] to the eyes. (51)
One should worship with "Salutation to Vāmanāya" for the forehead, "Salutation to Rāmāya" for the two eyebrows, "Salutation to Sarvātmane" for that head, and "Salutation" (namaḥ) for the rest. 52.
Thus is the mantra for worship.
Then, with a mind endowed with devotion and with a pure fruit, one should cause the arghya offering to be presented to the God of gods.
Then one should keep a vigil with a mind imbued with devotion, through dances, songs, instrumental music, religious narratives, and hymns of praise. (54)
Likewise, one should pass the entire night with Vaiṣṇava narratives;
then, one should perform circumambulation of the Dhātrī tree while reciting the names of Viṣṇu.
Either one hundred and eight or twenty-eight [verses];
then, at the time of dawn, having performed the *nīrājana* rite for Hari.
Having honored the Brāhmaṇa, one should offer everything to him;
there, a pair of garments and sandals should be given to the descendant of Jamadagni.
"May Keśava be pleased with me in the form of the son of Jamadagni.
Then, having touched an *āmalaka* fruit and performed a circumambulation, [he should offer it]. (58)
Having performed the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
thereafter, one should eat oneself, surrounded by one's family.
I shall now describe to you all the merit that arises from performing this;
it is equal to the merit found in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and the fruit obtained from all forms of giving. (60)
He obtains the fruit that is superior to all sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has been narrated to you in its entirety this supreme vow among all vows.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods vanished right there;
and all those sages likewise performed everything completely and without exception.
O best of beings, O lord of kings, you ought likewise to perform this vow, which is difficult to undertake and which liberates one from all sins. (63)

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Phālguna Śukla Āmalakī Ekādaśī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
(46) The Forty-sixth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
In the dark fortnight of Phālguna, the Amalaki Ekādaśī is heard of; but what is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of Caitra? (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Indra among kings, I shall relate this narrative that destroys all sins,
which Lomaśa spoke when questioned by me, the universal emperor Dhātṛ.
Māndhātṛ said to me:
"O Blessed One, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I wish to hear:
what is the name of the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) that occurs in the first fortnight of Caitra?"
Please, by your grace, tell me the ritual procedure for that [mantra] and its fruit. ||3||
Lomaśa said: In the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, there is the one known as Pāpamocanī Ekādaśī, which destroys the state of being a piśāca.
Listen, O King, for I shall relate to you her wondrous tale, which grants desires, bestows success, confers auspiciousness, destroys sin, and imparts righteousness. (5)
Formerly, in the region of Caitraratha, frequented by throngs of apsarases, when the spring season had arrived and the forest was filled with swarms of bees; ||6||
They take delight with the instrumental music of the Gandharva maidens; what need have they for men?
Those inhabitants of the third heaven, headed by Indra, the subduer of Pāka, engage in their play.
There is nothing else that bestows such happiness as the Caitraratha forest;
in that forest, sages perform intense austerities.
There, an Apsaras approached that best of sages, the ascetic named Medhāvin, who was staying there as a celibate student, in order to delude him. (9)
Extending his non-existence with the cry "She has devoured me!", she became renowned as Mañjughoṣā;
out of fear of him, she remained at a distance of one *krośa* near his hermitage.
Singing very sweetly while greatly distressing the female serpents,
he sang, having then beheld that [place] frequented by flowers and sandalwood.
Kāma, the son of Manas, also desired victory over the lords of sages who were devotees of Śiva; he took up residence within her body.
Having made her eyebrows the tip of the bow, her side-glances the bowstring, and her eyes—furnished with lashes—the arrows, in due order; ||13||
Having fashioned a tent out of his own breasts, he set out for victory;
the roar he uttered became like the very army of Kāma.
Seeing the wise sage, she too was afflicted by desire; yet that Medhāvin, though his body was blooming with youth, remained resplendent [in self-control]. (15)
Wearing a white sacred thread, he appeared like another god of love;
that wise youth dwelt in the auspicious hermitage of Cyavana.
Seeing that bull among sages standing there, having called out to her,
she fell under the power of passion and sang very softly.
Seeing her thus, with her bracelets, armlets, anklets, and girdle all jingling, and singing in that manner, the eminent sage was struck with wonder.
Having been forcibly brought under the sway of delusion by Madana along with his army, Indra, seeing the sage in such a state, approached him and cried out. (19)
The celestial nymph deluded him with her gestures, expressions, and sidelong glances;
setting aside her lute, she embraced that lord of sages. (20)
When the tree had been bent and shaken by the force of the wind,
that wise and eminent sage rejoiced together with her.
Then, having seen that supreme body of hers within that very [state],
it entered the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), while he himself fell under the sway of the principle of desire (kāmatattva).
That lustful man did not distinguish between night and day;
many years passed as he neglected the conduct of a sage.
Having addressed me thus, he set out for the world of the gods.
As he was departing, he spoke these final words to that best of sages:
"O Brahmin, let permission be granted for my departure to my own country. (24)
Medhāvin said:
"O fair-faced one, you have arrived this very day at the beginning of the evening;
remain in my presence until the twilight of dawn."
Having heard these words of the sage, she became terrified with fear.
O best of kings,
out of fear of the sage’s curse, they kept him confined for many years.
Fifty-five years, nine months, and three days passed for him like half a night, according to the calculation of the sage Sāreṇu. ||27||
Then, when the sage had departed at that time, Sāta spoke again:
"O Brahmin, let an instruction be given; I must go to my own home. (28)
Medhāvin said:
"It is now dawn; let my words be heard. While I perform my twilight devotions, you must remain steady. (29)
Having heard these words of the sage, Anasūyā became agitated with joy;
smiling slightly, she, of pure smiles, replied to him.
The Apsarā said: "O sinless lord of sages, how much time remains until your twilight prayers? Having shown me favor, please consider that the appointed time has arrived. (31)
Having heard these words of his, the best of Brahmins, his eyes wide with wonder,
then established the duration of the time that had passed.
Fifty-seven years passed while he was with her;
then he became enraged at her and turned into one wreathed in flames.
Extremely enraged, he emitted sparks from his two eyes;
seeing her in the form of Time (Kāla), who was the cause of the destruction of his ascetic merit.
Seeing that his asceticism, earned with great hardship, had been brought to ruin by her, the sage, his senses agitated, replied there to Saka-poṣṭha: ||35||
Then he cursed her, saying, "O wise one, become a *piśācī*!
Fie upon you, O sinful woman of wicked conduct, unchaste and fond of transgression! (36)
Burning with his curse yet standing bowed in humility, the fair-browed woman spoke these words to the sage, seeking his favor:
"O best of Brahmins, grant me your grace; show me favor by mitigating this curse. (37)
The company of the virtuous indeed occurs through seven steps of speech.
O Brahmana, many years have passed with you as my companion;
for this reason, O Lord of noble vows, grant me your grace. (38)
The sage said:
"Listen, O blessed lady, to this which brings about both curse and grace.
Why have you brought such great penance to ruin through your sinful desire? (39)
On the auspicious eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, there occurs the one named Pāpamocanikā, which brings about the destruction of all sins. (40)
"Even though his vow was not performed, he shall attain the state of a Piśāca.
Having said this, that Medhāvin also went to his father’s hermitage.
Seeing him arrived, Cyavana replied to him:
"O son, what is this that has been done by you? You have brought about the destruction of your merit."
Medhāvin said: "O father, I have committed a sinful transgression involving an Apsaras. Tell me the expiation, O father, by which the destruction of my sin may occur. (43)
Cyavana said:
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, there is indeed [a tithi] named Pāpamocanī. When this vow is performed, the heap of one's sins shall go to destruction. (44)
Having heard these words of his father, he performed that supreme vow;
his sin went to destruction, and he became endowed with the power of asceticism.

She too, having performed this supreme vow, was liberated from her state as a *piśāca* through the *Pāpamocanikā* vow; assuming a divine form, she became an excellent *apsaras* and departed to heaven. (46)
Lomaśa said:
O King, whatever sin the best of men commit, if they perform the Pāpamocanikā [rite], all that sin shall go to destruction. (47)

O King, by reading or hearing this, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows; even a killer of a Brahmin, a stealer of gold, a drinker of liquor, or one who violates the teacher’s bed [is purified]. (48)
By performing this vow, they become liberated from sin;
for by performing this excellent vow, one indeed gains great merit. (49)

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Liberation from Sin on the Eleventh Day of the Dark Fortnight of Caitra," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
(47) Chapter Forty-Seven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Salutations to you, O Vāsudeva; please tell me:
what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs during the bright fortnight of Caitra? (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O King Ikṣvāku, to this ancient and meritorious narrative which Vasiṣṭha formerly related to Dilīpa when he questioned him.
Dilīpa said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear; please tell me by your grace:
what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra?"
Vasiṣṭha said: "O King, you have asked well; I shall relate it before you.
In the bright fortnight of Caitra, there is a [tithi] known by the name Kāmadā."
The Ekādaśī is most meritorious; it is a forest fire to the wealth-granting demon Pāpaṃdha.
O King, listen to this story, which destroys sins and bestows merit. (5)
In the delightful city of Purānāgapura, adorned with gold and jewels,
dwell the exceedingly powerful nāgas who have Puṇḍarīka as their chief.
In that city, King Puṇḍarīka ruled his kingdom;
he was served by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Apsarases. (7)
The excellent Apsaras Tulalitā and the Gandharva Ulalita were both intensely inflamed by passion; thus, as husband and wife, they were tormented by desire.
Then, while you remain in your own delightful home, endowed with wealth and grain,
your husband shall dwell forever within the heart of Lalitā.
The passionate woman dwells eternally in his heart;
once, Puṇḍarīka was sporting while seated in that assembly.
He sang a song, yet without his beloved who was so charming;
remembering Lalitā, his tongue faltered over the words.
Having understood his state of mind, Karkaṭa, the best of nāgas,
informed Puṇḍarīka of his release from the fetters.
Having heard the words of Karkoṭaka, the serpent-king Ḍarīka became exceedingly terrifying, his eyes bloodshot with rage. (13)
O evil-minded one, that Rākṣasa, a flesh-eater and man-eater, became there a singer who was charming as a hare and afflicted by passion. (14)
O Indra among kings, because he was singing before me while under the influence of his wife, he assumed the form of a rākṣasa at her command. 15.
Raudrānana and Virūpākṣa cause terror by their mere sight;
their arms extend for a yojana, and their mouths resemble caverns.
His eyes resemble the sun and the moon; his neck is like a mountain; the nostrils are the openings of the Rāndhreta; and his two lips extend for a yojana.
O Indra among kings, his body rose to a height of eight yojanas;
having become such a Rākṣasa, he was experiencing the fruit of his own karma.
Beholding her husband thus transformed into a hideous form, Lalitā,
afflicted by great sorrow, pondered within her mind.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? My husband is tormented by a curse.
Thinking this again and again, she found no peace in her mind.
The Rākṣasa, capable of assuming any form at will, wandered through the dense forest of Lalitā together with his mistress, roaming through the difficult thickets of the great woods.
Cruel, devoted to evil, deformed, and a man-eater, he finds no happiness by night or by day, being tormented by his own sins. ||22||
Seeing her husband in such a state— both graceful and yet deeply distressed— Lalitā wandered with him through the dense forest, weeping.
Having seen the delightful hermitage and the sage whose form was perfectly tranquil, Lalitā quickly approached, paid homage, and stood before him. (24)
Seeing her, the sage, his heart filled with compassion, spoke to the sorrowful woman: "Who are you? Why have you come here? Speak the truth before me. (25)
Lalitā said:
"Know me to be Lalitā by name, the daughter of that great-souled Gandharva named Vīradhanvan, who has come here for the sake of a husband. (26)
O great sage, due to the fault of her husband, she became a Rākṣasa of fierce form and wicked conduct; seeing him, I find no happiness.
"O Brahman, instruct me now; O Lord, tell me what must be done. O auspicious one, perform that vow as I have described it according to the prescribed rites. (28)
The sage said:
O beautiful one, in the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight, there is the first day of that [fortnight];
it is the Ekādaśī known as Kāmada, which destroys sins and is supreme, O Lalitā. 29.
"O blessed lady, perform this vow exactly as it has been prescribed by me.
Whatever merit arises from this vow, let that be dedicated to your husband. (30)
"By the merit of that gift, the fault of his curse shall depart from the moment of that glance.
Having heard these words of the sage, Lalitā became filled with joy. (31)
O King, having observed the fast on the eleventh day, one should likewise do so on the twelfth day in the presence of a Brahmin and before Vāsudeva.
She spoke these words to her husband Lalita for his deliverance:
"Indeed, I have observed that vow—the fast of Kāmadā. (33)
By the power of his merit, let him too attain the state of a Piśāca at that very moment, even though he was acting according to Lalitā’s words.
Having been freed from evil, he became one of graceful movements and divine body;
his state as a Rākṣasa vanished, and he attained the status of a Gandharva once again.
Together with her, whose limbs were adorned with gold and jewels,
they ascended an excellent celestial chariot, appearing even more beautiful than their former forms.
"O best of kings, knowing this—that these two shall shine with splendor through the power of Kāmadā—this [rite] must be performed with great effort. (37)
For the sake of the gratification of the worlds, it has been declared by me at the beginning;
it destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and annihilates the state of being a piśāca. 38.
O King, there is nothing superior to this in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile;
by reciting or hearing it, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. (39)

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Caitra-Śukla-Akā," in the Uttara-Khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||47||
(48) Chapter Forty-Eight.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Āsudeva, salutations to you! Please tell me what the name of the Ekādaśī is in the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, and describe its greatness.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, in this world and in the next, she bestows good fortune;
in the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, she is indeed known by the name Varūthinī.
By the very observance of this vow, happiness arises at all times;
there is the destruction of sins and the attainment of good fortune as well. (3)
By making her thus unfortunate, she shall obtain the good fortune of women;
she is the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all people. ||4||
By the very vow of Varūthinī, which removes all sins for men and destroys the impressions of the womb,
the Creator has led me to the heavenly state.
Dhūmra, Dhumrākṣa, and many other kings likewise [perished];
the Lord Bhava was liberated from the skull of Brahmā.
A man who performs penance for ten thousand years,
or he who gives a bhāra of gold at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse,
obtains a fruit equal to that by practicing the Varūthinī vow.
But the man who, endowed with faith, performs the Varūthinī vow, shall obtain his desires both in this world and in the next. (8)
O best of kings, this [river] is indeed a purifier and sanctifier, the destroyer of great sins, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who perform its rites. 9.
O best of kings, the gift of an elephant excels the gift of a horse;
the gift of land excels the gift of an elephant, and the gift of food is even greater than that. (10)
Therefore, the gift of gold is indeed [great], but the gift of food is superior to that;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift greater than the gift of food.
Satisfaction of the ancestors, gods, and humans arises from food;
O best of kings, the gift of a daughter is declared by the wise to be equal to that. (12)
The Blessed One himself has declared that the gift of a cow is equal to that; furthermore, among all the gifts mentioned, the gift of knowledge is preeminent. (13)
A man who constructs a *varūthinī* (a defensive wall) obtains that same fruit as those men deluded by sin who live off the wealth of maidens. (14)
They go to hell, which consists of torment, through the exhaustion of their merit;
therefore, with every effort, the wealth of a maiden must not be accepted. 15.
O King of kings, he who, out of greed, takes a maiden after having purchased her for that wealth, will certainly become a camel in another birth. (16)
O King, Citragupta would not be able to calculate the measure of merit of one who gives [this] well-prepared [work], according to their ability. 17.
A man who, having prepared brass, meat, black gram, mung beans, chickpeas, and kodrava grain, obtains a fruit equal to that [of the aforementioned gift]. (18)
On the tenth day, a Vaiṣṇava who observes vows should avoid ten things: leafy vegetables, honey, meat, liquor, food, and sexual intercourse. (19)
Gambling, play, sleep, betel-leaf, cleaning the teeth, speaking ill of others, backbiting, theft, violence, and likewise sexual indulgence; ||20||
On the eleventh day, one should avoid anger, false speech, bell-metal, meat, liquor, honey, oil, and conversation with the fallen. (21)
On the twelfth lunar day, one should avoid physical exercise, travel, food, sexual intercourse, riding on the back of a bull, and lentil-based dishes. ||22||
O King, by this method, those by whom the army was thus arrayed,
having brought about the destruction of all sins, shall at the end attain the imperishable state;
for Madhusūdana, when worshipped, bestows this after one has kept a vigil through the night.
Those who are completely liberated from all evil go to the supreme destination;
therefore, those who fear evil should perform [this] with every effort. ||24||
A man fearing the son of Kṣapāritā should form an army;
by reciting or hearing this, O King, he obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. ||25||

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Vaiśākha-Kṛṣṇa-Varūthinī Ekādaśī," in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada within the Śrī Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(49) The Forty-Ninth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, tell me what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, what is its fruit, and what is the procedure for it?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O king of kings, this very same matter which you now ask me about was previously asked of Vasiṣṭha by the wise Rāmacandra.
Rāma said: O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the most excellent of vows, which destroys all sins and eradicates all suffering. (3)
I have not experienced the sufferings born of separation from my beloved;
therefore, O Great Sage, I am terrified and ask you about them.
Vasiṣṭha said:
You have asked well, O Rāma; this is the resolute mind of one who has renounced the world.
By the mere mention of your name, a human being becomes purified. (5)
Nevertheless, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, I shall describe this sacred vow,
the most excellent among all purifying vows.
In the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, there occurs Rāma-ekādaśī;
it is called Mohinī, the supreme remover of all sins. (7)
They are liberated from the snare of delusion and from the multitude of sins; by the power of this vow, I speak the truth, the absolute truth. (8)
For this reason, O Rāma, this [practice] must be performed by those such as you;
it brings about the destruction of sins and eliminates great suffering. (9)
Listen to this supreme narrative of Ekamanārāma, which removes all sins;
by the mere hearing of it, even great sin is destroyed. (10)
On the beautiful bank of the Sarasvatī is the auspicious city of Bhadrāvatī;
there, a king named Dyutimat indeed rules the kingdom.
There dwells a Vaiśya named Candravaṃśodbhava, who is steadfast and true to his word, and is abundantly prosperous with wealth and grain. (12)
Renowned as Dhanapāla, he was a promoter of meritorious deeds;
he was the builder of almshouses, wells, monasteries, gardens, tanks, and houses. (13)
Devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu and peaceful, he had five sons:
Sumanas, Dyutimat, Medhāvin, and Sukṛta. (14)
The fifth was Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, who was always devoted to great sins, intent on consorting with the wives of others, and skilled in the assemblies of libertines. ||15||
Addicted to vices such as gambling and the like, and longing for the company of others' wives,
he has no inclination toward the worship of the gods, nor toward the ancestors, nor toward the twice-born.
He was one who acted unjustly, possessed a wicked soul, and caused the depletion of his father's wealth;
he was a sinner who ate forbidden food and was constantly addicted to the drinking of liquor.
With his arms thrown around the necks of courtesans, he wandered wickedly at the crossroads;
he was driven out from his home by his father and abandoned by his kinsmen. (18)
