Indeed, he had his very ornaments for his own body brought to exhaustion by those courtesans; and, censured by them due to the depletion of his wealth, he was abandoned.
Then, as if born from the heat of anxiety, stripped of clothing and afflicted by hunger, he thought: "What shall I do? Where shall I go? By what means can I live? (20)
He began a life of thievery in that very city;
he was seized by the king’s men but released out of respect for his father. (21)
Bound again and released again, bound once more with great haste—that man of arrogant intellect and evil conduct was bound with firm shackles. (22)
Though struck and tormented again and again by lashes of the whip, O dull-witted one, you must not remain within the range of my domain. (23)
Having spoken thus, he was then released from his firm bonds by the king;
freed from fear of him, he departed and went into the dense forest.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, he ran hither and thither;
like a lion, he slew deer, boars, and spotted antelopes. (25)
He always remains like one intent on the consumption of worldly food;
holding a bow in his hand, with an arrow fixed against his back.
Wandering about in the forest, they kill birds that move on foot—cakoras, peacocks, partridges, francolin pheasants, and mice. (27)
This man of audacious intellect and merciless mind destroys these and others as well;
submerged in the mire of sin by the evil deeds committed in previous births, he sinks further into it. (28)
Overwhelmed by suffering and grief, and tormented day and night, he reached the hermitage of Kauṇḍinya at some point through the arrival of merit. (29)
Afflicted by a heavy burden of grief, Dhṛṣṭabuddhi approached the ascetic who had performed his ablutions in the Ganges during the month of Mādhava.
With his sins gone and his inauspiciousness destroyed by the touch of the reflection of that garment, he stood before Kauṇḍinya with palms joined in reverence and replied: ||31||
Dhṛṣṭabuddhi said: "O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, having shown compassion toward me, tell me that by the power of which merit liberation may be attained. (32)
Kauṇḍinya said:
Listen with an attentive mind to that by which the destruction of your sins shall occur:
in the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, there is the well-known day called Māhīnī. (33)
Prompted by her words, he observed the Ekādaśī vow;
the sins of embodied beings, even those equal to Mount Meru, go to destruction. (34)
"Accumulated over many births, this [merit] has been fully nourished by her through fasting.
Having heard these words of the sage, Dhṛṣṭabuddhi became clear-minded and serene. (35)
He performed the vow according to the rules through the instruction of Kauṇḍinya;
O best of kings, once the vow was completed, he became free from sin.
Then, having attained a divine body and being seated upon Garuḍa,
he went to the realm of Viṣṇu, which is free from all afflictions.
Such is this supreme vow of Rāmacandra, the deluding vow;
there is nothing superior to this in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (38)
Sacrifices, pilgrimages, and gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part [of its merit].
O King, by reading or hearing it, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. (39)

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ekādaśī of Mohanī in the Bright Fortnight of Vaiśākha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. 49.
The Fifty-fifth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha?
I desire to hear this greatness; therefore, speak it, O Janārdana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, you have asked well out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
this [account] bestows great merit and destroys even the most heinous sins.
O King of the Nāgas, he who serves Aparā becomes known in the world as one who grants sons and other [blessings]. (3)

Though overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin, as well as by the sins of destroying a lineage or killing an embryo, he was likewise a speaker of slander against others and one who took pleasure in the wives of others. (4)
O King, by not practicing these [vices], one certainly becomes free from sin;
whereas he who gives false testimony, employs false measures, or practices fraud with the balance scale— ||5||
He who recites false Veda and likewise false scriptures, a fraudulent astrologer and calculator, and a deceitful physician of Ayurveda; ||6||
One who is joined with false testimony should be known as an inhabitant of hell;
O King, by avoiding such [sins], they become liberated from evils.
That Kṣatriya who, having abandoned the duty of a warrior, flees from battle, goes to a terrible hell, being excluded from his own dharma. (8)
By not serving others, he too shall abandon evil and go to heaven;
so too for one who possesses knowledge, even if that disciple himself reviles his guru.
One who is joined with great sins goes to a terrible hell;
yet, by resorting to this [practice], even such a man shall attain a good state.
O King, listen as I describe the greatness of the other [river]; hear what fruit is obtained by men at Prayāga during the month of Māgha when the Sun is situated in Capricorn.
Just as the merit that is obtained by bathing during an eclipse at Kāśī,
so too is the satisfaction of the ancestors provided by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā.
O King, when Jupiter is situated in Leo, a man who has completed his Vedic studies should bathe in the Gautamī;
and when Jupiter has entered Virgo, he should immerse himself in the Kṛṣṇaveṇī.
Whatever fruit one obtains from the sight of Kumbhakeśvara and Kedāra, or even from visiting the sacred site during a pilgrimage to Badarikāśrama—[that same fruit is obtained here]. (14)

Whatever fruit one obtains at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse by performing a sacrifice with sacrificial fees, accompanied by gifts of elephants, horses, and gold—[that same fruit is obtained here]. (15)
One obtains such a fruit by observing the vow of Aparā;
likewise, by giving a cow that has recently calved, as well as gold and land. (16)
The fruit that a man obtains by means of this vow for Aparā is not attained even by another;
it is an axe to the tree of sin and a forest fire to the wealth of evil. 17.
He is the sun that dispels the darkness of evil and the lion that destroys the elephant of sin;
he is like a bubble in water and like a gnat among elephants.
Birth leads only to death without the vow of Ekādaśī;
therefore, having fasted on the following day and having worshipped Trivikrama, [one attains liberation]. ||19||
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, this has been told by me at the beginning;
O King, by reading or hearing it, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. 20.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Eleventh Day of the Dark Half of Jyeṣṭha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
(51) The Fifty-first Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, O speaker, I have heard all about the greatness of Aparā; now please tell me about the [greatness] of Jyeṣṭhā during the bright fortnight of that month.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The righteous Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, who knows the essential truth of the meaning of all scriptures and has reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, will speak of her. (2)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard these laws of Manu, and I have heard those of Vasiṣṭha; you should now speak to me correctly, O Dvaipāyana, concerning the Vaiṣṇava laws."
Śrī Veda-Vyāsa said:
"The duties of Manu and the Vedic duties have indeed been heard by you;
however, O lord of men, it is not possible to perform them all in the Kali age."
O Mahāmati, it is a means that is easy to practice, requires little wealth, involves little affliction, and yields great fruit; it is the very essence of all the Purāṇas. (5)
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
however, having become pure on the twelfth day, one should worship Keśava with flowers.
One should eat food with due respect, followed by the Brahmins;
yet one must not eat during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), nor during a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), O lord of men. (7)
O bull among men, this vow must be observed for as long as one lives by those who desire to attain the heavenly realm; regarding this, there is no doubt at all. (8)
Those who are sinful, of evil conduct, most wicked, and devoid of dharma—
yet who do not eat on the eleventh day— do not go to the presence of Yama.
Having heard those words, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena trembled like an *aśvattha* leaf; bowing down, he spoke to his preceptor. (10)
Bhīmasena said:
"O Grandfather of great intelligence, listen to my supreme words;
Yudhiṣṭhira, Kuntī, and likewise the daughter of Drupada [are also listening]. (11)
Arjuna, Nakula, and likewise Sahadeva—
those observers of excellent vows never eat on the eleventh day.
They always say this to me: "Do not eat, O Vṛkodara.
But I do not say that to them, dear father, for my hunger is unbearable.
"I shall give gifts according to the prescribed rites and I shall worship Keśava.
Having heard these words of Bhīmasena, Vyāsa spoke these words: 14.
Vyāsa said:
If heaven is desired by him, then meat, which is indeed wicked, must not be eaten on the eleventh day of either fortnight. (15)
Bhīmasena said: "O Grandfather of great intelligence, I speak before you:
I am able to subsist on a single meal; how could I, O Lord, endure fasting? (16)
That fire which is indeed called "Vṛka" is always within my belly;
when I eat excessively, it is then pacified.

“O Great Sage, I am not able to perform a single fast by which heaven is attained; rather, I shall perform that very thing exactly as it is. Therefore, having determined it with certainty, tell me that one thing by which I may obtain the highest good. (18)
Vyāsa said: When the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) falls while the sun is situated in Taurus or Gemini during the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should observe it with great care, abstaining from water.
A wise person should consume water for rinsing the mouth or sipping, but avoid drinking it; otherwise, there would be a violation of the vow. (20)
From sunrise until sunrise, a person who avoids water obtains the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs; listen! (21)
Then, at dawn on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), one should perform the ritual bath and,
according to the prescribed rule, give water and gold to the twice-born.
But having accomplished his purpose, the self-controlled one should eat together with the Brāhmaṇas;
O Bhīmasena, hear now what merit is gained when this is done. ||23||
Indeed, whatever Ekādaśīs occur throughout the year, one obtains their fruit; of this I have no doubt. (24)
Thus Keśava, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, said to me:
"A person, having abandoned everything else, should seek refuge in me alone. (25)
By fasting on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight], one is then liberated from sin;
in the Kali age, there is no purification of material objects, nor even the performance of Smārta rites.
But as for the Vaidika [tradition], since it has fallen into corruption from some cause in this Kali age—what need is there for me to say much more to you again and again, O son of the Wind? (27)
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
specifically, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should remain without water.
Listen, O Vṛkodara, to the meritorious fruit one obtains:
those [days] which are declared for the year, both bright and dark fortnights, O Vṛkodara. (29)
For all Ekādaśīs will undoubtedly have been observed as fasts;
they are meritorious, bestowing wealth, grain, sons, health, and auspiciousness. (30)
"O tiger among men, I tell you this as the truth:
the messengers of Yama are massive in body, terrifying, and black in form. (31)
The fierce ones bearing staffs and nooses do not approach that man;
rather, it is the gentle ones, clad in yellow garments, holding discs in their hands, and swift as thought, who approach him.
At the time of death, these lead the Vaiṣṇavas indeed to the city of Viṣṇu;
therefore, with every effort, one should fast, abstaining from water. (33)
Having then given a water-cow, one is liberated from all sins;
therefore, O son of Kuntī, you should perform the worship of Hari on this [day] while fasting.
Exert every effort for the pacification of all evils; even if there were an offense against me in a dream, or even due to the staining of my teeth, [let it be forgiven]. (35)
"I shall eat tomorrow, O Lord of Gods, after the day of Hari," having thus uttered this mantra, one should then become intent upon fasting. (36)
For the destruction of all sins, one endowed with faith and self-restraint [should perform this], even for the sin committed by a woman or a man that is as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara. (37)
All that is reduced to ashes by the power of Ekādaśī,
O lord of men, for those who are unable to give the water-cow (jala-dhenu).
A water-pot together with a cloth should be given;
indeed, he who observes the restriction of water during this [observance] partakes of merit. (39)
The fruit of ten million gold pieces is the merit heard for every watch;
whatever bathing, giving, recitation, or fire-offering a man performs upon this [day], [he gains that fruit]. (40)
All that has been spoken by Kṛṣṇa is attained as inexhaustible;
what need is there for any other dharma besides the Nirjala-ekādaśī? (41)
Having observed the fast correctly according to the prescribed rite, one shall indeed attain the state of Viṣṇu;
for gold, food, or clothing—whatever is bestowed upon her on this day [yields great merit].
Therefore, O tiger among the Kurus, all this shall be inexhaustible for him;
he who eats food on the eleventh day eats only sin. (43)
In this world, that outcaste, having died, attains an evil destiny;
whereas those who, having fasted on the twelfth day,
shall give gifts during the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, will attain the supreme state.
A killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, one who hates his teacher, and one who is always untruthful; ||45||
Those who fast on the day of Nirjala-ekādaśī are liberated from all sins; listen now to the special merit of this, O Kaunteya. (46)
That which must be performed by men and women endowed with faith is the giving of gifts;
the one who reclines upon the waters (Viṣṇu) should be worshipped, and likewise a cow made of water should be given. 47.
Or else, O best of kings, let there be a visible cow made of ghee, provided with abundant sacrificial fees and various kinds of sweet foods. (48)
O best among the upholders of dharma, the twice-born must be propitiated with effort;
for when the brahmins are satisfied, Hari, the giver of liberation, becomes truly pleased through them. 49.
Indeed, those by whom this [fast] was not observed have committed an act of self-betrayal;
they are evil-souled and of wicked conduct, for they have been robbed here—of this there is no doubt. (50)
A hundred future generations and likewise a hundred past generations, together with himself, have been led by them to the abode of Vāsudeva. (51)
By those who are peaceful, self-controlled, devoted to giving, and worshipping Hari, and by those who keep a vigil at night—by them has this fast been properly observed. (52)
Food, clothing, as well as cows, water, an auspicious bed and seat, a water-pot, and likewise an umbrella should be given on the day when no water is available. (53)
He who gives a pair of sandals to an excellent twice-born man who is a worthy recipient is honored in the heavenly world by means of a golden vehicle. ||54||
Whoever hears this with devotion and whoever recites it aloud—both of them attain heaven; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. ||55||

Whatever fruit a mortal may obtain by performing a śrāddha when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu during the Saṃnihati conjunction, that same fruit he obtains even from merely hearing of this [tīrtha]. //56//
One must observe the vow preceded by the cleansing of the teeth:
"On the eleventh day, fasting, I shall indeed abstain from water. (57)

On the twelfth day (dvādaśī), for the sake of pleasing Keśava, the Lord of the gods of gods, Trivikrama, should be worshipped, provided there is no other sipping of water (ācamana) [performed]. ||58||
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, incenses, flowers, and pleasing garments, one should recite this mantra: ||59||
O God of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, deliverer from the ocean of saṃsāra!
By the gift of this water-pot, lead me to the supreme goal. (60)
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the auspicious eleventh day of the bright fortnight, one should fast without water; here, one should offer water-pots along with sugar.
Having bestowed [these] upon the foremost of Brahmins, one rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu;
thereafter, water-pots should be given to the Brahmins with devotion.
Having fed the Brahmins, he, intent on that, should then eat himself. He who thus observes the full Dvādaśī, which destroys all sin— ||63||
Being completely liberated from all sins, he went to the state free from disease.
From that time forward, the auspicious Ekādaśī established by Bhīma became renowned in the world by the name Pāṇḍava-dvādaśī.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Jyeṣṭha-Śukla Anirjala Ekādaśī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||51||
The fifty-second chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha?
Please, out of your grace, speak of Vāsudeva before me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O King, I shall now describe before you the most excellent of all vows,
which destroys every sin and bestows complete liberation.
O best of kings, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, known by the name Yoginī, there is a [tithi] that destroys great sins.
She is the eternal boat for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, and she is the essence of the three worlds for those who observe the yoginī-vow. (4)
I shall relate before you an auspicious ancient tale:
in Alakā, there was a king of kings who was devoted solely to the worship of Śiva. ||5||
He had a flower-seller named Hemamālī;
his wife was beautiful and named Viśālākṣī.
Unattached to that [world] and having fallen under the power of the noose of desire, he brought a collection of flowers from the Mānasa lake and remained in his own home. (7)
Addicted to the flavor of love for his wife, he did not go to the abode of Kubera;
instead, Kubera performed the worship of Śiva in his own celestial residence.
At midday, O King, Hemamālī, observing the arrival of flowers,
rejoiced with his beloved in his own palace.
Then the King of Yakṣas, provoked by the delay of time, replied:
"O Yakṣas, why does that wicked-souled Hemamālī not come?
Let a decision be made regarding him! he said again and again.
The Yakṣas said:
"O King, you are a lover of women who stays at home according to your own will.
Having heard their words, Kubera was filled with anger. (11)
They quickly summoned the young ascetic Hemamālin;
perceiving the lapse of time, his eyes became agitated with fear.
Having arrived without having bathed, he stood before Kubera;
seeing him, the Giver of Wealth became enraged, his eyes bloodshot with anger.
Overcome with rage, his lower lip quivering with anger, he replied.
Dhanada said:
"Ah! O sinful, wicked, and evil-doing one, you have committed an insult against the gods! (14)
"Deprived of that beautiful woman, afflicted by the eighteen types of leprosy, and cast out from this place, go now, you lowest of men! (15)
As soon as this was said, he fell from that place,
overcome by great suffering, his body tormented by leprosy.
He finds no happiness by day, nor does he obtain sleep at night;
his body is tormented by the heat, suffering intensely in the summer sun while standing in the shade. (17)
By the power of the worship of Śiva, his memory is not lost;
even when overcome by sin, he remembers his former deeds.
Wandering and proceeding from there to Himādri, the best of mountains,
he beheld there the excellent sage Mārkaṇḍeya, a treasure-house of asceticism.
O King, he whose lifespan is equal to the age of Brahmā—
the evildoer stands far away from his feet.
Seeing him thus trembling, Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages, called out for the sake of helping others and spoke as follows: ||21||
"Why are you overcome by leprosy? From what cause do you become so exceedingly censurable?
Being thus addressed, he replied to the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
Hemamālin said:
"O Sage, I am a follower of the King of Kings, known by the name Hemamālin; every day I bring a collection of lotuses from Lake Mānasa. (23)
"At the time of Śiva’s worship, I offer [this] to Kubera;
on this very day, the time was unknown to me. (24)
O Vālmīki, while his mind was distracted by the pleasure of his wife and agitated by grief,
that king of kings then cursed me in anger.
Overcome by leprosy, I became separated from that beloved wife;
now, through the power of my auspicious karma, I have attained your presence. (26)
Knowing that by their very nature the minds of the virtuous are capable of benefiting others, O best of sages, command me, who have committed this offense. (27)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Since you have spoken the truth here and no falsehood has been uttered by you, I shall therefore describe to you the instruction for a vow that bestows auspiciousness. (28)
Observe the Yoginī vow during the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha;
by the merit of this vow, your leprosy will certainly disappear. (29)
Having heard these words of the sage, he fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff;
raised up by the sage, he became exceedingly joyful. (30)
Following the instruction of Mārkaṇḍeya, he performed the vow as prescribed;
consequently, all eighteen types of leprosy departed from him entirely.
Then, having properly observed the vow according to the sage’s word, he became happy.
O best of kings, such is the Yoginī-vrata that has been described. (32)
A man who performs the Yoginī vow obtains a fruit equal to that of one who feeds eighty-eight thousand brahmins.
It pacifies great sins and bestows the fruit of great merit;
by reciting or hearing it, a mortal is liberated from all evils. (34)

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Āṣāḍha-Kṛṣṇa-Yoginī-Ekādaśī," in the Uttara-Khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||52||
The fifty-third chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, there occurs the Kāca Ekādaśī."
Tell me this in detail: what is the procedure for her name?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall narrate the supremely meritorious Śayanī Ekādaśī, which bestows heaven and liberation, is known by this name, and is the supreme destroyer of all sins. 2.
By the mere hearing of which one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
this is the truth, the truth, as declared by me—there is nothing superior to this for human beings.
Created by the Creator for the destruction of the sins of sinners, this most excellent [river] exists;
therefore, O King of Kings, it remains the bestower of liberation even beyond that. ||4||
For this reason, O King, listen to the supreme goal that may be attained by men who merely hear the account, even through listening alone. (5)
O King, those who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu and dedicated to bhakti worship the Supreme Lord Vāmana during the month of Āṣāḍha. (6)
By whomsoever the lotus-eyed Vāmana was worshipped with lotuses on the Kāmikā day at the beginning of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha; ||7||
By him the entire world and the three eternal gods are worshipped,
by whom the Ekādaśī and the supreme day of Hari have been observed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Supreme Person, there is a great doubt in me regarding this; please listen.
How did you sleep, O Lord of Gods, and how did you take refuge in Bali?"
And how is one to sleep upon the ground? What do other people do? O highly wise one, tell me this; I have a great doubt. (10)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O tiger among kings, listen to this supreme narrative which removes all sins;
by the mere hearing of it, the destruction of all sins shall occur. (11)
O King, in the Tretā Yuga there was a man named Bala who was never before seen;
he constantly worshipped me, being my devotee and having me as his supreme goal. ||12||
O King, that Daitya, performing sacrifices and observing vows, worships me, the eternal one, with sacrifices according to the rules and with supreme devotion. (13)
Furthermore, after the Lord of the Day (the Sun) had deliberated in many ways with eloquent hymns,
I was worshipped in various ways by my preceptor along with the deities.
Then, in the fifth incarnation, He appeared in the form of a dwarf,
possessing an exceedingly fierce form that encompassed the entire universe.
The Daityas were defeated through a verbal trick; Śukra, relying on the truth, stood his ground and prevented him [from killing Viṣṇu], saying, "This one is Nārāyaṇa."
O King, when I requested three and a half paces of land,
it was granted by him with merely the water of his resolve placed in my hand.
O King, I have heard that his form was of such a kind:
he placed his feet upon the Bhūrloka and his knees upon the Bhuvarloka.
Having placed the hips in the world of the gods (Svarloka), the belly in Maharloka, the heart in Janaloka, and the throat in Tapoloka; 19.
The mouth should be placed at Satyaloka, and the head above that;
likewise, the moon, sun, planets, and the constellations [are situated there].
The gods, along with Indra, the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, likewise praised him with various hymns composed from the Vedas. ||21||
Taking up the sacrificial offering (bali) with my hand, the earth was filled with three steps;
then, I placed half of that step upon his back.
O King, that Dānava, who was a non-worshipper of Maheśvara, was cast down into the depths of the ocean;
what did he do after that? (23)
Bowing with discipline, he was well-pleased by Janārdana;
it was the day of Hari during the month of Āṣāḍha, in the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
Of those two, one form of mine remains there, having taken recourse to Bali;
the second is upon the back of Śeṣa in the midst of the Ocean of Milk.
O Great King, he sleeps in this manner until the upcoming Kārttikī festival;
during that time, he becomes a person of pure virtue, the most excellent among all who possess the highest Dharma. (26)
A mortal who performs this vow attains the supreme goal;
for this reason, O King, it should be performed with great effort. ||27||
There is nothing more purifying or more destructive of sin than this, wherein the Lord of Gods, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, goes to sleep. (28)
And on that [day], one should worship the God who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, having performed a vigil at night with special devotion. (29)
O King, even the Four-faced One (Brahmā) is not able to calculate the merit of her who thus performs this most excellent vow of Ekādaśī.
It removes all sins and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is always dear to the world of the living, even to one who cooks dog-flesh.
O beloveds of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, by the gift of lamps, by eating from palāśa leaves, and by the observance of vows,
one passes the four months of the rainy season without distress.
During the four months of the rainy season, a man should sleep on the ground;
he should avoid leafy vegetables in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise curd in Bhādrapada.
One should abandon milk in the month of Āśvayuja, clarified butter in Kārttika, and split pulses in Mārgaśīrṣa;
or else, remaining in celibacy, he attains the supreme goal. ||34||
By the vow of Ekādaśī alone, a person is liberated from sins;
it should always be observed, O King, and never forgotten. (35)
If the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇaikādaśī) occurs between the Śayanī and Bodhinī Ekādaśīs, that one alone should be observed as a fast by a householder; never any other dark Ekādaśī.
And whoever, O King, should hear this supreme narrative that removes sin, that person obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). ||37||

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Devaśayanī Ekādaśī," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||53||
The fifty-fourth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa?
Therefore, tell us that, O Govinda Vāsudeva; salutations be unto you! ||1||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall relate this narrative which destroys all sins, which was indeed previously told by Brahmā to the inquiring Nārada. 2.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, O Lotus-seated Lord, I desire to hear from you what the name of the Ekādaśī is in the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
"O Lord, who is her deity, what is her ritual procedure, and what is her merit? Tell me, O Master.
Having heard these words of his, Brahmā spoke these words: ||4||
Brahmā said:
Listen, O Nārada, with a desire for the welfare of the worlds, to [the account of] the Ekādaśī of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, known by the name Kāmikā. 5.
Merely by hearing this, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
in this [place], one worships the Lord of Gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Listen now to the meritorious fruit of him who worships and meditates upon Hari, Viṣṇu, Mādhava, and Madhusūdana, known by the name Śrīdhara. (7)
One obtains that same fruit which results from the worship of Kṛṣṇa at Nāgaṅgā, Nakāśī, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara. (8)
Whatever fruit one obtains at the Godāvarī, at Gurusiṃha, during a Vyatīpāta yoga, or at Daṇḍaka, that same fruit is obtained from the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
He who gives away the great earth together with its oceans and forests,
and he who performs the Kāmika vow— both are remembered as having equal fruits.
A man who gives a cow that is currently giving birth, along with its necessary accessories, obtains the same fruit as one who performs the Kāmikā vow. ||11||
The best of men should worship the god Śrīdhara in the month of Śrāvaṇa;
by that very act, the gods, gandharvas, uragas, and pannagas are all worshipped.
Therefore, with every effort, Hari should be worshipped according to one's capacity on the day of Kāma and other such occasions by humans who fear sin. (13)
For the sake of uplifting those who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, which is crowded with the mud of sin, this supreme Kāmika-vrata [is prescribed]. (14)
"There is nothing more purifying or more destructive of sins than this;
know this, O Nārada, for the Supreme Hari himself has spoken thus. (15)
Know that the fruit obtained by men devoted to the inner science (adhyātmavidyā) is far greater than that of those who observe the Kāmika vow. 16.
A man who keeps a vigil at night and performs the Kāmikā vow does not see the terrible Yama, nor does he go to an evil state of existence. ||17||
One does not see a base rebirth due to the practice of the Kāmikā vow;
by having performed the Kāmikā vow, yogins have attained absolute liberation (kaivalya). 18.
Therefore, with every effort, those of disciplined mind should worship Hari with leaves produced from the *tulasī* plant. (19)
He is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
he is like a single load of gold compared to four times that amount of silver.
One obtains that same fruit from worshipping with a tulasī leaf as one does when worshipped with jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, and the like. (21)
Viṣṇu is not so pleased by water with tulasī leaves as he is by one who worships Keśava with the dust of tulasī. ||22||
The moment it is seen, it pacifies the entire mass of sins; when touched, it purifies the body;
when smelled, it destroys all diseases; when sprinkled, it dispels the fear of Death;
and when planted, it brings about proximity to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa.
Homage to that peerless one, upon whose feet [the world] has placed itself, and who bestows the fruit of liberation. ||23||
If a mortal offers a lamp during the day or night on the day of Hari,
Citragupta is not at all able to calculate the extent of that merit.
If the "foremost lamp of Kṛṣṇa" is lit on the eleventh day, his ancestors dwelling in heaven are satiated with nectar. (25)
Having lit a lamp with ghee or again with sesame oil,
one goes to the world of the Sun, honored by the light of hundreds of millions of lamps.
This greatness of Kāmikā has been declared by me before you;
therefore, it should be performed by men, for it removes all sins. 27.
She is the remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin, the destroyer of the sin of destroying an embryo, the bestower of the station of Viṣṇu, and the giver of the fruit of great merit. ||28||
Having heard this greatness of her, a man endowed with faith attains the world of Viṣṇu and is liberated from all sins. ||29||

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Eleven Days of the Dark Half of Śrāvaṇa," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||54||
The fifty-fifth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa?
O Madhusūdana, please speak out of your grace before me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen attentively, O King, to this supreme narrative which removes all sins;
by the mere hearing of it, the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice is attained. (2)
At the beginning of the Dvāpara Yuga, in the city of Māhiṣmatī,
there was a king named Mahījit who ruled over his own kingdom.
For him who is bereft of a son, that kingdom does not bestow happiness;
for one without a son, there is no happiness in this world nor in the next. (4)
Thus, as this son of his reflected, much time passed away;
yet the king did not obtain a son who bestows all happiness upon men.
Seeing himself growing old, he became intent on meditation;
then, having come into the midst of his subjects, he spoke these words: ||6||
In this present life, no sin has been committed by me against the world;
nor have I cast into the treasury wealth acquired through unjust means. (7)
I have never seized the property of Brahmins or the wealth of the gods;
I have not committed the theft of a deposit, which brings great sin upon another.
I have protected the world like a son, and the earth has been conquered through righteousness.
Punishment was inflicted upon the wicked, even if they were like one's own kinsmen or sons; however, the virtuous were always honored, and no harm was done to the people.
O best of the twice-born, as I am speaking thus regarding the path endowed with dharma, consider this:
why was no son born in my house? (10)
Having heard these words, the twice-born, together with the subjects and the family priest,
consulted regarding what would benefit the king and went to that dense forest.
Looking here and there at the hermitages frequented by sages,
and desiring the welfare of the king, they beheld that best of munis.
He was performing terrible austerities, without support and free from affliction;
he was without food, self-conquered, with anger subdued, and eternal.
He was hairy, a knower of the essence of dharma, proficient in all the scriptures,
long-lived, high-souled, possessed of hair on his head, and equal to Brahmā.
As each kalpa passed, a single hair of his would fall out;
therefore, this great sage, who knows the three periods of time, is named Ato-lomaśa.
Seeing him, they were all filled with joy and approached his presence;
they paid him homage as was prescribed, according to custom, and as was fitting for each.
Bowed down in humility, they all said to one another, "By the power of our own good fortune, this most excellent of sages has arrived.
Seeing them along with their children in that state, the best of ṛṣis spoke: (17)
Lomaśa said:
"For what purpose have you arrived here? Tell me the reason;
for my mind is gladdened by the sight of you, and why indeed do you praise me?"
I shall create a doubt for you that will be for your benefit; there is no doubt that for those like me, birth is solely for the sake of helping others. (19)
The people said:
"Listen, we shall explain the reason for our arrival;
we have come into your presence for the purpose of cutting through our doubts. (20)
There exists no one superior to or more excellent than you, O Lotus-born One;
therefore, we have come into your presence on account of a certain task. (21)
O Brahmin, there is a king named Mahījita who is childless;
we are his subjects, O Brahmin, protected by him as if we were his own sons.
Seeing him bereft of a son, they were pained by his sorrow; having resolved upon a lifelong vow, they came here to perform penance.
O best of the twice-born, you have been seen by us only through our good fortune;
indeed, the accomplishment of men's purposes occurs simply through the sight of the great. (24)
"May the son of King Upadeśa become like me.
Having heard these words of theirs, the sage entered into meditation for a moment;
then, knowing his former birth, the sage replied: (25)
Lomaśa said:
"In a former birth, this man was indeed a Vaiśya who was destitute of wealth and cruel;
devoted to the business of trade, he wandered from village to village. (26)
Likewise, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
when the sun has reached the meridian, one should go to a reservoir of water at the boundary of the village.
Seeing the small well filled with water, he set his mind on drinking;
immediately thereafter, a cow together with her calf arrived there. (28)
When those afflicted by thirst and distressed by the heat of summer were drinking the cool water, he restrained them from drinking it and drank that water himself. (29)
By that sinful karma, the king shall become bereft of sons;
yet, through the merit of some previous birth, he has obtained a kingdom free from all thorns.
The people said: "O Sage, it is heard in the Purāṇas that sin goes to destruction through merit;
therefore, please tell us the instruction on merit so that there may be the destruction of our sins."
Just as by your grace, one becomes the son of a king. ||31||
Lomaśa said:
"O people, observe that vow on the Ekādaśī known as Putradā, which is renowned for bestowing sons, occurring in the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa. (32)
Having heard this and paid homage to the sage, they returned to their city and performed the vow according to the rules and in the proper manner, accompanied by a night vigil.
The people bestowed that most pure merit upon the king;
once the merit had been given, the queen then conceived a beautiful embryo.
When the time for delivery had arrived, she gave birth to a powerful son during the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
while the sun was situated in Cancer.
On the twelfth day, the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Vāsudeva is prescribed;
it should be performed with threads of gold, silver, copper, linen, silk, or lotus-fiber.
Having bathed with auspicious *kuśa* grass, *kāśa* grass, and cotton spun by a Brahmin woman,
one should purify the thread by tripling it and then folding it into three strands again.
At the time of milking the cows, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the preceding day;
having paid homage to the Brahmins and prostrated at the feet of the Guru.
Then one should perform the vigil with the resonance of singing;
likewise, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Bhillas, and Śūdras [should do so]. (39)
Established in their own duties, all should perform the *pavitraka* rite with devotion;
thereafter, one should offer the *pavitraka* to the guru according to the prescribed rules. (40)
One should worship the Brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇavas with fragrances, flowers, and other offerings; with the mantra "ato devā," the twice-born should offer [the oblation] to Viṣṇu. 41.
Just as with Viṣṇu, so too with Śiva, a Śūdra should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa rite every year using the Mūlamantra; this must be performed by men year after year.
For those who desire both worldly enjoyment and liberation in this ocean of sorrow that is saṃsāra, he who does not perform the Pavitrāropaṇa according to the prescribed rite [is lost]. (43)
For a Vaiṣṇava, the annual worship of that [goddess] becomes fruitless;
yet, by hearing her majesty, a man is liberated from sin.
Having obtained the happiness of sons in this world, he shall attain the state of heaven in the next.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled “The Ekādaśī of the Sons [Bestowed] by the Offering of the Pavitra on the Bright Fortnight of Śrāvaṇa,” in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||55||
The fifty-sixth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada?
I desire to hear this; please tell me, O Janārdana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O King Ikṣvāku, I shall describe it to you in detail;
it is known by the name Ajitā and is the destroyer of all sins. 2.
Having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa, whoever observes this vow on this [day],
his sins perish even from merely hearing of this vow.
O King, there is nothing higher than this for the welfare of both worlds;
what I have spoken is indeed the truth, for my speech is never false. (4)
In ancient times, there was a king renowned as Hariścandra;
he was a universal emperor (cakravartin), true to his word, and the lord of the entire earth.
Due to the ripening of a certain karma, he was deprived of his kingdom;
he sold his wife and son, and then he sold himself as well.
Even a king who has committed no meritorious deeds becomes a Pulkasa slave if he steals the garments of the deceased from a virtuous lord of men.
Thus that best of kings became one who had wavered from truth;
in this manner, many years passed for that monarch.
Then King Cintāpara became exceedingly distressed:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can there be atonement? (9)
While he was thus reflecting, submerged in an ocean of distress,
a certain sage arrived, having learned that the king was afflicted.
The twice-born were created by Brahmā for the purpose of assisting others;
seeing that best of the twice-born, the most excellent of kings bowed down to him. (11)
Having joined his palms in reverence, he stood before Gautama and related his own account, which was filled with suffering.
Having heard the words of the king, the sage Gautama was filled with wonder;
the muni then gave the instruction for this vow to the king.
O King, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the dark fortnight, the auspicious Ekādaśī has arrived; it is known as Ajā and bestows great merit. (14)
O King, this will be the curse of this sinful woman: by the power of your misfortune, she shall come to you on the seventh day. (15)
Being intent on fasting, perform a vigil at night;
when this vow has been thus observed, the destruction of your sin is certain. (16)
"O best of kings, I have come here by the power of your merit. Having spoken thus, the sage vanished from sight. (17)
Having heard the words of the sage, the king undertook the supreme vow; once that vow was performed by the king, his sin vanished in an instant.
Listen, O tiger among kings, to the power of this vow:
whatever suffering would have to be endured for many years shall come to an end. (19)
By the power of this vow, he crossed over the ocean of suffering;
through it, he attained reunion with his wife and the restoration of his son's life. (20)
Both were unable to divide it; then a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
By the power of Ekādaśī, he obtained a kingdom free of all thorns.
Hariścandra attained heaven along with his city and his retinue;
such is the vow that kings and men perform.
O King, those who are completely liberated from all sins go to heaven;
by either reciting or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of Bhādrapada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
The fifty-seventh chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs during the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya?
O Keśava, tell me this: who is his god, and what is his ritual procedure?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O protector of the earth, I shall relate this wondrous narrative,
which Brahmā once told to the high-souled Nārada.
Nārada said: O Four-faced One, salutations to you; please graciously tell me:
what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas?
I truly desire to hear this for the sake of propitiating Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said: "O best of sages, you are a Vaiṣṇava; indeed, you have asked well.
There is nothing in this world more purifying than the day of Hari."
The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas is renowned by the name Padmā;
on this day Hṛṣīkeśa is worshipped, and the supreme vow should be performed. (5)
I shall relate before you this auspicious ancient tale,
by the mere hearing of which great sin is destroyed.
I was the royal sage named Dhātṛ, born of the lineage of Vivasvat;
he was a powerful universal monarch who was true to his word.
He protected his subjects according to dharma like his own biological sons; in his kingdom there was no famine, nor were there mental afflictions or diseases.
His subjects were free from fear, and his wealth and grain flourished;
the king’s treasury was filled with riches acquired through righteous means.
All the social classes and stages of life likewise proceeded according to their own respective duties;
in the kingdom of that lord of the earth, the land was equal to the wish-fulfilling cow, Kāmadhenu.
As he was thus exercising his sovereignty for many groups of years, then,
at the arrival of a certain time, the ripening of karma indeed took place.
For three years, a new rain-cloud did not pour over that region;
consequently, his subjects were broken and afflicted by hunger.

Deprived of the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*, and devoid of the study of the Vedas, his kingdom became afflicted by fate through his own misfortune. Then the subjects, having assembled, spoke thus to the king: ||13||
The subjects said:
"O tiger among kings, you must listen to the words of your subjects.
In the Purāṇas, the wise have declared that 'āpaḥ' (the waters) are called 'nārāḥ'. (14)
Because he is the refuge (ayana) of the Blessed One, he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, existing as Parjanya, is established as all-pervading. 15.
He thus brings about rain; from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
In the absence of that, O best of kings, living beings go to ruin. Therefore, O best of the Kurus, act so that there may be security and prosperity.
The king said: "What you have spoken is true; nothing has been stated falsely by you anywhere. Food is declared to be Brahman, for everything is established in food. (17)
"From food beings arise; by food the world subsists"—thus is it heard in the world in the Purāṇas at great length. (18)
"Through the misconduct of kings, the oppression of subjects occurs;
yet, as I reflect with my intellect, I do not see any such thing as having been committed by myself. (19)
"Nevertheless, out of a desire for the welfare of my subjects, I shall strive [to do so]. Having formed this resolve, the king, accompanied by an immeasurable retinue, [set forth]. (20)
Having paid homage to the Creator, he went to the dense forest;
there he visited the foremost of sages and the hermitages inhabited by ascetics.
Then the king beheld the sage, the son of Brahmā,
illuminating the quarters with his splendor, like a second lotus-born creator.
Seeing him, the self-controlled king was filled with joy; descending from his vehicle, he bowed at his feet with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having greeted him with blessings for his welfare, the sage inquired after the king’s well-being regarding his kingdom and his seven limbs of sovereignty.
Having announced his arrival, the king inquired after his welfare;
then, having been offered a seat and received the water of honor (*arghya*), he sat down in his presence.
The king, being asked about the reason for his arrival, replied to the sage.
The king said: "O Blessed One, while I was protecting the earth according to the ordinances of dharma, a drought occurred; I do not know the cause of this. (27)
I have come here into your presence to cut through my doubts;
by providing for the security and well-being of the subjects, bring them peace.
The sage said:
O King, this is the Kṛta Yuga, considered the best among the ages; here people are devoted to Brahman, and here dharma has four feet. (29)
"In this age, O King of kings, the Brāhmaṇas are devoted to austerity, yet other people—this outcaste among them—is practicing penance in your realm. (30)
For this very reason, Navarṣatibalāhaka,
you must exert effort so that this fault may be pacified.
The king said:
"I shall not kill this innocent man who is performing penance;
instead, tell me an instruction on dharma that destroys calamities. (32)
The sage said:
"If it is so, O King, then observe the Ekādaśī vow during the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya; it is renowned by the name Padmā. (33)
By the power of his vow, there will certainly be a bountiful rain;
for this [vow] bestows all accomplishments and destroys all calamities. (34)
"O King of the Kurus, let him along with his subjects and his retinue observe this vow.
Having heard these words of the sage, the king returned to his own home. (35)
Then, in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, he performed the Padmā-vrata together with all his subjects and accompanied by the four social orders.
Thus, O King, when the vow was completed, the clouds rained down;
the earth, drenched with water, became abounding in crops. (37)
By the power of the lordly sages, the worlds attained happiness;
for this very reason, this supreme vow should be performed in such a manner. (38)
Having given to a brahmin on that [day] a water-filled jar filled with curd and rice, wrapped in cloth, along with an umbrella and sandals; ||39||
Salutations, salutations to you, O Govinda, known as Budhaśravaṇa;
having destroyed the multitude of my sins, be the bestower of all happiness. (40)
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and granting happiness to all people, O King, one is released from all sins by reciting or hearing it. ||41||

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ekādaśī of the White Lotus in the Bright Fortnight of Bhādrapada," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada. ||57||
The fifty-eighth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Madhusūdana, please tell me out of your grace.
In which month and on what name is the Ekādaśī that occurs during the dark fortnight? ||1||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, there is a vow known by the name Dirā.
By the power of that vow, even great sin is destroyed. (2)
O King, listen with focused attention to this supreme, sin-destroying narrative, which grants a higher rebirth to the ancestors who have fallen into lower wombs. (3)
O King, O delighter of kings, in a former age of the Kṛta Yuga, there was one who would obtain the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice merely by hearing it. 4.
Known as Indrasena, the lord of the ancient city of Māhiṣmatī,
that king, endowed with fame, protected the earth according to righteousness.
Accompanied by sons and grandsons, endowed with wealth and grain, he was the king of Māhiṣmatī, solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu. ||6||
O lord of men, King Japāgovinda spends his time according to the prescribed rule, contemplating the meditation on the supreme self (adhyātma-dhyāna) and bestowing liberation upon others.
One day, while the king was seated comfortably with his courtiers assembled,
the sage Nārada descended from heaven and arrived there.
Seeing him arrive, he rose to meet him with palms joined in reverence; having honored him according to the prescribed rite, he then seated him upon a throne.
The best of kings replied to the sage who was seated comfortably.
The king said:
"O best of sages, by your grace, everything is well with me. (10)
All the sacrificial rites performed today have become fruitful through the sight of you;
show favor, O divine sage, and tell us the reason for your arrival.
Nārada said:
"O tiger among kings, listen to my words which cause wonder.
O best of monarchs, I have come from the world of Brahmā to this world of Yama."
Honored with devotion by Śamena, he sat upon an excellent seat;
virtuous and truthful, he sat there worshipping the Sun.
Although he was a performer of many meritorious deeds, your father was seen by me in the assembly of Śrāddhadeva due to the fault of a deficiency in his vows.
O lord of men, understand that message which was delivered by him:
"The king known as Indrasena is the ruler of Māhiṣmatī. (15)
O Brahmin, he said before him: "I am standing in the presence of Yama due to some obstacle arising from a previous birth. (16)
"By the gift of double merit, send me, your son, to heaven.
Having been addressed thus, O King, I have come into your presence. (17)
O King, perform the Indirā-vrata for the sake of your father’s attainment of heaven;
by the power of that vow, your father shall go to heaven. (18)
The king said:
"O Blessed One, please graciously tell me of the Indirā-vrata;
by what procedure is it to be performed, in which fortnight, and on which lunar day? (19)
Nārada said: Listen, O king of kings, as I describe the auspicious procedure for this vow;
on the auspicious tenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
One should perform the morning bath with a mind endowed with faith;
then, having performed the midday bath at the time of noon, one should remain composed.
Endowed with faith, one should perform the śrāddha for the gratification of the ancestors;
then, having taken a single meal, one should sleep on the ground at night.
When the clear dawn has arrived and the eleventh day (ekādaśī) has come, [one should proceed].
One should perform the washing of the face, omitting the cleaning of the teeth;
then, with a spirit of devotion, one should undertake the observance of the fast. (23)
Having remained without food today and renounced all enjoyments, I shall eat tomorrow; O Acyuta, O Lotus-eyed One, be my refuge. (24)
Having made this resolve, one should likewise, at the time of midday,
perform the ritual bath before a Śālagrāma stone according to the prescribed rules.
Having thus worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa with incense, perfumes, and other offerings,
one should keep a vigil at night in the presence of Keśava.
Then, when the time of dawn has arrived on the twelfth day,
one should worship Hari with devotion and perform the śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules.
Endowed with faith, one should perform the śrāddha for the gratification of the ancestors;
the śrāddha performed with wheat flour becomes a source of purity. (28)
O King, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with barley, rice, sesame, black gram, wheat, and chickpeas, honoring them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Restraining his speech, he should eat himself along with his kinsmen, daughters' sons, sons, and others;
O King, perform this vow without sloth according to this rule. (30)
"O King, your ancestors shall go to the world of Viṣṇu," having said this to the monarch, O King, the sage vanished on the spot. (31)
In accordance with the prescribed rite, the king performed the supreme vow, accompanied by the inner apartments and attended by his sons and servants. ||32||
When the vow was completed, O son of Kuntī, a rain of flowers fell from the sky;
his father, mounted upon Garuḍa, went to the abode of Hari.
The royal sage Indrasena also, having made his kingdom free of thorns and having installed his son in the kingship, himself departed for the third heaven.
O King, I have thus recounted before you the greatness of the Indra-vrata;
by reading or hearing it, one is liberated from all sins. (35)
Having enjoyed all pleasures here, he shall dwell for a long time in the world of Viṣṇu. ||36||

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Ekādaśī of the Waning Moon of Āśvina," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||58||
The fifty-ninth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Madhusūdana, please graciously tell me this in my presence.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, what is the name of the eleventh lunar day? ||1||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Indra among kings, I shall describe this greatness which destroys all sins—
the Ekādaśī that occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
Another [tīrtha] renowned as Pāpakuśā is the supreme remover of all sins;
there, a person should worship me, who am named Padmanābha. ||3||
Having performed intense penance for a long time with his senses well-restrained, he attained the fruit of all his desires, which bestows heaven and liberation upon men. (4)
Having committed many sins, a man possessed by delusion attains that same fruit [of liberation] by bowing to the one whose banner is Garuḍa. (5)
Having bowed to Hari, who removes all sins and is beyond the reach of hell,
[I shall describe] whatever holy fords and sacred shrines exist upon the earth.
One obtains all of these through the chanting of the names of Viṣṇu—
those people who have taken refuge in the Lord Janārdana, Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
For those who have observed even a single Ekādaśī fast, even by chance, no torment of the world of Yama ever arises; such a person does not undergo the tortures of Yama,
even after committing a terrible sin.
That person who, having become a Vaiṣṇava, utters slander against Śiva, shall not go to the Vaiṣṇava realm;
he will certainly go to hell. ||9||
If a Śaiva, having become a Pāśupata, utters slander against Viṣṇu,
he is cooked in the terrible Raurava hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
Nothing so purifying exists in the three worlds as this vow of Padmanābha, which destroys all sins. (11)
O lord of men, sins remain in this body only so long as one does not fast on that auspicious day of Padmanābha.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the Ekādaśī day. 13.
No vow whatsoever is known in the world equal to Ekādaśī;
even those who perform it under a pretext go to the abode of the Son of the Sun (Yama).
This [vow] bestows heaven and liberation; it grants bodily health and freedom from disease;
it bestows a wife and sons; and it grants wealth and friends. (15)
O King, neither the Narmadā, nor the Gaṅgā, nor Prayāga, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara, nor even the Kaurava field is as meritorious as the day of Hari. 16.
O King, by keeping a vigil at night and fasting on the day of Hari,
one attains the station of Viṣṇu without any effort.
In this way, a man shall deliver ten ancestors on his mother’s side, ten on his father’s side, and ten on the side of his beloved wife. (18)
Possessing divine forms with four arms and other features, having abandoned the householder's life, adorned with garlands and wearing yellow garments, they proceed to the abode of Hari.
O best of kings, by fasting on Ekādaśī during childhood, youth, and old age, one certainly does not meet with an evil fate.
Having fasted at Pāpa-kuśā on the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, a person, completely liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Hari. ||21||
Having given gold, sesame seeds, land, a cow, food, water,
as well as sandals, umbrellas, garments, and so forth, a man does not behold Yama.
He whose days come and go devoid of merit does not truly live,
even though he breathes like the bellows of a blacksmith.
O best of kings, even a poor man should perform the *ava-dhyam* rite from heaven, always practicing the prescribed actions such as ritual bathing and giving charity. (24)
Those who perform meritorious deeds such as fire-offerings, ritual bathing, recitation, meditation,
and sacrificial sessions do not at all behold that terrible torment of Yama.
In this world, those who perform meritorious deeds are seen to be long-lived, wealthy, of noble birth, and free from disease; such are the results for those who practice virtue. (26)
What need is there for much speaking on this? By unrighteousness they ascend to a miserable state, and by righteousness they ascend to heaven; no deliberation is required here. (27)
O sinless King, I have thus related that which I was asked by you;
what else do you wish to hear regarding the greatness of the sinful Kuśā? (28)

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Kuśaikādaśī on the Tenth Day of the Bright Half of Āśvina," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||59||
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, out of grace and affection for me, please tell [me].
What is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika? (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, as I speak before you;
in the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, there is the most auspicious name of Ramā. (2)
The Ekādaśī is renowned as the supreme remover of great sins;
O King, in this context, I shall proclaim its majesty to you. (3)
In ancient times, there was a king renowned as Mucukunda;
O King, he shared a state of friendship with Devendra.
O King, he who maintained friendship in every way with Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and even with Vibhīṣaṇa.
There was a supreme king, a devotee of Viṣṇu, who was true to his word;
O King, while he was thus ruling his kingdom, it was cleared of all thorns.
A daughter named Candra-bhāgā, the best of rivers, was born in his house;
and she was indeed given in marriage to Śobhana, the son of Candrasena. ||7||
Once, O King, he arrived at his father-in-law’s house;
it was the day of the Ekādaśī vow, which bestows great merit.
When the day for the vow arrived, Candrabhāgā thought:
"O Lord of Gods, what will become of my husband, who is so exceedingly weak? (9)
He cannot endure hunger, and his father is one of fierce command;
for him, the drum is beaten when the tenth day arrives. (10)
"One must not eat, one must not eat, one must not eat on the day of Hari!
Having heard the resonance of the drum, Sobhana spoke to his beloved: ||11||
"What should I do, O beloved? Give me instruction, O fair-faced one.
Candrabhāgā said: "O Lord, no one should eat today in my father's house."
On the day of Hari, elephants, horses, young calves, and indeed other animals must not consume grass, food, or water. (13)
O beloved, why would human beings eat on the day of Hari?
If you, O beloved, should eat, then you will incur reproach. (14)
Having reflected thus with the mind, make your resolve very firm.
Śobhana said: "O beloved, these words are true; I shall observe the fast."
"Whatever is ordained by fate will surely come to pass exactly so. Having formed this firm resolve, he undertook a vow of religious observance. (16)
With his body tormented by hunger, he became exceedingly distressed;
as he was thinking thus, the sun went down behind the mountain.
For those Vaiṣṇava men who are devoted to the worship of Hari and whose minds are intent on keeping vigil, that night increases their joy.
O tiger among kings, it became a source of extreme sorrow for Śobhana;
at the time of sunrise, Śobhana passed away. (19)
The king had him cremated with woods fit for royalty;
Candrabhāgā, however, burned her own body together with her husband.
Having performed the funeral rites for him, Śobhana remained in the palace of Janaka,
O best of kings, by the power of the Ramā-vrata.
He reached the beautiful city of the gods upon the peak of Mount Mandara— a place unsurpassed, unassailable, and endowed with innumerable virtues.
It was adorned with golden-studded palaces decorated with gems and lapis lazuli,
and beautified by various kinds of wonderful crystal structures of diverse forms.
Seated upon a lion-throne, with a brilliant white parasol and chowries,
adorned with a crown, earrings, necklaces, and armlets,
he was being praised by gandharvas and attended by hosts of apsaras. ||24||
In that city, there lived one renowned as Somaśarman, who shone like the supreme king of kings. (25)
While wandering in the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, a brahmin saw him;
recognizing him as the king’s son-in-law, he approached his presence.
Having understood that it was auspicious, Somaśarman quickly rose from his seat upon seeing that he had arrived and paid homage to the best of the twice-born. (27)
He made inquiries regarding the welfare of his father-in-law, the king,
as well as of Kāntā, Candrabhāgā, and the city.
Somaśarman said:
"O King, all is well with your father-in-law in his home;
Candrabhāgā is in good health, and all is well throughout the city. (29)
"O King, let your own conduct be told; there exists a marvelous and wonderful marvel. A city so diverse and beautiful has never been seen by anyone anywhere. (30)
"O King, tell me this: from where did you obtain this?
Śobhana said:
"In the dark fortnight of Kārttika, there was the Ekādaśī known as Ramā."
O best of the twice-born, perform that by which this transient city of the lords of the twice-born, which was reached without being sought through fasting, shall become eternal.
The twice-born said:
"O Indra among kings, how is this unstable, and how indeed does it become stable? Tell me the truth; I shall act accordingly and not otherwise. (33)
Śobhana said:
"O Brahmin, I performed this supreme vow devoid of faith;
therefore, I consider what was certain to be uncertain. Listen to that. (34)
Mucukunda, the daughter of the Dasyus, who is as beautiful as the Candrabhāgā river—tell him this account;
this will certainly come to pass.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard his words, the twice-born Mucukunda went to the city and spoke to King Candrabhāga concerning the events that had occurred. (36)
Somaśarman said: "O auspicious one, whom have you seen as a beloved in person?
I have seen his city, which is unassailable and equal to that of Indra."
Therefore, that which is unstable has been described by him; make that [which is] stable.
Candrabhāgā said:
"O brahmin-sage, lead me there, for I am longing to behold my husband;
by the merit of my own vows, I shall surely bring that city here."
O twice-born one, bring about that by which our union may occur; for great merit is indeed obtained by those who were separated by performing a reunion. (39)
Having heard this, Somaśarman, unable to endure it, went to the hermitage of Vāmadeva in the vicinity of Mount Mandara. 40.
Vāmadeva heard the entire account related by the two of them;
he then consecrated the radiant Candrabhāgā with Vedic mantras.
By the power of the sage’s mantra and through his service on the day of Viṣṇu,
he attained a divine body and reached a divine state.
With eyes wide open in great joy, she went near her husband;
seeing her arrived, Śobhana rejoiced exceedingly.
Having summoned her, she seated her by her own side;
then Candrabhāgā, out of joy, spoke these pleasing words to her beloved.
Listen to those beneficial words which possess merit as they exist within me:
when I was born more than eight years old in my father’s house... (45)
From that time forward, whatever Ekādaśī vow has been observed by me,
performed according to the prescribed injunctions with a mind endowed with faith—
by the power of that merit, this city shall certainly become [prosperous]. 46.
And she, O tiger among kings, enjoyed herself together with her husband in this way, with all her desires fulfilled, until the dissolution of the world.
Adorned with divine enjoyments, a divine form, and celestial ornaments, he,
possessing a divine body, delights together with that beautiful woman.
By the power of the Rāmā-vrata, she [the goddess] was present upon the peak of Mount Mandara, like a cintāmaṇi gem or a kāmadhenu cow. 49.
O sinless King, I have recounted before you the greatness of the one named Ramā; all of it has been heard by you, O monarch. (50)
I have now declared before you the greatness of the Ekādaśī vows for both fortnights, which destroys all sins. (51)
Just as the dark Ekādaśī is, so too is the bright; one should not make any distinction between them.
For those who observe Ekādaśī, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Just as the milk of both a white and a black cow is the same, so too the two Ekādaśīs are remembered as yielding equal fruit. 53.
The man who hears the majesty of the Ekādaśī vows is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. ||54||

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of Kārttika," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||60||
The sixty-first chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, I have heard from you the greatness of Ramā exactly as it is.
O giver of joy, tell me what occurred during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe that which occurs on the white leaf of the coral tree,
just as it was told by Nārada to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
Nārada said:
Tell me in detail the greatness of Prabodhinī,
on which day Govinda, the promoter of righteous deeds, awakens.
Brahmā said:
O best of sages, listen to the majesty of Prabodhinī, which destroys sins, increases merit, and grants liberation to those of pure intellect. 4.
All sacred fords, from the oceans to the edges of the lakes, roar with pride only so long as the lunar day of Viṣṇu’s awakening in the month of Kārttika has not arrived. (5)
O best of Brahmins, the sin-destroying Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī roars upon the earth only so long as she has not arrived during the month of Kārttika, the awakener of Hari.
A man may obtain the merit of thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices by means of a single fast on Prabodhinī.
Even that which is difficult to obtain, unattainable, and beyond the scope of the three worlds—Hari-bodhinī grants that very thing as a son, even without being requested. (8)
When observed with devotion, the Hari-bodhinī fast bestows upon people sovereignty, prosperity, wisdom, kingdom, and the abundance of happiness. (9)
Whatever sins have been described as being as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara, the sin-destroying [fast] burns them away with a single fast alone. (10)
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of previous births, the night vigil dedicated to her consumes it like a heap of cotton. (11)
O tiger among sages, he who naturally observes the fast on Prabodhinī according to the prescribed rules obtains the fruit as it has been described.
O best of excellent sages, for that man who performs even a small good deed according to the prescribed rules as described, the fruit shall be equal to Mount Meru. 13.
But he who performs a meritorious act devoid of the prescribed rules, O Nārada, obtains from that dharma a fruit no larger than an atom, even if the act itself were as vast as Mount Meru.
Those who meditate with mental activity and those who shall perform the rite for awakening—
the ancestors indeed dwell joyfully in the world of Viṣṇu on their account.
Having committed even a terrible sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, a man goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, liberated from the sufferings of hell. (16)
By keeping a vigil for Viṣṇu, a man becomes cleansed of sin;
O Brahmin, that fruit which is difficult to attain through sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha is obtained thereby. (17)
That is attained with ease indeed by keeping vigil on the Prabodhinī day, even more so than by bathing in all the sacred fords and bestowing the entire earth as a gift. (18)
One obtains that very fruit by performing a vigil for Hari;
he alone is truly virtuous who has been purified by that very act. 19.
By this *Prabodhinī* composed by Kārttikeya, O tiger among sages, it is made certain that for men death is as impermanent as wealth and the body. (20)
Having understood this, O best of sages, one should observe the day sacred to Viṣṇu;
for whatever holy places exist throughout the three worlds, [they are all contained therein]. (21)
For one who properly observes the Prabodhinī vow in the house of Tānita, what need is there for many other merits? By him, the Prabodhinī has truly been performed.
This Kārttika Hari-bodhinī bestows sons and grandsons;
it is for the wise man, the yogi, the ascetic, and the one who has conquered his senses. (23)
For one who possesses this meditation on the awakening of Hari, there is both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for this is most dear to Viṣṇu and is the companion of the essence of dharma. (24)
The man who performs this with devotion shall become a partaker of enjoyment;
having fasted on Prabodhinī, that man does not enter a womb again.
Therefore, O Nārada, having renounced all things, one should perform [this] by means of action, mind, and speech, regarding whatever sin has been accumulated. (26)
Govinda washes away that [sin] during the vigil on Prabodhinī, when one performs bathing, giving, recitation, and worship dedicated to Janārdana. (27)
O child, whatever a person performs on Prabodhinī becomes inexhaustible;
those men who worship Lord Mādhava with devotion on that day [attain the same].
Having observed the fast, they are liberated from those sins born of a hundred lifetimes;
this is the Great Vow, which destroys the flood of great sins of one's sons. 29.
One should duly fast on the day of Viṣṇu’s awakening;
by means of this vow, one should gratify Janārdana, the Lord of Gods.
Illuminating all directions, it proceeds to the abode of Hari;
this should be performed with diligent effort by men who desire beauty and wealth. (31)
Whatever sin has been accumulated in childhood, in youth, or likewise in old age—whether it was committed over a hundred lifetimes, or whether it be small or great—[all that is destroyed]. //32//
Govinda washes away the sins of men who worship Him here;
this other [river] is holy, bringing wealth and grain, and removing all evils. (33)
By fasting on that day with devotion to Hari, nothing whatsoever shall remain difficult to attain;
indeed, whatever fruit is proclaimed for an eclipse of the moon or the sun [is obtained thereby]. (34)
A thousand times that merit is declared for one who performs bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and the worship of Hari during the Prabodhinī vigil. (35)
Whatever merit a man may have acquired since birth, all of that becomes multiplied ten millionfold when performed on Prabodhinī. (36)
All that becomes in vain for one who has not performed the Kārttika vow; that man who passes the month of Kārttika without observing the discipline of Viṣṇu [is lost]. (37)
O Nārada, one who has not accumulated merit through births does not obtain this fruit;
therefore, with every effort, [one should worship] Janārdana, the God of gods. 38.
O best of Brahmins, one who is devoted to Viṣṇu should serve [the deity] which grants the fruit of all desires; however, he should avoid the food of others during the month of Kārttika.
By avoiding the food of others, one obtains the fruit of the Vatsa-cāndrāyaṇa penance; and by constantly delighting in the scriptures during the month of Kārttika, one attains Madhusūdana.
He shall burn away all sins and obtain the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices;
yet he is not so pleased by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by recitations and the like. (41)
Those who, endowed with auspiciousness, engage in discourses on the scriptures concerning Madhusūdana during the month of Kārttika, or those who listen to the stories of Viṣṇu; ||42||
Whether it be half a verse or a single quarter-verse, the fruit is equal to that of a hundred cows;
having renounced all other duties, one should [recite] before Keśava during the month of Kārttika. (43)
O great sage, one should master the scriptures and listen to them;
whoever recounts the stories of Hari does so with a mind free from greed for worldly gain, seeking only the highest good.
O tiger among sages, that man who, by means of a religious observance during the month of Kārttika, listens to the Vaiṣṇava narrative, shall deliver a hundred of his lineages.
One who listens to the story of Hari on the day of Viṣṇu’s awakening (Prabodhinī) shall especially obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows, even if he possesses only a mere banner. 46.
O Sage, those who, having heard the divine narrative of Viṣṇu, honor the teller of that story, obtain this fruit: the merit of giving away the earth consisting of the seven continents.
O tiger among sages, it is taught that the world of those who spend the month of Kārttika in the diversion of singing and sacred scriptures is imperishable, according to their own capacity.
O sage, dear to the Kali age, I have seen that there is no returning again for one who performs song, dance, and instrumental music, as well as the auspicious narrative of Viṣṇu. 49.
That meritorious soul who performs this act abides above the three worlds,
[offering] with many flowers, many fruits, camphor, agallochum, and saffron.
O best of sages, worship of Hari must be performed on the day of awakening (Bodhavāsara) in the month of Kārttika, because by that means, immeasurable merit is obtained.
On the Prabodhinī day, during the vigil with various kinds of fruits and substances,
one should take water in a conch shell and offer it as an *argha* oblation to Janārdana.
Whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving—
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by offering the arghya on the day of enlightenment.
Thereafter, worship of the Guru should be performed with food, clothing, and other gifts,
as well as with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), for the sake of pleasing the God who holds the discus (Viṣṇu) and the celestial sages.
The man who listens to the Bhāgavata and reads this Purāṇa shall obtain for every single syllable the fruit arising from the gift of a Kapilā cow. 55.
O tiger among sages, for him who performs the Vaiṣṇava vow according to the rules during the month of Kārttika with his full capacity, liberation is indeed certain.
When the Garuḍa-bannered Lord Madhusūdana is worshipped with a single petal of a Ketakī flower,
he becomes well-pleased for a thousand years.
One should worship the Lord Yojanārdana with Agasti flowers;
by the sight of that divine sage, the fire of hell is extinguished.
Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, when worshipped with *munipuṣpa* flowers in the month of Kārttika,
