grants all desired objects of longing, just as [the planets] do during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
Having set aside all other flowers, Kārttikeya should worship Keśava with the *munipuṣpa* flower with devotion; he shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice (*vājimedha*).
Those people who offer Tulasī leaves and flowers to Janārdana during the month of Kārttika, O child, shall burn away all the sins of ten thousand lifetimes.
Whether seen, touched, meditated upon, praised, or even merely mentioned, the auspicious Tulasi, when planted, gathered, and constantly worshipped, [bestows these benefits]. 62.
O Sage, those who perform devotion to Tulasi nine times every day extend their merit for thousands of crores of yugas.
O Sage, as long as the male Tulasī plants that have been planted grow upon the surface of the earth with their branches, twigs, seeds, flowers, and leaves, [so long does the merit endure]. 64.
Those who are born as their descendants,
or those who have already gone [to them], shall dwell in the abode of Hari for a thousand years until the end of the kalpa.
O Nārada, whatever fruit is obtained from all flowers and all leaves is indeed attained by means of a single tulasī leaf during the month of Kārttika.
Seeing that the month of Kārttika has arrived, Mahāviṣṇu, who is Janārdana, should be worshipped with tender tulasī leaves even by one who lacks regular observances.
The merit gained by the gods through performing hundreds of sacrifices and giving gifts many times over is attained by worshipping Keśava with Tulasī leaves during the month of Kārttika.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Eleventh Day of the Bright Half of Kārttika," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||61||
The sixty-second chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the supreme vow among all vows."
It removes all sins of Viṣṇu and bestows fruit upon those who observe vows. ||1||
O Janārdana, tell us the narrative of the month of Puruṣottama;
what is its ritual procedure, what is its fruit, and which deity is worshipped therein? (2)
O Janārdana, when the intercalary month has arrived, please tell us:
what gift brings what merit, and what should be performed by men, O Lord? (3)
How is the bath performed, what is the mantra to be recited, and how is the ritual of worship prescribed?
What is the most excellent food to be eaten during this month of Puruṣottama? (4)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Indra among kings, out of affection for you,
I shall describe the greatness of the month of Puruṣottama, which destroys all sins.
When an intercalary month occurs, there is a day on which the eleventh lunar tithi falls;
it is known by the name Kamalā and is the most excellent among all lunar days.
By the power of that vow, Lakṣmī shall become favorable to him;
having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and recollected Puruṣottama.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule, the observer of the vow should perform his religious observance;
it is taught that the recitation of mantras performed at home has a single-fold merit, whereas at a river it is considered to have a two-fold merit.
In a cow-pen with more than a thousand cows, in a fire-sanctuary endowed with hundreds [of fires], in sacred fields of Śiva, at holy fords (tīrthas), and in the presence of the deities. ||9||
A hundred thousand Tulasī leaves were placed near Viṣṇu in his presence;
there was a certain excellent brahmin named Śivaśarman who lived in Avantī. ||10||
His son, named Tuṣaja, was possessed of faults;
at that time, he was abandoned by his father and forsaken by his kinsmen and relatives.
Due to the power of his evil deeds, he went to a very distant forest;
once, by the turn of fate, he arrived at the king of holy places (Prayāga).
With his face emaciated by hunger, he performed his ablutions in the Triveṇī;
afflicted by hunger, he searched there for the hermitages of the sages.
There he beheld the excellent hermitage of the sage Harimitra, frequented by Puruṣottama and visited by the assembly of people. (14)
There, in that hermitage, as the Brahmins were recounting stories that destroy all impurity, Kamalā heard them with faith from their mouths. (15)

Having heard this account of the lunar day sacred to Kamalā, which is most meritorious and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation according to the ritual prescribed by Jayaśarman, [one attains these fruits]. 16.
The Ekādaśī is most meritorious, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation; having stood with them in that empty abode, they then performed the vow.
When midnight had arrived, Lakṣmī came there and said, "O Brahmin, by the power of Kamalā, I grant you a boon. (18)

Jayaśarman said: "Who are you? Whose daughter are you? O timid one, tell me clearly how you came to be here. Are you Indrāṇī, the consort of the lord of the gods, or Bhavānī, the consort of Śaṅkara? (19)
O lady of auspicious countenance, neither a Gandharva woman, nor a Kinnara woman, nor even the wives of the Moon and the Sun have been seen or heard of by us as being like you. (20)
Lakṣmī said:
"O you who have become gracious, I have come here from Vaikuṇṭha, sent by the God of gods through the power of Kamalā. (21)
O Sage, on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Puruṣottama,
this vow was observed by you at Prayāga in the presence of the sages.
"O best of the twice-born, by the power of this vow, I shall undoubtedly come under your control; all human beings will likewise become subject to you. (23)
"By my grace, they shall obtain [their goal]; this which has been spoken by me is the truth.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Lotus-eyed One, since you are pleased, tell me the vow in detail."
O twice-born ones, those virtuous people who engage in these discourses—Lakṣmī said:
[it is] most pleasant for listeners to hear and the unsurpassed among purifiers. (25)
Therefore, one who is endowed with supreme faith should listen with effort to this meritorious [text] which destroys bad dreams—even if it be only a single verse or even half a verse. (26)
By reciting this, one is immediately liberated from tens of millions of great sins;
it is the supreme month among months, just as Garuḍa is the king among birds. (27)
Just as among rivers the Gaṅgā is foremost, and among lunar days the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is preeminent, even now all the gods desire to take birth in Bhārata. 28.
They worship that various [forms of] Nārāyaṇa, the one free from disease;
those who always worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa with devotion.
The hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā, constantly worship those who are devoted to the chanting of Hari's names, even if they are otherwise lowly. (30)
And those who are devoted to the worship of Hari have achieved their purpose in the Kali age, even if both Ekādaśīs—whether the bright or the dark fortnight—should occur. (31)

For householders, the previous [Ekādaśī] is prescribed for those seeking worldly prosperity, while the subsequent one is remembered for those seeking liberation. If the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) and the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) overlap such that the night remains until the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī),
then by breaking the fast on that Trayodaśī, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
"Having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat on the following day; O Acyuta, O Lotus-eyed One, be my refuge. (33)
Having recited this mantra with devotion for the God of gods, the wielder of the discus, one whose soul is satisfied should observe a fast. (34)
The observer of the vow, being self-restrained, should keep a vigil before the deity with songs, musical instruments, dances, the recitation of Purāṇas, and other such acts. (35)
Then, having risen at dawn on the twelfth day, the observer of the vow,
with his senses restrained, bathed and worshipped Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rules.
Having bathed Janārdana with the five nectars on the eleventh day,
one attains the same form as Hari by bathing Him with milk on the twelfth day.
O Keśava, for me who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance, be gracious through this vow; appearing before me, become the bestower of the vision of knowledge. (38)
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, the God of gods, the Bearer of the Mace, one should devoutly feed the Brahmins and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). ||39||
Then, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, he should perform the five great sacrifices together with his own kinsmen and eat himself while restrained in speech. (40)
Thus, he who, being self-restrained, performs the meritorious vow of Ekādaśī, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which a return to this world is difficult to obtain. (41)
Having spoken thus and granted that very boon to Kamala, she vanished.
That brahmin, having become wealthy, returned to his father’s house. (42)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, he who thus performs this supreme Kamalā-vrata, or hears of it on the day of Viṣṇu, is liberated from all sins. (43)

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Eleventh Day Known as Kamalā in the Dark Fortnight of the Month of Puruṣottama," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
The sixty-second chapter. ||62||
(63) The sixty-third chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord of the World, Janārdana, among the many dharmas and vows I have heard, has anything been heard that is equal to Ekādaśī? (1)
Speak again of the Ekādaśī that destroys sins and bestows merit,
by performing which a human being in this world may attain the supreme state.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O protector of the earth, whether it be the Śukla (bright) Ekādaśī or the Kṛṣṇa (dark) Ekādaśī, it must never be abandoned;
for it increases the happiness of liberation.
O King, Ekādaśī is the liberator from the bonds of worldly existence;
it is the granter of all desires and the destroyer of sins upon this earth. (4)
O best of kings, on a Sunday, at the new moon, or during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), Ekādaśī should be observed even with its defects; it increases one's sons and grandsons.
The Ekādaśī vow must never be abandoned by those who are dear to Viṣṇu;
it constantly bestows longevity and fame, as well as progeny, health, and wealth.
O protector of the earth, those who perform the Ekādaśī vow with supreme faith obtain liberation, beauty, and sovereignty; this vow is eternal.
O King, those who perceive through the vision described by the aforementioned method as being the form of Viṣṇu are seen to be liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (8)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, how is it that those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) are yet seen to possess forms of Viṣṇu, and at other times to possess forms of sin? Indeed, my curiosity is great. 9.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, those who in the Kali age perform with devotion this supreme waterless vow of Ekādaśī according to the rites prescribed by the scriptures; ||10||
How is it that they are not forms of Viṣṇu? How indeed are they not liberated while living? There is no meritorious vow equal to Ekādaśī, which removes all sins. (11)
O King, there exists nothing that bestows all desires upon men like this vow:
eating but one meal on the tenth lunar day, the Nandā, while abstaining from water. 12.
Having performed the breaking of the fast on the Bhadrā day, men become equal to Viṣṇu;
indeed, he who with faith performs this auspicious vow of Kāmadā [attains the same]. (13)
He too obtains his desires both in this world and in the next;
for this [river] is indeed purifying and sanctifying, and the destroyer of great sins. 14.
O best of kings, one should worship Puruṣottama according to the prescribed rite at Kāmadā, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who perform the ritual. 15.
With flowers, incense, and the like, as well as various kinds of food offerings;
[one should avoid] bell-metal, meat, lentils, chickpeas, and likewise kodrava grain. (16)
A Vaiṣṇava who observes the vow should avoid these ten things on the tenth day: leafy vegetables, honey, meat, food, eating again, and sexual intercourse. (17)
Gambling, sport, as well as sleep, betel, cleaning the teeth, speaking ill of others, slander, theft, violence, and sexual pleasure— (18)
On the eleventh day, one should avoid anger, false speech, bell-metal, meat, lentils, oil, and lying. (19)
On the twelfth day, one should avoid physical exercise, travel, food, sexual intercourse, riding on the back of a bull, eating the food of others, and leafy vegetables. (20)
O King, by this method, when she has been worshipped according to the prescribed rite as the granter of desires, Puruṣottama is honored after keeping a vigil at night.
Completely liberated from all evils, they go to the supreme goal;
by reciting or hearing this, O King, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.

Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada, [ends] the section titled "The Ekādaśī named Kāmadā of the bright fortnight of the month of Puruṣottama."
The sixty-third chapter. ||63||
(64) The sixty-fourth chapter.
Nārada said:
Some rules for the Cāturmāsya period are renowned on earth;
O Maheśvara, I wish to hear them—please tell me.

O Lord, tell me what fruit is obtained by the abandonment of the six flavors, by the growth of nails and hair, and by other observances, during the four-month period when Janārdana, Hari, is asleep? (2)
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the son of Atri (Dattātreya), with eyes wide open in joy, laughed and spoke to that best of the twice-born, Nārada, who was a treasure-house of asceticism.
Mahādeva said: Listen, O celestial sage, I shall tell you everything in detail.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, [one should proceed]. ||4||
One should undertake the Cāturmāsya vows here with devotion when Lord Hari has entered his yogic sleep and one has ascended to a bed upon the ground. ||5||
This shall continue for four months until the full moon of Kārttika;
likewise, the installation ceremonies, sacrifices, and other such rites shall proceed.
Marriage, vows, and family alliances, as well as other auspicious rites;
the king’s mounting of a vehicle, processions, and various other activities—[these are all performed]. (7)
Listen to the fruit of the vow for that person who performs a ritual observance while Acyuta, the Lord of the World, whose banner is Garuḍa, is fast asleep. ||8||
Whatever fruit a man may obtain through thousands of horse-sacrifices, that same fruit he shall fully attain by performing the Cāturmāsya vows. 9.
When the sun is situated in the sign of Gemini, one should cause Madhusūdana to sleep;
when the sun has entered the sign of Libra, one should awaken Hari once again.
Then, this sequence of ritual procedure applies even to one who has fallen into a great transgression:
one should install an image of Viṣṇu bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
O Nārada, one should place the gentle goddess, wearing yellow garments, upon a pure couch covered with a white cloth and provided with a pillow.
Furthermore, one who is a knower of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, or a devotee of Viṣṇu,
having bathed [the deity], should likewise offer milk, honey, parched grain, and ghee.
O Vāḍava, she has been honored with auspicious fragrances, incenses, and delightful flowers,
and worshipped with white blossoms by means of this mantra.
When you, the Lord of the World, are asleep, this entire world sleeps;
when you awaken, the whole world, including all that is moving and stationary, awakens. (15)
O Nārada, having thus installed that image of Viṣṇu,
he himself should then personally undertake the vow in its very presence by means of speech.
Whether a woman, a monkey, or a devotee of Him, according to the distinction between dharma and adharma,
[one should observe the vow] for four months of the rainy season until the rite of the deity's awakening (utthāpana).
One should undertake these observances, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth, having observed a fast continuously until the dawn becomes clear. (18)
Having performed the rites daily before Viṣṇu with a self-controlled mind,
I shall describe the fruits for those performers individually.
A wise man shall attain sweetness by abstaining from molasses,
and likewise, he shall obtain a long lineage by abstaining from oil.
By abstaining from ghee, a beautiful Brahmin is born;
by renouncing pungent oil, one attains the destruction of enemies. (21)
By renouncing fragrant garlands, one obtains incomparable good fortune;
by renouncing the enjoyment of flowers, one becomes a Vidyādhara in heaven.
But the person who practices yoga shall attain the state of Brahman;
[one should avoid] the six tastes: pungent, sour, sweet, salty, sharp, and astringent.
The man who avoids [betel] shall avoid deformity and shall not suffer from foul odors;
by abstaining from betel, an enjoyer of pleasures becomes one with a red throat. (24)
By the renunciation of ghee, one becomes possessed of unshakable beauty and a body that is always lustrous;
and by the renunciation of fruit, O lord of brahmins, one is born with many sons.
One who eats from a palāśa leaf becomes handsome and possessed of enjoyments;
radiant and a bringer of radiance, he becomes the very lord of wealth. ||26||
A person who renounces curd and milk attains Goloka;
he who observes the vow of silence shall have his command unimpeded. (27)
By the avoidance of the *sthālīpāka* offering, one attains the throne of Indra;
by the renunciation of such [duties], O son of Dharma, one becomes established in unrighteousness. (28)
By reciting "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" one hundred times, the fruit is multiplied a hundredfold;
indeed, alone, one shall become a lord of the Vidyādharas in heaven. (29)
By merely bathing at Puṣkara, one obtains the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā. ||30||
He who always eats on the ground shall become the lord of the earth;
and he who performs the smearing and sweeping in the house of Viṣṇu [attains great merit].
O learned one, there is no doubt that such a man shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha for an entire kalpa;
this applies to the man who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations here.
He goes together with Viṣṇu in a divine, well-yoked celestial chariot;
one who performs songs and instrumental music for Viṣṇu shall attain the world of the Gandharvas. ||33||
A wise man who subsists on the five products of the cow obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
moreover, he who constantly enlightens others through the diversion of sacred scriptures [attains the same]. 34.
By offering worship with the form of the *savyāsā* [mudrā] before Viṣṇu, one shall attain the station of Viṣṇu;
moreover, by performing worship with a *tulasī* leaf, one shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
By performing the divine sprinkling rite (prokṣaṇa), one obtains the station of the Apsarases;
by bathing in the house with cool water, one attains a stainless body.
By renouncing warm water, one obtains the merit of bathing at Puṣkara; and the man who eats from leaves obtains the fruit of Kurukṣetra. (37)
He who constantly eats from a stone slab acquires the merit born of Prayāga;
however, he who abandons the water of Dharmodaya is overcome by diseases.
One who eats from copper vessels obtains the fruit of Naimiṣa;
having abandoned the bell-metal vessel, one should employ every other type of vessel.
In the absence of all other vessels, an earthen vessel is the best;
one may also use vessels made from materials found at home or those produced from the leaves of the Palāśa tree.
But for the wise man who maintains the Agnihotra for a full year,
or who practices fasting with the sacrificial vessels, that is remembered as equal [in merit].
O learned one, eating from the leaves of the *brahma* tree is declared to be equal to the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance;
for one who eats even a single meal from *brahma* leaves, [the merit is great]. (42)
The merit that is proclaimed for fasting on Ekādaśī is said to be equal to three nights [of fasting] and is the destroyer of great sins. 43.
One shall obtain the fruit of all acts of giving and the fruit of visiting all sacred fords;
furthermore, by eating from lotus leaves, one shall not behold hell.
A Brāhmaṇa goes to Vaikuṇṭha, while another person attains heaven;
this is the great tree of Brahmā, which destroys sins and grants all desires.
O best of kings, the Śūdra caste must avoid the middle leaf;
by eating from it, he goes to hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras.
One should avoid the middle leaf and eat from the remaining leaves;
if a Śūdra eats from the middle leaf, O twice-born one, he becomes a Śūdra.
Purity comes from giving a tawny cow to a Brahmin; it does not come otherwise.
But if a Śūdra milks a tawny cow and consumes her milk in his own home, [he incurs sin]. (48)
For ten thousand years he is born as a worm in excrement;
once released from the womb of a worm, he attains the womb of a beast.
O Nārada, for as many years as there are hairs on that tawny bull which a Śūdra, having become such, causes to be driven, [he shall suffer].
That man shall be cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells; of this there is no doubt.
And his goat shall be seized, especially by a Śūdra. (51)
A Śūdra who drinks the milk of a cow that has not yet calved goes to the Raurava hell;
likewise, a Śūdra in whom association with Brāhmaṇas is observed [suffers the same fate]. ||52||
One who is outside the Vedic tradition is called a Śūdra, even if he is a Kaulika;
likewise, a Brahmin who is impelled by worldly affairs and carries out the commands of a Śūdra [is also so regarded]. (53)
As long as he does not move from his place, he remains a denizen of hell;
even so for a Brahmin who has been sent by a Śūdra to a house for the sake of water. (54)
Having drunk that water, which is equal to liquor, one shall go to hell;
therefore, a Śūdra must always and constantly give gifts to the twice-born.
One should especially practice devotion toward them;
having enjoyed happiness in this world, one goes to the next world.
This body, composed of the five elements, has been declared to be devoid of intrinsic purpose;
therefore, one should give it to the Guru, so that from this [act] one may obtain the fruit of immortality.
In this terrible Kali age,
O best of Brahmins, wicked-minded people of sinful conduct revile those who perform meritorious deeds.
Through censure one obtains suffering until the dissolution of all beings; O Great-Minded One, various dharmas indeed prevail in the Kali age. (59)
This Dharma, which bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation, is difficult to find in the world;
for who among men on this earth would actually lie upon the ground? (60)
For ten thousand years, that man is not afflicted by diseases;
endowed with many sons and wealth, he is born free from leprosy.
A man who eats only at night obtains the fruit of a pilgrimage to sacred fords;
and by eating without asking for alms, he obtains the fruit of constructing a large oblong pond or a well.
But he who avoids malice toward others and turns away from the injury of living beings—non-violence is proclaimed in the Vedas as the supreme dharma. (63)
I have heard it said everywhere that charity, compassion, self-restraint, and kindness [are the virtues];
therefore, these should be practiced with every effort, even by the great. (64)
They offer their very bodies, along with sons and grandsons, to the Guru;
by the power of that gift, they attain the state of being beloved to Viṣṇu.
He who is initiated by a Śūdra, and the Śūdra who initiates him—both of them are declared to be sinners until the dissolution of all beings. (66)
When a Śūdra, the most wicked of beings, gives rise to a mind intent on violence,
twenty-one generations of his family are cast into hell by that act.
O twice-born one, many heretics and Śūdras are seen on earth in this Kali age; by merely conversing with them, one falls into hell. 68.
O twice-born one, for those who delight in the knowledge of Brahman and who chant the Gāyatrī,
by the mere sight of them, sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa perish day by day.
The Brahmins who bear the conch and the discus are esteemed for their devotion to the dharma of Viṣṇu;
they are eternally devoted to the Vedic dharma and are the purifiers of purifiers. (70)
This Cāturmāsya rite must always be performed by those virtuous men;
O Vāḍava, what is the use of saying more, again and again? (71)
Blessed indeed are those men on earth who are Vaiṣṇavas in this world;
their lineage is considered most blessed, and their birth is remembered as most blessed. (72)
For him who consumes honey while the god Janārdana is asleep, great sin shall arise; hear now what results from abstaining from it.
One shall obtain that fruit which is gained by all various kinds of sacrifices;
however, one should avoid the pomegranate, the citron, and the coconut.
Having become a god in a celestial vehicle, he shall go to that realm of Viṣṇu;
he is born wealthy, fortunate, and into a noble family.
That man who, for four months, eats but a single meal a day during as many muhūrtas as there are from the time the sun has risen until it has reached its zenith; ||76||
That man who avoids rice, barley, and wheat is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for thousands of years. ||77||

Whatever fruit has been proclaimed by the sages for the performance of the horse sacrifice and other rites according to the rules with abundant sacrificial fees—that same fruit a person obtains [by this]. (78)
One who performs the libation (tarpaṇa) with *tulasi*, sesame seeds, and *darbha* grass becomes endowed with wealth and grain and is born with many sons. (79)
That fruit is multiplied ten millionfold, especially during the Cāturmāsya;
when Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, one should perform this [rite] endowed with the three.
They too rejoice in the presence of Viṣṇu for thousands of yugas, whether they have recited a full verse, half a verse, a quarter of a verse, or even half of that. ||81||
Those who sing the *pragāthas* at the beginning of Viṣṇu’s [sleep] are indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, he who avoids sexual intercourse while the god Janārdana is asleep— ||82||
He too is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for one Manvantara, [having offered] curd, milk, as well as buttermilk, jaggery, and likewise vegetables. ||83||
There is no doubt that those men who perform their bath with *āmalaka* fruit alone will partake in liberation from this very world through mere avoidance [of other things]. (84)
O Sage, day by day they obtain great merit;
the wise declare that the dhātrī fruit removes all sins. (85)
In ancient times, Brāhmaṇas were created as a means for the sake of delivering the three worlds;
he who observes silence during the twilight prayers and eats [only once] for four months [attains that goal]. 86.
Furthermore, he who himself eats cooked food for four months rejoices again in Vaikuṇṭha for as many as four Manvantaras. ||87||
He is honored in the world of Indra for ten thousand years;
he should observe silence during the four months of the rainy season. ||88||
One who goes to Śacī’s city of Viṣṇu and thereafter to the abode of Brahmā, and who eats while observing silence, never comes to grief. 89.
The Rākṣasas who ate while remaining silent went to the third heaven;
however, cooked food mixed with worms and insects becomes impure. (90)
O best of the twice-born, meat should be known as equal to the food of cows;
if a human should consume that food, it should be known as impure. (91)
This is declared to be the food of the Rākṣasas, which is always dear to them;
for in ancient times, Brahmā was gratified by that high-souled one, and it was granted by him.
Having eaten in silence, one undoubtedly attains heaven;
however, for him who eats while conversing, that food becomes impure. (93)
One eats the evil entirely by oneself; therefore, one should practice silence.
O Nārada, a meal taken in silence should be known as equal to fasting.
That best of men who eats in silence after performing the five offerings to the vital breaths—his five great sins perish; of this there is no doubt. (95)
O Brāhmaṇa, one should not use a stitched garment in rites for the ancestors;
a garment that has been worn while impure or has remained in a state of impurity shall itself become impure. (96)
One who voids feces or urine, or engages in sexual intercourse, while wearing a garment placed upon the hips or back, should discard that garment.
O sage, due to the specific nature of ancestral rites (pitṛ-karma), the worship of the Discus-wielder [Viṣṇu] by the wise should always be avoided during the time of the ancestors. 98.
These should be prepared without distinction by those who are pure and have conquered their senses, while Hṛṣīkeśa is fast asleep—consisting of grass, vegetables, and flowers. (99)
One should carefully avoid wearing stitched garments during the Cāturmāsya; indeed, he who avoids these while Hari is asleep [should be known as a true devotee]. 100.
One shall not go to hell until the dissolution of all beings;
likewise, one should not consume liquor, nor meat from a sheep, nor that of a rabbit, nor that of a pig. (101)
Especially during the Cāturmāsya period, when the god Janārdana is asleep, even that man who is devoted to non-violence attains divinity. (102)
O best of Brahmins, he who avoids false anger, as well as harshness and sexual intercourse outside the proper season, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Through celibacy, there is an increase in progeny as well as an increase in lifespan;
likewise, flowers, leaves, fruits, bedding, oil for massage, and unguents [are obtained]. (104)

One should avoid milk that has been needlessly drained and liquor that is fit for consumption; likewise, one must strictly abstain from what is forbidden during the Cāturmāsya festival when the Lord is asleep.
First, O Brāhmaṇa, that [debt] must be repaid; there is no doubt about this. O wise one, that wealth which is given to a twice-born man becomes inexhaustible. (106)
O best of Brahmins, there is no doubt that Hari, by whomsoever he may be worshipped according to this rule, bestows millions upon millions of times more merit. 107.
Viṣṇu grants him residence in his own abode; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
He who does not observe the prescribed rules while Hari is asleep during the Cāturmāsya period [shall suffer the consequences]. 108.
Even he attains hell, and his birth has passed in vain, who does not constantly perform the supreme rite prescribed by the twice-born. (109)
Likewise, by following these prescribed rules, one attains the supreme state;
however, a gift given devoid of the three aims of life becomes fruitless. (110)
Therefore, with every effort, the best of men should satisfy Janārdana, the God of gods, through observances and gifts according to his capacity. 111.
Without having performed ablutions and given gifts, and without honoring the Brahmins—all that is in vain, even for as long as fourteen Indras endure. (112)
Nārada said:
O Lord, Sovereign of the Universe, tell me what kind of celibacy (brahmacarya) it is, by the practice of which Govinda becomes fully satisfied with men? (113)
Mahādeva said:
"One who is devoted solely to his own wife is considered by the wise to be a celibate student (brahmacārī).
A learned man who abandons his own wife is more vile than a Cāṇḍāla. (114)
Having approached his wife during her season, he is enjoined to practice celibacy;
yet he who abandons a devoted wife who is free from fault [is censured]. (115)
In this world, one who commits evil deeds incurs the sin of foeticide;
yet [the merit of] thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices [is lost]. (116)
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and worship of the deities do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī). 117.
Whatever has been performed during the four-month period shall indeed become inexhaustible for him who listens to the Purāṇa once or twice a day. ||118||
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu; especially while Hari is asleep, by reciting and chanting the names of Hari.
O best of the twice-born, that Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa who indeed performs worship shall obtain a fruit multiplied ten millionfold. (120)
He alone is the soul of all dharmas and is indeed worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt.
This Cāturmāsya is meritorious, pure, and the destroyer of sins.
By hearing it, one attains incomparable merit and gains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. 121.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Cāturmāsya," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
The sixty-fifth chapter.
Nārada said:
O Lord, please describe the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the Cāturmāsya vows.
Once the concluding rite (udyāpana) is performed, everything certainly becomes complete. ||1||
Mahādeva said: "O highly fortunate one, if one performs the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) after having observed the vow, that performer of rites shall become a partaker of the full fruit. (2)
Having incurred a deficiency in his vows, he is born as a leper;
for this reason, O twice-born one, he should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having undertaken these observances and maintained them according to the rules,
when the Lord of the World has arisen from sleep, one should go into the presence of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should seek forgiveness from the God of gods according to the detailed injunctions.
It is traditionally taught that when oil is omitted, ghee should be offered; when ghee is omitted, milk is prescribed.
Silent rice-balls mixed with sesame and gold should be given to a twice-born man;
at the meal, one should provide food accompanied by curd and boiled rice.
One should especially give food accompanied by gold;
O best of sages, through the gift of food, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, he who eats for four months from a vessel made of *pālāśa* leaves should,
at the conclusion of the rite (*udyāpana*), give a vessel filled with clarified butter as a gift.
One should give a meal for six at the Brāhmaṇa-feeding;
at the night-meal, one should cause an ox along with gold to be given at the unasked-for fast.
Abstaining from eating black gram (māṣa), one should give a cow along with her calf to the best of sages; and by bathing with dhātrī fruit, a person should also give gold weighing one māṣa.
In the case of a vow regarding fruits, one should indeed cause fruits to be given;
in the case of a vow regarding grains, grain is prescribed, or alternatively, rice is traditionally taught.

Likewise, O best of the twice-born, he who has observed celibacy during the four months of the rainy season [should offer] a bed for sleeping on the ground, provided with cotton and accompanied by a pillow.
This meal should be given with devotion to both husbands, together with enjoyments, accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), as well as vegetables and salt. ||13||
One should offer ghee and barley flour without oil as a daily bath-offering;
likewise, for the vow regarding nails and hair, one should prepare a measure equal to a span (prādeśa).
By the renunciation of shoes, sandals are to be given;
by the total abandonment of meat, she is remembered as a tawny cow with her calf. (15)
One who constantly offers a lamp should bring a golden lamp;
he should indeed give that lamp, filled with ghee, to a twice-born man.

To a Brahmin who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and whose vow is perfectly fulfilled, one should give a gold māṣaka for the sake of fulfilling the desire of his vow regarding the restriction of eating only vegetables or beans. 17.
In the case of a restriction regarding sexual intercourse, one should give silver to a twice-born man;
but in the case of a restriction regarding betel leaves, one should give camphor along with gold.
O best of the twice-born, whatever has been performed according to the rules from time to time, that should be given away especially by one who desires to attain the next world. (19)
Having first performed his bath and other rites, he should manifest [the deity] before Viṣṇu:
"The God is without beginning or end, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace. Before whom do they perform [these acts], since Viṣṇu is the destroyer of sins? (20)

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Conclusion of the Cāturmāsya Vow" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
The sixty-fifth chapter. ||65||
(66) The sixty-sixth chapter.
Nārada said:
O best of gods, speak of the propitiation of Yama for my benefit;
how may a man, O god, not go to the hells? (1)
It is heard that in this world there is always the river Vaitaraṇī,
which is unassailable, shoreless, difficult to cross, and filled with much blood.
O Great God, O Lord, how can there be any ease for all these beings who are difficult to overcome? This is indeed a source of fear regarding the world of Yama. ||3||
O Blessed One, Lord of Gods and Goddesses, having shown compassion toward me, please explain in its entirety the ritual procedure for the purpose of liberating him. (4)
Mahādeva said: O brāhmaṇa, formerly, having bathed in the salt waters at Dvāravatī, I beheld that sage named Mudgala, who was a master of illusion. 5.
Having prostrated before me— who was like a blazing sun, my limbs radiant with ascetic heat— the sage Mudgala, filled with wonder, spoke.
Mudgala said:
"O Lord, I have suddenly fainted and fallen upon the surface of the earth;
my limbs are burning as I am seized by these helpless beings."
Dragged by force, I, a man no larger than a thumb,
was tightly bound by the soldiers and led to the presence of Yama.
In an instant, I saw Yama in the assembly hall—tawny-eyed, black-faced, most terrible, and accompanied by hundreds of deaths and diseases. ||9||
It was afflicted by the humors of wind, bile, and phlegm in embodied form,
and by body-wasting, fever, cough, eruptions, and skin diseases.
[One suffers] from fever, consumption of the head, pain in the private parts, hemorrhoids, weakness, and wasting;
as well as throat ailments, eye diseases, dysuria, fever, and ulcers. ||11||
By fainting spells, throat-seizers, heart diseases, spirits, and thieves—by such various, fierce, and manifold forms that cause fear. (12)
And with those holding skulls and heads in their hands, as well as Naraka, he was surrounded by fierce Rākṣasas and Dānavas who were seated or standing before him. ||13||
And here, there are officials of Dharma, such as scribes like Citragupta,
as well as tigers, lions, boars, peacocks, and serpents that are extremely difficult to restrain.
By scorpions, fanged beasts, spirits, insects, bugs, and the like; by wolves, leopards, dogs, crows, vultures, and jackals. (15)
By thieves, by spirits of poverty, by plagues, and by *ḍākinī* seizures;
by those with disheveled hair, by coughs and labored breaths, and by those whose faces are contorted with frowns. (16)
Yama shone resplendent in his assembly hall, attended by his retinue— punishers of evildoers who were themselves unafraid due to their vast majesty.
Just as a mountain inhabited by fierce forest-dwellers and wild beasts is not [feared] by people, so too the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara) laughed at those who were like servants. 18.
"How was the sage brought here by you, who were mistaken about his name—the son of Bhīmaka, named Mudgala, from the village of Kauṇḍinya? (19)
"There is a Kṣatriya whose life-span is exhausted; let him be released by means of the Āgneya [weapon].
Having heard this from them, they departed from there and returned once again.
Furthermore, all of them said to Dharmarāja, "We were rendered powerless; having gone there, we did not perceive that embodied being whose life-span was exhausted. (21)
Yama said:
"For what reason are those men generally invisible to you?
For those by whom the auspicious twelfth day (Dvādaśī) has been observed, the river Vaitaraṇī becomes as easy to cross."

Those who have attained immortality at Ujjayinī, Prayāga, or on the Yamunā, and those by whom daily offerings of sesame, elephants, gold, and so forth, as well as fodder for cows, have been given; ||23||
The messengers said:
"O Brahmin, tell us that vow in its entirety;
what must be performed there by men to bring you complete satisfaction? (24)
O best of men, how is one who has performed the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the dark fortnight released from sin by that very fast? (25)
O ocean of compassion, having shown mercy, please speak with a very gracious mind regarding the procedure by which that vow is to be performed correctly. (26)
Śrī Mudgala said:
Having heard the words of the messengers, he then spoke these sweet words:
"O messengers, I shall tell you everything exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard."
Yama said:
"O messengers, those days which occur during the dark fortnights of the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa— in those preceding days, one should duly perform the Vaitaraṇī-vrata."
An image should certainly be fashioned for as long as a year; having made it, one is liberated from that [debt], of this there is no doubt. ||29||
A restrictive vow for fasting, which brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu, must be observed:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, today my fast shall take place. (30)
Having worshipped Govinda on the twelfth day with a mind filled with devotion, one should avoid food and sexual intercourse until the senses have regained their clarity from sleep. 31.
"O Lord, having shown compassion toward me, please forgive all of that.
Having made this vow, one should go to the sacred bathing place at midday.
Having taken earth, cow-dung, and sesame seeds, one should proceed according to the prescribed ritual;
there, a bath should be performed for the sake of completing the vow. (33)
One should especially perform the ritual bath with this mantra:
"O Earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, and traversed by Viṣṇu! (34)
O Earth, take away this sin that has been accumulated by me in the past;
by that sin being destroyed, one is liberated from all sins. (35)
Moreover, sesame seeds produced in Kāśī are indeed forms of Viṣṇu;
by bathing with sesame seeds, Govinda removes all sin. (36)
O Great Goddess, born from the body of Viṣṇu and the remover of great sins, may you take away all sin; indeed, salutations be unto you. 37.
Having held a Tulasī leaf while pronouncing the name [of the Lord], the virtuous declare that bathing should be performed according to the prescribed injunctions. (38)
Having bathed in this manner, emerged from the water, and put on two clean garments,
one should satisfy the ancestors and the gods, and thereafter perform the worship of Viṣṇu.
Having established a flawless pitcher, joined with the five types of sprouts, endowed with the five jewels, and perfumed with divine garlands and fragrances; ||40||
It was filled with water, contained auspicious substances, and was provided with a copper vessel;
therein resided the god Śrīdhara, the god of gods and a treasure-house of asceticism.
O King, one should perform the most solemn worship according to the complete ritual;
one should cause an auspicious mandala to be prepared, fashioned from clay, cow dung, and other materials. (42)
One should have an image of Dharmarāja fashioned from rice grains that have been washed white and ground on a stone; it should be provided with hands and all other limbs.
Having placed the copper-colored river Vaitaraṇī before him,
he should worship it individually and properly, preceded by the ritual invocation (samāvāhana).
I invoke Yama, the lord of gods, who possesses universal form: O illustrious Keśava, come here and grant your presence! 45.
O Lord Hari, this water for washing the feet is offered to You, who are seated upon the splendor of Lakṣmī and who eternally delight in the garden of the universe; please show mercy toward me. 46.
"Salutation to Bhūtidāya for the two feet; salutation to Aśoka for the two knees;
salutation to Śiva for the two thighs; and salutation to Viśvamūrti for the waist. (47)
The glans penis is for Ka, the scrotum for Āditya, the fruit likewise;
the belly for Dāmodara, and the two breasts for Vāsudeva. 48.
One should offer salutations to Him as Śrīdhara for the face, to Keśava for the hair,
to Śārṅgadhara for the back, and to Varada for the feet.
"Obeisance to you, the Soul of All, who holds in your hands the conch, the discus, the sword, the mace, and the axe—by your own name, this is declared to be the head. (50)
Salutations be to you, who are the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, Rāma, Paraśurāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki! 51.
For the sake of destroying the entire flood of evil, I worship; salutations, salutations!
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu with all these auspicious mantras, one should worship him.
O Dharmarāja, homage be to you; O Dharmarāja, homage be to you!
To you, the lord of the southern quarter, who have a buffalo for a vehicle, homage! (53)
O Citragupta, salutations to you; salutations again and again to the wondrous one!
For the sake of pacifying the suffering of hell, grant me my desired wishes. (54)
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death and to the Ender, to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings. ||55||
Salutation indeed to Vṛkodara, to Citra, and to Citragupta;
one should always offer salutations again and again to Nīla and Dadhna. (56)
Thus, the Lord Dharmarāja is to be worshipped with these twelve names:
Vaitaraṇī, Suduḥpāra, Pāpaghna, and Sarvakāmada. (57)
"Come here, O highly fortunate one; accept this water-offering (argha) prepared by me.
On the terrible path of Yama's gate lies the river known as Vaitaraṇī. (58)

For the sake of lifting them out of that [suffering], she who transcends birth, death, and old age—who is difficult for evildoers to cross and who removes the fear of all living beings—[appeared]. (59)
O Goddess, salutations again and again to you, Jayā; out of fear of whom living beings devoted to torment plunge [into hell], yet who desires to cross over that terrible [state].
The gods preside over that river Vaitaraṇī;
it too is worshipped with devotion for the sake of pleasing Keśava.
On whose banks sages and ancestors likewise enter;
she too, in the form of a river, is honored as the remover of sins.
I shall give this [gift] so that you may cross it and be liberated from all sins;
for the sake of merit, I shall describe to you the Vaitaraṇī river.
I have worshipped you with devotion for the sake of pleasing Keśava.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World, lift me up from this cycle of existence! 64.
By the mere utterance of your name, take away all evil!
This supreme sacred thread has been fashioned from nine strands. ||65||
"Accept this, O Lord of Gods; being pleased, grant me my desired wish.
And here is this most beautiful betel for you, prepared according to my ability. (66)
Accept it, O Lord of Gods; deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence. This five-wick lamp, O Lord of Gods, is your *ārārtika* offering.
Devoted to the sun-like Lord who dispels the darkness of delusion and removes the suffering of worldly existence, [one attains] supreme food, well-cooked rice endowed with all flavors. (68)
"O Blessed One, please accept what has been offered by me with devotion, along with the recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra performed according to the prescribed number. (69)
May the Lord of Śrī be pleased with me; may He, being pleased, grant my desired wish.
Five cows were produced when the great ocean was being churned.

Among those cows, one should pay homage with "Obeisance, obeisance to the cow that gives milk" to the one intended for the vehicle; having worshipped the cow according to the prescribed rite, one should, with a concentrated mind, offer the arghya water.
O Goddess who milks all desires and wards off all destroyers, grant health, long-lasting progeny, and happiness to embodied beings day by day. (72)
Having been worshipped by Vasiṣṭha and the wise Viśvāmitra, O Kapila, take away the sin that was previously accumulated by me. (73)
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me.
O you who have golden horns and release from sin, may you establish me in heaven. (74)
O Goddess, who are composed of all the gods, O Subhadra, who are affectionate toward your devotees—just as fragrant cows of Surabhi [flow] from the rivers into the oceans. 75.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should give cows as a daily offering;
for cows are beneficial to all, pure, and destroyers of sin. (76)
O mothers of the three worlds, accept this offering;
salutations to Gaṅgā, Gaurī, and Bhūtī for the destruction of all sins. (77)
With this very mantra, the wise one should hold the trident and mace;
with "Oṃ, salutation to Padmanābha," the intelligent one should hold the lotus.
The wearing of the discus-form Viṣṇu is known as being born of the discus;
salutations to You, the giver of happiness, who take the form of the conch. (79)
The wearing of the conch is prescribed by this mantra;
likewise, the wearing of the four weapons is prescribed by the sages. (80)
Just as the Agnihotra sacrifice is obligatory, and likewise the study of the Veda,
so too for a Brāhmaṇa is this wearing of the heated seal and other marks.
It should be worn especially by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas, using fragrant sandalwood, specifically the sandalwood of Gopikā. 82.
Even a Cāṇḍāla becomes pure by wearing [this mark], of this there is no doubt, provided he wears the vertical, straight, and gentle Puṇḍra as a sign. (83)
Even if he were a Cāṇḍāla, one whose soul is pure is always worthy of worship by the twice-born;
for wherever Tulasī is seen in the house of Cāṇḍālas, [there the gods dwell]. (84)
The tulasī found there should be accepted with a mind imbued with the spirit of devotion. ||85||

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Worship of Yama," in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada, within the fifty-five-thousand-verse compendium of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in its Uttara-khaṇḍa.
(67) The sixty-seventh chapter.
Maheśvara said:
O Sage, having heard this from the mouth of Dharma, Mudgala, the best of the twice-born, spoke thus before me and departed as he pleased. (1)
O best of the twice-born, that house where Gopikā-candana remains is indeed said by Viṣṇu to be of the nature of a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha). ||2||
Neither grief nor delusion exists there, nor does anything inauspicious ever occur, in the home of that twice-born man where the sandalwood of the Gopikā remains. (3)
Happy are those ancestors whose lineage prospers forever, in whose home the sandalwood paste of Gopikā remains day and night. (4)
The clay born from the lotus of the Gopī is pure and purifies the body;
by its application as an unguent, all physical ailments and mental afflictions are indeed destroyed.
Therefore, that which is worn on the body by men bestows liberation and fulfills all desires;
so long as [this is not done], holy fords and sacred sites always continue to roar.

O twice-born one, as long as this Gopikā-candana has not been seen or heard of, it remains that which is to be meditated upon, that which is to be worshipped, and the destroyer of the impurity of faults. (7)
Merely by touching it, a human being becomes purified;
at the time of death for mortals, it is the supreme purifier that grants liberation. (8)
O best of the twice-born, what more shall I say? The sandalwood paste of the gopīs grants liberation, as does the wood of Viṣṇu’s tulasī and likewise the earth from its roots. (9)
Gopikā-candana, as well as Hari-candana—having combined these four, the wise person should rub them upon the body. 10.
By him, every sacred site throughout Jambūdvīpa has been established for all time;
he who makes a tilaka-mark with the liquid paste of Gopīcandana [attains this merit]. (11)
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
by him, indeed, the Śrāddha and other rites for his father have been performed after going to Gayā. 12.
Even by whatever person this Gopīcandana is worn—
whether he be a drinker of intoxicants, a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of cows, or likewise a killer of children—
he is liberated from that very instant by wearing the Gopīcandana. (13)
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gopīcandana," in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada within the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(68) The sixty-eighth chapter.
Maheśvara said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the characteristics of the fickle among the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having heard which, the world is liberated from great sins such as brahminicide;
such is their distinction, and such is their true nature as it may be.
O tiger among sages, listen as I speak this truth:
because he was born from Viṣṇu, he is indeed called Vaiṣṇava. (3)
Among all the social classes (varṇas), the Vaiṣṇava is said to be the most excellent;
for those whose food is most meritorious, their lineage is indeed Vaiṣṇava.
O twice-born one, for those in whom forgiveness, self-restraint, austerity, and truthfulness are firmly established,
sin is destroyed at the mere sight of them, like cotton.
Indeed, he whose mind remains free from attachment to similarity with others, and who constantly bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus—[that is Viṣṇu]. (6)
Since one should always wear a garland made of Tulasī wood around the neck,
a wise person should likewise constantly apply twelve tilaka marks.
He who understands dharma and adharma is called a Vaiṣṇava;
he is constantly devoted to the Vedas and Śāstras, and is always a performer of sacrifices. ||8||
They repeatedly perform twenty-four festivals;
their lineage is most blessed, and theirs indeed is called the illustrious one.
Those men who are devotees of the Lord (Bhāgavatas) are indeed born as the most fortunate in the world;
for even in a family where only one man has been born as a devotee of the Lord, [that entire lineage is purified].
By him that family was delivered, O Vāḍava, again and again—those born from eggs, those born from sprouts, and those whose birth is from a womb. ||11||
All of them, indeed, should be known as bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
by the mere sight of whom even a slayer of a Brahmin is always purified.
But what shall I say, O divine sage, regarding those most blessed on earth—those Vaiṣṇavas who are seen in this world, O great muni? (13)
Those indeed should be known as equal to Viṣṇu by those proficient in the truth;
they are the most blessed in the world during the Kali age—this I have heard, and there is no doubt about it. (14)
By him who performs the worship of Viṣṇu, the worship of all has been performed;
by him who has honored the Vaiṣṇavas, a great gift has been bestowed. (15)
Those who offer fruit, leaves, vegetables, food, or even clothing to the devotees of Viṣṇu are always blessed on this earth. (16)
For those by whom Viṣṇu has been worshipped, the worship of all [deities] has indeed been performed;
those by whom Viṣṇu has been honored are considered the most blessed. (17)
By the mere sight of them, a person is purified from sin;
O Vāḍava, what more need be said, and why speak again and again? (18)
Therefore, the sight of them bestows happiness upon the touch;
for as is Viṣṇu, so is this [person], and there is no difference between them anywhere. 19.
Knowing this, O child, the wise man should always worship him.
When even a single Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa is fed on earth, by him a thousand twice-born have been fed; of this there is no doubt. (20)

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Vaiṣṇavas," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||68||
The sixty-ninth chapter.
Nārada said:
O best of the immortals, for those who are always unable to observe fasts, [there is this alternative].
O sinless one, tell me the merit of a single Ekādaśī compared to those twelve.
Śiva said: In the month of Bhādrapada, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, that day bestows all merit; indeed, fasting on it yields great fruit.
Having bathed at the confluence of the rivers and fasted on that twelfth day,
one effortlessly obtains the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs.
If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) should coincide with the asterisms of Budha and Śravaṇā, it becomes exceedingly great;
whatever is performed on that day becomes inexhaustible.
O Nārada, when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
one who bathes at the confluence of rivers shall obtain the fruit born of the gift of a cow.
Then, having placed a water-filled pitcher there,
the wise one should set a vessel upon it and install Janārdana within it.
Then, the wise man should offer before him an oblation cooked in ghee,
and he should give nine new jars filled with water according to his capacity.
Having thus worshipped Govinda, one should observe a vigil there;
then, having bathed at the clear dawn and worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
With flowers, incense, and other offerings, with food oblations, fruits, and beautiful garments, one should then offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) and recite this mantra: ||9||
Salutations, salutations to you, O Govinda, who are endowed with the hearing of the wise;
having brought about the destruction of the flood of sins, be the bestower of all happiness. 10.
One should cause food, purified by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, to be offered according to the rules, especially to those who are knowers of the Purāṇas. ||11||
And by this very method, O best of men, even while remaining intent on a single-minded devotion, one should properly perform everything on the bank of a river.
In this regard, O god on earth, listen to this ancient history as an illustration of what occurred in a vast forest. (13)
Having heard which, one is liberated from great suffering in the world of Mānuṣa; in its western quarter is a region named Dāsāraka. (14)
There, O learned one, was the Maru desert, which causes fear to all living beings;
its ground consisted of intensely heated sand, and it was infested with wicked great serpents. (15)
It was filled with trees casting little shade and teeming with creatures that drink nectar,
along with *śamī*, *khadira*, *pālāśa*, *karīra*, and *pīlu* trees.
There, in some places, the ground is seen covered with dense thickets of formidable trees, bristling with firm thorns, and strewn with the lifeless bodies of people who have been devoured.
Nevertheless, all beings live and breathe due to the bondage of karma;
it is not because of water, nor because of reservoirs of water, that the clouds exist there.
Along with some thirsty young birds perched upon the wings, those best of winged creatures were seen by the brahmin as their lives departed. (19)
In that very region, by the power of destiny, a certain merchant,
having strayed from his own caravan, entered the throat of the desert-dwellers.
With a bewildered heart, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, he wandered about; he did not know where the village was, where there was water, or where he himself would go. (21)
Then he saw pretas, their senses agitated by hunger and thirst—loathsome, terrifying, hideous, fleshless, and fierce in appearance. (22)
She saw one of hideous appearance mounted upon a funeral pyre,
surrounded on all sides by many other pretas.
Seeing that man approaching— extremely fierce, preceded by the cries of hungry ghosts—
the ghost too beheld him as he entered that terrible forest.
Having gone to the earth, he approached the presence of that merchant;
having prostrated before the excellent merchant, he spoke these words: ||25||
"How did you enter this most terrible region?
The wise merchant replied to him, "In my journey, I became separated from my caravan. (26)
Due to the conjunction of destiny and by the force of past karma, thirst afflicts them excessively, and likewise hunger afflicts them intensely. (27)
This speech has reached the end of my life and seems to whirl about;
I see no means here by which I might live by any means whatsoever. (28)
When this had been said, the deceased spoke these words to the merchant:
"Taking refuge at the Śaṅkha tree in full bloom, wait for a moment. (29)
"Having been offered hospitality by me, you shall depart afterwards as you please.
Thus addressed, the merchant, afflicted by thirst, did exactly so.
When midday had arrived, a preta came to that place,
[to] a beautiful water-vessel containing cool water and blooming trees.
Then, having descended, he offered excellent food to the guest, consisting of rice mixed with curd and accompanied by a *vardhamāna* vessel.
Having attained supreme satisfaction by merely eating once,
he became free from thirst and fever within a single moment.
Then the pretas arrived, and he gave them their share from that [offering] in due order;
through the curd-rice and water, the pretas attained supreme satisfaction.
Having satisfied the guest and the entire realm of the departed spirits from all sides,
he himself then ate the remnants of the meal at his ease.
When he had finished eating his excellent food, the water was exhausted;
then, like a merchant, he spoke these words to Yama, the lord of the departed spirits.
"This supreme wonder appears to me in this forest: from where have you obtained such excellent food and drink? (37)
How is it that with such a small amount of food you satisfied even these many people whose bellies were not different from yours? (38)
How is it that you have made your dwelling in this most terrible forest?
Cut through this doubt of mine; my curiosity is supreme. (39)
Thus addressed, he spoke these words to the merchant: "O sinless one, in a past birth, I was devoted to trade. (40)
There was no one else in the entire city so wicked as me;
out of greed for wealth, I did not give alms to anyone at that time. (41)
Then, during the conjunction of Śrāvaṇa-dvādaśī in the month of Bhādrapada, there was a virtuous Brāhmaṇa who became my friend. (42)
Once, he went with me to the river named Tāpī,
where its confluence with the Candrabhāgā is meritorious.
The Candrabhāgā, the daughter of Candra, and the Tāpī, which possesses the heat of the sun—
into the cool and warm waters of those two rivers, he entered together with the twice-born.
On the occasion of the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī yoga,
the Rākṣasas fasted and gave a water-vessel filled with the waters of the Candrabhāgā river to a brahmin.
One should offer curd-rice together with full *vardhamānaka* vessels,
an umbrella, a pair of sandals, a garment, and likewise an image of Hari.
O high-minded one, for the sake of preserving my wealth, I gave [the land] to the foremost of Brahmins on its bank while I was engaged in a vow before Hara. ||47||
Having offered a single beautiful water-jar while observing a fast, I returned home; then, after some time had passed... (48)
Having attained the state of a *paśu* (animal), I fell into the condition of a *preta* (hungry ghost) due to my lack of faith;
thus, in this terrible forest, I am just like a pack of dogs. (49)
On the occasion of the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī yoga, water and grain were offered by me;
this [merit] is obtained every single day at the time of midday. (50)
All those who have committed sins, having attained the state of a *preta*, are of the nature of Brahmā;
some were those who approached the wives of others, and those who were intent on betraying their masters. (51)
Indeed, human beings born here in this desert region have taken on the forms of spirits, ghosts, and the aged; they have become my friends. (52)
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is inexhaustible, the Supreme Self, and eternal;
whatever is given with him as the intended recipient is proclaimed to be imperishable. (53)
Although they are repeatedly satisfied by inexhaustible food, they never at any time escape from their state as pretas or from their weakness. (54)
Having honored you, who have arrived as a guest, with food, I shall be liberated from the state of a preta and go to the supreme destination. (55)
But these, being devoid of me, will experience intense and terrible suffering born of their own past actions in this exceedingly dreadful forest.
Out of a desire to show favor to these highly fortunate ones,
please recite their names and lineages one by one, as they have been written down.
And there is an auspicious casket located at Astikakṣā;
having reached Himavat, you shall obtain that treasure there.
"O high-minded one, go then to Gayāśīrṣa and perform a śrāddha ceremony. Having thus instructed the merchant, that deceased spirit departed as he pleased. (59)
Then, eager because his life was nearly at its end, he dismissed him; having reached his home there, he subsequently departed for the Himalayas.
Then, having taken the treasure found there, he returned;
and after receiving his sixth share, he then went to Gayāśīrṣa.
Having gone there to Gayā, the high-minded one performed with faith the śrāddha for the pretas as prescribed, according to the proper ritual.
Having taken up the names and lineages one by one, he offered the funeral cakes;
whatever śrāddha each person had, the merchant performed it on that very day.
Then, in a dream, he showed his own body to Śaśabindu and said:
"O illustrious one, O sinless one, this is by your grace. (64)
"Having abandoned the state of a preta by performing this rite according to the rules at Gayāśīrṣa, I have attained the supreme goal. Thus spoke the noble-minded one.
Thereafter, meditating upon Viṣṇu again and again, that wise man returned to his own home when the month of Bhādrapada arrived during its bright fortnight.

On the occasion of the conjunction of the Śravaṇa asterism with the twelfth lunar day, he of incomparable intelligence, equipped with all necessary provisions, went once more to the confluence of rivers.
Having bathed at the confluence of rivers and fasted on that twelfth day (dvādaśī), and having likewise bathed there, given gifts, and worshipped Janārdana; ||68||
Immediately thereafter, with his mind focused on a single object, he offered the sacrificial oblations to the Brahmin according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. (69)
Then that wise merchant turned back [his caravan] every year when the month of Bhādrapada arrived.
Furthermore, on the occasion of the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī,
he quickly performed all these rites at the confluence of rivers, dedicating them to Viṣṇu.
After a very long time,
he met his end and attained the supreme state, which is difficult for all human beings to reach.
Even today he sports in Vaikuṇṭha, served by the messengers of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Brahmin, you too should perform this Śravaṇa-dvādaśī vow.
It bestows all prosperity both in this world and the next, generates sublime wisdom, and is the supreme remover of all sins. (74)
Whoever performs such a vow during the conjunction of the twelfth lunar day with the Śravaṇa asterism goes to the world of Viṣṇu by the power of this vow. ||75||

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Vow of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada.
The seventieth chapter.
Nārada said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation!
Tell me, O best of fathers-in-law, by what means one does not behold such suffering. ||1||
Maheśa said:
Listen, O Brāhmaṇa, I shall describe the auspicious Trirātra of the river, by the performance of which hell does not arise for men. 2.
Having attained incomparable longevity, health, good fortune, happiness, prosperity, and imperishable progeny, one is glorified in the heavenly world. ||3||
In the month of Āṣāḍha, joined by a rising river flood, she was formerly renowned as Purāṇasā, being constantly situated in water. ||4||

Just as a river, when completely filled by the floods of water during the rainy season, becomes full of all its currents; so too, she [the Goddess] should be worshipped with the vow of *āsā* (hope/expectation) when it is fully realized.

Having designated this as a three-night vow (vrata), it should be performed with great effort; the first day is the new moon, and that period of three days is for the purpose of beholding [the deity].
Just as women [take] the flood of a river from the water at its bank,
or else, O Kṛṣṇa, having placed that water in a jar, they should carry it home.
Having gone to a river, the wise twice-born man should bathe at dawn and perform worship;
he should observe a fast for three nights, or as much as he is able.
If one is unable, one may perform only a single meal [per day] or even a fast;
one should offer a lamp without interruption and perform worship in the morning and evening. (9)
Having invoked the great river by name as well as Varuṇa, and having established Keśava, who reclines upon the waters, at the base of the water; 10.
Salutations to the Goddess known as Gaṅgā, Gautamī, and Nadī; salutations to you, O Sindhu, Kāverī, and Sarasvatī! 11.
Salutations again and again to the Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Pūrṇā, Mahendrā, Sukhadā, Kāśyapī, Gaṇḍakī, and the Sindhu river. ||12||
Obeisance be unto you, Varuṇa, dweller in the waters, beloved of Hari!
O Lord of aquatic creatures, Sovereign of the element of taste, grant me perpetual auspiciousness. (13)
Accept this *argha* offered by me; grant me the fruit I desire, [offered] with *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds, coconuts, and auspicious fruits produced in their proper season. (14)
One should offer food oblations cooked in ghee to the river, saying:
"Obeisance to you, O Keśava, O Ananta; obeisance to you who recline upon the waters. (15)
"Protect me, O Lord; O Govinda, be the granter of boons.
In this manner, worship should be performed according to the proper time and in due order. (16)
Pure and observing the three-night vow with prayers and ritual services, one should worship and then perform the breaking of the fast by offering a vessel of water. (17)
Likewise, with fruits and flowers, accompanied by women and even children and men, together with songs and instrumental music, and with jars overflowing from the river. ||18||
Having placed them in water and water-mixtures, one should worship them with fruits and flowers, as well as with various kinds of grains and offerings of water. (19)
Having arrived at the house with laughter, songs, and dances, one should effortlessly worship vessels filled with the seven grains as if they were full. ||20||
One should fill seven, five, or three [vessels] according to one's capacity;
moreover, desiring one's own welfare, one should not drink river water for three nights.
If the sacrificial food for the one who is to cross over is stolen, it becomes otherwise;
likewise, river water should not be used once the ritual bathing and worship have been performed.
Likewise, he should cause pure foods fit for consumption to be brought;
there should be seven vessels made of bamboo and seven water-jars.
One should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) that is free from pungent, sour, and sweet flavors;
one should diligently avoid beans and food ground on a stone.
O best of the twice-born, one should observe this vow for three years;
having thus completed it after three years, one should perform its concluding rite (udyāpana).
O Nārada, one should give a black cow with black garments and sesame seeds;
having thus caused the husband and wife to be reconciled, one should also give gold according to one's ability.
O Nārada, one should fashion the northern [altar] out of gold in the form of a river;
furthermore, the mandala for Varuṇa should be the Sarvatobhadra.
Having established the water-pot there along with the offerings,
and having worshipped it according to the rules with devotion, one should then cause it to be given to a Brahmin.
One should feed Brahmins according to one's ability and in accordance with one's wealth, [offering them] to a preceptor who is of honored character and devoted to all the scriptures. (29)
O wise one, when this is performed in such a manner, the vow becomes complete;
there shall be good fortune, happiness, prosperity, and imperishable progeny. (30)
One does not fall into an evil rebirth, but is honored for a long time in heaven;
this practice was followed by the wives of the gods and likewise by the wives of the sages. (31)
This incomparable vow of three nights by the rivers was performed in former times by the Nāgas, Siddhas, and Gaṇas. What else do you wish to hear?
Through it, one always attains good fortune, progeny, and certainty. (32)
Thus ends the section titled "The Three-Night Vow of the River" within the *Umāpati-Nārada Saṃvāda* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The seventieth chapter. ||70||
[71] The seventy-first chapter.
The sages said:
O virtuous Sūta, may you live long! You, whose very soul is exceedingly compassionate, have indeed related this wonderful dialogue that took place between Nārada and Vyāsa. (1)
O Guru, tell us what kind of greatness of the name of the Blessed One was heard by the high-souled Nārada; we listen with faith. (2)
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, as I relate an ancient account;
O best of the twice-born, upon hearing which devotion to Kṛṣṇa increases. (3)
Once, Nārada, being well-composed, went to the peak of Mount Meru, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, in order to see his father. ||4||
There, O Brahmins, having bowed down to the god Brahmā, the lord of the worlds as he sat there, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke. (5)
Nārada said:
O Lord, Sovereign of the Universe, tell me the full extent of the power of this name;
what is the nature of the greatness of the name of that imperishable Great Soul?
He who is this Lord of the Universe, he is Nārāyaṇa, Hari himself;
he is the Supreme Self, Hṛṣīkeśa, present within all living beings.
Deluded by Māyā, all people in this worthless Kali age, being utterly infatuated, do not know the Blessed One, Adhokṣaja. ||8||
Brahmā said:
"In this Kali age, devotion should especially be practiced according to the rules preceded by the chanting of names; you ought to hear that from me."
The purification of unspoken sins committed by others has been observed;
however, the remembrance of Viṣṇu, the Victorious One, through diligent effort, is the destroyer of all sins. 10.
Therefore, by reciting and chanting the name of Hari, one is liberated from all sins resulting from false knowledge and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 11.
People always say, "Hari, Hari"—these two syllables;
by the mere utterance of them, they are liberated; of this there is no doubt. (12)
Of all expiations, the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is supreme;
remembering Him in the morning, at night, in the evening, at midday, and so forth. (13)
A person who remembers Viṣṇu, the god, attains Nārāyaṇa immediately and achieves the destruction of all afflictions through the immediate destruction of their sins. 14.
Liberation is attained and heaven is reached through the glorification of that Viṣṇu,
whose mind is fixed upon Vāsudeva during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and other rites.
One should know that to be imperishable for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
where, then, is the ascent to the back of Nāka, which is characterized by return? (16)
The recitation of the name of Vāsudeva is the unsurpassed seed-mantra of liberation;
His mouth is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), wherein she spreads her whirlpool.
The eastern Sarasvatī shines forth with the words "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa";
therefore, by remembering Viṣṇu day and night, one becomes the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||18||
"O son of excellent vows, you shall not go to hell, for the stains of the Kali age have been completely destroyed; I speak the truth, the truth, and again the truth. (19)
By the mere utterance of the name, one is liberated from great sin;
and by further chanting "Rāma, Rāma! Rāma, Rāma! [one is likewise freed]. 20.
Even a caṇḍāla becomes a purified soul; there is no doubt about this.
[The same applies to visiting] Kurukṣetra, as well as Kāśī, Gayā, and Prayāga. (21)
By the mere utterance of His name, all sacred pilgrimage sites have been visited by him;
for he is one who constantly chants and recites, "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! ||22||
Abandoning this world, he rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu, O Brahmin, constantly chanting and reciting the *Nṛsiṃha-hṛdaya* with joy. (23)
In the Kali age, a man who is a devotee of the Lord is liberated from great sin—
by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara.
Whatever one desires to attain, that one attains by chanting the name of Keśava in the Kali age;
knowing this, people have immersed themselves in Keśava, the Self of the world.
With all their sins completely exhausted, they go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu:
the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Nṛsiṃha, and likewise Vāmana. ||26||
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and then Kalki are remembered;
these are proclaimed as the ten incarnations upon the earth. ||27||
By the mere mention of these names, even a killer of a Brahmin is always purified, just as one who recites, chants, and meditates on the name of Viṣṇu in the morning [is purified]. (28)
"He is liberated; of this there is no doubt—he indeed becomes Nārāyaṇa.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Nārada was filled with the utmost wonder.
There he said to his father: "O best of gods, what was said?
There are thousands of gods; there are thousands of Rudras. (30)
There are hundreds of ancestors, as well as yakṣas, kinnaras, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and whatever other beings belong to the divine realm. ||31||
The greatness of their names has neither been heard nor seen by me in such a manner as the greatness of the name of Śrī Viṣṇu has been heard by me.
For one who is liberated by merely hearing its name, there is no doubt in this;
what need is there for wandering over the earth visiting various holy places, O God? (33)
He who, upon hearing of its greatness, attains liberation—that face is indeed a great holy ford (tīrtha), and that face is also a sacred field (kṣetra). ||34||
That face which utters "Rāma" is the fulfiller of all desires.
O observer of noble vows, what are its names, and how many are its powers?
"O Grandfather, tell me all of that in its entirety without omission.
Brahmā said: "This Viṣṇu is all-pervading, the eternal Supreme Self. (36)
May that glorious Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end, the self of all beings, and the creator of all beings— since I have indeed been born from him— protect me always.
This very one is indeed the time of time; he is my own ancestor, the imperishable, lotus-eyed, wise, and undecaying Supreme Person.
Viṣṇu, who always reclines upon Śeṣa, the thousand-headed, great Lord, who consists of all beings, is directly the universal-formed Janārdana. (39)
"O bull among men, this Viṣṇu, the slayer of Kaiṭabha, is the Creator and the Lord of the universe; yet I do not know his name or lineage. (40)
