"O father, though I am a proponent of the Vedas, I have never been a knower [of the truth].
Therefore, O celestial sage, go to where the Lord of the Universe resides. (41)
O best of sages, he will tell you all that truth;
he alone is the illustrious one who is forever the lord of Kailāsa. 42.
Among all devotees of Viṣṇu, he is the most excellent, higher than the highest; indeed, he has five faces, is beloved by Umā, and is the destroyer of all suffering. (43)
Viśveśvara, the Lord of the Universe, who is always affectionate toward his devotees—go there, O best of gods; he will tell you all of that.
Having heard his father’s words,
he set out from there toward the abode of Kailāsa to ascertain the greatness of that name.
Where the Lord Viśveśvara, the bestower of prosperity, eternally resides, there Nārada beheld that god worshipped by the deities. (46)
[He saw] the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, having five faces, ten arms, three eyes, and holding a trident in his hand. ||47||
He who carries a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, who wields a sharp spear and sword, who bears the Pināka bow, who is formidable, the giver of boons, and whose vehicle is the bull. ||48||
He was richly adorned with ashes and serpents, with the moon as his crest-ornament;
resembling a dark blue cloud, he possessed a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Having seen that Lord of Gods playing there, Mahādeva prostrated himself again like a staff with eight limbs, his eyes wide with wonder.
The supreme among Vaiṣṇavas said to the best of the Bāḍavas:
"O best of divine sages, tell me, why have you come here? (51)
Nārada said:
At one and the same time, I went to the presence of Brahmā;
there I heard the supreme majesty of the divine Viṣṇu.
O best of gods, that which was told by Brahmā there in my presence—
the full extent of this [name's] power— was heard from the mouth of Brahmā.
"In that regard, I previously asked about the thousand names of Viṣṇu;
then I was told by Brahmā: 'I do not know them, O Nārada. (54)
"O Mahārudra, he knows all of that and will tell it all;
having attained a state of great wonder, he has come into your presence. (55)
In this terrible Kali age, human beings are short-lived,
constantly devoted to unrighteousness, lacking steadfastness in their names, and devoid of purity.
Likewise, there were heretics and those who were not true Brahmins, always devoted to unrighteousness, neglecting the twilight prayers, fallen from their vows, wicked, and foul in appearance. (57)
Just as it was with the Brahmins, so too were the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas again and again;
likewise the Śūdras and others—these nine classes of men are Bhāgavatas. 58.
O Lord Viśveśvara, in the Kali age, those born from Śūdras who are excluded from the twice-born do not know dharma or adharma, nor what is beneficial or even what is harmful.
"O Lord, having understood this, I have come into your presence;
furthermore, I have heard the greatness of the Name from the mouth of a brāhmaṇa. (60)
You are the god of all gods; you are my protector at all times. You are the enemy of Tripura, the soul of the universe, and you are the creator again and again. 61.
By your grace, please recite the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu, which generates good fortune for men and always produces supreme devotion. (62)
It bestows the Veda upon Brāhmaṇas, grants victory to Kṣatriyas, constantly bestows wealth upon Vaiśyas, and gives happiness to Śūdras. ||63||
Therefore, O Maheśvara, I desire to hear that from you;
for you are always capable [of explaining] regarding Keśava for the sake of your devotees. (64)
O observer of noble vows, if it is not a secret, please tell me out of grace:
this is always supremely purifying and consists of all sacred fords.
"Therefore, O Lord, Sovereign of All, I truly wish to hear; speak!
Having heard Nārada’s words, his eyes were wide with wonder.
Then, covered in hair, he was born while recollecting the names of Viṣṇu. The Lord said:
"O Brahmin, this thousand names of Viṣṇu is a supreme secret."
Having heard this, O child, a person shall never fall into an evil state;
and once some time had passed, Pārvatī spoke to me.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord of Kailāsa, tell me truly:
O Lord of Gods, absorbed in supreme sovereignty, what do you recite?
O Lord Viśveśvara, tell me: how is it that you are always marked with ashes and always clad in animal skins; and how have you come to wear matted locks? 70.
You are the god of all gods; you are the teacher of all actions.
You are my lord, O Lord of the Universe, Protector of the World, Sovereign of the Cosmos. 71.
Mahādeva said:
"O Brahmin, when this was asked of me by Pārvatī again and again,
I then explained everything in detail before her."
Listen, Nārada, I shall tell you what was said to Pārvatī, by which the Blessed One, the giver of liberation, became pleased; of this there is no doubt. (73)
But this man is my father in person and has always been my kinsman;
I have always been devoted to him, for he is my husband forever. (74)
"Therefore, I shall fully declare it; listen as I speak.
Sūta said:
"O twice-born ones, having spoken thus, he indeed related it to Nārada."
That Thousand Names of Viṣṇu which was formerly proclaimed to Umā was indeed obtained by Nārada from Maheśa on Kailāsa. (76)
Once, by the turn of fate, he arrived from Kailāsa at the most wonderful sacred site known as Naimiṣāraṇya.
All the sages dwelling there, having seen that most excellent of sages,
performed a special worship for the high-souled Nārada.
Knowing that Nārada had arrived, those excellent Vaiṣṇava brahmins, their eyes wide with wonder, showered down a rain of flowers. (79)
Then, having offered water for the feet and the respectful oblation (arghya), and having performed the ritual waving of lights (ārati),
they offered fruits and roots and prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff.
And they said: "O great sage, we have accomplished our purpose; for in this place, the sight of you has occurred—purifying and destructive of sin. (81)
And by your grace, O Lord of Gods, the Purāṇas have been heard;
O Brahman, by what means may the destruction of all sins come to pass? (82)
Without charity, without austerity, without pilgrimages, penances, or sacrifices;
without gifts, without meditations, and without the restraint of the senses;
and even without the collections of scriptures—how can liberation be attained? (83)
Nārada said:
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, the god of gods, the teacher of the world, who was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa and beloved of Umā, he questioned him.
Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, you are the supreme deity, omniscient, and honored by all;
as such, you are worshipped even by the gods, beginning with Indra and Sūrya. (85)
All obtain their desired success by worshipping you, the bestower of boons;
you are free from birth and death, self-existent, and possessed of all powers. 86.
"O Lord, why do you always meditate upon the naked destroyer of Madana?
Why do you perform penance, matted-haired and grey with ashes? (87)
"Or what are you reciting, O Lord of Gods? I have a great curiosity, O observer of noble vows; since I am to be favored by you, tell me the truth."
Mahādeva said:
"This has not been told to anyone; it must be kept secret by me.
Nevertheless, O blessed lady, I shall speak to you, for you are my devotee and you are dear to me. (89)
O Goddess, in the former Satya-yuga, all beings were pure-minded; knowing Viṣṇu alone to be the Lord of all lords, they worshipped Him alone. 90.
O beloved, they attain supreme prosperity in this world and the next, which all the gods and the sages, burdened by afflictions, have not attained. (91)
Those who have formed a fixed conviction regarding the Name—even the gods who are averse to Viṣṇu—attain that goal after hearing it even from my own mouth. 92.
With minds bewildered by the Vedas, Purāṇas, and various philosophical systems, they do not attain certainty: "What is the reality? What is the supreme state? (93)
O beloved, [one does not attain this] through gifts such as the tulāpuruṣa, through sacrifices such as the aśvamedha,
or through bathing at sacred fords such as Vārāṇasī and Prayāga.

By means of ancestral rites such as the *śrāddha* at Gayā, by the recitation of the Vedas and other forms of silent prayer (*japa*), by severe austerities, by observances (*niyama*) and restraints (*yama*), and by compassion toward all beings and so forth; ||95||

Through service to the guru, through the duties to be practiced according to one's caste and stage of life, and through the proper conduct of knowledge, meditation, and so forth, over the course of ten million births. ||96||
They do not attain that supreme bliss by taking refuge with all their being in Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, the ancient Supreme Person. 97.
Mortals who have no other resort, though they enjoy worldly pleasures, suffer the highest torment when they are devoid of knowledge and dispassion and abandoned by celibacy and the like. (98)
Even all virtuous people do not attain that state which those who have abandoned all phenomena and utter only the name of Viṣṇu reach with ease. (99)
Viṣṇu should be constantly remembered and never forgotten;
all injunctions and prohibitions serve only to bring about this very end. (100)
However, the gods beginning with Brahmā and the sages, freed from all sin, have attained their desired state without fear solely through the name of Viṣṇu. (101)
And having failed to obtain honor for myself, Hari was properly propitiated by me, who,
with a disciplined mind, desired even something superior to this.
Then, O Lord of the World, Keśava, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being directly pleased, honored them with portions of his own self. (103)
The one whose nature is compassion honored the gods, the ancestors, and the twice-born with offerings of *havya*, *kavya*, and other gifts;
from that time forward, they have been worshipped throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (104)
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, by the grace of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, spoke thus to me: "You shall become more worshipful and superior even than I. (105)
O Śambhu, having thus propitiated you, I shall always receive a boon:
that at the beginning of the Dvāpara age, appearing through a portion of my power among humans and others, [I shall manifest]. (106)
By means of fabricated scriptures, you shall turn people away from me;
and you must conceal me, so that this creation may continue in its successive progression.
"I shall quickly create this delusion which will bewilder for many leagues;
and you, O mighty-armed Rudra, compose treatises of delusion. (108)
O mighty-armed one, show what is unreal as being real;
make yourself manifest and make me unmanifest. (109)
Then, having prostrated before that Supreme Lord, I said:
"How might the sin of a thousand Brahman-murders be somehow pacified? (110)
Yet, your lack of recognition [of me] cannot be overcome even in hundreds of millions of eons;
therefore, I have engaged in this rivalry with you, O Hari, so that I might become pure. (111)
"Tell me that, O Govinda, as the expiation you desire.
Thereupon the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke the truth concerning his own self. (112)
O daughter of the mountain, because of him I became superior;
therefore, I constantly worship, praise, and meditate upon him alone through ascetic penance.
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme reality; knowledge of Him is the means to liberation.
This is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures; anything else leads only to delusion. (114)
That there is liberation without giving, that I am equal to Viṣṇu, that knowledge comes from mere pilgrimage sites and the like, and that I am superior to Viṣṇu—[these are false]. (115)
"The non-difference between those like us, the liberated, and Hari"—all such statements are spoken for the sake of deluding everyone, and not otherwise.
Therefore, O Pārvatī, I possess non-dual majesty and am worshipful by the world. (116)
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of gods, O Śaṅkara, tell me that by which I too may become the peerless sovereign of all, equal to you, O Lord. (117)
Mahādeva said: "Excellent, excellent! O beloved, you have asked well regarding the Lord Viṣṇu.
I shall declare the thousand names, which are preeminent and grant liberation from the three worlds."
Of this *Śrī Viṣṇu Sahasranāmastotra*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Mahādeva, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Anuṣṭubh;

*hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *śrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *klīṃ* is the pivot (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation for the sake of the four aims of life: virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
*Oṃ vāsudevāya vidmahe mahāhaṃsāya dhīmahi.*
May Viṣṇu impel that for us.
If one recites the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa* according to the prescribed rule, the fruit thereof becomes multiplied ten millionfold; of this there is no doubt. (119)
Śrī Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman—this is for the heart.
Mūlaprakṛti is for the head. Mahāvarāha is for the topknot (śikhā).
"Banner of the Solar Dynasty" is the armor;
"Wondrous Childhood of the World, Desired by Brahmā and Others" is the eye.
"Yathārthakhaṇḍitāśeṣa" is the weapon-mantra.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) everywhere with "Namo nārāyaṇāya.
[The mantra is: *Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya puruṣāya mahātmane*.
We meditate upon the Great Swan, whose abode is the intellect of the pure being.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ.
*klīṃ* to Kṛṣṇa, to Viṣṇu; *hrīṃ* to Rāma, we meditate upon; may that God impel us. *kṣrauṃ* to Nṛsiṃha, let us know; *śrīṃ* to Śrīkaṇṭha, we meditate upon; may that Viṣṇu impel us.
Oṃ, let us know Vāsudeva; let us meditate on the son of Devakī; may that Kṛṣṇa inspire us.
Having uttered this mantra— *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ | klīṃ kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopī-jana-vallabhāya svāhā*— one should either recite it or meditate upon the imperishable Viṣṇu.
The wise person should recite the hymn of praise to Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the Universe. ||120||
Oṃ! Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest;
he is the supreme abode, the supreme light, the supreme reality, and the supreme state. (121)
The Supreme Śiva is the supreme object of meditation, the supreme knowledge, the supreme goal;
he is the ultimate reality, the supreme good, supreme bliss, and the supreme refuge. ||122||
He is beyond the manifest, higher than the ether, possessed of supreme prosperity, the Supreme Lord;
He is free from disease, changeless, free from conceptual construction, and without support. ||123||
He is without water, free from fear, untainted, unrestrained, devoid of qualities, partless, infinite, fearless, inconceivable, and beyond the reach of the senses. ||124||
Beyond the senses, the source of the measured, without a lord, without desire, undecaying, imperishable, all-knowing, all-pervading, all, the giver of all, the creator of all. ||125||
The teacher of all, the witness of all, worthy of worship by all, the remover of the suffering of all in every way;
possessing all power, the essence of all, the self of all, facing in every direction. ||126||
The abode of all, possessing all forms, the beginning of all, the destroyer of all suffering; the goal of all, auspicious in every way, the cause of all causes. ||127||
He who transcends all, the supervisor of all, the lord of all gods;
the twenty-sixth, the Great Viṣṇu, the Great Secret, the Great Pervader. 128.
He is eternally risen, eternally disciplined, the eternal giver of bliss, and the ancient one;
he is the Lord of Māyā, the Lord of Yoga, the Lord of Kaivalya, and the Self-born. 129.
Transcending birth, death, and old age; beyond time; having passed over worldly existence;
full; true; whose nature is pure and awakened; eternally consisting of consciousness. ||130||
He is the lover of yoga, accessible through yoga, the sole liberator from the bonds of worldly existence;
he is the Ancient Person, inward consciousness, and the Supreme Person. ||131||

He is the one to be known through the Vedānta, difficult to comprehend, free from the three types of suffering, the locus of the knowledge of Brahman, beginningless, self-luminous, and the self-existent Lord. ||132||
The Praṇava is indifferent toward all that is to be attained, equal in every respect, entirely irreproachable, difficult to reach, and beyond darkness. ||133||
He is the immutably fixed one, yet pervading all; he transcends the range of speech and mind.
He is Saṃkarṣaṇa, the destroyer of all, Time itself, who causes fear to all. ||134||
He whose movement is variegated and unsurpassed, the great Rudra who is difficult to approach, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the blissful one, Pradyumna, the deluder of the universe. 135.
Mahāmāyā is the seed of the universe, the supreme power, and the sole ground of bliss; he whose play is infinite and who is desired by all is the subduer of all beings. ||136||
I am Aniruddha, the life-force of all, Hṛṣīkeśa, and the Lord of the mind; I am the beloved of those free from worldly conditions, the Imperishable, and the director of all. 137.

The Lord of Brahman and Prāṇa, the sustainer of all beings, the leader of the body, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), primordial nature (prakṛti), the Master, the Person (puruṣa), and the upholder of the thread of the universe. ||138||
Aṃ is the inner controller, the one with three abodes, the witness, the Lord of the three qualities;
He is accessible to yogis, Padmanābha, the one who reclines upon Śeṣa, the Lord of Śrī. ||139||

Hari is the one whose lotus feet are eternally worshipped by Śrī, who possesses eternal Śrī, who is the abode of Śrī, who has Śrī ever residing upon his chest, who is the treasure-trove of Śrī, and who is the upholder of Śrī. 140.

The Lord who brings wealth under his control, the immovable one, the bestower of prosperity, Viṣṇu whose abode is the ocean of milk, whose chest is illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, Mādhava, the remover of the world's afflictions. 141.

He who has the Śrīvatsa on his chest, the vessel of boundless and auspicious qualities, the one clad in yellow garments, the Lord of the world, the protector of the world, and the father of the world. 142.

The upholder of the world, the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, the treasury of the world; he whose singular, throbbing valor is the world, who is free from egoism, the disputant, and identical with the universe. (143)
He consists of all wonders, he has accomplished all goals, he has conquered all passion;
his exertion is entirely unfailing, and his consciousness is superior even to that of Brahmā, Rudra, and others. (144)
He is the grandfather of Śambhu, the father of Brahmā, and the sovereign lord of Śakra and the other gods; he is beloved by all the deities, the embodiment of all the gods, and unsurpassed. ||145||
The sole refuge of all gods, the sole deity of all gods;
the enjoyer of sacrifice, the giver of the fruit of sacrifice, the Lord of sacrifice, and the creator of sacrifice. ||146||

The protector of sacrifice, the personification of sacrifice, wearing a forest garland, beloved by the twice-born; the sole object of honor for the twice-born, the deity of the brahminical lineage, and the slayer of demons. ||147||
The end-maker of all the wicked, the sole protector of all the virtuous;
the single belly of the seven worlds, the singular ornament of the seven worlds. ||148||
The wielder of the discus who effects creation, preservation, and destruction;
the bearer of the Śārṅga bow, the mace, the conch, and the lotus in his hands, whose vehicle is Garuḍa. 149.
His form is indescribable; he is worthy of worship by all, the purifier of the three worlds, possessed of infinite fame and boundless prowess, and the auspiciousness of all. 150.
He resembles ten million suns; he is as difficult to approach as ten million mountains;
he is the creator of the world through ten million Mayas; he possesses the great strength of ten million winds. 151.
He is the giver of ten million worlds, the Great Lord who is the peak of the three worlds;
he is the one whose beauty is ten million times more intoxicating than Cupid, and the crusher of ten million fortresses of enemies.
He is as formidable as ten million oceans, he is invoked by ten million heretics, he possesses the splendor of ten million Kuberas, and he is the enjoyer of the delights of ten million Indras. (153)

He who is the embodiment of ten million cosmic eggs, who is worth ten million Himalayas in ransom, who destroys the sins of ten million horse sacrifices, and whose worship is equal to ten million sacrifices. ||154||

He is the cause of health for millions of nectars, the fulfiller of desires for millions of wish-fulfilling cows, the embodiment of millions of forms of the knowledge of Brahman, the one pervaded by rays (or entered by the sun), and he whose fame is pure. ||155||

The sustainer of the universe, whose feet are the source of all sacred pilgrimage sites, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious, the primordial god, the conqueror of the world, Mukunda, the slayer of Kālanemi. 156.
Vaikuṇṭha is of infinite majesty, a festival for the great lords of yoga; he is eternally satisfied, radiant in his being, free from all fear, and the destroyer of hell.
The sole refuge for the poor and helpless, the remover of the world's singular distress, eternally capable of compassion for the universe, merciful, and the shelter of the virtuous. ||158||
The Lord of Yoga, eternally exalted, devoid of increase or decrease;
Adhokṣaja, the seed of the universe, the sovereign over hundreds of Prajāpatis. ||159||
His feet are worshipped by Śakra and Brahmā; he has gone to the supreme abode of Śambhu and Brahmā;
his eyes are the sun and the moon; he is the enjoyer of the universe and has reached the further shore of all things. 160.
He is the bridge for the world, the upholder of the bridge of dharma, and the bearer of the burden of the universe.
He is free from possessiveness, the lord of all worlds, unattached, yet possessed of wondrous enjoyments.
He who brings all under his control, the subduer of the universe, Viṣvaksena, the best of gods;
the Lord of all auspiciousness, adorned with divine and priceless ornaments. ||162||
He is endowed with all auspicious marks, the destroyer of the pride of all the lords of the Daityas, the entire essence of all the gods, and the leader of all deities. ||163||
He is the armor for all the gods, the crest-jewel of all the gods, the fortress for all the deities, and the destroyer of the thunderbolt for those who have sought refuge in him. 164.
The Lord Viṣṭaraśravas, whose name removes all fear, is the omnipresent one who brings about the welfare of all, who has slain his enemies, and who bestows the path to heaven. 165.
The Lord of the life-force of all deities, the ordainer of the Brahmins and others, Brahma-Śambhu, whose lifespan is a parārdha, the eldest of Brahmā, the Child, the self-ruling sovereign. 166.
Virāṭ is subservient to his devotees, worthy of praise, and the fulfiller of the purpose of those who offer hymns;
he acts for the sake of others, knows what must be done, and is eternally abandoned by actions for his own sake. ||167||
He is eternally blissful, eternally auspicious, eternally peaceful, eternally propitious; he is eternally beloved, eternally contented, eternally nourished, and eternally worshipped. ||168||
He who is eternally pure, the foremost purifier, the secret of the Vedas, Vṛṣākapi, the one with a thousand names, the one of three ages, the fourfold form, and the four-armed. 169.
The Lord of the past, future, and present; the progenitor of the Great Beings;
Nārāyaṇa; the Lord of the Muni; he who has emerged from all yoga. ||170||
The essence of the Vedas, the essence of sacrifice, the essence of the Sāman chants, and a treasury of austerity;
the one to be attained, the most excellent, the ancient seer, the ultimate peace, and the final refuge. (171)
He who destroys the trident of Śiva, the sole bestower of boons upon Śrīkaṇṭha;
he is Nara, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the son of Dharma, and the life of Dharma. 172.
The first creator of all truths, the destroyer of the pride of all women-jewels, the conqueror of the pride of the three times, the lover of Urvaśī, and the lord of sages. (173)
The first poet is Hayagrīva, the Lord of all masters of speech;
he is Brahmā, who embodies all the gods, the Guru, and the husband of Vāgīśvarī. 174.
Madhusūdana is the source of infinite knowledge, the destroyer of primordial ignorance (mūlā-vidyā), the bestower of omniscience, and the annihilator of the world's dullness. 175.
Lord of many tens of millions of mantras, the sole master who has reached the further shore of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman);
the primordial knower, the creator of the Vedas, the soul of the Vedas, and an ocean of sacred revelation (Śruti).
He is the one who brings about the realization of the meaning of Brahman, the birthplace of all higher knowledge,
the king of sciences, the embodiment of wisdom, an ocean of gnosis, and possesses indivisible intellect.
Matsyadeva, the great horned one, whose vision encompasses the vessel of the seed of the universe;
he who pervades the entire ocean through his divine play and is the promulgator of the four Vedas. 178.

The primordial tortoise, the support of all, who made the burden of the world as light as a blade of grass; he who turned the host of gods into immortals and was the cause of the production of the nectar of immortality. ||179||

He who is the support of the self, the support of the earth, the upholder of sacrifices, the supporter of the cow-like earth, the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the world, and the ordainer of the Śrāddha rites and other ceremonies. 180.

He is the destroyer of all fears of the ancestors, the life-giver to all the ancestors, the sole enjoyer of the offerings to gods and ancestors (havya and kavya), and the bestower of the sole fruit of those offerings. ||181||

He who has the ocean submerged within his body hairs, who agitated the entire sea, who is the Great Boar, the destroyer of those who obstruct sacrifices, and the refuge of those who perform sacrifices. 182.
The divine lion Śrī Nṛsiṃha is the destroyer of all undesirable objects and suffering;
he is the peerless hero of wondrous strength, the sole support for those who take refuge in his mantra. 183.

He possesses a form that is difficult for the world to behold, with nails more powerful than ten million vajras, and a brilliance as unbearable as the fire at the end of a yuga that terrifies even Brahmā and the other gods. (184)
The Lord of the great host of Mothers, who subdues the circle of the Mothers; rich in inconceivable and unfailing heroism, he is the devourer of all demons.
The destroyer of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Time (Kāla), the Lord of Saṃkarṣaṇī, the unbearable one who slays the enemies of the Dharma, and the destroyer of all fears. 186.
He is the destroyer of all obstacles, the bestower of all accomplishments, the fulfiller of all desires; he is the annihilator of all sins, known by the name Siddhamantrādhi. ||187||
The Lord of Bhairava, the destroyer of the suffering of Umā, difficult to approach even for ten million Deaths;
he whose roar caused the cosmic egg to burst and made the wombs of the Daityas miscarry. 188.
The protector of all upon being merely remembered, the one of wondrous form, the Great Hari;
he whose head is celibacy, who is the embodied guardian of the quarters, and whose ornament is the half-moon. 189.
He who has twelve suns for his head-garland and Rudra for his sole anklet;
he who is the protector of Girijā when she was seized by the Yoginīs, and who threatens with the *abhaya* mudrā. ||190||

The Lord of the Heroic Circle, exceedingly fierce, the incomparable enemy, the excellent Kālaśambhara, the Lord of Wrath, who devours the wicked, including the retinue of the fierce Caṇḍīs and others. 191.
The death of all immovable [forces], the death of death itself, he who turns back the death of time;
the destroyer of all incurable diseases, he who makes all malevolent planets auspicious. (192)
He who destroys the pride of ten million Gaṇeśas, who is unbearable and the destroyer of all enemy clans;
difficult for gods and demons to behold, he is terrifying and brings fear to the world.
He is the protector from all miserable states of existence, the devourer of the devourer of the world,
the fierce Śambaramārjāra, and the consumer of the mouse that is Time (Kāla).
He who has arms like staffs for weapons, the Man-Lion, the conqueror of Vīrabhadra.
The Lord of the Secret of the Yoginī-cakra, the consumer of the sacrificial animal of Śakrāri;
he is Rudra and Nārāyaṇa, whose form is a ram and who has Śaṅkara as his vehicle. ||195||

The protector from Śiva in the form of a ram, the consumer of thousands of wicked powers, the beloved of Tulasī, the hero, the one who follows the left-hand path (vāmācāra), and the bestower of all desires. 196.
Mahāśiva is mounted upon Śivā; Bhairava holds a single skull-cup;
Killī is the Lord of the Cakra, bestowing a divine, enchanting form like that of Indra. 197.
He is the bestower of fortune upon Gaurī and the abode of Umā; he removes the fear of Māyā;
he consists of the splendor of Brahman, consists of the glory of Brahman, and consists of the three Vedas. ||198||
Subrahmaṇya, the destroyer of Bali, the son of Aditi who removes her sorrow, Upendra, the king, Viṣṇu, the ornament of Kaśyapa’s lineage. 199.
Acyuta is the bestower of the kingdom of Bali and the giver of food to all gods and brahmins;
he is Urukrama (the wide-striding), Tīrthapāda (whose feet are sacred fords), Tripadastha (established in three steps), and Trivikrama (the triple-stepper). ||200||
With the sky as his feet, he has sanctified the three worlds with his own footsteps;
his head is saluted by Brahmā, Śiva, and others, and his swift-running feet leave no trace upon the earth.
Of inconceivable and wondrous extent, the universal tree of great power,
who went to the head of Rāhu and severed the head of Bhṛgu’s wife.
He who is ever afraid of sin, who possesses constant merit, who eternally shatters the hopes of the Daityas,
who fulfills the desires of all the gods, and who effects incarnations solely for the sake of the universe.
His own nature eternally concealed by his māyā, he is the wish-fulfilling gem for his devotees;
he is the constant bestower of boons, the sinless one who granted the sovereignty of kings such as Kārtavīrya.

The lord of sages, Dattātreya, whose immeasurable conduct is praised by the whole world, is eternally embraced by the Supreme Power; he bestows the bliss of yoga and is ever-intoxicated with divine rapture. 205.

He who steals away the splendor of all the enemies of Indra, the drinker from the lotus of the supreme nectar, the jewel born from the womb of Anasūyā, and the bestower of the happiness of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He who manifested wondrous power from Renuka, the sun of the Jamadagni lineage;
he who was untainted by the slaughter of his mother and other sins; he who conquered Skanda and bestowed a kingdom upon the Brahmins. (207)
The hero who brought an end to all kṣatriyas, the humbler of the pride of Kārtavīrya, the giver of the earth consisting of seven islands, the worshiper of Śiva, and the bestower of fame. ||208||
Bhīma, Paraśurāma, Śivācārya, Ekaviśvabhuk, Śiva—the treasury of all knowledge—and Bhīṣmācārya, whose presiding deity is Agni. (209)
The teacher of Dronacharya, whose bow was victorious over the entire world, who had conquered all that can be conquered;
he was the embodiment of peerless austerity, for whom celibacy was his sole sacrificial fee.
Manu was the best among the virtuous, the most venerable, the bull among men, and the sovereign;
he was the first king, the father of the earth, and the sole milker of all treasures.
Pṛthu, the sole expert in [granting] birth and other states; Gīḥ, Śrī, and Kīrti herself chosen by him;
the bestower of sustenance to the world; the most excellent universal monarch; the wielder of peerless weapons. (212)
He increases devotion to the Lord, which is attainable by sages such as Sanaka;
he is the creator, the expounder, and the promoter of the duties pertaining to the social classes and stages of life.
Rāghava, the descendant of the Sun, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, an ocean of excellent virtues,
a scion of Kakutstha, a sovereign of heroes, and a king who bears the yoke of royal dharma.

Having a basis that is eternally healthy, grasping all that is auspicious, and seeing only the pure; a jewel among men, a treasury of jewels, a presiding authority over the Dharma, and a great storehouse; the refuge of all that is most excellent, and possessing the power of the entire collection of the meanings of the scriptures. (215)
The conqueror of the world, the son of Daśaratha, the king who is the refuge of all jewels,
the father of all dharma, the seer of all dharmas, and the destroyer of all sins.
He was one whose wisdom and discernment surpassed the senses, possessed of patience and intelligence,
the most excellent among all refined men, and undisturbed by joy, sorrow, and other such emotions;
he had renounced his imperial sovereignty at his father’s command and was fearless toward the rise of calamities.

Having bestowed his sovereignty upon the cave-dwelling [Guha], wearing matted locks in emulation of Śiva, having obtained the jewel-mountain of Citrakūṭa, the Lord of the World became a forest-dweller. (218)
He who rendered all weapons infallible at will, the destroyer of the eyes of the son of the Lord of Gods (Indra),
the one who humbled Brahmā and Indra, the slayer of Tāraka, the killer of Kumbhakarṇa, and the destroyer of Virādha.
He who purifies the entirety of the Daṇḍaka forest, which had been struck by the curse of Brahmā;
he who alone wields the single arrow that slays fourteen thousand fierce rākṣasas.
He who destroyed Khara, Ari, Triśiras, and Hantā; the Janārdana who slew Dūṣaṇa; he who granted the attainment of Agni to Jaṭāyus; the King of Mantras who is the very essence of Agastya.
The great mass of Dumba’s bones was cast aside by the tip of his playful bow;
he pierced the seven palm trees and dragged down and destroyed the Dānavas of the netherworld.
Bestowing fearlessness with a mind solely intent on granting Sugrīva the kingdom,
he was the sustainer of the bodies of all the monkeys, headed by Hanumān and Rudra.
The ocean was once utterly agitated by the arrows of the Naga and Daitya Bāṇa alone;
now, the ocean has been dried up and consumed entirely by the arrows of millions of Mlecchas.
He is a unique bridge of bonds never before seen in the ocean, a treasury of glory,
one who accomplishes the impossible, and one skilled in the excellence of the root of the *ulmuka* plant.
He was the destroyer of the pride of the world, the uprooter of the clan of Paulastya (Rāvaṇa),
the slayer of Rāvaṇi, and the crusher of Prahasta, Chitti, and Kumbhakarṇa.

The cutter of Rāvaṇa’s single head, the bestower of the singular kingdom of Niḥśaṅka; the one who abolishes the distinction between heaven and non-heaven, and who stripped the Lord of the Gods of his sovereignty.
He who destroyed the nature of Rākṣasas, gods, and the principles of dharma and adharma; he who is praised by many;
he who humbled the ten-faced Rāvaṇa; and he who bestowed the kingdom upon Vibhīṣaṇa.
The sole reviver of his entire army, which had been slain by a rain of nectar; the creator of the very names of gods and brahmins; and the one worshipped by all the immortals.
He is the beloved of Satī, offered by the hosts of Brahmā, Sūrya, Indra, Rudra, and others;
he is the sovereign of all the kṣatriyas of Ayodhyā, and he is enchanting to all living beings.

He whose mercy and punishment are equal to his sovereignty; who regards the lowly and the exalted as equally dear; who perceives justice even toward his own faction and others; and who accomplishes the welfare of the humble more than that of the powerful. ||231||
Under the guise of a hunter, he performed deeds unbecoming of his station; he made all things equal by casting away his own eyes;
he attained the state of being liberated while still embodied (muktātmā); he was abandoned by his beloved Pārvatī; and he conquered the enemy of Smara (Śiva). //232//
Manifesting as Kuśala, Indradyumna, and others, he was invincible;
as the Lord of Kośala, Vīrabāhu, he abandoned his own brother for the sake of truth. ||233||
He caused the circle of the earth to rise up, shaken by the discharge of his arrows;
he made the gods, including Brahmā, who were once objects of desire, his own servants.
He brought benefit to the entire multitude of living beings, from outcastes and others up to the realm of Brahmā;
he performed many acts for the sake of the forest-dwellers of Ayodhyā, including his own donkeys, horses, and other animals.
Accompanied by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, having slain Indrajit, was content with the kingdom and the sandals, having obtained Rāmā through devotion to Viṣṇu. || 236 ||
Bharata was the slayer of ten million Gandharvas who were difficult to withstand; Śatrughna was the ender of Lavaṇa.
Śatrughna was the king of physicians, the master of Ayurveda, and the lord of medicinal herbs.
He who holds the eternal nectar in his hand, the archer, the one who crosses over, the sacrifice, the sustainer of the world;
the slayer of the enemy of the sun, the life of the gods, the lord of the south, and the beloved of the twice-born. ||238||
The sun over the land of Chinnamūrdha was set by the god who remains;
he whose form remained unharmed even after severing the head of Kadrāstra for the sake of the world. ||239||
The fire named Vājapeya and others, who is devoted to the dharma of the Vedas, the Lord of Śvetadvīpa, the propounder of Sāṃkhya, and the sovereign of all supernatural powers (siddhis). ||240||
He who dispels the darkness of delusion through the yoga of knowledge that illuminates the universe;
the perfected Kapila, son of Devahūti and grandson of Kardama. 241.
He is the master of yoga, the destroyer of meditation, the one who turned the sons of Sagara to ashes,
the bull among dharma, the lord of Surabhi, and one whose nature is purified by contemplation.
Śambhu is the sole support for the burning of Tripura and the driver of the universal chariot;
he is the ocean of nectar for his devotees who have conquered the Daityas through all their ascetic penances.
The divine Śeṣa, the sole sovereign of all serpents in the universe during the great dissolution, possesses a thousand eyes, a thousand mouths, heads, and arms. 244.
The earth, with its oceans, was joined to him by the rays from the jewels on his hoods;
he was the progenitor of Kālāgnirudra, and his weapons were the mace and the plow.
Wearing a blue garment, he was the destroyer of the defects of mind, speech, and body;
by the mere casting of his glance, he brought the ten-faced Rāvaṇa to a state of total defeat through his lack of contentment.
Bali, Saṃyamana, the terrible Rauhiṇeya, Pralamba, Muṣṭika-ghna, Dvivida-hā, Kāliṅga-dīrgha-karṣaṇa, and Bala. ||247||
The beloved of Revatī, born before Acyuta due to the exhaustion of his previous devotion, and the son of Devakī, Vasudeva, Kaśyapa, and Aditi. 248.
The descendant of Vṛṣṇi, the best of the Sātvatas, Śauri, the upholder of the Yadu clan, the Supreme Brahman in human form, Savyasācin, the giver of boons. 249.
He whose childhood was a wonder to the world through the graceful charm desired by Brahmā and others;
he who slew Pūtanā, shattered the cart, and destroyed the twin Arjuna trees. 250.
The enemy of the demon Vātāsura, the slayer of Keśin, the foe of Dhenuka, the Lord of the cows;
Dāmodara, the deity of the cowherds, the bestower of joy upon Yaśodā. ||251||
The subduer of Kālīya, beloved by all the cowherds and cowherdesses, who lifted Govardhana in sport, Govinda, the festival of Gokula. 252.
The destroyer of Ariṣṭa, the bestower of liberation upon the cowherd women maddened by desire, the one who instantly slew Kuvalayāpīḍa, and the crusher of Cāṇūra. ||253||

The enemy of Kaṃsa, who occupied himself with the administration of the kingdom for Ugrasena and others; he who made the Sudharmā hall his assembly hall, who brought the earth and its inhabitants under his control, and who was the destroyer of Jarāsaṃdha’s army.
He who restored the broken joints of Tyaktabhagna-jarā, who bestowed fame upon Bhīmasena, who kindled the fire, who gave back his deceased son, and who conquered Kāla, Antaka, and the rest. 255.
Protector of all hell-beings, conqueror of millions of all kings, lover of Rukmiṇī, subduer of Rukmin, and destroyer of Naraka. ||256||
Murāri, whose banner is Garuḍa, is the beloved of all beautiful women;
alone, he has conquered Rudra, Arka, Marut, and all other lords. ||257||
He who destroyed the pride of the Lord of Gods, who adorned the earth with wish-fulfilling trees,
who severed the arms of Bāṇa, and who conquered tens of millions of rivers and other hosts.
He who has conquered Mahādeva through his divine play, who is worshipped solely by Mahādeva, who granted victory to Arjuna in his defeat of Indra, and who is the sole upholder of the Pāṇḍavas. (259)

The severer of the head of the King of Kāśī, the sole crusher by the power of Rudra, whose eyes were [opened] by the grace of Viśveśvara, and the destroyer of the daughter of the King of Kāśī. ||260||

He is the destroyer of Śambhu’s vow, the one who consumed the leaders with the fire of Kāśī, the multiplier of millions of inhabitants of Kāśī, the teacher of the world, and the worshiper of the twice-born. ||261||

Formerly, by means of the vow of a young woman, he was brought under control; he who had granted boons to Śiva, who maintained the singular foundation of Śaṅkara, and who was a worshiper of his own Śaṅkara, [was subdued]. 262.
Lord of the Śivakanyā vow, possessing the form of Kṛṣṇa, destroyer of the enemy of Śiva; having the body of Mahālakṣmī, protector of Gaurī, and slayer of Vaidala and Vṛtra. 263.
He who caused Mucukunda to regain his own abode, who drove out Yavana from Ekacakrā, and who brought back the son of the twice-born who had been hidden away by the Lord of Yamunā. ||264||
The Lord of Dvārakā, who brought down the splendor of Indra for the sake of his devotee Śrīdāmaraṅka, and who alone granted liberation to the wicked Śiśupāla. 265.

He who makes millions of treasures available at the gateway for everyone from outcasts to the highest castes, and who grants liberation at his own will to his singular devotees headed by Akrūra and Uddhava. ||266||
He who turned the ocean into an immortal pool for the water-sports of children and women,
and who alone brought back to life Parīkṣit while he was still in the womb after being consumed by the Brahmā-missile.

He who removes the pride of Arjuna, by whom all the Kauravas beginning with Bhīṣma were swallowed up through his hidden seal-like form, and by whom the sons of the twice-born were utterly overwhelmed.
He who, by means of the divine weapons shattered according to their true purpose, removed the delusion of Arjuna;
and he who, under the pretext of the curse upon his embryo, destroyed the fear of the gods and the earth.

He who bestows freedom from old age, disease, and the states of existence; who grants all desired objects through mere remembrance; the god of love, the husband of Rati, the mind-born one, and the destroyer of Śambara. 270.

He is the conqueror of the earth, the Lord of Gaurī, the one who transcends all, the eternally desired, the flower-arrowed god, the one who conquers the universe, Smara, and the beloved of Kāmeśvarī. 271.
Lord of the Dawn, whose banner is the universe, who is all-proud, the Supreme Person;
the fourfold self, the fourfold manifestation, the ordainer of the four ages. ||272||
The soul of the four Vedas, the single universal self, the supreme among all, Vyāsa— the ancient seer who composed thousands of branches of the scriptures— [is present] by the tens of millions.
The lord of poets who composed the Mahābhārata, Bādarāyaṇa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, is the sole enlightener of all human goals. ||274||
The author of the Vedānta, the sole non-dual Brahman, the ancient one who acted with power;
the Buddha, the god who has conquered all other gods through meditation, the beloved of the world. (275)
He is victorious over the world even without weapons, the bearer of Śrī, and the deluder of the wicked;
he is the one who excluded the Daityas from the Vedas and the protector of the meaning of the Vedas and the sacred revelation.

The son of Śuddhodana, whose vision is faultless, the bestower of happiness, the lord of the assembly, who bestows compassion upon all according to their worth, is entirely empty [of inherent existence] yet grants the desires of all. (277)
The Lord of the Perfection of Wisdom, whose reality is distinct from the four alternatives; the Master of the paths of both heresy and the Vedas, who protects the heterodox scriptures. ||278||
The son of Viṣṇuyaśas, Kalkī, will be the destroyer of the Kali age;
he shall slay all wicked barbarians and act for the benefit of all refined twice-born castes.
He is the promoter of truth, the one who removes the long-standing hunger of gods and brahmins;
likewise, he is the horseman and others, the destroyer of the earth's misfortune. (280)
Immediately making the earth’s surface prosperous, he was a knower of all dharma that had been entirely lost;
he alone possessed the union of gold within iron, filling all the twice-born with pure gold.
The teacher of the single world who is beyond being cured, whose banner is the universal lotus, the lord of the principle of the Self, the supreme creator, the ordainer, and the husband of Umā. (282)
The best of husbands, the foremost of lords of subjects, Marīci, the leader of the Janakas, Kaśyapa, the king of the gods, Prahlāda, the king of the Daityas, and the Moon. (283)
The lord of the constellations, the sun’s splendor, the most excellent, Śukra, the sovereign of poets; Bhṛgu, the king of great sages, Viṣṇu, the lord of the Ādityas, Bali, and the self-ruling one.
He is the wind, the fire, the pure one, the most excellent, Śaṅkara, Rudra, the King, the Guru, the wisest of the wise, Citraratha, the foremost of the Gandharvas, and the supreme imperishable. 285.
Varṇādi is the foremost woman; Gaurī is the power (śakti) of Īśa; Agryāśī is Nārada, the king of divine sages; Arjuna is the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas; and Vāda is the king of discourse. 286.
The wind is the lord of purifiers; Varuṇa is the lord of aquatic creatures;
the Gaṅgā is the best of holy fords; gambling is the foremost of deceits; and [the Dhanvantari] is the best of medicines. (287)
Anna was the Sudarśana, the foremost of weapons; Vajra was the best of missiles;
Uccaiḥśravas was the king of horses; and Airāvata was the lord of elephants.

He is the wound-healer, the lord of the single-spoused goddesses, the holy fig tree, the sovereign of all trees; he is the supreme knowledge of the science of the self, the sacred syllable Om, and the best among the meters of the Vedas. ||289||
The lord of the Meru mountain, the path, the foremost month, the best of times; the primordial self of the day, the eternally perfected Kapila, the king of the Sāma Veda. (290)

He is Tārkṣya, the lord of birds; the foremost of seasons; the virtuous one; the wish-fulfilling tree (Kalpapādapa); the best among givers; the cow of plenty (Kāmadhenu); the foremost destroyer of suffering; and the most excellent friend. ||291||
He is the Cintāmaṇi jewel, the most excellent teacher, the mother who is most beneficial, and the father; he is the lion among lions, the serpent-king Vāsuki, and the best of men, the king. (292)
"O Lord of Castes, O Brāhmaṇa, O foremost in compassion—salutations, salutations!
This is the thousand names of Viṣṇu, the son of Vasudeva. (293)
It pacifies all transgressions, supremely increases devotion, and is the singular means for attaining all heavens, beginning with the imperishable world of Brahmā. ||294||
The sole staircase to the world of Viṣṇu, the destroyer of all suffering, the immediate bestower of all happiness, and the giver of supreme liberation. ||295||
It completely purifies the impurities of the mind, such as desire and anger; it bestows peace and sanctifies even those among men who are great sinners. (296)
It swiftly bestows the fruit of all desired objects upon all living beings;
it pacifies all obstacles and destroys all misfortunes. ||297||
It pacifies terrible suffering, destroys intense poverty, removes the three debts, and is a secret that brings wealth, grain, and fame. (298)
It bestows all sovereignty, grants all perfections, and confers all righteousness;
it yields the fruit of ten million pilgrimages, sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and vows. ||299||
It pacifies the dullness of the world, brings forth all branches of knowledge, bestows sovereignty upon those who have lost their kingdom, and removes every disease from the sick. (300)
It bestows sons upon the barren and grants life to those whose vitality is exhausted;
it destroys the afflictions caused by spirits, planetary influences, poisons, and the seizing of planets. ||301||
This is auspicious, meritorious, and life-prolonging; by hearing it, reading it, or reciting it even once, all the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and millions of mantras are mastered. (302)
O beloved, having heard and likewise studied the Purāṇas, the Śāstras, and the Smṛtis,
and having recited the single-syllable mantra, one recites even a single verse or a quarter-verse.
Everything desired is constantly accomplished without delay; how much more so everything else?
There is nothing like this for providing immediate conviction in all ritual actions. (304)
O auspicious lady, this must be guarded by you and recited solely for the sake of attaining your own goal;
it must not be given to one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, nor to one whose soul is afflicted by doubt.
It should be given with the desire for their welfare to a son, a disciple, or a friend who is devoid of devotion and faith, and who views Viṣṇu as being no different from others. ||306||
Without my grace, those of small intellect will not grasp this;
yet in the Kali age, Nārada shall lead the entire collection of ritual manuals to yield immediate results.
By means of this, the suffering of those unfortunate people in the world will perish; this shall come to pass among two or three Vaiṣṇavas in Āryāvarta. (308)
There is no abode higher than Viṣṇu; there is no austerity higher than Viṣṇu;
there is no dharma higher than Viṣṇu; indeed, there is no mantra that is not Vaiṣṇava.
There is no truth higher than Viṣṇu; there is no sacrifice higher than Viṣṇu;
there is no meditation higher than Viṣṇu; there is no goal higher than Viṣṇu. ||310||
What need has he for many mantras or for scriptures of great extent, or even for thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices, if his devotion is fixed upon Janārdana? (311)
Viṣṇu is composed of all sacred fords; the Lord is composed of all scriptures;
Viṣṇu is composed of all sacrifices—I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
All this that has been declared by me is the entire essence and the ultimate wealth of everything from Brahmā down. 312.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of the World, I am blessed, I am favored, and my purpose is fulfilled, since I have heard this hymn of praise, which is your secret and so very difficult to obtain. (313)
Alas! What great misery! While Hari, the remover of all suffering and the Lord of Gods, exists, the deluded suffer in the cycle of worldly existence. (314)
It is for the sake of this Protector that even Maheśa is seen by people as a naked ascetic with matted hair, his limbs smeared with ashes. (315)
There is no god superior to the enemy of Madhu, who is beloved by Lakṣmī and Kola, and whose true nature is indeed constantly contemplated by you, the Lord of Yoga. (316)
What higher state than that of Śrī Puruṣottama could there be?
Yet fools, who pride themselves on their knowledge, worship Him without truly knowing Him. (317)
I have been robbed by you, O Lord, since for so long this Master has not revealed to me your divine powers, beginning with yourself. (318)
Aha! Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, the highest among the best of all gods, the teacher of Brahmā and others, is viewed as merely ordinary by the deluded. (319)
They honor those who devote themselves to the greatness of the Great Ones;
endowed with forgiveness, they overlook even their enemies, disregarding their futile sins. (320)
In my youth as well, when my own father saw his subjects hungry, I was unable to nourish them out of distress; however, by propitiating Śrī, they were indeed sustained. (321)

And because of her, you and others like you, along with Śakra and the rest, together with your well-wishers, friends, and kinsmen, enjoy yourselves among the subjects who are gathered under her care. (322)
Without her, where is divinity, where is sovereignty, and where is possession?
All remain alive, yet they are established in nothing but torment.
By that very truth, Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and even Mokṣa are far away;
for those who are hungry and in distress, how can there be Yoga and Samādhi? (324)
He is the sole essence of saṃsāra, the unique leader of all the world;
even Śaṅkara, having abandoned her, remains under the sway of that one whose lotus-like fortune is ever-present.
Of that Great Soul, who was complete with lack of arrogance, purity, beauty, and the perfection of uprightness, and possessed of a vigor that surpassed all others. ||326||
Who can equal that God of gods, Viṣṇu, without whose partial incarnation everything would dissolve? (327)
Nevertheless, those who are deluded say that this world exists for the sake of defects;
yet for it there is neither birth nor death, nor is there anything unattainable, for its purpose is solely its own self-interest.
O Lord, Sovereign of All, it may be that because my mind is attached to sensual desires, or due to negligence arising from being absorbed in You, I am unable to recite [the mantra]. ||329||
O Lord whose banner bears the bull, please tell me that single name of Viṣṇu by which, when recited every day, one may obtain the same fruit as this thousand names. (330)
Mahādeva said:
"O Rāma, O Rāma, O Rāma! I delight in Rāma, the one who is most enchanting.
O lady of beautiful countenance, the name of Rāma is equal to the merit of a thousand names."
Thus ends the "Thousand Names of Viṣṇu" (Viṣṇu-sahasranāma) within the Umāpati-Nārada Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The seventy-first chapter. ||71||
(72) The seventy-second chapter.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Daughter of the Mountain, if Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or even Śūdras recite this daily without distinction, [they shall attain their goal]. (1)
Endowed with wealth and grain, they go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu—
whether it be a whole verse, or half a verse, or even a quarter, or even half a quarter.
O Goddess, by reciting this Thousand Names of Viṣṇu accompanied by the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one attains liberation until the dissolution of all beings.
Those best of men who recite this go to the imperishable state;
whether one recites it once, twice, or thrice a day.
His wealth and lifespan shall increase as much as the fourteen Indras;
likewise, he shall obtain sons, grandsons, and abundant fortune and prosperity. ||5||
O fair-faced one, what is the use of speaking further at length?
The Thousand Names of Viṣṇu repeatedly bestow supreme liberation.
Whichever person performs the worship of Him first,
when Viṣṇu has been fully worshipped by them, their own worship is considered equivalent to that performed for an entire year.
One should not be distracted, especially while reciting;
for if distraction occurs during the recitation, both one's lifespan and wealth will perish.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth throughout all of Jambūdvīpa, all those sacred fords are present right there in the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu. 9.
Right there are the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Veṇī; the Godāvarī and the Sarasvatī are also there.
All sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell where that Thousand Names reside. (10)
This is the supreme purifier, always dear to devotees;
it should indeed be meditated upon with a mind characterized by the spirit of service and the spirit of devotion. 11.
But those wise ones who recite the supreme work known as the Thousand Names, being liberated from all sins, go into the presence of Hari. 12.
Those who recite and chant this at the time of dawn—their lifespan, strength, and prosperity increase day by day. (13)
In the Kali age, when the occasion for a night vigil arises, a devotee of the Lord attains liberation through recitation for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
If one recites even a single name for the sake of Tulasī,
that worship should be known as yielding a fruit greater than that of ten million sacrifices.
O Pārvatī, those twice-born ones who recite [this] while traveling on the road—indeed, no faults arising from the road shall befall them. 16.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the majesty of Keśava;
those best of men who hear it are meritorious and embodiments of merit. (17)

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Greatness of the Thousand Names" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada.
The seventy-second chapter. ||72||
(73) The seventy-third chapter. Mahādeva said:
Oṃ. For this Rāmarakṣā Stotra, the great sage Viśvāmitra is the seer (ṛṣi);
Śrī Rāma is the deity (devatā).
The meter is Anuṣṭubh.
The application [of this mantra] is for the purpose of recitation for the propitiation of Viṣṇu. ||1||
Having meditated upon the imperishable Viṣṇu, Śrī Rāma, who resembles the flax flower, is clad in yellow garments, is free from decay, and possesses eyes as large as lotuses. ||2||
May Rāma protect my heart, and Śrīkaṇṭha my throat; may the protector from obstacles protect my navel, and the guardian of the universe my waist. ||3||
May the son of Daśaratha protect my hands; may he who assumes the universal form protect my feet;
and may the unsurpassed Lord of Sītā protect my two eyes. 4.
May the Soul of the Universe protect my crest; may the Granter of Desires protect my ears;
and may the Protector of the Gods, who is as difficult to approach as ten million Yamas, protect both my sides.
May the Leader of the Universe always protect my body;
may He who sets forth the instruction for the world protect my tongue and destroy my sins. (6)
May Rāghava protect me from falling; may Keśava protect those locks of hair;
may Vijaya grant me thighs; and may the Creator of the Universe protect my name.
Whoever should recite this protection accompanied by the power of Rāma shall become long-lived, happy, and wise, and shall obtain divine prosperity. (8)
The power of Viṣṇu provides protection from all beings; she indeed grants constant protection to whoever remembers [the names] "Rāma," "Rāmabhadra," and "Rāmacandra. (9)
Being liberated from sin, a person attains eternal liberation;
this was proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha to his guru, who was the very form of Viṣṇu. 10.
Then it was obtained by me from a brāhmaṇa, and I spoke it to Nārada;
by Nārada, it was brought here to the world of mortals among virtuous people. (11)
Whether they have slept or are traveling on the road, those best of men who recite this are partakers of merit. 12.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Hymn of Praise to Rāmakṣa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada.
The seventy-fourth chapter. Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme majesty of Dharma.
Having heard which, one is never again born on this earth at any time. ||1||
From dharma one obtains these three: wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
therefore, the wise man who seeks dharma is considered truly enlightened. ||2||
By means of austerity, charity, vows, and observances—through sattvic austerity, heaven is attained; such is the word.
Having come here, one who is free from anger and greed shall obtain a kingdom;
in another birth, there shall be liberation, and he shall attain the supreme state of Viṣṇu. ||4||

Through austerity, one is born here as a Rājasa or even a Rājasa-rājasa; having practiced austerity with a tāmasa disposition, one becomes a performer of cruel deeds, merciless, and full of malice. ||5||

That austerity which is said to belong to the *rākṣasas* and those of a *tāmasa* nature grants enjoyment; however, that austerity which is performed with a *sāttvika* disposition certainly becomes true austerity.

Even for those who dwell in the forest, restrained by passion and darkness, subsisting on air alone in a most solitary place, or even for ascetics who desire wealth and other such things, faults continue to arise despite being in the forest. (7)
Even at home, the restraint of the five senses and the performance of blameless deeds constitute austerity;
for one whose passion has ceased, the forest of austerity is his home. Therefore, the householder’s stage of life is declared to be one's own duty.

O daughter of the mountain, this most excellent and auspicious stage of life, the dharma of the householder, is extremely difficult for those who have not conquered their senses to traverse; yet it is the most eminent among the wise and has been proclaimed by Brahmā and the other gods.
Having performed austerities in the forest, an ascetic afflicted by hunger returns home;
with devotion, the giver of food provides him with that food, and he partakes in a portion of the merit of that person's penance.

A man who properly maintains the householder stage (gṛhāśrama), the foremost among the stages of life here, enjoys human pleasures even in this world and then proceeds to his own abode; there is no doubt about this. O Goddess, how indeed can sin accrue to those men who always maintain their home? (11)
The householder's stage of life is most meritorious; a home is like all sacred pilgrimage sites combined.
In this meritorious stage of the householder, gifts should especially be given.
Where there is worship of the gods, the feeding of guests, and shelter for travelers, that place is considered most blessed. (13)
Those men who, taking refuge in that house, worship the twice-born, shall never suffer any decline in their lifespan, prosperity, or sons. 14.
Listen, O Sundarī, I shall describe the gift that purifies great sins, which brings about all prosperity and bestows fruits both in this world and the next. (15)
When an auspicious time has arrived, having worshipped one's own deity, and having performed the daily and occasional rites, one should give gifts according to one's capacity. ||16||
If one takes the property of another and gives it specifically to Brahmins and deities,
having first seen hell, he subsequently attains the supreme state.
Just as Śatānīka, along with his son, was delivered by means of giving,
so too others, having given according to the Dharma to the twice-born, went to heaven.
O Goddess, listen as I shall explain in brief the gift of wealth, for which the merit of those who have given at the seats of Dharma has been proclaimed. (19)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift that purifies the body as this does;
by means of it, a man becomes free from sin—of this there is no doubt. (20)
Having enjoyed these pleasures, he then goes to the eternal Viṣṇu;
this was previously told by Brahmā to the high-souled Bhārgava.
O King, he was joined with evil, unrighteous, and of the nature of Libra and Taurus; he delighted in sinful deeds and was engaged in the activities that bind one to worldly existence. ||22||
Those who delight in eating forbidden food, those who kill an embryo, those who violate the bed of their guru, and those who speak falsehoods— these too are born into various wombs.

Having performed sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing and having caused the blameless to perform such sacrifices, they were constantly filled with anger and devoted to the harassment of the virtuous. (24)
Those who have violated trust and those who revile the Dharma—endowed with these sins and knowing their own life-span to be exhausted—[depart]. (25)
Having understood this, O Goddess, gifts should especially be given by them;
for there are many renowned Vaiṣṇavas on earth who are performers of dharma. 26.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Dharma of Giving," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||74||
The seventy-fifth chapter. Mahādeva said:
I shall describe the greatness of Gaṇḍikā according to its various aspects.
Just as the Ganges is, so too was that river described by the Sage in the scripture. ||1||
In this regard, the Śālagrāma stone arises in many ways;
its majesty has likewise been described by the best of sages. ||2||
O Pārvatī, by the mere sight of whom those of meritorious form—whether born from eggs, from sprouts, from moisture, or from a womb—become so [purified]. 3.
To the north, however, flows the great river Saṃbhūtāgaṇḍikā;
by remembering her again and again, one surely casts away sin. (4)
Where the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of prosperity, eternally resides,
those who bear the conch and the discus dwell in his vicinity.
Having attained death there, the sages and especially the gods remain in that place, possessing divine forms and four arms.
The Rudras, Nāgas, and Yakṣas—of this there is no need for deliberation.
Near her, indeed, stands this one who has assumed the form of Viṣṇu.
On this spot resides a multiform image that bestows supreme liberation;
indeed, the twenty-four classes of beings are present there.
One form is that of Matsya (the Fish), which bestows supreme liberation; another, known as Kṛṣṇa, is proclaimed by the wise to be present at the place named Viṣṇu-sthala.
Likewise, the one named Kalkinī is declared to be meritorious, as is Kapilā;
moreover, others are seen in various forms and in many ways. (10)
All her various forms stand in manifold ways;
she is the great Gaṅgā, the bestower of merit, dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation. 11.
On that very ground where Hṛṣīkeśa dwells even today, endowed with self-restraint, I too shall dwell there; of this there is no doubt. (12)
By the mere touch of her, one is liberated from all sins, especially the killing of a fetus, the killing of a child, and the killing of a cow. (13)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of other castes—all these indeed are liberated by the mere sight of Gaṇḍikāmbu. 14.
This Veṇī is indeed especially meritorious for both the virtuous and the sinful; even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated here—what need is there to mention others? (15)
O Pārvatī, I go there at all times, at every moment;
indeed, this king of holy places has been proclaimed by Brahmā. (16)
Bathing and giving gifts there have been ordained by the sages during that auspicious time in the month of Āṣāḍha; therefore, O beautiful one, I shall go there. (17)
And according to the ritual for one month, I perform my bath there; I recite the clear Tāraka mantra there without ceasing. (18)
Therefore, I am indeed born as a Vaiṣṇava, since I have come to this field of Viṣṇu;
that sacred field created by Viṣṇu is most excellent. (19)
O Goddess, this is remembered as the supreme purifier that grants the goal of the Vaiṣṇavas;
in this world, human birth is always difficult to obtain. (20)
The Gaṇḍikā-tīrtha is difficult to attain, and the sacred field of Viṣṇu is likewise difficult to reach;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, one must go there during the month of Āṣāḍha.
Having gone there, the wearing of the conch, the discus, and so forth should be performed without distinction by the best of the twice-born; it is remembered as the supreme purifier. (22)
Indeed, this conch-shell mark on the right side, marked with a wheel, is declared to be the bestower of liberation for the twice-born; it should be worn with great effort. (23)
Especially by the Brahmins, the conch, the discus, and other [emblems] are to be worn; O Great Goddess, when these are worn, those men are indeed Vaiṣṇavas. (24)
A sacred ford is equal to the Nagaṇḍikā, and the Navarātra vow is equal to the Dvādaśī;
O lady of beautiful countenance, there is no god other than Keśava—this is true again and again.
Those best of men who hear the greatness of Gaṇḍikā, having enjoyed happiness in this world, indeed go to the realm of Viṣṇu. (26)

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gaṇḍikātīrtha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umāpati and Nārada. ||75||
The seventy-sixth chapter. Mahādeva said: Listen, O beautiful one; I shall now speak of the hymn that brings about prosperity.
Having heard which, even a sinner who has killed a Brahmin is liberated; of this there is no doubt. ||1||
He spoke thus to Nārada regarding the elements; that I shall now tell you.
Then the god Svayambhū, of immeasurable splendor, said to him: (2)
Grasping his beautiful arm, he should remind him of the funeral rites:
"The Blessed One Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Lord Hari, whose weapon is the discus. (3)
The wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Ancient Supreme Person, the Unconquered, the bearer of the sword, the Victorious, Kṛṣṇa, and the Eternal One. ||4||
You are the one-horned boar, the essence of the past, the future, and the present; you are the imperishable Brahman, the truth, and the primordial cause of all that moves and is immobile, O Raghava.
You are the Dharma that protects the worlds, you are Viṣvaksena with four arms;
you are the commander of the army, you are the protector, you are Vaikuṇṭha, and you are the Lord of the universe.
You are the source and the imperishable; you are Upendra and Madhusūdana;
you are Pṛśnigarbha and Dhṛtārcis; you are Padmanābha and the end-maker of the battle.
The great seers, including Indra, declare you to be the refuge and the one worthy of seeking shelter;
the great seers call you the soul of the Vedas, the supreme essence of the Ṛg and Sāman, and the hundred-tongued one.
You are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*, you are the syllable *oṃ*, and you are the supreme austerity.
You were formerly Śatadhanvāvasu among the Vasus, and you are Prajāpati.
He is the self-effulgent Lord, the original creator of even the three worlds;
he is the eighth among the Rudras and the fifth among the Sādhyas.
The two Aśvins are your ears, and the Sun and Moon are your eyes;
you are seen at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end—you are the supreme austerity.
They did not know its origin or its end, asking, "Who are you?
You are seen in all the worlds, among the cows and among the Brahmins.
In all directions, in the sky, on the mountains, and in the caves,
he is the glorious one with a thousand eyes, a hundred heads, and a thousand feet.
You support all beings, as well as the earth with its mountains;
within the waters of the earth, you are the great serpent of all living creatures.
Supporting the three worlds, including the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas, he remains;
O Rāma, I am your heart, and the goddess Sarasvatī is your tongue.
The gods created hairs upon their limbs by means of their own creative power;
for them, the closing of the eyes was remembered as night, and the opening of the eyes likewise as day.
The body would be a mere conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*) without you; this entire world and the stability of the earth's surface likewise exist because of you. (17)
Agni is your wrath, while Śeṣa is your grace; you are glorious and possess the auspicious mark.
By means of your three ancient strides, the three worlds were traversed by you.
By you Indra was made king, and the great asura Bali was bound;
having withdrawn the worlds, you are Time who has established yourself alone. (19)
"You shall turn this world into a single, terrible ocean, both in what is visible and what is invisible; for you have assumed another supreme and divine lion-form. (20)
Hiraṇyakaśipu, the terror of all beings, has been slain;
you, having become horse-faced, have taken refuge in the depths of Pātāla.
The supreme oblation has been withdrawn; this secret is [revealed] again and again.
That which is heard as the supreme light, that which is heard as the supreme beyond. ||22||
That which is beyond the supreme, which is called the "beyond-the-supreme-soul" (parātpara),
that supreme mantra, that supreme splendor— you alone are declared to be that.
They say that you are the sacrificial offering to the gods and the ancestors, the means of purification, and the attainment of both heaven and liberation;
you are the existence, the origin, and the destruction of all things, yet you are beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
You alone are proclaimed by the Vedas as the sacrifice, the sacrificer, the hotṛ priest, and the adhvaryu priest, as well as the enjoyer of the fruits of the sacrifice. (25)
Sītā is Lakṣmī and you are Viṣṇu, the god Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Creatures;
for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa, you have entered a human body.
O best among the upholders of dharma, you have performed this fourfold deed: Rāvaṇa has been slain, and the gods have been made joyful by Rāma.
The divine power of the gods is not in vain; therefore, your valor is not in vain.
O Rāma, your vision is not in vain, and your praise is not in vain.
Those men on earth who are devoted to you, O God, the ancient Puruṣottama, shall become successful in their devotion. (29)
This meritorious hymn of the sages is an ancient history;
those men who shall recite it will never suffer defeat.
How indeed could these best of men meet with defeat here, for they are devoted to the Supreme Person? Indeed, in this world, there is no defeat for those who are dear to the Four-Armed One.
In this world, there exists the distinguished Tridaśa, the bestower of boons. ||31||
Even one who has committed great sins, if he should constantly recite this preeminent hymn among all hymns to the high-souled Rāghava at the three times of day, [is purified].
At the time of twilight, and especially at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, this should be recited with effort and a mind full of devotion by the best of the twice-born. (33)
This is indeed the supreme secret; it must never be disclosed to anyone at any time.
By reciting this, a follower of the Sāttvata tradition attains liberation; this shall certainly come to pass.
First, the Brahmins, the best of the twice-born, should perform the worship with the rice-balls;
this hymn should be recited so that one may obtain inexhaustible merit from the śrāddha. (35)
This supreme purifier grants liberation to people; having written it down, one should wear it at home with great concentration. (36)
The lifespan, fortune, and strength of that wise person who, having written it down, gives it to a Brāhmaṇa at any time, increase day by day. (37)
Those liberated ones who were born before go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
and whatever fruit there is in the recitation of the four Vedas, [that too they obtain]. (38)

A man who recites this hymn while performing japa attains the same merit as one who, having been invested with the conch, discus, and other marks by Brahmins devoted to the Vedas, performs the japa. (39)
O Mahādevī, at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, that [offering] will certainly become inexhaustible.
[One should wear] a rosary of lotus seeds around the neck and bear the marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth. (40)
Then one should perform the śrāddha while reciting and muttering this hymn;
performed according to the rules and with a spirit of devotion, it becomes complete, and not otherwise. (41)
Therefore, a person endowed with devotion should recite this with great effort;
by reciting it, that man obtains everything and prospers in happiness. 42.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Hymn for Prosperity and Post-Mortem Rites," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||76||
(87) The Eighty-Seventh Chapter—
Maheśvara said:
In the month of Caitra, Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, should be worshipped with great effort using either a *caṃpaka* flower or a *jātī* flower. (1)
One should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds and the Sovereign of all lords, with *damanaka* flowers, *maruka* flowers, or even with *bilva* flowers. (2)
O Goddess of the gods, in the month of Caitra, men, being well-composed, worship Viṣṇu with divine red lotuses and other offerings.
O God, this great Lord is always to be worshipped in the month of Vaiśākha;
one should take a ketaki leaf when the sun is situated in Taurus.
Hari, being worshipped with devotion by him, remains pleased for a hundred manvantaras;
moreover, one should worship Him with various flowers when the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived.
When the Lord of the gods is worshipped, all the gods are well-worshipped, even after one has committed thousands of sins and hundreds of great evils. (6)
O Goddess, they shall go to where Viṣṇu dwells together with Śrī;
when the month of Āṣāḍha has arrived, one should perform worship especially.
Those who perform the worship of Viṣṇu with karavīra flowers, red blossoms, or lotuses, and who offer perfumes, are to be known as partakers of merit.
Those who shall worship Govinda with kadamba flowers resembling gold— Viṣṇu— shall have no fear arising from the sun.
Dark as a rain cloud at the onset of the monsoon and honored with kadamba flowers,
he grants all desired objects for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Just as Mādhava becomes delighted upon reaching his lotus-abode, so does the Creator of the World become delighted upon obtaining the kadamba flower. (11)
O Goddess of the Asuras, Viṣṇu, when worshipped at all times with *tulasī*, *kṛṣṇatulasī*, or *vaṃjulī* leaves, constantly removes all suffering. (12)
When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, people worship Janārdana,
taking with them flax flowers as well as blades of dūrvā grass.
He should be worshipped with special effort using various kinds of flowers;
he grants vast desires until the dissolution of all beings.
When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, O Mountain-Dweller, listen:
[one should worship] with white lotuses, white flowers, and likewise with red sindūra.
By offering white water-lilies (*kahlāra*), one obtains the fulfillment of all desires, O Great Goddess.
In the auspicious month of Āśvina, the worship of Viṣṇu must be performed. (16)
He should always be worshipped with effort and preceded by devotion by people using fresh jasmine, jātī flowers, and various other auspicious blossoms. (17)
Those people who, having brought lotuses themselves, worship Janārdana, obtain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa on this earth. ||18||
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, Maheśvara is to be worshipped;
as many seasonal flowers as there are should be offered to Mādhava as well.
One should perform external worship with sesame seeds and sesame flowers;
when the Lord of Gods is thus worshipped, one enjoys the fruit of that [offering]. (20)
