Those gods among men who, in the month of Kārttika, shall worship Vāsudeva with Bakula flowers and ripe Punnāga fruits, [they shall attain the divine state]. 21.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Lord should always be worshipped with great effort using various flowers, along with food offerings, incense, and likewise with the waving of lights.
One should worship especially with divine flowers during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; O Great Goddess, worship in the month of Pauṣa is remembered as bestowing auspiciousness. (23)
In the month of Māgha, one should worship with various *tulasī* leaves, as well as with musk-water and various flowers. (24)
When the God of gods is worshipped with camphor, various offerings, and sweetmeats, one certainly obtains their desired object. (25)
When the month of Phālguna has arrived, one should perform the worship of Mādhava; having performed the proximate ritual service, one should take up flowers of every kind.
Then, O Lord of Gods, one should worship with all [materials], whether new or old;
for when the Lord of the World is worshipped, the imperishable state of Vaikuṇṭha is attained.
A person always attains this through the grace of Śrī Viṣṇu. ||27||

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Monthly Menstrual Cycle," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||87||
Now begins the eighty-eighth chapter: The Greatness of Kārttika (88).
Sūta said:
Hereafter, the majesty of the month of Kārttika is set forth.
Once, a sage came to Dvārakā with the desire to behold Kṛṣṇa.
And having taken divine flowers produced from the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpa-vṛkṣa). ||1||
Kṛṣṇa honored Nārada with a welcome, saying, "Here is the water of respect (arghya), here is the water for washing the feet (pādya)," as he offered him a seat. ||2||
Nārada presented those flowers to Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa distributed them among his sixteen thousand wives. ||3||
But having forgotten Satyabhāmā, the lord gave them all to the others;
Satyabhāmā, thereupon enraged, entered the chamber of wrath. ||4||
Then, having understood the situation, Kṛṣṇa went there with a concentrated mind;
he honored Satyabhāmā and, calling Garuḍa to mind, [proceeded].
As soon as he was remembered, Garuḍa then stood before him;
having swiftly mounted that bird, the Lord spoke thus to his beloved: (6)
O Satya, do not give way to anger on my account; for by opposing the king of the gods together with the deities, you would cause [the world] to sprout thorns. (7)
"O highly fortunate one, forgive my offense against the wish-fulfilling tree.
Having thus made this vow with Satyabhāmā, Kṛṣṇa—
He went quickly to the world of the gods, where that god, the slayer of Vṛtra, was;
having been requested for the sake of the wish-fulfilling tree, the Lord gave his reply. (9)
"O Lord, this celestial tree is not fit to be obtained by you from the earth.
Then the mighty-armed one, becoming enraged, uprooted the tree from its very foundation.
Then the exceedingly powerful one swiftly mounted his vehicle;
at that moment, the heroic wielder of the thunderbolt, with speed, raised his vajra.
He struck Garuḍa, saying, "Leave the wish-fulfilling tree!
Then, due to the weight of the thunderbolt, the leaf-chariot fell from its leaf.
He released one [arrow] and departed with haste;
by that stroke of the thunderbolt, three birds fell to the earth. ||13||
The peacock, the mongoose, and the blue jay went to Dvārāvatī;
having arrived, he placed them in the house of Satyabhāmā.
At that very moment, Nārada arrived and was greatly honored by Satyā. 14.
Satyabhāmā said:
"How may such a wish-fulfilling tree and such a lord as my husband be obtained in birth after birth? Pray, tell me that. (15)
Thus questioned, Nārada, the best of sages, then said:
"O Satyabhāmā, this [merit] is obtained through the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa. (16)
Then Satyabhāmā, having weighed Kṛṣṇa together with the wish-fulfilling tree according to the prescribed rite, gave him to Nārada;
and having drawn away all his belongings, Nārada departed for the third heaven. ||17||
Sūta said:
After the best of celestial sages had taken leave of the Lord of Śrī and departed, Satyā, her face blossoming with joy, then spoke to Vāsudeva. 18.
Satyabhāmā said:
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and my life is fruitful;
and blessed are those two parents of mine, who were the source of this jewel. (19)
Surely those two who begot me, the most fortunate woman in the three worlds, must have been such that I am now the beloved of sixteen thousand women, even as I am yours. (20)
Since I have properly entrusted this primordial Being, endowed with the wish-fulfilling tree, to Nārada according to the prescribed rite. (21)
Even the creatures dwelling upon the earth know of his fame;
yet here in my home stands this very wish-fulfilling tree at present. (22)
I am the most beloved of the Lord of Fortune, the sovereign of the three worlds;
therefore, O Madhusūdana, I wish to ask you something.
If you are one who does what is pleasing to me, tell me about this in detail;
having heard it, I shall indeed perform that for myself once again.
"O Lord, may I never be separated from you as long as this kalpa lasts.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his beloved, the elder brother of Gadā (Balarāma) smiled.
Having made Satyākara his guide, he went to the foot of the Kalpa tree, accompanied by his beloved, having dismissed his attendants and the world of people with playful grace.
Smiling and addressing Satyabhāmā, the Lord of the worlds,
like an elephant, spoke with his hair standing on end in joy, for the sake of her pleasure and satisfaction.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O beloved, there is no other woman dearer to me than you;
among my sixteen thousand wives, you are indeed as dear to me as my own life."
For your sake, the King of the Gods has come into conflict with the deities;
O Kāntā, hear what you have requested, which shall be a great thing. (29)

"Furthermore, O beloved, how could I not answer a question posed by you, even if it were something that ought not to be given, something that should not be done, or something that should not be spoken? Ask everything; I shall tell you whatever dwells within your mind. (30)
Satyovāca said: "Was it a gift, a vow, or perhaps asceticism that was performed by me in a previous life, by which I have indeed become like you, O immortal one, though born of a mortal? (31)
Constantly taking half of your body, traveling upon Garuḍa,
I have gone with you to the abodes of the gods, such as Indra.
Therefore, I wish to ask you: what inauspicious deed did I commit?
In another birth, what was my character and conduct, and whose daughter was I? (33)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen with an attentive mind; I shall tell you everything about the extent of her merit and the vow she performed in her previous birth.
In that city of Māyāpurī during the Kṛta Yuga, there lived an excellent brahmin named Devaśarman, a descendant of Atri, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Hospitable to guests, devoted to the service of the sacred fires, and dedicated to the solar vow, he constantly worshipped the Sun and was like a second Sun in person. (36)
That man, who was advanced in years and childless, had a daughter named Guṇavatī;
he gave her to his own disciple, named Candra.
The self-controlled son regarded him as a father, and the father regarded him as a son;
once, the two of them went to the forest seeking kusha grass and fuel for the sacrificial fire.
They roamed here and there through the forests at the foot of the Himalaya mountains;
then those two beheld that terrible illusion of the Rākṣasa.
With all their limbs overwhelmed by fear and unable to flee, they were slain by that Rākṣasa, whose form was like that of Death himself. ||40||
But by the power of that sacred field and again through their virtuous character, the two were led to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha by my attendants who are ever near me. 41.
As long as they lived, whatever worship of the Sun and other rites were performed by those two, by that very action I indeed became truly well-pleased with them. (42)
The Śaivas, Sauras, Gāṇeśas, Vaiṣṇavas, and worshippers of Śakti—here in this world, they all reach me alone, just as the waters of the rains reach the ocean. (43)
"I alone am born fivefold, as it were, playing with various names, just as a certain Devadatta is called by the names of his sons and other relatives. (44)
Then those two, dwelling in my abode, traveling in celestial chariots, both possessing the brilliance of the sun,
having forms equal to mine, remained in my presence.
The celestial nymphs enjoy the pleasures of sandalwood. ||45||
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā," in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||88||
(89) The Eighty-Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then Guṇavatī, having heard that both of those Rākṣasas were here, lamented piteously, afflicted by the grief caused by her father and her husband. ||1||
Guṇavatī said: "Alas, my lord! Having been abandoned, where are you going without me?
I am but a young girl; what shall I do now, left without you and without a protector? (2)
Who indeed will now, out of affection, protect me—who am unskilled in anything and distressed—while I reside in the home, provided with food, clothing, and other necessities? (3)
Wretched in fortune, deprived of happiness, with my lord slain and my life ruined—alas, I am a fool who, though having you as her protector, now seeks refuge in whom? (4)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having lamented thus at great length, like a female osprey, she who was deeply distressed fell to the ground, distraught, like a plantain tree struck by the wind. (5)
Having finally regained her breath after lamenting piteously at length upon the ground, she,
afflicted by grief, remained submerged in an ocean of sorrow.

Having sold all his possessions along with the household utensils, that performer of auspicious deeds performed for the two of them, according to his ability, the funeral rites pertaining to the next world. ||7||
From that time forward, she dwelt in that very city for the remainder of her life—tranquil, devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, truthful, pure, and having conquered her senses. (8)
She perfectly observed two vows from birth until death:
the vow of Ekādaśī and the proper observance of the month of Kārttika. ||9||
"O beloved, this substance for the vow is exceedingly dear to me;
it perfectly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, O son, and brings about prosperity. (10)
Those who daily bathe in the morning during the month of Kārttika, when the sun is situated in Libra— even those who are great sinners— are liberated.
Those men who perform the sweeping of Viṣṇu’s temple, the offering of svastikas and other auspicious signs, and the worship of Viṣṇu, are indeed liberated while living. 12.
Those men who perform ritual bathing, keeping vigil, lighting lamps, and attending upon the grove of Tulasī during the month of Kārttika are the very embodiments of Viṣṇu. (13)
Those who perform this even for three days in the month of Kārttika are worthy of worship even by the gods; what need is there to mention those who have practiced it from birth? (14)
Thus, endowed with virtues, she is properly led every year into the eternal retinue of Viṣṇu, a devotee whose mind is entirely intent upon Him. (15)
Once, O beloved, that slender-limbed woman, emaciated by old age and afflicted by fever, somehow went slowly to the Gaṅgā to bathe. (16)
As long as she remained within the water, trembling and tormented by the cold,
so long did she lament in distress until she saw a celestial mansion arrive from the sky.
[He was seen] nearby in the sky, bearing conch-shells, discs, maces, and lotuses in their hands,
perfectly assuming the form of Viṣṇu, and marked with the banner of Vainateya.
Placing her upon that celestial chariot attended by throngs of apsarases,
the attendants led her, being fanned with yak-tail whisks, to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then she, seated in that celestial chariot resembling a blazing crest of fire,
arrived in my presence by virtue of the merit of her Kārttika vow.
Then, according to the prayers of the gods beginning with Brahmā,
all those attendants who had come to the earth also departed along with me.
For all these Yādavas, O beautiful lady, are indeed my own attendants; your father Devaśarman was Satrājit, who has been cast down from his sovereignty.
O auspicious one, he who was Candraśarmā is this Akrūra, and she who was Guṇavatī is you;
by the merit of the Kārttika vow, you have increased my great affection.
"O auspicious one, previously you planted a grove of *tulasī* at my door; therefore, this desire-yielding tree (*kalpa-vṛkṣa*) has arisen from your courtyard. (24)
Because the festival of lights was performed by you in the past during the month of Kārttika, this Lakṣmī has become firmly established within the abode of your body. ||25||
And because you offered all those vows and other observances to Viṣṇu, who exists in the form of your husband, you have therefore come to be my wife. (26)
Because of the vow you observed during the month of Kārttika from birth until death, you shall never at any time behold separation from me. (27)
Likewise, those men who are devoted to vows in the month of Kārttika have attained my presence; they, too, are as pleasing to me as you are.
Indeed, men who perform sacrifices, charity, vows, and austerities do not obtain even a fraction of the merit of the Kārttika vow. ||29||
Having thus heard this from the Lord of the World at that time,
she was filled with joy born from the majesty of her existence resulting from the merits of her previous births;
[she beheld] the Lord of the Universe, who is the sole foundation of the three worlds.
Having prostrated before Kṛṣṇa, Satyā spoke these words.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Satyā’s Previous Birth," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(90) The Ninetieth Chapter. Satyā said:
O Lord, all parts of time are of the very nature of Time itself; why then are they not equal, and why is Kārttika the best among the months? (1)
Among the lunar days, Ekādaśī is dear to you, and among the months, Kārttika is dear; O Lord of the gods of gods, how is this so? What is the reason? Please tell me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
You have asked well, O Satyabhāmā; listen with a one-pointed mind to the conversation between Pṛthu, the son of Vena, and the celestial sage Nārada.
In this very way, O beloved, having been previously questioned by Pṛthu, the omniscient sage Nārada spoke regarding the reason for the superiority of Kārttika. (4)
Nārada said:
Formerly, there was an asura named Śaṅkha, the son of the Ocean, who possessed great strength and prowess and was unable to be overcome by the three worlds. ||5||
Having conquered the gods and cast them out from the heavenly worlds, the great asura likewise seized the offices of the world-protectors, such as Indra and the others.
Then, out of fear of him, those gods went to a cave in the Golden Mountain; together with Indra and their consorts, they dwelt there for many years. (7)
When the gods were stationed within the fortress of the cave of the Golden Mountain and remained under his control, the Daitya then reflected: ||8||
Even though the gods have been stripped of their authority and conquered by disease, they remain endowed with strength; what, then, is there for me to do here? (9)
Today I have realized, O gods, that you are endowed with the power of Vedic mantras;
I shall seize them, and then you will all indeed be deprived of your strength. (10)
Thinking thus, the lordly Daitya then observed Viṣṇu asleep and swiftly carried off the collection of the Vedas from Satyaloka.
But those Vedas, having been taken by him, fled out of fear of him;
they entered into the water here, accompanied by the sacrificial mantras.
Searching for them, Śaṅkha also wandered within the ocean,
yet that Daitya did not see them stationed together anywhere at all.
Then Brahmā, together with the Asuras, sought refuge in Viṣṇu;
taking the materials for worship, he went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
There, to awaken him, the gods performed acts such as singing and instrumental music, and repeatedly offered perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. (15)
Then the Blessed One, awakened and gratified by their devotion,
appeared there to those gods with a splendor equal to a thousand suns.
Then, having worshipped them with the sixteen types of offerings, the gods prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff; thereupon Keśava spoke to them.
Viṣṇu said:
"I am the granter of boons; with my throat, I shall grant you all the desires cherished by your minds, accompanied by the songs and instrumental music of the hosts of gods. (18)
From the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha until the day of Udbodhinī, one should [perform worship] at night during the fourth watch,
when a sliver of the moon remains, with songs, instrumental music, and other auspicious sounds.
"Whatever has been done by you for human beings at all times, those who constantly act in accordance with that indeed attain my state of union. (20)

Since the water for the feet, the respectful offering, the water for sipping, and so forth, which were prepared by you in whatever manner, have arisen with such marvelous qualities as to become the cause of your happiness. (21)
"All the Vedas have been carried away by Śaṅkha and remain submerged in the water;
I shall bring them back, O gods, after slaying the son of the Ocean."
From this day forward, you shall always perform sacrifices accompanied by the Vedic mantras and seed-syllables (bīja) every year during the month of Kārttika, while taking rest within the waters.
"From this day forward, I too shall dwell within the waters;
O lords of sages, you also must come with me. (24)
In this very time, the best of the twice-born perform their morning bath;
they would undoubtedly be as well-bathed as those who have completed the final purificatory rites (avabhṛtha) of all sacrifices. ||25||
O Śakra, those men who always properly observe the vow during Kārttika shall reach your abode and dwell there eternally. ||26||
"By my command, you must protect them from obstacles;
furthermore, you must grant them a lineage consisting of sons, grandsons, and descendants. (27)
"By my command, you must bring about an increase in wealth and act as the presiding lord over that wealth;
for by this means, men shall become the very embodiments of my form and shall be liberated while still living. (28)

From birth until death, this supreme vow has been properly performed by me through battle and other means, according to the prescribed rules, even while remaining amidst these [worldly] attachments. (29)
Since I have been awakened by you on this eleventh lunar day,
therefore this day of the moon’s waning must be honored as one that bestows divine favor.

O best of asuras, when these two vows are properly performed by men, they grant proximity to Kṛṣṇa; nothing else does so—not gifts, nor pilgrimages, nor austerities, nor sacrifices, which only grant the world of the gods.

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Preparation for the Slaying of Śaṅkhāsura," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(91) The Ninety-first Chapter.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, assuming a form resembling a small fish,
plunged into the waters at the abode of Kaśyapa on the Vindhya mountains.
Out of compassion, the sage quickly lifted Satam’s water-pot;
meanwhile, Satam himself descended into the well. ||2||
There too, the virtuous man cast me into a well;
thus cast into the ocean, I grew there as well. (3)
Then Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a fish, indeed slew the wicked Śaṅkha;
then, holding him in his own hand, he came to the forest of Badarī. ||4||
There, having summoned all the sages, the Lord gave this command.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "The Vedas have been scattered in the waters; you must recover them."
"Bring the water from the Jalāntarā quickly, along with its secret [mantras];
meanwhile, I shall remain at Prayāga accompanied by the hosts of deities. (6)
Nārada said: Then, by all those sages endowed with the power of austerity,
those six Vedāṅgas were recovered, together with the Vedas and the sacrifices.
O King, among them, each became a Ṛṣi according to the measure of what he had received; indeed, from that time forth, they were born as Ṛṣis of exactly that same measure.
Then all the sages, having assembled, went to Prayāga and presented the Vedas they had recovered to Viṣṇu, the creator of the world.
Having obtained the Vedas along with the sacrificial rites, Brahmā, filled with joy,
performed the horse sacrifice surrounded by hosts of gods and sages.
O Lord of Gods, the Siddhas, Pannagas, and Guhyakas fell prostrate upon the ground like staffs and offered this petition to you. (11)
The gods said:
"O Lord, O God of gods, O Master of the world, hear our petition!
This is a time for our joy; therefore, become the bestower of boons upon us. (12)
In this place, the sages recovered the lost Vedas by themselves;
and we have obtained our shares of the sacrifice through your grace, O Lord of Ramā. (13)
May this place also become the most excellent on earth, increasing merit and bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, forever by your grace. (14)
This time as well is of great merit, effecting the purification of even those who have slain a brahmin;
it makes what is given inexhaustible. Speak this boon to me. (15)
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"O gods, this which has been proposed by you is my own opinion as well. Let it be so; let this place attain the renown of being 'Brahmakṣetra'."
A king born of the Solar dynasty will bring the Gaṅgā here;
she shall unite with Kāla, the son of Sūrya’s daughter. ||17||
"And you all, beginning with Brahmā, shall dwell here together with me;
this shall become a most famous sacred site at the king of holy places. (18)
May acts such as charity, austerity, vows, fire-offerings, recitation, and worship always yield fruit for me, and may they never fail to bestow their rewards. (19)
Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed over many lifetimes go to destruction at that very moment upon the sight of this sacred ford.
In my presence, the wise likewise cast off their bodies;
indeed, those men do not undergo rebirth, as they enter my own form. (21)
All those hosts of ancestors who have assembled here to perform a śrāddha ceremony for their forefathers shall attain the same world as me. (22)
May this time also always bestow great merit upon virtuous people;
for those who bathe at dawn when the sun has entered Capricorn, it is the destroyer of sin. (23)

For those who perform the morning bath during the month of Māgha while the Sun is situated in Capricorn, all sins depart at the mere sight [of the ritual], just as darkness departs before the sun. (24)
I grant three things to men in succession for bathing in Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn: residence in the same world, the same form, and proximity [to me]. (25)
"O all you lords of sages, listen; I am the bestower of boons upon you.
Being omnipresent, I always abide here in the midst of the Badarī forest. (26)
Elsewhere, that fruit which is obtained through ten years of austerity is always obtained by you here in a single day. (27)
Those best of men who behold that place become liberated while living; at that time, sin does not remain within them at all. (28)
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to the gods, the God of gods, together with Brahmā, vanished right there.
All the gods remained there along with Indra; Indra and the others likewise attained invisibility.

Whosoever, being of pure mind, should hear this verse or cause it to be heard, that best of men shall obtain the same fruit as by visiting Badarīvana, the king of sacred fords, and shall attain me. (30)
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, within the *Kārttikamāhātmya*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā,
[is contained] the slaying of the demon Śaṅkhāsura, the arrival of the Vedas, and the majesty of Prayāga.
The Ninety-First Chapter.
(92) The ninety-second chapter. Pṛthu said:

O Sage Nārada, you have described the great fruit of the months of Kārttika and Māgha; you ought to explain to me correctly the procedure for bathing in those two months, as well as the rules and the ritual for their conclusion, exactly as they are.
Nārada said:
You are born from a portion of Viṣṇu; nothing remains unknown to you. Nevertheless, O unborn one, listen as I describe his majesty correctly. 2.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should, free from sloth, undertake the observance of the Kārttika vow. ||3||
When a quarter of the night remains and the moon has set, the one who is ever-vowed should rise with joy;
carrying a water vessel, he should go outside from his dwelling toward the southwest.

During the day and at the twilights, with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) worn over the right ear, facing north, having placed a blade of grass on the ground to hide [the private parts], and having covered the head with a cloth; ||5||
Restraining the mouth with effort and avoiding spitting or exhaling, one should void urine and feces; if it is at night, one should face the south.
Having held his penis and risen, and having taken impure clay, he should perform purification without lethargy so as to remove both odor and residue. (7)
One [application] should be given to the penis and the anus, ten to the left hand, seven to both [hands], and likewise three to the two feet. ||8||

This [standard amount] is declared to be two or three times greater for the student (brahmacārī) and the forest-dweller (vanastha), and four times greater for the ascetic (yati); at night, one should perform half of that purification.
One standing on the path [of purification] should perform half of that; for women and Śūdras, half of that again.
For one devoid of the acts of purification, all ritual actions are fruitless.
The mantras of one who is devoid of purification of the mouth are said not to yield fruit;
therefore, one should diligently perform the purification of the teeth and the tongue. 11.
O divine tree, grant us longevity, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, and wealth, as well as sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence. 12.
Having recited this mantra, one should always offer twelve finger-breadths of fuel-sticks from milky trees, even without fasting on the day of the sacrifice.
One should not perform oil massage on the first day of the lunar fortnight, the new moon, the ninth, the sixth, nor on Sundays;
likewise, one should not do so during lunar or solar eclipses.

One should avoid brushing one's teeth with wood from thorny trees, cotton plants, nirguṇḍī, or the brahmavṛkṣa; likewise, one should avoid those that are excessively fragrant, such as bilva or eraṇḍa. 15.
Then, with a serene mind and intent upon devotion, he should go to the abodes of Viṣṇu and Śiva,
taking with him perfumes, flowers, and excellent betel.

There, having performed the various services for the deity such as water for the feet and the respectful offering (arghya) individually, and having offered praise and bowed once more, one should perform auspicious songs and the like.
One should also honor the dancers accompanied by the sounds of cymbals, flutes,
and drums, as well as the singers, with flowers, perfumes, betel leaves, and other offerings.
The forms of Viṣṇu residing in temples are dependent on songs;
and penances, sacrifices, and gifts are performed for the sake of the Teacher of the World. (19)
"O King, you who constantly bestow contentment and wealth through devotion to the Lord, the True Master—where do you dwell, O Lord of Gods? This is what I have asked of you."
Viṣṇu, thus gratified by my devotion, then said:
"I do not dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the hearts of yogis."
O Nārada, I abide wherever my devotees sing;
having heard the narration of the true Purāṇas and the singing of my devotees, I remain there.
Indeed, those who are not deluded by passion and free from hatred do not desire [such things];
for it is by them that worship and the like, including perfumes, flowers, and so forth, are offered by men. (23)
From worshipping me in that manner, one attains joy and likewise freedom from fatigue;
[this is achieved] with flowers produced from the śirīṣa, unmatta, girijā, mallikā, and śālmalī trees.
Viṣṇu should not be worshipped with *arka*, *karṇikāra*, or *akṣata* flowers, nor with *japā*, *kunda*, *śirīṣa*, *yūthikā*, or *mālatī*. (25)
Likewise, Śaṅkara should not be worshipped with ketakī flowers;
Gaṇeśa should not be worshipped with tulasī leaves, nor Durgā with dūrvā grass.
One who desires prosperity should not worship the sun with *muni* flowers; however, fragrant and praiseworthy flowers are always appropriate for worship. (27)
Having thus performed the ritual of worship, one should ask forgiveness from the God of gods:
"O Lord of the Suras, [whatever was] deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion... (28)
"O Lord, may that which has been worshipped by me be fulfilled for me.
Then, having performed a circumambulation and prostrated like a staff, [he spoke]. (29)
Furthermore, one should ask for forgiveness from the Lord; one should ask for forgiveness from the primordial singer (Gāyana).
Those who properly perform the worship and other rites of Viṣṇu and Śiva during the night in the month of Kārttika—
Having shaken off their sins, those men go together with their ancestors to the abode of Viṣṇu. ||30||
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses,
in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the *Kārttika-māhātmya*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā, this is the chapter titled "Description of Observances."
The Ninety-Second Chapter. ||92||
[93] The Ninety-third Chapter.
Nārada said:
When two nāḍīs of the night remain, one who is pure should go to a body of water, accompanied by sesame seeds, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, lamps, and other offerings. (1)

Bathing in a human-made pond, a natural pool, a river, and at the confluence of two rivers is said to yield ten times the merit respectively; bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) is remembered as yielding infinite fruit.
Having first recollected Viṣṇu, one should then perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the ritual bath;
one should then cause the offering of water for the feet (argha) and other honors to be given in due order to the deities of the sacred ford and others.
Oṃ, salutations to the one whose navel is a lotus; salutations to you who recline upon the waters.
Let there be salutation to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; accept this water-offering (argha); salutations be unto you.
In Vaikuṇṭha, at Prayāga, and likewise at Badarikāśrama—
there Viṣṇu strode forth and thrice placed his foot.
Therefore, [I seek] protection from the gods, from whom Viṣṇu strode forth;
together with all of them, accompanied by the sages and the gods. ||6||
"O Supreme among Gods, O Lord of Devas, O Dāmodara, I shall perform the morning bath in the month of Kārttika together with you for your pleasure. (7)
Having meditated upon you, O Lord of Gods, I am prepared to bathe in these waters;
by your grace, O Dāmodara, may my sin be destroyed. (8)
O Kṛṣṇa, who destroys all sins, in this month of Kārttika dedicated to both daily and occasional rites, O Hari, together with Rādhā, please accept this arghya offered by me. (9)
O Hari, accompanied by Rādhā, accept this arghya offered by me, who have bathed according to the rules during the month of Kārttika while observing my vows.
Having remembered Bhāgīrathī, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Sūrya, one who observes the vow should enter the water;
standing in water reaching to the navel, he should bathe according to the prescribed rule.
A householder should perform his bath with the powder of sesame and *āmalaka* fruits;
for forest-dwellers and ascetics, it is the earth from the root of the *tulasī*. (12)
One should not bathe on the seventh, tenth, or ninth lunar days, nor on the second, tenth, or thirteenth, using *dhātrī* fruits together with sesame seeds.
First, one should perform the bath for removing impurities, and after that, the mantra-bath;
however, for women and Śūdras, it is not with mantras declared in the Vedas, but with those born from the Purāṇas.
The Bathing Mantras:
May that Viṣṇu, the destroyer of all sins, who formerly divided himself threefold out of devotion for the sake of the gods' work, purify me here by his grace. (15)
Having received the command of Viṣṇu for the purpose of performing the Kārttika vow, may all those gods protect me and always purify me. 16.
May the Vedic mantras, together with their seed-syllables, their secret teachings, and their potencies, and may the sages beginning with Kaśyapa, always purify me. (17)
May all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, all sacred fords that bestow the gift of water, and all reservoirs of water including the seven oceans, purify me. (18)
May the chaste wives, beginning with Aditi; the Yakṣas, Siddhas, and Pannagas;
the medicinal herbs, and the mountains—all born of the three worlds—purify me instantly. (19)
Having bathed with these mantras while observing the vow and having placed the purifier (pavitraka) upon his hand,
he should offer libations to the gods, sages, humans, and ancestors according to the prescribed rule.
For as many sesame seeds as are used in the libation for the ancestors during the month of Kārttika, for that same number of years do the ancestors dwell in heaven. (21)
Then, having emerged from the water, the practitioner, clothed in pure garments, shall complete the rites prescribed for the morning time and worship Hari once again. (22)

Having recollected the deities of the sacred fords and other such places, one should again cause the worship to be performed, endowed with perfumes, flowers, and fruits, with a mind intent upon devotion. (23)
The Arghya-mantra:
"O Destroyer of the Lord of Danujas, accept this arghya offered by me, who am observing the vow and have bathed according to the rules in the month of Kārttika. (24)
Then, one should devoutly feed Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, and one should prostrate before them again and again with perfumes, flowers, and betel. ||25||
The sacred fords reside in his right foot, and the Vedas take refuge in his mouth;
the gods are established in all his limbs, and they become honored through the worship of the twice-born. (26)

The true nature of Viṣṇu, who possesses an unmanifest form, is embodied on earth by the Brāhmaṇas; therefore, one who desires their own welfare should never treat them with contempt or oppose them. (27)
The observer of the vow should indeed worship that Tulasī, the beloved of Hari, O Goddess;
with a one-pointed mind, he should perform circumambulations and prostrations. (28)
You were created by the gods in the past and worshipped by the lords of sages;
salutations, salutations to you, O Tulasī, beloved of Hari, take away my sin! (29)
Then, having heard the ancient narrative of Viṣṇu, the devoted observer of vows, with a tender heart, should worship that brahmin sage and learned man with devotion. (30)
Thus, the devoted man who correctly performs the previously described complete rite attains the same world as Nārāyaṇa. ||31||
There is no cause for the removal of disease, the destruction of evil, the granting of supreme true wisdom, the attainment of sons, wealth, and other blessings,
nor the foundation of liberation, other than the Kārttika vow.
For there is indeed nothing else on the surface of the earth so dear to Viṣṇu. ||32||

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Bathing," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(94) The ninety-fourth chapter.
Nārada said:
O King, listen as I describe in their entirety those rules proclaimed for men observing the Kārttika vow. (1)
One observing the Kārttika vow should not consume any kinds of meat, honey, fermented gruel, nor even royal beans and the like. (2)
One observing the Kārttika vow should avoid split pulses, oil, and likewise food defiled by tears; he should also avoid that which is defiled in its essence or defiled by sound. ||3||
One observing the Kārttika vow should not accept food from others, nor harbor malice toward others, nor approach another's wife, nor accept gifts at a sacred site. (4)
During the month of Kārttika, the observer of the vow should avoid censuring the God of gods, the twice-born, his preceptor, those under religious observances, women, kings, and great men. (5)
The limb of a living being, meat, powder, that which is born from fruit, and "hero-meat" (vīra-āmiṣa);
likewise, lentils are declared to be grain, as is food that has been kept overnight.
The milk of goats, cows, and buffaloes, as well as other milks and the like, are considered meat;
likewise, all juices purchased from the twice-born and salt produced from the earth [are forbidden]. (7)
Cow's milk products kept in a copper vessel, water collected from a puddle, and food cooked for one's own sake—these are known as *āmiṣa* (impure) by the wise. ||8||
The practitioner of the vow should always maintain celibacy, sleep on the ground, eat from a leaf-plate, and consume food only at the fourth meal-time; he should thus perform his worship. 9.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Narakas, one should have an oil massage performed; on other occasions, one should not have an oil massage except during the Kārttika ablution.
One observing the Kārttika vow should avoid onion, garlic, drumstick, mushroom, leek, lotus stalk, radish, and hiṅgu. (11)
A follower of the Vaiṣṇava vow should avoid the bottle gourd, the eggplant, the pumpkin, the fruit of the brinjal, the śleṣmātaka, and the wood-apple. 12.
One observing the Kārttika vow should avoid a woman in her courses, and should not speak with Mlecchas, outcasts, or Vrātyas, nor with those among the twice-born who are outside the Veda. 13.
One who observes the Kārttika vow should avoid food seen by dogs or crows, as well as food from a birth-impurity; he should also avoid food cooked twice and burnt food. 14.

"One who avoids oil massage, as well as beds, food from others, and eating from bell-metal vessels during Kārttika shall be one whose vow is complete. A practitioner of vows should always avoid these in all religious observances.
One should also perform the Kṛcchra and other penances according to one's own capacity for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu. ||15||
In sequence: the kūṣmāṇḍa, the vṛntāka, the bṛhatī, the mūlaka, as well as the śrīphala, the kaliṅga, and likewise the fruit derived from the dhātrī. ||16||
Coconut, large gourd, patola, jujube fruit, leather, vaikataka, lotus stalk, and likewise kaṭa; ||17||
These vegetables are to be avoided in sequence starting from the first lunar day (pratipad);
likewise, a householder should always avoid the dhātrī fruit on Sundays.
A person should avoid even some of these things if it is for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu;
rather, having given that [which is permitted] to a Brāhmaṇa, he should always eat it himself. 19.
In this very same way, the observer of the vow should indeed perform the observances during the month of Māgha as well;
therein, he should also cause the vigil for Hari to be performed according to the prescribed rite.
Seeing a man who observes the Kārttika vow and acts according to what has been taught, the messengers of Yama flee like elephants tormented by a lion. (21)
Indeed, this vow of Viṣṇu is superior even to a hundred sacrifices;
the performer of sacrifice attains heaven, but the observer of the Kārttika vow attains Vaikuṇṭha. 22.
Whatever sacred fields exist here on earth that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, they all reside in the home of one who performs the Kārttika vow. (23)
Any bad dream or any evil deed born of the actions of mind, speech, or body, dissolves at that very moment upon seeing one who observes the Kārttika vow. (24)
Impelled by the words of Viṣṇu, Śakra and the other gods provide protection for the man observing the Kārttika vow, just as servants do for a king. (25)
Where those who constantly observe the vow of Viṣṇu remain ever honored, there indeed the planets, spirits, and piśācas do not dwell. (26)
Even the four-faced Brahmā here would not be capable of describing the merit of one who observes the Kārttika vow, performing it exactly as prescribed. (27)

The man who observes this vow with its prescribed restraints during the month of Kārttika— which is dear to Viṣṇu, destroys all sins, and everywhere brings about an abundance of sons, wealth, and grain— [attains these blessings].
What is the use for him of frequenting or serving sacred fords? ||28||

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Observances," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(94) The Ninety-Fourth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Now, O King, listen to the procedure for the proper conclusion of the Urjā-vrata as it has been narrated by me; what is the ritual injunction in brief? (1)

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the observer of the vow should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the sake of completing the vow and for the pleasure of Viṣṇu. ||2||
Above the Tulasī plant, one should construct an auspicious pavilion, adorned with beautiful archways, having four doors, and beautified by flowers and chowries. ||3||
At the gates, one should worship the gatekeepers individually, made of clay:
Puṇyaśīla, Suśīla, Jaya, and Vijaya. (4)
And at the base of the Tulasī plant, one should draw a Sarvatobhadra mandala, properly adorned with four colors, rich in beauty, and well-decorated. (5)
Having placed upon it a water-jar provided with a lid, endowed with the five precious gems, and joined with a large fruit.
There one should worship the Lord of Gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, who is clothed in yellow silk garments, and who is united with the Daughter of the Ocean. (7)
The observer of the vow should worship Indra and the other world-protectors within the mandala, for he was awakened by the gods on the twelfth day and [honored] on the thirteenth. (8)
Since he was seen and worshipped on the fourteenth day, he is therefore even more worthy of honor. On that day, one should fast with devotion, being peaceful and of restrained mind. (9)
With the permission of his guru, he should worship the Lord of the gods of gods with golden [images], using the sixteen types of offerings accompanied by various kinds of food. (10)
One should keep a vigil at night with auspicious songs, instrumental music, and other such festivities.
Those who sing with devotion during the vigil for the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrapāṇi)— ||11||
Those who perform song and dance during the day-long vigil for Viṣṇu are liberated from the accumulations of sins produced over hundreds of previous births. (12)
The fruit of those who give a thousand cows is declared to be equal to that;
one should perform singing, dancing, and so forth, and display various spectacles. (13)
He who, during the night vigil for Hari in the presence of Vāsudeva, recites the deeds of Viṣṇu and honors the Vaiṣṇavas; ||14||
He who performs the vigil for Hari with these dispositions—playing musical instruments with his mouth and displaying spontaneous speech—[attains the highest goal]. (15)
Day by day, his merit is considered equal to that of ten million sacred fords (tīrthas).
Then, on the full moon day, [he should feed] the best of the twice-born together with their wives. 16.
One should invite thirty, or many, or as many as one's own capacity allows;
for it was by granting boons that Viṣṇu then became the Fish-form. (17)
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or recited there is said to yield inexhaustible fruit;
therefore, the observer of the vow should feed those Brahmins with milk-rice and other such foods. (18)
With the two verses beginning "ato devāḥ," one should offer sesame and milk-rice (pāyasa) separately for the sake of pleasing the God of gods and the gods individually. (19)
One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and bow down to them;
then, having worshipped the Lord again, as well as the deities and Tulasī.
Then, there, the observer of the vow should worship a tawny cow according to the prescribed rite,
and honor the preceptor who instructed him in the vow with garments, ornaments, and other gifts.
Having worshipped him together with his wife, one should cause a cow to be given to him [the preceptor], saying:
"O Lord of Gods, may you then be pleased with me through your grace. (22)
Whatever sin has been committed by me through seven lifetimes because of this vow, may all that go to destruction, and may my progeny be stable. ||23||
May my desires always bear fruit through this worship of you;
may I attain your Vaiṣṇava body and the station that is exceedingly difficult to reach. (24)
Having thus asked forgiveness from those brahmins and propitiated them, he should dismiss them;
then the observer of the vow should give that image, together with jewels, to his guru. (25)
Then, accompanied by friends and teachers, the devoted one eats himself;
this very procedure is prescribed for the months of Kārttika or Māgha. ||26||
Thus, the man who properly observes the vow of Kārttika becomes free from sin and, being utterly liberated, shall attain proximity to Viṣṇu. ||27||
Whatever fruit is obtained through all vows, all sacred fords, and all acts of charity,
that should be known to be multiplied ten millionfold by performing this rite correctly according to its injunctions.
Blessed are they, highly meritorious are they, for them there is the arising of all fruits—those who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu and perform the vow during the month of Kārttika. ||29||
The evils residing within the body become anxious out of fear of him;
they say, "Where shall we go, if this man performs his vow? (30)
Thus, those devotees who hear these rules of the *ūrjavrata* and likewise recount them before a Vaiṣṇava shall obtain the full fruit from the proper performance of the vow.
They obtain all that which destroys defilement. ||31||

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Concluding Rite," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(96) The ninety-sixth chapter. Pṛthu said:
O Brahmin, regarding that vow of the month of Kārttika which you have described in detail,
you have spoken there of the worship of Viṣṇu at the root of the tulasī plant.
Therefore, I wish to ask about the majesty arising from Tulasī:
how is she so exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu, the god of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow? (2)
How did she come into being, and in what place, O Nārada?
Tell me this in brief, for you are considered by me to be omniscient. (3)
Nārada said: Formerly, when the lord of the Daityas, the son of the Ocean, had been struck down by Rudra,
the gods, headed by Brahmā, bowed their heads to Rudra and spoke.
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the majesty arising from Tulasī.
I shall relate to you all that ancient event as it occurred in the past.
Formerly, Śakra went to Mount Kailāsa to behold Śiva, surrounded by all the gods and attended by hosts of apsarases. (5)
As soon as he had reached the abode of Śiva, he quickly saw there a man of terrifying deeds, fearsome with his fangs and eyes.
Being questioned by him thus again and again—"O sir, who are you? Where has the Lord of the World gone?"—he did not speak, O King. (7)
Then the wielder of the thunderbolt, becoming enraged, rebuked them and spoke these words:
"O you! Even though questioned by me, you have not given an answer. (8)
"Therefore, I shall slay you with my thunderbolt; who is your protector in this matter, O evil-minded one?
Having spoken thus, the wielder of the thunderbolt then struck him violently with his bolt.
By that [act], his throat turned blue and his thunderbolt was reduced to ashes;
thereafter, Rudra blazed forth as if burning with his own splendor.
Upon seeing him, Bṛhaspati quickly joined his palms in reverence, and Indra, prostrating himself on the ground like a staff, began to offer praise. ||11||
Bṛhaspati said:
"Obeisance to the God of gods, to the three-eyed one with matted hair;
obeisance to Śarva, the destroyer of Tripura, the slayer of Andhaka. (12)

To the one who is deformed, the one who is exceedingly beautiful, the one who possesses many forms, the source of bliss, the destroyer of sacrifices, and the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices. ||13||
Salutation to the one who is Time, the ender of time, and the wearer of the serpent's coils; salutation again and again to the Brahmin, the slayer of Brahmā’s head. ||14||
Nārada said:
Thus praised, Śambhu then spoke to that bull among the twice-born, withdrawing the flame from his eye which was capable of consuming the three worlds. (15)
"Choose a boon, O Brahmin; I am pleased by this hymn of yours.
By granting life to Indra, may you live and attain great renown. (16)
Bṛhaspati said:
"If you are pleased, go to Indra, who has come to you for refuge;
let this Agni, born from the eye on your forehead, be pacified."
Īśvara said:
"How has he come to enter once again through the eye in my forehead?
I shall cast him far away so that he may not afflict Indra."
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, he seized him by the hand and threw him into the salt waters;
he fell at the confluence of the Sindhu, the Gaṅgā, and the ocean. 19.
Then he assumed the form of a young child and wept there;
by the sound of him weeping, the earth repeatedly trembled.
Both heaven and the world of truth (satyaloka) were deafened by that sound;
hearing it, Brahmā went there, wondering, "What is this? ||21||
Then he saw the boy standing on the shore of the ocean;
seeing that Brahmin approaching, the ocean also joined its palms in reverence.
Having bowed his head to the Child, he placed him on his lap;
then Brahmā spoke these words: "Whose child is this, so wonderful? (23)
Having heard these words of the Lord of Creatures, the Ocean spoke.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Rivers, from where was this very powerful boy obtained?"
At whose roar the gods, asuras, and great serpents were terrified.
The Ocean said:
"O Brahmin, this little son of mine was born in the Siddhu-Gaṅgā."
"O Teacher of the World, perform for him the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony.
Nārada said: While the Ocean was speaking thus, the son of the Ocean, still a child, [spoke]. (26)
He seized Brahmā by the beard, shaking him again and again;
as he shook his beard, water flowed from his two eyes.
When he had somehow freed himself from the beard, Brahmā then spoke to the ocean: ||| 27 ||
Brahmā said:
"Since this water of mine has been held by him with his two eyes, he shall therefore become famous by the name Jalandhara. (28)
Now he has become a youth, one who has mastered all weapons and missiles;
he shall be incapable of being slain by any living beings, except for Rudra.
Wherever he was born, there he will now go.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, he summoned Śukra and consecrated him in this kingdom;
then, taking leave of the lord of rivers, Brahmā entered into disappearance.
Then, his eyes blossoming at the sight of him, Sāgara [acted] at that time.
He requested Vṛndā, the daughter of Kālanemi, for the sake of making her his wife.
Then the asuras, headed by Tekālanemi, being greatly delighted, gave that daughter to him.
Having obtained those excellent allies, the self-controlled and powerful one, accompanied by Śuka, ruled the earth.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Jālandhara," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(97) The Ninety-Seventh Chapter.
Nārada said:
Those Daityas who were formerly defeated by the gods and reside in the netherworld (pātāla).
Those born on that lunar mansion were fearless in attending upon him.
Once, seeing Rāhu with his head severed, the king of the Daityas asked the brahmin Bhārgava: "O Lord, by whom has this been done? (2)
Then Bhārgava announced to him the severing of Rāhu’s head,
which had been brought about by the gods for the sake of the nectar from the ocean.
Having heard of the theft of the jewels and the defeat of the Daityas,
his eyes then became bloodshot with anger as he addressed his father.
He dispatched the messenger Ghasmara into the presence of Śakra;
the messenger, having gone to Triviṣṭapa, quickly reached Sudharmā.
Out of pride, with his head unbowed, he addressed the Lord of the Gods.
The messenger said:
"Jalandhara, the son of the Ocean, is the sovereign of all the Daitya hosts."
"I am a messenger sent by him; hear what he has said:
'Why was my father, the ocean, churned by you with a mountain? (7)
"Give me back all those jewels that have been taken; give them to me quickly!
Hearing these words of the messenger, the lord of the thirty gods was struck with amazement;
filled with fear and rage, he spoke to the voracious and terrible one. (8)
The Lord said: Listen, O messenger, to what was done by me in the past: just as the ocean was churned, so too were the mountains, terrified by fear of me, placed within my own belly.
Other enemies of mine, such as the Daityas led by Rākṣasa, were likewise [protected];
therefore, that collection of jewels was indeed seized by me as well.
Likewise, in ancient times, Śambara, the son of the Ocean, who hated the gods,
was slain by my younger brother and entered the belly of the ocean.
Therefore, go and tell him everything; there is no other reason for this.
Nārada said:
Thus dismissed by Indra, the messenger returned home and then related those words of Indra to the king of the Daityas.
Hearing that, the Daitya, his lips quivering with rage,
immediately made preparations with the desire to conquer all the gods.
Then, at the exertion of the Lord of the Gods, the sons of Diti arrived from the cardinal directions, from the intermediate points, and likewise from the netherworld,
by the hundreds and by the tens of millions.
Then, having gone to the third heaven accompanied by millions of army commanders such as Śumbha and Niśumbha, the Daitya took his stand for battle.
The gods, eager for battle, set out from Amarāvatī;
seeing the vast army of the Daityas, they stood surrounding the city.
Then a battle took place between the armies of the gods and the dānavas,
fought with maces, iron clubs, arrows, bludgeons, axes, and spears.
They rushed at one another and struck each other; in an instant, both armies became drenched in floods of blood.
With elephants, horses, chariots, and infantrymen fallen and being felled,
the battlefield shone like the sky filled with masses of clouds at twilight.
There, in that battle, Bhārgava restored the slain Daityas to life by means of the *amṛtajīvinī* spell and drops of water consecrated with mantras.
In that battle, the son of Gīrā brought divine medicinal herbs from the region of Droṇa again and again, and thus restored the gods to life.
Seeing the gods thus risen once again in battle, Jalandhara, overcome by anger, spoke these words to Bhārgava: ||23||
Jālandhara said:
"O Goddess, how is it that those slain by me in battle rise up again?
It is renowned that your science of restoration to life (saṃjīvanī-vidyā) exists nowhere else."
Bhṛgu said:
"Having brought divine medicinal herbs from Mount Droṇa, he quickly revives the gods; therefore, remove Mount Droṇa."
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus, the lord of the Daityas then took Droṇācala and quickly cast him into the ocean; he then returned once more to the great battle.
Then, seeing the gods slain, the preceptor went to Mount Droṇa;
however, there he, who was worshipped by the gods, did not see that king of mountains.
Having learned that Droṇa had been seized by the Daityas, Indra was despondent and overwhelmed with fear;
approaching from afar, his body agitated by sighs, he spoke.
"Flee! Flee! For he cannot be conquered;
for he is born from Rudra and Śaṅkara. Remember the deeds of Śakra! ||29||
Having heard those words, the gods, overwhelmed by fear,
then fled in the ten directions while being struck down by those Daityas.
Seeing the gods routed, the Daitya Sāgaradana entered Amarāvatī amidst the triumphant sounds of conchs and kettledrums.
When the Daitya had entered the city, the gods, led by Śakra and tormented by the Daitya, reached a cave in the Golden Mountain and took up residence there.
Then, having assigned Indra and the others to all the offices of the Asuras,
she herself went once more to the cave of the Golden Mountain, leaving the foremost Daityas such as Śumbha and others each in their respective positions.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Victory at Amarāvatī," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa within the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(98) The Ninety-eighth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Seeing that Daitya approaching once again, all the gods, including Indra, trembled with fear and began to offer praise to Viṣṇu. (1)
The gods said:
Salutations to the destroyer of suffering, who is ever intent on accomplishing the tasks of his devotees through various forms such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others.
May he who is the agent of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world beginning with Brahmā, and who holds in his hands the mace, conch, lotus, and discus, be victorious. ||2||
To the beloved of Ramā, the slayer of the Asuras, the lord of serpents and other beings, the wearer of yellow garments,
the one who brings to fruition sacrificial rites and the like, and the dispeller [of darkness].
To him, the worthy refuge, we bow; we bow. ||3||
Obeisance to You, Viṣṇu, the thunderbolt that shatters the mountain of suffering for the immortals tormented by the Daityas;
who reclines upon the couch of the lord of serpents, and who [possesses] the sun and moon...
To him who has two eyes, we bow; we bow. ||4||
Nārada said:
That man who constantly recites this hymn which destroys all distress shall never again be afflicted by distress through the grace of Hari. (5)
While the gods were thus offering praise to the enemy of the Danujas,
Viṣṇu then became aware of the calamity that had befallen the deities.
Rising suddenly, the enemy of the Daityas, his mind distressed with compassion,
mounted Garuḍa with speed and spoke these words to Lakṣmī.
Viṣṇu said:
"Your brother Jalandhara has caused the slaughter of the gods;
summoned by them, I shall go today with haste for battle."
Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord, if I am always your beloved and your devotee, then why, O ocean of mercy, is my brother to be slain by you in battle? (9)
The Blessed Lord said: "Because he was born from Rudra, because of the word of Brahmā,
and because of my own affection for you, this Jalandhara is not to be slain by me."
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu, mounted upon Garuḍa and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword, went with speed to fight where those gods were offering praise.
Then, oppressed by the fierce wind from the wings of Aruṇa’s younger brother,
the Daityas were whirled about like clouds scattered by a whirlwind.
Then Jalandhara, seeing the Daityas tormented by the wind, did not utter a word out of anger; instead, he rushed toward Viṣṇu.
Then a great battle took place between Viṣṇu and the lord of the Daityas,
as they filled the sky with their arrows until it was left without any space.
Viṣṇu, with a flood of arrows, cut down the demon's banner, umbrella, bow, and horses;
he then struck him in the heart with a single arrow.
Then, springing up with mace in hand and filled with haste,
he approached Garuḍa and struck him down upon the surface of the earth by his head.
Viṣṇu, as if laughing, cut the mace with his sword;
at that moment, [the opponent], together with his friend, struck Viṣṇu firmly with his fist.
Then those two of great strength fought with hand-to-hand combat,
making the earth resound with their arms, fists, and knees.
Having thus waged that most beautiful battle, the powerful Viṣṇu spoke to the king of the Daityas, Meghaga, with a voice full of fear: 19.
Viṣṇu said:
"Choose a boon, O Lord of Daityas; I am pleased by your valor. Even that which is not to be given, I shall grant to you, whatever dwells in your mind. (20)
Jalandhara said:
"If you are pleased with me, O Bhāvuka, grant me this boon:
dwell in my house together with my sister Satī and your attendants."
Nārada said: Having said, "So be it," the Blessed One, together with all the hosts of gods and accompanied by Ramā,
went to the city named Jalandhara.
And Jalandhara, having joyfully installed the Dānavas in the offices of the gods, returned once more to the surface of the earth.
The son of the Ocean, having brought under his own control whatever jewel was known among the gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, remained there.
Having established the Daitya Niśumbha of great strength in the subterranean abode of Pātāla,
the powerful one brought Aśeṣa and the others down to the surface of the earth.
Having made the hosts of gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, as well as yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans,
his own citizens, he ruled over the three worlds.
Having thus brought the gods under his control, Jalandhara protected his subjects according to dharma, as if they were his own biological sons.
While he ruled the kingdom according to Dharma, no one was seen who was diseased, nor distressed, nor emaciated, nor miserable. (28)
While the lord of the Dānavas was thus ruling the earth righteously and with perfect impartiality,
I once came there by chance to behold his splendor.
To behold Śrī Rāmaṇa and to serve him. ||29||

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Entry of Jalandhara," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā, in the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(99) The Ninety-Ninth Chapter.
Nārada said:
O best of kings, having duly honored Samā with great devotion according to the prescribed rites, the lord of the Dānavas then spoke these words with a smile.
Jālandhara said:
"O Brahmin, from where have you come, and what has been seen by you anywhere? O Sage, command me as to the purpose for which you have arrived here."
Nārada said:
O lord of the Daityas, I went to the peak of Kailāsa by chance;
there I beheld Śaṅkara seated together with Umā.
In a great forest of wish-fulfilling trees extending for ten thousand yojanas,
crowded with hundreds of wish-granting cows and brilliantly illuminated by wish-fulfilling gems.
Seeing that great marvel, a reflection then arose in me:
"Does such growth exist anywhere else in the three worlds, or does it not? (5)
O Lord of Daityas, your prosperity has been amassed by me for so long;
desiring to behold it, I have come here into your presence.
Beholding this prosperity of yours, which is surely lacking the jewel of a woman,
I conjecture that there is no one else in the three worlds more prosperous than Śiva.
Even though the apsarases and the daughters of the nāgas remain under your control, they certainly cannot equal Pārvatī in beauty. (8)
By her, in whose ocean of loveliness even the four-faced Brahmā was submerged and lost his former self-control—by whom else can she be compared? (9)
For even Madanāri, though free from passion, was brought under his own control by his mere sport;
and Viśvataṃtra, too, was made subject to him through asceticism. ||10||
Formerly, while wandering in the dense forest of Sauṃdarya,
the Creator repeatedly beheld her form even as he was engaged in the act of creation, [captivated] by her in the guise of a Śabarī woman.
He created those various apsarases, yet none among them was equal to her;
therefore, for one who enjoys such a jewel among women, his prosperity is unsurpassed.
Likewise, [I spoke] to Ananta and to the lord of all jewels, the king of the Daityas;
having spoken thus and taken leave of him, I departed while the king of the Daityas remained there.
Upon hearing of that form, he was overcome by a feverish distress;
then he dispatched a messenger, the son of Siṃhikā.
Then Rāhu, somewhat deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, went to Kailāsa, which was as white as all-pure moonlight. 15.
Having been introduced by the command of his own master, who had brought him in from the difficult-to-approach dark fortnight in its entirety, he was ushered in by the gatekeeper.
Then, impelled by the sign of her creeper-like eyebrows, she spoke these words: ||16||
Rāhu said:
"O bull-bannered one, listen to the command of the Lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, the master of all jewels, who is served by the gods and the serpents. (17)
How can the auspicious Haimavatī be the wife of one who dwells eternally in cremation grounds, who wears a garland of shaven heads, and who is naked? (18)
I am the supreme lord of jewels, and she is known as the jewel among women;
therefore, she is worthy of me, but certainly not of you who subsist on alms.
Nārada said:
While he was speaking thus, from the middle of the eyebrows of the wielder of the trident (Śiva), there emerged a fierce being with a voice like a sharp thunderbolt. 20.
With a lion’s face, a flickering tongue, and great blazing eyes, with hair standing erect and a withered body, he was like another Narasimha. ||21||
Seeing him, the sage began to devour him; terrified, Rāhu fled with extreme speed toward the outside, but the sage held him fast.
The mighty-armed Sacarāhu spoke with a voice as fearful as a thundercloud: "O Lord of the gods of gods, protect me, who have come to you for refuge! (23)
"O Lord of Gods, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge, protect me; Mahādeva has come here to devour me, a brahmin. (24)
Having heard the words of Mahādeva, he then spoke to the brahmin:
"He shall not be killed, for he is a messenger and is dependent on another."
Having heard "Muñca" (Release), O best of men, that person immediately released Rāhu;
having released Rāhu, that person prostrated before Mahādeva. ||26||
The man said:
"O Master, hunger afflicts me; I am completely emaciated by hunger.
O Lord of Gods, O Prabhū, please command me what food I should eat. (27)
Īśvara said:
"O Saṃtvan, quickly consume me with your hands and feet."
Nārada said: Thus commanded by Śiva himself,
that man ate his own flesh produced from his hands and feet until only his head remained.

Seeing him with only his head remaining, Sadāśiva was greatly pleased; filled with wonder, he spoke to that man of terrible deeds: 30. Seeing him with only his head remaining, Sadāśiva was greatly pleased; filled with wonder, he spoke to that man of terrible deeds.
Īśvara said:
"O Kīrtimukha, you are always the one who guards my door;
yet they do not perform your worship, nor do they act in a way that is pleasing to me. (31)
Nārada said:
From that time forward, Kīrtimukha has remained at the door of the Lord;
for those who previously did not worship here, their worship shall become fruitless.
Released by him, Rāhu fell upon the land of Barbar;
thus he became known as the progenitor of the Barbaras on earth, having spread across the world.
Then Rāhu, perceiving himself to have been born once again in this world,
approached Jalandhara and related everything regarding those deeds of the Lord.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Messenger" and the "Episode of Jālandhara," within the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand verses, in the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(100) The Hundredth Chapter. Nārada said:
Having heard that praise of Jālandhara, his body agitated with anger, he went forth swiftly, surrounded by tens of millions of Daityas. ||1||
As he went before her, Śukra became situated within the range of Rāhu’s gaze;
then his crown slipped and fell to the ground with great force.
Then, filled with hundreds of celestial chariots crowded with the Daitya armies, the sky shone as if filled with clouds during the rainy season.
Having observed his exertion at that time, the gods, led by Śakra,
arrived unobserved and informed the wielder of the trident [Śiva].
The gods said: "O Lord, do you not know how the gods address you?
Therefore, for our protection, slay the son of the Ocean."
Nārada said: Having heard these words of the god, the bull-bannered Lord laughed and,
summoning Mahāviṣṇu, spoke these words.
Īśvara said:
How was Jālandhara killed by you in battle with Viṣṇu?
Out of fear of him, he abandoned his own Vaikuṇṭha and fled. (7)
The Blessed One said:
"Because of your birth from the same source, because of your brotherhood, and likewise because of your shared prosperity, he was not slain by me in battle;
therefore, you must slay this Dānava."
Īśvara said:
"This one of great splendor cannot be slain by me with these weapons and missiles.
Let all the gods give me a portion of their own respective splendors for the purpose of a weapon."
Nārada said:
Then the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, emitted their own splendors;
seeing those splendors united into one, O Lord, it then became a great mass of light.
Therefore, Mahādeva suddenly fashioned an excellent weapon called Sudarśana,
a discus terrifying with its garlands of flames.
Then, with the remainder of his vital energy, Hara fashioned the thunderbolt;
at that moment, Jalandhara was seen upon the grounds at the base of Kailāsa.
Surrounded by tens of millions of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, all the gods, seeing him, were filled with joy and returned as they had come. (13)
And all the hosts, led by the general Dībhavaktra, equipped themselves with great haste for battle at the command of Śiva.
All the hosts, intoxicated by battle, descended from Kailāsa;
then a war broke out on the ground at the foot of Kailāsa.15.
It was a terrible conflict between the lords of the Pramathas and the Daityas, thick with various weapons and missiles,
and filled with the sounds of a multitude of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs that gladdened the hearts of heroes.
The earth resounded with the noises of elephants, horses, and chariots;
it was covered by showers of spears, javelins, arrows, clubs, darts, and battle-axes.
The sky shone as if completely covered by meteors, and then the entire earth shone with the slain elephants and horses. ||18||
It was covered as if with fragments of moving heads struck by the thunderbolt,
and likewise by the throngs of Daityas struck down by the Pramathas, and the Gaṇas struck down by the Daityas.
At that time, the earth became impassable due to the fat, blood, flesh, and bones [of the slain].
By the power of the *saṃjīvanī* [mantra], Bhārgava restored the hosts of Daityas, struck down by the Pramathas,
to life again and again in battle.
Seeing him, all the hosts became agitated and were overcome with fear.
Śaśin reported all of that conduct of Śukra to the Lord of the gods of gods;
then, from the mouth of Rudra, a most terrifying Kṛtyā emerged.
Pressing against trees with my breasts, which were as large as palm fruits and deep as caves,
I reached the battlefield and devoured those great asuras.
Holding Bhārgava in his own hand, he came forward and vanished;
then, seeing Bhārgava thus restrained, the hosts of the Daitya army [were struck with fear].
With their faces withered by pride, those warriors intoxicated by battle struck back;
then the host of Daityas' army, afflicted by fear, broke apart.
Just as a mass of scattered straw is struck down by the force of the wind, so too, seeing the army broken and devoid of fear, the hosts attained great joy. ||26||
Niśumbha, Śumbha, the commander-in-chief, and the valiant Kālanemi—
those three of great strength held back the army of the Gaṇas.
Then they released showers of arrows like clouds in the rainy season;
those floods of the Daityas' arrows were like swarms of locusts.
They obstructed all directions with a tumultuous roar;
the Gaṇas, pierced by hundreds of arrows, rained down a torrent of blood.
Then those hosts—already fallen, being felled, cut, and pierced—could no longer distinguish even the directions;
abandoning the field of battle, they all turned their backs in retreat. (30–31)
Then, seeing their own army broken, those wrathful ones— Gajāsya, Naṃdīśvara, and Kārttikeya— forcibly checked the foremost Daityas who had long been with them.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Daitya Army," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* within the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Satyabhāmā-saṃvāda*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī-Pādme Mahāpurāṇa*, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(101) The One Hundred and First Chapter.
Nārada said:
Seeing the lords of the Gaṇas—Dīpamukha, Ṣaṇmukha, and the others—the Dānavas rushed forward out of indignation for the sake of a duel with them. ||1||
On that day, Kālanemi, Śumbha, Lambodara, and Niśumbha rushed with speed and fury toward Ṣaṇmukha. ||2||
In the month of Kārttika, Niśumbha forcefully pierced him in the heart with five arrows; he then fell down, unconscious.
Then, as the enraged Śaktidhara was about to seize his spear, Niśumbha violently struck him down with his own spear.
Then the Lord pierced Kālanemi with arrows;
he struck down the horses with seven, the banners with seven, and cut off the charioteer with three. (5)
But Kālanemi, becoming enraged, cut off his bow;
casting that aside, he struck him firmly in the chest with a spear.
With his heart pierced by a spear, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
he too, having seized a mountain peak, cast down the mountain Śailādri.
Then Śumbha and Gaṇeśa, traveling on their vehicles— the chariot and the mouse—
fought one another and pierced each other with volleys of arrows.
Then the leader of the hosts pierced Śumbha in the heart with a feathered shaft,
and with five arrows he felled the charioteer to the ground.
Then Śumbha, exceedingly enraged and possessing a voice like a thundercloud, pierced the Lord of the Gaṇas with sixty arrows and the mouse with three from his mouth.
O King, the mouse, having been pierced by the arrow and experiencing intense pain,
emerged from the water and became a foot-soldier with a protruding belly.
Then Lambodara, having struck Śumbha in the heart with his axe,
felled him to the ground and once again mounted his mouse.
Both Kālanemi and Niśumbha, out of anger, simultaneously struck Lambodara with arrows, like a great elephant being struck with a goad.
Seeing him being thus oppressed, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra, accompanied by ten million spirits (bhūtas), then rushed forward with great speed. ||14||
The Kūṣmāṇḍas and Bhairavas, as well as the hosts of Vetālas and Yoginīs, and the multitudes of Piśācas and Yoginīs, also followed him. (15)
Then, with shouts of "kila-kilā," lion-roars accompanied by gurgling sounds, and the resonance of hand-drums, let it fall, shaking the very earth.
Then the bhūtas rushed forward and devoured the dānavas;
they leaped up and fell down repeatedly amidst the host of foot-soldiers.
In that month of Kārttika, those two who had arrived with great haste slaughtered the Daityas in battle with incessant volleys of arrows.
With the Daityas cut, split, struck down, felled, and likewise reviled,
that army then became agitated, their faces dejected.
Then, seeing his army utterly shattered, the powerful son of the Ocean advanced against the hosts of gods in a chariot adorned with many banners.
Then there arose the tumultuous roar of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the sound of kettledrums from the sky,
and the lion-like shouts of both armies.
By the multitudes of Jālandhara’s arrows, as if by masses of mist, the space between heaven and earth became completely covered. ||22||
Having pierced Gaṇeśa with five arrows and even the mountain with five,
he whose voice was like a thundercloud struck Vīrabhadra with twenty from his mouth.
Then, in the month of Kārttika, he swiftly pierced that Daitya with a spear;
struck by the spear and reeling, his mind became somewhat agitated.
Then, his eyes overcome with rage, Kārttikeya struck Jalandhara with a mace, and he fell upon the surface of the earth.
In that very manner, he violently cast him down upon the ground;
thereupon the Lord of the Gaṇas, enraged, shattered the mace with his axe.
Vīrabhadra pierced the Dānava in the heart with three arrows;
with seven more, he cut down the horses, the banners, the bow, and his shield.
Then the lord of the Daityas, exceedingly enraged, raised a terrible spear and struck down Gaṇeśa; he then mounted another chariot.
Then, filled with rage, he rushed impetuously toward Vīrabhadra;
thereafter, those two, resembling the sun, fought with one another.
Vīrabhadra likewise struck down his horses with arrows;
the lord of the Daityas cut off his bow and fought with a club as his weapon.
That Daitya, having approached Vīrabhadra with haste, struck him on the head with an iron club;
and that Daitya, too, had his head split open.
He fell to the ground, vomiting blood. ||31||

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Defeat of the Daitya Army," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā. ||101||
(102) The One Hundred and Second Chapter.
Nārada said:
Seeing Vīrabhadra fallen, the hosts of Rudra, out of fear, abandoned their flight and approached Maheśvara, crying out. ||1||
Then, having heard the clamor of the hosts, the moon-crested Lord [Śiva]— ||2||
Mounted upon his bull, he advanced toward the battle as if laughing;
seeing that Rudra approaching, the Gaṇas again let out lion-like roars.
Having returned, they approached and struck him with showers of arrows;
yet, upon seeing the terrifying Rudra, all the Daityas fled in every direction.
Seeing the one observing the Kārttika vow, the sins fled out of fear of him;
then, in the battle, he beheld the Jālandhara demons fleeing.
In a rage, Śumbha, Niśumbha, Aśvamukha, Kālanemi, and Balāhaka rushed toward Caṇḍīśa, discharging thousands of arrows.
Khaṅgaroman, Apracaṇḍa, and Ghasmara attained auspiciousness;
seeing the host of Gaṇas covered by Bāṇa’s arrows, Śiva [acted].
Having severed that mass of arrows with his own shafts, he then covered the sky;
and by means of gales of arrows, he then afflicted the Daityas.
With floods of fierce net-arrows, he struck [him] down to the ground;
then, out of anger, he severed the head of Khaḍgaroman with a battle-axe.
Having severed the head of Balāhaka with his sword, he split it in two;
then, having bound the Daitya Ghasmara with a noose, he struck him down to the earth.
Some were struck down by the bull, while others were repelled by his arrows;
