the asuras were unable to remain there, just like elephants tormented by a lion.
Then, his soul overcome with anger, Jalandhara, with a voice like the roar of a fierce thunderbolt, challenged Rudra to battle out of impetuosity.
Jalandhara said:
"Fight with me today! What is the use of these [others] being slain for you?
O wearer of matted hair, show whatever strength you possess!"
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, Bāṇa struck the bull-bannered Lord with seventy arrows;
but [the Lord], as if laughing, cut those arrows down with his own sharp shafts before they could reach him.
Then, with seven [arrows], he cut down the horses, the banner, the parasol, and the bow.
His bow being severed and his chariot destroyed, the valiant one took up a mace.
Śiva then rushed forward and split him in two with his mace and arrows; nevertheless, raising his fist, he advanced with the intent to kill Rudra.
Then Jālandhara the Daitya was driven back a distance of one krośa by Śiva’s volleys of arrows;
thereafter, he considered Rudra to be superior in strength.
He created the illusory cow, swift-moving, wonderful, and enchanting to Rudra;
then the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases sang and danced.
They played cymbals, flutes, drums, and cow-horns against one another;
seeing that great wonder, Rudra was bewildered by the sound.
Even though weapons fell from his hands, he was unaware of it;
observing Rudra thus become one-pointed in concentration, the Daitya Jalandhara [reflected].
Afflicted by desire, he went quickly to where Gaurī was staying,
having stationed the two very powerful ones named Śumbha and Niśumbha for battle.
With ten staff-like arms, three eyes, and wearing matted locks,
Jalandhara appeared mounted upon a great bull.
Then, beholding Rudra approaching, Bhavavallabhā emerged from the midst of her companions and came into the path of his vision. (23)
As soon as the lord of the Danujas beheld the lovely-limbed Pārvatī, he discharged his semen, and at that moment he became like a block of wood.
Then, having realized that he was a Dānava, Gaurī, overwhelmed by fear,
vanished on the spot and went to Lake Uttaramānasa.
Not seeing her, who was like a flash of lightning, for a moment, the Daitya then returned with speed to the battle where the bull-bannered god was.
Then Pārvatī also remembered Mahāviṣṇu in her mind;
at that moment, the goddess saw him seated nearby.
Pārvatī said:
"The Daitya Jalandhara performed a most wonderful feat against Viṣṇu;
is that deed of that evil-minded one not known to you? (28)
The Blessed Lord said:
"We too shall follow the very path shown by him;
otherwise, he could not have been slain, for he was well protected by his devotion to her husband."
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu departed for the city of Jālandhara;
meanwhile, Rudra remained at the battlefield, followed by the Gandharvas.
Then, seeing that the illusory power had vanished, Śiva was struck with wonder;
thereafter, his mind filled with astonishment, he went again in anger to battle Jalandhara.
Even though he was a Daitya, seeing Śiva returned once more, he covered him with a flood of arrows in the battle.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Deceit of the Daityas," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(103) The One Hundred and Third Chapter.
Nārada said:
Viṣṇu, having gone to Jālandhara, that city of the Daitya,
incited Vṛndā’s mind toward the violation of her devotion to her husband.
Then, in the midst of her dream, Queen Vṛndārakā saw her husband mounted upon a buffalo, smeared with oil, and naked.
Adorned with black flowers, frequented by hosts of carnivorous beings,
the shaven-headed one then proceeded toward the southern direction, enveloped in darkness.
Then her own city, along with herself, suddenly sank into the ocean;
thereupon the young woman awoke, reflecting upon that as if it were not a dream.
She repeatedly beheld the risen sun as motionless yet pierced by a hole;
perceiving this as an ill omen, she wept, overwhelmed with fear.
Finding no relief anywhere among the city gates, watchtowers, and palace rooftops,
she then went with two female companions to the city garden.
Even there, that foolish woman found no happiness anywhere;
as she wandered from forest to forest, she was not even aware of herself at that time.
Then, while wandering, those two boys saw two extremely terrifying Rākṣasas with lion-like faces, who were fearsome with their fangs and eyes.
Seeing him thus utterly distraught and intent on flight,
he then beheld [the other] with his disciples, their distress completely stilled and established in silence.
Then, out of fear, she spoke thus: "O Sage, protect me who have come to you for refuge, having clung my creeper-like arms to his neck. (10)
Then, seeing her distressed and pursued by the rākṣasas, the sage, out of anger,
made a terrible *huṃ* sound that turned them back.

Terrified by the fear of Yama’s messengers, they looked up toward the sky; then, prostrating themselves on the ground like a staff, they spoke these words to Vṛndā: yaddhuṃ kārabhayatrastaudṛṣṭvātaugaganaṃ gatau | praṇamyadaṇḍavad bhūmau vṛndāvacanam abravīt ||12||
Vṛndā said:
"O ocean of mercy, I have been protected by you from that terrible fear;
I wish to make a certain request, so please listen to it out of compassion. (13)
"O Lord, my husband Jalandhara has gone to fight Rudra; how will he fare in that battle? Tell me this, O observer of excellent vows. (14)
Nārada said:
Having heard those words, he looked upward out of compassion;
at that moment, the two lords of the monkeys arrived, bowed before him, and stood in his presence. (15)
Then, commanded by the signal of her creeper-like eyebrows, the two monkeys went into the sky; having gone there, they returned within half a moment and stood before him. (16)
Seeing the head, the trunk, and the hands of the Son of the Ocean,
she fell to the ground in a swoon, distressed by the calamity that had befallen her husband.
Then, sprinkled with water from his water-pot and comforted by the sage, she,
placing her husband’s forehead upon her own forehead, ascended the pyre without distress.
Vṛndā said: O Lord, why do You not speak today to me, Your beloved who am innocent, with whom You formerly took delight in pleasant conversations? (19)
How was he, by whom the gods along with the Gandharvas and Hari were conquered, slain by you, an ascetic—though you yourself are a conqueror of the three worlds? (20)
Nārada said:
Having thus wept, Vṛndā then spoke these words to the sage.
Vṛndā said:
O treasure-house of compassion, O best of sages, this life of mine is very dear to me.
"In my view, you alone are capable of restoring him to life.
Then, having heard those words, the sage smiled and said:
The sage said:
"He cannot be restored to life, having been slain by Rudra in battle;
nevertheless, filled with compassion for you, I shall restore him to life in this manner. (23)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, he vanished; at that very moment, the son of the Ocean embraced Vṛndā and, with a joyful heart, kissed her face. 24.
Then Vṛndā too, her mind filled with joy upon seeing her husband,
took delight in his company for many days while staying in the midst of that forest.
Once, at the conclusion of their amorous play, having seen that very Viṣṇu, Vṛndā, filled with anger, rebuked him and spoke these words. ||26||
Vṛndā said:
"Fie on this conduct of yours, O Hari, you who approach the wives of others!
You have been thoroughly recognized by me as a deceptive ascetic in person. (27)
Those two gatekeepers of your own whom you showed me through your magic power—they shall become Rākṣasas and carry off your wife. (28)
And you too, O wife, though afflicted by suffering, wander in the forest with him as your companion—he who has become your disciple, this Lord of All. (29)
Having spoken thus, Vṛndā then entered the fire, her mind fixed upon him even though she was being restrained by Viṣṇu. (30)
Then Hari, repeatedly remembering her, remained right there,
covered with the dust and ashes of Vṛndā’s funeral pyre,
along with hosts of sages and perfected beings.
Even though being awakened, he did not attain peace. ||31||

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Entry into the Fire of Vṛndā’s Funeral Pyre," in the Kārttika-māhātmya of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī-Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(104) The One Hundred and Fourth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Then Jalandhara, seeing Rudra of wondrous prowess,
created Gaurī through his illusory power (māyā) in order to delude the Three-eyed Lord at that time.
Then Śiva saw her standing atop the chariot weeping,
and he beheld her being struck by the Daityas Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Seeing Gaurī in such a state, Śiva too became troubled in mind;
forgetting his own prowess, he stood silent with his face cast downwards. (3)
Then Jalandhara, with speed, pierced Rudra with three arrows—
sunk up to their feathers— in the head, the chest, and the belly.
Then, awakened by Viṣṇu, he understood the illusion of the virtuous;
assuming a fierce form, he became exceedingly terrifying with garlands of flames. ||5||
Seeing his exceedingly great and terrible form, the great asuras were unable to stand before him and fled in the ten directions.
Then the god pronounced a curse upon those two, Śumbha and Niśumbha:
"Having fled from my battle, you shall both be slain by Gaurī. (7)
Again, Jalandhara swiftly rained down sharpened arrows,
so that the vast surface of the earth was completely shrouded in the darkness of shafts.
As Rudra, acting with haste, cut down his arrows,
the powerful one quickly struck the bull with an iron club.
By that blow, Vṛṣa turned away from the field of battle;
though being dragged by Rudra, he did not remain upon the battlegrounds. ||10||
Then Rudra, extremely enraged and assuming a fierce form,
swiftly hurled the Sudarśana discus, which possessed the brilliance of the sun.
Then, having reached Jalandhara while burning heaven and earth with its impetus,
it severed from his body that head which possessed large, wide eyes.
The body fell from the chariot onto the earth, making the surface of the ground resound;
and a radiance emerged from the body and entered Rudra.
Having seen that splendor arising from his body and having gone to the mountain of Gaurī’s Lord, Indra and the other gods then had their eyes wide open with joy. (14)
Having bowed his head to Rudra, he reported the deeds of Viṣṇu.
The gods said: "O Mahādeva, O God, we have been protected by you from the fear born of our enemies. (15)
Something else has arisen there; what shall we do?
Viṣṇu, bewildered by Vṛndā’s beauty, stands utterly infatuated. (16)
The Lord said: "O gods, go for refuge to Viṣṇu for the removal of this delusion;
seek the protection of Māyā, who is the dispeller of delusion; she will accomplish your purpose. (17)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished along with the hosts of elemental beings;
then the gods praised Mūlaprakṛti, who is affectionate toward her devotees. 18.
The gods said:
We bow to that pure primordial nature (prakṛti), from whose arising the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas proceed as the instrumental cause for creation, maintenance, and destruction;
and by whose will this entire universe expands through existence and non-existence. 19.
We bow to her who was formerly established throughout the entire world in twenty-three forms;
even the three gods, though they know her forms and actions, do not know her true nature. 20.

Those persons who are constantly endowed with devotion never encounter poverty, delusion, defeat, and the like; for we always bow to that Prakṛti of Viṣṇu, who is ever affectionate toward her devotees. (21)
Nārada said:
Whoever recites this hymn at the three junctions of the day with a one-pointed mind, poverty, delusion, and sorrows shall never touch him. (22)
Praising him thus, those gods beheld there in the sky a circle of splendor, which pervaded the quarters with its flames.
From within that [mass], everyone beheld Bhāratī moving through the sky, saying:
"I myself abide divided threefold by means of the three qualities (guṇas). (24)
Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Svarā, and Aceti, through the qualities of Rajas, Sattva, and Tamas,
shall go there and carry out that task for you, O gods.
Nārada said:
O King, as the gods were listening, that great light vanished from their sight;
at that moment, the eyes of the gods blossomed wide with wonder.
Then all those gods, having arrived as urged by his words,
bowed down with devotion to Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Svarā.
Then, O King, seeing those gods prostrate before them, the goddesses who are compassionate toward their devotees gave seeds to them and spoke these words.
The goddesses said:
"Sow these seeds of the field wherever Viṣṇu resides;
from that, your task shall attain success. (29)

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Jālandhara," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the *Śrī-Pādma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(105) The One Hundred and Fifth Chapter.
Nārada said:
O best of kings, from the seeds sown there, three kinds of plants arose: the dhātrī, the mālatī, and the tulasī.
The *dhātrī* is known as arising from *dhātṛ*, while *mālatī* is known as arising from *mā*;
and *gaurī* arises from *bhava*. These possess the qualities of *tamas*, *sattva*, and *rajas* respectively. ||2||
O King, upon seeing those two in the form of women, who were like goddesses of youth, Viṣṇu then rose up in agitation,
infatuated by their extraordinary beauty.
Then, out of delusion, he beheld them with a mind attached to desire; and Tulasī and Dhātrī also gazed upon him with passion. ||4||
That seed of Lakṣmī which had been previously bestowed by Māyā herself—because she was born from that, the woman became filled with jealousy toward her. (5)
Therefore, this extremely despicable plant called *ābarbarī*—which is a *dhātrī* and a *tulasī*—bestows affection upon that [Mādhava] because of its red color. (6)
Then, his suffering forgotten, Viṣṇu, who is saluted by all the gods, went joyfully to Vaikuṇṭha together with those two.
Therefore, on the full moon day of Kārttika, the rite of completing the vow for Viṣṇu is prescribed;
for she (Tulasī) is remembered as the bestower of delight when placed at the root of the Tulasī plant. ||8||
O King, that house in which a grove of Tulasī stands is indeed of the nature of a sacred pilgrimage site; the servants of Yama do not enter it. (9)
Those best of men who plant a grove of Tulasī— which removes all sins, is meritorious, and grants all desires— do not behold the Son of the Sun (Yama).
Beholding the Narmadā, bathing in the Gaṅgā, and contact with a grove of Tulasī—these three are considered equal. (11)
By planting, protecting, sprinkling, seeing, or touching it, Tulasī destroys the sins accumulated by men through speech, mind, and body. (12)
He who performs the worship of Hari and Hara with Tulasī sprouts does not enter the chamber of the womb; he attains liberation, of this there is no doubt. (13)
The sacred fords such as Puṣkara, the rivers such as the Gaṅgā, and the gods such as Vāsudeva all abide within a leaf of tulasī. (14)
If one gives up their life-breaths while holding a sprout of Tulasī, they attain union with Viṣṇu; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O best of kings. (15)
Even Yama is unable to look upon one who gives up his life while smeared with the earth of tulasī, even if he is joined by hundreds of sins. 16.
If a person wears sandalwood paste produced from Tulasī wood, sin shall not touch his body, even while it is being committed here. (17)
O King, wherever there may be the shade of a grove of Tulasī trees, there one should perform the Śrāddha; what is given to the ancestors there becomes inexhaustible. (18)
O best of kings, he who offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the shade of the Dhātrī tree causes his ancestors, even those residing in hell, to attain satisfaction. (19)
O best of kings, he who carries a dhātrī fruit upon his head, in his hand, in his mouth, and on his body, should be known as Hari himself.
He in whose body the fruit of the dhātrī, the earth from a tulasī plant, and earth from Dvārakā reside constantly is called liberated while living. (21)
The merit of bathing in the Gaṅgā is said to belong to that man who bathes with water mixed with dhātrī fruits and mingled with tulasī leaves. ||22||
A person should perform the worship of the gods even with *dhātrī* leaves or fruits;
he shall obtain the fruit of worship performed with various flowers made of gold. (23)
In the month of Kārttika, when the sun has entered Libra, all holy fords, sages, gods, and sacrifices constantly abide by resorting to the Dhātrī tree.
That man who plucks a Tulasī leaf on the twelfth lunar day, or a Dhātrī leaf in the month of Kārttika, shall go to most contemptible hells. (25)
Whoever eats food while taking shelter in the shade of a Dhātrī tree during the month of Kārttika, the sin arising from contact with impure food perishes for him for the duration of a year. ||26||
But that man who worships Viṣṇu at the root of a Dhātrī tree during the month of Kārttika has, in effect, always been worshipped in all the sacred abodes of Viṣṇu. (27)
Even the four-faced god Brahmā would not be capable of describing the greatness of the Dhātrī and Tulasī plants as fully as that of the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow.
Whoever hears with devotion the account of the origin of the Dhātrī and Tulasī plants, or causes others to hear it,
shall have his sins shaken off along with his ancestors.
He goes to heaven, seated upon a preeminent celestial vehicle. ||29||
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the *Kārttika-māhātmya*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā,
[this is] the chapter titled "The Greatness of the Dhātrī and Tulasī Trees."
The one hundred and fifth chapter. ||105||
(106) The one hundred and sixth chapter. Pṛthu said:
O Brahman, this great account of the majesty of Tulasī, which is full of wonders, has been properly heard by me as it was narrated by you. (1)
The great fruit that has been proclaimed for a man who observes the Ūrja vow—tell me again about that majesty, and by whom was this practiced, and how? (2)
Nārada said: In ancient times, in the city of Karavīra within the region of the Sahya mountains,
there was a certain Brāhmaṇa named Dharmadatta, who was highly renowned and well-versed in dharma.
Constantly performing the vows of Viṣṇu and always devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, he was intent on the recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra and fond of guests. ||4||
Once, in the month of Kārttika, for the sake of keeping a vigil for Hari,
he went to the temple of Hari at the fourth watch of the night when only a small portion of the moon remained.
Then, as he was going along carrying the implements for the worship of Hari,
he saw a demoness of terrifying roar approaching.
With curved fangs, face, and tongue, her bloodshot eyes were sunken;
naked, with parched flesh and hanging lips, she had a gurgling voice. (7)
Seeing her, trembling in every limb and terrified with fear, he then struck out in haste with the ritual implements and with water out of dread. (8)
And by remembering the name of Hari and using water mixed with tulasī, all her sins, along with their accompanying torments, went to destruction.
Then, having recollected her own condition arising from the ripening of the karma of her previous birth,
she prostrated herself like a staff before him and spoke it all.
Kalahā said:
"Indeed, I have reached this state as the ripening of my past karma;
how then shall I again attain the auspicious, supreme goal? (11)
Nārada said: Seeing her prostrated before him, speaking of her own deeds,
the brahmin was greatly amazed and then spoke these words.
Dharmadatta said: "By what ripening of karma have you come to such a state? From where do you come, who are you, and what is your character? Tell me all of that. (13)
Kalahā said:
O Brahmin, in the city of Saurāṣṭra there was a twice-born man named Bhikṣu;
formerly, I was his wife, known as Kalahā, and exceedingly cruel. (14)
Never have I performed even a single auspicious act at my husband's word; out of disregard for my husband's command, I did not offer him sweet food. (15)
Then that twice-born man, constantly agitated by fear because of his wife who was ever fond of quarreling, resolved to marry another woman. ||16||
Then, O twice-born one, having taken that house, my life was surrendered by me;
thereafter, the followers of Yama bound me as I was being bound and led me away.
Then Yama, having seen me, questioned Citragupta.
Yama said:
"O Citragupta, examine what karma has been performed by her."
"Let him receive the fruit of his actions, whether auspicious or indeed inauspicious.
Then Citragupta, rebuking him, spoke these words: ||19||
Citragupta said:
"Indeed, no auspicious deed whatsoever has been performed by her;
she ate sweet food that was offered by her husband."
Therefore, let her dwell in the womb of a bat, feeding upon her own excrement and the like;
for she constantly causes strife and acts as a source of hatred toward her husband. (21)
"O Hari, let her remain thereafter in the womb of a sow that eats excrement;
for she has always and constantly eaten from the cooking pot in this very manner. (22)
Therefore, because of that fault, this female cat, who devours her own offspring, has committed suicide by means of this woman on account of her husband. (23)
Therefore, let her remain among the most reviled ghosts and piśācas;
and from there, she must be brought to the region of Aruṇa along with the soldiers.
There, this [soul] remains for a long time in what is called the body of a preta;
thus, having experienced these three wombs, she who performs unwholesome deeds [remains]. 25.
Kalahā said:
"I am indeed that very one who has remained for five hundred years within a dead body, constantly tormented by hunger and thirst, suffering due to my own karma. (26)
Then, constantly afflicted by hunger, I, that merchant, went from my body to the southern region at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā and Veṇī rivers.
As long as she remained on its bank,
I was forcibly dragged far away from his body by the hosts of Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Then, O twice-born one, you were seen by me as I was emaciated by hunger;
I was one whose sins had been removed through contact with the water used for washing *tulasī*.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, show me your compassion; how may I attain liberation from this most terrifying triple-birth and from this body of a corpse? (30)
Having thus heard Kalahā’s words, the brahmin was filled with wonder and sorrow born from the ripening of that karma;
his mental state moved by compassion upon seeing her distress, he reflected for a long time and spoke these words out of grief.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kalaha," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa within the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(107) The one hundred and seventh chapter.
Dharmadatta said:
Sins are dissolved by means of pilgrimages, gifts, vows, and so forth;
however, for one who remains in the body of a *preta*, there is no eligibility for these [remedies]. (1)
Seeing this exhaustion of yours, my own mind is pierced with grief; it finds no peace at all until I have rescued you from your suffering.
Your extremely terrible sin, which brings about ripening in three wombs, cannot be exhausted by any other merits; nor can this most contemptible state of being a ghost. (3)
Therefore, by means of half the merit of this Kārttika vow which I have observed since birth, may you attain a good rebirth. ||4||
Sacrifices, gifts, pilgrimages, and even other vows can by no means equal the merit of the Kārttika vow; this is indeed certain. (5)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, as soon as Dharmadatta consecrated her with water mixed with *tulasī* while causing her to hear the twelve-syllable mantra, [the transformation occurred].
Then, liberated from her state as a preta, she appeared like a blazing crest of fire;
assuming a divine body, she illuminated the quarters with her extraordinary beauty.
Then, prostrating herself on the ground like a staff, she bowed to that twice-born man and spoke these words, her voice faltering with joy: (8)
Kalahā said:
"O best of the twice-born, by your grace I have been liberated from hell; for me, who was sinking in the ocean of sin, you have certainly become my boat. (9)
Nārada said: While she was speaking thus to the brāhmaṇa, she saw a radiant celestial chariot approaching from afar, yoked with hosts of attendants bearing the emblems of Viṣṇu.
Then Dharmadatta, filled with wonder, beheld that celestial chariot— which was attended by hosts of apsarases and ascended by Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla, the two gatekeepers of the preeminent Sāta-vimāna.
Seeing those two of meritorious form, he fell to the ground like a staff. ||12||
Having raised up the twice-born Puṇyaśīlasuśīla, who was bowed down,
those two virtuous ones spoke these compassionate words.
The two Gaṇas said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born! Since you are Viṣṇu, you are therefore always compassionate toward the wretched, a knower of dharma, and devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu. (14)
For this auspiciousness of hers, accumulated from birth, has been surpassed by half of the merit you have earned through performing the Kārttika vow. (15)
The sin accumulated over hundreds of previous births has dissolved away;
and through the vigil for Hari and other such acts, this celestial chariot has arrived.
Those who attain the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, the proximity of Viṣṇu, and his very own form—they are blessed, they have fulfilled their purpose, and their birth has become fruitful. (17)
Since Viṣṇu was propitiated by you with devotion just as he was by Dharmadatta, what indeed will Viṣṇu, when properly worshipped, not bestow upon embodied beings? (18)
By whom, the son of Uttānapāda, Dhruva was formerly established in his station;
by the mere remembrance of whose name embodied beings attain the supreme goal. 19.
In ancient times, the lord of serpents, seized by a crocodile, was liberated by the mere remembrance [of this name]; having attained his presence, he became known as Yojana. (20)
Therefore, Viṣṇu, being worshipped by you, will grant his own presence.
For many thousands of years, you have been accompanied by these two wives.
Then, when your merit has been exhausted and you descend to the surface of the earth,
you shall become a king born of the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa), renowned by name.
There was a king named Daśaratha, accompanied by two wives;
when he requested a third wife, she became the sharer of half his merit.
There, Viṣṇu will go to the surface of the earth due to the proximity of your penance;
having assumed himself the state of being your son, he will accomplish the work of the gods. (24)
Compared to this vow of yours, which brings such satisfaction to Viṣṇu, neither sacrifices, nor knowledge, nor gifts, nor sacred pilgrimage sites are superior. (25)
"Blessed are you, O Brahmin, for through your devotion this vow, which brings satisfaction to the Teacher of the World, has been performed by you;
by virtue of half the fruit of this, we are being led by you to the same world as Murāri. (26)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Quarrel," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
The one hundred and eighth chapter.
Nārada said:
Having heard those words in this manner, Dharmadatta was filled with wonder.
Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, he spoke these words: "Ha! (1)
Dharmadatta said:
"All indeed propitiate Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the distress of his devotees,
through sacrifices, gifts, vows, pilgrimages, and austerities, according to the prescribed rules."
It brings pleasure to Viṣṇu and creates His presence for them;
indeed, by performing it, all [other] observances are truly accomplished.
The two Gaṇas said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, you have asked well; listen with a one-pointed mind to this story, together with its history, which was told of old."
Long ago, there was a king named Cola, a universal monarch (cakravartin), in the city of Kāñcī; indeed, it is said that the countries were called "Cola" after his name.
While he ruled the circle of the earth, there was no man who was poor or distressed;
nor was there anyone with an evil mind or afflicted by disease.
Both banks of the Tāmraparṇī river belonging to that performer of endless sacrifices were richly adorned with golden sacrificial posts and resembled the celestial chariot of Indra.
O twice-born one, once the king went to that bed where the Lord of the worlds dwells in yogic sleep.
There, O King, having worshipped the Lord Śrīramaṇa according to the prescribed rites with divine gems, pearls, and beautiful golden flowers; ||9||
While he was prostrating like a staff and remained seated there,
he beheld that brāhmaṇa approaching in the presence of the God.
They saw that twice-born man, a resident of their own city and a servant of Viṣṇu, approaching there with Tulasī and water in his hands for the purpose of worshipping the gods.
Having arrived there, that brahmin sage worshipped the God of gods;
having bathed Him with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, he offered him the leaves of tulasī blossoms.
Seeing that his worship with jewels had been thus eclipsed by the worship of Tulasī, the king became enraged and spoke these words: ||13||
The King said:
"O Viṣṇudāsa, how is it that this [image], which was made by me and enriched with the splendor of worship with rubies and gold, has been covered here with tulasī leaves? (14)
"You do not know devotion to Viṣṇu; in my opinion, you are a wretch, you who indeed conceal this most splendid worship! (15)
Having heard those words, that best of brahmins, filled with anger and disregarding the king's dignity, then spoke these words. (16)
Viṣṇudāsa said:
"O King, you do not know liberation; you are arrogant because of your royal splendor.
Tell me, what vow to Viṣṇu did you perform in the past? (17)
The two attendants said:
Having heard those words of the brahmin, that best of kings laughed and then spoke these words to Viṣṇudāsa out of pride, O twice-born one. (18)
If you speak thus, O brahmin, being excessively proud of your devotion to Viṣṇu, then how great can your devotion to Viṣṇu be, you who are so poor and destitute? (19)
O Brahmin, you have never before performed sacrifices, acts of charity, or anything else that brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu, nor have you ever constructed a temple for the gods. (20)
Even for one such as this, devotion remains steadfast;
listen now to that [account] from me today, O best of the twice-born, for all these [others] are present here.
"This speech of mine shall lead to the direct realization of Viṣṇu;
through it, all of you shall likewise come to know devotion to both of us. (22)
The two attendants said:
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed for his own royal palace along with the king;
he then commenced a Vaiṣṇava sacrificial session, having appointed Mudgala as the officiating priest (ācārya).
It was frequented by hosts of sages and featured abundant sacrificial fees,
just like the prosperous sacrifice performed by Brahmā in the past at the sacred field of Gayā.
Viṣṇudāsa also remained right there in that temple, observing his vow.
Having always observed these five rules which bring satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
The vow of Māgha and Kārttika should be properly observed, as well as the protection of the Tulasī grove;
the Ekādaśī vow should be performed with the recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra.
With the sixteen types of offerings, including song, dance, and other such delights,
he performed the daily worship of Viṣṇu as well as these various vows.
Constantly remembering Viṣṇu even while walking, eating, or sleeping, he,
possessing equal vision, beheld Viṣṇu residing within all beings.
For the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, he constantly observed special observances during the months of Māgha and Kārttika, as well as the ritual for their formal conclusion.

Thus, as those two— the Lord of Cola and Viṣṇudāsa— remained steadfast in their vows, dedicated to Him, and performed actions with their organs of action fixed upon Him, a great deal of time passed while they were propitiating the Lord of Śrī.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the *Kārttika-māhātmya*,
within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā, in the narrative of the quarrel.
The one hundred and eighth chapter. ||108||
(109) The one hundred and ninth chapter.
The two attendants said:
Once, the brahmin Viṣṇudāsa, having performed his daily obligatory rites, was engaged in the work of cooking when someone, remaining unnoticed, carried it away. (1)
Even though he did not see that rice-porridge, the twice-born one did not prepare it again at that time; out of fear of breaking his vow, he refrained from performing the evening worship.
On the second day, having prepared the cooked food from that [same] source, just as he was about to offer it as an oblation to Viṣṇu, someone stole it once again. (3)
O twice-born one, when his food had thus been carried off by someone for seven days, he was filled with wonder and reflected within his mind as follows: ||4||
"Aha! Who comes daily and carries away my cooked food?
This place of those who have renounced their fields must by no means be abandoned by me. (5)
If I were to cook again and eat here, how could I then abandon this evening worship? (6)
"I must not eat this without having prepared some cooked food;
indeed, nothing that has not been offered to Hari is ever consumed by Vaiṣṇavas. (7)
Having fasted, how shall I remain here established in my vow? Today I shall properly perform the preservation of this cooked food.
Having thus prepared the food, he remained right there unobserved;
meanwhile, he saw a Caṇḍāla intent on taking away the cooked meal.
Seeing him emaciated by hunger, with a dejected face, and reduced to nothing but skin and bone, that foremost of the twice-born became filled with compassion in his heart.
Seeing the Brahmin carrying food, he said, "Stop! Stop! [The Brahmin replied: "Why do you speak so harshly? O sir, take this ghee. (11)
Seeing that foremost of brahmins speaking thus and observing that [other] person approaching, he ran forward with speed; out of fear of him, he fainted and fell down.
Seeing that Cāṇḍāla terrified and unconscious, that best of the twice-born approached him with speed and, out of compassion, fanned him with his own garments. (13)
Then Viṣṇudāsa beheld him who had just arisen—
Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Yellow-robed, four-armed, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark on his chest, wearing a crown,
resembling an Atasī flower, with the Kaustubha gem upon his broad breast— the all-pervading Lord.
Seeing him, that best of the twice-born was overwhelmed by ecstatic emotions; at that moment, he was unable even to offer praise or prostration.
Then Śakra and the other gods arrived at that very spot;
the Gandharvas and Apsarasas also sang and danced with joy.
At that time, that place became crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots, thronged by hosts of divine sages, and filled with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
Then Viṣṇu, having embraced his own devotee who was likewise of a sattvic nature,
granted him union with his own self and led him to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
In the presence of Viṣṇu,
King Cola, having been initiated, beheld Viṣṇudāsa seated upon the form of a supreme celestial chariot.
Upon seeing that servant of Viṣṇu who had gone to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, he hurriedly called his own guru, Mudgala, and spoke these words: ||21||
Cola said:
"That brāhmaṇa who, out of rivalry with me, performed these acts such as sacrifice and charity, now goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, having assumed the form of Viṣṇu. (22)

"By me, having been initiated, the oblation has been properly offered into the fire for Viṣṇu during this sacrificial session; and the brahmins have been satisfied by you with gifts and other offerings. (23)
Even now, the Lord has certainly not become fully propitious;
yet, solely through the devotion of that brahmin, Hari granted him a direct vision.
Therefore, Viṣṇu is not pleased by gifts or sacrifices;
devotion alone is the supreme means for the vision of the All-pervading Lord. (25)
The two Gaṇas said:
Having spoken thus and consecrated their own nephew upon the royal throne, [they departed],
for he had been initiated into sacrifice since childhood and had thereby attained the status of a son to them.
Therefore, even today in that region, the maternal nephews alone have always been the sharers of the royal portion, following the conduct established by him. (27)
Then, having approached the sacrificial ground, he stood before the fire-pit and loudly proclaimed three times, thereby awakening Viṣṇu at that moment.
"O Viṣṇu, grant me firm devotion through the actions of my mind, speech, and body.
Having said this, he fell into the fire while everyone was looking on. (29)
Out of anger at being praised by Mudgala, he plucked out his own crest-lock;
from that time until today, those of his lineage have been known as the Mudgalāviśikhas.
At that moment, Viṣṇu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared from the fire of the sacrificial pit;
Acyuta embraced him and caused him to ascend the foremost of celestial chariots.
Embracing him and granting him a form identical to his own, the Lord of Gods went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha together with him, surrounded by the deities.
Nārada said:
He who was Viṣṇudāsa was indeed of virtuous character,
and that king of Cola was named Suśīla.
Both of these, possessing forms identical to his own, were made by that beloved of Ramā to serve as his gatekeepers. ||33||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Quarrel," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(110) The One Hundred and Tenth Chapter.
Dharmadatta said:
I have heard that Jaya and Vijaya were the two gatekeepers of Viṣṇu; but what was performed by them in the past, because of which they now bear those forms? (1)
The two attendants said:
O twice-born one, in former times, by the mere glance of Kardama, two sons were born to him from Devahūti, the daughter of Tṛṇabindu. (2)
The elder was named Jaya and the younger Vijaya;
later, from another wife, there was Kapila, who was a knower of the dharma of yoga.
Both Jaya and Vijaya were always devoted to Viṣṇu; having fully restrained the collection of their senses, they became virtuous in character. (4)
Both were constant performers of the eight-syllable mantra and observers of the vow of Viṣṇu;
Viṣṇu always granted them direct vision during their perpetual worship.
Once, when Marutta had invited them to a sacrificial rite, those two,
who were skilled in sacrifice and honored by hosts of celestial sages, went there.
There, Brahmā became the Jayas and Vijaya became the Yājaka;
then they both performed the entire sacrificial rite in its full perfection.
After Maruta had performed the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*), he gave much wealth to those two;
taking that wealth, they both departed for their own hermitage. (8)
O Sage, at that time, while the two of them were dividing that wealth for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu through sacrifice,
they began to compete with one another.
Jaya said, "Let the portion be made equal," but there he was afraid; and Vijaya said, "In that case, whatever is obtained by whom, let that belong to him."
Then Jaya, his mind agitated by anger, cursed Vijaya:
"Having seized this [conch] of yours, you shall therefore become a crocodile. (11)
Having heard that curse, Vijaya also cursed him; because he had cursed him while deluded by intoxication, [Vijaya said]: "Therefore, go to the state of a female elephant. (12)
Having seen the omnipresent Lord Viṣṇu during his daily worship,
the two of them spoke thus and entreated the Lord of Lakṣmī for the cessation of their curse.
"O Lord, O ocean of mercy, how shall we two, who are your devotees, become crocodiles born from the womb of fish? Let that curse be revoked. (14)
The Blessed Lord said:
The word of My two devotees shall never become untrue;
even by Me, it can never be made otherwise.
Indeed, in the past, I manifested even within a pillar at the word of Prahlāda;
likewise, by the speech of Ambarīṣa, I truly appeared of my own accord on the road. 16.
"Therefore, having experienced these two curses of their own making, they shall surely attain my eternal abode. Having spoken thus, Hari vanished.
The two Gaṇas said:
Then, on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī, they became two female elephants;
remembering their former births, they remained steadfast in their vows to Viṣṇu even within that womb. (18)
Once, accompanied by his elephant, he went to the Gaṇḍakī river in the month of Kārttika to bathe; at that moment, a crocodile seized him as he remembered the cause of his curse.
Seized by a crocodile, that Nāga then remembered the Lord of Śrī;
at that moment, Viṣṇu appeared, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Then, having cast away the wheel of the demon Taugrāhamātanga, the Lord lifted them both up,
granted them his own form, and led them to Vaikuṇṭha.
From that time onwards, that place has been known as Harikṣetra;
for here, even a stone was split asunder by the friction of the discus.
"O twice-born one, these two who were mentioned by you as Jaya and Vijaya are world-renowned; they are the two gatekeepers who are eternally dear to Viṣṇu. (23)
Therefore, you too, O knower of dharma, who are eternally established in the vow of Viṣṇu, must abandon envy and malice and become one who perceives all things with equanimity. 24.
Always bathe at dawn during the months of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries;
remain steadfast in the vow of Ekādaśī as a protector of the Tulasī grove. ||25||
Always honor the brāhmaṇas, the cows, and the Vaiṣṇavas;
and do not eat masūra lentils, arānāla, or eggplants.
In this same way, O Dharmadatta, you too shall attain that supreme abode of Viṣṇu within the body, solely through devotion to Him, just as we have.
Therefore, compared to this vow of yours which brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu,
neither sacrifices, nor charities, nor pilgrimages are indeed superior.
"O foremost of Brahmins, you are blessed, for by you this vow, which brings satisfaction to the Teacher of the World, has been performed;
since we are being led to the same world as Murāri, which is the fruit obtained through a share of that merit. (29)
Nārada said:
Having thus instructed Dharmadatta, those two,
traveling in their celestial chariot, went together with that woman to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Dharmadatta, having conceived faith and remained steadfast in that vow,
reached that abode of the Lord upon the exhaustion of his body, accompanied by his two wives.
That man who hears this history of the past according to the prescribed rule obtains, through the grace of the Teacher of the World, an intellect that brings one into the presence of Hari. (32)
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the Kārttika-māhātmya, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā,
in the narrative of the quarrel, [this is] the chapter titled "The Description of the Former Merits of the Gaṇas."
The one hundred and tenth chapter. ||110||
(111) The one hundred and eleventh chapter. Pṛthu said:
O Lord, you have previously related how, on the banks of the Kṛṣṇaveṇī and other places, a quarrel arose between the hosts of Śiva and Viṣṇu due to the body of a merchant.
"Is this the power of those two rivers, or of that sacred field? Tell me that, O knower of dharma; for my wonder here is great. (2)
Nārada said:
Kṛṣṇa is the manifest form of Kṛṣṇa, and Maheśvara is the Lord of the Veṇī;
even the Four-faced One (Brahmā) is not capable of fully describing the power of their union.
Nevertheless, I shall proclaim its origin; listen to that.
Formerly, in the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu, there was the god Pitāmaha.
On the beautiful peak of the Sahya mountain, he prepared for a sacrifice;
having gathered all the sacrificial materials, he was surrounded by hosts of all the gods.
Accompanied by Hari and Hara, he went to the peak of that mountain during the hour presided over by Brahmā,
while Bhṛgu and other hosts of sages were present.
They performed the assembly for his initiation rites there;
then Viṣṇu had the twice-born invite his eldest wife, Svarā.
While he was approaching with haste, Bhṛgu spoke to Viṣṇu:
"Bhṛgu said:
'O Viṣṇu, she has been summoned by you, yet she does not come here with speed.'"
"If this initiation rite for the task is to be performed after a moment has passed, how can it be done?
Viṣṇu said: "If he does not arrive quickly, then let the Gāyatrī be employed here."
"Even she does not become his wife; who [else] is there for this meritorious deed?
Nārada said:
"In this very way, Rudra also approved of Viṣṇu’s words. (10)
Having heard those words of Bhṛgu, he then seated Gāyatrī on the right side of Brahmā and performed the ritual of initiation.
While they were performing his initiation ceremony according to the prescribed rules,
O King, Svarāja arrived there at the site of the sacrifice.
Then, seeing that Gāyatrī had been initiated along with Brahmā, Sarasvatī, out of jealousy, malice, and anger, spoke these words in a harsh tone: ||13||
Svarā said:
"Where those unworthy of worship are worshipped, and where there is transgression against those worthy of worship, three things will arise there: famine, death, and fear. (14)
This [power] of mine has been bestowed upon you by me with manifold ends;
therefore, you shall all become insentient and assume various forms. (15)
And because she sat upon this seat on the southern side,
therefore that river always carries a body that is invisible to people.
Nārada said:
Then, having heard that curse, Gāyatrī trembled; rising up even as she was being restrained by the gods, she cursed her own voice.
"Just as your husband is to Brahmā, so indeed am I to him;
since you have cursed me in vain, you too shall become a river. (18)
Nārada said:
Then all the gods, headed by Śiva and Viṣṇu, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!
[thinking], "Surely these three worlds will now go to destruction. (19)
The gods said:
"O Goddess, we all, beginning with Brahmā, have now been cursed by you;
if we all become inert and turn into rivers here. (20)
Indeed, these three lights will certainly perish;
therefore, this curse was uttered out of a lack of discrimination—let it be revoked. (21)
Svāhā said: "O best of gods, because the Lord of the Gaṇas was not worshipped at the beginning of the sacrifice, this obstacle has indeed arisen from my anger. (22)
Indeed, these words of mine do not turn out to be untrue;
therefore, O rivers, you have become paralyzed by your own [excessive] pride. 23.
"O Goddesses, we two shall also become co-wives of the Narmadā;
here, O gods, we shall flow toward the west. (24)
Nārada said: O King,
having heard those words, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara became as if paralyzed,
like rivers whose waters have been checked by their own banks.
There, Viṣṇu became the god Kṛṣṇaveṇyā and Maheśvara [became] Brahmā; at that time, the Gaṅgā Kakudminī appeared as something entirely distinct.
Having paralyzed the gods and the Asuras with his arrows,
those great rivers flowed separately from the peaks of the Sahya mountain.
The best of rivers, flowing eastward, became the Devaśai; and then Gāyatrī and Svarā flowed toward the west.
Through yoga, those two rivers attained the renown of being called Sāvitrī;
there, at that sacrifice, both Hari and Hara were installed by Brahmā.
Two goddesses named Mahābalā and Atibalā came into being.
O King, I am not capable of describing the majesty of those two rivers;
even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, have departed, and the streams remain as they were. (30)

Whoever listens with devotion to this supreme account of the origin of Kṛṣṇa, which destroys sins, or causes others to hear it, for him every action becomes meritorious; he obtains the fruit arising from seeing Him and bathing [in His presence].

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Kṛṣṇā and Veṇyā Rivers," in the Kārttika-māhātmya of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā. 111.
(112) The one hundred and twelfth chapter. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard those words, O beloved, Pṛthu, his mind filled with wonder, honored Nārada with devotion and then bid him farewell. (1)
Therefore, these three vows are indeed exceedingly dear to me:
those of Māgha and Kārttika, as well as the Ekādaśī vow. ||2||
Among forest trees, Tulasī is dear to me; among months, Kārttika is dear; among lunar days, Ekādaśī is dear; and among sacred fields, Dvārakā is mine. (3)
But he who, having conquered his senses, practices service toward these [deities], attains my favor; not so by means of sacrifices and the like. (4)
O beloved, by serving these [deities] through my grace, one need not fear sins, nor even from religious observances (niyama). ||5||
Satyabhāmā said:
"O Lord, that which you have told me is truly astonishing—that by the merit given by another, Kalahā attained liberation. (6)
Thus is the power of this month of Kārttika, which brings you prosperity,
since sins such as treachery against one's master have been removed through ritual bathing and charity.
O Lord, one obtains the merit that has been performed by another when it is given;
but by what means does a human being obtain even that which has not been given? (8)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen now to how merit and even sins, though not intentionally committed by men, are nonetheless experienced through their actions; hear this exactly as it is. 9.
In the [previous] ages, regions, villages, and families were the sharers of the results in rites such as the *bhāga-bhāj* (those entitled to a share);
however, in the Kali age, the agent alone is the enjoyer of the fruits of merit and demerit.
For this rule has been declared even in the absence of actual contact;
now learn how merit and demerit pass [to others] through contact. (11)
A mortal shall obtain half the fruit of merit or demerit exactly as it is from engaging in sexual intercourse, traveling together in a vehicle, or eating from a single vessel. (12)
Through teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or even eating in the same row, a human being constantly incurs a fourth part of the merits and sins [of those involved]. (13)
From sharing a single seat, a single vehicle, or even the inhalation and exhalation of breath, one becomes a partaker of a sixth share of the fruits of both merit and demerit. (14)
Through touching, speaking to, or even praising another, a human being constantly incurs ten parts of their merits and demerits. (15)
By seeing and hearing [others], and likewise by mentally reflecting upon them, a person may obtain a hundredth part of the merits and sins of others. ||16||
He who utters censure, slander, or reproach against another incurs the sin committed thereby and bestows his own merit upon that person. (17)
If a man performs service for one who is performing meritorious deeds—provided he is someone other than that person's wife, hired servant, or disciple—[he too gains merit]. (18)
Whatever substance is given to him in accordance with his service,
he too shall partake in the fruit of that merit in accordance with his service.
But he who, while others are eating in a single row, obstructs the serving of food— ||19||
One who serves food to that person,
or touches him, or speaks with him while he is performing his ablutions, twilight prayers, and other such rites, incurs a sin equal to that of eating the food of a patita.
One should certainly grant a gift consisting of merit and sixfold wealth to that man who, under the pretext of dharma, asks for another kind of property. (21)
Dhanada shall obtain the fruit of that merit-born action of the one who, having stolen another's property, performs a meritorious deed. (22)
In that case, the one who performs the work incurs the sin, while the fruit of that action belongs to the owner;
however, that man who dies without having discharged his debt to another [is bound]. (23)
The owner acquires merit corresponding to his own wealth;
likewise do the provider of the idea, the consenter, and the giver of the implements. (24)
The king also obtains a sixth part of the merit and demerit of his subjects;
from his subjects, the king extracts a sixth part of their merits and demerits. (25)
From a disciple, the teacher [receives merit]; likewise, a husband from his wife, and a father from his son;
even from her own husband, a woman obtains half of his merit. (26)
May she who constantly brings satisfaction remain ever devoted to my mind as I perform meritorious deeds, such as giving with my own hand to others. (27)
Except for a hired laborer and a son, the performer of the rite shall set aside one-sixth;
from the merit of the enjoyer of the maintenance, the performer shall set aside one-eighth.
If one does not cause oneself or another to perform service [to the teacher], [one incurs a fault]. ||29||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In this way, indeed, even the merits and sins accumulated by others constantly come to one.
Listen to this foremost ancient history, which is meritorious and bestows great spiritual benefit. (30)

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Portions of Merit and Sin," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, within the *Pādma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(113) The one hundred and thirteenth chapter.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Formerly, there lived in Tīpura a Brahmin named Dhaneśvara; he had fallen away from his sacred duties, was devoted to sin, and was very wicked-minded. (1)
He subsisted by the fraudulent sale of quicksilver, strength-giving herbs, hides, and other such items;
his mind was addicted to theft, harlotry, the drinking of liquor, and gambling. ||2||
Once, while traveling from country to country for the purpose of buying and selling,
he, together with his wealth, arrived at the city of Māhiṣmatī.
Because it was previously established by Mahiṣa, it became known as Māhiṣmatī;
in that city, the Narmadā river, which destroys sins, shines upon the slopes of its embankments.
Having seen the men who had come from various villages there for the Kārttika vow, he lived for one month while engaging in trade.
While wandering along the banks of the Narmadā for the purpose of selling [the cow],
Saṇatya saw Brāhmaṇas who had bathed and were devoted to the recitation of prayers and the worship of the gods.
Some were reciting the Purāṇas, some were devoted to hearing them,
and others were intent upon dancing, singing, playing musical instruments, and praising Viṣṇu.
Overcome with curiosity, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) saw here and there some who were marked with the Viṣṇu-mudrā and others wearing garlands of tulasī.
By constantly wandering there and by seeing, touching, and conversing with the Vaiṣṇavas, as well as by hearing the name of Viṣṇu and so forth, he obtained [merit].
Having thus remained for a month, he then, during the rite of concluding the Kārttika vow,
witnessed the vigil for Hari being performed by the devotees.
Then, on the full moon day, he saw various kinds of worship and other rites,
as well as offerings of sacrificial fees, food, and the lighting of lamps by those established in their vows.
Then, at the setting of the sun, he likewise beheld the ritual of the Festival of Lamps being performed for the sake of pleasing the Enemy of Tripura.

Since the marriage of the three cities was performed by Śiva on that day, therefore a great festival is celebrated for it by the devotees. Whoever shall offer even a small portion of my [gift] to Rudra, [shall receive great merit]. (13)

All his meritorious deeds would undoubtedly become fruitless. While wandering there, beholding the dancing and other performances, that lord of wealth was bitten by a black serpent and fell down, deprived of his senses.
Seeing him fallen, the people, filled with compassion, surrounded him.
Then they sprinkled his face with water mixed with tulasī. Thereupon, the servants of Yama bound him, having cast him off from his body.
Being beaten with whips, they led him in anger to Saṃyaminī;
but Citragupta, seeing him, then rebuked him and reported his case.
"Whatever evil deed was committed by him out of childishness,
Citragupta said:
'Not even the slightest good deed is seen in him anywhere from his childhood.'"
O Lord, even in a hundred years, one cannot describe the misdeeds of this wicked one, who is a personification of sin; he is seen only as such, O All-pervading One. (18)
"Therefore, let him be cooked in hell until the end of the kalpa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard these words, Yama spoke out of anger to his own servants. (19)
Revealing his own form, which possessed a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction,
Yama said:
"O Bhīma, release this man who is being bound with your mallets!"
In that place called Kumbhīpāka, where boiling oil was being cast [into the cauldron] with a shrieking sound,
as soon as he was thrown there, it became cool.
Just as the fire in the cauldron [of hell] was extinguished by the casting of Prahlāda, having witnessed that great wonder, the king of the pretas was filled with amazement. (22)
Then, having arrived with speed, he reported all of that to Yama;
and Yama, having heard the account presented by the leader of the pretas, was filled with curiosity.
"What is this? he asked, and as they were investigating it correctly, Nārada arrived there, laughing and hurrying along.
Having been properly honored by Yama, he looked at him and spoke these words.
Nārada said:
"O son of the Sun, this man is not capable of experiencing the hells."
For he has performed such karma that it brings about hell;
yet whoever should perform the acts of seeing, touching, or speaking with him would [reap the consequences]. (26)
A man certainly obtains a sixth part of that merit which he has performed for Hari throughout countless births. (27)
Therefore, this person who serves those observing the Kārttika vow for a month shall partake in a portion of their merit;
one who performs service for them partakes in the full merit of the completed vow. (28)
Therefore, there is no means of calculating the merit arising from this *ūrja-vrata*;
even great sins are [destroyed] for men who observe the *kārttika-vrata*. (29)
Viṣṇu, who is affectionate toward his true devotees, surely destroys all [sins] at the end with those very names, using water mixed with tulasī.
Because he has been favored by a Vaiṣṇava, he is not cooked in hell;
therefore, this man, his sins destroyed, deserves to attain a good state.
Just as the proximity of hellish enjoyments is attained through wet or dry sins, so too is the proximity of heavenly enjoyments attained through meritorious deeds. (32)
Therefore, one who possesses merit without desire, while remaining in the womb of a yakṣa, shall experience the reaping of evil after beholding all the hells. ||33||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
After Nārada had departed having spoken thus, the son of Surasūti (Yudhiṣṭhira), his virtuous deeds awakened by hearing those words, [acted accordingly].
He led that brahmin back again by means of his own servant,
intending to show him all those various hells.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Dhaneśvara," within the "Gloriousness of the Month of Kārttika" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(114) The one hundred and fourteenth chapter. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, having led the Lord of Wealth (Dhanesvara) to the hells, the attendant of Yama, the guardian of the dead, spoke, saying,
"I shall show you all those [hells]."
The messenger of the dead said:
"Behold these terrible hells, which inspire great fear even in the Lord of Wealth;
therein those who constantly commit evil deeds are cooked by the servants of Yama. (2)
This hell named Taptavāluka (Heated Sands) is terrible to behold,
wherein these evildoers, their bodies scorched, cry out in distress.
Those men who do not honor guests who have arrived at their home— emaciated by hunger— at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, are indeed cooked by their own karma.
Those who strike with their feet the guru, fire, brāhmaṇas, deities, and likewise consecrated kings—these very people shall be consumed by fire. 5.
This hell has six divisions, which one enters through various sins; likewise, the second great hell is called Andhatāmisra.
"O twice-born one, behold: the body of that evildoer is being torn apart by needle-mouthed worms with terrifying faces, which have come into contact with him. (7)
That [hell] is also established with sixfold divisions by horses, crows, deer, and birds;
there, those sinful mortals who pierce the vital organs of others are cooked.
This third hell is indeed called Krakaca, terrible to behold;
there, those mortals who have committed evil deeds are split apart by saws.
Furthermore, it is established that there are six types [of hells], such as the Forest of Sword-Leaves (Asipatravana) and others;
for they indeed cause one to experience separation from one's wife, children, and so forth. (10)
Men are cooked by others even more cruel than those they themselves desired;
being cut by sword-leaves, they flee out of fear of being sliced.
Behold, the sinners are being cooked here and there while being tormented;
this is indeed the fourth hell, most terrible, known as Argala.
Beholding those sinners bound with various kinds of nooses by the powerless Yama and being beaten with mallets and other instruments, they cry out in distress. (13)
Those men who obstruct virtuous people, such as Brahmins and others,
by seizing them by the throat and other such means, are cooked by the servants of Yama for their sins.
This [hell] also exists with six divisions, established through various forms of slaughter and mutilation;
behold the fifth hell, named Kūṭaśālmalī. (15)
O twice-born one, there stand these trees such as the Śālmalī, resembling iron spikes;
there these men are cooked in six ways by means of tortures.
Those who are always devoted to the wives of others, the wealth of others, and the injury of others—behold this sixth, wondrous hell, filled with blood and pus. (17)
There, those men who have committed evil deeds—those who ate forbidden food and were devoted to reviling others, backbiting, and the like—are cooked with their faces turned downwards. (18)
Being broken and struck, they utter terrifying cries;
moreover, this [world] is situated amidst the six kinds of odors rich in fragrance.
O Lord of Wealth, behold this seventh hell, Kumbhīpāka, which is terrible to behold; it consists of six types [of vats] filled with substances such as oil and others. (20)
There, the perpetrators of great sins are boiled by those who do nothing [to help them],
for many thousands of years, through repeated rising and sinking.
Behold these forty-one Raurava hells;
a sin committed unintentionally is called "dry," while one committed intentionally is declared to be "moist. (22)
[They are] established in two types through fresh, dried, and other such evils;
they are established through eighty-four distinct varieties. (23)
That which is miscellaneous, as well as that which causes impurity of the waters,
likewise that which causes the loss of caste— these are designated as minor offenses (upapātaka).
Excessive evil, great evil, and the sevenfold heinous crimes are thus remembered; by these one ripens in the hells in their respective order. (25)
Because you had contact with those observing the Kārttika vow, your hells have indeed been removed through the accumulation of that merit. (26)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having thus shown him the hells, the Lord of the Dead then led him away;
afterwards, he took Dhaneśvara to the world of the Yakṣas, for he remained there.
This follower of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) is remembered as Dhanayakṣa;
it was after his name that the son of Tugādhin created a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in Ayodhyā.

Such indeed is the power of this Kārttika month, which bestows liberation and grants emancipation, since even one who has accumulated many sins attains liberation merely by beholding one established in its vow. (29)

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Dhaneśvara," within the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(115) The One Hundred and Fifteenth Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to Satyabhāmā, his most beloved wife, Vāsudeva went to his mother's house to perform the evening twilight rituals and other duties.
Thus has been described this month of Kārttika, which destroys sins, is eternally dear to Viṣṇu, and always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||2||
The vigil for Hari, the morning bath, the service of Tulasī, the concluding rite, and the offering of lamps—these are the vows [to be observed] in the month of Kārttika. ||3||
By means of these fivefold observances, the Kārttika vow is fulfilled;
it is said that one obtains its fruit, which bestows the rewards of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The sages said:
O Romaharṣaṇa, this procedure for Kārttika has been declared to be dear to Viṣṇu, yielding great fruit, perfectly purifying, and destructive of sins. (5)
This must certainly be performed by those seeking liberation, or even by men desiring worldly enjoyments, in order to properly ward off the suffering that has been encountered. (6)
This being the case, suppose someone established in a vow finds himself in a crisis, or is situated in a difficult forest, or is tormented by diseases;
how should he perform the auspicious Kārttika vow? (7)
Sūta said:
O best of sages, listen as I shall relate everything that must be performed by men in order to obtain the fruit of their actions beyond measure.
One should perform the vigil for Hari in the temple of Viṣṇu or Śiva;
even in the absence of temples dedicated to Śiva or Viṣṇu, one may do so in the temples of all other deities.
Whether one is situated in a difficult forest or has gone elsewhere,
one should perform [the rite] at the root of an Aśvattha tree or even in groves of Tulasī.
By singing the names of Viṣṇu in the presence of Viṣṇu, a human being obtains the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows. ||11||
The man who plays musical instruments shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
the dancer shall attain the fruit arising from bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas). ||12||
A person who provides the materials for these [rites] shall obtain all this merit;
moreover, by praising and beholding them, one who desires their welfare shall attain the sixfold auspiciousness.
If one who has fallen into calamity should not obtain water for bathing,
or if one is ill, one should instead perform the cleansing of Viṣṇu by means of His names.
One who is established in a vow but is unable to perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) should feed Brahmins according to his capacity for the sake of completing the vow. (15)
Since he is the giver of the fruit of liberation, he must never be abandoned by men;
for on this earth, the Brahmins are the very embodiment of Viṣṇu, whose form is unmanifest. (16)
Through his satisfaction, may I always be perfectly satisfied; of this there is no doubt.
One who is unable to offer a lamp should instead kindle another's lamp. (17)
One should diligently protect them from wind and other such elements;
however, in the absence of *tulasī*, one should indeed worship a Vaiṣṇava Brahmin.
Since Viṣṇu is always present among his own devotees, in the absence of all else, the observer of the vow should offer [the sacrifice] to Brāhmaṇas or even to cows. (19)
Or perform service to the Aśvattha and Vaṭa trees for the sake of completing one's vow.
The sages said:
"How is it that by you the Aśvattha and the Vaṭa have been made equal to the cow and the Brāhmaṇa?
Why are those two made more worthy of worship than all other ancestors?"
Sūta said:
The Lord Viṣṇu himself is in the form of the Aśvattha tree; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, the Vaṭa tree is in the form of Rudra, and the Pālāśa tree bears the form of Brahmā.
Beholding, worshipping, and serving them are known to remove sin;
they certainly bring about the destruction of suffering, calamities, diseases, and evils. (23)
The sages said:
"How did Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara attain the state of trees? O Omniscient One, explain this to us, for our doubt in this matter is great. (24)
Sūta said: Formerly, while Pārvatī and Śiva were indeed engaged in amorous union with the gods, Agni was sent in the form of a brāhmaṇa to create an obstacle.
Then Pārvatī, enraged by the loss of the pleasure of the festival of love, cursed the inhabitants of heaven out of anger and indignation.
Pārvatī said:
"Even these worms, insects, and the like know the pleasure of sexual union;
by creating obstacles to that, O gods, you shall indeed attain the state of being born from plants."
Sūta said:
Thus, with her mind filled with wrath, that goddess Pārvatī cursed the gods;
consequently, it is said that all the hosts of gods attained the state of trees.
Therefore, O lords of sages, both Viṣṇu and Maheśvara became two *bodhivaṭa* trees;
on the day of the Sun (Sunday), the *bodhi* attained touchability, while [the other] attained untouchability due to its conjunction with the son of the Sun (Saturn) and the *viṣṭi* yoga.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Kārttika-māhātmya,
[this is] the section titled "The Praise of the Aśvattha and Vaṭa Trees."
The one hundred and fifteenth chapter. ||115||
(116) The one hundred and sixteenth chapter.
The sages said:
"How did this Sūtabodhitaru tree become untouchable, and how did it attain the state of being touchable on Saturday?
You ought to tell us all of this in detail. (1)
Sūta said:
Then the lords of the gods churned the ocean and obtained jewels;
the deities gave Śrī and the Kaustubha gem among those treasures to Viṣṇu.
As soon as Gīcaka had requested Lakṣmī for his own wife,
Lakṣmī informed him of the matter regarding Kṛpāṇin.
Lakṣmī said: "How can you marry a younger sister without first having consecrated the elder?
Therefore, O Madhusūdana, this Alakṣmī is my elder sister."
Afterward, this eternal dharma consists of marriage and the leading [of one's wife]. ||5||
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, the Creator of the World, together with Viṣṇu,
then [spoke] to the sage Uddālaka, who had performed very long penance.
In accordance with his own words, he indeed gave that Alakṣmī away—
she who had a large face, white teeth, and a body made of silver.
Having accepted her— who was wide-eyed, with blood-red eyes, and coarse tawny hair—
upon the word of Viṣṇu, the sage returned to his own hermitage.
The knower of dharma brought [the place] resounding with the sound of the Vedas,
enriched by the fragrant smoke of burnt offerings, and made to ring out with the chanting of sacred knowledge.
Beholding that hermitage, she was distressed and spoke these words.
Jyeṣṭhā said:
"This dwelling, filled with the sound of the Vedas, is not at all suitable for me."
"I will not come here, O Brahmin; take me elsewhere without delay."
Uddālaka said: "How is it that you do not grow weary? Or what practice is being followed here that is approved by you? And what dwelling would be suitable for you? Tell me that."
Jyeṣṭhā said:
"I shall certainly not dwell in that place where there is the sound of the Vedas, the honoring of guests, or [the performance of] sacrifices, charity, and so forth. (12)
Where there exists no mutual affection between husband and wife, and where there is no worship of the ancestors and the gods, I do not dwell there. (13)
Those who delight in gambling, those who steal the property of others, and even those who take pleasure in the wives of others—my mind has no delight in staying among them. (14)
I take delight in that place where the slaughter of cows and the drinking of liquor occur constantly,
and where sins such as the killing of a Brahmin arise;
where there is the humiliation of elders, virtuous people, and Brāhmaṇas.
I dwell constantly wherever there is harsh speech. (15)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, the sage Uddālaka became dejected in countenance;
remembering the speech of Viṣṇu, he did not speak.
He went there and, seeing the worship being offered to her, said, "I am not coming. Thereupon, due to that delusion, he became exceedingly distressed.
Then Uddālaka spoke these words to that Alakṣmī: "Ha! (17)
Uddālaka said:
"O Lakṣmī, stay for a moment at the root of this aśvattha tree while I go back to find a place of residence and return again. (18)
Sūta said:
Having thus established him there, Uddālaka then departed; he waited there for a long time, but when he did not see him, [he returned]. 19.
Then, distressed by the abandonment of her husband, she ascended the Karuṇā mountain;
while staying there weeping, she heard Lakṣmī in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, with agitated minds, they made their request to Viṣṇu.
Lakṣmī said: "O Lord, my elder sister is distressed by the abandonment of her husband;
if I am dear to you, go to comfort her, O compassionate one. (22)
Sūta said:
Then Viṣṇu, accompanied by Lakṣmī, arrived there filled with compassion;
he consoled that Alakṣmī and spoke these words.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"Having reached the Aśvattha tree, always remain there with unwavering devotion;
for this abode has been created by me, originating from my own body."
"O sister, may this younger sister Śrī remain steadfastly with those householders who worship you, Jyeṣṭhā, every day. (25)
Sūta said:
Those who hear or recite this greatness of Ūrja (Kārttika) shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu until the dissolution of all beings.

There is nothing else on this earth superior to Kārttika, which is dear to Viṣṇu, that removes disease, destroys great sins, bestows excellent intelligence, provides sons, wealth, and other means, and is the primary cause of liberation. (27)

O humans, perform the Kārttika vow with its prescribed observances, which is dear to Viṣṇu, destroys all impurities, and brings about the abundance of virtuous sons, grandsons, wealth, and grain; for what need has such a person for the service of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites? (28)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Alakṣmī," in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā.
(117) The one hundred and seventeenth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having then heard all those words from the son of Satrājit, the highly fortunate Satyā spoke these words to Hari. (1)
Satī said:
"O Lord, I have not heard the greatness of Kārttika in detail.
How is it that Kārttika is the most excellent among all the months? (2)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O saintly one, you have asked well regarding the Ekādaśī vow of Kārttika with great devotion;
it was formerly narrated to Śaunaka by the high-souled Sūta.
Sūta said:
Listen, for I shall declare this auspicious answer to your question,
which was formerly spoken by the Lord to the inquiring Ṣaṇmukha.
Kārttikeya said: "O Lord, many secrets of Padmanābha have been heard by me,
just as they are being proclaimed by you, a devotee of Viṣṇu."
For the sake of delivering those who have fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with vast waves of suffering, speak [to them] with diligent effort.
O best among speakers, tell me the procedure for the ritual bath in the month of Kārttika,
by which men shall cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
Tell me in great detail the fruit of the Vaiṣṇava dharma,
by the power of which dharma one indeed attains the state of Viṣṇu.
O observer of excellent vows, [tell me] the majesty of the gift of lamps and of flowers for the Sage;
likewise, O Lord, the majesty of Gopīcandana and of Tulasī.
Speak likewise of the greatness of the *mālatī* flower and of water-born flowers;
as well as the greatness of the *dhātrī* fruit and of the *damanaka*. (10)
O scorcher of foes, [I have heard] the greatness of the ketakī flower and of the food offering;
O Lord, [I have heard] the greatness of the water of sacred fords and the fruit of the Māgha bath. (11)
O best of gods, tell me the fruit of eating from the leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa*; O Sthāṇu, tell me the fruit of the *nīrājana* rite and of extinguishing another's lamp. (12)
The majesty of the Puṣkara field, as well as that of Śūkara, O Lord;
the majesty of the Śālagrāma and the ritual procedure for the Svastika. ||13||
O Lord, tell me the fruit of various gifts and of abstaining from the food of others; tell me the fruit of fasting for a month and of releasing one from a bed of suffering.
O observer of noble vows, tell me in great detail the majesty of Dīpāvalī, the majesty of Prabodhinī, and the majesty of Pañcabhīṣma.
The Lord said:
"Well asked by you, my child, for the sake of uplifting the world!
Why do I not speak? There is indeed no Vaiṣṇava equal to you. (16)
O child, by you, a virtuous son, I have undoubtedly been delivered;
your unwavering devotion to Keśava remains constant at all times.
That best of the twice-born who imparts the Vaiṣṇava dharma to men indeed obtains that same merit as one who gives a gift of the earth together with the oceans. ||18||
All holy fords and all acts of giving on one side do not equal even a ten-millionth part of the month of Kārttika. (19)
On one side are the gifts of cows and all sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees;
on the other side is dwelling at Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, and the Himālaya. (20)
On one side are Mathurā-tīrtha and Śūkara in Vārāṇasī;
on the other side, O child, is Kārttika, which is always dear to Keśava. (21)
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, O tiger among sages, Hara again uttered these words:
"I shall describe at great length the majesty of the Kārttika bath."
Īśvara said: The Kṛta age is declared to belong to the Brāhmaṇa, while Tretā belongs to the Kṣatriya himself;
they say Dvāpara belongs to the Vaiśya, and the Kali age is remembered as belonging to the Śūdra. (23)
O child, although in the Kali age there is laxity among men regarding the practice of bathing,
nevertheless I shall describe the ritual bathing during the months of Kārttika and Māgha.
That man whose hands and feet, as well as his speech and mind, are well-restrained,
