[He is] dark like the petal of a blue lotus, possessing four fangs and four arms. (79)
He had eight feet and one eye, ears like those of a dog, and a voice like a donkey; he was dull-witted, double-tongued, copper-eyed, and wore the skin of the king of beasts as his garment.
Mahādeva is to be meditated upon, for his form is not [perceived] by the senses;
this was told by Indrabhīṣma while he lay upon a bed of arrows.
Thus, O Bhīṣma, I have related to you this difficult-to-perform Pañcaka,
which is auspicious, meritorious, and a destroyer of sins— a great vow, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
by performing which even a slayer of a Brahmin or a killer of a cow is liberated from all sins. (82)
That which is celebrated on earth as Bhīṣmapañcaka,
lasting from the eleventh to the fifteenth [lunar day],
is said to be a prohibition against one intent on eating at that time.
In that vow, Viṣṇu bestows auspicious fruit. ||83||
Sūta said:
This merit, which is superior to all else and difficult to attain in the world, has been performed;
this secret, which is a compendium of the essence of the scriptures, has been narrated by me. 84.

O Goddess, having heard all this—which is protected by the gods, extremely secret, and bestows liberation—even those who were devoted to approaching women who should not be approached became [liberated] in a single step. 85.
One should liberate both the one who sells his daughter and the one who sells his sister;
this scripture, which bestows liberation, should be revealed to others only when they are not present. 86.
Having heard even a single word of this, a human being attains liberation;
it should be guarded with effort, for there are men who would abandon it.
O Six-faced One, the merit of those [who do not perform this] cannot be told; this is the truth, this is the truth.
Thus has all that which is the fruit of Kārttika been narrated. 88.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"The God of gods has spoken out of a desire for his son's welfare.
Having heard those words from his father, Ṣaṇmukha was filled with joy. 89.
All the aquatic beings said to that god, the life-force of the world:
"We have become fulfilled by hearing the fruit born of Kārttika."
Furthermore, there is nothing more to be heard; the fruit of my birth has been attained by him who, having heard this greatness, honors the reciter. (91)
Because he is equal to Viṣṇu, [he should be honored] with cows, land, gold, and garments;
for when the reciter is honored, Viṣṇu himself becomes honored. (92)

One who desires auspicious and fruitful results should always honor that which is suchness (tathātva), as well as the Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇas, and whatever constitutes Vedic knowledge and the like. (93)
One who desires the Dharma should give a book to the reciter;
indeed, those who bestow the knowledge of the Purāṇas enjoy the fruit of immortality. (94)
Whoever should recite this with devotion, and having heard it, should retain it in mind, is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||95||
Wealth, grain, fame, sons, long life, and even health are obtained simply by hearing of his greatness; of this there is no doubt. (96)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā," within the "Greatness of the Month of Kārttika" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
The Greatness of Māgha (125):
The One Hundred and Twenty-fifth Chapter.
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, you who desire the welfare of the world have narrated the account of Kārttika, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1)
Now, O Lomaharṣaṇa, as I speak of the majesty of the month of Māgha, by hearing which the great doubt of people is destroyed. (2)
O illustrious one, by whom was the greatness of the Māgha bath first proclaimed in this world? Please instruct us upon that, together with its ancient history.
Sūta said: Excellent, excellent, O best of sages! You are devoted to Kṛṣṇa, since you joyfully and repeatedly inquire about the topics of Kṛṣṇa with devotion. (4)
I shall recount the greatness of Māgha, which increases merit and destroys the sins of those men who listen to it and bathe at the break of dawn. (5)
Once, O Brahmins, Pārvatī, endowed with humility, touched the lotus-feet of Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, and questioned him.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, bestower of fearlessness upon devotees!
Be gracious, O Lord, Sovereign of the Universe; tell me now that which I ask.
O Lord, various kinds of teachings have been heard by me from you previously;
now I wish to hear—please tell me—the greatness arising from the month of Māgha.
By whom was this practiced in the past? What is the ritual procedure, and who is the deity?
Tell me all of that in detail, for you are affectionate toward your devotees. (9)
Maheśa said:
Having bathed in the final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*) of the sacrifice and having had auspicious rites performed for him by the sages,
he was honored by all the citizens and departed from his own city.
Dilīpa, the best among kings and a lover of the hunt, was filled with curiosity and surrounded by a vast array of hunters. ||11||
With his feet encased in sandals, wearing a blue turban as a head-covering,
with finger-guards made of iguana skin bound on, he moved along with bow in hand like a reptile.
He was surrounded by archers with their small swords fastened on, as well as by such foot-soldiers,
in the very beautiful and vast forests of the Gandhāras.
Having crossed the great stream, the youth, possessing the prowess of a lion, joyfully sports with them in the bowers, seeking deer. (14)
"Kill him! Kill him! This deer is indeed fleeing!"—thus prattling among his servants, he himself springs up and strikes. (15)
Wandering here and there once more, he beheld a forest region crowded with flocks of peacocks that had flown up from the branches in alarm and were now hiding there.
In some places it was terrifying due to the shrill howling of jackals, while in others, herds of does were fleeing in all directions with their fawns.
In some places they say she bears the splendor of herds of rhinoceroses;
in other places, she resounds with the hooting of owls peering from hollows.
In some places it was marked here and there with the footprints of the enemy of deer;
in other places, it was reddened by the blood of *rohit* deer torn open by the claws of tigers.
In some places, he pointed out the ground of the inner courtyard with herds of very affectionate female buffaloes, distressed by the weight of their full udders.
In some places it was covered by dense trees and fragrant with wild flowers;
in other places it was beautifully adorned by the humming of bees at the entrances of creeper-bowers.
It had a vast cave that was terrifying with half-sloughed-off snake skins,
and it was fearsome with pythons lurking in its crevices like slithering snakes shedding their skins.
In some places there were the flames of forest fires, beautiful with the light of glowing rocks,
filled with the sound of hissing, and teeming with deer and tigers.
Releasing the pack of hounds here and there among the hares, they rested at the pools and then proceeded once more into the interior of the forest.
Thus, O lord of kings, as the king was departing while the troop of hunters leaped about,
making a great clamor there, Sāraṅga emerged from the forest.
With the ground of the difficult path traversed by his surging momentum,
he at times ascended into the sky and at times moved upon the earth.
The king, following his footsteps, entered a perilous forest that was difficult to traverse due to its crooked currents, its fearsome nature, and its dense thickets of thorny trees. (27)
Having gone from one region to another, further and further away into desolate places,
his throat and neck were parched by the frantic pursuit of wild animals.

With his palate and mouth copper-colored, perspiring, exhausted, and suffering from heat, his voice faltering as he had traversed a long distance, he was afflicted by thirst when the sun reached the meridian. (29)
He beheld before him a lake that rivaled the lord of waters,
situated on the banks of dense trees, possessing excellent landing-stairs, stainless and auspicious.
It was vast, with full-blown lotuses and bees intoxicated by honey,
covered by the broad leaves of the lotus plants as if by emeralds.
It was clear, with fish darting out from beneath it, as pure as the minds of the virtuous;
it was mingled with moving aquatic creatures and adorned with rows of shimmering waves.

Like the minds of the wicked, it was cruel with swarms of crocodiles within; like the home of a miser, it was difficult to enter due to its mossy depths; [there he dwelt] day and night, pacifying the suffering of all the various birds.
Like a donor with all his possessions, he was the destroyer of the suffering of those in distress;
like one satisfying his own ancestors, he gratified the beasts of prey with his own blood. (34)
He removed all that distress, like the sun dispelling the frost;
upon seeing him, he became free from exhaustion, just as a cātaka bird is upon seeing a cloud.
There, having performed his midday rites at the Pītajalorāja [lake], the king, together with his companions, partook of the meat of game he had hunted. (36)
He dwelt on the shore of Lake Uvāsa, recounting delightful stories;
then, having fixed an arrow upon his bow, he remained at night upon a tree.
The hunters, having taken up their positions, blocked the paths of the quarters;
while the heroes remained thus, they spread a net throughout the forest.
At midnight, a herd of boars emerged from the marshy terrain;
having wandered here and there along the banks, they fell into a hunter-infested trap.
Pierced by the king and slain by many hunters, those boars fell to the surface of the earth in an instant, having been struck down. (40)
Seeing that tumultuous roar, the hunters became greatly emboldened;
running forward with great joy, they gathered together and surrounded the king. (41)
Taking them with him, he departed further from the shore of the lake with his soldiers;
desiring to go to his own city, he saw an ascetic on the path. (42)
He was the Brahmin Vṛddhahārīta, beautifully adorned with the Śaṅkha and Cakra,
his body emaciated by severe and difficult observances.
He was a great being whose body was reduced to mere bones, with coarse skin quivering upon it;
he bore a beautiful deer-skin and wore soft bark garments.
Seeing him, a forest-dweller who was reciting Vedic prayers and bearing nails, hair, and matted locks, he hurriedly made way for him.

Having bowed his head, the king stood with his hands joined in the *añjali* gesture before her who was seated upon a lotus. Then, the twice-born one, having ascertained that the lord of the earth was sufficiently adorned with ornaments, [addressed him]. (46)
He said: "O King, for the sake of spiritual welfare and with the desire to perform a service for another, for what purpose are you going at this most auspicious and meritorious time? (47)
Having abandoned the morning bath in the lake during the month of Māgha, he replied: "Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I do not know [the merit of it], O King. (48)
"What is the fruit of the Māgha bath? Tell me in detail.
Having heard these words of the king, the Vaikhānasa sage spoke.
"O King, the Blessed One, the sun-gem that swiftly dispels darkness, has now risen;
this is our time for bathing, not the occasion for conversation. (50)
"Having bathed, go to that Vasiṣṭha and ask him, the lord of your own lineage.
Having spoken thus, the ascetic remained silent and departed for his morning ablutions.
Having returned there as well and bathed according to the prescribed rites,
the heroic Dilīpa, filled with joy, went back to his own city.
Then, having reported the discourse on the forest-dweller (āraṇyaka) to the inner apartments once more,
he mounted a chariot drawn by white horses, accompanied by a very white parasol and fly-whisks.
Well-dressed and adorned with ornaments, he was surrounded by his ministers;
hearing shouts of "Victory! once again, he was praised by the bards and panegyrists.
Remembering the words of the ṛṣis, he went to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha; having arrived there, he bowed before the brahman-sage with humility and proper conduct. (55)
When the king had been offered a seat, received the water of honor (arghya), and was graced with blessings,
he was joyfully questioned by the sage regarding his welfare.
Then the king, of sweet appearance, spoke these words, gladdening the mind of the sage; he, in turn, questioned what had been said by the Vaikhānasa.
Dilīpa said: "O Blessed One, by your grace, I have heard in detail about conduct, the science of government, and those other duties of kings."
Whatever rites, gifts, their specific regulations, sacrifices, and ritual procedures belong to the four castes and the four stages of life; ||59||
I have heard of the vows prescribed by Him as well as the worship of Viṣṇu;
now I wish to hear what fruit is obtained from the Māgha bath.
O Brahmā, O Sage, tell me that which must be performed according to the proper ritual. (60)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"What has been spoken by that forest-dwelling sage is perfectly stated; it is the supreme good, bringing benefit to the three worlds, and a means of purification. (61)
O Sun, you who desire the gazelles, those women, unimpeded by your proximity, desire you with their side-long glances as you come to bathe in the river.

Without fire, without sacrifice, without meritorious works of charity and piety, and even without their beloved ones, people desire a good rebirth by bathing in the waters outside at dawn during the month of Māgha. (63)
O King, those who desire cows, land, gold, rubies, gold coins, milch-cows, and other such things, yet do not give them, [attain this state] after bathing in the Māgha at Ekārṇava.

Those who, desiring heaven, do not wither their own bodies through the three-times-seven-day vows, the *kṛcchra* penances, and the *parāka* fasts, but instead always delight in the bath of austerity; ||65||
The worship of Hari in Vaiśākha, austerity and worship in Kārttika, and likewise austerity, fire-offerings, and charity—this triad is especially distinguished in Māgha. (66)
The lord of the earth will certainly become one whose delusion is accompanied by its consequences;
furthermore, he will possess such an intellect that it gives rise to liberation.
O best of kings, that penance and charity performed during the month of Māgha is inexhaustible, as it is attended by divine eyes established through the worship of the feet [of the Lord]. 68.
Whether with desire or without progeny, or even without these,
having become one who observes the vow of bodily purity, one obtains the fourfold fruit born of ritual bathing.
Aditi, having fasted for twelve years during a time of distress,
obtained as sons the twelve Ādityas, who are the illuminators of the three worlds.
Subhagā, endowed with beauty like Śacī, was devoted to charity and virtue; she gave birth to Aruṇa in a seven-storied palace during the month of Māgha under the constellation Rohiṇī.
In that place, rich with purified splendor, was a courtyard graced by the graceful movements of dancers;
it was filled with beautiful women whose complexions were as radiant as those of the various continents.
It was beautified by the auspicious customs and the sound of singing and instrumental music; it was purified by the resonance of the Vedas and graced by learned Brahmins. ||73||

In this delightful place, devoted to the worship of the gods and constantly frequented by guests, you should perform your bath during the month of Makara while the sun is there, rejoicing with your kinsmen and loved ones. (74)

By those who gave gifts during the great festival of Māgha, and who worshipped and praised the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), through the renunciation of desired objects and the observance of religious vows; 75.
The source of Dharma is always free from impurity; it cuts away the root of sin.
Rooted in desire, it yields fruits through its results; but when free from desire, it always bestows knowledge. (76)
The world belongs to those whose conduct is rooted in knowledge, whose home is the forest, who are devotees of Viṣṇu, and who always bathe in the Māgha [month]. ||77||
O supreme ascetic, those men who are devoted to the Māgha bath sometimes return from the world of the gods by means of other merits, but they never fail to return [to heaven]. (78)
O best of kings, whatever number of hairs there are on all the limbs of that milch cow which a mortal gives after bathing in the month of Māgha, [for so many years shall he dwell in heaven].
He who performs the Māgha bath and offers sesame seeds with jaggery shall be honored in the heavenly world for as many thousands of years.
Having washed away his sin, that man indeed becomes exceedingly pure;
among all heaps of grain, sesame seeds are the destroyers of evil. (81)
Therefore, O best of kings, sesame seeds should be given with effort during the month of Māgha;
one performing the Māgha bath should provide a meal for a Brāhmaṇa. 82.
Having gratified the ancestors, the pure-souled one goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; therefore, with every effort, the month of Māgha is brought to pass through giving. 83.
O best of kings, one should never fail to give gifts during the month of Māgha;
having ascertained one's means, one should always give gifts in Māgha according to one's wealth. (84)
He who performs the Māgha bath and gives sandals and water-pots to Brāhmaṇas certainly dwells in heaven.
O King, one performing this supreme austerity of the Māgha bath must never neglect giving; for through giving, heaven is attained. (86)
By giving, heaven is attained; by giving, happiness is attained;
by giving, O King, even the evil born of great sins is destroyed. (87)
Without giving, penance, and splendor, it is like the sky without the sun; or like a family without progeny, or a house without proper conduct. (88)
There is nothing more purifying or destructive of sins than this song sung by the Vidyādharas to Bhṛgu on Maṇiparvata. (89)
The king said:
"O Brahmin, when did the sage Bhṛgu speak on the mountain?
Tell me out of curiosity how he gave him instruction in dharma. (90)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, in former times the clouds did not rain for twelve years.
Distressed by that, the subjects became emaciated and fled in all ten directions. (91)
O King, at that time, the central region between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains had become desolate,
devoid of the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭkāra, and abandoned by the study of the Vedas.
When this world is beset by calamity, its light obscured, its dharma lost, and its splendor vanished,
the circle of the earth will be as if empty of fruits, roots, food, and drink.
Having departed from his hermitage on the delightful banks of the Revā, which was shaded by various trees,
Bhṛgu went with his disciples to the Himālaya mountain.
There, situated to the west of Mount Kailāsa, stands a mountain renowned as Maṇikūṭa, a lofty peak composed of jewels, gold, and precious stones. (95)
With its lower parts white as crystal and its middle a mountain of blue stone, it shone like Śiva,
white all over with ashes yet possessing a blue throat.
Everywhere, like a dark cloud streaked with golden lines upon a blue stone, he shines, possessing a splendor more radiant than lightning, with his dark form shimmering like a flash of lightning.
With its peak of blue stone and its lower slopes girdled by gold, the mountain shines like Nārāyaṇa, encircled by his excellent yellow garment.
With its dark-blue girdle of forests and white stones amidst its center, that mountain shone like the sky with stars. 99.
Having regained his own radiant body and bearing glowing celestial herbs,
he shines with great luster like a second moon.
That mountain always shines with the beautiful music of Kinnarīs on its plateaus, with whistling bamboos, and with banners made of the leaves of Raṃbhā trees.
He was surrounded on all sides by the circles of radiant rays from emeralds, lapis lazuli, rubies, and white stones, as if by rainbow-bows.
Adorned with gold consisting of all elements and various jewels, it was completely surrounded on all sides by exceedingly high peaks that resembled tongues of fire. (103)
Upon his arrival, the Vidyādharīs, overwhelmed by passion, abandoned their husbands and ran toward him as if toward a god, even across grass, water, and stones. (104)
Those who have conquered the afflictions and are free from passion meditate day and night upon the cessation of that vital breath within the mountain caves of the delightful slopes of Brahmā.
With rosaries in their hands, these perfected ones (siddhas), their eyes half-closed,
worship the Lord of Beings within the slender waists of beautiful women.
The quarters of the sky are made fragrant by the scent of mandāraka flowers, and this place is always resonant with the warbling of water-birds from the mountain streams. 107.
With young elephants and forest-dwelling tuskers sporting happily in the foothills, and with herds of musk deer as well as beautiful and variegated wild animals; 108.
It was filled with herds of sporting yaks, various beasts of prey, as well as cooing pigeons, cakora birds, apes, and cuckoos. ||109||
With its royal swans and peacocks, it was ever delightful; together with its mountains, it was constantly frequented by gods, *guhyakas*, and throngs of *apsarases*. (110)
The King said:
"O Blessed One, this mountain is full of many wonders and is the refuge of all perfections; how great is its height, and how much is its length and breadth? (111)
The sage said:
Its height is thirty-six yojanas, and at its summit it is ten yojanas;
from root to top, its length and breadth together amount to sixteen yojanas.
It was resplendent with rows of yellow sandalwood, mandāra, and mango trees; it was filled with devadāru trees and beautified by sarala and arjuna trees.
This best of mountains, which always yields flowers and fruits, shines with houses formed by black aloe-wood creepers and by thickets of nikunja shrubs. (114)
Having seen that beautiful mountain, Bhṛgu, who was then afflicted by famine, made his dwelling there with a joyful mind. (115)
On that charming mountain, in its caves and forests,
Bhṛgu performed austerities for a long time, being well-disposed toward his penance.
O lord of kings, while that twice-born one remained thus dwelling in his hermitage— (116)
Having descended from Mount Aghata, those two lords of the Vidyadharas approached the sage, bowed, and stood there in great distress. (117)
Seeing them in such a state, the twice-born spoke these words:
"O Vidyādharas, why are you two so exceedingly distressed out of affection for me? (118)
Having heard the words of that sage, the Vidyādhara said to the twice-born:
"O best of ascetics, listen to the cause of my sorrow. (119)
Having obtained the fruit of my good deeds, I have reached this abode of the thirty gods;
yet even though I have attained a divine body, my face has become like that of a tiger. (120)
"Of what past action has this ripening come upon me?"—recollecting this again and again, my mind found no peace. (121)
Furthermore, O Brahmin, listen to this which agitates my mind:
may I be born as a beautiful woman, sweet-voiced and fair of form. (122)
At the time when this maiden, who was proficient in the arts of dance and song and endowed with every excellent quality, [was born], then by means of that pure vehicle— (123)
The sage Nārada, who was an expert in the aesthetic delight of playing the lute, was greatly gratified by the three [ladies] with seven *vipaṃcīs* and *parivādinīs*. 124.
Even while she was in a state of youthful innocence, the King of the Gods was delighted by this sweet-voiced maiden as she sang with her various melodic notes. 125.
Having heard that fifth-note resonance, so smooth with its various winding modulations, from her as she played the lute with her limbs agitated by curiosity; 126.
With his hair standing on end, Maheśvara, shaking his head, was gratified by her wealth of character,
nobility, a multitude of virtues, beauty, and youth.
There is no woman anywhere equal to her; she is not at all like others.
Where is this lovely lady with the face of a goddess, and where am I, a man with the face of a tiger? (128)
"Thus, O Brahmin, this is always burning within my heart, being inconceivable.
Having heard what was thus spoken by the Vidyadhara, the descendant of Ikshvaku [replied]: 129.
The three-eyed Bhṛgu, possessing divine vision, spoke laughingly:
"Listen, O best of Vidyādharas, to the wonderful fruit of karmas. (130)
Those whose minds are characterized by ignorance become deluded upon attaining wisdom; they are deluded because their intellects lack knowledge.
Just as even a space the size of a fly’s foot is dangerous when occupied by a venomous snake, so too is [the attainment of wisdom] perilous for the ignorant. (131)
"Even a minor action prescribed as a ritual duty can have such a terrible ripening;
for you, having fasted on the eleventh day of Māgha, performed an oil massage. (132)
Because you consumed oil on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) after fasting on the meritorious eleventh day (ekādaśī) during your previous existence, you have become tiger-faced in this body. (133)
In former times, Purūravas indeed obtained a body of such ugliness;
seeing his own wretched form, he was afflicted with great sorrow.
Having approached the king of mountains, he stood on the bank of the Devatā lake; having bathed and become pure, he remained there with supreme devotion upon a seat of kuśa grass.
Dark as a fresh blue cloud, with large eyes like lotuses, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and clothed in yellow garments. 136.
Contemplating in his heart that Hari, who shines with the Kaustubha gem and wears a forest garland, the king restrained all his senses.
For three months, he performed a most severe penance without food;
yet, being satisfied with even that small amount of austerity, he had performed worship throughout seven previous births.
As that king was thus recollecting [the Lord], He himself appeared before him on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, when the sun was in Capricorn.
Having quickly and joyfully sprinkled that Cakravartin with water from a conch shell,
Vāsudeva reminded him of his former conduct as a snake.
His form was exceedingly beautiful, lovely, and captivating—the very one by which the goddess Urvaśī, the leader of the gods, was enchanted. (141)
Having thus returned to his city, the king, who had accomplished his purpose by obtaining the boon, understood the course of karma; knowing this, why would a Vidyādhara be distressed? 142.
If you wish to avoid the deformity of the Dānava, then by my word alone, quickly [perform] the destruction of former sins. 143.
I shall describe the procedure for performing the ritual bath in the month of Māgha in the waters of the Maṇikūṭa river, which is frequented by sages, perfected beings, and gods. 144.
By the power of your misfortune, on the fifth day from now, beginning from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, you shall lie upon the bare ground near Māghona. (145)
For one month, abstaining from food, perform ablutions three times a day;
worshiping Viṣṇu at those three times, renounce enjoyments and conquer your senses.

O best of Vidyādharas, until the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, you shall remain with your sins burnt away; then, on the twelfth day, that auspicious occasion, [I shall grant you liberation].
"O god, having consecrated me with auspicious waters purified by mantras, I shall make your face like that of Kāma, O sinless one. (148)
"O best of Vidyādharas, having become equal to a deity, sport at your pleasure with this woman of excellent complexion. (149)
Having understood the power of Māgha, you should always perform the Māgha bath, so that the fulfillment of your heart's desires may occur for you at all times. (150)
Thus was it spoken by the all-knowing, great-souled Bhṛgu to that king of the Vidyādharas; O Indra among kings, further verses were then recited. (151)
Through the Māgha baths, misfortune perishes; through the Māgha baths, sins are destroyed.
Māgha is superior to all sacrifices and bestows the fruit of all gifts. (152)
Māgha roars from his sacrifices; Māgha roars from his yoga;
and Māgha roars with his intense asceticism, sounding like the roar of the Vidyādharas.
At Puṣkara, Cakratīrtha, Kurukṣetra, Brahmāvarta, Pṛthūdaka, Avimukta, Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean; ||154||
Whatever fruit is obtained by men through observances for ten years, that same fruit is obtained by bathing for three days in Māgha; of this there is no doubt. (155)
Those in whose minds there remains a longing for the heavenly realm must bathe in water wherever it may be found, even when the sun is in the sign of Capricorn.
Those who possess the qualities of long life, health, prosperity, beauty, and good fortune, and who have such desires, must not abandon their ritual bathing in the month of Māgha. (157)
Those who fear hell and the accumulated misery of poverty should,
by every means and with great effort, perform an immersion in the waters during the month of Māgha.
O best of kings, there is no other means for washing away the mire of poverty, sin, and misfortune than the ritual bath during the month of Māgha. 159.
Just as actions devoid of faith yield very little fruit,
so too does the Māgha bath bestow its fruit in its entirety.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, wherever one may be outside the water, the one who bathes in Māgha does not experience sufferings either in this world or the next. 161.
Just as the moon waxes and wanes during the two fortnights,
so too does sin diminish and the heap of merit increase in the month of Māgha.
Just as various kinds of jewels were produced from digging,
so too do meritorious jewels arise for men from the Māgha bath.
Just as the wish-fulfilling cow grants according to one's desire and the thought-gem grants what is thought of,
so too does this Māgha-bath bestow all heart's desires here.
In the Kṛta age, supreme knowledge was the highest; likewise, in the Tretā, sacrifice; in the Dvāpara, ritual action; but in all ages, the month of Māgha is supreme. 165.
O Lord of the Earth, for all castes and stages of life alike,
the ritual bath of Māgha rains down streams of dharma.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words of Bhṛgu, the Asura,
together with Bhṛgu, went to that very hermitage on the mountain bank of a mountain stream during the month of Māgha.
Having performed his bath together with his wife according to the prescribed rite,
he then attained that which was desired by his mind through the grace of Bhṛgu.
Having become a celestial voice, he rejoiced upon the Maṇi mountain; then Bhṛgu, desiring to favor him, arrived at the Vindhya mountains, filled with joy.
Merely by bathing in the month of Māgha at that king of mountains made of jewels, he became a Vidyādhara with a form as beautiful as the face of Madana.
Then, having completed his disciplined observances, Bhṛgu also descended from the region of Viṣṇu along with his disciples and arrived at the Revā.
This majesty of the month of Māgha, the essence of the entire world, was spoken by Bhṛgu, the best of the twice-born, to King Vidyādhara.
He who constantly hears this, which is variegated with diverse fruits, shall obtain all his beautiful desires here like a god. (171)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa," within the "Glorification of the Month of Māgha" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(126) The one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O best of kings, I shall now proclaim the greatness of the month of Māgha,
as it was spoken by Dattātreya in response to the inquiry of Kārtavīrya.
The king, the lord of Āhiṣmatī, went to that twice-born sage Dattātreya— who was Hari himself dwelling on the Sahya mountain— and questioned him.
Sahasrārjuna said:
"O Blessed One, best among yogis, all dharmas have been heard by me.
Out of compassion for me, O observer of noble vows, please tell me the fruit of the Māgha bath."
Dattātreya said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, to this auspicious answer to your question;
for in ancient times, this was told by Brahmā to the high-souled Nārada.
I shall relate all of that— the great fruit of the Māgha bath—
according to the location, according to the sacred ford, according to the rule, and according to the ritual performance.
In this land of Bhārata, and especially in this field of action (karmabhūmi),
the birth of those men who do not bathe during the month of Māgha is declared to be fruitless.
Just as the sky appears without the sun, nor the moon, nor the circle of stars,
even so, O King, it does not shine without the performance of virtuous deeds and the ritual bath in the month of Māgha.
Lord Hari is not so pleased by vows, gifts,
or austerities as Keśava is gratified by the mere act of bathing in the month of Māgha.
There exists no splendor whatsoever equal to the splendor of the sun;
likewise, there are no rites born of sacrifice equal to the ritual bath of Māgha.
For the sake of pleasing Vāsudeva, for the removal of all sins,
and for the attainment of heaven, a person should perform the ritual bath in the month of Māgha.
What is the use of protecting this body, though it be well-nourished, powerful, and strong, if it is transient, impure, and devoid of the purifying bath of sin? (11)
It is a pillar of bones bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, and a vessel for urine and excrement. (12)
Pervaded by old age, grief, and calamity, it is a sickly abode of disease;
it is full of passion, impermanent, and the refuge of all defects. (13)
The heat of tormenting others is a fire; the malice toward others is the supreme poison; likewise, one who is greedy, treacherous, cruel, ungrateful, and fickle [is to be avoided]. (14)
It is difficult to fill, difficult to restrain, and wicked, endowed with the three defects;
it leaks impurity, is full of holes, and is deluded by the three types of suffering. (15)
By nature devoted to unrighteousness, agitated by hundreds of cravings, and stationed at the gateway to hell—desire, anger, and great greed. (16)
In the end, it becomes worm-infested excrement and the sacrificial offering for dogs;
such is this body, rendered useless when deprived of bathing in the snowy Himalayas. 17.
Like bubbles in water or like husks within grain, those who are deprived of the Māgha bath are born only for the sake of death. 18.

A Brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava is ruined; a Śrāddha performed by one lacking yoga is ruined; a field where there is no devotion to Brahman is ruined; and a family that lacks proper conduct is ruined. (19)
Dharma is destroyed by pride, austerity is destroyed by anger, knowledge is destroyed by lack of firmness, and sacred learning is destroyed by negligence. (20)
An offering made by one who lacks devotion to the guru, by a woman, or by a celibate student is ruined;
an oblation offered into an unkindled fire is ruined; and enjoyment that is not witnessed by the eyes is ruined. (21)
The livelihood of one who harms others is ruined; the cooking for one's own sake by those who have daughters is ruined;
sacrifice performed by a Śūdra beggar is ruined; and the wealth of a miser is ruined. 22.
Ignorance destroyed by lack of practice causes enmity with the King;
a sacred ford destroyed for the sake of livelihood, and a vow broken for the sake of livelihood. (23)
A mantra uttered with untruth is defeated; likewise, one spoken with malice or slander is defeated.
A mantra recited with a distracted mind is defeated, and a recitation performed with an agitated heart is defeated. (24)
A gift given to one who has not mastered the Vedas is destroyed; the world of the atheist is destroyed;
and everything performed for the sake of the next world that is done without faith is destroyed. (25)
O King, just as this world is ruined for men who are destitute,
so too is birth ruined for human beings without the ritual bath in Māgha.
If one bathes during the Makara-saṃkrānti when the sun has not yet risen, how can one be liberated from sins, and how can one go to heaven along with one's ancestors? ||27||
A killer of a Brahmin, a thief of gold, a drinker of liquor, and one who violates the teacher’s bed—by bathing in Māgha, these shall be freed from sin; and the fifth is he who associates with them.
In the month of Māgha, when the sun has slightly risen, we purify that person—whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, or a thief of gold. 29.
All minor sins, as well as all major transgressions,
are reduced to ashes for the man who is intent upon the ritual bath of Māgha.
"Who will protect us from all evils at this gathering for the Māgha bath?
This is our time of destruction, if he does not bathe in the water. (31)
Thus do the wicked cry out upon seeing a man intent on the ritual bath;
yet those best of men shine like fires kindled by the Māgha baths.
They are liberated from all evils, like the moon from the clouds—whether moist or dry, light or heavy, and whatever has been committed through the actions of speech and mind. (33)
Just as fire consumes fuel, the Māgha bath destroys sin that causes suffering;
it likewise consumes whatever sin has been committed through negligence, whether done intentionally or unintentionally.
By merely bathing when the sun is situated in Capricorn, that [sin] shall perish; the sinless go to heaven, and even the most wicked attain purity.
O lord of men, no doubt should be entertained here regarding the Māgha bath; O King, all are qualified for the Māgha bath, just as they are for devotion to Viṣṇu.
For all people, the Māgha sacrifice is the giver of heaven; for all people, it is the destroyer of sin.
This alone is indeed the supreme mantra, and this alone is the supreme austerity. (37)
This supreme expiation is the unsurpassed ritual bath of Māgha;
through the repeated practice of births, the human mind becomes inclined toward the Māgha bath.
O King, proficiency in the knowledge of the inner self arises from lifelong practice;
it is skilled in washing away the smearing of the mire of saṃsāra. (39)
O King, it is the purifier of purifiers and superior even to the Māgha bath;
O King, one should perform the Māgha bath during this time which bestows the fruits of all desires. (40)
How did they enjoy those riches, comparable to the moon, the sun, and the planets?
O King, listen to this great marvel born from the power of the Māgha bath. (41)
A virtuous Brāhmaṇī named Kubjikā, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, afflicted by the suffering of premature widowhood, performed extremely difficult penance. 42.
In that great sacred field at the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā, she became observant of vows and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa. 43.
She was always possessed of virtuous conduct, constantly free from attachment, with her senses conquered and her anger subdued; she spoke the truth and was sparing of speech. (44)

Possessing the virtue of good conduct and the virtue of generosity, she emaciated her body; having given to the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born, and likewise having offered oblations into the fire. (45)
O King, she always subsisted on gleaned food, eating only at the sixth meal-time;
she performed penances such as the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, Pārāka, Taptakṛcchra, and others. ||46||
Thus, on the auspicious banks of the Narmadā, she lived upon a diet of fruits and roots;
in this manner, that ascetic woman, clad in bark garments and possessed of virtuous conduct, remained there.
Endowed with great being, steadfastness, and contentment,
she bathed for sixty Magha months at the confluence of the Revā and the Kapilā.
Then, O King, having died at that sacred ford after her penances were exhausted,
she went to the city of Viṣṇu by virtue of the merit gained from the Māgha bath.
She dwelt there, joined with great joy, for a thousand cycles of four yugas;
afterwards, for the destruction of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous, she was born again from the Lotus-born One.
She was brought down to the world of Brahmā under the name Tilottamā;
by the remainder of that merit, she became the singular abode of beauty.
Born not from a womb, a jewel among women who deludes even the gods, that slender-bodied one was the most excellent of the Apsarases, a mine of loveliness. (52)
Surely, having created that most wonderful masterpiece,
the Creator of the subtle rite was so pleased that he immediately granted his approval.
"O you with eyes like those of a young antelope, go quickly for the destruction of the Daityas!
Then that beautiful woman took her lute from the world of Brahmā.
Having gone by the path of Puṣkara to where the two enemies of the gods were, he bathed there in the pure and stainless waters of the Turaṅgā river. 55.
Having put on a beautiful red garment with the luster of the bandhūka flower,
she was adorned with jingling bracelets, lovely armlets, a girdle, and anklets.
Adorned with a necklace of shimmering pearls around her neck and beautified by swinging earrings,
she wore a crest of *mādhavī* flowers and stood before her lover.
She sang with a sweet voice, pressing the lute strings;
she brought the six musical notes to their full resonance, singing in a manner that was very smooth, tender, and melodious.
Thus, while Tilottamā was standing in the Aśoka grove, she was seen by the Daitya warriors; my heart, however, felt a joy as great as that of one whose limbs are tormented by suffering.
Seeing her, the soldiers were filled with great wonder and joy;
they hurried away without even looking back, driven by their longing for the life of the two [princes].
Having described it again and again with great agitation, he said:
"O Daityas, we do not know whether this is a goddess or a demoness."
She is the jewel among women, a Naga, a Ganapati, and a Yakshini, who is entirely devoted to you; she is a woman who has become a jewel for the world, O jewels of arms, and possesses great power. 62.
Not very far ahead stands the Aśoka tree that removes sorrow;
go quickly and behold it, which is enchanting even to the God of Love. (63)
Having heard those heart-stealing words of the army commanders,
he set aside his cup of *sīdhu* liquor and abandoned the sprinkling of water.
Leaving behind thousands of excellent women from that lake,
he took up a cruel iron mace weighing a hundred bhāras, resembling the staff of Death.
Having seized him who was both distinct and non-distinct, she rushed forward with speed;
whereupon Caṇḍī stood ready, equipped with her trident and bow.
O King, fanning the fierce fire of passion between the two Daityas, that rogue stood before her, utterly deluded by her beauty.
Intoxicated by the honey, those two brothers spoke to one another:
"O brother, let this woman of excellent complexion be my wife. (68)
"You alone, O noble one, must abandon this wife of mine,
whose eyes are like those of a madirā-flower," he said with such insistence that they became agitated like two intoxicated bulls.
Then, as their time had been ordained, they struck each other with maces;
by their mutual blows, they lost their lives and fell to the earth.
Seeing her at that time, the soldiers raised a great clamor:
"Who is this who resembles the Night of Doom? Alas, what is this that has arrived? (71)
While the armies were speaking thus, Tilottamā, like a lightning flash from a mountain peak, struck down the two Daityas, Suṃda and Upasuṃda.
Having swiftly ascended into the sky and illuminated the ten directions,
they then performed the task for the gods and returned before Brahmā.
Then, being pleased by the god Brahmā and having been approved by him,
I granted you, O moon-faced one, a place upon the chariot of the Sun.
"O King, enjoy manifold pleasures as long as the sun remains in the sky.
Having spoken thus, O King, that Brāhmaṇa woman became the most excellent of the Apsarases. (75)
One enjoys the great fruit of the Māgha bath in the world of Dyāpi-ravi;
therefore, O King, faithful men should always strive with diligence [to perform it]. (76)
Those desiring the supreme goal must bathe at Makarāditya; for one who has not bathed here, no human purpose whatsoever remains unattained.
No sin whatsoever remains undestroyed for the man who bathes in the month of Māgha;
all sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees weigh less than this [act]. (78)
O King of kings, there is no other act that bestows heaven, nor any other that destroys sin, than the ritual bath during the month of Māgha, especially at this sacred ford (tīrtha). (79)
And because there is nothing else on earth equal to the Māgha bath that bestows liberation. ||80||
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa,
in the Māgha-māhātmya, within the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa, in the praise of the Māgha bath,
[this is] the section titled "The Slaying of the Daityas Sunda and Upasunda."
The one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter.
(127) Chapter One Hundred and Twenty-Seven. Kārtavīrya said:
O great sage, by what cause is this most wonderful power described as being in the Māgha-bath? O you of excellent vows, tell that to me.
Having gone beyond sin, this Vaiśya went to heaven alone, without a second, through the merit of the month of Māgha; tell me of this wonder. (2)
Dattātreya said: By its very nature, water is pure, stainless, bright white,
a destroyer of impurities, O tiger among men, a solvent, and a quencher of burning heat.
It is the savior of all beings, their nourishment, and their very life. ||3||
The deity Āponārāyaṇa is recited in all the Vedas;
just as the sun is among the planets and the moon is among the stars, so too is Māgha the most excellent among all months for every ritual action. (4)
In the month of Māgha, during the pure morning hours,
even a bath in water as small as a cow's footprint bestows heaven even upon sinners.
O King, this yoga is difficult to attain in the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving;
even one who is incapable of this yoga should bathe for at least three days.
Even one who is incapable and poor should give something out of a desire for spiritual existence;
likewise, those wealthy men who perform the triple bath of Māgha become long-lived.
For fifty-seven days, the fruit increases like the moon;
when the sun has entered Capricorn, it bestows merit upon men according to their merit.
All the lunar days on which the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkārya-tithis) grant the performer of rites such as bathing and giving the imperishable and eternal state in this world.
Therefore, desiring one's own welfare, one should bathe outdoors during the month of Māgha. Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme procedure for the Māgha bath.
Some form of restraint in the shape of a vow should be undertaken by the best of men for the sake of an excellence of fruit; however, the wise man should eat something or abstain from eating. 11.
One should sleep on the ground and offer oblations of clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds;
one should worship Viṣṇu, the eternal Vāsudeva, at the three times of day.
An unbroken lamp should be offered, dedicated to Lord Mādhava.
[One should also give] gold, food, strength, clothing, sandals, saffron, and ghee. (13)
O lord of men, in the month of Māgha, one should give oil, a cotton pod, a cotton mattress, a cotton roll, a cloth, and food according to one's ability.
Likewise, O King, one who knows the Vedas should give even a single *rattikā* of gold;
that gift is inexhaustible for all time, like the ocean. (15)
One should not attend another's fire-sacrifice and should renounce the acceptance of gifts;
O lord of men, one should feed the Brahmins during the month of Māgha according to one's ability.
One who desires their own welfare should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to those [preceptors],
as well as perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the Ekādaśī vow according to the rules of Māgha.
This should be performed by one endowed with faith, desiring imperishable heaven, for the sake of attaining infinite merit and as a cause for the propitiation of Viṣṇu. (18)
O Lord Govinda, Acyuta, Mādhava, who resides in the ocean during the month of Māgha—O God, by this bath, may you grant me the fruit as it has been described! (19)
Having recited this mantra, one should bathe while observing silence and remaining composed;
one should then again remember Vāsudeva, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Mādhava. (20)
Even at home, a water-pot that has been shaken by the wind during the night makes one's bath equal to that of a sacred pilgrimage site, bestowing the fruits of all desires. (21)
In that regard, one should give food along with utensils as part of the vow;
by the power of that bath, a person shall not go to hell. ||22||
The bath performed by men at home with hot water yields the fruit of six years when the sun is situated in Capricorn.
O King, bathing externally in a large pond (vāpī) is said to yield the fruit of twelve years;
in a tank (taḍāga) it is double that, and by a river it is fourfold.
O King, the merit at the Devakhātas is a hundredfold, at the Mahānada it is a hundredfold,
and at the confluence of the great river it is four times a hundredfold.
O King, when the sun is in Capricorn, a human being obtains all that fruit multiplied a thousandfold simply by bathing in the Gaṅgā.
O best of kings, those who bathe in the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha do not fall from the abode of the gods for a thousand cycles of the four ages.
O Lord of the People, that man who bathes in the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha has given a thousand gold pieces every single day. ||28||
O best of kings, the sages have declared that a bath at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the month of Māgha is a thousand times more meritorious than [the aforementioned]. (29)
O King, for the sake of burning away the heavy burden of the flood of sins, Prajāpati, established in the welfare of all creatures, created Prayāga.
Listen, this place is indeed one where the waters are both white and black; it was ordained of old by Brahmā for those who are like sacrificial animals in the form of sin. (31)

Even one burdened with hundreds of sins who immerses himself in the white and black waters during the month of Māgha while the sun is situated in Capricorn (Makara) is never again immersed in the wombs of rebirth.
Even a mortal who delights in slaughter, if he should perform a bath at Prayāga during the month of Māgha, O tiger among men, attains the supreme state.
The Creator fashioned that path to the world of Viṣṇu, which is embraced by the Sarasvatī river whose twin streams are white and black. 34.
O lord of men, that invincible illusion of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the gods to overcome,
is consumed by fire at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures in the worlds consisting of light,
they subsequently merge into the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu) due to their immersion in the waters at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.

Even Citragupta is not capable of fully calculating the merit of one who performs ablutions on the full moon day of Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn, whether it be the bright or dark fortnight. (37)
In the month of Māgha, when the sun is situated in Capricorn, one who immerses oneself in the white and black waters—
Brahmā himself is not capable of describing the majesty of that merit.
Whatever fruit is obtained by one who remains without food for more than a hundred years,
that same fruit is obtained by bathing for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
The fruit that one obtains by giving a thousand bhāras of gold at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse is obtained day after day by bathing in the Veṇī during the month of Māgha.
O King, the fruit of bathing during the month of Māgha at the confluence of the white and dark waters (the Gaṅgā and Yamunā) is certainly not equal to that of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices. 41.
O best of kings, whatever sacred fords exist on earth and those seven cities likewise come to bathe in the Veṇī during the month of Māgha.
All holy fords that have become black due to the fault of association with sinners become white in color by bathing at Prayāga during the month of Māgha. 43.
O King, whatever sin has been accumulated by men over many births throughout an entire kalpa,
that is reduced to ashes for those who bathe at the confluence of the white and black rivers during Māgha.
The sin born of speech, mind, and body of a man shall certainly go to destruction if he bathes for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha. 45.
The person who bathes for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha casts off his sin and goes to heaven, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin. (46)
The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever she is plunged into; ten times more meritorious than that is the place where she is joined by the Viṃdhyā. 47.
Therefore, the north-flowing Gaṅgā at Kāśī is a hundred times superior;
and the Gaṅgā at its confluence with the Yamunā is said to be a hundred times superior to that [Gaṅgā] at Kāśī. 48.
O King, that river which flows westward becomes a thousand times more meritorious than that;
by the mere sight of it, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is removed.
The Ganges, flowing westward and joined by the Kālindī, destroys the sins committed ten million times; it is difficult for men to encounter during the month of Māgha, O King. (50)
O King, that which is called "Amṛta" is celebrated as being on the banks of the Sāveṇī;
in the month of Māgha, even a single moment there is difficult for even the gods to attain.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, the Rudras, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts; the Gandharvas, world-protectors, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Pannagas. ||52||
And those others who are perfected through qualities such as *aṇimā* and who propound the principles [of their own systems]—Brahmāṇī, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Śacī, Menā, Aditi, and Diti. (53)
O King, all those wives of the gods, as well as the hosts of nāgas—Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā—[all came there]. (54)
O lord of men, all the hosts of Apsarases as well as the hosts of Pitṛs come to the Veṇī at the time of Māgha to bathe.

The fruit that is obtained from bathing for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha is attained by those who manifest in their true form in the Kṛta Yuga and in concealed forms in the Kali Yuga.
One does not obtain that fruit on earth even by a thousand horse-sacrifices;
such is the fruit of bathing for three days in Māgha, as was declared of old by Kāñcanamālinī.
Released by him, that evildoer gave [the earrings] to the Rākṣasa.
Kārtavīrya said:
"O Blessed One, who was this Rākṣasa? And who was that woman wearing a golden garland? (58)
How did she bestow the Dharma, and how did she attain a good rebirth?
O Sun of the lineage of the Yogīs, tell me this, if you consider it fit to be heard; for I have a great curiosity. (59)
Dattātreya said:
Listen, O King, to this wonderful ancient history, by the mere remembrance of which one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. (60)
An Apsarā endowed with beauty, named Kāñcanamālinī,
having bathed at Prayāga during the month of Māgha, goes to the abode of Hara.
While he was staying in the hollow of the king of mountains in the form of a mountain,
that aged rākṣasa saw her ascended into the sky.
She possessed a radiant and golden luster, with beautiful hips and long eyes;
she had a moon-like face, lovely hair, and full, elevated breasts. (63)
Seeing her, endowed with such beauty, the Rākṣasa then said:
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, and from where have you come? (64)
Why is your garment damp? Whence comes this moisture on your braid?
From where have you come, O timid one? And whence do you possess the power of moving through the air? (65)
"By what merit, O blessed lady, has this body of yours become so full of splendor, endowed with such exceeding beauty, and so enchanting? (66)
O fair-eyed one, by the falling of a drop from your garment upon my head, my mind—which was always cruel—attained peace in an instant. (67)
"What is this greatness of water? You ought to explain this to me;
otherwise, my work would be devoid of merit despite its brilliance. (68)
The Apsarā said:
"Listen, O Rākṣasa; I am an Apsarā who can assume any form at will.
Having come from Prayāga, I am known by the name Kāñcanamālinī. (69)
"My garment is still damp; therefore, O dark and light river, I have already bathed well.
But I must go, O Rakshasa, to Kailasa, the best of mountains. (70)
There dwells the Lord of Pārvatī, worshipped by both gods and demons;
by the power of the waters of the Veṇī, your cruelty has been destroyed. (71)
I shall tell you all that merit by which I was born as the daughter of the wise Gandharva Sumedhas, possessing a divine form. (72)
I was a courtesan to the king, the lord of Kaliṅga;
endowed with beauty and charm, I was arrogant with the pride of good fortune. (73)
And among all the other young women in that city, I was the crest-jewel;
in that birth, O Rākṣasa, I enjoyed pleasures according to my desire. (74)
That entire city was infatuated by me through the excellence of my youth, as well as by various jewels, ornaments, and riches. (75)
Garments of variegated forms, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood—all this has been acquired by me through my enchanting form. (76)
"O night-stalker, I do not know the limit of my gold in my own abode;
young men, afflicted by desire, serve at my feet. (77)
By means of my power of illusion, I have deceived them all with their entire possessions;
some lustful ones have even died through their state of mutual rivalry.
Thus, while my entire movement was within that delightful city, when the time of old age arrived, my heart grieved:
"Nothing was given, nothing was offered in sacrifice, nothing was chanted, and no vow was observed by me. (79)
I did not propitiate the God who bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
I did not worship the Goddess Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune; and Viṣṇu, the remover of all sins, was not remembered by me, for I was greedy for worldly enjoyments. (80)
The Brahmins were not fully gratified, nor was the welfare of living beings accomplished;
not even an atom’s worth of merit was performed due to negligence. (81)
"O auspicious one, though a sin has been committed, my mind is not burning with remorse.
Having lamented thus in many ways, I sought refuge with the Brahmin. (82)
To the king's priest, who was devoted to Brahman and learned in the Vedas, he said:
"O Rakshasa, when questioned by me, how can there be atonement for me? (83)
O best of the twice-born, how shall I attain a good destination from this sin? For I am wretched, lowly-minded, and tormented by my own very actions. (84)
O twice-born one, lift me up from being submerged in the mire of sin by grasping my hair; shower upon me the water born of compassion with a glance of joy! 85.
"All virtuous people are good toward the virtuous, and the virtuous person is good even toward the wicked.
Having heard these words of mine, he granted me favor regarding my imprisonment. (86)
The twice-born said:
"O fair-faced one, I know all your forbidden conduct.
Quickly do as I say: go to the sacred field of Prajāpati. (87)
"Go there and perform a ritual bath; by that, your sins shall be destroyed.
O blessed lady, everything that was in your mind has been grieved over by me. (88)
I see nothing else that destroys your sin;
bathing at a sacred ford is remembered by the sages as the supreme expiation. (89)
However, O timid one, you should abandon even the evil committed mentally at a sacred ford;
having become purified by bathing at Prayāga, you will certainly go to heaven. (90)
O beautiful lady, by the mere act of bathing at Prayāga, heaven is attained by men without a doubt;
even the sin committed in another land [is destroyed] at that very moment. (91)
At Prayāga, sin perishes—except for that committed at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Listen, O timid one, to how in ancient times Śakra [abducted] the wife of the sage Gautama. 92.
Having seen her, he fell under the power of desire and went to meet that secret lover;
by that fierce evil deed, the fruit was produced at that very moment. (93)
Then, in the presence of Indra and that woman, as he approached the wife of the ṛṣi, his body became loathsome, censurable, and a cause for shame. (94)
Then, due to the greatness of his master’s curse, the king of the gods emerged with a thousand marks of the female organ [upon his body] and, turning his face downward, departed. (95)
Overwhelmed and filled with shame, he reproached his own deed on the summit of Mount Meru, which was rich in water and extended for a hundred yojanas.
Having gone there, he entered the bud of a golden lotus;
staying there, he constantly reproached himself as well as the god of love. (97)
Fie upon that state of being possessed by desire in this world, which instantly brings about sin;
for by it one goes to hell, censured by all the world. (98)
Fie upon that wicked Manmatha, the constant source of calamities, who thus destroys life, fame, glory, virtue, and fortitude! (99)
"While the enemy residing in the body— difficult to subdue, ever-pleased, and always uncontrollable—
is thus speaking, while Vāsava remains hidden in his lotus-abode," (100)
O timid one, the world of the gods does not shine without Ākhaṇḍala;
therefore, the gods, along with the gandharvas, the world-protectors, and the kinnaras, [approached him]. (101)
Having come together with Śacī, they questioned Bṛhaspati:
"O Blessed One, we do not know the god who is the slayer of Bala. (102)
Where does he stay? Where has he gone? Or where shall we search for him?
Without him, even heaven, together with the hosts of gods, does not shine.
Just as a family, though illustrious and endowed with virtues, [is diminished] without a good son, let a means be devised immediately by which it may shine in the heavenly world. (104)
"He has a protector and is endowed with great fortune; therefore, delay is not appropriate here.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Guru spoke this speech: ||105||
I know that Indra, having impetuously achieved his purpose, now reaps the fruit of his deed wherever he stays out of shame for his own transgression. (106)
For men, the abandonment of ethical conduct leads to terrifying consequences;
alas, intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty, one fails to consider what ought and ought not to be done. (107)
For fools, their intellects struck down by fate, perform there that which is censurable and causes the destruction of both seen and unseen merit. (108)
Since through this offense our birth here and hereafter will be fruitless, let us now go to where Śakra resides. 109.
Having spoken thus, all of them, led by Bṛhaspati, departed;
they saw a grove of golden lotuses in a vast lake.
They praised the King of Gods so that awakening might arise;
then, through the teacher’s awakening, he emerged from the lotus bud. (111)
Indra, dejected and disfigured with eyes contracted by shame, grasped the feet of his preceptor, that foremost of the twice-born. 112.
"Save me! O Bṛhaspati, tell me the atonement for this sin.
Having heard these words of the king of the gods, the brahmin Bṛhaspati spoke.
Listen, O Lord of Gods, I shall declare the means for the destruction of sin;
by the mere act of bathing at Prayāga, one is freed from that very moment of transgression. (114)
"You shall be released from your status as king of the gods; let us go there together.
Then, having arrived along with his domestic priest, the crusher of armies—
He bathed at the confluence of the white and black waters and was instantly liberated from his sins;
then the preceptor of the gods, being pleased with him, granted him a boon.
O sinless one, your sin has been destroyed merely by bathing at Prayāga;
O Śakra, since your sin is destroyed, by my grace you shall soon [attain your goal]. (117)
A thousand of these wombs, and a thousand of such forms as yours, [shall be yours];
at that very moment, by the word of the twice-born, the Lord of Śacī shone forth.
Then, he was honored by all the gods and sages, who were like a thousand lotuses for his eyes, as if they were the minds of those [beings] themselves.
Being praised by the Gandharvas, Śakra went to Amarāvatī;
thus, at Prayāga, the subduer of Pāka was instantly freed from sin.
For you too, O auspicious lady, should go to Prayāga, which is frequented by the gods, for the immediate destruction of sin and firmly for the sake of attaining heaven. (121)
Having heard these auspicious words of his, together with their historical context, she was immediately overcome with agitation; she bowed at the feet of the twice-born man.
Having abandoned all kinsmen, as well as male and female servants and the household,
and having clearly renounced all sensory objects which are like the consumption of poison by a demon, ||123||
Indeed, seeing my body destroyed by the gaze [of the king], I have emerged from within the terrible fire of falling into the ocean of hell. 124
Then, O tiger among corpses, with my heart burning with that [remorse],
I went and performed a ritual bath at the confluence of the white and dark rivers during the month of Māgha.
O aged night-stalker, hear the majesty of that bath:
the destruction of sin occurred after three days, and [the final result] was achieved in twenty-seven days. (126)
"By whatever merit remained for me, through that I attained the state of a goddess;
thus, Girijā is my dear companion, delighting on Kailāsa. (127)
Thus, by the power of Prayāga, she became one who remembers her past births;
remembering the majesty of Prayāga, she said, "In every month of Māgha, I go [there]. (128)
Thus, O Rākṣasa, all that was asked by you with a mind full of wonder has been related by me in its entirety for your pleasure. (129)
O Rākṣasa, for my pleasure, tell me your own life story;
by what deed were you born so deformed and exceedingly terrifying? (130)
Bearded and possessing long fangs, the wheel-eater (Cakravyāda) was in a mountain cave.
The Rākṣasa said:
"He gives what is desired, he takes [it], he speaks of secrets, and he asks [about them]. (131)
For a virtuous person acts out of affection, O blessed lady, and all that resides in you;
indeed, O lovely-eyed one, I believe you have surely honored me. (132)
"An immediate atonement for this cruel deed must be made by you;
therefore, O blessed lady, I shall tell you of the evil deed that you yourself have committed. (133)
Having disclosed one's suffering to a virtuous person, one shall thereafter become happy in every way.
Listen, O lady of beautiful hips: in Kāśī, I was a scholar of the Rigveda who had mastered the Vedas. (134)
O fearless one, in former times he was born as an excellent twice-born man in a great and stainless family of kings, as well as of Śūdras and Vaiśyas who had committed evil deeds. (135)
In Vārāṇasī, I committed a terrible act of accepting gifts from the wicked; though forbidden many times and in many ways, I repeatedly rejected my own reproach. (136)
I did not even reject the acceptance of gifts from a caṇḍāla;
moreover, another sin occurred there for me, whose mind was deluded.
There is no evil deed that has not been committed by me. (137)
Moreover, O lady of excellent complexion, hear another defect of that field:
whatever sin, even as small as an atom, exists in Avimukta, it becomes as vast as Mount Meru;
yet no merit whatsoever was accumulated by me there in that birth. (138)
Then, after a long time had passed, I died there in that beautiful place;
by the power of Avimukta, I did not go to hell. (139)
No sinner who dies in Avimukta goes to hell;
whatever sin is committed in Avimukta becomes as firm as a thunderbolt.
By that sin, which was like a coating of adamant, my birth-demon became fierce,
most cruel, and evil, arising on the Snowy Mountain.
Born twice previously in the womb of a vulture, thrice as a tiger, and twice as a reptile; once as an owl, and thereafter as a dung-worm. (142)
But this, O beautiful lady, is my tenth birth as a Rākṣasa;
thousands of years have passed since my birth.
"O blessed lady, there is no escape for me from this ocean of suffering;
O fair-browed one, I have indeed cleared this area of three yojanas of all living beings. (144)
And since the destruction of many innocent beings has been wrought by you through your actions, O fair-browed one, my mind is constantly consumed with grief. (145)
My mind, sprinkled with the nectar of your sight, has attained coolness;
a sacred ford bears fruit in time, but the company of the virtuous bears fruit instantly. 146.
Therefore, O fair-browed one, the wise praise association with the virtuous.
Thus I have told you all this, my own sorrow that was in my heart. (147)
O fair-browed one, that virtuous person is rare whose own self does not suffer;
you surely know what is appropriate here, so I shall say nothing further. (148)
Reflecting, "How shall I go to the further shore of this ocean of suffering?
one finds that the company of the virtuous is the sustenance for all. (149)
"Does the Ocean of Milk give its milk to a crane that has swallowed a fish?
Dattātreya said:
"Having heard these words of his, her mind was moistened with compassion. (150)
Having set her mind upon the gift of the Dharma, Kāñcanamālinī said:
"O Protector, I shall now provide atonement; do not grieve. (151)
Having made a firm vow, I shall strive for your liberation;
indeed, many *māgha* fasts have been performed by me year after year according to the prescribed rule. (152)
"O noble one, O Rākṣasa, preceded by faith, I have sown [seeds] in the field of Brahmā, both white and black; I shall now declare the enumeration of that Dharma. (153)
For the wise say that dharma must be practiced in secret;
the sages who proclaim the Vedas praise the giving of gifts to those in distress. (154)
O auspicious one, what fruit would there be for a cloud raining upon the ocean?
O Rākṣasa, I myself have experienced that very fruit born of merit. (155)
O friend, I shall give that to you immediately; it is the destroyer of sin.
Then, having squeezed out the garment and placed the water in my lotus-like hand— (156)
She bestowed upon that aged Rākṣasa the merit born of the Māgha vow;
hear now, O King, the wonderful power arising from the dharma of Māgha. (157)
Then, having thus obtained that merit, he was liberated from his rakshasi body and was reborn with the form of a deity, a body radiant with splendor like the sun. (158)
Mounted upon the celestial vehicle, his eyes wide with joy, he then shone in the sky, illuminating the quarters with his splendor. (159)
Bearing a divine form, he shone like a second sun; then he greeted Satī, who was adorned with a golden garland. 160.
O blessed lady, the Lord Vettīśvara is the deity who bestows the fruits of actions;
all that you have done for me is such that there can be no recompense from my side. (161)
Even now, out of compassion, be gracious and show me favor;
O Goddess, bestow upon me auspicious instruction that embodies all principles of conduct.
Having heard that which surely accomplishes all dharmas so that I may not commit sin, I shall go to the abode of the gods afterwards with your permission. (163)
Dattātreya said:
Having heard these pleasing words, full of righteousness, spoken by him, O King, Kāñcanamālinī spoke with great affection regarding dharma. (164)
Constantly devote yourself to Dharma; abandon violence toward living beings; serve virtuous men; slay the enemy that is desire;
and quickly cast off the practice of proclaiming the faults and virtues of others.
Speak the truth, worship Hari, and go to the world of the gods.
Abandon the notion of "self" regarding this body of bone, flesh, and blood;
forever relinquish the sense of "mine-ness" toward wife, children, and the like.
Indeed, behold this world incessantly as being subject to momentary decay.
Be one who relishes the flavor of the state of detachment, remaining steadfast in yoga. ||166||
Out of affection, I have proclaimed the path of Dharma to you;
O Citta, endowed with the discipline of existence, take it all to heart. Having cast off your demonic body, assume the form of a god.
Go quickly to heaven, which consists of light, as you please.
Having heard the Dharma, the Rākṣasa was thrilled and, being well-pleased, said:
"May you always be joyful; may all be auspicious for you at all times. (168)
"May you rejoice on Kailāsa in the presence of Śiva as long as the moon and sun endure;
O woman of excellent complexion, may your love for Umā remain unbroken. (169)
O Mother, may you always be established in Dharma and established in austerity;
let there be no greed for your body, and always remove the suffering of those in distress. (170)
Having spoken thus and then bowed down to Satī Kāñcanamālinī,
the Rākṣasa, praised by many Gandharvas, departed for heaven.
Then the celestial maidens, overwhelmed with joy, arrived and rained down showers of flowers upon her head, who wore a golden garland. (172)
Then, embracing her, the maidens spoke these kind words:
"O blessed lady, you have performed a marvelous feat in liberating the Rākṣasa."
Out of fear of this wicked one, no one enters this forest;
now, indeed, we roam here at our ease, free from fear. (174)
O King, having heard those words of theirs, Kāñcanamālinī was delighted; at that time, being virtuous, she felt she had accomplished her purpose through their gift.
Having quickly liberated that rākṣasa, the excellent gandharva maiden Kāñcanamālinī set out for the abode of Hara, sporting with those [other maidens].
And she was filled with joy through her desire to help others. ||176||
Any person who listens with supreme devotion to this dialogue between the bridegroom and the bride shall never at any time be afflicted by rākṣasas.
For his mind indeed becomes intensely focused upon the Dharma. ||177||

Thus ends the section titled "The Liberation of the Rākṣasa" within the dialogue between Dilīpa and Vasiṣṭha, in the Māgha-māsa-māhātmya of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter. ||127||
(128) The One Hundred and Twenty-Eighth Chapter:
The Hymn on the Essence of Yoga (Yoga-sāra-stotra)
Vasiṣṭha said:
The greatness of Māgha has been told as spoken by Dattātreya;
now I shall proclaim the fruit that comes from the Māgha bath. (1)
The ritual bath in Māgha is the most excellent of all sacrifices, yet it yields fruit at all times; equal to all vows and austerities, it is the supreme penance. (2)
Having purified their minds through the ritual bath of Māgha and having established the ancestors of both lineages in heaven,
they themselves proceed to the radiant celestial realm, free from all obstructions.
And with beautiful celestial chariots that travel at will.
Those men who, though they have committed sins, are always devoted to wicked conduct and follow the wrong path—
if they bathe during Māgha and worship Hari, [they are purified].
Those who steal also accumulate great debt in this world. ||4||
Those men who are devoid of truth, who cause suffering to their father and mother, who do not abide by the stages of life (āśrama), who are bereft of family dharma,
and who are hypocritical— they too [do not attain] the goal of the virtuous.
For indeed, they go there by means of baths performed during the month of Māgha. ||5||
Bathing in sacred fords during the month of Māgha is extremely difficult for men to attain on this earth;
therefore, by means of that [bath], the state of those who know Brahman is reached by men.
It is attained; herein I have no further deliberation. ||6||
O King, in the month of Māgha, the practice of austerity, charity, and recitation, as well as the worship of Hari, yields inexhaustible results;
therefore, men should diligently perform these according to their capacity.
Having bathed, one should give garments, but not gold.
In the month of Māgha, a man who gives food becomes an immortal drinker in the abode of the gods; a giver of gold goes into the presence of Indra;
and one who always gives lamps, fire, and clothing likewise attains that state.
He dwells in the world of the sun, consisting of light. ||8||
In this world, even those who perform sacrifices, give bountiful gifts, practice intense and radiant austerities,
and engage in the service of celibacy, worship,
and yoga do not become pure unless they are free from sin.
Just as by means of meritorious baths taken during the month of Māgha. ||9||

Those who bathe in an excellent sacred ford during the month of Māgha do not undergo even those various torments of unbearable agony and the scorching heat of the flood of suffering that even evildoers do not experience.
And they perform [this] when the orb of the sun has half-risen. ||10||
Those who, having bathed during the month of Māgha, worship Hari, become kings upon descending from heaven—
gracious, handsome, fortunate, and sweet-spoken.
Endowed with righteousness, possessing abundant wealth, and having a lifespan of a hundred years. ||11||
Just as a piece of wood offered into a blazing fire becomes nothing but ashes in that very instant,
so too is one dissolved through the ritual bath of Māgha.
Even a small accumulation of a flood of sins becomes a great burden. ||12||
Whatever sin has been committed by men through body, speech, or mind— whether consciously or unconsciously— the bath taken in Māgha at a preeminent sacred ford is sufficient to purify it.
Like Viṣṇu, it quickly burns everything once it has entered the heart. ||13||
O King, for even here on earth, the fruit of sin being experienced by men sometimes arises from negligence;
therefore, the ritual bath of Māgha is undertaken.
At that very moment, it certainly goes to its destruction. ||14||
The Gandharva maidens, who were born from the curse of the lord of the earth and were experiencing the difficult-to-overcome fruit of their sin,
have indeed been liberated through bathing during the month of Māgha.
Before the speech, there was a marvelous growth of hair. ||15||
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the king, with joy, bowed at his lotus-like feet;
then, bowing low with supreme faith, he questioned that priest.
"O Blessed One, please tell us: from where did the curse come upon these maidens? Whose children are they, what are their names, and what is their age? (17)
How, by the words of Lomaśa, were they liberated from the curse arising from the ripening [of their karma]? Where did they bathe for a month, and how many were they in number? (18)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, to this supreme narrative pregnant with dharma,
which is like a fire-stick containing fire within it, or like a source of dharma that gives birth to fire.
The Gandharva was Sukhasaṃgīti; his daughter was Pramodinī. Suśīla’s [daughter] was Suśīlā, and Svaravedin’s was Susvarā. (20)
Sutārā, Candrakā, and Candrikāsuprabhā—
these, O King, are the names of those apsarases.
Furthermore, all five maidens were equal in age;
they emerged like rays from the moon and were as radiant as moonlight. (22)
