With moon-like faces and beautiful hair, their lips possessed the nectar-like flavor of the moon; they brought joy to the eyes, just as moonlight does to night-lotuses.
Born from a mass of loveliness, possessing beautiful and enchanting forms, with budding breasts like lotuses, they were like lotus-ponds in the month of Mādhava.
Whom did she not cause to blossom with the fresh sprouts of her forest-like creeper of youth? Golden-hued, radiant as gold, and adorned with golden ornaments. (25)
They were adorned with golden necklaces and garments of brilliant hue, and they possessed beautiful voices through various melodic scales (*grāma*) and diverse modulations (*mūrchanā*). ||26||

In the delights of providing rhythmic clapping, and in the playing of flutes, reeds, and lutes; in the blending of the sound of the mṛdaṅga drum, and in the gestures of the lāsya and mārga dances. (27)
Expert in various amusements such as painting and skilled in the fine arts,
being thus endowed with such qualities, they were captivated by the maiden during their play in the grove.
Cherished by their fathers, they lived truthfully in the abode of Kubera.
Once, in the month of Mādhava, five of them gathered together out of curiosity and went from the grove to the forest,
searching for mandāra flowers for the maidens.
Once, in order to propitiate Gaurī, excellent women went to the Acchoda lake;
they returned from there taking choice golden lotuses along with choice blue water-lilies.

Having bathed in a pond made of pure lapis lazuli, clear crystal, and translucent coral, and having put on fine garments, they fashioned an image of Umā out of gold, using molds made of earth from a sacrificial altar, while remaining in silence.
Having worshipped Gaurī— who had already been honored with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron— with excellent lotuses and other offerings,
the young maidens, moved by deep devotion, danced with various services and rhythmic clapping of their hands.

Then, relying on the excellent note of Gāndhāra, those fawn-eyed women sang with very high-pitched sounds and beautiful modulations; they sang verses of artistic syllables and charming compositions with harmonious movements and perfect pitch.

Then Agnipa, the son of the sage Vedanidhi, arrived at that most excellent of tirthas, Acchoda, which bestows both sorrow and joy through its sounds and so forth, and where the performance of unrestrained dancing was intense.
With a face more boundless in beauty than the moon, with eyes as long as lotus petals, broad-chested, with fine arms, exceedingly handsome, and dark-complexioned—he was like another Kāmadeva. (35)
Wearing a topknot like his fellow celibates, he shone with a staff as the God of Love shines with his bow;
clad in a deer-skin, wearing a fine sacred thread and a golden-colored girdle-string around his waist. (36)
Seeing that brahmin on the shore of the lake, those young women were filled with curiosity and rejoiced, saying, "Who is this who has become the guest of our eyes? (37)
Having abandoned their dancing and singing, they became intent on gazing at him,
like does pierced by the arrows of Kama, as if by a hunter.
Crying out "Look! Look! with great agitation, those simple women fell into the delusion that the best of brahmins was the god Kāmadeva himself.
Having worshipped him again and again with their eyes as if with lotuses,
those maidens thereafter engaged in mutual deliberation.
If this were the god of love, Kāmadeva, how could he proceed deprived of Rati? Or if these were the two Aśvin gods, they surely move about as a pair. (41)
Whether he was a Gandharva, a Kinnara, or a Siddha capable of assuming any form at will; or perhaps a son of a Rishi, or some other being superior to humans. ||42||
Or perhaps this man was created by the Creator for our sake; he is like a treasure hidden by past karmas for the benefit of those who are fortunate. (43)
In the same way, for us maidens, Gaurī has brought an excellent bridegroom, her heart moistened by the waves of the water of compassion. (44)
"O best of kings, he was chosen by me and you, and likewise, you were chosen by him and me"— thus did she speak to the five maidens, Tīṣu, and the others.
Having heard those words, he performed his midday rites there, and reflecting in his heart, [thought], "This obstacle has arisen. (46)
Even the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Giriśa, as well as the ancient Siddhas and sages,
though powerful through yoga, were wonderfully deluded by the playful charms of those women.
Whose deer-like mind does the god of love not strike down with his sharp arrows—the eyes of women—discharged from the very firm bows of their creeper-like eyebrows? 48.
Only so long does the intellect of right method shine; only so long does the multitude experience fear;
only so long is there intense firmness of mind; and only so long is there the agitation of calculation. (49)
The prowess of asceticism and the steadfastness of men endure only so long as non-human beings do not delude them with the arrows of women's glances, which are full of great intoxication. (50)

By what qualities do women—who delude and intoxicate those possessed by passion with their most graceful and charming ways—delude and intoxicate me, who am devoted solely to the protection of Dharma? (51)
O merciless one, those whose minds are utterly deluded imagine beauty in the impure bodies of women, which are composed of semen, excrement, and urine, and thus they fall prey to Māra.
For the proximity of women has been proclaimed as terrible by the wise of pure intellect;
therefore, as long as these [women] are not yet near me here, I shall go home. (53)
Before the excellent women could reach his presence,
the twice-born man vanished through the power of Viṣṇu.
Then, having seen that miraculous feat of the wise son of the seer, the king’s inability to see him while he was on the ground was due to the power of his yoga.
With eyes trembling in terror, the young women, overwhelmed by fear,
looked toward the ten directions with bewildered gazes as if they were empty.
They said to one another: "We clearly perceive this as a net of Indra, or rather, we recognize it as an illusion; though seen, it has become as if unseen. (57)
Their hearts were perpetually pervaded by the fire of separation,
like a lush sandalwood forest consumed by a blazing wildfire.

Having abandoned this illusory science (*māyājālikī vidyā*), show us quickly what you have; for you have presented yourself before us with a mind joined to it, like a fly at the very first morsel of food. (59)
"Alas! Why have you been shown to us? By what Creator were you fashioned again? It is now known that you were not created for our sake, but rather as a cause of great torment. (60)
Is your heart merciless? Do you have no thought for us? Are you a rogue, O beloved? Are you stealing away our hearts? (61)
I hope you have no suspicion toward us; I hope you are merely testing us. I hope you are one whose nature is fond of jesting and who is skilled in the arts of deception. (62)
Do you know the agility of consciousness for entering into the mind? And how much less do you know the means for its departure? (63)
I hope you do not become angry with us without cause;
I hope you understand the suffering that others experience when deceived. (64)
Without the sight of you, O Lord of our hearts, we certainly do not live now;
yet we live again through the hope of beholding you.
Lead us also to that place where you have gone so swiftly;
the Creator, who deprived us of the sight of you, has acted as a cutter of our very sprouts.
Grant me your vision in every way; practice compassion in every way.
For virtuous people never perceive an end in any respect.
Having lamented in this manner and waited for many moments, the maidens,
out of fear of their fathers, quickly began to set out for home.
Bound by the fetters of love for Him and deeply distressed by separation, they somehow summoned their courage and returned each to her own home. (69)
Having arrived, they all fell down near the water-machine;
asked by their mothers, "What is this? Why has there been such a delay? (70)
The maidens said:
"While he was joyfully engaged in music together with the Kinnarīs, he remained there; therefore, he did not notice the day and so forth at the lake. (71)
O Mother, we are weary from the journey; our bodies are consumed by this great distress.
Because of this profound delusion, we do not have the strength to say anything at all.
Having spoken thus, the young maidens rolled there upon the jeweled floor;
concealing their true feelings, those charming girls prattled with their mothers.
At that time, one woman did not joyfully dance with her toy peacock,
nor did another, out of curiosity, teach the parrot in its cage.
She fondles the mongoose and not others; she does not cause the sarika bird to sport.
She is exceedingly bewildered by another and does not play at all with the cranes.
They took no pleasure in diversions, nor did they find delight in their palaces;
they spoke not with their kinsmen, nor did they play upon the lute. (76)
They did not drink the sweet honey, produced from the wish-fulfilling tree, which was flavorful like nectar and fragrant with the scent of mandāra flowers. //77//
By that very yoginī, those maidens were made to fix their eyes on the tip of the nose, their stream of meditation becoming imperceptible, with their minds fixed upon Puruṣottama. (78)
Standing for a moment at the window, which was covered by moonstones from which drops of water were trickling, he gazed for a moment and then, in an instant, began to weep.
For a moment they prepare a bed with the petals of lotuses from the long pond,
while being fanned by their friends with cool plantain leaves.
Thus perceiving that night to be equal to an eon, those women of the lower realms somehow summoned their fortitude, though they were overwhelmed as if with fever. (81)
In the morning, seeing the jewel of the sky and considering it their own life, they informed their respective mothers and went to worship Gaurī. (82)
Having bathed according to that rite and having performed the worship of the Goddess with flowers and incense in the prescribed manner, they remained there singing. 83.
In the meantime, that brahmin also arrived at the Acchoda lake from his father’s hermitage in order to bathe. (84)
Upon seeing Mitra, those maidens of the excellent night became like lotuses with eyes wide open at the sight of that celibate student. 85.
Having approached the celibate student, those maidens who had him as their deity formed a noose of arms by binding them in a left-and-right interlacing fashion.
The rogue sword departed yesterday; you are unable to go today.
You have surely been chosen by us; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (87)
Thus addressed, the Brāhmaṇa, held by the noose of Bāhu’s arms, spoke:
"Blessed one, you have spoken words that are favorable and pleasing. (88)
But for one devoted to the first stage of life, who is habituated to the study of the Vedas, how can his vow reach its completion even now while remaining in the house of the teacher? (89)
"In the hermitage, this dharma must be protected by the wise;
therefore, I consider this marriage to be dharma for my daughters. (90)
Having heard his words, they then spoke these words to him,
longing for every sound like cuckoos for the month of Mādhava.
"From dharma comes wealth, from wealth comes desire, and from desire arises the fruit of dharma"—thus do the wise describe the teaching as definitively established. (92)
"Since your desire has been fulfilled due to the abundance of merit, you have arrived here first;
therefore, let this heavenly realm be enjoyed with various pleasures. (93)
Having heard those words of theirs, he spoke with a timid voice:
"Your speech is true; however, first complete your own vow here. (94)
"Having obtained the permission of the guru, one should perform all the marriage rites and no others"—having said this, they spoke again clearly: "O handsome one, you are a fool! (95)

Divine medicine, the Brahman-elixir, spiritual perfection, treasures, excellent arts, women, mantras, as well as the elixir of accomplishment—all these, when obtained through righteousness, should not be rejected by the wise. (96)
If a task has arrived as accomplished by fate or other means, one who follows the principles of policy should not neglect it;
for neglect does not yield fruit again, and therefore, procrastination is not praised. (97)

In this world, only fortunate men—and no others—obtain daughters who are deeply affectionate, of noble birth, pure, whose hearts are moist with love, who speak sweet words, who choose their own husbands, and who possess beautiful forms and lovely youth. (98)
"Where are these most beautiful women, and where is this young ascetic?
Indeed, the Creator must be considered extremely clever for bringing about such an impossible union. (99)
Therefore, you should now accept us; otherwise, there shall be no auspiciousness for you, nor even life itself for us. 100.
Then the Brahmin, the most knowledgeable in dharma, having heard their words, said:
"O deer-eyed ones, how can dharma be abandoned by men whose wealth is dharma? (101)
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—this fourfold set should be understood as fruitful when practiced as prescribed; however, if practiced contrarily, it is fruitless.
Therefore, observing my vow, I shall not take a noble wife at an improper time;
for he who does not know the proper time for an action does not obtain the fruit of that action. (103)
Since my mind has become intent upon this investigation of dharma, therefore listen, O maiden, for you yourself shall choose your own husband. (104)
Having thus understood his intention and observed one another, they released their hands from each other's grasp, and then Aṅghripamodinī took hold of him.
Suśīlā embraced him with her arms and neck, while Svarā likewise did so;
and Sutārā kissed the face of Candrikā.
Nevertheless, though he was changeless and resembled the fire of universal dissolution, that celibate student, utterly overwhelmed by rage, cursed them. (107)
"Since you have clung to me while I was a Piśācī, you shall likewise become Piśācīs.
Having been thus swiftly cursed by him, they abandoned him and remained in the city.
Why, O sinless one, have you committed such a wicked deed? Having done what is disagreeable while intending to do what is pleasing, fie on your knowledge of dharma! 109.
We have heard that for a man who commits treachery against those who are devoted, loyal, and friendly, happiness in both worlds comes to an end. (110)
"Therefore, you too shall quickly become a piśāca due to our curse.
Having spoken thus, the young women ceased speaking, sighing heavily and distressed by hunger.
Then, O King, due to their mutual agitation at that lake, all those maidens and that celibate student became piśācas. (112)
The Piśācas, together with the female Piśācī, subduing that most terrible wheel, exhaust the ripening of that karma previously acquired. (113)
O King, the auspicious and inauspicious karma previously acquired certainly bears fruit in its own time, being as unavoidable even for the gods as one's own shadow. (114)
Kraṃ, Daṃ, Ti, Pitaraḥ, and Tāsām Mātaraḥ; therein lies the heedfulness of children, for destiny is indeed difficult to overcome. 115.
Thereafter, those Piśācas, greatly distressed for the sake of food, ran hither and thither and remained on the bank of the lake. (116)
Thus, after a great deal of time had passed, Lomaśa, the best of sages, came to the Acchoda lake on the fourteenth day of the month of Pauṣa to bathe. ||117||
Seeing that brahmin, all the piśācas, agitated by hunger, gathered together in a herd and ran forward, desiring to kill him. (118)
Scorched by that intense splendor of Lomaśa,
they were all unable to stand before him and remained at a distance.
There, O King, the Brahmin Vedanidhi arrived at that very moment; having beheld Lomaśa, he prostrated himself before him with his eight limbs touching the ground. 120.
Having bound his hands in *añjali* at his head, he spoke these truthful words:
"The meeting of the virtuous occurs only through the dawning of great fortune. (121)
Between a man who constantly bathes in all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā, and one who cultivates the company of the virtuous, the company of the virtuous is superior. (122)
The company of gurus on this earth yields both seen and unseen fruits; it bestows heaven and removes disease—how then can it be considered fraught with obstacles? (123)
Having said this, he related that wonderful former event:
"These are those Gandharva maidens; this is that very boy, my own son. (124)
O best of sages, all of them, deluded by mutual curses, stand before you with dejected faces in the form of piśācas.
"By the sight of you, the salvation of the ignorant shall come to pass today; would the mass of darkness not dissolve in its cave at the rising of the sun? (126)
O King, having heard that, Lomaśa, his heart moistened with compassion, replied to that highly effulgent sage who was distressed for his son: 127.
"By my grace, let memory suddenly arise in these children, and let them speak the Dharma by which this mutual curse may come to an end. (128)
Vedanidhi said:
"O Great Sage, let that dharma be told by which children are liberated;
this is no time for delay, for the fire of the curse is terrible. (129)
Lomaśa said: "If you perform the Māgha bath according to the prescribed rites along with me, they will be released from the curse; otherwise, there would be no atonement. (130)
A curse is the fruit of sin; yet for men, the destruction of that sin occurs through bathing at a sacred ford during the month of Māgha—this is the firm conviction of Caitanya. (131)
Sin committed over seven lifetimes and present transgressions—
all this is destroyed by a bath in the month of Māgha, especially at a sacred pilgrimage site.
Even that sin for which the lords of sages see no expiation,
even such a transgression shall perish at a holy pilgrimage site through the month of Māgha.
The month of Māgha, when practiced with a mind focused on knowledge, bestows the fruit of liberation;
at the sacred fords on the slopes of the Himalayas, it destroys all sins.
The month of Māgha, which removes all sins and bestows liberation, has been prescribed by the exponents of the Vedas as being like Indra’s world for those who bathe at Badarīvana. 135.
It destroys sin, removes suffering, and bestows the fruits of all desires; it grants the world of Rudra, and in Māgha, the Narmadā is the destroyer of sins. ||136||
The Yamunā leads one to the world of the Sun and destroys impurity;
the Sarasvatī destroys sin and bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā. (137)
O best of the twice-born, on the full moon day of Māgha at Viśālā, the giver of vast fruits is like a forest fire to the sinner, destroying the very causes of rebirth. 138.
The Jāhnavī is proclaimed for liberation from the world of Viṣṇu;
likewise the Śarayū, Gaṇḍakī, Sindhu, Candrabhāgā, and Kauśikī. (139)
The Tāpī, Godāvarī, Bhīmā, Payoṣṇī, Kṛṣṇaveṇikā, Kāverī, Tuṅgabhadrā, and other rivers that flow into the ocean. ||140||
One who dies at Āśumāghīna goes to the heavenly world free from sin;
at Naimiṣa, one attains union with Viṣṇu; and at Puṣkara, proximity to Brahmā.
Indeed, the world of Indra is attained at Kurukṣetra during Māgha;
at Devahrada, the month of Māgha bestows the fruit of success in spiritual practice. 142.
By bathing at Prabhāsa in the month of Makarāditya, one becomes a member of the retinue of Rudra;
by means of Māgha, a man attains a divine body from Devakī.
O Brahmin, by bathing during the month of Māgha at the Gomati, there is no rebirth;
likewise at Hemakūṭa, Mahākāla, Oṃkāra, and Amareśvara. (144)
O Brahmin, by bathing at the confluence of all rivers during the month of Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn, one is glorified in the world of Rudra, which is the abode of blue-throated deities.
Through bathing, the attainment of all desires arises for men;
yet, O best of the twice-born, the month of Māgha is obtained by the fortunate at Prayāga, because there the white and black waters grant freedom from rebirth. 146.
The gods dwelling in heaven constantly sing: "Alas, for us there will be no Māgha at Prayāga,
where men, by virtue of their bath, do not experience the pains of the womb."
They behold [him] and remain in the presence of Viṣṇu. ||147||
Even those men who, though burdened by a multitude of sins, bathe here for three days at this Prayāga tīrtha, go to heaven as righteous ones; they do not enter the hells.
They move about beautifully in the auspicious heaven like gods. ||148||
When both were placed upon a scale by the Creator in the past, along with holy fords, vows, gifts, austerities, and sacrifices,
it was [the merit] of Prayāga in the month of Māgha that outweighed them both.
Therefore, Māgha is more venerable; for that very reason, he is superior. ||149||
Even by means of fierce austerities— accumulated over a long period— consisting of emaciating the body through subsisting on wind, water, and leaves,
and by means of yogic practices, men do not attain that goal.
Indeed, by bathing in the month of Māgha, one attains that same destination. ||150||
And for those who have bathed at the sacred ford of Prayāga, where the celestial river meets [the Gaṅgā], at the rising of the sun in Capricorn—
does their house door not shine with splendor?
A swarm of bees, struck by the ears of an elephant, [scatters]. ||151||
That which bestows a fruit greater than that of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices from its mere bathing,
effortlessly destroying all sins.
Surely, why is that Prayāga not resorted to? ||152||
In ancient times, there was a king named Vīrasena in the region of Avanti;
having come to the bank of the Narmadā, he performed the Rājasūya sacrifice. ||153||
He also performed sixteen horse-sacrifices according to the prescribed rites, which were resplendent with golden enclosures and enriched by sacrificial posts adorned with gold ornaments.
Generous, devoted to the gods, a giver of cows and a giver of gold, he bestowed upon the twice-born heaps of grain resembling mountains. (155)
There was a Brahmin named Bhadraka, who was foolish and of low birth;
he was a farmer of wicked conduct, excluded from all righteous dharma. ||156||
Distressed by his labor in agriculture and not supported by his kinsmen, he wandered here and there and departed, tormented by hunger. (157)
Having entered a merchant caravan by divine providence, he arrived at Prayāga;
honoring the great Māghī full moon, he bathed there for three days. ||158||
O best of the twice-born, having become sinless here merely by bathing, he departed from Prayāga and returned there once again. ||159||
On several occasions, both the king and the brahmin met with misfortune;
their fate was observed by me in the presence of Śakra. (160)

Their splendor, their form, their strength, their devotion to women, their celestial vehicle, their ornaments, their garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers, and their dancing and singing were all equal. (161)
Thus has the greatness of the snow [of the mountain] been seen; how can the greatness of this sacred field be described?
O Brahmin, the month of Māgha at the confluence of the white and black rivers is considered equal to Rājasūya sacrifices.
At the confluence of the white and blue [waters], extending three hundred bow-lengths, one who performs the Rājasūya sacrifice in the month of Māgha shall not return to rebirth. 163.
Even the wind of the month of Māgha may touch cold and dark water, but one who slays a great sinner— O, alas!— shall certainly not touch what is unrighteous.
O twice-born one, what is the use of much speaking here? Listen to this certainty:
Māgha at a sacred ford destroys sin once its fruit has manifested. (165)
In this regard, I shall tell you a story; listen with an attentive mind—this ancient history known as "The Liberation of the Piśāca."
"Listen, O young Apsarases; let your son likewise listen, for by my grace he shall regain his memory and desire liberation from the state of a Piśāca.
(1) Formerly, there was a Brahmin named Devadyuti, a devotee of Viṣṇu who had mastered the Vedas. (166)
With a mind overflowing with compassion, he liberated them from the piśācas. ||167||

Dilīpa said: Where did he reside? Whose son was he? What was his religious observance? What was his sacrificial offering? By whom was he initiated into the Vaiṣṇava way of life, and which piśācas were liberated by him? (168)
O great sage, recount all of this in detail; through your grace, we shall listen to this most meritorious account with great curiosity. (169)
Vasiṣṭha said:
At Plakṣaprasravaṇa, on the auspicious and holy bank of the Sarasvatī,
he established a beautiful hermitage there, taking refuge at that mountain.
With *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, with *bilva*, *bakula*, and *pāṭala*, with *tiṃtiḍī*, *ciribilva*, and with mangoes (*cūta*) and *campaka*. (171)
With *karañja*, *kovidāra*, and *kesara* trees; with *kuṣmāṇḍa*, *tilaka*, *karṇikāra*, *kumbha*, *khādira*, and *tiṃduka* trees. ||172||
With *vānīra*, *sālvaja*, *bīra*, *pīlu*, *uduṃbara*, and *vetasa*; with *śākoṭa*, *aṭarūṣa*, *karahāṭa*, and *vaṭa* trees. ||173||
With *ghoṇṭā*, *kuṭaja*, and *pālāśa* trees; with *aśoka* trees that dispel sorrow; and with *jaṃbū*, *nīpa*, *kadaṃba*, *kṣīrikā*, and *karamardaka* trees. ||174||
With *bījapūra* fruits together with *nāraṅga*, shining with the luster of gold;
with *panasa* trees bearing juice, and with coconut trees that bear fruit at all times. ||175||
With *saptacchada*, *tripatra*, auspicious *śirīṣa* and *āmalaka*, *karkaṃdhū*, *lakuca*, *akṣa*, *pāribhadra*, *vacā*, and so forth. ||176||
With *ketaka*, *siṃduvāra*, *tagara*, *kunda*, and *mallikā* flowers;
with *padma*, *indīvara*, *kahlāra*, *mālatī*, *yūthikā*, and others. ||177||
With *mālatī* and *mōgara* flowers, adorned with *jātī* fruits, as well as with *punnāga*, *kiṃśuka*, *barbarī*, and *tulasī* trees. ||178||
O King, that hermitage was delightful with its various kinds of trees;
in the midst of the forest flows the Sarasvatī river, whose waters are sacred.
There, the cranes always warble with a sweet and melodious cry of passion;
the cuckoos utter their notes, and the bees hum "guṃ jaṃ ti. (180)
That forest was filled with much clamor from parrots and sarikas;
various beasts of prey roamed there in that most excellent of woods. (181)
Then the entire forest was covered all over with honey-trees, always bearing fruit, always in bloom, and grey with particles of pollen. 182.
It was embraced on both sides by creepers heavy with the weight of blossoms produced from fresh sprouts,
like a lover embraced by his beloveds.
Terrified by the fear of his curse, the wind thereafter blew with equal force;
and the sun, for nine years, dried up the clouds with its rays.
For that forest was free from affliction, constantly frequented by perfected beings (siddhas),
and eternally producing delight, like the Caitraratha grove.
While he was dwelling there, that virtuous soul, the best of the twice-born, possessed a divine luster;
he obtained a son named Sumitra through a boon from the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Listen to the rule for him whose self was always unrestrained:
in the summer, he constantly practiced the five-fire penance, with his eyes fixed upon the sun. (187)
Restraining his anger even while it rained down like a cloud, he remained under the open sky during the rainy season;
when the wind blew fiercely, he stood firm and unshaken, like the Himavat mountain.
O twice-born one, he dwells at the confluence of the Apas, the Saha, and the Sarasvatī;
at the proper time, he performs ablutions three times in the pure water. (189)
He constantly gratifies the ancestors, the gods, and the sages with faith;
he is eternally devoted to the Brahma-sacrifice, truthful in speech, and has his senses subdued. (190)
Resting on the ground, he meditated while longing for Hari;
with wild forest produce, he offered the agnihotra sacrifice, honoring guests with faith.
He always passes his time according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa fast;
he seeks his livelihood solely from fruits and leaves that have fallen of their own accord. (192)
Free from agitation, devoted to asceticism, and having mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary branches,
his body was reduced to mere bones with his veins standing out prominently.
In this manner, a thousand years passed for him in that forest;
then, by the power of his asceticism, that mountain blazed forth.
O twice-born one, the splendor of that great-souled one cannot be endured by living beings;
blazing with ascetic power, he shines like Vaiśvānara.
In that forest, deer, tigers, rats, and cats—having become free from enmity and equal by birth—played together with one another, devoid of fear. (196)
Listen also to another rule for him, which is exceedingly difficult to attain:
he should worship Nārāyaṇa constantly at the three times of day. (197)
With a thousand blossoming and fragrant flowers, according to the ritual procedure of Vedic hymns, he should remain intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu. ||198||
The Brahmin performs every action solely for the pleasure of Viṣṇu;
by virtue of the boon granted by Dadhīci, he has become an excellent Vaiṣṇava. (199)
Once, on the eleventh day of the month of Vaiśākha, the great sage,
having performed a beautiful worship of Hari, offered a wonderful hymn of praise.
At that very moment, the god Hari himself, mounted upon his celestial vehicle,
arrived before him, exceedingly delighted by her hymn of praise.
Having seen him mounted upon Garuḍa, manifest before their eyes with the hue of a cloud, four-armed, large-eyed, and adorned with every ornament; ||202||
With his hair standing on end and his eyes filled with tears of joy, that brahmin, his mind feeling its purpose fulfilled, then touched the ground with his head.

Indeed, due to that joy born of the *namo-mūla-mantra*, even within the interior of the entire universe (*brahmāṇḍa*), he did not remember his own body; he became one who has realized Brahman. ||204||
Then the sage, a devotee of Viṣṇu, was addressed with affection by Hari:
"O Devadyuti, know this: you are my devotee and you have taken refuge in me. (205)
O sinless one, you who have renounced all actions, whose nature is now mine, and who are always focused on me—by this hymn of praise, I am pleased; choose a boon. 206.
Having heard these words of Hari, the great ascetic replied:
"O God of gods, O Lotus-eyed One, You who have assumed a form through Your own Māyā! (207)
O God, compared to the sight of you, there is no other boon more difficult to obtain;
[this includes] all the gods beginning with Brahmā, and the yogis beginning with Sanaka. (208)
The perfected ones, such as Kapila and others, desire to realize you directly;
yet they are bound by the snares of "I" and "mine," along with delusion, greed, and [the notions of] good and evil. (209)
O you who have seen the highest and the lowest, these things are seen by me as having causes;
the fruit of my birth, my actions, and my intellect has now manifested. (210)
O Lord of the World, you have been worshipped; what more could be requested than this? O Lord of Gods, for the sake of the new [auspicious] purpose, I hold your lotus feet within my heart.
With my inner self absorbed in you, I always meditate with devotion;
I pray for this very boon: may my devotion to you be unshakable. (212)
"Let it be; indeed, let him request no other boon than that of the Lord of Kamalā.
Having heard these words of his, Hari, with a gracious countenance, [replied].
He replied with a serene mind: "So be it, O best of the twice-born!
No other obstacle shall arise for your asceticism. (214)
Those people who shall recite this hymn composed by you will possess unwavering devotion toward my domain.
And their entire religious activity will become pure;
moreover, their supreme and ultimate wisdom will remain unshakable. (216)
Having thus addressed you there, Janārdana, the God of gods, departed;
from that time on, Devadyuti became devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
Dilīpa said:
"O great sage, I am favored and purified by this narrative;
through this association with Viṣṇu, I have truly become like one who has bathed at Gayā today. (218)
Tell me what that hymn is by which Mādhava was propitiated;
I have a great curiosity regarding that sinless Brahmin. (219)
"By your grace, O Brahmin, I consider my heart's desire attained;
for to whom does association with the great not lead to greatness? (220)
Out of your grace, please tell me the unsurpassed hymn of Viṣṇu,
by which the Blessed One was pleased and granted him a vision.
Vasiṣṭha said:
I shall tell you that supreme hymn, free from secret mysteries, which was formerly received by Suparṇa and then passed to me through Garuḍa. 222.
It is the essence of the inner womb, bringing about great prosperity and auspiciousness;
it removes all sins and is supreme, bestowing upon kings the knowledge of their own self. 223.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva; salutations to Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, to Kṛṣṇa who is dear to his devotees, the Lord of the World, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow. ||224||
When the praiser, the object of praise, and the act of praising—the entire world—is permeated by Viṣṇu, then by whom is he praised? Devotion alone brings joy to human beings. (225)
What praise can there be for that God whose very breath is the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs and their commentaries? Yet, out of devotion for Him, I have become eloquent. (226)
The entire three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, revolves like a wheel;
therefore, you alone are sung of as Cakrapāṇi, whose excellent weapon is the discus.
The Vedas do not directly declare Him; neither speech nor mind knows Him.
How then can one like me praise Him, or how can one become devoted to Him? ||228||
You are Brahmā and the others, you are Brahmā and Viṣṇu; you alone are the refuge of all. You are the creator, the source of Brahman, and indeed the pure Brahman itself.
"Who is this yogin, O Lord, who, having pierced through the body, touches the embodied one, yet is not tainted by the defects of the body? Homage to him!
He remains awake in the state of divinity within his own self; he does not sleep."
From whom the intellect consisting of a mass of bliss arises, you are Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
The great elements such as Mahat, as well as the qualities of the Vaikārika [ego], all these are You alone, O Lord; their diversity is a construction of the deluded. (231)
Just as Brahmā is fashioned by his sons and others, so too are you fashioned by the three conceptualizations whose forms are like hair upon a hair.
I bow to that stainless Viṣṇu, who is the single reality free from defects and devoid of qualities, yet appears as the entire world in the form of consciousness to the poets. 233.
By whose knowledge they perform even those actions prescribed by the Vedas, being free from desire, friends of the world, pure, and immeasurable Brahman—[to him I bow]. (234)
I bow to Hari, who is praised as the true form existing within all beings, whom yogis worship through awakening as pure existence alone, with all else destroyed. (235)
Knowing Him alone as the Supreme, the best of the twice-born sing "I am Brahman";
seeing no deity equal to You, I bow to Mādhava. (236)
Salutations to that Self of Consciousness, who, through his illusory power (māyā), destroys the manifold delusions of "I" and "mine," as well as the floods of sins of human beings.
Salutations to that Self of Consciousness, by remembering whose name the floods of sins of men are instantly destroyed, whether they are on the move or at rest. 238.
In worlds that are perpetually ablaze with the flickering flames of the fire of delusion, one who has entered the shade of his lotus feet is not burned. (239)
I bow down to that Ananta, by the mere remembrance of whom there is neither delusion nor an evil rebirth, neither diseases nor sufferings. (240)
Those who dwell solely in the Buddha do not desire offspring born from their wombs; they behold the world as the Self alone. (241)
If the meaning of the word, the meaning of consciousness, and the supreme name of Viṣṇu are one and the same, then by that truth, O Mādhava, may saṃsāra not touch me. 242.
By that truth that Nārāyaṇa is all-pervading throughout the universe, as is agreed upon by the Vedas and other scriptures, may my devotion to Viṣṇu indeed be free from obstacles. (243)
Without the seed-syllable of the womb, there is no seed;
that which has been cultivated by the seed-syllable of the womb—let that seed of existence, along with Viṣṇu, be cut down by me with the sword of knowledge. 244.
May that Hari be gracious to me, who, like an actor, appears through the qualities (guṇas) in the tasks of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
May that Hari, who has descended here in ten ways solely for the protection of Dharma and who was entreated by all the gods, be gracious toward me. (246)
May that Lord Hari, who dwells alone and untainted within the palace of the hearts of all living beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be gracious unto me. (247)
In the beginning, Hari alone was indeed the sixfold wheel, and likewise he became one and many;
having entered the deities as their creator, may that Hari be gracious to me. (248)
The bird of the heart, equal to space, beginning with space, transcending space, whose activity is space, and moving through space;
you are the void that is Brahman, the enjoyer of what begins with space, the one whose form is space, and the consumer of the sacrifice.
That by whose light the world is illuminated with joy, and by whose illusion it is bound—stupidity, suffering, and unreality are merely its inherent nature. (250)
The universe created by you rejoices; that which is abandoned by you becomes impure.
Although associated with it, you are unattached; therefore, there is no modification in you whatsoever.
The Cārvākas worship consciousness as arising from the combination of the elements;
the Buddhists, however, through their reasonings, declare you to be the intellect, which is momentary and subject to destruction. (252)
The Jinas and deities consider you to be the size of the body;
the Sāṅkhyas meditate upon you as the Puruṣa, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). ||253||

Those who are devoid of birth and other such conditions, and who previously possessed the characteristic of bliss—such people contemplate You alone as Brahman, according to the Upaniṣads, among themselves. (254)
The elements, the body, the mind, the intellect, and the senses—knowledge and ignorance are you alone here; there is nothing whatsoever other than you. (255)
You are the sustainer of all beings; you alone are my refuge.
You are the fire, you are the oblation, you are Śakra, the priest, the mantra, and the fruit of the ritual action.
O Vaikuṇṭha, you are both existence and non-existence; I have gone to you for refuge.
You are the giver of the fruits of action and the fruit of the rites performed by those initiated.
You are the cause of all beings; you alone are my refuge.
Just as [the passion] of young women for a youth, and that of youths for a young woman. ||258||
Just as the mind finds delight therein, may my love find delight in you;
even if he be a sinner or one of evil conduct, O Hari, toward a man who bows before you— (259)
The servants of Yama do not look upon him as owls avoid the sun;
yet, until then, the threefold suffering and the flood of sins continue to afflict people. (260)
O Protector, as long as one does not remember your lotus feet with devotion... [261]
That which the qualities, the birth-species, the body, and the dharmas do not touch, and which all the sense-faculties do not touch—
that which the sages, having abandoned attachment and delusion, do touch.
To that Blessed One, Hari, I pay homage. ||262||
Having dissolved the gross into the instrument, the instrument into its cause,
and that cause into that which is devoid of both cause and instrument—
having thus dissolved [all], the sages enter therein.
Salutation be to that Hari, who is served by the sages.
For those who possess the beautiful quality of sovereignty, having embraced that Fortune of happiness and liberation— made submissive by the swaying motion of their carried meditation—
they lie here, enjoying only their own bliss.
Let there be salutation to that Hari, who is served by the sages.
In that whose nature is free from the transformations of existence such as birth and so forth, this group of six waves is utterly shaken off;
and whom the defects of passion and the like do not constantly torment.
I bow down to that stainless Vāsudeva, who dwells within the heart.
That meditation which, when joined with it, is sufficient to abandon ignorance;
that fire of meditation into which the world falls and meets its destruction; and that wisdom which, shining forth, destroys the enemy of doubt.
I bow to you, Hari, the dense mass of awakening through the power of self-control. ||266||
All beings, both moving and unmoving, are under the control of Hari;
by this truth, may Hari stand before me. 267.
"Just as Nārāyaṇa pervades the entire world, both the stationary and the moving—by that truth, may Keśava manifest his form. (268)
"If my devotion to Hari is as great as that which I have for my preceptor, by that truth, may Keśava reveal himself. (269)
Thus reflecting upon his devotion through those truthful oaths,
Puruṣottama, being well-pleased, revealed himself to him.
Then, having granted him the boon and fulfilled his heart's desire,
the Beloved of Kamalā departed, gratified by the Brahmin’s hymn of praise.
Having accomplished his purpose, that twice-born man, devoted solely to Vāsudeva,
remained in that penance grove together with his disciples, chanting the hymn of praise.
Whatever human being recites this hymn or even listens to it, they obtain the abundant fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). ||273||
The Brāhmaṇa always attains the awakening of self-knowledge;
his intellect is never born to evil, nor does he ever perceive anything inauspicious.
Through the recitation of this hymn, all men attain stability of intellect, stability of mind, and likewise stability of the senses. (275)
The man who, being devoted and full of faith, recites this while reflecting upon its meaning, shakes off his sins in this world and attains the station of Viṣṇu. (276)
By reciting this constantly, one obtains one's desired objects, as well as sons, grandsons, and cattle; likewise, one attains long life, strength, and valor. (277)
Whatever fruit is obtained by [giving] a thousand sesame vessels or a thousand cows, that same fruit one attains who recites this hymn of praise. (278)
Whatever among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa a person always desires, he shall attain it without delay by means of this hymn. (279)
May there always be steadfastness for men who hear this praise concerning conduct, discipline, the Dharma, wisdom, austerity, and self-restraint. (280)
Whether one is burdened by great sins (mahāpātaka) or by secondary sins (upapātaka), one’s soul becomes instantly purified by reciting this hymn even once. 281.
It increases wisdom, fortune, fame, renown, knowledge, and virtue;
it pacifies malevolent planets and destroys all that is inauspicious. ||282||
This hymn, which removes all diseases, is wholesome, destroys all misfortunes, and enables one to cross over the miserable states of existence; it should be recited by the twice-born.
In times of affliction from the stars or planets, and during fears of kings, thieves,
fire, robbers, or falling [meteors], one should immediately recite this.
There is no fear of lions or tigers, nor likewise any fear of malevolent spells; nor is there any fear from bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, or rākṣasas. (285)
When this [mantra] is proclaimed here, there shall never be any fear for men from Pūtanās, Jṛmbhakas, or obstacles. (286)
He who, having performed the worship of Vāsudeva, recites this hymn, is not smeared by sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (287)
That goal which is not attained even by bathing at holy pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā, one attains that very goal by reciting this meritorious hymn. (288)
Whoever recites this once, twice, or even thrice a day—at all times and at every moment—shall enjoy imperishable happiness. (289)
Whatever fruit is obtained by reciting even the four Vedas three times, a person who studies this hymn once obtains that same fruit. (290)
One who, with faith, constantly remembers Hari attains inexhaustible wealth and becomes beloved by women; he receives worship in this world. (291)
One who constantly recites this hymn is always endowed with prosperity and never encounters misfortune; indeed, such a person cannot be led away by cattle. 292.
Misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts perish instantly for those devotees who hear this hymn. (293)
He who, having risen early in the morning, recites [this] while pure and devoted to Viṣṇu, obtains imperishable happiness both in this world and in the next. (294)
It is indeed led by divine splendor, auspicious, and pleasing to Viṣṇu;
it generates the grace of Viṣṇu and brings about the vision of Viṣṇu. ||295||
Whoever constantly recites with devotion this hymn named *Yoga-sāra*, which is supremely purifying, goes to the world of Viṣṇu. (296)
Thus has this secret hymn, which destroys all sins, been told to you.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the liberation from the state of a piśāca. ||297||
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Māgha-māhātmya, in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa,
this is the section titled "The Narration of the Yoga-sāra-stotra."
The one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter. ||128||
(129) The One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen to those piśācas who were liberated by him in that forest:
formerly, there was a king named Citra in the region of Draviḍa.
Born of the lunar lineage, Mahāvīra was a hero who had mastered all weapons and missiles;
he was always endowed with a multitude of elephants, horses, and chariots, and was ever valorous. (2)
With his treasury filled with various kinds of gold and jewels, possessing great wealth,
he was constantly intent on sporting in the midst of a thousand women.
That king was devoted to women, ever lustful, greedy, and of fierce temper;
he did not act according to the righteous words spoken by his ministers.
He reviles Viṣṇu excessively and always hates the Vaiṣṇavas.
"Who is this Viṣṇu? Where has he been seen? Where does he exist? By whom is he glorified? (5)
Thus King Sahadevi, deluded by fate, [sought refuge] with Viṣṇu;
for who indeed would oppress those who worship Nārāyaṇa? ||6||
Established in the state of heresy, he does not consider Brahmins, the Vedas, Vedic rituals, vows, or even the act of giving gifts to be worthy of respect. ||7||
Through unrighteousness and harsh punishments, he causes suffering to his subjects;
he is cruel, merciless, fierce, and averse to virtuous deeds. (8)

One whose conduct has fallen away, who hates what is undecaying, who has cast off the sacred fire, and who has abandoned his duties—that king instructs the people like another personification of Death. (9)
Then, after a great deal of time had passed, King Āpaṣcata died;
his funeral rites were performed according to the Vedic injunctions by Lelaha alone.
Then, being severely tormented by the herd of elephants,
he proceeded along a path made of iron spikes, which was filled with heated and poured molten lead.
Scorched by the rays of the fierce sun, devoid of the shade of trees,
strewn with glowing embers, and filled with flickering tongues of flame.
He was struck by extremely terrible crows with iron beaks,
and he was devoured by wolves with fearsome fangs and by dreadful dogs.
Hearing of the suffering of other men who had committed sins,
he went to the world of Pārthiva, which brings fear even to Antaka (the God of Death).
Listen to the course of that king in this world, which is so difficult to endure:
from hell to hell he went, passing through them one after another. (15)
First, he enters Tāmisra, which is dreadful and brings manifold suffering;
and again, he enters Andhatāmisra, where suffering is incessant. (16)
Immediately thereafter, he went to the most fierce Mahāraurava and Raurava hells,
as well as the Kālasūtra and the Mahānaraka hells.
Afterwards, submerged along with the king in the difficult-to-cross [hells],
he fainted from suffering in Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tāpana, and Pratāpana.
The king [fell] into the Pratāpana hell, his mind scorched by the fire of suffering;
and into the Saṃpāta, Sakākola, Kuḍūmala, and Pūtimṛttika hells. ||19||

Then he entered the iron city, the deer-eyed woman, the syllable *traṃ*, the syllable *paṃ*, the place, the silk-cotton tree, and the river; it was again most terrifying, difficult to behold, and hard to traverse.
And likewise the Forest of Sword-leaves and the Iron Prison;
having fallen into all these, O King, the evildoer [suffers].
For twenty-one yugas, he experienced the terrible torment and agony of Avīci hell due to his proclamation of hatred toward Viṣṇu.
O King, having experienced the torments of Yama and emerged from hell,
he then became a great Piśāca on Mount Meru by the power of his vow.
Wandering through all directions and regions, hungry in this world,
he does not find food or water even on Mount Meru, the eternal mountain.
Once, while wandering about, that piśāca, afflicted by grief,
entered the Plakṣaprasravaṇa forest with the hope of future fruit.
Taking refuge in the shade of a *bibhītaka* tree, deeply distressed, he cried out repeatedly and loudly in a terrible voice, "Alas! I am struck! (26)
For me, who am deluded by hunger and thirst and who have harmed all living beings, how will there be an end to this long cycle of birth? (27)
In this ocean of sin, who will provide a hand to support one who is submerged in the waves of suffering? (28)
Thus Devadyuti, while engaged in his studies, heard the piteous and compassionate lamentation of that piśāca, whose mind was dejected. (29)
Having arrived there, he then beheld that piśāca,
with a distorted and terrifying face, yellowish-red eyes, and emaciated.
With hair standing erect on his head and a dark-complexioned body, he was like another messenger of Yama;
with a lolling tongue, protruding lips, long shanks, and covered in veins. ||31||
With long legs, a withered snout, sunken eyes, and a dried-up skeleton, the preeminent sage, filled with curiosity, then questioned him. (32)
Devadyuti said:
"Who are you, with such a terrifying form? Why do you weep so piteously?
From what cause has this state come upon you? Tell me, and what may I do for you? (33)
For indeed, no living beings who have entered my hermitage experience suffering;
they all find only joy, just as in the abode of Viṣṇu. (34)
"Speak quickly, O gentle one, the cause of this suffering;
for the wise do not delay when the matter at hand has arrived. (35)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words, the Piśāca was pleased; ceasing his weeping, he then spoke with a piteous voice, bowing down in humility. (36)
The Piśāca said:
Your words have removed all the distress within me, just as a cloud raining upon a mountain dispels the heat produced by a forest fire in summer. (37)
"O twice-born one, it is because of some merit I have performed that you have been seen by me;
for there is no meeting with the virtuous in one place for those who have not accumulated merit. (38)
Having said this, he related his former history:
"Through the fault of my hatred toward Viṣṇu, I have come to this state. (39)
O twice-born one, since even a most sinful person, upon being released from his life-breaths, would go to the abode of Viṣṇu by remembering Him, hatred toward that Hari arose within me. (40)
He who protects all beings and upholds dharma throughout the three worlds, he who is the inner self of all beings—toward him I have conceived this hatred. (41)
He who is proclaimed here in all the Vedas as the bestower of the fruits of actions is worshipped by Brahmins through austerities, having come under the sway of both passion and aversion.

O twice-born one, Hari—who is the object of meditation for those ascetics at the end of the Vedas who have abandoned ritual action, who love the forest, and who wander alone without attachment—is my enemy. (43)
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, and the yogis, beginning with Sanaka, worship Viṣṇu here for the sake of liberation; he has been reviled by me. (44)
He who is the eternal creator of the universe in the beginning, the middle, and the end—he whose beginning, middle, and end do not exist at all—attained the state of equanimity. (45)
Whatever evil karma I had committed in my previous birth, which was scorched by the fire of hatred for Viṣṇu—all that has been reduced to ashes. (46)
If I should somehow behold the limit of this sin, I shall not worship any deity other than Nārāyaṇa. (47)
Having long endured the torments of hell due to my hatred for Viṣṇu,
I have emerged from that infernal realm and entered this demonic womb.
By which ritual mantras has he now been brought to your hermitage, where the darkness consisting of suffering was destroyed by the sun of the sight of you? (49)
Wherever death, bondage, prosperity, happiness, or a wife may be obtained, there one is led by one's own karma, which acts like a hand upon the neck. (50)
Now, tell me the appropriate rite that destroys the state of being a *piśāca*;
for those who go to heaven are blessed when they perform deeds that benefit others. (51)
Devadyuti said: Alas! This illusion of Māyā steals away the memory of gods, asuras, and humans, by which even among the gods hatred arises that destroys dharma. (52)
I am the creator and protector of those worlds, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), and the Self of all beings; how can a fool harbor hatred toward me? (53)
Since all actions become fruitful through devotion to Him, what mortal, being devoid of such devotion, would not fall into a miserable state in this world? 54.
Devoting themselves always to Nārāyaṇa, members of the four castes should perform only those actions prescribed by the Śruti, the Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous. 55.
Otherwise, they go to hell unless they resort to the sacred scriptures;
therefore, one should abandon any action taught in the scriptures that contradicts the meaning of the Vedas. (56)
Having deceived those who are ignorant of logic with treatises composed by their own intellects, they create obstacles on the path to the highest good solely for the destruction of the world. //57//
Those who revile Viṣṇu, the Vedas, the three fires, austerity, and the three classes of twice-born go to hell for that very reason, due to their devotion to false scriptures.
This very Draviḍa king, having been hostile toward Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods and the Lord of the universe, has gone to hell. (59)
Therefore, one who desires merit should abandon hatred toward the gods and especially toward Brahmins; in this world, he should also abandon any action that is outside the Veda.
Having spoken thus, the sage told the piśācas what was beneficial:
"Go to Prayāga; may you be blessed; observe the month of Māgha."
Wherever one has attained certain liberation from the state of a Piśāca, there is no doubt in this matter;
having bathed there, they go to heaven—this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
There, a person abandons their former evil karma;
indeed, there is nothing else superior to bathing at Prayāga. 63.
Know that Prayāga is the expiation for even the most sinful, consisting of austerity, charity, and ritual action, and surpassing sacrifice and yoga. (64)
The gateway to heaven and liberation is opened upon this earth;
there is no other on earth than these two rivers, the white and the dark, which flow together as a single stream.
For one bound by the shackles of sin, where is Viṣṇu—the sole axe for cutting them—nor the fire of the sun’s brilliance, nor the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā? (66)
Where is that wretched, trivial heap of human sins, which is like an offering of straw to a mass of dark clouds, compared to the autumnal moon? (67)
A man shines after the destruction of his sins once he has bathed in the waters of the Veṇī;
I am not capable of describing the greatness of that which is both white and black. 68.
"Even a Keralaka twice-born man who has been touched by a drop of its water is liberated"—having heard these words of the sage, the piśāca was delighted in his heart. (69)
Freed from suffering and filled with joy, he affectionately questioned the sage:
"O great sage, how was the twice-born man of the Kerala country liberated? (70)
Relating this account, rely upon your compassion for me. (71)
Devadyuti said:
"O Piśācas, listen as I tell you this auspicious and meritorious tale:
there was a certain Brāhmaṇa named Vasu in Kerala who had mastered the Vedas. (72)
His wealth having been seized by his heirs, he was rendered penniless and abandoned by his kinsmen;
leaving his native land, he was tormented by great suffering. (73)
After wandering from country to country for a long time,
he entered a great forest, slightly afflicted by disease.
While traveling across sacred fords, exhausted, hungry, and parched on Mount Vindhya, he met his death due to famine; neither cremation nor funeral rites were performed for him. ||75||
By the ripening of that karma, he dwelt for a long time as a hungry ghost in that mountain cave within the desolate forest.
Afflicted by cold and heat, without food and without water, naked, without shoes, he cried out for food while sighing deeply. (77)
Wandering here and there like the wind, accompanied by Kerala,
the twice-born man found no refuge and obtained no happiness anywhere at that time.
Afflicted by grief, he lamented as he beheld his own good destiny;
having always given gifts, he now enjoys the fruit of his own actions. (79)

Those who do not offer oblations into the fire, those who do not worship Govinda, those who do not cultivate the knowledge of the Self, and those who turn their backs on the excellent holy places; ||80||
Those who do not give gold, clothing, betel, jewels, food, fruit, or water to those in distress—all of them have failed in their duty. (81)
Those rogues who, through force or by means of deception, seize the property of Brahmins, the wealth of others, or the assets of women; those who are deceivers and exploiters of others. (82)
Those who are hypocritical, deceitful, thieves, and those whose livelihood is like fire;
those who are merciless toward children, the elderly, the sick, and women; and those who are devoid of truth—[these are the ones who go to hell]. (83)
Those who set fires, those who administer poison, and others who give false testimony;
all those who approach women who should not be approached, and others who act as priests for entire villages. ||84||
Those who abandon their father, mother, daughter-in-law, offspring, or their own wife; those who are miserly, greedy, atheistic, and corrupters of dharma—[these are the ones excluded]. (85)
I shall deliver from danger one who abandons his master in battle, one who abandons one who has sought refuge, those who harm cows, land, or other jewels [of virtue]. (86)
Those who speak ill of others, who are sinful, who revile deities and gurus, and those who are intent on accepting gifts in all the great fields of merit; ||87||
Those who delight in harming others, those who injure living beings, and all those who accept gifts from the wicked—they are born again and again. (88)
Among the states of hungry ghosts, rākṣasas, piśācas, animals, trees, and other evil births, there is not even a trace of happiness for them, neither in this world nor in the next. (89)
Therefore, having abandoned prohibited matters, one should perform prescribed actions;
one should worship sacrifice, charity, austerity, sacred fords, mantras, deities, and the guru. ||90||
Having seen that the ripening of karmas is difficult to traverse throughout millions of births, the Dharma must be practiced continuously by those of all four castes. (91)
Having thus seen the state of a hungry ghost, which indeed arises from the seeds of evil, the brahmin gave him instruction in the Dharma and spoke to him again: (92)
Thus, while that Kerala ghost was dwelling on the mountain at that time, after passing a long period, he saw a traveler on the road. (93)
They were carrying two baskets containing the water from his braided locks,
while singing praises to the foremost deity, Janārdana, whose fame is holy.
Seeing him, that hungry ghost suddenly blocked the path;
he revealed himself and said, "Do not be afraid. (95)
"I wish to drink water from you, O best of pilgrims;
if you do not give me water, my life-breaths will surely depart. (96)
Having heard these words of the ghost, the traveler replied out of curiosity.
The pilgrim said: "Who are you, overcome by suffering, emaciated, withered, and clad only in the directions as your garment? (97)
With only his life-breath remaining, he was on the verge of death, deformed, and terrifying; he had the appearance of fresh smoke, was fierce, and his eyes were darting about. ||98||
"You do not touch the ground with your feet, and you have no flesh on your arms and sides.
Having heard these words, the preta then spoke this speech: (99)
The preta said:
"Listen, O most virtuous one, I shall tell you by what means I became such as I am.
I was a brahmin who gave no gifts, greedy, and of impure conduct. (100)
I always ate the food of others alone, enjoying delicious meals; yet not even a single alms-offering was given by me here, nor did I provide even a small amount of curd. (101)
The Vaiśvadeva offering has not been performed, nor has the external bali-oblation been cast;
indeed, the thirst of living beings tormented by thirst cannot be quenched by mere water. (102)
Wandering the earth, he once failed to satisfy his ancestors with libations, nor did he ever perform the śrāddha rite, nor were the deities ever worshipped by him anywhere. (103)
I did not give protection against rain and sun, nor did I provide footwear;
I gave no water-vessel, no betel-leaf, and no medicine. (104)
I did not dwell in my own home, nor was hospitality ever offered to anyone;
yet the aged, the wealthy, the protectorless, and the wretched were satisfied with drink and food. (105)
Indeed, by giving a mouthful of grass to cows, one is liberated from disease;
and by offering sesame-based oblations that have not been previously given or sacrificed, the Brahmins are purified.
On this earth, there are no givers like you;
for even a small amount of gold given during the Vyatīpāta yoga yields great fruit. (107)
O twice-born one, transits, eclipses of the sun and moon, and all other festival days became devoid of offerings. (108)
The lunar days (tithis) of the month of Kārttika are always my primary favorites;
yet, [the merit of offerings] was never given by me to the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days or during the Maghā asterisms. (109)

No offense was committed against the twice-born on the anniversaries of Manu and other progenitors at the beginning of the yugas, nor was a lamp fed with sesame oil offered by me during the month of Kārttika. (110)
"O you who desire beauty and fortune, I have not bathed during the month of Māgha;
[therefore, grant me this] for a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas at the Gautamī river when Jupiter is in Leo. (111)
In a previous birth, I did not give wealth intended for a religious purpose, nor did I bathe in the Kṛṣṇaveṇī river when my preceptor had entered the state of a bridegroom. (112)
Having kindled a fire with heaps of wood for the Brahmins who had bathed during the months of Pauṣa and Māgha and were afflicted by the cold, he did not suppress their shivering. (113)
In the months beginning with Mādhava, I did not give cool water;
I did not plant an Aśvattha tree, nor was an Nyagrodha ever made to grow by me. (114)
O Vam, I have never anywhere granted liberation from the house of death to living beings;
nor have I protected one who has come for refuge, terrified by the fear of life. (115)
O twice-born one, without fasting for three nights, Madhusūdana is not pleased; likewise, [one must perform] the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, Pārāka, and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Now, there is another, the *taptakṛcchra*, as well as the *ātapanas*;
these meritorious vows were practiced by the gods, beginning with Indra. (117)
"O best of the twice-born, having previously practiced these [austerities] until his body was completely withered away, he was thus born from the sky in a former life. (118)
He beheld there, in this very birth, the most cruel and wondrous course of his own unprecedented karma, which was difficult to comprehend.
On this mountain, those seeking peace have abandoned all other fruits found on the paths frequented by wolves and tigers, as well as those dropped everywhere by parrots. (120)
The roots are meritorious, easy to digest, yielding fruit and juice, excellent as food, soft, and sweet. (121)
Various kinds of honey exist in great abundance;
and there are waters from streams and waterfalls in every direction. ||122||
"O Mountain, although all these objects are easily available, I do not see any food anywhere, as if I were always struck down by fate. (123)
I live by subsisting on air, just as serpents live;
yet I live again, O Brahmin, through the power of my divine birth. (124)
A person does not obtain what is unobtainable through strength, wisdom, constant effort, spells, human exertion, valor, nor even through companions and friends. (125)
In gain and loss, in pleasure and pain, in marriage, death, and life, in enjoyment, disease, and separation—destiny alone is indeed the cause. (126)
Those who are ugly, of low birth, fools, censured for their despicable conduct, and devoid of heroism and prowess, may by fate enjoy kingdoms. (127)
One-eyed men, those born blind, the incompetent, those devoid of conduct, the wicked, and even eunuchs are seen established in sovereignty by the power of fate. (128)
By those who have given sesamum seeds, cows, gold, and garments;
by those who have given away daughters as brides for Gaurī; and by those who have given the earth.
Beds, seats, betel-leaf, palaces, and wealth; as well as various kinds of food, both solid and soft, sandalwood, and aloe-wood, were all bestowed [as gifts]. (130)
Whether in the forest, on a mountain peak, in a village, or even in a city, their enjoyments stand ready before them at every turn through diligent effort. (131)
On Mount Saṃtyatra there are also other, even more powerful rākṣasas—rākṣasas, piśācas, and most dreadful piśācīs. ||132||
Sometimes, in various ways and in different places, they wander from forest to forest and obtain food and drink through their own past actions. (133)
Having heard this, [he said: "May you grant fearlessness to those who have come here;
they are not even able to look upon you, O Govinda-bhakta, for you are pure. (134)
Rākṣasas, pretas, and pūtanas do not touch nor do they even look upon one who has devotion to Viṣṇu as their armor and is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa. 135.
Bhūtas, vetālas, gandharvas, śākinīs, āryakas, and grahas;
revatīs, vṛddharevatīs, and likewise the mukhamaṇḍya grahas. ||136||
The cruel and wicked yakṣas and bālagrahas, those who are vṛddhagrahas, as well as the terrifying mātṛgrahas and other vināyakas; ||137||
Malevolent spirits, serpents, kūṣmāṇḍas, and whatever other wicked creatures there may be, do not behold the supreme Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇa who is pure. (138)
The deities of the planets and constellations do not afflict one who is pure, protected, and most righteous; yet they constantly afflict one who is unprotected and impure. (139)
The name Govinda is at the tip of your tongue, while the Veda resides within your heart;
you are pure, you are of a charitable nature, and you are everywhere free from fear.
"O Brāhmaṇa, knowing thus that one abides by the fruit of one's own actions, and having reflected upon it again and again, I do not grieve. (141)
O Bālinī, on the bank of that river, I heard a statement uttered by a crane while I was wandering about. (142)
The Brahmin said:
"What kind of speech uttered by the crane did you hear?
I wish to hear that; O Preta, tell me quickly. (143)
The preta said: "O best of Kārpāṭikas, listen to the words of the sārasa bird:
'In this thicket is a river named Dhūsarā, which originates from both mountains and streams. (144)
It was filled with swarms of intoxicated cranes exulting on the ever-present waters;
it was rich in the beauty of great *kakubha* trees and enchanting with lush *jaṃbū* fruits. (145)
I reached its bank and entered the dense forest;
I remained there indeed with the desire to eat fruit. (146)
Flying up from the forest, accompanied by ten thousand cranes marked with the *sārasa* bird,
he came to the riverbank to enjoy it with many birds.
Having drunk water there and enjoyed himself with his wife, he fell asleep, placing his head and face within the hollow of my left wing. 148.
At that very moment, having descended from his vehicle, a man was seen—red-faced, with deeply bloodshot eyes, carrying a staff, and possessing a row of firm nails. (149)
Lomaśa, the long-tailed monkey of restless movement,
arrived with great speed to the place where that crane was sleeping.
Having approached, she seized the crane firmly with both hands with a cruel intent while many birds looked on. (151)
All the sky-dwellers have flown away, soaring up one after another;
the female crane, terrified, remains there uttering cries of distress.
Then the crane, his sleep broken and his eyes darting in alarm, quickly looked about with his neck craned upward. (153)
Beholding the wicked monkey, who was extremely cruel and desirous of killing him,
the bird then addressed him with sweet speech.
Why do you oppress this branch-monkey without any offense?
A person who has committed an offense is to be executed even by kings before the eyes of the people. 155.
Noble persons such as you ought not to oppress us, for we are virtuous men who have turned our backs on the livelihoods of others. (156)
They subsisted on water and moss, were wanderers of the sky dwelling in the forest, were devoted to their own wives, and were entirely abstinent from the wives of others. (157)
O best of monkeys, it is not right for one such as you to harass Brahmins who are devoted to others, even if they engage in slander and backbiting. (158)
I know that you are innocent in every way, O monkey, yet I was born from you; you do not, however, know me. 159.
Having heard those words of his, the fickle monkey then quickly released the crane; standing at a distance, he spoke swiftly. (160)
The monkey said:
"Tell me, how do you know this ancient birth?
You are a bird devoid of knowledge, and I am a forest-dwelling animal."
The crane said:
"I know clearly that you are one who remembers your past births;
for in a previous existence, you were the king of the Vidyādharas, Parvateśvara. (162)
"I am that most venerable brahmin, the family priest of Daśaratha;
therefore, O best of monkeys, I recognize you perfectly. (163)
While you were protecting this earth, all the subjects were oppressed; being devoid of discrimination, you accumulated wealth excessively. (164)
O monkey, you were previously burned by the flames of fire arising from the heat and suffering caused to living beings;
now you have been cast again into the most dreadful Kumbhīpāka hell.
Again and again you have been burned, and again and again born; thirty such years have passed for you with this hellish body.
Uttering terrible cries and weeping again and again,
he experienced intense torments in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Having crossed over hell, you have now attained this birth as a monkey due to the remainder of your sin; it is for this reason that you desire to kill me.
Previously, from the brāhmaṇa’s grove, you forcibly took ripe bhāpha fruits and ate them without having asked for permission. (169)
Beholding the terrible ripening of that karma, you now exist as a monkey dwelling in the forest. (170)
Even for one who has previously performed both auspicious and inauspicious deeds, the experience [of their results] plays among living beings, unobstructed even by the gods of the three realms. (171)
Thus I know your birth exactly as it is, along with its cause; for although I have attained a body of vital essence, I am not deluded by ignorance. (172)
The preta said:
Having heard this, the brahmin monkey also spoke to the sārasa bird:
"You surely know everything; how is it that you have come to the state of a bird? (173)
The crane said: "I shall tell you that deed by which I fell into misfortune and entered the womb of a bird; you ought to hear all of this. (174)
In the past, during a solar eclipse at Carmadā, you gave away more than a hundred khārīs of grain to many brāhmaṇas. (175)
Out of pride in my office as priest and out of greed, having likewise insulted the twice-born, I took everything from them after giving them only a trifle. (176)
Due to the sin arising from seizing property that was not common to the Brahmins, I have fallen into the Kālasūtra hell, in the mire of red blood. (177)
There, submerged up to the navel in a place filled with wriggling worms, foul-smelling, and frothy with pus,
I remained with my face turned downward, licking the pus.
Likewise, my body is being devoured by great vultures above and by crows, while it is incessantly tormented by worms. (179)
In that mire of blood, I then became breathless;
even a single moment seemed to me like a great kalpa.
I have experienced torments for thirty thousand years;
I am unable to describe that suffering, whether as a monkey or as a denizen of hell. (181)
The office of domestic priest is extremely terrible and, by its very nature, a source of sin;
for it is there that the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa consists of subsisting upon the gods.
The acceptance of gifts from a king is terrible; by it, the twice-born are consumed.
The domestic priest who seizes even their property becomes a denizen of hell.
Whatever sin a king commits, he is first afflicted by it through his own body;
this is proclaimed by those who perceive the truth regarding that priest. 184.
By some means, through fate, I have somehow attained deliverance from hell;
yet now, by the turn of destiny, the state of being a bird has come upon me. (185)
Having previously stolen a vessel of wine from my sister's house and given it to a gambler out of fear, because of that, this fate as a female crane has befallen me. (186)
And who was this Brāhmaṇī in a former life, that she was so extremely cruel? Because of that, she has been born as a crane, sharing the same nature as me. (187)
"O Vānara, thus has the entire fruit of action been told—past, present, and future; listen with attention. (188)
"I shall be beautiful, and you shall be beautiful;
I shall be Sīta, your wife, and Sārasī shall also be yours. (189)
We shall dwell at ease in the land of Kāmarūpa;
immediately after that, we shall go to the Yoginī Bhāvikalyāṇī.
Then, having attained a human birth which is difficult to obtain again, [beings] achieve therein both that which is beneficial and its opposite. (191)
Thus, having utterly deluded all beings with his own māyā, he enjoys them through both pleasures and pains; it is not us alone whom he does so. (192)
This path, which has proceeded in the world and is fashioned in various ways, consists essentially of dharma and adharma, and has for its nature the fruits of pleasure and pain. (193)
It is constantly and repeatedly resorted to by all living beings—by gods, asuras, tigers among men, worms, insects, and aquatic creatures. (194)

This thorn of suffering has not been overcome even by the slightest effort; it cannot be transcended except by dispassionate yogis who have reached the further shore of the Vedas through meditation. 195.
Whether it be a small or even a great deed, whether meritorious or non-meritorious, Maheśvara, having taken account of the place and the time, bestows its fruit here in this world. (196)
Thus, having understood the illusion of the Lord as being governed by the laws of destiny, those of great intelligence neither grieve, nor suffer, nor feel distress. (197)
The ripening of past karmas cannot be altered in any other way, neither by means of expedients nor by wisdom, nor even by the gods, who are like monkeys leaping from branch to branch. (198)
First you were born as a king, and afterwards you were born as a hell-being;
now you have become a monkey, and you shall obtain such a birth again.
Thinking thus, O monkey, remain free from sorrow and dwell at ease;
enjoy yourself here in this forest while awaiting the right time.
I too, bound by the illusion of the Lord, shall spend my life from forest to forest,
maintaining the fortitude of one who has grasped the essential truth.
The monkey said:
"I have honored you before, and even now I bow to you.
You remember your former births; I know everything regarding my previous life."
Stay, O male and female crane; may there always be well-being for you.
Through your words, my delusion has vanished, and I shall wander forever [in peace]. (203)
The preta said:
"O twice-born one, I have heard this beautiful, wonderful, and most purifying dialogue between a bird and a monkey on the riverbank. (204)
At that moment, my own awakening occurred, and by it, my grief was destroyed;
now I have realized the supremely wonderful majesty of the waters of the Jāhnavī.
Having seen you here, O best of Brahmins, I, being tormented by intense thirst and desiring to cross over from the state of a ghost (preta), beg for the water of the Jahnavi. (206)
O twice-born one, another marvel was seen by me on this very mountain;
indeed, I wish to drink that water of the Gaṅgā. (207)
A certain Brahmin born in Pāriyātra, who served as a village priest, became a brahmarākṣasa in this world due to officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing. (208)
Out of greed for our company, he remained there for eight years;
O best of the twice-born, his bones were collected by his virtuous son.
Having been cast into the pure Gaṅgā at the Kanakhala tīrtha,
he was instantly liberated from that most terrible state of being a rākṣasa.
Such is the great and wonderful majesty of bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
this water was requested by Indra himself, who had performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice, when he went to heaven.
Previously, at a sacred ford, I accepted many possessions; however, no remedy for that was performed, such as the recitation of prayers and other rites. (212)
Therefore, for him who has the form of a preta, water and food are difficult to obtain;
there, on the Vindhya mountain, a thousand years have passed.
Thus I have told you everything, casting aside my great shame;
now, O best of the righteous, quickly [fulfill your purpose] by means of the gift of water. (214)
Satisfying those whose life-breaths had reached their limit and were hanging by a mere thread, he reflected:
"Even in the state of being a ghost, life is difficult for living beings to obtain in this world. (215)
Indeed, the body must be protected by people at all times and in every way;
for even those afflicted with leprosy and other such diseases do not desire the abandonment of their bodies. (216)
Devadyuti said:
