Having heard those words, the traveler was struck with great amazement; bearing compassion for the ghost, he reflected: 217. Devadyuti said: Having heard those words, he was filled with supreme wonder; the traveler, cherishing pity for the ghost, began to reflect.
Indeed, the fruit of sin and merit is clearly seen in this world:
[the states of] gods, demons, humans, and even insects and worms. (218)
Birth in various wombs, affliction by various diseases, death for both the young and the old, as well as lameness and hunchbackedness—[these are the sufferings]. (219)
Prosperity and poverty, wisdom and likewise folly—how else could these arrangements exist in the world? (220)
Blessed are those in the land of action who bestow upon worthy recipients the wealth earned through the path of righteousness, and thereby accomplish their own welfare. (221)
Land, jewels, gold, cows, grain, houses, elephants, chariots, horses, clothing, villages, prepared food, fruit, and water. ||222||
A maiden, divine herbs, food, an umbrella, sandals, an excellent seat, a bed, betel, garlands, a palm-leaf fan, and a noble throne. (223)
All this should be given by those desiring to conquer the three worlds;
for what is given is obtained in heaven, and it is only by giving that one enjoys [the fruits]. 224.
Parasols, chowries, and vehicles; excellent horses and noble elephants; palatial mansions and superior couches; cows, buffaloes, and beautiful women. ||225||
Food, ornaments, pearls, sons, female servants, and noble lineage; longevity, health, sovereignty, the arts, sciences, and great skill—[these are obtained]. (226)
All the fruit of giving is obtained by human beings on earth;
therefore, one should give with effort, for what has not been given does not accrue [to one]. (227)
Having sung this verse with a righteous and gentle voice, the preta, hearing it, spoke again with a distressed mind: ||228||
"You are surely like one who knows the Dharma; of this there is no doubt.
Grant me life, as a cloud grants water to the cātaka bird. (229)
"In this matter of giving life, do not delay for long. Then the king replied with words imbued with justice: [230]
Listen, O Lord of Bhṛgukṣetra; for the sake of the two ancestors who have become pretas and remain in that state, I have brought this water from the King of Tīrthas.
That water, both white and black, was requested by you from the middle;
I do not know [the outcome] due to this doubt regarding dharma—what is appropriate here? (232)
For the sake of investigating strength and weakness, I shall follow the more powerful method;
I do not rely on mere pride regarding the Vedas and the Dharmaśāstras. (233)
The protection of the life-breaths of living beings is considered by the sages and the deities to be superior even to all sacrifices, such as the horse-sacrifice (hayamedha). (234)
Having thus granted the boon and performed the protection of the deceased,
I shall take up water again for the sake of the ancestors and carry this purifying water.
This method, which bestows the perfectly pure Dharma, shines forth as most powerful;
the wise have declared everything other than assisting others to be insignificant. (236)
Even if my very life-breaths were joyfully given away by men who assist others, could there not be service rendered to others through water? What more, then, have I not already attained? (237)
This verse, sung by Dadhīci in ancient times, is heard upon the earth;
it is the essence consisting of all dharma, and is approved by those who know all dharma. (238)
One should perform service for others even at the cost of one's life or wealth;
the merit born of helping others is equal to that of a hundred sacrifices.
Having spoken thus, that most virtuous brahmin gave water originating from the Gaṅgā and Yamunā to the deceased for the sake of protecting his life-force.
Having drunk the water and likewise sprinkled it upon his head, the hungry ghost was satisfied;
he abandoned that ghostly body and in an instant became possessed of a divine form. (241)
Having witnessed that great marvel, the entire assembly of people exclaimed: "Aha!
This man has been liberated from the state of a ghost by the drops of water from the Veṇī! (242)
Even Brahmā is not able to describe the quality of the waters;
otherwise, how could Mahādeva bear the water of the Gaṅgā?
Whoever should drink even a drop of the water of the Gaṅgā, which possesses inconceivable power,
he becomes a god or an accomplished one (siddha) and shall not enter a womb again.
Accomplishment is like the celestial Gaṅgā; wisdom is like the celestial Gaṅgā;
liberation is like the celestial Gaṅgā; for the [physical] Gaṅgā is superior to all. (245)
Therefore, O righteous one, with every effort and great devotion, he who constantly practices the limbs of yoga has liberation within his grasp. 246.
Venerable Bhavapaṃtha, do not abstain from the Dharma;
by you I have been instantly rescued through the gift of a drop of water to the Gaṅgā.
Having spoken thus, that Piśāca of Kerala departed for heaven after honoring the traveler, that excellent kinsman, with blessings. (248)
Having released the deceased from the waters, he took that water once again and returned by the same path, mindful of the ritual splashing of water at the sacred ford.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus heard the greatness of Prayāga and having bowed to that sage, the piśāca went quickly to Prayāga at the time of the month of Māgha. (250)
Having bathed at the confluence of the Asitā and Sitā during the month of Māgha, O best of the twice-born,
that Piśāca, his sins exhausted, abandoned his Piśāca body.
Then, having attained a divine body, the Dravidian king,
free from all faults, praised the god Nārāyaṇa with devotion.
Being praised by the Gandharvas and unvanquished by the women of heaven,
he went to the city of Purandara in a most excellent celestial chariot.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, I have related to you this curious ancient account of the brahmin, a history that instantly destroys all sins. (254)
O Brahmin, this which bestows knowledge, grants liberation, is renowned, and destroys miserable rebirths—thus has all this ancient account been told to you with interest. (255)
O best of the twice-born, you have heard this history which destroys misfortune;
now, along with me, let these daughters and your son [depart].
And you too should come to Prayāga, O Vaisravana, for those who desire the supreme goal;
here we shall perform the Māgha bath, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (257)
There they shall be instantly liberated from their state as Piśācas, which arose from their evil deeds.
Maheśa said:
Having thus drunk with joy the sweet nectar of the story from the lotus-mouth of Vasiṣṭha, they were all delighted and crossed over the ocean of hell.
Delighted, they set out swiftly through the sky together with him;
O Dilīpa, hear all about that sacred ford, which is both white and black.
Then, having swiftly reached Kāma by way of the sky, those unbearable ones arrived there with hearts full of joy. 261.
Then Lomaśa spoke there with compassion to the assembly of celestial beings:
"Let everyone behold with faith this king of sacred fords on earth. (262)
Even without [specific] knowledge, all living beings are liberated at this Prayāga;
it was here that Prajāpati, desiring to create, performed a great sacrifice. ||263||
Then, possessing the power of emission, he performed creation;
there, Nārāyaṇa, desiring a wife, bathed at the confluence of the white and dark waters.
Therefore, having obtained the fortune of Lakṣmī as his wife at the churning of the nectar,
he dwelt there for six months and bathed in the Veṇī according to his desire.
The wielder of the trident destroyed Tripura with three arrows;
these are the three sacrificial pits, blazing with perpetual fires. (266)
The fire, which is satisfied by whatever it consumes, has attained satisfaction here; at this, the thirty-three gods rejoiced exceedingly. (267)
The Great Lord, blue-throated and bearing a skull-cup, manifested here;
served incessantly by the gods, he arrived like a young ascetic at the water's edge.
In the *Mṛkaṇḍasūnu-kalpa*, it is said that Janārdana, in the form of Yoga, entered the mouth of the son of Mṛkaṇḍu and remained there while the world was filled with flames. ||269||
O friend, this Goddess of the Bhagirathi, who removes all suffering and bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, is resorted to by the Siddhas for the sake of attaining perfection.
This river Bhāgīrathī is the goddess who incessantly bestows prosperity, who is unsurpassed on the path to heaven, and who is the very cause of heaven. 271.
That river is Yamunā herself, by the mere act of bathing in whom all living beings attain the same world as the Sun, the cutter-away (Vikartana).
O Sage, the confluence of these two rivers of merit bestows happiness;
those who have bathed here and are purified by knowledge are not cooked in hell. (273)
Even without knowledge, all living beings are liberated here at Prayāga;
moreover, O Brahmin, hear another ancient history. (274)
This destroys all sins for those who hear it and annihilates all diseases.
Formerly, a Gandharva cursed by Ṛcīka became a crow. (275)
Having bathed right there at the confluence of the white and dark waters, he immediately released the curse;
for by the curse of Vāsava, the Apsaras Urvaśī had been fallen from heaven.
Desiring heaven, she bathed and soon thereafter attained heaven; and O Sage, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, obtained a son named Śaṅkara.
O best of the twice-born, in ancient times Śakra, desiring sons, bathed here at the holy confluence of the white and black rivers at Prayāga; likewise, one desiring wealth should bathe well here.
He seized all the treasures of the Giver of Wealth by means of his illusory power;
meanwhile, Kaśyapa performed penance there, intent on the worship of Śiva.
At this sacred ford, Bharadvāja attained perfection in yoga;
at this sacred ford, in ancient times, the lords of yogis with tranquil minds [attained their goal].
Āsana and the other [limbs of yoga] attained the fruit-stage of yoga;
those who bathed in this month of Māgha at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā [attained it as well]. 281.
All these are in the form of stars; by them the entire world is pervaded.
Through them, those who desire enjoyments attain their desires, while those seeking liberation attain liberation. 282.
O best of the twice-born, twenty-three seekers of perfection have attained success here at Prayāga;
now your daughter and your son also desire liberation. (283)
By my word, let all of you, O Sitā and Asitā, plunge into this water;
by the power of the waters of the Veṇī, may there be the destruction of the sins committed in former times.
Thus, he obtained that entire fortune, which was the great fruit of the curse received;
such were the words of the sage, true, beyond the senses, sufficient, and profound. (285)
Having heard this, they all became filled with longing and prepared for their bath;
upon reaching Prayāga, which is difficult to attain, they were instantly freed from their state as Piśācas.
Released from the suffering of the curse, they each regained their own bodies;
and the Knower of the Vedas, seeing his sons and those maidens of divine form, [was filled with joy].
He was pleased with Aulomaśa out of affection, his inner self being serene;
"By your mere grace, the great ocean of sin has been crossed. (288)
"Now, O best of sages, speak what is appropriate for these children.
Lomaśa said: "This youth has studied the Vedas and completed his observances. (289)
"Therefore, by the word of Lomaśa and at the command of her father, she then took the lotus-hand of those women who were filled with passion for him."
According to the marriage rite, he was a fellow religious student (brahmacārī) who had performed auspicious ceremonies with pure substances and mantras by the sages.
And he took the hands of those five maidens according to the sacred law;
then all the maidens were filled with divine joy, their desires fulfilled.
He became joyful and well-pleased;
then, having granted his permission, that sage Lomaśa was saluted by them.

He went to his own hermitage on Mount Meru, which is frequented by the gods; then, O King, that treasury of the Vedas, filled with joy, set forth for the city of Kubera, placing his five daughters-in-law and his son at the forefront.

Thus, by the words of the eminent sage, the five Gandharva maidens— freed from all impurity through the merit born of bathing at Prayāga, the king of holy fords, during the month of Māgha— attained their desire and departed, having secured their great gain.

Whoever here constantly hears this supreme, purifying history, which is like a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and the cause for the dissolution of all afflictions, shall indeed become fulfilled with all desired objects; endowed with dharma, he goes to the world of the gods, which is difficult to attain. (296)
Whoever, having heard this history, should honor the reciter with cows, gold, and garments—he is indeed equal to Brahman. (297)
Since Viṣṇu becomes honored when his reciter is honored, one who desires that existence be fruitful should always worship him. (298)
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the Māgha-māhātmya, within the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa,
[this is] the chapter titled "The Marriage of the Gandharva Maiden."
The one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter. ||129||
The Greatness of Devotion to Viṣṇu (130):
The One Hundred and Thirtieth Chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, I have heard the greatness of the month of Kārttika and that of Māgha;
now I desire to hear of the supreme rite that bestows liberation. (1)
O Lord Viśveśvara, please describe that which is called the supreme devotion, by the mere knowledge of which men may attain happiness. (2)
Mahādeva said: That person whose mind is absorbed in Him, who possesses devotion, is considered supreme;
he is eternally devoted to the dharma of compassion and intent upon the religious duties dedicated to Viṣṇu. (3)
Subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, and bearing the conch and discus, one should worship Viṣṇu at the three times of day; that is considered sattvic devotion. (4)

The highest devotion is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvikī), that of the middle quality (rājasī) is middling, and that of the lowest quality (tāmasī) is the least; thus devotion is declared to be threefold. (5)
Śrīdhara, however, should be practiced by those desiring liberation and the fruits of their desires, [yet] through egoism, hypocrisy, envy, and deceit. (6)
That devotion which people perform for the purpose of destroying another, or for the sake of mere verbal ostentation, is declared to be tāmasī.
That devotion which is performed toward a deity while focusing on sense objects, or for the sake of fame and power, is proclaimed as tāmasī (tamas-born). ||8||
He who worships me in an image or the like with a sense of duality is characterized by passion (rājasa).
Ritual actions should be performed by Brahmins devoted to knowledge for the sake of exhausting their past karma. 9.
Indeed, that intellect which offers itself to Viṣṇu is considered Sāttvika devotion;
therefore, O Goddess, Hari should always be served in every way. 10.
Tamas-ness is attained through a tamasic state;
rajasic [nature] through a rajasic one; but the sattvic [nature] through a sattvic one. (11)
A glorious Brahmin who is devoted to the study of the Vedas and is free from passion and hatred, yet bears the conch and the discus, is said to be always impure. (12)
He who is engaged in the ritual section of the Veda (karmakāṇḍa) yet always reviles Viṣṇu, and who reviles His devotees, is called a great outcaste (mahācaṇḍāla). ||13||

O Goddess of the Gods, those who are constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas, who are always performers of sacrifices and officiants of rites, and who are ever intent on the *agnihotra*— yet remain averse to the religious duties of Viṣṇu— I despise them, O Mistress of the Gods, for they are outside the Vedic fold and hostile to the dharma of Viṣṇu. (14)
The gods, greatly rejoiced, bestow peace; the Grandfather (Brahmā) and others ensure security;
and the preeminent sages grant blessings to those men who carry devotion to Govinda. (15)
The hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, accompanied by auspicious grahas, bhūtas, and piśācas, are well-pleased;
and Lakṣmī remains steadfast in the home of those men who bear devotion to Govinda. (16)
The Gaṅgā, Gayā, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Kāśī, Prayāga, and Kurujāṅgala remain within the bodies of those men who, having first performed acts of devotion, carry devotion to Govinda. (17)
Thus, the wise man should propitiate the Blessed One along with Śrī; that brāhmaṇa shall always be one who has accomplished his purpose—of this there is no doubt. (18)
O best of goddesses, whether he be a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, every man who practices devotion with particular intensity attains liberation. (19)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Devotion to Viṣṇu," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(131) Chapter One Hundred and Thirty-One.
Pārvatī said:
The Śālagrāma stone is pure; there are various forms [of deities] upon the earth.
How many kinds of worship for those very forms are traditionally taught? (1)
O Lord of the Asuras, tell me how these [deities] are to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas, or by Kṣatriyas, or by Vaiśyas, or likewise by Śūdras, or even by women. (2)
Mahādeva said: The Śālagrāma stone is meritorious, pure, and the performer of dharma;
by the mere sight of it, even a man who has committed the murder of a Brahmin is purified. (3)
That house is declared by the Vedas to be the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrtha), wherein this auspicious Śālagrāma stone, the very form [of the Divine], is ever present. (4)
The five should be honored by Brāhmaṇas, and likewise four by Kṣatriyas;
three should be honored by Vaiśyas, and one should be honored with great effort. ||5||
Merely by the sight of her, a Śūdra may attain liberation;
O Goddess, those men who indeed worship according to this rite [shall likewise attain it]. ||6||
Having enjoyed all pleasures there, they go to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu;
this is that great form which always removes sin. (7)
O Goddess, because the fruit beginning with Kailāsa arises from worshipping there, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Sarasvatī are present in that place. (8)
Wherever the stone remains, everything [is accomplished] there; of this there is no doubt.
What is the use of speaking much more on this, O fair-faced one? (9)
O Goddess of gods, worship must be performed properly by men who desire liberation; those people who worship Janārdana with a spirit of devotion [attain their goal]. (10)
By the mere sight of them, even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified—those Śūdras who always perform their own worship in the state of being servants. (11)
O Goddess of the gods, even Brahmā and the other lords of the deities do not know the merit of those brāhmaṇas who indeed worship Hari with a spirit of devotion. (12)
In those births, twenty-one generations of their family were delivered by them;
for that brahmin who bears the marks of the conch and the discus and performs worship [is likewise saved]. (13)
By that worship of Viṣṇu, the entire world is indeed worshipped; the ancestors declare, "In our lineage there have been Vaiṣṇavas. (14)
That family is indeed delivered by them until the dissolution of all beings;
having rescued us as well, they lead us to the abode of Viṣṇu.
That very day is blessed; blessed are his mother and kinsmen;
his father indeed is blessed, and likewise blessed are his friends. (16)
All those who are solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu should be known as most fortunate;
by the mere sight of them, one is liberated from great sin. (17)
All minor offenses and all major sins—indeed, all of them—are destroyed by the mere sight of Vaiṣṇavas. (18)
Those men on earth who are devotees of Viṣṇu shine like fires;
they are liberated from all sins, like the moon from the clouds. ||19||
Whether moist, dry, light, or heavy, whatever has been committed through speech, mind, or action—all that comes to destruction by the mere sight of Vaiṣṇavas. (20)
Whatever sin there may be, such as violence and the like, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, all of that comes to destruction through the sight of a Vaiṣṇava. (21)
The sinless go to heaven, and even the most wicked attain purity through the mere sight of the virtuous; this truth has been spoken by me to you. 22.
One who is devoted to Viṣṇu is skilled in washing away the smearing of the mire of saṃsāra; he is the purifier of purifiers—of this there is no doubt. ||23||
Those devotees of Viṣṇu who remember Madhusūdana every day should be known as being composed of Viṣṇu; there is no doubt that Viṣṇu is present therein. ||24||
Dark blue like a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes as long as lotuses, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and clothed in yellow garments. ||25||
Hari, resplendent with the Kaustubha gem, wearing a forest garland, and possessing the beauty of a face and cheeks illuminated by the radiance of shimmering earrings. (26)
Adorned with a crown, bracelets, armlets, and anklets; possessing a serene lotus-face, four arms, and endowed with splendor. ||27||
O Pārvatī, those brahmins who meditate in this way upon Viṣṇu are indeed the very form of Viṣṇu; they are Vaiṣṇavas, without a doubt. ||28||
O Queen of Gods, by the mere sight of them, or through devotion, or by feeding them, or by worshipping them, one certainly attains Vaikuṇṭha. (29)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Worshipping the Śālagrāma Stone," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(132) Chapter One Hundred and Thirty-Two.
Pārvatī said:
What kind of remembrance of Ananta-Vāsudeva is traditionally taught, by hearing which delusion does not arise again for human beings? (1)
Mahādeva said: "O Queen of the Gods, those who have perceived the ultimate reality remember Viṣṇu constantly;
just as one afflicted by thirst [remembers] water, so do I remember Viṣṇu. (2)
Just as the entire world, when agitated by snow, remembers the fire, even so do the gods and others remember Viṣṇu. ||3||
Just as a woman devoted to her husband constantly remembers her husband, so do they remember Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds and the Lord of the lords of the universe. ||4||
Just as one afflicted by fear seeks refuge, just as one greedy for wealth seeks riches, and just as one desiring a son seeks a son, so do I remember Viṣṇu. (5)
Just as the cātaka bird remembers its home even when far away, and just as one who knows Brahman remembers Mādhava, so do I, a knower of Brahman, remember Viṣṇu and the knowledge of Brahman. (6)
Swans desire Lake Mānasa; sages desire the remembrance of Hari;
and devotees desire devotion—likewise, I remember Viṣṇu. (7)
The body is dear to living beings because it is where the self resides;
those living beings desire long life—likewise, I remember Viṣṇu. (8)
Just as bees [cling] to a flower, as ruddy geese to the sun, and as devotion [clings] to one's own beloved, so do I remember Viṣṇu. (9)
Just as people bewildered by darkness long for a lamp,
so indeed do men in this world long for the remembrance of Keśava.
Just as one afflicted by fatigue longs for rest, just as one addicted to sleep longs for waking, and just as one free from sloth longs for knowledge, so do I remember Viṣṇu. 11.
As elephants [fear] mountainous ground and lions [fear] forest elephants and the like, so too must those who fear sin practice the remembrance of Viṣṇu. 12.
Just as fire is produced in a sun-crystal through contact with the sun, so indeed is devotion produced toward the Earth through association with the virtuous. ||13||
Just as the beloved water of the cool-rayed moon resorts [to the earth] through conjunction with the moon, so indeed does eternal liberation arise from union with a Vaiṣṇava. 14.
Just as a night-lotus pond blossoms upon seeing the moon, so too does devotion offered to the Lord always grant liberation to all people. 15.
Just as one who is terrified of fire should practice the recollection of a female bee,
through that yoga of recollection, one attains a state of similarity with the female bee.
The Gopīs performed the remembrance of Viṣṇu with the thought that he was their lover;
they were led to the state of union (sāyujya), and in that same way, I remember Viṣṇu. 17.
Some contemplate Janārdana with a spirit of scholarship, some with a spirit of hypocrisy, and others with a spirit of greed. ||18||
Some [worship] with devotion, some with a feeling of affection, or again with a feeling of hatred; some with a sense of ownership, some with their intellect, or even without prior conscious intent.
By whatever means people may contemplate Janārdana,
having enjoyed happiness in this world, they go to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu.
Oh, how wonderful is the majesty of Viṣṇu, which causes the hair to stand on end;
even a spontaneous remembrance of him bestows liberation from the three worlds. (21)
Neither by great wealth nor by extensive knowledge is [the Lord] seen;
rather, by the single yoga of devotion, He is perceived immediately as being near.
Although He is present nearby, He is far away, like a person out of sight to those whose eyes are closed;
likewise, the Eternal One is invisible to devotees who lack the yoga of devotion.
"This is reality, this is reality"—thus one is deluded by the divine illusion;
but when the reality of devotion is attained, then the entire world is permeated by Viṣṇu.

O beautiful one, listen: although the nectar was obtained by Indra and the others for the sake of happiness, they were nonetheless as miserable as if they were without Viṣṇu, because they lacked devotion to Him.
Having attained the nectar of devotion itself, suffering does not arise again;
having reached the station called Vaikuṇṭha, one rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu.
Just as a swan, having abandoned water, constantly drinks milk,
so too should one, having relinquished other duties, take refuge in devotion to Viṣṇu.
Abandoning devotion to any other, one should take refuge in devotion to Viṣṇu;
for how can a task be accomplished by tying up water with a cloth? ||28||

Without devotion, even if one attains a body, all such effort is in vain. Those people who teach religious duties without devotion to Viṣṇu will surely fall into a terrible hell; of this there is no doubt. (29)
Just as a fool desires to cross the ocean with his two arms, so does a man [desire to cross] the ocean of worldly existence without devotion to Viṣṇu. (30)
If one who practices devotion to Viṣṇu is cast down by the performance of ritual acts,
he remains free from possessions yet filled with longing, just as Mount Meru maintains its desire [for the sun].
O God, such a longing for devotion to you is created by me here in this life;
indeed, that devotion of mine shall bring about its fruit in another birth. (32)
Just as even a tiny fire here burns down a vast forest in various ways,
so too does devotion to me, even when performed in the measure of an atom.
Devotion is heard of among hundreds, and even understood among thousands;
yet among them, O Goddess of Gods, only one is truly born as a devotee.
Many kinds of people in the world will give their wisdom to others;
yet such a person who practices it himself is seen only once in ten million.
Devotion is mocked by worship, and it is ridiculed by victory;
O Lord of Gods, such is the nature of devotion that it is accepted only through that very [attitude].
Just as one might fall into the ocean or take refuge in a well for protection, so too is devotion grasped by him whose disposition is like that. //37//
Just as when a tree is watered at its root, its leaves are seen upon the branches;
so too, O Goddess, by means of worship alone, the fruit is established before one.
Just as the mind is fixed upon a water-pot by one who fetches water, so too, having fixed the mind upon Lord Hara, one shall attain liberation. 39.
Just as a mother gives a small amount of molasses to her child during infancy, yet the child begs for more molasses out of greed; (40)
Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes one, so too they perceive no difference [between themselves and the Lord] by the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu. (41)
Just as the sun is omnipresent and just as fire is omnipresent, so too does devotion abide within the devotee; he is never obstructed by actions.
Ajāmila, having abandoned his own duty and committed sinful acts, attained liberation for certain by remembering his son Nārāyaṇa. (43)
Those devotees who, day and night, subsist on nothing but my name alone—they indeed dwell in Vaikuṇṭha; in this matter, the Vedas are the witnesses. 44.
The fruit of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha is seen even in heaven; yet, having fully enjoyed that fruit, one inevitably falls back down. (45)
O Goddess, likewise for those who possess devotion to Viṣṇu, having enjoyed manifold pleasures and attained Vaikuṇṭha, when will there ever be a return for them? 46.
He by whom devotion to Viṣṇu has been practiced dwells in the world of Viṣṇu;
O Lord of Gods, behold him through the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu. (47)
Hundreds of stones situated in the midst of water were carried across by him;
yet, for one devoted to Viṣṇu, the mind is like the Soma-plant without water. 48.
Just as a six-legged bee dwelling in a lotus pond on the shore of a forest perceives the fragrance of the night-lily, so too is one devoted to Hari devoted to the devotee. 49.
Some dwell on the banks of the Gaṅgā for as many as a hundred yojanas;
one knows the fruit of the Gaṅgā, while another likewise possesses devotion to Viṣṇu.
Indeed, a buffalo constantly carries a load of camphor and agallochum, yet it does not perceive their fragrance; likewise, those whose faces are turned outward do not know Viṣṇu.
Just as deer, desiring the scent of musk, smell a *śāla* tree but do not recognize it as being in their own navels,
so too do those whose faces are turned outward fail to know Viṣṇu.
Just as instruction given to fools is a futile exertion of breath, so too is instruction in devotion to Viṣṇu given to one who is turned away from Him. 53.
Milk drunk by a snake indeed turns into poison; likewise, devotion to Viṣṇu becomes like poison for those who are devoted to others. 54.
Just as those with sightless eyes, having seen a lamp and even a mirror, do not perceive objects situated nearby, so too do those whose faces are turned outward fail to see Viṣṇu.
Just as fire is covered by smoke, or a mirror by dirt,
or as an embryo is enveloped by the membrane within the body, so too is Kṛṣṇa thus covered.
Just as clarified butter remains in milk and oil always resides in sesame seeds, so too Viṣṇu pervades all moving and non-moving beings, yet he is not seen by gods or humans.
Just as many clusters of jewels are strung together upon a single thread,
so too is the entire universe woven together within Brahman, which consists of pure consciousness.
Just as fire residing within wood is seen only through friction, so too is Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, perceived only through meditation. 59.
The lamp would be one at the beginning, from which thousands are born;
even so, Viṣṇu remains as one, abiding as the all-pervading.
Just as light always resides within the lotus at sunrise,
yet is seen in many ways upon the water, so indeed is Viṣṇu perceived in the world.
Even though the wind remains in its natural state, it always carries various fragrances; likewise, the Lord, residing within all living beings, experiences the qualities born of nature.
Just as water becomes of such a nature through contact with sugar or poison,
so too the self, having come into being, experiences the fruit of its own karma.
Just as various trees are produced from the union of the earth and water,
so too is one born into various wombs through the union with the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Whether in an elephant, a mosquito, a god, or even a human,
he remains firm within the body, neither superior nor inferior, fixed in his state.
Brahmā and the others were seated there, as well as the inhabitants of the earth and the celestial realms—
the gods, the sacrifices, the nāgas, the gandharvas, the kinnaras, and so forth.
In all of them, He is seen like the moon reflected in water;
indeed, Śiva, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, is seen as Maheśa.
Thus it is declared that Viṣṇu is everything; he is this all-pervading Hari, the Lord of all, known through the Vedānta, who transcends time and is indeed nameless.
Thus, O Goddess, he is undoubtedly a devotee of the assembly of the Vedas;
for he who is one is to be known as manifold, and he who is manifold is indeed one. (69)
Through the differentiation of name and form, it is described in many ways on earth;
by the eye, the light of the sun is perceived, and by the sun, the eye is made to flourish.
Likewise, the Supreme Self and the individual self always exist within every body;
just as space remains within each jar even when that jar is broken.
For when this state of being both form and formless has been shattered, one becomes perfectly immovable;
like a wooden figure, it falls without a master.
The body, which consists of various types of worms, perishes along with the self;
yet the colors of gold remain, and through fire they return to their original state.
In the same way, living beings who have attained devotion reach a previously non-existent state;
just as fools perceive the sun, though it be covered by its own clouds, as being devoid of luster.
Likewise, those deluded by ignorant minds do not know that Lord, who is free from conceptual construction and formless; yet by them, He is proclaimed through the Vedas.
And from that which is formless, it manifests with form according to its own will;
from that, space was born—devoid of sound and free from qualities.
From space, the wind was born, and it then became accompanied by sound;
from the wind, light was born, and from light, water came into being.
Within those waters was Virāṭ, whose interior is golden and who assumes the universal form; and in the lotus of his navel were millions of cosmic eggs.
From that [Prakṛti] arose Prakṛti and Puruṣa; from them, the threefold world was fashioned.
And from the union of those two, the conjunction of the principles (tattva-yoga) was born.
The origin of Viṣṇu is said to be Sāttvika, that of Brahmā Rājasa, and Śiva is declared to be Tāmasa; by these, everything is set in motion. (80)
There is one state of Brahmā in the world, which follows the seeds of karma;
by means of that, Viṣṇu withdraws all the worlds without exception. (81)
At that time, the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu remains there;
thus Viṣṇu is all-pervading, being the very beginning, middle, and end.
Indeed, people bound by their actions do not understand due to ignorance;
he who should perform at the proper times the duties appropriate to his social class.
That karma which has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity and is the cause of the Nābhigarbha is deliberated upon by the sages in all the Vedānta scriptures. (84)
I shall now fully proclaim this knowledge of Brahman within the body:
indeed, the mind alone is both the cause and the effect of the auspicious and the inauspicious. 85.
When everything is purified by the mind, then that is the eternal Brahman; the mind alone is always one's kinsman, and the mind alone is always one's enemy. 86.
Some have crossed over by means of the mind, while others have reached the further shore by means of the mind;
in the midst of all renunciation, one likewise performs external action.
In this very way, one who performs an action while acting is not defiled, just as a lotus leaf is not defiled by drops of water. //88//
Just as fire cast into fire [is extinguished], what purpose is served by devotion? When the essence of devotion is tasted, then liberation does not seem desirable. (89)
Viṣṇu is not attainable in this birth even through the eightfold yogas;
however, Viṣṇu is attained through devotion and may become easily accessible at all times.
Through these Vedas, knowledge is attained; through knowledge, the object of knowledge itself.
But when that object of knowledge is reached, then this world is empty. ||91||
Is Viṣṇu attained through physical force or by means of the eightfold yogas? For all states of being, purity of intention is what is praised. (92)
Just as one embraces according to one's desire, so is the result according to the nature of the object;
for indeed, one whose feet are shod with sandals walks upon the earth as if it were made of leather. (93)
Whatever kind of intellect one possesses, in that same way one perceives the world;
even a neem tree, though sprinkled with milk, does not abandon its bitter nature. (94)
All beings follow their own nature; instruction is useless.
Indeed, having cut down a mango tree, how could one obtain its fruit and leaves?
How could one lead this birth in vain for the sake of the pleasures of the senses?
It would be like cooking medicine in a vessel made of lapis lazuli. (96)
Likewise, one who has given away [wealth] is not burned; how could his birth be in vain?
Having placed a treasure in his house, how could an auspicious man perform menial service? (97)
Having abandoned that Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, how could one find delight in another path? What is the purpose of reciting the four Vedas by those devoid of devotion? 98.
A hunter, when endowed with devotion, is honored even by the gods;
having bound a single berry in his own hand, what need has he for mirrors? (99)
Their attendants have been granted sovereignty by the gods, such as Brahmā and Rudra;
yet they do not accept even the slightest thing offered by their Lord.
Having gone to one who possesses nothing and is unable to give food to a guest, how could there be meditation there on the bodiless Kṛṣṇa? (101)
Having seen it with form, many have come to that state out of devotion.
How can the wise explain how worshipful devotion can exist toward that which is empty, yet possesses form? 102.
How can a person travel on the path of emptiness without a support?
He who is with form is himself the master; he who is formless is the Lord. (103)
The one with form is seen through bliss alone; the formless is not perceived.
Devotion is found in that which has form, while enmity resides in that which is formless. 104.
Indeed, the formless is realized by itself through that which possesses form;
when the body's hair stands on end through the grace of the remembrance of Hari. (105)
When one sheds tears of joy, liberation then becomes a servant;
how could the sin committed in childhood not be destroyed? (106)
Having abandoned one's own duty, how could one practice terrible austerities through worship, charity, vows, pilgrimages, recitations, and burnt offerings not offered to you? (107)
Death in accordance with one's own duty is better; a supreme duty that brings about both [worlds] is preferable.
Having abandoned the scriptural injunction, how could one practice a terrible penance? (108)
A deluded person who is devoid of the stage of life (āśrama) shall never attain perfection.
The castes were created by Brahmā and assigned to their respective duties. (109)
Wealth acquired through one's own lawful duty is called "pure wealth" (śukla-dravya).
Whatever gift is given with that pure wealth, accompanied by faith, [is considered a true gift]. (110)
Even with very little, his great merit is beyond calculation—[the merit gained] by whatever wealth was brought for household tasks through association with the lowly. (111)
Whatever gift has been given by humans and others using that substance, its fruit does not accrue to them; indeed, they do not partake in that fruit at all.
Whatever kind of action one performs with the desire for sensory pleasure, such a womb does that fool obtain, for he is weak in knowledge. (113)
Whatever action one performs here, that is experienced there; if suffering should arise for a person practicing merit. (114)
Therefore, one should not practice self-mortification; for a man who commits sinful deeds born of his previous body, only suffering arises. 115.
O Goddess of the gods, one should not feel elation at that pleasure, just as animals bound by ropes are under the control of their master according to his will. 116.
Even men on this earth are led away by the bondage of their karma;
like forest-dwelling monkeys, they dance from house to house.
Thus, having led living beings through all wombs by means of their own karma, they sport like a ball thrown at will by a master. (118)
By means of their own karma, living beings are driven toward pleasure and pain; bound by their own actions, they are powerless to restrain that bondage. 119.
The gods are bound by their own actions, as are the ṛṣis and others;
on Mount Kailāsa, they reside within the body of Rudra, subsisting on the food of serpents and bulls.
Those who are unable to consume the nectar [of immortality] have karma as their powerful source;
he who bestows a healthy body is indeed called "Sūrya" (the Sun) by the wise. 121.
The charioteer of that chariot was Paṅgu, whose womb was born of karma; he was the powerful Indra-dyumna, a royal sage who had attained this state through his own actions. 122.
Since he is the capable Lord, the origin of action was rendered futile by him;
so too were Rudra, Brahmā, and the other gods, as well as humans and those who are asuras. (123)
Bound by all their karma, they wander upon the surface of the earth;
the entire world is dependent on karma, having been created by Viṣṇu in the beginning. 124.
That karma, dependent on Keśava, perishes by the name of Rāma;
for water situated everywhere bestows liberation, whether it be white or black. (125)
For those who act in this manner, the worship of Keśava grants liberation from karma; yet he who acts with body, speech, and mind for the sake of the pleasure of the senses [is bound]. (126)
Thinking that I have committed a sin against the One who is alone, and remembering Him in my mind, one should perform the appropriate expiation. 127.
One is the enjoyer of past karma, yet new karma does not increase further;
some praise the planets, while others praise the pretas and piśācas. (128)
Some praised the gods, while others spoke of medicinal herbs;
some [praised] the mantra and its accomplishment, and others [praised] intelligence and prowess.
Some follow exertion, others daring, others patience, as well as policy and strength;
through praise of their respective actions, they all pursue their desires. (130)
The ancient sages have described this as the intellect that is certain [of its object]:
when one possesses merit and not even the slightest sin exists within us. (131)
For knowledge is indeed twofold: meritorious and auspicious, or sinful.
When one's [karma] consists of sin, merit, and their equilibrium, it is found within actions. ||132||
When one attains the state where duality becomes non-dual through equanimous yoga, one shall proceed to the stage of bliss;
having renounced everything externally, one should become free from longing in the mind. ||133||
That conduct of his is in vain; he does not experience the fruit of that sin.
He performs external actions while remaining free from desire in his mind. (134)
Renunciation is to be known as mediocre; it does not, however, yield the full fruit. Having abandoned both the external and the internal through the intellect, one takes refuge in the void. 135.
That renunciation should be known as the highest, which is difficult even for yogis to attain;
some abandon everything out of anger, while others do so through the power of debate. (136)

Abandoning everything with great difficulty, you have practiced universal renunciation; endowed with excellent intelligence and faith, you have not fallen under the sway of anger and other such passions. ||137||
For by means of his actions, even a man who is defiled attains a happy rebirth in the homes of the pure, the prosperous, the wise, and even the yogis. (138)
But one who has fallen from yoga shall be born into a family preceded by the twice-born;
and in a very short time, he attains the fullness of yoga once again.
Through the grace of yoga and devotion, one may reach the state of consciousness-bliss, just as mud is removed by mud and blood by blood itself. (140)
How can an act consisting of violence ever be capable of washing away karma?
How can a sacrifice composed of violent acts be capable of exhausting karma? (141)
Sacrifices performed by those desiring heaven grant only a small amount of happiness in heaven; moreover, even though such pleasures are many, they are impermanent. (142)
For those who bow with devotion to Hari, there is never any separation from eternal happiness;
nor is there even the happiness of universal sovereignty, kingship, or likewise the bliss of heaven. (143)
I do not fear any other desire whatsoever as much as dwelling in a womb;
even iron may be split by stones, but a ruby is never split.
Devotion to Viṣṇu is not divided by a mind full of various desires;
the heron eats aquatic creatures while avoiding frogs and the like. (145)
Likewise, this Yama should avoid all those who serve Kṛṣṇa; he who protects them as well as he who slays them is called a protector. 146.
Even though he was endowed with hundreds of offenses, Kṛṣṇa, who bestows compassion, acted toward him according to the nature of his transgression by causing him to dwell in his own place. 147.
If one asks what the guardian of a field does today when he receives the fruit [of his labor], so too is the self in this body dependent on others and subject to their mercy. (148)
Having reached the further shore, he was slowly led by the wrestlers to the place of execution;
though he was the giver of liberation even to hunters, he himself was dragged away by the hunchbacked woman.
In that palace comparable to the celestial abodes easily attained in dreams, which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to reach,
they were themselves delivered when the remnants of the cowherd’s meal were consumed.
O Goddess, having seen that glorious, imperishable Puruṣa, the Supreme Self Janārdana, who is eternally sung of by yogis, they were filled with wonder. ||151||
Those who recite this divine remembrance day after day, being liberated from all sins, go to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu. (152)
By means of this realization of non-existence, one who recites [this] in the presence of Viṣṇu shall enjoy happiness in this world and attain the supreme state. ||153||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Remembrance of Viṣṇu," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(133) Chapter One Hundred and Thirty-Three.
Pārvatī said:

O you of excellent vows, tell me of whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist on this island; for this king of islands has always been fashioned upon the earth. O Lord, having shown compassion toward me, please state their number. (1)
Mahādeva said:
"The omnipresent one is to be seen within all beings everywhere on earth;
whatever is seen in the seven worlds, whether moving or unmoving."
Without him, that truth has neither been seen nor heard by me. Therefore,
O Goddess of the gods, Viṣṇu, the Great God Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions,
exists in the form of a sacred ford upon this very island.
I shall describe those sacred fords (tīrthas) in their entirety; there is no doubt about this.
First is the field of Puṣkara, the most excellent and auspicious of all sacred fords;
second is the field of Vārāṇasī, which bestows liberation. ||4||
The third sacred field is remembered as Naimiṣa, the purifier of sages;
and the fourth is Prayāga, remembered as the most excellent of all holy fords (tīrthas). ||5||
The fifth is said to be Kārmuka, which arose on Mount Gandhamādana;
the eleventh is Kānyakubja, where Vāmana resides.
The seventh is Viśvakāya on the auspicious lower mountain;
the eighth is named Gautama, which was fashioned long ago by Maṇḍara.
The ninth was Madotkaṭa, the tenth Rathacaitraka,
and the eleventh Kānyakubja, where Vāmana resided.
The twelfth is Malaya, and after that Kubjāmraka;
then Viśveśvara, Girikarṇa, and Kedāra, which bestows liberation.
On the back of the Himalayas is Bāhya; likewise Gokarṇa and Gopaka;
Sthāneśvara on the snowy mountain; and Bilvaka and Bilvapattrika.
On Śrīśaila, Mādhava is the sacred site; likewise, Bhadra is at Bhadreśvara.
Vijaya is proclaimed at Vārāha, and Vaiṣṇava is on the Vaiṣṇava mountain.
Raudra at Turudrakoṭi, Paitrya at Kāliñjara, the Kapila tīrtha at Kaṃpila, and likewise Karkoṭaka at Mukuṭa.
O Goddess of the gods, the sacred site originating from Śālagrāma is located on the cheek;
that called Śiva is on the Narmadā, and Viśvarūpaka is on the Tumā. (13)
Utpalākṣa and Sahasrākṣa were born on Mount Vairata;
likewise, Pitṛtīrtha is in the Gaṅgā, as is Viṣṇupādodbhava.
At the Vipāśā [river] is Vipāpa; at Pāṭala is Puṇḍravardhana;
Nārāyaṇa is at Supārśva; and at Trikūṭa is the temple of Viṣṇu. ||15||
On Mount Malaya is the auspicious place named Vipula-vipula;
on Koṭitīrtha is Kaurava, and on Gandhamādana is Sugandha. ||16||
One should remember Kubjāmraka at the three junctions of the day, the lofty Gaṅgā, the mountain dear to Hari, Viṃdhyapradeśa, Badarī, and the Sārasvata [tīrtha]. (17)
Kāli is remembered as the sky, Kālarūpa as the arrow, Cāṃdra as the region of the moon, and Turamaṇa as the leader of the holy places (tīrtha). ||18||
On the Yamunā is the one called Mṛga, on Karavīra that born of the Kurus,
and on Vināyakaparvata the holy site (tīrtha) called Vaimūka.
O Earth, in the region of Bhāskara, at Mahākāla, there is the great lord Maheśvara; there is a holy ford named Abhayada, known as Amṛta, which bestows immortality.
In Maṇḍapa is Viśvarūpa; in Īśvarapura is the one called Svāhā;
in Vailāla is Vailāleya; and in Marakaṇṭaka is Cāṇḍika, located in the direction of Pracaṇḍā.
Likewise, Someśvara at the holy site of Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Devamātra on the Sarasvatī, and the one situated on the bank of the Pārāvata. (22)
Mahālaya is at Mahāpadma; Piṅgaleśvara is at Uyoṣṇī;
likewise, the holy site named Saurava is at Siṃhikā. (23)
One should worship Kārttika at Kṛttikākṣetra, Kara on Śaṅkara Hill, and the divine one named Utpala at the confluence of the Subhadrā and the Asi. (24)
Then there is Gāṇapatya, and then Parvata at the place named Viṣṇu;
thereafter Jālaṃdhara is proclaimed, as well as the holy site (tīrtha) called Viṣṇumukha.
Tāra is proclaimed as Tāraka on Mount Viṣṇu;
Pauṇḍra is in the Devadāru forest, and Pauṣka is in the region of Kaśmīra. ||26||
The Bhauma, Hima, Himādri, and Catuṣṭika are the four Puṣṭikas;
likewise, the Kapālamocana Tīrtha arose at Māyāpura.
Then, from Śaṃkha came Uddhāra, and from him indeed Deva Vaiśaṅkhadhāraka;
from Piṇḍa was born Piṇḍanāman, and from Siddha came Vaikhānasa. ||28||
On the northern bank of the Acchoda river in Kuśadvīpa, there is the medicinal water of Kuśa, which fulfills the desires of Viṣṇu and bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. (29)
They call Manmatha the Hemakūṭa, and Tīrtha the Kuṃude Satyavādana; Āvāśvaka is known as a sacred ford, and Vindhya is remembered as the Vaimātṛka.
The sacred ford consisting of Brahman within the mind is remembered as the purifier of all sacred fords;
O beautiful one, hear that which is the most excellent among all these sacred fords. 31.
The sacred ford consisting of the name of Viṣṇu has never existed before, nor will it ever cease to exist;
for even a slayer of a Brahmin, a stealer of gold, a killer of a child, or a killer of a cow [is purified by it].
One is indeed liberated by the mere name through the grace of Keśava;
in the Kali age, Dvāravatī is beautiful, and the Lord Janārdana is blessed.
For those men who behold this God, their liberation is most firmly established—[those who behold] Viṣṇu, the Lord of all, the Sovereign, the most blessed God. (34)
O Mahādeva, we have reflected upon Janārdana, who dwells within the wise;
this has been declared as the one hundred and eight sacred fords (tīrthas). 35.
Whoever recites, causes others to recite, or even hears [this], is liberated from all sins;
and whoever, having bathed in these sacred fords, beholds Nārāyaṇa Hari.
Freed from all sins, one goes to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu; that great holy place (tīrtha) is remembered as the purifier of the worlds and the Lord of the Universe. ||37||
Even those who do not travel [to sacred sites], O best of men, attain the supreme goal;
one should cause the highly meritorious "Eight Hundred" to be recited during rites for the ancestors.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of this world, one attains the eternal state of Viṣṇu through the gift of a cow,
the performance of śrāddha, or by giving daily, again and again.
Through the ritual of worshiping the deity, the wise person attains the supreme Brahman. ||40||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Holy Places of Jambūdvīpa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(134) Chapter One Hundred and Thirty-Four.
Mahādeva said:
O beautiful lady, I shall now proclaim the greatness of the Vetravatī; listen!
By bathing there, people are liberated until the dissolution of all beings.
A well named Mahāgambhīrasaṃjñaka was dug by Vṛtra;
from that well emerged the Goddess who destroys the multitude of great sins.
O best of goddesses, just as this Ganges is the most excellent of rivers,
so too does the mere sight of her pacify the floods of sin.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall relate an ancient history, hearing which even sinners are liberated from faults and the bondage of karma. (4)
And in the city of Campaka, he acts as king;
he is always wicked, of evil appearance, and an oppressor of the people. ||5||
Adharma appearing in the form of Dharma, he was devoted to Viṣṇu’s destruction; he was a slayer of gods and twice-born brahmins, and a defiler of the stages of life (āśramas).
The second [son] was Vedani, illustrious yet foolish, merciless, deceitful, devoted to false scriptures, and a violator of others' wives. ||7||
Named Vidāruṇa, he was indeed a fool;
once, by the turn of fate, he came to that river. (8)
O Goddess of the gods, he himself became a leper due to his addiction to hunting;
this great sin arose from his reviling of Brahmins. (9)
He was a speaker of falsehoods, evil-minded, deceitful, and indeed merciless toward animals;
he was constantly a reviler of the Vedas and a defiler of the scriptures concerning cows. ||10||
Wandering thus in the forest, afflicted by thirst and accompanied by his friends,
that king dismounted from his horse, drank water, and went home.
By that very drinking of water, leprosy was cured; of this there is no doubt.
Moreover, the intellect of that king became especially pure.
O Goddess of the Asuras, when devotion to Viṣṇu arose within him,
from that time forward he always performed his ritual bathing at the proper hour.
O Goddess of the Gods, having been born there stainless and enriched with many forms, he enjoyed happiness in this world after performing numerous sacrifices. (14)
Having given sacrificial fees to the Brahmins, he indeed attained the state of Viṣṇu; knowing this, O Goddess, [one should perform rites] especially at the Vetravatī. ||15||
O best of goddesses, whether they be Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, those who perform their ablutions here attain liberation in this world. (16)
Those who perform their ablutions there—whether in the month of Kārttika or Māgha, whether they are outsiders or knowers of the Vedas—are liberated from the bondage of sin. (17)
Having bathed at the confluence of rivers, one is liberated from sin;
that place where the union of the Sābhramatī with her [the Devikā] is clearly seen. ||18||
Having bathed there without distinction, even a slayer of a Brahmin is always liberated;
O sinless one, that divine city of Kheṭaka is indeed like heaven itself.
O Queen of Videha, many separations from Brahmā were brought about there;
having bathed and eaten there, one is not subject to rebirth again.
O Goddess, she is remembered as the peerless Gaṅgā, especially by the gods;
those men who desire happiness and those men who desire wealth [should worship her]. 21.
Those people who desire heaven bathe here again and again;
having enjoyed happiness in this world, they go to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu.
Those born of the solar lineage and likewise those of the lunar lineage,
having arrived at the Irāvatī and bathed there, attained supreme bliss.
By seeing it, one removes suffering; by touching it, one removes mental sin.
O Goddess, by bathing and eating there, one becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt.
One enjoys infinite fruit from bathing, recitation, and likewise from fire-offerings;
having gone to the sacred site of Vārāṇasī, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance with devotion. (25)
O best of goddesses, having gone there, that merit which was previously unearned becomes truly meritorious; especially so if one meets their end at the Vetravatī.
Having become four-armed, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
whatever holy places there are on earth, as well as the gods and the ancestors, [are all present]. ||27||
And all of them dwell here at the Vetravatī, O Goddess of the Suras;
what more need be said, O fair-faced one, after saying it again and again? 28.
O Anasūyā, there is no sacred ford on earth equal to that of the Vetravatī;
there I am Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā, the gods, and the supreme sages.
O Maheśvarī, all the deities reside at the Vitastā,
especially at one time, two times, or three times a day.
Those who perform their ablutions there are undoubtedly liberated. ||31||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Vetravatī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(135) The one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, I shall describe the majesty of the Sābhramatī exactly as it is;
indeed, Kaśyapa, the best of sages, performed great austerities there.
For many years,
he performed great austerities on the beautiful Arbuda mountain, which was densely covered with various trees.
Having gone there, penance was indeed performed by the sage Kaśyapa,
where the delightful Sarasvatī flows— pure and the destroyer of sins.
O Goddess, one day he went toward Naimiṣa;
at that time, all the sages engaged in many conversations.
Then, having been properly questioned by those twice-born ones, that sage Kaśyapa said:
"O Lord Kaśyapa, for our pleasure, let Gaṇeśa be brought from his home."
"By your name, this best of rivers shall become the river Ātusaṅgā.
Having heard their words and having paid homage to those twice-born ones, [he departed].
Having arrived in the Arbuda forest near the banks of the Sarasvatī,
he then performed there a penance that was exceedingly difficult to accomplish.
Indeed, I was propitiated by that brahmin Kaśyapa;
at that time, I appeared visibly before that best of brahmins.
Choose a boon—may it be auspicious for you—whatever dwells within your mind. ||9||
Kaśyapa said:
"O Lord of the gods, O Lord of the universe, you are capable of granting a boon;
grant me that pure, sin-destroying hymn which resides upon your head. (10)
"O Mahādeva, salutations to you who are non-different from me;
O Goddess, at that time I said: 'Accept this, O best of the twice-born.'"
Then, having relinquished a single matted lock, it was given by me to Gaṅgā;
taking it, that best of the twice-born went joyfully to his own abode. 12.
There is a sacred ford named Keśarandhra, which is the dwelling place of Kaśyapa;
having gone there, the Lord of Gods was surrounded by sages.
The excellent river Kāśyapī was brought forth by Kaśyapa;
it is said that by the mere sight of her, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated.
Pārvatī said:
Tell me, what merit is gained merely by bathing at that sacred ford?
You are compassionate toward Viśvanātha; please show mercy upon me. (15)
O King of Gods, what merit is there in beholding [it], and what is said regarding bathing [there]? O Brahmin, what is its greatness like? You ought to tell me all of this. (16)
Mahādeva said: "O Lord, by the grace of the illustrious Viṣṇu, I have heard of many sacred fords (tīrthas) and shrines, as well as the rivers that flow into the ocean."
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Revā, and the great river Tāpī;
the Godāvarī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Kauśikī, and likewise the Gallikā. ||18||
The Kāverī, the Vedikā, the Bhadrā, and the Sarayū which removes sin;
as well as various other rivers on earth that take away all sins. (19)
Prayāga, the king of holy places, as well as Kāśī, Puṣkara, the sacred site known as Naimiṣāraṇya, and Amara-kaṇṭaka. ||20||
The field of Dvārakā is supreme, and the Arbuda forest is supreme;
such are the various and diverse divine fields.
O Goddess of gods, there the Śrutis were heard by me through the grace of Viṣṇu;
previously, O Pārvatī, I was indeed entreated by Bhagīratha.
Then this Gaṅgā was given by me to Kaśyapa, who desired the world of Viṣṇu; she was subsequently given back to me at the request of the sages. (23)
This Gaṅgā of Vaikāśyapa always removes the defects of disease;
this is what is called by that very name in the world throughout the ages. (24)
Therefore, I shall describe it; listen to its true nature as it is: she was named Kṛtavatī in the Kṛta age, and Girikarṇikā in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age she was known as Candanā, and in the Kali age she is remembered as Sābhramatī;
indeed, O people, she is especially for the purpose of bathing day after day.
O Goddess, those who are liberated from all sins go to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu at the Plakṣāvataraṇa-tīrtha on the Sarasvatī. ||27||
Whatever fruit may arise for humans from bathing at Kedāra and Kurukṣetra, that same fruit is surely obtained daily by those [who bathe] in the Sābhramatī and other such rivers. 28.
"There is no doubt that this occurs," according to the words of Vyāsa;
O Queen of the Asuras, it happens every day during the second fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Whatever fruit is obtained from performing a śrāddha ceremony correctly on the new moon day and other such occasions, a man attains that same fruit by bathing in the Sābhramatī. (30)

On the full moon day of Kārttika, when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation, whatever fruit a mortal obtains by standing before Mādhava at Śrīsthala, that same fruit he obtains from bathing in the Sābhramatī. 31.
O Goddess, this is the most excellent purifier among all the worlds;
it is the most blessed, O Goddess, sacred, and indeed the destroyer of sins. (32)
In that Vaiśā, on the Bhramatī river, they always remain—those who were their kinsmen in the east and likewise those in the north. (33)
All those from the west and the south constantly go to the village of Kheṭaka in the presence of Brahmā, under the very pretext of a pilgrimage to sacred sites. 34.
They always arrive, there is no doubt, on the full moon day of Kārttika;
there they perform the Śrāddha rite as well as the feeding of Brahmins.
People constantly perform various religious duties and various sacrifices;
they always practice diverse kinds of giving.
In all the four ages, there is no need for deliberation on this point:
Yavakrīta, Raibhya, Kākṣīvata, and Uśija likewise [attained their goals]. (37)
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Kaṇva, Medhāvī, and Punarvasu—
endowed with the qualities of initiation (dīkṣā)— reside in the eastern direction.
Likewise, in the north were the illustrious Madhumat and others,
as well as the highly fortunate Subandhu and the powerful Dattātreya.
Śikhī, Dīrghatamas, Gautama, Kaśyapa, Śvetaketu, Kahoḍa, Pulaha, and Devala; ||40||
Viśvāmitra and Bharadvāja, the heroic Jamadagni,
Garga the son of Ṛcīka, and likewise the sage Uddālaka.
Devaśarmā, Dhaumya, Āstīka, Kaśyapa, Lomaśa, Nābhiketu, and Lomaharṣaṇa as well. ||42||
The sage Ugraśravas, as well as Bhārgava Cyavana and those such as the Vālakhilyas— all of them indeed go there.
Having performed their ablutions, abstaining from food, and always devoted to Viṣṇu,
they stand eternally on the bank bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The sacred ford named Gayā is the most auspicious of all holy places;
there dwells the Lord of the gods, the Grandfather himself. (45)
"O Gītā, those ancestors who desire a share in the śrāddha ceremony should wish for many sons, so that even if just one among them goes to Gayā. (46)
One should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice, or one should release a dark-colored bull;
likewise, Vārāṇasī is meritorious and always beloved by the ancestors. 47.
And since this very [river], by my meditation, bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, let there be a tree named Madhava here at my command, O Lord of Gods. 48.
O Lord of Gods, I dwell eternally here, especially in Vārāṇasī;
therefore, this city is always the most blessed and supreme among my [abodes]. 49.
The holy pilgrimage site of Vaivimaleśvara is beloved by the ancestors,
as is Prayāga, the sacred ford of the ancestors, which is endowed with all other holy sites.
O Goddess, at my word, they shall come to the waters of the Sābhramatī, as will the Lord Vaṭeśvara accompanied by Mādhava. (51)
O Goddess of the gods, by my command, they dwell at the meritorious Daśāśvamedhaka and likewise at Gaṅgādvāra, as well as along the Sābhramatī river.
There is the Nadāthalalitādevī Tīrtha, which possesses seven streams; likewise, there is the place named Amitrapada, Kedāra, the abode of Śaṅkara. (53)
They call the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean auspicious, as it consists of all sacred fords;
likewise, there is the Brahma-lake in the pool of the waters of the Śatadru.
The sacred ford named Tuṇaimiṣa is always under my command; there is no doubt that the goddesses dwell in the waters of the Sābhramatī. (55)
Then, from the holy Śvetāvalkalinī, there flows the Śvetā and the Hiraṇmayī;
then the Hastimatī and the Vārttaghnī, both rivers that flow toward the ocean.
These [waters] are indeed beloved by the ancestors and bestow the fruit of ten million śrāddhas;
therefore, sons should offer śrāddhas there for the benefit of their ancestors.
O beautiful one, there is a city there called Pāṭala, also known as Vāḍava;
on the Sābhramatī river, these rivers always flow there in particular.
Those people on earth who perform bathing and giving of gifts there, having enjoyed happiness in this world, go to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu. (59)
Jambūdvīpa is of great merit, where merit increases;
therein lies the region called Ārya, which is of great merit and bestows the fruits of all desires. (60)
The holy site known as Nīlakaṇṭha, as well as the lake Dahrada, and likewise the sacred Rudrahṛada and the meritorious Rudramahālaya. ||61||
Due to my great merit as a ḍākinī, the great river Acchodā likewise flows into the Sābhramatī, having made herself visible to me. (62)
Likewise, Dhūmrāmitra, Vaijanātha, Dṛṣadvara, Kṣiprānadī, Mahākāla, as well as Ākali and Jarogiri; ||63||
The wise have declared that Gaṅgodbhūta, Harodbheda, and Narmadākāra are equal to the Gaṅgā in terms of the merit gained from offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas). ||64||
O Lord of Gods, these Brahma-tīrthas on the northern bank of the Sābhramatī have been protected by the gods, with Brahmā at their head.
O Maheśvarī, this [rite] destroys the sins of people even by mere remembrance;
how much more so for those men who offer it during a śrāddha, O Sureśvarī!
Oṃkāra, Pitṛtīrtha, the waters of the Kāverī and Kapilā, the confluence of the Caṇḍavegā, and likewise Amarakaṇṭaka; ||67||
O Goddess, bathing and other rites performed here in the confluence of the Vārtaghnī, preceded by Gaṇeśvara, shall be a hundred times more meritorious than at Kurukṣetra.
The collection of sacred fords brought from Sābhramatī by the Gaṇas in ancient times has thus been described by me in brief,
along with the confluence of these holy sites.
Even Vāgīśa (the Lord of Speech) is unable to fully describe the detailed reality of sacred fords;
the truth is the sacred ford, compassion is the sacred ford, and the restraint of the senses is the sacred ford.
One should diligently perform a bath at its sacred ford; of this there is no doubt.
The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the saṅgava period is of the same duration.
Therefore, bathing and other rites at a sacred ford (tīrtha) bestow pleasure upon the gods.
Midday consists of three muhūrtas; afternoon follows after that.

The bathing, offering of rice-balls, and libations that generate joy for the ancestors should be performed during the three-muhūrta period of late afternoon; one should not perform a śrāddha at that time.
That period known as Rākṣasī is censured for all ritual acts;
it is always proclaimed to consist of fifteen muhūrtas of the day. (74)
Among those, the eighth muhūrta is traditionally known as the time of *kutupa*;
for at midday, the sun is always in its meridian. (75)
Therefore, midday is the giver of infinite fruit for the ancestors through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa); likewise are the sword-vessel and the Nepalese bali-offering.
Silver, darbha grass, cows, a daughter's son, kutapa wool, and sesame seeds—these they call "pāpa," meaning that which is contemptible; they cause torment for such a person. (77)
Therefore, these eight are renowned as *kutapas*;
from the *kutu* moment upward, there are four *muhūrtas*.
And this five-muhūrta period is prescribed as the time for the śrāddha;
kuśa grass and black sesame seeds are known to have originated from the body of Viṣṇu. (79)

For the sake of protecting the *śrāddha*, the denizens of heaven have thus declared: "An offering of sesame seeds and water must be made by those residing at sacred fords while standing in the water. (80)
With darbha grass in hand, one should perform the śrāddha rite alone;
thus, by those known by the name Sābhramatī, there is entry into this sacred ford (tīrtha). 81.
Having caused it to be made for me, O Goddess, it was given to Kaśyapa Vaikhaṇasa;
that Kaśyapa is my devotee and has always been dear to me. 82.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, this Gaṅgā, which is purifying and destroys sin, [is present] at the Vaibrahmacārika tīrtha on the Sābhramatī. 83.
Having established myself under that name, I am indeed Śaṅkara;
I stand for the welfare of the world as one known by the name Brahmacārīśa. (84)
On the banks of the Sābhramatī, at the place known as Brahmacārīśa, when a devotee performs worship with particular devotion during the Kali age, [the fruit is attained]. 85.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of this world, he attains the great state of Śiva;
even if he departs while afflicted by great diseases, he reaches that same goal.
O Maheśvarī, by the mere sight of which a disease quickly perishes;
having gone to that sacred site, one who has conquered his senses and observes a fast—87.
While he performs worship with devotion, standing perfectly steady during the night vigil,
I indeed come into his sight in the form of a yogi.
"I grant the desired objects of longing; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one! Especially for those people who come to my abode," (89)
I shall bring about the pacification of their diseases after a long time;
eighty-four types of disease have been described by me. (90)
O beautiful one, by the mere sight of this, he shall perish along with his disease; there exists no sign of my presence there in the mountain valley. (91)
O great ascetic, there is no doubt that at this very time, on this very spot of earth, this [place] is my own for the mere act of bathing. (92)
O Goddess of the Suras, King Brahmadatta, the son of Vaiśvānara, was possessed of great valor;
by that king, penance was performed for a long time.
Furthermore, he performed the fire-sacrifice in many ways, and he practiced various austerities, such as month-long fasts and the like, on numerous occasions. (94)
O lady of excellent complexion, after the king had thus performed such great asceticism for a very long time, I appeared before him in person to grant a boon.
O Brahmadatta, O lord of men, listen to these great words: whatever you constantly desire, all that shall be granted to you by me without a doubt. (96)
He said: "O Lord of Gods, if that which is desired by me is to be granted, then let only one boon be given to me forever. (97)
"O Lord of Gods, may an Īśvara be born on earth under my name.
O sinless one, being satisfied by those words, a boon was granted by me.
Then, O Goddess of the Suras, I dwelt together with him;
staying here without food, I performed devotion in its entirety. (99)
I shall grant the desired objects of their wish, as many as fourteen Indras [might rule].
And those Brahmins who come here and perform the recitation of the Rudra-mantras and other rites—[to them I shall grant these].
They perform these especially; listen as I describe them:
they bring the happiness of women, the happiness of sons, and furthermore, the increase of fortune. (101)
Fame, sovereignty, as well as the destruction of diseases and other ailments—all that which is desired is indeed swiftly attained in the Kali Yuga. (102)
O Pārvatī, in this terrible Kali age, my devotees shall come to this earth,
establish [the deity] here, and dwell for five days.
"O Goddess of the Gods, I grant you your desired objects; this is the truth, the absolute truth!
He shall be known by the name Brahmadatta, a second Brahmā, and he shall be a celibate student. (104)
Having installed Gaṅgādhara and stayed for five days,
the king then returned once more to his own kingdom.
The most renowned and supreme great Brahmadatta, who was a knower of dharma, ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years. 106.
Then, after having enjoyed the kingdom for some time, that king went to that world of Śiva, the supreme state known as Brahman. 107.
Two gods reside there, designated by these names: one is indeed known as Brahmacārīśa, and the other is remembered as Gaṅgādharas. (108)
To those people who perform worship especially at my sacred site, I grant all their desires here; of this there is no doubt. (109)
That very place should always be embraced as the Linga, and it should always be visited by men;
there, flowers, incense, and various kinds of food offerings should likewise be presented. (110)
The wise man who performs [this worship] with bilva leaves, flowers, and likewise with sandalwood and other [fragrances], certainly obtains everything. (111)
They offer worship to those who abide in me; to them I grant everything.
Whoever should constantly hear this narrative concerning the student (brahmacārin), [to him I grant everything]. (112)
Having attained happiness in this world, he goes into the presence of Śiva,
where the Lord who wears the Gaṅgā dwells eternally, bestowing prosperity.
The second [state] is always present, known as the Lord of the Vow of Celibacy (brahmacārīśa).
Through the union of meditation with these two, one certainly attains the state of Śiva. ||114||
By seeing [the deity], disease perishes; by worshipping, one attains long life;
and by bathing there at that Lord of Gods, one becomes a partaker of liberation—of this there is no doubt. (115)
Listen, O Sundarī, I shall describe a most wonderful sacred site (tīrtha), renowned as Rājakhaḍga, which is especially [efficacious] on the Sābhramatī river. 116.
Born of the solar lineage was King Vaikartana;
he was of evil conduct, sinful in nature, and a reviler of the Brāhmaṇas. ||117||
He was always hostile toward his guru, an obstacle to all ritual actions, eternally devoted to the wives of others, and a constant reviler of Viṣṇu. ||118||
He constantly inflicts various kinds of oppression upon the subjects;
such is that wicked-souled one who always dwells upon this earth. (119)
Listen, after some time had passed in this manner, due to the power of his own evil deeds and the turn of fate, he became afflicted with leprosy. (120)
Having gazed upon his own body and reflected upon it again and again, he became absorbed in anxious thought, meditating on what ought to be done. (121)
Once, by the turn of fate, he went to the forest for the sake of sport;
having reached the bank of the Sābhramatī river there, he remained.
There he performed his ablutions and drank the excellent water;
by that bath, his body immediately became known as divine. (123)
A form made of pure gold was seen in the mountain and in the sky; at that very moment, he became a king—of this there is no doubt. (124)
O Lord of Gods, having attained a divine form, the king enjoyed sovereignty for some time and then indeed went to the supreme state. 125.
Thus, this became known as the royal sword-tīrtha;
those who perform ablutions here and whoever bestows gifts likewise [attain merit]. (126)
Having enjoyed the pleasures of this world, they attain the eternal state of Viṣṇu;
for them, there is never any disease, nor does sorrow ever arise at any time.
The man who performs his daily bath in this sword named Rājasa shall attain heaven and be honored by Brahmā and the other gods. (128)
In the Kṛta age he is named Īśvara; in Tretā, Bhuvaneśvara; he is known as Rājeśvara in the Dvāpara age, and in Kali, Naga-nandin.
In this terrible Kali age, the Lord of the Universe (Viśvarāṭ) has become concealed;
therefore, he has manifested as the royal sword known by the name Tīrtha.
Those men who perform the libation for the ancestors here with faith are proclaimed on earth as performers of meritorious deeds. (131)
Those who perform their ablutions here [at Bālahaṃtāra], even if they are slayers of Brahmins, are freed from those faults and go into the presence of Śiva. (132)
Those men who shall perform the release of a dark-colored bull at the Sābhramatī,
their ancestors will remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
This divine narrative, known as the "King’s Sword," for those men who hear it, O Devī, no fear exists. 134.
Diseases and defects are destroyed by hearing and reciting it. ||135||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Sābhramatī," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. 135.
(136) Chapter One Hundred and Thirty-Six.
Pārvatī said:
Tell me which countries she purified as she flowed from Naṃdikuṇḍa;
tell me which lands she sanctified on her way,
and which holy sites she established after reaching Mount Arbuda.
Sūta said:
When the Goddess had spoken thus there, Mahādeva, the sovereign of the universe,
addressed these words to Pārvatī, who enchants the entire world.
Mahādeva said: Prior to the supremely purifying Naṅdikuṇḍa tīrtha, the Kapālamocana tīrtha was proclaimed by the sages. (3)
This sacred site possesses a splendor exceeding all others; it is the supreme purifier among purifiers.
Here, I cast down the skull known as Brahma.
O Pārvatī, from this [event] the Kapālamocana Tīrtha was born;
it is purifying for all beings, manifest, and renowned throughout the world. (5)
That sacred ford is known as Kapālakuṇḍa, the king of all holy places;
where the gods, as well as nāgas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and others [reside].
