Great-souled beings dwell at this pure and auspicious holy ford (tīrtha),
a ford renowned throughout the three worlds that bestows gifts and grants liberation.
Having bathed there and become pure, one should worship Kapāleśa after fasting for one night and providing a feast for the Brahmins.
There too, by the gift of clothing, one obtains the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice;
and whoever at that sacred site undertakes the vow of beholding [the deity], ||9||
Having abandoned the body, he will certainly go to the world of Śiva;
for in ancient times, Saudāsa was freed from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter by bathing in this sacred ford.
O Goddess of the Suras, having been liberated, he attained stainless knowledge;
born in the lineage of Bhāgīrathī, he was the mighty one named Sudāsa.
His son was Mitrasaha, also renowned as Saudāsa;
due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha, Saudāsa attained the body of a Rākṣasa.
Having performed his ablutions in the Sābhramatī, he was liberated from the sin born of the curse;
for here flow the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Sarasvatī. (13)
These pure and merit-bestowing goddesses always dwell at Nanditīrtha;
likewise, there is the gift of cows, the gift of land, and the gift of beds. (14)
The gift of a daughter in marriage should especially be performed by wise men;
immersion in the Sābhramatī is declared to be equal to this gift. 15.
Wherever all these very things have fallen upon the ground, they too attain purity by the mere touch of water. (16)
A man who performs a śrāddha here with devotion, his ancestors, being fully satisfied, go to the supreme abode. ||17||
Those men who always hear this divine narrative shall be liberated from all sins and attain union with Viṣṇu. ||18||
For those who praise Maheśvara through action, mind, and speech, no suffering exists as long as the dissolution of all beings. 19.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Nanditīrtha," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(136) The one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Then, from that region, the river Sābhramatī arrived,
scattering [the remains] at the hermitage frequented by brahmin-sages.
By the force of its waters, it split the mountain ridges in many ways;
divided into seven streams, it flows toward the southern ocean.
The first is the meritorious Ābhramatī; the second is Seṭikā;
the third is the meritorious Valkinī; and the fourth is Hiraṇmayī.
The fifth is called Hastimatī, declared to be the remover of all sins;
and that sixth is Vetravatī, which was created in ancient times by Vṛtra.
This is that supreme goddess who emerged from the well of Vṛtra;
she was born there as the Vetravatī, the destroyer of great sins.
Bhadrāmukhī, Śubhaprāyā, and Saptamī, the purifier of the world— O Goddess,
by these seven [deities], protect those people and their lands.
Having purified it with one [mantra], he who shall offer a śrāddha at the Vikīrṇa-tīrtha, dedicated to the ancestors, establishes [them] in the seven streams.
Whatever fruit there may be from the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā,
that shall belong to those who have fallen away from their vows and for whom the rites of water and funeral cakes have been neglected.
Those for whom the rites of offering rice-balls and water have been performed are liberated in that scattered [place].
Whoever performs a *śrāddha* there will certainly attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (*gāṇapatya*).
Therefore, one should perform the śrāddha with faith according to the injunctions of the three Vedas at this sacred ford; O brahmins, by this, seven rivers shall rise up even for a pauper.
"O best of Brahmins, perform your ablutions if you desire the world of the Ṛṣis.
Thus was it specifically said by Kaśyapa to the twice-born. 11.
If one performs a bath here, which always removes all suffering, it is the most excellent of sacred fords (tīrthas) and the highest of the highest among holy sites (kṣetras). 12.
This sacred ford is widespread, bestowing auspiciousness and removing the afflictions of disease;
those who perform their ablutions here especially during the Kali age shall always [attain these benefits]. (13)
Therefore, those who possess merit are indeed born here; of this there is no doubt. This supreme purifying site, scattered [throughout], is equal to the sacred ford of Gayā;
it constantly bestows merit upon the ancestors and destroys the suffering of the worlds. (14)
Thus ends the section on the scattered holy fords.
Beyond this sacred ford (tīrtha) is the unsurpassed sacred ford called Śvetodbhava, where the river Śvetā was born from the ashes on my back and belly.
Renowned throughout the three worlds as the destroyer of all sins, she was born from the union with the ashes of Hara and is honored by the gods. 16.
Having bathed in that [tirtha], being pure and self-controlled, and having stayed for three nights, a man who beholds Mahākāleśvara is glorified in the world of Rudra. ||17||
If one should offer the piṇḍas to the ancestors on its bank with kuśa grass and sesame seeds, his ancestors will become well-satisfied; of this there is no doubt. (18)
The Śvetagaṅgā is of great merit and liberates one from suffering and poverty; O Goddess, by bathing there, supreme bliss is attained. (19)
O Pārvatī, I always reside at that meritorious confluence;
O beautiful one, those who perform ablutions and offer gifts there [attain great merit].
For him, there shall be that fruit of infinite result; of this there is no doubt. There, the god Bhūteśvara certainly resides at the confluence.
In that regard, those best of men who offer incense, lamps, flowers, and the waving of lights (ārārtika) are people whose very nature is merit. ||22||
If one takes a bilva leaf and offers it upon Śiva on the day of Śvetā in the presence of Śiva, one constantly obtains whatever is desired. (23)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Śvetā-tīrtha," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(138) The One Hundred and Thirty-Eighth Chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Then, one devoted to pilgrimage should go to Gaṇatīrtha, which is said to be Triviṣṭapa, located on the banks of the Candanā by the Gaṇas. ||1||
A man who, being composed in mind, bathes at Triviṣṭapa on the full moon day, incurs no doubt; he is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O highly fortunate one, even he whose stay in heaven lasts for only the four months of the rainy season is honored in the world of Rudra because of his merit.
Having bathed at Gaṇatīrtha on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and observed a fast, and having bathed at the confluence of the Bakulā, a person goes to heaven. ||4||
Having bathed at that sacred ford and beheld Bakuleśa, a man shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati through the grace of Gaṇeśvara. ||5||
This is the supreme purifier, increasing merit and longevity;
by hearing it, a person obtains incomparable merit equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Remaining here, abstaining from food, with senses subdued and mind composed,
he thus chants the name of the supreme deity, the delightful Lord of the Gaṇas.
O fair-faced one, he attains all enjoyments; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Here, King Somavaṃśī Viśvadatta, possessed of great prowess, [attained them]. 8.
O Goddess of the Gods, having performed great austerities for a long time,
he then attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas through the grace of Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Hoḍa, the sage Kauśītaka, Bharadvāja, Garga, Viśvāmitra, and Vāmana; ||10||
O Maheśvarī, all these sages, who are embodiments of merit, constantly perform service by the grace of Śrī Gaṇeśa. ||11||
One who is childless obtains children; one who is destitute obtains wealth;
one who is ignorant obtains knowledge; and one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation. 12.
O fair-faced one, what is the use of speaking further at length?
Whoever performs a bath here, or likewise offers worship again and again, [attains the fruit]. (13)
Completely liberated from all evil, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
[salutation] to Śiva who has the form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu who has the form of Śiva. ||14||
O Goddess, by the grace of Śrī Viṣṇu, I do not perceive any interval between them. ||15||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Gaṇa Tīrtha at the Confluence of the Bakulā," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-Khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(139) The one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
On the northern bank of the Sābhramatī, there is a famous place known as Agnitīrtha;
it is situated not very far to the northeast of that river, having made its abode there.
The sacred ford (tīrtha) named Pāleśvara is established by Caṇḍīyatra;
it is the seat (pīṭha) of the Yogamātṛs, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). ||2||
There, the Mothers of all the gods remained for the sake of their mission, exerting supreme effort for the purpose of bestowing grace upon the worlds. ||3||
Having stayed for three nights at that sacred ford, one of firm vows should approach that Īśāna, the Lord of Gods, Caṇḍikeśvara.
Having performed his ablutions in the Sābhramatī river in the vicinity of Mātṛtīrtha, and being disciplined in the practice of meditative absorption (samādhi), he should proceed to Vaimātṛmaṇḍala.
A person obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows by bathing at Agnitīrtha and beholding Cāmuṇḍā.
No fear shall arise for him from demons, spirits, or piśācas; for the Gokhurā and Acana rivers meet there with the Sābhramatī. (7)
O Goddess of the lords of gods, thousands of sacred fords (tīrthas) reside there;
O Pārvatī, one should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) there with powdered rice (lacaūrṇa).
Having offered funeral cakes and fed the twice-born, one shall attain the imperishable state.
There, King Kukardama was a most sinful, wicked, and uncontrollable rogue. (9)
I am deluded, filled with arrogance, and a reviler of the twice-born; I am a killer of cows, a destroyer of strength, most sinful, and always difficult to subdue. (10)
O Goddess of the gods, while he was ruling his kingdom in the city named Piṇḍāra,
his death occurred at that time through the practice of yoga in dharma.
O Maheśvarī, having died there, he was reborn in the form of a preta;
his face was yellow, his mouth was parched, and his hair was yellow and coarse.
Extremely tall, with abundant body hair, and tormented by hunger and thirst, he wanders here and there, subsisting only on air. (13)
Accompanied by many ghosts, he wailed piteously with cries of "Alas! Alas! Then those ghosts standing near him said, "What should be done? (14)
Then those other evil-minded *preta*s, weeping and tormented by hunger, thirst, and other afflictions, came into the presence of the king. (15)
They travel together with the king through many desolate regions;
neither water nor food is ever seen on their path. (16)
Possessing hideous forms, they roam the surface of the earth; they always devour the flesh of corpses and drink blood. (17)
Thus King Kukardama, constantly surrounded by wicked men, once, by the turn of fate, went to the hermitage of his preceptor. (18)
"Through that yoga, he was joined with the merit performed in a previous birth.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord Viśveśvara, tell me, what merit was performed by him? (19)
"This wicked and evil-souled man is a bringer of suffering to the brāhmaṇas; tell me, how did he come to have the company of the virtuous? That is most difficult for me to understand. (20)
Mahādeva said: "O mountain-dweller, listen as I shall relate everything that was performed by this king in his previous birth."
In a previous birth, O Goddess, this man was a Brāhmaṇa who recited the Vedas;
having worshipped Mahādeva and performed the honoring of guests, he [attained this state]. ||22||
That best of Vāḍavas ate his meals there constantly;
by the power of that merit, even in the city known as Piṇḍāraka, [he attained his goal].
It is heard that a king named Kukardama was born there;
indeed, he performed no meritorious deed whatsoever, whether by action or by thought.
By that very exertion, he became a king of the dead (Pretarāja), with a parched mouth, a withered form, a yellowish complexion, and a terrifying appearance. ||25||
O Goddess of the Suras, the merit performed in a previous birth does not perish;
by the power of that merit, he was joined with his preceptor at the hermitage.
Kahoḍa was present there, and by him the King of the Dead (Yama) was seen—his mouth parched, his form withered, yellowish in color, and terrifying. ||27||
He was joined by fearful, highly sinful, and wicked pretas; his hair stood erect, he wore matted locks, and he was as terrifying as the form of Death itself. ||28||
Having seen this, Vāḍava then became utterly distraught.
Kahoḍa said:
"In this delightful and most wonderful place..."
"O King, we always reside at the Agnipāleśvara Tīrtha;
how have you become our sacrificer, O Lord of the Dead? (30)
O auspicious lady, by what ripening of karma was this evil-souled one, of wicked form, appearing like Time itself and terrifying, born upon the surface of the earth? (31)
The preta said:
"O Brahmin, listen to the sin committed by me in a previous birth.
I was a king in the city named Piṇḍāraka, in the land of Kukarda. (32)
Listen now to what was done by me while staying there:
indeed, the killing of brāhmaṇas and the speaking of untruths and other such things in former times. (33)
I am one who constantly oppresses subjects, harms living beings, causes suffering to cows, and violates the vows of Brahmins. (34)
Always remaining unclean, he was a reviler of virtuous people, constantly censuring Viṣṇu, and a slanderer of the Vaiṣṇavas. (35)
Of wicked conduct and evil soul, always united with a low-caste woman, he considered himself a master everywhere, yet was not devoted to purity. (36)
Then, due to the force of that karma, the king of the twice-born died;
having entered this womb, I was born miserable in many ways. (37)
For one who has no mother or father, and no kinsmen or relatives, the spiritual teacher is his kinsman; the teacher is indeed both his mother and his father. (38)
Knowing this, O Brahmin, you ought to grant me liberation. (39)
Kahoḍa said:
"Listen, O best of kings; you shall indeed perform it for me.
You will surely attain liberation here today; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Even the pretas who have gathered here, led by Ekādaśa, attain liberation especially at this excellent tīrtha. ||41||
Then, O Goddess of the Asuras, that Brahmin went to the sacred ford and caused all the rites of water and rice-ball offerings to be performed for them.
O Goddess, having gone to the sacred ford again and again, one should perform the rites of śrāddha and other ceremonies as previously described by Brahmā to me. 43.
O Lord of Gods, once their deeds are completed at that king of holy places, they are liberated;
mounting an excellent celestial chariot, they go to my city.
O Goddess of the Asuras, where the Gokhura, Ayatrasa, and Śābhramatī rivers meet, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices by bathing and giving gifts there. 45.
Where the Agnitīrtha exists, known by the name Kapāleśvara, there liberation is proclaimed; this is the truth, the absolute truth, it is certain. 46.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Majesty of Agnipāleśvara," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
(140) Chapter One Hundred and Forty:
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, I shall now describe another great confluence with the Hiraṇyā,
when in ancient times the Sābhramatī became the Gaṅgā of seven streams.
Then that daughter of Brahmā became renowned as the Saptasrotā;
that seventh stream is designated by the name Hiraṇyā.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, even a sinful man shall attain a [higher] state.
Between the Ṛkṣu and Mañju mountains lies the mountain named Satyavān. (3)
To the east of that is the great and auspicious holy site (tīrtha) at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā;
having bathed and drunk there, one shall attain a blessed state. ||4||
Then one should go to Vanasthalī after having seen Hari Nārāyaṇa;
[there is] the meritorious tīrtha of the Apsarases and Hiraṇyā-saṅgameśvara.
Where Urvaśī, the auspicious one among all the Apsarases, was born,
there Nara and Nārāyaṇa performed supreme austerity.
In that auspicious place, beautiful with the confluence of the Hiraṇyā, which removes great sins,
all the sages indeed bathe, freed from all taints.
O Lord of Gods, at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā, the sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, as well as the Vālakhilyas and other brahmins, immerse themselves.
Wherever that golden form certainly manifests through bathing,
the fruit obtained there is indeed equal to the merit of giving a thousand tawny cows.
One always attains that fruit at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā;
whatever merit is gained at Daśāśvamedha during an eclipse of the moon or the sun [is obtained there]. ||10||
Furthermore, it is declared that at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā, one obtains an infinite number of times that merit;
indeed, one attains whatever fruit is gained from the gift of one's weight in gold (tulāpuruṣadāna). ||11||
One always obtains that fruit at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā.
There, the great Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa performed intense penance. 12.
In former times, at that place where King Janamejaya performed his ritual ablution, his body became like gold. (13)
O Goddess, at that time, on the banks of the Hiraṇyā, the royal sage Viśvāmitra arrived there for the purpose of bathing. ||14||
Having performed his bath especially well, he went to my city, Māmakī.
O Goddess of the gods, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who perform their ablutions here go to the abode of Śiva. (16)

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Confluence of the Hiraṇyā Tīrtha," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara Khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. 140.
(141) The one hundred and forty-first chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Thereafter, O Goddess, I shall describe what follows after the confluence of the Hiraṇyā:
the river Dharmāvatī, where she meets with the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed there at Anarodhanī, one goes to heaven without a doubt;
whoever beholds the Dharmakṛta-tīrtha there becomes a partaker of merit.
If one performs a *śrāddha* ceremony there, one is liberated from the debt owed to the ancestors;
thereafter is the Madhurā-tīrtha, which destroys all sins. ||3||
One should bathe at Madhurātīrtha and behold Hari, the slayer of Madhu,
where Kṛṣṇa took rest, agitated by fear of Jarāsaṃdha.
After the slaughter of the asuras had occurred, the Lord, desiring to go to Kuśasthalī,
stayed for seven nights on the bank of the Candanā.
Having reached the Madhurā tīrtha, which is protected by the heroes of the Bhoja, Vṛṣṇi, and Dhaka clans— the bulls among the Yādavas— he performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites.
There Hari established one named Madhurāditya,
along with eighteen thousand brahmins who were devoted to sacrifice.
Having established them and having given various gifts,
O Goddess of the Suras, thousands of sacred fords (tīrthas) remain there.
A śrāddha ceremony should be performed there with the desire for the welfare of the ancestors;
those dwelling at my sacred ford need never fear Jarāsandha.
Having spoken thus to those twice-born ones, Kṛṣṇa departed for Dvārakā;
a man, having bathed in that sacred ford, should worship Madhurārka.
By the gift of a tawny cow on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
one shall enjoy happiness for a long time in this world and thereafter attain the state of the Sun.
Listen, O Sundari, I shall relate an ancient history;
by hearing which, the world is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Once upon a time, O Goddess, Māṇḍavya, the best of sages,
performed great and highly meritorious penance at Gaṅgādvāra.
He always subsisted on leaves, fruits, and water, or lived on air alone;
O God, he was constantly devoted to the meditation upon Viṣṇu day and night. ||14||
O Goddesses, in that very region dwelt King Viśvamohana, who was constantly devoted to the practice of yoga and eternally dedicated to dharma.
On this earth, he possessed abundant wealth consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
his son, endowed with auspicious marks, was renowned as Somacandra.
Once, O Goddess, he went to a forest for hunting;
having gone there, he then performed the acts of hunting. (17)
Surrounded by his own people, he delighted himself;
O Goddess of the Asuras, as the king was thus intent on pleasure, night fell.
On that night, the king stayed in the Kheṭaka forest;
when that night had passed, during the hour known as Brahma-muhūrta.
Then the horse was specifically stolen here by an evil-minded thief; at that time, a cry of "Alas! arose: "Where has he gone? Where has Hari gone? (20)
Then, out of fear of the king, they all became eager to depart;
for they were saying, "The horse has indeed been stolen by a thief. (21)
While they were all looking on, they arrived at Haridvāra,
where the sage Tumaṇḍavya was constantly performing austerities.
Then those soldiers saw him engaged in meditation, saying, "This man is a thief and a constant evildoer; he stands here merely by practicing meditation. (23)
Having bound the horse, they arrived; then, recognizing him, the king's soldiers seized that great sage and all deliberated thus. (24)
They reported that best of sages to the king, saying:
"O King, this thief who stole the horse has indeed been brought here; he is the thief, always [at large]. (25)
Then, at the command of Ādatta, he was again placed upon a stake;
thereafter, all those soldiers joined together and bound him.
Immediately thereafter, he was indeed impaled upon a stake;
yet at that moment, he did not perceive that act of being transfixed by the stake.
Since he had ascended to yoga and was devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu,
it was only after some time that he became aware of being impaled upon the stake.
"I am Māṇḍavya, the best of sages; by whom has this deed been committed?
Thus the Blessed One, the omniscient knower of the three periods of time, reflected. (29)
And this is the work of Dharma alone, never of anything else;
established in yoga, his soul possessed of dharma, he has come into the presence of Dharma. (30)
Having gone there, he said this: "Listen to this summary of dharma;
you are always renowned in the world and in the Vedas as Vaidharmya. (31)
The impalement on a stake and the performance of the ritual act were indeed carried out by you;
O God, I wish to hear all of that from you, for I have no doubt.
Dharma said:
Listen, O best of the twice-born, to the sin committed in your previous birth;
I shall relate it to you, so please show me your favor.
"O highly wise one, listen to this: due to my childhood, this sinful act committed in a previous birth has caused me to fall in this present life. (34)
Once, having attained the state of a Brahmin in a lonely forest, you went there and [killed] a Brahmin living being named Śalabha. (35)
"O you of excellent vows, having been impaled upon a stake by that man due to his own actions, you have now been placed upon a stake by this king because of your own deeds. (36)
In every way, the performed karma—whether auspicious or inauspicious—must be experienced;
there is no doubt that you have experienced only a small portion of this karma. (37)
"O best of Brahmins, may you be happy; go indeed wherever you desire.
Having heard these words, Māṇḍavya, the most excellent of the twice-born, [replied]. (38)
There, with eyes fierce with anger, he spoke these words.
Māṇḍavya said:
"O most sinful one of wicked conduct, what great transgression have you committed? (39)
"Because you committed this act of piercing with a goad upon the trident out of anger at my words, you shall become a Śūdra in every respect. (40)
After some time had passed, there was born one named Vidura, devoted solely to the worship of Viṣṇu, in the lunar lineage known as Śeva. ||41||
Under the very pretext of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, he went to the river Sābhramatī,
where the Dharmāvatī confluence exists, O Goddess of the Lord of the Asuras.
There, Vidura, possessing a righteous form, performed the bath that removes transformation;
for there, in Dharmāvatī, his status as a Śūdra was abandoned—of this there is no doubt. (43)
For this reason, O Goddess, those virtuous people who perform their ablutions there go to the supreme state. 44.
Those men on earth who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) and acts of charity here shall attain supreme prosperity in this world and rejoice in heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Majesty of Madhurāditya," within the "Majesty of the Sābhramatī" section of the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||141||
The one hundred and forty-second chapter.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Having bathed at Kambu-tīrtha and having performed the libations for the ancestors (pitr-tarpaṇa), a man...
One should worship Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the lords of gods, who is beyond name. ||1||
Having given gifts to Brahmins according to the rules and in accordance with the injunctions, one attains the world of Viṣṇu through the power of this sacred ford. ||2||
O beautiful one, in this place, the wise royal sage Viśvāmitra formerly performed intense austerities out of a specific desire for offspring.
Subsisting on air and taking no food, he lived there consuming only wind;
he was constantly devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu and intent upon meditation on Viṣṇu. ||4||
Through this austerity, he attained his desire for progeny;
indeed, any man who desires offspring and goes to Kambu-tīrtha shall likewise obtain it. (5)
He constantly obtains progeny; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one.
Thus ends the majesty of Kambu-tīrtha.
From there, O best of goddesses, one should go to the sacred ford named Kapīśvara,
which is present and destroys even the greatest of sins.
Formerly, when that battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa was being waged, the monkeys especially seized the best of mountains. (8)
They established an unsurpassed sacred site (tīrtha) named Kapīśvarāditya;
at which sacred site, having bathed and performed the libations for the ancestors, a man [attains merit].
Having beheld Āditya, the Lord of Monkeys, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
one should perform a bath there, especially on the eighth day of the month of Caitra.
Hanumān and his foremost companions bathed there for three days;
this is the power of Kapitīrtha that has been described to you. (11)
Having bathed at this sacred ford and having worshipped Kapīśvara, a man becomes handsome and possessed of great enjoyments; of this there is no doubt. ||12||
Whatever power, worldly dharma, or even a son one desires, all that shall be obtained eternally through the power of Kapitīrtha. ||13||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Eka-pitṛ-tīrtha," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter One Hundred and Forty-three:
Then one should go to the supremely purifying holy ford Ekadhāra.
Having bathed at Ekadhāra and fasted for one night, a man [attains merit]. ||1||
By worshipping the Lord of Devas, the Master, one may deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage;
that holy ford where one performs immersion should be known as equal to Svāmitīrtha.
By the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha), one goes to the world of Rudra free from disease;
and having bathed and drunk [its water] there, one goes to the world of Brahmā. ||3||
Indeed, those who have performed meritorious deeds in the three worlds dwell upon this bank. ||4||
No fear exists for them regarding the edge of a sword or similar dangers;
indeed, all such things quickly perish at this sacred site which possesses a single stream.
Thus ends the description of the Ekadhārā Tīrtha.
From there, one should go to the supreme holy site among all holy sites, which has seven streams and is named Saptasārasvata, so called because it was established by the sages.
In the Tretā Yuga, this holy site was established by whom? By which sage was it made? In the Dvāpara [Yuga], it was set in motion with seven streams by the sons of Pāṇḍu.
The sacred ford, which fell from the matted locks of Hara, attained a sevenfold flow;
for the Gaṅgā possesses seven forms throughout the seven worlds.
Carrying those merits, I am at this sacred ford, Saptadhāraka;
a Śrāddha performed here in seven ways bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors.
Listen, O Goddess; I shall relate an ancient history, hearing which, O Sovereign of the Gods, one will certainly go to the world of Brahmā. (10)
The son of Kauṣītaki was indeed well-known by this name;
he was constantly devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu and was a worshiper of the world of Viṣṇu. ||11||
There was one who studied the Vedas and was devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice;
in his house lived two wives, Surūpā and Viśvarūpā. ||12||
Seeing them bereft of their son, Devaviśa was immediately struck with wonder;
reflecting on what ought to be done, he became deeply absorbed in anxious thought.
The lineage is indeed sustained by a son; otherwise, one would go to hell.
Thinking in this way, one never finds happiness anywhere. (14)
Then, having abandoned his own home, he went into the presence of the Guru.
Homage to you, O Guru, who are the benefactor of the gods. (15)
You are the protector of all the worlds and the guardian of the Brahmins;
you are the performer of sacrifices—O King of the twice-born, salutations to you. 16.
"O great sage, I am childless;
O Lord, tell me what must be done so that, in every respect, a son may certainly be born. (17)
There is no destination for one without a son, neither in this world nor even in heaven;
therefore, by whatever means possible, one should bring about the birth of a son. (18)
This statement, indeed, has been remembered as having come into your presence. 19.
The Guru said:
"Go, O tiger among sages, to where the Sābhramatī river flows;
having gone there, O best of sages, you will certainly obtain sons."
Having heard those words and having prostrated himself like a staff,
the king of brahmins went toward the Sābhramatī river.
Then, having gone there, the brahmin-sage named Maṅki performed great austerities for four years, O Goddess.
O Goddess, at that time, in the Tretā Yuga, this most wonderful holy place (tīrtha) was established by that knower of Brahman, Maṅkin.
Born there, it is beyond doubt that this place bestows sons and fulfills all desires; even today, no other holy site equal to this has ever existed, nor will there ever be one.
Having obtained sons together with the best of the twice-born, and having enjoyed various kinds of pleasures according to his desire, he has gone to my abode. (25)
This divine narrative is purifying, supreme, and great;
by hearing it, one obtains everything, including the happiness of having sons. (26)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Saptadhāra Tīrtha," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Pādma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(144) Chapter One Hundred and Forty-Four. Mahādeva said:
O Goddess of the gods, from there one should go to the great pilgrimage site of Brahmavallī;
O best of gods, hear directly the true nature of that sacred place.
Where the waters of the Asābhramatī join with the Brahmavallī by means of its radiance, that Brahmatīrtha is remembered as equal to Prayāga. ||2||
There, by the offering of a *ḍipa*, the ancestors certainly attain satisfaction for twelve years, according to the word of Brahmā. (3)
The merit of performing a śrāddha at Gayā is especially attained at Brahmavallī;
having learned this, those who perform it there shall cause their ancestors to obtain satisfaction. 4.
The gift of a cow, the gift of land, and likewise the gift of food—merit equal to these gifts is found especially in the Brahmavallī. ||5||
Right here, Sanaka and the others, having bathed according to the prescribed rites and through meditation on the state of the Supreme Brahman, attained the world of Viṣṇu. (6)
O Lord of Gods, whatever fruit a man obtains by going there to Puṣkara, to the Gaṅgā, and to the sacred field of Amarakaṇṭaka— [he obtains that here].
One attains that fruit specifically through the Brahmavallī; it is the same as the merit that men obtain by giving gifts during an eclipse of the moon or the sun. ||8||
O Goddess of the gods, one attains that fruit upon the Brahmā-vallī;
they assume divine forms and bear the conch, the discus, and the mace. ||9||
O Goddess of the Asuras, even they go to heaven after performing their ablutions and wearing the tulasī leaf while remembering Nārāyaṇa; indeed, they attain the divine,
blissful, and imperishable state of Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus ends the majesty of the Brahmavallī-tīrtha.
Thereafter, one should go to Vṛṣatīrtha, which is highly renowned as Khaṇḍatīrtha;
having bathed there, cows formerly attained heaven and Goloka. (11)
O Mothers of the World, because you were protected by Dharma in the form of Khaṇḍa after falling from heaven due to a curse,
it is therefore called Khaṇḍatīrtha.
Pārvatī said:
Whose curse was it that befell the world-mothers, the cows, in ancient times? How did they fall from their place in the world, and how were they protected by Dharma? (13)
Mahādeva said: Formerly, while sporting with his mothers in Goloka, Vṛṣeṇa discharged excrement and urine, which fell upon the head of Hara.
Then, because of that fault, Hara indeed pronounced a curse upon them:
"Having lost your consciousness, you shall go from your own world to the earth. (15)
"The cows, having been cursed by the Blessed One, requested the Lord, saying: 'Having propitiated Hara once again, may we regain our world. (16)
When you have bathed at the Khaṇḍa lake near the Brahmavallī in the Āsābhrama-tīrtha, you will certainly attain heaven.
Then, having bathed in that lake together with the cows and the cowherd,
they, being utterly purified, went to heaven into the presence of Mahādeva.
Having bathed at Gohrada-tīrtha and performed the libations for the ancestors,
a person attains the world of cows, which is free from burning and dissolution.
Staying there, even though he is without food, that man indeed gives a ball of rice;
he prospers in happiness for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Whatever fruit is certainly obtained by the gift of ten million cows, one attains that same fruit at Khaṇḍatīrtha; of this there is no doubt. ||21||
If a man takes bull urine and drinks it at Khaṇḍatīrtha, he shall attain purification at that very moment; of this there is no doubt. (22)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy place superior to Khaṇḍatīrtha;
those men who go there, O best of gods, shall be partakers of merit.
Having gone there, O best of Asuras, one should perform the worship of cows;
then, having bathed with a concentrated mind, one should worship the bull.
By worshipping [it], one’s doubts regarding rebirth are destroyed and one shall dwell for a long time in Goloka;
having gone there, one who gives a golden cow with particular devotion [attains the highest state]. (25)
By that [act], he enjoys happiness in heaven for as long as fourteen Indras [reign];
then, having given ten cows, he bestows them upon a twice-born man.
O best of gods, this is remembered as yielding infinite fruit at Khaṇḍatīrtha;
having gone there, the planting of a Pippala tree should be performed by the wise. (27)
O Goddess of the gods, when that is performed, one goes to the world of the ancestors; they perform the planting of five divine *vāmalakī* trees. (28)
Having enjoyed the pleasures of this world, they go to the realm of Hari. ||29||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Sacred Site of Khaṇḍatīrtha," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The one hundred and forty-fifth chapter.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"Thereafter, you should go to the great and supreme holy site, Saṅgameśvara."
Where the holy Hastimatī and the Sābhramatī rivers are joined together.
Having received the curse from the sage Uḍinī, the river became dried up;
she subsequently attained fame in the world by the name Bahiścaryā.
I shall fully describe that holy ford, meritorious and renowned throughout the three worlds;
it is merit-bestowing, a remover of all sins, and famous even in the three worlds. (3)
Having bathed at that sacred ford and beheld the god Maheśvara, a person is liberated from all sins and proceeds to the world of Rudra. ||4||
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the cause of this curse,
by which we have become dry in form here due to the reason for that curse.
Where the meritorious great river named Sābhramatī flows, there the river named Hastimatī has joined with the Gaṅgā. 6.
There, the sage began a most great and supreme penance;
thus much time passed for that ṛṣi, whose self was the Supreme Self.
Having propitiated Hṛṣīkeśa, the eternal Nārāyaṇa,
he remained on its bank for many years, O Lord of Devas.
O Pārvatī, these days passed for that sage without distinction;
however, by the turn of fate, the rainy season eventually arrived.
O lady of excellent vows, at that time, due to the turn of fate, the river there became completely full;
then, during the night, that place was abandoned by the sage Kauṇḍinya.
Great suffering arose during the night; crying out "Alas! Alas! with compassion, he lamented.
Reflecting on what ought to be done, he became deeply absorbed in anxious thought. (11)
Accompanied by the great and divine sage Āśramī,
he went by means of the yoga of water to Hastimatī, O best of goddesses.
O beautiful one, fruits, roots, and even many books have likewise gone into that [river] by means of the water's flow. (13)
It is said that the best of sages, along with Kauṇḍinya, cursed that river:
"In the Kali age, you shall be devoid of water. (14)
O Maheśvarī, having thus pronounced that curse upon Hastimatī,
that most excellent of brahmins departed for the eternal realm of Viṣṇu.
Even today, the sacred ford known as Saṅgameśvara exists;
by seeing it, even a sinner is liberated from such sins as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Someśvara Tīrtha," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara Khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The one hundred and forty-sixth chapter. Mahādeva said:
From there, O Lord of Gods, one should go to the Tīrtha Rudramahālaya, which is truly incomparable to Kedāra and was personally created by Rudra himself. ||1||
A *śrāddha* ceremony should be performed there as a means of satisfying the ancestors;
by the offering of that *śrāddha*, the fathers along with the grandfathers [are satisfied]. (2)
Satiated, they go to the supreme abode of Rudra—
those who release a bull there in that great sanctuary of Rudra.
On the full moon day of either Kārttika or Vaiśākha, one rejoices together with Rudra;
having drunk the water at Kedāra, there is no further rebirth.
By merely bathing here, one becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus at one time, he departed for Kailāsa. ||5||
Having recognized the Sābhramatī as the great Gaṅgā for the welfare of the world,
he bathed there, drank [of its water], and established that unsurpassed sacred site (tīrtha).
Then, O beautiful lady, I departed for my own abode, Kailāsa;
immediately thereafter, that place became the highly meritorious holy site known as Mahālaya.
This Rudramahālaya shall attain great fame.
O best of goddesses, for those who go there on the full moon day of Kārttika or Vaiśākha,
no suffering born of the entire cycle of worldly existence shall exist again.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Great Holy Site of Rudra," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The one hundred and forty-seventh chapter. Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, listen to the account of that holy place (tīrtha) which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
It is renowned as Khaṅgatīrtha, which destroys all sins. ||1||
Having bathed at Khaṅgatīrtha and beheld the auspicious Lord Khaṅgeśvara, a person shall not go to a miserable state; he proceeds to the heavenly world. ||2||
O best of gods, whoever beholds the deity Khaḍgadhāreśvara should especially perform worship there on the full moon day of Kārttika.
This Lord Viśveśvara is always beloved on earth;
the Lord of All grants everything, bestowing all desired objects. ||4||
One who desires sovereignty or wealth in the month of Vaiśākha beholds that Lord;
by the grace of Viśvanātha, he quickly attains that objective. ||5||
Then, one should worship Viśveśa with flowers, incense, food offerings, lamps, betel nuts, fruits,
and bilva leaves in every direction.
By worshipping Śrī Viśveśvara here, one shall obtain wealth, grain, and the prosperity of sons, grandsons, and so forth; of this there is no doubt. (7)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Sacred Site of Khaṅga," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The one hundred and forty-eighth chapter. Mahādeva said:
On the bank of the Sābhramatī is the unsurpassed Gayātīrtha.
The auspicious [city] named Citrāṅgavadaṇa, presided over by Mālārka. ||1||
It was adorned with rows of wish-fulfilling trees and mandāra flowers,
as well as with mango, *niṃbaka*, *dāḍima*, *kāśmarya*, *aśvattha*, and *tiṃduka* trees.
Therefore, one should remove leprosy by means of the confusion of memory regarding the *yojana* [distance];
for him in whom leprosy arises, *Mālārka* shall remove it.

If she undergoes an initiation there according to the various rites prescribed in the Yajurveda, she becomes like one dead, or else she obtains a son only after a long time—though he may be as barren as a sonless woman. ||4||
The twilight ablutions, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and worship of the deities—when performed by a devotee of the Sun, these become inexhaustible at Mālārka. ||5||
Having come here, O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the vow of the illustrious Sun;
having enjoyed happiness in this world, one indeed goes to the realm of the Sun.
Having gone there, the royal sage Mṛtavatsa performed austerities;
by the grace of Śrīmālārka, that king obtained a son. ||7||
Having gone there, one who is distinguished by fasting and has conquered the senses—whoever indeed worships Mālārka—will certainly partake in liberation. 8.
The Brahmins headed by Vasiṣṭha and the gods led by Indra always dwell in Mālārka, the best of divine abodes, in the presence of the Sun. (9)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Sacred Site of Mālārka," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(149) The one hundred and forty-ninth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Beyond this sacred ford, situated on the Mālārka river, one should go to Candaneśvara, the supreme abode of fragrance. ||1||
Having drunk the blood of Duḥśāsana,
the mighty Bhīma fulfilled his entire most dreadful vow.
Having bound Draupadī’s hair with his two blood-stained hands and having given [the wealth] to the twice-born, he then set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Having gone with his brothers to the lovely bank of the Sābhramatī, he brought from heaven a sandalwood tree to the Sābhramatī. (4)
Born with the characteristics of a woman due to the power of a sacred pilgrimage site (puṇyatīrtha),
he bathed there, drank [the water], and performed the libations for his ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa).
One would not go to hell, but would attain the world of Rudra;
then, having seen Candaneśa, the Lord of the Universe who brings welfare to the world.
One should worship [the deity] according to one's ability, going there so that one does not grieve;
for there, King Kaivartaka performed worship many times.
He has gone to that world of Śiva, reaching which one no longer grieves;
there the eternal God dwells, where even the sages are immersed.
Viṣṇu himself, the Supreme Soul, eternally resides here as the bestower of prosperity;
this is that blessed Sābhramatī, and here is the blessed Lord Viśveśvara.
O Pārvatī, where many sacred fords (tīrthas) have arisen upon the earth, here [is the place] with the various auspicious and meritorious fruits of the Āmardakī tree. (10)
O beautiful one, the offering of arghya should be performed there according to the prescribed rite.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Candaneśvara," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||149||
The one hundred and fiftieth chapter. Mahādeva said:
From there, one should go to Jaṃbū-tīrtha for the purpose of bathing, which destroys sin.
In this age of Kali, that which stands for men like a staircase to heaven— ||1||
Where, on that most excellent mountain, the lord of the bears (Bhṛṅgiriṭi) formerly established the Jālandhara Liṅga, which is worshipped by hosts of gods. (2)
When the asura Vairocana was previously slain by Rāma,
at that time the earth resounded with the blaring of kettledrums and other musical instruments.
Victory has been won by Vairāmacandra; Rāvaṇa was slain at the gateway, and having recovered Sītā and proclaimed it, he bathed in that auspicious, excellent sacred ford.
O Goddess of the Suras, a *liṅga* was installed there by him under his own name;
having bathed there, a man should immediately remember Rāma along with his younger brother.
O Jābāli, having bathed at Teśvara, one is glorified in the world of Rudra. Indeed, O Goddess, wherever the remembrance of Śrī Rāma is performed,
liberation from the bonds of worldly existence is seen, throughout all that is moving and unmoving.
I am Rāma, and Rāma is to be known as me; Rāma is indeed Vīra and Ugra as well.
Knowing this, O Goddess, no distinction exists anywhere.
Those who mentally recite "Rāma, Rāma, Rāma" will attain the fulfillment of all their goals in age after age. (8)
O Goddess, I shall always practice the remembrance of Śrī Rāma;
having heard which, O Goddess, rebirth never occurs again anywhere. 9.
O Goddess, dwelling constantly in Kāśī, I remember Śrī Rāma, the lotus-eyed one, perpetually with devotion according to the prescribed rites. (10)
Then, remembering the most beautiful Arāma from before,
he dispatched that one known as Jāmbava, the teacher of the worlds.
Having bathed there, eaten, and performed the worship of the God,
one attains the world of Śiva for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
For here, by the mere act of bathing, one attains strength just like that of Jāmbavat, through the grace of the illustrious Lord of the Universe. (13)
Indeed, whatever man comes here and performs a gift-offering, he shall obtain a thousandfold fruit from the sight of you. (14)

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Jāmbavat-tīrtha," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||150||
(151) The one hundred and fifty-first chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Beyond this sacred ford, there is another sacred ford known as Indragrāma,
where in ancient times Śakra, having bathed, was liberated from terrible sin.
Pārvatī said:
"O Śakra, by what deed here did he incur this terrible sin? And how did he become free from sin? Tell me this in great detail. (2)
Mahādeva said: Formerly, Indra, the lord of the gods, and Namuci, the lord of the asuras, made a mutual agreement that neither should slay the other with weapons. (3)
Then, at the direction of the voice from the sky, Indra took up foam and struck Namuci; at that moment, the sin of killing a Brahmin arose.
Śakra questioned his preceptor regarding the means for the destruction of sin;
then, by the instruction of Bṛhaspati, she [the goddess] wandered along the northern bank of the Bhramatī.
Having arrived at this place, the Lord of the Gods established a shrine;
by merely bathing here, one's sins depart at that very moment.
A full stream of pure white milk was produced from his body;
the slayer of Vṛtra then installed the Lord Dhavaleśvara.
That liṅga is renowned on the surface of the earth by the name of Indra;
likewise, [one should worship it] on the full moon day, during the new moon, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), and during an eclipse.
When a Śrāddha is performed for the ancestors at Dhavaleśvara, their satisfaction lasts for twelve years, provided one feeds the Brahmins after reaching that place. (9)
When one Brahmin has been fed, it is as if all have been fed;
gold, land, and garments should be given according to one's own ability. (10)

A white, milch cow along with her calf should be given to a Brāhmaṇa; then, having come here, whatever Brāhmaṇa performs the recitation of the Rudra-mantras and other rites, [he shall attain the fruit]. 11.
By the grace of the illustrious Maheśa, that merit performed here at this sacred ford becomes multiplied ten millionfold for the man who observes fasts and other such rites. 12.
He indeed becomes enriched with all desires; of this there is no doubt—[this applies to] whoever, having brought bilva leaves, worships that Lord. (13)
A man obtains dharma, wealth, and pleasure on this earth, especially when those best of men go [to bathe] on a Monday. 14.
Havaleśvara shall pacify their disease as well as their affliction, especially when they perform worship on a Sunday. ||15||
The greatness of those [deities] has never been known by me, O Goddess, whether through *dūrvā* grass, *arka* flowers, white water-lilies, lotuses, or their petals. (16)
Those people who perform worship with this [rite] become partakers of merit;
having brought a Śvetārka flower, one should worship Dhavaleśa. (17)
By the grace of the Lord of Dhavala, one constantly obtains whatever is desired; when Nīlakaṇṭha is worshipped, Śaṅkara is always present for everyone. 18.
In the Tretā Yuga, the Lord and Master was indeed the renowned Hara; in the Dvāpara, he was known as Śarva; and in the Kali age, he is Vaidyanātheśvara. 19.
In this regard, O Queen of the Asuras, hear that ancient account which occurred in the past:
formerly, a Vaiśya named Nandin lived in a village of the Draviḍas.
Devoted to the meditation on Śiva, he performed the worship of Śiva;
daily, he attended upon the white-colored liṅga known as Dhavala, situated in the forest of penance.
Rising every day at dawn, Śivavallabha became exceedingly devoted to the worship of the *nandī* liṅga. ||22||
He became devoted to the worship of flowers according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
Once, there was a Kirāta hunter who was intent on the chase.
A wicked man of sinful conduct, wandering on the banks of the Sābhramatī in a place infested with many beasts of prey, was slaughtering deer with his arrows. ||24||
Wandering in this manner, that Kirāta,
who was intent on harming living beings, went by chance to a place where a well-worshipped Liṅga was located.
The Liṅga renowned as Dhavaleśvara, adorned with many wonders, was seen and well-worshipped with various flowers and fruits. (26)
Having thus embraced the linga, he departed; she wandered along the bank.
There, having drunk water, he then filled his mouth with a mouthful. (27)
Having taken up the deer meat with one hand,
he held bilva leaves in his other hand for the purpose of worship.
Having arrived quickly, he performed worship at the Liṅga;
all those flowers were then scattered here and there.
Having performed the bathing of that *liṅga* with the water from his mouth-rinse,
he offered *bilva* leaves for worship with one hand.
With his second hand, he likewise offered the deer meat;
joined with a prostration like a staff, he made a mental resolve.
"From this day forward, O Śaṅkara, I shall perform worship with great effort;
you are my master and I am your devotee, from this day forth. (32)
Having thus become observant of his vows, the Kirāta returned home;
likewise, at the time of dawn, he went to the temple of the god. (33)
Seeing all that had been done by the Kirāta,
and seeing that chaotic and impure state in the presence of Śiva, he was struck with wonder.
And all these things were shaken by that evil-minded one; filled with anxiety, he thought: "What is this strange thing that has arisen today? (35)
"Indeed, those obstacles which were said not to exist for one devoted to the worship of Śiva have now appeared before me due to the reversal of my own good fortune. (36)
Having reflected thus for a long time, he washed the temple of Śiva and returned to his own home by the same path by which he had come. ||37||
Then, perceiving that his mind was directed toward Dinna, the priest spoke these words to him: "Why is your mind gone elsewhere? (38)
Then, addressing the priest, he spoke these words:
"O Brahmin, today I beheld something impure in the presence of Śiva. (39)
"I do not know at all who caused this to be done there. Then he spoke likewise to the words of the priest and to Nandin.
He who performs the worship of flowers and other offerings there without hesitation is, without a doubt, deluded regarding what ought and ought not to be done; do not entertain such an opinion.
Therefore, O Lord, you should not worry further;
at dawn, you must go with me to that abode of Śiva.
"I shall inflict punishment upon that wicked one for the sake of investigation.
Having heard these words of the enraged priest, [he spoke]. (43)
Staying in his own house at night with a grieving heart,
when that night had passed, he summoned his domestic priest.
He went to the abode of Śiva along with that great-souled one;
having washed [the deity] and performed worship, he offered various ornaments made of jewels. 45.
And having performed the ritual services together with the Brahmins, two watches of the night passed in this manner while the Lord was being praised. (46)
That Mahākāla, of such a form and great strength, arrived—having the appearance of Time (Kāla), most fierce, bow in hand, and full of majesty. ||47||
Seeing him, the king, terrified with fear, hid there;
and the domestic priest also suddenly became overcome with fear.
Having brought that offering there exactly as before without any error, the Kirāta presented a bilva leaf.
With that very offering of food, the Kirāta worshipped Śiva;
prostrating himself on the ground like a staff, he rose and went to his own home. (50)
Seeing that great marvel, the priest, his mind agitated by grief, reflected for a long time.
Then those brahmins were asked: "Let it be told exactly as it is.
Thereupon, they all gathered together and deliberated according to the treatises on dharma.
Then all those brāhmaṇas, their joy having vanished, said:
"An obstacle to the Lord has arisen, which is difficult to ward off even by the gods. (53)
"Therefore, O best of Vaiśyas, bring that liṅga to your own home.
Thinking "So be it," he [the king] undertook the great uprooting of the Lord Śiva. ||54||
Having brought it to his own home and installed it according to the prescribed rite,
he fashioned a golden pedestal, most excellent and radiant with splendor.
Then they worshipped him with many offerings;
thereafter, on the following day, the Kirāta arrived at the temple of Śiva.
As long as he gazed [there], he did not see the phallic emblem of Īśa; suddenly abandoning his silence, he spoke these words of lamentation: ||57||
"O Lord, you have come to this place; show yourself to me today!
If they do not grant me a vision, I shall cast off my body this very day. (58)
"Ho! O Lord of the World, Destroyer of Tripura, Maker of the Śaṅkha!
O Rudra, O Mahādeva, reveal yourself by means of your own self! (59)
Having thus reviled the inauspicious one with words that were both taunting and sweet, that Kirāta,
undaunted, plunged his knife into his own belly.
Having pierced him with an arrow and reached his arm, Uṣā cried out loudly:
"O Lord, show yourself! Why do you depart, abandoning me? (61)
Having thus thrown [the spear] and then lifted this protector (Aṃtrāṇi) up from all sides,
that Kirāta suddenly hurled her into that pit with his very hand.
Having made his heart pure, let him immerse himself in the Abhramatī;
likewise, having quickly brought water along with a bilva leaf.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, he fell prostrate on the ground like a staff;
at that moment, the Kirāta was situated there in the presence of Śiva.
Then Rudra appeared, surrounded by his attendants;
he was white as camphor, radiant, with matted hair and the moon as his crest-ornament.
Having seized him, Rudra said: "O you who wander through the assemblies!
O hero of great wisdom, O high-minded one, you are my devotee."
"Choose a boon, O devotee, whatever dwells in your heart.
Thus addressed by Rudra, Mahākāla was filled with joy.
Endowed with supreme devotion, he fell to the ground like a staff;
then he spoke this to Rudra: "I pray for nothing else. (68)
"I am your servant, O Rudra; you are my master, without a doubt.
This is the most praiseworthy thing in the world, birth after birth. (69)
You are my mother and you are my father; you are my kinsman and my friend.
You are my teacher, you are the great mantra, and you are always to be known through mantras. (70)
Having heard those desireless words of the Kirāta at that time,
Bhava granted him the status of a chief attendant and the position of gatekeeper.
Then the three worlds were made to resound by the sound of that damaru drum,
by the booming sound of the kettledrums, and by the clamor of the conchs.
Then, both of them and thousands of drums sounded;
hearing that terrifying roar, he went forth in haste out of wonder. (73)
Then, for four days, he gazed intently at that penance grove where Śiva was stationed, surrounded by his attendants, appearing as a Kirāta hunter.
Filled with great wonder, he spoke these words to Sana; desiring to praise the Kirāta, he did so with supreme concentration.
"O Śambhu, you have brought me here; you are a supreme devotee of penance. I too am your devotee who has arrived here; report this to Śaṅkara. (76)
Having heard those words of his, the Kirāta, filled with haste, took up his bow and approached Śaṅkara.
Laughing, the Blessed Lord Rudra spoke these words to the Kirāta: "Tell me, who is this that you have brought here into the presence of my attendants? (78)
The Kirāta said:
"O Lord, he was your devotee; indeed, he was always intent on your worship here with various gems, rubies, and flowers offered every day. (79)
"He has been honored with both his life and his wealth; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Master, compassionate toward your devotees, please bring him back today. (80)
Mahādeva said:
"O illustrious one, O high-minded Mahākāla, I know that you are a Vaiśya by conduct; yet you are my devotee and my friend. (81)
Those who are free from worldly conditions and those whose minds are sincere—
they are dear to me, they are my devotees, and they are the most distinguished among the best of men;
both of them have been accepted by the Auspicious One as his personal attendants.
Then many celestial chariots of great splendor gathered there;
they were all raised up by that illustrious Kirāta, along with those two excellent Vaiśyas.
Having reached the world of Kailāsa by means of most rapid celestial chariots,
they attained the very same form as the Great-Souled Lord.
Both Gaṇas were honored like sons by the daughter of the mountain, who performed the lustration ceremony for them.
Then the goddess, who moves with the gait of an elephant, smilingly said this:
"O Great God, there is no doubt that your mind is exactly as you are. (86)
Through their resemblance, their manner of movement, and their well-honored gestures of mirth, the Kirāta and the Vaiśya, having heard those words of the Goddess, [recognized her]. (87)
Turning away immediately while Śaṅkara was looking on, the two attendants of Rudra spoke with great haste as he watched. (88)
O Three-eyed One, you have shown compassion toward both of us;
since Bhava always stands at your side, salutations to you. (89)
Having understood their disposition, the Blessed Lord Bhava, smiling, said:
"By your supreme devotion, let your desire be fulfilled. (90)
From that time forward, these two became the gatekeepers;
stationed at the door of Śiva, they beheld the Goddess at midday. (91)
These two, Ekona and Dīmahākāla, are dear to Śiva;
even those who are sinful, most unrighteous, deaf, mute, or lame [attain the goal]. ||92||
Those of low birth, the wicked, outcasts such as dog-cookers, and others of whatever kind they may be, should worship Dhavaleśvara. (93)
They have gone there, and they will go there as well; no hesitation should be felt in this matter.
Here, bathing, giving gifts, and the worship of Śaṅkara bring about the attainment of treasures.
Those who have performed their ablutions in the Sābhramatī and worship Dhavaleśvara go to the world of Rudra; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (95)
Those best of men who perform bathing and giving here,
having enjoyed the pleasures of dharma, artha, and kāma, go to the abode of Hara.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains during an eclipse of the moon or sun, or on the anniversary of his father's death, he shall certainly attain that same fruit [by this means]. 97.
From heaven, she constantly and in every way arrived from the wish-fulfilling cow;
having arrived, she worshipped that god Śiva in whatever manner was appropriate. ||98||
O best of gods, there is no doubt that he goes to heaven;
by his persistent milking, that liṅga has been turned white. (99)
From that, the place named Dhavaleśvara has forever become renowned upon the earth.
O Goddess, living beings who die here, impelled by Time, go to the state of Śiva for as long as the moon and sun endure. (100)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Dhavaleśvara," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||151||
Mahādeva said:
There is a preeminent sacred site among all holy places situated on the bank of the Sābhramatī;
it is renowned as Bālāpai and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1)
There, at that sacred ford maintained by ascetics and frequented by the gods,
a maiden of most firm vows performed supreme penance.
The daughter of the sage Kaṇva, a maiden named Bālāvatī who was a celibate student, was a virtuous woman whose beauty was peerless on earth. ||3||
Endowed with many observances, that beautiful woman performed a vow dedicated to Sāvitrī, having resolved: "May Bhāskara become my husband. (4)
Ten years passed for her as she wandered along the shore,
practicing those various rules of conduct which, though extremely difficult to perform, were undertaken with devotion.
By that vow, by her asceticism, by the performance of her religious observances,
and by her supreme perfection of devotion, the Blessed One was pleased with her.
The god of gods, the Sun, arrived at the hermitage;
assuming the form of a brahmin seer, the high-minded one entered. (7)
Seeing that most excellent sage of fierce asceticism, the foremost knower of Brahman,
Sātī honored that twice-born man according to the rules for forest-dwellers.
Sākalyāṇī said to that ascetic devoted to the Sun:
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, O Lord, what do you command? (9)
"I shall give you everything according to my ability, with the exception of my own body; I am a devotee of the Sun, so I will by no means give my hand [in marriage]. (10)
O you whose wealth is asceticism, the Sun, the god who is the lord of the three worlds, must be propitiated through vows, observances, and austerities.
When she had spoken thus, he, as if smiling, looked at her;
then, like the sun beholding one established in religious observance, he spoke to her.
O auspicious one, you have practiced fierce asceticism that is most difficult to perform;
and for what purpose you undertook it, that remains exactly as it was, O child. (13)
Everything is obtained through austerity; everything rests upon austerity.
O blessed lady, even the state of divinity and liberation itself are attained through austerity. 14.
"O fortunate one, accept these five jujube fruits.
Having said, "Cook them after giving the jujube fruits to her," Aravī departed. (15)
Without having asked that auspicious lady, who was like Brahmā herself, that highly illustrious one remained not very far from that village. 16.
Having remained there with the desire to test its nature, the Brāhmaṇa Ravi,
the Sun, caused a grove of jujube trees to be established.
Then that young girl, free from fatigue, with palms joined in reverence, carefully placed the fire upon the hearth for the purpose of cooking the jujube fruits.
O Queen of the Asuras, as that goddess of supreme splendor was cooking the jujube fruits,
a very long time passed while she was cooking them.
A great heap of wood, once ignited by fire, followed the path of destruction throughout the day,
turning into a mass of ashes.
Having washed his feet with water, he then, out of a desire to do what was pleasing to the brāhmaṇa, offered an oblation into the beautiful-looking fire for the sake of the jujube fruit.
O sinless one, having been burnt again and again, her feet were placed upon [the fire] once more;
then, seeing her through her karma, the divine Sun was pleased.
Then he showed her his own form through various maidens and, being exceedingly pleased, spoke to that maiden of firm vows: 23.
Sūrya said:
"O girl, I am pleased with your devotion, your austerity, and your observance of vows;
therefore, O girl, let your desired wish be fulfilled. (24)
"In this sacred ford (tīrtha), you shall dwell in my house, engaged in ascetic penance;
and this most excellent of fords shall be marked by your name. (25)
Renowned as Bālāpai, it stands upon the bank of the Sābhramatī;
it is famous throughout the three worlds and was praised of old by the brahminical sages.
Having bathed at Bālātīrtha and remained pure for three nights, a man,
facing the rising sun, beholds the face of Raktāditya.
One attains the world of the Sun; there is no need for hesitation in this matter—especially on a Sunday, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or on the seventh lunar day (saptamī). ||28||
At the equinoxes, at the solstices, and also during lunar and solar eclipses,
having bathed, one should offer libations to the gods, the ancestors, and the grandfathers.
Then one should give a cow made of jaggery and rice mixed with jaggery to Brāhmaṇas;
and the worship of the Sun-god should be performed with Karavīra and Japā flowers.
Those men who perform these [deeds] indeed dwell in the world of Yama;
a man should give a red cow and a single yoke-bearing bull.
A person obtains the fruit of performing a sacrifice and shall not go to hell;
one who is diseased is freed from disease, and one who is bound is released from bondage.
By the gift of food at this sacred site, the ancestors attain satisfaction.
Mahādeva said:
O one rich in asceticism, listen also to another greatness of this sacred ford (tīrtha), which is a great ancient account related by Vyāsa.
Formerly, an old buffalo, worn out by age and unable to carry its burden, was abandoned by the caravan leader. (34)
In the heat of summer, he went to a great river to drink water;
by fate, he was swallowed by a crocodile and thus fell under the power of death.
By the power of this holy ford, the son of the Lord of Kānyakubja, having bathed in the pure waters, became a king who remembered his former births. (36)
Recalling his own past conduct and the great power born of the sacred ford,
he returned, bathed in its waters, and gave away gifts many times over.
There he installed Maheśvara, the God of gods;
having bathed in this holy ford and having fully worshipped Mahiṣeśvara, a man [attains the fruit]. (38)
Upon seeing the face of Raktāditya, one is liberated from all sins;
where the waters of the Sābhramatī flow from east to west. (39)
Even greater than Prayāga is that great merit which grants all desires;
whatever is given to the best of the twice-born, offered into the fire, performed as a śrāddha, or recited here shall become inexhaustible. (40)
By the gift of cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, garments, grain, beds, seats, vehicles, or umbrellas, a person obtains whatever desire they may wish for. (41)
By the grace of the illustrious Maheśa and through the power of this sacred ford, this Bālāpendra Tīrtha is always the remover of both merit and sin. 42.
Having seen which, all the sages are forever free from passion;
that place named Māhiṣa, also called Śveta, is a great bestower of merit. 43.
O Lord of Devas, where there is no rebirth for one who has bathed;
such is the fruit that a man obtains by performing a bath in the Godāvarī. ||44||
O Goddess, one obtains that fruit at this sacred site; of this there is no doubt. ||45||
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Holy Site of Bālāpendra," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(153) The one hundred and fifty-third chapter. Mahādeva said:
I shall now describe another supreme holy site, Durddharṣeśvara, by the mere remembrance of which even a sinner becomes meritorious. (1)
When the war between the gods and asuras had ended and the Daitya had met his death, Danu,
having undertaken an invincible vow, went to the hermitage of Bhārgava.
Having propitiated Mahādeva, the invincible cause of the world,
he obtained from the crane the science of the "Life-restorer" (Mṛtasaṃjīvanī), which is beneficial to the three worlds.
The sacred ford of Uśanas, renowned upon the surface of the earth for the sake of the Daityas, is known as Kāvya-tīrtha;
having performed his ablutions at Kāvya-tīrtha, he worshipped the god Maheśvara.
By [visiting] the one known as Durddharṣeśvara, one is liberated from all sins;
furthermore, you must hear the account that occurred there, which is not to be found anywhere else.
Long ago, when a battle occurred here between Vṛtra and Vāsava,
the gods were defeated by the Asuras; then Indra, the lord of the gods,
having reflected on what ought to be done, went to his preceptor.
Indra said: You are our direct preceptor and the eternal protector of the gods;
you are the most excellent and glorious among the sages. O ocean of mercy, please show us compassion! (7)
"O observer of excellent vows, I have been defeated by Vṛtra; where shall I go? [8]
Bṛhaspati said:
Listen, O Lord of the Gods, for I shall tell you that by which you will indeed always be happy;
act upon my words if you desire your own welfare. (9)
Come then to the Sābhramatī; having gone there, become happy, for the god named Durddhara, the bestower of prosperity, dwells there eternally. (10)
"O Lord of the Gods, he grants all desired objects; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Having heard the words of his preceptor, he went toward that river. 11.
Having bathed there, the lord of gods worshipped that Maheśa;
and from that bathing and worship, the illustrious Maheśvara was well-pleased.
Mahādeva said:
"Whatever you constantly pray for, all that I shall grant.
Having heard these words, the Lord of Gods spoke this supreme speech: [13]
Indra said:
You are the lord of all worlds; you alone are the cause and the goal.
Indeed, you are the Lord of the Universe, O God, and you are always perceived by me. 14.
O Lord of the Universe, O Lord of the Gods, if you are pleased with me, then slay Vṛtra; O Mahādeva, this is my great desire.
Mahādeva said:
"O Lord of Gods, it was at your word that this Vṛtra was slain by me.
O Lord of Asuras, take up whatever weapon I am about to give."
And by that very same method of breath-control, you will slay him; of this there is no doubt.
Indra said: "O Lord of the Universe, what weapon do you speak of with which I may slay Vṛtra?
When was that weapon, which is superior even to the thunderbolt, fashioned by you?"
Mahādeva said:
"This Pāśupata weapon was indeed fashioned by me in the past;
it has not been given to anyone, O Śakra, but has been guarded by me for your sake."
"O God, you have performed worship without fear;
therefore, take this weapon by which you shall slay Vṛtra. (20)
Then, having obtained it from Śrī Maheśa through his grace,
Maghavan [Indra] used that Pāśupata weapon to slay the exceedingly powerful Vṛtra.
All of that has arisen here by the grace of the invincible Lord;
O Goddess of gods, it occurs simply through bathing and through the worship of the Lord. 22.
"O fair-faced one, what has been attained is truly true by the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Knowing this, O Goddess of the gods, one should perform a bath there;
for the sight of Maheśa destroys all sins. (23)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Durdharṣeśvara," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||153||
(154) The one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter:
A supremely purifying sacred site, well-concealed, on the bank of the Sābhramatī.
It will be known as Khaḍgadhāra, and it will be protected by Kalaugupta. ||1||
If, while on a journey, one happens by chance to bathe or drink water there, being liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Rudra. ||2||
There, the meritorious Asābhravatī, having followed Kaśyapa,
was held by Rudra in his mass of matted hair as she was about to descend to the netherworld.
O Goddess of the Suras, Rudra is established there under the name Khaṅgadhārī;
having bathed there, even sinners have gone to heaven.
In this very context, I shall relate this ancient history concerning the vow performed by a hunter,
which was exceedingly difficult to accomplish.
Pārvatī said:
Who was this Vaikīrāta by name, and what vow was undertaken by him?
I wish to hear all that exactly as it happened; let it be told.
"Indeed, there exists no one else in the world besides you who is the best among speakers;
therefore, O Lord, tell us everything that is beneficial, for we wish to hear it."
Mahādeva said:
In former times, there was a most terrible and wicked-souled man named Caṇḍa;
he was cruel, deceitful, treacherous, and a source of fear to all living beings.
Then that evil-minded man incessantly slaughters fish with a net,
as well as deer, wild beasts, black antelopes, and porcupines with arrows.
Having scattered various kinds of birds, he, being enraged, caused them to fall down;
he killed the winged creatures, especially peacocks.
The hunter was a man of great sin, wicked, and beloved by evil people;
his wife was likewise, and he had a great disease of impotence.
As he was dwelling in this manner, a great deal of time passed.
Once, during the night, the Evil One (Māra) stationed himself atop a śrīvṛkṣa tree.

O Daughter of the Mountain, having joined an arrow to his bow, I stood there with bow in hand; thus, while he was awake as night approached, remaining unwinking on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Though filled with rage, he cut down many leaves of the *śrīvṛkṣa* tree there;
those [leaves] fell upon the *liṅga* that was situated at the foot of the *śrīvṛkṣa*. (14)
Even the leaves of the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, by the power of divine destiny, become entirely an act of worship to Śiva. ||15||
By that wicked-minded Puṣkasa, who was ignorant and used to rinsing his mouth [with water], a great ablution was performed. (16)
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, at the rising of the moon,
the Puṣkasa of wicked conduct became purified, his sins having been cast away.
His wife, Pracaṇḍā, came into his presence;
she was despondent and had abstained from food, while that Puṣkasa remained there.
Neither the boar, nor the deer, nor even the buffalo had yet arrived;
however, for the sake of food, that beautiful woman took his very own meal.
Not seeing Pracaṇḍāsā, that cruel-eyed woman, his wife, threw herself into the middle of the water of that very river. 20.
Then the fierce-souled one was told by her: "Come quickly and eat;
fish-flesh for your sake has now been brought by me."
"What was done by you, fool? Yesterday morning I was seen by your side; yet today, O fool, you have destroyed my family. May this sin be yours! (22)
Having heard these words of Caṇḍā, he who possessed a fierce form [replied]:
"By fasting on Śivarātri and by keeping a vigil during the night... (23)
Born of a pure disposition and observing pure vows, he went to bathe in the river; while that evil-minded man was bathing, a dog arrived there.
O Mistress of the Gods, when all that meat had been devoured by the dog,
Caṇḍā became enraged and set about to kill the dog.
Then, by the fierce Caṇḍa who was greatly enraged, they were restrained:
"He must not be struck by you; what evil has he done? (26)
She said, "The food has been eaten by this very wicked soul;
why, O fool, do you wish to eat it today when you are not hungry? (27)
The Puṣkasa said:
"I am fully satisfied by that food which was eaten by the dog;
what use have I for this transient body whose life has departed? (28)
O beautiful lady, those who nourish their bodies with their whole being should be known as deluded sinners, excluded from both worlds. (29)
Therefore, having abandoned pride, desire, and wickedness, and being free from the notion of a self-existent state, remain steadfast through the realization of reality. 30.
"O lady of beautiful hips, today I shall abandon this body by means of the vow of holding a wooden staff; what is the use of my living on for long? (31)
Having spoken thus, as soon as he drew his sword and was about to cut his own throat,
many hosts impelled by Śiva arrived there.
Many celestial mansions have arrived here in its vicinity;
having seen those very mansions as well as the hosts [of deities], he [acted] thus.
He spoke with supreme devotion even toward those Puṣkasas: "Why have you all come here, wearing rudrākṣa beads? (34)
All resemble crystal, all have the crescent moon as their crest-ornament;
they wear matted hair and are clothed in animal skins, with necklaces and ornaments fashioned from the coils of serpents upon their arms. ||35||
"Endowed with glory and possessing prowess equal to Rudra, tell me truly and appropriately what is fitting. Thus questioned by the Puṣkasa, the attendants of Rudra then spoke.
The Gaṇas said:
"We have been sent by the supreme lord Caṇḍaśiva;
come quickly, mount the vehicle together with your wife."
Because you performed the worship of the Linga of Śiva during the night,
