by the ripening of that karma, you have attained the supreme goal.
Thus addressed by Vīrabhadra, he spoke as if laughing:
"What good deed have I, a sinful Puṣkasa, ever performed? (39)
"Being a fool and evil-minded, and always delighting in hunting, I am indeed of sinful conduct; how then shall I dwell in heaven? (40)
How was the worship of the Liṅga first performed? Let that be told. Having become filled with great curiosity, I ask you; please speak out of compassion. (41)
Vīrabhadra said:
"O Caṇḍa, Mahādeva, the God of gods, known as the bearer of the Gaṅgā on his head and the Lord of Umā, is today well-pleased with you and your wife."
Furthermore, you have performed worship incidentally today, while looking at a *kola* fruit and indeed at *bilva* leaves. (43)
At that very moment, those fierce beings were struck down by you;
since you have severed their heads from the *liṅga*, O Lord, you are a man of great merit.
Thus, a great and steadfast tree of wakefulness arose for you;
by that very wakefulness, the Lord of the World was truly pleased. (45)
Indeed, by the mere sight of the illustrious Kola, even on the occasion of a hunter, the day of Śivarātri was observed as a fast. 46.
Pleased indeed by this fast and vigil, that noble-souled, excellent god,
through your grace, being a granter of boons, bestows all great powers and excellent boons.
Thus addressed then by the wise Vīrabhadra,
even the Puṣkasa ascended the foremost of celestial chariots while all were looking on.
Then, for all the hosts of deities and even for all living beings, many kinds of drums and musical instruments resounded loudly. 49.
The lords of the gandharvas sang accompanied by lutes, flutes, drums, singing, laughter, and dance, and the hosts of apsaras danced.
Being fanned with chowries and various types of umbrellas,
he was indeed brought into the presence of Śiva with a grand festival.
Even a Puṣkasa attained [liberation] then through bathing at a sacred ford and worshipping Śiva;
how much more so one who, with faith and devotion, [worships] Śiva as the Supreme Self? ||52||
Those in this world who offer flowers and the like, fruits, perfumes, betel, and unbroken grains—they are Rudras; of this there is no doubt.
Mahādeva said:
From that time forward, that holy place became renowned as Khaḍgadhārā.
O Queen of the Gods, this tīrtha shall remain hidden during the Kali age.
Those who perform their ritual bath specifically during the month of Māgha, Vaiśākha, or Kārtika,
are liberated and go to the world of the gods.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Bharadvāja, and Gautama also arrived there for the purpose of bathing, desiring to behold the god Pinākin.
O Pārvatī, the Liṅga exists in the three Yugas, but not in the Kali age;
for at that time, I was cursed by the sage Viśvāmitra.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord of the Asuras, how was the curse bestowed by the Ṛṣi? O God, I desire to hear that from you; I have no doubt. 58.
Mahādeva said: O Goddess, once upon a time, Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic,
arrived at this most wonderful sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Khaḍgadhāra.
Having performed his ablutions in the Sābhramatī river, he beheld me;
he remains there eternally, performing worship in manifold ways.
O beautiful lady, there was a certain great villain, a Kaulika who bore the form of sin; he then placed me upon Śiva as a deceptive offering.
Having seen that as well, Viśvāmitra then spoke to me once again: "A wicked deed has been committed here by a sinner."
Indeed, no punishment was ever inflicted upon him by Śarva, the Supreme Self;
therefore, having reached this certainty, I shall undoubtedly bestow a curse upon him.
Having reflected thus at that time, O Goddess, I was then cursed by him.
"In this terrible Kali age, you must remain hidden in every way.
Having thus pronounced this curse, the most excellent of sages departed.
From that time forward, O Goddess, I have been hidden due to the sage's curse;
yet, if one performs worship especially at my location, [the fruit is attained].
Indeed, whatever evil they possess perishes even at that very moment, for those who fashion an image of me made of clay and worship it. (67)
In this particular place, my banner indeed resides;
in the Kali age, it is renowned by the name Khaḍgadhāreśvara. 68.
In the Kṛta age it was indeed named Mandira; in Tretā it is remembered as Gaurava;
in Dvāpara it is renowned as Viśva; and in Kali it is remembered as Khaṅgeśvara. ||69||
O Goddess of the gods, having understood that this place is my southern quarter, the wise man should always fashion an image there. (70)
One who performs worship constantly shall obtain their desired fruit;
such a person on earth attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (71)
O Maheśvarī, O fair-faced one, those who offer incense, lamps, food offerings, as well as sandalwood and other such things to the Lord of Gods, the Protector of the World— truly,
truly, there shall be no suffering for them. (72)
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Dhāreśvara," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(155) The one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
To the south of Khaḍgadhārā is a supremely purifying sacred site (tīrtha) known as Dugdheśvara, which destroys all sins. ||1||
Having bathed at that sacred ford and beheld Hara as Dugdheśvara,
a man shall be instantly liberated from the suffering born of sin.
Dadhīci performed austerities on the auspicious bank of the Sābhramatī;
the Candrabhāgā, possessing great merit, flows along after joining with the Gaṅgā. ||3||
There, bathing, giving, recitation, worship, and likewise austerity—all these attain imperishability through the power of the Dugdha-tīrtha. (4)
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, I desire to hear about the origin of Dugdheshvara;
O Lord of the Gods, let the greatness of the Dugdha-tīrtha be told."
Mahādeva said:
Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, the gods were defeated by the daityas; becoming intent on flight, they came to the hermitage of Dadhīci.
Having abandoned their weapons there, the gods fled in the sixteen directions;
afterwards, Dadhīca heard the tumult arising from the Daityas.
Having immersed those weapons in water, Bhārgava drank them;
in due time, all those gods became eager to retrieve the weapons.
Accompanied by their preceptor, they were all filled with mutual joy;
even the snakes played together with the mongooses.
Beholding such numerous wonders in that hermitage at that time, all the gods were filled with the utmost amazement.
They beheld that best of sages seated upon his throne at the place where the holy Sābhramatī unites with the Candrabhāgā.
He was resplendent with supreme luster like the sun,
appearing like a second fire-god together with his wife Suvarcā.
Just as Brahmā is [seen] from the Sāvitrī, so too was that best of sages seen by all the foremost gods, preceded by prostrations. 13.
Then the gods, led by Bṛhaspati, said to him:
"You have long been known throughout the three worlds as a donor. (14)
We have all come into your presence for the sake of a request;
we are all terrified by fear, so you ought to grant us weapons. (15)

Thus addressed, that highly intelligent chief of sages spoke to the gods: "O gods, these [flowers] have been drunk; therefore, O lords, they must be revived by sprinkling them with water while reciting the mantra. (16)
Then the gods said to the brahmin, "Give [us] the bones for the destruction of the Daityas. The twice-born replied, "They must be given quickly. (17)
Having said this, he sent his wife back to the hermitage;
then the delighted brahmin, having remembered the gods, spoke with great intelligence.
"O gods, take these yellow and black [substances] exactly as they are. Having spoken thus, O Goddess, the twice-born one, a knower of yoga, entered into a state of yogic union.
Then, smiling and deceiving that brahmin with words, he said:
"O venerable Brahmin, while you are alive, how can we obtain bones? (20)
Laughing, the brahmin-sage said: "Stay together for a moment;
O gods, I myself shall cast off this body this very day."
Having spoken thus, O Goddess, that knower of yoga, accompanied by the twice-born, entered into yogic union and immediately went to the world of Brahmā, from which one does not return again.
Then all the gods, seeing him there reduced to destruction, the hosts of deities reflected: "How indeed shall we prevail? (23)
They both called for Surabhi, and the Lord of Śacī said to her: "Lick the body of this best of the twice-born at my command. (24)
Because of his words being true,
at that very moment the body was made fleshless by that cow and was instantly licked away.
The gods seized those bones and fashioned them into weapons;
from his backbone, the weapon known as Brahmaśiras was likewise produced.
Having fashioned weapons and missiles, those gods of great strength and prowess went forth with haste, intent upon the slaying of Vṛtra.
Then Suvarcā, sent by the wife of Dadhīci for the sake of accomplishing the Asura’s task,
arrived there and beheld her husband dead, his body then dissected.
Having understood all that deed of the asuras, the virtuous Suvarcā, the wife of the eminent rishi, then became enraged; being exceedingly provoked, she then uttered a curse.
"All the asuras became even more wicked; indeed, they were cursed many times and likewise became greedy.
Therefore, all of them, including Indra, the asuras, and the others, became childless," he said.
Having sat down at the foot of an Ashvattha tree on the bank of the Ashramati, that ascetic woman thus pronounced a curse upon those gods.
While she was pregnant, chaste, and virtuous, her own womb burst open;
the embryo emerged from the belly of the high-souled Dadhīca.
This great lord Pippalāda was an actual incarnation of Rudra;
smiling, he spoke these significant words to his mother’s womb: 33.
"O highly fortunate one, remain for a long time in the presence of Suvarcāta Pippalāda; O Aśvattha, become the bestower of auspiciousness upon all. (34)
Speaking thus to her son,
the virtuous Suvarcā returned to her husband with supreme concentration.
Thus, having ascended to heaven together with their husband, the wife of Dadhīci, those gods became eager for the sake of the Daityas who possessed weapons and missiles. (36)
And those leaders headed by Indra, possessed of great strength and prowess, arrived;
Kāmadhenu flowed forth and went to the place where the twice-born had met his end.
Through the power of the Sage, milk manifested in the form of a Liṅga;
it became renowned as Dugdheshvara on the bank of the river Sābhramatī, O Goddess. (38)
From that time forward, the holy site became renowned on earth by the name Hitā;
its greatness is incomparable, and merely hearing of it destroys all sins. (39)
Those men who listen with devotion to the account of the origin of Dugdheśvara are also liberated from sin and go to the great abode of Rudra. 40.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Dugdheśvara," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(156) The one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter. Mahādeva said:
To the east of Dugdheshvara is a supremely purifying holy site (tīrtha),
where the river named Chandrabhāgā indeed confluences.
There, the Lord Candreśvara dwells eternally, bestowing merit;
he is the great Hara, all-pervading at all times, who grants happiness to the worlds. (2)
Those who perform ablutions here and constantly practice meditation shall indeed obtain that same fruit from worshipping Śiva at the Sābhramatī. ||3||
Indeed, it is said that Soma performed penance here for a very long time;
therefore, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) was established there under the name Candreśvara. ||4||
Śukra performed austerities near the Candrabhāgā;
therefore, this sacred site is superior to all other tīrthas on earth and is purifying at all times. (5)
O Goddess of the gods, the Kālāugupta shrine was established by the sage;
there a golden liṅga is seen, of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed here, drunk [the water], and performed the worship of Śiva,
those men who shall come together will obtain dharma, wealth, and pleasure.
Those who especially perform rites such as the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) and others,
having enjoyed the state of heaven, afterwards go to the abode of Hara.
O Goddess, those people who come daily to the vicinity of the Candrabhāgā for the purpose of bathing are to be known as partakers of merit. 9.
Having gone to the very opposite bank, they worship that auspicious Śiva there,
known by the name Candreśvara, the glorious Hara who destroys the accumulation of sins.
Those best of men who, having come here, perform the recitation of the Rudra-mantras and other rites without distinction, are to be known as being of the very form of Śiva. (11)
Wherever the best of gods and givers perform their ablutions, those [waters] should be known as forms of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt. (12)
Those who perform a śrāddha ceremony here, or even with a sesame ball (piṇḍa), go to the abode of Viṣṇu by the power of that offering of the piṇḍa. ||13||
Here, charity should be bestowed and bathing performed according to the prescribed rites;
by bathing here, people are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Those who especially plant a banyan tree on this bank go to the abode of Śiva for as long as the moon and sun endure. (15)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Umā, Candeśvara, and the Candra-bhāgā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(157) The one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter. Mahādeva said:
Near Dugdheshvara, however, there is an exceedingly purifying and delightful holy site (tīrtha) renowned on earth by the name of Pippalāda. ||1||
Having previously performed austerities at that place, the sage, following his mother’s word,
brought forth a magical creation (kṛtyā) equal to the submarine fire.
Seeking to discharge his debt to his father, the high-souled Dadhīca, one who bathes there and drinks [the water] is cleansed of the sin of killing a Brahmin. (3)
On the bank of the Sābhramatī, there is the well-guarded Pippalāda Sureśvara;
by bathing there, O Goddess, a man shall become a partaker of liberation. ||4||
The planting of *pippala* trees must be performed according to the prescribed rite;
O Great Goddess, when this is done, one is liberated from the bondage of karma.
Pārvatī said: "O Lord, tell me for what reason she was born as Sātukṛtyā;
tell me, O Master, what was previously done by her through that transformation?"
By which son she was brought [here] for the sake of discharging his debt to his father.
Mahādeva said:
"That excellent sage Dādhīca has arrived here for the sake of penance;
great austerity has been performed here by that supreme-souled ṛṣi."
There, a demon named Kolāsura arrived for the purpose of creating obstacles;
by him, many obstacles were indeed created there—of this there is no doubt. (9)
O Goddess of the Suras, a *kṛtyā* was then produced there by his beloved son, the wise Kahoḍa, for the purpose of killing him.
By her, the great asura named Kola was slain;
therefore, O Pārvatī, a great holy site (tīrtha) was born there, which remains hidden during the Kali age.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Sacred Site of Pippalāda," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(158) The one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Then, at the Pippalāda-tīrtha, one should visit the excellent Picumanda-arka;
this sacred site on the banks of the Sābhramatī river destroys diseases, sins, and mental anguish. ||1||
Long ago, in the battle at Kolāhala, the gods were defeated by the Dānavas;
seeking to preserve their lives, they entered into trees there in minute forms.
There, Śambhu resides in the Bilva tree; the imperishable Hari in the Aśvattha; the thousand-eyed one in the Śirīṣa; and the god Prabhākara in the Niṃba. (3)
In this manner, the gods [resided] appropriately among the trees;
meanwhile, the Daitya Kolāhala was confronted by the all-powerful Viṣṇu.
Having been slain in that great battle, they remained there for so long, taking refuge in trees;
for whichever tree each deity had taken shelter in, [there he stayed].
Since he has become one with that [essence] through constant recitation, one should therefore not destroy it;
thus, from the repose of the Sun, the *picumandārka* is supreme. (6)
A holy ford (tīrtha) that removes disease arose on the bank of the Sābhramatī through bathing;
having gone there, if one should especially worship that Sun-god, [one attains liberation].
Having worshipped the best of gods, one obtains the desired fruit;
and those who, having gone there, indeed recite the twelve names. ||8||
Those men of meritorious deeds, for as long as they live, have no doubt [of this]:
[they worship] Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Ravi, the illuminator of the universe. ||9||
Likewise, [he praised] Tīkṣṇa, Śuṃ, Ārtaṇḍa, Sūrya, Prabhākara,
Vibhāvasu, Sahasrākṣa, and Pūṣan as well.
Thus, the wise person who, being self-restrained, recites these twelve names, shall obtain wealth, sons, and grandsons, as well as celestial vehicles in the sky. (11)
Whosoever on earth should worship by relying upon each individual name shall become a Brahmin for seven births, wealthy and devoted to the Vedas. (12)
A Kṣatriya obtains a kingdom, a Vaiśya acquires wealth, and a Śūdra attains devotion; therefore, one should recite this supreme Sūkta. 13.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy place superior to Nimbārka;
having bathed and drunk [the water] here, one will certainly partake in liberation. (14)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Holy Tīrtha of Nimbārka Deva," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(159) The One Hundred and Fifty-ninth Chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Therefore, O Goddess, much further away is an unsurpassed field of the Siddhas, where Aniruddha was formerly confined by Citralekhā for the sake of Uṣā. ||1||
In former times, he was led to the city of the demon Bāṇa and remained in his house, confined by nooses and arrows; there, he then remembered Koṭarākṣī.
She who is the manifest power of Viṣṇu, ever intent on protection— this very goddess was installed here on the riverbank by Kṛṣṇa.
Having conquered the asura Bāṇa in battle, as he was returning to Dvārakā,
she appeared in person through the hymn of praise offered by Aniruddha.
Having bathed with diligence at that sacred ford for one year and having beheld the face of Koṭarākṣī, a man attains abundant prosperity.
Having bathed at Siddhatīrtha and beheld the goddess Akotaravāsinī,
a man is glorified in the world of Rudra by means of a vehicle yoked with lions.
O lady of beautiful countenance, because he was addressed thus simply by means of remembrance of her,
people go there and thereby become partakers of liberation as spoken by him.
Having gone there, O Pārvatī, and having performed a bath without distinction,
one should then recite the hymn of Koṭarākṣī with full awareness.
She who has eyes like hollows, whose form is universal, who possesses the power of great illusion,
the conqueror of the three cities, the slayer of Tripura, the auspicious one, and she who is the very form of Śiva.
She is proclaimed as Kanyāsārasvatī, the remover of misfortune from Durgā;
she is Bhairavī with terrifying eyes, the goddess Lakṣmī, beloved by the people. (10)
O Goddess of the gods, these names have been declared in many ways;
those best of men who recite them go into the presence of Śiva.
O fair-faced one, those wise ones who recite this hymn composed by Aniruddha are liberated from painful bondage; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
The supreme among all sacred fords on earth is that which was fashioned from a hollow tree;
by its mere sight, heaps of sins are likewise destroyed.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Holy Site of Koṭarā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(160) The One Hundred and Sixtieth Chapter. Mahādeva said:
Beyond this sacred ford is another, renowned as Tīrtharāja;
there, seven rivers flow carrying water mixed with sandalwood.
A bath here is distinguished as being a hundred times superior to that at any other sacred ford,
for it is here that Vāmana himself resides as the foremost of all gods.
He who gives a sesame-cow on the twelfth day of the month of Māgha,
being liberated from all sins, shall deliver a hundred generations of his lineage.
A self-controlled man should offer even water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
by him a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years—this is a secret that the ancestors declare. (4)
Whoever feeds Brahmins at this sacred ford with jaggery and milk-rice, by feeding a single Brahmin, it becomes as if a thousand have been fed. ||5||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "Vāmana-tīrtha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||160||
(161) The One Hundred and Sixty-first Chapter. Mahādeva said:
From there, one should go to Somatīrtha, a secret place on the bank of the Sābhramatī;
it was there that Bhava, having emerged from Pātāla, became Kālāgni.
Having bathed at Somatīrtha and beheld the auspicious Someśvara Śiva, a person directly obtains the fruit of drinking the Soma juice; of this there is no doubt. ||2||
In this world, such a man becomes handsome, fortunate, and possessed of enjoyments, and is proficient in all the scriptures; moreover, he shall go to auspiciousness in the next world. (3)
In this regard, I shall relate an ancient history; listen, O beautiful one, to it as it truly is.
Having heard it, one is liberated here from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
The sage Kauṣītaka performed intense austerities;
having become entirely abstinent from food, he was devoted exclusively to subsisting on leaves.
Then, subsisting on air alone, he became devoted to meditation upon the Self;
in this manner, he performed great penance there for many yugas.
"O Brahmin, by the power of fate, Maheśvara has become well-pleased at some point;
whatever you pray for, I shall grant all of that to you."
Kauṣītaka said:
"O Lord of Gods, by your grace, let a liṅga be produced here;
let there be a god eternally renowned here as Someśvara. (8)
Whereby, having bathed and eaten, one may obtain the desired fruit;
especially in this sacred place, if one performs the recitation of the Rudra-mantras and other rites.
O best of men, those who perform these dharmas obtain wealth and prosperity;
one without a son obtains a son, and one without wealth obtains wealth. (10)
One who desires a kingdom shall obtain that kingdom; of this there is no doubt.
If you are pleased with me, O Lord, then grant all of this to me. 11.
Īśvara said:
Then everything was given to the twice-born by the lord of the asuras;
from that time forward, that sacred site became renowned as Somaliṅga. 12.
Those who always worship Sadāśiva with sandalwood paste or bilva leaves obtain happiness arising from sons and other blessings within a human body. ||13||
Likewise, when Monday arrives during the Yoga known as Chaturdaśī, one who goes to the abode of Hara always obtains their heart's desire through the grace of the Somaliṅga.
O Goddess, whoever goes there and offers fruits and the like according to their specific desire, they shall certainly obtain that very thing. 15.
Furthermore, those who worship that god, the illustrious Maheśa, the wielder of the Pināka bow, with white Akaravīra flowers and Pārijāta blossoms; ||16||
Thus, O best of gods, they attain this unsurpassed state of Śiva. ||17||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Soma-tīrtha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(162) The one hundred and sixty-second chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Then, O Goddess, one should go again to the Kāpotika Tīrtha,
where the waters of the Sābhramatī flow towards the east.
There, on every festival day, he offers a ball of food preceded by the libation to the ancestors, using wild fruits and flowers. (2)
Furthermore, that man who offers oblations even to crows, dogs, and the like,
shall easily cross over the path of Yama.
Having bathed at that sacred ford on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, a person should worship the supreme Lord Īśāna, Prācīneśvara, with white mustard seeds.
He shall then deliver himself, as well as his fathers and grandfathers,
where a pigeon joyfully gave its own body to a guest.
Praised by all the hosts of gods who had ascended to heaven in celestial chariots,
from that time forth that sacred ford became renowned as Kāpota.
Having bathed there and drunk [the water], a man casts off the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, tell me how the body was given by the pigeon."
O Lord of the Gods, what is that sign? I do not know it thus, O Sovereign of the Suras.
Mahādeva said:
"O supreme mistress of the gods, in this sacred place there is indeed a most great banyan tree;
its infinite branches are seen spreading across the vast earth. (8)
There, O Goddess of the Gods, many birds dwell; likewise, a pigeon has built its nest there in that house. (9)
There dwells the lord of birds, eternally devoted to Viṣṇu;
accompanied by his family, he resides permanently upon a branch. (10)
One day, O Goddess, on the twelfth lunar day, the day of Viṣṇu, a hawk arrived there as a guest, O beautiful lady. (11)
"O pigeon, give me the flesh from your own body;
otherwise, I shall cast a curse," thus it was said, O daughter of the mountain. (12)
"O Lord, today on the day of Viṣṇu, I have arrived afflicted by hunger;
therefore, O Master, that meat of the snow-mountain must be given to me who am tormented by hunger. (13)
Having heard what was said by the hawk, O Goddess, that great Vaiṣṇava pigeon then gave up his body; of this there is no doubt.
By the power of that gift, O best of gods, a great sacred ford (tīrtha) called Kāpotaka was born, which is the purifier of all purifiers. (15)
O best of goddesses, having bathed at this sacred ford and performed the worship of Śiva, a man gives sweet food to guests.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu;
for the pigeon indeed gave his own body to the Great-Souled One. (17)
He indeed goes to the realm of Viṣṇu for as long as the moon and sun endure. Therefore, O Goddess, having gone there, one should always honor the guest;
when the guest is honored there, one certainly obtains everything. ||18||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Pigeon Tīrtha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(163) The one hundred and sixty-third chapter.
Mahādeva said:
The most excellent of sacred fords, which destroys even the greatest sins, is renowned as Go-tīrtha, located near the Kāśyapa lake. ||1||
Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the killing of a Brahmin, by bathing at Go-tīrtha one is freed from them; of this there is no doubt. (2)
Having attained black bodies due to the influence of their former sins, cows bathed at a certain sacred ford and thereby regained their whiteness once more. (3)
Having bathed at that sacred ford and having given daily fodder to the cows, a man shall become free from debt to his mothers through the grace of the Cow-Mothers. ||4||
Having gone to Go-tīrtha and bathed there, a man who gives a milch cow to the foremost of Brahmins goes to the abode of Brahmā. ||5||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Go-tīrtha," in the Sābhramatī-māhātmya of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(164) The one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter. Mahādeva said:
O Goddess of the gods, there is another great sacred site here called Kaśyapa,
where there was a large lake fashioned by the god of the mountain.
There shines the deity named Kuśeśvara,
where there is likewise a beautiful pool constructed by Kaśyapa.
Having bathed there, O Goddess, neither a man nor a woman shall go to hell;
[there dwell] Brahmins who maintain the sacred fires and are constantly devoted to the Vedas. ||3||
The learned Mahādevikāśyapas dwell here;
this city, fashioned by the Ṛṣis, is just like the sky.
Kāśyapa performed even more extensive austerities here;
it was by his ascetic power that the Gaṅgā, born from the matted locks of Śiva, was brought down.
She is the daughter of Aṅgākāśyapa, the great destroyer of sins;
by the mere sight of her, people are liberated from evil transgressions. (6)
They praise the gift of a cow and likewise the gift of a chariot;
having performed a śrāddha there, one should diligently offer the gift of land.
In the terrible Kali age,
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy place equal to the one named Kaśyapa, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
Indeed, it is there that all the deities and the sages, free from all taint, eternally reside by the grace of the Lord of Devas, the King of Tīrthas. (9)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Kaśyapa-hrada," within the "Greatness of the Sābhramatī" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(165) The one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Thereafter, one should go to Bhūtālaya, a sacred ford that removes sin and is a place of refuge;
it is where the Baṭu tree stands and where the Prācī Candanā river flows.
A man who, having bathed at Bhūtālaya on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and observed a fast,
gives black sesame seeds as a gift, is never reborn as a preta.
Whoever offers a water-pot together with sesame seeds intended for the ancestors will undoubtedly deliver their forefathers from the state of being a preta. (3)
By bathing in pure water at dawn on the fourteenth or the eighth day under the name of such a person, a man is liberated from the state of a preta. (4)
Having bathed at the holy ford, the abode of spirits, and having beheld the banyan tree known as Bhūtālaya, one shall not experience fear from spirits by the grace of Bhūteśvara. ||5||
Thus ends the sacred site of Śrī-Bhūteśvara-tīrtha.
Therefore, the sacred site beyond this one is remembered as Ghaṭeśvara;
having bathed there and beheld Him, one will certainly partake in liberation.
Where the Ghaṭa-tīrtha, the supreme great one, and the Sābhramatī-tīrtha are located;
having seen Mahādeva there, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Having gone there, the man who performs the special worship of the Plakṣa tree obtains all his desired objects on earth through the power of his mind. (8)
Thus ends the Ghaṭeśvara Tīrtha.
Then, a man should go with devotion to the place renowned as Vaidyanātha;
having bathed there in the sacred ford, he should be intent upon the worship of Śiva.
By satiating the ancestors according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Born from the gods, Vijaya brings about the destruction of all sins;
by beholding him, men shall always attain various desires. (10)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vijayī-tīrtha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(166) The one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter. Mahādeva said:
Beyond Vaidyanātha is a supreme sacred site that bestows all spiritual perfections;
it is renowned as Devatīrtha, the most excellent among all sacred sites. (1)
Having received tribute by force from Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) commenced the great sacrifice, the Rājasūya.
O Goddess, on the bank of the Sābhramatī, there is a place renowned as Pāṇḍurārya, where the Pāṇḍu clan was born from the lineage of Dikpāla Dakṣiṇa.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sābhramatī and having bowed to Pāṇḍurāryā, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation through devotion established by others; ||4||
A man certainly attains the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as supreme intelligence; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (5)
Having paid homage to Pāṇḍurāryā with a pure disposition, worship performed for a year should be offered by those possessing the intellect of reality.
Having cast off his body at that sacred site near Pāṇḍurāryā,
he reaches the peak of Kailāsa and becomes an attendant of Caṇḍeśvara.
In ancient times, Hanumān performed extremely difficult penance there;
by the power of that sacred ford, he acquired the ability to leap across the ocean.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Holy Site of Pāṇḍurāryā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(167) The one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter:
Beyond this sacred site is another sacred site, renowned as Caṇḍeśa.
And where the god Caṇḍeśvara, the bestower of prosperity, eternally resides. ||1||

O Maheśvarī, having seen him, one is liberated from sin, whether committed through ignorance or intentionally; and all the deities, having come together, established a city renowned by the name Caṇḍeśa.
Thus concludes the Caṇḍeśa Tīrtha.
Beyond this sacred site, there is another sacred site on earth known as Gāṇapatya; it is situated near the Sābhramatī river and was fashioned by the gods. ||3||
Having bathed there, a person is liberated from sin; of this there is no doubt. I believe she exists on the bank of the Sābhramatī out of a desire for the welfare of people. 4.
Abandoning all those holy fords on earth and all those in the oceans, one should resort to this most wonderful holy ford.
He who, with his senses subdued, performs a *śrāddha* there out of devotion to Rudra,
being pure in soul, obtains the fruit arising from all sacrifices.
Whatever is offered at Gaṇatīrtha dedicated to the ancestors, all that quickly comes to fruition through the grace of Gaṇanātha. ||7||
Having bathed at that sacred ford, if a man bestows a bull upon a brahmin, he shall transcend all worlds and attain the supreme goal. ||8||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Holy Site of Gaṇa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(168) The one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
From there, O Great Goddess, one should go to Vārtraghni, where Śakra obtained union with that virtuous daughter of the mountain. ||1||
There, men of restless minds perform their ablutions;
one who performs the bath shall obtain the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices. (2)
In that place, whoever performs a śrāddha offering cakes made from sesame powder purifies his lineage—seven ancestors and seven descendants. (3)
Having bathed at the confluence and worshipped Gaṇanāyaka according to the prescribed rites,
one shall not be overcome by obstacles nor ever be deprived of prosperity.
Pārvatī said: "O Purandara, for what purpose have you come here to this world from the heavenly realm? You ought to explain this to me. (5)
It is proclaimed by the Vārtraghni verses, by the Nadīka hymns, and by the Nirukta;
it is the City-Opener (Puraṃdara), resounding with the chanting of the gods and the Vedas.
Tell me, what is that union which he who constantly honors [it] attains?
Mahādeva said: Long ago, in this very world of Bhūrloka, there arose this question concerning a great king renowned as Yudhiṣṭhira, who was exceedingly righteous.
O Goddess, I shall now declare before you that which was spoken by him when he was questioned by Bhīṣma, who is righteous and the very embodiment of knowledge.
The battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava lasted for ten thousand and ten hundred years, causing the hair to stand on end.
Then Śakra, having been defeated and having made a pact with Vṛtra,
abandoned his refuge in non-injury and came to me for protection.
At the confluence of the Vārtraghni, he propitiated Śaṅkara at that holy place;
then, O Goddess, I appeared before him in the sky. 11.
O God, whatever ash fell from my body onto the slopes of Kāśyapī became that meritorious Liṅga fashioned by you.
Bhūteśvara, whose body is smeared with ashes and who was established by Brahmā—by the mere sight of him, even the sin of killing a Brahmin shall depart. (13)
By performing a śrāddha on the days marking the beginning of the yugas, one is liberated from all sins;
thus, I became well-pleased with the high-souled Indra.
"Whatever you may desire, O God, I shall grant all of that to you.
By means of this vajrayoga, you will swiftly slay Vṛtra. (15)
Śakra said: "O Blessed One, by your grace, O best of gods, I shall slay the son of Diti,
that oppressor of the world, with my thunderbolt while you look on."
Having spoken thus, Indra then went toward the Asura;
at that time, both sides, and especially the divine army, raised a great roar.
There was clay, as well as many ḍamarus, ḍiṇḍimas, kettledrums, and various musical instruments;
and all the asuras felt a great greed for their livelihoods.
In an instant, Maghavat became powerful;
then, perceiving him thus possessed, the sages and the serpents likewise [acted].
As he went into the presence of Śakra, who was desirous of battle, being praised by the sages with hymns of "Victory! Victory! to the lord Tiśakra, his form became exceedingly difficult to behold.
Mahādeva said:
O Devī, listen now to these signs that appeared suddenly upon the body of Vṛtra at the front of the battle. 21.
His mouth became blazing and terrible, and an extreme paleness came over him;
his body trembled greatly and a hot, heavy breath was produced.
A violent horripilation occurred and his breath became very labored;
most terrible meteors fell and reached his side. (23)
Vultures, hawks, crows, owls, and other most dreadful birds all circled above Vṛtra like a wheel. ||24||
Then Indra, mounting his elephant, arrived there;
with thunderbolt raised in hand, Śakra approached that Daitya.
The Lord of the Asuras let forth a superhuman roar of fury;
then Śakra hurled his thunderbolt at the striving Vṛtra-asura.
Possessing a vajra, endowed with great majesty, and as vast as the fire of cosmic destruction, Śakra struck down the Daitya Vṛtra like the shore [restrains] the ocean. ||27||
Then,
seeing Vṛtra— who was the terror of all the gods— slain, a great roar arose once again from every side.
Then a great rain of flowers fell upon the tops of the trees;
having slain Vṛtra, the terrifying lord of the Dānavas, the Blessed One [remained].
Being praised by the immortals, he entered Devadānī together with them;
then, the most excellent splendor emerged from Vṛtra’s body.
The most terrible and horrific sin of killing a Brahmin, which causes fear to the worlds, has a formidable face, a distorted form, and black matted hair. 31.
And Kapālamālinī, who is very emaciated, rides upon a cloud; she is smeared with blood, most sinful, and exceedingly terrifying as she rides upon a fish. 32.
Having gone forth, O great goddess, she of such a form, bringing fearlessness,
then began to search for Indra, O best of the Vaisyas.
Having seen Śakra of great splendor, she rushed out from there; she seized the Lord of the Gods by the neck and then became firmly attached to him.
While terrified by the fear arising from that act of brahmin-slaughter,
he hid within the midst of lotus stalks and remained there for many groups of years.
Seized by her, O Goddess, he became motionless;
Śakra then made an effort to dislodge him from her. (36)
O Great Goddess, he was not able to dispel the sin of killing a Brahmin;
as soon as he was seized by it, the Lord of the Gods assumed a hideous form.
Having approached his grandfather, he honored him by bowing his head;
and [the grandfather], knowing that Śakra had been seized by the sin of killing the foremost of the twice-born, [spoke].
Then, while Brahmā was reflecting upon this, O best of asuras,
she, being thus meditated upon, approached Brahmā and spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, O Himavat, I have arrived here in your presence;
O Lord, you ought to tell me what must be done by me. (40)
Then the Grandfather spoke to that Brahmahatyā in a sweet voice, briefly and exactly as it was: 41.
"Let this king of the gods be released; do what is pleasing to me, O beautiful lady!
Tell me, what desire of yours shall I fulfill today? What do you wish for here? (42)
Hatyā said: "O best of men, by your word I shall depart from Śakra;
salutations to you, O God of gods, and grant me a dwelling place. (43)
Mahādeva said: Having thus promised her, the Grandfather (Brahmā) then [considered] the means for Śakra to remove the sin of killing a brahmin.
Then, having summoned Agni, Brahmā spoke these words:
"O Jātavedas, accept for me one-fourth of the sin of Śakra’s murder."
Agni said:
"O Lord, honored by the worlds, what is the cause of my liberation from this brahmin-slaughter? I wish to know this according to the truth."
Brahmā said: "O Fire, that man who, having approached you while you are blazing, should offer anywhere seeds, medicinal herbs, sesame, fruits, roots, sacrificial fuel, or kuśa grass... (47)
At that very moment, she will dwell there as if she were your own body;
furthermore, the fever of your mind shall be the vehicle for carrying away the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Then the blessed Grandfather, the consumer of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors, accepted those words along with his retinue, and thus he obtained what was dear to him.
Then, having summoned the trees, herbs, and grasses, the Grandfather,
O highly fortunate one, began to speak on this matter.
Then, O Goddess, the trees, herbs, and grasses, having been addressed exactly as they were,
became distressed like fire and spoke these words to Brahmā.
O Grandfather, tell us how we may be freed from this sin of killing a Brahmin; you ought not to strike us again for that which was committed by our own nature.
O God, we constantly endure fire as well as cold rain driven by the wind, as well as cutting and piercing. (53)
Brahmā said:
"That man who, out of great delusion, shall commit the act of cutting or piercing you without cause— she shall follow after him."
Mahādeva said: Then, having uttered "Om" with great medicinal herbs and grasses,
those high-souled ones worshipped Brahmā as well and departed just as they had come.
Then the god, the Grandfather of the worlds, summoned the Apsarases and spoke with sweet words to Sāntvayanī, the most excellent of those dwelling there.
"O excellent women, this Brahmahatyā has followed after Vṛtra;
now accept a fourth part of her as I have prescribed. (57)
The Apsarases said:
"O Grandfather, since we have resolved to be taken as wives by the Lord of Gods, you must consider the time for our liberation from your abode. (58)
The Grandfather said:
"Whoever should engage in sexual intercourse with women who are menstruating, she shall quickly seize him; let the fever of your minds depart. (59)
Mahādeva said:
Thus addressed with joyful minds, the hosts of Apsarases returned to their own respective abodes and then rejoiced upon the mountain.
Then the divine Grandfather, the creator of the worlds,
again meditated upon the waters, and they immediately appeared.
And all of them, having assembled and bowed down before the Grandfather Brahmā of immeasurable splendor, spoke these words to him.
"O Lord of the Immortals, O Master, these have arrived here in your presence by your very command; please give us your orders, O Lord. (63)
Brahmā said:
"This terrifying Brahman-slaughter has come after Vṛtra, O Puruhūta; you four should accept a share of it for the sake of peace."
The Waters said:
"O Lord of the World, let it be as you, our Master, have spoken;
yet you ought to consider for us the time for our liberation. (65)
For you alone, O Indra, are the supreme refuge of the entire world;
for who else could even grant such grace as to rescue us from our distress? (66)
Brahmā said:
"The man who, having formed such a small-minded view, is deluded in his intellect," ||67||
He shall quickly depart from you, having released his phlegm, urine, and excrement; he will go there and dwell right there.
From that, liberation will indeed come to pass—this I tell you as the truth.
Mahādeva said:
Then, O Sovereign Goddess of the Asuras, having released the Lord of the Gods from the sin of Brahman-slaughter, she departed;
and by the command of the God, the Lord of the Gods became exceedingly joyful.
Thus, in a former age, Śakra incurred the sin of Brahman-slaughter;
having performed penance at this sacred site, he became pure in soul and went to the third heaven.
Then, having performed the horse sacrifice, he became free from sin;
thus, O daughter of the mountain, at the Sābhramatī tīrtha, [he attained] the state of Vārtraghnī.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vārtraghnī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(169) The one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter.
Maheśa said:
Thereafter, it is said that from the confluence of the Devanadī and Vārtraghnī,
she entered the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, together with the Bhadrā.
Even the ocean, desiring to do what was pleasing and wishing to come, brought about a reunion with his beloved out of affection for the Sābhramatī. ||2||
Bhadrāvāpī, Subhadrāyā, Vayasyāsā, Nadīpurā—she who had assumed the form of Śrī herself—became his companion on the path. ||3||
The confluence of those two is meritorious on the northern shore of the ocean;
having bathed at that sacred ford, the man who gives pure water [attains merit].
Having paid homage to Varāha, one shall attain the realm of Varuṇa;
the Lord Viṣṇu entered the ocean by that path.
Having conquered all the Dānavas who were the adversaries of the gods,
the divine Yajña-varāha,
having agitated the abode of the Makaras and sported for a very long time, emerged from the mud with Kardama.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord, tell me in detail about the entry of Devayajña-Vārāha into the Sābhramatī river and his emergence from the Kardamāla forest.
Mahādeva said:
"O mountain-dweller, listen as I shall relate all that ancient sport of the Boar-form Hari within the waters."
This very Lord, the sovereign of the gods, who for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the deities assumed the form of a boar, having taken on that body in person. ||9||
Having supported the goddess Earth, he emerged from the abode of Kardama;
there, O beautiful one, a great sacred site known as Varāha was born.
Any man who bathes there becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt. One should perform a śrāddha ceremony here for the sake of the liberation of one's ancestors.
Released, he goes together with them to the great, bliss-bestowing world. 11.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Vārāha Tīrtha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(170) The one hundred and seventieth chapter. Mahādeva said:
Beyond this sacred site, there is another sacred site known as Saṅgama, where the Sābhramatī and the Gaṅgā meet with the ocean. ||1||
There, bathing and giving gifts should be performed according to the prescribed rules;
by bathing there, even those who have committed great sins are liberated.
In that regard, one who desires the welfare of their own kin should perform a śrāddha ceremony there;
for when a śrāddha is performed at this very place, one shall certainly dwell in the world of the ancestors.
Where the god Sāgara always meets Gaṅgā, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated there; what need is there to mention other sins? (4)
Where people of deluded intellect do not recognize a sacred ford (tīrtha), at that time one should establish that supreme ford under an unknown name. ||5||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Holy Site of Saṅgama," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(171) The one hundred and seventy-first chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Near Saṅgama is a famous holy ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the world called Āditya; superior to it has never existed, nor will there ever be.
Indeed, for one who must perform the vision [of the deity], there should be bathing with lotuses, and worship with *arka* flowers as well as with oleanders. (2)
In that place, the inhabitants of the celestial realms always perform acts of faith and charity;
this Ādityaka Tīrtha is pure and a destroyer of sins. ||3||
By the mere sight of it, this sacred ford bestows merit even upon those who have committed great sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Holy Tīrthas," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(172) Chapter One Hundred and七十二 (Seventy-two):
Mahādeva said:
Therefore, there is a holy place superior to that holy place, renowned as Nīlakaṇṭha;
its sight must always be performed by one who desires liberation. (1)
O Goddess of the Asuras, by means of bilva leaves, incense, or lamps, a mortal obtains his desired object simply from the sight of Nīlakaṇṭha. ||2||
Always established in the excellence of the world-renouncing vow of fasting, he grants to the people whatever they desire.
Kalausātī was the great goddess, renowned indeed as Kāśyapī. ||4||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Nīlakaṇṭha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(173) The one hundred and seventy-third chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Where the river Sābhramatī meets the goddess Durgā, there is a confluence with the ocean; one should perform a ritual bath there. (1)
In the Kali age, they will become free from defects; there is no doubt about this.
One should perform the Śrāddha ceremony there, as well as at the confluence of the Durgā.
Having gone there, one should provide food to Brahmins without distinction and perform the gift of cows and buffaloes according to the prescribed ritual.
This [river] is auspicious, most auspicious, purifying, and the destroyer of sins;
by merely seeing her, O Goddess, a man is released from his transgressions. (4)
Just as it is with the Gaṅgā, so too should this river Ābhramatī be known;
in the Kali age, O Goddess, she especially bestows the fruits of many ages.
Even if a hundred tongues were to issue from my mouth,
I would never be able to describe her virtues.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Sābhramatī," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(174) The one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the vow that is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
by hearing which, the world is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. (1)
The manifestation of the Self-luminous One for the sake of the happiness of His devotees has become a meritorious occasion, whether it be a specific lunar day or even an entire month. ||2||
O Goddess, by chanting whose name one attains eternal liberation—he alone is the Supreme Self, the cause of all causes. (3)
The Lord, the master of all, the soul of the universe and the universal form,
by whom the twelve suns were supported— that very same high-souled Nṛsiṃha has become manifest out of a desire for the peace of his devotees. 4.
Pārvatī said:
O best of gods, you have indeed described innumerable incarnations;
O Lord, Sovereign of the Universe, tell me of the supreme abode known as Nṛsiṃha.
By means of which mere consciousness one may attain the world of bliss. ||5||
Mahādeva said:
Having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu, he stood upon the lap of the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, as He sat at ease, and spoke these words. (6)
Prahlāda, the best among the wise, [saw] his father’s slayer as supreme.
Prahlāda said:
O Blessed One, Viṣṇu, obeisances unto You who possess the wondrous form of Nṛsiṃha! I am Your devotee, O best of gods; I ask You about the truth. ||8||
"O Lord, my undivided devotion toward you has indeed arisen in manifold ways;
tell me, O Master, what is the reason why I have become dear to you? (9)
Nṛsiṃha said:
O highly wise one, listen with a one-pointed mind; I shall tell you, my child, what the cause of devotion is, and furthermore, what the cause of being dear [to the Lord] is. (10)
Formerly, you were born as the son of a certain brahmin, yet you did not study;
indeed, by name you were Vasudeva, excessively addicted to a courtesan.
In that very birth, he did not perform even the slightest virtuous deed;
instead, longing for union with a courtesan, he consumed honey and ghee.
"O sinless one, through the power of my vow, devotion has arisen in you.
Prahlāda said: "O Lord of Gods, tell me in detail: what was the vow of Kaśyapa’s son?"
"By some means, I have been insulted while staying with a courtesan;
having shown compassion toward me, please tell me everything regarding her. (14)
Nṛsiṃha said:
In ancient times, for the purpose of creation, Brahmā indeed performed this unsurpassed vow; by the power of my vow, the world of moving and non-moving beings was brought into existence. 15.
A vow was performed by Īśvara for the purpose of slaying Tripura;
indeed, by the power of this vow, Tripura was brought down. ||16||
This supreme vow was also performed by many other gods, ancient seers, and highly wise kings.
By the power of this vow, may all attain perfection;
indeed, they shall obtain manifold enjoyments, such as beloved wives and so forth, just as I have. (18)
"O you who have dissolved away my disease by eating [it], enter me with joy!
For the sake of your purpose, you have descended as an incarnation, since you have emerged from my body as something distinct. (19)
For them, there is no returning again even after hundreds of great eons;
they obtain a fortune such as that of Kubera, which a poor man cannot find.
Then, one who desires love shall obtain love; one who seeks a kingdom shall obtain a supreme kingdom; and one who desires long life shall obtain a lifespan such as that of Śiva himself.
It ensures that women do not become widows, and likewise bestows sons and good fortune;
it brings wealth and grain, and likewise destroys all sorrow.
Whether they be women or men, whoever performs this supreme vow, to them I grant happiness as well as the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. (23)
O child, what is the use of speaking at length? For neither I nor Śaṅkara is able to describe the fruit of this vow, which is indeed my own vow.
Prahlāda said:
O Blessed One, by your grace I have heard of this unsurpassed vow. Now I am filled with devotion to hear the fruit of this vow from you. (25)
Now I wish to hear the supreme procedure for this vow;
O Lord, in which month and on which day should it take place? (26)
O Lord, you ought to explain this in detail, according to which procedure one may indeed become a partaker of the complete fruit. (27)
Nṛsiṃha said: O Prahlāda, may it be well with you; listen with one-pointed attention to the vow.
One should observe it on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha. (28)
O son, listen to the account of my own manifestation and the cause of my satisfaction—my birth—intended for the sake of the happiness of my devotees. 29.
Because it arose from the western direction, this field of Mālasthāna is sacred and a destroyer of sins. (30)
In that field, there was a renowned Brāhmaṇa who had mastered the Vedas, known by the name Hārīta, and devoted to knowledge and meditation. ||31||
O Lord, that woman was exceedingly virtuous and possessed great merit;
she was always devoted to her husband’s will and was known by the name Līlāvatī.
O son, by those two great penance was performed for a very long time;
twenty-one yugas passed there, of this there is no doubt.
And in that sacred field, he indeed became manifest before their eyes at that time.
Nṛsiṃha said:
"O Brahman, whatever you desire, I shall grant it to you; of this there is no doubt.
Then those two said to him: "If this boon is to be granted to us, [then let it be so]."
"May one like you become my son this very moment," he said;
but I replied, "In that case, I already have a son, so there would be a contradiction. (35)
For I am Viśvakarman, the manifest Supreme Self, higher than the highest;
I shall dwell within the womb, for I am indeed the eternal.
Hārīta then said: "Let it be so, there is no doubt;
from that time forward, I have remained on this earth for the sake of my devotees. (37)
Having come here, that best of devotees shall perform a vision [of me];
I shall incessantly destroy all his afflictions. (38)
For this very reason, O best of men, there exists no fear for those who perform the vow according to its various prescribed rites. (39)
Having meditated upon the form of the Child (Bāla) together with those two in a special manner,
he who performs worship at night shall become Nārāyaṇa himself.
Four-armed, with great fangs, possessing the form of Time (Kāla) and difficult to approach; resembling ten million suns and as unassailable as ten million Yamas;
his face like that of a lion and his limbs endowed with those of a man. ||41||
One should always worship Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the divine lion in the form of Time;
having understood this specifically, whoever goes to my abode [attains it]. (42)
This vow is supremely purifying, bestowing prosperity, granting great strength, and indeed bestowing liberation upon devotees; of this there is no doubt. (43)
By performing this vow on a Saturday in conjunction with the Svāti nakṣatra, one obtains the fruit of twelve thousand [repetitions] of the Vaikriya rite. 44.
The union with the yoga of accomplishment (*siddhiyoga*), likewise the application in the marketplace, and the conjunction with all yogas—this is the destroyer of ten million killings. (45)
A day joined with either of these destroys sin; he who, knowing this day to be such, would treat it as equal [to an ordinary day], is a doer of evil. (46)
One who does not perform [this] goes to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure;
therefore, having first performed circumambulation, one should always obtain my day on this very day. 47.
"Today, I, your devotee who has conquered his senses, shall perform my vow of observance before you; grant that it be free from obstacles. (48)
One observing a vow must avoid conversation with the wicked and similar activities;
thereafter, at the time of midday, one should [bathe] in pure water such as that of a river.
Whether at home, or at a shrine for the gods, or at a beautiful lake, a wise person should perform his bath with a Vedic mantra. (50)
One should bathe according to the prescribed rules with clay, cow dung, as well as with the fruit of the *adhātrī*, and with sesame seeds, for the sake of pacifying the entire flood of sins.
Having dressed oneself in beautiful garments, one should commence the daily rites;
then, having smeared the house, one should prepare an auspicious eight-petaled lotus.
Having placed there a copper pitcher provided with a cloth,
one should set upon it a vessel completely filled with rice.
And having fashioned there an image of me made of gold, accompanied by Lakṣmī,
one should bathe it with water and the five nectars using one's own power.
Then, having summoned a brahmin teacher who is not overly greedy and placing him at the forefront— one who is learned in the scriptures— he should worship the deity.
One should have a pavilion constructed there, adorned with clusters of flowers;
I am to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite with flowers produced in their respective seasons. (56)
He who [performs worship] with the sixteen services, with mantras, and with observances—therefore, he should especially be worshipped with the Purāṇic mantras. ||57||
Sandalwood mixed with camphor, combined with thick saffron, as well as flowers that bloom in the rainy season and tulasī leaves. ||58||
He who would offer incense made of black agallochum, which is always dear to Hari, to the illustrious Nṛsiṃha, is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (59)
One should offer [this] to Hari, the Guru, for the accomplishment of all desires and goals.
A great lamp should indeed be prepared to destroy the darkness of ignorance;
one should perform the Great Lustration (Mahānīrājana), preceded by the sounding of the bell.
O Beloved of Ramā, I offer you this food offering, including sugar and various kinds of eatables and edibles; please effect the destruction of all my sins. (61)
The mantra for the food offering (naivedya):
"O Nṛsiṃha, O Acyuta, O Lord of Gods! On this auspicious day of your birth, I shall observe a fast, renouncing all enjoyments. (62)
Therefore, O Lord, be pleased and dispel the sins of this birth;
a vigil should be observed at night with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
One should constantly read the Purāṇas centered on the narrative of the illustrious Nṛsiṃha;
thereafter, at the time of dawn, one should indeed perform the ritual bath.
Satisfying me according to the previously described procedure, one should worship me; with a mind fixed on my presence, one should perform a Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha in my presence.

Furthermore, for the sake of conquering both worlds, one should give to worthy recipients who possess true wisdom those gifts which are to be given and those which are not to be given, as will be described hereafter.
That god, made of gold, brings me great satisfaction;
he bestows cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and other gifts upon the twice-born.
A bed with a cotton mattress should be given, along with the seven types of grain;
other items should also be given according to one's ability and according to one's own means. (68)
One should not practice stinginess with wealth, for [the merit] resulting from what was prescribed would otherwise perish;
afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and give them excellent sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Even those who are destitute must perform this; it should be given according to one’s capacity.
All castes indeed have the right to this vow of mine, but it must be performed especially by my devotees who are solely intent upon me. (70)
Then, this prayer was offered:
"O Lord of Gods, deliver those born of my lineage and those humans who are yet to be born from the ocean of worldly existence which bestows suffering. (71)
For me, who am submerged in the ocean of sin, assailed by diseases that move within my body, overcome by living beings, and fallen into great suffering; (72)
O Lord of the World reclining upon Śeṣa, grant me the forest of Karāvala;
O Lord of Gods, by means of this vow, become the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (73)
Having thus prayed to the deity and dismissed him according to the prescribed rite,
one should offer all the sacrificial gifts and other items to the preceptor (ācārya).
Having satisfied the Brahmins with sacrificial fees, he should dismiss them;
then, absorbed in meditation upon me, he should eat together with his kinsmen.
Even one who possesses nothing, by fasting on the fourteenth day, is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever hears this vow, which destroys sins, with devotion, shall be cleansed of even the murder of a Brahmin merely by hearing it. (77)
Whatever human being recites this supreme, secret, and purifying [text],
he shall always obtain all his desires as the fruit of this vow.
By the grace of Śrī Nṛsiṃha, he performed this with the Ṛṣi together with Līlāvatī at the time known as midday through his own power. 79.
One who goes to that sacred field and worships Śrī Nṛsiṃha shall worship with supreme devotion and attain eternal liberation. ||80||
By the grace of Śrī Nṛsiṃha, one constantly obtains one's desires;

Salutations to you who are Bhairava, the destroyer of the afflictions of those who take refuge, and who possesses the form of a child; salutations to the glorious Nṛsiṃha, who is both the Supreme Form and the Child, appearing in the form of a youth.

Salutations to the one whose body is all-pervading and auspicious, who manifests his own form, whose body consists of all living beings, who is the Lord of the universe, and who is the self-sounding Ātman. 83.
Salutations to you, the lion of compassion residing within the orb of the sun;
salutations to you who possess twenty-four forms and whose nature is the fire of Kālarudra.
Salutations to you, Nṛsiṃha, whose singular form is the universe; the Lord Nṛsiṃha who bears [the mark] on his forehead and who conquered Vīrabhadra. 85.
There are twelve solar discs, intensely heated according to their proportions;
therein flows the meritorious river Siṃdhumaṃhā, which is especially beautiful.
Near it, O beautiful one, there exists even today a city renowned as Maulistāna, which was built by the gods at all times. (87)
The abode of the high-souled Hārīta is situated there;
Līlāvatī resides right there—of this there is no doubt. (88)
There, near the river Sindhu, there will be an echo;
for when the Kali age has arrived, the mlecchas will indeed be practitioners of sin.
Many indeed dwell there; of this there is no doubt.
Just as at the birth of Nṛsiṃha, a supreme and wondrous sound arose. (90)
When a man cries out loudly, "O Nṛsiṃha! O Nṛsiṃha!", a corresponding echo indeed arises in the mountains, the sky, and the quarters.

Whether they be killers of a Brahmin, stealers of gold, drinkers of liquor, or violators of the Guru’s bed—those people who, having gone to the Siṃdhu, perform their ablutions without distinction [are purified]. ||92||
One is liberated from this, there is no doubt, by the grace of the illustrious Nṛsiṃha;
indeed, such people exist among men for a duration of ten nights.
O you of meritorious deeds, know that my word is not false:
during the Kali age, the castes, with the twice-born at their head, shall dwell there. 94.
They should be known as outsiders to the Veda, like Mlecchas, by the best of the gods;
there they constantly ate my flesh and drank wine. (95)
Therefore, there is no doubt that these most wicked ones are of the nature of unrighteousness;
they are like Brahmins who have abandoned their twilight devotions and are likewise outside the Veda.
O Goddess of the Gods, in that city, in the western quarter, there dwells a single, supreme, and very extensive holy site known as Nṛsiṃha;
by hearing of it, a man is immediately liberated from sin—of this there is no doubt. (97)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Nṛsiṃha," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
The Greatness of the Gītā (175–192) (175)

That which yogis perceive in their hearts with an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, and which those who investigate intensely regard as the essence of the Vedas—[that is this]. (8)
Thus, this imperishable light is the nature of the Self, nameless, consisting of an unbroken mass of bliss, and devoid of duality. (9)

That upon which the world depends for its existence, that of which it is composed and through which it is experienced—there is nothing in the reality of the moving and unmoving world that is devoid of this principle. 10.
When the wise Dvaipāyana, having churned his intellect which had thoroughly scrutinized the Vedas and various sciences, composed the scripture of the Gītā, he bestowed it [upon the world]. 11.

Having heard these words of measured length from the enemy of Mura, Lakṣmī—her tremulous eyes wide with joy—was filled with wonder. (13)
Śrī said: "O Hṛṣīkeśa, you alone are always the object of meditation for those who practice self-restraint;

The attainment of the splendor of pure consciousness, the supreme bliss, the most excellent, the form of the Lord accessible through identity with the Self, as gloriously proclaimed in the Gītā. (18)

The Lord said: Having heard the words of Śrī, which were joined with historical narratives, the Master taught the Gītā, which provides a vision that follows after the Self.
I am the Self, the Supreme Lord, divided into two by the distinction between the higher and the lower; beyond that is the Witness, Śiva, who is devoid of qualities and partless.

When the five-faced Maheśvara became dependent upon practice,

Therefore, the wise person who practices even a single chapter, or half of it, or a single verse, or even half a verse, is liberated and attains supreme bliss. (29)
Śrī said: Who was he named Suśarman? O Goddess, what was his caste and what was his nature? From where did his liberation come, and by what cause did it arise? (30)
The Blessed Lord said:
There was one named Suśarman, of wicked intellect, who became the foremost among the evil-minded;
he was born into a lineage of Brahmins who were ignorant of the Self and performers of cruel deeds. (31)
Neither meditation, nor recitation, nor sacrifice, nor the honoring of guests—nothing but the objects of the senses alone proceed with his great strength. (32)
Constantly devoted to agricultural work, subsisting on leaves, and fond of liquor,
he spent a very long time in this manner, offering me oblations.
Desiring to fetch leaves, he wandered through the hermitage;
there, that man of deluded intellect was bitten by a black cobra.
Having met his end in due time and having gone to many hells, he returned once more to the world of mortals and attained the state of a bullock. (35)
Sold by his own father for five coins for the sake of his livelihood,
he spent seven or eight autumns leading [the oxen] on his back with great hardship.
Once, having been whirled around for a long time by the force of his speed, Pañcaguṇa fell violently to the ground and fell into a swoon. ||37||
With eyes turned toward the cows, vomiting forth a continuous stream of foam from his mouth, he was neither living nor did he meet death; he remained suspended by the power of his own karma.
In that gathering of people, where the world was drawn by curiosity, some meritorious person bestowed merit for the sake of his welfare. (39)
Some others, recollecting their own past deeds, gave [gifts];
there was also a courtesan staying there, who followed the ways of the world.
Unaware of her own merit, she had cast aside a small portion [of food], when she was led away by the servants of Time to the city of the departed. (41)
Released from the state of being "meritorious" by the merit given by the courtesan,
he returned once more to the world of mortals into the home of those endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct.
Remembering his own birth among the twice-born,
and desiring to know the truth after a long time, he sought that which brings about the cessation of his own ignorance for the sake of the highest good.
Having approached a courtesan and made it known that [the gift] had been given, he asked her;
she replied, "A parrot constantly recites this to me, for he is aged."
I purified myself with that [water] and mentally dedicated that merit to them;
then Śuka, being questioned by those two, began to explain.
Remembering an ancient narrative and his own previous birth, Śuka said:
"In the past, having been a learned man, I was deluded by the pride of my scholarship. (46)
Due to passion and hatred, I was envious even of those who were wise and possessed of good qualities;
consequently, after death, I attained worlds that are loathsome. (47)
Thus, I was born into the family of a Kīra as one who was exceedingly devoted to his virtuous guru;
yet, due to my evil karma, I was separated from my parents by Time. (48)
Exhausted by the heat on the road during the summer, I was brought here by the sages;
now, being old and weary, I have been placed in this hermitage, which provides great refuge. (49)
Having heard with reverence from the young sages the first chapter of the Gītās as they recited it, I repeated the lesson again and again. (50)
In the meantime, a certain hunter, a doer of thievish deeds, seized me and then sold me; such is the account related. (51)
The Blessed Lord said: This chapter was proclaimed of old by him through whom sin was dispelled;
it is by this that the best of the twice-born attained purification and liberated his own soul. 52.
Having thus addressed one another and praised his greatness, those wise women attained liberation while remaining in their homes, chanting his name night after night.
Therefore, for one who reads, hears, remembers, or practices this first chapter, the ocean of worldly existence—which is so difficult to cross—shall no longer exist. 54.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the dialogue between Satī and Īśvara, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||175||
(176) The one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter. The Blessed One said:
Thus has been proclaimed the unsurpassed narration of the first [chapter];
now listen as they proclaim the majesty of the other chapters as well. (1)
In the southern direction, in the city named Purandara, there lived one renowned as Devaśarman, a glorious master of the Vedas among those who proclaim the Āmnāya. ||2||
He honored guests, was learned in the Vedas and Shastras,
performed multitudes of sacrifices, and was always dear to ascetics.
For a long time, that righteous-souled one gratified the gods with oblations and the fire-god with offerings; yet, he did not obtain even a single moment of peace or tranquility therefrom.
Desiring to know the means to the supreme good, he daily attended upon ascetics whose resolves were true,
providing them with no small amount of requisites.
As he was practicing in this manner, a great deal of time passed;
then, at one point in the past, a certain man who had been liberated from karma appeared on earth.
With his desire for experience dispelled, his eyes fixed upon the tip of his nose,
his mind tranquil, he meditated upon the Supreme Brahman, overflowing with bliss.
Having clasped his feet with a bowed body and a humble heart,
the learned man performed for him the hospitable rites due to a guest according to the prescribed rules.
And bowing down to that ascetic who was content with his own pure state, he inquired about the attainment of nirvāṇa for himself. (9)
He told this story to his friend Ajāpāla, who was named Purana and was a teacher of self-knowledge.
Having approached the feet of that illustrious one, he went toward the mighty city;
in the northern part of it, he beheld a vast forest.
The breeze from the Māruta mountain, wafting the exquisite fragrance of many swaying flowers,
filled the quarters of the sky with the songs of intoxicated bees.
Then, as he was sitting on that stone slab on the bank of the river in the forest,
he saw his friend Sānanda, whose eyes were closed in meditation.
Even while the sun was shining, this garden was filled with beings who, having abandoned their natural enmity, were at peace with one another. 14.
With a desire to subdue the ten-faced one, he who was tranquil toward the herds of deer drenched the earth with his nectar-like compassion. 15.
Approaching him with humility, his mind uplifted and his heart full of joy, he was likewise honored by that king, who bowed his head slightly.
Then the wise one, with undistracted mind, attended upon his friend Maitreya;
when the time for meditation had concluded, he questioned him with full composure.
Devasharman said:
"I desire to know the Self; therefore, you ought to instruct me in the means for attaining success in this my aspiration. (18)
The Blessed Lord said:
Having reflected for a moment, that Mitravan spoke as follows.
Mitravan said:
O learned one, understand this ancient account as it is being told by me.
On the banks of the Godāvarī, there was a city named Pratiṣṭhāna;
therein lived one named Durdama, born in a lineage of wise men.
There, a king named Astivikrama reigned;
though he received gifts every day, he lived as one who merely filled his belly.
Bound by the noose of Time, he was led to the abode;
having experienced torments in all the hells. (22)
Born into a certain family of ill-behaved twice-born men,
you were preceded by a knowledge that followed the ways of worldly existence.
He married that unassailable maiden from a lowly family;
in time, she left childhood behind and reached youth.
With full breasts, beautiful hips, and eyes unsteady with intoxication,
she could not endure her ill-behaved husband and desired other men besides her own.
Desiring to obtain a livelihood, she went out from this city long ago and united with a man of Cāṇḍāla birth who was seeking a lover.
She conceived a child from him, and thus she was born as a maiden;
yet, due to the persistence of her former sins, she became his wife.
In time, from that very old Śaiva, an Ḍākinī was born;
through evil association and contact with wicked women, she became one of corrupt mind. (28)
Lusting for the taste of blood, she devoured a diseased hunter;
wandering through a terrible forest, she was seen by people and cast out.
Having reached the world of the departed, he encountered a tiger in his illness, as a result of the power of his violence toward living beings after having experienced terrible hells. (30)
In the course of time, that evil-minded woman, having encountered the onset of death, went to hell and was reborn as my daughter, Durddharṣa, in my house. (31)
O learned one, while I was protecting her as we crossed the forest,
I saw a fierce tiger that seemed intent on devouring everything.
Behold the herd of goats, which has fled in terror from the illusion, abandoning its mother out of fear for her life. (33)
Remembering his former enmity, the tiger rushed toward him;
remembering that [enmity], he went quickly to the bank of the river in its vicinity.
Thereupon, having cast off fear and abandoned hostility without restraint, he remained as a protector of the island, silent and free from envy. (35)
Beholding him in such a state, he began to speak:
"O tiger, lift me up with respect and eat me as you desire. (36)
"How is it that this wisdom has not occurred to you, that you abandon your hostile intent?
Having heard these words, the leopard, free from malice, spoke.
In this place, both fatigue and the distress of hunger and thirst have departed;
therefore, I do not request you, though you are standing close at hand.
Thus addressed, she spoke again: "How have I become fearless? You know what the cause here is; you ought to tell me. (39)
Having been addressed thus, Dvīpin said again, "I do not know;
I shall go forth to ask this great being who stands before us. Thus they both departed. 40.
Having approached them both, I was questioned with great astonishment;
and together with them, I questioned the lord of the monkeys. (41)
Being thus questioned by me, the monkey spoke this with reverence:
