"Listen, I shall relate here the ancient account of Ajāpāla."
Behold this great sacred precinct situated before the forest;
here indeed is the Bakaliṅga established by Brahmā. 43.
A wise man named Sukarman, practicing austerities, gathered forest flowers and approached Purojava, who was worthy of worship by the gods. 44.
Having bathed in the waters of the river and having completed his ritual duties,
after a long time, a certain guest arrived at his hermitage.
Having brought forth food consisting of fruits, he prepared it for him;
pleased by that hospitality, he addressed Sukarman.
What is this root of action that you persist in after having enjoyed its fruit?
Or do you strive for it solely out of the habit of following others? (47)
Thus addressed by that knower of the self who was for the most part pleased,
he then replied with clear words that were excellent and beneficial to himself.
O learned one, the fruit of this action is the state of not knowing that [Brahman]; by which [action], another person, desiring to know, serves Śambhu solely for that purpose. (49)
This is the fruit of serving the one with matted hair (Kapardin):
that you have favored me by touching my heart's desire.
Having heard these truthful words of his, the ascetic was pleased;
he then inscribed a second chapter of the Gītā upon the surface of the rock.
He quickly commanded the brahmin to recite and practice it, saying:
"Your own desire will surely bear fruit all around. (52)
Having spoken thus, the wise one vanished while he looked on;
and, filled with wonder, he remained there incessantly following his instructions.
Then, after a long time, his self was purified and his intellect became serene;
wherever he wandered, that very place became a peaceful grove of asceticism.
Know that for one who recites this second chapter, there is neither cold nor heat, nor hunger nor thirst, nor even fear, all because of his austerity. 55.
Mitravān said:
Having been addressed thus by him, and after I had related another story,
I was permitted by his grace to depart together with the goat and the tiger.
Having gone there, he saw the *Madhyama* written upon a stone slab;
by reciting it, he attained the supreme perfection of his penance. (57)
Therefore, you too, O auspicious one, ought to practice this constantly;
by it, liberation will not remain far away for you. (58)
Commanded by Devaśarman, he himself, having honored and bowed down to that Tena-mitravat, went to the city of Purandara.
Having approached a knower of the Self there in a certain temple of a deity and first reported this occurrence, he then recited that chapter.
Having purified his soul through that training and reciting the chapter with devotion,
he reached the second, supreme, and faultless state.
This narrative of the second has been told; listen now with attention.
Furthermore, O Indra, I shall speak of the majesty of the third as well.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the dialogue between Satī and Īśvara, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(177) The one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter. The Blessed Lord said:
In Janasthāna, there was a twice-born man named Jaḍa, a descendant of Kauśika;
having abandoned the dharma appropriate to his caste, he set his mind upon the livelihood of a merchant. (1)
Addicted to the wives of others, gambling with dice, drinking wine,
and constantly devoted to hunting, he thus passed his time.
Then, when his wealth was exhausted, he began to practice theft at night;
by means of that, he obtained the riches of those who were performing sacrifices and seeking to offer them.
He traveled a great distance to the northern direction for the purpose of trade,
[bringing] musk, aloe-wood, black [sandalwood], and yak-tail fans as bright as mountains.
Having taken it, he returned and brought it from a distance of five yojanas;
then, on another day, while he was suffering from the pain of not seeing his beloved, [the king] said: ||| 5 ||
When the sun had set after traversing the long path,
darkness spread freely through the ten directions beneath the trees.
Having fallen under the power of the Sadasyus, he was swiftly struck down by them;
due to that lapse in dharma, he became a terrible and most fierce graha.
Thirsty and afflicted by hunger, licking the corners of his mouth,
with hair standing erect, exceedingly emaciated, and possessing a large belly clinging to his back.
His body became mere skin and bone, and his eyes were deeply distressed by wicked conduct;
at that time, his son was virtuous and well-versed in the Vedas.
He protected [him] exceedingly; desiring to see him, he came there, constantly seeking news from the villagers but not obtaining it. ||10||
Then, once when his companion, the son of Manu, had arrived, he,
having learned the news from him, grieved greatly for his father.
Then, having reflected and desiring to perform what pertains to the next world, the wise man,
equipped with the necessary provisions, set out to go to Vārāṇasī.
Having traveled seven or eight stages along the road,
he proceeded to perform his twilight devotions at the foot of that tree where his father had been slain.
There, he recited the third chapter of the *Gītās*, which destroys all sins;
then, with a terrible voice, he struck out into the midst of the sky.
Then he beheld his father falling from the sky, a terrifying sight;
his consciousness was overwhelmed by both wonder and fear. (15)
He beheld before him in the sky a vast expanse pervaded by splendor;
it was filled with millions of tinkling bells, and its every direction was suffused with light.
He of supreme intellect beheld a celestial chariot before him;
there he saw [his father] seated, surrounded by divine women.
Beholding his father, who was dressed in yellow garments and being praised by the sages, he bowed down and joined him with a benediction.
Then he asked about this event, and he (the sage) explained it to him:
"It was due to the cause of merit from the calf-form, even though that action was difficult to abandon. (19)
"By chance, I have been liberated by you while reciting this chapter in your presence; therefore, desist from your recitation, for the time has now arrived for you. (20)
"That for which he went to Vārāṇasī—that which he has performed for himself—the Lord spoke;
thus addressed, he replied to his father of radiant splendor. (21)
Suta said: "Having instructed me in what is beneficial, what else remains for me to do?
The Blessed Lord said:
Then the father said to his son: "O sinless one, this task must be performed by you."
"Whatever deed was committed by me, that was done by my brother;
he has gone to a terrible hell, and you ought to release him. (23)
"Others in this lineage have indeed fallen into hell;
it is my heart’s desire that they too shall be liberated. (24)
Thus addressed, the son, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him again:
"By what action may I liberate all of them? Please instruct me. (25)
When he had thus addressed these words, the father spoke to his son.
The father said:
"O child, you ought to perform that by which I have been liberated."
Having performed that [practice], dedicate the merit arising from it to them;
then, like me, they all shall abandon their torments.
"I shall go very soon indeed to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Being thus instructed, the son said, "If it is so, O father, [then] regarding the denizens of hell..."
"I shall liberate all of them as well, if such is your word;
let it be so—may there be auspiciousness, for this great favor is most welcome. (29)
Having thus instructed his son, he departed for the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
he too, having turned back from there, reached Janasthāna.
Then, at the command of his father, Sunda set out for the city of Śauri, arriving there at the appointed time;
he performed everything exactly as had been instructed by his father.
He performed meritorious acts at Utsarasa with the intent of liberating those in hell—
those who, in this very interval, had fallen into the state of torment belonging to Viṣṇu.
Thinking, "I shall liberate those in hell," why have they come to me?
Therefore, they were all honored by him with various kinds of hospitable rites.
Being questioned about their welfare, they all spoke of universal happiness; then that wise lord of the world of the ancestors, having honored him, [spoke]. (34)
They asked him about the reason for his arrival and informed him of it;
"Know, O Lord of the Kīnāśas, that you are reclining upon the serpent Śeṣa. (35)
"Sent by Śauri to instruct us in your presence, the Lord asks after your welfare through our mouth. (36)
"And he restrains himself in order to liberate all sentient beings in the hells.
Having heard this command of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor, [he acted accordingly]. (37)
With his head bowed in salutation, he reflected with his mind upon something inconceivable,
beholding all those [beings] who had been liberated from hell and were now intoxicated with pride.
Then, followed by all those virtuous ones, he went by an excellent vehicle to the abode of Viṣṇu,
where the Ocean of Milk was situated.
Then he beheld the Teacher of the World, whose radiance was equal to many tens of millions of blazing suns, and who was dark-complexioned like the petals of a blue lotus. 40.
His splendor was intermingled with the rays from the jewels on the hoods of the serpents serving as his couch;
he was being gazed upon with intense joy by Ananda, whose mind was filled with delight.
It was gazed upon repeatedly with eyes that were false to appearances yet followed the true nature of things, by Śrī and Premā;
it was attended on all sides by yogis whose pupils had become fixed through meditation.
He was being praised by Mahendra, who was unable to overcome his adversaries,
with the words of the Vedas issuing from his mouth.
His multitude of virtues was being sung by embodied words;
he was both fully pleased and yet indifferent toward all states of existence.
For those who have accumulated merit through yoga, there arises simultaneously a vision of themselves as the Self, encompassing the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings.
He gladdened himself with his own splendors filled with radiance,
bearing a body that pervaded and was illuminated by the luster of the serpent.
Beholding him, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, like the sky illuminated by moonlight, she bowed with a vast and satisfied mind. (47)
Yama said:
Salutations to the Creator, whose mind has become purified by all acts of creation, who has vomited forth the Vedas from his mouth, and who is the universal form. 48.

Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is established in strength, whose impetuosity is difficult to withstand, who is hostile toward the lord of the Dānavas, who abides in goodness, and who is the support of the universe. 49.
Salutations to the conqueror of the multitude of sins of all embodied beings,
whose flames arise from the fire of the slightly opened eye on his forehead.
For you are the teacher, the self, and the supreme lord of the entire world;
having set aside all the Vaiṣṇavas, you show compassion toward us. 51.
Pervading the entire world with his expanded māyā, you are neither overcome by that [māyā] nor by the qualities (guṇas) produced from it. ||52||
Even while moving within the tree, you are not overcome by those two eyes directed toward their objects, even though your mind has not been restrained. (53)
Through that [attainment] which leads to the fruit, you dissolve into the Self alone;
there is no limit to your own greatness, just as [the ocean] itself is boundless.
"Silence alone is appropriate for me here; how can you be an object for my words?
Having thus praised him, he then spoke these words with palms joined in reverence.
"O Teacher of the World, since I am devoid of qualities and free from attachment due to this application [of yoga], there is another purpose for me; please instruct me in it. (56)
Having been thus informed by him, Madhusūdana addressed him with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, sprinkling him with the nectar of his words.
The world shall be uplifted from evil by me, who abide by my vow; having entrusted the burden to you, I do not grieve for embodied beings. (58)
"Performing your own duties, go now to your own abode.
The Blessed One said:
"Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished, and he too returned to his own city. (59)
He too, having repeatedly uplifted all those born of his own lineage who were situated in hell,
went himself to the world of Viṣṇu by means of the supreme vehicle.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(178) The one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter. The Blessed Lord said:
Now I shall proclaim the majesty of the fourth [tīrtha] as well; listen.
By which [act], having abandoned the state of being a jujube tree, the maiden went to heaven. (1)
Śrī said:
"O God, how did the maiden go to heaven after indeed relinquishing her state as a jujube fruit? What were those two like formerly, and how did she attain preeminence?"
I wish to know this; O Lord, you ought to speak it.
Indeed, I am not satiated while hearing this supreme narrative. (3)
The Blessed Lord said: On the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, there is a city named Vārāṇasī;
there, in the abode of Viśveśvara, dwells one named Bharata, whose mind is disciplined.
Constantly delighting in the Self, he devotedly recites the fourth state as his meditation;
through that practice, the pure-souled one is not overcome by dualities.
Once, while sporting at a certain time, that ascetic went outside the city,
desiring to see the gods who dwell upon Mount Ujjayanta.
Having rested at the foot of those two banyan trees, he fell upon their fruit;
leaning against one, he supported the other with his arm, which was scorched by the sun's heat.
When those two ascetic women had departed,
both Badarī and Ārdrā became withered and leafless within five or six days.
Then, in the house of certain Brahmins, two daughters were born;
that pair grew for seven full years.
Having approached from nearby regions, he beheld that ascetic;
taking hold of his feet, he spoke these truthful words.
"By your grace alone, this pair has been liberated;
casting off their state as jujube fruits, they shall attain human form. (11)
Thus addressed by them, the sage, having forgotten [them], replied: "When will you two come again? For what reason were you not recognized by me? (12)
"Tell me the reason for both of you being jujube fruits; I do not know it. The two maidens told him the reason for their own state as jujube fruits.
At the very beginning, for the sake of liberation from this cause which is so difficult to abandon, there exists on the banks of the Godāvarī a sacred ford that bestows merit upon men. (14)
Known as Chinnapāpa, he attained the highest pinnacle;
there, one named Satyatapas performed most rigorous penance.
In summer, he stood in the midst of great blazing fires;
in the rainy season, his hair was constantly drenched by torrents of water.
In the cold season, wearing wet clothes and bearing a body covered in bristling horripilation, the self-restrained sage, remaining pure, constantly performed austerities at that time. ||17||
Having attained perfect peace, he fixed his mind upon the Self alone,
like a bird resting in trees that bear fruit in all seasons and provide excellent shade.
Having bound even supreme joy to beings who are free from envy, it was brought about by his skill in pursuing the fruits of asceticism. (19)
Brahmā himself would approach him every day, questioning him; because he was free from any sense of contraction, Brahmā followed after him daily.
For his asceticism increased as he followed those meditations,
considering himself almost liberated from his own exalted state.
Then, terrified by that hundredfold obstacle,
Purandara summoned us from among the Apsarases and commanded us equally.
"Both of you must create an obstacle to that penance performed by him—he who, seizing me by the foot, desires to enjoy my kingdom. (23)
Having received this message in the presence of Indra,
we went to the Godāvarī, where the sage was residing.
With soft, sweet-sounding flutes made of clay, stone, and bamboo,
a melodious song was commenced, accompanied by slender voices.
Carrying her broad-hipped form, with thick and full breasts,
her face smiling with a smile, and her curls slightly disheveled, she was borne by the Bhoja king.
She was adorned with jeweled earrings, her eyes were radiant like white lotuses, she possessed a slender waist and well-rounded thighs, and her two feet were even and beautiful.
She showed him the entire course of youth, following the movements of emotion, accompanied by the rhythm of notes, beats, and tempo.
As those two were dancing, the sound "maṃ daṃ maṃ daṃ," which had arisen with a gentle onset and was gradually increasing, caused the entire circle of the quarters to roar.
Then, with the force of her sighs, a very cool breeze [blew] through her garments;
as her clothes were slightly raised, she revealed her breasts.
Increasing our intense pride with their fierce gait,
they provoked the anger of the sage whose mind was otherwise unchanging.
Then, out of anger, he cast water with his hand and uttered a curse:
"O two [trees], you shall both become jujube trees on the banks of the Jāhnavī. (32)
"We two have committed a three-year transgression; O Sage, please forgive us who are bowed down in humility. Thus he was later propitiated.
Then the sage of meritorious intellect, with the truthfulness that "the waters shall flow upon the arrival of Bharata," ordained the release from our curse.
Among mortals, there was the attainment of birth and the recollection of past lives; then, having gone to our hermitage at Badarī, we both became trees. (35)
"O Smara, you have performed atonement for the offense committed against the four [gods];
therefore, we bow to you, not merely because of the curse. (36)
"You have liberated Ghorādevī from this terrible saṃsāra.
The Blessed One said: "Having been addressed thus by the two of them, the sage was then exceedingly pleased in mind. (37)
Having worshipped the Tathāgata Amitābha, he departed;
those two maidens should daily recite the fourth chapter with devotion. (38)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(179) The one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter. The Blessed One said:
O Goddess, beloved, I shall now describe in brief the majesty of the fifth [chapter], which is honored by the world; listen with focused attention.
O twice-born one, there was a man named Piṅgala in the city of Purukutsa; he was born into a distinguished family of renowned Vedic scholars. ||2||
Having abandoned the scriptures appropriate for his family as well as the Vedas,
he set his mind upon the triple symphony of music, playing drums and other instruments.
Having exerted himself there in singing, dancing, and instrumental music,
he attained supreme renown and entered the royal palace.
Formerly, this king lived with that virtuous woman in a state of equality;
having taken another's wife, he enjoyed her with undivided attention.
Then, his pride swollen and his mind agitated,
Kuśa incessantly sought out the faults of that very person in private.
He had a wife named Aruṇā, born of a noble family.
Wandering about at night in search of her, she who was sporting with her lover perceived her own home as a dense forest.
Having severed his heads, he struck them down upon the surface of the earth;
deprived of life by him, the demon departed for the abode of Yama.
Having experienced difficult-to-conquer hells, he was born as a vulture in a lonely forest;
she too, having abandoned her inferior body due to a disease that destroyed her virility, [was born there].
Having approached the terrible hells, that parrot in the forest saw her,
who was wandering here and there, desiring to take some grains.
Remembering his enemy, the vulture, he tore at her with his sharp talons;
then, she fell into a human skull filled with milk. ||12||
The vulture also rushed toward its own slayer, and he [the hunter] was captured by the netters;
then, separated from his wife, he lost his life in the waters of the human-skull lake.

Right there, that exceedingly cruel bird dove into it; led by the servants of Yama, he reached the world of the ancestors. Remembering their previously committed evil deed, both of them became partakers of the consequences.
Then Yama, beholding their loathsome deed, [reflected]:
"By this very act of bathing, a great merit has been produced for death. (15)
He permitted these two to go to their desired world,
for their minds were invincible even by the multitudes of great sins.
Then, filled with wonder and remembering their own misdeed,
they approached Vaivasvata, bowed down, and questioned him.
The evil deeds accumulated by us both in the past are now censured;
tell us, therefore, what is the cause for the desires of the world? (18)
Thus addressed by the two of them, Vaivasvata then spoke these words:
"Having realized the eternal Brahman by means of the path known as Gaṅgātaṭa. (19)
Solitary, free from the sense of "mine," peaceful, devoid of passion, and without envy, he constantly recites the fifth chapter of the Gītā. (20)
Purified by that merit and having realized the eternal Brahman,
even though he had been a sinner, he heard this and cast off his body.
Having obtained that water from his skull-cup, you two shall attain purity, for your bodies have been cleansed and your souls purified by the Gītās. 22.
Therefore, go you both to those worlds situated on the path of your desires,
having been purified by the greatness of the fifth chapter of the Gītā.
Thus enlightened and gladdened by that Samavartin,
the two ascended a celestial vehicle and went to the abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(180) The one hundred and eightieth chapter. The Blessed Lord said:
O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall proclaim the majesty of the sixth chapter, by hearing which liberation lies within the very palms of men. (1)
O lady with smiling eyes, there is a great city named Pratiṣṭhāna on the banks of the Godāvarī, where I reside under the name Pippaleśa.
There, by the cool sprays from the banks of the Godāvarī scattered by the flapping of the wings of swans,
the fatigue of those observing the vow of silence was dispelled.
The waters of the Godāvarī, made fragrant by the pollen from the calyxes of rows of blooming lotuses, are praiseworthy; by means of them, men become like gods. 4.

"Alas, O lords of sages, upon the wives of the great Maratha kings—who were like the very wives of the moon, the lord of medicinal herbs—there fell a calamity that caused their decline and destruction. (5)
There, they touched faces that resembled blooming lotuses,
where great kings played, their jeweled earrings jingling as they moved.
He [beheld] the faces of celestial women sporting on the peaks of exceedingly lofty palaces, which surpassed the beauty of the ascetics whose minds were absorbed in the three sounds of Hara.
Where, day after day, the deer-skin cloak of [the ascetic] wears thin as he gazes upon the rays of the great jewels on the high balconies of the palaces. (8)
In that place, the winds from the fluttering banners— blown by the gusts of air— carried the fragrance of *cūta*, *campaka*, *muni-gandha*, *dūrvā*, and *candana* flowers.
There were vehicles for those whose fatigue had vanished, as well as elephants and horses;
and there were countless groups of merchants with heaps of sandalwood from the Malaya mountains.
On which the Malaya mountain is seen reduced to nothing but its stones;
and where even the pearls are seen as mere lifeless objects.
There, a lord of the earth named Jñānaśruti reigned, who was like a cluster of flower-buds for the laughter of the city’s tutelary deities on all sides. 12.
Upon whom this Śeṣa supports the earth, which resembles a jewel,
even amidst the intense brilliance of the solar orb of his majesty.
The Kalpa trees, eternally darkened by the smoke of the sacrifices,
appear as if out of shame at his extraordinary generosity.
The garments of the gods did not abandon the city of Pratiṣṭhāna even slightly, as they were fully satisfied by the taste of chewing the sacrificial *puroḍāśa* cakes.
Upon whom the clouds, nourished by the streams of his charity, the moonlight of his majesty, and the smoke of his sacrifices, rained down incessantly at the proper season.
While he ruled the earth, calamities did not find a foothold even for a moment, nor did political intrigues find any scope to spread.
Under the pretext of inspecting the ponds, wells, and tanks every day,
he searched for the treasures hidden in the earth that were located within his heart.
His palace, shining with white banners, gleams like the Himalaya mountain with its peaks reaching toward the sky. (19)
Pleased by his gifts, austerities, sacrifices, and protection of his subjects, the inhabitants of heaven assembled to grant him a boon.
Then, shaking their wings,
those divine swans, white as lotus stalks, emerged from the goddess and departed by way of the sky.
As they were approaching in haste and conversing with one another,
two or three of them, led by Bhadrāśva, went forth quickly from the front.
As they all gathered together, they said to him who was departing with speed:
"How is it that you have gone forth with such velocity, while we remain standing before you? (23)
"All of you must proceed together along this difficult path;
do you not see the mass of light shining clearly before you? (24)
Having clearly heard these words of King Jñānaśruti, whose very form was merit, those standing behind him spoke properly to those in front. (25)
Having insulted him, they spoke these words loudly and irreverently to the one named Raikya,
whose splendor was invincible and who was a teacher of the Veda.
"Is the majesty of this King Jñānaśruti even more intense?"—
thus did I hear the voices of the sages, O King, concerning Jñānaśruti.
Having ascended a very lofty palace and remaining there comfortably, the king, filled with wonder, then summoned his charioteer. (28)
That high-souled one gave this command: "Let Raikya be brought here.
Then, having reflected upon the king’s words, which were filled with the nectar of wisdom, [he set out].
The charioteer named Mahas, spreading joy, set forth for the city named Vārāṇasī, which bestows liberation. (30)
Where the Lord of the Universe, the Teacher and Master of the World, resides—
namely at that sacred field called Gayā where the God who wields the mace (Viṣṇu) dwells.
With eyes wide open in joy, he dwells there in order to uplift all the worlds;
thereafter, by means of all the various holy sites (tīrthas), he resides at the side of Gaurī’s father.
I traveled to where Kedāra, the destroyer of sins, is located;
by beholding him even once, mortals shall be liberated—of this there is no doubt. (33)
Freed from great sins and having enjoyed pleasures as desired,
he then departed for Gauḍa, where Puruṣottama resides.
By the mere sight of whom gods and men go to their own celestial worlds;
from there he went to the city of Dvāravatī, which bestows liberation. (35)
Having bathed at the Gomatī-tīrtha and beheld the five Kṛṣṇas, [he went] where Hari, the beloved of Rukmiṇī, resides on the bank of the Gomatī.
A mortal attains liberation after having enjoyed pleasures as desired;
then, having reached the ocean and beheld Somanātha, [he is liberated].
Then the wise one departed from that god who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
and reached the city of Avantikā, which likewise grants enjoyment and liberation.
Where Mahākāla, the bestower of welfare, sports with Umā in happiness;
having reached the syllable Oṃ on the bank of the Narmadā,
which grants joy and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, he departed from there with haste.
Then, wandering through the city named Aśvamedhaka,
he reached the place where Śārṅgadhara, the Lord of Lakṣmī himself, was personally present.
Then Viṣṇu arrived at Gayā, reaching the pool known as Loṇāra;
having bathed and drunk there, a person is liberated from bondage. (41)
From there he went toward Rudragayā, known as Kolhāpura,
where the blessed Goddess Lakṣmī resides, bestowing her grace upon her devotees.
Having bathed in the Pañcanadī river and beheld Mahālakṣmī, a man enjoys pleasures according to his desire and attains devotion. ||43||
Then, having reached the city named Amalagiri and having ascended Mount Nandikeśvara, [he arrived where] Somanātha is located.
Upon seeing the four-armed Lord Śiva, Somanātha, intent on granting boons, liberation certainly comes to men; of this there is no doubt. (45)
Then, having beheld Harihara on the bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā river, whose arms fall upon the circle of the earth in every age; 46.
Beholding which, all men perceive the beautiful form of Hari-Hara; having enjoyed pleasures according to their desire, those men are liberated from bondage. 47.
Having remained in heaven for a hundred kalpas, their bonds to saṃsāra being released,
they then beheld their Lord, the all-pervading Sovereign of the worlds.
Beholding this, men never again see hell;
having remained in heaven for a hundred kalpas, they are liberated from the latent tendencies of saṃsāra. (49)
They shall grant liberation; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Then, having reached Śrīśaila, which is frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, [he should proceed]. (50)
There, the beloved of Girijā, known by the name Mallinātha, [resides] in order to deliver all the worlds from the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra. 51.
Having remained in heaven for a hundred kalpas, those whose bonds of saṃsāra have been released shall attain liberation; therefore, no deliberation is required in this matter. (52)
Then, having reached Śrīśaila, which is frequented by siddhas and gandharvas,
there resides the beloved of Girijā known by the name Mallinātha.
To uplift all worlds from the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra,
he himself reveals the supreme light from time to time.
Even for those men who were looking on and even for those who were mindful of Yama,
the torments of hell remained far away, yet they were terrified as if standing at a great distance from them.
Having enjoyed happiness in the heavenly world and being freed from the bonds of saṃsāra, those men shall attain liberation; of this there is no doubt. (56)
Rāma, along with his younger brother and Jānakī, also went there;
having bathed and drunk [the water] there, one is certainly liberated from hell. 57.
Having enjoyed the happiness of the heavenly realm for hundreds of millions of eons,
men who have abandoned the path of saṃsāra attain liberation without a doubt.
Returning from there and arriving, he beheld on the bank of the Bhīmarathī the two-armed Lord Viṭṭhala, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||59||
There is the birthplace of the Godāvarī, the great Brahmagiri,
and having reached the abode of Gautama, there dwells Tryambaka, the destroyer of Baka.
Between the Aruṇā and the Varuṇā, where the river Godāvarī flows—
having bathed and drunk there, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is dissolved.
Having beheld Abrahmagiri, which is endowed with innumerable sacred fords (tīrthas), men attain liberation itself and are freed from the suffering of saṃsāra. (62)
O Gautamī, eager to seek out sacred fords situated on both banks,
Sūta then departed for Mathurā, the destroyer of sins.
Wherein gods, asuras, and humans worship the divine Svāyambhuva;
that is the primordial, great abode of the Blessed One, which bestows liberation.
It is renowned in the Vedas and Shastras as the birthplace of the Lord of the Three Worlds;
it is frequented by various hosts of gods and served by throngs of the best of the twice-born.
He who shines like a half-moon adorning the banks of the Kālindī, who is the sole full moon dwelling in all sacred fords (tīrthas), and who bestows fearlessness. 66.
Resembling Mount Govardhana, it is covered with holy trees and creepers;
it is the highly meritorious forest of the twelve [sages], which bears the essence of the sacred scriptures for rest.
Then he beheld the city of Kaśmīra to the north-west;
thereafter, he saw the field of Kurukṣetra, level and a sacred site bearing the weight of Dharma.
There, rows of cloud-kissing mansions,
white as the moon, appeared like the manifest outbursts of the loud laughter of Śiva.
It was adorned with golden pitchers for the garlands of grace bestowed by devotion,
like golden lotuses fallen from the hands of celestial nymphs, shaken by the winds.
On the pinnacle of the palace, blue silk banners appeared like creeping vines of the celestial river,
resembling circles of moss.
If the Goddess of Speech does not dwell eternally there, having taken refuge in Kashmir, then how could she write this scripture all at once? (72)
These [beings], languid from intoxication, have long been resting at the banks of the Sarasvatī;
they move about with their vehicles, carrying lotus stalks and betel leaves.
Then, in order to discern the specific skill of the one who had sent forth the arrow, Vīrañcī, like Tārā, shone forth; she then approached them all together.
The land-lotuses were visible there, along with the pleasures of the touch of their hands;
and the couches and seats provided by the enemy of the Dānavas were arranged therein.
Where the eloquent discourses of the twice-born were clearly not heard,
even a mute celestial became a master of the surging waves of speech through his words.
The circle of the sky, pervaded by the smoke of his sacrificial rites, does not even now lose its blackness, though it has been washed by the clouds. (77)
Where the place of the nectar that had fallen was seen in the moon under the guise of frost, due to the great radiance of the sacrifice.
By the power of practice from birth, even the young recite [the scriptures] by themselves; for there, relying on the presence of their teachers, they master all the arts.
Where the "kaṃ-kaṇa" sounds and "huṃ-kṛtis" of the wives of Brahmins daily resound, there the humming of wandering bees is like the cry of "luṃ. (80)
Where the wind blows gently, repeatedly touching the surface of the cheeks of the wives of non-Brahmins, as if out of fear of their curse. (81)
There, the god named Māṇikyeśvara, who has Śītāṃśu as his crest-jewel, dwells daily for the sake of granting boons to embodied beings. 82.
Having conquered the venerated kings and being honored by Maṇikeśa, he thereafter assumed the name Māṇikyeśvara. (83)
Since he was highly honored with rubies and abundant riches by the King, the Lord of Kashmir, who was celebrating his conquest of the quarters; ||84||
He saw Tārā sitting upon the cart, resting in its shade, scratching her limbs as she sat there. ||85||
Recognizing him instantly by those various signs described by the king,
the charioteer bowed down and, having saluted Raikva, spoke to him.
The charioteer said:
"O Brahmin, who are you and what is your name? You appear so pure and exceedingly tranquil. For what purpose have you come here to rest, and what do you intend to do? (87)
Having heard those words and being filled with supreme joy, he remembered his charioteer and said, "Now our desires are fulfilled. (88)
Furthermore, there must be someone who performs extensive service, knowing very well our state of mind. (89)
Taking with him that which resided in his heart, out of respect for the intention of oneness,
he slowly departed from where the lord of the earth remained.
Then, having prostrated before the king, the charioteer, joyful at the sight of his master, joined his palms in reverence and reported everything exactly as it had happened. (91)
Then, having heard those words, the king, his eyes smiling with wonder,
became full of faith in the practice of the realization of identity.
Taking a small cart yoked with a pair of mules, as well as pearl necklaces, silken garments, and a thousand cows, the king departed. (93)
That yogi went to Kashmir, where he was received by the king;
having informed him of this, the king prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before him.

"O wicked lord, you have insulted me with harsh words out of anger toward the King, even though I am a Śūdra who has attained my status through supreme devotion to the two [Viṣṇu and Śiva]. You do not know my conduct. (95)
"Take this cart yourself, having raised it up along with the mules; take also the garments, the pearl necklaces, the cows, and even the milch-cows. (96)
Having thus commanded, the lord of the earth felt fear regarding their unity;
then, out of fear of a curse, the king [offered] his pair of lotus-feet.
Accepting it with devotion, he himself said, "O Brahmin, may you be pleased. ||98||
The king said:
"O Blessed One, from where does this most wonderful greatness of your praise come?
O Blessed One, being gracious, please explain this to me according to its true nature. (99)
Raikya said:
"O King, I recite the sixth chapter of the Gītā every day;
by that alone, this mass of splendor of mine has become unbearable even for the gods. (100)
By diligently practicing the sixth chapter of the Gītā with one-pointed concentration, the wise King Jñānaśruti attained liberation. 101.
Raikya also attained happiness in the presence of Lord Māṇikyeśvara, chanting the sixth chapter of the Gītā, which bestows liberation. (102)
Having assumed the guise of crows, even the inhabitants of heaven came forth at will to grant a boon, filled with wonder. ||103||
If a person should constantly recite even this single chapter, he too shall undoubtedly attain that very state of Viṣṇu. 104.
Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(181) The one hundred and eighty-first chapter. The Blessed Lord said:
Now I shall describe the majesty of this seventh chapter, by hearing which the ears become filled with a flood of nectar. (1)
There was a fortress named Pāṭaliputra with lofty gate-towers;
there lived a brāhmaṇa named Śaṅkukarṇodayārṇava.
Having adopted the livelihood of a Vaiśya, he acquired great wealth;
he gratified his ancestors and honored the gods.
Devoted to the acquisition of wealth, he caused kings to be fed;
for the sake of auspiciousness, he performed the taking of a fourth hand in marriage within his own home.
Once, during a night as virtuous as the Dharma itself, he set out together with his sons and kinsmen while he himself was drowsy at the foot of a tree.
A venomous snake may come from anywhere and bite this person;
as soon as it has bitten, the soul becomes incurable by means of gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like.
Then, within just a few moments, his life departed;
his body was covered by the petals and stalks of the *picumanda* tree.
Having placed him upon their shoulders, the sons of the cowherd returned home;
then, after a long time, a serpent was born from him. (8)
My soul, bound by those latent impressions, remembering my previous birth, has come out from the house after leaving these children behind. (9)
There, they deposited wealth equal in number to ten million of their own selves; then, endowed with supreme faith, they performed the Nārāyaṇa-bali sacrifice.
Once, while the son of that twice-born man was away, he returned in a dream, afflicted by one born of a serpent.
The father spoke of his mental state before his sons;
then, having risen in the morning, they were struck with supreme wonder and confusion.
They sat around, whispering to one another;
there, out of affection for his father, one of them even desired to pull him up. (13)
One strives to kill a serpent out of greed for another's wealth, while the other has his mind deluded by the essence of affection for his father. (14)
Or rather, why should he merely grieve and weep for one born of a snake?
Then the middle son, having consoled his two brothers, spoke as follows: ||15||
Having departed for his own abode under some pretext,
he then slowly summoned his virtuous wife.
With a spade in hand, he went to where his father, the serpent, was staying; having ascertained the truth through signs, even though his father was unaware of his wealth.
Having come to that anthill, he, out of a greedy mind, tried to dig it up;
his wife was driven away by him, and he himself dug into the earth.
From an extremely fierce anthill being dug up, a serpent emerged;
then, with unbearable mouthfuls of venom that issued forth, [he struck]. (19)
The serpent spoke these words with the winds of his hissing breath.
The snake said:
"Who are you? For what purpose have you come? And how is it that the hole is being dug? By whom has this fool been sent? Tell me all this before me. (21)
The son said:
"I am your son, named Śiva; having come here out of curiosity to seize gold, I am greatly amazed by a dream obtained during the night. (22)
Śiva said:
Having thus heard the words of his son, which were censured by the world,
he then began to speak clearly while laughing loudly with his hoods raised high.
The serpent said:
"If I were truly your son, you would quickly release me from this bond—a serpent born of my previous birth for the sake of a deposit. (24)
The son said:
"O father, tell me how liberation may be attained;
I have come before you having abandoned the entire world, just as one might depart in the night. (25)
The father said: "O son, neither pilgrimages, nor gifts, nor penances,
nor sacrifices are in any way capable of liberating me from this calamity arising from you."
The seventh chapter of the Gītās, which is like nectar and the cause for dispelling the suffering of old age and death, [is explained] by me. (27)
O son, on the day of my śrāddha, feed with faith a brahmin who has studied the Saptamādhyāyin; by that, liberation will be attained, without a doubt. (28)
Furthermore, endowed with supreme faith, he should feed other twice-born ones who are experts in the knowledge of the Vedas and their branches, according to his capacity. (29)
Having heard these words of their father, who had attained the state of a serpent,
all those sons did even more than what was commanded.
Then the illustrious Śaṅkukarṇa, having cast off his serpent body and made a division among his sons, assumed a divine form.
The wealth that had been divided and given by his father was [given] to them in numbers reaching into the millions;
because of that, all those sons, who were of virtuous conduct, rejoiced.
Then those sons, whose minds were fixed on righteousness, constructed a food-distribution hall for the purpose of building tanks, wells, lakes, sacrificial altars, temples, and palaces.
Therefore, by chanting the seventh chapter, one becomes a partaker of liberation;
having recognized the sixth as most desirable, those whose vision is fixed upon Nirvāṇa [attain it].

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(182) The one hundred and eighty-second chapter.
Śiva said:
O Pārvatī, listen as I shall describe the majesty of the eighth chapter,
by the mere hearing of which you will attain supreme joy.
In the southern region, there was a city renowned by the name Āmardaka;
there lived a twice-born man named Abhayaśarman, who was the master of a courtesan.
Eating meat, drinking liquor, stealing the wealth of the virtuous, taking pleasure with the wives of others, and being fond of the sport of hunting; (3)
The most venerable one fulfilled the exceedingly intense desire of his friends by means of a circle of jesters, [offering] the nectar-like juice of the *catālī* fruit. ||4||
Having drunk [the poison] down to his throat, that evil-souled man, severely afflicted by its indigestion, died; in due time, he was reborn as a great palmyra tree.
Resorting to its dense and exceedingly cool shade,
two certain husband and wife who had become brahmarākṣasas took up residence there.
The Goddess said: "Tell me, of what nature are they, what is their essence, and what is their conduct? By what action, O God, have these two become Brahma-rākṣasas? (7)
Śiva said:

There was a certain twice-born man named Kuśīvala who was an expert in the true essence of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, proficient in the meaning of all the scriptures, and possessed of virtuous conduct. (8)
Driven by excessive greed, that evil-minded one, named Kumati, together with his wife, accepted great gifts from the petitioner. (9)
Day after day, he failed to bestow upon the twice-born his queen, his personified Time (the executioner), his horses, and other possessions,
while giving them not even a single cowrie shell obtained as a gift.
In due course, these two, who had become Brahma-rakshasas, wandered this earth with bodies distressed by hunger and thirst. (11)
Then, having approached the foot of a palm tree, the two of them rested there, wondering, "How shall this great suffering of ours come to an end? (12)
"How can liberation from the womb of a Brahmarākṣasa be attained?"—
thus questioned by his wife, that Brāhmaṇa replied.
Without the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman, without inquiry into the inner self, and without the knowledge of the rules for ritual action, how could one be liberated from this distress? 14.
The wife said:
"O Supreme Person, what is that Brahman, what is the inner self (adhyātma), and what is action?
Listen to this wonder which occurred when she had spoken thus to her husband. (15)
Then, upon hearing half a verse from the eighth chapter, that excellent brahmin immediately abandoned his form as a palm tree and became [a human]. (16)
Their souls shaken by immediate wisdom, they were liberated from the mass of evil;
through that majesty, they became completely freed from it. (17)
When he had spoken thus, and [the deity] had emerged from his mouth,
then from the sky there came a beautiful, tinkling sound of small bells.
It was adorned with divine lotus-faces and circles of celestial maidens; it was filled with bees wandering about the faces of the Apsarases like honey-bearing lotuses.
It was graced by chowries as white as the foam on the shores of the ocean of milk being churned,
beautiful with their handles and their tips.
Mounted upon a divine celestial chariot, where Gandharvas sang and hundreds of celestial nymphs danced, the couple ascended to heaven. 21.
This entire account occurring therein was truly marvelous;
therefore, the intelligent man respectfully inscribed this half-verse.
He went to the city named Vārāṇasī, which bestows liberation,
desiring to propitiate Janārdana, the God of gods.
The noble-minded one began to perform supreme penance continuously.
In the meantime, Janārdana, the Lord of the World and God of Gods, [appeared].
"Having been questioned by the daughter of the ocean of milk, who joined her hands in a hollowed gesture, he remains without even leaving the path of sleep; let it be told. (25)

The Blessed Lord said: On the banks of the Bhāgīrathī in Kāśī, there was a twice-born man named Bhāvaśarman, who was exceedingly wise and filled with the essence of devotion to me; he practiced intense austerity. (26)
O Goddess, with my senses restrained, I was greatly pleased by his penance as he recited half a verse from the eighth chapter of the *Japangītā*. (27)
O beloved, while reflecting for a long time upon this fruit worthy of such asceticism, I am now eager to grant it; therefore, do not return again.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord, even though Hari became pleased, if he did not grant her that [boon], what then was the fruit obtained by Bhāvaśarman, the devotee of Hari? (29)
Śrī Mahādeva said: Then, having obtained the grace of the pleased enemy of Mura,
that best of brahmins, Bhāvaśarman, attained ultimate happiness.
Even all his descendants attained that same state. ||30||
It is solely by the power of that karma that you previously attained this state; is this not indeed the majesty of this eighth chapter? O Goddess! 31.
It has been said that she with the eyes of a young deer should always be beheld. ||32||
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(183) The One Hundred and Eighty-Third Chapter.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the ninth chapter with reverence;
listen and remain steadfast, O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain. (1)
There is a city named Māhiṣmatī on the bank of the Narmadā;
there lived a twice-born man named Mādhava, who was devoted to Śiva.
A knower of the true nature of the Vedas and their auxiliary branches, fond of guests from time to time, and possessing a purified intellect, he acquired great wealth solely through his learning. (3)
Once, he began to perform a great sacrifice;
a goat, its body worshipped, was brought there for the purpose of being offered. ||4||
Seated there, causing wonder to the world, he spoke these words aloud:
"What is the use of these many sacrifices, even though they have been performed according to the rules? (5)
"Behold this very state of affairs, which yields only perishable fruits and serves as the cause of birth, old age, and death. (6)
Having heard these words of the goat, the people dwelling within the pavilion were filled with great curiosity and were struck with wonder. (7)
Then the twice-born, with palms joined in reverence and eyes fixed in stillness,
bowed to him with faith and respectfully questioned that goat.
The twice-born said: "Of what lineage are you, what is your nature, and what is your conduct? Tell me this; and by what action did you come to be a goat—what is the cause? (9)
Chāga said:
"In former times, there was one in an exceedingly pure lineage of the twice-born, who was an expert in Vedic knowledge and the performer of numerous sacrifices. (10)
Once, for the sake of curing her son's illness,
my mother-in-law, bowing with devotion to Caṇḍikā, requested a goat from me.
Then, while the goat was being slaughtered at the site of Caṇḍikā’s pavilion, the mother of the goat, a knower of Brahman, uttered this curse: 12.
Since you desire to kill my son through an unrighteous path and by means of evil, you shall, by virtue of being the lowest of the twice-born, enter the womb of a goat. (13)
Then, O best of the twice-born, after passing away in due time, I became a goat;
having thus traversed the various kinds of agonizing torments of rebirth. (14)
The Brahmin said:
"Even for one who has entered the womb of an animal, there exists the recollection of former births;
my mind is now turned toward it, eager with the flavor of curiosity to hear about your birth. (15)
The goat said:
"O all you twice-born ones, tell me that in its entirety as well:
at one time, through the instruction of a snake-charmer, I became a monkey. (16)
Beheld by the ḍimbhas playing about, he danced from house to house among the Gaṇas,
even as he gazed upon his own noble sons who were likewise noble.
He became averse to action, having abandoned the excitement of dancing;
then the snake-charmer [attacked] with unbearable, circular staffs.
With eyes red with rage, he struck me violently;
thereupon I fell unconscious, with a stream of blood flowing from my wounds. (19)
Smelling food, I went toward water and met my end through the law of time;
thereafter, I became a dog, wandering from house to house.
Seeking food, I wandered about eating the remnants of others' meals;
at one point, I entered my own house and its kitchen.
Hungry, he smelled the rice placed in the cooking pot;
out of fear, he looked at the surface of the earth and the ten directions in an instant.
Seeking peace from the clamor of people and as if licking his flanks,
he was then once seen by his own sons who had come there.
And I was beaten by my old wife with clubs and other weapons;
consequently, with my hips broken and shedding much blood, I departed. (24)
Agitated by fainting, he somehow emerged from the house;
his limbs were foul-smelling due to the presence of worms within them over time.
Thereafter, O learned one, having reached the state of a horse in the house of a vintner, I became a horse after dying here in the course of time.
Once, he was brought by that man to a crowded marketplace for sale; there, a row of teeth, decayed and worn out by old age, lay prostrate.
His wife, repeatedly preparing for a pilgrimage to Dvārakā,
was striving to purchase a horse for a very small price.
Having been seized by her with only a small amount of wealth, I, being old, set out to go along with my sons, the twice-born, as they helped me mount [the vehicle]. (29)
Gradually, I sank into the thick mud on the bank of the lake;
there, with my neck bent, I fell deep into the mire.
Being struck repeatedly by my sons with clubs and stones in their hands,
and being raised up many times, I have preserved my life.
Then, having ascertained that he was dead there, his sons, their efforts frustrated,
departed from the house after covering their wretched mother with cries of lamentation.
Then, after passing through a long time, he was born as a goat;
having crossed over the torments of the succession of many low and inferior births.
The twice-born said: "What is the use of this constant mass of suffering born from the great goat? Tell me truly and clearly how my ultimate happiness may come to pass. (34)
The goat said:
O twice-born one, I shall tell you another wonder as well, if you have the curiosity to hear it while you remain composed and inquire further. (35)
There was a city named Astināma, Kurukṣetra, which bestows liberation;
there, Candravarman, of the Solar dynasty, became the lord of the earth. (36)
At the time of the solar eclipse, being restrained by supreme faith,
he began to give a gift consisting of a man along with the appropriate time.
Having summoned a twice-born man who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, he went with his family priest to bathe in the holy, merit-bestowing waters.
Then the Great Being (Mahāpuruṣa), as if laughing, spoke these words aloud:
"He grasps something else entirely, even though it is right before his field of vision. (39)
"O twice-born one, how is it that you wish to seize the personified Kāla at this time and place called Kurukṣetra during the moment of a solar eclipse? (40)
Even though you have ascertained that all this is a cause of sin, how can you proceed to do it with a mind blinded by greed for wealth? (41)
Having heard these words of his, which caused the world to marvel, the brahmin said, "What is this fear of a great gift? (42)
I alone truly know the means to properly cross this unfathomable ocean of great sin consisting of such a gift. (43)
Then, having bathed and put on two garments, the protector of the earth was pure,
with a serene heart, adorned with white garlands and unguents.
Avalambavyakara, the Bhoja king, arrived accompanied by his attendants and domestic priests, being served by people appropriate for that occasion.
Having arrived, the king, with devotion, presented that Kālapuruṣa to that twice-born man according to the prescribed rites.
Having mercilessly pierced the heart of the man of Time, that evil-souled Cāṇḍāla, his eyes bloodshot with rage, emerged somewhere with a pitiless onset. (47)
Moreover, when the time for another's wedding festival had arrived, Niṃdā, the Cāṇḍālikā, approached the side of the body of that twice-born man. 48.
Then that pair of Cāṇḍālas, having emerged with bloodshot eyes,
proceeded to forcibly devour the twice-born man.
While reciting the ninth chapter of the Gītā with his mind fixed within his heart, he looked silently at the king, wondering which brahmin was the one being honored.
The wise twice-born man [perceived] Govinda sleeping there, his consciousness as if intoxicated by wine, and the sinner taking refuge nearby due to the swaying of the winds.
Then, that pair of Cāṇḍālas, their efforts rendered fruitless, was pursued by Vaiṣṇavas who had arisen from the syllables of the Gītā as they fled.
That supreme [weapon], which was present within the body of the twice-born as he stood by his side during the joy of his marriage, emerged with great force.
Having thus ascertained her conduct, the lord of the earth,
his eyes smiling with wonder, questioned the twice-born man in her very presence.
"How was this terrible, great, and un-crossable calamity overcome by you? While reciting what mantra, or remembering which divine abode? (55)
"O twice-born one, tell me: who was that man and who was that woman; how did these two appear there, and how did they attain peace? (56)
The twice-born said:
"Having assumed the form of a Cāṇḍāla—a form of intense impurity—I consider this pair to be composed of the very essence of woman. (57)
O Lord of the Earth, you should understand all this greatness of the garland of mantras from the ninth chapter of the Gītā, which has been remembered by me. 58.
"O King, I recite the ninth chapter of the Gītā every day;
by that, I have crossed over the calamities arising from improper acceptance of gifts. (59)
As the king practiced this ninth chapter from that twice-born man,
they both attained supreme and ultimate bliss.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||183||
(184) Chapter One Hundred and Eighty-Four. The Goddess said:
O Guru, who are omniscient, the consciousness of all, and the Lord of all speech—blessed am I that you, who are honored by Śiva, have been beheld by me. 1.
This meritorious majesty of the ninth chapter has been described;
it is honey consisting of many wonderful and sweet narratives. 2.
O Lord of the gods, no satiety ever arises from hearing of You;
O Bull-bannered One, my longing to hear of You increases without abating.
O Ocean, there was once a greatness belonging to me, which was the very life-breath of the Gītās;
even therein, the sages declared the tenth chapter to be the most preeminent. (4)
With reference to that great chapter, relate the narrative.
Śiva said:
Listen, O fair-hipped one, to this ladder to heaven, which is difficult to attain.
In the city of Kāśī, there lived a Brahmin devoted to meritorious fame, whose supreme and purifying story was like a boundary mark for spiritual powers.
With a tranquil mind, free from malice, harshness, and rashness, he was constantly devoted to renunciation through the mastery of his senses.
Renowned as one of steadfast intellect, he was devoted to the island of Nanda;
having crossed the ocean of the Vedas, he was skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures. (8)
As he was returning, his mind entirely dependent on meditation, his inner self deeply immersed in contemplation, and his vision fixed upon reality; ||9||
"O Karāvala, I shall give you this forest with affection;
why then has the sage become dejected, causing such wonder? (10)
Having attained a gaze that was focused on the tip of his nose and exceedingly gentle,
he remained as if his senses were asleep.
O large-eyed one, he will place his broad chest against the threshold of the door;
for how long can that fawn-eyed youth lie there at night without fear? 12.
Having prostrated at my lotus feet, Bhṛṅgiriṭi asked me:
"By what method was this vision of you brought about? (13)
What need is there for this great soul to perform austerities, offer oblations, or recite prayers, when the God himself provides him support at every step by taking hold of his hand? (14)
"Why is this Nala not permitted to go outside of this city? When he reaches the very limits of the sky by his own will," ||15||
At that time, he did not see even all the embodied beings standing at his side;
I wish to know the reason for this as explained by my master. (16)
"If you are worthy of being favored and if it is appropriate to speak, then utter that.
Having heard this question from Bhṛṅgiriṭi, I spoke.
Once, on the slopes of Kailāsa, in a grove of Punnāga trees,
where the forest was filled with clusters of blossoms and the sounds of celestial nymphs with beautiful hips.
The quarters of the sky were made resonant by the warbling of flocks of sweet-voiced cuckoos,
and the air was filled with the cries of the multitude of *dātyūha* birds, such as the *garutmata*.

In this swift [chariot], the wooden water-wheel (ghaṭī) revolves, the copper [fittings] gleam with beauty, the sāraṇī-reed is fully awakened, and the plantain trees at the corners are motionless in their leaves. 20.
O you who are infatuated by the human voice, what is the use of this place frequented by musk deer, and by deer with hair standing on end and trembling? 21.
In that place, crowded with parrots displaying their cleverness by mimicking the sound "haṃ saiḥ," the water was stirred by winds blowing from the direction of the Nirvindhyā mountain.
In which the bees were intoxicated by the honey-wine dripping from the *mādhavī* flowers,
and which was filled with the fragrance of clusters of blossoms whose three folds had unfolded.
In that place where the bees were intoxicated by the fragrance of blossoming bakula flowers, and where the circle of the earth was washed with nectar produced from the moon; 24.
Having ascended a certain altar, I remained there for a moment,
amidst heaps of blossoms bursting forth from the mouths of bees as they were jostled by the swaying branches of the trees.
A fierce wind blew, casting a shadow like that of a mountain;
thereafter, a great roar arose, making the slopes of the caves resound.
Then, from the depths of the sky, a certain bird descended,
possessing the luster of autumnal clouds, like a mass of soot.
Like a mass of darkness or a mountain whose wings have been clipped,
he prostrated himself before Padmāvatī, having firmly grasped the earth with his feet.
Having brought a fresh lotus, he placed it at my feet;
then, with clear speech, the bird uttered a hymn of praise.
O Lord of the World, Jayadeva offers his body as an ocean of nectar; O You whose form is the joy arising from the waves of constant association with the contemplation of the Real. 30.

O you who have abandoned the impurity of the latent impressions of non-duality, who are free from the three stains, and whose form is attained through samādhi that has conquered the senses and transcends dependence on others. 31.
O You who are free from limiting conditions, formless, and free from disease;
O You who are boundless, devoid of ego, unobstructed, and beyond all qualities. ||32||
O you whose lotus feet are expert in protecting those who have come for refuge;
O you who have consumed the mind-born god of love with the flames of the great serpent Bhīmāla! 33.
O Great Lord, who has swallowed the demon Andhaka split by your axe;
O Wipe-away-of-the-dust-from-the-foreheads-of-the-wives-of-the-Tripura-demons! 34.

Salutations to the one whose breasts are like those of Kātyāyanī, who is adorned with the finest ornaments, who is far beyond the reach of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and who possesses the form of supreme wisdom.
Salutations to Caitanyanātha; salutations to him whose form is the three worlds, the lotus-feet of whom are kissed by the foremost of yogis. (36)
Even Vācaspati is not bold enough to offer praise for Your wonder, which enables one to cross to the further shore of the ocean of endless existence.
O Mahādeva, even the serpent with a thousand faces possesses no skill in describing you; how much less so I, a bird of small intellect? 38.
Having heard this hymn composed by that bird, I said to him: "Who are you? From where have you come, O bird? (39)
Your body is like a swan, yet your color resembles a crow; for what purpose have you come here, O lion? Let that be told.
Thus questioned by the bird, the Lord of the Earth—the best among those who know how to speak—replied with gentle words to the bird who stood bowed in humility. (41)
"O Lord of Gods, O Dhūrjaṭi, this swan of Svayambhū has now become entirely black through its own actions, O All-pervading One. (42)
Listen to that which was asked by the Omniscient One, as it is told:
having gone from Lake Mānasa to the earth, I have fallen into distress. (43)
Near the city of Saurāṣṭra, at a lake where lotuses were blooming, I [ate] mouthfuls of lotus stalks as white as the crescent moon. 44.
Having summoned my strength and relied upon it, I quickly ascended into the sky;
then, from that height in the air, I suddenly fell to the earth.
Then, his soul overwhelmed by delusion and with all his senses unimpaired, his body trembling from delusion as he was touched by cold breezes, [he spoke]. (46)
Then, having awakened and seeing no cause for his own fall, he thought: "Alas! What is this that has happened? How can there be a fall for me today? (47)
"Upon this body, which is as white as refined camphor, there is a dark stain"—filled with such wonder, I began to reflect. (48)
At that moment, I heard such a voice from the lotus:
"Arise, O Haṃsa; I shall explain the cause of your sin and blackness. (49)
Then, having risen and come together, she was seen in the middle of the lake,
accompanied by five beautiful lotuses and stalks of water-lilies.
Then he began to ask the cause of their blackness and their falling;
there he saw those who were dark as a rain-cloud, yet possessed of golden complexions and covered in fine garments.
Four-armed, holding the mace, conch, discus, and lotus as weapons,
they were resplendent, adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, and earrings.
We saw sixty thousand men stationed in the sky;
having bowed and circumambulated the five-lotus lake, Sarojinī, [they departed].
"Starting from my own flight, I have related all that was asked.
Padminī said:
"O Kalahaṃsa, you have come to me through the sky, having traversed a great distance. (54)
By that very act of falling, I have fallen upon the surface of the earth;
by that same act, O best of birds, my body is perceived as black. (55)
Beholding him fallen, with a heart full of compassion, he spoke to that lotus of his, which had not yet produced fragrance, using this middle voice. (56)
Having smelled [this fragrance], sixty thousand bees went to heaven;
these were seen by you, possessing a luster equal to that of blue lotuses. (57)
All of them were the sons of a sage in their seventh previous birth;
on the bank of this very lake, they performed supreme penance.
Once, a certain passionate woman, whose breasts were like clusters of ripened blossoms, her body trembling with the passion of love, was deeply absorbed in the delight of singing.
With the radiance of her smile kissed by the moonlight of her pearl necklace,
she placed her lute upon her breasts and sang sweetly in this forest.
Hearing that song, which was like the cry of a deer, all those brahmins approached her and looked at her simultaneously.
"She was seen by me; she is mine alone! they said to one another.
Then a battle with fists ensued among those brothers.
With their chests crushed by each other's fists, they gave up their lives;
having experienced those terrible hells, they became cranes on earth.
Then they killed the wild beasts that had been burnt by another fire;
thereafter, having reached Mātaṅgavatī, they struck down those who were on the path.
Having drunk the water of the Veneviṣa forest, they went to the realm of Yama;
having undergone births as donkeys, camels, monkeys, and cats, they returned in due order.
Then, having smelled the fragrance of that cloud which had arisen from the bees in the whirlpool of this lake, they indeed attained the state of Viṣṇu.
Listen, O bird, I shall tell you of my power by which I exist; prior to this birth, in my third previous birth on earth— (67)
I was the daughter of a twice-born man named Sarojavadana;
I was solely devoted to my husband and intent upon the service of my elders.
Once, while I was teaching a female sarika bird, you became agitated;
out of anger, you cursed me, saying, "May you become a sarika bird. (69)
Having attained the state of being summoned after death through the grace of her devotion to her husband,
a certain maiden nourished me as if I were one of the sages' own daughters.
I heard that this Brahmin recites every morning the tenth chapter of the Gītā, known as the "Vibhūti," which destroys all sins. (71)
In time, having cast off this body as a sārikā bird, I went to heaven; by the greatness of the tenth chapter, I became an apsaras in the celestial realm.
The one renowned as Padmāvatī, the beloved of Padmā and full of happiness, once traveled through the sky in a celestial chariot with me. (73)
Having beheld this beautiful lake with its stainless lotuses,
as soon as I descend and begin my water-sports— (74)
Durvāsas arrived, and she was seen by him naked;
out of fear of him, I myself assumed this form of a lotus-pond. (75)
With my two feet there are two lotuses, with my two hands there are two, and with my mouth there is a fifth; thus, O Bhoja, I am indeed the five-lotus one.
With eyes blazing with anger, that lord of sages said:
"O sinful one, remain in this very form for a hundred years! (77)
Having thus uttered this curse, he vanished from sight in that very moment;
by the greatness of his meditative absorption in the Lord’s power, his speech dissolved away.
"O best of birds, by the mere touch of my body you have fallen upon the surface of the earth;
today the end of your curse has arrived, so stay here."
Listen to this supreme chapter being recited by me,
by the mere hearing of which you shall be liberated this very day.
Thus he recited this tenth chapter in a smooth voice;
having heard it, she took the lotus offered by him.
"I offer this most excellent lotus from the Padminī lake to you," having said this,
he cast off his body, and that was like a marvel.
Bhṛṅgiriṭi said:
How did this one become a slayer of a Brahmin in a previous birth?
For what reason did he cast off his body in your presence? (83)
Having heard these words of Giriṭi, I then spoke: "In a previous birth, he was born in the house of a brahmin. (84)
Renowned as Sutapāti, a celibate student with his senses subdued, he dwelt in the preceptor’s household, performing the study of the Vedas every day. (85)
He performed service to his guru perfectly and with devotion;
while the guru was lying down, he would lie down himself, and while the guru slept, he would touch him with his feet.
Due to that evil deed, he attained the state of an animal even while in heaven;
thereafter, he was born as a twice-born among the swans of the lotus-born Brahmā.
In this life, in that [previous] life, and from the past until the end of this world,
the tenth chapter of the Gītā was then narrated by Nalinī.
Having heard this, Vihaga attained the unsurpassed knowledge of Brahman; he was born into a family of brahmins by the power of the tenth chapter. 89.
By the power of lifelong habit, even from the lotus-like mouth of this infant, the tenth chapter of the Gītā shines forth at all times. (90)
By transforming his mind toward that goal, he always perceives the Lord, who dwells within all beings and bears the conch and the discus. 91.

Whenever and wherever the vision of this incorporeal being is affectionate toward him, that person—whether he be a drinker of liquor or even a slayer of a Brahmin—becomes liberated from all [sin]. 92.
Having realized that, the Brahmin, by means of his own nature which is the form of the Supreme Self, was brought to this city, a field of liberation. 93.
Liberation for the people residing here is held in the palm of their hand;
therefore, by his mere glance, no other distinction arises. (94)
I do not permit him to go outside; for through the greatness of the tenth chapter, the knowledge of reality—which is very difficult to attain—has been gained. 95.
This sage has likewise attained this liberation while living;
therefore, I place my hand upon his shoulder as he walks along the path. (96)
"This great mountain is the bearer of the majesty of the tenth chapter. Thus was this narrative told in the presence of Bhṛṅgiriṭi. (97)
This which has been told to you is the destroyer of all sins;
whether it be a man, or a woman, or even a *yāpika*. (98)
By merely hearing this, one obtains the fruit of all stages of life (āśramas). ||99||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(185) The one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter. The Goddess said:
This history is the supreme means for attaining the welfare of the Lord; having heard it, which is filled with compassion, the state of being free from the "I" and "mine" proceeds. ||1||
O first of speakers, Virūpākṣa, describe the greatness of the eleventh chapter based on its narrative.
Īśvara said:
Listen to this story concerning the description of the Gītā,
as well as the purifying majesty of that which is named Viśvarūpa.
It is impossible to recount even a single chapter of the Viśālākṣī;
there are thousands of stories therein, and only one is told by me.
On the bank of the river Praṇītā, there is a city renowned as Meghakara,
which possesses ramparts and gate-towers that serve as a support for its great majesty.
It was adorned with beautiful golden ornaments upon the spacious halls of the hermitage.
By those who are illustrious, happy, peaceful, of virtuous conduct, and who have conquered their senses. ||6||
It was presided over by swift [beings], charming with beautiful peaks and delightful;
it was adorned with golden marketplaces and courtyards shimmering with jeweled pillars.
Resounding with the tinkling of banners and the sweet warbling of cranes, its horizons were made vocal by the resonant sound of Vedic recitation. ||8||
The vast circle of the sky was filled with the resonant sound of musical instruments,
while its physical form was overcome by the wind stirred up by the fluttering of banners and streamers.
The city shines with the sounds of lutes and flutes, and with songs sung by women at the excellent gates along the royal highway, which surpass even the neighing of horses in the stables.
There dwells the Lord of the World, resplendent with the śārṅga bow in hand, as if constantly gazing upon the cities of the guardians of the quarters.
He is the embodied Supreme Brahman, the life of the eyes of the world,
his majestic form honored by the lotus-eyes of Lakṣmī.
Having the body of Trivikrama, dark as a cloud, with tender luster;
his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, like a royal lotus, and adorned with a forest garland. ||13||
Adorned with many ornaments, he was like the ocean filled with jewels;
his splendor was equal to a cloud flashing with a garland of moving lightning.
Upon her crown resides the Supreme Person himself, holding a śārṅga bow in his hand;
by seeing him, one is instantly liberated from the bondage of birth and worldly existence. (15)
In that city there exists a great sacred ford named Mekhalā, by bathing in which men constantly attain the station of Viṣṇu. ||16||
There, by beholding Narasiṃha, the Lord of the World and ocean of mercy, a person is liberated from the terrible evil deeds accumulated over seven lifetimes. (17)

The man who beholds the Lord of the Gaṇas on the Mekhalā mountain shall always cross over even those obstacles that are difficult to overcome; he becomes devoted to celibacy, free from possessiveness, and devoid of egoism. (18)
In that [village] there was a certain excellent brāhmaṇa named Megha, who was highly renowned as Sunanda and was well-versed in the Vedas and the Śāstras. ||19||
O beloved, having brought the collection of senses under control and being devoted to Vāsudeva,
one should recite this chapter on song in the presence of the Lord who possesses the Śārṅga bow.
He recites the eleventh chapter, which reveals the universal form;
by the power of this chapter, he attains the knowledge of Brahman. 21.

By means of a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consisting of a praiseworthy consciousness that was the result of tenfold milkings of supreme bliss, he attained an unwavering state as if facing [the object] directly with his own senses. (22)
That yogi, liberated while living, remained constantly in that state.
Once, when Jupiter was situated in Leo, that great yogi— ||23||
He set out to perform a pilgrimage to the Godāvarī;
on the first day, he arrived at the excellent Viraja-tīrtha.
Beginning at his navel, he worshipped the deity in the sacred bathing places;
then, repeatedly immersing himself, he beheld Kamalā, the sustainer of the world.
Having worshipped that Mahāmāyā, who bestows the fruits of all desires,
one should then bathe at Tārātīrtha and subsequently at Kapilā-saṅgama.
Having performed the ritual purification at the eight holy sites (aṣṭatīrtha) and offered libations to the ancestors, he bowed to the Lord Śiva Kumārīśa and proceeded to the gateway of Kapilā. ||27||
There, having bathed and washed away the evil deeds of previous births,
and having worshipped, bowed down to, and heard from the Lord Madhusūdana in this manner, [he remained].
Having stayed there for that night, he went forth in the morning together with the twice-born and men to that holy site where Rāma’s oblation-pool is located,
wherein the Man-Lion himself, worshipped by Prahlāda, resides.
Having seen that Lord of the Gods of gods and having worshipped him with devotion,
he spent that day there and departed for the city of Ambikā.
Out of grace toward his devotees, he remains present there,
fulfilling all the desires of human beings whatsoever.
Having worshipped Bika with devotion through flowers, incense, and unguents, as well as with various offerings, hymns of praise, and prostrations; ||32||
Therefore, that Brahmin arrived long ago at the city named Kaṇṭhasthāna.
There dwells the supreme power, Mahālakṣmī, of great splendor. ||33||
Beholding her, whose orb possessed the luster of the moon, the sun, and fire, and who, like a stream of nectar for the lotus, severed the heat of worldly existence; 34.
The heart-lake of the king of yogis, frequented by the swan-king Bhoja, consisting of the great unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*), and possessing a non-dual form. ||35||
Having propitiated the divine Mahālakṣmī, who bestows the fulfillment of desires, with a mind imbued with devotion, that lord of sages [attained his goal]. (36)
Accompanied by the Brahmins, he reached the marriage pavilion in the city;
there, in that city, he requested lodging in every house.
The twice-born man found no dwelling to stay in, not even in a single house;
however, the village headman showed him a spacious, two-roomed residence.
Having entered, that brāhmaṇa, together with his companions, took up residence there.
Then, when the morning had become clear, that best of the twice-born [spoke] to Sunanda.
He looked out from his dwelling and beheld his own body,
as well as all the travelers who had arrived there by chance.
As he was traveling along the road, the village watchman saw him and spoke to him: "O long-lived one, you are everything in every way. (41)
