You are the merit of meritorious men who possess their rightful fortune;
O child, a power that is truly transcendent exists within you.
"O tiger among sages, where have those companions gone, and how did they get outside that palace? Behold; I shall tell you before you. (43)
But what other ascetic here do I see who is your equal? Do you know some great mantra, or upon what science do you rely? (44)
By whose compassion has this supramundane power been bestowed upon you?
O best of Brahmins, by the force of that very compassion, remain in this village. (45)
"O Blessed One, I shall perform every form of service for you.
Having said this, he caused the lord of sages to dwell in that village.
And he performed service for him with devotion day and night;
when several days had passed, after seven or eight days had gone by, [he approached]. (47)
Coming before him in the morning, he wept, deeply afflicted by grief: "Today, for me who am devoid of fortune, my virtuous and devoted son [has departed]. (48)
"O you whose fangs are blazing, I have been devoured at night by a snake!"—when the guardian had spoken thus, the self-restrained one questioned him. (49)
"Where is that Rākṣasa? Tell me, how was your son devoured?
The village guardian replied: "There dwells in the city a terrible night-stalker who preys upon men. (50)
"Since he constantly devours the men who frequent the city, he was long ago besought here by all the citizens and men. (51)
We offer all these Rākṣasas as food;
O Rākṣasa, devour those travelers who sleep at night! 52.
In that dwelling, for the protection of their own lives, they prepared food for those village guards who had been ushered in by the village headman.
"O best of the twice-born, while you were sleeping in this house surrounded by ill-fated others, they were indeed seized by him; you alone have been released. (54)
O best of the twice-born, you alone know my power;
today a certain friend of my son has arrived. (55)
Though he was unaware of this, that dear friend of his son was ushered into that house along with other travelers by the servants. (56)
Having heard that my son had entered there at midnight,
he went to bring him back, but he too was devoured by that rākṣasa.
In my distress, I said to that flesh-eater in the morning:
"O evil-minded one, you have devoured even my son during the night! (58)
This son of mine is submerged in the belly of existence;
tell me, O night-stalker, what means there is by which he may live. (59)
The Rākṣasa said:
"O King, having entered the interior without knowing it was your son, I devoured him;
unaware, I ate that son of yours along with the ants. (60)
Just as he lived within my womb and was protected there, so too has this been ordained by the supreme deity, Fate. (61)
O twice-born one, by the power of that person who recites the eleventh chapter of the Gītā incessantly, there is liberation for me and the rebirth of the deceased. (62)
The village guardian said:
"How is it that this power of the eleventh chapter is so wonderful? (63)
Thus questioned by me, the night-stalker, the best of Brahmins, spoke.
Long ago, a certain vulture traveling through the path of the sky dropped a fragment of bone from the tip of its beak somewhere into the water.
Then, having arrived at that reservoir of water, a certain wise lord,
recognizing it as a great sacred site (tīrtha), performed the libation for his ancestors.
All the people said to him: "Tell us, how is this a sacred ford (tīrtha)?
One who has restrained his senses recites the eleventh chapter [of the Bhagavad Gītā] here at the three junctions of the day. (67)
Having observed a vow of silence, that brahmin was killed by thieves on the road;
a fragment of his bone fell from the beak of a vulture into the water.
Thus, this divine ford (tīrtha) was born, which destroys all sins;
thereafter, all those men bathed there in that pool.
And thus, through their stainlessness, they attained the supreme state by the power of this eleventh chapter; so it shall come to pass.
My liberation as well as the resurrection of the dead is at hand; whatever Brāhmaṇa has been uttered by me remains right here. (71)
And he recited the eleventh chapter incessantly;
with that mantra of the chapter, it was consecrated seven times.
"If the lord of Brahmins (the preceptor) were to place this upon his head after performing the water-rite, then my liberation from that sin would occur;
of this there is no doubt.
Thus was I instructed by him, and I have come into your presence.
The Brahmin said:
"O protector of the wood-apple tree, by what sin was this Rākṣasa born, that he devours men while they sleep in this house during the night? (74)
The village guardian said:
"In this village there was formerly a certain Brahmin who was a farmer. Once, that twice-born man was preoccupied with guarding a field of śāli rice. (75)
Not very far away, a great vulture was devouring a piece of earth;
out of compassion, the ascetic felt pity for it from a distance and sought to liberate it.
Having eaten and drunk, the bird then departed by way of the sky;
thereupon, out of anger, that ascetic spoke to the farmer. (77)

"Shame on you, O plowman of wicked intellect, cruel-minded and pitiless! Shame on this wretched life of yours, which lasts but a moment and is averse to saving others from the dangers of thieves, tigers, serpents, enemies, fire, poison, and water! (78)
And those struck by vultures, rākṣasas, bhūtas, vetālas, and the like; ||79||

If a capable person neglects people [in distress], he shall obtain the fruit of their slaughter; likewise, he who, though being a master, does not liberate a Brahmin seized by thieves and the like, incurs the same.
He shall go to a terrible hell and is born again as a wolf,
being struck down in the forest and tormented by vultures and tigers.
The one who releases a cow at a sacred shrine (caitya) attains the supreme goal;
likewise, those killed by tigers for the sake of cows, or by wicked kings and others, [attain that same goal]. 82.
The three steps of Viṣṇu are difficult to attain even for yogis;
[they are equal to] thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices. (83)
The sixteenth part of the merit gained from protecting one who has come for refuge is not equal to the neglect of a distressed living being who seeks protection out of fear. (84)
Even a meritorious person is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell in the course of time;
you yourself see even a mere speck of dust being devoured by a wicked vulture. (85)
Although you were capable of preventing it, you did not do so;
therefore, because you are merciless, you shall become a night-stalker (a demon).
Having heard this curse, O Sage, the plowman, his body trembling with fear, bowed down to the Brahmin and spoke these piteous words: (87)
"Long occupied here with guarding the field, my eyes were cast far away; thus I did not perceive this man being struck down by the vulture so close at hand. (88)
Therefore, you ought to show favor to this wretched man.
The Brahmin said:
"He who knows the eleventh chapter and who recites it daily," (89)
Therefore, when this water consecrated by him falls upon your head, O Śitāvakī, then by his curse you shall obtain liberation. ||90||
Having spoken thus, the ascetic departed; the plowman became a Rākṣasa.
Then, O best of the twice-born, he approached with that meditation and mantra;
with his own hand, he poured the water from the sacred ford upon his head.
Mahādeva said:
Having heard that request of his, he was overwhelmed with compassion;
saying "So be it," together with Pāla, the sage went to the Ṛkṣavant mountain.
By that eleventh [son], Viśvarūpa, this mantra was entrusted to Trita by the brahmin Śiśita, who was a yogin.
By the power of the chapter on the Gītā, he obtained release from the curse; casting off his demonic body, he thereafter became four-armed. 94.
Thousands of people were swallowed by that demon and became four-armed, bearing conchs, discs, and maces in their hands. ||95||
Having ascended these celestial chariots, they then spoke to the Rākṣasa:
"O night-walker, who is my son? Show him to us! (96)
When the village guardian had spoken thus, the Rākṣasa, possessing divine intelligence, said:
"Know him to be the four-armed one, with a luster dark like a tamāla tree. (97)
He wore a crown of rubies, was adorned with divine jeweled earrings,
possessed a great chest made beautiful by necklaces, and was decorated with golden armlets.
[He saw] his son, who had attained divinity, with lotus-like eyes, affectionate, holding a lotus in his hand, and mounted upon a divine celestial chariot. 99.
Having heard these words of his and seeing his son in such a state, he began to lead him toward his own home; then, together with his son, he laughed.
"O protector of mine, how many times have you been born as my son?
Previously I was your son, but now I am a god. (101)
"By the grace of this brāhmaṇa, I shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
even though he was a night-stalker, behold his body now possesses four arms. (102)
"Because of the greatness of the eleventh [chapter], one attains heaven equally with the people;
therefore, study this chapter from this Brahmin and recite it constantly. (103)
"There is no doubt that your own destiny will also be like this, O father;
therefore, the company of the virtuous is difficult for people to attain in every respect. (104)
He too has arisen today to accomplish his own desired goal;
what is the use of wealth, or enjoyments and gifts, or sacrifices, or even penance? 105.
What is the use of sacrificial merits or other higher goods than reciting the *Viśvarūpa* hymn, and hearing this chapter concerning that supreme form of Viṣṇu? (106)
That which emerged from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa-Brahmā, the essence of the ten-fold assembly of the Full One, O friend Arjuna, is this elixir of absolute liberation at Kurukṣetra. 107.
"For men who fear worldly existence, I see nothing else that removes the fear of mental and physical ailments, nor destroys the suffering of many births— remember that!
Śiva said.
Having spoken thus, accompanied by all his attendants, he went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Then the village guardian recited that chapter from the Brahmin;
both of them, having laughed at him, went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, this narrative of the greatness of the eleventh [day] has been described to you;
by the mere hearing of which, there is the destruction of great sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the dialogue between Satī and Īśvara, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(186) The one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter.
Mahādeva said:
There is a city named Kolhāpura in the southern region;
it is an abode of happiness for the virtuous and the holy, and a source of spiritual perfection. ||1||
The supreme seat (pīṭha) of the Supreme Power (paraśakti), frequented by all the gods, which is renowned in the Purāṇas and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||2||
There, at that place known as Rudragayā, which is vast and world-renowned, there exist millions of sacred fords (tīrthas) and millions of Śiva-liṅgas. ||3||
There, you saw a golden banner atop the palace, its archways shimmering with cow-hides from the great mountain-like ramparts.
It was adorned with the splendor of the balconies of great palaces made of moonstones,
and its courtyards were perfumed by the incense smoke rising through the lattice windows.
It possessed the expansive shade of fluttering banners and was endowed with temples.
[They were] clever, very beautiful, affectionate, endowed with prosperity, and pure in mind. ||6||
It was presided over by men of virtuous conduct adorned with many ornaments— women with eyes like those of a doe, with faces like the moon, and with curling locks of hair.
They possess the luster of full-blown campaka flowers, with plump breasts like firm tumgas,
slender waists, and naves deeply indented and adorned by three folds.
They possessed broad hips and beautiful pairs of breasts,
with lower garments that were noisy with the jingling of jeweled girdles and anklets.
Where women, with their tinkling bracelets and the shimmering rays of light from the jewels on their lotus-like hands, intoxicate even the sages. 10.

Having heard the series of syllables of the song as the king was reading the letter,
the horse then attained the state of liberation and fell down with speed.
Then, having cut the reins and removed the saddle-cloth,
as he was attempting to raise the king of horses, the horse rose up dead.
Then, having addressed King Sarabhabheruṇḍa with a melodious voice,
he ascended a divine celestial chariot and departed for the abode of the gods.
Then, having ascended the mountain, he beheld an excellent hermitage, provided with *punnāga*, plantain, mango, and coconut trees. (38)
The king [beheld] a grove of grapes, sugarcane, betel-nut trees, and *nāgakeśara* flowers, filled with frolicking young camels and dancing flocks of peacocks. (39)
Having prostrated before the twice-born one who was staying beyond the hermitage,
he, whose latent impressions of saṃsāra had been cast off, questioned him with supreme devotion.
"Tell me, by what means did he go from the horse to heaven?
Having heard these words, the king spoke to the twice-born one. (41)
After a long time had passed, he died and became a horse due to that sin;
then, in some place, half a verse from the fifteenth chapter was written down. (42)
Then, having heard [the words] from the mouth of the reciter, the horse departed for heaven;
thereafter, he was surrounded by his retinue who had assembled there.
Having prostrated before the twice-born man, with his hair standing on end with joy,
he emerged [and saw] that very leaf inscribed with the fifteen syllables of the Gītā.
While this was being recited, the great protector of the earth, his eyes blossoming with joy,
consecrated his own son together with three ministers well-versed in counsel.
The one of pure intellect attained liberation through the power of these lion-thrones. ||46||
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(190) The one hundred and ninetieth chapter. Īśvara said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the majesty of the sixteenth chapter; listen, O you who are overflowing with longing and joy at the sight of the elephant-destroyer! 1.
In the Gurjara maṇḍala, there was a city named Astisaurāṣṭrika;
there lived a king named Khazgabāhu, who was like a second Indra.
In the ocean, whose interior was made fragrant by the garlands of flowers belonging to her,
Hari lay comfortably with Lakṣmī.
When the particles of camphor that were his fame were scattered across the expanse of the sky by the winds of the sighs of his enemies, they appeared under the guise of stars.
The enemy kings who bathed in the sword-blade tirthas of that [river] have turned back from heaven even today, utterly bewildered by the words of the celestial women.
He had an elephant named Arimardana, fierce with rut,
whose temples were surrounded by swarms of bees buzzing in the water of the streams of ichor flowing from them.
Turbid with streams of ichor flowing from the surface of his temples,
he shone like Mount Meru with its lofty peaks, its sources of rivers overflowing with water.
In that [city], yak-tail fans, brilliant as the moon,
shone like the cool rays of the moon fallen into the interior of a forest.
The surface of the royal golden vessel, filled with thick layers of water, shone like a portion of the sky pervaded by evening clouds. ||9||
Having once again freed himself from the fetters and shackles of the wicked, and having broken that firm iron bond, he emerged by force in the night.
Disregarding all the elephant-drivers with their heels kicking and goads brandishing,
he angrily destroyed his own stables.
Though being pierced on all sides by sharp arrows with iron tips and struck by bamboo staffs, the riders did not cause him even the slightest bit of fear.
Then the king, having arrived and heard of this marvel,
went there together with princes who were experts in the science of elephants.
Then, having arrived unseen, that exceedingly powerful one,
displaying a fierce arrogance that bewildered the king, seized the rows of watchtowers.
Standing at a great distance from him, the citizens beheld that most terrifying being;
out of fear, they kept their children hidden, and their curiosity was extinguished.
There, the paths were blocked by people intent on flight,
and the air was made fragrant by the spray from the streams of their fierce ichor.
Having bathed and traveled by that path, a certain twice-born man arrived from a lake,
reciting several verses from the sixteenth chapter of the Gītā.
Though being forbidden in many ways by the citizens and even by the elephant-drivers. ||18||
Not considering [the danger], he moved away from the terrified elephants,
covering the people with his trumpeting and crushing them.
Touching his lotus-feet, the twice-born man departed safely;
thereafter, a great wonder arose there that was beyond the reach of words.
Then, while the citizens and even the king of Mānasa were looking on,
the lotus-eyed king summoned his ministers.
Having dismounted from his vehicle and bowed down, he questioned that brahmin.
The king said:
"O Brahmin, this great deed you have performed today is extraordinary.
How did you emerge from that elephant which was like a mountain? (23)
"O Lord, which god do you worship? Which mantra do you recite?
And what siddhi do you possess? O twice-born one, tell me. (24)
The twice-born said:
"O King, I recite daily a few verses from the sixteenth chapter of the Gītā; by these, all perfections [are attained]. (25)
Then, leaving behind his curiosity for the elephant,
the king returned to his own palace, taking the twice-born man with him.
Having observed an auspicious moment and having gratified the best of the twice-born.
With gold pieces numbering one hundred thousand, he acquired the Gītā-mantra,
as well as several verses from the sixteenth chapter of the Gītā.
The king, full of curiosity, practiced [the arts] with great hospitality;
then, on one occasion, he went out to the outer courtyard accompanied by his soldiers. (29)
He released that very elephant from its intoxicated mahout,
clearly disregarding the pleasures of sovereignty through such explicit words.
Then, regarding his life as a blade of grass, the king entered before the elephant; taking hold of its temples and its trunk smeared with rut-fluid, he grasped it firmly.
The king, a leader among the daring, entered the triple fortress with confidence,
just as an unrighteous man enters the mouth of Rāhu or the mouth of the Kali age for his own destruction.
A virtuous man indeed emerged from the mouth of the wicked like a man from an elephant;
having returned to the city, the king consecrated the prince.
From the sixteenth chapter of the Gītā, he attained the supreme goal. ||34||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||190||
(191) The one hundred and ninety-first chapter. The Lord said:
O Śivā, listen as I describe the power of the sixteenth chapter;
now hear clearly the greatness of the seventeenth chapter, which is like an ocean. 1.
Duḥśāsana was the servant of the son of Khazgabāhu;
having come to seize that elephant, he fell from the elephant and attained this imperishable state. ||2||
With his soul bound by those latent impressions, he was born as an elephant;
yet, having heard the seventeenth chapter of the Gītā, he attained the supreme state.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I have heard that Duḥśāsana attained the state of an elephant and was then liberated;
tell me that very thing in detail, O Illustrious One."
Īśvara said:
A certain dull-witted man, having made a high-stakes wager with the sons of the circle of ministers, mounted an elephant. Then—
Having gone only a few steps, unopposed by anyone, the fool named Duḥśāsana uttered these arrogant words: ||6||
Then, having heard those words, Krodhāndha became heavy with the burden of rage;
his feet faltered and he fell, along with the princes who were his equals.
Then Kuśa, with the force of his thighs, uprooted that small portion which had fallen and was slightly breathing, having been made into a raft by the elephant's fury.
Then, out of anger toward that deceased man, the intoxicated elephant scattered the heap [of bones] by trampling them apart with its foot.
Then, after some time had passed, he died and was born into the womb of an elephant;
he spent a great length of time as the elephant of the king of Siṃhala Island.
Together with King Khazgabāhu, who was preeminent in his devotion to loving-kindness (maitrī),
he was then brought by way of the water-path to the realm known as Vāruṇa.
Jayadeva was brought out of affection by King Akhaṅgabāhu, who, remembering his own birth, beheld his kinsmen and brothers. (12)
With great sorrow, he passed a few days;
he dwelt silently in the house of Khazgabāhu, offering no instructions.
Content with a single verse to complete the stanza,
he gave that elephant as a gift to a certain poet.
By this poet Śatānanda, fearing the afflictions of disease, the temple-tower was sold to the ruler of Mālava. (15)
After some time had passed, although he was being nurtured with great effort, he became one on the verge of death there, afflicted by an incurable fever like that of an old jar. (16)
The elephant did not smell the cool water, nor would he take a morsel of food;
he could not sleep in peace and shed nothing but tears.
Thereupon, the king heard the account as related by the mahout. (17)
Having heard this, he arrived together with his attendants at the place where the feverish elephant was;
and having beheld the king, [he saw] that which causes wonder to the world.
O King, ocean of the waters of royal policy and knower of all scriptures, the elephant uttered these words properly, his fever and pain having been completely released. (19)

O beloved of the feet of the Enemy of Mura, who has conquered the hosts of his foes! What is the use of medicines, what need for physicians, what with mantras, and what with those who recite prayers? (20)
"Bring a twice-born man who recites the seventeenth chapter of the Gītā;
by him this disease of mine will be pacified, of this there is no doubt. (21)
The lord of men did exactly as he was instructed by the elephant;
then, casting off his elephant-form, Duḥśāsana was liberated.
Then, when that supreme [object] was thrown into the consecrated water by that brahmin,
the lord of the earth ascended a divine celestial chariot.
He beheld that Duḥśāsana, who possessed the splendor of Indra, the subduer of Pāka.
The king said: "Of what caste are you, what is your nature, and what is your occupation? Tell me this. By what action were you born as an elephant, and how have you come here? (25)
Questioned by the king, Duḥśāsana, remaining in his celestial chariot, spoke with steady syllables in due order concerning his own conduct as it had occurred.
By reciting the seventeenth chapter of the Gītā, Naravarmā, the king of Mālava, became liberated from that [sin] in a very short time. (27)
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(192) The one hundred and ninety-second chapter. Pāvartī said:
O Śiva, you have described the greatness of the seventeenth chapter; now, please proclaim the majesty of the eighteenth chapter. (1)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Citrānanda, to this meritorious greatness of the eighteenth chapter, which establishes the conclusion of the Upaniṣads, as told by Giri on the mountain.
The entire essence of all scriptures, an elixir reached through the ears, it is devoted to tearing asunder the net of the torments of saṃsāra. ||3||
The supreme secret of the perfected ones, capable of uprooting ignorance, is consciousness—the foremost and highest state belonging to the slayer of Kaiṭabha. 4.
It is the root of the creeper of discernment, the remover of the impurities of lust and anger, and the city that brings rest to the minds of the gods, beginning with Indra. ||5||
He who delights the minds of great yogis such as Sanaka and others, who is the cause of Janaka,
and whose roar of "Kiṃkara" (the servant of Time) has surpassed Time itself by mere recitation.
It is the uprooter of the one hundred and eight diseases;
there is no secret superior to this, O Haṃsagāminī.
It removes the three types of affliction and destroys great sins;
it is like the wish-fulfilling cow that yields desires whenever and wherever they are sought.
Just as Vyāsa is among the sages, as the best knower of Brahman among the Vyāsas; just as Śakra is among the gods, and Guru is the foremost among those beginning with Śakra.
Just as nectar is the supreme among all juices and is renowned throughout the universe, so is Kailāsa among mountains, and just as Indra is among the inhabitants of heaven. 10.
Puṣkara is the foremost among sacred fords (tīrthas), just as the lotus is among flowers; Arundhatī is the foremost among virtuous wives in the worlds. 11.
Just as the Aśvamedha is among sacrifices, as Nandana is among gardens, and as Vīrabhadra, my follower, is among all the Rudras; ||12||
Just as the gift of land is the foremost among gifts, as Gautamī is the foremost among rivers, and as the field of Hari is praised in the world for religious acts; ||13||
In that same way, O Pārvatī, listen with devotion to this meritorious narrative concerning the greatness of the eighteenth chapter, which is supreme among all worlds. 14.
Merely by hearing this, a living being is liberated from sins.
On the peak of Mount Meru is the beautiful city of Amarāvatī. (15)
It was fashioned by Viśvakarman for the amusement of Purāma,
endowed with inexhaustible virtues, and served by ten million gods.
There, the splendor is manifestly like the *puṃjavatī* [mantra], renowned as the very knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*);
and the palaces there, constructed from *cintāmaṇi* stones, grant all desires.
Victory! [I shall describe] from the peak of Mount Meru as far as the city of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), where the daughter of Puloman sits comfortably in the shade of the Kalpa tree.
There he hears the songs of the celestial nymphs sung with dark-hued voices,
where the enemy of Bala dwells, having shattered the lives of the gods.
The celestial river became crimson with the waves of the Daityas' blood;
the gods, repeatedly remembering the taste of the nectar of old, [lamented]. (20)

Formerly, on that mountain which was like the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), where the deer were emaciated by hunger and thirst and where the female deer were exhausted day after day, there dwelt Śatakratu.
Accompanied by Śacī, glorious, and served by all the gods,
the illustrious one was once seated comfortably upon a throne occupied by the messengers of Viṣṇu.
He beheld that supreme Person, who was like a thousand-eyed illusion;
then Indra was overwhelmed by his splendors.
As soon as Hari had descended from the lion-throne into the pavilion of the assembly, his soldiers [surrounded him].
They spread the imperial crown of sovereignty over the host of gods;
then, for that consecrated Mahendra, Pulomajā [appeared].
He quickly mounted his left [side], a divine elephant that resounded with "duṃ-duṃ" cries;
then the gods, accompanied by their celestial music and filled with joy, [approached].
The celestial women honored the gods with divine jewels;
then the sages likewise offered blessings through the Vedas. (27)
Before him, the hosts of Apsaras danced with the syllable *raṃ* at their head; and the Gandharvas, with charming speech, sang songs of wonder with the syllable *gaṃ*. (28)
Thus, seeing that new Indra being honored with many festivals while his own sacrifice was being destroyed, Śakra was filled with amazement. (29)
He constructed tanks on paths not previously made, and planted great trees that provide rest for travelers. (30)
Never before had the god Tripurabhairava been seen by me;
nor had the goddess, who dwells in Nidhivāsa, been worshipped by me—she who is languid with pride.
Megha did not behold the wielder of the Śārṅga bow standing before him;
he performed no bath at Virajā, nor did he go to the city of Kāśī. ||32||
Narasiṃha himself was not seen by the resident of Nadevavāṭikā;
nor was Eraṇḍaviṣṇu, nor Heramba ever attended upon by him. (33)
The goddess who dwells in the city of Ājātu was beheld by Reṇukā;
the goddess who dwells in the city of Dānā was worshipped with devotion. 34.
Out of devotion, he himself beheld the three-linga Tryambaka at Tripura;
he did not see Somanātha while staying at the Śārdūla pond. ||35||
The god Ghusṛṇeśa, situated in Revāpura, has not been seen by me;
nor has Nāganātha, renowned in the city of Nāgadaṃta, been seen by me. ||36||
The great Amṛteśvara was seen by him while staying at Parṇagrāma;
likewise, Harihara himself was seen by him while staying on the bank of the Gabhadrā. 37.
In the ninth [chapter], Śrīnivāsa, whose abode is on the mountain, is well-described;
he is beheld at Śrīraṅga on the banks of the Kāverī, the very center of the ear. 38.
The wretched and helpless cried out, yet they were not released from prison;
during the famine, living beings were not honored with the gift of food. (39)
Even when performed night after night in a place devoid of water, it does not possess the power of water.
A bath was performed at the Nagautamī, yet Hariṇeśvara was not seen;
nor was a bath performed at the Kṛṣṇaveṇī when Jupiter had entered Virgo. (41)
Neither was a fragment of land given away, nor were poets honored;
no sacrificial session was performed at sacred fords, nor were sacrifices offered in the villages. (42)
Many lotus ponds containing abundant water were not constructed along the way, nor were any palaces ever built anywhere for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva).
Those who have come for refuge are never overcome by fear while protected;
how could Devadatta have acquired such merit here all by himself? (44)
Becoming agitated by such thoughts, the destroyer of cities (Śiva),
distressed and hurried, went to the abode of Hari, which is like the depths of the ocean of milk.
Having entered there, the cow, having been made to fall asleep by new hymns of praise,
suddenly spoke of the sorrow caused by the loss of her own sovereignty.
Indra said:
"In the past, a hundred sacrifices were performed by me out of a desire for Ramā and solely for your pleasure;
by that merit, I have attained this supreme state, free from fear. (47)
Now a certain new Indra has arisen in heaven;
by him dharma has been established, and by him sacrifices have been performed. (48)
O Acyuta, how has this divine throne of mine been ascended? 49.
Mahādeva said:
Having heard these words as he was speaking thus, the Lord of Ramā, his eyes brightened with a smile, spoke these sweet words. (50)
The Blessed Lord said:
What is the use of gifts that yield meager fruit, what use of austerities, or what use of sacrifices?
While dwelling upon the surface of the earth, you have already gratified me in the past. (51)
Indra said:
"O Blessed One, by what deed did that twice-born man please you,
such that out of affection the Blessed One granted him the station of Paurandara?"
The Blessed Lord said: By the merit of reciting five verses from the eighteen chapters of the Gītā, this supreme sovereignty has been attained by you. (53)
"Be firm, you who have become the crest-jewel of all merit.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Indra, having learned the means, [acted accordingly].
Assuming the guise of a brahmin, he went to the bank of the Godāvarī;
there he beheld the holy city, the excellent village of Kālikā.
Where the Lord Kāleśvara, the crusher of Time, resides, there on the bank of the Godāvarī stands a most righteous [shrine]. (56)
He beheld a compassionate Brahmin, a master of the Vedas,
who was constantly reciting the eighteen chapters and whose mind was self-controlled. Then, with supreme joy, he rolled at the pair of his feet.
He recited the eighteenth chapter; by that, he was instructed.
Then, by that merit, he attained union with Viṣṇu,
abandoning the meager station of the gods, such as Purandara and the others.
Having realized this, he was filled with exceeding joy and went to the city of Vaikuṇṭha;
therefore, this is the supreme reality and the highest truth for sages. (60)
I have related this divine majesty of the eighteen chapters;
by the mere hearing of it, one is liberated from all sins. (61)
Thus has been told the greatness of the Gītā, which destroys sin;
it is meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging, leading to heaven, and a great source of well-being. (62)
O highly fortunate lady, the man who hears this endowed with faith shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices and attain union with Viṣṇu. ||63||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gītā," within the Dialogue between Satī and Īśvara, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The Greatness of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (193–198) (193)
The one hundred and ninety-third chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, omniscient bestower of all goals!
Having bestowed supreme compassion upon me, please tell me that which I ask.
Having heard the greatness of the Gītā, which contains many wonderful stories,
devotion has arisen in him to hear the supreme discourse concerning Kṛṣṇa.
Among all the Purāṇas, however, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is supreme;
for in it, Kṛṣṇa is sung at every step by many sages.
Now, I shall relate its greatness exactly as it is, along with its historical accounts. (3)
Īśvara said:
Having saluted the high-minded Sūta as he sat at Naimiṣa,
Śaunaka, who was skilled in tasting the essence of the nectar of sacred narratives, spoke.
Śaunaka said:
[It is] the destroyer of the darkness of ignorance and the annihilator of the sins of ten million births. (5)
How can discernment, enriched by devotion, knowledge, and detachment, increase through this nectarine elixir of the narrative known as the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, which was recounted by Sūta? (6)
And how can the Vaiṣṇavas effect the dispelling of great delusion? In this terrible age, for the most part, the living being has become demonic. ||7||
Now, what is the elixir for the purification of each person overcome by afflictions—that which is the most excellent among all that is excellent, and the purifier among all that purifies? (8)
Now tell me that practice which brings pleasure to Kṛṣṇa,
which is like a wish-fulfilling gem, which bestows worldly happiness, and the wealth of the station of Indra.
The Guru, being pleased, bestows even Vaikuṇṭha, which is exceedingly difficult to attain. ||10||
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am pleased with you; I shall relate that which I have heard—the essence of essences, which destroys the fear of saṃsāra. (11)
O virtuous one, listen attentively as I relate that which increases devotion and is the cause of Kṛṣṇa’s satisfaction.
The scripture Śrīmad Bhāgavata, spoken by Kṛṣṇa in the Kali age, provides protection for the world that is being devoured by the mouths of the serpents of Time. 13.
There is nothing else superior to this for purifying the mind;
it is attained by the virtuous through the merits accumulated over many previous births. 14.
Having learned of King Parīkṣit’s liberation,
the Lotus-born One weighed the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, and the Mahābhārata.
There, the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is present as the most venerable on earth;
the discourse of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is difficult to obtain even for the gods. 16.
Thus, after reflecting many times, the pure and virtuous sages considered the Śrīmad Bhāgavata to be the very form of the Blessed Lord upon this earth. (17)
For that person who attains the abode of Hari through recitation or hearing [this], hearing it for a year bestows abundant happiness upon them. (18)
O best of the twice-born, by practicing devotion for one month, one attains the manifestation [of the deity];
and by doing so for seven days, this [practice] grants liberation in every respect. (19)
O wicked one, what is the use of speaking at length? The nectar of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, which reveals the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa, should be constantly drunk by the virtuous. 20.
In ancient times, Sanaka and others, devoted to compassion, proclaimed to Nārada—
the one who had previously heard it from Brahmā— the ritual procedure for the seven-day recitation.
Śaunaka said: Having received from his father the knowledge known as the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, Nārada, the knower of the reality of the worlds, wanders the earth at all times. (22)
With whom among the great-souled ones did Nārada have a meeting, where the procedure for the seven-day recitation was heard by the divine sage? 23.
Sūta said:
In this regard, I shall describe to you this narrative filled with devotion,
which was formerly told to me by the compassionate Brahmārāta.
Once, in Viśālā, Sanaka and the others saw Nārada sitting with his head bowed down, dejected in mind. (25)
Seeing his own brother on that celestial chariot, the divine sage, filled with wonder, questioned those sages who were intent upon discerning the truth. ||26||
The princes said:
"O Brahmin, why do you worry so, appearing so dejected and distressed? This state is not fitting for one like you who is detached from worldly liberation; tell us the cause. (27)
Nārada said:
"Having learned that she was the most excellent of all, endowed with various kinds of holy places, bestowing merit, and being of the nature of purity, I have arrived upon this earth. (28)
At Puṣkara, at Prayāga, at Kāśī, on the banks of the Godāvarī, at Harikṣetra, at Kurukṣetra, at Śrīraṅga, and at Setubandha; ||29||
Wandering here and there among these and other sacred fords,
I did not see anywhere anything that brought me peace or satisfied my mind.
Now I am oppressed by Kali, the friend of unrighteousness;
truth, purity, compassion, and charity do not exist anywhere on this earth. (31)

These wretched people of the world, who bear their bellies, who give false testimony, who are devoted to great heresy, and who possess minds that grant [only] what is good and pleasant—[they do not know me]. 32.
Householders were dominated by their wives; those of the [other] castes were devoid of vows;
forest-dwellers resided in cities; and renunciants were intent on worldly enjoyment. (33)
Out of greed, they sell their daughters; devoted solely to agricultural labor, they have fallen from right conduct, are divided among themselves, and exhibit only self-willed behavior. (34)
Hermitages, groves, sacred fords, rivers, and lakes, as well as temples of the deities, have been destroyed there by the wicked. (35)
Neither a perfected yogi nor a man of knowledge performing virtuous deeds is seen here;
today, by the forest fire of the Kali age, spiritual practice has been reduced to ashes. (36)
The countryside has its pillars of commerce, the twice-born have their pillars of auspiciousness, and women have their pillars of passion; thus is the world seen everywhere upon the earth. (37)
Once I reached the auspicious bank of the Yamunā, where that Vṛndāvana forest was seen, the place where the pastimes of Hari took place. (38)
In that regard, O lords of sages, hear that wonderful thing which was seen there:
a young woman sat there with a weary mind. (39)
Two aged men, fallen and breathless at his side, were unconscious;
before them stood two women, one seeking to rouse them and the other weeping.
She was being watched by those standing on the shore as if they were her own guardians; she was fanned by many women and repeatedly exhorted again and again. (41)
Having seen her from a distance, I approached out of curiosity;
upon seeing me, that young woman rose up and spoke these words: ||42||
The boy said:
"O holy one, stay here for a moment and dispel my anxiety;
for the sight of virtuous men, O auspicious one, wards off the entire flood of sins."
It is solely through past merit that this vision of you has arisen. ||43||
"O giver of honor, I am capable of cutting away even this minute mental suffering.
Nārada said:
"Having been addressed thus by her, my mind became tender with compassion."
Overcome with curiosity, I questioned that woman of beautiful hips.
"O auspicious one, who are you, and who are these lotus-eyed women?
Tell me everything before me regarding the cause of your sorrow. (45)
Thus questioned by me, the girl, her mind distressed,
spoke of all her suffering and the cause of her own misery.
Bālā said: I am known as Bhakti; these two are my sons, named Jñāna and Vairāgya, who have been worn out by the yoga of old age. 47.
O Nārada, the Gaṅgā and other rivers have come here for the purpose of serving Him;
they serve Him constantly with great honor. (48)
"O Sage, I have been exhausted on all sides and have gained no spiritual merit whatsoever.
O best of Brahmins, first hear my story."
Because of him, though born in Draviḍa, I have attained growth in Karṇāṭa; yet, due to this [separation], I have become miserable and find no peace anywhere. (50)
It remained somewhat in Mahārāṣṭra and fell into decay in Gurjara;
there, due to the influence of the terrible Kali age, it was shattered by heretics.
"I am weak and have been long deprived of my children; give me some food. (52)
"O Nārada, by the turn of fate, I have arrived at this forest;
though I am but a young girl, I have become possessed of a beautiful form. (53)
Having abandoned these two sons of mine, who are sleeping here with untroubled minds and are both very old, I am not now able to depart. (54)
"How was I born as a young girl? Whence came my son and my aged husband? How has this reversal occurred among these three who were once of one mind? (55)
"Thinking, 'I am an aged mother and these are my young children,' I therefore grieve for myself, my mind filled with wonder. (56)
If you know, O knower of dharma, compassionate one, protector of the distressed,
tell me everything according to the truth, and whatever the cause of this may be.
Thus questioned by her, I reflected for a moment and, addressing her with devotion, spoke after a long time: (58)
O sinless one, through my knowledge I perceive your entire conduct;
O wise lady, do not despair, for Hari will bring you well-being.
This terrible Kali age is a yoke that seizes all beings;
by it, the eternal conduct and the path of yoga and austerity have been destroyed.
People are full of sin and drink liquor; they commit acts of deceit and evil.
The virtuous here are afflicted by great suffering, while the wicked are joyful in their minds. (61)
A wise man, though steadfast in mind, is seen neither as such nor otherwise; this earth, burdened by the weight of the wicked, is unfit to be touched or even looked upon.
Day by day, O beautiful lady, this swelling of your throat diminishes as the year gradually passes;
yet no one perceives these two sons of yours.
You, having been abandoned by many horses and having reached a state of decay,
have again become young through union with the forest fire.
Blessed indeed is this forest where devotion has become new;
for here, due to the absence of those who seize [the devotee], novelty has not been lost. (65)
"It appears that something here is asleep due to the bliss of its own self.
Bhakti said:
"How is it that Kali has been established today as pure by King Parīkṣit?"
Was unrighteousness indeed overlooked by Hari, who is devoted to compassion? ||66||
"O twice-born ones, having cut through this doubt of mine with your speech, I have become happy; having heard her words, I spoke again. (67)
O child, listen with love to that which was asked by you:
when the Blessed Lord Mukunda, having abandoned the earth, departed for His own abode.
The Kali age, which began on that very day as a subverter of truth,
was seen by the King during his conquest of the quarters to have sought refuge with him, just like a low-born man.
One who perceives your qualities is not defiled; for this fruit is common to all, which is not attained through austerity, nor by yoga, nor by meditative absorption.
In the Kali age, the wise man obtains that fruit through the chanting of Keśava's names;
having seen such a Kali as this, which yields a result more essential than the essence itself.
Viṣṇurāta established [this] for the benefit of those born in the Kali age;
however, due to the performance of evil deeds, its essence has now departed from all sides.
Just as seeds devoid of husks lie scattered upon the ground, so too did the stories of the Bhāgavata exist in every house and among every person through the Brahmins. (73)
Then, out of greed for wealth acquired through their actions, the essence of their discourse vanished;
those people became atheists, performers of exceedingly fierce and manifold deeds, and beggars. (74)
While he was staying at all the sacred fords, he then departed for Tīrthasāra;
[he saw those] whose minds were agitated by desire, anger, great greed, and thirst.
The wheel of saṃsāra was shattered by his actions; thereafter, the essence of karma departed from him due to the conquest of the mind, through greed, and by resorting to heresy. (76)
And because they did not study the scriptures, they lost the fruit of meditation and yoga; those so-called scholars took pleasure in their wives like buffaloes. (77)
They are indeed skilled in producing sons, yet they are not skilled in the means for liberation; for where is their Vaiṣṇavism, which is led by the true tradition? 78.
All are intent on giving to the gods, and all are devoted to giving to the virtuous;
this, however, is the nature of the age (yuga-dharma)—to whom can blame be given? (79)
Therefore, by remembering the lotus-eyed one, you shall attain happiness. ||80||
O best of the twice-born, having heard these words spoken by me, she was filled with wonder; after praising me, she spoke these words once more.
Bhakti said:
"O divine sage, you are indeed blessed to have come here through my good fortune;
for in this world, the sight of holy men bestows all spiritual perfections. (82)
O Sage, O Brahmin, instruct me now so that there may be for me an easy means [to attain this]; for you, the omniscient one, there is indeed nothing here that cannot be accomplished. (83)
Having contemplated even a single composition of his words, one who was previously Dhruva attained the state of Dhruva through his grace— he by whom the unconquerable Māyā was conquered.
I bow to that son of Brahmā, who has become free from all conflict. ||84||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Bhāgavata," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(194) The One Hundred and Ninety-Fourth Chapter.
Sūta said:
O compassionate brahmins, listen to that which I indeed related when I was thus entreated by her with such exceedingly piteous devotion. ||1||
Nārada said:
"O young girl, do not grieve in vain; fixing your mind within your heart, remember the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and you shall obtain the bliss of love. (2)
And he by whom Draupadī was rescued from the distress caused by the Kauravas, and the beautiful cowherd women were protected—that Kṛṣṇa has gone away somewhere. (3)
But you, O Devotion, are his constant beloved, dearer to him than his own life;
for when summoned by you, the Blessed One goes even to the homes of the lowly. (4)
In the three ages beginning with the Kṛta, realization and dispassion are the means for achieving liberation;
but in the Kali age, devotion alone brings about union with Brahman. (5)
Having thus resolved, He whose form is consciousness and supreme bliss, with a delighted mind, created you from His own body as His beloved.
Having joined his palms in reverence, Hari was asked by you, "What shall I do?
Thereupon Kṛṣṇa commanded you, "Sustain my devotees."
When you had likewise accepted that, Hari became pleased at that time;
he gave you Muktidā as a handmaid, and Jñāna and Vairāgya as his two sons.
You eternally nourish your devotees while residing in Vaikuṇṭha; and on earth, for the sake of sustaining your devotees, you have assumed the form of a shadow. ||9||
Together with the knowledge of liberation and dispassion, you have indeed arrived; for they abide in liberation throughout the ages, beginning from Kṛta up to Dvāpara. (10)
When the Kali age reached its decline, afflicted by the diseases of heresy, she quickly returned once more to Vaikuṇṭha at your command;
even today, liberation comes swiftly as soon as she is remembered by you. (11)
Having adopted these two as your own children and protected them by your side, your sons have become dull-witted and aged due to your neglect in this Kali age. (12)
Nevertheless, abandon your anxiety; I shall devise a means.
O fair-faced one, there is no age equal to the Kali age. (13)
In that [age], I shall proclaim you in every house and among every person, setting aside other doctrines and placing great festivals at the forefront. (14)
If I do not set you forth, then I am indeed not a servant of Hari;
for those living beings who will follow you here in the Kali age [will likewise not be servants]. (15)
Even sinners shall go fearlessly to the abode of Hari, provided that devotion in the form of love always exists within their hearts. (16)
Those of stainless form do not see a plowman even in a dream, nor a hungry ghost, nor a piśāca, nor a rākṣasa, nor even an asura. (17)
The Lord is accessible through the touch and sight of those whose minds are endowed with devotion;
He is not attained by austerities, nor by the Vedas, nor even by knowledge or ritual action.
For Hari is indeed attained through devotion; in this matter, the cowherd women are the authority.
Devotion arises for fortunate men only after a thousand births. (19)
In the Kali age there is devotion; in the Kali age there is devotion. Through devotion, Kṛṣṇa stands before one.
But those who commit acts of hostility toward devotion perish within the three worlds. 20.
In former times, Durvāsas fell into misery because he reviled devotion: "Enough with religious observances! Enough with sacred fords! Enough with yoga! Enough with sacrifices! (21)
Enough with discourses on knowledge; devotion alone grants liberation.
Having spoken thus, he indeed heard my own greatness being proclaimed.
To her, who was filled with all kinds of joy, he spoke these words again:
"O Nārada, you are truly blessed; your devotion toward me is unwavering. (23)
Never again shall this mind of mine be joined with that [state of] delusion;
O Compassionate One, you have quickly dispelled my suffering and distress. (24)
"Awaken me to the consciousness of my two sons.
Having heard those words of hers, I was indeed filled with compassion. (25)
Setting out to awaken the two of them, he touched their faces with his hand, pressed their ears together, and uttered a loud sound.
May there be a swift awakening to knowledge and an awakening to dispassion, through the sounds of the Vedas and Upanishads, and by the repeated recitation of the Gītā. 27.
Though being awakened by that breeze, they somehow attained consciousness;
yet both remained sluggish and languid, their eyes not even glancing about.
With hair as white as a crane's and resembling dry wood, the two of them, emaciated by hunger, merely looked at each other and fell back asleep. (29)
Then I became absorbed in thought, wondering, "What should be done by me?
Alas, how can sleep depart, and how can the extreme old age of these two be removed? (30)
O best of the twice-born, while I was reflecting upon Govinda and remembering him, a voice from the sky suddenly spoke: "O sage, do not be distressed. (31)
Your exertion will undoubtedly be fruitful;
for this purpose, O celestial sage, perform virtuous deeds. (32)
The virtuous, who are adorned by goodness, will declare that act to be their own;
for when that noble deed was performed, the sleeping of these two [parents] was an act of old age.
"Within a moment, devotion shall depart and spread everywhere"—even after clearly hearing these words from the sky, O twice-born ones, I [remained] out of fear. (34)
It was not known that what had been described as being hidden by the voice from the sky was [the truth];
why then have these two become endowed with knowledge through the accumulation of their past actions? (35)
Where will those virtuous ones be? How will they speak of the reality of karma?
What must I do here regarding that which was spoken in the language of the sky? (36)
Then, O twice-born ones, having established those two there, I went outside;
from the Vṛndā forest, I questioned the best of the twice-born wherever I found them.
Then, having heard the entire account, they were all struck with wonder in their minds; indeed, being ignorant of the serpent's power, they offered no reply at all. (38)
Some declared it to be incurable, while others said it was incomprehensible;
still others remained silent, reflecting upon it again and again.
Being awakened again and again by the sounds of the Vedas and Vedānta and by the recitations of the Gītā, that triad indeed arose; oh, what a marvel! (40)
"Even by the yogi Nārada himself, that which cannot be known—how can it be accomplished here by other mere humans?
Therefore, distressed with anxiety, I have come to the Badarī forest. (41)
Having made a firm resolve for that purpose, I was performing penance right here when I beheld before me the lords of sages, Sanaka and the others,
who possessed a radiance equal to ten million suns; I then spoke to those best of sages.
Now, by great good fortune, you have indeed been seen by me;
therefore, O highly fortunate ones, with minds well-pleased, tell me the means for that. 43.
Sirs, you are the best among yogins, wise and highly learned;
though but five years of age, you are the ancestors even of those who came before. (44)
Always residing in Vaikuṇṭha, they were intent on chanting the glories of Hari;
intoxicated by the nectar of stories of His divine play, they were devoted to the remembrance of Hari. ||45||
Therefore, even now, the venerable son of Time does not trouble those for whom,
in former times, the two gatekeepers of Hari were struck down by a mere knitting of the eyebrows.
Having become two Daitya women, they both returned to that same place for three births;
tell me the means by which that which was spoken by the bodiless voice may be accomplished. (47)

O wise ones, being compassionate, please speak clearly on how and where that which is to be practiced may be explained, so that devotion, knowledge, and dispassion may arise with ease, and so that your fame may spread throughout all the worlds. (48)
The princes said:
"O divine sage, do not worry; bring joy to your heart.
There exists here a means that is easily accomplished and bestows happiness upon the whole world. (49)
O Nārada, you are most blessed; you are the crest-jewel of the detached, the foremost among those who are vessels of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s love, and the best of speakers. (50)
O celestial sage, it is not surprising that you are intent upon the practice of devotion;
for those who are servants of Kṛṣṇa, such wandering on earth for the sake of devotion is entirely appropriate. (51)
In this world, the sages have devised many methods for the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi);
yet all of these are achieved through great exertion and generally yield only heaven as their fruit. (52)
The path that leads to Vaikuṇṭha exists within the worlds;
a virtuous teacher of that path is generally obtained through good fortune. (53)
O Lord of Sages, that which has been described as the action of the sky-voice should be understood here by the omniscient ones of old as the sacrifice of knowledge (jñānayajña). 54.
The discourse on the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata, which is the sacrifice of knowledge spoken by Śuka, appears to me as a bestower of happiness for devotion, knowledge, and detachment. 55.
All these defects of the Kali age, terrified by the sound of the glorious Bhāgavata, flee toward their destruction like wolves at the mere sound of a "ha! (or a lion's roar).
Devotion endowed with knowledge and dispassion, bringing forth the essence of love, will bring about joyful play in every house and among every person. (57)
Sūta said:
Having heard what was spoken by Kumāra, the venerable Nārada, with a delighted mind,
spoke again, contemplating his excellence.
Nārada said:
Though awakened by the sounds of the Vedas and Vedāntas and by the recitations of the Gītā, that triad did not rise, being obscured by the defects of the Kali age. (59)
"How will he attain awakening here through conversation with the devotees of the Lord? O you whose vision is never in vain, please sever this doubt of mine. (60)
Those who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge must not delay;
therefore, Sanaka and the others, being dispassionate and with vital energy drawn upward, praised him.
The eternal Siddhas spoke with reverence to the Brahmin Nārada.
The princes said:
"The narrative of the Bhāgavata is born from the essence of the Vedas and Upaniṣads;
it shines as the most supreme, appearing distinct with its exalted fruit. (63)
Just as there is flavor from the root to the tip within the fruit of a mango tree, so too is this [flavor] present;
yet, when separated from its husk, it becomes enchanting to the whole world.
Just as clarified butter existing within milk is not perceived as sweet [while still mixed], yet once it has become separate, that divine substance increases the delight of the gods. (65)
Just as sugar permeates the beginning, middle, and end of a stalk of sugarcane, so too does the narrative of the Bhāgavata remain distinct from yet pervading all things. 66.
The Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is indeed a Purāṇa of aesthetic rasa; it has been revealed for the sake of the happiness of devotion, knowledge, and renunciation. (67)
For indeed, by the grace of the Brahman Kṛṣṇa,
this entire *Catuḥśloka* appears as the Brahman itself.
This account of his life was proclaimed to you by Brahmā;
and it was also proclaimed by you, O divine Vyāsa, to [Śuka] for the sake of removing his suffering.
By the mere remembrance of whom Bādarāyaṇa immediately became despondent with worldly life, and composed this great work, which is enchanting for those who delight in the Self. (70)
In this matter, what wonder is there that you should ask again and again about the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the scripture capable of attracting Kṛṣṇa?
Sūta said: Having heard these words uttered by the lords of yogis, headed by Sanaka, which were most desirable—
Having devoutly supported their feet and bowed his head,
he joyfully spoke to those who remove the world's afflictions.
Nārada said:
"The very sight of you destroys the flood of sins for those tormented by the forest fire of worldly suffering and extends their ultimate welfare."
May he who went to the battlefield for the sake of manifesting his love—by drinking the entirety of the stories sung from your mouths without exception—be for your protection. 73.
If, through the arising of merit accumulated over many births, a person of merit should attain the company of the virtuous,
then the great darkness of delusion caused by ignorance will be dispelled.
For then that great discernment arises and flourishes. ||74||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(195) Chapter One Hundred and Ninety-Five.
Sūta said:
Then the celestial sage, having honored the princes there, spoke these words with humility, being devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge. (1)
Nārada said:
"I shall perform a sacrifice of knowledge, radiant with the stories of Śuka and the scriptures, through diligent effort for the sake of establishing devotion, knowledge, and detachment. (2)
"O twice-born ones, let that place where I must perform the sacrifice be told;
you four alone have been chosen by me as the carriers of the sacrifice."
Over how many days should the glorious Bhāgavata narrative be heard? What procedure should be followed therein, O you who are experts in the sacrifice of knowledge? (4)
The princes said:
"Listen, O Nārada, we shall tell you that narrative of men which destroys the heap of sins for those who hear it and increases their merit."
Near Gaṅgādvāra, however, there was a great city named Kāmadā.
To the north of the Golden River is the meritorious bank named Ānanda,
frequented by various hosts of sages and resorted to by gods and Siddhas.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, possessed clear and soft sands,
was situated in a delightful secluded spot, and was adorned with golden lotuses.
By the very power of that field, the mutual enmity that existed in the minds of the living beings dwelling nearby vanished, as their hearts became affectionate toward one another.
Indeed, you must perform a sacrifice of knowledge there with great effort;
for there, a narrative that bestows unprecedented delight shall take place.
Devotion will come there, placing her two sons before her, to him who stands at the threshold of the forest of old age with a body worn out by decrepitude. (11)
Wherever there is devotion to the discourse concerning the Lord, there she, along with her son, will become like a young woman who has drunk the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s glory. 12.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, those Kumāras, together with Nārada, then went quickly to Gaṅgādvāra for the sake of the sacrifice of knowledge.
O bull among the Bhārgavas, when they reached the bank of the Gaṅgā,
a great clamor arose throughout the seven worlds, beginning with the world of mortals (Bhūrloka).
Those ancient Vaiṣṇavas who had attained the worldly state through the mere touch of the cloth [used for] tasting the nectar of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam arrived, running again and again. 15.
Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Cyavana, Gautama, Medhātithi, Devala, Devarāta, Rāma, as well as Gādhija, Śākala, Mṛkaṇḍaputra, Atri, and Japippalāda. (16)

Vyāsa and Parāśara, the two lords of yoga, as well as Śuka and others who are foremost among the devotees of the Lord (Bhāgavatas), accompanied by their disciples and learned in many scriptures, have made the tasting of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa their primary goal. (17)
The four Vedas, the six Vedāṅgas, the three Upaniṣads, the three Saṃhitās, the seventeen Purāṇas, and likewise the six Śāstras departed. (18)
There are the rivers such as the Gaṅgā, the lakes such as Puṣkara, all the sacred fields in every direction, and the forests such as Daṇḍaka. (19)
There, Himavat and the other mountains, the gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, the continents, the oceans, the guardians of the quarters, and those dwelling in the netherworld likewise went forth. (20)
Then, during the initiation ceremony, Nārada offered an excellent seat; the two Kumāras, along with Aviditā and Sarvā, sat down, intent upon Kṛṣṇa.
The Vaiṣṇavas, those deeply detached, the renunciants, and the celibate students stood at the forefront; Nārada stood before them.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, on the left side are the hosts of sages, and on the right are the dwellers of heaven; elsewhere are the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, and the sacred fords.
The sound of "Victory!", the word "Homage!", and likewise the sound of conch shells,
reached the very limits of space, resounding through the ten directions.
Having ascended their celestial chariots, the delighted inhabitants of Nākavāsa scattered flowers from the Kalpa trees over that assembly hall.
Sūta said:
When Bhṛgu and the others had thus sat down as was fitting, they recounted the majesty of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam to Nārada. (26)
The princes said:
"Listen, O Nārada, we shall describe the most wonderful majesty of that scripture known as the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata, according to the prescribed rules. (27)
The Bhāgavata narrative should always be cultivated by virtuous men;
by the mere hearing of it, they attain the fulfillment of their purpose. (28)
The work known as the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata consists of eighteen thousand verses and twelve cantos; it contains the dialogue between Parīkṣit and Śuka. (29)
One wanders in this wheel of existence, deluded by ignorance,
for as long as the Śuka-śāstra has not reached one's ears. Of what use are many scriptures, Purāṇas, Saṃhitās, and Āgamas?
If the *Bhāgavata* has not been heard by men with a spirit of devotion; ||31||
That house in which even a portion of the Bhāgavata is always present is indeed a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) for men, destroying their sins. (32)
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of royal consecrations do not equal even a sixteenth part of the narrative of the Bhāgavatī. (33)
O best of sages, sins remain in this body only so long as the glorious Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is not properly heard by men. (34)
Neither the Nagaṅgā, nor Nagayā, nor Kāśī, nor Pratiṣṭhāna, nor Puṣkara is equal to the fruit of merit obtained from the Bhāgavatapurāṇa. ||35||
If you desire the destruction of worldly existence, recite daily from your own mouth even half a verse or a single quarter-verse originating from the Bhāgavata. (36)
It is the beginning of the Vedas, the mother of the Vedas, and indeed the Puruṣa-sūkta.
And likewise the Trayībhāgavata, as well as the twelve-syllable and eight-syllable mantras. ||37||
The twelvefold Prayāga is Time itself, consisting of the year;
it is the Brāhmaṇa, the Agnihotra sacrifice, the cow, and the twelfth lunar day. ||38||
Tulasī, the spring season, and Puruṣottama himself—O Lord of Sages, in reality there is no separate existence among these. (39)
O twice-born Nārada, whoever should explain this scripture of the Bhāgavata day after day, the sins committed throughout ten million births are destroyed for him. 40.
When the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam is heard, recited, and meditated upon by men, it bestows either liberation or devotion; likewise, the service of Tulasī and the sacred fire [grants the same]. (41)
But when the time of death has arrived, he who casts fear far away and listens to the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam with devotion shall partake in liberation. 42.
On the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada), one should give the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, adorned with a golden lion-throne, to an eminent brahmin after having it duly decorated. 43.
Endowed with devotion, possessing a celestial vehicle, moderate in diet, and having conquered his senses, he who hears [this] from the beginning shall attain the world of union with Kṛṣṇa. ||44||
Alas, those who, even for the mere duration of their birth, have not properly restrained their deceitful minds on this earth and have not drunk the stories of Kṛṣṇa,
have lived like outcasts or like cattle.
Falsehood is the mother of one's own birth, and it has tormented me intensely. ||45||
Those by whom the Bhāgavata Purāṇa has not been heard, nor the Ancient Person (Puruṣa) worshipped,
have certainly not offered oblations into the mouths of the gods on earth.
The birth of those men has passed in vain. ||46||
But that man whose mind, corrupted by sin through association with the wicked, finds no delight in the stories of Hari—
fie on that man, who is equal to a beast and a mere burden upon this earth!
Thus indeed say the sages who were perfected in former times. ||47||
The discourse originating from the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata is indeed rare in this world;
it is obtained only through merit accumulated over ten million lifetimes. (48)
Therefore, O virtuous one, storehouse of yoga, you should listen to the Sātvata narrative every day; in truth, O twice-born, there is no fixed rule regarding the number of days. (49)
Since it is held that his hearing [of the scripture] occurs through truth and celibacy, therefore in the Kali age there is indeed a specific rule consisting of seven days. (50)
Due to the difficulty of conquering the mind, due to disease, due to the decline of human lifespan, and due to the abundance of defects in the Kali age, the seven-day recitation is prescribed. 51.
The restraint of the mind and likewise the practice of observances can be accomplished within seven days; therefore, the arrangement of these observances is prescribed.
Whatever fruit is obtained from constant listening with faith, that same fruit was attained by Śukadeva through listening for only seven days. (53)
Whatever fruit is not obtained through austerity, yoga, or meditative absorption—all that one may obtain without effort by listening [to this] for seven days. (54)
Compared to sacrifice, vows, austerity, meditation, knowledge, and visiting sacred fords, the observance of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Saptāha is indeed considered supreme. (55)
When Kṛṣṇa, having abandoned the earth, was intent on going to his own abode,
the wise Uddhava, perceiving this, spoke these words to Govinda.
Uddhava said:
O Blessed One, all the work of the gods has been accomplished by you;
now you desire to go to your own abode beyond darkness.
Therefore, O Lord, anxiety has arisen in me through fear of separation from you;
O Lord of Gods, dispel that [anxiety], for I have come to you for refuge. (58)
"This terrible Kali age has arrived; all people here will become wicked.
Therefore, O Lord, command what should be done then. (59)
O delighter of the Yadus, this earth, burdened as it is, to whom else but you will she go for refuge? No protector other than you is seen here. (60)
Therefore, O Ocean of Compassion, show us mercy and remain right here;
for it was for the protection of the virtuous, O Lord, that you manifested yourself.
Though devoid of qualities and formless, You possess a body of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
yet, separated from You, how shall these devotees endure upon the surface of the earth?
"Therefore, perform that which is for our benefit—the difficult practice of the worship of the Nirguṇa.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Uddhava, Hari reflected for a moment.
O twice-born one, filled with supreme compassion, he bestowed the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam upon him, having deposited his own splendor within the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam.
Having given this to Uddhava, the Blessed One entered His own abode;
by him, this form of the earth of speech exists here as Śrī Hari.
By constant service to her, the sin of men is destroyed in an instant;
therefore, listening to it for seven days is declared to be superior to all else.
O twice-born one, the listener, the speaker, and the questioner attain absorption in that [divinity] for the sake of washing away suffering, poverty, misfortune, and sin. (67)
For the sake of conquering desire and anger, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is sufficient;
otherwise, the Vaiṣṇavī Māyā is difficult to overcome even for the gods. How can it be turned away from men without the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam? (68)
Sūta said:
Having thus spoken the majesty of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata,
they began to relate the divine narrative of the Bhāgavata.
While the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the essence of the Vedas and Upaniṣads, was being commenced by the twice-born, devotion suddenly manifested there as if it were already present. (70)

Taking her two handsome young sons, who were full of joy, by her arms, she whose body was beautiful with love repeatedly uttered the names "Śrī Kṛṣṇa," "Govinda," and "Murāri, O Lord" within her heart. (71)
Seeing her arrive—adorned with the essence of the Bhāgavata and dressed in most beautiful attire—the compassionate ones gazed upon her;
and all of them, their eyes wide with wonder, reflected: "How? From where has she come? (72)
Then, having heard these words from the prince— which were uttered with the purpose of making his own goal accomplished—
the daughter of the Lotus-born (Brahmā), her face bowed down, spoke to the prince.
Devotion said:
"Even though I have perished in the Kali age, I have been nourished by you this very day through the essence of the narrative."
"Where shall I stay? Point out to me a dwelling place that is pleasing to both of them. (74)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of Brahmā, the Kumāras reflected upon them thoroughly and fixed them in their minds.
And they spoke of devotion, which removes the disease of worldly existence and bestows the singular gift of love upon those who possess devotion to Hari. ||75||
The princes said:
"Toward those who are devoted to Govinda, toward the virtuous, and toward those intent on compassion for the distressed..."
Having restrained the mind that has strayed onto a wrong path, one should make it single-pointed upon the lotus feet of Hari.
Therefore, these defects born of the Kali age are not able to behold you, even though they are powerful in this world; for in the Kali age, you alone exist for the welfare of the universe.
It shall be proclaimed by Nārada. ||77||

In the midst of all the worlds, those who possess exclusive devotion to Śrī Hari are the most fortunate, even if they are destitute; for even Hari himself, having swiftly abandoned his own realm, dwells within their hearts.
He enters the hearts of those who are bound by the thread of love. ||78||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||195||
(196) Chapter One Hundred and Ninety-Six.
Sūta said:
Or rather, having perceived the extraordinary devotion within the hearts of the Vaiṣṇavas, Hari abandoned his own realm and came to this earth. ||1||
Wearing a forest garland, dark as a rain cloud, clad in yellow garments, and bearing a crown; his shimmering makara-shaped earrings were set with a multitude of gold chains. ||2||
With three folds gracefully descending his neck, he shone brilliantly with the beautiful Kaustubha gem;
possessing the loveliness of ten million gods of love, he was anointed with divine sandalwood paste.
The embodiment of supreme bliss and consciousness, the sweet-sounding holder of the flute, entered the stainless hearts of his own devotees. 4.
Those residents of Vaikuṇṭha who are Vaiṣṇavas of peaceful mind have arrived in hidden forms to hear the narrations of Hari. (5)
Then a loud cry of "Victory! Victory! arose, accompanied by the sound of conchs, by which the most terrible inauspiciousness born of the Kali age was brought to its end.
Having observed there the forgetfulness of both the dwellings and the people regarding their own homes,
Nārada, the knower of the truth of the supreme self, spoke to the Kumāras.
Nārada said:
"O lords of sages, this supermundane majesty has been observed by me today, arising from the seven-day rite."
Even the deluded, the deceitful, and even beasts and birds go to that state known as the Supreme;
therefore, in this world of men, no other scripture than this has been ordained as pure for the sake of its purification. (9)

O youths, tell me: in this Kali age, which is a reservoir of faults, by what means—other than the Saptāhajajña consisting of sacred narratives—can people achieve the destruction of the flood of sins and attain their ultimate purpose? 10.
"A new path has been revealed by you, who are compassionate and devoted to the welfare of the world.
The youths said:
"Those men who are evildoers, extremely wicked, always addicted to evil conduct, and full of envy—" (11)
Those who are consumed by the fire of anger, crooked, and devoid of desire, go to Hari through the sacrifice of seven days.

Those who are devoid of truth, who revile their father and mother, who are agitated by craving, who are outside the pale of the stages of life and the social orders, who are hypocritical in their study of the Vedas, who live by harming living beings, and who perform sacrifices lasting seven days— they go to Hari.
Those who commit the five heinous sins, those who act with deceit, the cruel, those as merciless as *piśācas*,
those nourished by the property of Brahmins, and those who are unchaste— even they go to Hari by means of the seven-day sacrifice.

Those who are deceitful, impulsive, base, ungrateful, defiled, and evil-minded, and who constantly commit sins through body, speech, and mind—even they go to Hari by means of the seven-day sacrifice. 15.
Sūta said:
Then, when Nārada, who is worshipped by the gods, had thus become satisfied in mind,
the Kumāras were pleased and spoke again to Nārada.
The princes said:
"In this regard, we shall proclaim an ancient history, by the mere hearing of which the destruction of sin is produced. (17)
Formerly, you [dwelt] in a city named Kōhalā on the bank of the Gabhadrā river,
which was filled with wealth and grain and endowed with the conduct of the various castes and stages of life.
There lived a most excellent brahmin known as Ātmadeva, who was wise in the Vedas, the sciences, and the ritual injunctions, and was ever devoted to his daily duties. ||19||
Devoted to her own welfare, she was fond of the impermanent wealth of this world;
yet, born of a noble family, she was intent on establishing the truth of her own words. (20)
Due to the ripening of past karma, she is generally a talkative woman;
though brave, she is harsh in domestic duties and fond of quarreling. (21)
As the couple lived there thus without offspring,
their age passed away until it reached the measure of fifty years.

Now, if a couple of the same lineage, who are suffering and childless, reside in the house, one should cause offspring to be produced for them, and their wealth and other assets should also be given to them. (23)
Although many gifts of cattle, land, gold, and garments have been bestowed, neither a son nor a daughter is born due to past karma. (24)
Once, O best of the twice-born,
that king, having become weary of himself and distressed by his childlessness, abandoned his home and went to the forest.
Wandering here and there with a mind agitated by the pain of delusion, emaciated by hunger and overcome by thirst, he happened by chance to reach a body of water. (26)
O Nārada, having drunk water in that lake, that best of the twice-born sat down there, taking refuge in the shade of a tree.
Then, at that very moment, a certain Siddha who was wandering the earth arrived there;
having drunk water from that pond, he too came to that place. (28)
Seeing him seated there in tranquility, the noble-minded Ātmadeva rose up with due honor and grasped his feet as if they were those of his own guru.
Then those two sat down and questioned one another,
their minds becoming very affectionate like a teacher and a disciple in a hermitage.
Then Sayatī, seeing him sighing with inner sorrow, questioned that compassionate lion, the god whose essence is the burden [of others], who stood before him. (31)
The Siddha said:
"O best of the twice-born, what anxiety dwells in your heart that causes you suffering? O knower of dharma, tell me of that which brings you such distress. (32)
Having heard those words of that great-souled Siddha,
Ātmadeva then spoke of the cause of his own suffering.
Ātmadeva said:
What can I say of this suffering accumulated by my past karma?
My ancestors are drinking lukewarm water. (34)
The ancestors and the deities do not accept the offering given by me;
distressed by that suffering, I have come here to give up my life. (35)
