"Fie on this life, devoid of offspring, and on this house, wealth, and lineage! Even this cow that is being tended by me is now approaching death. (36)
Even the tree planted by my own hand has come to this state;
for one as unfortunate and childless as I, what is the use of life beyond this? (37)
The princes said:
Having spoken thus, he wept aloud before him, afflicted by grief;
at that moment, great compassion arose in the heart of the Lord.
Having seen and understood the garland of syllables on the forehead,
that wise practitioner of yoga spoke again at length to the twice-born Ātmadeva.
The Siddha said: Listen, O Brahmin, I have today examined your *prārabdha*;
the attainment of a son for you is not seen even for the duration of seven births. (40)
"Relinquish your obsession for the sake of your subjects; the course of karma is all-powerful. But having attained discernment, O high-minded one, be happy.
Having heard these words of the Siddha, the best of the twice-born—
But with his mind fixed on the hope for offspring, he spoke of his success, though he was deeply distressed. ||42||
The Brahmin said:
"What use have I for discernment? Give me a son, even by force!
Otherwise, overwhelmed with grief, I shall give up my life before you. (43)
Seeing such persistence on the part of the brahmins, that one whose wealth was asceticism spoke: "Sagara, the lord of subjects, suffered grief because he was childless. (44)
Citraketu has gone to his misery because of the erasure of the lines of fate;
therefore, O knower of dharma, if you too should obtain a son— ||45||
"Having become happy through what was heard, fate is indeed more powerful.
Having said this to the best of the twice-born, the perfected one, esteemed by the virtuous, departed. (46)
Out of persistence, she gave one fruit to him who requested a son, saying:
"O twice-born one, this fruit is given by me to you for the sake of obtaining a son. (47)
"A son shall be born to you from your wife; of this there is no doubt. Truthfulness, purity, compassion, charity, and eating but a single meal a day—" (48)
"The rite must be performed for three years; by that, the son shall become pure.
Having spoken thus, the yogi departed, and the brahmin returned to his own home. 49.
Having given that fruit to her wife, she spoke as instructed by the Siddha;
then the cruel Dhulī, eager to establish her own position, addressed the virtuous man.
She told her friend everything that had been said by her husband regarding the speech of the Siddha:
"If I were to eat this fruit offered by the Siddha... (51)
If I were to become pregnant, how could I endure it? I have little appetite for food and lack the strength for household chores. (52)
If he has entered the womb in a transverse position, then my death will surely come;
how can I, so delicate, endure the agonizing pain of childbirth?
While I am weak, Nanda will never cease from seizing all my possessions. (53)
"O lady of pure smiles, anxiety has come upon me; what shall I do?
O twice-born one, having heard those words, she [remained silent] out of fear of breaking her affection. 54.
"So be it," she said to her with affection, her face beaming with a smile;
"thus, by means of this clever reasoning, the fruit has not been consumed at all. (55)
When her husband asked, "Has the fruit been eaten? she replied, "It has been eaten.
Once, her sister went to that house of her own accord. (56)
"All that was told before has indeed become a great anxiety for me.
What shall I do, for I am pregnant? Tell me the truth. (57)
She said, "I am pregnant; I will give [the child] to you after my delivery.
Until then, remain comfortably at home, well-concealed as if still with the fetus. (58)
"I will nourish that boy in your house forever;
O fair-faced one, give me the fruit of the cow today for the sake of testing it. (59)
Having spoken thus, with a joyful heart, she went to her own house at the end of the day;
and Dhūlī also did exactly as had been instructed by her sister.
Then, having given birth to the boy, she quickly entrusted him to Dhūlī;
she reported to her husband that the child had been born safely.
When happiness had arisen for the world through the birth of himself, his deity, and his subjects,
he gave gifts to the foremost of the twice-born and performed the birth-rite.
The sound of singing and musical instruments was exceedingly auspicious in his house;
the high-minded Ātmadeva was filled with joy. (63)
Then she said to her husband: "O Lord, there is no milk in my breasts;
how shall I now sustain the infant who has just been born?"
Long ago, a boy was born from my sister who had given birth;
bringing her to our home, you shall protect and nourish that child.
Having heard these words of his, that best of brahmins,
his soul deluded, performed exactly so, filled with joy as if he were a god.
The son of his mother’s sister was given the name Dhūm by his mother according to its true meaning; he constantly received nourishment from her breast-milk.
Then, when three months had passed, that cow gave birth to a child who was divine,
stainless, with a golden luster, and possessed of all auspicious marks.
Seeing him, the Brahmin was pleased and personally performed the purificatory rites;
all the people, desiring to see him, arrived there filled with great wonder.
And through the arising of great fortune for the brahmin Ātmadeva, a boy resembling a god was born from the cow, causing great wonder. (70)
That secret was not known by anyone through the application of ritual injunctions;
seeing that son, Gokarṇa addressed him as "Gokarṇa. (71)
After some time, both of them reached their youth:
Gogakarna, the wise and learned one, and Dhundhukarin, the great rogue. (72)

Devoid of the practices of bathing and purification, eating both what is fit and unfit to eat, overwhelmed by anger, a thief, hateful toward all people, and associated with wicked outcasts (caṇḍālas). ||73||
For he would seize children playing and forcibly throw them into a well;
in this manner, through his addiction to prostitutes, he brought his father's wealth to ruin. (74)
Like a wretched man for his father, he wept aloud in grief;
a sonless man is always happy, whereas a bad son is a giver of suffering. ||75||
The word spoken by the Siddha is true; I have now experienced it myself. Where shall I go? Where shall I stay? May he remove my suffering. (76)
"I shall give up my life in water, in fire, or I shall throw myself from a precipice"—while he was thinking thus with his face turned downward, [the sage] approached him. (77)
Gokarṇa awakened Janaka to the truth.
Gokarṇa said:
"O Father, this world is essence-less; it bestows upon men suffering and delusion. (78)
Who is a son? What is wealth? Whose is a wife? Who is a husband, O father?
The world, its soul bound by delusion and rendered wretched, suffers in various ways. (79)
There is no happiness whatsoever for Indra, nor is there any happiness for a universal monarch;
but there is happiness, O Father, for the sage who is dispassionate and devoted to solitude. (80)
Abandon ignorance in the form of the people and delusion, which is the cause of hell; free from duality, devoid of fear, and without pride, go forth, having renounced the entire forest.
Then, having heard those words, the virtuous twice-born one spoke to Gokarṇa.
The twice-born one said: "O sage, tell me in detail what must be done by me in the forest. (82)
O Treasure of Compassion, lift me up, for I am bound by the noose of delusion, deceitful, wretched in mind, and fallen into the pit of saṃsāra. 83.
Having heard these words of his father, Gokarṇa, who was learned in wisdom, spoke with a joyful heart to his distressed and despondent father. (84)
Gokarṇa said:
Quickly abandon your sense of ownership and attachment toward this body of yours— a mere heap of flesh, bone, and blood— as well as toward your wife, children, and the like.
Behold this world incessantly as being grounded in momentary destruction; O Knower, become one who relishes dispassion and is devoted to the Lord. ||85||
Constantly devote yourself to the Dharma; abandon worldly ways. Having served holy men, cast off the thirst for desire.
Quickly relinquish the habit of contemplating the faults and virtues of others.
Therefore, drink deeply the essence of the stories of Viṣṇu. ||86||
The princes said: "Thus, having understood the experience described by the son, free from worldly desire and firm in mind, he abandoned his home at sixty years of age."
Constantly followed by those dear to Hari, that great-souled one, dwelling in the forest, attained the state of Hari which is difficult to reach.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter in the Śrī Bhāgavata-māhātmya, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(197) Chapter One Hundred and Ninety-Seven:
The Kumāras said:
When his father had thus departed for the forest, O Nārada, that great villain Dhundhukārin later returned and began to threaten his mother.
"O Nārada, tell your mother where the treasure is located;
otherwise, I shall certainly kill you. (2)
Terrified by his words, her mind filled with grief that night, she threw herself into a well and died; when discovered by people, she was taken out.
O Sage, having caused her to be taken away by twice-born men who were her kinsmen and husbands, the wise Gokarṇa,
equanimous in pleasure and pain, set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Dhum remained in the house of Dhukārī, surrounded by his own courtesans;
his intellect was deluded by the maintenance of that [household] through extremely fierce conduct and practices. ||5||
Desiring to obtain ornaments, the courtesans said to him:
"O dear one, we are all here, having come together with you as our protector. (6)
O giver of honor, no other than Dhanada (Kubera) ever comes here;
therefore, his garments are fine and his ornaments are radiant.
"If we, O embodied beings, were to go from your presence to another man,"—
having heard these words of theirs, he reflected for a moment.
At night, disregarding his own home and mindful of death,
he went out and stole clothes and ornaments from someone's house.
Filled with joy, Sanārada gave them those priceless garments and ornaments out of affection for them, having seen them. (10)
Those women reflected and, having determined among themselves that "these have been brought here by him through theft," they deliberated together.
"He constantly commits theft; the king will surely seize him. Having taken his wealth, the king will certainly put him to death. (12)
"Having killed that thief with great delight, we have seized much wealth; why then do you not go there? (13)
Then those cruel-hearted women, having bound him while he slept by the neck with very sharp nooses, prepared to kill him.
When he had died and was being held tightly by the neck,
they then repeatedly threw coals into his mouth.
Distraught by the extreme suffering of the flames of fire, he met his death;
then those mostly reckless women cast his body into a pit. (16)
O best of sages, that conduct was not known by anyone;
when questioned by the people, they said, "Our husband has gone far away. (17)
After a long time, he will arrive, tormented by the lack of wealth;
therefore, the best among the wise should never place their trust in women. 18.
They utterly destroy the one who trusts them, while constantly seeking ever-new [objects of desire];
their speech consists of nectar that increases the passion of lovers. (19)
The heart of women is like the edge of a razor; who is dear to them?
Having taken a great deal of wealth, they then cast their husbands aside. (20)
Extremely overwhelmed by fear of the king, they quickly fled to another village;
then the great preta, a doer of evil deeds, let out a "dhun-dhu" sound.
Constantly assuming the form of a whirlwind, he runs toward the quarters, driven by the fear of death;
afflicted by cold and heat, he is without food and parched with thirst.
Finding no happiness anywhere, he cried out repeatedly, "Alas!
Alas! After some time had passed, he realized that this [body] was indeed dead.
Gokarṇa performed the śrāddha at Gayā during his pilgrimage;
having completed the pilgrimage, he returned to his own city.
Honored with affection by the citizens and his own kinsmen and friends,
the twice-born dwelt in his own home for several days.
Knowing that Gokarṇa was fast asleep at night, the extremely wicked Gaṇeśa, the doer of "dhuṃ-dhū" sounds, manifested a terrible form. ||26||
For a moment he became an elephant, for a moment a camel, and for a moment a great buffalo;
for a moment he was fire, for a moment a serpent, and in an instant he became a man.
Seeing this reversal, the wise Gokarṇa, endowed with fortitude, reflected in amazement, "What is this? ||28||
"This is some base man who has fallen into a miserable state," having thus resolved in his mind, he spoke to him with compassion. (29)
Gokarṇa said: "Who are you that have come to me in this most terrible night, terrifying me? Are you a ghost (preta), a vulture (uccāṭa), or a piśāca? Or from where have you attained this state?"
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, tell me what must be done by me for you now, since you have approached my presence at night in such a terrible form. (31)
Having heard these words of his brother, the great villain Dhundhukārin, having attained the state of a ghost, wept intensely in great distress.
Deluded by his state as a preta, he was not at all able to speak;
then, thirsty, he pointed toward water with a gesture of recognition.
Then that highly fortunate Gokarṇa, esteemed by the virtuous, having made his own water into a vessel, cast it forth while uttering this: ||34||
That water was poured by his high-souled brother Gokarṇa; it arrived for the sake of satisfying the deceased who had been making the sound "dhūṃ-dhūṃ. (35)
Then Nārada, possessing the knowledge of what had occurred, said: "O Agokarṇa, by this water offered by your meritorious brother, you have made it your own. (36)
The preta said:
"I am your brother, known by the name Dhundhukārin;
through the fault of my own actions, I have come to this state of being a preta. (37)
Having been repeatedly threatened by me out of fear for my mother’s death, he subsequently became eager to support his mistress for the sake of wealth. (38)
Out of greed for wealth, such as through theft and other means, I committed forbidden acts;
once, however, I was requested by them to provide more excellent ornaments. (39)
Having stolen those [jewels] from the house of a wealthy man at night, I then, out of greed for that wealth, forcibly bound him by the neck with nooses. (40)
O giver of honor, they all seized my vast wealth out of fear of the king and caused me to be executed by casting me into the fire. ||41||
Having fled from this city, their friendship uprooted by self-interest,
they have therefore attained the state of ghosts today, O brother, because of you.

I have been sprinkled with [the water of] realization by one who is exceedingly compassionate through his merit; I live now on air alone, for the arising of this desired fruit has come to pass today. (43)
I saw you, my brother, asleep in the midst of the host in your own home; then, thinking me ignorant of your presence, you made an effort to violate me. (44)
"O wicked one, I have suddenly become known to you; O brother, by the rising of compassion for the wretched, release me quickly! (45)
"From this state of being a preta, you have undoubtedly achieved your purpose.
Having heard these words of his brother, the wise and knowledgeable Gokarṇa [reflected].
With a distressed soul, Gokarṇa spoke to his brother, who was grieving and uttering cries of "dhun-dhuka":
Gokarṇa said—"I have offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to you at Gayā; I have supported you. (47)

"O brother, having heard from Lokamukha how you came to the state of a preta, [I know that] even one who is destitute attains an auspicious destination by offering the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Gayā. (48)
"There is no doubt that you have attained this; how is it that you have not gone to heaven?
Having heard these words of his high-souled brother Gokarṇa, [he replied: 49.
Dhum, whose soul was afflicted by suffering, stood before him and said:
"Even by performing a hundred śrāddhas at Gayā, my liberation will not come to pass. (50)
"Another means must be devised by you for my deliverance from this delusion.
Having heard these words, Gokarṇa was filled with wonder.
"If liberation is not attained through faith, then your goal is unattainable;
now, remain in your own place, free from fear of ghosts. (52)
"Having reflected, I shall perform the supreme means for your liberation.
Having heard these words, Dhundhukārin then departed.
After that, O Nārada, together with Gokarṇa, he remained in his own place within the cremation ground, contemplating the *kalidruma* tree for the remainder of the night.
Standing there, he sought liberation but did not find the means to achieve it;
then, in the morning, he along with Gokarṇa went to his own kinsmen, clansmen, and relatives.
He reported the events of the night to the Brahmins learned in the Dharmaśāstras;
having deliberated upon those events extensively according to the scriptures, O twice-born ones, they [spoke]. (56)
When they had become unaware of that event, they then praised the Sun.
The twice-born said:
"Salutations to you, O Bhāskara, Āditya, dispeller of darkness, possessor of rays! (57)
O witness of the world, abode of the universe, saluted by gods and asuras;
O twelve-fold self, whose steeds are like the sun, awakener of the worlds! (58)
You are the constant refuge for all people who are devoted to righteousness;
you are Brahmā, you are Hari, and you are the wielder of the trident—the creator, sustainer, and destroyer.
O Lord, there is no refuge for living beings in this world other than you;
you are Śarva in the form of earth, and you are Bhava assuming the form of water.
You are Agni; you are Rudra in the highest place; you are Vāyu, the bearer of a fierce form.
O Bhīma, you are the one whose body is space; you are yourself the sacrificer and Paśupati.
Mahādeva is the embodiment of Soma, and Īśāna is indeed the Sun; your eight divine forms are worshipped by those who proclaim the Vedas.
For the sake of fulfilling all desires and pervading the three worlds,
you are the Fish, the upholder of the Vedas, the Tortoise, and the supreme bearer of the mountain.
You are the upholder of the earth as Varāha; you are Trivikrama, the sustainer of the worlds.
You are Bhārgava, the slayer of those who harm the Vedas; you are Rāghava, the slayer of those who harm the world.

O Kṛṣṇa, you are the remover of the earth's burden; O Buddha, you are the deluder of the asuras; and O Kalki, you are the slayer of the mlecchas—thus you appear in age after age when dharma has declined.
Assuming the form of Brahmā, you are the creator of the various kinds of living beings— gods, asuras, and humans, as well as those that move on the earth and those that fly in the air.
O Lord of the Cow-herds, you are Indra, you are Dharmarāja, you are Varuṇa, and you are the Lord of Wealth;
you exist in the form of all the world-protectors.
The embodiment of the three Vedas, worshipped in the three periods of time, possessing three abodes and consisting of the three qualities—
you alone, O Sun, are worshipped by the worlds as divided into three forms.
"O Lord of the World, you alone are the one who awakens the lotus";
having spoken thus to the best of the twice-born, O Lord of Sages, they stood there. (69)
Then, while they were listening, the illustrious Sūrya, moving through the sky, laughed aloud and said:
"O best of the twice-born, O lords of sages, listen as long as you remain here. (69)
Then, moving through the sky, the illustrious Sūrya laughed aloud while they were listening, and said:
"Listen, O best of the twice-born, to the purpose for which I have been described."
By the merit of your own selves as gods, for the sake of pacifying the great sins of the son of Dhūlī (Dhūlisūnu),
this Gokarṇa Ohaṇa shall indeed be his deliverer through the Śrī Bhāgavata Saptāha.
This hymn which has been composed by you is a description of my own majesty.
O Brahmins, by praising him, a man shall obtain the path of the gods;
likewise, one who desires sons, wealth, dharma, or liberation [shall attain them]. (73)
"By reciting this *Vāñchācintāmaṇi-stotra*, one shall attain the supreme state.
Having spoken thus, the god Bhāskara, stationed in the celestial realm, became silent. (74)
Then those twice-born ones, with delighted minds, exclaimed "Excellent!
to Gokarṇa in that assembly of brahmins on the auspicious bank of the Bhadrā river.
A great curiosity arose there among the citizens,
and Gokarṇa, who knew the true meaning of all things, sat upon his seat and spoke.
Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa and the others, he composed for seven days this scripture of the praises of Śrī Hari, which originated from the lotus feet of the Lord of the Holy Tīrthas.
"If this be true, then may he attain the state of Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda"—with such a thought conceived in his mind, [he recited] that which is named the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata. (78)

He addressed that [deity] with the words, "From whom [comes] the birth of that by which [the world is known]," while looking here and there for a place to stay after arriving at the cremation ground. (79)
Then, O Nārada, assuming the form of the wind, he entered the syllables *vaṃ* and *śaṃ*, which were joined with the seven notes (*saptasvara*),
while the foremost Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas were listening.
On the first day, Nārada, stationed within a hole in the ground, listened daily to the fierce speech of Dhundhu’s son whenever the discourse came to an end. (81)
Then, it was truly marvelous: a single knot burst open;
and in this same manner, one knot after another burst open on each of the subsequent days. (82)
Upon being pierced by those seven arrows, he immediately abandoned his state as a ghost;
assuming a divine form, he became adorned with a garland of tulasī.
Clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, and adorned with ornaments, he who perceives the reality of all things bowed to his brother Gokarṇa and spoke. (84)

By your grace, I have been liberated from the bondage of the defilement of being a ghost; blessed is the narrative of the Bhāgavata, which I have heard and which uproots the state of being a preta. (85)
Likewise, even a seven-day fast is auspicious and grants access to the world of Viṣṇu;
by its power, I have been liberated from the state of a ghost, from which I was deeply afflicted.
Whether wet or dry, light or heavy, committed through speech, mind, or physical actions—this [mantra] reduces sin to ashes in seven days, just as fire consumes fuel. (87)
In this land of Bhārata, which is desired even by the gods, those who listen to the scripture of the Lord shall attain the most supreme goal. (88)
The body is said to be a collection of sinews, bones, marrow, flesh, and blood;
its impurity is understood through the tasting of its pure constituent parts. (89)
The body, corrupted by the impurities of karma, is the vessel for hell;
therefore, this alone is indeed the means for the cessation of those defects. (90)
Like bubbles in water or like mosquitoes among living beings, those devoid of the Lord’s scripture are born only for death. (91)
O twice-born ones, when the *Bhāgavata* is heard, the knot of the heart is pierced, all latent impressions are severed, and one's karmas are exhausted. (92)
While he was speaking thus, that excellent celestial chariot arrived;
having boarded it from Vaikuṇṭha, he departed for the abode of Viṣṇu.
When he had gone to the world of Viṣṇu, all those best of the twice-born became filled with wonder and questioned Gokarṇa.
The twice-born said:
"The Bhāgavata has been heard by all of us gathered here. O highly fortunate one, what is the reason that you alone, O brother, have taken refuge in Hari? (95)
Gokarṇa said:
"Listen, I shall declare the reason for the brothers' attainment of the supreme state;
having heard it, you too shall go to Goloka. (96)
One should perform the seven-day recitation while devoted to fasting, with a mind single-pointedly focused on Kṛṣṇa; this bestows the attainment of Goloka. (97)
O twice-born ones, listen again for seven days to the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, which bestows the nectar of love for Kṛṣṇa, with your minds always one-pointed. (98)
O best of the twice-born, having heard these words of Gokarṇa,
they settled down once more for seven days in order to hear the Bhāgavata.
O Nārada, with their minds fixed one-pointedly on Kṛṣṇa and according to the prescribed rule,
all those twice-born ones again heard the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam.
At the conclusion of the discourse, the lotus-eyed Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared before the best of sages, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with a garland of forest flowers, clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, and decorated with bracelets and a mace. ||102||
Seeing him accompanied by Viṣvaksena and the other foremost attendants, all those twice-born ones were filled with joy and, prostrating themselves upon the ground, bowed down to him.
O Sage, at that time the sounds "Victory! and "Homage! arose on all sides;
then Hari, gladdening the twice-born, uttered the sound of "Śam" and "Kh".
Then many celestial palaces arrived from Vaikuṇṭha while the twice-born looked on, accompanied by the foremost of the Lord’s attendants.
He gave Gokarṇa and Tuṣāli forms resembling his own,
while the other listeners were dark as a rain cloud and dressed in yellow silken garments.
Wearing crowns, earrings, and beautiful forest garlands,
he performed a great marvel there at that very moment, and it was truly extraordinary.
O Sage, those Cāṇḍāla people who were staying in that village,
having ascended those celestial chariots by the command of Kṛṣṇa, went to heaven.
Accompanied by Gokarṇa, Kṛṣṇa, who is beloved by the cowherds and cowherd-maidens,
reached Goloka, which is situated above all worlds;
there lies the beautiful Vṛndāvana forest, surrounded by a hundred peaks.
Surrounded on all sides by that very same Vijayā forest, which shines most wonderfully, there is a grove where many excellent pavilions, crystal ponds, and lakes are situated;
where cows that yield all desires rest in the shade of rows of celestial trees; and where the Son of Nanda, surrounded by cowherds whose minds are intent on play, sports with delight. (110)
In the midst of this beautiful grove, by the will of the Lord of Vṛndāvana, there stands a magnificent enclosure, radiant with a wall inlaid with jewels and precious stones;
and there, a vast banyan tree, possessing a wondrous form and great splendor, provides shelter for the calves while being inhabited on every side by the gopīs.
Gokula shines.
In its center shines a radiant palace presided over by Hari, wherein dwell the Lords of the House of Nanda, worshipped together with Rādhā.

Even the great fortune of Umāpati and the other gods is always contemplated by those within; that fortune of their son, whose form is sweet, excels with auspicious splendors that illuminate the multitude of cosmic eggs.

Even that which is unattainable through fierce austerities— such as subsisting on air, water, or leaves, and emaciating the body— as well as through the acts of recitation and sacrifice, [is achieved] by one born from the iron cow.
He did not enter the world because he did not engage in the performance of sacrifices known as *gāha*. ||113||
Whoever reads or even hears this meritorious history, he too goes to Goloka; what then need be said of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam? ||114||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Bhāgavata," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(198) Chapter One Hundred and Ninety-Eight— the Kumāras said:
Now we shall proclaim the procedure for the seven-day recitation,
by which the Bhāgavata becomes perfected for those men who have dedicated their souls to Kṛṣṇa.
Having summoned an astrologer skilled in the scriptures and honored him with wealth and parrots, a devoted man should repeatedly inquire about an auspicious moment.
The Muhūrta called Savadadya is highly praised there;
[these months] are Nabhas, Nabhasya, Īṣa, Ūrja, Sahas, and Śuci. (3)
The months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa are excellent; the month of Kārttika is best, and the full moon day is auspicious.
Days of the week excluding Tuesday and Sunday, as well as the asterisms Bharaṇī, Dhruva, and the Mṛdu group, are favorable. (4)
O Lord of Sages, the commencement [of a rite] is always recommended when there is an auspicious yoga and an auspicious lagna, even during the daily recitation of the Purāṇas.
A wise person should avoid the twelfth day because of the occurrence of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*);
some, however, [avoid it] for the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* itself even during the seven-day period.
O celestial sage, those who know the ancient lore say that there is no prohibition [against this];
the wise have declared the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Saptāha to be a great sacrifice (mahāyajña). ||7||
Therefore, O best of Vaiṣṇavas, this vow must be observed by all Vaiṣṇavas equally; thus, there shall be an assembly of the virtuous for seven days.
Therefore, Vaiṣṇavas who desire to hear [the teachings] should come here;
for those who have assembled, one should provide them with lodging. (9)
Whether at a sacred ford, in a forest, or even in a village,
one should carefully construct a pavilion on ground that has been thoroughly purified.
O Sage, a high seat made of plantain wood and covered with ashes, adorned with banners on its four sides, is prescribed for the speaker to sit upon before him.
The seats for the listeners, who are free from attachment to both sides, should be arranged;
and in this assembly, the best among the learned shall face north as the speaker. (12)
A speaker should be made who is an excellent Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiṣṇava, one who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras, skilled in providing illustrations, wise, and utterly free from desire. 13.
One who removes all doubts should indeed be made the speaker;
however, another wise scholar should be stationed by the side of the speaker for the purpose of assistance. (14)
One who cuts through the doubts of listeners and brings about awakening for the ignorant should first worship Gaṇeśa for the purpose of destroying obstacles to the narration. (15)
Then, having worshipped Durgā, Hara, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Bhāskara, and the twice-born according to the rules with devotion, he should offer libations to the deities and the ancestors.
First, one should worship Hari in the earthen image, and thereafter in the book;
then, having performed circumambulation, [one should offer] substances, garments, and fruits.
O Sage, having placed the book containing [the description of] Hari upon water, one should pray:
"In this world, you, O Bhāgavata, are yourself established as Kṛṣṇa. (18)
This desire of mine, which has taken refuge in you, the protectorless one, for the sake of liberation from the ocean of existence, has been made entirely fruitful by you. (19)
"O Keśava, I shall perform [this] without obstacle; I am your servant," having spoken thus, O Sage, one should offer the materials before the book. (20)
Prostrating with palms joined in reverence, he should pray to the speaker:
"O best of the twice-born in the form of a boar, you who are learned in all the scriptures! (21)
"Destroy my ignorance through the exposition of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata";
having thus prayed, one should choose five Brahmins as recitators.
O best of sages, for the purpose of reciting the twelve-syllable mantra,
one should worship those who know the rules of song and instrumental music, as well as those who seek wealth, beginning with Śuka and others.
O Sage, he who has cast aside anxiety for his wife, wealth, home, and sons should, according to the prescribed rule, establish this narrative for the purpose of its recitation. (24)
One who listens with a one-pointed mind shall obtain the complete fruit [of the merit] from sunrise until three and a half watches have passed. (25)
Having recited it, one should explain the meaning, whether of a single verse, a chapter, or even the entire book;
O Nārada, one may even pause at midday for a period of two ghaṭikās.
At the conclusion of the discourse, the glorification of Keśava must be performed;
and a fast should be observed by the listeners who desire its fruit. (27)
If one is unable to do that, one should collect a small amount of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) once a day,
whether with water, fruit, milk, or ghee.
The maintenance of the body must be performed solely by oneself, free from obstacles;
O Nārada, hear now the rules for men who observe the vow for seven days. (29)
It is proclaimed that those who are devoid of Viṣṇu-initiation have no entitlement here [to this practice].
Celibacy, sleeping on the ground, and eating from a vessel made of leaves [are required]. (30)
O best of sages, one should always observe these for seven days:
avoid double-dhal grains, honey, oil, food from others, and the juice derived from sugarcane.
The observer of the vow should avoid food that is defiled by intention, defiled by action, or stale;
likewise, onions, garlic, leeks, radishes, and turnips.
A man observing the vow of *kathā* should not eat the *nālikā* or the *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd.
He should also avoid lust, anger, intoxication, greed, violence, and envy. (33)
Indeed, one who observes the vow of discourse should never harbor delusion, hatred, or violence. //34//
One who observes the vow of sacred discourse should avoid reviling the Vedas, Vaiṣṇavas, and Brahmins, as well as gurus, cows, those observing vows, women, kings, and great souls. (35)
A wise person observing the vow of discourse should practice truthfulness, purity, compassion, silence, straightforwardness, humility, and serenity of mind. (36)
One who desires prosperity, one seeking a son, one desiring victory, or one whose mind is set on liberation—should listen to the *Bhāgavata*; even one free from desire shall attain Śrī Hari.
On the seventh day, at the conclusion of that [recitation], one should perform the *laṅghana* (fasting);
furthermore, worship of the speaker should be performed with gifts such as cows, land, gold, and other excellent offerings.
One should bestow upon the listeners a garland of *tulasī* from the temple and likewise hold a festival with those skilled in song and instrumental music. (39)
On the following day, the wise one should listen to the meaning of the Gītā and offer oblations for each verse with the Gāyatrī mantra, according to the prescribed rule.
Milk-rice, honey, clarified butter, sesame seeds, rice grains, barley, sugar, priyāla, grapes, vāta, and dates. 41.
Aṃ, camphor from the Bhoja country, sandalwood, agallochum, and resin; cloves, nutmeg, and a thousand bilva leaves—each of these separately. ||42||
For the purpose of removing obstacles, for the correction of omissions and excesses,
and for the sake of one's own purification, one should recite the Thousand Names.
Then, one should feed twelve or eighteen Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa) along with an abundance of faith; gold and a cow shall be the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Or else, for the sake of accomplishing the vow, on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada,
one should fashion a golden lion and place [the image] upon its back.
Having had the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam written by hand and presented [to the preceptor], when this procedure is performed, there is the removal of all sins. 46.
When heard, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam bestows excellent fruit upon the listener;
it is the means for attaining dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa, and it grants devotion. (47)
There is no task to be found in the world that cannot be accomplished by this;
therefore, the Bhāgavata is considered superior to all other Purāṇas in the world. 48.
The speaker is proclaimed by the wise to be one who is free from the eighteen defects, and the listener is considered to be one who is free from the thirty-two transgressions. (49)
The Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is a Purāṇa that grants all desires to men;
likewise, hearing it even without desire bestows pure devotion. 50.

The celestial wish-fulfilling tree named Śrīmad-Bhāgavata has its roots established in the Tāraka-mantra; it flourishes with twelve sturdy trunks through the emergence of its basin of radiant devotion.
It possesses thirty-two thousand branches and eighteen thousand leaves, which are easily accessible and bestow all desired fruits, standing preeminent above everything else. (51)
Thus everything was told, and that which was desired by you was accomplished—the youthfulness of knowledge, dispassion, and devotion, which grants liberation to the world. (52)
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, those Kumāras, drenched by the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s words, desisted from their intent to uproot the devotees of the Blessed One. (53)
Having heard those words, Nārada, the beloved of the Blessed One, spoke to them with hands joined in reverence, his voice faltering with love.
Nārada said:
"I am blessed and I am graced by you who are full of compassion,
since Hari has been revealed to me in the vicinity of the Bhāgavata-saptāha."
While that Nārada, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, was speaking thus,
Śuka, the lord of yogis, arrived there while wandering about.
Having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, with lotus-like eyes, the son of Vyāsa— a moon to the ocean of wisdom—
was constantly reciting the Bhāgavata in his heart, satisfied by his own attainment at the conclusion of the narrative.
Seeing him of immense splendor, the members of the assembly immediately rose from their excellent seats and rejoiced;
and as soon as he was seated comfortably upon his throne, the lotus-eyed Hari appeared.
Then Lord Brahmā, the lotus-seated one, arrived there with his sons for the sake of hearing the recitation and seeing [the scene];
the chief gods and the deities also arrived in their celestial chariots, and the sky became filled with them. (59)

Prahlāda became the cymbal-player with a graceful and agile movement; Uddhava was the conch-blower; the celestial sage (Nārada) was the lute-player due to his mastery of musical notes; Arjuna became the creator of melodies (*rāga*);

the sons of Indra were the drummers, proclaiming cries of "Victory! Victory!"; the Kumāras were the chanters of truthful words; and the son of Vyāsa (Śuka), possessing unsurpassed virtues, became the proclaimer of the true nature of reality.
Seeing that very dance of the three female students there, which was endowed with the nine forms beginning with knowledge and was truly extraordinary, Hari, his heart filled with joy, spoke thus:
61. "Having beheld this extraordinary *kīrttana*, he, with a delighted mind, spoke as follows."
Choose a boon from me, O best of devotees; I am well-pleased with you because of your intense narration and glorification of my stories.
Having heard those words, they became exceedingly joyful and, their hearts moist with love, spoke to Hari.
The princes said:

"O Enemy of Mura, by this seven-day sacrifice being performed, you will become instantly propitious toward men in this most terrible Kali age—men of short lifespans and beset by hundreds of obstacles. (63)
Thus, O Lord, we choose this boon from you, the Soul of all and the cause of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe:
that there may be no mutual conflict of desires among us who serve your lotus feet. (64)
Having said, "So be it," Hari vanished right there;
Nārada, with a deeply serene soul, then paid his respects to the Kumāras.
Then those beginning with Sanaka, those beginning with Bhṛgu, and those beginning with Śuka,
having drunk that nectar of his discourse, departed for their own hermitages filled with joy.
O Śaunaka, from that time forward, devotion accompanied by the two sons [of the Lord] was propagated by Nārada throughout the entire circle of the earth.
Śiva said:
O beloved, having heard this great narrative, Śaunaka, with a pleased soul, again questioned Sūta, who destroys all doubts. (68)
Śaunaka said:
When was this spoken by Śuka? And when by King Gokarṇa?
And when by the celestial sages and the Brahmins? O giver of joy, please relate this to me.

Sūta said: Thirty years after the departure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, when the Kali age had arrived, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, Śuka performed the *vaikunthārambha* (the commencement of his ascent to Vaikuṇṭha) under the asterism Bharaṇī.
Two hundred years after the passing of Parīkṣit,
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śuci, Gokarṇa related this story.
"O twice-born one, four thousand years of the Kali age have now passed;
let this sacrifice be brought to completion from the time of Parīkṣit’s birth. (72)
Īśvara said: Having heard these words of his, Śaunaka, the best of sages,
completed that sacrifice which lasted for a thousand years.
The Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Kaurmya, Mātsya, Vāmana, Vārāha, Brahmavaivarta, Nāradīya, and Bhaviṣyaka [Purāṇas]. ||74||
They heard the Āgneya Purāṇa from Vaiśampāyana, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa;
indeed, these Purāṇas were heard by them during the Dvāpara age.
Formerly, this place was the site of sacrifices for the best of sages, such as Śaunaka and others;
however, it was when Valadeva arrived on a pilgrimage that [the transformation occurred]. (76)
In the place called Naimiṣa Miśrika, summoned by the lords of sages,
they saw Sūta seated there upon his high seat.
O Pārvatī, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the day of breaking the fast, the Blessed Lord Rāma was agitated like the great ocean during a full-moon tide.
During the hour of the first watch of the night, Rāma, having been deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Kṛṣṇa, struck the hair-raising Darbha grass with his hand. ||79||
Then all the hosts of sages, intent on the sound "Alas!", became exceedingly distressed in their inner selves with grief and sorrow, crying out, "O Mountain! (Nagaja).
The sages, devoted to forbearance, spoke with humility to Rāma, the Lord of the World.
The sages said:
"O Rāma, O Rāma, O mighty-armed one, by you who brings light to the world—" (81)
"Because she acted out of ignorance, this crime does not amount to the murder of a Brahmin;
for he is a direct disciple of Vyāsa, a great seer of antiquity and one of immense ascetic power. (82)
We, having made ourselves available for the sacrificial rite, have bestowed this seat upon him, the reciter of the eighteen Purāṇas. (83)
O giver of honor, in this discourse on the Lord of the World, there is also the account of his long life;
for you, in order to protect the world, are the one who establishes the bridge of dharma.
"O beloved, having said, 'The Lord of the World, capable of both restraint and grace, has appeared,' those sages stood before Baladeva. (85)
They suddenly became silent, remembering the power of destiny;
then the Blessed Lord Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, spoke.
Delighting those brahmins and following the path of the worlds and the Vedas, Śrī Rāma said: "O brahmins, listen; may it be well with you; having cast your anger far away... (87)
"That which I know to be desired by you and which grants success in your undertaking—by my boon, his son shall become one of great wisdom. (88)
He will explain every scripture desired by you;
let that task for which I have been summoned be stated. (89)
Īśvara said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Rāma,
they urged Īśvara to carry out the slaying of Balvala.
Then, having slain Bāṣkala and propitiated the bull among sages,
he bowed down and, being granted permission, set out on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords.
When Rāma had departed on his pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), the lordly sages, headed by Śaunaka and others, summoned Lomaharṣaṇi, honored him, and spoke to him in the forest.
They established that portion for the sake of recitation, from the greatness of the Āgneya-parvan up to the end of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata. 93.
With delighted minds, they heard the seven Purāṇas along with their supplement;
having composed seventeen Purāṇas, the son of Satyavatī [completed his work].
O beautiful lady, even with the Mahābhārata, Nārada, the seer of the gods, did not find satisfaction for his mind; having perceived his heart to be distressed, he departed. 95.
The Blessed One arrived at the excellent hermitage of Vyāsa;
seeing him, the son of Vasu’s daughter honored him by first offering a seat.
They honored Nārada with rites prescribed by rule;
then Nārada said to him, "Why are you thus troubled in mind? (97)
"O meditator, explain all this, for it is the cause of my doubt.
Thus questioned by the sage, the son of Parāśara spoke.
"O Brahmin, what is the cause of this delusion of the mind? Since you are skilled in higher knowledge, please explain that after having understood it yourself. (99)
Thus requested by him, Nārada, who was skilled in the knowledge of the supreme self (adhyātma),
spoke that supreme truth which had been declared by Brahmā to himself.
Nārada said: Listen to me, O son of Parāśara, the reason why even this mind of yours, O Lord, though born from the Vedas, appears to you as incomplete. 101.
O sinless one, having descended into this world, you have divided the Vedas into their respective parts and composed the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas. 102.
In this Kali age, where the lifespan of men is short, he observed that the entire dharma of the three Vedas had been prescribed for those residing in the various castes and stages of life. (103)

Where the eligibility of all is seen for hearing [the teachings] and so forth—including women, Śūdras, and even those born of mixed castes—for them, association with the virtuous is the means to become virtuous. (104)

O Sage, although you have described dharma and the other goals of life as eternally extolled, you have not likewise described the greatness of Hari as preeminent among them— He who is devoid of all ritual actions and is a singular storehouse of faults.
There is no path for evildoers except the nectar of the stories of Kṛṣṇa;
this indeed is the virtue found in this terrible Kali age among men.
By the mere chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names, one is thus released from the bondage of karma;
[otherwise,] sacrifice, charity, austerity, ritual action, knowledge, and meditation were practiced in the Kṛta and other ages. (107)
And likewise, O Brahman, the chanting of names grants success in the Kali age; therefore, you have appeared for the sake of uplifting men born in the Kali age. 108.
May he fully describe the Purāṇa named Śrīmad-Bhāgavata, by the recitation of which the minds of living beings will certainly become absorbed in the Lord. 109.
The worlds will attain satisfaction and achieve the fulfillment of their purpose. ||110||
Ishvara said:
Having thus instructed Vyasa of immeasurable splendor,
O beloved, the Sage departed at his own will, constantly singing the virtues of Hari.
After Nārada had departed, Vyāsa, who perceives all things, composed this supreme and glorious Śrīmad Bhāgavatam. 112.
Having taught the four Vedas to Paila and the others according to the prescribed rules,
he then imparted all the Purāṇa collections to Sūta.
He taught the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, a Purāṇa equal in extent to the Vedas, to Śuka, who was untiring in his study of both the world and the Vedas. 114.
O King, while Śruta was thus conversing with the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, who was full of beneficial intent, Vaiśampāyana spoke to the descendant of Uttara.
Having been proclaimed in its true meaning by Śaunaka and other sages, this [work] stands preeminent above all the Purāṇas, O Mountain-souled One.
In this [river], for those men whose minds are attached, no suffering arises;
there, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, shines within the heart. 117.
As for that which was asked by you, O auspicious lady, for the sake of the world's deliverance:
"Proclaim to me the majesty of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata. (118)
All of that has been pointed out to you by me, O leader of the Gaṇas, together with various historical accounts, bestowing both devotion and liberation. 119.
The man who hears this greatness with devotion, or even reads it, or even rejoices in it, shall attain the supreme goal. (120)
A twice-born man, having studied it, shall attain the Vedas; a Kṣatriya shall obtain victory;
a Vaiśya shall likewise acquire wealth; and a Śūdra, merely by hearing it, attains the supreme goal.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(199) Chapter One Hundred and Nineteen— the Sages said:
O Sūta, tell us in detail the majesty of the Kālindī, for whom it was revealed and by whom, together with its narrative account. (1)
Sūta said:
Once, the son of Pāṇḍu, desiring to hear the auspicious knowledge of Saubhari, approached that place, bowed to him, and questioned him as follows. (2)
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Brāhmaṇa, tell me of that auspicious holy place (tīrtha) on the banks of the son of Mārtaṇḍa (the Yamunā),
which is higher than the highest, the birthplace of Vaikuṇṭha.
Saubhari said:
Once, while the two best of sages, Nārada and Parvata, were traveling through the sky toward Khāṇḍava, they beheld it as exceedingly beautiful.
Having descended there from the sky, they sat upon the auspicious bank of the Kālindī; after resting for a moment, they entered the water to bathe.
King Śibi Uśīnara, while wandering in the forest on a hunt,
saw them and sat down on the riverbank, waiting for their departure.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rites and donned their garments, those two sages were saluted with their heads by the king, and they sat down upon the riverbank.
There, beholding thousands of golden sacrificial posts in the camp, he, free from pride, spoke to Nārada and Parvata: (8)
Śibi said:
"O tigers among sages, let it be told whose sacrificial posts these are;
by whom has this sacrifice been performed here—by a god or by a man? (9)

Having abandoned sacred fords such as Kāśī and others, what man here would worship with sacrifices? What distinction does this [place] have over those other sacred fords, other than the presence of higher knowledge? (10)
Nārada said: In ancient times, Hiraṇyakaśipu, having conquered the gods headed by Śakra and having attained sovereignty over the three worlds, assumed immense pride. (11)
His son was Prahlāda, who was solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
yet that evil-souled one, whose auspiciousness had perished, constantly sought to do him harm.
Out of enmity toward him, Viṣṇu immediately assumed the form of Narasiṃha;
having slain the lord of the Daityas, he restored the kingdom of heaven to the Lord of the Gods. (13)
Having attained his own abode, the Lord of the Gods, remembering the qualities of Nārāyaṇa, bowed his head at Bṛhaspati’s feet and spoke to him. (14)
Indra said: "O Guru, the Lord Hari, the sustainer of the world, has granted me the sovereignty over the gods; I now desire to worship Him with sacrifices. (15)
O Teacher, tell me of a sacred place and also of the brahmins;
you, who act for our welfare, must not delay in this matter. (16)
Bṛhaspati said:
You possess the lovely Khāṇḍava forest, which is supremely purifying, filled with ketakī, aśoka, and bakula trees, and with bees intoxicated by honey. (17)
There flows the holy Yamunā, auspicious and the purifier of the three worlds;
she grants heaven upon remembrance and the station of Brahmā at death. (18)
O Lord of Gods, perform sacrifices with many offerings on its bank for Keśava, if you desire the perpetual welfare of your own people. (19)
Nārada said:
Having heard the words of his preceptor, Śakra quickly mounted his vehicle and returned to his own forest, which bestows auspiciousness.
Having come here together with his preceptor, the gods, and the sacrificial implements,
he beheld this forest and attained supreme joy.
Urged by his preceptor, Śakra, having invited the seven sages— the sons of Brahmā,
Vasiṣṭha and the other twice-born ones— performed a sacrifice for the Lord of the World.
The Blessed One, pleased with him, arrived together with Brahmā and Īśa at the sacrifice of Śatakratu, where a great festival was taking place.
Then Śakra, perceiving the three deities to be virtuous, his mind becoming crooked, rose quickly from his seat and paid homage along with the sages. (24)
Quickly descending from their vehicles and sitting down at their edges upon seats made of fine gold, they shone like sacrificial fires upon altars. (25)
Between Śambhu and Brahmā, whose bodies were white and red respectively,
Hari shone with his dark-blue complexion and yellow garments, like a lightning-charged cloud between two mountain peaks.
Śakra, having washed his feet, took that water upon his head;
filled with joy, he spoke these words in sweet syllables: ||27||
Indra said:
"O Lord, this sacrifice ordained by me has today become fruitful."
O Viṣṇu, if even this [form], which has attained visibility though it is difficult to perceive even for yogins, has been made into a single embodiment consisting of the three Vedas by you alone; (29)
Nevertheless, O Lord, your diversity through qualities is as false as that of a crystal;
it is like fire hidden within wood, which cannot be manifested without friction. (30)
You do not manifest to beings in such a way through mere mental devotion;
rather, devotion to You alone is that which benefits all living beings. (31)
The gods became happy because of the joy produced by Prahlāda;
we, however, are seekers of sense-objects, our minds veiled by your māyā. (32)
We do not know your true nature, even though we are servants at your feet;
O Brahman, O Mahādeva, you two are indeed the teachers of the world.
Because it is like that [reality] in its lack of substantiality, it is not separate from it;
therefore, no pause (*yati*) is mentioned, nor is anything conceived by speech or mind.
For him who has thus arrived at this state, all that belongs to the dualistic path remains far behind. (34)
One should contemplate that this entire multitude of phenomenal appearances which is perceived is indeed unreal;
those who take refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu cross over it—that which you bear upon your head as a crown.
My devotion is intensely fixed upon the two lotus-feet of the younger brother of Vidhi (Viṣṇu), from whose eyes, when agitated, this entire universe—beginning with Mahat—is born. (36)

O supreme one, you who are compassionate toward those like us, you who dispel the sorrow of your own people by bestowing happiness upon the side of your enemies—this which is called compassion would indeed be ignorance if it were practiced only for that purpose. (37)
Nārada said:
Having thus praised Keśava, the Lord of gods, he bowed down before him and stood with his mind intent on listening to His words, being greatly honored.
Having thus heard that praise of the Lord of Ramā performed by him in the assembly, the sages exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! to Indra.
Even those who perform great austerities for a hundred years, O Śatamanyu,
do not possess such devotion as you have for Mādhava.
That yoga is easily attainable through which the desired goal is reached;
and the renunciation of those [desires] with equanimity—that devotion is the refuge for human beings. 41.
Whatever action is performed according to the prescribed rules with wealth earned through one's own duty—that offering of the work to Viṣṇu is devotion that bestows auspiciousness. 42.
One should not worship another deity with the thought that they are Viṣṇu, nor should one abandon the Vedic statements; such a devotee is dear to this Lord Hari.
Those who daily hear the virtues of Hari, those who perform his glorification, those who remember the Lord, and those who worship Him—they likewise attain victory.
Those who bow down before him, those who serve him with devotion, those who offer him friendship, and those who declare themselves his own—they do not desire liberation and the like for him. (45)
Out of devotion to Indra, you too should propitiate this Teacher of the World;
do not desire anything for yourself, and you will have accomplished all that needs to be done.
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of instruction from the sages, which are worthy of being served by all and which grant the state that lies beyond the three worlds,
Hari, the eternal teacher, spoke sweet words to his own devotee in the assembly.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Indra’s Sacrifice," in the *Kālindī-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the *Pādma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(200) The Two Hundredth Chapter— The Blessed Lord said:
This is not surprising: the sages, who are most proficient in knowledge, follow my path and practice profound, honored devotion. ||1||
For these teachers of knowledge, who dwell upon the surface of the three worlds,
constantly set forth the lost path of the Veda.
Since you have taken refuge in me with devotion— even though you are subject to worldly existence and attached to the enjoyments of heaven—
what wonder is there, for your teacher is the Great Teacher himself?
Worship me, O tiger among asuras, with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
as you depart, you will quickly attain this state that stands near you.
"Bestow many prasthas of jewels at every sacrifice;
by this name, this place of yours shall become Indraprastha. (5)
Having performed the rites here, he established Prayāga, the foremost of sacred fords (tīrtha),
having brought together the Sarasvatī and the Gaṅgā, the purifier of people.
O Lord, establish yourself in Kāśī, Caśivakā, and Cī;
and always make Gokarṇa and Samaṅgā your dwelling place.
O you sons of Brahmā, you who are experts in knowledge and discernment, by the power of your own yoga, create here the seven sacred fords (tīrthas). ||8||
O Guru, please point out to me that sacred ford which awakens one to the Vedas;
for even without formal study, awakening occurs for those in distress through bathing there.
And may there arise a memory of my previous birth and of the Supreme Self, wherein I established the most enchanting city of Dvārakā. (10)
Where the confluence with the Gomati occurred, equal to the ocean;
where Vāsava made Kośalā and established Madhuvana.
I shall descend through the two bodies of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
at Badarikāśrama, which is the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
O Leader of the Suras, I always establish myself wherever I dwell;
these two unsurpassed holy sites, Haridvāra and Puṣkara, are such places. (13)
Therefore, out of a desire for your very welfare, I shall establish here those sacred sites of Naimiṣa which have existed for a long time on Mount Kālāja. (14)
"I shall indeed establish [the deity] here on the bank of the Sarasvatī.
Nārada said:
Having heard these most auspicious words of Hari, Śiva understood that it was already accomplished.
Having seen that, Brahmā, Śiva, and the others, along with the lords of the gods, also performed it in this place which embodies all sacred fords. 16.
Having repeatedly worshipped the Lord of Ramā with many sacrifices featuring golden sacrificial posts,
he presented heaps of jewels to the brahmins in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
May Nārāyaṇa, the soul of all, who is beyond measure, be pleased;
from that time forth, this sacred site was called Indraprastha. (18)
In that place which consists of all holy fords, one who dies is not born again;
having obtained the prasthas of jewels bestowed by Indra, the Brahmins [prospered].
Therefore, O Earth, grant me such a blessing in this assembly;
may Govinda be pleased by this gift for the sake of Indra.
O Lord of the World, he in whom devotion to you shall be unwavering has,
in this land of action, performed a hundred sacrifices in the city of the gods.
By that merit, you obtained the abode of the gods according to your desire;
now, however, Viṣṇu has been worshipped by you with sacrifices free from desire.
Falling from your own station, you will become a preeminent twice-born on earth;
even there, worshipping Viṣṇu through your own duty, you [shall attain your goal]. (23)
He will remember his own past deeds, such as the performance of sacrifices and other rites;
through that remembrance, he will abandon his home and wander to various sacred fords (tīrthas).
Together with Janaka, he will arrive at this Śakratīrtha and,
having entered the fourth stage of life (saṃnyāsa), he will cast off his body here.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot brought by the hosts of attendants and shining with the brilliance of the sun,
you shall become divine and attain the abode of Śrī Hari.
Nārada said:
Having thus heard the blessings of the brahmins and their words portending the future, the lord of the gods attained supreme joy in Śiva.
Having completed the sacrifices according to the prescribed rites, he dismissed the gods, headed by Mādhava, after they had been worshipped with golden sacrificial posts.
Having honored the sons of Brahmā, the officiating priests, with wealth and other gifts,
Śakra, placing Bṛhaspati at the head, departed for the third heaven.
Having established his rule there, Indra, endowed with devotion to Śiva and Hari,
descended to the city of Hastināpura on earth when his merit was exhausted.
There was a certain twice-born man named Śivaśarman, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas;
his wife was named Guṇavatī, whose name was truly significant of her virtues.
Born at that auspicious hour, Indra became a servant of the Lord of Śrī;
the summoned astrologers, having observed the ascendant, spoke as follows. (32)
The astrologers said:
"Śivaśarman, this boy shall be dear to Hari; he will deliver you. We speak thus for your welfare; it is the truth, not a falsehood. (33)
He whose body is thirteen years old, having studied the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and being perfected in knowledge, shall indeed perform his marriage. ||34||
Having again procreated a virtuous son, he will become a forest-dweller; wandering among sacred fords, the steadfast man will embrace renunciation.
In Indra’s Khāṇḍava forest there is the Yamunā, the best of rivers;
on its bank lies Hari-prastha, where he will meet his death. (36)
Nārada said:
Having heard the auspicious words uttered by the astrologer, Śivaśarman then gave his own son the name Viṣṇuśarman.
Having dismissed them with wealth, the wise man reflected:
"I am blessed, for my son shall be a devotee of Viṣṇu. (38)
"This son of mine shall accomplish my four stages of life (āśramas) and shall die at a sacred ford (sattīrtha);
who else besides me is so fortunate? (39)
Reflecting thus in his mind, Śivaśarman had the birth-rites and other ceremonies performed for the infant by the most eminent of the twice-born on an auspicious day. (40)
Then, when seven years had passed, that best of the twice-born performed his son's initiation ceremony in the eighth year, during the month of Caitra.
Having taught the Vedas to his son until he was twelve years old,
Śivaśarman, together with his wife, entrusted him to King Aśiva.
Having fathered a son with his own wife, the wise Viṣṇuśarman made his own mind free from attachment to worldly objects by embarking on a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā).
Approaching his father, the highly wise Viṣṇuśarman, recollecting the words of the sage, prostrated himself at his two feet.
Viṣṇuśarman said:
"Father, give me leave; I shall worship Viṣṇu, having entered the third stage of life which brings about association with the virtuous. (45)
Wise people do not become attached to wives, homes, wealth, children, and friends, which are as momentary as bubbles upon the waters. (46)
By means of Vedic study, the two debts incurred through birth have been discharged;
now, free from desire, I wish to worship Keśava at sacred fords.
Having renounced attachment to the qualities [of nature], I now desire to dwell for a while in some supreme sacred place (tīrtha), as long as my prārabdha karma remains.
Having been addressed thus by his son, that most intelligent father, having become indifferent to worldly existence, recalled the words of the astrologers and said: (49)
Śivaśarman said:
"This is the time for the fourth stage of life even for me, who am free from egoism; having abandoned sense objects like poison, I shall enjoy the nectar of Keśava. (50)
Today, in my old age, I have brought this son of mine from the forest to my home by force,
like an elephant captured from the wild and led into a king’s palace.
This Suśarman will cause your younger brother to suffer imprisonment, just as one who has been abandoned by us—deprived of learning, fortune, and noble lineage—is treated like a common man. (52)
But as I am departing for the religious life, my mother, devoted to her husband,
will follow me just as the twilight follows the sun at the end of the day.
Therefore, let us both go, reflecting upon the lotus feet of Śrī Hari, so that we may attain the state of being known by Him. 54.
Nārada said:
Having reflected thus, at midnight while the world was shrouded in darkness, those two seekers of liberation abandoned their sleeping family, departed from the house, and went forth.
Wandering together at those two excellent holy sites, free from ego and accomplished, the two met here at this auspicious Śivada-tīrtha in Śakraprastha.
Having arrived here and beholding the sacrificial posts erected by himself in his previous birth,
Viṣṇuśarman remembered his union with Hari.
The wise one said to his father: "Formerly, I was Śakra;
I performed sacrifices here with the desire to please Mādhava. (58)
Right here, Keśava, who is affectionate toward his devotees, became thus pleased;
the virtuous ones, the seven sages, and I were satisfied by him with measures of jewels.
By those very [deities], devotion to Viṣṇu was granted, and liberation was bestowed both in this world and the next;
indeed, all [the gods] beginning with Viṣṇu performed acts of pilgrimage there.
This Indraprastha has been made a sacred ford (tīrtha) embodying all holy fords;
it was here that death [is attained] by those very eminent sages, as they have declared.
From that [state], I remember all this— the attainment of Hari’s feet—
and these two, Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, who have come from the world of Viriñci.
The conjunction of these two [rivers] when brought together is called Prayāga;
this Kāśī, the city of Śiva, lies in the region to the east of Prayāga.
In the western part of Kāśī, within a distance of fifty-two dhanus, one who has died there is not reborn; [this extends for] twenty-one dhanus.
This Śivakā was established by Śiva himself; it bestows immortality and liberation.
This sacred field named Gokarṇa is the supreme favorite of Lord Śambhu. (65)
Situated on a plot of land measuring two bow-lengths to the west of this holy Dvāravatī, the king of sacred fords (tīrtharāja), [is the temple]. (66)
Since he was to become four-armed at a distance of seventy bows from that place,
this city, which is affectionate toward its people, is called Kośalā, situated in the eastern direction.
At a distance of eighteen dhanus, she is seen, a sight of merit;
this Madhuvana was established here by Viṣṇu himself.
To the west of Kośalā, at a distance of ten bow-lengths,
and further to the north, O Father, is the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
This stands at a distance of eleven dhanus from the ground;
this sacred site, Haridvāra, is situated to the south of that.
In this land of Śaddhanu, there is seen that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
this is the sacred ford named Puṣkara, the crest-jewel of all holy places.
The region of the earth extending twelve *iṣu*-measures stands out due to its fearlessness;
it is the *gavyūti* of Prayāga and other sites belonging to the high-souled Seven Sages. (72)
In the eastern direction, there are seven sacred fords; that is the group of seven tīrthas.
There are many sacred fords (tīrthas) in Kāśī, including the seven primary ones. ||73||
At every step, one who dies here is born as a four-armed being,
at a distance of only one *gavyūti* west of Prayāga.
In ancient times, the holy site named Nigamodvodhaka was established by the Guru;
there is a great distance between this site and the Nigamodvodha of the seven holy sites.
O dear one, this sacred field of Indraprastha was established by the gods in ancient times; it extends for one yojana from east to west. (76)
This boundary of Indraprastha, extending for four yojanas to the south of the Kālindī, has been described by the great sages.
And where, among the three gods, the Unborn One abandons his body, he becomes unborn.
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of his son, the twice-born Śivaśarman [spoke] auspiciously.
Doubting him, Śivaśarman said to his son who spoke the truth:
"How may I know this—that you were formerly a lord of the gods? (79)
"O son, you have performed sacrifices here by which the twice-born were gratified with jewels;
act in such a way that I may become possessed of the knowledge spoken of by you. (80)
Have you heard of this boundary at Indraprastha, from which time your resolve was born and you no longer left your home? (81)
"The four Vedas with their auxiliary limbs were studied by you alone;
from where did this knowledge come to you regarding the deeds performed in a previous birth? (82)
Viṣṇuśarman said:
"The sages granted me this [boon] which bestows the recollection of previous births;
from them alone did I hear this account of this sacred ford."
O son, perform your bath here at the holy ford known as Nigamodbodhaka;
you shall obtain rare knowledge that grants the recollection of your previous births. 84.
"O father, you shall also remember the activities of my previous birth through the touch of the water of this sacred ford; I tell you this as the truth. (85)
Nārada said:
O best of brahmins, having heard this, Śivaśarman prepared to bathe in that sacred ford which awakens one to the Vedas and recalls his previous birth. 86.
A certain Bhilla, pursued by a lion, arrived running;
overcome with extreme terror, he was gasping for breath and overwhelmed by exhaustion. (87)
Violent by nature, a destroyer of paths, and a constant plunderer of merchants;
he had blackish-brown hair, was short of stature, and had eyes like those of a cat. (88)
The two of them beheld from afar that terrifying form of the Lord, which was like a mass of sin, and they saw the lion not very far behind him. 89.
The father and son climbed a tree standing nearby and remained there, saying, "O Kṛṣṇa, deliver us from this untimely death! (90)
Seeing a tree that was more swiftly growing than the king of horses, the terrified Kirāta proceeded to climb it in order to seize him. 91.
Ascending it with the speed of a lion or a tiger,
he threw him down at his feet upon the back of the chariot and mounted him.
Then even the Kirāta standing below pierced his belly with a spear,
so that it was drenched in a stream of blood and its entrails and lotus-like heart were cast out.
Then, having uttered an exceedingly terrible roar,
the lion, seized by pain, crushed the Bhilla’s head and killed him instantly.
O King, when those two had passed away and their bodies had perished,
two celestial chariots descended from the sky along with two hosts of attendants.
It was fashioned from crystal stones by two [beings] with the color of fresh clouds, whose ears were adorned with beautiful earrings and embellished with clusters of jewels. (96)
Holding in his two hands a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, he wears beautiful and variegated garments;
he is adorned with golden ornaments and clad in yellow robes. 97.
With her lotus-like eyes fully blossomed, she possessed windows made of rubies; with her steady, firm, and beautiful gait, she was adorned with tinkling anklets.
With their forearms adorned with rows of bracelets and beautiful armlets, and with chests made captivating by pearl necklaces, they appeared as if possessed of canopies.
With its face of curved locks of hair, it was adorned with a lofty banner;
with its pair of eyebrows, it possessed a high archway that surpassed the bow of the five-arrowed god of love.
Adorned with hundreds of turrets that resembled parrots on their noses,
it possessed floors with the luster of fresh coral and was as pure as a mirror.

Having abandoned their divine forms as Gaurī, Bhilla, and Pañcāsya, they remained in their ordinary human states even before the departure of their life-breaths, through the power of this sacred site (tīrtha). ||102||
Then, having brought those two attendants of Hari—
who possessed forms, attire, and appearances identical to his own— into their presence, they spoke.
O Bhokirāta, best among men, O lord of beasts,
know us to be two attendants of Śrī Hari who have arrived from Vaikuṇṭha.
"We shall reach that true state where there are no waves for you both;
mounting each your own celestial chariot, go quickly and without delay."
Having mounted their respective celestial chariots, the Kirāta and the Lord of Beasts,
filled with wonder, spoke to the two attendants of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
O tigers among the thirty gods, listen to our words:
through the sight of you two, the ultimate knowledge has been born within us. (107)
In this birth, very little merit has been performed by us;
yet, through your grace, the memory of our past deeds arises within us. (108)
Devoted to killing living beings for the sake of food, with cruel internal faculties, born into a family of sinful conduct, and inspiring fear by their very appearance—[these two]. (109)
"We two were indeed sinners in such a world;
by what merit has the sight of us been granted to you both? (110)
"And by what merit shall we attain the state of similarity [to Śrī Hari] and go to the abode of Śrī Hari?
The two attendants said:
"O Preceptor of the Gods, it is certainly because of death at this sacred site [performed] in the past. (111)
The sight of you both has occurred, and our wonderful resemblance is striking;
furthermore, the attainment of the station of the Lord of Lakṣmī shall be yours for a long time. (112)
Indeed, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin roar only so long as the vision of this holy site of Bṛhaspati has not arisen. (113)
Just as darkness perishes here upon the rising of the sun, so do sins vanish at the sight of a Nigama-dvodbhaka. 114.
This sacred field called Indraprastha is indeed purifying for Indra;
therefore, Viṣṇu was worshipped here with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Listen to the boon granted by the gratified Viṣṇu to him:
"O Śakra, in your field, which consists of all sacred fords (tīrthas), people... [116]
Those who cast off their bodies are indeed equal to me, for they too are non-violent. ||117||
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, those two foremost attendants led the two of them to the abode of Hari, where, having gone, one never again sinks into the ocean of worldly existence. 118.

Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "The Ascent of Bhillasiṃha to Vaikuṇṭha," in the Kālindī-māhātmya of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||200||
(201) Chapter Two Hundred and One: Nārada’s Utterance.
Then, having descended from the tree, both father and son were greatly amazed to see that even they,
though sinners, had attained the state of Hari.
Then Śivaśarman, the best of brahmins, having heard that praise of the holy place spoken by the Gaṇa,
spoke to his own son Viṣṇuśarman.
Śivaśarman said:

"Behold the majesty of this king of holy places (tīrtharāja), by which even a Śabara and a Daṃṣṭrin attained that state which is not easily obtained by the twice-born, even through accomplished penance, as if in play. (3)
What praise can be sufficient for this preeminent holy place, by the power of which even two sinners, from birth until death, attained a form identical to that of the son of Hari? 4.
Even a form of pure being belonging to the Lord is difficult for the gods born from lotuses to attain;
yet here are two dark-natured ones, a lion and a hunter—what a sacred place this is, with its wondrous deeds!
Having reached that state which is the goal of all actions and is known as the supreme abode of the Father and Mother (Brahmā and Śakti),
one attains death here at the feet of the Divine Teacher (Viṣṇu) and never falls away from the station of Mādhava.
Nārada said:
O King, having thus personally witnessed the greatness of this sacred ford (tīrtha), that best of the virtuous twice-born proceeded to bathe there.

Having performed the purification of his mouth, teeth, and feet, as well as that of his mind, he—wearing the five-fold sacred thread and having bound his topknot while remembering Mādhava—[proceeded]. ||8||
Reciting the verse beginning with "aśvakrānte," he touched the earth of the riverbank and,
applying a tilaka mark with that very [mud], entered the water.
There, having submerged himself facing the current and emerged again, he submerged once more, remembering Hari and Gaṅgā, the purifier of the world. 10.
Remembering Ayodhyā and the other seven cities, he rose up once more; yet, with his mind surrendered to Govinda, he submerged again into the water.
Having performed his bath according to the prescribed rules, that best of the twice-born put on clean garments; then, having gone outside, he applied the *tilaka*.
Binding darbha grass around his hands, feet, and head with a thread,
the self-controlled one performed the twilight devotions according to the rules, as well as the threefold libation.
Having respectfully offered arghya with water and *sūryāyaka* flowers,
that best of brahmins, with palms joined and head bowed, paid homage.
Then, O king of brahmins, he performed the worship of Viṣṇu— whose lotus feet are worshipped by the entire world— from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of food (naivedya).
Having performed his duties and being well-seated, he spoke to his son in such a manner,
recollecting his actions in a previous birth in their entirety.
Śivaśarman said: "O Viṣṇuśarman, this speech of yours is not false, for my memory of my former births and deeds has arisen here through this bath. (17)
"O noble one, listen as I speak before you: formerly, I was born in the lineage of wealthy and virtuous Vaiśyas. (18)
A man named Pitāmeśvara lived in the city of Kānyakubja;
relying on the great wealth of dharma, he earned his fortune through trade. (19)
A great deal of time passed, yet no son was born to him,
whose body was seized by old age and whose mind was distressed by that anxiety.
Then that excellent Vaiśya reflected day and night:
"Without my son, this vast wealth that I have accumulated is indeed useless. (21)
In this world, even one who possesses wealth is like a debtor without a son;
he is like a rain-cloud laden with water that fails to rain for the cātakas.
That man conquers the entire universe by means of his threefold power, which is pre-eminent in righteousness, just as a king overcomes an invincible enemy.

The pure assembly of well-wishers, including the ancestors and human beings, was delighted when she spoke words of truth that were as pleasing to her friends and rivals as they were to those seated nearby.
The father’s own glory increases through his son who has risen to eminence, just as the pure water of the ocean increases by means of the moon, the king of the twice-born. 25.
