Therefore, strive for the birth of a son by means of either your body or your wealth;
for without him, these two things are in vain for people whose lives are as fleeting as lightning.
While he was thinking thus, the eminent sage Devala, who possessed supreme knowledge of the Vedas, arrived at his house at that time to bestow a boon.
Beholding him arrived, the father rose from his seat,
offered him the arghya and pādya water, and then bowed his head at the feet of the sage.
Having seated me on a seat provided by his own hand, my grandfather questioned Devala, the best of sages, who possessed divine vision. (29)
Welcome, O best of sages! May there be peace in your family, and may your austerities, Vedic study, and observances proceed without hindrance. (30)
Do guests ever arrive at your hermitage at the proper time?
And do the trees of the hermitage bear fruit according to one's heart's desire? (31)
Do tigers and other predators not harbor enmity toward deer and other animals, having come to your hermitage as if they were brothers with their own brothers? (32)
How can your wandering on this earth bring joy to householders?
For those who are submerged in the attachments of home, where is there a sight such as yours? (33)
O Sage, for one who has awakened to the dust of Hari’s feet, desire no longer exists anywhere;
nevertheless, tell me quickly the reason for your arrival.
Śivaśarman said:
Having been addressed thus by him, the sage Devala, who is honored by the gods, spoke to the lord of the people, desiring to know his inner thoughts. (35)
Devala said:
O best of Vaiśyas, you have accumulated abundant wealth through righteousness;
for you, who know the dharma, perform the daily and occasional rites. (36)
A man gains respect in the royal assembly through his wealth, just as a brave warrior gains victory in battle against the enemy through his prowess. ||37||
But the householder, having acquired wealth, attains great prosperity, O Lord of the People, like a bull at the ripening of the autumn harvest. (38)
Relatives and other people do not abandon the wealthy when their fortune has vanished, just as honey-drinkers do not leave a tree laden with honeyed blossoms. (39)
Through the absence of wealth, a state of emaciation arises for householders, just as it does for the waters of lakes during the season of summer. (40)
O lord of the people, that vast wealth of yours remains in your house;
why then is there this emaciation of your limbs? If it is something to be hidden, speak of it at once.
The Vaiśya said:
"You are like fathers who delight in giving beneficial instruction;
what is there that ought to be hidden from you by those like me who have attained the status of sons? (42)
O best of sages, by your grace all is auspicious for me in every respect;
yet even in my old age, this lack of a son remains my sole sorrow. (43)
Therefore, O bull among sages, know that this emaciation of my limbs is for that reason.
I am afraid of my ancestors, for from them comes the downward fall of men.
O sage, by employing that means, I shall become the father of a son through her;
for there is nothing on this earth that cannot be accomplished by those such as you.
Śivaśarman said:
Having heard these words of that excellent Vaiśya, Devala steadied his mind for a moment and meditated with eyes closed. (46)
Seeing the cause of his father’s obstruction to the continuity of his lineage,
he spoke as if performing a sacrifice to the gods, invoking the memory of the Vedic rites.
Devala said:
"Once in the past, this woman, though a Vaiśya by birth, was a practitioner of dharma;
I shall now relate the desire that she formed within her own mind. (48)
"O Gaurī, beloved of Śambhu, if I become pregnant, then I shall gratify you with meals endowed with the six flavors. (49)
With incense, lamps, garlands, betel leaves, and dancers, with songs emerging from the mouths of the three-faced one, and with various kinds of ointments; ||50||
Having thus given her word before her friends,
she remained there, filled with devotion for you, her beloved, awaiting that appointed time.
In that very month, a fetus was formed in this woman of yours;
then all her friends, their hearts full of affection, spoke to her. (52)
"O fortunate one, since this Chitragarbha was presented by you to Gaurī, therefore perform the worship of the Goddess as promised. (53)
Otherwise, an obstacle arises from its improper performance;
for here the goddesses, when either gratified or provoked, bestow boons or curses. (54)
When her friends had thus related this to her husband, that illustrious and devoted wife, filled with joy, spoke to you with humility. (55)
O Lord, I wish to worship Gaurī, who grants all desires, so that by her grace I may attain my desired goal, just as you two have done. (56)
Having heard these auspicious words of hers, he considered his mistress of the house to be already pregnant, for she was indeed the best among Vaiśyas.
Rejoicing in the supreme joy of the festival, Sadyobhava himself commanded his servants to procure the materials for the worship.
Then, O Father, they brought all those items and gave them to him—honey, food, grapes, perfumes, and so forth. (59)
Then, having summoned all her own companions, she spoke these words: "O friends, all the materials for the worship of the Goddess have been brought together. (60)
"Taking the articles for worship, you must go to the temple of Bhikṣāṭana;
there, being virtuous, satisfy the Goddess with worship performed according to the prescribed rites. (61)
"In our family, a pregnant woman does not go outside the house;
therefore, I will not come, so you all go for that worship. (62)
Thus commanded and praised, the friends took the necessary materials and went to the temple of Ambikā,
where the banner bearing the emblem of a bee was wandering about like a madman.
It was filled with flocks of cuckoos and clusters of blossoming mango trees, adorned with swans, cranes,
and ruddy geese, and possessed of clear waters.
It was filled with parrots and mainas that spoke of the virtues of Mahādeva,
and it supported the friend Umā, who was intent on sprinkling the creepers of her pearl necklaces.
The ground of which was purified by the placement of the feet of Umāpati; its reservoirs of water were composed of crystal stones, and it possessed celestial trees. 66.
It resounded with the songs and dances of Gandharvas accompanying the Lord of Pārvatī,
and its mango buds were slightly stirred by a gentle breeze.
The bower of creepers resounded with the cries of dancing peacocks;
it shone like a mountain of sport, radiant with the glittering luster of jewels.
Having gone there, those women, accompanied by their husbands, bowed to the Daughter of the Mountain;
then, having circumambulated her with devotion, they addressed her.
"O beloved of Śiva, grant us peace;
accept this offering brought for the purpose of your worship. (70)
There was a Vaiśya named Śarabha; he had a wife named Lalitāṅganā. He desired a child by her, and upon obtaining that [desire], he performed your worship. (71)
O beloved of Śambhu, by your grace she has become pregnant;
this very Bali has been sent by us for your worship. (72)
"In her family, pregnant women do not go outside the house; therefore, O Goddess, since she has not yet arrived, please be gracious and accept [this offering]."
Having spoken thus, his female friends then led Bāli to him;
having presented him according to the prescribed rite, they worshipped him with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Failing to obtain an answer from Gaurī, they returned home;
dejected, they told their own friends that the beloved of Śiva was despondent.
Having heard their words, that Vaiśya woman became distracted in mind and thought: "How is it that even Gaurī does not love me? (76)
She knows that just as devotion was offered by me in her worship, what among humans—whether external or internal—is unknown to such beings? (77)
Since I had not gone there, he knew the reason for that as well: "How could she have been satisfied by me, who am weak and have given nothing? (78)
I know of no other cause for my dissatisfaction here than that I shall surely take delight in that abode once I have gone there. (79)
Since that which is past cannot be done today, I shall depart from the womb; for its sake, [I have come] to this temple. (80)
"Salutations to that wife of Mahādeva; may she grant peace!
Having said this, the Vaiśya woman stood there, bearing a child in her womb.
Śivaśarman said:
"O Viṣṇuśarman, having learned of this past event, my father questioned Devala, the tiger among sages and possessor of superior knowledge. (82)
The Vaiśya said:
O Sage, tell me how that daughter-in-law Pārvatī, having failed to perform the worship as she had promised, became the cause of your grief. (83)
Since Śivā herself knew that she had gone there, and because she had told her friends about it, she became despondent and wondered from where this danger could have arisen.
Devala said:
O best of Vaiśyas, listen to this;
I shall tell you the reason why Pārvatī became despondent, which resulted in the destruction of her embryo.
When her friends had departed after honoring Skanda’s mother,
Vijayā, filled with curiosity, spoke to Pārvatī.
Vijayā said:
"O Girijā, this offering has been given to you with faith by human women; O fair-faced one, why have you not become pleased with them? (87)
Since you have been worshipped with incense, lamps, and food offerings for the sake of satisfaction, why, O Goddess, have you instead displayed a causeless form of dejection? (88)
Devala said:
Having heard these words of her friend, the Goddess, who is worshipped by the best of gods, spoke to Vijayā, her friend, regarding the cause of the Vaiśya’s despair. 89.
Pārvatī said:
"O Vijayā, like the wife of a Vaiśya, you have gone outside the house;
having become unable to endure it, you have departed from the womb due to a lack of discernment. (90)
"Having been summoned by her friend for my worship, they have assembled;
yet those like me do not accept an offering made by another's hand. (91)
If her husband had arrived, there would have been misfortune; for, due to his intoxication, she would have suffered a miscarriage. (92)
O friend, whatever vow or worship the woman is unable to perform herself, the Lord causes her to do; thus, for those two, there shall be success in the heavens.
Or rather, since she did not come herself, this worship was performed by her for me without having first asked her husband, who is the chief of the Vipras and whose mind is fixed on no other. (94)
"Furthermore, this pregnancy longing (dohada) shall not be fruitless, for it was not brought about by my husband;
provided that both husbands come together again with faith toward me. (95)
"A son shall be born to him who worships me; that will be for both of you.
Devala said:
"That curse was not [imposed] by you, O Vaiśya, nor indeed by your wife. (96)
Her friends had heard of this favor bestowed by her;
however, because of their ignorance, no son was born to that Vaiśya couple. (97)
O Vaiśya, this has been told to you: that lack of remedy due to ignorance, which bestows neither happiness here nor in the next world, is the cause for the absence of peace. 98.
Just as Vasiṣṭha formerly [acted] for King Dilīpa,
having heard that, the king likewise gratified Nandinī.
Likewise, you who possess a wife, please Gaurī, the bestower of desires, who, when propitiated,
granted a son to King Dilīpa.
Propitiate Gaurī in such a way that she will grant it to you.
The Vaiśya said:
O Sage Kācasānandin, who was that king named Dilīpa? 101.
Having propitiated her, that best of kings obtained a son, setting aside Maheśa and the other gods who grant the fruits of only three castes. (102)
"O Sage, tell me all this that I have asked: how was she propitiated by that king for the sake of a son?
Having heard it, I shall then serve the Daughter of the Mountain together with my wife. (103)

Śivaśarman said: Having heard these words spoken with humility by my father, the leader of men, Viṣṇuśarman, that sage set forth to relate the history of Dilīpa, which is most purifying in the world. (104)

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Kālindī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||201||
Chapter Two Hundred and Two:
Devala said:
Listen, O highly wise one, to [the account] of King Dilīpa.
Listen to this divine and wonderful discourse, which destroys all sins. ||1||
In the lineage of Vaivasvata Manu, there was Dilīpa, the best of kings,
who was like Prācīnabarhis in the lineage of Svāyambhuva Manu.
Protecting the earth according to dharma, that best of upholders of the true dharma,
the lord of the earth, swiftly conquered the worlds by means of his exalted virtues.
The daughter of the lord of Magadha was the chief queen of that king; she was renowned by the name Sudakṣiṇā, and was like Śacī to the lord of heaven. ||4||
But when no son was born to the queen after a long time, that emperor,
the lord of Kośala, reflected thus within himself.
The circle of the earth, adorned with jewels such as oceans, Mount Sumeru, and cities, was held by him for the sake of adorning his arms; it was not for the sake of pride. (6)
Just as the three groups [of duties] when practiced at the proper time without conflict bring happiness, so too for one who possesses these, there is no lack of bliss in the heart. (7)
Viṣṇu was propitiated with sacrifices, as were Indra and the other foremost gods;
and throughout the entire earth, large ponds, groves, and wells were constructed.
With cows, land, gold, and garments, and with meals endowed with the six flavors, I have satisfied the Brahmins and guests who were present there with devotion. (9)
Having raised up the protectors of the earth from battle in accordance with righteousness for the sake of service, I have indeed augmented my treasury with great wealth. (10)
Those who have gone astray, who are intoxicated, and who violate their own dharma—those who turn their faces away from the ancestors and the gods—should be punished; they have been punished by me.
On the five parvan days, on the day sacred to Viṣṇu, during rites for the ancestors, and on the lunar days of the tenth and eleventh, I have not engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman. (12)

I did not neglect my own wife when she had bathed at the conclusion of her menstrual period; nor did I refuse her when she requested me even outside that time, provided it was an appropriate occasion. (13)
Thus, with her who was full of desire, I took my pleasure with desire; in this way, dharma, artha, and kāma were pursued by me according to their proper time. (14)
"By what fault was this multitude of mental afflictions born in the queen?
Our preceptor Vasiṣṭha alone possesses knowledge of the past and the future. (15)
"He will speak of that fault because of which no son is born to me.
Devala said:
Having reflected thus, the king, intending to go to the hermitage of his preceptor, departed.
He entrusted the prosperity of the treasury and the prosperity of magical power to his ministers.
Then, having worshipped the god Prajāpati and the hermitage of their guru,
the two, desiring a son, set out on an auspicious day.
After traversing the road for several days, staying together in a single carriage,
the two of them reached the auspicious hermitage of their preceptor in the evening.
The sage, who performed the hospitable reception of guests upon the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite,
was [surrounded] by a wreath of smoke spreading from the substances offered into the sacrificial fire.
He sanctified certain sages dwelling within himself,
while that mountain had its interior filled with herds of deer and a profusion of spreading dūrvā grass.
The area around the pavilion was filled with the tumultuous clamor of flocks of birds gathering on the trees as herds of deer approached from all sides.
There, tigers, deer, and other wild animals were free from mutual enmity;
it was a place where sages devoted to recitation and meditation were heard for a moment as they rested, their voices echoing with the sound of sacred scripture.
In that place, the two of them saw Vasiṣṭha, who had completed his daily rites, while young boys, enamored of play, were engaged in games during a time not intended for study.
The queens and the women of the harem, having approached with devotion, bowed down to the feet of their lord and teacher as he sat calmly upon a grass mat.
The preceptor also joined him with a blessing that he might attain the state of Aruṇadhaṭī.
Then the preceptor honored that guest with offerings such as the madhuparka.
Having been honored with offerings, he asked the most excellent of Arhats, "O Vasiṣṭha!
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O best of kings, is all well with your kingdom? (26)
O hero, is the earth protected by you according to dharma, while the world follows its own dharma with skillful discernment? (27)
O King, both the rural folk and the city-dwellers increase their own prosperity through you, just as a virtuous woman increases her household wealth through her wisdom.
O Lord, do the wise not abandon those who possess substance because of affection, companionship, or living together? (29)
O Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa,
you who grant the city of heaven, do your desired vows bear fruit for the king and his subjects in this city, just as the celestial sandalwood tree fulfills the wishes of those in heaven? (30)
Devala said:
Having thus questioned him, the best of sages, Vasiṣṭha, that bull among munis, fed the king with foods brought forth through the power of yoga. (31)
The noble-minded Arundhatī, filled with great respect, fed the queen with various kinds of cooked foods prepared by the people.
When the king had finished his meal and was seated at ease, the healthy sage took hold of the king— who was also healthy—
with his hand as he bowed low, and questioned him once more.
Vasiṣṭha said:

[He ruled] a kingdom endowed with the seven constituent elements, whose subjects were devoted to their own duties, whose kinsmen and ministers were pleased, and whose warriors were skilled in the proper use of weapons and missiles. (34)
For that king whose friends are under his control, whose enemies have been subdued, and whose mind is devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa—what need has he for the kingdom of heaven? (35)
O Lord, the righteous kings of the Ikṣvāku lineage, having procreated sons, entrusted the kingdom to them and themselves retired to the forest for asceticism. (36)
"You are young, have not yet seen the face of a son, and are not qualified for the practice of asceticism;
for what purpose have you come here, having abandoned such a kingdom? (37)
The king said:
"O Brahmin, I have not come to your hermitage to perform penance, having abandoned my kingdom here out of a desire for heaven. (38)
O Brahmin, this which you have said is true: having installed their kingdoms upon their sons, those born of the Ikṣvāku lineage have retired to the forest hermitages. (39)
Even though those great kings have gone to heaven, this kingdom has not been abandoned by them;
for their very forms remain here in this assembly, dwelling with troubled minds.
Just as childhood passed away from my father and youth has arrived, so too has it come to pass.
Just as he will depart even before that time, so too will old age certainly arrive. ||41||
After old age, death inevitably follows for a person; there is no doubt of this.
O Brahmin, when I have met death, it will be without the birth of a son. (42)
"O Guru, tell me, to whom will this sovereignty over the earth belong?
For although I am childless and have established myself in the kingdom, I possess no sense of ownership here;
for that [ownership] existed previously only because of the absence of such a person."
O you who perceive the disharmony within my group, please understand this from me, your disciple.
"O treasure of asceticism, by what fault is a son born blind?
Having perceived the fault through meditation, tell it to me, O Guru, quickly. (45)
"I shall perform a remedy for him so that he may not obtain those [sons].
Devala said:
Having heard these words of that lord of the earth, Vasiṣṭha...
Having perceived the cause through meditative absorption, Saṃtati spoke to him.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O tiger among kings, in a former age you served the leader of the gods."
Remembering this bride who has bathed, you have departed from your own palace;
as you go with haste, O Father, may you be filled with longing for her.
Once, while she was standing on the path at the foot of the celestial tree (Kalpavṛkṣa), you produced an excessive anger toward her venerable foot-dust. 49.
Because you did not perform the customary practice of circumambulation and salutation, she cursed you in great anger: "No son shall be born to you. (50)
"Go quickly to give me my season, you who are so eager for your son, before you cease to attend to my service. (51)
With your mind fixed on her, you heard the curse from the sound of the chariot wheels:
"Her cow Nandini, the mother of my daughter, [is yours]. (52)
"Propitiate her with this daughter-in-law, and she will grant you a son.
Devala said:
When the sage Vasiṣṭha had spoken thus, that Nandinī—
Having returned from the penance grove with her breasts flowing with milk out of affection for her calf,
Vasiṣṭha, the preeminent among sages, his heart gladdened upon seeing her,
spoke again to the king after presenting Nandinī to him. (54)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, she has indeed arrived, whose auspicious name brings welfare as soon as it is remembered;
therefore, know that the accomplishment of your purpose is now close at hand. (55)
"By following her into the forest and enduring such hardship, you have propitiated her;
through her grace, O son, she will grant you a son—of this there is no doubt. (56)
O King of kings, O wielder of the bow, graze her in the forest in such a way that no predatory creature born of the woods might overcome her. (57)
Devala said:
Having replied "So be it" to the king and his daughter-in-law who spoke with such humility, the ascetic gave them that hut for the purpose of sleeping there for the night.
There, with a restrained mind, the lord of men lay down upon the ground strewn with darbha grass together with his wife and passed the night.
Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Kālindī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||202||
The two hundred and third chapter.
Devala said:
Then the lord of men worshipped Uṣas with flowers and other offerings.
Having taken the cow Anandinī, the queen's favorite, he went to the forest. ||1||
As she went along eating those [fruits], the king followed her like a shadow;
as she ate the grass and other such things, he too consumed their roots and so forth.
As she sat in the shade of a tree, Anusūya also sat down;
as she drank her after-drink, the king too drank water.
By taking small, soft morsels, by removing his teacher's pain with his teeth,
and by scratching him, he served the preceptor like a wish-fulfilling cow.
Then, O lord of the earth, I returned each evening to the king's hermitage,
sanctifying his path with particles of dust raised by the hooves of my horses.
As she proceeded with her heavy lower garment, she appeared unsteady,
like the daughter of Nanda oppressed by the weight of the great task of protecting the earth.
The queen went out to meet her near the sage’s hermitage,
having brought sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, food offerings, incense, and other such items.
Having worshipped her according to the prescribed rites and having prostrated before her again and again, the queen,
after performing a circumambulation, stood before her with palms joined in reverence.
Having accepted that worship performed with such faith by the king, and remaining steadfast in his resolve, he went with those two to the hermitage.
Dilīpa served her with firm resolve;
twenty-one days passed in this manner. ||10||
Then, desiring to test his true nature,
that daughter of the mountain entered the cave of the Himavat, which was filled with young grass and free from fear.
While that lord of the earth was beholding the beauty of the slopes of the Himalayas,
a lion, its approach unnoticed, seized Nandin by its strength.
Like a cow in distress, that bow, though without wheels, let out a loud cry;
it produced intense pain for him who held the bow in his hand.
Hearing that she had been violated, the lord of the world immediately withdrew his gaze from the slopes of the Himalayas.
Seeing the lion above him—with its sharp teeth and claws, its face streaming with tears—the king became deeply distressed. (15)
Observing that she had been seized by him with a lion-like roar,
the wielder of the bow extended his right arm to draw forth an arrow from its quiver.
Having extracted an arrow from his quiver to slay that lord of beasts, the king fixed it with a string and drew it back. (17)
Stunned by the sight of the entire host of gods, the king was unable to release his arrow; he remained there, filled with wonder. ||18||
Observing such a king, the lord of beasts spoke these words in a human voice, causing him great astonishment. (19)
Siṃha said:
"O King, I know you to be Dilīpa, born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku; and you should know me to be Śaṅkha, a member of the Bhṛgu clan named Kuṃbhodara. (20)
This is the Devadāru tree that stands within the range of your vision, O Hero, protected like a son by Pārvatī with her affectionate heart. (21)
Once, as a wild elephant rubbed its temple against him,
it tore away the very soft bark garment of the great king.
Observing him in such a state, Ṛḍānī, filled with compassion,
stationed me here, making me his protector.
"O Goddess, listen to what I say:
whatever creature comes here, you shall devour it while dwelling in this womb. (24)
From that time forward, O lord of kings, obeying your command, I have been dwelling here in Kandaraka, which was protected by all the gods. (25)
"You should feel no wonder at the inertness of your own body;
for here on this Himalayan mountain, the great power of Śiva’s Māyā operates. (26)
On whomsoever I am unable to strike with my trident, that lord shall mount upon my back and ascend the bull. (27)
Return to your own body, which protects all means of accomplishing one's goals;
O hero, this Gaurī has been brought here by fate for your consumption.
Devala said:
Having heard those words of his, which were accompanied by an address to a hero, Dilīpa, his body rendered motionless, replied to him. (29)
The King said:
[I salute] Śiva, the auspicious cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world;
Ambikā, the mother of the universe; and Gaṇeśa, who has the face of an elephant and the lion as his mount. (30)
O lord of beasts, you are honored by me as my servant;
having heard the words I speak, why do you stand with your hair standing on end? (31)
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, is known to you as our preceptor;
this is his cow named Nandinī, who fulfills all purposes.
This [practice], which has been properly cultivated by me for several days, was undertaken by me in order to propitiate him who is difficult to please. (33)
"O small deer, this mother of yours was held by me in the cave of the mountain;
she was unable to be released from you by me, as she was forcibly held by that mountain-dweller. (34)
I went before that sage, wondering how this world-renowned daughter of Kāmadhenu could have become his wife. (35)
There is no other cow like this one by whom I have been satisfied;
therefore, release her and take for yourself the foremost of your own food. (36)
I give my own body, though it is stained by infamy;
in this way, there shall be no loss of dharma for you, O Sage, nor will there be a lack of food.
For me too, who gives up my life for the sake of the cow, there will be a supreme destination. (37)
Devala said:

let my mind be fixed upon the state of Brahmā, Maheśvara, or Indra.
Constantly praying to that very Puruṣottama, my father,
I have dwelt here at this great sacred ford, having rendered my mind free from worldly objects.
Viṣṇuśarman said:
"If your death occurred while you were dwelling in this great sacred place (tīrtha), how did you obtain birth again? This is my doubt. (11)
Having abandoned the boundary of that sacred ford out of greed for wealth,
those travelers and their porters met their death at the hands of the Rākṣasas.
By drinking the water of this most excellent sacred site (tīrtha), those who had gone to heaven likewise attained it;
even a Rākṣasa, having met his death there, attained that same state.
Nakrāta went to heaven by his own will while you were looking on;
surely death must have occurred there, since [the fruit of] that birth is now visible.
Nārada said:
Having heard the inauspicious words of his son, Śiva spoke of the former events that were the cause of his own birth. (15)
Śivaśarman said:
"O Viṣṇuśarman, listen to this cause of my birth;
I shall tell it before you, and having heard it, become free from doubt. (16)
Once, while I was absorbed in meditation during the worship of Viṣṇu,
Durvāsas, whose nature is prone to anger, arrived at my hermitage.
Unaware that he had arrived, I remained in that same state, devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu and recollecting my name, Cirantana. (18)

Having stood for a moment before me, the sage, overcome with anger and his eyes bloodshot red, spoke these words aloud to himself: 19. Having stood for a moment before me, the sage, overcome with anger and his eyes bloodshot red, spoke these words aloud to himself:
Durvāsas said:
"Alas! I am the son of Atri, born from the womb of Anasūyā;
I have been insulted by this wretched mortal."
By me, Śakra was overthrown from his sovereignty over the three worlds;
yet this evil-minded man treats even me with contempt. (21)
O World, you are that very one from whom I am afraid, as if from the fire of time; for, having abandoned the triad of gods, you are the most excellent of Arhats to me.
Why does Yama, stationed within that very form, not awaken this fool who, having resorted to meditation, meditates upon that deity? (23)
"Surely this man meditates upon the god Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world;
for, satiated by the nectar of his meditation, he possesses no external knowledge. (24)
Whether he meditates on Hari, Brahmā, Śambhu, or anyone else, I must punish him by all means, for he has shown me contempt. (25)
Śivaśarman said:
Having reflected thus, he awakened me, Sumati;
and with eyes red with anger, he cursed me once I had regained my senses. (26)
Whatever desire one has in the mind while meditating, having disregarded me, how indeed could that ever come to pass in this world in any way? (27)
Having spoken thus, O dear one, when that sage, the son of Atri, set out,
I, terrified with fear, grasped his feet.
Thus addressed, O best of sages, [he said]: "Forgive me; let my anger be released.
Those like me do not fully understand the actions of those such as you. (29)
"You have now bestowed a terrible curse, yet they did not believe it;
be gracious to me who am bowed before you, and grant me favor by ending the curse. (30)
Thus addressed, Durvāsas cast off his anger like one greedy for cold water, saying:
"O dear one, why is this not appropriate, since he is the moon-crested Lord? (31)
Having become that best of Brahmins, the wise one said to me:
"Having met your death right here, you shall not undergo birth again. (32)
Having thus shown me favor,
O dear one, he who was clothed only by the directions departed after staying that day, honored by me with hospitable rites.
Even when thinking "I am," the speech of the Sage is not false. //34//
He went to his own home, carrying remorse in his heart, thinking: "Alas! Even though he was constantly pure in mind and lived as a hermit at sacred fords, [he fell thus]. (35)
The sight of the Lord of Śrī has become difficult to obtain in this birth,
like that of a cloud for a cātaka bird during the summer season that causes such intense heat.
From where has this come to me, who obstructs my path to Vaikuṇṭha—a cloud that has appeared for people like a mouth of dark rainwater at the time of death? //37//
There is surely no fault in the Sage; indeed, his will is like that of Hari.
For even after granting me the Sudarśana, he has brought about another birth for me.
Terrified by saṃsāra, I must take refuge at the lotus feet of Hari, just as a traveler scorched by the heat of the summer sun seeks shelter under a tree. (39)
What is the use of wealth, children, wives, or other transient kinsmen, for me who constantly mutters, "Govinda! Supreme Bliss! Rāma!"? (40)
Remaining as if indifferent toward the household, while worshipping Hari, he will experience only that karma which has already begun, without being affected by other actions. (41)
Reflecting thus, my dear father, after bathing in the water that had washed the feet of Hari, I reached my own home within a few days.
The father's death was announced to the mother and to the kinsmen;
having heard it, they too were overcome with grief, for they did not realize that this [world] is impermanent. (43)
Free from desire for the worlds such as Satyaloka while dwelling at home, I indeed met my death on the banks of the Gaṅgā, which is frequented by the virtuous. (44)
Born into a Vaiṣṇava family due to the curse of the sage Durvāsas,
I shall attain the abode of Hari after meeting my death here at this sacred pilgrimage site.
Nārada said: O highly fortunate one, when that sacred ford (tīrtha) had thus been fashioned by the preceptor of the gods, those two performed their ancient rites there.
Having spoken thus to one another, those two best of the twice-born remained there, their minds fixed in meditation upon the sprout-like feet of Hari. 46.
They meditated upon Hari, the lotus-eyed one,
with four arms and a body dark blue like a rain cloud,
resplendent with his own weapons as ornaments.
Having remembered this, they attained a form similar to that of Hari.
The narrative of him whose field is this supreme and meritorious place called Indraprastha has been told; now hear its fruit, O auspicious one. 48.
Whatever merit is gained from bathing in the Gaṅgā and whatever merit arises from the gift of a daughter, a man obtains that same merit through faith by listening to this. ||49||
When a son is born, and when Jupiter is in the constellation Rohiṇī, whatever fruit arises on earth from bathing in the waters of the Godāvarī; [that fruit one obtains by this]. (50)
The fruit of that [merit] arises from hearing of this; there is no doubt in this matter.
Therefore, there is no other holy place superior to this supreme *tīrtha* which bestows all goals, wherein even animals, by dying, certainly become four-armed [deities]. (51)
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa,
in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses,
in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the *Māhātmya* of the Kālindī.
The two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Awakening at Nigama."
The two hundred and sixth chapter. Saubhari said:
The illustrious Śibi, King of Dharma, heard those words of the sage.
With a delighted mind, he spoke this supreme [teaching] to Nārada. ||1||
Śibi said:
O Sage, this greatness of this most excellent holy place, which awakens one to the Vedas, has been correctly described by you; it is destructive of sins, and I have heard it well. (2)
O Muni, there are indeed hundreds of sacred fords here in Indraprastha;
please describe the greatness of any other one as well, if such exists.
Nārada said: O King, this Dvārakā lies within the territory of Indraprastha;
hear from me as I relate to you what occurred there in ancient times. 4.
Now, in Kāmpilya, there was a certain twice-born man who, like the god Puṣpeṣu (Kāmadeva) incarnate, captivated the hearts of all women with his supreme charms. (5)
Skilled in the science of music, with a voice as sweet as the cuckoo’s,
he once held a lute in his hand and played it repeatedly.
O King, with a voice as sweet as the song of the cuckoo,
that high-minded one wandered through the city, singing at every crossroads.
Hearing the sound of his singing, accompanied by melodic modulations and musical elaborations,
the women of the city abandoned their own household chores and came to him.
Enchanted by his beauty, they could not withstand the impulse of desire;
their fortitude faltered upon hearing that song right before their eyes.
By him Brahmā’s mind was enticed toward Bhāratī, and by him half of Śiva’s body was bestowed upon Pārvatī. (10)
In this world, even one who is devoid of wealth and lacks wisdom—anyone other than those two—is capable of conquering Smara (the God of Love), for women are by nature fickle. (11)
Even though they were difficult to subdue, they could not endure the onset of passion;
O King, what more need be said? Desire is indeed invincible in this world.
Then they would go wherever he went,
singing along with him, their voices like lutes, as he sang, enchanted by his own melody.
Then, O King, their husbands, sons, brothers, and fathers arrived, rebuked them, and led them back to their respective homes.
Having searched for her, they all returned to his presence;
then, when the citizens gathered there, they spoke thus to the Lord.
The king summoned the twice-born Rāhasi and asked him: "O Brahmin, by what mantra have those city women been deluded? (16)
Therefore, tell me that, O best of Brahmins; I shall give you much wealth.
Otherwise, I shall undoubtedly expel you from my own kingdom. (17)
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of the king, that best of the twice-born, an ocean of speech, form, and virtue, spoke the truth before him. 18.
The twice-born said: "O King, there is neither mantra nor medicine in me, a mendicant.
However, all the women in that city have their senses unsubdued. (19)
O King, having beheld my form and likewise heard the sound of my song,
the women in the city of Stavapura were overcome by the force of passion.
"What shall I do, O Great King? What offense have I committed against you, O Lord?
My command, O Ruler of the Earth, is as inviolable as that which was performed in a former life. (21)
Nārada said:
O King, while the twice-born was speaking thus concerning Uśīnara Śibi, all the citizens gathered together and addressed the monarch as follows. (22)
The citizens said:
"O King, the women of the city have been deluded by this brahmin;
they no longer remain in their homes, for they are not restrained by us. (23)
"O Lord, if this deluder of women should dwell in the city, then we shall indeed go to other regions today;
for our bull-like god, who is the essence of the rites of *havya* and *kavya*, has departed. (24)

O Lord of Men, like a cow abandoned by its owners, this earth has fled from that kingdom which was pursued [by you], seeking refuge with him who is without sin, while her own splendors have been forsaken.
Then they will follow him away like cows following a bull;
how can Fortune remain in an empty house even with effort? (26)
Since these three—dharma, artha, and the home—are under the control of women, what remains for those two once their dharma and wealth have perished? (27)
Nārada said:
While the virtuous citizens were speaking thus, their women arrived;
having sat down near the king, they spoke to one another as follows. (28)
The women of the city said: "Having obtained this Brahmin of such lovely form, our hearts rejoice, just as lotuses in the water do upon reaching the lord of day. (29)
They shriveled up like water-lilies scorched by the heat of the sun;
having come together and met him, they held him before the king. (30)
"He is not to be killed, and what can our king do to him?
Having said this, they hurriedly seized that best of the twice-born. Nārada said: [31]
Then, while their own husbands and the king were looking on, they said to him: "O lord of our hearts, come to the house of the god of love."
"O Śamaya, because of our extreme hunger, we are truly unable to remain standing.
Having heard these words of theirs, he, together with the brāhmaṇa, replied.
The brahmin said:
"I am your son; you are my mothers. For what reason have you abandoned your homes and are wandering about? (34)
By propitiating one's own lords, both worlds are certainly secured;
for when the Lord is propitiated, Viṣṇu, the sovereign of all gods, is likewise pleased. ||35||
He becomes pleased with you; when he is pleased, what is difficult to obtain?
That woman who, abandoning her own husband, serves another out of a desire for pleasure— [36]
He incurs reproach and falls into a most terrible miserable rebirth;
having dwelt there for as many eons as there were instances of his deception of his wife. (37)
Emerging from that again, it attains the state of being immobile;
from that as well, it acquires the state of a beast over many births. (38)
Then, having been liberated from the human state, she will become a cow;
thus, knowing such a miserable rebirth, turn away from this person. (39)
"Because you have reviled me, you shall go to a most dreadful hell;
if you desire worldly existence and its pleasures, you shall not obtain them here, for it is only through sin that men fall downward. (40)
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of his and having seen the pleasures of her husband,
she stood with her face bowed down in shame, like a palm tree struck by the wind.
But the exceedingly fierce fire of passion within those city women was extinguished by the cooling water of that young brahmin’s words.
O King, they all rose up and began to dance, forgetting everything—including this world—which causes even the delusion of gods such as Brahmā and Śakra. 43.
The women said:
"Fie on this man of evil deeds, who is an axe for the wood of virtuous conduct!
Blessed is that Smara (the God of Love), by whom he was struck, for the sake of pleasing the lovely-eyed women. (44)
What can we say of Rukmiṇī, who is worshiped by the world, and by whom he who was named Pradyumna—[that very Rāhu who devours the moon of feminine virtue]—was borne in her womb? (45)
If that which is with the gods comes within the range of our vision, we shall cast it again into the fire of the gaze of the Lord who performs meditation. 46.
By that Viṣṇu, who delights in the Self, this evil man was created;
he was made beloved of sixteen thousand women—what more need be said? (47)
While they were thus censuring desire, they praised that best of the twice-born,
O King, by whose conduct their own virtue was protected.
Blessed is the mother of this man, by whom this best of Brahmins was created in this world as a conqueror of Cupid and a protector of the supreme dharma. (49)
Fie upon those women who were laughed at by the world of kings, conquered by passion, and by whom a manifest evil was produced through both speech and mind! 50.
Nārada said:
Having reflected thus, all those women, having abandoned their anger and being enlightened by the words of the twice-born, went each to her own home. (51)
Then the king also honored that self-controlled twice-born man with garments and ornaments, and sent him back to his own home.
Then, at that time, the powerful lord of Kārūṣa arrived and besieged the city of the lord of Kāpila with his armies.
A terrible battle took place between the two; he was slain in that fight.
The city was plundered, and all the heroes were killed on every side.
Those women, having consumed the kālakūṭa poison, did not die;
yet they did not perform any expiation for that sin.
By whatever sin those [beings] belonging to the Rākṣasa named Bhīṣaṇa were produced, they were born in the city of that Rākṣasa with massive bodies and terrifying forms. (56)
There, all those city women were gathered by Hanumān at the banner of the chariot of the victorious one, as he moved about performing sacrifices or stood still.
Furthermore, those very same rākṣasīs appeared amidst the sounds of battle, afflicted by hunger and thirst, and inspiring terror by their mere sight. (58)
Thus, by that evil committed through speech and mind, they obtained two births mixed with the womb of a rākṣasī. ||59||
By that sin, both cities, along with their kings, were destroyed;
therefore, one must never indulge in another's beloved.

O Lord, even by women who fear sin, their own husband— whether he be diseased, dull-witted, impoverished, or even deprived of sight— must not be abandoned through speech or thought if they desire a good rebirth. (61)
I have related to you at great length this accumulation of sin produced by mind and speech through devotion to another lover, as well as the very fruit that has been obtained by these women. (62)

These women from Indraprastha, having seen the sinless one [Kṛṣṇa] from Dvārakā, attained heaven through their thoughts and words; yet, due to their devotion to another lover, they were released from that intense state of being flesh-eating demons and, falling into the water like drops, obtained the status of celestial nymphs, which brings joy to the gods. (63)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Dvārakā," in the *Māhātmya of the Kālindī*, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The two hundred and seventh chapter. Saubhari said:
Having heard these words of that great-souled one, the son of Dharma [Yudhiṣṭhira]...
King Śibi spoke these words to Nārada with humility. ||1||
Śibi said: O best of sages, while you were staying on the path of the desert,
how did these two Rākṣasīs obtain water from this Dvārikā?
Nārada said:
Listen, O King, to this divine, pure story that destroys all sins,
concerning a brahmin named Vimala who dwelt in a cave of the Himavat mountains.
In a valley of the Himalayas, there was a certain Brahmin named Vimala;
he was a worshiper of the gods, sages, ancestors, and the sacred fires, and a hospitable host to guests. ||4||
Devoted to the worship of Hari’s feet, he was a knower of the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, and Dharma;
his mind was filled with the ancient scriptures describing the multitude of virtues of Vāsudeva.
In his old age, by the grace of the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), a son was born to him;
then Janaka gave him the name Haridatta.
He performed for him the rites of tonsure and so forth according to the prescribed rules;
and from his preceptor, Haridatta received the sacred thread initiation.
Having studied the Vedas according to the prescribed rules and having given the teacher's fee, he,
becoming dispassionate, renounced both stages of life along with their roots.
Realizing that this was not his doing, his mother, who was devoted to her son, lamented, bathing her pair of breasts with tears born of separation from her son. (9)
The mother said: "O father, why have you abandoned me, who am without a protector, and departed from here?
You leave me like a bee leaving a weak lotus stalk, while your father is already seized by old age."
I have attained the status of Vārddhaketa through service at the feet of the Lord of Śrī;
yet, abandoning me, you have resorted to His feet for the sake of liberation. (11)
O father, you have been deluded; you have sought the impermanent for the sake of attaining happiness, having cut off the permanent Hari while pursuing that which is transient.
O wise child, since you yourself worship Viṣṇu for the sake of all goals,
this unstable world having been understood by you, you too have become stable.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? This knowledge of illusion cuts through me—this fierce, root-like [ignorance] that produces excellent fruit, though it belongs to the realm of the scriptures. (14)
Blessed is King Daśaratha who died from grief for Rāma;
shame on me, who, despite separation from my son, continues to cling to this life! (15)
Come, O bestower of sight; deliver me completely from this distress.
O ocean of virtues, speak words consisting of the Vedas before your father.
Nārada said:
O King, having lamented thus, his mother fell upon the ground like a streak of clouds shattered by the teeth of Rāhu. 17.
Then the eminent brahmin-sage Vimala arrived;
seeing her fallen upon the ground, he spoke, "What is this? (18)
Why is she with disheveled hair and scattered garments and ornaments, fallen upon the ground? O auspicious one, what calamity has befallen him? (19)
O King, all those female companions said to that Vimala.
The companions said: "O son, having studied the Vedas and having given the teacher's fee," (20)
Having become devoted to Nārāyaṇa, Haridattaka went forth as a renunciant;
due to the grief of separation from him, she fell to the surface of the earth. 21.

Nārada said: Having heard their words, Vimala, who was exceedingly wise, enlightened his own wife with these nectar-like words: 22. [Nārada said: Having heard their words, Vimala, who was exceedingly wise, enlightened his own wife with these nectar-like words.
Vimala said:
"Arise, my wife, and hear the words spoken by me; why do you lie fallen here in despair?
Blessed is your son, who, having realized this world to be perishable, has taken refuge at the lotus feet of Hari. (23)
Blessed indeed are you, O auspicious one, who grants birth to such a son as this, whose portion is the feet of Hari;
he will undoubtedly deliver me, his family, and even the ancestors born of that lineage.
"Where is this universe, which is both one and yet moving and falling away? Where is the service of Hari, which grants the eternal world?
Thinking thus, O virtuous lady, kings such as Bharata and others devoted themselves to Hari; and in the very same way, so did your son.
Wives, sons, houses, bodies, and kinsmen—these bring suffering in every birth;
therefore, until one reaches the sprout-like feet of Hari, a wise man should remain free from all desires. (26)
Nārada said:
Thus enlightened by that steadfast one, she rose from the surface of the earth and spoke to her husband in a piteous voice.
The wife said:
"O beloved, I know everything that you have spoken so unkindly; however, I do not see a successor to our lineage, and for that reason, I am tormented exceedingly. (28)
What is the use of the great holy site of Putreśatīrtha, or even of service to Keśava?
If our death should occur right here in our own home, then both worlds will be ours. (29)
Human beings must indeed exert effort to produce virtuous sons;
for sons rescue their ancestors from the ocean of saṃsāra. (30)
O high-minded one, if you desire a son who shall be the bearer of the family lineage, worship the Creator and Sustainer of all living beings with the longing for a son. (31)
Nārada said: Having heard her words, the twice-born Vimala replied:
"Indeed, I am going to Prayāga, the field of Brahmā, out of a desire for a son. (32)
Having spoken thus, that twice-born man set out and went to Haridvāra;
having bathed there according to the prescribed rites, he then proceeded to Indraprastha.
After several days, at the time for the heroic meal (vīrasāyaṃ), which grants all desires, he bathed and ate; then, during the night on the bank of the Yamunā, he caused [the others] to sleep.
While Vimala was sleeping at midnight,
the Lord of the Gods, having mounted his swan and followed by all the sacred fords (tīrthas), approached him.
Having arrived, he raised up Vimala, the son of Śakra;
and that best of asuras spoke these words in sweet syllables.
Brahmā said:
"I know the desire and the thought residing in your mind; however, it is not possible to fulfill it—listen to the reason for that. (37)
Once, all the deities assembled on the summit of Mount Meru and, for the sake of accomplishing their purpose, praised Mādhava, who was present in the mouth of my father, Śiva. 38.
Praised by us and the other gods, the Lord Hari was pleased;
then Viṣṇu appeared and said, "Choose [a boon]. (39)
Having been addressed thus by him, the gods, having obtained the boon as desired from the Lord of Śrī, all departed to their respective abodes. (40)
I said: "O Lord of Gods, grant me this supreme boon:
let there be a sacred field named Prayāga that fulfills all desires. (41)
Therefore, O sinless one, my second field situated at Indraprastha, which has been properly maintained by me from you, shall be a hundred times more meritorious.
Having heard these words of mine, the Blessed One said to me at that time, "So be it," and spoke these words again: "Listen to my speech. (43)
The Blessed Lord said:
In the Khāṇḍava forest of Indra, there is an auspicious sacred field named Indraprastha on the bank of the Kaliṃdā; those who die there become equal to Me. (44)
There, Virinca fashioned his own city of Dvārakā, which surpassed the city situated on the shore of the ocean by hundreds of qualities. 45.
If a person disregards that [Tīrtha] and resorts to another Tīrtha, he does not obtain the fruit of the Tīrtha; this which has been spoken is not false. 46.
A person obtains at Śakratīrtha the merit arising from all sacred fords;
moreover, by coming to the city of Dvārakā, one protects other sacred fords as well. 47.
Having performed various rites at other sacred fords and sacrificial sites,
one shall obtain from them a fruit that is certain to be attained here.
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished; I too went to my own world, O best of the twice-born, situated below Vaikuṇṭha.
Kāśī is remembered as being a hundred times superior to my own sacred field of Prayāga;
likewise, the holy site that awakens one to the Vedas is a hundred times superior to Kāśī.
These three groups of seven sacred fords (tīrtha-saptaka) are remembered as yielding equal fruit;
by practicing these three without transgression, one attains both the white and the black [paths].
I shall indeed grant you both that which you desire;
for some great seers have said that [the merit of] seven cities is equal to this. ||52||
From Ayodhyā and other cities, they say there are one hundred [tīrthas] leading to Indraprastha;
O best of Brahmins, you have come here, O bestower of the fruits of all desires! 53.
At the sacred ford known as Śrī Dvārakā, he performed an ablution with the desire for a son;
indeed, all the holy fords that exist within the interior of the jar of the universe [were present there]. (54)
The merit from chanting the hundred names is immeasurable compared to that;
this sacred site shall grant you a son who will be the leader of your lineage. (55)
"From bathing [there], Govinda will become gracious in soul.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, the Lord of the gods of gods, vanished on that spot.
Then Vimala, having bathed, offered libations even to the gods and others;
that righteous-souled one spoke thus at Dvārakā, the beloved abode of Kṛṣṇa. (57)
"Give me that Śakara which was heard; salutations to you, my devotee.
When this was said by that brahmin, a divine voice then arose: 58.
The divine voice said:
"O son, through the grace of this holy place, the crest-jewel of all sacred sites, you shall become a knower of the essence of dharma and a performer of meritorious deeds. (59)
"Since he delayed coming home for a month, let him perform an ablution [for that].
Nārada said:
"Having heard these words of the virtuous, he became confident regarding the birth of his son."
Taking water from the moving river in his water-pot, he set out for Dvārakā;
on the way, a Brahmin friend whose banner was the Malaya mountain joined him as a companion.
Having visited all the sacred fords, Mīlita returned home and related to him his own life story, which consisted of dialogues with Brahmā.
Having heard what had occurred at the sacred ford of Dvārakā, he too was struck with wonder;
that righteous-souled one said, "O friend, listen to these words of mine."
"As many sacred fords as have been established in the land of Bhārata, I desire to create that many of this supreme ford spoken of by you. (64)
"O friend, take me and show me that sacred ford which grants all desires;
for those friends who assist their companions on the path of life are truly the best of friends. (65)
In this world, neither father, mother, nor son will bow down to a man who is destitute;
indeed, all kinsmen abandon such a person in this world.
But his friends do not grieve, for they are already pained by his suffering;
rather, it is the friend who rescues his friends who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having taught me the path of devotion to Hari, which is a fire to the forest of worldly existence, you are therefore my best friend; O friend, please do me this favor.
O twice-born one, show me this best of boons, the place called Dvārakā, which is known as a sacred ford (tīrtha).

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Kālindī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compilation consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||207||
The two hundred and eighth chapter.
Nārada said:
Vimala, having led that twice-born man away, has now returned here to Dvārakā.
O King, once again those two wise ones, desiring devotion to the Lord of Śrī, bathed; then once more, a voice as deep as a cloud arose from the sky. 1.
The Voice from the Sky said:
"Listen, O tigers among the twice-born! This is the auspicious holy place (tīrtha) of Hari. By the grace of this holy place, devotion to Viṣṇu shall arise within you both."
By which this world abandons the intense delusion of ignorance. ||2||
Nārada said:
Having heard these words from the unembodied voice, O best of the twice-born,
they said to one another, "This is the grace of Hari."
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites and having attained supreme devotion to Hari,
they both prostrated themselves and then set out, conversing thus with one another.
The two birds said:
"Just as our union on this path has arisen through reflection,
so too does the union with home, wife, and other such things arise upon the earth."
Now a separation is about to occur, as if we were two traveling upon the path of the sea.
Likewise, among wives, sons, and others who exist only for a limited time, blessed is that virtuous man in this world who experiences the company of wife and children. (6)
One should take refuge in the eternal Lord of Śrī, who is the knower and momentary; one should worship Him.
Nārada said: "O Mādhava, I must remember You; I am one who has taken refuge at Your feet. (7)
Having said, "A message must be sent to me," they both went to their own homes.
O King, listen now to how that friend [acted] toward Vimala.
The liberation of the rākṣasīs was ordained by him as he traveled along the path.
Traveling along with a Brahmin, he reached that region devoid of water. ||9||
There, those rākṣasīs, scorched by their sins and distressed by hunger and thirst,
saw that best of the twice-born from afar as they were traveling along the path.
Seeing him with a water-pot in his hand, the female demons spoke thus among themselves:
"The female demons said:
'Some traveler is approaching, carrying a vessel of water in his hand. (11)
"Even a slight alleviation of our hunger and thirst will come about;
we shall devour him and drink what is held in his hand. (12)
"A vessel, water, and we, afflicted by thirst and hunger for a hundred years.
Nārada said:
"A certain woman spoke thus: 'In former times, I [ate] this warm liver. (13)
"Having devoured him and drunk his blood, I shall return to life.
Another said, "O Gajānanā, how much wealth does he possess? (14)
"Neither for Mamā nor for Vyāghrānanā, nor even for Tuṣā, is it seen;
listen to my words regarding the others known as Rathacakrā. (15)
"I shall make earrings for him; another said, 'I shall make a triple-girdled waistband'; yet another said, 'I shall [make them] with teeth made dark on one side. (16)
"Rāma is skilled in dice; let us play with him in the gambling hall.
Having said this to one another, they all ran toward that brahmin. (17)
Seeing those women with gaping mouths, lolling tongues, and great arms shining like torches,
the brahmin was overwhelmed with fear.
O King, he performed on all sides of himself the protection prescribed in the Vedas;
then those two Rākṣasīs of terrifying prowess approached and stood not far away.
O King, repulsed by his splendor and his mantras, they said:
"Who are you here? From where have you come? Tell us that."
By the sight of you, our minds attain serenity;
what fruit then will not manifest from the touch of your feet? Therefore, O Lord, place your own lotus-feet upon my head.
Nārada said:
Having heard their words, the son of Haridatta spoke.
The twice-born one said:
Having made [these] holy bathing places, I, a Brāhmaṇa, have arrived. 22.
"What do you ladies now desire from Puṣkara?
Therefore, let it be requested; if I am able to give it, then I shall grant it. (23)
The Rākṣasīs said:
"O best of Brahmins, tell us of those holy fords where you have bathed;
let all those meritorious places liberate us from this base birth."
[Protect us] from this [world], which bestows the most intense suffering through thirst and hunger.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Previously, from this hermitage, I went from here to Haripurī;
from there, having bathed in the waters born of Soma at Dvārakā, I departed.
Then I reached the sacred ford named Prabhāsa, situated on the shore of the ocean; there, at that most purifying place where the bridge is bound, I bathed.
Therefore, I have come to this highly meritorious Kiṣkindhā, where Rāma slew Vālin, the lord of the monkey hosts, by means of a stratagem. ||27||
Therefore, I have come to this monastery situated on the banks of the Narmadā, where Sarasvatī, who is served by all, resides. (28)
Then, having bowed to that Veṇī at Āveśa in Dakṣiṇāpatha,
I beheld there the two cities of Śivakā and Viṣṇukā.
Since from the death of these two, a living being becomes Śiva and Viṣṇu, I have therefore come to Oḍhra, where Hari, the Lord, resides. (30)
The bestower of the four goals of human existence, he directly fulfills even the desires of his devotees;
having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites and having consumed what has been offered to him, [one attains the fruit]. //31//
Having reached that very confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, which is a source of grace,
he offered libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors there according to the prescribed rite.
I arrived at the place where the Gaṅgā becomes hundred-mouthed;
then, having gone to Gayā, I offered the funeral cakes according to the prescribed rite.
He offered to the ancestors flowers of tulasī, sandalwood paste, and water,
along with the Kośalā, Śarayū, and Vārikarṇadhāra rivers, using the wind as a vessel.
I arrived there, having purified all people by my very touch;
for there exists a sacred ford named Gopratāra, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (35)
There, I performed my duties such as bathing and other rites;
thereafter, I reached Kāśī, the capital city of the Lord of Umā.
Having bowed to the Lord Viśveśvara and to Viṇḍumādhava,
he bathed with devotion in Maṇikarṇikā and in the Jñānavāpī.
Having stayed there for three nights, I returned again to Prayāga on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, where Prajāpati himself is visibly present.
Having performed his ritual bath at dawn during the month of Māgha,
he returned once more from there to Naimiṣa on the bank of the Gomatī.
Where all sacred fords dwell by means of my own illusory power,
from there I reached Mathurā, where Viśrāntisaṃjñaka resides.
In its vicinity is that supreme and meritorious holy ford (tīrtha) named Asikuṇḍa, which contains the Kṛṣṇatīrtha, Gaṅgātīrtha, Dhruvatīrtha, Ākrūratīrtha, Keśitīrtha, and Kālītīrtha. 41.
There flows the Yamunā, a river of great merit that bestows all goals;
on both its banks stand twelve shrines of Śrī.
There are celestial beings who shine with splendor and accomplish all purposes;
having bathed in them and drunk [their waters], a man is not born again. 43.
From there, I came to the meritorious and supreme city of Hastināpura,
where the Ganges, the best of rivers, was born from the lotus feet of the Lord of Śrī.
Then, having come from the abode of Nārāyaṇa situated on the slopes of the Himavat mountains and having seen Mādhava, I arrived at Kedāra. 45.
Having worshipped Viśveśvara there and drunk the water once more,
I arrived at the highly meritorious Haridvāra on the bank of the Jāhnavī.
Having bathed there and offered libations to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages,
I arrived at Kurukṣetra, where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows.
There too, with my senses restrained, I performed all the prescribed rites after worshipping the lotus feet of the Lord of Śrī at Puṣkara.
But while I was traveling on the road, a friend of mine named Vimala met me as I was going home from the sacred site at Indraprastha. (49)
I was led back again to that place by that twice-born man,
to Śakraprastha, which bestows all desired objects and is renowned as a sacred ford (tīrtha).
There, the meritorious city of Dvārakā was personally created by Viṣṇu;
there, Viṣṇu himself was perceived through his speech, though not in physical form. (51)
There, having both bathed together, for the sake of attaining devotion to Viṣṇu, this [mālā] was given to me by Viṣṇu, who exists in the form of Kṛṣṇa; and it was given to him by me. (52)
Having heard Hari's speech there and having beheld his form, devotion was attained by me; from that place, I have come toward Puṣkara.
I shall now describe this meritorious water of the lord of holy places named Dvārakā, which was contained within his water-pot and belongs to the night-wanderer (Niśācarī).
I have been questioned by you, and that which was asked has thus been explained;
seeing this wretched condition of yours, compassion arises in my heart. (55)
"Tell me, what shall I do today? For I am under your command.
"May you possess knowledge," he said, and he sprinkled them with ashes. (56)
By the touch of that water, they all remembered their births and deeds and cast off their formidable demonic bodies.
Having reached a celestial chariot that had descended from the seventh heaven,
they ascended it and, having become Apsarases, bowed down before the twice-born sage.
And they said, "O best of the twice-born, through contact with the waters of Dvārakā, we have been released from our state as Rākṣasas; we are now going to the abode of the gods. (59)
O twice-born one, this Dvārakā, situated within Indraprastha, has come;
there is no other holy place in the world superior to this which bestows all desired objects. (60)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, O lord of the earth, they ascended their celestial chariots and departed toward the eastern direction,
by the command given by that twice-born sage.
O Lord of the Earth, by hearing this greatness of Dvārakā situated on the banks of the Yamunā, a person is liberated from sins.
The fruit that arises from hearing this *Mahimnaḥ-stotra* is equal to that which results from feeding a hundred Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas according to their desires. ||63||
O King, just as the senses find perfect happiness in the worship of Govinda,
so too do they find it through hearing the greatness of this Dvārakā.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving twenty palas of gold during a solar eclipse,
that same fruit is attained by one who hears this greatness.
Having heard of Vimala’s attainment of a son, one obtains a son here; and having heard of his friend’s attainment of devotion, supreme devotion is obtained. (66)
He who hears this liberation of the Rākṣasīs endowed with faith,
O best of men, goes by means of a celestial chariot to the abode of the gods.

The greatness of Dvārakā, the best of cities, which is served by the people of the three worlds and situated at Śakratīrtha, has been described as being like the majesty of the most excellent of kings.
What further, most meritorious thing shall I describe before you? For one who speaks must indeed avoid delay in his own spiritual welfare. 68.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Dvārakā," in the *Kālindī-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The two hundred and ninth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Saubhari, what is the greatness of this single tīrtha? [Tell me] the sage Nārada..."
And he described [the glory] of Śakra’s Tīrtha to Śibi, who had gone there. ||1||
Therefore, O foremost of sages, my failure to listen has arisen;
please tell me the meritorious dialogue between Śibi and Nārada, for I am bowed before you.
Saubhari said:
Having heard the majesty of Dvārakā as described by Nārada, King Śibi, the lord of the Śibis, questioned him with great reverence.
Śibi said:
O Brahmā, O best of the Gajasuras, I have heard the supreme and wonderful majesty of Dvārakā situated on the banks of Indraprastha.
Tell me whatever sacred account of the sage Yati exists in Ayodhyā; for me, who am parched with thirst, your words are nectar.
Nārada said:
There exists a meritorious account that destroys even great sins—the story of that barber and that brāhmaṇa Mukunda. 6.
O King, although that twice-born man had committed the murder of a Brahmin and met an untimely death,
both he and his father attained the celestial realm through the grace of Kośalā.
On the bank of the river Candrabhāgā, there was a settlement called Purīśāka; there lived a wicked and despicable barber named Caṇḍaka.
He is a doer of evil who steals the wealth of others by theft;
he is a slayer who kills travelers with weapons, nooses, and the like, and a plunderer of wayfarers. ||9||
Constantly addicted to gambling and intoxicants, with senses agitated by another's wife, he broke through the wall of a temple and sold bricks and stones. (10)
O King, there lived in a place near Satasṛṣṭi a Brāhmaṇa endowed with prosperity, who was devoted to the duties of Brahman and named Mukunda. (11)
Once, having embraced his own young wife,
Goniśin slept fearlessly, her body relaxed from the exhaustion of amorous play.
Then, at the dead of night, he entered that residence together with Caṇḍako,
in order to seize whatever ornaments and articles were on the palace belonging to Mukunda.
Having taken that which was situated outside the guest-house, he went to his own cave;
and then he entered again the house of that brahmin.
Desiring to tear open the door-panel, he exerted himself with great effort;
yet, being obstructed by the iron bolt, he was unable to open it. (15)
Then he ascended and entered the house of that brahmin;
having entered that house, the cruel man placed his hand upon the wretched man.
The most wicked barber, acting like a thief, saw there in the tower his two husbands fast asleep and extremely distressed. (17)
Desiring to seize the golden ornaments from the two of them, he went to their side;
taking many ornaments situated on one part of the bed, [he departed].
Having gone there with the intent to seize it, that barber lunged forward; at the touch of the thief, the brahmin woke up, overcome by fear. (19)
When that wicked thief, having seized his bodily ornaments, stood there with his eyes closed as if saying nothing at all; ||20||
Seized by his two arms by the wind-god Vāyu, he was shaken;
then, unable to endure the destruction of his wealth, he returned from behind.
By that very sword of the king-thief, the twice-born man was struck; with the middle of his belly ripped open, he uttered the words, "O father! O mother! (22).
"What is this? What is this? saying thus, the people approached his side;
they saw him with his armor fallen away and his body smeared with blood.
They asked Camukuṇḍa, "By what deed was such a thing done?
And he, with great difficulty, spoke this to his own kinsmen: ||24||
Mukunda said:
"This is indeed the ripening of my own previously accumulated karmas; there is no one at all who bestows pleasure or pain upon any embodied being."
"Dharma and adharma are indeed the roots of those two [results] from past deeds.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, he was deeply afflicted by a great burden of sorrow.
Then, while his friends were looking on, O King, that lord of the earth gave up his life-breaths; at that time, O King, his mother, a virtuous brahmin woman, lamented for him.
With his head resting upon his own arms adorned with beautiful earrings, his mother said:
"Alas! I am ruined by you, who have departed from me while still in your youth."

O high-minded one, just as the beauty of day perishes with the sun upon its setting behind the western mountain, so too is this body of yours no longer fit for the application of sandalwood paste. (29)
Drown me in this ocean of pain and grief, which is grey with the dust of heaven.

That very practice of chewing betel which was formerly established by you will surely now be performed with a mixture of vomited blood; for those two eyes of yours once conquered the beauty of the lotus.
Therefore, now that you have arisen like one who has emerged from being shrouded by a mass of darkness, arise, O virtuous one, and teach your own disciples! 32.
Just as one honors a guest who has arrived at a Vaiśvadeva sacrifice,
so do those friends of yours standing at the door call out to you, urging you to come forward.
"Whatever is to be given, give it to them; whatever is to be taken, take it. Alas! Alas! Come! Give an answer! Fall at your feet! [34]
Otherwise, I shall give up my life in your presence.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, Mukuṇda’s mother then fainted.
His wife, placing her head upon her own lap, lamented aloud.
The wife said:
"O Ocean, listen to my words through this path of names. (36)
If you were angry, why did you not speak equally before your mother? Never before have you observed such silence toward the wicked;
surely some insignificant brother has insulted you.
"This parrot is old and eats food only with you;
feed him well-prepared food, as well as this sweet-voiced sārikā bird. (38)
"Rāma, Rāma, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu"—reciting this string of names, these two clever birds, a myna and a parrot, rose up. (39)
"What offense have I committed against you, that you do not speak to me?"
"That which was given by you, O Ameghananda, was not properly protected by me. ||40||
I shall not neglect the time for the delivery of that child which you, O Lord, have entrusted into my womb; I shall follow you. 41.
Nārada said:
Having lamented thus, that chaste woman, with her mind following her husband who was dearer than life, wept for Mukuṇḍa. 42.
Then, O King, his preceptor named Vedāyana,
who was a wandering ascetic (saṃnyāsī), arrived at his house while traveling across the earth.
"Where has his mother gone, and where is the wife of that wise man?
She is not to be seen," he asked, and then the maidservant replied.
The maidservant said: "O Master, by some thief my master was slain at night;
the daughter-in-law's ornaments and all her silk garments have been taken away. (45)
Having fallen from the top of the palace, he lay dead upon the ground;
his mother, his wife, and his brothers stood near him.
"O Guru, fallen into an ocean of great sorrow, we lament.
Nārada said: Having heard these words spoken by the maidservant, the wandering mendicant (parivrāj) spoke.
Having ascended the palace roof, he saw his own attendant lying dead;
beholding him close by, he lamented intensely before his kinsmen.
Intending to rescue them from this ocean of grief, the wise one spoke to them.
Vedāyana said:
"Is this grief being felt by you on account of the body or on account of the self? (49)
"O Mother, tell me the truth: is this body suitable for both of us?
This body is a mere collection of elements, acquired through the force of past karma. (50)
When those [elements] have been exhausted, a state of distinctness arises among beings;
that which is their becoming one again through their actions is the birth of men.
The separation resulting from that destruction is known as death; for this reason, the wise understand the separation of the elements to be dependent upon karma. (52)
Therefore, one should not feel grief for this body, which is insentient and dependent on others;
for birth and death are seen to occur through beginningless ignorance.
Because of the false notion of "I" regarding the body as the self, you do not perceive that [Brahman] there;
when that [notion] ceases, that Brahman is revealed, which is pure and devoid of form.

Self-luminous, the cause of the world yet transcending all causes, exalted by its qualities, eternal, and consciousness—He who, through the light of His own blissful nature, illumines the universe. (55)
The eye does not lick with the tongue, nor does it see; the ear does not hear, nor does the nose smell; the skin never touches at any time.
That which is past the senses, self-luminous, and the vision of the Self, is not an object [of the senses], is remote from the mind, and is not even within the range of the intellect. (57)
The deities who are beings of pure essence worship his forms of descent;
yet they do not know that form which is beyond both being and non-being.
Thus, since the self is of such a nature, the fool who directs anger toward it generates anger that neither arises nor ceases. (59)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Kālindī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||209||
Chapter Two Hundred and Tenth.
Nārada said: Having thus awakened them all with words concerning the ultimate truth, [he spoke].
He caused that sacrifice to be performed; its constituent rites were produced from his own self.
A young woman, persistently urging her husband— who was already with child—
to take another wife, was restrained by that wise man.
O King, his brother took those bones and went together with that ascetic to cast them into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
O King, after these two renunciants had spent several days there,
they reached Indraprastha by way of the caravan and dwelt in that holy place.
O King of Kosala, this [city] situated within Indraprastha is Ayodhyā;
here, at the end of the night, we slept upon the ground on the bank of the Yamunā.
In the space between the two of them,
the other [the corpse] had reached a state of deep sleep, its bones and skin shriveled by the exhaustion of the journey.
Then, at midnight, while the people of the caravan were fast asleep, a certain dog arrived there with the desire to steal cooked food and other provisions.
He wandered throughout the entire camp, repeatedly sniffing at the cooking stations; licking the vessels with his head, he sometimes endured blows from sticks.
Struck on the head by someone, he fled from there without making a sound,
powerless like a man conquered by his own wife.
Where he had been scratched by dogs, sticks, stones, bricks, and the like,
he entered there again out of a desire for food and drink.
Just as a destitute person, out of a desire for enjoyment, remains attached to a courtesan,
so too does he wander here even though both his parents are sleeping there.
From between the two of them, a dog snatched away the cloth bundle; having carried that cloth bundle some distance on his teeth, he dropped it. (12)
Having torn open her bones and observed that they were devoid of flesh,
he cast them into the midst of the waters of this Kośalā.
O King, as soon as those bones were cast into the water by that arrow, they became like this.
Mounting a divine celestial chariot, Mukunda has arrived here.

O King, seeing that his elder brother and younger brother were asleep, he of divine form then gently awakened them; having paid homage to his elder brother (Guru) and his father (Ru), he spoke these words. (15)
Mukunda said:
