"O preceptor Vedāyana, salutations to you; O younger brother, may blessings be upon you.
By your grace, my bones have indeed fallen here into this sacred ford."
Having encountered death and reached that fruit which is hell, it is by the grace of this sacred ford that this divine state has been attained by me. (17)
I have come here to pay homage to you, my guru, who are like a sacred ford;
for I am departing by means of a divine celestial chariot for the abode of the gods.
"You have been saluted by me; this is the sight of the sacred ford along with Śiva. You have been seen; grant me leave, for I am going to heaven, the source of happiness. (19)
Nārada said: Having heard these words of his, Vedāyana, the preceptor of Mukunda,
then spoke to him as he sat in the celestial chariot, his own wonder having vanished.
Devāyana said:
"O Mukunda, tell me truly: having obtained death, where have you gone?
To which world have you gone, dear one, that you now go to heaven?"
"What occurred there, O dear one? Who was the lord of that world? What was the nature of the subjects, and what was the dharma there? Tell me all of it. (22)
Mukunda said: "O Guru, I shall relate to you what occurred after my death;
by the grace of this sacred ford (tīrtha), memory has now arisen within me. (23)
When I was struck down by that wicked barber Caṇḍaka,
the servants of Yama, most terrible to behold, arrived there.
Their hair was reddish-brown, their bodies, nails, and lips were dark, their feet were sometimes short and sometimes long, and their noses were small. ||25||
"Let him be led, let him be led away by the command of the King of Dharma to the city of Saṃyamanī"—thus did they speak to one another. (26)
Having spoken thus, they cast him with great fury into the ground of torment,
bound him with cruel nooses, and struck him with iron hammers.
As I was being led by them along that path of scorching sand, I wept, afflicted by intense suffering; and I was struck again and again by them. (28)
"Having made it certain, they will surely revile me greatly.
The messengers of Yama said:
"Because you have not violated your teacher while speaking with unwavering firmness regarding Brahman," (29)
"What are you doing? This dreadful face of yours must be seen; you shall have to experience the terrible fruit of that evil deed. (30)
"By that very sin, O sinner, you have met with untimely death," he said, and in a moment, [he transported] me to a place many yojanas away.
They led him to the city of Saṃyamanī, where King Yama himself resides;
having bowed before the King of Dharma, they established him at the very front.
"O sinful ones, this brahmin has been brought here";
having seen me, Dharmarāja then spoke to the members of his assembly. (33)
Yama said:
"O sages, listen with great concentration to my words regarding the authority in which I have been appointed by Brahmā. (34)
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said to him, "No.
Brahmā said:
"You shall be the punisher of unrighteous men, the lord of Yama. (35)

O son of Caṇḍakara, inflict punishment upon those who commit the highest crimes: he who, though capable, does not support his parents, and he who is ungrateful toward his guru—these two are great sinners who must be cast into the hells. (36)
For all of them, up to ten thousand years for each;
you must never act toward these two in such a way that they become angry. (37)
Yama said:
"O members of the assembly, because of these words of Brahmā, I do not perform the funeral rites for that man who betrays his own guru, nor for one who fails to support his parents. (38)
"This Brahmin is a traitor to his guru; because of that treachery, he has met with an untimely death.
By my command, he has been brought here by my servants, though he is unfit to be seen. (39)
"O servants! First, let him be cast into the terrible Aurava hell for ten thousand years;
and having been extracted from there, let him be cast again into whichever [hell] he ought to be cast. (40)
At that very time, this sinful man was a violator of his guru's bed.
In all the hells, he remains for as long as time permits, moving swiftly. ||41||
Mukunda said:
"O Master, O Teacher of Vedāyana, by your command, these servants of mine seized me,
bound me with nooses, and cast me down into the terrible Raurava hell."
There, O dear one, I obtained that most heavy and exceedingly terrible [vision],
such that a certain moment was then passed by me as if it were an eon.
For thirty days I endured that suffering while staying there;
indeed, on this thirty-first day, I have now emerged. (44)
When fragments of bone fell into this most excellent of sacred fords, the sin arising from the transgression against my guru was instantly destroyed for me. (45)
By the grace of this sacred ford (tīrtha), the state of heaven has been attained by me;
I shall dwell happily in heaven for as long as the fourteen Indras endure. 46.
Those women who dwell in that city of Yama are indeed terrifying to sinners, yet enchanting to the righteous. (47)
They have the faces of lions, elephants, and boars, with large fangs and protruding bellies;
they have the faces of cats, tawny hair, are passionate, and possess long, excellent arms. 48.
When I became free from sin through the grace of this sacred ford (tīrtha),
then my subjects were seen by me in my abode as possessing divine forms.
All of them were speakers of truth, endowed with disciplined conduct,
wearing divine ornaments and adorned with celestial garments.
O sinless father, I have thus related all that I was asked by you;
now grant me permission to depart for the city of the Lord of the Immortals.
Nārada said: O King,
having heard those words spoken by his disciple,
that virtuous ascetic again questioned the twice-born Mukuṇḍa.
Vedāyana said:
"From my childhood until now, you have studied everything from me—the entire Veda along with the science of grammar (śabdaśāstra), including the padapāṭha and kramapāṭha. (53)
By virtue of your service to me, which was performed without any sense of "mine," you have become most excellent;
O virtuous one, the qualities of the wise, such as tranquility and self-restraint, reside in you. (54)
How did the sin committed by violating the guru arise for them? O father, tell me this so that I may understand it according to reality. (55)
Mukunda said: "I have disobeyed the command of the creator of births, the sacred thread, and daughters, as well as the giver of the sacrificial thread, and of the Vedas. (56)
Service to my mother-in-law and father-in-law was performed by me like that of a servant;
yet, even toward you, the giver of the scriptures, I have committed the offense of disregarding your command. (57)
The family preceptor, the royal priest, is one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta;
you ought to hear from me what offense he has committed against him. (58)
"If a son is born in our family who is skilled in the Dharma, then we shall give a single cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to that priest. (59)
"Having given [it], it is cut off; 'this is not enough'—such is the state of desire.
Long ago, on an auspicious day, as soon as my son was born," (60)
Because of my deluded intellect, I failed to perform the family rites prescribed in the Āgamas;
by that very omission, I became a transgressor against my guru. (61)
I have related all this to you exactly as it happened regarding my transgression against my guru; may you grant me permission for the sin that has occurred, so that I may go to the abode of the gods.
Vedāyana said:
"This auspicious Kośalā, situated within Indraprastha, reveals through its grace the memory of their previous birth. (63)
"O sinless one, by what merit have these bones fallen into this sacred ford? Tell me the name of that [place], for you possess the memory of it. (64)
Muka said:
"Once, a certain Brāhmaṇa came to my house in the evening;
I gave him a place to stay and food according to the prescribed rites. (65)
Having eaten according to his desire, he slept upon an auspicious bed;
at midnight, a most terrible fever seized his entire body.
Afflicted by that [poison], the virtuous twice-born man obtained a sleep like that of a cow;
as death approached, he gave up his life-breaths at the very break of dawn.
O Guru, the rites of cremation and so forth were performed for him by me;
his bones were cast into the Ganges according to the prescribed ritual. (68)
Due to that lack of merit, his bones fell in this auspicious place, at this sacred ford (tīrtha) named Kośala, which was established by the god Brahmā. 69.
Nārada said:
O King, that virtuous twice-born man, having recounted his own life story, immediately departed by means of a celestial vehicle to the heavenly garden, which is so beautiful it captivates the gods.
Although he had not mentioned that he was destined to meet death at the hands of a thief, he attained heaven through the grace of this king of sacred fords (Prayāga).

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter [210], titled "The Narrative of Mukundā," within the "Greatness of the Kālindī" section of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The two hundred and eleventh chapter.
Nārada said:
O Śivā, I have related before you this entire, supreme narrative known as Muka.
And it was also told by Caṇḍaka; listen to that as well.
On that day, O King, the Brahmin Mukunda was killed by Caṇḍaka; at that time, the citizens heard of this event.
Having heard this, they reported it clearly before the king.
The citizens said:
"O King, the excellent brāhmaṇa Mukunda has been killed by Caṇḍaka. (3)
That vast wealth has been led away; whatever is appropriate, let that be done.
For you are the protector and the punisher of the wicked for us, your subjects. (4)
Nārada said:
Having heard this, the king, his eyes reddened with anger, spoke to the minister standing at his side: "Listen to what is being said by these men! (5)
"Bring that sinner here quickly; otherwise, I shall have you executed! Arise, arise, O most wicked one! Let justice be done for the virtuous! (6)
If the subjects in a king's realm are oppressed by fierce robbers, that king goes to hell; yet he goes there even more so if he fails to protect them from those very robbers.
Nārada said: Having heard these words of the king, that minister, together with Śiva, mounted his horse with speed, accompanied by a hundred foot soldiers, O King.
She asked the relatives of that Mukunda who were in the house: "By whom was Mukunda killed? Tell me the truth before me. (9)
"I shall destroy that wicked one by the command of the king.
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of the minister, the kinsmen of the Brahmin replied. (10)
The Brahmin kinsmen said:
"O minister, this turban of that Mukuṇḍa, who was struck down by Caṇḍaka and fled away, has indeed fallen here. (11)
He who is seen with one's own eyes on the path is indeed the bringer of happiness.
What can we do, having been submerged by that evil in an ocean of grief?
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of his kinsmen and that brahmin, the king,
together with his minister, went to the house of that sinner as well.
Having quickly dismounted from his horse, he entered that house himself;
there, together with a few foot soldiers, he saw him lying down.
Commanded by him, the servants immediately dragged that wicked and lowest of barbers by his hair and raised him up from the couch. (15)
"What? What?"—thus lamenting, he opened his eyes;
just then, that wicked barber was seen standing right before him. (16)
Remembering that sin he had committed during the night of his own karma,
he stood for a moment with his face cast down, beholding Yama stationed at the tip of his nose.
Having caused him to be seized by his own wicked soldiers, the minister led him to the presence of the king and spoke thus to the monarch: (18)
"O King, this Chandaka the barber, the slayer of a Brahmin, has been brought here;
whatever you command, O Master, I shall perform it with speed. (19)
The king said:
"O long-lived one, listen to my words, O best of ministers who are learned in dharma. This is the Candrabhāgā, the most excellent of rivers, whose waters are stainless. (20)
Those who give up their lives here attain the auspicious abode of the gods;
therefore, this sinful soul should not be shaven here. (21)
If this slayer of a Brahmin should go even a short distance outside of these boundaries, he shall without delay go to the terrible hells.
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by the king, O monarch, that best of ministers dispatched the outcastes (śvapacas) to kill him by the king's command. (23)
The Śvapacas, having raised him up on the opposite bank of the Candrabhāgā,
severed his head from a stretch of ground two yojanas in extent.
In the land of Aparānta, the sinful one became a serpent with a terrifying form;
dwelling within the hollow of a tree trunk, his face was formidable with the flames of poison. ||25||
By the fire of his breath, the dry and withered tree was consumed,
just as a lake is dried up by the heat of the sun.
Because of his departure, that evil [place] became a desert at the roots of all its trees;
the various kinds of grass and other growth were cut away, and it then became unfavorable for cattle.
O King, on one occasion a caravan arrived there from the southern region,
traveling toward the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa known as Badarī.
There, a certain Brahmin joined a caravan on the road.
[He saw] a wooden vessel, free from cracks, joined with the bones of his father and mother. ||29||
O King, O highly fortunate one, the Ganges, who fulfills the desires even of sinners, descended to cause those who had transgressed to fall [into her waters]. 30.
He too arrived there in that forest where a serpent was present;
he cast away his secluded gaze upon a needle made of iron, which was being held in the hand.
Then, having arrived, that serpent joined its hood to the handle of the ladle;
as soon as the vessel was slightly opened, it entered inside.
Then, having returned to his own place among the voting sticks, he stood there motionless like a snake with its coils, full of virulent poison within its mouth.
Then at dawn, O King, they all departed from that place;
and that Brāhmaṇa also went toward Mañjuṣā, which was surrounded by an army.
Having placed the crest-jewel upon his head, O lord of kings, he set out toward the Ganges;
after some days, the caravan of those traveling to the holy ford arrived.
Right here in Kośalā, O lord of the earth, in Vaipulyanītā, a certain Brahmin, afflicted by the cold, then summoned his inner strength. (36)
On that auspicious bank of Ayodhyā, Jūṣāvaraṇa was shining;
there, that serpent, having obtained the wind as his food, remained without any other sustenance.
Having lifted up a fine stick, he went out from there;
and seeing him emerged, [the other] cried out "A snake! A snake! in anger. (38)
As all the people, shouting and with clods of earth in their hands, rushed forward,
the snake was struck down by one man just as it was fleeing.
Then, while those going to the holy ford were looking on, he gave up his life-breaths;
having abandoned his body along with his arm, he attained the state of divinity so difficult to achieve.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, the serpent spoke these words to the people here: The serpent said:
"O Brāhmaṇas of the South, listen to my words. (41)
Formerly, I was a barber named Caṇḍaka, the lowest of men and a slayer of a Brahmin;
due to the sin of killing a Brahmin, I became a serpent in a desert region.
Having experienced the sufferings of hell for five hundred thousand years,
he passed two ten-thousand-year periods in the womb of a serpent.
By the grace of this sacred ford (tīrtha), supreme divinity has been attained.
Therefore, this ford named Vaikośala should not be abandoned, for it bestows all goals; through it, even heaven was reached by me, though I am a sinner.
Nārada said: Thus instructed by his barber, that sinner, having attained a birth unknown [to him],
went today to heaven seated in a celestial chariot, by the grace of this sacred ford.
Having become like those from the south (Dakṣiṇātyas) in their conduct, they lived there among the heretics, having beheld the majesty of the lotus feet of Govinda within their own minds. 46.
Having witnessed the majesty of this sacred ford, that best of Brahmins conceived faith in it and cast his parents’ bones into the tīrtha.
As soon as the fragments of his bones had fallen, his two parents,
having become divine, arrived there mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot.
And they both spoke to their own son while the people were indeed listening:
"O child, live long in this world; may you be possessed of wealth, grain, and happiness. (49)
"By granting us liberation, you shall indeed attain liberation; this is not false.

Whatever fruit may arise from the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the Gaṅgā, and whatever destination is attained by the ancestors through that—both of these shall result from the falling of our bones here. (50)

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Narration of Mukunda," in the *Kālindīmāhātmya* of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, within the *Śrī-Pādma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The two hundred and twelfth chapter.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the parents of that brahmin appeared in divine forms.
Having ascended the excellent celestial chariot, they went to the city of Śiva.
Their son, however, having stayed there in Ayodhyā for three days,
departed for his own home, reflecting upon the majesty of the sacred sites.
O King of Kośala, this alone is what should be told to you by the wise;
I shall relate it to you, whose mind is eager to hear.
The forest-dwellers of the south, desiring to die, remained in that [forest];
let them perish in Kośalā, which bestows wealth upon those who are capable. (4)
Then, one among them, disregarding his skill in archery,
set out for the abode of Nārāyaṇa, but was stopped on the path by Viṣṇu.
And it was spoken to the twice-born one in the form of an old brāhmaṇa.
The old brāhmaṇa said: "O best of brāhmaṇas, where are you going, having abandoned this auspicious Kośalā?"
O twice-born one, this sacred site of Indraprastha is the most excellent of all sacred sites.
Wherein this Kośalā exists, which bestows liberation and is beloved by Viṣṇu, through her son. ||7||
Wherever you go, having abandoned her who bestows the state free from desire, there no success shall be yours; Viṣṇu will turn his face away from you.
If you desire liberation, O Vipra, take up renunciation at the Tīrtha;
it will grant whatever group [of desires] one has wished for upon bathing there. (9)
Even though they had strayed beyond the range of her vision, they attained the state of gods;
by her grace, the two brahmin husbands were liberated and established in heaven.
Even though you have developed confidence through this vision of his majesty, why do you abandon her now that you have obtained her through the dawning of good fortune? (11)
Just as someone afflicted by thirst, having found an ocean of nectar, might abandon it and go toward a leather bag—so too are you seen to be deluded in your vision. 12.
Just as someone, deluded, might throw a wish-fulfilling gem into a well, yet its movement is seen even while it remains in his hand—such is your movement. (13)
Just as some person of dull intellect, having propitiated Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, might beg for the mere trifling pleasure of the senses—such is your course. (14)
Having abandoned this treasury of the method, which bestows all goals, there is no attainment of heaven for one who has bathed here, nor is there the state of immortality for one who has died. (15)
Nārada said: O King, having heard these words of Hari, who upholds the welfare of the twice-born, that brāhmaṇa spoke to the best of brāhmaṇas regarding Badarikāśrama.
The Brahmin said: "O best of Brahmins, by your trustworthy words, the former glory of my small village has been brought to light for me, who have now heard it. (17)
"I have never heard of this sacred site, Indraprastha. O elder, how could Kośalā be situated within it? (18)
O twice-born one, how can one not praise that hermitage where Nārāyaṇa himself is present and where yogis, having attained liberation, remain? 19.
"Just as Viṣṇu himself would have restrained me by saying that there is no other destination [for me], so too, O twice-born one, this Indraprastha is a sacred field superior even to Badarī. (20)
Therefore, even if that hermitage were shaken, I would not leave it;
for one who desires liberation does not depart from his own dwelling, just as I remain here.
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by that brāhmaṇa, Hari appeared with four arms, casting off his ordinary form and assuming a divine appearance. 22.
He spoke to that illustrious twice-born man who was desirous of liberation.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Brahmin, this Indraprastha is the most excellent among all the best of holy places."
He was like Śambhu among all those who know Brahman, and like the Gaṅgā among rivers.
He was like Himavat among mountains, like the king of birds among birds,
like Śakra among the gods, and like Nārada among the devotees of Viṣṇu.
He was like the sun among luminous bodies, like the ocean of milk among oceans, like the Brahmin among the social classes, and like the Grandfather (Brahmā) among all created beings. ||25||
Just as the son born of Kauśalyā was the most excellent among the sons of Viṣṇu, so too is this Śakraprastha the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas). 26.
Whether free from desire or possessing desire, a man may cross over at some sacred ford.
In each and every instance, I alone am indeed the bestower of the fruit for the entire self.
Having abandoned Ayodhyākośala, which lies within Indraprastha, a devotee who visits it obtains the fruit of a bath at Prayāga from the feet of the Giver of Boons. 28.
Nārada said: Having thus heard those words and beheld that supreme form,
the twice-born sage prostrated before the Lord of Ramā and returned to her very presence.
The Lord, the all-pervading soul of the universe, entered into him;
and that Brahmin was honored by Him with that very disposition, as he was pointed out as the true reality.
Having arrived there in Kośalā, O lord of men,
that brahmin related the entire account to all his own companions.
Having heard this from that illustrious southerner, the twice-born ones undertook a fast unto death upon her and abandoned their ordinary bodies.
Then, mounted upon Garuḍa, he approached Śrī Viṣṇu together with his own attendants in as many celestial chariots, all radiant with brilliance.
Seeing him approaching with his retinue in a celestial chariot,
she fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff, her body possessing a divine form.
All the twice-born ones, possessing bodies of divine knowledge, praised him who was of divine form, the god of gods, whose feet are the source of the Vedas. (35)
The Brāhmaṇas said:

Salutations to You, who bear a body with a luster like the *atasī* flower, clothed in yellow garments; to You whose ears are adorned with shimmering earrings set with various gems, and whose long, pervasive dark hair is bound in a topknot. (36)

Devotion to you is indeed like a wish-fulfilling creeper; it grants whatever is desired by the mind. O Lord, just as that [creeper] is obtained through the skill of its cultivation, so too is this [devotion] attained through your grace. 37.

Oṃ! This lotus-foot of the Giver of Boons, which is worshipped by hosts of lords such as Śiva, and which is meditated upon in the hearts of multitudes of yogis—[it is the cause] of that supreme bliss, liberation, from which there is no returning. (38)
O Lord of Śrī, we have indeed attained Your own form, characterized by beautiful marks such as the Śrīvatsa;
nevertheless, we desire Your state of servitude, which is honored by all, including Nārada and others. (39)
O Lord of Śrī, that bliss which belongs to those who have attained the state of Your servants is not possessed by us, even though Lakṣmī dwells within our chests;
O Maheśa, no one else in the world knows it, nor has anyone else experienced it.
O Lord of Śrī, even among us, Your dispassionate servants, he is not to be honored;
therefore, the great sages such as Nārada and others worship the Lord of the World through those who have attained devotion to You. 41.
Granted that the inner self transcends the bliss of Brahmā, yet Śambhu attains satisfaction through service to you;
intent on your devotion and absorbed in you, he dances aloud again and again to grasp your virtues.
For this reason, those embodied beings who have attained servitude to you are not subject to the waves of worldly existence;
they reach that very abode which belongs to the two gatekeepers of Gauda, who bear your marks, though they do so through delusion. 43.
Because you can appear within this very world at will, no sudden arrival from another world is required;
who could understand your power of illusion here, which is difficult even for gods such as Brahmā and Śiva to comprehend? (44)
Nārada said:
Thus being praised by them, the Lord, intent upon returning to his own abode, spoke to those southerners with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O twice-born ones, by the grace of this Kośalā,
you shall attain even my own form (sārūpya) and you shall become my servants."
O Brahmins, from this day forward, this unsurpassed sacred site shall be widely renowned by the name Dakṣiṇakośalā. ||47||
There, having become the son of Daśaratha, he shall slay the ten-headed Rāvaṇa;
that land is called Uttarakośalā by all the best of sages. 48.
Even one who has failed [in other duties] but possesses knowledge ascends to Vaikuṇṭha;
and even he who dwells here without that [knowledge] goes to heaven.
They say that this Dakṣiṇakośalā possesses ten qualities;
some lords of sages correctly declare it to possess eleven qualities. (50)
There is only this much difference between her and me:
my hosts of attendants lead those who have died in her to Vaikuṇṭha. (51)
When he has died in this [state], I myself shall place him, whose mind is focused on no other,
upon Garuḍa and, having granted him the state of being of like form (sārūpya), lead him there.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to those twice-born ones and having led them away, Viṣṇu departed for Vaikuṇṭha,
O King, while himself praising the majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha).
All this cause has been told to you, O Lord of the Earth, by which this land here is called Dakṣiṇa-Kośalā by the wise. (54)
The destroyer of the lineage of the impurities of the Kali age, who has severed the desires of those men who hear [his name] by means of attaining the lotus-eyed one’s feet—
the majesty of you, the best of kings, has been described in Kośalā.
I shall relate to you the account of what occurred in Madhuvana as you listen.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Kośalā," in the Kālindī-māhātmya of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
[213] Chapter Two Hundred and Thirteen. Nārada said:
O dear one, this supremely purifying Madhuvana is auspicious;
it is here that the city was established by Viṣṇu, who was pleased with the King of the Gods.
This sacred ford named Viśrānti is the most excellent in the three worlds;
it bestows liberation upon those who know it, purifies men, and is frequented by the virtuous.
Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, eternally dwells here in the form of the auspicious boar at this most excellent and meritorious holy site, O King, which is known as Viśrāntisaṃjñaka.
O King, for one by whom Viṣṇu has been constantly propitiated throughout many births, death indeed occurs at this sacred ford (tīrtha). ||4||
On the very bank of the Kālindī, Hari performed his second [act];
at the holy site known as Viśrānti, Kaṃsa was struck down.
O King, these two are equal in their qualities that bestow Vaikuṇṭha;
through some rise of fortune, they are obtained, granting all desired objects.
Now, I shall describe before you the greatness of Athīrtha;
having heard which, you will obtain the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O King, in a beautiful city of the Kirātas at the foot of the Himalayas,
there lived a Brahmin named Kuśala who was destitute.
His wife was ill-behaved and devoted to men of wicked conduct; that most unchaste woman deluded her husband with her actions. (9)
Deluded by her, the husband was unable to restrain himself; intent on obeying her command, he became wretched, as if purchased for a price.
The people used to bring that twice-born man, the husband of an unchaste woman, before them;
out of fear of ridicule, that foolish man would even flee from his own house.
The evil-minded one took possession of costly fine silks and ornaments given by paramours; he did not feel shame even when laughed at.
A wicked woman who, out of contempt, gives her husband an old garment that has fallen from her body after she has emerged from the service of a slave. (13)
Thus, having been thus despised by that unchaste woman, her own husband fell into extreme misery and died from poison at night.
Then that wicked woman, acting out of her own will and driven by fear of the king, spoke a falsehood, saying: "I shall follow my husband. (15)
O Lord of the Earth, her friends, who had been thus instructed, approached her and restrained her, speaking as follows.
The friends said:
"O deer-eyed one, why do you bring about such misfortune for yourself, that you are intent on destroying this body of yours which resembles gold? (17)
"O friend, what happiness have you seen for this man who is industrious yet poor and powerless, and who can only fill his own belly? (18)
Protect this young son; who else but you is his protector? O beautiful one, we shall all die if you pass away.
Look upon this house; arise, O fair-faced one!
May this son of yours live long, bestowing happiness upon his wife. (20)
All your kinsmen desire your life;
arise and fulfill the heart's desire of your own relatives. (21)
O virtuous lady, all your friends are weeping out of affection for you;
console them with your own words so that they may be well-comforted. 22.
Nārada said:
Having heard those words of theirs, which were ill-spoken and contrary to dharma,
he raised his face and spoke, making his kinsmen hear him.
The female friend said:
"I know that the speech and dharma spoken by you are indeed true;
nevertheless, one's own husband must be honored by women, for he is the bestower of both worlds. (24)
O friends, listen to these words spoken by me, which are in accordance with the treatises on dharma; if they are reasonable, then approve them. (25)
That woman who, intent upon following her husband who has met his end, follows him—even if she is sinful—dwells for a long time in heaven together with him. (26)
A husband must not be abandoned by women, even if he is destitute or diseased;
he must be followed even if he is as good as dead while living—this is the eternal Vedic injunction.
Reflecting thus within her own mind, she said to her friends:
"He will live according to his own destiny; what indeed can I do for him? (28)
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by her friend, those wicked women who bestowed evil thoughts upon her spoke with words of righteousness to her, who was deluding all people. 29.
The friends said:
"O fair-browed one, first abandon us who are wretched; O beloved, go after him! We are all unable to endure the pain of separation from you. (30)
"O you who are devoted to me, why do you wish to follow those others and leave your own husband?
Dharma is minimal, while sin is abundant; what kind of heaven could there be [for such a one]? (31)
"This husband of mine lives; he has been well protected by you. O friend, whatever was said by the husband and wife, that has been carried out by you. (32)
As long as he is unable to provide for his own livelihood, so long shall your son live by means of your own good fortune. (33)
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus, she desisted from following her husband; then, by means of her son, she caused the funeral rites for him to be performed.
Then, after some time had passed, he caused his son's initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) to be performed by Brahmins, having given them wealth bestowed by the king. (35)
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, the young Kuṇḍa, possessing knowledge of the true reality,
departed from his home and immediately became devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Having attained the company of the virtuous and abandoned his own natural body,
he ascended to his own world, which is unattainable even by yogis.
Then, when her son had departed, she indeed experienced mental anguish; yet on that very same day, O King, she again took pleasure with her paramours.
Thus, O King, while she was being measured by them with her paramours,
she arrived at the time of old age, destroying her beauty and passion.
Abandoned by her lovers, her body seized by old age, she became another messenger, a destroyer of family and character. 40.
For at that time, O King, he had stolen a cow with its calf from a certain Brahmin; she had been sold for some small amount of wealth, and he had not yet paid her price. ||41||
O King, for some time he was sent by her as a messenger;
subsequently, his body became withered and devoid of its natural qualities.
O King, when leprosy arose in her, five parts of her body fell away: the two hands, the two feet, and then the nose as the fifth. (43)
When such a person does not obtain food from anywhere, he should then go to the marketplace with the intention of begging that has arisen in him. (44)
There, having implored the world-protectors with a piteous voice, reproaching herself for her fallen state and her sinful outlook, she filled her belly.
Then, O King, a certain twice-born man who was devoted to practice, a knower of the meaning of all the scriptures, and a great orator, beheld her and spoke these words. (46)
Sin brings suffering to people both in this world and in the next;
therefore, sin should not be committed by men who fear suffering. (47)
If a person, having committed a sin, indeed performs an act of expiation, he shall not practice that [sin] again, nor shall he obtain its fruit. 48.
He who, having committed this [sin], repeatedly performs this *siprā-prāyaścitta*, finds refuge from this very sin both in this world and in the next. 49.
By this [deed], a mass of evil has been accumulated by him in this world;
he experiences its fruit right here, and he shall also experience it in hell.
In all the scriptures, an expiation is indeed seen for all those who have committed evil deeds;
however, there is no expiation for women who turn their faces away from their duties.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, that best of the twice-born bowed to the Sun and departed,
repeatedly remembering Viṣṇu, remaining fearless because of his vision.
Thus, O King, having experienced the fruit of her own actions, she who had acquired it herself died after only a few days. ||53||
The cremation of that woman of evil deeds was performed;
having been dragged by her hair, she was brought out of the city by the *śvapacas*.
At the time of her death, these servants of his arrived;
having caused her to obtain a body of torment, they led her to the city of Bhāskara.
The god was gentle toward those of like dharma, yet manifest as Guhya to sinners;
however, due to her lack of vision, he once again became averse to her.
Yama himself, with his face turned away, commanded his servants: "Let her, together with him, be cast into the terrible Raurava hell. (57)
Having been addressed thus, those servants then brought her and cast her headlong down into the terrible Raurava hell, according to the karma she had committed.
Having remained there in that Raurava hell for the duration of one manvantara,
he was subsequently reborn as a lizard in a cremation ground, where he ate the flesh of the dead.
There too, for a hundred years, she experienced the suffering that is the fruit of her own karma, subsisting on a coarse diet of the flesh of the dead. (60)
Once, the son of the sage Ekadama, who had been born from her womb,
having entered the womb of a Brahmin, was wandering there in the cremation ground.
Beholding her being praised by the sons of sages as she devoured the flesh of the dead,
they meditated for a moment and realized in their own minds that she was their mother.
Having spoken thus to himself, the son of the sage addressed his own mother, who was in a state of delusion:
"I shall today deliver her from this difficult-to-cross ocean of suffering. (63)
A living being is called "ahona" (destitute) when, due to sinful karma acquired by oneself, there is no limit to the duration of its experience [of suffering]. (64)
The time known as the Nāraka-manvantara has passed for her;
and now, a hundred years have gone by there according to the reckoning of men.
"How much further must she endure this intense evil?
Nārada said:
Having reflected thus, he again meditated with his eyes closed through the power of his knowledge.
O King, having seen with his divine eye that terrible course of that sinful woman,
he once again assumed his own body along with his excellent Brahmin companions.
The son of the sage said: "Alas! Even in a hundred kalpas, no deliverance from this is seen, except for death at a sacred ford or taking refuge in the Lord of Ramā."
Or else, even by the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā on my behalf, she shall not attain a good rebirth even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (69)
Neither of these two pairs shall ever occur for her in this womb:
death in the vicinity of that sacred ford, and a lack of devotion to the Lord of Śrī during his service. (70)
For her who is submerged in an ocean of sin, the cause of her deliverance shall be the *vaihtraka* Śrāddha performed by me at Gayā. (71)
Nārada said:
Having reflected thus, that virtuous soul went to his father’s hermitage and related everything to his father regarding the cause of his mother’s grief.
Having heard his son’s words, which announced the mother’s suffering, the best of sages spoke to his son, who was bowing down in reverence. (73)
The sage said:
A king who knows the ways of policy should quickly rescue his own mother from misfortune,
just as one seeks the fortune of victory over an enemy in battle.
A son who rescues his own mother and father from suffering would go to hell, even if he were capable of saving them. (75)
Having obtained water from their own son at the excellent Tīrtha of Piṇḍāśca,
the ancestors go from hell to heaven, and from heaven to the abode of Hari.
Therefore, rise up quickly and go to the Khāṇḍava forest;
there lies the holy Yamunā, frequented by the best of sages.
On its bank is Astihariprastha, which contains all sacred fords;
there is the meritorious Madhuvana, established there by Viṣṇu himself.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rules and performed his own daily rites, he—
Aiming for her, they performed the śrāddha rite and carried out the funeral ceremonies for their own mother.
When you have performed the *śrāddha* ceremony there, desiring her to attain a good rebirth,
she shall abandon this formidable iguana body and reach the world of Hari.
O father, the merit that arises from the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā is said by the wise to be a hundred times greater when performed in Madhuvana. 81.
"Now, O dear one, the Sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo;
perform the śrāddha for your ancestors and kinsmen while the Sun is in the sign of Leo. (82)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter [213], titled "The Greatness of Kālindī," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
The two hundred and fourteenth chapter.
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of his father, he departed with great haste.
O King, the Madhuvana forest is meritorious, being a hundred times superior to Gayā. ||1||
Having invited the Brahmins residing at that holy site in the evening, the knower of mantras summoned them again at the proper time and spoke words of welcome.
Then, having washed his feet and honored him with perfumes and other offerings,
he affectionately gave him water for the feet (arghya) and sipped water himself.
Then, having led those brāhmaṇas to the place for the śrāddha,
he seated them together with kuśa grass, tulasī flowers, perfumes, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds.
Having filled the vessel for the ritual action, that twice-born man meditated upon the lotus-eyed Lord;
he recited three times the verse beginning with "devatābhyaḥ. (5)
Then, he should perform the binding with *satila* (sesame) and purified *kuśa* grass,
using the mantra beginning with "agniṣvātta," in sequence for the directions starting from the east.
With the mantra "rakṣobhūte," he tied his lower garment;
then, having made a solemn vow, he offered a seat of kuśa grass to the twice-born.
Then that best of Brahmins summoned the ancestors;
having offered them water for their hands (arghya), he turned the vessel face down.
Having offered perfumes and other gifts, and having again sipped water with the right hand,
the virtuous twice-born man should then give the vessels with both hands, right and left.
Permitted by those brahmins, he then performed the *agnaukaraṇa* rite;
O King, he filled those vessels with sacrificial offerings such as clarified butter and other oblations.
With his hands neither too low nor too high, holding the edge of his alms-bowl, he recited the *Pṛthvī* [verse] for the twice-born, having been taught it by the Brahmins. (11)
With the mantra "asaṃskṛtapraṇītānām," the virtuous twice-born man offered the seat of scattered food (vikiropana) upon the Darbha grass with its tips pointing toward the south.
With the mantra beginning "agnidagdhāḥ," he scattered food mixed with ghee along with water upon the seat prepared with kuśa grass for the king of kings.
Having sipped water again with the right hand, he offers a handful of water for life; then, having asked, "Are you satisfied?", they reply, "We are satisfied. (14)
Having received the permission of those twice-born ones to eat the remaining food, the brahmin prepared an altar measuring one span for the sake of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas). ||15||
O King, facing southward, she drew a line with a blade of darbha grass while reciting the mantra "ye rūpāṇi," and she placed a firebrand toward the direction of Agni.
O Lord of the Earth, those who were his mother and father in a previous birth, and their parents who were his paternal grandparents, O King—[all these were born as his sons]. (17)
O best of kings, he who, according to the prescribed rule, intends for his great-grandfather, as well as his two fathers, and the six ancestors beginning with the father, together with their wives—
Having provided auspicious seats and offered six morsels of food,
and having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform the dismissal of the Brahmins at midday.
Having smelled his left arm, he should place the alms-bowl down;
then, taking the water-vessel, he should recite "vāja vāje. (20)
Having again offered water for the feet and the respectful oblation (arghya), he gratified them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and other gifts;
then, having followed them as far as the gate and received their instructions, [he departed].
And he himself, O King, along with his kinsmen and six hundred twice-born ones, partook of the meal.
Thus, O Indra among kings, that best of virtuous twice-born men completed the śrāddha ceremony. (22)
When that self-controlled one departed from that auspicious Madhuvana tīrtha toward his father’s hermitage, he was accompanied by those who were previously connected to him.
Then all those who had eaten at the śrāddha met on the road;
mounted upon six celestial chariots and adorned with divine ornaments, wearing divine garments, O King, they spoke thus to that best of the twice-born: ||24||
The ancestors said:
"O child, O tiger among brahmins, choose an excellent boon!
By performing a śrāddha here at this sacred ford (tīrtha), we have been delivered by you."
"O one of great intelligence, by your grace we have attained the status of a spiritual assembly (gaṇa) under the Lord of Śrī; therefore, ask for whatever is desired in your heart. (26)
The son of the sage said:
"Who are you? From where have you come? And from where have you attained this state of being a host of attendants? Why do you suddenly grant me a boon without having received any benefit? (27)
Nārada said:
Having heard those words concerning his previous births, his father spoke out of grief: "He died after consuming poison. (28)
The father said:
"In a previous birth, O Brahmin, I was a learned man (bhūsura) who was your father;
I was greatly tormented by my wife, who was your mother and remained unfaithful. (29)
Having consumed poison at night and fallen into extreme suffering, I met an untimely death; because of that, I became a night-stalker (rākṣasa).
In this way, O dear one, one hundred and fifteen manvantaras passed while I remained in that state of being a rākṣasa.
Now, because you performed a śrāddha here at this meritorious sacred ford (tīrtha) of Madhuvana at the age of sixteen, I have indeed attained godhood.
This celestial chariot, dispatched by Indra from heaven, is approaching with its attendants and a host of apsarases for the purpose of my ascent. (33)
"Then, in order to grant you a boon, I departed for heaven, ascending my excellent celestial chariot accompanied by my attendants and hosts of Apsarases. (34)
Choose a boon, O auspicious one; therefore, let us not delay.
Seated upon the elephant Airāvata, the Lord of the Gods gazes upon me.
Nārada said:
Having thus related his own history and having bestowed devotion to Hari— which had been requested by him— upon his own son, O King, he departed for the celestial realm.
Then his mother spoke to that son from a previous birth.
The mother said: "By your grace, I have been born as a goddess and am liberated from sin. (37)
O best of the twice-born, even though I am a sinner, I have attained the friendship of Śacī because you performed this śrāddha at this holy place known as Viśrānti.
"O illustrious one, pray for that which is desired by your own heart;
we shall grant it to you, for the word of goddesses is never false. (39)
O best of the twice-born, you know the truth of that sin by which I was born as a lizard in the forest of my ancestors after dwelling for a long time in hell.
O son, O daughter of Puloman, O daughter of the gods, grant me leave;
I am being watched from the sky by hosts of gods and celestial nymphs.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to her desireless son, O King, his mother,
having been saluted by him with his head bowed, departed for Triviṣṭapa.
Then the Grandfather spoke again to that best of the twice-born, his own grandson, regarding his state as a partial incarnation of Hari.
The Grandfather said:
"O child, child, may you live long! You have obtained your own desired wish.
By your grace, we have crossed over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of worldly existence."
"I am your grandfather, O child, and this is your grandmother; that virtuous woman has followed me in death and has shortly attained residence in the same world as mine. (45)
Now that you have rested on this journey and the śrāddha rite has been performed, we two have attained the very nature of Hari in his world. (46)
Nārada said: O best of kings, having spoken thus, that twice-born one, together with his own wife,
passed beyond the world of Brahmā and went to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then the great-grandfather spoke these words to the lord of kings:
"O twice-born one, listen with a focused mind as I tell you that which you have asked. (48)
The great-grandfather said:
"O dear and illustrious child, I am your great-grandfather.
Due to the fruit of killing an embryo, I have entered the womb of a sow. (49)
Thereafter, O dear one, I emerged from that state, afflicted by sin;
then, O best of mountains, I attained the state of an immobile being through my lack of meditation.
There too, having remained for a long time and possessing stability,
it was forcibly uprooted from its base by a certain elephant.
At that very time, you committed an act of faithlessness;
because of this, O best of sages, I was released from my stationary state by you at this supreme sacred ford.
"I have arrived at this excellent residence in the city of the King of Yakṣas;
O best of the twice-born, by your grace, grant me permission for this immeasurable stay. (53)
Desirous of seeing you, I have come here; you, of auspicious appearance, have been seen by me. Among all sacred fords, Madhuvana is the most excellent.
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by him, the son of the sage, who was well-versed in dharma, bowed his head to that lord of kings, his own great-grandfather, and questioned him.
The sage said:
"O father, you were born into a most noble family of brahmins;
how, O teacher, could you have committed the sin known as the killing of an embryo?"
O illustrious one, explain that supreme and highest womb into which you have entered, which is beyond reproach, if it is within your memory. (57)
The Great-grandfather said:
"O tiger among the twice-born, formerly, in the birth of a certain brāhmaṇa, I established my own livelihood through the proper application of mantras. (58)
Out of greed for wealth, and with my mind struck down by fate, I gave medicine to women for the sake of conceiving a child, which led instead to their destruction. (59)
For people deprived of wealth, greed indeed brings about knowledge,
just as the sun, the lord of the day, provides the means of subsistence for those with irrigation channels during the dry season.
O Father, when one's wisdom is destroyed, a person certainly commits sin;
from sin one attains hell, and from that, one reaches a most wretched state of rebirth.
Then a certain woman, who was pregnant, asked me:
"O Brahmin, shall I give birth to a son or to a daughter? (62)
Then I said to her, "She will become the daughter of Vīta-vaka;
for the sake of producing a son for you, I shall give you this great medicine."
Having been addressed thus, that woman of evil intellect, the crest-jewel of wicked women,
seized my feet and gave me a *pala* of gold.
Thus he spoke to me: "Six daughters have been born to me; this seventh one was mentioned by you. I shall live only upon the birth of this one. (65)
"O you of great intelligence, act in such a way that I may give birth to another daughter who will destroy my own life. (66)
Having heard her words, I spoke to her again:
"I shall provide the medicine at the time of delivery once a son has been born. (67)
Having assented to my words with "So be it," she went home; awaiting that time, she remained there, intent on fulfilling her word.
When she had gone, O tiger among the twice-born, I became distressed with anxious thought; listen as I relate that to you. (69)
"This woman has given me a fruit that is known to produce a son; I do not know what kind of gold will come from it. (70)
What should I do in this matter? How can this gold, weighing one *pala*, remain in the house of a poor man like me? (71)
Reflecting thus, that thief caused his maidservant to administer to her father a terrible and violent medicine that induces abortion. (72)
Then, due to that medicinal herb, there occurred a miscarriage of her fetus in the third month; at that time, no sign was known as to whether it was male or female.
Then, having arrived at our house, they were despondent due to the miscarriage;
they requested gold from us, being hopeless of the birth of a son. (74)
Then I showed him brick powder mixed with ashes, combined with turmeric powder, along with water. (75)
"O Mother, this powder has been prepared by me for the birth of your son;
through your gift, twice as much wealth has accrued for its accomplishment. (76)
Having spoken thus, she abandoned the powder and went home according to her custom;
then she said to me, "O best of the twice-born, I shall take [the powder] from you at the proper time. (77)
Thus, this most terrible matricide and foeticide committed by me has caused me to wander through three most loathsome wombs. (78)
"By your grace, I am now liberated from this state of being stationary;
O best of sages, grant me permission, for I shall go to the auspicious Alakā. (79)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, O king of kings, his great-grandfather was saluted by him with his head bowed; he then departed toward the northern direction.
[He ascended] a variegated celestial chariot, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells,
inhabited by dancing gandharvas, and beautified by walls of jewels.
Then the great king’s great-great-grandmother,
seated upon that excellent celestial chariot, spoke to her own great-grandson.
The great-grandmother said:
"O you of excellent vows, by this merit you shall not go anywhere at all, except for a temple marked with the lotus-feet of the Lord of Padmā. (83)
"This sinful husband of mine, O sage, was your great-grandfather;
though restrained by me, he of wicked intellect committed sin. (84)
Thus, that evil-souled one was rescued from the ocean of suffering by you;
by whom indeed could the praise of your virtues be fully expressed? (85)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, O lord of kings, she departed for the world of her husband;
and in Alakā, she rejoiced for a long time with that very husband.
Then all the maternal grandfathers and others of the Sage’s son, together with their wives, ascended celestial chariots and went to heaven. (87)
That best of the twice-born, having gone from that sacred ford to his father’s hermitage,
related the entire account to his father.
He too went there with his family and,
for the sake of rest, constructed a leaf-hut near the hermitage of Atri.
There, performing his ablutions three times a day at the Viśrānta-tīrtha,
that best of sages felt no longing even for the world of Viṣṇu.
O King, once while the sage was performing his ablutions in the midst of the water, he made this wish: "When shall I behold Hari? (91)
O best of sages, while that king was thus longing, Hari, whose seat is the king of birds, arrived with haste. 92.
Hari, possessing four arms, stands together with Lakṣmī who resides upon his chest;
he is clothed in garments the color of fresh clouds and the hue of lightning.
His chest was radiant with the Kaustubha gem; he bore the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
his neck was graced by a forest garland, and he wore earrings in the shape of makaras. ||94||
With eyes like full-blown lotus petals, his face adorned with beautiful locks of hair,
and his chest marked by the red hue of coral-like palms, he held her hand.
Illuminating him with the luster of his teeth and casting away the darkness of the quarters like the autumnal moon, he spoke to that best of the twice-born.
The Blessed Lord said:
O best of the twice-born, this auspicious Madhuvana is my own sacred ford;
it grants rest to the knower and, through bathing therein, fulfills all desires.
At this time of your bathing, you desired a vision of me; for your benefit, I have granted it to you—something difficult even for the gods, beginning with Brahmā, to obtain. (98)
"Abandon this human body of a brahmin and attain a divine one;
ascend the lord of birds and come to my abode along with me. (99)
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of the Lord of Śrī, the lord of sages, O ruler of the people, bowed down and offered praise while remaining in the water itself. (100)
The sage said:

O Lord of Śrī, I bow to that which bestows the glory of fortune upon the Bhojas, which crushes the pride of the foot-soldiers, which destroys the cycle of worldly existence, and which is worshipped by the thirty gods. 101.
For those beings here who are deluded by your own Āryānātha, their liberation will never occur without your compassion. 102.
O Lord, through the service of sacred fords and the like, as well as through association with the virtuous, devotion arises in those men indeed by Your grace. (103)
Having heard the chanting of Your qualities,
which destroys all sins, uttered by many holy men, one who recites it shall enter the womb of a singer and attain liberation.

O Lord of Śrī, the minds of Your people, having fallen into the great battle of worldly existence, are covered by the dust [of passion] and thus lose their purity, like a supreme gem [covered in dust]. (105)

That man who, as he falls, touches Your lotus feet like a staff while his body is covered in horripilation—he leads both his own lineage and himself to Your state, which is sought after by all yogis. (106)
O Lord, the individual soul alone, deluded by Your māyā, wanders through the paths of the universe;
yet by the tremulous glances of Your gracious eyes, it crosses that ocean of the world in an instant. 107.
Nārada said:
Having thus praised Govinda, that best of sages fell prostrate like a staff at His feet, repeatedly uttering, "Victory! (Jaya). 108.
The Lord of Śrī, having quickly raised that best of sages who had prostrated like a staff upon the ground with His arms, placed him upon Garuḍa. 109.
The Supreme Soul then went to Vaikuṇṭha along with that family;
thus, O King, has this account of Madhuvana been told to Śiva. 110.
This majesty, which destroys all sins—what else do you wish to hear?
By hearing it as it is being told, a mortal is liberated from all sins. (111)

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Madhuvana," within the "Greatness of the Kālindī" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||214||
The two hundred and fifteenth chapter. Saubhari said:
Having heard these auspicious words of Nārada, Yudhiṣṭhira—
King Śibi Auśīnara, who was ill-behaved, spoke to him.
Śibi said:
"O Sage, I have heard from your mouth the greatness of Madhuvana; however, there remains one doubt in my mind."
How could he, by whose virtuous nature all his own kinsmen were delivered, have been the son of an unchaste woman throughout two lifetimes? (3)
"O Blessed One, O Nārada, you who know everything in its true essence—tell me this:
what has passed, what is present, and what is yet to come."
Nārada said: Once, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha— a day endowed with all sacred festivals— all the sages assembled at Haridvāra.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites and performed their auspicious daily duties,
they sat down upon the ridge of the Himalayas with tranquil minds.
There, Budha, the son of Tārā, arrived among the assembly of sages;
endowed with an abundance of beauty, he was like another Smara incarnate. ||7||
Seeing him arrive, the lords of sages rose;
once he had saluted them with his head bowed low, they sat down again.
O Lord, observing the respect shown to Buddha by the foremost of sages,
the son of a sage questioned his own father in this manner.
The son of the sage said:
"Who is this who has arrived with my father, appearing like another Smara in beauty?
Great respect has been shown toward him by Vyāsa and other eminent sages. (10)
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of his own son, that virtuous soul,
the tiger among sages, spoke to his son who was full of persistence.
The father said:
"This son of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, born from the womb of Tārā, is wise, named Budha, and is the supreme benefactor of the moon. (12)
The son said: "O father, what irrelevant words have you spoken?
How can he who is the son of Bṛhaspati be the dung of the moon?"
How can this son of the preceptor of the gods be the founder of that lineage which was established by Jajña, Sūrya, Yātātapa, Vidhu, and Atri, the lord of sages? (14)
A great doubt exists within my mind regarding these; O best of Brahmins, dispel it for me, a child who is full of uncertainty. (15)
The father said: "Formerly, O Father, the illustrious Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, was carried off by the powerful Candra through force. (16)
Having stolen her and brought her to his own home according to the prescribed rite, he enjoyed that wife of his Guru for a long time with her.
Then, after some time, a fetus was conceived;
subsequently, Bṛhaspati requested his own wife back from him. (18)
Overcome by intoxication and arrogant in his strength, even the Moon did not grant it;
then, O dear one, Bṛhaspati, together with the gods headed by Śakra, [approached].

Having been thus addressed by Indrajit, Śukra, equipped for battle, began to fight alongside the powerful Indrajit; and Vṛhaspati, for the sake of assisting the Moon, joined together with the sons of Diti and the Dānavas.
Then, O dear one, having assembled for that exertion in battle, a fierce war indeed commenced on account of Tārā. ||21||
In that most terrifying battle, which all people will regard as the foremost, the gods and the dānavas shall be slain. (22)
O dear one, there was neither victory nor defeat for anyone;
then Brahmā arrived and restrained that fierce battle.
Having informed the Lord of Night (the Moon) regarding Tārā,
Bṛhaspati then beheld her as she was pregnant; enraged, he brought about a confrontation between the gods and the Daityas in the very presence of Viriñci (Brahmā).
Bṛhaspati said:
"Listen to my words, O lady with eyes as beautiful as the *tāra* and *itarā* stars!
Whose embryo is this held within you—is it yours, or mine? (25)
The father said: When that auspicious girl, though asked again and again in this manner, did not speak anything before him due to her bashfulness, [he thought: "What is in her mind? (26)
Then, while those gods and enemies of the asuras were looking on, he was born; filled with wrath, he spoke thus to his mother: ||27||
Budha said:
"O wicked one, why is my father not being mentioned by you?
Cast aside your shame and behold the power of my curse! (28)
The father said:
Having spoken thus, when he took up water and was prepared to curse, then Sāmanta spoke this to him: "Your father is Sudhākara. (29)
When this had been said by that virtuous woman, Candra took his son Budha with great joy and went to his own palace.
Having taken Tārā, who was praised by Bṛhaspati, he went to his own home;
Brahmā, the gods, and the Daityas also each went to their respective homes. ||31||
All this that you have asked me has been explained:
how you were born of Bṛhaspati’s wife, and how you were cast out by Candra.
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of his father,
the son of the sage laughed loudly and said to his father, "This man is a base-born son (kuṇḍa), the offspring of an unchaste woman."
And his father said to his son: "Alas, my son! Do not speak this;
he who knows the hearts of all beings will curse you when he understands what you have said."
Nārada said:
O King, having been addressed thus by that sage, Aṅgiras understood what was spoken and spoke as follows while all the sages were listening. (35)
Budha said: "O tigers among sages, listen to my speech;
whether it be good or bad, deliberate upon it without delay. (36)
I have come here for the purpose of seeing you who possess the realization of the ultimate nature;
I have not committed even the slightest offense against anyone. (37)
"Why do these arrogant ones treat me with contempt out of envy? It was for the sake of making my own birth fruitful that I became eager for the sight of you. (38)
The very nature of the wicked causes even the virtuous and sinless to tremble with fear, just as cuckoos, though sweet-voiced, do so elsewhere.
The wicked do not abandon their evil nature even through association with the virtuous,
just as the ocean does not lose its saltiness even by contact with the waters of the Ganges.
Alas, what wickedness there is in this hunter!
For he kills even those deer who follow the conduct of sages and roam the forest like ascetics, even though they are well-versed in singing.
What offense have the fish committed against those evil-minded fishermen, that they kill them while they are moving in the water? That is simply their nature: violence. (42)
Even the virtuous do not abandon their own nature when they associate with the wicked,
just as sandalwood trees do not lose their coolness even when surrounded by serpents whose venom is like fire.
Do the virtuous ever dance at the rise of another's prosperity?
Just as the peacock, O best of sages, dances at the rising of the cloud. 44.
The virtuous maintain their own limbs even for the sake of others;
for the benefit of their parents, gods, and men, they regard their own limbs as their very fathers. (45)
The rising of the virtuous is a cause of joy for the pure-hearted, just as the rising of my father, the cool-rayed moon, is for the night-lotuses. (46)
Nārada said:
Having spoken these words in anger, Budha cursed that young sage, saying,
"You too shall quickly become a cauldron upon the surface of the earth."
Having thus heard the curse uttered by Budha, his father caused his own son to fall into the two fires, saying, "May it be forgiven. (48)
He said: "This boy does not know your majesty; it is not fitting for those like you to show anger toward such a child. (49)
O virtuous one, when a person who is naturally forgiving becomes angry for some reason, it is like the coolness of water being heated by fire. (50)

Therefore, quickly show favor toward someone upon whom you may bestow it; for the virtuous have forgiveness as their essence, especially toward those who are like children, devoid of discernment. (51)
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by that sage, the son of Śūta then abandoned his anger; with a tranquil mind, he bestowed his grace upon him.
Budha said:
"O sage, this boy of yours, having attained the state of a sacrificial vessel on the surface of the earth and having been given the sacred thread and the soma-juice, shall soon reach his own abode."
Thus, O best of kings, the son of the sage attained the state of a sacrificial pit on earth due to the curse of a deity,
by whom his ancestors were liberated.
Having heard this purifying majesty of Madhuvana, a person obtains the entire fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). ||55||
For the sake of that supreme majesty which I have maintained,
it remains within their hearts, so that they are not overcome by sense objects.
Those of great intelligence who shall recite this majesty and listen to it will, without a doubt, go to the same world as Viṣṇu after leaving their bodies. 57.
This sacred narrative of Madhuvana, which brings delight to the Lord of Śrī, has been described by me;
it is capable of severing the mass of impurities of the Kali age and is the cause for blocking the path to the eyes of those whose bodies are merit. 58.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Madhuvana," in the *Kālindī-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the *Pādma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||215||
(216) Nārada said:
O King, this Badarikāśrama is [situated] beyond the Aṭomadhuvana forest.
It occupies a portion of ground measuring eleven dhanus. ||1||
I shall describe before you the most wonderful majesty of this best of sacred fords, hearing which one is liberated from fear. (2)
There was a certain king of Magadha named Devadāsa; he was a Brāhmaṇa, truthful and self-controlled, like another Dharma incarnate. (3)
He was proficient in all branches of knowledge like another Bṛhaspati,
and through his devotion he brought joy to Hari, just as Prahlāda did for the king of the Daityas.
Though possessed of a wife, he was a conqueror of passion, like the beloved of Pārvatī;
he was constantly devoted to righteous conduct, like the sage Viśvāmitra.
This wealth was in the house of the Lord of Magadha; now let Drona take it to his own home, for he is as generous toward worthy recipients as Bali, the lord of the Daityas.
His wife was the most excellent of women, like Lakṣmī herself, preeminent in virtues,
devoted to the service of her husband, and the delight of her kinsmen.
O King, he had one son named Gada, who was wise;
and he had one daughter named Valayā, who was endowed with auspicious marks.
The elder son of those two was a girl, and from him [the king] was born a younger daughter;
that best of the twice-born performed their marriages in due order.
O King, after her marriage, that girl endowed with auspicious marks went to her father-in-law’s house after some time had passed.
Aṅgada, possessed of great intelligence and adorned with the splendor of youth, bore the burden of the household like his father, being learned in all the scriptures. ||11||
Once, O best of Brahmins, having recognized that his son was capable of performing the household duties,
that lord of kings spoke to his own wife.
Devadāsa said:
Listen, O virtuous lady, to these words appropriate for this time;
then, O blessed one, let that which is fitting be performed immediately. (13)
This old age, having arrived, will cause the body to fall, just as a fierce wind knocks down a ripe fruit from its stalk. 14.
"O lady of virtuous vows, at dawn, she will surely take away even the splendor of my eyes, as well as that of the stars together with the moon. (15)
This old age will cause my gait to falter, with stumbling steps and a tottering stride, just as a wicked woman causes one to stumble with her anklets.
Therefore, O auspicious one, since this old age arises before our strength has even matured,
we must quickly perform that which is for our own souls.
Sons, friends, brothers, and parents are perishable, as are wealth and other such things; O fortunate one, a wise person should not become attached to these. (18)
Therefore, wandering among all the sacred fords with my senses conquered,
I shall behold the Lord Hari according to the rule of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
Then, having performed the ritual renunciation (saṃnyāsa) at some auspicious and supreme sacred ford (tīrtha),
I shall cast off this body of mine, bringing an end to my prārabdha karma.
If one's life-breath were thus released, liberation would occur; of this there is no doubt—for me, whose mind is perfectly established in the lotus-feet of the Lord of Śrī. (21)
Uttamā said:
Whether a man or a woman, in this perishable world, one who is devoid of consciousness does not, apart from Mādhava, find the eternal refuge. (22)
Therefore, having brought me as well— who serve Your lotus feet—
as a co-dweller with Yourself, quickly ferry me across this vast ocean of the universe.
This illustrious son Aṅgada has become capable of bearing the burden of the household, and this auspicious daughter-in-law is his helper. (24)
Whether it be a foolish man or a woman capable of bearing children,
that fool who does not feel revulsion for these two is one whose mind is obstructed from the highest good.
Nārada said:
Having thus consulted with one another in private at that time,
the two lords summoned their son Aṅgada and spoke these words to him.
Then the two said to their husband: "O Aṅgada, know us to be those whose limbs have grown frail with the onset of old age;
we shall strive for our own spiritual welfare somewhere on a holy ground. (27)
Worship of Hari with devotion is said to be the supreme good;
for that purpose alone do the saintly ones on earth strive without desire for personal gain.
They have no attachment to sense objects, equanimity toward all living beings, and never experience joy or grief, nor pleasure or pain. (29)
Therefore, those virtuous ones in the world who serve the feet of Govinda—by the mere sight of them, a person becomes one who has accomplished his life's purpose. ||30||
A wise man, wandering among sacred fords and eager for the sight of him, may obtain that vision through some arising of good fortune. (31)
Therefore, O Angada, having placed the burden of the household upon the two long arms of the master of the house, set out for the pilgrimage to the holy ford of Nausarjasvatī.
If, in the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, one should ever behold a holy man, then the two sons would have their purpose fulfilled. (33)
Nārada said:
Thus addressed by his parents, the son uttered a cry of "Well said!
Nārada said:
This, which brings about the liberation of the entire family, has been proclaimed by you two. ||34||
"Do not despise Āśumā; what can I do for your benefit?
I am always carrying out the commands of you two whose feet are worthy of worship. (35)
"Take this excellent wealth, which was acquired for the purpose of giving at sacred pilgrimage sites;
send me as well, your servant, to attend upon you in your own presence. (36)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus and taking their wealth, he went two krośas away;
then, with some difficulty, he was turned back by those two as they followed him to their home.
Taking some wealth with him, Viṣṇu said, "Let us go by boat.
Having stayed there for three days, subsisting on roots and fruits, [he departed]. (38)
O Lord of the Earth, when they had moved out from there, a certain great Siddha encountered them on the path. (39)
Having been saluted by both of them with their heads, he sat down;
once seated, that king of the Siddhas was then questioned by them as follows.
"O noble one, from where have you come and what do you wish to do? Tell me that.
The Siddha said:
"I am a Siddha, O best of ascetics; my home is in Kalpagrāma."
Having arrived from Indraprastha, he witnessed a great marvel there:
the perfected sage Kapila, who was equal to Nārāyaṇa in his qualities.
Therefore, studying Sāṃkhya, I lived in that hermitage.
Once, my illustrious teacher Kapila departed from his own hermitage. 43.
To bathe in the waters of the Yamunā at the highly meritorious place known as Badarī.
There, a buffalo from the Ikṣvāku forest was thirsty for the waters of the Yamunā. ||44||
Having entered the water and drunk it, he remembered his former births;
remembering his past deeds, the buffalo who had been born in the forest [reflected]. (45)
Emerging quickly from the water, he approached his preceptor, the venerable Kapila;
and as the ascetic was listening, he spoke with a human voice:
"Listen, I shall today tell you that which is most wonderful."
Mahiṣa said:
"O Kapileśvara, you who have become a portion of Viṣṇu and are the lord of the Siddhas!
What is the name of this great holy place (tīrtha)? O protector, please tell me. (47)
O highly fortunate one, due to the touch of the waters of this best of holy places, even the great sin of my previous birth has been destroyed. (48)
The Siddha said:
Having heard these words of Mahiṣa, the great sage,
though already knowing his conduct, laughed and spoke as follows.
Kapila said: "In a previous birth, you were a tiger among buffaloes. What action did you perform there, by which you obtained this buffalo womb?"
The buffalo said:
"Listen, O tiger among sages, to the account of my previous birth. In former times, I was a powerful king, the lord of Kaliṅga. (51)
Deluded by lust, I did not distinguish between my own wife and another woman;
I was a thief of the wealth of virtuous merchants who were free from sin. (52)
O King, I wander fearlessly through the city at midnight to sport with beautiful women who are the wives of others, in the playful dalliance of love. (53)
When I saw that beautiful woman in her house, I was deluded by passion;
I dwell there like an elephant in the midst of a field of sharp swords. (54)
Having played there without hesitation and having taken wealth from that house, in how many days shall I return again to my own home? (55)
Seated in the midst of the assembly, [Rāma said: "O children of the city, I shall fight with my own arms during the day, provided you two remain awake. (56)
"O Sage, thinking that he is a mere child, I shall forcibly seize his father's wealth, whether it be small or great. (57)
"O Great Sage, he who is defeated therein due to cowardice is not worthy to dwell in my city; thus have I resolved. (58)
Even so, while this king was reigning, the citizens abandoned the city and departed for other regions. (59)
Once, while the tiger among sages, Durvāsas, was wandering the earth, that Durvāsas, born of Rudra, arrived at my city.
Having kindled the funeral pyre, all the citizens came into his presence;
having prostrated themselves, they spoke these words to him, making known their own suffering: ||61||
The citizens said:
O tiger among sages, O ocean of compassion, show mercy!
Enjoin this king, who is devoted to unrighteousness, to the path of dharma. (62)
By the dawning of our good fortune, you have come to us;
like a boat, you shall carry us across this overflowing ocean of the king’s misery. (63)
O bull among sages, our wealth was stolen by that greedy father, and virtuous women were defiled by that lustful and sinless man. (64)
O great sage, many children about ten years of age have been killed; this king is a treasury of countless vices. (65)
Mahiṣa said:
Having heard these words of the citizens, the sage Atri’s son reflected,
"This one deserves punishment," and then approached me as I sat in the assembly.
Seeing him approaching, naked and like a wandering ascetic,
I had my servants block him, saying, "He is not worthy of being seen."
"Covered entirely with dust, she has indeed taken the form of a cow or a buffalo; 'Let her be driven away!'—thus I repeatedly commanded those standing by my side. (68)
Then his other servants approached to restrain him;
however, with a mere "hum" sound, the sage reduced them all to ashes.
Just as you protected the sacrificial horse from the ocean, your own father,
I shall reduce all those servants to ashes by my fiery power.
Perceiving this, he rose up suddenly and prepared to enter the house; then that best of sages addressed me, saying, "O you sinner! (71)
"In this great forest, become a buffalo at once!
Having spoken thus, he was indeed cursed by him, and then he cast off his royal body.
O sage, I was born as a buffalo in the great forest of Maru;
O best of sages, I dwelt there for a long time. (73)
Listen also to that merit by which I have come here: many step-wells, wells, and lakes were caused to be constructed by me. (74)
The planting of mango and other trees along the road was ordained;
by this merit, O Lord, my fall into hell has not occurred. (75)
"I have indeed reached this confluence of waters at this sacred ford (tīrtha).
Thus, I have told you all of my auspicious and inauspicious deeds in my previous birth. (76)

"O Sage, tell me how this buffalo-cow, who was born from my womb and by whom this excellent holy place was reached, might attain liberation from this wretched birth; for through the mere touch of the water of this best of tirthas, she has become a rememberer of her past lives."
Kapila said:
"This is the highly meritorious sacred ford (tīrtha) called Badarī belonging to the Lord of Ramā.
Bathe here quickly, and you shall obtain the desire residing in your own heart."
The Siddha said:
O great sage, having heard these words of that buffalo,
the shadow of the celestial dweller entered that excellent holy place (tīrtha) in order to bathe.
Having bathed there with a desire for heaven, as he emerged from the water onto the bank,
Śakra mounted his elephant at that very moment and arrived from heaven.
Indra said:
"O Lord ofekaliṅga, abandon this body born of a buffalo;
having obtained a divine form, return with me to heaven."
"Because you bathed with the desire for heaven, that abode of the gods has been attained by you. (81)
The Siddha said:
Thus addressed by Satadūta, he abandoned his buffalo body,
