assumed a divine form, and mounted the king of elephants.
Having mounted the king of elephants and remained gazing at the sky,
he bowed his head to the god and praised the sage Kapila.
Kaliṅga said:
Salutations to you, O Supreme Lord, the cause of absolute knowledge; the bridge for the Vedas and sciences, and the enemy of those who oppose them. (84)
O Lord, from you has arisen the Sāṃkhya system which brings about the realization of truth for embodied beings whose minds are seized by Māyā, like a father to his children. 85.
O Muni, you punish those who, having abandoned what was ordained by the Vedas, turn back according to their own will;
you punish those deserving of punishment by immersing them in the states of animals and other lower births.
Indra and all the other guardians of the world are your subordinates; terrified of punishment for any harm they might do, they follow your will.
In every age, throughout the cycles of the gods and the past, those who opposed the dharma of the three Vedas were incarnated by you, O Soul of All, for their destruction.
O Lord of the Wheel, those enemies of the gods who were slain by you have abandoned their bodies composed of darkness and have gone to Vaikuṇṭha.
O Lord of the World, command me to go to the abode of the gods;
favor Indra as well with the nectar of your glance. 90.
O Lord of Gods, O Master, it was solely through your grace that he, at the sacred ford named Badarī, cast off his tamasic body and attained a sattvic one.
Having ascended with Indra to the abode of the thirty gods, I shall go at my own will by the grace of you, O Lord, the ocean of compassion. (92)
The Siddha said:
Having thus praised Kapila, the Lord of Gods, the ruler of Kaliṅga bowed at his feet and departed for the abode of the thirty gods.
This wonderful thing was seen by me, O brahmin, at the hermitage of Badarī:
the liberation even from sin for one who serves his guru. (94)
There is no holy place in the three worlds superior to this, which bestows all goals;
go there with your wife if you desire the highest welfare. (95)
O twice-born one, I went to the house named Badarī to bring my own aged father, who was free from worldly desire and longing for liberation. (96)
Nārada said:
O King, having thus extolled the greatness of this best of holy places called Badarī, that Siddha departed for his own home. 97.
Then, after some time, that wise brahmin, wandering through sacred fords together with his wife, arrived at Indraprastha. 98.
O King, with that very same body, he brought those three to his own abode;
and though he was already a perfected being (siddha), he quickly brought his father from his house as well.
There, desiring liberation, he bathed in that sacred ford;
and he too was then honored by Śrī Vāsudeva, whose father had attained perfection.
Then, praised by the gods, the Lord went to his own abode located within Indraprastha, known as Sadvadarya. By bathing there, one obtains every desired object for the mind.
Its pure majesty has been described by the king Nṛpatimati; having heard it, a person never again falls into a mother's womb. (101)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of Badarikāśrama," in the *Kālindī-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||216||
(216) Chapter Two Hundred and Seventeen.
The King said:
O Sage, you have described to me the greatness arising from Badarī,
hearing which my mind has attained a state of stainless purity.
O tiger among sages, this entire supreme place known as Śakraprastha possesses such wonderful majesty that it bestows the four aims of human life.
O Nārada, beyond this world there is a supreme sacred site (tīrtha) that bestows liberation even upon those who have fallen; it is the most excellent destroyer of all sins, simply by being seen.
O Nārada, I desire to hear from you, who bring satisfaction to the virtuous, the greatness of this Haridvāra situated within this [region]. 4.
O Sage, uplift me, who am wretched, through the description of this sacred ford situated at Śakraprastha, which [liberates one] from ignorance, desire, and karma. (5)
Nārada said:
Listen, O highly fortunate one of immeasurable speech; I shall describe before you the majesty of Haridvāra, which bestows the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
In this regard, O Lord, I shall now relate to you how a certain sinful outcaste attained the way to heaven; listen with an attentive mind. (7)
In the past, there was a dog-eater (śvapaca) of sinful deeds known as Kāliṅga, who lived outside the city at Dharmakṣetra, Kurukṣetra. ||8||
Having forcibly gathered children of the city-dwellers, about five or six years of age, he led them away and killed them. 9.
The base king, having killed them, seized their ornaments made of silver and gold, as well as the jewels and other valuables they wore on their bodies.
Desiring to seize the wealth of travelers, he entered the dwelling of a virtuous man at night; observing that the travelers possessed riches, he struck down the solitary man in the forest.
O King, once on the occasion of a lunar festival (parvan), people from various directions gathered at Kurukṣetra with the desire to receive various gifts.
O King, having bathed according to the prescribed rites on that day of the sun’s change (the new moon),
and having given gifts as was fitting, the people returned to their respective homes.
A certain eminent man among the Vaiśyas, who was possessed of great wealth, later set out from among all the people toward his own home. (14)
Placing twenty foot-soldiers in front of him, the horseman Kāliṅga,
though a great sinner, set out after him for the sake of prosperity.
O King, after traveling for several nights, that lowest of men, a pariah, was unable to find an opportunity to seize his wealth.
He was not even able to seize his wealth by force;
for that Vaiśya alone was joined with twenty thousand people. (17)
O King, having come here for the sake of a Vaiśya, that evil-minded man entered his camp at midnight in order to steal his wealth. (18)
As that evil-souled man was entering, he was noticed by one of the Vaiśyas, who struck him with his own weapon. ||19||
O King, as he approached the Tamāla tree, the attendant who was to strike him seized him by both feet while he was still asleep.
Having seized other people and awakening them [to the truth], he was one who bestowed [merit] at every watch;
yet he was indeed struck down by that very hand of the sinful thief.
Having heard this, as he was fleeing, he was seized by other people;
then, having suddenly killed his captor, he fled once more. ||22||
O King, by a certain archer-servant, that base man was swiftly struck from afar with an arrow and fell dead. (23)
O King, as soon as they were struck by that arrow,
both of the Vaiśya’s followers, who had been slain by the thief, instantly gave up their lives.
O King, having ascended those four excellent vehicles brought by the hosts and remaining in the sky, they spoke thus to the Vaiśya:
25. O King, having ascended those four excellent vehicles brought by the hosts and remaining in the sky, they spoke thus to the Vaiśya.
The followers of the Kalinga merchant said:
"O noble master of the merchant, this is an unsurpassed holy place (tīrtha);
it is Haridvāra at Indraprastha, which brings about the welfare even of sinners. (26)
We three, though having met with untimely death at this excellent sacred ford, shall now go to heaven; O Vaiśya, may it be well with you.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, they went to heaven, the auspicious abode created by Śiva,
where various objects of enjoyment are obtained at will.
Then, when the night had passed, in the morning, that best of the Viśas performed the cremation of his own servant's body and cast down the bones.
O Lord, while those bones were being cast into the sacred ford, those two servants returned here from heaven and spoke thus to that Vaiśya:
30. "O Lord, while those bones were being cast into the sacred ford, those two servants returned here from heaven and spoke thus to that Vaiśya."
The two servants said:
"O noble lord of the Vaiśyas, by dying here at this sacred ford on earth, even for beings who are sinners, there is the attainment of heaven; of this there is no doubt. (31)
If the bones of a creature who has died on dry land fall into the water of this sacred ford,
then, O Vaiśya, that person shall attain residence in Satyaloka.
By the falling of our bones into the water after we both died on land, we have attained a station in the world of Brahmā that shall endure as long as the existence of Brahmā. (33)
The bones of the thief who had died on dry land fell into the waters;
from that place, O Lord of the people, he stood in the abode of the gods.
O best of gods, quickly cast his body as well into this sacred ford,
so that he too may attain the supreme state.
The virtuous should always perform acts of benefit even for others;
however, harm inflicted by the wicked must be endured with patience. (36)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, O highly fortunate one, those two departed toward the city of Hari;
by casting their bones into the waters of the sacred ford of Haridvāra, they attained liberation.
O King, that illustrious merchant searched for a fire to burn the body of that thief, but he did not find it. ||38||
Returning once more to that very place, the crest-jewel of all sacred fords,
the great king bathed at Haridvāra according to his desire.
Having procreated virtuous sons and having propitiated Viṣṇu through sacrifices, I shall satisfy the Brahmins and my kinsmen with wealth acquired through righteous means. (40)
Having met such a death in you, we have gone to the abode of Hari;
O King of Tīrthas, salutations to you—this is what must be done for you.
O King, having thus bathed in that sacred ford (tīrtha) according to his desire, the Vaiśya Kāmada returned to his own home together with all his servants. ||42||
Having gone there, the wise man begot sons upon his wife who had no other co-wife,
and he satisfied his kinsmen with wealth acquired through righteous means.
O King, by propitiating the Lord of Kamalā with supreme devotion, one who meets death at this sacred ford shall attain Vaikuṇṭha. ||44||
Thus, O King, has the greatness of this sacred ford been described to you;
now hear the fruit that comes from listening to this account of the meritorious Haridvāra. 45.
By the gift of a drona of sesame seeds, one obtains that fruit which belongs to the Māgha [month].
A person obtains that fruit by listening to its greatness. ||46||

Whatever fruit is obtained from the gift of gopīcandana and from eating from brahmapatra leaves, that same fruit is attained simply by hearing the greatness of this [rite] during the month of Kārtika. 47.
O King, the fruit that is obtained by staying awake during the final watch of the night at Prabodhinī is equal to that which arises from hearing the greatness of this sacred ford. 48.
Indeed, there is no sacred site on the surface of the earth that bestows the fruits of the four aims of life like Śakraprastha, which is truly equal to Haridvāra. 49.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of Haridvāra," in the Indraprastha-māhātmya of the Uttara-khaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||217|| ||cha||
(218) Chapter Two Hundred and Eighteen.
Nārada said:
Furthermore, listen to the most wonderful majesty of the highly fortunate Puṣkara, that sacred site situated here which bestows auspiciousness. (1)
By the grace of that sacred ford (tīrtha), Viṣṇu, the lord of all gods, being pleased,
dwelt for one month in the house of Puṇḍarīka;
there, even his younger brother, though devoted to sin, attained liberation.
Śibi said: "Who was that virtuous-souled Puṇḍarīka, and what deed did he perform?"
Because the Blessed One was pleased with him, he dwelt in that house for a month.
O Sage, tell me everything: how did his younger brother, that sinful soul, attain the abode of Śrī Hari through the grace of this sacred ford? 4.
As I listen to this, a sense of shame arises within me regarding the greatness of Śiva and Umā. ||5||
Nārada said: O King, in the city of Vidarbha, there was a highly illustrious Brāhmaṇa named Mālava, who was a knower of Brahman, tranquil, learned, and devoted to Viṣṇu.
He is the nourisher of gods, sages, ancestors, spirits, and humans;
he is unattached to sense objects and free from greed, delusion, and other such vices.
Once, when the highly fortunate Bṛhaspati had arrived, Siṃha said:
He set out to bathe in the highly meritorious Godāvarī. ||8||
To give there, he took ten thousand palas of gold from his house;
while traveling on the road, that righteous-souled man thought this in his mind: (9)
Mālava said:
"Ten thousand palas of gold were brought by me from my home for the purpose of giving;
it must not be given to just anyone, but should be given to a venerable and virtuous person. (10)

That which is given at the proper place and time to a worthy recipient—a Brahmin who is a vessel for the nectar of the Vedas and who does not seek personal gain—becomes inexhaustible and attains the state of imperishability. //11//
Having given what was brought through the practice of gleaning to Durvāsas, the righteous sage,
who lived by the vow of śiloñcha, abandoned his own body and went to the supreme state.
Recognizing Vāmana as a worthy recipient, King Bali, the lord of the Dānavas,
gave him the three worlds— which he had acquired by his own arm— even though they were the very opposite of his own side.
Therefore, wealth earned by me through righteousness should be properly given to a worthy recipient for the satisfaction of Govinda; its fruit should not be sought [for oneself]. 14.
But Puṇḍarīka, whose nature is dharma, the crest-jewel of all worthy recipients, will come from the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura), summoned by me as my nephew. 15.
"O Ānī, I shall give half of that wealth to my worthy son, and the remainder of my sister's dowry to learned Brahmins according to the prescribed rule.
Nārada said:
Having reflected thus, O King, that best of virtuous brahmins reached the holy Godāvarī river after some days at Mālava.
The righteous Puṇḍarīka, the son of his sister, met him;
he had previously come from Mālava, the land of the Mahīpati.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite on the day of the lion’s stride (Siṃhasaṃkrama), he gave half of his wealth to the Puṇḍarīka [temple], saying, "May Hari be pleased."
The virtuous Puṇḍarīka, having bathed in the waters of the Godāvarī,
joyfully gave a fourth part of his own wealth to those learned in the Vedas.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites and having given gifts according to his ability, O King, he said to his sister's son as he was departing for his own home: (21)
Mālava said:
"Salutations should be offered to the elders, and blessings to the juniors;
for this meeting of those of our age has indeed been but momentary. (22)
Thus, for all living beings, [attachment] occurs together with sons, wives, and so forth;
therefore, what wise man would [cling] to this cyclic existence, which consists of such momentary conjunctions? ||23||
One who is an object of compassion may certainly become detached; through the mercy of Śrī Hari, such a living being becomes devoted to the company of the virtuous. 24.
In him, a desire to hear the pastimes of that Hari arises;
and having heard them, he himself will even chant the pastimes of Hari when they are being narrated by the virtuous. (25)
Then, reciting with longing, he remembers the power of Govinda;
thereafter, there arises for him love in the service of Govinda’s feet.

Just as a man then swiftly crosses the great ocean by means of a boat, so too, O righteous-souled one, for this very purpose do the virtuous and the wise exert effort toward their actions; therefore, you too must be diligent. (27)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the son of Vidarbha somehow dismissed his sister's son,
who had a tearful face and eyes clouded with tears, and departed.
The virtuous Puṇḍarīka also departed for his own home;
after some days, O King, he arrived here at this auspicious place.
He beheld his younger brother named Bharata fallen upon the ground, gasping for breath and smeared with blood flowing from his wounds.
Weeping aloud, he asked: "O brother, by whom have you been brought to such a state? For what purpose have you come here from your home? (31)
When the lord of kings, Puṇḍarīka, asked this with great distress,
Bharata was immediately so overcome by pain that he gave up his life.
Then, while the people of the land and even his preceptor were looking on, that wondrous aerial chariot with its single pole descended from the sky.
Then, having ascended that divine cow, even though he was a doer of evil deeds, Bharata spoke these words to his elder brother while bowing down: 34.
Bharata said: "O Puṇḍarīka of great intelligence, by the grace of this holy ford, Puṣkara, even though I am a sinner, I have attained residence in heaven. (35)
"O brother, although you know my cruel deed, nevertheless I shall tell you something today that is unknown to you. (36)
Just as that house was consumed along with Amita by me, while possessed by Aprabhāvatī, so too was abundant wealth squandered for the sake of wine.
Whatever was lost by me at gambling, whatever was acquired through the act of theft, and whatever remains of Śambhu’s offerings (nirmālya) were consumed by me on the night of Śivarātri. (38)
"O Puṇḍarīka, you know that this deed was committed by me, for which reason the Brahmin named Jebuka was insulted by you. (39)
O brother, that deed which I performed when you had gone to the Godāvarī is not known to you; oh, I shall tell it to you as well. 40.
When you had departed, having overcome the side of the clouds, I then heard from the people in the world these words, difficult for the heart to bear: "Hari has gone. (41)
Summoned by his maternal uncle to give the wealth of Puṇḍarīka,
he then killed his own brother and brought back that wealth.
"I shall take the abundant wealth offered by the Mālava king;
with that great fortune, I will satisfy Prabhāvatī. (43)
"I play at dice with those skilled in the art according to my own will;
having reflected thus, I have remained here, blocking your path. (44)
"O high-minded one, having killed you and seized much wealth, I have surpassed all in riches;
O brother, I have obtained this from some caravan that arrived. (45)
O Great-minded One, while I was fast asleep there at night among the merchants,
a certain thief then [arrived] at midnight to [steal] the wealth of the merchants.
Having entered there into a caravan crowded with people in order to steal, that thief, having taken some wealth, fled;
his servants immediately pursued him while shouting aloud. (47)
The servants said:
"Seize him! Seize this thief! He flees with great haste, having stolen much wealth from the midst of many of us. (48)
Bharata said:
Having heard those words of theirs, which were being praised daily before me, O brother, I ran forth suddenly with the desire to seize them. 49.
Then, having recognized him as the merchant's servant and his protector,
they all, with swords in hand, swiftly attacked him who was armed with a sword.
Among them, a certain excellent twice-born man, claiming "I am a Brahmin," was struck by me,
a most sinful person, with a sharp-edged sword.
I was killed by those servants of the merchants who were as sharp as sword-edges;
the merchants departed at dawn for their own native land. (52)
Then you arrived here and saw me, who was gasping for breath, my body smeared with flowing blood, and unconscious from the delusion of agony. (53)
"O brother, that for which I have come has been told to you;
I have also explained how I met with an untimely death."
Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter [218] in the Kālindī-māhātmya of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(219) The two hundred and nineteenth chapter.
Nārada said:

Having heard these words of his, the high-minded Puṇḍarīka spoke to that kinsman in the hearing of his own companions: 1. Having heard these words of his, the high-minded Puṇḍarīka spoke to that kinsman in the hearing of his own companions: 1.
Puṇḍarīka said: "By what merit did death occur for Bharata at this sacred ford?
If you know it, tell me; your sin is indeed well known. (2)
Bharata said:
"O Puṇḍarīka, listen to this which I shall relate before you;
this meritorious gift of a holy ford (tīrtha) was performed here in this very birth. (3)
Once, having won wealth and returning to my own home,
I saw a dead child, the helpless son of one who had died, lying in the marketplace.
Having placed that most excellent [body] upon my head and brought it to the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā,
I adorned it with garments and other offerings, and performed the funeral rites, beginning with cremation.
All the wealth acquired through gambling has been spent by me;
by that merit, this auspicious sacred ford has been attained by me.
Perform the consecration of my body, beginning with cremation.
Śrī Nārada said: O King, although Bharata was a sinner, once the purificatory rites were performed,
he went to heaven by the grace of this Puṣkara tīrtha.
Just as Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, dwells for one month in the abode of Puṇḍarīka.

Listen now to how, by the grace of this sacred ford, that righteous-souled one attained the supreme goal; having witnessed Bharata’s attainment of the highest state at this very tīrtha, my heart considers this place to be the granter of all desires.
Thereupon, Puṇḍarīka, who was exceedingly eager and wise,
[prayed that] Hari might dwell in his house during the month of Māgha in His own form.
O best of kings, having thus bathed at this sacred ford that bestows all goals, Puṇḍarīka returned to his own home without any further desire.
He told his kinsmen that his brother had died;
they too, their intellects veiled by illusion, fell into grief upon hearing this. (12)
Then Puṇḍarīka, performing his own domestic duties within his home, dwelt there in great bliss, thinking: "Hari will come here for the sake of ascetic penance."
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, he celebrated a supreme festival, thinking:
"Tomorrow, Hari will certainly come to my house. (14)
By sprinkling sandalwood water and by smearing it with cow dung,
he prepared the sacrificial altar with a square of pearl powder.
He fed two hundred Brahmins with various kinds of food and gratified them with abundant sacrificial fees. ||16||
Accompanied by his kinsmen, he likewise performed a night vigil, singing with sweet-voiced singers skilled in various musical instruments.
Then, at dawn, having dismissed all those singers and others,
he sat down within his house, longing for the arrival of Govinda.
Then, having turned his own vehicle back from near the house,
he entered the interior of the residence in order to fulfill the desire of his kinsmen.
O King, seeing that Mādhava had arrived accompanied by Puṇḍarīka,
he rose quickly from his seat and bowed his head to him.
And that righteous-souled one, finding bliss in the sight of Govinda, honored him with offerings such as arghya and seated him upon a seat. ||21||
Puṇḍarīka said:
You have very clearly performed that which destroys both existence and non-existence;
meanwhile, you who maintain the stability of the world must remain here for Viṣṇu.
This shall continue until the completion of his penance, during which time you and your servants must dwell there to attend upon him. (23)
In that regard, O Lord, Vaikuṇṭha is indeed free from all defects;
its deeds within its abode are worthy of being described by the virtuous.
It has been heard that Hari dwells there with Sanmukha and others;
by their words, his heart was captivated by that beautiful form. (25)
O Lord, those alone are truly virtuous who attribute virtues to your ears; for it is through their service that your heart becomes inclined toward you.
O Lord of Lakṣmī, those alone are truly virtuous whose minds are equal toward both enemy and friend. (27)
Indeed, they alone are truly virtuous who do not allow their minds to become disturbed even when there is a cause for such change, amidst both gain and loss. (28)
"Undoubtedly, they alone are truly virtuous who are devoted to the Lord of Lakṣmī;
where you are, there the virtuous are, and where the virtuous are, there you are.
Therefore, O Blessed One, recognizing me as a virtuous man, please dwell in my house during this month of Māgha. (29)
Nārada said:
Having heard those words of Puṇḍarīka, Mādhava spoke these words, illuminating the quarters with his splendor.
The Blessed Lord said:
O high-minded one, you are the best of the virtuous on this earth,
since you have bathed at this holy ford while in My company.
"Arise, O twice-born one, and perform your bath in the waters of the Ganges during Māgha!
On the full moon day of Māgha, I shall bathe you at Puṣkara. (32)
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing for the entire month of Māgha at Prayāga, all of that is attained by bathing for a single day at the Puṣkara tīrtha. 33.
Nārada said:
Thus addressed by Murāri,
O chief of Brahmins, Puṇḍarīka performed his bath in the waters of the Gaṅgā when the sun had slightly risen.
He worshipped the lotus-eyed Lord, who was like a white lotus,
with blossoming *tulasī* flowers, barley, saffron, and sandalwood paste.
With incense made of agaru and guggulu, he performs the lustration (nīrājana) of the Lord of Ramā,
who is dark as a cloud, with five camphor lamps while smiling.
Having fed the Teacher of the World with foods consisting of the four kinds of delicacies,
some immortals fanned him as he slept upon his jeweled couch.
He offered a footstool with wheels for the Lord of Ramā, as well as a betel-roll prepared with camphor. ||38||
Then, as the Lord of Śrī was binding his turban, the best of Brahmins stood before him,
holding up a mirror with his hand.
Thus, while he was dwelling in his own home,
a certain Brahmin performed worship for him and spent the entire month of Māgha in his company.
Then, at the conclusion of the month of Māgha on the full moon day, he saw Tārkṣya standing before him, arrived there by the mere act of being remembered by the Lord of Ramā.
Seeing him, the lotus-eyed Lord spoke to Puṇḍarīka.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of the twice-born, listen to the words that I shall speak to you. (42)
At the sacred ford of Puṣkara located in Indraprastha, I stayed for one month and gave [this gift] for the sake of bathing there by chance. ||43||
O high-minded one, having climbed this tree today, I have endured great exhaustion;
therefore, let us go to that very Prati-puṣkara, the crest-jewel of all sacred fords.
O twice-born one, if you so desire, I shall grant you whatever you wish from that bestower of the four goals of life, for I am under its control.
Where even a sinful brother, like Bharata, has gone to heaven upon death—desiring the bliss of heaven—what else remains to be described of him? (46)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to the best of Brahmins and the most excellent of kings,
the lord of gods placed the king of birds upon his vehicle and proceeded to the best of all sacred fords.
From the body of Puṇḍarīka, that light, together with his vital breath,
emerged and entered the abode of Govinda.
Thus, O King, having gone to Indraprastha at this Puṣkara-tīrtha, Puṇḍarīka attained union with the Lord through his bath. 49.
Thus, O King, Govinda also dwelt happily for one month in that house, following the wishes of the holy man, like his own kinsman.
Who indeed is able to describe the greatness of Puṣkara?
I have described only ten millionth part of it as it exists at Śakraprastha.
O King, by hearing of its greatness with faith, a person obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice; indeed, one also gains it by reciting it.

Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Puṣkara," within the *Kālindī-māhātmya* of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, in the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||219||
(220) The Two Hundred and Twentieth Chapter.
Nārada said:
In your presence, O Śiva, king of holy fords, I shall describe with faith to you the highly meritorious majesty of Prayāga. ||1||
Once, the world-renowned Gandharva Viśvāvasu, the protector of the earth,
went to Mount Sumeru to sing in the assembly of Brahmā.
There, King Viśvāvasu beheld the best of gods seated upon a magnificent throne, attended by hosts of deities,
near the seat of Brahmā. O King, he was seated upon an excellent seat.
He beheld Indraprastha, like a second Lord of the World on earth. ||4||
O King, at Surarājatīrtha and Rājendra-prastha,
he saw those two performing the fanning of his head with chowries.
O Lord of the Earth, other sacred fords belonging to different deities, situated far from those two,
were seen by him with their palms joined in reverence.
In their presence, the Gaurāṅga gāndharva melody, the most excellent of ragas,
went to Satyaloka along with the holy pilgrimage sites after the gods had been dismissed.
Then the wise Viśvāvasu, O king of kings, having beheld the majesty of that sacred ford at Indraprastha, exclaimed "Hā hā! and spoke as follows: ||8||
Viśvāvasu said: O tiger among Gandharvas, this most wonderful sacred ford (tīrtha) named Indraprastha is, within this ocean of worldly existence, the king among all sacred fords.
Brahmā, the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, whose lotus-feet are the refuge for the hosts of gods and demons,
sat upon a seat close to his own throne.
Even the king of holy places (Prayāga), standing behind him with a fly-whisk over his head, has now become like a servant; what then can be said of other holy sites?
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist upon the earth that bestow the fruits of the three aims of life (trivarga),
this sacred ford of Indraprastha bestows the fruits of all four aims of life (caturvarga).
O Dhruva, even with the remainder of your life, it would not be possible for you to praise the great qualities of such holy places situated here as these, which are endowed with such virtues. (13)
Nārada said:
O King, having thus beheld the splendor of Indraprastha, the wise Viśvāvasu went to his abode, which is purifying and grants all desires.
Just as among all the gods Śakra, the lord of Śacī, is the most excellent, so too among all sacred fords (tīrthas), this Prayāga is the most excellent. 15.
Therefore, O Great King, this Śakraprastha is even more excellent; for within it is seen this Prayāga, O King. (16)
O King, listen to what happened there at the city of Āhiṣmatī on the banks of the river Narmadā concerning the courtesan Mohinī.
There lived a courtesan named Mohinī, who possessed great wealth, was endowed with beauty and youth, and was highly proficient in dancing and singing. (18)
Driven by greed for wealth, she committed many sins;
she committed seven murders of Brahmins and killed many servants. (19)
And by that sinful woman, many of their fetuses were caused to fall;
thus she spent her youth in evil deeds. (20)
Then, after some time, old age overcame that body;
her frame seized by decrepitude, she ceased to have any longing for sense-objects.
O King, the minds of young men are not like a wheel;
they do not trust anyone with their own wealth acquired through sinful means. (22)
He did not eat himself what was not given, nor did he ever deposit anything anywhere;
once, however, at midnight, he awoke and reflected thus: [23]
When I have died, this wealth acquired by sinful means will lead me to that terrible and most dreadful hell. (24)
Their maidservants and their husbands shall enjoy my wealth;
why then am I not provided with a good rebirth by myself right now? (25)
Having thus reflected and established the highest resolve for the practice of dharma,
he constructed gardens, lakes, ponds, wells, and temples.
O Great King, she established water-stations all around the city for the sake of travelers during the summer heat, and she also gave food to them.
She established a dharma-śālā near her own residence for the lodging of travelers from foreign lands,
and she further provided them with excellent food.
While these phenomena were thus proceeding, she who was deluded by worldly existence became afflicted with fever at one time, thinking thus: (29)
Although much wealth has been spent by us for the sake of the Dharma, nevertheless, there remains an abundance of gold, silver, and other riches. (30)
"I shall give this to the Vedic scholars through my knowledge," he thought;
having thus reflected, O twice-born ones of the city, he summoned Mohinī.
O protector of the earth, having learned that they had not arrived because of the terrible reception [of their guest],
he then divided that wealth of his into two portions.
O King, one portion was given to the indifferent women and another to those from foreign lands;
she herself, however, became destitute, O Sāttvat, though she was enchanting.
Realizing that death has arrived in such a manner, some depart;
having abandoned their wealth and taken it with them, they go wherever they please. (34)
Thinking thus, when she has been freed from the fever, she will surely take back whatever wealth was given at that time for her benefit. (35)
Then, O lord of the earth, after [the tree] had been struck eighteen times with a thick sala-wood mallet,
he became free from fever at the remainder of his own lifespan.
O Lord of the Earth, she, who had no friend other than her single aged cow,
tirelessly attended to him with wholesome food and other necessities.
After some days, she gave birth to a full-grown calf;
out of shame, we used to eat in the house of that old cow. (38)
"I have remained here happily until now, but today suffering has arrived;
because of poverty I must depart from here"—thinking thus, he went elsewhere. (39)
O King, that enchanting woman goes along with thieves who carry away her wealth.
Thinking thus, he seized the one whose [enemies] had been destroyed and returned to his own house.
O King, having failed to obtain wealth from her, she was abandoned by highway robbers while still gasping for breath in that very forest.
Or rather, O King, a certain Vaikhānasa ascetic, carrying a water-pot filled with the water of this Prayāga, arrived here in the forest. 42.
Then, O King, seeing her fallen with her body mangled by weapons, she was thus entreating him for the gift of life from the palm of his hand: 43.
The Vaikhānasa said:
Who are you, whose body has been wounded by various weapons?
For what purpose have you come alone to this desolate forest? (44)
This [place] at the auspicious waters of Prayāga, situated within Indraprastha, has been brought here by some rise of fortune out of a desire to do what is pleasing. (45)
Having been addressed thus by him, she was unable to speak; she opened her mouth with the desire:
"May I become his chief queen to drink that water. (46)
Then, O King, when that Prayāga had been thrown into the mouth of the well,
that enchanting courtesan gave up her life.
At the time of her departure from life, she chose the status of queen for me;
therefore, I became the queen of Vīravarmā of Rāḍhīva. (48)
O King, through drinking the water of the holy ford at the house of the lord of Kerala, which was gathered together, he became endowed with noble lineage, character, wealth, and sovereignty. 49.
Then the lotus-eyed lady bore him, who was golden-hued and possessed of all limbs;
therefore, his father gave him the name Hema. ||50||
Once, adorned with golden garments and golden ornaments,
she went to the house of her friend Kalā, the daughter of a minister.
There, O King, she was bathed with oil of *yāvaka* and fed various kinds of food, and then she sat down upon an excellent seat.
Her hair-braid was entwined with flowers, she was adorned with a thin silk garment dyed with lac,
and she spoke to Kalā while holding a betel-roll in her mouth.
Hemāṅgī said:
"O you who speak with the sweet voice of a cuckoo, show me that wonderful thing which you mentioned as being in the house. (54)

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Indraprastha," in the *Kālindī-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the fifty-five thousand verse compendium of the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*. ||220|| ||cha||
(221) The two hundred and twenty-first chapter.
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by that queen, the wife of King Sākalārāja,
she brought a golden crown from her own treasury and placed it before him.
He said, "O Great King, there is a great wonder concerning this wife of yours; O Queen, there is a book here, and indeed, there are paintings within it. (2)
Open it and see what is within this book;
surely the mind will find delight there upon beholding the paintings. (3)
Having spoken thus, he opened the mouth of the king’s wife;
then, with his hand, he took up the manuscript situated there within the vessel.
There he surveyed briefly the incarnations;
first the terrestrial globe, which is fifty crores of yojanas in extent.
There, the earth is seen joined with the letter *aṃ* and joined with the letter *tha*;
between these two is the salt-water ocean and the Lokāloka mountain. (6)
Then, O Great-Minded One, having seen the seven continents surrounded by the seven oceans, [he saw] the rivers, mountains, and regions within them.
She beheld this land of Bhārata,
and she gazed upon the rivers, chief among them the Yamunā and the Jāhnavī, which are dear to the lord of the earth.
O King, that highly fortunate one beheld this auspicious Indraprastha situated on the bank of the Yamunā, O monarch, along with the sacred ford of Vraja.
Having seen this Prayāga, a sacred ford created by Brahmā, at this place,
that wise woman remembered the karma she had performed in a previous birth.
Then, rising up silently, she went quickly to her own home;
having resolved, "I shall not eat from now on until I have set out for a sacred ford," she departed.
On that very day, the virtuous beloved spoke thus to Vīravarman, who was seated beside her on the golden couch and was dear to her as her own life: "This is the king of sacred fords (Tīrtharāja)."
Hemāṅgī said:
"O Lord of my life, listen to my words which bestow righteousness; O highly fortunate one, act upon them quickly, and they shall be fulfilled. (13)
Formerly, during my youth, I was a deluded courtesan who committed many sins; it was only in old age that a sense for dharma arose within me.
"O King, wealth acquired through evil was spent by me according to dharma;
yet when I departed from my own city, O King, I was destitute. (15)
Then, in that desolate forest, thieves struck us—those tormented by useless poverty, out of a desire to seize our wealth through sin. (16)
Seeing me lying there, wounded by a cold weapon, gasping for breath and deprived of consciousness, the thieves abandoned me and departed with their hopes shattered. (17)
Then a certain Vaikhānasa, carrying water from Prayāga, arrived there in that forest as if he were traveling toward Indraprastha. ||18||
Seeing me fallen there in such a state, that ascetic asked: "Who are you? From where? For what purpose have you been brought here? (19)
At that time, I said nothing at all; I merely requested merit.
Therefore, he placed it in my mouth, and then I abandoned my body.
O Lord, having heard that at the time of the departure of life this [mantra] wards off all obstacles and grants all desires, the queen said, "I shall become [your] wife. (21)
O King, by the grace of that holy ford (tīrtha), I have become the mistress of your house, born from a noble family and endowed with excellent conduct and character. (22)
O King, I now desire to see Prayāga, the king of sacred fords, which grants all desires, located at Śakraprastha along with you. (23)
"O King, O Lord, when I set out for the king of holy places (Prayāga), then I shall eat food"—thus was the wager established. (24)
The king said:
"O lady with tremulous eyes, how may I know that this is what you have said? O auspicious one, make it certain; I shall do as you have told me. (25)
Nārada said:
When the king had spoken thus, there was suddenly a voice from the sky.
The celestial voice said:
"O King, what has been spoken by this wife of yours is true."
At Prayāga, the preeminent among sacred fords, situated in the meritorious Indraprastha—
go there and perform your ablutions, and you shall obtain whatever you desire.
Nārada said:
Having heard that voice arising from the sky,
the king then prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and said, "I bow to its speaker."
Then, having summoned his minister and entrusted the kingdom to him there,
he ascended a chariot together with her and went to that most excellent of sacred fords.
After several days, the king arrived here together with Hemāṅgī;
accompanied by his wife, he offered milk at the king of holy places (Prayāga).
O Kāmadā, may those two lords bathe here at this auspicious tīrtha;
by means of this very body, may I attain Vaikuṇṭha at Prayāga. ||31||
O King, while they were merely bathing out of mutual desire,
two tigers among the gods arrived there on their swift vehicles, I and the bird-god [Garuḍa].
Beholding the two who had arrived, King Vīravarman bowed his head to the two gods and,
with a one-pointed mind, offered praise.
The king said:
"Obeisance to you two, tigers among gods, who bear dark and ruddy bodies, are clothed in silken garments, and possess golden armlets that shine from afar. (34)
Salutations to You two, whose natures are dominated by *rajas* and *sattva*, who are the causes of the maintenance and creation of all things moving and unmoving;
Lords of the wonderful worlds Vaikuṇṭha and Satya, possessing four and two arms respectively, and mounted upon the king of birds (Garuḍa).

I bow my head with true devotion to those whose lotus feet are worshipped by the gods, who bestow both liberation and worldly enjoyment upon people according to their state—whether they possess passion or have attained dispassion. (36)
Even Govinda, the foremost of the gods, does not fully know your true nature;
for you are beyond primordial matter (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa), remaining far removed from both mind and speech.

Blessed is that man in this world who, having contemplated this entire universe as momentary within the Supreme Self, with a mind focused on nothing else, worships the lotus feet of Yours, which are the object of veneration for the hosts of sages. (38)
This service of your feet is a sacred ford (tīrtha) that is difficult to attain;
for people who worship you, it bestows the fruit of their desired goals. (39)
Nevertheless, these two should be cultivated for the sake of liberation and not for the attainment of anything else; he who cultivates them with a desire for something else is indeed a fool. (40)
The virtuous, having served that Lord and this sacred ford which bestows liberation, do not desire anything else;
having transcended all worlds, they seek only the conquest of birth. 41.
Nārada said:
O King, when the lord of the earth had thus praised the Lord of the Gods, the master of the worlds, he stood still; at that moment, Hiraṇyākṣa spoke.

O Lord of Padmā, O lotus-petal-eyed one, O Brahmā, O Guru of Bhāratī seated upon the formidable throne! Salutations to you both; may you be gracious toward this wretched-minded one and deliver him from the ocean of worldly existence. (43)
"O Lord, by the grace of this sacred ford, I have become your queen;
I have obtained the vision of you two, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (44)
"O you two who know the minds of all, grant us that which is desired in our hearts; for at the time of our bath, we have performed that which is ultimate. (45)
Thus, having been praised by both of them, those two preeminent among gods, with faces beaming with favor, spoke these words to the lords of the earth: 46.
Hari and Brahmā said:
"O Hemā, you are blessed, since this husband of yours has been delivered by you from this state, even though his mind was attached to the pleasures of sovereignty through this union. (47)
For kings who are attached to sense-objects, such liberation as this is difficult to attain;
yet it has arisen for your husband through the grace of this sacred ford (tīrtha). 48.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus and gazed upon Garuḍa, the foremost of birds, those two best of gods departed for Satyaloka, O lord of men. 49.
There, O King, they were all duly honored by Brahmā;
and in accordance with his wish, they remained for a single moment.
Then, O King, Hari, having mounted Garuḍa together with those two consorts, went to the glorious Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus has been narrated to you, O King, the majesty of the king of holy places (Tīrtharāja),
which is meritorious, destructive of all sins, conducive to fame, and bestowing sons.
The person who would constantly hear this and also recite it shall go to the desired abode; this which has been spoken by me is the truth. (53)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Prayāga," within the "Glorification of Indraprastha" in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||221|| ||cha||
(222) Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Two.
Nārada said:
Listen, O King Śibi, as I describe before you the supreme majesty of Kāśī, which is meritorious, conducive to fame, and bestows long life. (1)
O King, in ancient times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a single tree named Śiṃśapā on the banks of the Indraprastha at Kāśī.
There, a female owl had built her nest in a tree;
beneath it, a great serpent dwelt together within a hollow.
Once, having deposited two eggs in his nest, that crow’s wife went away somewhere and did not return to her own nest.
O Lord of the Earth, that very crow himself, guarding his two eggs,
sat high upon that same Śiṃśapā tree.
Then once,
O King, a great whirlwind arose at night and uprooted the Śiṃśapā tree, even though it was very firm.
As the thunderbolt was being hurled down by Vātyāyana,
the crow and the serpent were crushed upon the surface of the earth and their lives departed.
Having become three divine cows, they uttered a curse;
then, having ascended three celestial chariots, the crows and others went to the abode of the Lord of Śrī.
Śibi said:
"O divine sage Nārada, tell me everything: by what merit were those three cities, which bestow liberation, previously obtained by them?"
Nārada said: There was a Brāhmaṇa named Śravaṇa from the region of Kurujāṅgala;
his wife was named Kuḍā, and he had a brother named Kuraṇṭaka.
Because he was constantly one who ate without bathing, and because he was greedy for eating mouthfuls of delicious food, Śravaṇa, due to that fault, became a village crow. (11)
His brother, Kuraṇṭaka, was a fierce atheist;
he was a destroyer of the path of the Śruti and Smṛti, and a reviler of the deities. ||12||
Due to that fault, he indeed became Kālakuṇḍalī;
and she, the daughter of Kuṇḍaśravaṇa, became a woman, partaking of the defects of both.
Therefore, having abandoned her state as an immobile being, she became dependent on both.
O King, this account of her conduct in her previous birth has been told to you. 14.
Henceforth, O King, I shall proclaim the merit by which these three attained that beautiful city of Kāśī, belonging to the Lord of the Universe. 15.
Then, having returned from another village to his own home,
he saw a milch cow of a certain traveler sunk in a well.
Urged by him, the two of them observed and effected his rescue;
having heard what was said by them, Kuṇḍa exclaimed, "Excellent! (sādhu).
Having attained the rare death through the merit of that [pilgrimage],
they ascended to Vaikuṇṭha at Kāśī, situated on the banks of Indraprastha.
O King, although this city belongs to Maheshvara of Kashi,
nevertheless, a living being who dies here shall find happiness in Vaikuntha, the abode of Hari.
O King, this supreme majesty of Kāśī has been recounted to you. What else do you wish to hear? Tell me what remains to be known. 20.
Śibi said:
"O Sage, you have mentioned the three sacred fields of Maheśa:
Kāśī, Śivakāñcī, and likewise Gokarṇa as the supreme. (21)
O great sage, the greatness of one [place] has been described by you; now let the greatness of Gokarṇa, Śivakāñcī, and Cyavana be told, if it exists.
Nārada said:
Gokarṇa is a purely Śaiva holy place (kṣetra) that is supremely purifying.
O King, a man who dies there becomes Śiva; of this there is no doubt. (23)
If a living being should die there on land, in water,
or in the sky, then Śiva, having manifested upon the peak of Kailāsa, sports there.
O King, for one who dies here at the sacred site of Gokarṇa, there shall be no rebirth;
he will eventually attain liberation together with Śiva.
O high-minded one, O Lord, I shall describe the greatness of this Gokarṇa, which I have heard from the mouth of Brahmā.
Situated at a distance of one gavyūti from Prayāga and near the Gurus Tīrtha, this mountain which is seen here is a boundary-mountain of auspicious appearance. (27)
There was a very cruel Bhilla named Ika-Karkaṭa;
his wife, named Jarā, killed five husbands. (28)
Then, having heard [the news] from his sister, he prepared the sixth sweetmeat, which was mixed with the poison of old age, in order to kill her. ||29||
O King, at the very sight of her, that most cruel crab, along with the high-souled Bhilla, began to kill the young girl. (30)
When the Bhilla chief arrived with sword in hand for the purpose of killing him, she,
having learned of his intent to slay her husband, approached him.
Frightened and desiring to save her own life, she fled into the forest;
O Lord of the Earth, she was pursued by that Arkakaṭa.
Here, at the Gokarṇa Tīrtha, having taken up a sword in his hand,
he severed his head with that sword and cast his body into the water.
He returned to his own abode from that Gokarṇa Tīrtha;
there at Gokarṇa, Sājarā met her end through her sins.
O King, on the peak of Kailāsa, I became a companion to Pārvatī;
thus have I related to you this majesty of Gokarṇa. (35)
O Lord, I shall describe to you the sacred and purifying majesty of Śivakāñcī, which is situated on the banks of Indraprastha. (36)
That supreme state was declared by Aṅga to Karṇeya;
herein, the illustrious Mahādeva [spoke] to Viṣṇu, the lord of all the gods. 37.
Having propitiated him, he attained the status of the king of devotees and authentic knowledge.
Therefore, we are all the sons of that Great Lord, Brahmā. (38)
We constantly propitiate [the Lord] out of a desire for true devotion and knowledge;
here, O King, Bāṇāsura propitiated Maheśvara. (39)
Desiring to attain the status of his attendant, he remained without food for a hundred years;
pleased with him, the Blessed One granted him his own status as an attendant.
And he himself was always its city guardian;
O King, this city formerly belonged to the high-souled Viṣṇu.
Formerly, Viṣṇu, pleased by his ascetic penance, granted a boon to him;
in this regard, there is one great and wondrous event from the past.
O King, just as that Brahmin who was a devotee of Śiva attained Vaikuṇṭha,
there was once a certain unrighteous Brahmin named Heraṃba.
Always delighting in the worship of Śiva through body, mind, and speech,
that highly fortunate one once wandered among the sacred shrines of Śiva.
O King, a devotee of Śiva, having come here to Śivakañcyā, this wise man did not abandon this charming woman. 45.
Afterwards, he gave up his life there within the waters of that lake;
there, the hosts of Śrī Mahādeva [honored] that best of Brahmins.
Having led Mount Kailāsa, they proceeded according to his command;
then, in the midst of their journey, the hosts of Gaṇas arrived from Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Hari.
As they endeavored to seize that best of the twice-born by force, a great battle ensued between those hosts and Hari and Śarva. 48.
In that battle, some achieved victory while others suffered defeat;
then Viṣṇu, seated upon Garuḍa, arrived there from Vaikuṇṭha.
From Kailāsa, Maheśa, the sustainer of the three worlds, mounted upon his bull, and [Viṣṇu]—
those two lords of the universe, having looked at each other with joy, smiled.
Behold that great battle waged in the sky itself by the hosts;
then Viṣṇu [withdrew] his own hosts and those of Śiva from the celestial combat.
Having restrained the bird and placed him upon his back, Mādhava went to the abode of Śiva,
accompanied by Śiva and his own attendants.
Proceeding on the path, the illustrious one, praised and honored by the thirty gods,
went forth and entered that mountain with Mahādeva leading the way.
Then, while demonstrating its beauty to that brahmin,
[the mountain] was honored by Mahādeva and departed from that Kailāsa.
Then Mādhava went to Vaikuṇṭha through supreme devotion;
that illustrious twice-born man also [went there] by the grace of this sacred ford.
Having obtained the sight of Govinda in the presence of Hara, he rejoiced. O King, this majesty of Śiva’s grace has been recounted to you. May there be prosperity. 56.
Listen with a well-concentrated mind to that which is named Tīrthasaptaka;
this holy site, O Great King, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. (57)
O King, through seeing, touching, meditating upon, or even remembering it,
this [practice] was performed by the great sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others.
O King, we two remained there performing great austerities for the sake of creation;
and the righteous Marīci also performed his ritual ablutions for the sake of obtaining a son.
There, the highly fortunate Atri obtained an excellent son, Kaśyapa; there, too, he satisfied the preeminent gods through his ascetic penance.
There, by the grace of this holy place (tīrtha), that righteous-souled one obtained the Soma and Durvāsas whom he had received from them through the power of his speech.
From that lineage, the twice-born obtained sons through their speech;
Pulaha also obtained a son who was even more endowed with virtuous qualities.
O King, it was here at this very holy site that Agastya was born in former times through immersion;
and here at this same tirtha, a son was obtained by Pulastya while he was performing austerities.
The highly fortunate Kubera was he who was the friend of the Lord of Umā;
and from Kratu were born thousands of Ālakhilyas.
By the grace of this sacred ford (tīrtha), all these indeed became perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas);
even Vasiṣṭha, the great ascetic, obtained sons such as Rajas and the others.
O tiger among kings, his greatness has been described as sevenfold;
furthermore, O lord of the earth, there are many other sacred fords (tīrthas) as well.

O King, even with millions of years, or even with infinite time, the majesty of those [shrines] such as Kapilāśrama, Kedāra, Prabhāsa, and others cannot be fully described by me; how much less so by those like me? (67)
Saubhari said:
Having spoken thus, Nārada, the best of sages and the foremost among ascetics,
went through the sky toward Śiva while chanting the virtues of Nārāyaṇa.
O King, having heard from the mouth of the sage the splendor of Śakraprastha, the capital of Śibi Auśīnara, he considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites at Indraprastha, that lord of the earth performed all the customary honors and departed for his own city.
O Lord, this majesty of Indraprastha, which purifies all people, has been described by me to you as the sacred site on the bank of the Yamunā. (71)
O King of kings, in the Kali age, those devoid of faith will show no respect for Indraprastha, the crest-jewel of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Whatever fruit arises from hearing the eighteen Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata, that same fruit is produced by [hearing] the Mahimnaḥ-stotra at Indraprastha. ||73||

Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing a hundred thousand times during the month of Māgha at the time of dawn, that same fruit shall be attained by hearing the majesty of this [text] with faith. (74)
O Lord of the Earth, whoever listens with faith to its greatness has thereby gratified the ancestors, the gods, and likewise the sages. (75)
Whatever fruit is obtained through the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, Pārāka, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such vows, that same fruit arises from hearing the majesty of this [teaching] even without faith. (76)
O Lord of the Earth, whatever fruit results from all the sacrifices, such as the Aśvamedha and others, that same fruit arises from hearing the majesty of this [text] with faith. (77)
Sūta said:
Having thus heard from Śaunaka and Saubhari the greatness of Indraprastha, King Yudhiṣṭhira departed for the city of Hastināpura.
Then, having disciplined his brothers with Duryodhana at their head,
he went to the holy Indraprastha with the desire to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having come from Dvārakā to Govinda, the family deity,
that lord of the earth performed the Rājasūya sacrifice for him.
Thinking, "This sacred ford (tīrtha) bestows liberation even upon one who has uttered a curse," Hari slew Śiśupāla there.
Śiśupāla also, by dying at that very sacred site, attained union (sāyujya) with Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of all goals, upon the earth. 82.
Where Śiśupāla was slain and where the two performed [the rites], there Bhīma fashioned a very extensive pool with his mace. ||83||
The Bhīmakuṇḍa, known as the purifier of the earth, came into being on the surface of the ground half a gavyūti to the south of the Kālindī. (84)
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing in the Kālindī at Indraprastha, that same fruit is produced there in that pool; of this there is no doubt. ||85||
Sūta said:

A living being who resides in a place that is not a sacred field (akṣetra) should, year after year, seek forgiveness for his own offenses through religious duties such as circumambulation and other rites toward that [true] field. ||86||
Furthermore, the man who circumambulates [the earth] every year shall not be tainted by the faults arising from the transgressions of the fields, nor by sinful deeds. ||87||
One who does not perform circumambulation does not attain the perfection of the sacred field;
therefore, those seeking the fruit [of their actions] should offer circumambulation at the holy site.
Chanting the name of Hari while performing circumambulation,
one obtains at every step the fruit arising from the gift of a Kapila cow.
The fortunate man who performs a circumambulation of Śakraprastha on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra is liberated from all sins. (90)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Seven Tīrthas— Indraprastha, Kāśī, Gokarṇa, Śivaka, Cīta, Bhīmakuṇḍa, and others," in the *Kālindī-māhātmya* of the Uttara-khaṇḍa within the *Śrī-Pādma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. || 222 || ||cha||
(223) Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Three. Śaunaka said:
O highly fortunate son of the charioteer, you are truly wise;
please grant us, who are deeply immersed in distress, a flood of nectar. (1)
O holy one, please instruct us on that mantra which delivers one from this world, which is pure in its essence, and of which the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is composed. (2)
Sūta said: Listen, O Śaunaka, I shall declare this most wonderful jewel of a mantra,
which was spoken by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha to Dilīpa.
Once, however, Dilīpa, having prostrated before his preceptor Vasiṣṭha, that tiger among the twice-born, asked this very same question as you have.
Dilīpa said:
O Blessed One, you have explained all duties in their particular details—
the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life, as well as the constant, occasional, and ritual actions.
The duties of kings, sacrifices, pilgrimages, gifts, vows, and so forth—
O best of sages, these consist of the knowledge derived from scripture and bestow the enjoyment of imperishable heaven.
Now I desire to hear of the eternal path to liberation;
O Brahmin, it behoves you to tell me that by which I may go, for this is my good fortune. (7)
What mantra is the sole medicine for the disease of existence among all mantras?
Who else is the supreme bestower of liberation for all embodied beings? (8)
Because of the affection and reverence [he feels] toward me, due to my being endowed with that very same designation. ||9||
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, you have asked well, you who desire the welfare of all the worlds. I shall speak of one supreme secret that delivers one from the cycle of worldly existence.
In ancient times, all the auspicious great sages, devoted to sacrifice and charity,
questioned Nārada, the son of Brahmā and the best of munis.
The great sages said:
"O Blessed One, by what mantra shall we go to the supreme state?
Tell us that, O highly fortunate one; it behoves you to show us your favor. (12)
Nārada said: In ancient times, all the yogis, headed by Sanaka, questioned the Grandfather (Brahmā) regarding that single path to liberation which is so difficult to attain.
Brahmā said:
"Listen, all you yogis, to this wonderful secret."
Neither all the gods nor the sages whose wealth is austerity know [this];
the immutable Lord Nārāyaṇa himself declared it to me at the beginning of creation. (15)
I worshipped Īśvarī and Sahadevī perfectly;
thereupon, the blessed and imperishable Nārāyaṇa was pleased with me. (16)
We gave to him the Prājāpatya sacrifice, all the knowledge born of the Vedas, and the illuminating mantras, both those that are pervasive and those that are non-pervasive. (17)
Then I spoke to that God, the Ancient Supreme Person:
"O Blessed One, by what mantra is there a crossing over the cycle of worldly existence for men? (18)
Tell me that in its true essence for the benefit of all the world:
what mantra among all mantras is free from the requirement of preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa)? (19)
"By a single recitation, it bestows the supreme state upon men.
The Blessed Lord said: "O highly fortunate one, you have asked well, desiring the welfare of all the worlds. (20)
Therefore, I shall declare this secret to you, by which men may attain me.
Among all these mantras, this jewel of a mantra brings auspiciousness;
by merely remembering it once, it bestows the supreme state. (22)
The placement of the two jewel-mantras, the practice of restraint, taking refuge, and the mantra "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa" bestow all fruits. ||23||
Listen to the enumeration of the jewel of the Name-mantra;
by its mere utterance, I am perpetually and completely satisfied. (24)

Whether he be of noble birth, a householder, an ascetic, or one who has mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas; whether he be devoted to sacrifice and charity, or a visitor to all sacred pilgrimage sites—(25)

One who observes vows, one who speaks untruths, one who is envious, or even one who lacks knowledge—such a person is not qualified for the recitation of mantras; one should avoid him with great effort.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, Śūdras, and others as well—all these are qualified for this, provided they are my devotees. (27)
This supreme mantra should be spoken for those who have no other refuge, likewise for those who serve no other, and for those who practice no other. (28)
Bestowing fruit immediately upon those who are distressed, this [practice], even when performed but once, prevents rebirth in another body for living beings, even those who are arrogant. (29)
Whether one is afflicted by suffering, seeking knowledge, desiring wealth, or even a seeker of wisdom, or even Prajāpati himself—if he seeks refuge in me but once, he shall attain his desires. (30)
This should not be told to one who has not been initiated, nor to one who is not a devotee, nor to one who is arrogant;
nor to an atheist, nor to one who is greedy, nor to one who lacks faith and is averse [to the teaching]. //31//
It should not be spoken to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who has not resided [as a disciple] for a full year;
rather, it should be taught to one who is free from desire and anger, and devoid of pride and greed.
And to him who serves me with devotion through the yoga of service and alms-gathering,
the unsurpassed jewel of a mantra should be spoken according to the prescribed rule.

The purification of place, time, and so forth, as well as the removal of enemies, friends, and others; the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), mudrās, and the like, together with the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). ||34||
Having a body marked with my wheel-signs, likewise performing worship unto me, having entrusted all actions to me, and being one who has no other refuge but me. (35)
The surrender of all fruits [of action] preceded by great faith, the effort consisting of no other means, and the state of one's own self being "possessing nothing" (akiñcanatva). (36)
One should avoid conversation, salutation, and other such interactions with those who are not Vaiṣṇavas; likewise, one should perform salutation and worship only for those who have no other deity.
These and other such rules have been proclaimed for one who has entered [the path];
the supreme mantra should be imparted to him who is endowed with such qualities as these. (38)
Of that [purification], I am Nārāyaṇa, the eternal sage Viṣṇu;
and I am the deity together with Śrī, an ocean of affection. (39)
The glorious Lord of all worlds is of excellent conduct and likewise fortunate;
he is omniscient, omnipotent, and his desires are always fulfilled. (40)
I am the all-pervading one, the friend of all, an ocean of the nectar of compassion;
I am the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, proclaimed as the supreme deity. (41)
I am the goddess Gāyatrī, consisting of twenty-five syllables;
one should apply the six, seven, six, three, five, two, and six limbs [to the mantra]. (42)
One should meditate upon Him who possesses universal form, whose divine appearance holds the discus, conch, mace, and lotus in His hands, and who never departs from Lakṣmī. 43.

Pure and self-restrained, one should worship Śrī, who dwells on the left [side], along with this jewel of a mantra, using offerings of perfumes and flowers. O Prajāpati, even when worshipped but once with this, I am well-pleased. (44)
Brahmā said:
You have correctly spoken this supreme secret of Anātha;
it is the power of the jewel of mantras that bestows all perfections upon men. 45.
You are the father of all worlds, you are the mother and indeed the guru;
you are the master, the friend, the brother, the refuge, the resort, and the well-wisher.
O Lord of Gods, I am indeed your servant, disciple, and likewise your friend; therefore, O ocean of compassion, you have spoken this supreme teaching to me. 47.
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, please explain the initiation for the jewel of mantras according to the correct procedure and in its entirety. (48)
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, O Vidura, I shall explain the supreme procedure for initiation into the mantra.
First, one should take refuge in a spiritual preceptor (ācārya) for the sake of attaining shelter in Me. 49.
The preceptor should be perfected in the Vedas, a devotee of Viṣṇu, free from envy, knowledgeable in the mantras, devoted to the mantras, always taking refuge in the mantras, and pure. (50)
One who is endowed with the tradition of the virtuous, proficient in the knowledge of Brahman, possessing no other means of accomplishment, and likewise having no other purpose; ||51||
A Brāhmaṇa who is free from passion, devoid of anger and greed,
a teacher of virtuous conduct, desirous of liberation, and a knower of the Supreme Self.
An Ācārya is one who is endowed with such qualities as these, who is impartial toward all and friendly, and who instructs others in right conduct;
he is thus called an Ācārya. ||53||

But that disciple who is dependent upon the teacher, who is instructed in virtuous conduct, and who remains firm in his conduct during that instruction, is described as a true disciple by the virtuous. (54)
One should cause a disciple endowed with such characteristics and possessed of all virtues to study this supreme jewel of mantras according to the prescribed rule. (55)
On the twelfth lunar day, or under the asterism Śravaṇa, or whenever it may be on a day sacred to Viṣṇu,
one should perform the initiation there, provided that the true preceptor is well-pleased.
One should encircle the Sudarśana and the Pāñcajanya with gold,
or else one may encircle them with silver, copper, or even bell-metal.
Having bathed [the deity] with the pure five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship it before me.
One should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, according to the rule and with the mantra. ||58||
There, the preceptor— the best of the twice-born— should establish the fire according to the procedure prescribed in his own *gṛhya-sūtra* and then offer clarified butter with the mantra.
One should perform oblations with the jewel of mantras one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times, or likewise with other auspicious Vaiṣṇava mantras.
With mantras such as the Puruṣasūkta and others, one should offer oblations of clarified butter and milk-rice;
into that fire, the best of the twice-born should cast a discus and a conch shell.
The Guru should offer clarified butter twenty times with the six-syllable mantra;
likewise, taking up the heated disc with mantras, he should proceed in that manner.
One should perform the *añjana* (anointing) on the right and left arms with *śaṃkha* [sandalwood paste];
then, having completed the remainder of the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should again perform the worship (*pūjā*).
Then, having taken a jar filled with purified water and having consecrated it with the mantra, one should sprinkle it upon his head.

The Guru should teach the mantra to a disciple who is wearing white garments, who has properly sipped water for purification, who is endowed with humility, and who bears the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
The meaning of the mantra and its commentary (vṛtti) should be explained in detail;
then, having received the mantra, one should honor the teacher with ornaments and other gifts.
He who studies the mantra according to this method from a Vaiṣṇava guru,
O best of gods, then attains the state of a Vaiṣṇava.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to the Creator, Hari, the God of gods and father,
cut him with his own discus and then personally imparted the mantra to him.
O best of sages, the Lord Brahmā, the sovereign of all the worlds, was my father;
he too duly bestowed the mantra upon me according to the prescribed rites.
Therefore, O best of sages, having taken hold of the Sudarśana, go each of you, O twice-born ones, for refuge to the two feet of Nārāyaṇa. (70)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, all those sages, who were qualified for both paths, went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu along with the celestial sage Nārada. (71)
Therefore, O royal sage, if you too desire union with Viṣṇu,
you must wear the Sudarśana according to the procedure for the path of initiation.
Go for refuge to that one pair of Nārāyaṇa’s feet;
he is the manifest Lord of all worlds, Brahmā, the sovereign of the three realms. (73)
He spoke this supreme mantra to me and to Nārada as well,
in the presence of the great sages such as Śaunaka who dwell in the Naimiṣa forest.
Nārada bestowed the mantra of surrender and seeking refuge;
O King, even the great sages do not know this most profound secret. (75)
Neither the gods, nor the Siddhas, nor the Sādhyas, nor the Dānavas know [this];
even by me has the mantra been imparted to Parāśara, the son of Śakti.
O King, I shall here declare this supreme secret, the dual hymn of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, which consists of surrender and seeking refuge. (77)
There is no mantra more supreme than this; I speak the truth.
There is no dharma whatsoever in all the worlds more supreme than this. (78)
Truth, truth, and again truth—this was declared by Brahmā in the past:
there is no god higher than Nārāyaṇa who bestows liberation upon men.
The service of that [deity] itself becomes liberation, which cuts away all karma. ||80||

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Instruction on Knowledge," in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||223||
(224) Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Four.
Dilīpa said:
O Blessed One, tell me everything concerning the nectar of devotion to Hari;
for as I listen to this devotion to Viṣṇu which brings such happiness, I am never satiated. (1)
O best of sages, for those humans who are constantly scorched by the great flames of the threefold fire of suffering, there is the nectar-ocean of devotion to Viṣṇu. ||2||
In this terrifying forest of worldly existence, what other refuge is there besides You?
O Great Sage, please explain in detail the various types of devotion toward the Supreme Self, which are constantly practiced by the sages. (3)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Indra among kings, you ask well concerning that devotion to Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Lord, which brings eternal happiness and enables men to cross over the ocean of worldly existence. (4)
In former times, upon the peak of Kailāsa, the goddess Girijā asked this very great question of Śaṅkara, who is honored by the world. (5)
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, destroyer of Tripura, Lord of the gods!
Tell me of devotion to Viṣṇu, which grants liberation to all embodied beings.
The various forms of the object of worship, the mantras, as well as the rules for his worship;
the true nature of that Viṣṇu, his manifestations, his qualities, and so forth—[all these are described]. (7)
And its nature as the world, reaching which one does not return;
that by means of which the Blessed Lord Hari effects creation, maintenance, and dissolution. ||8||
That supreme abode of Hari, having gone to which they do not return,
is the highest state attained by whatever action or means of practice.
Sinful men whose minds are attached to sense-objects undergo these [consequences].
Out of affection for me, tell me everything in full detail and without omission. (10)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus questioned by the Great Goddess, Hara, the destroyer of Tripura,
then spoke with supreme affection after having paid homage to Janārdana.
Rudra said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess, you who desire the welfare of all the worlds!
Well done, O Goddess, that you ask me about the supreme majesty of the Lord of Śrī. (12)
O Pārvatī, you are blessed, you have performed meritorious deeds, and you are a devotee of Viṣṇu.
I am always well-pleased with you, O blessed lady, because of your virtue, beauty, and qualities. (13)
Now, O Girijā, I shall describe the supreme devotion to the Blessed One,
as well as the ritual procedure for His mantras and the true nature of that wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The Reality is Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, the eternal Vāsudeva;
he is the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Light, higher than the highest. ||15||
The infallible Person, Kṛṣṇa, the eternal, the auspicious, the Lord;
the constant, the all-pervading, the immovable, Rudra, the witness, the Lord of Creatures. ||16||
He is the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, and indeed the manifest Lord of Brahman;
he is Hiraṇyagarbha, Savitṛ, the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the all-pervading one. ||17||
The Lord expressed by the syllable *a* is the Sovereign, the husband of Śrī, Bhū, and Nīlā;
he is the master of immortality, through whose food one grows beyond. 18.
The Universal Soul, with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet, having touched the earth on every side, stands transcending it by the measure of ten fingers. 19.
He is infinite, the Lord of Śrī, Rāma, the bearer of qualities yet devoid of qualities, the Great One;
the sovereign of all worlds, the illustrious one, the omniscient, whose face is turned in every direction. (20)
O Pārvatī, I shall tell you that greatness of Vāsudeva, the foremost in the world and the Lord of the universe, which is possible for me to describe.
It is impossible for me to describe that meaning of all the Upaniṣads, as determined in the Vedānta, even together with Brahmā and the gods. (22)
Listen as I speak again of the various types of its worship separately:
the first is declared to be Vaiṣṇava, consisting of the marking of the conch and discus of Hari. 23.
The wearing of the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the acceptance of their mantras, worship, recitation, meditation, and likewise the remembrance of His names. ||24||
Chanting [His names], hearing [them], bowing down, serving His feet,
using the water from washing His feet, and eating what is offered to Him— (25)
And [he described] their service, the observance of the Dvādaśī vow, and the planting of Tulasī for Viṣṇu, the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. (26)
Devotion has been declared to be sixteenfold for the sake of liberation from the bondage of existence;
it belongs to all deities alike, as well as to me, O Supreme Person. (27)
Hari is always to be worshipped, especially by Brāhmaṇas;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should always worship Hari according to the prescribed rules. (28)
Marked with those signs, one attains the abode of the Lord of Śrī without doubt;
a Brāhmaṇa should have the conch and discus marked upon the roots of his two upper arms. (29)
Having purified [the disciple] by means of the fire-oblation itself for the removal of all sins, [one should mark him with] a discus, or a conch and a discus, or likewise the five weapons. (30)
Having worn [the sacred thread] according to the prescribed rule, one should commence the ritual of Brahman;
indeed, having placed the fire-purified purifier (pavitra) at the roots of both arms. 31.
Having abandoned the terrible city of Yama, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
yet he who worships Keśava while being devoid of the mark of the discus [is not so]. ||32||
All that—worship, mantra-recitation, and so forth—becomes fruitless for a Brāhmaṇa who [marks] the base of his arms with a wheel heated by fire. (33)
Having made the *aṃ* syllable and recited the mantra, one shall attain liberation from *saṃsāra*;
having worn the *sudarśana* discus heated by fire, O best of the twice-born. (34)
Having initiated him according to the prescribed rite, one should subsequently employ him in ritual duties;
however, he who shall feed at a śrāddha one who is devoid of Viṣṇu’s discus [is guilty].
All that becomes useless, and the ancestors depart in despair;
therefore, one should honor a Brahmin marked by Viṣṇu’s discus during the śrāddha rite. (36)
One should diligently avoid that which is devoid of the discus of Viṣṇu;
however, one should indeed give cows, land, gold, and other gifts to one who bears the mark of the discus.
Whatever was given to that one who was deprived of his discus all went indeed to the asura;
they were cut at the base of their arms by a discus heated by fire.
Those whose bodies are marked with the discus heated by fire and offered as an oblation go, liberated from all sins, to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (39)
For him, sacred fords and sacrifices have been attained; of this there is no doubt.
Without having worn the discus according to the prescribed rite, a Brāhmaṇa remains merely an ordinary man.
One should not eat anything at all from such a person, even if he performs a thousand sacrifices;
for a Brahmin who has not maintained the Cakra according to the rules is difficult to find through mere knowledge.
