He becomes censured in all the worlds and fallen from the status of a Brāhmaṇa;
for Hari, the God who bears the conch and discus, is to be worshipped by them as their very self.
In the same way, he who is marked with the signs of the discus and other emblems is to be honored by all, whether he be a knower of all the Vedas or an expert in all the Śāstras. ||43||
By not wearing the discus according to the prescribed rite, a Brāhmaṇa becomes fallen;
likewise, one who is devoid of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and bereft of the conch and discus [is fallen]. ||44||
Having mounted him upon a donkey, one should lead him out from one's own city;
for Vāsudeva Janārdana is devoid of contact with the primary elements.
In the same way, O Goddess, a Brāhmaṇa is marked by the discus of Viṣṇu;
therefore, [the mark] of Hari burns away the flood of sins arising from contact with Prakṛti. 46.
One should wear the heated discus and conch at the roots of the arms;
women and Śūdras should always wear them with fragrant sandalwood paste.
One should indeed inscribe a heated wheel on the upper arm of a Brāhmaṇa;
according to the prescribed rule for a Brāhmaṇa, one should likewise make a mark with heated gold.

For the sake of accomplishing the Śrauta and Smārta rites, as well as for the perfection of mantras, and likewise for the purpose of attaining the right to worship Hari, one should wear the mark according to the prescribed injunctions. (49)

For the sake of attaining the state of being a Vaiṣṇava and for the sake of attaining knowledge itself, one should perform the fire sacrifice according to the rules, offering oblations with the discus and the conch. 50.
A Brāhmaṇa should not have his body marked by anyone other than one who bears the mark of Hari;
nor even for the sake of Hari himself, should he be marked by anything other than the conch, the discus, the mace, the sword, and the Śārṅga bow.
One should burn the body according to its specific characteristics; one who has not been burnt by another is not eligible for the rite.
One should avoid from afar a Brahmin who does not wear the sacred thread. 52.
One should not look upon a Brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava as if he were a dog-cooker (outcaste) in this world;
for a Vaiṣṇava, even if outside the [four] castes, purifies the three worlds. 53.

Therefore, O lady of auspicious countenance, the wheel should be worn by Brahmins according to the prescribed rite, for the sake of the perfection of Vedic mantras, for the perfection of knowledge, and for liberation. (54)
Those great souls who have been marked by the discus of Viṣṇu are extraordinary;
however, those Brāhmaṇas who are devoid of the discus of Viṣṇu are considered ordinary.
For Brahmins residing in any of the stages of life (āśramas), especially so,
the Vaiṣṇava discus must indeed be worn according to the prescribed rite, as enjoined by the Vedas.
The wise who know Brahman understand that a brahmin should carry the Sudarśana on his right arm and should carry the conch on his left.

O lady of auspicious countenance, the wearing of the *cakras* and other marks as proclaimed in the *Mahopaniṣad*, the *Atharvaveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, and the *Yajurveda*, and as declared in the *Ṛgveda*, has thus been described.

O Viṣṇu, the lords of men, in order to cross the ocean of birth, place the lotus, the discus, and the purifier (the conch) at the base of their arms; others hold ancient emblems, while still others offer these [modern] ones to you.
The ancient, auspicious, and pervasive Vedic scripture is a pure foot;
by means of that wheel, those who are heated may cross the ocean of sin.
The purifying power belonging to Brahmās-pati always pervades the world of Hari.
Those whose bodies have not been heated by austerity do not attain the supreme state.
Those whose bodies have been heated by that [fire] proceed to the supreme abode;
the Sudarśana, the discus of Hari, has a rim consisting of purified rays.
It has a thousand spokes, destroys the material world, is the gateway to the higher realms, and possesses great splendor;
learn from me its names according to the sequence of Viṣṇu’s discus.
Purify us with your pure, fire-refined Brahman-nature;
purify us with that which is your stainless, purifying brilliance.
By that very means with which the gods always purify themselves through the filter, may the Pāvamānī verses purify me with its thousandfold stream. 65.
The purifier belonging to Prajāpati is golden and has a hundred strands;
purified by that, we, the knowers of Brahman, purify ourselves with the Veda.
The wheel of his sovereignty is stainless and his vision is undecaying; for when these two were maintained by this Great-Souled One, the gods attained their most exalted station.
Therefore, weapons such as the conch and the discus should be worn in two ways;
especially by Brāhmaṇas, and particularly by Vaiṣṇavas. (68)

That noble-souled one who, having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark and bearing the discus, meditates upon the foot of Viṣṇu with his voice and mantras, being pure in mind, goes to that which is higher than the highest and ever resides within the heart. (69)

Those who have a garland of *tulasī* and a lotus-seed rosary resting upon their necks, whose upper arms are marked with the conch and discus, and who bear the shimmering vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhva-puṇḍra*) upon the surface of their foreheads—they alone quickly purify the world, O Vaiṣṇavas! (70)
Those protectors who do not properly carry out the well-extended purifying rite of the Lord of Heaven for the sake of enjoyment—those beings do not truly grieve. ||71||
Those who carry the wheel for the sake of enjoyment, having swiftly attained stability through ritual means,
occupy their supreme station in the highest heaven by virtue of their splendor.
Marked with the sacred thread purified by the heat of the sacrificial fire at the base of his two arms, he shall cross the great ocean of worldly existence and reach the Supreme Self, Hari.
The defiled one goes to the world of others. ||73||
One should mark the roots of one's own arms with heated wheels and other symbols;
likewise, one should mark one's wife, children, servants, and even domestic animals and the like. (74)
Thus do all the Śrutis declare, O fair-faced one;
likewise, it is told in the Itihāsas and the Purāṇas as well. (75)
The Vaiṣṇava path is said to be twofold: external and internal.
The external consists of [bearing] the conch, the discus, and so forth; the internal is freedom from passion. (76)
That which consists of the equality between the external and the internal is indeed declared to be Vaiṣṇava;
therefore, the mark of the discus and so forth is traditionally held to be the primary Vaiṣṇava sign. (77)
Internal vision of one's own self, free from the defects of passion and the like;
compassion for all beings, tranquility, and lack of greed for the objects of the senses. ||78||
Freedom from attachment to children, wife, and so forth; likewise, delight in the practice of yoga; and the worship of the Supreme Lord through the yoga of exclusive devotion. ||79||
Therefore, the marking with the discus and other weapons is indeed remembered as the mark of a Vaiṣṇava;
because of being devoid of the marks such as the discus, the status of a Vaiṣṇava is not attained. ||80||
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara,
[this is] the section titled "The Greatness of Sudarśana and Others."
The two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter. ||224||
(225) Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Five. Śaṅkara said:
O lady of auspicious appearance, I shall declare the greatness of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra);
by its mere wearing, the best of the twice-born is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. (1)
In the center of the vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra), which is broad and very beautiful, Janārdana, the God of gods, is seated together with Lakṣmī. ||2||
Therefore, the body of one upon whose person the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is worn becomes the pure and auspicious temple of the Blessed One. (3)
That Vaiṣṇava who wears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with pure clay has effectively bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices. ||4||
The Brahmin who wears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is honored in all the worlds;
ascending an excellent celestial chariot, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. ||5||

The best of the twice-born should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) at the three junctions of the day for the sake of purifying all sins and for the attainment of the fruits of sacrifices and charitable works.
Upon seeing one who wears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, one is liberated from all sins;
or by bowing with devotion, one obtains the fruit of all possible gifts. (7)
If one feeds a Brahmin who wears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* at a *śrāddha* ceremony, his ancestors will remain satisfied for ten million kalpas; of this there is no doubt. (8)
O fair-faced one, he who wears the vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) and performs a śrāddha ceremony shall obtain the fruit of a śrāddha performed at Gayā for thousands of crores of kalpas. ||9||

Whatever sacrifice, charity, performance of austerity, recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and so forth one may perform while wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra), its merit shall be infinite. ||10||
But whoever performs any rite whatsoever while devoid of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*—all his acts, such as sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and public works (*pūrta*), shall be fruitless; of this there is no doubt. ||11||
That body of human beings which is devoid of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark should not be looked upon at all; it would be like a cremation ground. ||12||
But he who is devoid of the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark—whatever rites such as the *saṃdhyā* prayers he performs—all that is taken away by Rākṣasas, and he goes to hell. (13)
A learned Brahmin who follows the Vedic tradition should wear the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark with white clay; he should never wear it horizontally, even in times of distress.
The vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark belongs to the Brahmins, while the *tilaka* mark belongs to the Kṣatriyas;
that in the shape of a cloth-band (*paṭṭākāra*) belongs to the Vaiśyas, and the triple horizontal line (*tripuṇḍraka*) indeed belongs to the Śūdras. (15)
The *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* should be made with clay, and likewise the *tilaka* with musk;
the *paṭṭākāra* mark should be made with sandalwood paste, and the *tripuṇḍra* with sacred ash alone. (16)
The vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra), however, is never forbidden for anyone;
even a Kṣatriya who is a devotee of Viṣṇu should wear it. 17.
Brahmins must never wear horizontal stripes or similar markings;
nor should they perform the worship of anyone other than Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. (18)
O Goddess, even if he be a Brahmin born of noble lineage and learned, if he should become a wearer of ashes, one should avoid such a person just as one avoids a jar containing the dregs of wine. 19.
The rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) applies likewise to those who are like Śūdras and to Śūdras themselves;
by wearing the triple mark, a Brāhmaṇa would undoubtedly become an outcast. ||20||
The single-minded ones of great fortune, who delight in the welfare of all beings, should apply the *puṇḍra* in the shape of Hari’s foot, including the intervening space. (21)
One should fashion the vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) in the shape of Hari’s foot according to the prescribed rule; for that mark, provided with a central gap, is indeed the temple of Hari. 22.
One should fashion the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) as straight, gentle, well-proportioned, and very beautiful;
it should be shaped like a staff, richly adorned, and provided with a hollow in the middle. 23.
Therefore, a beautiful vertical mark (puṇḍra) in the shape of a staff, provided with a gap at the top, should always be made by Brahmins and by women of auspicious appearance. 24.
In the center of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), which is broad and very beautiful, Hari dwells together with Śrī, seated within the space between the lines.
That lowest of the twice-born who makes an upward sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) without leaving a gap between its parts indeed drives away both Viṣṇu and Śrī who reside therein. ||26||
Those lowest of the twice-born who apply an unbroken vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) will have the paw of a dog permanently upon their foreheads; of this there is no doubt. (27)
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the same world as Hari, a Brāhmaṇa should always wear a mark accompanied by turmeric, provided it possesses auspicious gaps. 28.
Having taken earth from the lake on Mount Veṅkaṭa with supreme devotion, one should apply the vertical marks (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) for the sake of attaining union with Hari. 29.
Taking earth from the root of the sacred Tulasī of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the devotee should apply the vertical marks (ūrdhva-puṇḍra); thereupon, Hari becomes pleased with him. ||30||
Then, having taken beautiful clay produced there in the auspicious and delightful Dvārāvatī at the Vāsudeva-lake, that best of the twice-born [proceeded]. (31)
One should wear the vertical marks (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) for the attainment of the fruits of all desires,
having taken with supreme devotion the clay originating from the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, one who wears upright *puṇḍra* marks obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
as do those who use sandalwood, turmeric, and likewise the ashes produced from the *agnihotra*.
It is declared that the wearing of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) brings everything under one's control.
One should indeed fetch the clay from wherever there is a holy place sacred to Hari. (34)
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, at the root of a bilva tree, by a reservoir of water, on the shore of the ocean, at an anthill, and especially in a sacred field of Hari. ||35||
One should take the clay from that place where the water used for Viṣṇu’s ablution flows constantly, for the purpose of applying the sectarian marks (puṇḍra).
At Śrīraṅga, on Veṅkaṭādri, at Śrīkūrma, in auspicious Dvārakā, at Prayāga, on Nārasiṃhādri, and at Vārāha in the Lasī forest; ||37||
Having taken clay with devotion along with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, and having applied the *puṇḍra* marks upon the limbs, one shall attain union with Viṣṇu. ||38||
In whatever place the highly fortunate Vaiṣṇavas reside, from that very place the clay should be taken for the application of the vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra). 39.
The dark [color] is said to bring peace; likewise, the red brings subjugation.
They say the yellow brings prosperity, while the auspicious white brings liberation. (40)
Circular, horizontal, without gaps, short, long, extended, thin, crooked, deformed, with a bound tip, with a severed base, or displaced from its position; ||41||
They say that a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) which is impure, coarse, attached [to the skin], fashioned with fingers, foul-smelling, or unbearable is useless. 42.
Beginning from the base of the nose up to the forehead, one should draw with clay;
starting from the middle of the eyebrows, one should fashion the intervening space. ||43||
The space between [the lines] should be two finger-breadths wide, and the sides should be the measure of one finger-breadth;
one should draw a straight and auspicious *puṇḍra* with pure clay. (44)
One should meditate on Keśava at the forehead, Nārāyaṇa on the abdomen, Mādhava on the chest, and Govinda in the hollow of the throat. (45)
He should place Viṣṇu on the right side of the belly, Madhusūdana on the arm,
Trivikrama on the neck, and Vāmana on the left side.
One should place Śrīdhara on the left arm, Hṛṣīkeśa on the neck, Padmanābha on the back, and Dāmodara on the hips.
With the water used for that washing, one should [apply it] to Vāsudeva on the head, the forehead, the two arms, the two backs, and the hollow of the throat. 48.
One should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) measuring four finger-breadths;
it is prescribed that on the belly and its two sides, it should be extended for ten finger-breadths. 49.
On the two arms and the chest, a mark (puṇḍra) of eight finger-breadths is prescribed;
thus, a Brāhmaṇa should always wear twelve marks. (50)
Having meditated upon those respective forms [of the deity] within each of those *puṇḍra*s, one should apply them with the mantra;
in all the intermediate spaces, one should apply turmeric for the sake of prosperity (*śrī*).
They say there are four marks for the mountain-dwellers (kṣatriyas), two are prescribed for the vaiśyas, while a single mark is ordained for women and śūdras. (52)
One should wear four marks on the forehead, the heart, and the two arms;
however, it is prescribed that there be two on the forehead and the heart, and one on the brow.
The vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) on the forehead is prescribed as the first for all;
its application is ordained specifically in the sequence beginning with the forehead. (54)
One should bear the forms beginning with Vāsudeva upon the four *puṇḍra*s;
on two, Govinda and Kṛṣṇa; and on one, Nārāyaṇa. (55)
Thus, O Girijā, the procedure for the *puṇḍra* has been declared by me for all;
it resembles the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree and likewise has the shape of a bamboo leaf. (56)
Resembling a lotus bud, these three are known as the deluding marks;
the pure, great devotee of Hari [should apply] the sectarian mark in the shape of Lord Hari’s foot. (57)
Or else, O Goddess, one should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) in the shape of a staff. ||58||
With the roots of their arms marked by the *sudarśana* [discus], with all their limbs marked by vertical *puṇḍra* [tilaka] lines,
wearing garlands and lotus-seed beads, they are pure.
They protect the worlds from contact with the flood of misfortune. ||59||

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Urdhvapuṇḍra," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||225||
(226) Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Six. Śaṅkara said:
Whether performing ritual placement (*nyāsa*) or worship (*arcana*), one who is single-mindedly devoted should rely upon a mantra taught by a Vaiṣṇava;
through a mantra instructed by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, the supreme goal is not attained. (1)
If the excellent two-fold mantra was previously taught by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, one should again properly receive it from a Vaiṣṇava guru according to the prescribed rite. ||2||
Even one who has studied a thousand branches of the Vedas, or is initiated into all sacrifices, or is born into a great family, cannot be a Guru if he is not a Vaiṣṇava. (3)
But that Vaiṣṇava who correctly teaches the two mantras is to be known as an Ācārya, the shatterer of the bonds of worldly existence. ||4||
Then, having taken refuge with a teacher, the twice-born student should serve him for one year;
once the teacher has ascertained his conduct, he should instruct him in the mantra. ||5||

Having performed the purificatory rites such as heating and so forth, the Guru should subsequently utter the mantra; indeed, having performed the heating, the marking with the *puṇḍra*, and the naming according to the prescribed rule.
Afterwards, one should teach the mantra to a disciple whose mind is stainless;
when [the disciple] has been refined by the rite of the wheel, this is designated as "tāpa" (heating). ||7||
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is likewise declared; it is indeed called the Vaiṣṇava name.
Thereafter, the Guru should teach the mantra to the disciple according to the prescribed rule. ||8||
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) using the eight-syllable mantra or another Vaiṣṇava mantra;
indeed, O lady of auspicious countenance, for the Vaiṣṇavas, ritual placement alone is supreme in this matter. (9)
Therefore, among these, nyāsa alone is said here to be the most excellent;
that brahmin who is devoted to the science of nyāsa is called the best. ||10||
There is nothing higher than Nyāsa; I tell you this as the truth.
Understand from me that nyāsa and prapatti are two [forms of surrender] which are synonymous. 11.
One should perform all ritual actions preceded by the instruction on the two;
one who does not possess the qualification for the two is not fit for any ritual actions. (12)
Therefore, having first completed our studies, the best of the twice-born should thereafter properly practice the unsurpassed, glorious eight-syllable mantra. (13)
The eight-syllable mantra is said to be a condensation of the *praṇava* itself;
however, the wise state that the mantra begins with the innate *praṇava*. (14)
Nowhere else [is there anything] apart from the *praṇava* in all mantras, due to its own inherent nature;
one should first join the auspicious *praṇava* to all mantras. (15)
The syllable Oṃ is the Praṇava, the Brahman, and the leader among all mantras;
one should employ it at the beginning of all mantras, O lady of auspicious countenance. (16)
From its own nature, the syllable *praṇava* is established within that root mantra:
first the single syllable *oṃ*, and then the two syllables *namaḥ*. (17)
Then, "nārāyaṇāya" consists of five syllables in their proper order;
thus, this eight-syllable mantra should be known as the accomplisher of all goals. ||18||
The remover of all suffering, glorious, the essence of all mantras, and auspicious;
its seer is Nārāyaṇa, and its deity is indeed the Lord of Śrī. (19)
The goddess Gāyatrī is the meter, the Praṇava is said to be the seed-syllable, and the eternal, inseparable goddess Śrī is called the power (śakti) of the mantra. (20)
The first word is "Oṃ," the second is said to be "Namaḥ," and the third is "Nārāyaṇāya"; thus the three words have been proclaimed. ||21||
The syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m* following them—this *praṇava*, consisting of the three Vedas, is declared to be the state of Brahman. (22)
By the syllable *a* Viṣṇu is expressed, and by the syllable *u* Śrī is expressed;
the syllable *m*, however, is proclaimed as the servant of these two, the twenty-fifth [tattva]. ||23||
That form of Vāsudeva is expressed by the letter *a* by the wise;
the form of the goddess Śrī is expressed by the letter *u* by the sages. (24)
By the syllable *ma*, the individual soul (*jīva*), the twenty-fifth principle, is expressed;
by the *ka*-group, the elements (*bhūta*); and by the *ca*-group, the sense organs (*indriya*).

Knowledge is expressed by the *ṭa*-group and the *ta*-group, as well as by the letters beginning with *dha*; the mind is said to be denoted by the letter *pa*, while the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*) is denoted by the letter *pha*.
By the letter *ba* and by the letter *bha*, the Great Nature (*mahā-prakṛti*) is expressed;
that which is the letter *ma* is the Self (*ātman*), proclaimed as the twenty-fifth principle. ||27||

Distinct from the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and so forth, having no means other than [the Lord], existing as a subordinate to the Blessed One, he is the conscious being known by the letter "M. (28)
Some say that the syllable *u* expresses the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*);
and because it is partial to that side, the syllable *śrī* is also expressed by the syllable *a* alone. (29)
Just as the radiance of the sun is eternally inseparable from it, so Viṣṇu, the ocean of auspicious qualities, is expressed by the syllable *Ā*. (30)
The Lord of Śrī is the remainder of all souls, the supreme Person who is the seed of the universe;
he is the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, the Sovereign, and the kinsman of the world. (31)
The eternal sovereign of the worlds, never departing from Viṣṇu, she is the mother of the entire universe and the delightful consort of Viṣṇu. 32.
Śrī, who is the support of the world, is expressed here by the syllable *u*;
by the syllable *ma*, the wise declare the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) to be the servant of those two. (33)
He is the abode of knowledge, possessed of the quality of knowledge, conscious, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
He is not insentient, is changeless, and possesses a singular, uniform essential nature. 34.
The self (aham-artha) is atomic, eternal, pervasive by nature, and consists of consciousness and bliss; it is imperishable, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), distinct in form, and ancient. (35)
Indeed, it is unburnable, indestructible, undampened, and likewise unwithering and imperishable;
endowed with such qualities as these, it is truly the remainder of the Supreme.
By the syllable *ma* is expressed the individual soul (*jīva*), the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), who is always dependent on another;
he belongs solely as a servant to Hari, and never to anyone else. (37)
In this way, his very state of servitude is established as being in the middle [syllable].
Thus, O sinless one, the meaning of the *praṇava* has been explained by me for you to know. (38)
O auspicious one, this is the exposition of the meaning of the *praṇava* by means of the remainder of the mantra:
for one who has become a servant of the Supreme, no independence exists here. (39)
Therefore, one should mentally turn away from the notions of "the Great One" (mahat) and "I" (ahaṃ).
Even that which is to be done with the thought of one's own means is prohibited.
The syllable *ma* represents the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*), and the syllable *na* is its negation.
Therefore, however, the liberation from egoism should come about through salutation alone. ||41||
Through *namaḥ* (reverence), all success shall be attained; otherwise, one meets with destruction.
Whatever is accompanied by *namaḥ* is called *ahaṅkāra* (the creative utterance). 42.
For one joined with egoism, not even the slightest happiness exists;
one whose self is deluded by egoism sinks into blinding darkness. 43.
Therefore, by means of the word "namas" (homage) here, his independence is negated; for he lives only as one who is dependent upon the Blessed One. 44.
Therefore, the status of being an agent of proof does not belong to a conscious being;
rather, the entire world of moving and non-moving things proceeds solely from the volition of the Lord. 45.
Therefore, one should abandon all injunctions based on one's own capacity without exception;
for through the power of the Lord, there is nothing that cannot be attained by him. //46//
Having surrendered one's existence to Him, one should rest; one should perform only His work, [thinking]:
"Lord Hari is the Supreme Self, the Master, and I am always His. (47)
"Indeed, he is to be employed according to his own will, for he is the Lord of the Self.
Thinking thus, I mentally abandoned that [body], which was devoid of the ego and strengthened by the realization of the Unmanifest (Amata). 48.
The notion of "I" regarding the body is the root of involvement in the cycle of rebirth and the bondage of karma;
therefore, a wise person should restrain the mahat, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the mind. 49.
Now, O auspicious daughter of the mountain, I shall declare the word "Nārāyaṇa":
the term "nārāḥ" refers to the multitudes of individual souls (ātman), and this Supreme Person is their goal (gati). (50)
He alone is the refuge of that [universe]; therefore, He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
For the entire world, consisting of all sentient and insentient entities, is both heard of and seen.
He who abides eternally pervading all is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
The term "nārāḥ" is proclaimed to be the collective designation for all groups of men. ||52||
He is their refuge, support, and forest; therefore He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
The wise know that the principles (tattvas) born from Nara are called Nārāṇi.
He whose course (āyana) consists of those very [kalpas] is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
he by whom the entire universe is held after having swallowed it at the end of the kalpas.
Furthermore, because he by whom the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is emitted, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
the whole world, both mobile and immobile, is designated as "nāra. (55)
Because his abode and resort is that [mass], he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa; "nāra" is a collection of men, and he is their refuge (ayana) and goal (gati). ||56||
Therefore, he is eternally called Nārāyaṇa by the sages, from whom the worlds arise like vast foam upon the great ocean. (57)
Furthermore, because all things dissolve therein, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
he who is eternal by virtue of his eternal nature, eternally liberated, and the sole possessor of enjoyment. (58)
Nārāyaṇa, together with Śrī, is remembered as the Lord of the entire world.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate reality.
Whatever exists in the world, whether it is seen or even heard, Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that within and without. (60)
The Person whose nature is free from evil, who dwells within all beings—the divine, singular, eternal, and imperishable Hari, Nārāyaṇa. ||61||

He who is the seer and that which is to be seen, as well as the hearer and that which is to be heard; he who is the toucher and that which is to be touched, and the meditator and that which is to be meditated upon—[all these are non-existent]. (62)
The speaker and the spoken, the knower and the knowable, the world of consciousness and the unconscious—all that is Hari, the Lord of Śrī, who is declared to be Nārāyaṇa. (63)
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
pervading all worlds on every side, he transcends them by the measure of ten fingers.
Whatever has been and whatever is to be, all that is Nārāyaṇa, Hari;
moreover, he is the Lord of immortality, as well as the Virāj, the Supreme Person, who exists through food. 65.
He alone is the Puruṣa, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, Acyuta, and Hari;
he is the golden one, the Blessed Lord, the immortal, the eternal, and the auspicious Śiva.
The Lord of the entire world, the sovereign and master of all realms, is Hiraṇyagarbha, Savitṛ, Ananta, Soma, and Maheśvara. ||67||
This word "Bhagavān" as well as the word "Puruṣa" applies without any limiting adjuncts to Vāsudeva, who is the Self of all. (68)
Lord Viṣṇu is the Sovereign, the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, and the friend of the world; he is the sole ruler of all that is moving and unmoving, and the ultimate refuge for ascetics. 69.
He who was declared at the beginning of the Vedas as the Lord, in whom the Vedas are established—
he whose supreme state is beyond that which is dissolved in primordial nature (prakṛti), is the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
He who is Viṣṇu, he who is Nārāyaṇa, and he who is Hari—he alone is the eternal Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord (Maheśvara). (71)
Because sovereignty has arisen from him, and because he abides within everyone,
the word "Īśvara" (Lord) is likewise applied to him by the sages;
for lordship free from all limiting conditions is established in the Divine Being alone.
"He is called the Self and the Lord by the eternal Vedic injunctions;
therefore, the state of Maheśvara is established in Vāsudeva. (73)
Moreover, by the mere play of his power, the Lord is the master of the two-fold manifestation; such is the sovereignty of that Universal Self.
That Lord who is proclaimed by the wise as the husband of Śrī, Bhū, and Nīlā—from him alone is the status of being the Lord of All established in Vāsudeva. (75)

He is the Lord of sacrifice, the sacrifice itself, the enjoyer of sacrifice, the performer of sacrifice, and the all-pervading one; He alone, the enjoyer of sacrifice, is the Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord.
Lord Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, the imperishable soul who partakes of all *havya* and *kavya* offerings, is the Sovereign here;
by His presence, all demons and all obstacles immediately depart. (77)
He who, having attained the state of Virāṭ and become Hari, is Janārdana—
he alone is the Supreme Lord who gratifies the three worlds.
With that full oblation with which the gods performed the sacrifice, from that sacrifice were born those creatures who have two rows of teeth. (79)
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were born;
from it were produced horses, cows, men, and other beings. (80)
Indeed, from this Person, whose body is the sacrifice of all, the entire world—both stationary and moving—has arisen from Hari. (81)
His mouth, arms, thighs, and feet became the social classes in their respective order;
from his feet the earth arose, and from his head the sky was born. (82)
From his mind was born the Moon, from his eye the Maker of Light (the Sun),
from his mouth Agni, and from his breath the thousand-eyed Vāyu, who moves ever on.
From the navel of Viṣṇu arose the sky and the entire world, both moving and unmoving;
for from that eternal Viṣṇu everything has emerged. (84)
Therefore, Viṣṇu is proclaimed as Nārāyaṇa, who consists of all things;
having thus created the entire universe, Hari again devours it. 85.
Like a spider, he produces from his own play Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Varuṇa as well. (86)
Because he seizes and carries away [all things], he is therefore called Hari;
he is that Person who, when the world has become a single ocean, remains enveloped by Māyā.
Having placed the universe within his own belly, the eternal one sleeps therein;
for here, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the infallible Acyuta, was indeed alone.
Neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Rudra, nor the gods, nor the great sages;
neither heaven nor earth, nor the moon, nor the sun can reach him. 89.
The stars, the worlds, and the great cosmic egg are not encompassed by anything else;
rather, O auspicious one, the entire universe is encompassed by Hari.
Since he was created again in that same manner at the beginning of creation, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
O Pārvatī, his servitude is declared by means of the fourth mantra.
This entire world, beginning with Brahmā, has become his servant;
having understood this meaning, one should thereafter employ the mantra. (92)
But without knowing the meaning of the mantra, one does not attain accomplishment at all; nor, O fair-faced one, does one attain enjoyment, devotion, or liberation. 93.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Meaning of Mantras," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(226) Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Six. Pārvatī said:
Explain to me in detail the gravity of the meaning and words of the mantra, as well as the true nature of Īśvara and his manifestations and qualities. (1)
O Lord of all the gods, tell me in truth everything regarding that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, as well as the various manifestations of Hari.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the true nature of the Supreme Self—
the collection of manifestations and qualities, as well as the states of being of Hari.
He who is the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu, declared as Nārāyaṇa, is the Lord of the worlds, the eternal Supreme Self. (4)
With hands and feet on every side, with eyes on every side, the all-pervading Lord, in whom indeed all worlds and supreme abodes reside. (5)
Bearing that [form], He also transcends the minds of the wise.
Thus, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama, possessing a divine and auspicious form, exists with the Goddess for the sake of enjoyment in His many forms. (6)
Possessing a massive body, with a form like fire, the youthful Hari, though having attained the state of a youth,
took delight with Śrī, the mother of the worlds.
Like the moon with its own radiance, he is a ray of nectar. ||7||
And this prince of Jagadīśvarī, eternally youthful and possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, remained in the supreme abode. (8)
The supreme ether exists for the sake of enjoyment, and the entire world exists for the sake of sport;
thus, through enjoyment and sport, the two-fold manifestation of Viṣṇu’s glory is established. (9)
His constant abiding in enjoyment sometimes withdraws his play;
both enjoyment and play are maintained by him through his possession of power.
His three-quarters are pervasion in the supreme abode; his one-quarter has come into being here again.
The three-quarter manifestation is eternal, while the quarter consisting of lordly power is impermanent.
The auspicious form of the Lord, situated in the supreme abode, is eternal, infallible, perpetual, divine, and forever endowed with youth. (12)
Constantly surrounded by sovereignty, fortune, and the earth, this Śrī, the mother of the world, is eternal and inseparable from Viṣṇu. 13.
O fair-faced one, as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, so too is Lakṣmī;
she is the sovereign of the entire world, the consort of Viṣṇu, and eternally auspicious. 14.
With hands and feet extending everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, Nārāyaṇī, the Mother of the World, is the refuge of the entire universe. 15.
Upon whose sidelong glance rests the entire world, both the stationary and the moving;
by whose opening and closing [of her eyes] come the maintenance and dissolution of the universe. (16)
The primordial Mahālakṣmī of all, the Supreme Goddess consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), whose nature is both perceptible and imperceptible, stands pervading the entire universe. 17.
Beholding that entire universe as empty,
the Supreme Goddess filled that entire emptiness with her own splendor.
She is Lakṣmī and Dharaṇī, renowned as the goddess Nīlā;
she is the support of the world, having assumed the form of the earth. (19)
In the form of the essence of water and so forth, she herself becomes the blue body;
having attained the nature of Lakṣmī, she is indeed embodied as wealth and speech. ||20||
Thus, she who is the very form of the Goddess, the Fortune of the world, delighted Hari;
O fair-faced one, all the various branches of knowledge are of the nature of Lakṣmī. (21)
Indeed, all beauty whatsoever is said to be her very body;
for loveliness, virtuous conduct, and auspicious fortune reside in women, yet her form, O Girijā, stands at the head of all womankind. (22)
By whose glance, as fierce as a falling thunderbolt, Brahmā, Śiva, Mahendra the lord of heaven,
the moon, the sun, Kubera, and even Agni [were struck].
They attain abundant sovereignty. ||23||
Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Vidyā, Mātā, Viṣṇupriyā, Satī, Padmālayā, Padmahastā, Padmākṣī, and Lokasundarī. ||24||
The eternal sovereign of all beings, the patient one, omnipresent and auspicious;
the consort of Viṣṇu, the Great Goddess, the daughter of the Ocean of Milk, Ramā. 25.
The earth is the mother of infinite light, blue in color, and the bestower of all happiness;
likewise, she is Rukmiṇī, Sītā, and the auspicious Sarvavedavatī. ||26||
She is Satī, Sarasvatī, Gaurī, Śānti, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Rati;
she is Nārāyaṇī, the lady of excellent form, the eternal and inseparable consort of Viṣṇu.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites these names of merit, shall attain great fortune, as well as wealth and grain free from blemish. (28)
The golden-hued, tawny goddess Lakṣmī, adorned with garlands of gold and silver, moon-like and made of gold, who never departs from Viṣṇu. (29)
I invoke here Śrī, the fragrant one, the unassailable, ever-nourishing, and bestowing of prosperity, the sovereign mistress of all beings. 30.
Thus, in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, the Great Goddess, being praised, bestowed the bliss of all sovereignty upon Śiva and the other inhabitants of heaven. (31)
She is the sovereign of the universe, the eternal consort of Viṣṇu;
the entire world, both moving and unmoving, rests upon her sidelong glance.
He upon whose chest that goddess resides, shining like a flame—
he is indeed the Lord of All, the manifest Imperishable, the Undecaying Person.
The glorious Nārāyaṇa is all-pervading, an ocean of the quality of affection, a master of virtuous character, fortunate, omniscient, and omnipotent. (34)
He is eternally one whose desires are fulfilled, a natural friend and companion, an ocean of the nectar of compassion, and the refuge for all embodied beings. 35.
To that glorious Viṣṇu, the mine of compassion who bestows the happiness of heaven and liberation upon his devotees, I perform all service as his servant. (36)
In all circumstances of place, time, and so forth, one shall attain the bliss of servitude, which is established as the very nature of the Lord of Kamalā. ||37||
Having understood the meaning of the mantra in this way, one should properly practice devotion toward it;
for this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has become its servant. (38)
The glorious Nārāyaṇa is the Lord, the Master, and the Sovereign of the worlds;
he is mother, father, son, kinsman, abode, refuge, and ultimate resort. (39)
The Lord of Śrī, who possesses auspicious qualities and bestows the fruits of all desires,
is that very Lord of the World who is described in the scriptures as being "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa).
Inferiority is said to consist in being joined with qualities that are natural and subject to rejection;
wherein there is the state of false manifestation through statements within the scope of the Vedānta. 41.
It is also said that all this which is perceived is impermanent;
even here, it is merely the destruction of the mundane form of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa). ||42||
Thus it is said that the two forms of Prakṛti are impermanent;
O Great Goddess, this is the meaning concerning the emergence of Prakṛti from Hari. (43)
For the sake of sport, [it was created] for Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who possesses the authority for divine play,
together with the fourteen worlds and the oceans accompanied by the continents.
This beautiful cosmic egg, born of primordial nature, is completely filled with the four kinds of beings and with mountains of great height. 45.
Endowed with tenfold increasing qualities and enveloped by the seven coverings,
he is Time who revolves in the form of *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, and so forth.
The creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world occur precisely according to time;
a thousand cycles of the four yugas constitutes a single day of Brahmā.
For as many years as there are nights for Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
when that period of Brahmā’s life is exhausted, he who brings about the dissolution of all shall arrive.
Just as the worlds within the cosmic egg are consumed by the fire of time,
so too are all the individual selves of Viṣṇu dissolved into primordial nature (prakṛti).
The elements that constitute the covering of the egg shall attain dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛti).
That primordial nature, the support of the entire universe, rests upon Hari.
By her, the Blessed One, the God of gods, always effects the creation and dissolution of the world; for the sake of sport, she was created as the world-encompassing Māyā.
Ignorance (avidyā) is primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting eternally of the three qualities (guṇas); it is the eternal cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. 52.
She is yogic sleep, the great illusion, primordial nature endowed with the three qualities,
the unmanifest, and the primary matter (pradhāna) of Viṣṇu, who undergoes transformations for his divine play.
The creation and dissolution of the world always proceed from Prakṛti alone;
the abode of the innumerable Prakṛtis is an imperishable mass of dense darkness. (54)
Above the boundary is Virajā, and below the boundary is Sanātanī;
by her, the entire world is upheld in its various states, such as gross and subtle.
In this state of expansion and contraction, the creation and dissolution are remembered;
thus indeed all beings are contained within primordial nature (prakṛti). 56.
Therefore, all this is empty, for it is contained within the Great Nature (mahat).
Thus, the form of Nature is the supreme form of manifestation. 57.
O daughter of the mountain, listen now to the form of the manifestation consisting of the three quarters:
between the Pradhāna and the supreme ether flows the Virajā river.
With the waters produced from the dissolution of the Vedas, her impurities were washed away;
on the further shore of that [ocean], in the supreme ether, resides the eternal Tripādbrahman.
It is the nectar, eternal, constant, infinite, and the supreme state;
it is pure, consisting of sattva, divine, imperishable—the station of Brahman. (60)
Possessing a splendor equal to the fire of many millions of suns, imperishable, consisting of all the Vedas, pure, and devoid of creation and dissolution. ||61||
Innumerable, undecaying, eternal, devoid of waking, dreaming, and the like, golden-hued, the state of liberation, it brings the bliss of Brahman-joy. (62)
Free from equality or superiority, devoid of beginning or end, auspicious, most wonderful in its splendor, delightful, and an eternal ocean of bliss. (63)
That supreme abode of Viṣṇu, endowed with such qualities as these, is not illumined by the sun, nor by the moon, nor by fire. (64)
That which, once reached, one does not return from—that is the supreme abode of Hari;
that is the supreme, eternal, and constant abode of Viṣṇu, the imperishable.
Indeed, it cannot be described even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
The abode of Hari cannot be described by me, nor by the Creator, nor by the hosts of lords of sages;
for even the Lord Acyuta, in whom that abode resides, my dear friend, does not know it even during the day.

That which is the imperishable secret of the Vedas, wherein all the gods have taken their seat—whosoever knows that, what shall he do with the Ṛg-verses? But those who know this, they sit together [in bliss]. //67//
The wise always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu—the imperishable, eternal, and divine, O Goddess, spread out like the eye. 68.
It is impossible for deities such as Brahmā and Rudra to enter it;
it is perceived by the foremost of yogis through knowledge according to the path of the scriptures. (69)
Neither I, nor Brahmā, nor the gods, nor the great seers know the meaning of all the Upaniṣads; having perceived it, O lady of virtuous vows, I shall speak.
For in the supreme station of Viṣṇu, that which is called auspicious,
there the many-horned cows— meaning the subjects— dwell in great happiness.

Regarding this, it is said: That supreme abode of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is dressed as a cowherd, shines forth with its rays of light—those very rays being the cowherds known as "Sukha" (Bliss). 72.
The world of Brahmā, which is of the color of the sun, beyond darkness, an unshakable light, the support of Brahman, and eternal, is composed of pure sattva. (73)
In this eternal state, upon the ground made manifest through commonality, the two youths, Śrī and Sanātana, remained ever-vigilant. (74)
Since the two sisters, the youthful Earth and Nīlā, are beloved of Viṣṇu;
and here [dwell] the ancient Sādhyas and the eternal Viśvedevas who were present in former times. (75)
Those great ones, beautiful to behold, attain the celestial vault;
there the wise sages, ever-watchful, kindle their light.
To that state, O wise brahmins, the knowers go, desiring communion;
that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is designated as liberation.
In that [state], those liberated from bondage attain the state of bliss;
having attained it, they do not return, and therefore it is called liberation (mokṣa). ||78||
Liberation, the supreme state, the divine, the immortal abode of Viṣṇu, the imperishable, the highest realm, Vaikuṇṭha, the eternal station. ||79||

I shall describe in detail the form of that Acyuta, whose supreme abode— the eternal, supreme, and most excellent sky— is expressed by these synonymous terms, and who possesses a three-quarter manifestation. (80)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Threefold Manifestation of Sovereignty," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
(228) Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Eight.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
The worlds of the three-quarter manifestation are proclaimed to be innumerable;
they are all composed of pure *sattva* and are designated by the bliss of Brahman-joy. (1)
All are eternal, immutable, and free from passion and other defects to be abandoned;
all are golden-hued, pure, and possess a splendor equal to ten million suns. ||2||
All these divine beings, free from desire and anger, were devoted solely to the singular essence of devotion for the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa. ||3||
They have taken refuge in the uninterrupted and perfectly complete bliss of chanted song.
All the Upaniṣads are of the nature of the Vedas and possess Vedic splendor. ||4||
They are surrounded by divine men and women who are embodiments of the Vedas, and they are graced by lakes filled with water whose sole essence is the Veda. ||5||
Accompanied by the immobile entities in the form of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth,
it is impossible for me to describe everything that extends throughout the world.
The interval between the stainless supreme ether and [the individual soul] is known as Kevala;
that state is to be experienced by those who serve the unmanifest Brahman. (7)
The state that bestows the bliss of the joy arising from the experience of one's own self, which is absolute, is called *niḥśreyasa*, *nirvāṇa*, *kaivalya*, and *mokṣa*. ||8||

Therefore, those of small intellect desire liberation devoid of happiness;
but the high-souled and highly fortunate ones are the servants of the Lord’s feet. (9)
They go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu which bestows the bliss of Brahman;
that station of Hari is Vaikuṇṭha, filled with various inhabited lands. 10.
Surrounded by walls, celestial chariots, and palaces made of jewels,
in its center stands that divine city renowned as Ayodhyā.
It was surrounded by walls variegated with many jewels and adorned with archways;
it possessed four gates and was encircled by a jeweled gateway.
It is guarded by the gatekeepers Caṇḍa and others, such as Kumuda and the rest;
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are at the eastern gate, while Bhadra and Subhadra are at the southern gate.
In the west are Jaya and Vijaya; in the north are Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ;
[and] Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, or Manaḥ.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—these, O fair-faced one, are declared to be the guardians of the directions here in the city. (15)
It was surrounded by rows of houses as radiant as ten million fires, and was filled with divine men and women who were eternally in the prime of youth. (16)
In the center of the city was the enchanting inner palace of the god, enclosed by a wall of jewels and adorned with jeweled archways. ||17||
It was filled with celestial chariots, preeminent mansions, and many palaces,
and was adorned on all sides by hosts of divine apsarases and women.
In the center was a divine pavilion, a lofty royal hall,
auspicious and composed of jewels, adorned with thousands of pillars made of rubies.
It was strewn with divine pearls, graced by the singing of the Sāmaveda, and featured a beautiful, auspicious lion-throne in its center composed of all the Vedas.

This [universe] is eternally enveloped by the deities beginning with Dharma, who consist of the nature of fire, and whose bodies are the four feet consisting of dharma, knowledge, sovereign power, and dispassion. ||21||
He is eternally surrounded, in due order, by the forms of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas;
he is Śakti, Ādhāra-śakti, Cit-śakti, and Sadāśivā.
And the powers of the deities beginning with Dharma are proclaimed;
there, in the center, reside Fire, Sun, and Moon. (23)
Kūrma, the king of serpents (Nāgarāja), Vainateya, and the Lord of the Three Vedas (Trayīśvara)—all the meters and all the mantras have assumed the form of the sacred seats (pīṭhas). ||24||
The divine seat of yoga is known to consist of all letters;
in its center is an eight-petaled lotus, radiant like the rising sun. (25)
In the center of that, within the pericarp of the lotus, O lady of auspicious appearance, the Supreme Person, the Lord of Sahadeva, sits together with Īśvarī. (26)
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns, he is a youthful prince, tender and endowed with delicate limbs. (27)
Resembling a blooming red lotus, he possesses tender lotus-feet;
he is fully awakened, with eyes like white lotuses, and is marked by a pair of beautiful, creeper-like eyebrows.
He possessed a fine nose, was endowed with beautiful cheeks, and had lovely ears and a lotus-like face; he was adorned with teeth like pearls and a coral-like lower lip that was ever-smiling.
Resembling the full moon, with a lotus-face graced by a beautiful smile, he shone with two earrings possessing the hue of the rising sun. (30)
He is adorned with glossy, dark blue, and curly locks of hair,
his tresses being enriched by Mandāra and Pārijāta flowers.
Adorned with the brilliance of the thousand-rayed sun rising at dawn and the Kaustubha gem,
he shone forth, his conch-like neck graced by a necklace and a golden garland.
He was resplendent with broad, high, and full shoulders, and adorned with four arms that were thick, rounded, and long.
He was adorned with rings, bracelets, and armlets,
and further embellished with excellent ornaments such as the Kaustubha gem, which shone like ten million rising suns.
He is adorned with a forest garland upon his magnificent, radiant chest,
and graced by the lotus of his navel, which is the source and dwelling place of the Creator.
Adorned with smooth yellow garments resembling the morning sun,
his feet are variegated with various jewels and resplendent with two bracelets.
Endowed with a row of nails resembling the moon in its radiant splendor, Acyuta is a treasury of pride, loveliness, and beauty, like ten million moons.
Anointed with divine sandalwood paste and adorned with a divine garland,
he shone with his two uplifted arms grasping the conch and the discus.
With her two hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and likewise with her other two hands, the goddess Mahālakṣmī, the Great Sovereign, is seated upon his left lap. (39)
Golden-hued, tawny, adorned with garlands of gold and silver,
endowed with all auspicious marks, she possessed a body in the full bloom of youth.
Adorned with jeweled earrings, her hair was decorated with blue lotuses;
she was anointed with divine sandalwood paste and graced by celestial flowers.
Adorned with *dāraka*, *ketakī*, and *jātī* flowers, she was delicate of limb;
she possessed beautiful eyebrows, a fine nose, shapely hips, and full, elevated breasts. (42)
Her lotus-face was adorned with a gentle smile that dispelled all suffering;
she shone with two earrings possessing the hue of the rising sun. ||43||
She has the luster of the color of molten gold, is adorned with ornaments of molten gold,
is endowed with four hands, and is decorated with golden lotuses.
She was adorned with a golden lotus garland enriched with various wonderful jewels,
and graced with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings.
Adorned by a pair of prominent lotuses held in her two arms, she is graced by hands holding what are known as a citron and a jambu fruit. 46.
Thus, the Lord Maheśvara always rejoices eternally in the supreme, eternal, and imperishable ether with Mahālakṣmī, who is likewise eternal and never-departing. ||47||
On the two sides, on auspicious seats, sit Dharaṇī and Nīlā;
and at the tips of the petals in the eight directions are the Śaktis, Vimalā and the others.
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and likewise Yoga, Prahvī, Satyā, and Īśānā are the powers (śaktis) of the Supreme Self. 49.
Taking divine whisks that possessed a luster like the moon and were endowed with every auspicious mark, they fanned the Lord Acyuta with joy.
There were five hundred celestial nymphs as women, inhabitants of the inner apartments, adorned with every kind of ornament. ||51||
All of them held lotuses in their hands, possessed the radiance of ten million fires,
were endowed with all the auspicious marks, and had faces as cool and pleasant as the moon.
Surrounded by them, the King, the Supreme Person,
shone like the Lord of the Gods (Indra) surrounded by Ananta, Vihageśvara, Senānī, and the other lords of the deities.
Surrounded by other constant attendants and those who have been released,
that man, devoted to pleasures and sovereignty, rejoices together with Rāmā.
Thus does this Lord of Vaikuṇṭha shine in the supreme station;
O auspicious Girijā, I shall describe His various manifestations and the worlds associated with them. 55.
In the east is the temple of Vāsudeva, belonging to the world of Vaikuṇṭha;
in the southeast is the world of Lakṣmī, and in the south is the abode of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Sārasvata is in the southwest, Prādyumna likewise in the west;
Ratiloka is in the northwest, and Aniruddha’s realm is in the north. (57)
In the north, there shall be the world of Śānti; this is remembered as the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
Following that, in sequence, are these twenty-four worlds beginning with Keśava.
The second enclosure of Vaikuṇṭha is declared to be named Śubha;
the auspicious third enclosure consists of the worlds of Matsya, Kūrma, and the others. 59.
Satya, Acyuta, Ananta, Durgā, Viṣvaksena, Gajānana,
the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures, and the worlds constitute the auspicious fourth enclosure.
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas were established in the great quarters beginning with the East,
as well as the Sāvitrī, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), Dharma, and Makha.
The fifth enclosure is declared to be imperishable and consisting of all speech;
likewise, it contains the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, Śārṅga bow, and plow. 62.
Likewise, the Mausala [weapon], along with all the *śastra*s and *astra*s, is declared to be the sixth enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), consisting of imperishable mantra-weapons. (63)
The regions of Indra, Agni, Yama, as well as Nairṛta, Varuṇa,
Vāyu, Soma, and the seventh, Īśāna, are recorded by the sages.
The Sādhyas and the hosts of Maruts, as well as the Viśvedevas, all the eternal ones in the supreme abode, and whatever other inhabitants of heaven there may be— 65.
Indeed, those lords of the thirty gods are impermanent in this world of Prakṛti;
"those majestic ones attain the celestial realm (nāka)," so indeed says the Śruti.
Thus the Lord, the Sovereign, shines with his supreme state, accompanied by eternal, liberated beings devoted to enjoyment and by his divine queens.
Neither the sun illumines that, nor the moon, nor the fire;
having gone there, the yogins of firm vows do not return. 68.
Those who are devoted solely to the single mantra of duality go to that imperishable state; they do not reach it through Vedic sacrifices, study, gifts, or auspicious vows.
Neither by austerities, nor by fasting, nor by ritual acts of propitiation,
can [the goal] be attained as it is by this single mantra, through devotion to You alone.
"That eternal and imperishable state, attainable through devotion, [is thus described].
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, you have well described the supreme nature of heaven. (71)
How did he, who eternally resides in the supreme void, come to abide in the sphere of primordial nature? For what reason? Was it out of sport, or for some specific purpose? (72)
How is it that the Supreme Lord, who abides in this world consisting of pure sattva, has established himself through a manifestation mixed with rajas and tamas? ||73||
Rudra said:
In the manifestation of the three-quarters, the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, who is the sole object of enjoyment for those eternally liberated, that all-pervading one rejoices perpetually. (74)
Then Mahāmāyā, the primordial nature (prakṛti) who is the support of the universe,
having joined her palms in reverence, praised that Supreme Lord, the Sovereign.
Mahāmāyā said:
Homage to you, the abode of the three worlds; homage to you, whose form is the universe.
Homage to you, the ancient one, the cause of the world's origin. (76)
Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā;
salutations to you, the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. ||77||
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the victorious one, whose very nature is that of all the gods;
salutations be to you, the infinite one, who possesses a thousand forms. (78)
Salutations again and again to the one who is infallible, immutable, whose nature is pure being, and whose essential form is devoid of beginning, middle, and end. (79)
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Knowledge, to the Supreme Self;
to you who are the self of all beings and the refuge of all beings. 80.
Salutations to you, O Brahman, the light; salutations to you who possess all forms.
Salutations to you, the dweller in purity, the supreme swan.
Salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa, to Rudra, and to the sustainer of all beings;
salutations to Hayagrīva, the radiant one, to Kāla, and to Hari.
Homage to you, O Sacrificial Person, whose very nature is the sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors. (82)
Salutation to this Prajāpati, to Sūrya of auspicious luster;
salutation to that Agni, the consumer of oblations, whose self is sacrifice. 83.
Salutations to you, the progenitor and the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
salutations to him who is known through the Vedānta and whose nature consists of the fourfold self.
Salutations to you, O Brahmā; salutations to you, O Viṣṇu; salutations to you, O Śiva; and salutations to you, the performer of auspiciousness.
Salutations to you, the one of three qualities (triguṇa), the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
Salutations to you who are devoid of qualities, who abide within the inner self of all;
salutations to that unmanifest Viṣṇu, the witness of the worlds. ||86||
Salutation to Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, whose form is the perfection of the six divine attributes;
salutation to Him who is full of infinite qualities and the bestower of all goals. 87.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, whose nature consists of the five states;
salutations to you who possess the forms of the ninefold and fivefold manifestations. 88.
Salutations again and again to Govinda, the Supreme Sacrificial Boar;
salutations to the changeless, the pure, and the adversary of all that is to be abandoned. 89.
Salutations to Rāma, to Kṛṣṇa, and to you, Narasiṃha;
salutations to you, Keśava, the remover of the afflictions of the worlds. (90)
You alone are the refuge for all the worlds, the Supreme Person;
be gracious, O Lord of the gods, for the welfare of all the worlds. 91.
All sentient beings residing within me are without support or refuge;
they are devoid of bodies, formless, and entirely free from sense faculties. ||92||
Deprived of all religious observances and constantly experiencing suffering, O Keśava, it behoves you to grant them both worlds and bodies. (93)
O Omniscient One, fashion once again, as before, the manifestation of Your divine play—the entire world, both sentient and insentient, moving and stationary. (94)
O Supreme Lord, behold how I have been deluded; for the sake of your divine play, O Puruṣottama, create the material egg together with me. (95)
"Merit and demerit, pleasure and pain—these are not cast aside in this cycle of birth and death;
therefore, you ought without delay to manifest your divine play by presiding over me. (96)
The illustrious Mahādeva said: Thus addressed by that goddess Māyā, the Supreme Lord, while Māyā was being established within her, proceeded to create the world. 97.
He who is called here the primordial Puruṣa, the Imperishable (Acyuta), is that very Lord Viṣṇu who entered into Prakṛti. (98)
He created within primordial nature (prakṛti) the beginning of the elements, which has the Great One (mahat) as its support;
from this Puruṣa, who is the Great One, the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra) was born. 99.
From this very principle of ego (ahaṃkāra), the three qualities (guṇas) were born;
from those three qualities, the creator of the universe produced the subtle elements (tanmātras). 100.
From those subtle elements (tanmātras), the gross elements (mahābhūtas) were born at that very moment;
first, the syllable Om was born from Brahmā, whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas). ||101||
From space arose wind; from wind, fire was born; from fire, water emerged; and from water, the earth is said to have arisen. (102)
The elements beginning with space were indeed created one after another;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their respective qualities. (103)
Having created those qualities in an ascending order and having taken them up, the Great Lord,
having mixed them together, created a vast cosmic egg;
therein, he created the fourteen worlds according to their enumeration.
In that [egg], Puruṣottama created the thirty gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as the fourfold [creation]: the divine, the animal, the human, and the immobile. 105.
Thus created at the end of the great creation, O lotus-eyed one,
[beings] are born there among the wombs of the gods and others, in accordance with their karma.
For they arise from the primordial Self, established within its own nature. ||107||
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa,
in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa,
[this is] the section titled "The Description of Paramavyoma and Other Realms."
The two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter. ||228|| ||cha||
(229) Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Nine.
Pārvatī said:
Tell me in detail this unsurpassed account of the creation of the gods:
how were the eternal ones, the foremost of the three heavens beginning with Brahmā, born? And tell me that in detail—the incarnations and portions of the Lord.
Rudra said:
Having created ether, air, fire, water, and earth in their proper sequence,
Brahmā created within them the ocean of unfathomable waters.
When this world had become a single ocean, Hari took all beings onto the leaf of the banyan tree of the illusion of water and entered the sleep of yoga.
Desiring to create the world with all its beings, Madhusūdana entered into yogic sleep; by means of that Māyā, he sported for a long time.
In her, he— the soul of Time— begot the unsurpassed [Time] who consists of units such as kalās and kāṣṭhās, and whose form comprises pakṣas, months, and so forth.
At that time, the lotus from the navel of Hari was in the form of a bud;
it was radiant, the seed of the entire universe, and blossoming.
There, Brahmā, the one of great intelligence, arose and emerged;
impelled by the quality of *rajas* and desiring to create the world,
he praised the Supreme Lord who was reclining in the yoga-sleep.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to you, O Viṣṇu, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe;
to the one adorned by the ornament of the world, the glorious one who possesses the universal form.
Salutations to the god who is devoted to Brahman; salutations again and again to Govinda, Kṛṣṇa, who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins and who works for the benefit of the world. (9)

Salutations to the one whose forms are Pradhāna and Kāla, to the Puruṣa and the Īśvara; salutations to the one whose form is the phenomenal world, yet whose true nature is beyond the phenomenal world.
Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇa, the Universal One, the Lord of the Universe;
salutations to the Supreme Self, the Brahman, the sovereign lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā.
Salutations to Vāsudeva, whose form is the universe, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
to Hari, the Lord of the three Vedas, who is the very embodiment of the Lord of the universe.
Homage to you, who are filled with infinite auspicious qualities;
when you sleep, the entire world sleeps, for you are composed of the world. 13.
The entire world, including all things moving and unmoving, is pervaded by you;
you alone are the cause, the agent, and the effect arising from the three qualities.
You alone are the Supreme Lord, the creator, the ordainer, and the disposer;
you remain awake, established in pure *sattva*—O Lord, whence could there be sleep for you?
The eternal worlds abide in you as deities, sustained by your meditative concentration.
Śiva said:
Thus addressed by Brahmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Lord,
rose from that bed, released from his yogic sleep.
Having restrained that yogic sleep,
the inconceivable Lord Acyuta, the sovereign of the worlds, proceeded at that very moment to create the universe.
Having reflected thus, that Puruṣa then created the entire world.
Then all the worlds indeed became a golden mandala of the Sugata. ||18||
The Lord created the seven islands and oceans, together with the earth and its mountains, along with the shell of the cosmic egg, within the lotus of his navel.
Then Hari, the Lord, established his abode within that egg;
who, indeed, could then meditate upon Nārāyaṇa with a mind focused on the Self? (20)
From his forehead, as he was meditating, a drop of sweat was produced;
that drop, in the form of a bubble, instantly fell upon the earth.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, I was born from that bubble;
I am three-eyed, with a trident in my hand, adorned with a crown of matted hair. (22)
Filled with humility, I said to the Lord of Gods, "What shall I do?
Thereupon, the god Nārāyaṇa, full of joy, spoke thus to me.
O fair-faced one, you are the creator of the two worlds and the destroyer of Rudra, appearing with a terrifying form; you are the manifest power of Saṅkarṣaṇa for the purpose of destroying him.
Therefore, O Goddess, I have been born from Nārāyaṇa as the bringer of fear;
yet Janārdana shall surely withdraw me once again when he so commands.
From his two eyes he created the moon and the sun, which remove heat from above;
from his two ears he created the wind and the quarters; and from his mouth he created Indra and Agni.
From his two nostrils, the lotus-eyed one created Varuṇa and Mitra;
from his two arms, he created all the gods, along with the Sādhyas and the hosts of Maruts.
From all his pores of the skin came jewels and medicinal herbs;
likewise, from his skin came mountains and oceans, as well as cattle and other animals.
The Brāhmaṇa was created from the mouth, and likewise the Kṣatriya from the two arms;
the Vaiśya was born from the thighs, and the Śūdra indeed arose from the feet. (29)
Having thus created the entire world, which remains insentient,
the Lord of Gods presides within it in his universal form.
Since there is no manifestation of that [Lord] without the withdrawal of his power (śakti), therefore Viṣṇu alone is the eternal life-force of the entire world. ||31||
That very Supreme Self, remaining in an unmanifest form,
Himself brings about the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of Brahmā.
This eternal Vāsudeva, who is complete in the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), manifests the world in four forms from his own self consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa). ||33||
The Blessed One in the form of Pradyumna is endowed with all sovereign powers over Brahmā,
the Prajāpatis, Kāla, and all living beings.

Having attained the state of being his inner controller (antar-yāmitva), he indeed performed the formal dismissal (samyak-sarga); thereafter, he gave the Vedas along with the Itihāsas to that Great-Souled One.
This Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, is a portion of Pradyumna; born from a fraction [of him], he performs the entire creation and maintenance of the universe. (36)
And the Blessed Lord Aniruddha is endowed with power and splendor over the Manus,
the kings, time, and all living beings.
The Blessed One, established as the Antarvyāmī, brings about stability;
he is Saṅkarṣaṇa, the Great Viṣṇu, endowed with the power of knowledge. ||38||
Assuming the role of the inner controller (antaryāmin) of Time, of all beings, and of Rudra and Yama, the Lord withdraws the universe. ||39||
Thus, in the state of the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), the inner rulership of the Self [is established];
[the incarnations are] the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, and then the Dwarf. (40)
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki—these ten are the states of manifestation (vibhava-avasthā) of Brahman, the Supreme Self. ||41||
The sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) has been proclaimed in relation to Nṛsiṃha, Hara, Kṛṣṇa, and Iṣu;
it is like one lamp produced from another lamp of the Supreme Lord who exists in the state of Parā.
O auspicious Girijā, listen to this state of Hari’s assistance:
the supreme world of Vaikuṇṭha, the unsurpassed realm of Viṣṇu. 43.
Śvetadvīpa is His essential form, as is the supreme Ocean of Milk;
thus has the fourfold manifestation been correctly described by the great seers.
In the midst of the veil of water is the auspicious causal Vaikuṇṭha,
resembling ten million fires, entirely virtuous and imperishable.
It was filled with fragrant trees and fires,
divine, composed of various jewels, and joined by tens of millions of celestial chariots.
As for that which was described as the supreme abode, established with such characteristics,
in that city of Vaikuṇṭha, resplendent with various jewels— (47)
In the center of Devajayārāma was a beautiful and unsurpassed city,
provided with four gates and featuring golden ramparts and archways.
It was guarded by the gatekeepers beginning with Caṇḍa, as well as by Kumuda and others, and it was surrounded by rows of divine mansions made of various jewels. (49)
It was spread out for five padmas and yojanas in extent,
and was surrounded by tens of millions of palaces rising a thousand yojanas high.
It was graced by divine men and women who had reached the prime of youth;
both the women and the men therein were adorned with all auspicious marks.
And they were all identical in form to Śrī Viṣṇu, adorned with every ornament, clothed in divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine sandalwood paste. ||52||
O Lord of Gods, those who have attained perfection through the eight-syllable mantra rejoice there with devotion in that self-delighting realm, by means of the sixteen-fold form of devotion. 53.
Having entered that state, those who are chosen rejoice as they desire in their minds;
having gone there, they do not return, remaining forever established together with Viṣṇu.
The auspicious ones are joined with Viṣṇu, whose nature is uninterrupted.
The wise attain that same bliss eternally. ||55||
Entering the worlds of Hari here and there with pure minds,
living beings attain heaven once again, just like those already dwelling in heaven.
Just as Saumitri and Bharata, and just as Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others, so too they are born in Satyaloka according to their will. (57)
Furthermore, by that very [means], they shall go to that supreme, eternal state;
for Vaiṣṇavas, there exists neither the bondage of karma nor rebirth. ||58||
For the wise have declared that service to Viṣṇu is indeed liberation;
servitude to the Lord of the Immortals is not proclaimed to be bondage. (59)
The servants of Hari are free from all bonds and are beyond affliction;
whereas the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are characterized by the necessity of returning again.
They cause suffering born of the bonds of karma, bestow fear through the loss of friends and kin, yield fruits of great exertion, and are the causes for the destruction of living beings. ||61||
The enjoyment of pleasure by men is like eating food mixed with poison;
having seen the men established in heaven when their karma is exhausted, the deities [depart]. (62)
When provoked, they surely cause one to fall from the bond of duty that has been undertaken;
therefore, O Goddess, the happiness of heaven is achieved through manifold exertions.
The yogi should abandon that which is impermanent, fragile, and mixed with suffering;
he should constantly remember Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the flood of all miseries. 64.
By the mere utterance of His name, they attain the supreme state;
therefore, a wise person should earnestly pray for the world of Viṣṇu from Gaurī.
One should thus worship the compassionate intellect with unswerving devotion; He who possesses all knowledge and virtues will surely protect one—of this there is no doubt. (66)
Therefore, by reciting this eight-syllable mantra, which is exceedingly blissful and auspicious, one attains the supreme Vaishnava realm that grants all desires. ||67||
Seated upon that divine celestial chariot, on a gem-studded couch radiant as the rays of a thousand suns, the Blessed Lord Hari shone forth.
And there, upon a golden pedestal supported by the foundational powers (ādhāra-śakti) and others, which is divine, composed of various jewels, and endowed with many colors; ||69||
In that auspicious eight-petalled lotus, within the syllables of the mantra,
upon the beautiful pericarp, lies the auspicious syllable of the seed-mantra of Lakṣmī.
In that [palace], which possessed a radiance equal to a thousand times ten million rising suns,
the glorious and divine Nārāyaṇa was seated upon a lotus throne.
On his right side was the Mother of the World, made of gold,
holding divine whisks and adorned with celestial garlands and ornaments.
Holding a vessel of wealth, a citron, and a golden lotus in her hands, she is on the left side; the goddess Pṛthivī has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus.
Adorned with various ornaments and decorated with diverse, excellent finery,
she holds two beautiful red lotuses aloft with her two raised arms.
Likewise, the goddess held a pair of vessels for grain with her other two hands,
while the Śaktis, beginning with Vimalā, took up divine whisks.
Seated upon the tips of the petals, they were all adorned with every auspicious mark;
in their midst sat the Blessed Lord Acyuta Hari.
Adorned with divine ornaments, he is graced by armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and other jewels, holding in his hands the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Resplendent with two earrings like the rising sun at dawn,
the Supreme Lord is eternally served by the aforementioned thirty deities.
He indeed dwells in the eternal and true city of Vaikuṇṭha, enjoying [the fruits of his merit],
having mastered the glorious eight-syllable mantra for the sake of the perfected ones who possess wisdom.
That Vaiṣṇava world is indeed accessible [only] to them, and not to others by any means.
Thus, O fair-faced one, has the first manifestation (vyūha) been described to you. (80)
O lady of excellent vows, listen as I describe the second world of Viṣṇu;
this world, known as Nitya, is remembered as the foremost of all worlds belonging to Viṣṇu. ||81||
Then that world was vast, meritorious, pure, composed of sentient beings, and auspicious, illuminated simultaneously by the light of a thousand midday suns. ||82||
Even for you, it would not dissolve even in an eon; this world of mine is most vast. It cannot even be seen by the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
It was entirely filled with groves of wish-fulfilling trees extending evenly in all directions,
and it was provided with oblong ponds completely filled with nectar-like water.
It was adorned with divine lotuses made of gold and jewels,
and surrounded by tens of millions of divine ornaments resembling water and fire.
It was adorned with *puṣpaka* flowers and with *gandharva* trees being carried along by cuckoos and other birds warbling with continuous melodies. ||86||
He was surrounded by divine men and women who were slightly less than sixteen years of age, endowed with the splendor of all auspicious marks and adorned with celestial ornaments. ||87||
In those delightful regions,
the women, together with their joyful husbands, worshipped the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Attaining happiness obtainable through His grace, they always enjoy it;
they sing of the supreme bliss found in the great deeds of Kṛṣṇa. (89)
