With lotus-eyes, lotus-hands, and beautiful forms resembling the lotus, those excellent women, adorned with divine garlands and garments, were sporting. 90.
Adorned with ornaments and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, those men standing there were garlanded and dressed in yellow garments. ||91||
Because there is no contact with anything else while the man and woman are sporting there, the blissful nectar of devotion to Hari increases day by day. (92)
In its center was the beautiful city of Vāsudeva,
adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and water.
It was completely adorned on all sides with various flowers, celestial chariots, and other ornaments;
in its center, beneath the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree, upon a lotus seat— (94)
It was covered with various smooth rugs and cushions,
and adorned with coverings of diverse flowers, richly beautified by divine fragrances.
Seated upon that divine throne which delights the mind,
the eternal Vāsudeva, the Lord of gods, dwells together with his sovereign Śrī.
Resembling the tip of a parrot's beak, adorned with divine ornaments,
he had a pair of smooth nostrils as bright as gold and a face marked with auspicious signs.
He shone with two cheeks that were smooth, broad, and most beautiful, adorned with dark, curly hair, and possessing eyes like the petals of a red lotus. 98.
He has fashioned his crest from jasmine, *ketakī*, and white water-lily flowers;
his lips have the luster of smooth bimba fruit, and his lotus-face bears a beautiful smile. (99)
Adorned with bees, he shone like a priceless pearl;
smeared with yellow sandalwood paste, he was marked with a tilaka of musk. (100)
He is graced by four long arms that are elevated,
and he is adorned with sprout-like hands that resemble the color of the *japā* flower.
And he was adorned with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem upon his broad chest.
He is adorned with divine garlands, exceedingly beautiful and composed of pearls,
and is wrapped in a yellow garment that possesses a luster like the rising sun.
He shone with lotus-petal-like feet adorned with anklets of rubies, and was resplendent with rows of nails resembling the spotless moon. ||104||
His lotus-like hands are smooth and white, resembling red lotuses; he possesses feet, a chariot, and garments, and is resplendent with a pair of arms. (105)
Embracing the body of Śrī with his other two arms upon his own chest,
he shines like a dark cloud streaked with flashes of lightning and rising thunder.
Upon this [island] with its seven mountain ranges, smooth and beautiful, the eternal Lord of Gods, Vāsudeva, sports with his pair of lotus-feet. 107.
Adorned with all ornaments made of molten gold and kashaya cloth,
she shone like the night illuminated by the moon, her hair being very glossy, dark blue, and curled.
Adorned with divine flowers such as the coral tree and the pārijāta, her hair is richly beautified by ear-ornaments and resembles the tālīsa leaf. 109.
Adorned with armlets, maces, necklaces, and other ornaments, they press their full, uplifted breasts against the chest of Hari. 110.
Having reached the prime of youth, she who is eternally the most beautiful woman in all the worlds sports there with her husband Lokeśa without interruption. (111)
He alone is Vāsudeva here, the captivator of the hearts of all beings;
he sports in this entire world, bestowing all desires upon men. 112.
Here, the eight powers, the embodiments of Lakṣmī, are stationed all around:
Ramā, Rukmiṇī, Sītā, Padmā, Padmālayā, and Śivā. (113)
They possess auspicious marks and virtuous conduct, and they bestow pleasure and desire;
likewise, they are endowed with weapons such as the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and bow.
It protects that world on all sides with forms shaped like lotuses;
thus, O lady of auspicious appearance, you have correctly seen its second form.
I have spoken this in brief, for it cannot indeed be told in detail:
those who recite the twelve-syllable mantra called Sukhāhvaya.
They constantly attain that which is eternal, auspicious, and inexhaustible;
[it is] not through the study of the Vedas, nor by sacrifices, nor by vows, nor by fasting. ||117||
The world of Viṣṇu cannot be attained anywhere without giving;
therefore, with a mind focused on no other, one should worship the devotee of Hari who serves him. 118.
One attains the supreme accomplishment that liberates from the bondage of karma.
Thus, O Goddess, the second imperishable array is proclaimed. (119)
But listen, O Pārvatī, as I shall describe the third supreme array: on the northern shore of the ocean of water, in Śvetadvīpa, O high-minded one. (120)
For the sake of revealing the yogas to the great-souled ones beginning with Sanaka—
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana— ||121||
Sanatkumāra, Jāta, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha— these seven sons of Brahmā were yogins of exceedingly great power.

Always dispassionate toward all enjoyments, pure, and characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva), they partake solely in the singular flavor of the bliss arising from the vision of the Blessed One. ||123||
And for the purpose of beholding those such as Nara and Nārāyaṇa who dwell in Śvetadvīpa, Hari is present there.
In the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), which shines with the brilliance of ten million moons, resplendent with jewels of every kind, served by great yogis, and free from all fear; 125.
There, the gardens were delightful, resembling the Pārijāta tree,
filled with clusters of blossoming creepers, and adorned with sandalwood trees.
It is filled with blooming lotuses and water-lilies, and endowed with various reservoirs of water;
in its center is a beautiful city named the auspicious Airāvatī.
It was adorned with divine celestial mansions made of various jewels,
filled with divine men and women, and crowded with many palaces.
In its center was a beautiful inner apartment, filled with jewel-trees and surrounded by many palaces with turrets resembling the rising sun.
In its center was a divine pavilion, adorned with jewels and gold,
and perfumed by the fragrance of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron.
It was beautifully adorned with canopies richly decorated with various flowers,
filled with divine apsarases, and graced by the singing of Sāman chants.
In its center is a seat possessing the radiance of the sun and Vaiśvānara;
in the middle of that is an eight-petaled lotus, like another lunar disc.
Seated in the pericarp in the center of that [lotus] is Janārdana, resembling pure saffron in luster and adorned with strings of pearls. (133)
He has four hands holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
he is adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings. (134)
His pair of feet shone like golden lotuses,
and they were resplendent with rows of nails as bright as refined silver.
He was resplendent with the beauty of youth at the age of sixteen,
and his broad forehead was adorned with fragrant saffron.
Adorned with a vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on his forehead, he was beautifully dressed in white garments resembling the foam of churned nectar. ||137||
He was resplendent with two bright earrings made of pearls, seated upon a lotus throne, his form enchanting to the world. ||138||
On his left side sat a goddess of divine form;
in her beauty, character, and excellent virtues, she was like Lakṣmī herself. (139)
Adorned with saffron robes as radiant as lotus filaments,
she was endowed with all auspicious marks and decorated with ornaments of refined gold.
Adorned with divine garlands and garments, her hair was dark and curly;
she shone with four arms, decorated with armlets and bracelets.
This wife of Citaśīrṣaja shines with pearl necklaces;
she possesses smooth nostrils and is adorned with beautiful, slow-moving teeth. 142.
Her nose-tip was adorned with a musk tilaka and set with pearls;
her full and elevated breasts were as radiant as golden jars. (143)
Smeared with divine saffron paste, adorned with a garland of lotuses, she holds a garment, a vessel, a citron, a mirror, and a golden lotus. (144)
The goddess held in his lotus-hand grants all desired objects with her mind; his similar Śaktis are situated there all around Hara. 145.
Īśāvāsyā, Mahādevī, Jāhnavī, Kamalālayā, Sāvitrī, Sarvagā, and Padmā are proclaimed to be the Śaktis. ||146||

Faith, intelligence, fortitude, wisdom, retentive memory, and tranquility; as well as sacred learning, mindfulness, steadfastness, the increase of intellect, and the wise discernment of the mind. 147.
These glories are said to be the maidservants of that which performs every action;
they are the eternal attendants of the deities such as Ananta and Vainateya.
The hosts of Sādhyas and Maruts, as well as the eternal deities,
dwell in palaces, celestial chariots, forests, and cities.
Delighting here in the enjoyments obtained through his grace, they sport constantly, eternally free from what is to be abandoned and devoid of the fruitless. (150)
Those who constantly recite the mantras of Viṣṇu endowed with faith, or those who are devoted to the vow of Dvādaśī, go to that imperishable state. (151)
O Daughter of the Mountain, the eternal world of Viṣṇu cannot be attained even by sacrifices, gifts, rituals, or religious observances. (152)
The station of Viṣṇu can be attained by men through exclusive devotion;
therefore, one should always worship the god Janārdana with devotion. 153.

One should always perform kīrtana, which is merely the name; one should meditate, recite the mantra, offer oblations, and satisfy [the deity] with devotion—the all-pervading one who grants all desires. 154.
Thus has been described, O lady of beautiful hips, the third manifestation of the Supreme Self, its essential nature as it was proclaimed by the ancients. (155)
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the fourth and most excellent manifestation (vyūha): for the protection of the inhabitants of heaven, the Supreme Lord [appeared] from the Ocean of Milk. 156.
In the ocean of milk, which was agitated by the herds of [the mountain] Puraṃdara and adorned with a thousand eyes, Kāśa produced nectar in the measure of ten million parrots.
Upon that vast and auspicious bed of infinite extent lies Acyuta Hari, Padmanābha, seated upon a divine throne. 158.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with eyes as broad as lotus petals, he was resplendent with a crown that shone like ten million suns. ||159||
Resplendent with two divine earrings blazing with various jewels,
he was wrapped in a yellow garment that possessed the luster of the rising sun.
Adorned with a hand resembling a throbbing red lotus, graced by a glistening ornament, and resplendent with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and rings. ||161||
Adorned with hands holding a conch, a discus, a mace, a bow, and a sword, he is resplendent with kalpa-trees rich in beautiful flowers, fruits, and branches. ||162||
Adorned by the lotus-navel from which the birth and death of the universe proceed,
his body is smeared with yellow sandalwood paste and decorated with all manner of ornaments.
[He saw him] with beautiful celestial flowers such as māndārava and pārijāta,
and with hair arranged in a very glossy, dark-blue, curly braid.
Adorned with smooth, elevated, and beautiful nostrils, he shone with a pair of symmetrical knees;
his feet were graced by anklets richly set with branches of jewels and coral. (165)
He is resplendent with rows of nails shining like the full moon, and his lotus-face has lips as red as *aśoka* flowers. (166)
He was resplendent with rows of teeth shining like priceless pearls, and his face was beautifully adorned with a smile resembling the full moon. ||167||
Having attained full youth, glorious, with radiant and delicate limbs, he is the refuge of all worlds and the bestower of the fruits of all worlds. (168)
A queen worthy of him in beauty, character, virtues, and other qualities—shining like molten gold and adorned with ornaments of molten gold—[was found]. (169)
Endowed with the qualities of youth, beauty, charm, splendor, and virtuous conduct, she was clothed in auspicious garments resembling the foam of the ocean of milk. ||170||
Her hair was honored with flowers of the *dāraka*, *ketakī*, and *jātī*; she was adorned with a musk tilaka and graced by a jeweled parting of her hair. (171)
Richly adorned with the beautiful splendor of various colors, she was decorated with earrings reaching to her ears;
she was utterly amazed by the red streams of moonlight resembling coral.
She was beautifully adorned with glossy locks of hair resembling intoxicated bees;
she possessed a slender waist, large eyes, and full, elevated breasts. (173)
Shining with four hands and adorned with all ornaments,
the Goddess held a pair of auspicious golden lotuses with her two upraised arms.
Embracing her husband firmly with her other two arms, she stood there,
constantly gazing at the gods with sidelong glances.
O Śivā, those who are constantly beheld by that Goddess are truly blessed;
there, the gods, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras remain stationed in their celestial chariots.
With eyes overflowing with tears, they constantly sing praises to the Goddess while being oppressed by the Daityas and by the gods, such as Brahmā and Rudra. (177)
Being thus praised there, the Lord granted fearlessness to the gods;
having granted fearlessness to the gods, Hari, the sovereign of all deities, [remained]. ||178||
He began to slay the Rākṣasas for the sake of protecting the world;
thus, O sinless one, the fourth array of Hari has been described to you. 179.
What else do you wish to hear, O fair-faced one? Speak;
you are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you are devoted to Puruṣottama. (180)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Varieties of Viṣṇu’s Manifestations," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
The two hundred and thirtieth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, tell me where the Lord of Gods, Madhusūdana, [slew] the Rākṣasas."
Tell me how he struck him with a certain form; you ought to speak thus.
O Maheśvara, out of affection for me, describe in detail the majesty of that earth whose forms are the fish, the tortoise, and so forth.
Mahādeva said: Listen, O Goddess, with a tranquil mind; I shall describe the majesty of Hari’s incarnational forms, such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others. 3.
Just as a lamp is produced from a lamp, so it will be for the Supreme Lord; the states of manifestation, dissolution, and so forth, belong to another. (4)
Thus have been described the auspicious incarnations of various forms;
these are the manifestations of the glory of the Supreme Self, the Lord, in his embodied (arcā) form. ||5||
Brahmā, the sovereign emperor of the highest festival, [created] through the Prajāpati-rite Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, Dakṣa, and Kardama.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Giriśa, and likewise Kratu—
these are declared to be the lords of the nine progenitors in their proper order.
There, the blessed Marīci begot Kaśyapa;
and O lady of auspicious appearance, Kaśyapa had four wives.
Aditi, Diti, Kadru, and likewise Vinatā—
of these, Aditi, who was beautiful to behold, gave birth to the gods.
Diti gave birth to sons who were Rākṣasas, characterized by darkness (tāmasa), and great Asuras:
Śambūka, Hayagrīva, and the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa. ||10||
Hiraṇyakaśipu, Jambha, Maya, and others of great ascetic power,
as well as the exceedingly heroic Makara, have all attained the world of Brahmā.
Having deluded Brahmā, that valiant one seized the Vedas;
and having swallowed the Śruti, he then entered the great ocean.
Then the entire world became a void, a confusion of dharma;
no one studied the nine or sixfold Vedic hymns, and it was devoid of the system of castes and stages of life.
Then the divine Prajāpati, surrounded by all the hosts of gods,
went to the churned ocean and, having sought refuge, praised the Lord.
Brahmā said: Be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Master of the serpent-throne, O Sovereign of all, O Soul of all gods, O Acyuta who consists of all the Vedas! 15.
You are the primordial seed of the world and its existence; yet, in the midst of all, you are superior to everything.
You are the Lord of the bound souls (paśu), and by your own will, you have descended into that very state.
You alone sustain this entire eternal world in its conscious form; for you are the unmanifest source of all beings, the primordial matter (pradhāna), and the imperishable Puruṣa.
O Supreme Lord, you are the very body of the world’s beginning, middle, and end;
you alone are the refuge of all worlds, the Supreme Person. 18.
You are the origin of the elements, the Great Being, the cause of the multitude of beings;
relying upon you alone as the cause, the self-possessed one rejoices in the abode of light.
You are the beginning and you are the end; you are the great, all-pervading wind.
You are the origin and you are without origin; you are the fire, the treasury of splendor. 20.
You are the waters, the life of all the worlds, the Supreme Lord;
you are the earth, the support of the universe, and you are the mountain, O Great-minded One. 21.
You are the river and you are the ocean; you alone are the origin of the universe. You are the celestial sage, you are all beings, and you alone are the Supreme Person. 22.
Impelled by you alone, people act toward both the good and the evil;
the Vedas, harassed by the Daitya, have entered the great ocean.
This entire world, both stationary and moving, has the Vedas as its foundation; indeed, the Vedas alone constitute the ultimate basis for all duties. ||24||
"Through the Vedas, there will be eternal satisfaction for all the gods;
therefore, O Keśava, you alone are worthy to bring back the Vedas. (25)
The illustrious Mahādeva said: Thus addressed by Brahmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Lord, assumed the form of a fish and entered the great ocean. 26.
Then, having assumed the form of a makara, he tore that most terrible Daitya with the tip of his snout and struck him down— he who was honored by the immortals.
Having slain him and taken all the Vedas together with their limbs and sub-limbs,
that one of great splendor presented them to Brahmā.
The Vedas, which had been mixed together and swallowed by that Rākṣasa, were made manifest by that wise Blessed One in the form of Vyāsa. (29)
The Vedas, which had become divided, were unified by the high-souled Vyāsa;
likewise, all the deities were protected by the Fish incarnation.
Then, having rendered the three worlds free from fear by bestowing the Vedas, O wonder,
the Consort of Ramā was praised by hosts of gods and perfected beings.
He whose feet are worshipped by yogis vanished from sight.
For the venerable Vāsudeva is Hari, who embodies all the gods. ||32||

Thus ends the description of the Fish Incarnation, titled "The Dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara," within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The two hundred and thirtieth chapter. ||230||
The two hundred and thirty-first chapter.
Śrī Rudra said:
Listen to the glory of Viṣṇu in his tortoise form, which is honored by all the worlds.
I shall speak of that; listen well with a one-pointed mind. ||1||
The son of Atri, renowned as Durvāsas, possessed great splendor;
he was fierce toward all the worlds, a disturber of them, and a performer of great austerities. ||2||
Then the Brahmarṣi, a treasure-house of asceticism, went to the peak of the Himalayas;
he was a portion of myself, a Brahmarṣi who always causes fear to all.
Having stayed there for a year, honored by the kinnarīs,
that sage, desiring to see Mahendra, departed for the heavenly world.
At that time, the one of great splendor beheld Maheśvara mounted upon an elephant, the Lord of Śacī being worshipped by all the gods.
And having seen that, the great ascetic Durvāsas, his soul filled with joy,
respectfully presented him with a garland of *pārijāta* flowers.
Having taken that garland and placed it upon the head of the elephant,
the Lord of Devas departed from there toward the Nandana grove.
Then the elephant, overflowing with rut, took the garland with his trunk,
crushed it, and threw it down upon the surface of the earth.
Then the highly effulgent Durvāsas, his eyes red with rage, being incensed,
cursed Mahendra with the fire of his burning anger.
Durvāsas said:
"Since he, though endowed with the singular glory of the three worlds, treats me with contempt, therefore let the glory of the three worlds perish; of this there is no doubt. (10)
Rudra said:
Having been thus cursed, Śakra then returned once more to his own city;
thereafter, Śrī, the sustainer of the worlds, vanished of her own accord from sight.
Inauspiciousness vanished, and the three worlds were then restored;
for everything in the world, both stationary and moving, was supported by the waters.
Within that city of Antarddhānavatī, everything became utterly lost;
all the thirty gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as the gandharvas, yakṣas, and kinnaras, [vanished]. (13)
The Daityas, Dānavas, Nāgas, humans, and likewise Rākṣasas;
beasts, birds, insects, and all things both stationary and moving. ||14||
All those who were looked upon by that Mother of the World, Alakṣmī, were made outcasts by her;
they were all rendered partakers of suffering by poverty alone. 15.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, the gods, losing their composure, cried out;
the clouds had not yet rained for nine years, and all reservoirs of water were dried up. (16)
At that time, all the trees were withered and devoid of fruits and flowers;
likewise, the gods along with the gandharvas, daityas, dānavas, and rākṣasas [were distressed].
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they approached Brahmā of immeasurable splendor;
they spoke to him, the Lord of the gods, the lotus-born Grandfather.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, the three worlds are afflicted by hunger and thirst; they have not offered oblations, they do not utter the sixfold *vaṣaṭ* call, and they are devoid of all religious duties. (19)
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, all the gods, dānavas, and humans sought refuge in Bhava, the Lord of all worlds, as their protector. ||20||
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to protect these people who are afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Rudra said:
"Having heard these words of theirs, the Grandfather of all the worlds [spoke]."
The bestower of boons, Brahmā, being supremely pleased, spoke to them all. Brahmā said:
"Listen, all you deities, Daityas, Gandharvas, and humans! (22)
All this has come to pass through the transgression of Mahendra;
this great and terrible calamity has arisen, which will bring about the dissolution of the world.
O gods, because the high-souled Durvāsas became possessed by anger,
these three worlds were destroyed by that very wrath.
His soul not overcome by pride or anger, yet defiled by wrath, that evil-minded one said: "Let the three worlds be deprived of their prosperity! (25)
Due to that curse, Lakṣmī, the mother of the worlds and beloved of Nārāyaṇa,
the goddess and supreme sovereign mother of the universe, vanished from sight.
For just as people become happy by the light of a glance from the corner of the eye, they surely become partakers of suffering when even the mere sight of the world is not obtained. 27.
Therefore, let us all go and worship the eternal Lord Nārāyaṇa, who dwells there in the supreme ocean of milk. 28.
"If this Lord of Gods, Śiva, is pleased, this world shall become [auspicious]";
having thus resolved in his mind, Brahmā, accompanied by the hosts of gods, [proceeded]. 29.
Together with the sages headed by Bhṛgu, he went to the Ocean of Milk;
on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk were the deities beginning with Brahmā and Rudra.
They worshipped Viṣṇu according to the rite prescribed for Puruṣa,
while reciting the eight-syllable mantra and the Puruṣasūkta.
Meditating with undistracted minds, they offered oblations to the Supreme Lord;
they praised him with divine hymns and prostrated themselves in manifold ways.
Then the Blessed One became gracious toward all the inhabitants of heaven;
he remained visible to them while being praised by the great seers.
Having mounted Vainateya, the all-pervading Lord who embodies all the gods,
they beheld that Sovereign of the worlds, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
He wears yellow garments, has four arms, and eyes resembling lotuses;
his chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and he is adorned with a forest garland.
Adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, and anklets, they praised him with shouts of "Victory! and bowed down to him incessantly.
Then the Blessed One, out of compassion, spoke to all the deities: "I am the giver of boons; choose a boon, O gods," he said. (37)
Having heard this, all the gods, led by Brahmā, then spoke these words with palms joined in reverence to the Lord, the Sovereign.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, by the sage's curse, this entire triple world—along with its gods, asuras, and humans—is now afflicted by hunger and thirst. (39)
Therefore, O Supreme Person, we have gone to you for refuge;
protect this entire world, for no one else anywhere is capable of doing so. (40)
Rudra said:
Having been thus addressed by all the deities, Acyuta, the Supreme Lord,
reflected upon this and spoke these words to those gods, headed by Brahmā.
The Blessed Lord said:
Due to the curse of the sage, the son of Atri, Lakṣmī had vanished;
however, by his glance, she returned endowed with sovereignty over the universe. 42.
Therefore, all you gods, led by Śiva and Brahmā,
having uprooted Mount Mandara and placed it in the Ocean of Milk, [proceed].
O gods, having made the churning-stick resonant with a deep gurgling sound and encircled it with the king of serpents, perform the churning together with the Daityas, Gandharvas, and Dānavas. 44.
And this Goddess of Misfortune arises indeed for the protection of the world;
gladdened by her, O highly fortunate ones, you shall become [prosperous], of this there is no doubt. (45)
Enveloped in the form of a tortoise, I myself support the mountain;
by my power, I have entered all the exceedingly strong asuras.
Rudra said:
Having been addressed thus, all the deities, led by Brahmā, spoke to the Lord of Gods regarding the deer-eyed woman who possessed the marks of desire: "Excellent! Excellent! (47)
While being praised by the best of the gods, the illustrious Lord Acyuta,
who is honored by all the worlds,
the support of all, the god of all, and the one whose vision is equal toward everything, then vanished from sight. ||48||

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Curse of Durvāsas," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-Khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||231||
Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Two.
Śaṅkara said:
Then all the hosts of gods, the Dānavas, and others of great strength...
They uprooted Mount Mandara and hurled it into the ocean.
Then the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, the creator of beings and possessor of immeasurable prowess,
supported that mountain in the form of a tortoise.
The eternal Lord of the Universe, whose body has no beginning, middle, or end, who possesses universal forms, and who is worthy of worship, supported the best of mountains. (3)
Likewise, with only one arm, the omnipresent and imperishable Lord [performed the task];
then all the gods and asuras churned the ocean of milk.
Then, as the ocean of milk was being churned by the gods of great power, Mount Mandara was encircled by the king of serpents, who made a gurgling sound.
For the sake of generating prosperity, all the great sages likewise fasted, observed their vows, and chanted the Śrī-sūkta.
On the pure eleventh day, while the great ocean was being churned, those best of divine brahmins performed the recitation of the Thousand Names.
Having observed the fast, all the sages chanted the supreme Śrī-mantra;
desiring what, did they chant it—to worship Hari, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa? (8)
Having meditated thus, the foremost of the twice-born and the best of sages performed their worship;
then, at that very moment, the great ocean was being churned.
There, first of all, the great poison Kālakūṭa appeared—inflicting great suffering, most terrible, and possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction. ||10||
Seeing him, all the gods and dānavas fled, afflicted by fear;
then, seeing those best of the gods fleeing and tormented by fear, [he pursued them]. (11)
Then, O lady of auspicious gaze, I spoke these words to them there:
"O hosts of gods, none of you should fear the poison."
"I shall consume the great poison Kālakūṭa," thus was all those gods, led by Indra, addressed by me.
Bowing down deeply, they praised me with words of "Excellent! Excellent!
Then, seeing that great poison, resembling a dark cloud, manifest itself, [they were struck with fear].
Having meditated upon the god Aniruddha, who bears the banner of Garuḍa upon his heart, who resembles the rising sun, and who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace; 15.
Having meditated with one-pointed mind upon the Lord, who is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, who wears earrings of molten gold, and who is the Sovereign who removes all suffering; 16.
Having recited the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as a great mantra, accompanied by the syllable *alakṣmī*, that poison indeed becomes most terrible, primordial, and the cause of all fear. (17)
By the power of the three names of the omnipresent Viṣṇu,
that poison which causes the destruction of the world was indeed digested.
One who is self-restrained and devoted should recite with devotion these three names of Hari, the infallible one: "O Govinda," preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*. (19)
For him who, with a disciplined mind, recites the great mantra of the three names, there exists no great fear of death arising from poison, disease, or fire. (20)
"And for him, there is no fear even of untimely death; what need is there to mention anything else? O Goddess, by these three names alone, the poison has been drunk up by me. (21)
Then the thirty gods, greatly delighted and filled with wonder, praised me;
having bowed to me, O Goddess, they once again churned the Ocean of Milk. While it was being churned by me and the gods, O beautiful lady—
Born from Jyeṣṭhādevī, clothed in garments and adorned with jeweled garlands, she who had appeared spoke to the gods: "What must be done by me? indeed.
I spoke to that goddess who was being intensely praised by all the hosts of gods.
The gods said:
"O beautiful one, those in whose homes internal strife breaks out—" (24)
"Therefore, we grant you that place; dwell there, joined with misfortune, constantly speaking harsh words and uttering falsehoods. (25)
But those of wicked mind who sleep during the time of twilight—residing in their houses, she bestows suffering and poverty upon them. (26)
Wherever there are skulls, hair, ashes, bones, husks, and charcoal, there shall be their constant dwelling place; of this there is no doubt. ||27||
In that place which is marked by the shards of his house, bones, ashes, hair, and other such signs, he dwells constantly with impurity, forever overcome by the Kali age.
O Mahādevī, serve that evil-minded person who sips water for purification without having first washed his feet, for he is utterly overwhelmed by impurity. 29.
The lowest of men will become those who use husks, cow-dung, leaves, stones, sand, cloth, or leather for cleaning their teeth. ||30||
O Goddess, always delight in their houses with Kālīnāda;
[enjoy] sesame paste, kalañja, kāliṅga, and the sprout of the śigru tree.
Those lowest of men who eat mushrooms, village pigs, bilva, the fruit of the kośātakī, bottle-gourd,
and onions— in their houses, O Goddess, poverty shall always reside. (32)
Rudra said:
Having thus commanded all the asuras, they made Kāli, the beloved of Kali, their elder sister;
then, with great composure, they once again churned the ocean of milk.
Then, O lady of auspicious countenance, the goddess Vāruṇī was born; subsequently, Ananta, the king of serpents, took that fair-eyed woman as his wife.
Then she, born from the liquor and adorned with all ornaments,
graced with every auspicious mark, became the wife of Vainateya.
Then hosts of celestial nymphs and Gandharvas of great prowess,
endowed with beautiful forms and devoted to singing and dancing, began to celebrate.
Then Airāvata was born, as well as the horse Uccaiḥśravas;
Dhanvantari, the Pārijāta tree, and Surabhi, the cow who grants all desires. (37)
The thousand-eyed one (Indra), with a delighted mind, accepted all of these;
then, at the time of dawn on the twelfth lunar day, when the sun had risen.
Furthermore, while that [ocean] was being churned by the gods led by Indra, she was praised by the great ṛṣis with joyful countenances. ||39||
The auspicious Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of all worlds, is the goddess Śrī who has arisen;
she shines like ten million rising suns and is adorned with golden ornaments. 40.
Seated upon a golden lotus, she was adorned with all auspicious marks;
her large eyes were like lotus petals, and her hair was dark and curly. 41.
She was anointed with divine sandalwood paste, adorned with celestial flowers,
and endowed with all kinds of divine ornaments made of various jewels.
She has a slender waist, is the sustainer of the world, possesses full and elevated breasts, has four arms, large eyes, and a face like the full moon. 43.
Holding a vessel of wealth, a citron fruit, and a pair of auspicious golden lotuses with their lotus-like hands, which are adorned with all ornaments. ||44||
Wearing a garland of unfading lotuses upon her chest,
they beheld that Great Goddess, who desires the welfare of all the worlds.
The sovereign of all beings, the Mother adorned with a garland of lotuses, Nārāyaṇī, the sustainer of the world, whose abode is the heart of Nārāyaṇa. ||46||
Beholding that Mahālakṣmī, all the deities were overjoyed; the hosts of gods in heaven sounded their drums most vigorously. ||47||
The forest goddesses rained down showers of flowers without interruption;
the lords of the gandharvas sang, and the hosts of apsarases danced.
Likewise, auspicious winds blew, the sun became radiant,
the fires blazed peacefully, and the ten directions became clear.
Immediately thereafter, the cool-rayed one arose from the ocean of milk;
Soma, the brother of Mātṛ, who possesses rays consisting of nectar, brought happiness. (50)
And Candra became the lord of the stars and the maternal uncle of the three worlds;
then, from the merit of that [birth], Tulasi, the purifier of the world, became the wife of Hari.
Then all the gods and inhabitants of heaven, their minds filled with joy, arose for the purpose of worshipping Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow and the sustainer of the world. 52.
Having restored that mountain as it was before, with their desires still unfulfilled,
all of them, led by Śiva and Brahmā, gathered together and approached their mother.
Having praised her with a thousand names, they recited the Śrīsūkta;
then the Goddess, being pleased, spoke to all the gods.
Śrī said: "Choose a boon, O best of gods; I am the giver of boons; may it be well with you.
Rudra said:
With palms joined in reverence and their bodies bowed low, the gods spoke to Śrī. ||55||
The gods said: Be gracious, O Goddess Kamalā, beloved of the Lord of all worlds; O Goddess, you who are eternally inseparable from the chest of Viṣṇu. (56)
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, you are eternally the protectress of the three worlds;
for everything in the world, both moving and unmoving, is supported by the waters. 57.
All the inhabitants of heaven become powerful when beheld by you;
the sovereignty of Rudra and the other gods arises from your glance. (58)
"O Goddess, Mother of the World, we desire this; salutations be unto you!
Rudra said: "Having been addressed thus by all the deities, the Great Sovereign, the Mother of the World—" (59)
"So be it," said Nārāyaṇapriyā to those gods;
then Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, [appeared].
In that very same manner, Brahmā appeared from the ocean of milk as before;
then the gods, having paid homage to Janārdana, offered him praise.
All of them, with auspicious and joyful countenances, spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The gods said:
"Accept the Goddess, the beloved of the Lord of all and the consort of Śiva."
"For the sake of protecting the world, [grant] Lakṣmī who never departs.
Rudra said:
"Having spoken thus, all the gods, led by Brahmā, together with the sages... (63)
Having seated both the Goddess and the God upon a divine throne composed of various jewels and resembling the rising sun, they were overwhelmed with tears of joy.
They worshipped Acyuta, who was seated with Lakṣmī, adorned with divine garments, divine garlands, and various jewels. 65.
They worshipped the Goddess with perfumes, incenses, lamps, and food offerings made of nectar, as well as with divine, non-worldly fruits. (66)
The auspicious and tender Tulasī goddess arose from the nectar;
with it, they immediately worshipped the pair of the Lord’s feet.
Having performed three circumambulations and bowing down again and again,
the gods, overwhelmed with tears of joy, praised him with hymns of praise.
Then the blessed Lord Hari, the sovereign of all gods, being pleased,
together with the Goddess, granted them their desired boons.

Then, the gods, humans, and others were greatly delighted; purified by the glance of Lakṣmī’s side-long look, they attained supreme, uninterrupted happiness and remained entirely free from disease, endowed with abundant grain and wealth. (70)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Birth of Lakṣmī," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||232|| ||cha||
The two hundred and thirty-third chapter.
Śaṅkara said: Then the Blessed One spoke to the gods and the great sages.
With a heart greatly rejoiced along with the Goddess, for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds. ||1||
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O all you sages and gods of great power;
Ekādaśī is supremely meritorious and the destroyer of all calamities.
Because it was observed by you for the purpose of beholding Lakṣmī, this Dvādaśī, dear to me, is therefore always meritorious. (3)
From this day forward, those people who have resided here on the previous day, endowed with supreme faith, [shall do so] on the twelfth lunar day when the sun has risen. (4)
Those who worship me with incomparable devotion along with Tulasi and Lakshmi—
all of them, liberated from bondage, attain my state.
And those men of sinful deeds, deluded by my māyā, do not worship Puruṣottama on this twelfth day. ||6||
Those most wicked men who go to hell worship those very sins— those objects of the senses that bind them and turn them away from my worship.
She incessantly casts [beings] into this cycle of existence, which is difficult to cross due to illusion and pride.
Rudra said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the eternal Supreme Self, [departed]. (8)
Being praised by the sages, he proceeded to the abode of Kamalā in a celestial chariot resembling the sun, where he rested upon the serpent Śeṣa as his couch in the Ocean of Milk.
There, the Supreme Lord remained present together with the goddess, whose eyes were large and beautiful, for the purpose of being seen by the gods. ||10||
Then all the hosts of gods, having worshipped the eternal one in the form of the tortoise with devotion, praised him with joyful minds. ||11||
Then the Lord Janārdana, appearing in the form of a tortoise, became gracious;
the Blessed One said:
"O lords of gods, choose a boon, whatever dwells in your minds."
Rudra said:
Then all the hosts of gods [beheld] Janārdana in the form of a tortoise.
With palms joined in reverence and their minds overflowing with joy, they all spoke.
The gods said: "O one of great strength, for the sake of assisting Śeṣa and the elephants of the quarters... (13)
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to sustain the earth consisting of the seven continents.
Rudra said:
"So be it," and the blessed Lord, the creator of the worlds, was delighted in his heart.
They supported the earth, encompassed by its seven continents;
then the gods, along with the gandharvas, daityas, dānavas, and humans, [rejoiced].
Permitted by the great seers, they returned to their own worlds;
from that time forward, all the gods, with Brahmā at their head, [acted accordingly].
The Siddhas, humans, yogins, and the best of sages, placing the command of Viṣṇu before them, were endowed with supreme devotion. ||17||
Having fasted on the eleventh day, O woman of excellent complexion, they then worshipped Janārdana with devotion according to the prescribed rite on the twelfth day.
All this, O fair-faced one, has been narrated regarding the birth of the Goddess and the tortoise-incarnation of Viṣṇu; what else do you wish to hear? (19)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fasting on the Ekādaśī," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-Khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Pādma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
[234] Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Four.
Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the ritual procedure for the twelfth day (dvādaśī) and the method for the worship of Viṣṇu that must be performed there, O Lord. (1)
O Maheśvara, out of affection for me, describe in detail the power of Ekādaśī, which removes all sins of human beings.
Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for the twelfth day (dvādaśī);
by the mere remembrance of it, Janārdana becomes gratified. (3)
When the eleventh day has arrived, a person who observes a fast here becomes liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. ||4||
The sin accumulated over seven lifetimes, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, dissolves in an instant through the worship of Hari on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī). ||5||
Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the eleventh lunar day.

Indeed, the twelve-day vow (dvādaśī) of excellent complexion is said to be the granter of Dharma, the granter of wealth, the granter of desires, and the granter of liberation; it is the cow of plenty for all the desires of men. //7//
O lady of auspicious gaze, there exists no protection against sin equal to Ekādaśī;
there is no vow equal to Ekādaśī. (8)
He who, having abandoned Ekādaśī, performs another vow, is like one who, having renounced a great kingdom held in his own hand, begs for alms. ||9||
O beloved, whatever sin has been committed through the eleven sense organs, all of that shall go to dissolution by fasting on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī). ||10||
O fair-faced one, the ancient scriptures proclaim here again and again:
"One must not eat, one must not eat when the day of Hari has arrived. (11)
"O excellent woman, it is declared that [meat] is always unfit to be eaten; how much more so during the bright and dark fortnights for all the castes and stages of life? (12)
The fast of Ekādaśī must indeed be observed; there is no doubt in this matter—even when the anniversary of the death of one’s mother or father falls on an Ekādaśī. (13)
It should be offered on the twelfth day, never on the day of fasting;
for neither the ancestors nor the gods consume food that is censured. (14)
One should not eat on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), nor should one ever drink liquor;
one must never kill a Brahmin—for these three are considered equal. ||15||
Therefore, one should observe the fast on the pure Ekādaśī; he who exerts effort through the three states of mind, speech, and body [should do so]. 16.
One should carefully avoid that [eleventh day] which is mixed with the tenth;
for it may be mixed with the tenth at the time of dawn. (17)
Having abandoned that pure twelfth day and fasted here without hesitation while even a fraction [of the eleventh] remains at the time of sunrise; ||18||
Likewise, O Goddess, if the thirteenth day is found to be conjoined with the twelfth, and if the twelfth is pure, then fasting is prescribed on that [twelfth] day. ||19||
At the time of sunrise, one should perform all the prescribed rites;
it is ordained that the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place there, even if it is during the final minute (kalā) of the twelfth lunar day.
One should certainly not abandon even a pure Ekādaśī on this matter; there is no doubt.
Wherever even a fraction of Ekādaśī exists when the sun has risen on the Dvādaśī, [that day is to be observed].
Having abandoned all other Ekādaśīs, a twice-born man should fast there;
having thus determined this rule, he should observe the fast on the day of Hari.
Of those two days, the first is the evening; [one should observe] the evening and morning [fasts] in the middle one. Therein, one should perform the fast, having abandoned the four meals.
On the tenth day, he should eat only one meal, avoid sexual intercourse with women,
sleep on the ground, and remain pure on the following day.
Having anointed oneself with the fruit of the *dhātrī*, one should perform the ritual bath and the twilight prayers;
then, being intent on fasting, one should worship Hari during the night.
A Vaiṣṇava should not look upon, converse with, or touch a heretic, one who persists in forbidden acts, an outcaste, or likewise a dog-eater. 26.
That brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava is proclaimed to be a heretic;
he who abandons the topknot and the sacred thread is said to be one established in improper conduct. ||27||

One who is joined with great sins or minor sins is called fallen (patita). Regarding this, the Vedas have reached a firm conclusion: such a person is declared to be an outcaste (antyaja) or a dog-cooker (śvapaca). ||28||
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods at night, one should perform a vigil with perfumes, flowers, lamps, garments, and auspicious ornaments. (29)
One should worship with devotion at night through recitations, hymns of praise, and prostrations;
then, at the time of dawn, [one should worship] with water mixed with tulasī.
Having bathed according to the proper ritual and having fully gratified the ancestors and the deities,
one should worship Janārdana, the Lord of the worlds, together with Lakṣmī.
There, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with tender tulasī leaves and fragrant flowers, one hundred and eight times.
One should properly present a garland made of lotuses to those two, and offer incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel leaf. (33)
One should offer divine milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar, and one should also present betel-leaf (tāmbūla) combined with camphor. ||34||
Having performed this prostration with devotion,
one should likewise offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter into the fire.
Reciting the Puruṣasūkta and the Lakṣmīsūkta verse by verse,
he should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice (pāyasa), and he himself should eat while remaining silent and restrained.
One should pass that great day by reciting the Purāṇas and other scriptures;
sleeping on the ground and observing celibacy, one should sleep during that very night.
Thus being worshipped on the twelfth day, the Lord, the husband of Kamalā, will certainly become pleased in an instant and grant all desired objects. (38)
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme Dvādaśī vow has been told. What else do you wish to hear? I shall speak that which is to be said. (39)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Twelfth Day (Dvādaśī)," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(235) Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Five. Śrī Pārvatī said:
And as for what was said by you, that one should avoid conversation with heretics; ||1||
"The Blessed One has told me here that [those who eat] even from a dog-cooker (outcaste) are censured.
By what characteristics and marks are such people described as being on this earth?
Rudra said:
Those who, deluded by ignorance, declare another deity to be supreme. ||2||
Those who wear skulls, ashes, and bones, and who bear non-Vedic marks, are indeed considered heretics by Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World. ||3||
Except for those in the forest-dwelling stage of life who wear matted hair and bark garments,
those who perform non-Vedic rites are indeed heretics.
O Goddess, those twice-born who are devoid of the most beloved marks of Hari, such as the conch, the discus, and the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), are indeed remembered as heretics.
But that twice-born man who does not practice the conduct prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis should be known as a heretic, despised in all the worlds. (6)
Indeed, those who act without the pleasure of the Blessed One are considered heretics;
for Viṣṇu is the enjoyer of all sacrifices and the supreme deity of the Vedas. ||7||
He who offers oblations and gives gifts specifically for the sake of deities alone should be known as a heretic, acting independently in all ritual acts. (8)
He who, out of independence, performs the great rites prescribed by the Veda,
yet [regards] the god Nārāyaṇa as being equal to deities such as Brahmā and Rudra— ||9||
He who looks upon others with equanimity in the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] through the actions of mind, speech, and body—he shall always be a true ascetic (pāṣaṇḍin). ||10||
He who does not know Vāsudeva would be a heretic, even if he be a twice-born; what need is there for much speaking on this matter? Those Brāhmaṇas who are non-Vaiṣṇavas [are likewise]. (11)
"They are never to be questioned, nor spoken to, nor looked upon.
Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, O best of gods, I ask about a supreme secret."
Out of affection for me, please explain this: a great doubt remains within me;
the wearing of skulls, ashes, skins, and bones is censured by the Vedas. (13)
O Lord of Gods, for what reason is this, which is censured by the gods, being maintained by you? O Great-minded One, I ask you about this fickleness of women.
"O Great Lord, it was previously stated by you in detail that nothing whatsoever should ever be done out of great power. (15)
"O Lord, you ought to forgive me for this question regarding what should not be done.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus was the speech of the Goddess asked in secret, in a place devoid of people. 16.
He spoke of that which was his own supreme secret, whatever he had practiced.
Śiva said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is a most wonderful secret. (17)
"O Goddess, what has been told by me among people must not be spoken by you; however, O lady of excellent vows, because there is no difference between [my] body and yours, I shall speak it to you."
In ancient times, on this very earth, there were great Daityas such as Namuci and others—possessing great strength, great heroism, great valor, and great splendor. (19)
All were devoted to Viṣṇu, pure, and entirely free from sin;
all were established in the dharma of the three Vedas, with Indra at their head. ||20||
Having approached Viṣṇu, they, afflicted by fear, went to him for refuge.
The gods said:
"They are unconquerable by all the gods, having shaken off their impurities through austerity. (21)
"O Keśava, you alone are worthy to conquer these great Daityas.
Mahādeva said:
Having heard these words of the gods, which were full of fear, Hari [acted]. 22.
Having consoled those guardians of the quarters, Puruṣottama said to me:
The Blessed Lord said:
"O mighty-armed Rudra, you were indeed created for the purpose of deluding the enemies of the gods. (23)
"O best of gods, practice the dharma of heretical conduct;
speak those *purāṇas* which are characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*) to them. (24)
O you of great intelligence, compose treatises that lead to delusion;
by me, the brahmins and the great seers shall be liberated. (25)
Having entered into them through devotion to me, speak to those sages:
Kaṇāda, Gautama, Śakti, Upamanyu, and Jaimini.
Kapila, Durvāsas, Mṛkaṇḍu, Bṛhaspati,
and Bhārgava Jāmadagnya— these ten are the ṛṣis characterized by tamas.
Having entered into the power of their own nature, they bring misfortune to the world;
yet they are themselves thoroughly immersed in your power through the intense increase of darkness.
Those Brahmins will become *tāmasa* in an instant, there is no doubt; they will proclaim *tāmasa* doctrines throughout the three worlds. (29)
The Purāṇas and the Śāstras have been augmented by you with falsehood;
likewise, the emblems of skulls, skins, ashes, and bones have been entirely spread abroad by you, O Immortal One. (30)
You alone have sustained the worlds; delude the three worlds as you wish!
Likewise, being well-honored, you alone shall establish the Pāśupata scripture. (31)
Due to divisions such as Kālamukha, Śaiva, Pāṣaṇḍa, and Mahāśaiva, this doctrine—which is unrecognizable and outside the Veda—is [followed by] the lowest of men. (32)
Indeed, all those devoid of consciousness will become wearers of ashes and bones;
those characterized by darkness (tāmasa) will proclaim you as the Supreme Being in all their scriptures. (33)
Relying upon their doctrine, all the eternal Daityas shall undoubtedly become averse to me in an instant. (34)
O Rudra of great strength, I too, along with you, worship [the Lord] in every age during the incarnations for the purpose of deluding those characterized by tamas.
"Adhering to this opinion, they will surely fall; of this there is no doubt.
Mahādeva said:
"O beautiful lady, having heard what was thus spoken by Vāsudeva, I..."
O lady of beautiful countenance, he became deeply distressed with a most sorrowful face;
then, having paid homage to that god, the Supreme Lord, I spoke to him. (37)
"O Lord, if I were to do this on the surface of the earth as you have said, then, O Protector, it would lead to my own destruction; of this there is no doubt. (38)
In this matter, O Hari, that task can now be accomplished by me;
yet your command must not be transgressed—this is a great and most painful dilemma. (39)
When this had been said, O Goddess, Hari comforted me once more and said to me: "Let there be no destruction for him here. (40)
"For the benefit of the deities, carry out my word; O best of gods, I shall also tell you the means for your own survival. (41)
Out of compassion, he bestowed upon me a thousand names of himself,
and having established this mantra within my heart, he gave it to me as an imperishable recitation.
The six-syllabled great mantra is called the Tāraka Brahman; for those who recite it with devotion, there is liberation—of this there is no doubt. (43)
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes like lotus petals, bearing a conch, a discus, a mace, a bow, and arrows, and adorned with all ornaments. ||44||
Having uttered this supreme mantra: "Obeisance to Śrī Rāma, who is clad in yellow garments, possesses four arms, and is the beloved husband of Jānakī. (45)
This [mantra] removes all suffering and grants liberation even to sinners;
by constantly reciting this mantra, you shall become pure. (46)
Whatever sin was produced in you from the wearing of ashes, bones, and so forth,
all that has become entirely auspicious through the auspicious recitation of my mantra.
O best of gods, O observer of noble vows, being satisfied, I shall destroy all my sin; may devotion to no other deity than me arise [in me]. 48.
Worship this Lord Puruṣottama within your heart with the mind alone;
carry out my command out of love for me, and all this shall be auspicious for you. 49.
Having thus instructed them, O Goddess, she dismissed the hosts of Maruts;
once dismissed, those gods returned and went to their own hermitages.
Then the gods, led by Indra, entreated me.
Indra and the others said:
"O God, quickly do what is beneficial for us, as it has now been commanded by Hari. (51)
Mahādeva said: O auspicious one, for the sake of the welfare of the gods, I have adopted this conduct of the heretics— the wearing of skulls, skins, ashes, and bones.
O auspicious lady, I have composed the Tāmasa Purāṇas as described by Viṣṇu, as well as the heretical Śaiva scriptures, as previously stated. (53)
O sinless one, having entered even the twice-born such as Gautama through my power, I have correctly expounded the scriptures that are outside the Veda.
Adhering to this view, all those wicked spies became averse to the Blessed One; shrouded in darkness, they all turned their backs upon him.
Having smeared themselves with ashes and other substances, and being engaged in most formidable austerities,
they worshipped me alone with blood, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.
Having obtained the wind of the gift of pride, they are arrogant with the power of intoxication;
they are excessively attached to sense objects and possessed by desire and anger. ||57||
Then, devoid of strength and lacking in vigor, defeated by the hosts of gods and fallen away from all dharma, the Kāleyas went to that most wretched state. 58.
Relying on this very misconception, they wander upon the surface of the earth;
devoid of all virtuous qualities, they constantly behold hell. (59)
Thus, my conduct for the sake of the welfare of the gods has been censured by the gods;
yet, honoring the command of Viṣṇu, I have performed the wearing of ashes and bones. (60)
O Goddess, this external mark is for the purpose of deluding enemies;
however, one should always meditate within the inner heart upon the Lord Janārdana.
And while muttering that very mantra which expresses the saving Brahman,
it is indeed equal to the thousand names of Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa.

O Goddess, O auspicious one, by constantly reciting the six-syllabled great mantra that increases the lineage of the Raghus, we indeed remain perpetually immersed in the nectar of eternal bliss and enjoy the ultimate happiness of Brahman.
All this that was asked by you has been told to you, O lady of auspicious countenance.
What else do you wish to hear? Ask me with pleasure.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of Heretics," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(236) Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Six.
Pārvatī said:
O sinless one, O Lord of Asuras, please describe to me those tamasic scriptures proclaimed by those brahmins who are devoid of devotion to the Blessed One; tell me their names in due order.
Rudra said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the tamasic [scriptures] in their proper order. 2.
By the mere remembrance of them, even the wise would fall into delusion;
for it was by me alone that the Śaiva, Pāśupata, and other systems were first proclaimed. (3)
Now hear what was proclaimed by the Brahmins who were inspired by my own power:
the great Vaiśeṣika scripture was indeed propounded by Kaṇāda. (4)
Likewise, Gautama proclaimed the Nyāya system, Kapila indeed [proclaimed] the Sāṅkhya, and Dhiṣaṇa likewise spoke that which is utterly despised by the intellect of Cārvāka. (5)
For the sake of destroying the Daityas, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a Buddha, proclaimed the false Buddhist scriptures, such as those concerning the naked ones and those wearing blue garments. (6)
The doctrine of illusion (māyāvāda), an untruthful scripture, is said to be Buddhism in disguise; it was taught by me alone, O Goddess, in the Kali age through the form of a Brāhmaṇa. (7)
Demonstrating that the words of the Vedas are meaningless and censured by the world, it is established right here that your own karmic nature must be abandoned. (8)
That which is described by those who have fallen away from all [proper] action is called heterodoxy;
however, it is the oneness of the Supreme Lord and the individual soul that is established by me. ||9||
I shall describe the own nature of this Brahman as being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), for the purpose of deluding the entire world here in the Kali age. (10)
O Goddess, this great scripture, which possesses the meaning of the Vedas yet is non-Vedic through illusion, was fashioned by me alone for the purpose of destroying the worlds. (11)
At my command, Jaimini formerly composed that great treatise, the Mīmāṃsā Śāstra, which, through a doctrine devoid of a Lord, rendered the Veda meaningless. (12)
O Girijā, understand from me those scriptures which are tāmasa;
I shall describe the Purāṇas that are tāmasa in their proper order. (13)
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, and likewise the Śaiva; as well as the Bhāgavata, the Nāradīya, and the Mārkaṇḍeya as the seventh. (14)
The eighth is declared to be Āgneya, and likewise the ninth is Bhaviṣya;
the tenth is Brahmavaivarta, and the eleventh is remembered as Liṅga. (15)
The twelfth is Varāha, and Vāmana is the thirteenth;
the fourteenth is declared to be Kaurma, and Mātsya is remembered as the fifteenth. ||16||
The sixteenth is declared to be the Gāruḍa, the seventeenth is remembered as the Skanda, and the eighteenth is the Brahmāṇḍa; such are the Purāṇas in their proper order.
Know from me that these six—the Mātsya, Kaurma, Laiṅga, Śaiva, Skānda, and Āgneya—are tāmasa. 18.
The Vaiṣṇava, the Nāradīya, and likewise the auspicious Bhāgavata;
the Gāruḍa, the Pādma, and the Vārāha, O lady of auspicious appearance. (19)
The Sāttvika Purāṇas are indeed to be known as auspicious;
namely, the Brahmāṇḍa, the Brahma-vaivarta, and likewise the Mārkaṇḍeya. (20)
Now learn from me of the future Vāmana incarnation, which consists of portions of the *rājasa* mode.
Those incarnations characterized by *sattva* are said to bestow liberation, while those characterized by *rajas* are always inauspicious. (21)
In the same way, O Goddess, those characterized by tamas are causes for attaining hell;
likewise, the Smṛtis are declared by the sages to be endowed with the three guṇas. ||22||
O lady of auspicious appearance, there are those of sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic natures;
likewise, Vāsiṣṭha, Hārīta, Vyāsa, and Pārāśara. ||23||
The Bhāradvāja, Kāśyapa, Sāttvika, Muktida, Śubha, Yājñavalkya, Ātreya, Taittiri, and Dākṣa [recensions] are the words. 24.
The auspicious Kātyāyana, Vaiṣṇava, and Rājasā are bestowers of heaven;
likewise, the Gautama, Bārhaspatya, Sāṃvarta, and Yama are remembered as such. (25)
The Sāṅkhya and the Auśanasa [systems] are likewise characterized by tamas and lead to hell;
what need is there for much speaking here regarding the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis as well? (26)
A wise person should avoid those who are characterized by darkness (tamas), for they lead only to hell.
All this has been told to you incidentally as a vision of the auspicious;
now listen, for I shall describe to you the remaining state of Hari’s manifestation.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Tāmasa Scriptures," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||236|| ||cha||
The two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter.
Śrī Rudra said: Hiraṇyaka and Hiraṇyākṣa, the two sons of Kaśyapa, were possessed of great strength.
Both Diti’s sons, the two lords of all the Daityas, possessed great heroism.
The two of great strength, named Jaya and Vijaya, went to Lord Hari on Śvetadvīpa;
there, they encountered Sanaka and the other lords of yogis who had entered [the divine abode]. ||2||
O Goddess, those two gatekeepers, the best of asuras and possessed of great heroism, were cursed by them for preventing those who were eager to behold Hari. ||3||
Sanaka and the others said:
"Having abandoned that [body] on earth, what will the two hands of the God do?
Rudra said:
Having thus pronounced the curse upon them both, the lords of sages remained there. ||4||
Having understood that matter to be ruined, he summoned those two as well. ||5||
Then the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, rose up and spoke there.
The Blessed One said:
"O you two of great prowess, you have committed an offense against the high-souled ones."
"O gatekeepers, this must not be transgressed by you two;
for seven births, you two shall be my sinless servants. (7)
"Or even for one who undergoes three births from the state of enmity.
Rudra said:
"When they had been addressed thus, those two of great prowess spoke to the Supreme Lord."
Jayavijayā said:
"O giver of honor, we are unable to go to the earth for a long time;
therefore, O Lord, grant us birth as enemies, and let us both depart. (9)
"By you alone as a deity shall he be slain; we shall obtain [him] as our food.
Rudra said:
"Having spoken thus, those two gatekeepers were born in former times, possessed of great strength. (10)
From Kaśyapa, who was possessed of great heroism, two great Asuras were born from Uditā:
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the younger.
Both were world-renowned and exultant in their great heroism and strength;
Hiraṇyākṣa was of immeasurable stature and exceedingly haughty.
Having uprooted with thousands of arms the earth together with its mountains, its oceans, its islands, and all living beings; ||13||
Having torn it out and placed it upon his head, he entered the netherworld (rasātala).
Then all the hosts of gods, afflicted by fear, cried out. ||14||
They went for refuge to the god Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment;
then, having perceived that wonder, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace [appeared].
Assuming the form of a boar, Janārdana—
the omnipresent Lord whose body has no beginning, middle, or end, and who consists of all the gods— manifested his universal form.
With hands, feet, eyes, and great tusks on all sides, and possessing mighty arms, the Supreme Lord slew the Daitya with a single tusk. 17.
Seeing his great body crushed and fallen upon the earth, that lowest of demons and titans seized him with his teeth and restored him to his former state.
Then, having established himself, he who is Śeṣa assumed the form of a tortoise;
seeing that Great Hari in the shape of a boar, all the gods and sages, their bodies bowed with devotion, offered hymns of praise. (19)
The gods said:
"Salutations to the Sacrificial Boar; salutations to you, the hundred-armed one!
Salutations to you, the God of gods; salutations to you, whose form is the universe! (20)
Salutations to you whose nature is stability, who are the embodiment of all sacrifices; salutations to you whose form is time, consisting of kalās, kāṣṭhās, and nimeṣas. ||21||
Salutations to you, the elemental self, whose body is the Ṛgveda;
likewise, salutations to you, the divine self, and salutations to you, the Sāmaveda. ||22||
Oṃ, salutations to you, Oṃkāra, whose nature is the Yajurveda,
who is the very form of the Ṛgveda, and who consists of the four Vedas.
Salutations to you, who possess the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Sāṅga and Upāṅgas; salutations to you who sing [the hymns].
Salutations to you, Govinda, who are without beginning or end.
Salutations to You, the knower of the Vedas, whose singular nature is most excellent; salutations again and again to the Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā, the Father of the universe. 25.
Rudra said:
Having praised the Lord in the form of a boar with these and other hymns of praise,
they worshipped Hari, the Lord of the Self, with fragrances, flowers, and other offerings.
Being worshipped by those gods, Hari joyfully granted them their desired boon while being sung to with delight by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Being praised there by the great seers, he vanished from sight.
Having thus praised him with devotion, the devoted man, rising early in the morning, [should recite] these [verses]. (28)
He obtains his desired land, which for a long time is endowed with crops and fruits.
All this majesty of Hari as the Boar has been recounted to you;
likewise, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall now describe the Nārasiṃha [incarnation], so listen. 29.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Varāha Incarnation," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(238) Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Eight.
Rudra said:
Then, having learned that his brother had been slain, the great Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu performed penance on the side of Mount Meru directed toward me.
For thousands of divine years, subsisting on air alone, the mighty one,
while chanting the five-syllabled mantra, worshipped me, O auspicious lady.
Then, with a joyful mind, I spoke to that great asura:
"Choose a boon, O Daitya, whatever dwells in your heart.
Thereupon, O lady of auspicious countenance, the Daitya spoke to me who was well-disposed toward him. (3)
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Among gods, asuras, and humans; among gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas; and among beasts, birds, wild animals, and the great-souled siddhas—" (4)
Grant me invulnerability against the yakṣas and vidyādharas, as well as the kinnaras; likewise, against all diseases and weapons, and against all the foremost of sages. (5)
Rudra said:
"So be it," O lady of lovely appearance;
having obtained that great boon from me, that son of Diti became possessed of immense strength. ||6||
Having conquered Mahendra and the gods, he became the lord of the three worlds;
and by force, he himself took possession of all the sacrificial shares.
The deities, having been defeated by him, find no protector;
all the gandharvas, gods, and dānavas are like his servants. ||8||
Yakṣas, nāgas, siddhas, and sādhyas were all brought under his control;
he took as his wife the auspicious daughter of Uttānapāda, a maiden named Kalyāṇī.
The mighty king of the Daityas married her according to the prescribed rites.
From her, the illustrious Prahlāda, the king of the Daityas, was born during that auspicious time.
He who is devoted to Hṛṣīkeśa, even while dwelling in the womb, [is devoted] to Hari in all states and in all activities through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
With a serene soul, the wise one knew no other than the eternal Lord of Gods;
even when the time had come, he remained humble while dwelling in the house of his guru. 12.
Having studied all the Vedas and various treatises,
after some time had passed, the son of the Daitya [went] together with his preceptor.

Approaching his father, he paid homage with humility. Embracing that son of auspicious marks with both arms and placing him upon his lap, the lord of the Daityas spoke these words in great wonder: 14. Approaching his father, he paid homage with humility.
Embracing that son of auspicious marks with both arms and placing him upon his lap, the lord of the Daityas spoke these words in great wonder: 14.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Prahlāda, you have been residing in the house of your preceptor for a long time. O observer of noble vows, tell me what knowledge was taught to you by your preceptor. (15)
Rudra said:
Thus questioned by his own father, Prahlāda, who was a Vaiṣṇava by birth, spoke with affection these words that dispel all impurity to the lord of the Daityas. (16)
Prahlāda said:
Having bowed down to that Viṣṇu, who is the Lord, the Person, and the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, and who is omnipresent, I shall speak to you. 17.
Rudra said:
Having heard this hymn of praise to Viṣṇu, the king of the Daityas was filled with wonder;
out of anger, he said to that preceptor, "What have you said regarding my son? (18)
"O evil-minded one, for what purpose did you speak such praise of Hari to my son? This is a foolishness, an improper act unworthy of a brahmin. (19)
"O lowest of the twice-born, this praise of my enemy, composed even by a child, ought not to be heard in my presence; yet it has been done through your grace. (20)
Having spoken thus and looking all around, the king of the Daityas, overwhelmed with rage, said to one Daitya: "Bind this lowest of brahmins! (21)
Having heard these words of the king, he bound the son of Bhṛgu.
Seeing his guru being bound, Prahlāda, who was devoted to brahmins, said to his father: "Father, my guru did not tell me this. (22)
By the grace of the God of gods, O Lord Hari, I have been instructed;
there is no other teacher for me, for that very Hari is my inspirer.
The listener, the thinker, as well as the speaker, the seer, the omnipresent Lord, Hari himself is the imperishable creator and the controller of all embodied beings;
therefore, O Lord, this sinless Brahmin, who is my preceptor, must be released. (24)
Rudra said:
Having heard these words of his son, Hiraṇyakaśipu then released that brāhmaṇa and spoke to his own son with amazement. 25.
"O child, why do you wander thus with false words, deluding the mind of a twice-born?
Who is Viṣṇu? What is his form? And where is that Hari situated? (26)
"I alone am the Lord in this world, for I am the sovereign of the three realms;
therefore, worship me alone as Govinda and abandon your invincible enemy. (27)
Or else, O leader of the asuras, worship the god Śaṅkara, Rudra, the Lord and teacher of the world, the auspicious one who bestows all sovereignty. (28)
Having applied the triple mark with ashes worshipped by the Daityas,
and having worshipped Mahādeva according to the path taught in the Pāśupata [tradition], ||29||
Rudra said:
Having heard these words of the lord of the Daityas, the priests of the Daityas [spoke]. (30)
The family priests said: "O illustrious one, do exactly as your father says.
Abandon the enemy, the foe of Kaiṭabha, and worship the Three-eyed Lord. (31)
There is no god higher than Rudra, who bestows everything upon men;
even you became a lord by his very grace. (32)
Rudra said:
Having heard these words of theirs, Prahlāda, who was born as a Vaiṣṇava, [spoke]. (33)
Prahlāda said:
"Oh, how excellent is the Lord, by whose māyā the world is deluded!
Oh, how wonderful that those who know the Vedānta are honored in all the worlds! (34)
Even Brahmins, filled with pride, speak thus out of fickleness:
"Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate reality. (35)
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditator; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditation; he is the goal of the entire universe, the eternal, auspicious, and infallible one. (36)
Vāsudeva, the eternal, is the sustainer and the ordainer of the world;
this entire universe is indeed the Puruṣa, and it is he who lives upon this universe. ||37||
He possesses a golden body, is eternal, and has eyes resembling lotuses;
he is the gentle Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā, stainless and of auspicious form. ||38||
By that very [power], Brahmā and Īśa were created as the two supreme gods at the beginning of creation;
honoring his command alone, Brahmā and Śaṅkara abide. (39)
Out of fear of him the wind blows; out of fear of him the sun rises;
out of fear of him Agni, Candra, and Death as the fifth run on. 40.
In the beginning, there was the one divine Lord Hari, the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
there was no Brahmā, no Indra, nor Īśāna, nor the moon and sun. (41)
Neither the wind nor the earth, nor the stars, nor the dwellers of heaven—only the wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 42.
O best of the twice-born, having thus abandoned the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, why do you speak before me out of passion, greed, or even fear? (43)
Having abandoned that Lord Hari, the protector of all and the sovereign of all, how can I resort to heresy and worship Śaṅkara? (44)
The Lord of Lakṣmī, the God of gods, the Infinite, the Supreme Person—
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, and adorned with all ornaments. ||45||
Always [worship] the Youthful One, the Lord of All, who bestows the bliss of eternal joy. ||46||
The high-souled yogis, Sanaka and others, meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, whom the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā, Śiva, and Indra worship. (47)
By the side-long glance of whose wife the gods were beheld—namely Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Varuṇa, Yama, Soma, and the Lord of Wealth. ||48||
Merely by remembering his name, even for sinful beings, liberation occurs swiftly—a liberation that is very difficult even for Brahmā and others to attain. (49)
He alone is thus the protector and the glorious Lord even of the gods at all times;
him alone, the infallible one, joined with Lakṣmī, I shall worship.
"I shall attain that supreme abode of Viṣṇu with ease indeed.
Rudra said:
Having heard these words of his, Hiraṇyakaśipu then [acted]. 51.
Overcome by great anger, he blazed like another fire;
looking around at the Daityas, he spoke thus, faint with rage: ||52||
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "By my command, have the evil-doing Prahlāda, who is intent on worshipping his enemy, slain with terrifying multitudes of weapons. (53)
Thinking, "Hari alone is my protector," he protects me out of affection;
today, indeed, may I behold Hari’s protection to be fruitful. (54)
Rudra said: Then, with weapons raised, the Daityas, by the command of the lord of the Daityas, surrounded the high-souled son of the Daitya king and stood ready to slay him.
Prahlāda likewise, having meditated upon Viṣṇu within the lotus of his heart and chanting the eight-syllabled mantra, stood firm like another mountain. (56)
The heroes struck him from all sides with spears, javelins, and pikes;
yet Prahlāda’s body remained auspicious there due to his remembrance of Hari.
Through the power of Viṣṇu, which is difficult to withstand, it became intensely like a thunderbolt;
then, having reached his body, it [absorbed] the great weapons of the enemies of the gods.
Like petals of the blue lotus, they fell, severed upon the auspicious earth;
yet the Daityas were not able to pierce even the slightest part of his body. (59)
Filled with wonder, the soldiers stood with their faces turned toward the King of the Daityas,
having beheld such a high-souled son of great strength.
Having fallen into a state of supreme astonishment, the king of the Daityas, overwhelmed by rage,
then commanded all the highly venomous serpents.
Then, commanded in anger by that king with the words, "Devour Vāsuki and the other terrifying [serpents]," those mighty ones set out.
With flaming mouths and terrifying forms, those whose weapons were poison devoured that one of great strength,
biting into him who was a devotee of the one whose banner bears Garuḍa.
The wind-eaters became fangless and venomless;
their limbs mangled by a thousand sons of Vinatā, they were utterly overwhelmed.
Seeing such great serpents at that time, the lord of the Daityas fled in all directions, vomiting blood profusely.
Then, filled with rage, he commanded the elephants of the quarters who were possessed by great intoxication;
and thus directed by that king, the elephants of the quarters became arrogant with rut.
Then, surrounding him, they struck him violently with their massive tusks;
thereupon, the tusks of the elephants of the quarters fell to the earth, severed at their roots.
Deprived of their tusks, the elephants, afflicted by fear, fled away;
seeing those great elephants, the powerful lord of the Daityas became enraged.
And having kindled a great fire, he cast his own son into it;
yet, seeing Prahlāda, who is dear to the one who reclines upon the waters, the carrier of oblations [the Fire-god] [refrained].
The fire, though cool, did not burn that steadfast man;
seeing the boy unburnt, the king was greatly amazed. (70)
Then he gave him a terrible poison that was beneficial to all beings;
and by the power of Viṣṇu, that poison became nectar for him. ||71||
By offering that [oblation] to the god, one consumes even poison as nectar;
