through such means of slaying—terrible in form and exceedingly cruel—[the goal is achieved].
Having deluded his son and observed his invincibility,
the king of the Daityas, overwhelmed with wonder, then spoke to his son with conciliatory words.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Viṣṇu, you have correctly described the supremacy [of the Lord] before me.
Because He pervades all beings, He is designated as 'Viṣṇu'. (74)
That god who is omnipresent is indeed the Supreme Lord;
demonstrate to me directly his very state of being omnipresent. (75)
Sovereignty, power, and splendor, as well as knowledge, heroism, and strength—these are the supreme form and the manifestations of the qualities of that Supreme Being. (76)
Having observed this with effort, I consider Viṣṇu to be the foremost among the inhabitants of heaven;
there is no one among the gods in the world who is my equal in strength.
O giver of honor, by the granting of this boon from Īśāna, you have obtained invincibility among all beings and unassailability by all creatures;
yet even Viṣṇu might attain lordship over me by conquering me through his strength and heroism. (78)
Rudra said:
Having heard these words of his, Prahlāda, filled with wonder, spoke;
that one of noble vows described the power of Hari to Dainya. (79)
Prahlāda said:
He who is the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self, is called Vāsudeva because he dwells within all beings. (80)
Viṣṇu is designated as the creator of the entire world;
indeed, there is nothing else in this world, whether stationary or moving, other than him. (81)
In every respect, his form consists of both conscious and unconscious entities, and not otherwise;
his pervasion extends through three-quarters of the supreme ether, while the wonder of his pervasion by a single quarter is marvelous.
That Janārdana, who holds the discus and mace in his hands and wears yellow garments, is seen by yogins through devotion; he is never seen by one lacking devotion.
Janārdana cannot be seen through anger or through envy,
among gods, animals, humans, or even among stationary beings.
It remains pervading all things, both the small and the great. //84//
Rudra said:
Having heard these words of Prahlāda, the chief of the Daityas, his eyes copper-red with rage, then spoke while repeatedly rebuking his son. (85)
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"If this Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, is indeed the Supreme Person, show proof of it today; what is the use of much talk? (86)
Mahādeva said:
Having spoken thus, the Daitya suddenly struck a pillar of his own palace with his hand and said this to Prahlāda: 87.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"Show me Viṣṇu in this place, if he be omnipresent;
otherwise, I shall slay you, you who prattle with false words. (88)
Rudra said:
Having spoken thus, the lord of the Daityas suddenly drew his sword and, in a rage, hurled it at Prahlāda’s chest to slay him with the blade. (89)
At that moment, a great sound was heard intensely from the pillar,
as if the interior of the sky were bursting with the roar of the thunderbolt at the end of an aeon.
By that great sound, which shattered the ears of the Daityas, they were all cast down upon the ground like trees severed at their roots. ||91||
Trembling with fear, the Daityas indeed perceived the three worlds as submerged;
then, from that pillar, the immensely radiant Mahāhari emerged.
He made a most terrible sound, resembling the destruction of the world;
by that great roar, the stars fell upon the earth.
Assuming the form of Narasiṃha, Hari appeared there as if manifest, enveloped in a splendor equal to many tens of millions of suns and fires. (94)
With a face like that of a five-faced lion and a body in human form,
his countenance was formidable with fangs, and he was towering with a flickering tongue reaching toward the sky.
The omnipresent Lord has the ends of his hair wreathed in flames, his eyes are like glowing embers,
and he possesses a thousand long arms equipped with all kinds of weapons.
He shines like Mount Meru surrounded by many-branched trees;
he wears excellent divine garlands and is adorned with celestial ornaments. ||97||
He stood there in the form of a man-lion to destroy all the demons;
having seen that Narasiṃha of great power, who appeared terrible. ||98||
With his eyelashes scorched and his limbs trembling, the lord of the Daityas fell down.
Then Prahlāda beheld Hari, who resembled a man-lion. 99.
With shouts of "Victory!", he paid homage to Janārdana, the Lord of Gods;
he beheld [the marks] upon the limbs of that high-souled Nṛsiṃha.
The worlds, along with the oceans, islands, gods, gandharvas, and humans—a thousand such cosmic eggs—are seen upon the tip of his mane. (101)
Within his eyes, the moon, the sun, and the other [planets] are seen;
likewise, in his ears, the two Aśvin deities, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate directions are seen. (102)
On his forehead are Brahmā and Rudra; in his nostrils are space and wind;
Indra and Agni are in his mouth, while Sarasvatī is in his tongue. 103.
In his fangs are lions, tigers, śarabhas, and great serpents;
on his neck Mount Meru is seen, and upon his shoulders are the great mountains. (104)
The gods, animals, and humans were on the arms of that Great-Souled One;
the intermediate space was in his navel, and likewise the earth was at his feet.
All herbs and plants were on the rows of hair from his feet to his toenails, and the Vedas, together with their limbs and sub-limbs, were in his breaths. (106)
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts, as well as those Gandharvas and Apsarases, were seen manifest in all his limbs. (107)
Thus are the manifestations of that Supreme Self seen by you:
[the Lord] whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, and who is adorned with a forest garland. (108)
Having perceived the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, the son of the lord of the Daityas was endowed with weapons such as the conch, the discus, the mace, the sword, and the Śārṅga bow. (109)
His limbs drenched with tears of joy, he bowed down again and again;
yet the lord of the Daityas, upon seeing Hari, stood under the sway of death out of rage. ||110||
Raising his sword to fight, he rushed toward that Man-lion;
then all the hosts of Daityas, possessed of great strength, regained their senses. ||111||
Taking up their own weapons, they rushed forward in haste and struck Hari,
like many stalks of straw cast repeatedly into a fire.
In that very same way, the great weapons were reduced to ashes upon the body of Hari;
then, seeing those armies of the Daityas, Narahari [acted].
And with the clearly manifested garlands of flames arising from his mane, he utterly consumed the Dānavas by means of the fire produced from the mane of the Man-Lion. 114.
All the hosts were reduced to ashes;
that army was utterly destroyed, leaving behind only Prahlāda and his followers once they beheld their forces turned to ash.
In his anger, the lord of the Daityas drew his sword and rushed forward;
but [Viṣṇu] seized the lord of the Daityas by one arm as he held the sword in his hand. (116)
The Lord of Gods caused him to fall, just as a great wind fells a branch;
having seized him as he fell to the ground, the man-lion [tore apart] his massive body. 117.
He placed him upon his own lap and beheld the face of Hari;
[he saw] the sin committed by slandering Viṣṇu, as well as that born from the fault of being a Vaiṣṇava.
Then, by the mere touch of Nṛsiṃha, the body of the lord of the Daityas was instantly reduced to ashes; thereafter, the Man-lion [consumed] the great frame of the demon king.
The lord of the Daityas, whose soul was pure, tore [the mountain] apart with dense, sharp claws resembling thunderbolts, as he beheld the face of Hari directly before him.
With his heart pierced by claws, the Great Lion, having achieved his purpose,
gave up his life after tearing that body into a hundred pieces with his sharp talons.
Having dragged out their long intestines, they hung them around the necks of their beloveds;
then all the hosts of gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism [were struck with wonder]. (122)
Placing Brahmā and Rudra at their head, they approached slowly to offer praise,
being afraid to propitiate him who blazes with faces on all sides.
They meditated upon the Mother, the sustainer of the worlds, the Sovereign Goddess, golden-hued and radiant, the destroyer of all calamities. (124)
Having meditated upon the auspicious Nārāyaṇī, whose limbs are eternally faultless, they devotedly paid homage to the eternal Goddess with recitations of the Devī-sūkta. 125.
As they were meditating upon her, that goddess then appeared right there—four-armed, large-eyed, and adorned with all ornaments. (126)
Seeing her, who was adorned with fine *dukūla* garments, divine garlands, and unguents—the beloved of the God of gods—all the inhabitants of heaven [were filled with wonder]. (127)
With palms joined in reverence, they said to the Goddess:
"Act so that our beloved Lord may grant his favor and bestow fearlessness upon the three worlds. (128)
Rudra said:
Having been addressed thus, the Goddess, having suddenly attained her beloved Janārdana,
prostrated herself, paid homage, and said to him, "Be gracious."
Upon seeing his own beloved queen, Hari, the Lord of All,
instantly cast off the anger born of the demon's body as if he were pleased.
Having embraced the goddess Lakṣmī,
who had approached him, Hari, the ocean of compassion, gazed upon the gods with eyes moistened by the nectar of mercy.
Then, as they praised him loudly with cries of "Victory! Victory!
and bowed down, a joyful agitation arose among those who were beheld by his compassionate gaze.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with joy, bowed down to the Lord, the Master of the Universe, and spoke with palms joined in reverence. (133)
The hosts of gods said:
"O Lord of the Universe, we are unable to behold this most wonderful splendor;
this form is exceedingly marvelous, adorned with many arms and feet. (134)
All of us, the inhabitants of heaven, are unable to behold or even stand before your exceedingly sharp splendor, which pervades the three worlds. (135)
Mahādeva said: Thus entreated by the gods, the Lord of Devas withdrew that most terrifying splendor and became pleasant to behold.
The autumn moon, with eyes like white lotuses, is difficult to behold;
it is auspicious, resembling a flash of lightning amidst a mass of nectar-like rays.
With divine arms adorned with armlets and bracelets made of various jewels,
they resembled the branches of the wish-fulfilling tree laden with excellent fruit.
The Supreme Lord is endowed with four soft, divine [hands], beautified by lotus-like hands that resemble the hibiscus flower. ||139||
The Man-Lion is resplendent with his two upraised arms holding the conch and the discus, while his other two hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (140)
Adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, and a forest garland, he shone with two earrings resembling the rising sun. (141)
Adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, and endowed with the glory resting upon his left hand, the lion among kings shone brilliantly. (142)
Upon seeing that Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha, the gods along with the great ṛṣis were drenched by tears of joy, their hearts overflowing with rapture. (143)
Immersed in that ocean of bliss, they offered continuous salutations and worshipped the Lord of the Self with offerings of divine flowers. (144)
Having consecrated the Eternal One with jars of jewels filled with nectar, and with garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and delightful incenses; 145.
Having worshipped the lion among men with divine and offered lamps, they praised him with divine hymns and bowed down to him again and again. 146.
Then Lakṣmī’s Lord, being pleased, granted them their desired boons;
thereafter, the Lord of All, who is affectionate toward his devotees, [departed] together with the hosts of gods.
Having consoled his devoted son Prahlāda, he had him consecrated by the foremost of the asuras and established the imperishable Prahlāda as the king of all the daityas.
He granted him his desired boons and unwavering devotion;
then the Man-Lion was praised by all the hosts of gods.
There, as if with bodies composed of scattered flowers, he vanished;
thereafter, all the hosts of gods returned each to his own abode.
Furthermore, with delighted minds, they consumed their own sacrificial portions;
then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, became free from all distress.
When that great Daitya had been slain, everyone was filled with joy;
then Prahlāda, the devotee of Viṣṇu, ruled the kingdom with righteousness.
Having obtained the kingdom through the grace of Hari, that best of Vaiṣṇavas worshipped the Man-Lion with numerous sacrifices, gifts, and other offerings. (153)
In due time, he attained the eternal abode of Hari, which is accessible only to yogis.
Those who constantly hear this account of Prahlāda’s life [attain the same]. (154)
They shall all be liberated from sin and go to the supreme goal.
This majesty of Hari as Nṛsiṃha has been told to you, O Goddess;
now listen, O Goddess, to the remaining states of his majesty in due order. 155.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Nṛsiṃha," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(239) Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-nine.
Rudra said:
Prahlāda’s son was born known as Virocana;
his son was the powerful Bali Vaiśvānara, who possessed mighty arms. (1)
The best among those who know the true Dharma, faithful to his word, with senses conquered, the most beloved devotee of Hari, eternally devoted to righteousness, and pure. ||2||
Having conquered the gods along with Indra and the hosts of Maruts, as well as the three worlds, that one of great strength established them under his own control and ruled the kingdom. ||3||
The earth yielded crops without being ploughed, providing abundant grain and fruit;
all the cows gave milk in full measure, and the trees were laden with flowers and fruit. (4)
All men, devoted to their own duties and free from sin,
constantly worship Hṛṣīkeśa, being devoid of all mental anguish.
Thus, by the power of his conduct, the mighty lord of the Daityas ruled the kingdom;
Indra and the other gods of the three worlds stood before him as his servants. (6)
Having enjoyed sovereignty over the three worlds, his pride in his strength humbled, he saw his son deprived of his kingdom; out of a desire for his welfare, [he acted]. (7)
The righteous Kaśyapa, together with his wife Aditi, performed austerities directed toward Hari,
observing a vow of milk.
He worshipped Janārdana, Padmanābha, the Lord of Gods;
thereafter, Hari was fully propitiated by him for thousands of years.
There, the eternal Lord appeared before her;
seeing him, the lotus-eyed one, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Dark as a sapphire gem, adorned with all ornaments, and beautified by a shimmering crown, armlets, necklace, and earrings. ||11||
His chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, he was clothed in yellow garments,
and he sat together with Śrī upon the great-souled Maṇḍaleśa.
Having beheld that Lord of the worlds with a heart overflowing with joy, that best of brahmins, together with his wife, prostrated and offered praise. (13)

Kaśyapa said: Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Lakṣmī, Omniscient One, Sovereign of the Universe! O Soul of All, Lord of all gods, you who are the cause of the creation and destruction of the world. 14.
Salutations to you, whose form is without beginning or end and is infinite; to the sustainer of the universe;
to you whose body is the Veda and its auxiliary sciences, and who are the eye of all. 15.
Salutations to You, the Self of all; salutations to the most subtle;
salutations to the one filled with auspicious qualities, whose nature is the object of meditation for yogis. ||16||
Homage to the youthful prince, the sovereign of Śrī, Bhū, and Īlā;
to Him who eternally enjoys solitary bliss and abides in the supreme abode. ||17||
Salutations to you, the fourfold self; salutations be to you, the fourfold manifestation. Salutations to you who abide in five states; salutations to you, whose nature is fivefold.
It should always be worshipped by yogins who are devoted to the fivefold essence; it abides as the fivefold consecration for those who know the reality of the fivefold meaning. (19)
Furthermore, O Hari, whose self is eternally complete in fourfold ways, the wise know that your essential nature is always to be understood as fivefold. (20)

The twice-born, who are devoted to ritual action, consist of the three Vedas, and are compassionate toward their devotees; with their hands raised in worship, they purify the entire world, which is your own progeny. (21)
Salutations to the creator of the three worlds, the self-existent soul of all, by the mere sight of whom there occurs liberation from the bonds of worldly existence. 22.
Salutations to you, O Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, to the All-pervading One who possesses all forms!
Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, to Kṛṣṇa, to Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; salutations to you, Viṣṇu, the Victorious One, whose nature is pure goodness (śuddhasattva). ||23||
Mahādeva said:
Being thus properly praised with these and other hymns by the great sage, Janārdana, being well-pleased, spoke in a deep voice. 24.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am pleased with you, having been worshipped with such devotion.
Choose a boon; may it be well with you, for I shall grant your heart's desire."
Mahādeva said: Then Kaśyapa, together with his wife, spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa. ||26||
Kaśyapa said:
"O Lord of Gods, having attained the state of being my son, act for the benefit of the gods;
the three worlds have been forcibly conquered by Bali."
Having become the younger brother of Indra, he became renowned as Upendra;
by whatever means possible, having conquered Bali through his illusory power (māyā),
he gave the three worlds eternally to my son Śakra.
Mahādeva said: Having been addressed thus by that brahmin, Janārdana replied,
"So be it," and while being praised by the gods, he vanished right there.
And at that very time, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, entered the womb of Aditi as the son of the high-souled Kaśyapa.
At that time, Bali, a man of great austerity, commenced a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) according to the prescribed rites,
together with eight great ṛṣis.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Vāmana," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||239||
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Then, after a thousand years, Aditi gave birth to Viṣṇu, the infallible Vāmana, the Great Lord of all the worlds. 1.
I bow to Hari, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, whose splendor is like that of the full moon,
who is beautiful, lotus-eyed, and possesses a very short stature.
The Lord, wearing the guise of a young brahmin student, who is the range of all the Vedas, and marked by the signs of the girdle, deerskin, staff, and so forth. ||3||
Seeing him, all the deities, led by Śatakratu,
together with the great seers, offered praise and paid homage to the one of great splendor.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke to the best of the gods.
Vāmana said:
"O best of gods, what should be done by me today? Tell me that."
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Then the thirty gods, being greatly delighted, spoke to that Supreme Lord.
The gods said:
At this time, O Madhusūdana, the sacrifice of Bali is taking place.
O Lord, this is not the time for refusal regarding that lord of the Daityas;
having requested the world of the triple heaven, you ought to grant it to us. (7)
Śaṅkara said:
Having been thus addressed by all the gods, Hari went to Bali,
who was seated at the place of sacrifice together with eight sages.
But seeing that he had arrived, the king of the Daityas rose up suddenly, accompanied by his ministers, thinking, "Viṣṇu himself has come as a guest. (9)
Having seated him upon a seat of flowers according to the prescribed rite,
she prostrated herself, paid her respects, and spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
Bali said:
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose; my life has become fruitful.
Having worshipped you, O lord of brahmins, what can I do that is pleasing to you?"
"O best of the twice-born, for what purpose have you come here seeking me?
Grant that to me quickly; speak, O foremost among those who know the Vedas. (12)
Śaṅkara said:
Then, with a delighted mind, Vāmana spoke to that lord of the earth.
Vāmana said:
Listen, O Indra among kings; I shall tell you the reason for my arrival.
"O Lord of Daityas, grant me the ground of the fire-pit; I desire nothing other than the space of my three strides, O giver of honor. (14)
Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of land is supreme; that king who gives land to a Brahmin who possesses nothing at all [attains the highest merit]. (15)
Even one who possesses only a thumb's breadth of land may become a lord of the earth;
there is nothing found here in this world as purifying as the gift of land. (16)
He who accepts land and he who bestows land—both of these are performers of meritorious deeds and go to heaven upon death. (17)
Therefore, O Great King, grant me this three-footed plot of land.
O Lord of the Earth, do not enter into the effort of giving this small amount of ground;
for that shall become the granting of the three worlds. (18)
Śaṅkara said: Then, with a joyful countenance, the lord of the earth replied,
"So be it," and he resolved to perform the gift of land for him according to the prescribed rites.
Seeing that king of the Daityas, his priest Uśanas then spoke these words: "O King, let the earth be given back."
Śukra said:
"O King, this is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, who, having been entreated by the gods, has come here after covering the entire earth in order to obtain it from you. (21)
Therefore, O King, you must not give away the earth; instead, O Great-Souled One, grant me another object according to my word, O Lord of the Earth. (22)
The illustrious Śaṅkara said: Then, laughing, the king spoke to that preceptor with fortitude.
Bali said:
As if for the pleasure of Vāsudeva, all this merit has been performed by me. ||23||
Today I am fortunate indeed, since Viṣṇu himself has come here; today my life and great happiness must surely be offered to him. (24)
"Therefore, give even the three worlds to him without delay.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Having spoken thus, the king reverently washed his feet.
Having first offered water according to the prescribed rite, he gave her the chosen land;
then, having performed the circumambulation and paid homage, he bestowed wealth as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
With a joyful inner soul, they both spoke again to the brahmin.
Bali said: "I am blessed, I have fulfilled my duty, O twice-born one; please speak of the earth."
"O best of Brahmins, accept this earth as you desire.
Śrī Śaṅkara said: Viṣṇu spoke to that king, the lord of men, while standing near Stava.
"I shall measure out the earth today with my foot while you look on.
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord abandoned that dwarf form.
Assuming the body of Trivikrama, he seized this earth, extending fifty crores [of yojanas] along with its oceans and mountains. 30.
Madhusūdana stepped with a single foot upon the earth, together with its oceans, its continents, and its gods, asuras, and humans.
The eternal Lord spoke to the king of the Daityas, "What shall I do?"—
referring to that very three-strided form of the Greatly Resplendent Ishvara.
Even for the sake of the welfare of the gods and the high-souled sages,
it would not be possible to behold even Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
O auspicious Girijā, having traversed the entire earth,
that foot became extended for more than a hundred yojanas.
The eternal Lord granted him divine vision; he revealed his own form as Janārdana to that king of the Daityas.
Having beheld that universal form of the Lord, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, attained incomparable joy and was overwhelmed with tears of bliss. (36)
Having seen him thus, and having paid homage and offered praises with hymns of praise,
he spoke with a faltering voice and a joyful inner soul.
Bali said:
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, having beheld you, the Supreme Lord!
O Supreme Lord, you yourself take possession of these three worlds. (38)
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
Then Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, the Infallible, extended his second imperishable foot upwards as far as the world of Brahmā.
O lady of auspicious countenance, the world, accompanied by the stars and planets and surrounded by all the gods, became completely filled with the footstep of Acyuta.
Then the Grandfather, his heart overflowing with joy, [gazed upon] that foot of the God of gods, which was marked with the signs of the Brahma-wheel, the lotus, and other symbols.
Saying, "I am blessed," Brahmā took his own water-pot and,
with devotion, washed [the Lord] with the water contained therein.
By the power of that Viṣṇu, this [water] became inexhaustible;
that pure water fell from the peak of Mount Meru as a sacred bathing place (tīrtha). ||43||
For the sake of purifying the world, [the waters] were made to flow in the four directions as the Sitā,
Cakṣu, Alakanandā, and Bhadrā, respectively.
Then, to the south of Mount Cāmara, the river that purifies the worlds is known as the Tripathagā; she flows in three ways and is called by three names. (45)
The Dakini spoke of this heaven, as well as Bhogavati below;
and in the middle is the Ganga, Végavatī, for the sake of purifying men, O Auspicious One. (46)
O lady of beautiful countenance, having seen that auspicious stream in the midst of Mount Meru,
I bore it upon my head for the sake of purifying myself.
O Goddess, having held the auspicious water of the Gaṅgā for a thousand divine years, I attained the state of Śiva, honored in all the worlds. 48.
He who would carry on his head the Gaṅgā originating from Viṣṇu’s foot, or drink it, will undoubtedly become worthy of worship by the lords of the gods. 49.
Even if one should say "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" across hundreds of yojanas,
one is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then King Bhagīratha and Gautama, the great ascetic,
having honored me through their penance, made a request for the sake of Gaṅgā.
I affectionately gave that best of rivers, the auspicious Gaṅgā belonging to Viṣṇu, which exists for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, to those two.
Brought by Gautama, she was celebrated as Gautamī;
because she was brought by that king, she became renowned as Bhāgīrathī. (53)
In this context, the most excellent birth of Gaṅgā has been narrated;
thereafter, the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa [confronted] Bali, the lord of the Daityas.
He who is affectionate toward his devotees granted the auspicious world of Rasātala to all the Dānavas, as well as to the Nāgas and the aquatic beings.
He made King Bali perform sacrifice until the dissolution of all beings;
having accepted the worlds from Bali, the slayer of the Daityas departed in the guise of a young brahmin.
Then the imperishable Viṣṇu, the descendant of Kaśyapa, affectionately gave it to Mahendra;
thereafter, the gods along with the Gandharvas and the sages of great luster [were present].
They praised Acyuta with divine hymns and worshipped him;
then, he contracted that great form for the very purpose of being seen by them.
Being worshipped by the thirty gods, Hari vanished;
thus was Śakra well protected by the all-powerful Viṣṇu.
The Lord of the Three Worlds obtained great sovereignty over the three realms.
All this auspicious majesty of Vāmana has been narrated to you;
O Goddess, I shall now describe his remaining majesty in due order.

Thus ends the two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Vāmana," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||240|| ||cha||
Chapter Two Hundred and Forty-One.
The Lord said: There was a great son of Bhṛgu, Jamadagni, the best among the twice-born.
He was a master of all the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and possessed of great ascetic power. ||1||
O beautiful lady, that virtuous-souled one performed austerities directed toward Mahendra for a period of a thousand years on the auspicious banks of the Gaṅgā.
Then the blessed Lord Pākaśāsana, being pleased, spoke to Indra. Indra said: "O best of Brahmins, choose a boon that is in your heart. (3)
The Lord said: Then the brahmin-sage Jamadagni spoke to the highly gratified Śatakratu. Jamadagni said:
[He gave] Surabhi, the cow of the gods, who always yields all desires.
Īśvara said: Then the Lord of Gods, being pleased, gave to that brāhmaṇa, the destroyer of [his] lineage,
the goddess Surabhi, who yields all desires.
Having obtained the goddess Asurī, Jamadagni, of great asceticism and immense power,
dwelt like another Śatakratu.
The great ascetic Jamadagni married according to the prescribed rites the beautiful daughter of Reṇuka, known by the name Reṇukā.
With her, that righteous-souled lord took delight for many years,
just as the powerful Indra did with the auspicious goddess Paulomī.
Then, desiring a son, that most righteous king performed a sacrifice;
through that sacrifice, he gratified the Lord, the subduer of Pāka.
Being fully satisfied, the husband of Śacī gave him a son of great strength,
of immense luster, with mighty arms, who was a scorcher of all enemies.
Then, O lady of pure smiles, in due time the lord of sages begot upon Reṇukā a son of great heroism and endowed with strength.
By a portion of a fraction of a fraction of Viṣṇu’s splendor, he was endowed with all auspicious marks;
that son of great heroism had Bhṛgu as his grandfather.
Then, out of great joy, he gave him the beautiful name "Rāma," which is characterized by the syllable of Viṣṇu.
Born from Jamadagni, he was called Jāmadagnya;
that bull among the twice-born also grew up within that lineage of Bhṛgu.
Having been presented [to him] and praised by him, he who was proficient in all branches of knowledge then went toward the Śālagrāma mountain to perform austerities.
There, the twice-born son of Marīci beheld the Brahman-sage Kaśyapa of immeasurable splendor; filled with joy at that sight, he [stood] there. 16.
He duly bestowed upon him that imperishable Vaiṣṇava mantra;
having received the mantra from the high-souled Kaśyapa, Ārāma then [proceeded].
Then he worshipped the Lord of Kamalā according to the prescribed rites,
while muttering the great six-syllabled mantra day and night.
Meditating upon the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Hari,
the righteous-souled Bhārgava performed austerities for many years.
At that time, the great ascetic Jamadagni, a brahmin-sage who had conquered his senses and was restrained in speech, was staying on the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā.
He performed great religious acts, such as sacrifices and gifts, according to the prescribed rules; by the grace of Indra’s cow, his riches became complete.
After some time, however, the lordly sovereign of the Haihayas,
surrounded by his entire army, having conquered all kingdoms, [arrived].
Having reached the hermitage of Jamadagni Bhārgava, the lord of the earth beheld that highly fortunate one and paid homage to the best of sages. (23)
Having inquired after the welfare of that great seer of purified soul,
the king presented him with garments and ornaments.
They honored the king who had come to their home; having worshipped that best of monarchs according to the prescribed rite with the *madhuparka* offering, they paid him due respect.
The sage offered food to the lord of men along with his army;
he was requested by that wise descendant of Bhṛgu, who desired a divine cow.
Then, that one of great asceticism created a complete abundance of food, drink, and other provisions;
he created it as inexhaustible food, drink, and so forth.
That best of sages presented her to the king, the lord of men;
and upon seeing that brindled cow, the king was filled with wonder. (28)
That wicked-minded king, filled with longing for her, requested Surabhi from Jamadagni there, O best of kings. (29)
Kārtavīrya said:
"O Brahmin, give me Śabalā, the tawny cow who grants all desires;
I shall give you thousands of other cows, O you of excellent vows."
The Lord said: Having been addressed thus by that king, Jamadagni of great asceticism then spoke. Jamadagni said:
O King Aśabalāraja, O lord of the earth, you have gone to the state of death. 31.
"O King, this wealth belongs to the gods and is protected by Śakra, the lord of the gods; how could it be given away by me? (32)
Īśvara said: Thus addressed, the king, defiled by anger, surrounded by his entire army, forcibly seized Śabalā. (33)
Then, O woman of excellent complexion, the highly fortunate Śabalā became enraged and struck his armies with her horns as well as the soles of her hooves.
Having destroyed that army in a mere moment by means of her variegated forces,
the Goddess vanished and in an instant went to the vicinity of Śakra.
Seeing his own army slaughtered, Arjuna was overwhelmed with rage.
He struck Bhārgava, the best of the twice-born, with his fist.
Struck many times by that thief, his limbs rendered mangled, that best of brahmins, Māra, suddenly fell to the ground. (37)
Having slain the best of sages there, the sinful lord of the Haihayas,
surrounded by a vast army, entered his own city.
Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, worshipped the Lord of the gods;
being thus fully honored by him, the delighted Keśava spoke.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O brahmin, I am pleased with the austerity of you, whose self is restrained;
I shall bestow upon you a supreme and auspicious power."
Then, possessed by my power, abandon these wicked and best of kings for the destruction of the earth's burden and truly for the welfare of the gods. 41.
The Lord said:
Having spoken thus, the God gave him an axe that crushes enemies,
the great bow of Viṣṇu, and numerous divine weapons.
Having given it, the Blessed One Janārdana spoke to Jāmadagnya.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of the twice-born, having slain many kings who were intoxicated with pride, accept the entire earth bounded by the oceans, for you are a slayer of enemy heroes."
And protect [the earth] according to dharma, endowed with great heroism;
in due time, through my grace, you shall also go to my own abode.
The Lord said:
Having spoken thus and granted a boon to the twice-born, the God vanished;
and Rāma then immediately departed for his father’s hermitage.
Seeing his father slain, the descendant of Bhṛgu was overcome with rage;
desiring to rid the earth, which was crowded with kings, of the Kṣatriya caste, he set about his task. (46)
He went to the city of the lord of the Haihayas, which was surrounded by kings;
with his body blazing from the onset of anger, he stood there with his weapon raised high.
Seeing that son of Jamadagni, possessed of great majesty,
they regarded him as the fire of cosmic destruction blazing with his very body.
Afflicted by fear and fleeing in all directions, they all reported to the king, the lord of the Haihayas, that great being who was equipped with every kind of weapon. ||49||
Having heard those words, the king, his mind filled with wonder, spoke.
The Lord of the Haihayas said:
"Who is this that stands by force at the gate of my city, equipped with weapons? (50)
Neither Mahendra, nor Yama, nor Rudra, nor even the Giver of Wealth (Kubera),
though armed, would ever be able to stand at the gate of my city.
Mahādeva said:
Having spoken thus, that lord of kings dispatched very powerful tax-collectors to see him; the evil-minded one commanded them, "Seize him! (52)
Having gone there, they beheld the hero of great strength standing at the city gate,
blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction and difficult to look upon because of his own splendor.
Even those of great strength, who were unable to even catch sight of him,
set out with great haste, O dear one, desiring to seize that hero.
Seeing all those kings, the servants of the lord of the earth, equipped with weapons, the great and powerful Jāmadagnya, the best of Brahmins, spoke while smiling: ||55||
Paraśurāma said: "O lowest of men, I am Rāma, the son of Bhārgava;
having arrived here, I shall slay all these excellent kings because of the death of my father."
I shall offer the blood of Kārtavīrya mixed with sesame seeds as an oblation to my father, and I shall indeed offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) using his head as the lotus.
Mahādeva said:
Having been addressed thus, those of great prowess, asking "What shall we do for that king?", struck him with arrows as fire is covered by straw. 58.
Then the highly heroic Rāma, whose prowess is truth, being enraged,
drew the bow of Viṣṇu and produced the sound of its twanging string.
The three worlds were filled with that great roar;
even among the gods, a great and wonderful terror arose.
Then, with arrows resembling fire, that one of great strength struck those heroic and mighty warriors who were asking, "What shall we do? (61)
Having slain Atukiṃkara, he stood before that high-souled king like the fire of cosmic destruction, inspiring fear in all living beings.
Having heard that his own Atakinkaras had been slain by the wise Rāma,
the heroic lord of the Haihayas, his eyes bloodshot with rage, [spoke].
They set forth with their army to where the imperishable Bhagavān was;
they beheld him, blazing with his own splendor and appearing formidable.
All the people there were terrified, seeking welfare and fearing the destruction of the people;
then, at that time, there occurred a most terrible battle with King Rāma.
Then, as the two [warriors] rained down terrifying showers of weapons and missiles like two clouds,
the highly effulgent Rāma [assailed] that army of the king at that time.
With the Vaiṣṇava weapon, he effortlessly burnt everything to ashes in an instant;
thereafter, Nārāyaṇa of immeasurable prowess struck with a sharp axe.
He severed the thousand arms of the evil-minded Kārtavīrya;
that king of great prowess was unable to fight with Rāma.
There, that evil-minded one became devoid of vigor due to his own sin;
then the powerful son of Reṇukā, filled with rage, severed that head.
Just as the powerful Lord of the Gods [Indra] struck down the great mountain peak with his thunderbolt,
so did the majestic son of Jamadagni slay that thousand-armed one.
Enraged in battle, he struck all the kings with his axe;
seeing that most terrible Rāma upon the surface of the earth, the kings [fled]. (71)
Afflicted by fear, they all fled like female elephants before a lion;
even the kings who had previously fled out of anger at their father’s death now ran away.
Enraged like the Lord of Birds against serpents, the descendant of Bhṛgu,
the powerful son of Jamadagni, struck them down and rendered the entire world devoid of Kṣatriyas.
The Blessed One protected that very great family of Ikṣvāku alone,
both because it was the lineage of his maternal grandfather and because of the word of Reṇukā.
Having deprived those born of his maternal grandfather’s lineage of their kingdom, Rāma—the ender of royal dynasties—did not slay them, out of regard for his own kin. 75.
But the powerful son of Jamadagni, having performed austerities, destroyed the lineage of all the kings and rendered the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas.
The twice-born performed the great horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) according to the prescribed rites; he bestowed the earth, consisting of seven continents, upon the foremost of the Brahmins.
Having given the earth to the Brahmins, the powerful son of Jamadagni then went to the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa to perform austerities.
O Goddess, this account of the high-souled Jamadagni, the Lord Śārṅgin who descended through the infusion of his power (śakti), has been narrated to you. 79.
Indeed, because of the penetration of power (*śaktyāveśa*) by that Great Soul, he would not be an object of worship;
rather, he is to be worshipped by the great-souled and foremost Brahmins who are devotees of the Blessed Lord.
The incarnations of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are indeed complete in all excellent qualities;
being worshipped by the sages, they bestow liberation upon men. 81.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Life of Paraśurāma," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||241|| ||cha||
Chapter Two Hundred and Forty-Two.
Rudra said:
Formerly, Svāyambhuva Manu [taught] the great mantra of twelve syllables.
He performed his recitations on the banks of the Gomatī in the pure and auspicious Naimiṣa forest.
Having been worshipped for a thousand years by him, the Lord Hari, the husband of Kamalā, said to him: "Choose a boon from me. (2)
Then Svāyambhuva Manu spoke with joy to Hari.
Manu said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Acyuta, accept the state of being my son for three births."
"Out of longing for a son, I worship you, the Supreme Person.
Rudra said:
Having been addressed thus by him, the Lord of Lakṣmī spoke with a very great voice. 4.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of kings, that which you have desired in your mind shall come to pass;
I am indeed greatly pleased with you for the sake of granting you a son."
O best of kings, O you of excellent vows, at the time for the purpose of [the world's] stability, when you were born in various places, I too was born there.
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I have come into being, O sinless one.
Rudra said:
Having thus granted him the boon, Hari vanished on the spot;
this was his first birth during the era of Svāyambhuva Manu.
Formerly, in the lineage of the Raghus, there was King Daśaratha;
and in the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis, the powerful Vasudeva became the second [incarnation]. (9)
At the end of the Kali age, which measures one thousand divine years,
that Brāhmaṇa will be born in the village of Śambhala.
Kauśalyā indeed became the wife of King Daśaratha; she was renowned by the name Devakī for the sake of serving the lineage of Yadu. 11.
The wife of the brahmin Harivrata, Devaprabhā, likewise attained the state of motherhood to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) across three births. ||12||
O lady of virtuous vows, I shall first relate to you the life-story of Rāma, by the mere remembrance of which even sinners attain liberation. (13)
Hiraṇyaka and Hiraṇyākṣa took up their second birth; from them were born the two of great strength, Kumbhakarṇa and Daśagrīva.
O sinless one, Pulastya had a righteous son, the brahmin named Viśravas;
his wife was the large-eyed daughter of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
From the mouth of Sukeśitanaya and the Dānava Sumālī, there was a daughter named Kekasī;
she became his wife, firm in her vows.
At the time of twilight, the goddess Tulasī, whose form was slender and whose appearance was auspicious, being overflowing with passion, delighted the great sage as she desired by singing.
Because they were born during the twilight of desire (kāmasandhyā), those two Rākṣasas of great strength,
Rāvaṇa and Kuṃbhakarṇa, became world-renowned.
To that maiden named Śūrpaṇakhā, who was born with an exceedingly deformed face, Vibhīṣaṇa was born after some time had passed. (19)
Rāvaṇa, who was of excellent character, a devotee of the Blessed Lord, truthful, righteous, and pure, as well as Kuṃbha and Karṇa, were on the excellent Himavat mountain. ||20||
Then Rāvaṇa, that evil-minded one, intensely worshipped those two of great and fierce asceticism with his own auspicious lotus-like heads.
O Goddess, you worshipped me with a most terrible deed;
then, O fair-browed one, I spoke to him with a joyful inner soul.
"Choose a boon, whatever dwells within your mind.
Then that evil-minded one spoke [to the lord] of the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas: 23.
Desiring to conquer all the worlds, I granted him invincibility;
then I bestowed it upon that wicked-souled Rākṣasa.
O fair-faced one, he is unslayable by gods, dānavas, and yakṣas;
this rākṣasa is of great prowess and is arrogant because of the granting of a boon.
He oppressed the three worlds—the gods, the dānavas, and human beings. Being tormented by him, the gods, led by Brahmā, [sought refuge].
Afflicted by fear, they sought refuge in the Lord, the Consort of Kamalā;
then, perceiving their agony, the Eternal One granted them freedom from fear.
The Blessed Lord spoke to all the gods, headed by Brahmā and Rudra:
"I shall take birth in the lineage of King Daśaratha, the descendant of Raghu."
I shall slay the evil-minded Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen;
assuming a human form, I will destroy this thorn in the side of the gods.
O lords of the quarters, even though you have attained the state of monkeys,
O best of Gandharvas and Apsarases, grant me your assistance.
Rudra said:
Having been addressed thus by Viṣṇu, the god of gods, all those deities assumed the form of monkeys and were born upon the surface of the earth.
This earth, girt by the oceans, was bestowed upon the great-souled Raghus of old by Bhārgava and previously granted by the great sages.
The son of Vaivasvata Manu, a king of great strength and the best among those who know all dharmas, was renowned as Ikṣvāku. (33)
Following him was the mighty King Daśaratha, of great splendor,
the son of King Aja, who was truthful, virtuous, and pure.
By his valor, he protected the entire earth along with its kings, and he established all the best of monarchs in their respective kingdoms. ||35||
Then that king married the daughter of the King of Kosala, a maiden named Kausalya, who was beautiful in every limb.
Then there was the daughter of King Māgadha,
a woman of radiant smiles named Sumitrā, who was his second wife.
Then, the third daughter of King Kekaya likewise became his wife, the lotus-petal-eyed one known by the name Kaikeyī. (38)
Endowed with righteousness, that descendant of Kakutstha took delight with those three wives of the king of the Śakas while protecting the earth. ||39||
The city named Ayodhyā is situated on the bank of the Sarayū;
it is completely filled with all kinds of jewels and abounds in wealth and grain. (40)
Adorned with walls and gate-towers, and filled with golden ramparts,
it was like the city of Mahendra, with its excellent elephants and horses.
In that city, the righteous-souled king dwelt together with the best of sages,
and with his high-souled priest, the brahmin Vasiṣṭha.
He caused the entire kingdom to be governed with all thorns removed,
because in her the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, would be born.
Therefore, O auspicious lady, that city was celebrated as Ayodhyā because of its merit;
indeed, it became the supreme abode for that very name.
Wherever the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu has set, that alone is the supreme state;
there, liberation occurs instantly, which completely destroys all karma.
O lady of auspicious countenance, when Mahāviṣṇu was born there, all the men attained great joy; and that king, having protected the entire earth, [departed]. (46)
Desiring a son, he indeed worshipped Hari, the infallible Acyuta, with a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
thus was the Lord of Śrī, King Hari, who pervades all, fully honored by him. (47)
At that Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, Keśava, the bestower of boons, spoke; then Hari appeared in the fire in the form of the sacrifice. 48.
Resembling pure Jāmbūnada gold, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, wearing white garments, glorious, and adorned with all ornaments. ||49||
Adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, and a forest garland; with large eyes like lotus petals, he has four arms and is the ocean of noble majesty.
Lord Śiva appeared together with Śrī seated upon his left side;
affectionate toward his devotees, he said to the king, "I am the giver of boons."
Seeing that Lord of All the Worlds, the king, overwhelmed with joy, bowed together with his wife with a delighted inner soul. (52)
With palms joined in reverence and bowing down, he spoke to Janārdana, the God of gods, with a voice faltering with joy: "Accept the state of being my son."
Then the blessed Lord Acyuta, being pleased, spoke to the king.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of kings, I shall indeed be born for the welfare of the world of the gods."
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the Rākṣasas, for granting liberation to the worlds, and for the establishment of Dharma. ||55||
Mahādeva said:
Having spoken thus, Hari gave to the king the divine, bright milk-rice (pāyasa) cooked in a golden vessel,
which rested in the hand of Lakṣmī.
Viṣṇu said:
"O King of excellent vows, give this Vaiṣāsa to your wives;
from them your sons shall be born as my elephants. (57)
Mahādeva said:
Having spoken thus, Janārdana, being praised by all the sages,
revealed his own self-bliss and then vanished right there.
Having seen both his elder and younger wives there, the king,
being composed, divided the divine milk-rice and gave it to them.
In the meantime, his middle wife Sumitrā,
beautiful-eyed and desiring a son, approached him.
Seeing her there, Kausalyā and the slender-waisted Kaikeyī each gave him half of their own porridge of milk-rice.
Having consumed that divine milk-rice porridge, all those slender-waisted queens,
now possessing full-grown embryos, shone with radiant splendor.
Then, O Lord of Gods, Hari Janārdana, clothed in yellow garments and holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, appeared to them in their dreams.
At this delightful time, O lady of pure smiles, in the month of Madhu, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight, under the pure constellation presided over by Aditi; (64)
At the hour of midday, when all the planets were auspiciously aligned with the ascendant,
Kausalyā gave birth to Hari, the Lord of the World.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with ten million heads resembling [the peaks of] Mount Meru, with large eyes like lotus petals, and adorned with all ornaments. ||66||
His chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; he was adorned with all ornaments and shone with two earrings resembling the rising sun.
Resembling many suns, enveloped in great splendor,
it is the beautiful body of the Supreme Lord, like a lamp produced from another lamp.
The Lord of all worlds, the eternal object of meditation for yogis, the infinite Supreme Lord who is the meaning of all the Upaniṣads. (69)
The cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, free from affliction, the refuge of all beings, the all-pervading one who consists of all beings. (70)
When the Lord of the World had arisen, the celestial drums resounded in the sky, and the best of gods rained down showers of flowers. (71)
From the very mouth of Prajāpati, the gods, standing in their celestial chariots in the firmament, filled with joy and overwhelmed with emotion, praised him together with the sages. (72)
The lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced;
auspicious and pure breezes blew, and the sun became brilliantly radiant.
The fires blazed up, and the ten directions became peaceful and stainless;
then the king, seeing his eternal son, was filled with joy.
Then the family priest Vasiṣṭha performed the birth-rite for him;
at that time, the venerable Vasiṣṭha gave him the name Ramya.
This great Lord is the beloved of Śrī, whose abode is the lotus;
therefore, O Rāma, His ancient name is established as Śrīrāma.
Among the thousand names, this one is equal to the name of Śrīśa; it grants liberation to men.
Because he was born from the mouth of Viṣṇu, he is called "Viṣṇu. (77)
Having thus spoken his name, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, having led him around, paid homage, and praised him with hymns of praise; ||78||
Having recited the thousand names of the Great-Souled One for the sake of auspiciousness,
he of great splendor departed from that most meritorious house.
Then the king joyfully gave much wealth to the foremost of the Brahmins;
he also performed the gift of ten thousand cows according to the sacred law.
The best of the Raghu dynasty gave away a hundred thousand villages,
along with garments, divine ornaments, and incalculable wealth.
For the pleasure of Viṣṇu, he gratified the Brahmins there;
and Kausalyā, having seen her lotus-eyed son Rāma, [was filled with joy].
O lady of excellent countenance, his hand bears a full-blown lotus, and he holds a lotus in his lotus-like hand; [I bow] to his glorious lotus feet. 83.
Having seen [him] marked on his chest with the signs of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, banner, garments, and so forth, as well as the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha gem, and a forest garland; 84.
Within her, the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—resided;
within her smiling face were the fourteen worlds, O large-eyed one. (85)
O woman of excellent complexion, from the breath of that great-souled one came the Vedas along with the Itihāsas; and upon his hips were the continents, the oceans, and the mountains. 86.
In his navel were Brahmā and Śiva; in his ears, the auspicious directions;
in his eyes, fire and the sun; and in his nose, the wind of great speed.
Having perceived the meaning of all the Upaniṣads and their entire manifestations,
she bowed down again and again with palms joined in reverence;
her eyes filled with tears of joy, she spoke these words.
Kauśalyā said: "O Lord of the gods of gods, O Master, I am blessed to have obtained you as my son.
Be gracious, O Lord of the world, and show me the affection due to a son. (89)
Īśvara said:
Thus addressed, Hari, the omnipresent Hṛṣīkeśa, assuming the illusory state of a human, wept aloud out of his childhood nature. 90.
Then Queen Pramuditā, skilled and endowed with auspicious marks,
the slender-waisted one, embraced her son with joy and gave him her breast-milk.
The eternal Lord, the husband of Umā and the great sovereign, drank her breast milk from childhood and dwelt upon his mother’s lap.
In that auspicious and delightful region, which grants all desires to men, the delighted citizens and the people of the countryside held a festival. (93)
Impelled by the people, Kaikeyī gave birth to Bharata,
and Sumitrā gave birth to Lakṣmaṇa, who was endowed with auspicious marks.
And the highly fortunate Śatrughna, the scorcher of the enemies of the gods;
and Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, who was born from the portion of Ananta. 95.
Śatrughna, of immeasurable prowess, begot Sudarśanā;
they all grew up there in the lineage of Vaivasvata Manu.
Those sons were duly consecrated by the highly powerful Vasiṣṭha;
all those kings had studied the Vedas and were likewise learned in the sacred scriptures.
They were experts in the true meaning of all treatises, firmly established in the practice of archery, supremely noble, and the increasers of joy for the worlds. ||98||
There, the two kings Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa became a pair;
likewise, Bharata and Śatrughna became a pair for those two. 99.
Then, in the residence of her father, the goddess Lakṣmī, the sovereign of the world,
appeared at an auspicious field where the plow had turned the soil, under the favorable gaze of the lord of the plow (Balarāma).
Her lotus-like hands hold red lotuses as radiant as ten million rising suns;
she is endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
Holding a garland of unfading lotuses against her beautiful breast,
that lovely woman appeared as if she had been born from the face of Sītā in her childhood state.
Having seen that auspicious maiden who was composed of the Vedas, King Janaka,
the lord of Mithilā, took her up and nurtured her as his own child.
In the beautiful palace of Janaka, the beloved of the Lord of all worlds, the Goddess of the gods grew up for the sake of protecting all the worlds. 104.
Not far from that place, on the auspicious bank of the Bhāgīrathī at the highly meritorious Siddhāśrama, there was the world-renowned Kauśika. ||105||
There, the great sage began to perform that preeminent sacrifice; now, as this sacrifice of the twice-born was proceeding—
The night-stalkers became destroyers of Rāvaṇa’s resolve;
then Kauśika, having reflected, [saw] Hari, born from the lineage of Raghu.
Desiring to bring [him] back out of a wish for the welfare of the worlds, that righteous-souled one went to the beautiful city of Ayodhyā, which was protected by the descendant of Raghu. (108)
The best of sages beheld Daśaratha, the best of kings;
and the king, seeing Kauśika, rose from his seat and joined his palms in reverence.
Accompanied by his sons, the one of great splendor bowed down to the best of sages;
saying "I am blessed," he spoke with joy to the delight of the Raghus.
Having seated him upon the supreme throne and honored him according to the prescribed rite, she circumambulated him, paid her respects, and said to him, "What shall I do? (111)
Then, with a joyful heart, the great ascetic Viśvāmitra spoke.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O King, give me this descendant of Raghu for the protection of my sacrifice."
"May there be success for the immeasurable Raghava in the presence of the Lord;
therefore, O Adorned One, you ought to grant Rama for the sake of protection. (113)
Ishvara said:
Having heard those words of the best of sages, the foremost among all knowers, he gave Raghava along with Lakshmana to that excellent sage. 114.
Having taken Rāghava with him there, Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic and best of the twice-born, departed for his own hermitage, well-pleased. 115.
Then, as the best of sages departed, the gods were overjoyed;
they rained down showers of flowers and praised him of great majesty.
Then the mighty Vainateya, his soul gladdened, arrived;
having become invisible to all beings, he reached the best of the Raghus.
Having given them two divine bows, two quivers with inexhaustible arrows,
and various divine missiles and weapons, the twice-born departed.
While the heroes Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were traveling through the forest with the high-souled Kauśika,
a demoness of terrifying appearance was encountered.
Then those two great heroes slew Tāḍakā, the wife of the demon Sumdāsa, with arrows discharged from their divine bows.
Then, having been slain by Rāghava, that Rākṣasī of terrible appearance cast off her horrific body and assumed a divine form.
With her body blazing with light and adorned with all ornaments,
she departed for the world of Viṣṇu after bowing down to the two best of the Raghus.
Having slain her, the glorious Rāghava, endowed with great majesty, entered the auspicious hermitage of Kauśika together with the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the delighted sages, having gone out to meet the best of the Raghus and having seated him, worshipped that Supreme Soul with offerings of water for the feet and other honors.
Having undergone the initiatory rites, Kauśika, that best of sages, together with the other sages, began that unsurpassed sacrifice according to the prescribed ritual. (125)
During this great sacrifice, a Rākṣasa named Mārīca,
together with his brother Subāhu, stood there intent on creating obstacles.
Seeing those fierce throngs of Rākṣasas, Rāghava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
struck Subāhu, the lord of the Rākṣasas, with a single arrow.
With the Pavana weapon, he cast the great Rākṣasa Mārīca into the ocean, just as the wind blows a withered leaf away.
Having seen the great prowess of Śarāma, that best of Rākṣasas laid down his weapons and departed for a great hermitage to perform austerities.
When the great sacrifice was completed, the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra,
with a joyful heart, honored Rāghava there.
He embraced the Great-Souled Hari, who wears the side-locks of a youth, who is dark as the petals of a blue lotus, and whose eyes are as broad as lotus leaves. (131)
Then, having smelled his head, that best of men offered praise;
at that very moment, the king who was the sovereign of Mithilā arrived.
We have begun to perform the Vājapeya sacrifice with the most excellent sages;
all [the kings], led by Viśvāmitra, set out to witness it. ||133||
The sages, whose minds were virtuous, accompanied by Aghuśārdūla,
followed the lotus feet of that high-souled Rāma as he was departing.
That ground became a cursed land, having been stepped upon by that great stone;
for it too had previously been cursed by her husband, the twice-born Gautama.
Ahalyā became auspicious through the touch of the feet of Raghunātha;
then, O best of sages, having reached the city of Mithilā— (136)
Accompanied by the two descendants of Raghu, they became joyful in heart;
seeing those illustrious ones arrived, the king of great power [was filled with joy]. (137)
Then the King of Mithilā, having gone out to meet him and bowed down,
worshipped Rāma, whose eyes were as broad as lotuses and who possessed the luster of the petals of a blue water-lily.
Wearing yellow garments, smooth and radiant with delicate limbs, he surpassed the pride of ten million Cupids with his supreme beauty. 139.
He who is Hari, the body of the Supreme Lord, endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with all ornaments, resides within the lotus of one's own heart. 140.
Seeing that Lord of the Raghus, who was like a lamp lit from another lamp through his supreme virtues such as excellent character, Janaka’s heart was filled with joy.
The king regarded the son of Daśaratha as the Supreme Lord himself;
saying "I am blessed," he paid homage to the descendant of Kakutstha.
The lord of men, the sovereign, reflected in his mind that he should grant his daughter to Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, out of favor toward him. 143.
Having learned that his son was a descendant of Raghu, the best of kings honored him there according to dharma with garments and auspicious ornaments.
I honored the sages with offerings such as the madhuparka;
thereafter, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the lotus-eyed Rāma—
Having broken that divine bow of Śiva, he won the daughter of Janaka;
then, he was fully gratified by her great bride-price of valor.
The Lord of Mithilā joyfully gave her to him,
just as in former times the great ocean gave its splendor to Keśava.
The righteous lord of Mithilā dispatched a messenger to Rāghava;
accompanied by his two sons, he then entered Mithilā.
Accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and others who were well-pleased, that lord of the earth, the best of charioteers, resided in the delightful city of Janaka.
At that very time, during an auspicious moment, the King, honored by the people of Mithilā, performed the marriage of Rāma with the daughter of the Earth.
Then, Lakṣmaṇa took as his wife Ūrmilā, the daughter of Janaka born from Janaka’s younger brother,
who possessed auspicious radiance.
The king then performed the marriage of Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti— both endowed with every auspicious mark— to that son of Sumitrā, Bharata.
Having completed the wedding rites there, the powerful and illustrious King Daśaratha set out for Ayodhyā, surrounded by the citizens and the people of the countryside.
Having accepted the wedding gifts and being honored by the King of Mithilā,
he departed with his son, his daughter-in-law, his horses, his elephants, and his army and followers.
Then the son of Jamadagni, possessed of great heroism and majesty, took up his axe and bow like an enraged lion. (155)
Desirous of fighting, the destroyer of kings rushed toward the descendant of Kakutstha;
having reached and beheld Rāghava, Bhārgava spoke these words.
Paraśurāma said: O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, listen to my words;
having slain numerous kings of great prowess throughout many ages. (157)
"Having given the earth to the Brahmins, I went away to perform austerities;
but having heard of your heroism and strength, I have come here to fight with you. (158)
The Ikṣvākus, born of my maternal grandfather’s lineage, are not to be slain by me; yet, having heard of their valor and the strength of the Kṣatriyas, it is impossible for me to endure them. (159)
O King, O best of the Raghus, since even that formidable and unassailable Raudra bow was shattered by you,
let the battle of liberality be granted instead.
But this bow belongs to Viṣṇu; O subduer of enemies, string it with your own prowess, for it was indeed conquered by you alone.
Or else, cast down your weapons before me, who am stronger;
seek refuge with the descendant of Kakutstha, for you are timid at heart.
The Lord said:
Thus addressed by the descendant of Bhṛgu,
the majestic Rāma took up that bow as well as its Vaiṣṇava power.
Then that powerful son of Jamadagni, though not yet separated from his power,
became devoid of heroism and lost his luster, like a twice-born man who has failed in his religious duties.
Seeing Bhārgava’s splendor destroyed, the best of kings praised Kākutstha again and again, saying, "Excellent, excellent! (165)
The descendant of Kakutstha, having taken up that great bow and strung it with ease,
fixed an arrow upon it and spoke to the astonished Bhārgava.
Rāma said:
"O twice-born one, what is to be done by you with this preeminent arrow?
Whether it be for cutting asunder this world, or the netherworld, or heaven, my ascetic power is your vehicle. (167)
The Lord said: Having seen Bāṇa, who resembled Aghora, and having recognized him as the Supreme Self (Paramātman), the descendant of Bhṛgu was delighted and spoke to Rāma. ||168||
Paraśurāma said:

"O Rāma, O Rāma, O mighty-armed one! Though I did not know you as the eternal one before, I know you this very day, O descendant of Kakutstha, by virtue of your prowess, qualities, and other attributes. (169)
You are the primordial person, the manifest Supreme Brahman, the supreme and imperishable;
you are Ananta, Mahāviṣṇu, Vāsudeva, higher than the highest. (170)
You are Nārāyaṇa, you are the Lord of Śrī, you are the Sovereign; you consist of the three Vedas.
You are Time, you are the entire universe, and you alone are that which is called the letter 'A'. (171)
You alone are the Supreme Lord, the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer;
you are inconceivable, you are the form of the Great Being, and you are the great Manu.
Possessing the four, six, and five qualities, you alone are the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama);
you are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, you are the syllable Om, and you are composed of the three Vedas.
You are the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest; you bear the qualities yet are beyond them as the Supreme.
I am unable to praise You, who are beyond even the reach of the Vedas.
O Lord, whatever rashness I have committed by desiring to fight you, that must be forgiven by you out of pure compassion for one who has no protector. (175)
Having conquered all kings by his own power and having bestowed the earth upon the twice-born, he attains ultimate peace solely through the grace of you, O Lord. (176)
The Lord said:
Having spoken thus to the descendant of Kakutstha, the son of Jamadagni, who was possessed of great ascetic power,
circumambulated and paid homage to Rāghava, the protector of the world.
Then Rāghava, possessed of great splendor, informed that great sage of the heaven won by the performance of a hundred sacrifices, and he comforted that great muni.
He worshipped him according to the prescribed rites with water for the feet, the guest-offering, water for sipping, and so forth;
thus honored there by him, the son of Jamadagni, a man of great asceticism, [remained].
Then King Daśaratha, accompanied by his sons and his wife, went to the delightful hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa to perform austerities. 180.
At an auspicious moment, the mighty Rāghava, along with Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata, entered his own city. ||181||
Having approached their respective wives, they rejoiced with delighted minds;
there, O Raghava, Rama dwelt for twelve years together with Sita.
The righteous-souled Nārāyaṇa delighted him with his splendor;
then, at that very time, King Daśaratha [summoned] his son.
Out of affection, the lord of the earth desired to invest his eldest son with the kingdom;
however, his beloved wife Kaikeyī, who had previously received boons from him, [intervened]. (184)
They entreated the best of kings for Bharata’s consecration, saying, "We shall live in exile for fourteen years. (185)
Then, his mind struck by grief due to those false words, the king banished Rāma, his beloved son, from the kingdom.
Although Rāghava was capable, he righteously renounced the kingdom for the sake of slaying the Ten-necked one, on account of his father’s command.
The descendant of Kakutstha went to the forest with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā,
while the king, afflicted by the separation from his son and overwhelmed by grief, was on the verge of death.
Though being urged by his ministers to that kingdom, the virtuous-souled Bharata did not desire the sovereignty, keeping his brotherly affection in view. (189)
Then, having come to the forest, he entreated his brother, the descendant of Kakutstha; however, Rāma, the subduer of enemies, did not desire the kingdom because of his father’s command.
Out of devotion, he gave his own sandals to him, and Bharata likewise accepted them; having obtained the kingdom through Rāma's sandals, O auspicious lady, he [ruled].
Worshipping daily with perfumes and flowers, that best of kings, the son of Kaikeyī, remained standing upon his knees, engaged in the practice of austerity. (192)
Until the arrival of that high-souled descendant of Raghu,
all the city-dwellers remained devoted to their religious observances.
On the auspicious Citrakūṭa mountain, in the beautiful hermitage of Bharadvāja, Rāghava delighted Vaidehī in the pure waters of the Mandākinī.
Once, while the high-minded Rāma was sleeping on the lap of the daughter of the Kekayas, a crow approached and began to walk upon him. 195.
Having seen Jānakī there, who was afflicted by the arrows of pride,
he tore at her full and elevated breasts with his sharp claws.
Seeing that crow, Rāma, the upholder of the earth, seized Kuśa with his hand,
joined it with the Brahmā weapon, and hurled it.
Seeing that blade of ghōrasaṃkāśa grass, its form composed of flames, the crow fled, uttering a piteous cry. ||198||
The extremely terrible weapon of Rāma pursued that crow;
the crow, tormented by fear, wandered through the three worlds. (199)
Wherever that crow, seeking refuge, went,
there that weapon entered him, bringing fear.
Afflicted by weapons and seeking refuge, the crow quickly went to Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Varuṇa. (201)
Seeing that crow, all the gods, Dānavas, and others led by Rudra said,
"O wise ones, we are not able to protect ourselves.
Then the Blessed One, Brahmā, the lord of the three worlds, spoke.
Brahmā said:
O best among the eaters of offerings, go for refuge to him alone;
he is the glorious protector of all, a treasure-house of compassion. (203)
The Lord of all beings, endowed with virtues such as good character, protects those who have come for refuge and those who are dear to him, being a treasury of patience. (204)
O twice-born one, even though his livelihood is protected by his father, mother, friends, and kin, a man should go for refuge to the Lord of Gods, in whom all find shelter. 205.
Mahādeva said:
Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, the consumer of oblations (Agni),
he approached the descendant of Raghu and suddenly fell prostrate upon the ground, overcome with fear.
Seeing the crow in a life-threatening danger, Sītā then spoke with humility to her lord, the All-pervading One, saying, "Save me! Save me! (207)
Then Jānakī placed the head of the crow, which had fallen before her onto the ground, at his feet.
Then, the ocean of the nectar of compassion, possessing infinite virtues and moved by pity, rescued the crow by lifting it up with his trunk. (209)
Rāma, the ocean of compassion, said to that crow, "Do not fear;
I shall grant you freedom from fear. Go, go as you please. (210)
Having bowed down repeatedly to Rāghava and to Sītā as well, he quickly departed for the heavenly realm,
protected by Rāghava.
Then Rāma, together with Vaidehī and the wise Lakṣmaṇa,
dwelt on Mount Citrakūṭa while being praised by the great seers.
Being thus honored by Bharadvāja, Rāghava,
the best of the Raghus, proceeded to the very extensive hermitage of Atri.
Seeing the best of the Raghus arrived, that most excellent of sages,
whose soul was devoted to dharma, went out to meet him with his wife, filled with joy.
Having seated him together with Sītā upon a most excellent and beautiful seat, he offered water for the guest-offering, water for washing the feet, water for sipping, and various garments. (215)
With affection, she gave him the madhuparka offering, as well as ornaments and ointments;
his wife Anasūyā, however, gave him unsurpassed divine garments. (216)
He affectionately presented Sītā with radiant ornaments and caused Rāghava to be feasted with divine foods, drinks, and delicacies.
Honored there by him with supreme devotion, the king,
together with Lakṣmaṇa, dwelt there for a day, his heart filled with joy.
At dawn, Rāma, having risen, circumambulated and prostrated before the great sage, and then prepared to depart.
Then, having been granted permission by him, the lotus-eyed Rāma set out for the Daṇḍaka forest,
which was densely populated by great sages.
Having slain there the most terrifying and formidable rākṣasa named Virādha, he then went to Śarabhaṅga and entered his auspicious hermitage.
Then, upon seeing Kākutstha, his impurities were instantly destroyed;
he departed for the world of Brahmā, which was filled with Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Rāma proceeded in due order to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa, and then to that of Agastya, and likewise to that of Agastya’s brother; he was thus honored by them all.
Having cooked the medicinal paste on the auspicious bank of the Godāvarī,
he remained there for a very long time in supreme happiness.
Having gone there, those best of sages, practitioners of the dharma of asceticism,
worshipped Rāma, the lotus-eyed Lord of the Self.
They reported that fear instigated by the hosts of Rākṣasas;
Kākutstha, having consoled them, gave them the gift of safety.
Honored by him with the *tetu* [offering], they returned to their own hermitages;
for thirteen years after he had passed away, they remained there in a state of bliss.
On the delightful bank of the Godāvarī, at the charming Pañcavaṭī,
after some time had passed, there appeared a Rākṣasī of terrifying form.
There, Rāvaṇa’s sister Durāsadā entered;
she beheld that best of the Raghus, who was like a peak of Mount Kailāsa and possessed of great pride.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes as broad as lotus leaves,
tall, mighty-armed, with a neck like a conch shell and a large jaw.
His lotus-like face was smiling and resembled the full moon, framed by glossy,
curly locks of hair that were dark like a swarm of bees.
With eyes like red lotuses, his palm marked by a lotus, partless like the full moon, and resplendent with rows of nails. ||232||
Resembling smooth and tender dūrvā grass, a beautiful treasure-house of delicacy, clad in yellow silk garments and adorned with all ornaments. ||233||
Seeing that Rāma, who possessed the age of a youth and a form that deludes the world, which Rākṣasī, afflicted by the arrows of pride, [approached]? 234.
Then, approaching the lotus-eyed Rāma, the rākṣasī said:
"Who are you that dwell here in the Daṇḍaka forest in the guise of an ascetic? (235)
"Why have you come to this place of the Rākṣasas, which is so difficult to approach?
Speak quickly according to the truth; you ought not to speak a falsehood. (236)
Maheśvara said: Thus addressed, Rāma, together with Sītā, laughed and spoke these words. Rāma said:
I am the son of King Daśaratha, known by the name Rāma; and this sinless younger brother of mine, armed with a bow, is named Lakṣmaṇa.
This is my wife Sītā, the beloved daughter of Janaka;
by the command of my father’s word, I have come here to the forest.
"We wander through the great forest out of a desire for the welfare of the sages;
O beautiful one, for what purpose have you come to my hermitage? (239)
"Who are you? In whose family were you born? Speak everything truthfully.
Maheśvara said:
Having been addressed thus by the hunter, she, though distressed, spoke these words without hesitation.
The Rākṣasī said: "O King, I am the daughter of Viśravas and the sister of Rāvaṇa; by name I am Śūrpaṇakhā, renowned throughout the three worlds. (241)
"O Lord, this Daṇḍaka forest was given to me by my brother;
devouring multitudes of sages, I roam about in this great forest. (242)
But having seen you, O best of sages, by whom shall I be afflicted with the arrows of pride?
Therefore, out of desire for you, I have come here together with you, entirely without fear. (243)
"O tiger among kings, you ought to become her master;
O protector of the earth, I desire to devour this Sītā who dwells here. (244)
"In the forests and on the foremost mountains, [I shall dwell] with you and Rāma.
Maheśvara said:
Having spoken thus, he saw the rākṣasī preparing to devour Sītā.
Śrī Rāma, raising his sword, cut off [her] nose and ears.
Weeping and terrified, the ogress with her deformed face quickly entered Khara’s abode and reported Rāma’s actions to him.
Surrounded by thousands of Rākṣasas and accompanied by Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras,
that slayer of enemies arrived to fight most fiercely with the descendant of Raghu.
There in the terrible forest, Rāma effortlessly struck down those massive-bodied rākṣasas with arrows resembling the Destroyer at the end of time.
With arrows resembling venomous serpents, he struck down Khara, Triśiras, and the exceedingly powerful Dūṣaṇa in battle.
Having slain all the rākṣasas dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
he was honored by hosts of gods and praised by the great seers.
He dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa;
and hearing of the slaughter of the Rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa was overwhelmed with rage.
Having been driven from Janasthāna by the evil-minded Mārīca,
the ten-necked Rāvaṇa arrived at Pañcavaṭī together with his rākṣasas.
By means of a deer-form created through illusion by the Rākṣasa Mārīca,
the two sons of Daśaratha were lured far away from the hermitage.
Just as he was about to carry off Sītā, the wife of Rāma, who was his own slayer due to his own destruction,
the powerful Jaṭāyu, king of the vultures, saw her being carried away.
Out of friendship for Rāma, that subduer of enemies fought there with the Rākṣasa;
having slain him by the strength of his arms, he [confronted] Rāvaṇa.
He entered the city of Laṅkā, which was filled with many Rākṣasas,
having deposited the daughter of Janaka in the midst of the Aśoka grove.
Having brought about his own destruction by Rāma’s arrow, he entered his own home;
meanwhile, Rāma, having slain the Rākṣasa Mārīca who had assumed the form of a deer, [proceeded]. ||258||
Then, having learned that his wife had been abducted by a rākṣasa, the son of Daśaratha entered there once again along with his brother, the son of Sumitrā.
Greatly tormented by abundant grief, the high-minded one lamented aloud;
while searching for Sītā in the forest, he encountered a mighty vulture on the path.
Seeing him fallen upon the surface of the earth with his wings severed from his body and his entire body filled with blood, he was struck with amazement. ||261||
The glorious one asked Rāghava, "By whom and for what purpose are you seeking to kill me?
