Seeing Rāghava, the vulture spoke these words of self-restraint to Dama-dama.
The vulture said:
"Your wife was carried away by the powerful Rāvaṇa;
I have been slain in battle by that chief of the rākṣasas."
Maheśvara said:
Having spoken thus, he suddenly gave up his life in the presence of Rāghava; Rāma then performed his funeral rites according to the Vedic injunctions.
And by the grace of Rāghava, that vulture attained his own eternal state, the supreme station accessible only to yogis. (265)
The best of birds attained liberation through the common form of Hari; then, having gone from there to Mālyavat, he went to the auspicious hermitage of Amataṅga.
Having approached the highly fortunate Śabarī, who practices righteousness, that best of devotees saw Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. (267)
Having gone out to meet him and paid homage, and having seated him upon a cushion of kuśa grass, one should wash his feet and honor him with other fragrant flowers. ||268||
With minds overflowing with joy, she indeed worshipped with devotion,
offering fragrant fruits and sweet roots.
Then, having tasted the fruits, Rāghava, whose vow was firm, granted her supreme liberation. 270.
Then, having gone to Pañcapaṣāra, Rāghava, the slayer of enemies,
slew the Rākṣasa Kabandha of terrible form there.
Having slain him, the one of great heroism burned his body and ascended to heaven;
thereafter, the lotus-eyed Rāma went to the Godāvarī.
He asked Gaṅgā, "Do you know that beloved woman?
Then Gaṅgā, shrouded in darkness, did not answer him.
Then, out of fear, the people became greatly agitated and, placing the great sages at their head, fled to the river whose waters had turned red with anger due to Śaśāda’s transgression.
Having joined their palms in reverence and sought refuge in Rāghava,
all the great sages then spoke to the eternal Rāma.
The sages said:
"The Gaṅgā, born from the lotus-feet of you, the Lord of the Three Worlds, purifies the three worlds;
indeed, you alone, O Lord of the Universe, ought to release us from this curse. (276)
Maheśvara said:
Then the righteous-souled Rāma, who is compassionate toward those seeking refuge, spoke.
Rāma said:
By the mere act of bathing in this Gaṅgā, which destroys all sins, may the Śavarīs, having been joined with auspicious waters, be liberated from my curse. (277)
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Kakutstha, possessed of great strength, made that supreme Śabarī-tīrtha equal to the Gaṅgā and the Gayā with the tip of his bow.
And since his body became a sacred ford for the great devotees of the Lord in its waters, that body will undoubtedly become the world and the heavens. (279)
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Kakutstha went to Mount Ṛṣyamūka;
then he was met on the bank of the Pampā lake by the monkey Hanumān.
Having come together at his word, he met with Sugrīva;
and by Sugrīva's command, having slain Vālin, the lord of monkeys.
Rāma consecrated Sugrīva himself in that kingdom;
he, however, dispatched him forth, desiring to see the daughter of Janaka.
The lord of monkeys, having encouraged the heroic monkeys headed by Hanumān, [spoke];
meanwhile, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, had crossed the ocean.
Entering the city of Laṅkā, he beheld Sītā, firm in her vows,
emaciated by fasting, miserable, and utterly devoted to grief.
"Having presented her with the token of recognition, let it be reported whether she is smeared with poison, whether she is singing, and whether she is wearing soiled garments. (285)
There, the monkey himself uprooted the archway, having struck down the son of Rāvaṇa as well as the seven sons of the ministers.
Having consoled Vaidehī, he then addressed the forest guards,
the servants, and the five leaders of the vanguard of the army.
O Lord, having been captured at will by the son of Rāvaṇa,
he beheld the lord of the Rākṣasas and likewise conversed with him.
The monkey burnt the city of Laṅkā with the fire from his own tail;
having taken the token of recognition given by her, he returned once more.
Approaching the lotus-eyed Rāma, that lord of monkeys, possessed of great splendor, reported the truth: "Sītā has been seen. (290)
Accompanied by Sugrīva and surrounded by many monkeys,
Rāma went to the shore of the great ocean and encamped his army there.
The younger brother of Rāvaṇa was known as Vibhīṣaṇa;
he was righteous, true to his word, and the most excellent among the great devotees of the Lord. ||292||
Having learned that Rāma had arrived, he abandoned his elder brother,
the kingdom, his sons, and his wife, and sought refuge with the descendant of Raghu.
Having accepted that [offering] at the word of Māruti, the Lord granted him safety and consecrated that gentle one in the kingdom of the Rākṣasas. ||294||
Then Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, desiring to cross the ocean, approached it; and beholding its waters to be perfectly clear, the mighty Rāma [was filled with joy]. (295)
Taking up his Śārṅga bow, he dried up the ocean with floods of arrows;
then the Lord of Rivers [the Ocean] addressed the descendant of Kakutstha, that treasury of compassion.
Having sought refuge with the Lord, the Ocean worshipped Him;
then Rāghava refilled the ocean once more with the Varuṇa weapon.
At the command of the Ocean, Nala constructed a bridge across the sea, the abode of makaras,
using mountains brought by the monkeys.
Then, having gone to the city of Laṅkā and stationed his great army,
he properly arranged the battlefield for the monkeys and the rākṣasas.
Then the powerful Rākṣasa, the ten-faced son of Śakrajit,
bound both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with serpent-nooses.
Vainateya arrived and discharged those weapons;
all the Rākṣasas were slain by the mighty monkeys.
In battle, Rāma slew the heroic and mighty Kumbhakarṇa, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa,
with arrows resembling tongues of fire.
Enraged, Indrajit struck down the monkeys with the Brahmāstra;
however, Hanumān brought back a mountain containing great medicinal herbs.
From the touch of his [the enemy's] spear, all [his followers] rose up;
then the heroic younger brother of Rāma [Lakṣmaṇa] [attacked] the conqueror of Śakra in battle.
He struck Vṛtra down with his arrows, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt [Indra] did;
then the descendant of Pulastya went forth to fight Rāma in battle.
Then, accompanied by his fourfold forces and his ministers, the exceedingly powerful one engaged in battle with the monkeys and the rākṣasas. (306)
And likewise, the lord of the rākṣasas struck down both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, along with the son of Sumitrā, using his spear. 307.
Then the highly effulgent Rāghava, the destroyer of rākṣasas, being enraged,
struck down the heroic rākṣasas with arrows resembling the Destroyer at the end of time.
With thousands of blazing arrows that were like the staff of Death,
the descendant of Kakutstha completely covered the ten-necked Rākṣasa as he moved about.
With all his limbs pierced by the weapons of Rāghava,
that night-stalker fled in fear from Laṅkā toward the forest.
Seeing the world as consisting of suffering, he entered his home out of world-weariness;
then Hanumān brought the great mountain containing the potent medicinal herbs.
By that means, Rāmānuja then quickly attained perfect knowledge;
thereafter, Daśagrīva began the fire sacrifice for the sake of destroying his enemies.
That malevolent spell of the enemy, which had been destroyed by the leaders of the monkeys, was cast anew;
then the descendant of Pulastya set out once more for battle with Rāma.
Then, having ascended Indra’s divine chariot yoked with bay horses, he was joined by many rākṣasas.
The wise one dispatched a messenger drawn by horses of the Rāghava and monkey breeds;
then the best of the Raghus ascended the chariot brought by Mātali.
While being praised by the hosts of gods, he fought with that Rākṣasa;
then a great and terrible battle took place between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
All the gods, stationed in their celestial chariots, beheld there that most terrifying age-long battle with weapons and missiles, which lasted for seven days and nights.
The best of sages severed the heads of the ten-necked one,
which had repeatedly reappeared due to a boon granted by Kapardin.
Rāghava swiftly discharged the Brahma-weapon, most terrible for the destruction of that evil-minded one, possessing a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Then that weapon, released by Rāghava, having pierced the chest of Rāvaṇa,
split the earth and entered the depths of the netherworld.
Being worshipped by the serpents, it went to the hand of Rāghava;
that great Daitya, his life-breath departed, fell down and died.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with joy, rained down showers of flowers upon the Great-Souled One, the Teacher of the World. (322)
The lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsarases danced;
likewise, pure breezes blew and the sun became radiant.
Having consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa as the foremost of the Rākṣasas in Laṅkā, the sages, Siddhas, gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras offered their praise.
The best of the Raghu dynasty considered himself as one who had accomplished his purpose;
there, after consecrating Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāma spoke these words: 325.
Rāma said:
"As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth remains,
and as long as my story persists in the world, so long shall the kingdom remain with Vibhīṣaṇa."
Having gone to my divine, eternal abode, which is accessible only to yogis,
may you, endowed with great strength, attain it together with your sons, grandsons, and your retinue.
The Lord said: Having thus granted him that boon, the one of great strength, Rākṣasa, reached Maithilī there in the midst of a gathering of people. 328.
Rāghava spoke many censurable words to Sītā;
thus reproached by him, that virtuous woman entered the great fire.
Then all the hosts of gods, led by Śiva and Brahmā,
seeing the Mother entering the fire in her state of terror,
approached the best of the Raghus and, with palms joined in reverence, all spoke.
The gods said:
O Rāma, Rāma, you of mighty arms and exceeding valor, listen!
Sītā is exceedingly pure, virtuous, and never departs from the path of righteousness. (331)
Like the radiance of the sun that cannot be cast aside in vain, she has appeared upon the surface of the earth for the sake of the welfare of the world. 332.
She is the mother of the entire world and the refuge of the whole universe;
Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa were her servants, devoted to her from of old.
Due to the curse of Sanaka and the others, those two were born upon the surface of the earth;
for the sake of their liberation, Vaidehī was taken [as a wife] by them in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Both of those foremost of Rākṣasas, having met their death at your hands,
have been liberated and have gone to heaven along with their sons, grandsons, and followers.
You are Viṣṇu; you are the supreme Brahman, the eternal object of meditation for yogis;
you alone are the beginningless, endless, and imperishable one among all the gods.
You are indeed the glorious Nārāyaṇa, and Sītā is the eternal Lakṣmī;
she is the mother of all the worlds, and you, O Supreme Lord, are the father. 337.
This mother of the world is indeed eternal, never departing from you;
for as you are omnipresent, O best of the Raghus, so too is she. (338)
Therefore, O gentle descendant of Kakutstha, accept Sita— pure in conduct, virtuous, and firm in her vows— without delay, as one would take [the nectar] from the ocean of milk.
Ishvara said:
In that very interval, the witness of the world, together with Agni,
took Sita and presented her to Rama in the presence of the gods.
Then the Fire-god, residing within his entire body, spoke there to the descendant of Kakutstha.
Vahni said:
"O Lord, this Sītā is of pure conduct and free from blemish; accept her without delay, O Rāma. What we have told you is the truth, the absolute truth. (341)
Ishvara said: Then, having accepted Sita according to the word of Agni, Rama, the scion of Raghu,
became joyful while being honored by the foremost of the gods.
Although these best of monkeys were slain in battle by the rākṣasas,
they quickly rose up alive due to the boon of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Then the Lord of the Rākṣasas took from his brother in battle the aerial chariot named Puṣpaka, which resembled the sun and belonged to Kubera.
He presented those garments and ornaments to Rāghava;
thus honored by him, the illustrious and majestic Rāmacandra [departed].
The son of Daśaratha ascended that foremost of celestial chariots together with his wife Vaidehī and his heroic brother Lakṣmaṇa.
Together with hosts of bears and monkeys, the high-souled Sugrīva,
the heroic Vibhīṣaṇa, and the rākṣasas of great strength.
Just as in the Vaikuṇṭha celestial palace by the great-souled ones who are eternally liberated,
so did all the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas ascend.
Being praised by the foremost of the gods, Rāma, whose prowess is truth, set out for Ayodhyā; having reached the hermitage of Bharadvāja, Rāma [proceeded on]. (349)
There, in the presence of Bharata, he dispatched Hanumān;
having gone to the abode of the Niṣādas, he saw Guha, a devotee of Viṣṇu.
The bull among monkeys told him of Rāghava’s arrival;
having gone from there to that region of the forest, he saw the younger brother of Rāghava.
Bharata likewise announced to him the festival of Rāma’s arrival; and having heard that the best of the Raghus had come with the monkey, [he prepared for his reception]. (352)
Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, having returned once more to the descendant of Kakutstha, experienced incomparable joy along with his younger brother and his circle of friends. (353)
Rāghava, together with his younger brother, descended from that foremost of celestial chariots and related everything— the slaying of Rāma’s enemy and his own conduct— to him.
Then the sage honored Bhāradvāja, that treasure-house of asceticism, together with his wife, as well as Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, along with his younger brother.
Having honored him there with cooked foods, fruits, roots, and so forth, as well as garments and ornaments,
he bowed down to that most excellent of sages.
Then, having been permitted, Rāma, surrounded by his friends and accompanied by his followers, ascended the Puṣpaka chariot and departed for the village of Nandigrāma.
Accompanied by his younger brothers, the son of Kaikeyī, together with his ministers, the city leaders,
and the foremost kings with their armies, joyfully went out to meet his elder brother.
Having reached the tiger among the Raghus, who was surrounded by his followers from various regions,
Rāghava, the scorcher of enemies, then descended from the Puṣpaka chariot.
He embraced both Bharata and Śatrughna,
as well as the family priest Vasiṣṭha, his mothers, and his elders and kinsmen.
The one of great splendor prostrated himself before Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
as well as before Vibhīṣaṇa, Sugrīva, Jāmbavanta, and Nala.
There, Bharata, together with his brothers and their followers, embraced Hanumān and Suṣeṇa after first performing an auspicious ceremonial bath.
Wearing divine garlands and excellent garments, and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
he ascended the auspicious, divine chariot driven by Sumantra.
He was being praised by the thirty gods, as well as by Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa,
and also by Bharata, Sugrīva, Śatrughna, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Aṅgada, Suṣeṇa, Jāmbavān the son of the Wind-god, Nīla, Anala, Subhaga, Śarabha, and Gandhamādana. ||365||
And other heroic monkeys, Guha the lord of the Niṣādas, Rākṣasas of great prowess, and mighty lords of kings [were there]. (366)
Then, having properly mounted many auspicious elephants and horses, accompanied by various auspicious musical instruments and abundant hymns of praise, [he set forth]. (367)
Accompanied by bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, as well as the elite soldiers of the Niṣādas,
he of great splendor entered the imperishable city of Sāketa.
Having beheld the royal city on the way and reflecting upon his father, the king himself,
Rāma entered the palace, which had been purified by the movement of the holy feet of Sugrīva, Hanumān, and Vibhīṣaṇa.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Entry of Rāma into Ayodhyā," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Pañca-pañcāśat-sāhasrī Saṃhitā of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||242|| ||cha||
The two hundred and forty-third chapter.
Śaṅkara said:
Now, on that meritorious day, at an auspicious moment endowed with favorable aspects, [he performed the rites].
The people performed auspicious rites for the sake of Maṅgala’s consecration. ||1||
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, Kaśyapa, Mārkaṇḍeya, Maudgalya, Parvata, and likewise Nārada. ||2||
Then those great ṛṣis and sages performed an auspicious consecration for that best of kings there, preceded by recitation and fire-offerings.
Having seated him together with Sītā upon a divine golden throne adorned with various jewels, like Janārdana with Śrī; ||4||
With divine golden jars made of various jewels and auspicious, filled with the holy waters of all sacred fords and combined with auspicious substances. ||5||
The sages of firm vows [performed the rite] with pure water consecrated by mantras, combined with the tips of dūrvā grass, tulasī leaves, flowers, and fragrances.
Chanting the auspicious Vaiṣṇava hymns consisting of the four Vedas,
they performed the auspicious consecration for Kākutstha, the lord of the world.
When that auspicious and excellent moment arrived, celestial drums resounded in the sky,
and showers of flowers fell from all sides.
The descendant of Raghu, together with the Goddess, adorned himself with divine garments, ornaments, celestial perfumes,
ointments, and various kinds of divine flowers.
Adorned by sages who had mastered the Vedas, he shone resplendently;
at that time, Lakṣmaṇa held a divine parasol and a fly-whisk.
On his sides, Bharata and Śatrughna shone like two palm-leaf fans;
the illustrious Vibhīṣaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, presented him with a mirror.
Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, held a full water-pot,
and the highly effulgent Jāmbavān held a captivating garland of flowers.
The son of Vālin gave betel-leaf with camphor to Hari;
Hanumān gave a divine lamp, and Suṣeṇa a beautiful banner.
Surrounding the Great-Souled One, the ministers sat in attendance:
Sṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Saurāṣṭra, and Rāṣṭravardhana. ||14||
Akopadharmapāla and Sumantra are remembered as ministers;
and there were kings, tigers among men, lords of various provinces. (15)
The citizens, the merchants, and the elders waited upon the king,
as did the bears, the lords of the monkeys, the ministers, and the sovereigns of the earth.
Surrounded by Rākṣasas, eminent Brāhmaṇas, and Kimpuruṣas, he was like the Lord of Kamalā merged in the highest heaven among the deities. ||17||
Thus, at that time, the illustrious and excellent king shone forth in Sāketa,
[beholding] Him who was dark as the petal of a blue lotus and whose eyes resembled the petals of a lotus.

He saw the descendant of Kakutstha, whose arms reached his knees, who wore yellow garments, who was dark-complexioned like Hari, broad-chested, and adorned with various ornaments—Vibhīṣaṇa and Sugrīva. (19)
The hosts of gods, stationed in their celestial chariots with minds overflowing with joy, beheld the best of the Raghus seated upon the throne, consecrated by the Goddess. 20.
The hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases praised him with shouts of "Victory!
Then Rāma was consecrated by Vasiṣṭha and the other great sages.
He shone with the goddess Sītā as Nārāyaṇa does with Śrī;
and because he was beyond the mortal state, they were afraid to approach his lotus feet for worship.
Having seen him, Śaṅkara was filled with joy and his soul was thrilled; he approached with great delight, joining his palms in reverence, his voice choked with emotion,
gladdening all the gods, sages, and monkeys.
Mahādeva said:
Salutations to the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the eternal Supreme Self, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is the universal form, the Creator. 24.
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the root of the bulb of uninterrupted bliss;
to him whose divine form is the embodiment of joy for the three worlds. ||25||
Salutations to the one worshipped by Brahmā and Indra, the bestower of fearlessness;
salutations to the one whose nature is Viṣṇu, who possesses all forms—salutations, salutations! (26)

Salutations to the Great Soul, whose nature is free from all limiting adjuncts, who is the self consisting of the three qualities, and who effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world]. 27.
Salutations to you two—you, the Goddess of this ignorance, and its presiding authority—the male and female principles for the sake of the worlds. (28)
Salutations to the mother and father of the world, and to Jananī and Īśvarā; salutations to her whose form is manifold manifestation, and to her whose essential nature is beyond all manifestation.
Salutations to her whose nature is meditation, whose form is the self contemplated by yogis;
salutations again and again to her who is devoid of both transformation and non-transformation. (30)
To Sītā, who is the immutable seed-form, and to the son of Raghu;
you are Lakṣmī and Sītā, you are Viṣṇu; you are Gaurī and Sītā, you are Śiva.
Through Sītā you became Brahmā, the four-faced one;
through Sītā you became Śakra, the husband of Śacī; through Sītā you became Anala, whose wife is Svāhā. ||32||
O best of the Raghus, this goddess who has carried away Sītā has assumed a form; for Sītā is indeed all prosperity, and you are Kubera.
Sītā is the goddess Carudrāṇī, and you are the mighty Rudra;
Sītā is the goddess Rohiṇī, and you are the moon who bestows happiness upon the world. (34)
Sītā is night, O Lord, and you are the sun; Sītā is day, and you are the day.
Sītā is the goddess Mahākālī, and you are eternally Mahākāla. 35.
O twice-born one, whatever exists in the three worlds that bears a feminine gender, all that is Jānakī; and whatever is marked by a masculine name, all that, O Lord, is indeed you. (36)
At that time, you too shall protect her, for you are the Lord of all gods, the sustainer of everything everywhere,
and the power that upholds the universe.
Therefore, the merit marked by you two is ten million times greater;
that conduct, marked by Śiva and Śakti, bestows peace upon you. (38)
We two are always worthy of worship by Rāma and the world, and worthy of worship by you;
Gaurī is one who mutters your name, and I am one who performs the recitation of your mantra. 39.
To one who is about to die at Maṇikarṇikā while residing halfway in the water,
I shall impart the Tāraka mantra, the bestower of Brahman, which reveals the directions.
Therefore, you are certainly the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Jānakī;
deluded by your māyā, all do not know you in truth. (41)
The Lord said: Having been addressed thus by Śambhu, Nārada became inclined toward grace;
he assumed a divine form, glorious and of most wonderful appearance. ||42||
Thus, having beheld that form, those men, monkeys, and gods were not even able to look upon it, for it was a great and wonderful radiance.
Out of fear, the foremost of the thirty gods prostrated with extreme devotion;
and Rāma, though he was not afraid, perceiving their terror, assumed his illusory human form and spoke again to the gods and the men and monkeys.
Rāmacandra said:
"Listen, O gods! Whoever shall praise me daily with this hymn spoken by Śambhu, that man shall become equal to a god. (45)
Liberated from all evils, he attains my own nature;
he obtains victory in battle and is never struck down. 46.
One is not afflicted by spirits, vetālas, kṛtyās, or even by planetary grahas;
a sonless man obtains a son, and a maiden finds a husband. 47.
The poor man attains prosperity, and the one possessed of courage becomes virtuous;
endowed with glory, he is born with strength equal to his own—of this there is no doubt. (48)
May there be freedom from obstacles in all undertakings and in all endeavors for men; whatever difficult-to-attain desire a mortal may cherish, may it be fulfilled. (49)
Within six months, one attains perfection through the grace of this hymn.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices—that fruit is obtained multiplied ten million times by means of this hymn. (50)
The Lord said: Having spoken thus, Rāmacandra dismissed Maheśvara, and he dismissed all the gods who had assembled, beginning with Brahmā. (51)
All those humans, men, monkeys, and deities were filled with supreme joy; having been dismissed by Rāmacandra, they departed. (52)
Thus dismissed, they all indeed returned in great joy and extreme happiness,
reciting the supreme hymn spoken by the Lord.
Remembering Rāma, whose form is the supreme universal manifestation. ||53||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Vision of the Universe," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.
(244) Chapter Two Hundred and Forty-Four.
Śaṅkara said:
Then Rāma, protecting all directions, enjoyed delightful royal pleasures with Vaidehī for a thousand years. ||1||
All the people of the inner apartments censured Vaidehī for staying in the house of the Rākṣasa, as did the people of the countryside.
Out of fear of public censure, we, the warders of the enemy, observed human custom by attending upon the pregnant princess. (3)
In the sacred hermitage of Vālmīki, on the bank of the Gaṅgā in the great forest,
the one of great luster released the pregnant woman in the assembly of sages.
She, having left her husband's home, took up residence in the abode of a sage;
honored by the wives of sages and protected by the sage Vālmīki. ||5||
There, two sons named Kuśa and Lava were born to her;
and there, by that sage, they were consecrated and grew up in the Vedic tradition.
Rāma, endowed with virtues such as self-restraint (yama) and others, and devoid of all worldly enjoyments, protected the earth together with his brothers.
Constantly worshipping Viṣṇu, Hari, who is without beginning or end,
and ever devoted to the practice of celibacy, the king ruled the earth.
Having slain Lavaṇa, the righteous Śatrughna, along with his two sons, protected Mathurā, which was established by the gods, O descendant of Raghu.
Having slain the Gandharvas on both banks of the Indus, Bharata established his two sons of great strength in that region.
Having slain the Madras in the western land of Madra, the immensely powerful Lakṣmaṇa consecrated his two sons of great heroism.
Having returned to Ayodhyā, he touched the feet of Rāma,
[informing him] that the Brahmin’s young son had met his end through the law of time.

Taking him up in wonder, she gave her breast to the Great-Souled One,
upon whom the Lord of the Universe was then fastened by the mere mention of his name.
In that place, he was addressed as Dāmodara by all the great seers;
meanwhile, the two Yamalārjuna trees, having been liberated, attained human form through Tautuki.
Then all the elder cowherds, led by Nanda Gopa, perceiving this great portent, departed for another location. (95)
In the beautiful Vṛndāvana, on the auspicious bank of the Yamunā,
they established lovely dwellings for the cows and the community of cowherd girls.
There, the two very powerful Taurāma and Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Vatsapāla, were then tending the calves. 97.
While Kṛṣṇa was in the midst of the calves, the great asura named Baka prepared to kill that best of the Yadus by assuming the form of a crane.
Seeing him, Vāsudeva also playfully lifted up a clod of earth and struck him;
that great asura fell to the ground with his wings.
Then, after tending the calves in the forest for several days, he fell asleep on soft sprouts in the shade of a *jaṃbu* tree. (100)
Then, immediately after that, Lord Brahmā, surrounded by hosts of gods, arrived to see Kṛṣṇa; having come there, he saw the two best of the Yadus asleep.
Having carried off the calves and the young bulls, he returned once more to the third heaven;
then, having awakened and looked about, [Nanda] saw that the calves and the young bulls were lost.
Seeing that the calves, the cowherds, and the boys had all returned, they were filled with wonder; and Kṛṣṇa, having understood that this deed was performed by Prajāpati, [remained silent].
In that very same way, the eternal Madhusūdana created children and calves, according to their forms and with such speed. 104.
The Lord of the worlds created calves, cowherds, and sheep;
and seeing them at the time of evening, the cows indeed became their mothers. (105)
Just as they had proceeded before, each approaching its own respective calf,
so it was when one year had passed for that high-souled one.

Then Prajāpati, having joined his palms in reverence and circumambulated and prostrated before him, spoke out of fear to Govinda, the Lord of the three worlds: "Having joined his palms in reverence, having circumambulated and prostrated, Brahmā, the lord of the three worlds, spoke out of fear to Govinda. (107)
Brahmā said:
Salutations, salutations to You, the Soul of all, whose very nature is the knowledge of reality;
to the Great Soul, the beloved Self, whose nature is eternal bliss. 108.
O you who are atomic, vast, and of even more massive form; all-pervading and imperishable;
whose nature consists of no beginning, middle, or end—homage be to you, O Self! 109.
And salutations to you, whose nature consists of eternal knowledge, power, sovereignty, valor, and splendor; to the Great Powerful One, the embodiment of the six perfections in their fullness.
O Brahman, you are the Veda-Purusha and indeed the Mahāpuruṣa; you are the Puruṣa who bestows the state of being the Śarīra-puruṣa, and you are the Puruṣa himself. ||111||
There are four persons, and you are the ancient Puruṣottama;
O Brahman, the earth, fire, wind, and the rest are your manifestations.
O Lord of the Universe, from Your speech arose the subtle elements of earth and fire;
O All-pervading One, the intermediate space and the wind were created by Your vital breath. 113.
O sinless one, from your eye the sky and the sun were created,
and likewise the directions and the moon were created from your ear.
O Varuṇa, the flow of the waters is yours; you are the Great Lord in the mind. When this great inquiry has been uttered, that Brahman shines forth. 115.
In the very same way, this is [the case] in the sacrifices, this is so in the Mahāvrata; this is the *chaṃdogeya*, this is the *nabhya*, this is the *dviyajña*, and this is indeed Vāyu. 116.
This very same [nature] exists in space, likewise in these herbs, and in the same way in all the lunar mansions, the planets, and the sun. (117)
Thus, regarding these very beings, the Śruti declares them to be Brahman;
that alone is the supreme Brahman, known as the immortal on all sides. 118.
"He is the golden, imperishable sacrifice; he is the pure one, dwelling in purity"—these are Vedic designations for Him, yet they do not apply to Him in any [literal] sense whatsoever. (119)
The supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, who consists of sight, hearing, touch, mind, and speech—He is Peace, according to the Śruti. 120.
O lotus-eyed one, you are the meaning of all the Upaniṣads;
I am not able to praise you, who have reached the further shore of all the Vedāntas.
This great offense of yours, the abduction of my child, has been committed by me;
therefore, O Lord who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, please forgive it. 122.
Maheśvara said:
Having thus praised Hari and having prostrated before him again and again,
the Creator (Brahmā) gave back the calves to him and returned to his own abode.
Always keeping Hari in the form of a child within his heart, O Goddess, the creator Brahmā,
possessed of great austerity, dwelt together with the gods, joyful and well-nourished.
The calves and the children that had been created by Kṛṣṇa became one with the original calves and children even as the inhabitants of heaven looked on. 125.
Kṛṣṇa departed for Nanda’s Gokula accompanied by the cowherd boys; after several days had passed, that preeminent scion of the Yadu dynasty was joined by other cowherds.
Then, having gone to a lake of the Kālindī, Acyuta [encountered] the king of serpents, who was situated there, exceedingly fierce, and possessed of the strength of a thousand heads.
Having effortlessly crushed a thousand fruits with a single foot,
Madhusūdana brought him to the brink of death.
Having attained perfect knowledge at that very moment, he went for refuge to him;
then the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa protected the serpent, who had relinquished his venom.
Fearing Vainateya,
the preeminent scion of the Yadus banished him from the lake to the summits of Mount Aṅka by his own power.
Quickly abandoning that lake of evil, accompanied by his sons and wife,
he then paid homage to Govinda and departed from Kāliya.
But those trees standing on its banks that had previously been scorched by poison, as soon as they were gazed upon by Kṛṣṇa, quickly became laden with flowers and fruit. (132)
Then, in the course of time, having attained boyhood, the Lord Madhusūdana, who embodies all the gods, began to tend the herd of cows. (133)
Accompanied by cowherd boys of his own age, Rāma, the best of the Yadus,
wandered about the delightful Vṛndāvana.
There, having slain that most terrible great asura in the form of a serpent,
he struck down its massive body, which was as heavy as Mount Meru.
Having reached Dhenuka’s forest, which was a dense thicket of palm trees,
he entered that beautiful grove filled with fruiting palms.
There stood Dhenuka, who was always shaped like a mountain and bore the form of a donkey.
Seizing his feet and lifting him up, he struck him with a rhythmic blow (*tāla*);
at that very moment, those guardians were then crushed by him.
Having quickly departed from that forest, they arrived at the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree;
there they played with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in the sports of childhood. 138.
There, a Rākṣasa named Pralamba arrived in the guise of a cowherd;
placing Rāma upon his back, he quickly departed into the sky.
Recognizing him as a Rākṣasa, Rāma struck him on the head with his fist in a fit of rage; then, his limbs overwhelmed by that blow, he fell down.
With his head and body shattered there, drenched in blood, that very Rākṣasa let out a terrifying cry. ||141||
Then, at the time of dusk, the delighter of Nanda dwelt in the cow-pen,
sporting with the cowherd girls in the splendor of the full moon.
The lord of the Daityas named Ariṣṭa, having assumed the form of a bull, went there;
arriving to slay Kṛṣṇa, he let out a great roar.
Seeing him, all the cowherds fled, oppressed by fear;
Kṛṣṇa also saw that fierce lord of the Danujas approaching.
Having uprooted a palmyra tree, he crushed him in the middle of his horns;
with his head broken, that horned beast vomited much blood.
He fell with a terrifying force, letting out a roar and casting off his life;
thus he slew the massive-bodied Ariṣṭa, the lord of the Danujas. ||146||
Having summoned the cowherd boys there, as it were, into the cow-pen where they dwelt,
then after some days, the great Asura named Keśin [arrived].
Assuming the body of a horse, he went to Vraja to slay Govinda; having reached the beautiful cow-pen, he then let out a loud neigh.
The three worlds were filled with that great sound; all the hosts of gods were terrified, thinking, "Alas, the end of the age has come! (149)
There, all the cowherds and cowherdesses, overcome by that power and rendered distraught, regained their senses and then fled together from there. (150)
The gopīs went to Kṛṣṇa for refuge and said, "Save us! He, who is affectionate toward his devotees, said, "Do not fear, do not fear! (151)
Then, having quickly consoled him, the younger brother of Vāsava playfully struck that Daitya on the head with his fist.
With his teeth and eyes wide open and emitting a great roar,
he lifted up a massive boulder and hurled it at the son of Gavi.
With his entire body crushed like powdered sesamum, the great asura Māra fell suddenly to the ground with a terrifying sound like the bellowing of a bull. 154.
Seeing Keśin slain, the hosts of gods in heaven released showers of flowers and cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (155).
Thus, having slain the Daityas who were fierce in their strength while still in his childhood,
Hari rejoiced in happiness together with Balarāma.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes resembling lotus petals, wearing yellow garments, adorned with garlands, and decorated with a forest wreath. ||157||
His chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem; he was adorned with variegated garlands and unguents, endowed with diverse ornaments, and resplendent with two earrings. ||158||
Wearing a garland of tulasī, adorned with a tilaka of musk, and possessing hair arranged in a very glossy, dark-blue, curly braid; 159.
Adorned with various kinds of bound flowers as ornaments for his peacock-feather crest, his palms, soles, and lips are like red lotuses. ||160||
His face, with its creeper-like eyebrows, resembles the crescent moon situated in the middle of the fortnight;
he is resplendent with necklaces, anklets, armlets, and two bracelets. ||161||
In the most delightful Vṛndāvana, resplendent with fruits and flowers,
the joy of the Yadus dwells there, charmingly sounding his flute.
Seeing Acyuta, whose beauty surpassed that of ten million Cupids, all the cowherd women were tormented by the weapon of the god of love. (163)
Formerly, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
upon seeing Rāma, who was Hari himself there with a most beautiful form, desired to eat him.
They all attained the state of womanhood and were born in Gokula;
having obtained Hari through desire, they were thereafter liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
Just as the Daityas, having encountered Madhusūdana with anger, attained liberation upon meeting their death in battle. ||166||
Having approached Hari with true devotion, the gopīs were liberated from their enemies—the gods—despite being the cause of the world's lust, anger, and falsehood, as if they had been cast out. 167.
Those people who resort to Janārdana out of desire, fear, or even hatred attain Vaikuṇṭha; how much more so, then, through the yoga of devotion! 168.
Hearing the sound of his flute at night, all the cowherd women rose from their beds with their fine hair disheveled. (169)
Abandoning their husbands, sons, and wives, and casting aside shame and their own families, whom else—afflicted by the arrows of pride—would they not have approached as the Lord of the World? (170)
Having all come together, the cowherd women embraced Keśava with their arms and drank his lip,
just as the goddesses drink the nectar of immortality.
The Lord of the Self sported with all of them in Govraja;
and all those women, being fearless, took their delight with him in Vraja.
In this manner, they delighted Keśava day after day in the delightful Vṛndāvana and likewise on the banks of the Kālindī.
Pārvatī said:
Having descended into this world for the sake of protecting dharma,
how could that Janārdana commit the act of approaching another's wife?
Rudra said:
"O lady of auspicious countenance, there is no distinction between one's own body and the bodies of others; the entire world is that [single] body, and nothing exists here as separate from it. (175)
For that great-souled Puruṣa, there is no distinction between female and male, because he possesses innate lordship and is the self-master, the Lord of the universe. (176)
Likewise, O fortunate one, due to the power of having cast off all evil, there is no defect whatsoever in this all-pervading Lord, the Supreme Self. (177)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus spoken to the Daughter of the Mountain, Rudra, the illustrious destroyer of Tripura,
proceeded to relate the remaining life-story of Kṛṣṇa.
Rudra said:
When the autumn season had arrived, the cowherds, led by Nandagopa, began to perform a great festival for the Lord of the Gods. 179.
Then the powerful Govinda, having prevented that festival of Śatakratu, caused a festival for Govardhana, the king of mountains, to be celebrated.
Then, enraged, the thousand-eyed Indra rained down a great deluge incessantly for seven nights upon Nanda Gopa’s cow-pasture.
Janārdana, for the sake of protecting the cows, playfully held up the great mountain Govardhana, which he had uprooted. 182.
O lady of virtuous vows, having reached the shade of that mountain, the cowherds and cowherd-maidens dwelt there in perfect happiness, as if they were inside their own palaces.
Then Śakra, the thousand-eyed one, terrified and with a bewildered mind,
warded off that rain as it fell upon Nanda’s cow-pen.
Kṛṣṇa then set that great mountain back in its original place;
all the elder cowherds, led by Nandagopa, [did likewise].
Having worshipped Govinda, they were filled with supreme wonder.
Then the god Śatakratu, approaching Madhusūdana,
stood with palms joined in reverence and praised him with a voice faltering with joy.
Indra said:
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, omniscient one, you who have taken three strides!
Salutations be to you, the Lord of all, the Self of the universe, who transcends the three qualities (guṇas). ||187||
You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call, you are the syllable *oṃ*, you are the ritual intention, and you are the oblation;
O Keśava, you alone are the father and the mother of all the gods. 188.
At the beginning, you were Hiraṇyagarbha; from him the world came into being.
You alone are the sole Lord, the Puruṣa, the golden one. 189.
O Lord of the Universe, you alone have sustained this earth and this heaven; you are the giver of self and the giver of fruit to this world. 190.
That nectar of the Lord of the worlds was obtained by the gods, while death became their shadow; thus, light and darkness became eternal. (191)
To that very God we offer worship with oblations;
from Him, O golden one, these golden worlds have emerged.
O Keśava, he whose tongue is the ocean—
his vehicle is the wind that moves through these cardinal and intermediate directions, O Imperishable One.
To that very god, you, we offer worship with this oblation, by whom the earth, having been ascended [by you], has flourished once again. (194)
O Brahman Maheśvara, by you that heaven was pierced;
you dwell in the intermediate space like dust, all-pervading and imperishable.
To that very God we offer worship with an oblation—He who is the King of the Krantis, shining like heated gold and endowed with all virtues. (196)
Prosperity and Fortune always gaze with their minds upon that place where the Sun has arisen and shines in the supreme station. (197)
To that very God, to You who exist, we offer worship with oblation, since You, O Janārdana, are the waters, the vast expanse, the universal Brahman, and the creative power. 198.

Conceiving embryos in this creation, he brought forth the progenitors; the one, imperishable, and all-pervading Lord, who creates the flood of shores, existed as the sole sovereign of both gods and asuras.
To that very god, who by his greatness beheld the waters and Prajāpati, we offer worship with an oblation. 200.
There, at the beginning, those who were establishing the sacrifice produced the oblation as a male;
he who was the one and only among the gods, the supreme deity beyond the transcendent.
To that very God, who is Bhava, we offer worship with an oblation;
may He not harm us—He who is the inexhaustible, primordial Male, the progenitor of the earth. 202.
He who, as the Lord, generated the primordial Speech from the eternal Truth and Dharma;
he who produced the moon, the Bṛhatī meters, the waters, and the entire world.
To that very God, who has become all these, we offer worship with oblations;
for he, O Lord, has brought forth all these created beings on every side. 204.
O Acyuta, we worship you—the overseer of the beings born from you, who are both future and past—so that whatever desires we have may be fulfilled for us in brief. (205)
May we become lords of the three worlds through your compassionate glance;
may there be the Person named Hiraṇmaya, possessing golden beard and hair. 206.
From the tips of the nails, everything is gold; Savitṛ has become one who possesses gold.
That all-pervading Brahmā, who is established as the Āditya, is this very one. ||207||
We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ;
may it inspire our thoughts so that we may attain well-being. (208)
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, O Śrīśa, O Lord of all, O Keśava!
Salutations be to you, who are known through the Vedāntas, the Lord of sacrifice, and the embodiment of sacrifice! 209.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva; salutations to you in the guise of a cowherd.
May all that [suffering] be destroyed right now, for this offense was committed by me.
Therefore, O Lord of the World, O Ocean of Compassion, O Supreme Person, please forgive this;
slay Kaṃsa, who is difficult to overcome, in a very short time.
Having accomplished what is beneficial for the gods, may you dwell happily upon the earth. (211)
Mahādeva said: Having thus praised Govinda, Hari, the lord of all gods,
consecrated him with nectar and ambrosia and divine, excellent ornaments.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods, he returned once more to heaven;
and the elder cowherds and the cowherd women, having seen Śatakratu there, [were filled with wonder].
Thus honored by them, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, those two of great heroism adorned with divine ornaments, experienced incomparable joy.
Nanda and [Yaśodā] remained there in the beautiful cowherd settlement with great happiness; in the meantime, the best of sages, the divine Nārada, arrived.
Having gone quickly to Mathurā, he entered the presence of Kaṃsa;
there, honored by the king, he sat upon an auspicious seat.
Then he reported all the activities of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
including the exertion of the gods and the birth of Keśava.
Likewise, by Vāsudeva there was the entrusting of his sons to Vraja, the destruction of the Rākṣasas, and the banishment of the king of serpents. (218)
Having reported everything concerning Kaṃsa’s meeting with Śatakratu in its entirety to that mountain-like Dhāraṇa, [he departed]. (219)
Honored by that Rākṣasa, he departed for the abode of Brahmā;
meanwhile, Kaṃsa, his mind deeply agitated, was surrounded by his ministers.
They deliberated together regarding their own destruction;
there, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Dānavas spoke of a course of action for his own benefit to Akrūra, the best among the wise and a lover of righteousness. (221)
Kaṃsa said: "Out of fear of me, all the gods, led by Indra, having approached Viṣṇu, went to him for refuge, afflicted by terror. (222)
Having granted them freedom from fear, the Blessed One, the creator of beings,
Madhusūdana, was born from the womb of Devakī in order to slay this one.
The evil-minded Vasudeva, having deceived me at night,
placed his son in the house of the wicked-souled Nanda.
Though he is but a child, he is difficult to overcome; he has slain the great asuras.
There is no doubt that he would even prepare himself to slay me. 225.
He cannot be slain by new [means] even by the gods and asuras together with Indra;
he must be subdued through a stratagem alone, having been brought here by me at that time.
By means of elephants intoxicated with rut, by wrestlers, or by excellent horses—
by whatever method possible— he can be slain right here.
Therefore, O best of the Yadus, having gone to the cow-pen, bring here Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, along with all the elder cowherds headed by Nanda Gopa,
so that they may partake in the bow-sacrifice.
Mahādeva said:
Having said "So be it," the heroic best of the Yadus mounted his chariot and set out for the beautiful Gokula, eager for a sight of Kṛṣṇa.
Akrūra, the most excellent of great devotees, full of humility, beheld Kṛṣṇa, who was free from all fatigue, standing in the midst of the cows.
Resembling a dark blue rain cloud, adorned with all ornaments,
with eyes as broad as lotus petals, long arms, and free from ailment.
Clad in yellow garments, beautiful in all his limbs,
his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and adorned with jeweled earrings.
There he beheld Janārdana, adorned with a forest garland of *tulasī*, wearing wild flowers as ear-ornaments, and surrounded by cowherd maidens.
With his entire body bristling with horripilation and his eyes overflowing with tears of joy,
the best of the twice-born descended from that chariot and prostrated himself.
Having met Gopāla with joy, they circumambulated and prostrated before him;
his two feet, resembling red lotuses, were marked with the signs of the vajra and the wheel. (235)
Placing [his head] upon his own crown and bowing again and again at his lotus feet,
[he beheld] the Lord, who resembled the peak of Mount Kailāsa and wore blue garments.
Then, seeing Balarāma, who resembled the full autumnal moon and was adorned with a necklace of pearls,
that Yādava bowed down to him.
Filled with joy, the hero embraced those two best of the Yadus and raised them up;
then, O hero, accompanied by that Vṛṣṇi Akrūra, they both returned home.
Having seen the best of the Yadus arrive, praised by Nanda the cowherd,
the one of great splendor approached him and seated him upon an excellent throne.
They joyfully honored him according to the prescribed rites with offerings of water for the hands and feet and other gifts;
they worshipped him with devotion using divine garments and articles of worship.
The Yādava Akrūra presented garments and ornaments to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and gave [gifts] to Nanda the cowherd and Yaśodā as well. 241.
Having inquired after his welfare with composure while seated upon a kusha-grass mat,
the wise king, being questioned, spoke of all matters of state.
Akrūra said: "This Kṛṣṇa, of great splendor, is the imperishable Nārāyaṇa himself, for the sake of the welfare of the gods and for the protection of the virtuous. (243)
For the destruction of the earth's burden, for the re-establishment of dharma, and for the slaughter of all the Daityas, beginning with Kaṃsa; ||244||
Requested by the hosts of gods and the high-souled sages,
he was born in the womb of Devakī during the great night of the rainy season.
Out of fear of Kaṃsa, Ānakadundubhi brought the Lord of Gods and,
during the night, deposited his son Hari in your house.
Even during that very season, the illustrious Yaśodā gave birth to a daughter named Māyā, born from Śaśa, who possessed a beautiful countenance. (247)
By her, this entire auspicious community of Vraja was deluded;
while Yaśodā lay unconscious upon her bed, that bull among the Yadus [remained there].
Having placed Kṛṣṇa [in the basket] and taken the girl, he went to his own home;
having deposited her on Devakī’s bed, he came back outside.
Then Devakī, lying upon her bed, wept quickly;
hearing that, O observer of good vows, Kaṃsa suddenly seized the girl.
Having whirled him around, the powerless one leaped up and threw him onto the surface of a stone.
But she, having risen up, possessing eight arms equipped with weapons, stood in the sky and spoke to Kaṃsa with a deep voice in anger: ||251||
The maiden said:
"O lowest of Dānavas, he who is the infinite one, the lord of all gods, and the Supreme Person, has gone to the cowherd settlement for the sake of slaying you. (252)
Akrūra said:
Having spoken thus, that great illusory power (Māyā) departed for the Himavat mountains;
from that time forward, the evil-minded one remained with a mind agitated by fear.
They dispatched the Dānavas to their destruction before that great-souled one;
yet they were all slain effortlessly by this wise youth as if in play.
The Supreme Lord performed most wonderful deeds:
the lifting of Govardhana and other mountains, and the expulsion of the king of serpents. ||255||
Having heard from the celestial sage the account of the encounter with Mahendra and the destruction of all the rākṣasas, he was exceedingly afflicted by fear.
Having led away the mighty-armed Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who are difficult to overcome,
he prepared to have them beaten by intoxicated great elephants and by wrestlers.
I dispatched him here for the purpose of bringing Kṛṣṇa;
that evil-minded one has carried out the subjugation of Vasudeva.
All this conduct of that most wicked soul has been fully described;
you all, O inhabitants of Vraja, must go to partake in the bow sacrifice.
"O cowherds, having taken curd, clarified butter, and other offerings, you should go together with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice today. 260.
Kaṃsa will be slain by Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, casting aside all fear, you shall depart at the king’s command.
The Lord said:
Having spoken thus, the highly intelligent Akrūra remained silent.
Upon hearing those words of his, which were harsh and hair-raising, [the Lord spoke]. (262)
Led by Nandagopa, all the elder cowherds, overcome with fear and deluded by grief, spoke while submerged in a great ocean of misery. (263)
Having seen them there, the lotus-eyed and valiant Hari comforted them, saying,
"Do not fear," and then struck the Rākṣasa.
"I shall go to Mathurā together with Rāma and accompanied by you all, in order to bring about the destruction of this evil-minded Kaṃsa. (265)
Having slain there the evil-souled Kaṃsa, the foremost of the Dānavas,
and having killed all the Cāraṇas and Rākṣasas, I shall protect the earth.
"Therefore, casting aside your grief, go to the city of Mathurā. Thus addressed by Hari, the cowherds, led by Nanda, [departed]. (267)
Again and again they embraced him and smelled his head,
reflecting upon the immeasurable deeds of that great-souled one.
And at the word of Akrūra, all the cowherds went forth with various pure items consisting of milk, curd, and clarified butter. ||269||
Yaśodā gave Akrūra a large, gentle meal consisting of many cooked foods that were wholesome, savory, sweet, and delicious. (270)
Accompanied by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, as well as by Nanda and the other excellent cowherds, and by friends— both young and old— he entered the house which had been beautifully decorated.
The gentle food, which removes impurities and wards off disease, was given by Yaśodā; the best of the Yādavas then ate that auspicious meal. (272)
Having fed them according to the rule and having given them water for rinsing the mouth, she,
firm in her vows, gave them camphor and betel leaf.
When the sun had set,
the descendant of Yadu, having sat through the twilight with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, ate excellent milk-rice.
Accompanied by those two, Ākrūra sat down upon that bed in that most excellent palace, which was beautiful, illuminated by lamps,
furnished with a smooth and variegated couch, and adorned with fresh flowers.
Upon him Hari Kṛṣṇa lay, as Nārāyaṇa lies upon Śeṣa.
Seeing him, Akrūra was suddenly overcome with tears of joy and his hair stood on end; casting off his deep sleep, he indeed gazed upon that supreme auspiciousness.
The best of devotees massaged the feet of Viṣṇu;
by this much alone, his life was fulfilled and his existence was well-lived. (278)
This is sovereignty over the three worlds; this is the supreme bliss;
this is kingship; this is righteousness; this is the ultimate happiness of liberation. ||279||
It is impossible for Śiva, Brahmā, and other deities, for Sanaka and the other sages, or for Vasiṣṭha and the other great seers, to remember it even with their minds. ||280||
That pair of feet of the Lord of Śrī, radiant as an autumnal lotus,
was touched by the hands of Indirā’s companions, bringing supreme and great happiness.
"By good fortune, O Viṣṇu, I have obtained the auspicious pair of your lotus feet;
because of the weight of that bliss of Brahman, the night and its moments have passed away. (282)
Then, at the clear dawn, while being praised by the foremost hosts of celestial beings, Hari awoke from that bed.
Having performed the ritual ablution according to the rules together with the wise Rāma, he fell at his mother’s feet and announced his intention to depart.
Having raised him up, she—filled with a mixture of grief and joy over her loss of fame and his birth—her face bathed in tears, embraced her son with great affection. (285)
The goddess Dṛḍhavrata bestowed her blessing upon the two sons and, having embraced the two great heroes again and again, bid them farewell. (286)
Akrūra also, having bowed to Yaśodā, spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Akrūra said:
"O illustrious one, O sinless lady, grant me your favor; I shall go.
This mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, having slain the exceedingly powerful Kaṃsa," [288]
"He will become the king of the entire world, of this there is no doubt; therefore, O lady of beautiful countenance, cast away your grief and be happy. (289)
The Lord said:
Having been addressed thus and dismissed by her, Akrūra, the best of the Yadus,
mounted his excellent chariot together with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Then, being praised by hosts of apsarases, he departed quickly for Mathurā;
all the elder cowherds, headed by Nanda Gopa, followed after him.
Taking up again clarified butter and various fruits,
the cowherd women watched Hari as he departed from Gokula.
They followed Madhusūdana as he departed seated upon his chariot;
Hari, however, caused all those cowherd women to turn back.
With hearts tormented by grief and eyes clouded with tears, she wept repeatedly, crying out, "O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! O Govinda! as she gazed upon the lotus-eyed one.
Those who were stationed there wept with eyes full of tears;
then Akrūra urged the divine chariot forth from the cowherd settlement.
Accompanied by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the Yādava proceeded toward Mathurā;
having quickly crossed the Yamunā, he stationed his excellent chariot on the bank.
Having descended from that chariot, he proceeded there to bathe;
likewise, having immersed himself in the auspicious water, he then performed his necessary duties.
There, reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn correctly, that best of devotees beheld Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, endowed with auspiciousness, in the water. (298)
The Lord wore a blue garment as radiant as the kasha flower at the end of autumn;
he was anointed with divine sandalwood and possessed the luster of ornaments made of pearls. (299)
He beheld Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were red with anger, who wore garlands of sylvan flowers, and who resembled dark blue clouds. (300)
Wearing divine yellow garments, with eyes as long as lotus petals,
his body smeared with yellow sandalwood paste and adorned with various jewels.
Seeing them there, the best of the Yadus was filled with supreme wonder;
rising up, he beheld those two of great strength in that place.
Furthermore, having immersed himself there and recited the two mantras,
he beheld Hari upon the couch of Śeṣa in the ocean of nectar, accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Seeing the God of gods in that water, being praised by Sanaka and others and worshipped by all the deities, the best of the Yadus was filled with supreme wonder;
he then offered praise to Hari, the omnipresent Lord.
Akrūra said:
Salutations to You, the soul of time, who are without beginning or end;
salutations to You, the unmanifest, and salutations to You, the changeless.
Homage to you, the sustainer of beings; homage again and again to you, O tiger among beings!
Homage to you, the supreme self, the controller of all beings. (306)

Salutations to you, the subject of transformation and the subject beyond transformation, the perceptible person, and the sustainer of the qualities; salutations again and again to you, the one who is self-restrained.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Self, who is devoid of distinctions such as place and time; salutations again and again to You, the infinite and infallible Acyuta.
Salutations to you, Govinda, the Lord of the Triple Veda, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, the Universal One, Vāsudeva. ||309||
Salutations again and again to Viṣṇu, who possesses manifold forms and is eternal;
salutations to the lotus-eyed one, the perpetual one, and the bearer of the conch and the discus. ||310||
Salutations again and again to Hari, the Lord of all worlds, whose supreme splendor is enhanced by ornaments resembling ten million rising suns. ||311||
Salutations again and again to Savitṛ, the seed of all worlds, the Supreme Self; to Saṅkarṣaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Pradyumna. ||312||
Salutations to you, Aniruddha, the Sustainer and the Ordainer, the source of the universe,
who possess a thousand forms and many heads, feet, and arms.
Salutations again and again to the eternal Puruṣa of a thousand names;
salutations to you who lie upon the serpent-couch and possess a gentle form.
Salutations to you, O Keśava, who wear yellow garments;
salutations to you, O Śrīdhara, whose radiant splendor is enhanced by the friction of the embrace of Lakṣmī’s firm breasts; salutations to you, the Lord of Śrī, who possesses infinite forms. (315)
The Lord said: "That man who, at the time of bathing, recites this hymn with devotion while meditating upon the eternal God, is indeed liberated from great sins. (316)
Having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords, he shall attain union with Viṣṇu;
thus, having praised the Lord within the water, the best of devotees [attains this]. (317)
He worshipped [him] with waters and fragrant flowers;
having performed his duty, Akrūra then emerged from the waters of the Yamunā.
Having approached, he, endowed with auspiciousness, prostrated before Rāma and Kṛṣṇa; seeing him humble and amazed, Govinda, Hari, spoke to him. (319)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Yādava, what wonder did you see in that water? The Lord said:
Then Akrūra spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the best of the Yadus and possessed of great splendor.
Akrūra said:
O Lord of all, Master of the greatness of the universe, O Hṛṣīkeśa, what wonder is there? For you alone are indeed the entire world.
You are the waters, you are the sky and fire; you are the earth and likewise the wind. You are this entire fourfold world, both the stationary and the moving.
There is nothing other than you, O Vāsudeva, just as there is no nectar other than the cloud;
you are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the syllable *oṃ*, and likewise the sacrificial offering.
You alone are the eternal and immutable Lord of all the gods;
you are neither without cause nor with cause, and you are beyond both cause and non-cause.
O Lord of Gods, you have assumed a physical body for the protection of the Dharma;
you have attained the majestic manifestations of the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, and so forth.
O All-pervading Lord, you alone behold this entire world as being composed of yourself.
The Lord said: Having thus praised Govinda and bowed down to the Lord of the worlds,
that best of the Yadus ascended the divine chariot together with those two.
Then, having quickly reached Mathurā, which was built by the gods,
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa stationed him at the city gate and he entered the inner apartments.
Having informed the king of their arrival at that time,
he was honored by the monarch and then entered his own home.
Then, at the time of evening, the two of great strength, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
having grasped each other's hands, arrived together in Mathurā.
As those two great heroes and supreme messengers were traveling along the royal highway,
those two high-souled ones saw a washerman who was washing clothes.
As Acyuta was entering the royal palace clothed in divine garments,
the powerful Rāma, as if begging for them, took those clothes from him.
At that time, the son of Vaśiṣṭha, standing on the road, did not give anything to him;
instead, he uttered a harsh cry and spoke many bitter words there. (333)
The immensely powerful Kṛṣṇa struck him with his palm;
thereupon, he fell as if slain on the road, vomiting much blood.
Those two heroes, Rāma and Keśava, together with their kinsmen the cowherds, put on those beautiful garments just as they pleased.
Having reached the florist's house, they were seen and saluted;
filled with joy, they were worshipped with fragrant, divine flowers. (336)
The two preeminent heroes of the Yadu clan gave him the desired gift of the *taubara* weapon; then they returned together to the street and saw that woman of auspicious countenance.
O highly fortunate one, seeing a woman who was hunchbacked, carrying a vessel of sandalwood paste, with a crooked gait and a bent back, you asked her for perfume. || 338 ||
Laughing, he gave excellent sandalwood to the past and future [Tathāgatas];
taking that divine sandalwood, he smeared it upon himself as he desired.
Having bestowed upon him a most exquisite form, they met him on the road— those two delicate youths with beautiful faces, gazed upon by women.
The two high-souled ones entered the sacrificial hall along with their followers;
there Keśava beheld the divine bow duly worshipped.
Then Madhusūdana, having seized it with ease, broke it;
hearing that bow being broken, Kaṃsa became greatly distressed.
Having summoned the wrestlers, the charioteers, and the foremost leaders of the Daityas,
and having deliberated with his ministers, that preeminent Daitya spoke to Cāṇūra.
Kaṃsa said:
"Rāma and Kṛṣṇa have arrived, the destroyers of all the Daityas;
at dawn, let them be slain by means of an unhesitating wrestling match."
By whatever means possible, I shall [overcome] those two who are arrogant due to their physical strength—either by means of elephants in rut or by the foremost of wrestlers—with great effort. (345)
Īśvara said:
Having been thus instructed, the king, together with his younger brother and his ministers, quickly ascended to the top of the divine palace out of fear. (346)
At the gates and on all the paths, he stationed rutting elephants;
he placed wrestlers fierce with pride and [wild] tuskers everywhere.
Having understood all of that, Kṛṣṇa, together with the wise Rāma and his followers, stayed there for the night in the sacrificial hall.
Then, when the night had passed and the morning was bright and clear,
the two heroes Rāma and Kṛṣṇa rose from their bed and performed their water-rites.
Having performed their auspicious rites and eaten, the two, eager for the battle, departed from that house like two lions from a great cave. (350)
The elephant named Kuvalayāpīḍa, who stood at the king’s gate like a peak of the Himalayan mountain, increased the victory of Kaṃsa.
Having seen that great elephant, who was the destroyer of the pride of the host of gods, possessed of a massive body, and intoxicated with rut, Keśava then became five-faced.
Grasping one hand with the other, the Supporter of the Earth leaped up gracefully,
whirled him around, and then hurled him down upon the ground.
The great elephant of Māra fell suddenly to the ground with a terrifying sound like the bellowing of a thousand bulls, as if a hundred mountains were being pulverized.
Having killed Danta and Upananda and having seized Arāma and Keśava,
they then entered the arena to engage in combat with the wrestlers.
Having witnessed Govinda’s prowess there, all those kings, terrified by his seizing [of the earth], fled and returned to their own cities. (356)
Having fastened the two door-panels very firmly, they stood there by the thousands;
but seeing the door-panels thus securely bound, Kṛṣṇa, with ease, [proceeded].
Having struck him with his foot, the valiant one caused him to fall;
those two, broken and cast down, lay there while the army remained stationed.
There, all those struck down in their positions had their necks crushed;
then, those two of great strength entered the palace of Kaṃsa.
While he was thus causing them to whirl about, O illustrious one,
those two high-souled wrestlers, Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika, who were eager for the arena, beheld him with their arms raised.
Kaṃsa, too, having seen Govinda and Rāma of great strength,
was overcome with fear and then spoke to Cāṇūra, the best of wrestlers.
Kaṃsa said:
"At this moment, I shall effortlessly grant half of my kingdom to those two wrestlers, the cowherd boys."
Īśvara said:
At that moment, Kṛṣṇa was seen by the two wrestlers in the midst of the forest-battle like another great Mount Meru. (363)
In the range of Kaṃsa's vision, Acyuta was like a fire of destruction;
yet he was like Madana himself before the women, and like another infant to his parents. (364)
Like Hari among the thirty gods, or like a friend among cowherds,
they beheld Hari there, omnipresent, in his manifold forms.
Vasudeva, as well as Akrūra and the high-minded Nandagopa,
having ascended another palace, beheld the great carnage.
There, Devakī, standing among the women of the inner apartments,
gazed upon the face of her son with her auspicious eyes filled with tears.
Comforted by them, the queen entered the interior of the palace;
then all the hosts of gods remained in their celestial chariots in the sky.
They praised the lotus-eyed Acyuta with shouts of "Victory!", while the hosts of gods and Maruts cried out loudly, "Slay Kaṃsa! (369).
Then, in that very place resounding with the noise of musical instruments, those two great wrestlers of immense strength approached the bull. (370)
Cāṇūra fought with Govinda, and Muṣṭika with Halāyudha;
those two great-souled ones resembled blue and white mountains respectively.
Through the methods of hand-to-hand combat, with fists and kicks,
a terrible slaughter occurred that brought fear even to the gods.
After sporting with Cāṇūra for a long time,
Janārdana then crushed the wrestler's body and cast him to the ground with ease.
Vomiting much blood upon the surface of the earth with a great crash,
that great wrestler, who caused suffering to both gods and demons, was struck down.
In that manner, the valiant Rāma fought with Muṣṭika for a long time;
he struck him on the chest with his fists.
With his bones and sinews shattered, he fell to the surface of the earth;
then, seeing that prowess, all the wrestlers fled.
Afflicted by intense pain, Kaṃsa was overcome by a great and fierce terror;
at that very moment, the two invincible heroes, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, arrived.
The two great-souled ones ascended the lofty temple-palace;
there, Janārdana struck Kaṃsa on the head with his palm.
Hari cast him down from the pinnacle of the palace onto the surface of the earth;
with all his limbs pierced, he gave up his life upon the ground.
When Kaṃsa had been slain by Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, who was also possessed of great strength,
struck his younger brother Sunāman with his fist alone.
Having slain the evil-minded Kaṃsa along with his younger brother, Rāma and Keśava caused their younger brother [Balabhadra] to fall upon the earth, O upholder of the earth.
Approaching their parents, they both bowed down with devotion;
Devakī and Vasudeva, in turn, embraced them again and again.
Out of affection and longing for their son, they both smelled his head;
above them, Devakī’s breasts poured forth milk. (383)
Then, after Rāma and Kṛṣṇa had consoled their parents and gone outside,
in that very interval, divine drums resounded in the sky.
The lords of the thirty gods uttered cries of joy and showered rains of flowers;
having praised Janārdana with divine hosts of Maruts and having paid him homage, they departed.
Having attained supreme joy, they returned to their respective worlds;
having paid homage to Nanda the cowherd and the elder cowherds, Keśava [departed].
The righteous-souled Janārdana joyfully embraced Rāma and,
out of affection, gave him many jewels and wealth.
Keśava honored all those elderly cowherds with garments, ornaments, and the like, as well as with abundant wealth and grain.
Dismissed by that Kṛṣṇa, those led by Nanda the cowherd departed for the divine cow-pen, filled with both joy and sorrow.
Having approached their maternal grandfather, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa— those two who are difficult to overcome—
liberated him from his bonds and consoled him again and again.
Madhusūdana then caused the coronation of Cakraka in that kingdom by means of the best of the twice-born, and performed the funeral rites for Kaṃsa.
Having established the leaders of the Yadu clan,
headed by Akrūra, in the kingdom, and having installed Ugrasena as king, the righteous Hari, son of Vasudeva, protected the earth according to dharma.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Kaṃsa," within the *Śrīkṛṣṇacarita* section of the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious *Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||245|| ||cha||
(246) Chapter Two Hundred and Forty-Six.
Śrī Maheśvara said:
Then Ānakadundubhi performed the initiation ceremony for his two sons, Vairāja and Kṛṣṇa, according to the Vedic rite. ||1||
Rāma and Keśava were consecrated by the preceptor Garga with divine,
pure, and auspicious purificatory baths performed by Vaiṣṇava scholars.
Having performed the purificatory rites, the two of great strength, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
went to the house of the high-souled Sāndīpani and paid their respects to him.
Having studied the Vedas and the Shastras from that preeminent among the twice-born,
they brought back the deceased son and gave him as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having received the words of blessing from that high-souled elder and having bowed down to him,
those two best of the Yadus then departed for Mathurā.
Then, having heard that the invincible Kaṃsa had been slain by Kṛṣṇa,
his father-in-law, King Jarāsandha of great strength, [was moved].
Then, having arrived with thousands of akṣauhiṇīs— armies of great strength—
he besieged the city of Mathurā in order to kill Kṛṣṇa.
Having departed from that excellent city, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, possessed of great heroism,
beheld that flood of troops crowded with elephants and horses.
Vāsudeva then remembered his eternal primordial form;
by the mere act of remembering him, Dāruka became Viṣṇu’s charioteer.
The great chariot named Sugrīvapuṣpaka was brought forth;
it was eternal, drawn by divine horses adorned with flowers and other ornaments.
It was equipped with divine weapons such as the conch, discus, and mace;
it was adorned with the banner of Vainateya and was invincible even to the gods.
Having reached the earth and bowed down to Govinda, the charioteer of Hari presented him with a brilliant chariot, complete with weapons and horses.
Having seen this, Kṛṣṇa too, with great joy, mounted the great chariot after his elder brother had already ascended it, while being praised by the hosts of Maruts.
Assuming a four-armed form and bearing a conch, a discus, a mace, and a sword, he—
wearing a crown, earrings, and garlands— advanced toward the battlefield.
The powerful Baladeva, seizing his mace and plow,
began to destroy that army like a second Maheśvara.
Dāruka quickly urged the chariot forward in that battle, like the wind driving a fire through a forest overgrown with grass, shrubs, and creepers. 16.
Then the soldiers of Jarāsaṃdha covered that chariot with maces, iron clubs, spears, and hammers.
With his very discus, Hari swiftly and effortlessly cut those many blades of grass and pieces of wood,
just as a great fire consumes them with its flame.
Then, taking up his Śārṅga bow, he cut down those armies with sharp, inexhaustible arrows; nothing at all could be discerned.
In that great battle, some of those mighty warriors had their lotus-faces severed by discs, some were crushed by maces, and others by various other weapons.
Some were cut by swords, while others were struck by spears; some had their necks crushed by the tips of ploughs, and others had their heads smashed by mallets.
In an instant, Madhusūdana, the best of the Yadus, having destroyed that entire army,
blew his conch shell with a sound like a thunderbolt unleashed by fate.
With their hearts pierced by the sound of the conch, those mighty warriors—along with their horses and elephants—fell down, having abandoned all hope for life. (23)
That army, consisting of twenty-one akṣauhiṇīs along with its elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers, was completely destroyed by Kṛṣṇa alone; it was utterly annihilated.
Slain by Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, in half a moment;
then all the hosts of gods, their hearts overflowing with joy. ||25||
They rained down showers of flowers and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
Then the mountain, having cast off the entire burden of the earth, [departed].
Being praised by the thirty gods at the head of the battle,
the exceedingly powerful Jarāsaṃdha beheld his own army being slaughtered.
The evil-minded one quickly advanced to fight with Baladeva;
a terrible battle took place between those two who never retreat in combat.
Taking up his plow, Rāma struck down his chariot along with its driver in battle; then, seizing that one of great strength, the wielder of the spear [Śiva] took hold of him.
Raising his pestle quickly,
he set about to kill Jarāsaṃdha, that best of kings, who had fallen into a life-threatening peril.
Having seen that the mighty Rāma had slain the great elephant like a lion, Kṛṣṇa struck the elder brother [Balarāma] and said, "I shall slay him," O Lord.
The righteous and high-minded Saṅkarṣaṇa,
the imperishable one, released Jarāsaṃdha at the word of Kṛṣṇa, having liberated his enemy.
Having mounted his chariot with his younger brother, he entered Mathurā;
there he encountered the immensely powerful Kālayavana, who was accompanied by a great force.
He related the prowess of Vasudeva’s two sons,
as well as the slaughter of the Dānavas and the death of Kaṃsa.
He reported the slaughter of the akṣauhiṇīs as well as his own defeat,
and related the entire great deed of Kṛṣṇa.
Hearing that, Ayavana became enraged and was surrounded by thousands of millions of Mlecchas, who possessed great strength and prowess and were filled with intoxication.
For the sake of assisting that lord of Magadha, he, possessing great strength,
quickly went to the city of Mathurā accompanied by him alone.
Having covered the earth, which is filled with various provinces, with his forces,
he then besieged the city of Mathurā after encamping his great army.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having reflected upon the welfare of the citizens, requested land from the ocean for the sake of a dwelling place for the people. (39)
The Ocean gave to Kṛṣṇa a site thirty yojanas in extent;
there, in the midst of the waters, he built the city of Dvāravatī.
It was endowed with many palaces, with golden walls and arched gateways,
and surrounded by rows of divine houses made of various kinds of jewels.
The lotus-eyed Lord created it, endowed with delightful gardens and many lakes, just like Indra’s Amarāvatī.
While the citizens of Mathurā were fast asleep, Janārdana suddenly lifted them up during the night and settled them in Dvārāvatī.
All those people, having awakened together with their sons and wives,
sat upon the floors of golden palaces and were struck with the utmost wonder.
They were surrounded by many riches and grains, divine garments and ornaments, and excellent houses filled with every enjoyment.
Delighted, they stood together like hosts of gods in heaven,
as the two mighty ones, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, were about to fight with the Yavana.
Then Rāma, the great chariot-warrior, taking up his plow and his pestle, went out from Mathurā with his brother. 47.
Enraged in battle, Kṛṣṇa struck down the great army of the Yavanas; having strung his Śārṅga bow, he [assailed them] with arrows resembling tongues of fire.
The son of Devakī burnt away the entire strength of the Mlecchas;
seeing his own army destroyed, the powerful Kālayavana [fled].
The lord of the Yavanas fought as if with a mace against Vāsudeva,
while Kṛṣṇa, remaining unhurt, engaged in a struggle with him for a long time.
