Turning his face away, the lotus-eyed one fled from that battle;
pursued with great speed, he cried out, "Stay! Stay! (51)
With great speed, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa entered a mountain cave;
there lay sleeping the king, the great sage Mucukunda.
The Lord Hari remained invisible to that king;
meanwhile, the great hero Yavana, raising a mace in his hand, [advanced].
Having set out to kill Kṛṣṇa, he entered that cave.
Seeing the king lying there, he thought that Kṛṣṇa was Janārdana.
I struck the great sage Mucukunda with my foot;
thereupon, the blessed great sage Mucukunda awoke.
Out of anger, his eyes became blood-red and he uttered the syllable *huṃ*.
By that sound of *huṃ* and by his wrathful gaze, [the world was shaken]. ||56||
Having been consumed by fire and reduced to ashes, Yavana gave up his life;
thereafter, the Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared before the royal sage.
Janārdana is dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes resembling white lotuses;
he holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and is clothed in yellow garments.
Seeing him of immeasurable splendor, the royal sage rose up suddenly and exclaimed, "O, what fortune!
O, what fortune!"—thus spoke the great muni.
With his entire body covered in horripilation, his face bathed in tears,
and uttering cries of "Victory!", he bowed down again and again.
Mucukunda said:
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, O Supreme Lord, by the sight of you!
Today my birth has become fruitful; my life is successful."
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
salutations to the divine Dāmodara, the treasury of splendors. (62)
Salutations with joined palms to the son of Adhokṣaja, Hari;
salutations to you, Rāghava, the lotus-eyed one.
Salutation to You, the infallible and unchanging Tathāgata;
salutation to You, Govinda; salutation to Viṣṇu, the Victorious One. ||64||
Salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self; salutations to you, Mukunda, and salutations to you in your fourfold manifestation.
Salutations to the supremely auspicious one; salutations to you, the Supreme Self;
salutations to Vāsudeva, the bringer of peace and the lord of the Yadus.
Maheśvara said: Having thus praised Govinda, he bowed down to him again and again; then the Blessed One spoke to the great sage Mucukunda.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O royal sage, choose a boon, whatever dwells in your heart.
Maheśvara said:
He then requested liberation that is free from returning [to this world] again. ||68||
Then, having abandoned his human form, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa granted him that eternal, divine world. 69.
Assuming a form identical to that of the divine Supreme Self,
he mounted Vainateya and entered the eternal abode.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Mucukunda," within the Life of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, in the Dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||246||
(247) Chapter Two Hundred and Forty-Seven.
Rudra said:
Then, having slain the Yavana there, the delighter of the Yadus, together with the wise Mucukunda,
granted him a boon and attained liberation as he departed.
Hearing that Cāyavana had been slain, the evil-minded Jarāsaṃdha marched forth against Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by his own army.
The entire army of that evil-minded one was slain by Kṛṣṇa;
the lord of Magadha fell unconscious upon the surface of the earth. ||3||
Having regained consciousness after a long time, his limbs trembling and afflicted by fear,
the Lord of Magadha was unable to fight with Rāma.
Turning his face away, he fled swiftly, followed by the remnants of his army,
thinking that Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were invincible and possessed of great strength.
Then, having abandoned their mutual hostility, they entered their own city;
thereafter, those two sons of Vasudeva, accompanied by their army, [proceeded].
Leaving the city of Mathurā, he entered the city of Udvārikā;
there, Vāyu, sent by Indra, [entered] the assembly hall of the gods.
Out of affection, he gave to Kṛṣṇa a throne fashioned by Viśvakarman,
constructed of diamonds and lapis lazuli, and adorned with many seats.
Having reached that delightful assembly hall, which was resplendent with divine golden umbrellas made of various jewels, King Ugrasena and the other monarchs [entered].
He rejoiced together with his kinsmen like the hosts of gods in heaven.
There was a king named Raivata, born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
He affectionately gave his daughter, named Revatī, who was endowed with all auspicious marks, to Rāma.
He married that Caravatī according to the prescribed rites and delighted her, as the Lord of the Gods does with Śacī. ||12||
The righteous King of Vidarbha was named Bhīṣmaka; he was a man of dharma, and he had auspicious sons, the foremost of whom was Rukma. (13)
Their youngest daughter was Rukmiṇī, of excellent complexion, born from a portion of Kamalā and endowed with all auspicious marks. (14)
She was Sītā during the incarnation as Rāghava and Rukmiṇī at the birth of Kṛṣṇa;
she is the companion of Viṣṇu in all other incarnations as well. (15)
In the Dvāpara age, Hiraṇyaka and Hiraṇyākṣa were born again,
endowed with the names Śiśupāla and Dantavakra.
Born in the lineage of the Cedis and endowed with great strength and prowess, his son desired to give Rukmiṇī to Śiśupāla. (17)
But that woman of beautiful countenance did not desire Śiśupāla as her husband;
rather, from childhood onwards, she was firmly devoted to Viṣṇu, being steadfast in her vow. ||18||
Always performing the worship of the gods with Kṛṣṇa as her husband in mind, Rukmiṇī, while still a maiden, gave various kinds of gifts. (19)
Devoted to the practice of her vows and meditating upon Puruṣottama, the Lord of her own self and her husband, she dwelt in her father’s house. (20)
The best of kings made every effort, with the approval of his son Rukmin, to arrange that marriage for Śiśupāla.
Rukmiṇī sent a brahmin, the son of the family priest, with a message concerning her husband Kṛṣṇa; he departed quickly for Dvārakā. ||22||
Having approached Kṛṣṇa and Rāma and being duly honored by them both,
he related to them everything that Rukmiṇī had said.
Having heard that from the wise brahmin, the two lords, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
[received] a chariot that travels through the sky and is fully equipped with all weapons and missiles.
Having ascended with the great-souled Dāruka, the foremost of charioteers, those two Supreme Persons proceeded swiftly toward the city of Vidarbha. 25.
Kings from all kingdoms, headed by Jarāsandha, had come from everywhere to witness the marriage of the wise Śiśupāla. ||26||
At that time of the wedding, Rukmiṇī, adorned with golden ornaments,
went out from the city with her companions to worship Durgā.
At that very moment, however, the son of Devakī arrived;
the powerful Madhusūdana seized her as she stood upon the chariot.
Having placed him upon his chariot along with his charioteer, he departed quickly for his own abode.
Then the kings, headed by Jarāsaṃdha, were overcome with rage. ||29||
Accompanied by the prince Rukmin, they stood ready for battle;
filled with wrath and endowed with a fourfold army, they followed after Hari.
The mighty-armed Balabhadra, having descended from his excellent chariot and seizing his plow and club, struck down his enemies in an instant.
In the battle, he forcibly struck down chariots, horses, great elephants, and even those who travel on foot with his plow and pestle.
By the stroke of his plow, the rows of chariots were pulverized, and the elephants fell to the ground like mountains struck by a thunderbolt. (33)
With their heads split open and vomiting much blood, that entire army was indeed destroyed by Balarāma in a mere instant. 34.
In that great battle, rivers of blood flowed everywhere throughout the conflict, carrying away horses, elephants, chariots, and foot soldiers.
All the kings, utterly shattered and oppressed by fear, fled away;
meanwhile, the powerful Rukmī, driven by anger, wrought a slaughter under Kṛṣṇa.
Raising his bow, he struck the wielder of the Śārṅga with floods of arrows;
then Govinda, laughing, took up the Śārṅga bow with ease.
With a single arrow, Dharaṇīdhara struck his chariot-horses and charioteer;
he also cut down his chariot, banner, and standard.
Deprived of his chariot, he took up a sword and stood upon the ground;
however, the heroic Kṛṣṇa cut that sword asunder with a single arrow.
Then, raising his clenched fist, he struck Kṛṣṇa on the chest;
Hari seized that hero by the throat, binding him tightly.
Laughing, Madhusūdana took up a sharp razor-edged arrow;
having shaved off his head, Janārdana released him.
Overcome with grief and sighing like a serpent,
he entered his own city and remained there as if dwelling within it.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Destruction of Vidarbhasena," in the *Śrīkṛṣṇacarita* within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||247||
(248) Chapter Two Hundred and Forty-Eight.
Rudra said:
Then Kṛṣṇa, having ascended a divine chariot together with Rāma, Rukmiṇī, and Dāruka, went swiftly to his own abode.

Then, having entered the city of Dvārakā at an auspicious moment under a favorable lunar mansion, Hari, the son of Devakī, [performed the rites] according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas. ||2||
He married the princess Rukmiṇī, who was adorned with gold;
at that time of the wedding, divine drums resounded in the sky.
The best of the gods shouted and rained down showers of flowers;
so too did Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Akrūra, and the foremost of the Yadus.
The highly effulgent Balabhadra and the other leaders of the Yadus performed the marriage of Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī with great joy.
Then Nanda Gopa arrived together with the cowherd boys and the herds of cows, and Yaśodā arrived accompanied by well-adorned women.
All the wives of Vasudeva, headed by Devakī, as well as Revatī, the goddess Rohiṇī, and whatever other women of the city there were. ||7||
Filled with joy, they performed all the marriage rites; there, Devakī affectionately performed the worship of the gods.
Then, according to the prescribed rites, the aged royal women performed all the marriage ceremonies along with the festivities by the most excellent of the twice-born.
He fed the Brāhmaṇas and honored them with auspicious garments and ornaments;
Ugrasena and the other kings there were also highly honored. ||10||
Nanda Gopa and the other cowherds, as well as the women such as Yaśodā and the rest,
[were honored] with many golds, jewels, garments, and ornaments.
Honored and greatly delighted at this great festival of their wedding,
they both embraced their husband and bowed down before the sacrificial fire.
Blessed with the benedictions of the foremost brahmins who were learned in the Vedas,
the bride and bridegroom shone resplendently upon that marriage altar.
The Kṣatriya son of Devakī, together with his wife, gave cows to the Brāhmaṇas, to the elders,
and likewise to his eldest brother.
Having thus completed all the wedding rites, Madhusūdana dismissed all the kings and everyone else who had assembled there. (15)
Having been honored there by the departing deer, those most noble Brahmins, the best among kings, departed for their own abodes. 16.
The virtuous and imperishable son of Devakī dwelt with great happiness upon the auspicious floor of a celestial palace together with Rukmiṇī.
With her he took his delight, as Nārāyaṇa does with Śrī,
while being praised by sages and even by the hosts of celestial deities.
Day after day, with a joyful soul, Janārdana,
the eternal one, dwelt in happiness in the most beautiful city of Dvārāvatī.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara,
in the account of the life of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, this is the section titled "The Narration of Rukmiṇī’s Marriage."
The two hundred and forty-eighth chapter. ||248||
(249) Chapter Two Hundred and Forty-Nine.
Śrī Rudra said:
Satrājit’s daughter, Satyabhāmā, renowned for her fame, was born from Śini on earth; she was another wife of Kṛṣṇa. (1)
The third wife of that illustrious one was known by the name Kālindī, daughter of Vivasvat; she approached him with playful grace. (2)
Janārdana married Viṃdānuviṃdāsuta, the daughter of Mitravinda, who possessed a radiant smile and was standing ready for her own choice of husband (svayaṃvara).
With a single noose, he who had eyes as broad as lotus petals seized those seven intoxicated bulls and her for whom valor was the bride-price.
The lord of the earth gave that great jewel known as the Syamantaka to his younger brother,
the high-souled Prasena.
Once, Madhusūdana requested this excellent jewel;
then Prasena spoke forcefully to that Vāsudeva.
Prasena said:
"This gem constantly produces eight measures of gold;
therefore, this stone called Syamantaka must not be given by me to anyone."
Mahādeva said:
Having understood Kṛṣṇa’s intention, he remained silent.
Once, Kṛṣṇa went out to hunt together with all the best of the Yadus.
Accompanied by great forces such as Prasenajit and others, they entered the vast forest,
followed by thousands, each intent on slaying the deer.
Thus, while Prasenajit had gone far into the great forest alone,
a lion, having seen him and approached, killed him and carried off his jewel.
Having slain that lion and seized the jewel, the exceedingly powerful Jāmbavān quickly entered the cave, which was inhabited by celestial women.
When he had departed like the sun set behind the mountain, [Rāma], accompanied by his followers,
beheld Vāsudeva on the fourth day as the moon had risen, and entered his own city.
Then all the citizens said to one another regarding Kṛṣ�a:
"Having killed Prasena in the forest under the pretext of hunting, Govinda—"
Śyāmā took the excellent jewel and entered with Takṣaka;
then Hari heard the words spoken by the people of Dvārakā concerning that matter.
Out of fear of public censure, he went into the forest with all the Yadus;
there, in the woods, he showed them all his son slain by a hunter.
Having attained purification of self and stationed his great army there,
he alone, with the Śārṅga bow and mace in hand, entered the dense forest.
Having seen the great cave, Kṛṣṇa entered it with a fearless mind;
there he was in a spotless dwelling illuminated by various excellent jewels.
Having been heard by Jāmbavān, who had playfully placed the Child upon the nurse’s swing;
holding a jewel at the front of the swing, he sang joyfully while swinging it. 18.
The lion killed Prasena; the lion was slain by Jāmbavat. Do not weep for the little child; this is surely the end of your [enmity]. 19.
Having heard that, the powerful Vāsudeva then blew his conch;
by that great sound, Añjanā’s son Jāmbavān emerged.
A terrible battle took place between the two of them for ten uninterrupted days,
involving fists like thunderbolts and inspiring fear in all living beings.
Observing Kṛṣṇa’s increase in strength as well as the depletion of his own power, he understood the previous words of the Supreme Soul.
This very Rāma has descended here once again for the protection of dharma;
he, my lord, has come to grant me my heart's desire.
Having understood this, the Lord of the Bears (Bhīṣma) completed his task of battle;
then, with palms joined in reverence, he spoke to Govinda out of great wonder: "Who are you? (24)
Turning back the slaughter, Śauri spoke with a deep voice.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "I am the son of Vasudeva, known as Vāsudeva. (25)
"You have fearlessly stolen my jewel known as Syamantaka;
let it be returned to me quickly, lest you meet your death. (26)
Mahādeva said:
Having heard that, Añjaneya was delighted and prostrated himself like a staff; then, having circumambulated and offered salutations with humility, he spoke to Keśava.
Jāmbavān said: "O Lord, I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose through the sight of you.
O son of Devakī, I am your servant by virtue of our former relationship. (28)
"O Govinda, you have previously granted me this slaughter;
yet this slaughter was committed by me through delusion, even though it was performed by you, my Lord.
Therefore, O Eternal One, O Lord of the World, O Mine of Compassion, please forgive this. (29)
Mahādeva said:
Having spoken thus, and having bowed down and offered salutations again and again,
he placed the Lord with humility upon a seat composed of various jewels.
Having washed his feet, which resembled autumnal lotuses, with auspicious water,
he worshipped the leader of the Yadus according to the ritual of the *madhuparka* offering.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites with divine garments and ornaments,
[he gave] his daughter, a girl named Jāmbavatī, endowed with great beauty.
He gave that jewel among maidens to him of immeasurable luster as a wife; and with other excellent gems, he gave him the gem known as Syamantaka.
There, having led forth the maiden as if for marriage, the monkey Jāmbavanta, who slays the heroes of his enemies, joyfully bestowed supreme liberation upon him out of affection.
Having joyfully taken his daughter Jāmbavatī, the maiden,
he emerged from that cave and set out for the city of Dvārakā.
The best of the Yadus gave the jewel known as Syamantaka, which Satrājit had brought, to his daughter; he, in turn, gave that supreme gem to his daughter.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the sight of the moon is called "false accusation" (mithyābhidūṣaṇa); therefore, one should avoid it. ||37||
There, on the fourth day, a person obtains a vision of the cool-rayed moon;
by hearing his story, one is liberated from false speech. (38)
The three daughters of the King of Madra—Sulakṣmaṇā, Nāgnajitī, and the illustrious Suśīlā—were all maidens of beautiful countenance. (39)
Standing at their own *svayaṃvara*, those radiant women chose Kṛṣṇa as their husband; on a single day, the best of the Yadus married them all.
All eight queens of that great-souled one were headed by Rukmiṇī:
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Kālindī, and Śucismitā; ||41||
Mitravindā, Jāmbavatī, Nāgnajitī, Sulakṣmaṇā, and the slender-limbed one named Suśīlā is recorded as the eighth queen. (42)
The son of the Earth, a Rākṣasa named Naraka of great prowess, having conquered Śakra, the lord of the gods, and all the deities in battle; ||43||
He forcibly seized the two radiant earrings of Aditi, the mother of the gods,
as well as the various treasures of the deities.
Airāvata, the elephant of Mahendra; likewise Uccaiḥśravas, the horse; the wealth of Dhaneśvara, such as rubies and other gems; and likewise the treasures Śaṅkha and Padma.
He carried off our women and the celestial nymphs, as well as the river of the earth; and he forcibly seized the weapons of those dwellers of heaven, such as the thunderbolt and others. (46)
Having slain the gods with those very [weapons], he dwelt in a celestial assembly hall fashioned by Maya, moving through the sky in that stainless atmosphere.
Then all the hosts of gods, placing the Lord of Śacī at their head, sought refuge with Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds, being afflicted by fear. 48.
Kṛṣṇa, having heard all of Naraka’s activities,
granted fearlessness to the gods and thought of Vainateya (Garuḍa).
Before that Lord Viṣṇu, the mighty Vainateya, who is honored by all the gods, stood with palms joined in reverence. (50)
Having ascended that best of birds together with Satyabhāmā, Keśava,
being praised by the sages, proceeded toward the abode of the Rākṣasa.
It blazed in the sky like the orb of the sun,
surrounded by many Rākṣasas and adorned with divine ornaments.
Kṛṣṇa beheld that city, which was impenetrable even by the gods;
then the powerful Lord, having observed its enclosures, [struck them] with his discus.
Then, as if with his splendor and radiance, the Sun-god cut down all those Rākṣasas by the hundreds and thousands.
Then, raising their spears, they went forth to face the battle;
thereafter, with divine *tomaras*, *bhiṇḍipālas*, and excellent *paṭṭiśas*... [55]
They struck Keśava as if striking fire with straw;
thereupon, the Blessed One, whose banner is Garuḍa, took up his Śārṅga bow.
With arrows resembling tongues of fire, he severed their divine weapons, as well as the necks of those elephants and the swift horses. 57.
The valiant Puruṣottama cut them down with his very discus;
some were severed by the discus, while others were struck by his arrows.
Some Rākṣasas were struck down by the mace on that battlefield;
thus all those Rākṣasas were felled to the surface of the earth. 59.
Having slain all the Dānavas, the lotus-eyed one appeared like the mountains shattered by the thunderbolt hurled by Śakra.
Puruṣottama blew his great conch, Pāñcajanya;
then the powerful Daitya Naraka took up his bow.
Mounting a divine chariot, he went forth to battle against Keśava;
a terrible and hair-raising combat took place between the two of them.
Then, as the two showered many thousands of arrows like two clouds raining,
the eternal Vāsudeva [struck] with a crescent-shaped arrow.
The heroic one severed the bow of that Rākṣasa-faced one and discharged a great divine weapon at Naraka’s broad chest.
With his heart pierced by the spear, the great asura fell to the earth,
roaring like a massive mountain shattered by Indra’s thunderbolt.
Then Kṛṣṇa approached that Rākṣasa;
requested by the Earth, he said to the Rākṣasa, "Choose a boon.
And that Rākṣasa [beheld] Kṛṣṇa seated upon Garuḍa.
"O Bestower of Boons, I am likewise a human being;
for the sake of the welfare of other worlds, I choose this supreme boon. (67)
O Lord of all lords of beings,
O Madhusūdana, dispeller of fear, may there never be the attainment of hell for those who perform the auspicious ritual bath on the anniversary of your death. 68.
Mahādeva said:
"So be it," the Lord Govinda granted him that boon;
then he beheld directly from Hari two hands resembling lotus buds.
His feet, adorned with vajra- and vaidūrya-studded anklets,
were worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, and other gods as well as by sages.
Having renounced his life-breaths, the son of the Earth attained the same form as Hari;
thereafter, all the hosts of gods were their minds filled with overflowing joy.
As the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa was entering that city, the great ṛṣis rained down showers of flowers and offered hymns of praise.
By force he seized the jewels of the inhabitants of heaven,
as well as the two earrings of the divine mother and the horse Uccaiḥśravas.
Airāvata, the best of elephants, and the blazing mountain of jewels—
all this the best of the Yadus gave to Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Having conquered the kings from all kingdoms,
that powerful Naraka then carried off sixteen thousand maidens.
Then, within the inner city of all the hells,
those who had been suppressed and censured saw Kṛṣṇa of great heroism, who resembled a hundredfold pride.
They all chose as their husband the Lord of the universe, the omnipresent one;
at that very moment, Govinda appeared in an infinite form.
Then Puruṣottama took their hands in marriage according to the prescribed rites,
while all the sons of Naraka placed Mahī at their head.
They went to Govinda for refuge, and he, the treasury of compassion, protected them;
out of respect for his word, he established all of them in that kingdom upon the earth.
Having placed Draupadī upon a celestial chariot along with all her other women,
the illustrious messengers of the gods settled them in Dvāravatī.
Mounting Vainateya together with Satyabhāmā, Keśava went swiftly to the heavenly world to behold that mother of the gods.
Entering the city there, O best of the twice-born, the mighty Janārdana, having descended from the king of gods, went together with his wife. 82.
There, Aditi, who is deeply affectionate toward her sons, embraced with both arms her mother Vaṃ and that Vaṃ, the consort of the dwellers of the triple heaven.
Having seated them upon the principal seats, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and those led by Śatakratu worshipped them with devotion. 84.
There, having arrived at the chamber of Śacī, the illustrious Satyabhāmā worshipped the Supreme Lord as was fitting. 85.
While she was seated upon a comfortable throne, having been worshipped by that goddess,
at that time the attendants of Pārijāta brought excellent flowers.
Urged by the thousand-eyed Indra out of affection for Queen Śacī, those flowers were taken up by the slender-waisted Goddess Śacī.
And he bound his own hair, which was dark and pure, upon his head,
having there disregarded the illustrious Satyabhāmā, who had surpassed Śacī.
Thinking, "This woman is unworthy of these auspicious flowers fit for a god," he [the king] gave her those flowers. (89)
Having departed from that city, the lotus-eyed Satyabhāmā, filled with indignation, approached her husband Kṛṣṇa and spoke to him.
Satyabhāmā said:
"O Govinda, this Śacī, arrogant because of her excellent Pārijāta tree, bound me by my hair without giving it to me. (91)
Mahādeva said:
Having heard what was spoken by Satyabhāmā, the mighty Vāsudeva uprooted the Pārijāta tree and placed it upon Garuḍa.
Having swiftly mounted the immensely powerful Vainateya, the son of Devakī set out for the beautiful city of Dvārakā. 93.
Then Śatakratu, the king of the gods, overcome with anger,
[was joined] by the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts.
Having mounted Airāvata, he went forth to battle against Keśava;
then all the hosts of gods approached Janārdana with great joy.
They rained down showers of weapons upon him like clouds upon a great mountain;
Kṛṣṇa, however, cut those missiles of the gods with his discus.
But the powerful Vainateya, filled with rage,
struck down those gods with his wing-beats, just as the wind scatters stalks of straw.
Then the thousand-eyed lord and master of the gods, filled with rage and desiring to slay Kṛṣṇa, suddenly hurled his blazing thunderbolt.
Kṛṣṇa playfully seized that thunderbolt with a single hand;
thereupon, the thousand-eyed Indra became afraid and descended from the king of serpents.
Standing before him with palms joined in reverence and having paid homage to Janārdana,
he spoke with a voice faltering with emotion, after first praising him with hymns of praise.
Indra said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, this Pārijāta tree, which was fit for the gods and previously given by you to me and the Asuras, how will it remain among mortals? (101)
Mahādeva said:
Then the Blessed One spoke to the thousand-eyed one who stood before him:
"O Lord of the Gods, you have been humiliated by Śacī in your own home because of your truthfulness."
Without having given the *apārijāta* flowers to Satyabhāmā, the beloved Pulomajā herself wore them upon her own head. (103)
O Lord of Gods, the *pārijāta* tree was taken by me for her sake;
O Sovereign of the hosts of gods, it was promised by me to be given to her. (104)
"O Vāsava, I shall place the Pārijāta tree in your house;
therefore, O Lord of the Gods, the Pārijāta must not be given away today. (105)
"For the benefit of the deities, I shall bring [the Pārijāta] to the surface of the earth;
therefore, O Lord of the Gods, let the Pārijāta remain in my abode for now. (106)
"O Śakra, when I have gone to heaven, take [this] as you desire.
Mahādeva said:
Having spoken thus, the best of the Yadus himself gave the thunderbolt to him. 107.
Saying "So be it," the wielder of the thunderbolt paid homage to Govinda and departed for his own divine city, surrounded by hosts of deities.
Kṛṣṇa also, seated upon Garuḍa together with Queen Satyabhāmā and being praised by the sages, entered Dvārakā.
Having established the celestial tree Pārijāta near Satyabhāmā, Hari,
who pervades all things, delighted her with all his wives.
In the houses of all those daughters of Niśā, the glorious Madhusūdana, assuming his universal form (viśvarūpa), dwelt, bestowing happiness. 111.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Marriage of Śrī Vāsudeva," within the *Śrīkṛṣṇacarita* section of the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||249|| ||cha||
(250) Chapter Two Hundred and Fifty: Śrī Rudra said:
From Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, Pradyumna was born from the god of love, Madana. ||1||
Having become the destroyer of Madana, that one of great power struck down the excellent Śambara. ||2||
To that Rukmī, a son named Aniruddha was born from his daughter.
He married the daughter of Bāṇa, a maiden named Uṣā. ||4||

In a dream, she enjoyed for sixteen years one who was dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes like white lotuses, long-armed, and adorned with various ornaments; yet upon waking, not seeing him before her,
she became bewildered, tormented by passion.
But having abandoned her life-breath, she lamented in many ways: "O red-lotus-faced one, where are you? Where have you gone? (5)
Then her friend, a maiden named Citralekhā, seeing her reduced to such a state, asked, "For what reason is your mind so bewildered? (6)
She, too, related exactly as it had happened her husband whom she had found in a dream.
She too, having depicted all the most excellent among gods, humans, and others upon a cloth, showed it to her. ||8||
He also correctly described those born of the Yadu lineage, such as Kṛṣṇa, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and others. ||9||
Having honored Kṛṣṇa and seen Aniruddha immediately after Pradyumna, she embraced him, saying, "This is he! ||10||

Then Citralekhā, accompanied by many illusory demonesses, went to Dvāravatī; having seen Aniruddha sleeping at night within the inner apartments, she seized him, enchanted him, and cast him onto the bed of Bāṇa’s daughter in Māhiṣmatī, a place filled with shrines, palaces, and other structures belonging to Bāṇa’s harem. ||11||
Then the awakened one, seeing Uṣā— who was situated in the Ananga-pāvaka grove, endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with various ornaments, garments,

perfumes, and garlands, golden-hued, with beautiful hair and well-formed breasts— firmly embraced her as an elephant does a female elephant, and being filled with great affection, he enjoyed her pleasure as she desired. ||12||
Thus, as he continued to sport without interruption for the duration of a month, some elderly Daitya women living in the inner apartments eventually discovered him and reported it to Rāhu. ||13||
The king, his eyes copper-red with anger and filled with great astonishment, dispatched attendants before him, saying, "Bring that man here! ||14||
They too, having quickly ascended the royal palace, arrived to seize Aniruddha as he lay upon the princess’s bed. ||15||
Seeing the virtuous ones who had exerted themselves, he playfully uprooted a single palace with his hand and, in a mere moment, reduced millions of them to mere dust. ||16||

Then the lord of the Daityas, seeing his servants slain, was filled with curiosity; having been told by the celestial sage that this youth was the grandson of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he took up his bow and approached Aniruddha himself to seize him. Aniruddha, seeing the thousand-armed king coming to fight, whirled his iron club and hurled it at Bāṇa. With an arrow released from his own bow, [Bāṇa] cut that iron club to pieces.

Immediately thereafter, having bound Aniruddha tightly with the serpent-missile (*uragāstra*), he confined him within his own inner apartments. (20) Then Kṛṣṇa, having learned of this very situation from the celestial sage (*devarṣi*), ascended his aerial chariot (*vimāna*) together with Baladeva and Pradyumna and his own army, and arrived there to sever the forest of Bāṇa’s arms. (21) Formerly, Śaṅkara had been worshipped by the son of Bali; being pleased, he said, "Choose a boon. (22)

Bāṇa requested this boon of the Lord: "Please remain seated at the gate of my city at all times for its protection, and destroy any enemy army that approaches. (23) Having said "So be it" to him, Śaṅkara likewise sat at the gate of his city, equipped with weapons and accompanied by his son and his hosts. At that very moment, seeing Vāsudeva approaching with his own army in a state of wrath, he mounted his bull and, endowed with all his weapons and surrounded by his son and his hosts, went forth to fight. (24)
Kṛṣṇa, too, beheld that Lord of Beings—wearing an elephant hide, a skull, and ashes; adorned with blazing serpents; tawny-hued, three-eyed, and bearing a trident;

the destroyer of all hosts of spirits, the source of fear for all beings, radiant as the fire of universal dissolution, accompanied by his two sons and surrounded by his entire retinue—the Destroyer of Tripura.
Having stationed his army at a great distance behind him, he stood together with Balabhadra and Pradyumna, laughing in the presence of that Rudra.
He began to blow his age [upon him]. ||25||
At that time, there first occurred a terrible encounter between Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara,
with arrows resembling thunderbolts released from the Pināka and Śārṅga bows.
Rāma fought with Bāṇa, and Pradyumna with Ṣaṇmukha;
those two of great heroism fought like two lions fierce in their strength.
Vināyaka struck the Yādava on the chest with his own tusk;
Rāma, seizing a mace, struck his tusk.
With his tusk shattered, he whose vehicle is a mouse suddenly fled;
from that time forth, the Lord of Gaṇas has been known in this world as Hatadanta (the One with the Broken Tusk).
Addressed as "Ekadanta" by the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas,
he whose vehicle is the peacock engaged in battle with Pradyumna.
The wielder of the plow, Hala-yudha, drove away the hosts with his mace;
that Nīlalohita fought with Kṛṣṇa for a very long time.
Having fixed upon that arrow a burning fever of great intensity,
he, his eyes bloodshot with rage, released it violently.
Then Kṛṣṇa warded off that weapon with the Śītajvara;
those two fevers were indeed discharged by Hari and Hara.
By the command of those very two, Hari and Śaṅkara, men who hear of their battle enter intensely into the world of mortals.
They all became free from fever and attained a state of health;
then Hṛṣīkeśa [discharged] the invincible Mohanāstra.
Madhusūdana fixed an arrow to his bow and discharged it at Bhūteśa;
repeatedly expanding [his power], he was not bewildered by that non-dual weapon.
Śaṅkara, the lord of the thirty gods, fell to the ground unconscious;
seeing his father thus deluded, the heroic one raised up his spear.
The six-faced one, whose vehicle is the peacock, advanced to fight Kṛṣṇa;
but with a mere "huṃ" sound, Kṛṣṇa turned him away from the battle.
Having thus conquered the three-eyed wielder of the trident, that best of the Yadus,
the majestic one, blew his loud-sounding conch shell, Pāñcajanya.
Having heard then that his son Śaṅkara had been defeated by Kṛṣṇa,
Bāṇa mounted his chariot and went forth to battle Keśava.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa suddenly stationed upon Garuḍa,
he covered Govinda with showers of many weapons and missiles.
[The battle was] continuous with maces, iron clubs, spears, javelins, and even lances; with slings, swords, discuses, and arrows.
Janārdana cut all of them with his discus alone;
he discharged the Sudarśana for the purpose of severing his arms.
The thousand-spoked Sudarśana, hurled by the king of the Danujas,
was swiftly cut into a thousand pieces upon his arm by Ananta.
Then, immediately after that, the goddess Pārvatī, firm in her vows,
approached the presence of Hari and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Pārvatī said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Universe, Nārāyaṇa, ocean of mercy!
O Lord of Gods, best of the Yadus, may I be Your maidservant in my previous birth. 46.
O gentle one, on Mount Ākauśala, that boon was granted to me by you, the high-souled one, who were pleased with me, [granting] eternal good fortune. (47)
O All-pervading Lord, You are the foremost among the thousand names, one of which is celebrated by the sages as "Gaurī-saubhāgya-dātā" (the Giver of Good Fortune to Gaurī). 48.
O eternal one, mounted upon Garuḍa, O Govinda, let that be true;
therefore, you ought to restore my husband to life as a god. (49)
Rudra said:
Having been addressed thus by the Goddess, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa,
whose husband was deluded by him, then withdrew his weapon.
Released by the *kṛṣṇa* weapon, Śiva, the lord of all beings, rose up with palms joined in reverence and praised the Lord of the worlds. (51)
Śaṅkara said: O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World, Bhava, Puruṣottama; Supreme Lord, Highest Sovereign, without beginning or end, undecaying!
Among humans, this intense energy consists of the assumption of a body;
all this activity of yours is characterized by pride alone.
Be gracious to me, O Eternal One; be gracious to me, O Impermanent One.
Be gracious, O Lord of the moving and unmoving world; be gracious, O Acyuta, O Keśava! 54
You alone are the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the worlds; you are the teacher of the world.
You alone, O Lord of Gods, are Brahman, appearing in the form of both the conscious and the unconscious.
You are the beginning, you are the beginningless, you are the Lord, and you are indeed Śeṣa;
you are the Great Principle (Mahat), you are the Supreme Brahman, and you alone are the inner self (pratyagātman). 56.
You are the foremost among all the immortals; you are the immortal one, O Lord of the gods.
You are the lord of mortals, yet you possess a physical form, O Lord, by virtue of your excellent character.
The eternal Upa and Rajīva were born from your breath;
therefore, they are protected by you out of affection and respect.

I have placed you—who are beyond the perishable and the imperishable, who eternally shine as the supreme abode of the gods, and who reside within the universe—within my heart for the sake of the service of a servant. 59.
But he who, deluded in this world, does not know you—the creator of all beings, the Lord of the high and the low, the abode whom the wise know as the servant—[he is lost]. (60)
Devoted to them, they dwell for twenty-five years in that state equal to the gods;
however, one who shares in common with them remains far from your eternal state.
But for you, O eternal one of the Yadu clan, the states of Ruci and Ārūkeśī are possible; they declare that these pairs are under your direct supervision.
Their names, karmas, qualities, and eternal sovereignties—these supreme ones are said to transcend all attributes. (63)
These two forms, consisting of karma and jñāna, were heard of previously and subsequently;
they are the two sons of the Lord of Youth, the praisers of Tvaṣṭṛ and Keśava. 64.
You are supreme consciousness, the eternal Brahman; by you, who are conscious, O eternal one, let [all beings] be enlivened through this supreme consciousness, which is indeed your own self.
Therefore, having departed from that body out of compassion,
you have bestowed upon me the realization of the Self in the supreme otherworldly heaven.
One attains wisdom, discernment, intelligence, vision, and likewise fortitude;
one obtains all desires and then becomes immortal. (67)
This very consciousness is the self, which is that which is in the heart and the mind;
it is also intention, resolve, deliberation, reasoning, memory, and volition.
O Lord, austerity, the Vedas, desire, joy, coolness, and so forth—these are merely names for that which is primordial consciousness, O treasury of compassion. (69)
You are this supreme Brahman; you indeed are Prajāpati.
You are Indra and Rudra; you are all the deities.
All these beings are indeed you alone, O Supreme Lord; sons, friends, living beings, life-force, and likewise all others, O Eternal One. (71)
Those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouting;
horses, cows, humans, elephants, and others as well. (72)
Whatever living beings there may be— whether moving creatures or stationary entities— all of them indeed come into existence from you.
For they say that Hari, the object of their sacred learning, has entered into you; it is by you alone that people are impelled toward what is right or wrong in their actions. (74)
Therefore, O Lord, ocean of compassion, please forgive whatever offense I have committed against you by virtue of your most auspicious qualities. (75)
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, Govinda, Acyuta, Mādhava;
O Vāsudeva, glory of the world, Nārāyaṇa, let there be salutation to you! (76)
I bow to you, O Lord of the universe, the destroyer of suffering, the mine of compassion!
O Śrīśa, omnipresent one, glorious Supreme Self, let there be salutation unto you! 77.
O Lord worshipped by the eternally liberated ones in your own abode of Vaikuṇṭha, O Rāma, lotus-eyed Lord of the Triple Veda, salutations to you! 78.
Obeisance to You, O delight of the Yadus, who take the form of Kṛṣṇānanda for the destruction of the earth's burden; obeisance to Viṣṇu, the victorious one. 79.
Having thus praised Govinda and prostrated before him, Umāpati, the Lord of Beings, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words in a profound voice: 80.
Rudra said:
"O Lord, this Bāṇa, the son of Bali, has been granted a boon by me;
and I myself previously granted him a boon when he requested it. (81)
O best of the Yadus, you are capable of accomplishing everything, including immortality;
therefore, you ought to protect this son of Bali, who is dear to me. (82)
Having said "So be it," the Blessed One then [addressed] Bāṇa, the son of Bali,
who had fallen into a life-threatening crisis with his arm severed and drenched in blood.
Having withdrawn the discus, Govinda, the ocean of compassion, released him;
and Śaṅkara, whose vows are firm, having liberated the son of Bali, [departed]. (84)
Having mounted his lordly bull together with Pārvatī, the Lord went to his dwelling place,
Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth.
Having paid homage to the two of great strength, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
Satrāyaṇa went with them to the city and released the son of Madana.
Having honored him as was fitting with divine garments and ornaments,
he gave Uṣā to that descendant of Śūra, the grandson of Kṛṣṇa.
Then Bāṇa worshipped Rāma and Kṛṣṇa— who had married Aniruddha according to the prescribed rites— along with Pradyumna.
Then Janārdana, having placed Aniruddha there together with Uṣā upon his divine chariot, departed for Dvāravatī.
Accompanied by Rāma and Pradyumna and joined by his army, Hari entered the beautiful city, just as Maghavan enters [heaven] with the gods.
Aniruddha, filled with joy, constantly delighted Bāṇa’s daughter in a palace made of various jewels with manifold enjoyments. ||91||

Thus ends the two hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Battle with Bāṇāsura," in the Umā-Maheśvara Saṃvāda of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī-Padma Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||250||
(251) Śrī Rudra said:
Now, Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva, or rather the King of Kāśī, was worshipping Maheśvara for twelve years in a secluded place at Vārāṇasī while remaining without food.
He recited the five-syllable mantra. ||1||
At the time of the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), he worshipped Lord Śaṅkara with his own lotus-like eye. ||2||
Then the trident-bearing Lord of Umā, being pleased, said: "Choose a boon."
He said, "Grant me that five-faced Śiva, the lord of all beings, who is gracious, the bestower of boons, and whose form is equal to that of Mādhava-Vāsudeva. ||4||

Requested by him, saying, "O Śiva, grant to me also the four arms joined with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; eyes resembling the petals of a white lotus; a beautiful crown and earrings like those of Vāsudeva; and the marks such as yellow garments and the Kaustubha jewel," Śiva bestowed all of that upon him. ||5||
He deluded all the worlds by saying, "I am Vāsudeva. ||6||

Once, having come from heaven, Nārada approached the Lord of Kāśī, who was arrogant with the pride of his own power, and said: "As long as you have not conquered the son of Vasudeva, you do not truly possess the status of a Vāsudeva."
In that very moment, having mounted a swift chariot adorned with the form of a Garuda banner, he reached Dvārakā with an army of one Akṣauhiṇī.

There, stationed upon a golden chariot at the city gate, I, Vāsudeva, sent forth a messenger, saying: "I have arrived for the sake of battle; until you have defeated me, your status as Vāsudeva does not exist. (9)

Viṣṇu, having heard that, mounted Garuḍa and went forth from the city gate to fight with Pauṇḍraka; he beheld Pauṇḍraka seated upon a chariot with an akṣauhiṇī of troops, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in his hands.

Then Kṛṣṇa, taking up his Śārṅga bow, completely incinerated that great army of one akṣauhiṇī— consisting of dogs, elephants, and foot soldiers— with arrows as bright as blazing fire in a mere moment.
With a single arrow, he effortlessly severed even the weapons—the conch, discus, mace, and others—held in his hands. ||12||
Having severed his lotus-like head—adorned with a crown and earrings—with the Sudarśana discus as a purifier, he caused it to fall within the inner apartments in Vārāṇasī. ||13||
Seeing that, all the inhabitants of Kāśī were struck with wonder, wondering, "What is this? ||14||

Having heard that his father Pauṇḍraka had been slain by the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, Daṇḍapāṇi, who was already afflicted by the death of his mother, was urged by his own priest and performed a sacrifice to Śaṅkara according to the ritual of the Great Lord (Māheśvara). ||15||
Being well-pleased, Śatru gave to him with great affection a Māheśvarī Kṛtyā, who was capable of slaying Kṛṣṇa. ||16||

King Śaka beheld that great goddess, whose body was thickly covered with flames, whose mass of manes was ablaze, whose eyes were tawny, whose terrifying face was glowing, who held a trident in her hand, who was smeared with ashes and red sandalwood paste, adorned with a garland of human skulls, and who struck fear into all the gods; seeing her—whom Rudra had granted—he urged her, saying, "Kill Kṛṣṇa along with his sons, wife, and kinsmen. ||17||
Causing fear to the entire world, burning the whole earth with his own splendor, and uttering a roar like the thunderclap of the dissolution, he entered the city of Dvārakā. 18.
There, all those people, seeing her and thinking it was the great dissolution of the world, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! and informed Kṛṣṇa. ||19||
Kṛṣṇa, having told them all, "Do not fear," and seeing that most terrible *kṛtyā* stationed at the gateway of the rampart,
suddenly released his thousand-spoked Sudarśana discus— which is capable of warding off all weapons and missiles— at that *kṛtyā*.

But she, beholding the Great Sudarśana—which possessed a splendor equal to ten million suns at the end of an eon, rose a hundred yojanas high, was equipped with all radiant weapons, golden-hued, filled with light, capable of causing the dissolution and maintenance of the entire world, thousand-spoked, saluted by all the gods, and serving as the refuge of the universe—fled toward Vārāṇasī, crying out, her own luster destroyed and afflicted by fear. ||21||
Sudarśana also followed that Kṛtyā very closely. ||22||
Afflicted by fear and crying out, she entered the inner apartments of that lord of Kāśī. ||23||

Sudarśana, having reached that city of Vārāṇasī, reduced to ashes even that city of the Lord of Maheśvara—which was garlanded with many palaces and mansions—along with the son of Pauṇḍraka, the King of Kāśī named Daṇḍapāṇi, together with his servants, army, and mounts; and being honored by all the gods and great sages, he returned once more to Dvāravatī and entered the very gentle hand of Kṛṣṇa like a well-ordered ritual. ||24||
And here these verses are sung:
"Having burned that inexhaustible power [of the enemy] by means of his own vigor, he reduced the discharge of their weapons and missiles to mere ashes; then he went to the city of Vārāṇasī. (25)
Abounding in chariots, elephants, and horses, and filled with men and women;
containing all its treasuries and granaries, it was difficult even for the gods to behold.
The discus of Hari completely incinerated that entire city, including its gates, the rest of its houses, its walls, and its courtyards.
With its power of movement unimpaired and having accomplished what was impossible to achieve,
that wheel, blazing with radiance, approached the hand of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Destruction of the Sorcery Created by Pauṇḍraka’s Son," within the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Carita* in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttara-Khaṇḍa of the *Śrī-Pādma-Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(252) Chapter Two Hundred and Fifty-Two.
Śrī Rudra said:

Then, after the killing of Kaṃsa, the lord of Magadha, remaining hostile toward the Yādavas, constantly oppressed them; being distressed, they spoke to Kṛṣṇa. (1) And Kṛṣṇa, having summoned Bhīma and Arjuna, deliberated with them: "By him, Rudra was worshipped; therefore, by his grace, he cannot be slain by weapons, yet he must be killed by some other means. (2)
Then, having reflected, he said to Bhīma, "Engage in this wrestling match with him"; that was promised by him.

Then Vāsudeva, who is worshipped by the entire world of moving and unmoving beings, went to the city of Jarāsaṃdha accompanied by Bhīma and Arjuna, and having assumed the guise of a brahmin, he entered his inner apartments.

He too, having conquered powerful Kṣatriyas in battle and taken them by force, confined them in his own residence; then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of every month, he killed one of them and offered a sacrifice to Bhairava with their blood alone. ||5||
While Jarāsandha was thus engaged in the slaughter of all people and kings, Bhīma and Arjuna, exerting themselves together, entered his palace in the very guise of brahmins.

But having seen them, he prostrated himself like a staff, seated them on appropriate seats, and honored them according to the ritual of *madhuparka*, saying: "I am blessed; I have fulfilled my purpose. For what reason have you come to me? Let that be told, and I shall give all of it to you. ||7||
Smiling, Vāsudeva said to that king: "We have come for the purpose of battle with Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Arjuna; approach one of us and choose him for a duel. Thus he spoke.
He replied, "So be it," and then chose Māruti for a duel. ||9||
Then, a terrifying wrestling match between Bhīma and Jarāsandha took place continuously for twenty-five days. ||10||
Then, urged by Kṛṣṇa himself, the son of Vāyu (Bhīma) split his body in two and cast it to the ground.
Having thus slain Jarāsandha, Vāsudeva also liberated those kings who had been imprisoned by Jarāsandha by means of the sons of Pāṇḍu. ||11||
Having caused the son of Vāyu to slay both Jarāsandha and Sandha, the upholder of the Yadu lineage liberated the kings who had been imprisoned in his palace.
And having there paid homage to and praised Madhusūdana, they all, protected by Kṛṣṇa, returned to their respective districts. 13.
Then, having gone to Indraprastha with those two, Vāsudeva caused Yudhiṣṭhira to perform there the great royal sacrifice, the Rājasūya.
There, when the sacrifice was completed, he offered the foremost honor to Kṛṣṇa with the approval of Bhīṣma. ||15||
There, Śiśupāla addressed many insulting words to Kṛṣṇa. ||16||
Kṛṣṇa, too, severed his head with the Sudarśana [discus]. ||17||
At the conclusion of three births, he attained the same form as Hari. ||18||
Then, having heard that Śiśupāla had been slain, Dantavakra came to Mathurā to fight with Kṛṣṇa. ||19||

Having heard that, Kṛṣṇa mounted his chariot and went to Mathurā to fight with him. A battle took place between Dantavakra and Vāsudeva at the gate of the city of Mathurā on the bank of the Yamunā for a day and a night; then Kṛṣṇa struck him with his mace.
But he, with all his limbs crushed like a mountain split asunder by a thunderbolt, fell lifeless upon the surface of the earth. ||22||
He too attained the supreme state of union with Hari—a state accessible to yogis, characterized by eternal bliss and happiness, and forever abiding. ||23||

Thus, Jaya and Vijaya, having descended into the cycle of worldly existence solely for the sake of the Lord's pastimes under the pretext of the curse of Sanaka and the others, were slain by Him himself even during three births; at the conclusion of those three births, they attained liberation. (24)

Kṛṣṇa, having slain him and crossed the Yamunā, went to Nanda’s cowherd settlement; there he saluted his former parents and comforted them, being embraced by them with throats choked with tears. Having bowed to all the elder cowherds and comforted them, he gratified those present there with jewel-ornaments and other gifts. ||25||
On the delightful bank of the Kālindī, surrounded by sacred trees,
Keśava played incessantly with the cowherd women.
Indeed, through the very joy of delightful pastimes, Hari, wearing the dress of a cowherd,
dwelt there for two months, bound by the essence of love.

Then all the people staying there, such as Nanda and Gopā, together with their sons and wives, as well as the beasts, birds, and wild animals, by the grace of Vāsudeva, assumed divine forms, ascended a celestial chariot, and reached the supreme realm of Vaikuṇṭha. ||28||
But Kṛṣṇa, having granted His supreme, stainless abode to all the inhabitants of Nanda-gopa’s Vraja, entered the glorious city of Dvāravatī while being praised by hosts of gods in heaven. ||29||

There, assuming His universal form (*viśvarūpa*), He took delight with Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Akrūra, and others, as well as with His sixteen thousand wives who were honored daily by them, and with His eight divine queens, within various mansions made of celestial jewels; there, upon very smooth couches strewn with flowers, He enjoyed their company. ||30||

Then a brahmin, a fellow student of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa and their childhood friend, who was constantly tormented by extreme poverty, tied together in a worn-out garment the flattened rice he had obtained by begging in a mere handful and came to the glorious city of Dvārakā to see Vāsudeva. ||31||
He, however, stood silently for a moment at the door of Rukmiṇī’s inner apartments.

Kṛṣṇa, perceiving that the brāhmaṇa had arrived, was saluted by Pradyumna; taking him by the left hand and seating him on a comfortable seat within the house, he washed the feet of the trembling brāhmaṇa—who was quivering with fear—with water from a golden pitcher held in Rukmiṇī’s hand, and honored him with the madhuparka offering. ||33||

Having gratified him with food, drink, and other offerings comparable to nectar and ambrosia, he himself took from between his own worn-out garments the puffed rice obtained through begging, and laughing, he ate it with his own hand. ||34||
At the very moment Kṛṣṇa ate the *pṛthuka* grains, he attained great sovereignty, consisting of abundant wealth, grain, clothing, and ornaments. ||35||
But he, having been dismissed by Kṛṣṇa, entered his own city thinking, "Kṛṣṇa has not given me any garment or wealth. ||36||

Then, seeing his own home filled with abundant wealth and grain, and saying, "This was obtained through His grace," he, with a joyful inner self, enjoyed all desires together with his wife, adorned with divine garments and ornaments; and having performed many sacrifices for the satisfaction of Hari, he attained by His grace the supreme, eternal bliss of heaven. ||37||
Then Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having seized the kingdom from the sons of Pāṇḍu under the pretext of a fraudulent game of dice, banished them from his own realm. ||38||

Those [Pāṇḍavas]—Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva—having gone to the great forest together with their noble wife Draupadī and remained there for twelve years, and having all stayed undetected for one year in the residence of Virāṭa, the lord of the Matsya country, returned with Vāsudeva as their ally to fight the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. ||39||

Between those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, along with kings who were lords of various lands, there occurred a great battle at the highly meritorious Kurukṣetra, which struck fear even into the gods. ||40||

Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, acting as Arjuna’s charioteer and infusing him with His own power, caused him to slay all the kings led by Duryodhana, Bhīṣma, and Droṇa, along with their eleven akṣauhiṇīs of forces at Kurukṣetra; having thus established the Pāṇḍavas as the preeminent men and completely removed the entire burden of the earth, He entered His own city. ||41||

Then, after some time had passed, on a certain day, a Vedic brahmin arrived at the palace gate carrying a five-year-old boy who was his only son; placing him there and lamenting profusely, he addressed Kṛṣṇa with many words of reproach. (42)
Having heard that reproach, Kṛṣṇa remained silent.
"But my five sons were killed previously; this is the sixth. Kṛṣṇa will not let him live, and then I shall die at the king's gate," he said. ||44||
At that time, Arjuna arrived to see Kṛṣṇa and beheld him in such a state, lamenting out of grief for his son. ||45||

Arjuna, too, seeing the five-year-old boy who had met his end through the law of time, was overcome with compassion; he granted the brahmin assurance of safety and promised, "I shall restore your son to life. (46)
Reassured by the praise of the Brahmin, he was delighted. ||47||

Then, seeing that the Brahmin boy had not regained life despite being consecrated with many life-restoring mantras, and having thus failed in his vow, he was overcome with great grief and desired to give up his own life by that very means.

Kṛṣṇa, having understood all of that, emerged from the inner apartments and said to Vaidika, "I shall give you all your sons. Having thus consoled him, he mounted Garuḍa and, accompanied by Arjuna, went to the realm of Viṣṇu. ||49||
There, having seen Nārāyaṇa seated together with the Goddess in the vicinity of a celestial jewel-pavilion, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna paid their respects.
Embracing them with both arms, he said, "For what purpose have you come? (51)
And the Blessed Kṛṣṇa said, "Give me the son of the Vedic man. ||52||
Satunārāyaṇa gave those sons of Brāhmaṇas, who were of his own age, to Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, filled with joy and accompanied by Arjuna, placed them upon the back of Garuḍa; then, having mounted it himself while being praised by the hosts of gods in heaven, he entered Dvāravatī.
He gave those six sons, who were five years of age, to that brāhmaṇa; and he too, filled with extreme joy, bestowed the blessing: "May you cause Kṛṣṇa to prosper. (55)
Arjuna, having fulfilled his vow and paid homage to Kṛṣṇa, returned to his own city, which was protected by Yudhiṣṭhira. ||56||
From Kṛṣṇa’s sixteen thousand wives, ten million sons were born; it is impossible to recount the number of their sons and grandsons. ||57||
Regarding this, there is also a verse:
"There were eight hundred, a thousand, and likewise ten thousand sons;
Pradyumna was the first among them all, the son of Rukmiṇī. (58)
This earth became completely covered by those Yādavas, who were beyond counting.
Furthermore, wishing to remove the burden of the earth, Kṛṣṇa desired to bring about his own destruction under the pretext of a curse from the Ṛṣis.
Once, all the Kumāras came to sport upon the Narmadā. ||61||
There, having seen the great seer Kaṇva performing austerities, she disguised herself as a woman, tied an iron mace to the belly of that son of Jāmbavatī,
approached the presence of Aṅgiras, paid obeisance to everyone, and placed that boy— who was her husband in disguise— before him.
"Tell us," they said, "whether there will be a woman or a man in her womb. ||62||
Unable to endure their contemptuous disregard, he said to them all: "By this mace, you shall all be slain! ||63||
With their minds agitated, they all approached Kṛṣṇa and reported that deed which had been spoken by the great sage.
Kṛṣṇa also then threw that iron club, which had been pulverized, into the lake.
Then, great spaces resembling diamonds arose, produced from seeds that had been reduced to powder. ||66||

There, a fish swallowed that remnant of the pestle which was the size of the little finger; a fisherman, having caught that fish, took the fragment of the pestle from its belly and fashioned a blade for the tip of an arrow.
Once, all the Yadavas—Rama, Krishna, Pradyumna, and the others—became intoxicated after drinking the Vāruṇī liquor sent by Indra.
Taking up *vīraṇa* grass against one another and uttering many words of abuse, they fought and met their destruction. ||69||
Kṛṣṇa, exhausted from battle, lay down to rest in the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree; then, taking up his bow and arrows along with a quiver, he went out for the purpose of hunting.
Thus, having completely renounced their lives, they all attained their respective celestial realms.

Having thus withdrawn everything by means of the *mūśalena-saṃhṛti*, the one God alone, sleeping in the shade of a great tree crowded with many thickets, meditated upon himself as Vāsudeva abiding in the fourfold array (*caturvidhavyūha*); then, placing his foot upon his knee, he sat down, intending to cast off his human form.

In that interval, a hunter who made his living by hunting saw, through the power of his accumulated merit, the lotus-foot of Hari— marked with the signs of the discus, thunderbolt, banner, and kusha grass, and exceedingly red—
and pierced it. ||73||

Immediately thereafter, recognizing him as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he was overcome with great fear; bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he, having committed a great offense, prostrated before him, saying, "May my entire transgression be forgiven. (74)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa, seeing him in such a state, raised him up with his nectar-filled hands and, saying, "No offense has been committed by you," spoke while consoling him who was afflicted by great fear. ||75||
Then he bestowed upon him the world of Viṣṇu, which is accessible to yogis, eternal, from which there is no return, and which consists of all the Upaniṣads. ||76||

At that very moment, he abandoned his human form and, together with all his sons and wife, ascended a divine celestial chariot—resplendent like the light of a thousand suns, filled with hosts of divine apsarases, and made of gold—and went to the radiant Vaiṣṇava realm consisting of the five Upaniṣads, crying out "Vāsudeva! alone. (77)
At that time, having mounted a chariot made of wood, he entered into the presence of Viṣṇu.
Kṛṣṇa also sent word to Arjuna, saying, "Bring me first to my own form. ||79||
Having mounted the chariot swift as thought, he approached the presence of Arjuna. ||80||
Then, having ascended that very chariot and circumambulated it, Arjuna, with palms joined in reverence, said, "What shall I do? ||81||
Kṛṣṇa said to Pārtha: "I shall go to my own world, but you, having gone to Dvāravatī, should bring Rukmiṇī and my other seven wives from there and send them to me in my physical body. [82]
Accompanied by Sadāruka, he arrived at the city. ||83||

Then, from within that [chariot], the gods stationed in their celestial mansions in the sky, seeing Kṛṣṇa together with the sages about to depart for the heavenly world, offered praises and rained down showers of flowers.

Kṛṣṇa also, assuming a human form—that body which is the cause of the maintenance and destruction of the entire world, which is the inner witness of all fields of experience (*kṣetrajña*), the object of meditation for yogis, free from affliction, and whose essence is Vāsudeva—mounted upon Garuḍa and departed while being praised by the great sages. 85.
Arjuna related all of that to Vasudeva, Ugrasena, and his principal queens, headed by Rukmiṇī. ||86||

Having heard that, all the citizens and women, abandoning Dvārakā and emerging from the inner apartments, all those beloveds of Kṛṣṇa went quickly into the presence of Hari, accompanied by Vasudeva and Ugrasena. ||87||
All of them—Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Akrūra, and all the elders of the Yadu clan—abandoning their seats, approached the eternal Vāsudeva.

Revatī, having embraced the body of Balabhadra and entered the fire, attained a divine celestial chariot upon reaching that [fire] and reached the divine realm of Saṅkarṣaṇa, the abode of her husband. ||89||
In the same manner, Pradyumna with his golden daughter, as well as Aniruddha with Uṣā, and all the Yādava women, having honored the bodies of their respective husbands, entered the fire. (90)
Arjuna performed the funeral rites for all of them. ||91||
At that time, Dāruka also arrived, having mounted a divine chariot named Sugrīva, which was yoked with celestial horses and endowed with every kind of jewel. ||92||
The Pārijāta tree went from the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods to the world of Indra, Tridaśa. ||93||
At that time, the city of Dvāravatī was submerged in the great ocean. ||94||
Then, as all his sixteen thousand wives were going to Indraprastha with Arjuna, bandits seized them. ||95||
Formerly, when the wives of the gods and Gandharvas saw the great sage Aṣṭāvakra, they laughed; consequently, he cursed them, saying, "You shall become prostitutes.

Later, having propitiated and honored him, and by his grace having obtained Vāsudeva—who is saluted by all the worlds—as their husband, they nevertheless fell into the hands of a bandit because of that very same [past] act.

Arjuna, too, defeated by bandits and overwhelmed with grief, thinking that all his sovereign power and heroic strength of arm had vanished along with Kṛṣṇa, returned to his own city like the evening sun whose brilliance has completely perished, saying, "Today my good fortune has come to an end. (97)

Thus, for the benefit of all the gods and for the destruction of the entire burden of the earth, He descended into the Yadu lineage; having brought about the destruction of all the *rākṣasas* and having eliminated even the great burden of the earth, He liberated all inhabitants— both mobile and immobile— of Ānanda-vraja, Dvārakā, and Mathurā from the bonds of time and worldly existence, and established them in the supreme, eternal, golden, beautiful, and pure (*sāttvika*) heaven accessible to yogis.
Vāsudeva dwelt there, impermanent though he was, being served by celestial queens and others. ||98||
Regarding this, there are these verses: All other incarnations are but parts; the great life-story belongs to Kṛṣṇa.
The Lord of Ramā has appeared for the destruction of the earth's burden. (99)
This life-story of Kṛṣṇa is for the purpose of destroying the wicked;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion, rejoices eternally in Vaikuṇṭha. 100.
This most wonderful and auspicious account of the deeds of Kṛṣṇa has been told by me to you in brief; it bestows all fruits. 101.
Whoever recites the life-story of Vāsudeva in the presence of Hari, or remembers it, or hears it with devotion, goes to the supreme abode. (102)
Whether one is burdened with great sins (mahāpātaka) or likewise joined with minor offenses (upapātaka),
by hearing the life-story of Bālakṛṣṇa, one is liberated from all evils.
By remembering Hari seated in Dvāravatī together with Rukmiṇī, one undoubtedly attains great sovereignty through this [practice]. ||104||
In battle, in a narrow pass, or when surrounded by enemies, one will become thoroughly victorious by meditating upon the leader of all the gods. 105.
Whoever remembers Him playing with the cowherd girls in the auspicious Govraja attains all desires and indeed obtains good fortune. (106)
He who, though afflicted by great calamities, diseases, and the like, remains steadfast in the city of Kāśī, shall conquer even the most terrible *kṛtyā* stationed there. (107)
What is the use of saying much more in this matter? At all times, O auspicious lady, a wise person should simply utter the mantra: "Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa. (108)
Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, to Vāsudeva, to Hari, the Supreme Self; salutations to Govinda, who destroys all afflictions, to him who is bowed down to. 109.
O Goddess, by reciting this mantra every day with devotion, a person, being completely liberated from all sins, shall attain the world of Viṣṇu. ||110||
Janārdana is indeed the lord of all the gods;
for the protection of the worlds, he truly assumes various different states of existence.
Desiring to destroy Tripura, I worshipped Hari;
the glorious one, assuming the form of Buddha, deluded those enemies.
Deluded by that scripture and deprived of all righteousness,
the enemies of the gods have been slain by me with the Nārāyaṇa weapon.
Having descended into the portion of that Brahmin’s dwelling,
Janārdana shall likewise slay all the fierce Mlecchas.
Through those various states, O fair-faced one, all the conditions of the Lord of the World have been described by me; what else do you wish to hear? Tell me.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Departure for His Own Abode," within the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-carita* of the *Umā-Maheśvara-saṃvāda*, in the *Uttara-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-Pādma Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
(253) Chapter Two Hundred and Fifty-Three.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, everything concerning the states of existence of Hari has indeed been told;
they were utterly amazed by that account of the deeds of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. (1)
O Lord of Gods, even after hundreds of other kalpas, my hearing of the life-story of Rāma and the high-souled Kṛṣṇa never ceases! (2)
O Lord of Beings, the heart is never satiated with the nectar of Hari’s stories;
now I desire to hear the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu, and likewise, O God, I wish to hear the procedure for his worship. (3)
Śrī Rudra said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the installation of the most high-souled Hari;
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds: that which is established by others and that which is self-manifested (svayam-vyakta). ||4||
Having fashioned an image of Hari out of stone, clay, wood, metal, or other materials, one indeed establishes the performance of rites as prescribed in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgama. ||5||
Listen to me as I explain that which is called "establishment" (sthāpana), for it is self-manifested;
in that [image], Viṣṇu himself is indeed ever-present on earth for the sake of men. (6)
The Lord is himself present in stone and wood; indeed, that is remembered as being self-manifested (svayam-vyakta).
One should worship Madhusūdana whether he is self-manifested or installed [by others]. (7)
For the purpose of worshipping the deities and the great sages,
Keśava, the eternal Lord of the World, himself comes into their presence.
Whatever was to be enjoyed by whomsoever in their respective forms appeared on earth as such;
one should always worship that very thing and always take delight in that alone. (9)
The Lord of gods, the best of deities who reclines at Śrīraṅgam, is to be worshipped according to the injunctions;
he alone appeared on earth through the ascetic penance of the lords of the Ikṣvāku dynasty. 10.
In Kāśī as well, Mādhava, the remover of impurities, is to be fully worshipped by me—wherever that eternal one has manifested himself in a beautiful house. (11)
Having come together here and there, I delight while remaining fully established;
for the Lord of Sacrifice is not found by men through the eightfold yoga, but rather in worship.
Having come within the range of the eyes, it grants the desired boon;
accessibility in all circumstances is obtained by people through worship of the image. (13)
The presence of these [deities] is always found upon the surface of the earth, in the highly meritorious Jambūdvīpa, specifically in the auspicious land of Bhārata. (14)
Viṣṇu is present in the image, but never in others;
therefore, in this land of Bhārata, [he is worshipped] by sages and even by the gods. 15.
O Goddess, Hari is eternally present in this great land of Bhārata, which is constantly served through austerities, sacrifices, ritual acts, and the like. 16.
Likewise at Indradyumna, at Kaurma, on Siṃhādri and Karavīraka;
at Kāśī, Prayāga, Saumya, and on the Śālagrāma mountain. ||17||
In Dvāravatī, in Naimiṣa, as well as in Badarikāśrama, at Kṛtaśauca, and at Pauṇḍarīka and Daṇḍaka, one may take away sin. 18.
In Mathurā, on Veṅkaṭādri, on Śvetādri, and on Garuḍācala; in Kāśī, at Anantaśayana, in Śrīraṅga, and on Vāsavādri. (19)
On the gentle Nārāyaṇācala, at Vārāha, and at Vāmanāśrama—these and others are self-manifested (svayam-vyakta) and bestow the fruits of all desires. (20)
For the auspicious sages declare that in whatever place Janārdana himself manifests his presence, in that very place he is self-manifested.
The most excellent of great devotees, having installed Keśava according to the prescribed rite, should effect His presence through the mantra; that installation is considered preeminent.
One should worship the Lord in that [image] both in villages and in homes;
however, the worship of the Lord in the home is prescribed by the virtuous to be performed upon a Śālagrāma stone. (23)
Worship of the Great Soul consists of the recitation of mantras, sacrificial yoga, the chanting of His names, service, and likewise the marking of one's limbs with His symbols. (24)
And his worship, O auspicious one, is divided into nine types;
the performance of each respective rite is constantly prescribed for the Brahmin. (25)
The most excellent brāhmaṇa is a great devotee of the Lord and indeed the guru of men;
he is to be worshiped by all the worlds just like Hari himself. 26.
A Brahmin who performs the five purificatory rites beginning with heating, who carries out the work of new worship, and who knows the fivefold purpose, is remembered as a great Bhāgavata. ||27||
The performance of various ritual acts and sacrifices is ordained for the Kṣatriya;
likewise, he is to be marked with their symbols and to perform service to them and worship them. (28)

The chanting of the syllables of the mantra, the proclamation of the names of Hari, and the salutation of the Viśas are declared to be their six duties according to the rules for sacrificial rites. (29)
Proclaiming His name, service, worship, salutation, and likewise honoring His devotees—these five forms of sacrifice are for one born as a Śūdra. (30)
O Beloved, for all men, the mental worship of the Lord of the World should be performed collectively, and it should also be performed according to one's own specific qualification. (31)
By those devoted to no other deity, who seek no other fruit;
by those who know the Vedas, who know the reality of Brahman, who are free from passion, and who desire liberation. ||32||
Hari should always be worshipped by Brahmins and others as well—by those who are endowed with devotion to the Guru, who are very serene, and who are excellent holy men. 33.
The worship of Hari by men should be performed according to their respective social classes (varṇa);
likewise, auspicious Vaiṣṇavas must carry out duties in accordance with their class and stage of life (varṇāśrama). 34.
One should always properly perform here those duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti;
a wise person should not transgress the actions declared in the Śruti and Smṛti. (35)
That Vaiṣṇava who does not practice the conduct prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis has fallen into heresy and shall dwell in the Raurava hell. (36)
Therefore, one should indeed perform the worship of the Lord of the World in accordance with one's own caste;
therefore, a human being should always practice the conduct prescribed by the Smṛtis. //37//
For mental worship is common to all men in auspicious matters;
having observed one's own qualification, one should perform the rite with diligence. (38)
Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, truthfulness, avoidance of worldly pleasures, non-stealing, and non-violence are the means for achieving dharma for all. (39)
Therefore, one should worship Madhusūdana according to one's own caste; having risen at dawn during the night and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules. 40.
Having paid homage to his own gurus, he should remember Acyuta within his heart;
being pure and restrained in speech, he should recite [the Lord's names] with devotion according to the Thousand Names.

Having gone outside the village and discharged the excrement according to the rule, he should perform purification as prescribed, sip water for ritual sipping (ācamana), and become restrained and pure. ||42||
Having first cleaned his teeth, he should perform his bath according to the prescribed rule,
taking with him earth from the root of a *tulasī* plant along with its leaves.
O lady of auspicious countenance, having consecrated [the water] with the root mantra and the Gāyatrī,
and having performed the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, one should bathe while anointed with that very mantra.
Having invoked the Gaṅgā, which originates from the feet of Hari, into that very pure water, one should bathe and quickly recite the supreme Aghamarṣaṇa hymn. 45.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the purification (mārjana) according to the sequence prescribed for the Puruṣasūkta;
thereafter, having submerged oneself quickly, the wise person should recite the root mantra.
Having consecrated it with the Vaiṣṇava mantra twenty-eight times, or one hundred and eight times, the Vaiṣṇava should then pray while using that water.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should offer libations to the gods, the sages, and likewise the ancestors;
then, having wrung out his garment and sipped water again, he should be clothed in a clean, washed garment. ||48||
Then that best of the twice-born, the Vaiṣṇava, having taken beautiful, pure clay and consecrated it with a mantra, [applied it] upon his forehead and other parts of the body.
The wise man, free from sloth, should apply the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) according to the prescribed number;
having performed the twilight worship according to the rules, he should mutter the Sāvitrī mantra.
Having gone home with self-restraint, having washed his feet, remaining silent,
and having sipped water (performed *ācamana*), he should enter the pavilion for worship with a one-pointed mind.
Having seated that Lord, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, upon that beautiful and exceedingly white pedestal adorned with an abundance of flowers; 52.
One should worship correctly according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings;
or, in the case of an installation, one should perform the worship of the manifest [deity] in the home according to the injunctions.
A twice-born man, with a restrained mind, should perform the worship of Viṣṇu according to the rules prescribed in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgama, with devotion and as is appropriate. 54.
A Vaiṣṇava should act exactly as instructed by the Guru.
That which is proclaimed as Śrauta is the Vaikhānasa, while that which is called Smārta is the Vāsiṣṭha.
The ritual procedure of the Pañcarātra is declared to be a divine scripture;
one must not omit any part of the rite, for the worship of Viṣṇu is supreme. (56)
With invocations, seats, water for the hands (arghya), and so forth; with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and the like;
with incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), betel leaves (tāmbūla), and other items, accompanied by prostrations. ||57||
A Vaiṣṇava, filled with joy, should perform the worship of Viṣṇu according to his ability, reciting the Puruṣasūkta verse by verse along with the root mantra. (58)
