Devotion to the Dhātrī and Tulasī plants, as well as the honoring of guests—these are briefly declared to be the constituent parts of Kriyā-yoga. ||5||
Without the yoga of action, one does not attain perfection through the yoga of meditation alone;
he who is devoted to the yoga of action reaches that supreme state of Viṣṇu.
Jaimini said: O Lord, O Master, if you have favor toward me, please tell me the greatness of those which have been declared as the constituent parts of kriyā-yoga.
O Brahmin, what are the virtues of the Gaṅgā, and what is the fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu? What are the most excellent gifts, and what is the devotion of the twice-born? (8)
What is the fruit of Ekādaśī? What is devotion to Bādhātrī like? What is devotion to Tulasī like? Or what is the honoring of guests like? (9)
O Sage, tell me all of this; I have the desire to hear it.
No one other than you is able to explain it within the three worlds. (10)
Vyāsa said:
Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born! Your mind is certainly pure, since you possess such faith and curiosity to hear this secret narrative. (11)
It is indeed not possible to fully describe the virtues of the Bhāgīrathī;
therefore, I shall speak of them in brief—listen with a one-pointed mind. (12)
Even if one recites the two syllables "Gaṅge" with extreme tenderness, I believe that even so, sin departs; it is indeed an elixir for the great elements. (13)
The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere; however, she is difficult to find at the three places: Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. ||14||
O sage, all the gods, together with Indra, having arrived at the beautiful Gaṅgādvāra,
perform rites such as bathing and giving gifts.
O Sage, those humans, animals, insects, and others who, by the turn of fate, cast off their bodies there, attain that supreme state which is difficult even for gods to reach. (16)
O brahmin-sage, listen now to this ancient history (itihāsa) being told by me;
by merely hearing it correctly, one is liberated from all sins. (17)
Formerly, there was a king named Manobhadra, born of the Lunar dynasty, who was powerful and a knower of all dharmas in this world. (18)
His queen, named Hemaprabhā, was a speaker of pleasant words, devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and endowed with all auspicious marks. (19)
Having slain all his enemies in battle along with the king,
the one of great power ruled the entire earth, including its oceans and islands.
Once, that highly illustrious protector of the earth, having summoned his ministers, spoke these words with affection in the midst of the assembly.
Manobhadra said:
"O ministers, this entire earth has been protected;
all enemies, along with their sons, armies, and vehicles, have been slain. (22)
His own kinsmen were protected by gifts, and the Brahmins were satisfied; likewise, all the gods, along with their sons, armies, and vehicles, were honored. (23)
All these kinsmen of his own lineage, who had been protected by him through all sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees—this entire power has been snatched away by this great old age. (24)
Indeed, being weak, I am not able to perform certain actions;
for royal splendor does not shine upon men who lack capability. (25)
Adorned with all ornaments, like a passionate woman with full limbs,
even all the enemies on the surface of the earth remain in fear for that long.
As long as they have not attained proficiency, they do not desire her with their beautiful eyes—
even though she is endowed with every virtue and their minds are fixed upon her.
The earth abandons an aged king, just as a wanton woman leaves one who has been protected by her own will;
all virtues are attainable through devotion, and great fame is attainable through virtue. (28)
The earth is to be obtained through strength, not through the gift of final liberation; one who is devoid of capability is considered a wretch under the command of the enemy.
That king, who accepted the words of fools alone, was destroyed by his enemies;
therefore, I divided the entire kingdom among the excellent ministers.
"I wish to give [this] to my two sons, if it is approved by you.
The ministers said:
"O King, this speech which has been uttered by you, the knower of policy—" (31)
Thus, O most excellent of beings, we have no doubt regarding this matter;
nevertheless, by the king's command, we two have come here together.
He had two sons named Vīrabhadra and Yaśobhadra;
both were endowed with all virtues, youthful, and sweet-spoken.
They were always devoted to their father, peaceful, strong, and dedicated to dharma;
then that king, the best among those who know the science of statecraft, [acted] with haste. (34)
Out of curiosity, he divided his entire kingdom and gave it to those two.
In the meantime, a certain vulture arrived accompanied by his own wife.
Having arrived and sat down in the midst of that assembly, O best of the twice-born,
they beheld those two birds who had come there and were exceedingly joyful.
"O King, tell us why this auspicious arrival of yours has occurred.
The vulture said:
"I am a vulture; O protector of the earth, behold this woman of immeasurable ascetic power. (37)
I have come with joy to behold the prosperity of your two sons;
yet, a great misfortune was seen to have befallen them in a previous birth. (38)
"We have come together here to see Indra, who has attained prosperity in this very birth.
Having heard these most wonderful words of the vulture, the king, his mind filled with astonishment, spoke again, O Brahmin. (39)
The king said:
"O vulture, I have heard from you this most wonderful speech;
how is it that you know the former history of these two?"
If you know the previous history of these two in its true nature,
then tell me all of this in its entirety, O best of birds.
The vulture said:
"O King, these two śūdras named Garasaṅgara, sons of Satyaghoṣa, were present during the age known as Dvāpara. (42)
At one and the same time, while the king was dying within his own palace, those servants,
rendered powerless, came to lead these two [princes] to the royal throne.
Arriving by the thousands of millions upon millions with nooses in their hands,
they bound these two, who were intoxicated with pride, with leather nooses.
And they led them to the abode of Death by a path exceedingly difficult to traverse.
Having seen these two, Dharmarāja said to Citragupta: "Ha! (45)
"Let Citragupta deliberate upon the entire conduct of these two;
by his command, Citragupta [shall record] all their deeds, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (46)
He then questioned them from the very beginning, and thus spoke to Antaka.
Citragupta said: "O mighty-armed one, these two are indeed truthful, possessed of meritorious vows and great magnanimity. (47)
If there is some misdeed observed in all one's actions, it is surely because one has personally renounced giving and has not bestowed gifts upon the twice-born. 48.
O King, by that very same action, both of these are destined for hell;
the one who gives having renounced the act of giving, and the one who does not give to a twice-born man.
One who gives a gift does not remember it, and the recipient does not beg for it; thus one may go to a terrible hell that brings fear to all beings. (50)
"Both of them shall dwell in hell as long as the moon and the sun exist; therefore, O Lord, these two are great sinners, for they have stolen the property of a Brahmin. (51)
Perform this rite quickly, for hell is most dreadful. ||52||
Then, by the command of Yama, messengers with their lips bitten in rage cast these two into a terrible hell, O Lord of the Earth.
On that very day, O King, having been approached by the messengers of Yama along with this wife of mine, I was led to the abode of Yama. (54)
O King, listen to this deed performed by me as well;
I shall relate it from the very beginning, for it will cause wonder to those who hear it. (55)
Formerly, I was a Brāhmaṇa named Sarvaga, born of a noble lineage;
I was a resident of the Saurāṣṭra country and had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (56)
This illustrious wife of mine, named Jūkaṣā, is devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and born of a pure lineage. (57)
"O illustrious one, being intoxicated by my learning, youth, and wealth, I once, while still young, committed an insult against my parents even in my mind. (58)
I am one who dwells in youth, praised in great assemblies, a performer of all duties, wealthy, handsome, wise, and devoted to the nourishment of those who know me. (59)
My father and mother were likewise devoted to sin;
they were devoid of the rising of virtue, and were greedy for the company of heretics.
Manliness, life itself, wealth, as well as family, learning, and fame—all his possessions have been rendered fruitless by his parents. (61)
Reflecting thus repeatedly in my mind upon the king, I abandoned the service of my parents, which bestows auspicious merit, out of contempt. (62)
"O King, by this karma, at the command of Yama, I was cast along with my wife into hell by the messengers of Yama, where those two were the foremost of sinners. (63)
O King, listen now to this: together with these two sinful ones and my wife, I remained in that terrible hell for as long as that period of time.
O best of kings, for thousands of crores of yugas and hundreds of crores of yugas,
you have experienced great suffering in hell.
O King, after passing through the hells, I was born together with my beloved in the lineage of vultures, both of us likewise eaters of the flesh of the dead.
And these two as well, O King, having reached the end of hell and desiring its cessation, were born into the lineage of locusts to experience the fruit of their own karma. (67)
Listen as I relate that deed performed by these two during their birth as the royal locusts, which will strike wonder into the ears of the listeners.
Once, O Lord of the Earth, a most powerful wind arrived.
In the exceedingly pure interior of the Gaṅgā, where the waters have fallen from Uḍḍīya; ||69||
Having fallen thus into the waters of the Gaṅgā, these two of delicate limbs immediately met their end, which removes all impurities.
Then these women of beautiful eyes were sent to fetch him;
they arrived with celestial chariots endowed with every luxury.
Those two, liberated from all sins and adorned with garlands of light,
ascended a divine celestial chariot and departed for the city of Viṣṇu.
O King, for that duration of time Brahmā remained in his unmanifest birth;
then, by the command of Brahmā, he arrived at the city of Indra.
O King, they remained there for that length of time, enjoying a happiness difficult even for the gods to attain, while consuming the earth which was so hard to endure.
These two of great renown, born in your lineage which is a sacred purifier, shall cast off their bodies in the Gaṅgā; for them, there will be no further birth. (75)
Nevertheless, these two, born of the highest merit, shall enjoy the earth;
having enjoyed the entire world for a long time together with their sons and grandsons. (76)
Having reached death at the Gaṅgā, which is difficult even for yogins to attain,
these two kings shall go to union with Nārāyaṇa.
All this former history of these two, who are the crest-jewels of the class of kings, has been told by me through the power of their recollection of past births.
Having reached the banks of the Ganges and come to this state, who will provide protection for us two, so wicked-souled? (79)
O protector of the earth, this contempt for friends, which brings the suffering of hell upon men, has been seen by me alone; it is nothing but that. (80)
O best of the twice-born, devotion to one's father yields suffering both in this world and the next;
it leads to the destruction of prosperity here and to hell hereafter. (81)
I consider even such sins as the killing of a Brahmin to be preferable, O protector of the earth, for eventually an atonement for them may occur, whereas this [sin] is eternal. (82)
Human beings on this earth cut down with the axe of disrespect toward their parents the tree of merit, which was earned through hardship and destroys all afflictions. (83)
O King, whatever is given into the mouth of the ancestors, O supreme ascetic, Viṣṇu himself eats that, because Hari exists in the form of the ancestors. (84)
Those who thus serve Pratyakṣadeva and his parents day and night shall attain all perfections through the grace of that Lord of the World. (85)
Those men who remain devoid of devotion to their father stay in hell for as many thousands of kalpas.
Therefore, this great suffering has arisen for me;
I do not know when I, together with my wife, shall attain liberation. (87)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his and having accepted them, O best of the twice-born, the king became filled with joy and was struck with wonder again and again. (88)
The king said:
"It is indeed a marvel that this has been heard from your mouth, O vulture; yet no conviction regarding this arises in my heart or in theirs. (89)
Then, O best of kings, a voice arose loudly from the intermediate space:
"This is true, true, true; there is no doubt about this. (90)
Then, O brahmin-sage, together with his wife and his bird,
he suddenly became as he was before, due to the narration of the majesty of the Gaṅgā.
The best of the Gandharvas sang with joy at both [events], the Apsaras danced in groups, and a rain of flowers fell. (92)
A divine celestial chariot, endowed with all enjoyments, arrived;
and hosts of messengers sent by the enemy of Kaiṭabha came forth.
Then he, together with his beloved wife, who was dear to all cows and brahmins,
immediately ascended a celestial chariot and went to the abode of Hari.
O best of the twice-born, having heard of this wondrous deed, the king, together with his sons and wife, became devoted to the service of the Gaṅgā. (95)
There is no holy place equal to Bhāgīrathītīrtha in all the three worlds, by the mere utterance of whose name one attains liberation from all sins. 96.
O best of the twice-born, the greatness of Gaṅgādvāra, which destroys all sins, has been told to you; what else do you wish to hear? (97)
Those gods and humans who recite this chapter with supreme devotion in a temple, and those who listen to it with devotion toward the assembly of the twice-born—their sins perish instantly. (98)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kriyā-yoga-sāra* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. ||3||
(4) The Fourth Chapter. Jaimini said:
Through your grace, I have heard the greatness of Gaṅgādvāra;
now I wish to hear the greatness of Prayāga. (1)
O Sage, let the greatness of the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean also be told; for in this world, no one other than you is able to describe it correctly. (2)
Vyāsa said:
"O child, I am not able to describe fully the fruit of Prayāga and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean; listen, O twice-born one, to a brief summary. (3)
O Sage, whatever sacred fords exist within the midst of the millions of cosmic eggs, do they all attain a likeness to Prayāga? (4)
At the confluence of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī, all the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, offer their praise. (5)
For those who perform their ritual bath there during the month of Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn (makara),
there shall never be a return from the world of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, thousands of millions of cows, horse-sacrifices as the foremost of rites, and other gifts of gold equal to Mount Meru—[all these do not equal the merit of that gift]. (7)
Whatever fruit is obtained by the wise through performing fire-sacrifices and giving gifts to Brahmins at Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, Prabhāsa, and Gayā; ||8||
By bathing at Prayāga during the month of Māgha, the merit becomes ten million times greater than that;
therefore, Prayāga is remembered as the supreme among all sacred fords (tīrthas). ||9||
O best of the twice-born, when the sun was situated in the zodiac sign of Leo,
I performed severe penance for a long time at the Godāvarī through bathing, giving gifts, vows, and other such practices.
Whatever merit is declared in the Vedas, Agamas, and Puranas to be inexhaustible, that same merit is obtained by bathing at Prayaga during the month of Magha; of this there is no doubt. (11)
Listen as I describe the fruit that one who has fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna obtains in Kāśī. (12)
Freed from the sins accumulated over ten million births, assuming all forms,
and having delivered ten million persons, he rejoices together with Śiva.
O twice-born one, whatever fruit is obtained by worshipping Viṣṇu for a hundred crores of kalpas, that same fruit is attained by bathing even once at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
If one worships for even a single day while the sun is situated in Capricorn, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth: everything shall indeed become inexhaustible. 15.
As many days as a person remains there during the month of Māgha,
for that many hundreds of kalpas he rejoices together with Viṣṇu.
Whoever has performed a single bath in the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is immediately liberated from all sins and transgressions by the mere sight of that [Tīrtha]. (17)
If people desire to cross over the extremely difficult bondage of saṃsāra, they should bathe with devotion in the Gaṅgā and Yamunā and behold Mādhava. 18.
O brahmin-sage, whatever humans sacrifice there, having offered it while their bodies are still intact, they obtain that very thing immediately; of this there is no doubt.
I shall relate a historical account right here; listen to it, for by hearing it, a person becomes liberated from all sins. (20)
In that place, there was a certain wealthy Vaiśya named Praṇidhi, who was solely devoted to the worship of deities and guests, and to his singular devotion toward the Brahmins. (21)
His lawful wife was named Padmāvatī; she was devoted to her husband, possessed of beautiful limbs, endowed with virtuous character, born of a noble family, and spoke kindly. 22.
O best of the twice-born, whatever qualities suitable for women were created by the Supreme Lord, those very qualities reside within their bodies. 23.
Then that Vaiśya, Asaupraṇidhi, having taken much wealth, set out for trade, O Brahmin,
under an auspicious lunar mansion and on a favorable date.
From wealth dharma arises, and from wealth comes extensive fame; through wealth one attains noble lineage; indeed, there is nothing in this world that cannot be achieved without wealth. (25)
Seeing a person devoid of wealth, even a friend flees;
like a cloud in autumn that has lost its water, he would be reduced to fragments upon fragments.
Relatives remain only so long as there is wealth to be consumed;
he who has wealth has a family, he has intelligence, and he is a scholar. (27)
A man devoid of wealth, even while living, is like one who is dead;
for his intellect turns away from the acquisition of dharma, wealth, and knowledge. (28)
It should be known that for one who is exceedingly foolish, the fruit of even greater effort is meager;
therefore, dharma must be practiced constantly and wealth must always be acquired. (29)
Learning should always be cultivated by wise men;
for through giving, both wealth and knowledge increase day by day. (30)
Dharma indeed increased for those men who protected it;
having obtained even a piece of wood, grass, or chaff, they would not abandon it. (31)
Even a man who is habitually acquisitive never comes to ruin;
therefore, this Vaiśya should be appointed as the guardian over his wife. (32)
Skilled in domestic affairs, he went abroad for trade.
Then, on one occasion, his wife took up ointments and other such items. (33)
Then, for the purpose of bathing, he went with his friends to the hermitage of the brahmin seer;
at that time, the one named Dhanurdhvaja himself took refuge in a boat.
Acting according to her own will, she beheld her performing the act of bathing—she who was enriched with blossoming golden flowers and whose face was like a full-blown lotus. (35)
Beholding that wife of the Vaiśya, who had eyes like those of a young deer and lovely, full, and elevated breasts, that dog-eater became afflicted with passion.
Laughing, and without considering his own form, Dhanurdhvaja spoke these words:
"O auspicious one, O lady of beautiful hips, O sweet-smiling beauty! (37)
O beloved, O slender-waisted one with broad hips, my mind has been captivated by you alone through the essence of your exquisite youth, along with me, who am likewise endowed with virtues. (38)
"O virtuous one, may you experience every happiness.
O twice-born one, having heard these words from her bow and banner, her friends then [spoke]. (39)
Thus, with their lips bitten in rage, they spoke these words.
The friends said: "O fool! O you of wicked conduct! O you born of a family of evil-doers! (40)
Not even a glance at his feet is granted to him;
for this woman is a devoted wife, solely intent upon her religious duties. ||41||
Those who desire their own happiness do not perceive evil through their vision; they always gaze upon the faces of others' wives and covet the wealth of others. (42)
Seeing them, their minds deluded and tormented by the fire of lust, they said:
"Go far away, you sinful woman! Do not speak such unbearable words. (43)
"We ourselves do not even touch your lordship with our feet.
Dhanurdhvaja said:
"Fie upon this word 'caste' (jāti), while you yourself recognize every quality!"
"Because you have honored me, I shall now [grant] this state of being a dog-cooker;
however, there is gold filling the palace, situated within a pitcher. (45)
"What man, knowing the multitude of her virtues, would not take her upon obtaining her?
Therefore, I shall employ a stratagem so that I may obtain this young woman. (46)
"O you who are called 'He' (the Lord), act accordingly; I have come for refuge from fear of worldly enjoyment.
O best of the twice-born, he spoke thus to that fool again and again. (47)
Filled with extreme curiosity, they spoke these words;
the friends said:
"O evil-minded one, if you truly desire this beautiful woman... (48)
"O twice-born one, quickly cast your body at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā; there you shall laugh, looking at one another's faces. 49.
Taking that virtuous wife, they went into their own home;
meanwhile, due to delusion, that dog-eater became as one who had committed a thousand killings of Brahmins.
Having performed sacrifices at the confluence of the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, he passed away;
he was powerful, possessed of all virtues, and his form resembled that of his master.
And that very dog-cooker (outcaste), remembering his own past life, became that same Vaiśya named Praṇidhi on that very auspicious day. 52.
Having completed his trade, he returned toward his own home;
then that outcaste, though a brahmin, entered his dwelling. (53)
Beholding those two mines of virtue standing before him, identical in form, age, and even in qualities that corresponded to their vow, [the king was amazed]. (54)
"Whose beloved am I? Who is my husband? she wondered.
Then that virtuous woman, filled with wonder, gazed upon those two husbands.
He praised the god Mādhava with words of tender syllables. ||56||
Padmāvatī said:
I bow to Govinda, whose form is infinite, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the gods headed by Śakra;
the Lord of Yoga, who is free from desire among those who know yoga, the bestower of yoga, and worthy of worship by yogis. (57)
Salutations be to you, the crusher of Kaiṭabha; salutations to you, the destroyer of Madhu.
Salutations be to the annihilator of the demon Kaṃsa; salutations be to the one who struck down Cāṇūra.
Salutations be to you, the eternal foremost among those who rescued the Vedas; salutations be to you, the one who raised up the earth.
Homage be to you, who are capable of supporting the earth; homage be to you, the destroyer of the Daityas. ||59||
Salutations to you who washed the Gaṅgā with the pair of your feet; salutations to you, the end-maker of the royal dynasties.
Salutations to you who crushed Rāvaṇa along with his army; salutations to you, the destroyer of the Daityas of the three worlds.
Salutations to you, the reviler of sacrificial rites; salutations to you, the destroyer of the Mleccha tribes.
Salutations to you, whose seat is the lotus of the heart; salutations to you, the banner that fells all enemies.
Be gracious, O Lord, beloved of the cowherd women; O God of gods, who holds the mountain with one hand!
Be gracious, O bee at the lotus-face of Lakṣmī; be gracious, O Viṣṇu, eternal salutations to you! ||62||
Be gracious, O lotus-eyed one, wielder of the discus, you who hold the Kaumodakī mace in your hand!
Be gracious, O Viṣṇu, who holds the conch; let there be constant salutation to you, the bearer of the lotus.
In this temple of the wonders of saṃsāra, where delusion is the darkness and discernment is the lamp, I wander perpetually, utterly bewildered by the māyā of Keśava, which is yours. (64)
O Enemy of the Asuras, even the leaders of the Vīraścis, Indra, and the Sun do not know your illusion;
how then could I, a mere human, understand your illusion? Out of compassion for me, remove this delusion before my eyes. (65)
Vyāsa said: Having heard her hymn of praise, the Lord Mādhava,
the Master of the Universe and bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life, looked upon her.
He suddenly appeared, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
looking toward the earth with his head bowed, he paid homage at those two feet.
Salutations to you, O bestower of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, who have dispelled the delusion of my own mind caused by my lack of knowledge. 68.
The Blessed Lord said:
Abandon this delusion, O lovely one; these two are indeed your husbands.
O woman of beautiful hips, serve them both always with single-minded devotion.
O Lord, since your vow was that he who is devoted to me, young, and wise, should enjoy the fruit of happiness, you yourself have become twofold for the sake of fulfilling it. (70)
O lady of beautiful hips, just as Lakṣmī, who possesses formless beauty, sports with me, so may you also always enjoy happiness with these two. (71)
Padmāvatī said:
O Lord of the Island, O God, men praise you as the one who alone bestows peace;
O Compassionate One, lift me up from this ocean of shame in which I am submerged! (72)
The Blessed Lord said: "O fair-faced one,
when you were censured and became truly afraid on earth, O virtuous lady,
then come to my city along with these two."
Then, by the command of the Blessed One, a celestial chariot arrived immediately;
taking the two of them with him, he began to depart for Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, O Jaimini, as she was traveling along the road with her two husbands,
she saw a certain great-souled being seated in a chariot accompanied by a woman.
It was supported by hosts of messengers with four arms, whose eyes were like lotus petals and whose complexion was like the *atasī* flower, as they sat upon Garuḍa.
Then that virtuous woman asked those excellent messengers of Viṣṇu, who possessed the forms of Viṣṇu: "Who is this man standing in the chariot? (77)
Who are you, O great-souled ones, with eyes like white lotuses?
You are all equal to Viṣṇu, bearing conchs, discs, and other weapons in your hands. (78)
Then all those messengers of the Blessed One, whose prowess was equal to that of Viṣṇu, laughed repeatedly and spoke, filled with supreme joy.
The messengers of Viṣṇu said: "O virtuous lady, we are the messengers of Viṣṇu; taking this meritorious person with us, we shall go to our noble station, the supreme world. (80)
Padmāvatī said: "O high-souled messengers of Viṣṇu, tell me this: by the power of what merit has he attained such a state? Oh, tell me! (81)
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"This is a Rākṣasa named Bṛhaddhvaja, who causes grief to the world;
he dwells in forests and other such places, and possesses great strength and prowess. (82)
One who steals the wives or the wealth of others, one intent on committing crimes, one who eats beef, one who speaks harsh words, and one who reviles the gods; ||83||
Whatever action is devoted to sin has always been performed by him;
O devoted wife, he has never performed an auspicious deed even in a dream.
Constantly afflicted by desire, he mounted this chariot and wandered through the sky for the sake of abducting the wives of others, O lady of beautiful hips.
Whichever young woman he beholds wherever he goes, afflicted by passion, he forcibly embraces her right there. (86)
Then, on one occasion, he beheld the beloved wife of the king named Abhīmakeśa— a beautiful woman in the prime of her youth— standing in the midst of a pleasure grove.
Then, beholding her who possessed the luster of golden flowers, he spoke these words with affection: "O beautiful one, what are you doing here? (88)
Then she herself said: "I am Keśinī, adorned with that name, and I am an expert in the science of sexual union (surata-śāstra) belonging to King Bhīmakeśa. (89)
The lord of the earth does not look upon me—even for a moment—with eyes gladdened by love, though I am the daughter of his own lineage, endowed with every virtue, and free from fault. (90)
My husband remains here constantly, his discourse uninterrupted;
while I remain here, scorched by the fire of separation, lamenting my own past deeds. (91)
"Who are you, O best of beings, and how have you come to this garden?
You have arrived here; please tell me everything with a gracious mind. (92)
Then he spoke these words to her whose face resembles the full moon:
"O lady, I am the illusory Rākṣasa Vīra; I have come here to embrace you. (93)
Abandon your angry husband who always sees only faults; O slender one, resort to me, and I shall grant you every supreme happiness. (94)
Then, laughing joyfully, that virtuous woman bound this lord of the rākṣasas by the arm with her vine-like arms, pressing his face against her own.
He mounted the divine chariot together with this woman of beautiful hips, who was a young bride to the virtuous, overwhelmed by the agitation of discernment. 96.
Relying on their state as husbands, they were filled with great curiosity; mounted upon a chariot with the speed of the wind, they traveled through the path of the sky. 97.
Then he said to her, "O lady with the beautiful face, look!
We have arrived from your husband's country at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. (98)
Then this woman, standing upon her chariot, reached the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean and immediately met her death, as she was gazed upon by those filled with extreme terror.
Having lamented in many ways over that unchaste woman, this Rākṣasa too, seeing her with her life-breaths departed, immediately met his own death. (100)
By the command of the one whose banner bears the son of Vinatā, we two, whose sins have been washed away and who are performers of meritorious deeds, are now leading [them] toward Vaikuṇṭha.
Whether in water, on land, or in the sky, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, even sinners go to the supreme goal by abandoning their bodies. 102.

Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one attains that holy site at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean which is difficult to find even in the three worlds. (103)
There, even a killer of a Brahmin attains purification; of this there is no doubt—having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and having beheld Hari, Mādhava. (104)
Upon seeing the face of Kārttikeya, rebirth no longer exists;
for Kārttikeya is Hari himself—thus has their non-difference always been established. (105)
All those who behold even a single suffering person are destined for liberation;
hear now of the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, a sacred ford superior to all other holy places. 106.
"Whether in water, on land, or in the sky, the deceased shall attain liberation.
Vyāsa said:
O Jaimini, having spoken thus, those messengers of Viṣṇu took them both with them.
They all went suddenly through the path of the sky to the abode of Viṣṇu;
the virtuous Padmāvatī went along with her two husbands. 108.
O best of the twice-born, having attained a form similar to that of Viṣṇu, the bestower of the four goals of life, he enjoys there all the pleasures that are difficult to obtain. (109)
Having attained supreme knowledge, they reached a state of identity with Hari;
for the Gaṅgā embodies all sacred fords, and Hari embodies all sacred fords.
Therefore, devotion to both Gaṅgā and Hara is enjoined.
Formerly, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, there was a king named Mādhava. (111)
Having practiced austerities there for a long time, he attained eternal liberation.
Jaimini said:
"O best of beings, who is this Mādhava of whom you spoke? What deeds did he perform? How did he practice penance? Tell me all of that."
Vyāsa said:
O high-minded one, listen as I shall relate in brief the life-story of that great-souled brahmin-sage Mādhava. 114.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Prayāga," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini. ||4||
(5) The Fifth Chapter. Vyāsa said:
The city of Astitāladhvajā was like the realm of the thirty-three gods;
it was renowned throughout all the worlds and filled with throngs of virtuous people. (1)
There lived a king named Vikrama, born of a pure lineage, who was righteous, truthful, and devoted to the protection of his subjects. (2)
His beloved, named Hārāvatī, was difficult to find on earth;
she surpassed the splendor of the moon with the radiance of her own face. (3)
That very same [queen] remained dear to that king even while she stayed among the multitude of women,
just as Gaṅgā remains dear to the Lord of Rivers even while she stays among the multitude of streams.
O twice-born one, after some time had passed while he was devoted to the gods and the brahmins,
a son endowed with all auspicious marks was born to him from her.
Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, that universal monarch, who was learned in all the treatises,
gave him the name Mādhava.
Then, after some time, that powerful Brahmin Mādhava reached the further shore of the river of all sciences and was endowed with excellent qualities.
Then that lord of men consecrated his son with the position of crown prince and then with the kingship—
him who was a worshiper of the gods on earth and of all the hosts of deities.
And on one day, surrounded by his troops, the king, being very clever,
went out of curiosity to the great forest for the sake of hunting.
Having slain many wicked beings there at the time of midday,
he then made an effort to depart from the forest toward the city.
Accompanied by his army, Mādhava joyfully returned to his own city;
there he beheld a certain young woman intent on bathing in a lake. (11)
Her body was made manifest by garments and materials fit for bathing;
she surpassed the full moon with the beauty of her own face. (12)
Her cheeks were radiant with a pair of golden earrings;
her navel was covered by very long locks of hair, and she possessed a beautiful smile.
She was like a golden lotus bud, with beautiful, uplifted breasts;
her waist was slender as a lion’s, and she possessed the voice of a cuckoo.
That beautiful woman became like a banner raised by the high-souled Kandarpa over the kingdom of the hearts of young men. 15.
Beholding her of such a form in the wilderness, devoid of all company, what man on earth bearing life would not fall under the sway of desire? (16)
Then Vikramaputra, his heart pierced by the arrows of pride upon beholding that lovely-faced woman, thought to himself: "What [shall I do]? (17)
No one like her has been seen on the circle of the earth;
by embracing her here, one's birth shall be made fruitful.
"I am the best of all the worlds by virtue of my age, splendor, and qualities; even if Indra were to come here today, he must nevertheless be led away. (19)
The fault that arises from abducting another's wife is well known;
who indeed is able to describe it, since even my father was a king? (20)
Having reflected thus with a very firm mind, that lustful man left his armies stationed at a distance and went to where Sītā was.
Sovereignty, wealth, and desire on this earth—these three destroy the splendor of discernment; what is more wonderful than that? (22)
Your father is the destroyer of misfortune and the protector of dharma for men;
shame on this Kāmadeva himself, who deludes the entire world! ||23||
Then, beholding him approaching with great speed,
that noble-minded woman, being alone, became deeply overwhelmed with anxiety.
Seeing her alone, standing upon the star, in the full bloom of youth, this man runs toward her with great speed; this thought dwells in my mind. (25)
All sages declare that the protection of the Dharma is itself protected;
there is nothing here to be known, nor will anything of this kind come to pass.
When enemies advance against a place that is bereft of allies, flight there is praiseworthy; staying would lead to the destruction of one's life. (27)
Having reflected thus, that woman of noble form then tucked her water-pot under her left arm and set her mind on fleeing from the lake out of fear. (28)
Then, O twice-born one, that Mādhava also, having gone before her with great speed, stood with his hand outstretched. (29)
Śrī Mādhava said:
O beautiful woman of lovely form, by the power of your exquisite youth, you have stolen my heart and are fleeing; I am ruined, rendered senseless. (30)
"O lady of tremulous glances, O lovely-limbed one, what is your name, and who is your husband?
Where have you come from, for you have surpassed heaven; there is no woman equal to you on this earth. (31)
O beautiful one, you are the most excellent here, endowed with all auspicious marks;
why do you carry water like a maidservant, O lotus-faced one? (32)
O lady of delicate limbs, you always carry two golden jars upon your breast, yet you carry a water-pot under your arm; this is truly marvelous! 33.
On the path intensely scorched by the rays of the sun, the reddened spaces between her toes shine like the buds of *japā* flowers. (34)
"O lady of beautiful hips, love me with affection; O fair-faced one, abandon this jar!
My suffering has come to an end merely by the sight of you. (35)
"O beautiful one, I am the son of the illustrious King Vikrama, named Mādhava;
with all my being, I shall become yours, O lady of excellent limbs. (36)
You shall possess great charm in the midst of my circles of women, just as the *mālatī* flower does among flowering creepers for the sake of the bee. (37)
Or perhaps, out of pride, you wish to transgress my word;
nevertheless, I shall not strike you down, for I am the son of a king. (38)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words spoken by him, O Brahmin, she abandoned the path and stood with her face cast down; then she spoke very slowly. (39)
Even if he should never listen to my words, even from another person, nevertheless, casting aside all shame, I shall surely speak before you. (40)
For thus I am Subāhu, the beloved of the Kṣatriya Mahāvīra;
I am indeed Candrakalā, bringing water for the worship of the gods. (41)
The words spoken by you are not worthy of your family;
for all those born in your lineage are as eunuchs toward the wives of others. (42)
I am a woman alone, and you are the source of heroes;
what fame will come to you by embracing me here by force? (43)
Embracing another’s wife may yield pleasure for a mere moment;
however, it brings infamy in this world and suffering for more than a hundred eons thereafter. (44)
O hero, this is a land of action; let merit alone be cultivated here.
Never set your mind upon seizing another's wife. (45)
From greed desire arises; from desire evil arises;
from evil comes death; and even after death, there is residence in an insurmountable hell. ||46||
All your virtues are rendered useless and even your birth is fruitless, since you have fallen under the sway of desire and wish to dally with another's wife. (47)

Thus he asked the Kirātas—who were unable to do anything else—with sweet words, accompanied by a Brahmin and devoted to Hari. (34)
Dharma said:
"Who are you, with such deformed appearances, holding nooses and mallets in your hands, with mouths made terrible by tusks, and possessing a radiance like that of charcoal? (35)
All of you are great heroes with eyes blazing like fire;
nevertheless, this misfortune has been brought upon you by someone. (36)
The messengers of Yama said:
"O twice-born one, we are all messengers of Yama who always carry out his commands; this great staff of ours is always ready for the onset of slaughter. (37)
Dharmasva said:
"O you of great strength and prowess, you have arrived here unexpectedly;
by whom and how was this wretched state brought about? (38)
The messengers of Yama said:
"O best of the twice-born, cast away your fear; hear the entire account of how this suffering of ours came to be so utterly unbearable. (39)
"We are servants sent by Dharmarāja to lead away that one who was torn apart by the two horns of the bull like Time itself; what shall we do? (40)
Therefore, commanded by him, we have all come here with weapons in hand, having bound that most wicked sinner, to take him away. (41)
Then, his time having come, that evil-minded one,
who was like Death itself, was torn apart by the two horns of a bull acting as the cause.
Then, being compassionately sprinkled there by the droplets of Ganges water,
that foremost of sinners began to mutter the name of the Gaṅgā.
Although he was already cleansed of all impurity by the sprinkling of droplets from the waters of the Gaṅgā,
they made an effort to lead him away, having bound him firmly with nooses.
To bring him [back] as well, the Lord of Gods, the protector of those who seek refuge,
dispatched his own messengers of great strength and prowess.
Then, O best of Brahmins, certain messengers arrived from Narayana and spoke to us with anger on the path.
The messengers of Viṣṇu said: "O great-souled ones, who is this? How have you bound this noble-minded man with a noose and brought him here? What service do you perform for Vākya? (47)
"Abandoning this Great-Souled One, flee as you please;
otherwise, we shall cut off your heads with the edge of our discus. (48)
O best of the twice-born, having heard these arrogant words of the messengers of Acyuta, they were addressed by us in this manner. (49)
"We are all the messengers of Daṇḍapāṇi, the lord of all living beings;
having taken this foremost of sinners, we shall depart for the abode of Śamana. (50)
All of you are great souls, adorned with garlands of tulasī, with eyes like the petals of blooming lotuses, strong, and bearing the banner of Garuḍa.
Divine, wearing garments as beautiful as a peacock's neck,
you possess four arms bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
"How is it that you all, who possess such qualities and are endowed with every auspicious mark, desire to bring this foremost of sinners? (53)
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"We are all messengers of Viṣṇu, and we have now come here to lead this meritorious man toward Vaikuṇṭha. (54)
"O messengers of Yama, release this devotee of the Blessed Lord, our own kinsman who is cleansed of all sin, if you wish to live! (55)
O twice-born one, having heard these words of theirs once more, listen as we relate that which was spoken by us out of anger, pervading all directions. (56)
This wicked man of evil conduct has committed a thousand killings of Brahmins;
he is ungrateful, a killer of cows, a betrayer of friends, and evil-minded.
"Many gold pieces, as large as Mount Meru,
were constantly stolen by this most wicked-souled man from the wives of others."
Thousands of millions upon millions of Viṣṇukīṃkaras were created,
and likewise many killings were committed, as well as the killing of women.
Every single day, he committed the theft of deposits, incest with his own mother,
and likewise the eating of beef.
The burning of another's house caused by the injury of others, censuring another in an assembly, and causing the miscarriage of a widow’s fetus; 61.
O best of men, like a Yavana, he struck down with sharp swords a guest who was entering his house at night out of greed for wealth.
This base and deluded man committed these and other great, innumerable sins; not even the slightest thing conducive to merit did he do. (63)
Therefore, this great sinner is led to the house of torment; O best of beings, you should know that sinners are to be punished by Dharmarāja.
If you are indeed the messengers of the Blessed One, the God of gods, then why do you wish to lead away this foremost of sinners? (65)
The messengers of Viṣṇu said: "What you have spoken is indeed the truth; there is no doubt about this. All sinners are always subject to punishment by the Lord of Life. (66)
This man has been liberated from evil by being sprinkled with the droplets of the Gaṅgā;
therefore, let us all lead him to the abode of Hari.
So long do the sins of embodied beings remain within their bodies,
until they touch the most rare water-sprays of the Ganges.
Just as all darkness is destroyed by even a single digit of the moon, so too is sin destroyed by even a single drop of the water of the Gaṅgā. (69)
By remembering the name of Gaṅgā, one is released from sin;
what wonder is there in this, that by seeing her water directly, one is liberated? (70)
Even the cold water of the Ganges acts like fire in the forest of sins;
just as fire burns a lotus grove, so does that coldness cause burning.
Therefore, this Keśava is a peerless performer of meritorious deeds;
go, O messengers of Śamana, if you desire your own welfare. (72)
Having heard these words from those messengers of Keśava, we spoke this further reply; listen now as we laugh loudly and speak it. (73)
How wonderful, how truly wonderful! This man, who was once an abode of impurity, has been liberated from all his sins simply by being sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, a mortal is not released from karma acquired by his own hand even after hundreds of millions of eons, without having experienced its fruit. (75)
"We have all assembled here at the command of Yama to bring him;
by whose word shall this foremost of sinners be released by us? (76)
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"You are surely of sinful nature and utterly devoid of discrimination, since you do not recognize the virtues of the daughter of Jahnu. (77)
That action which is prohibited by the Veda is remembered as a sin (pātaka);
that action which is approved by the Veda is said to be righteous (dharmya).
We have heard that Devanārāyaṇa is himself manifest as Svayambhū;
as is Viṣṇu, so is Gaṅgā—Gaṅgā indeed is the destroyer of all sins. (79)
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious karma wrought by one's own hand, Hari removes it;
when Hara is pleased, where can the sins of embodied beings remain? (80)
"Having reached this state because of sins acquired in previous births, you who are still performers of evil deeds—why do you desire further sin even now? (81)
"You are revilers of the Gaṅgā and likewise revilers of Viṣṇu;
therefore, we shall slay you sinners with the edge of the discus. (82)
Having spoken thus, O best of beings, those messengers of Viṣṇu, their eyes red with anger,
waged a fierce battle against us.
"Kill this one! the messengers of Jīveśa cried out, and becoming enraged, they struck us repeatedly with the edge of their discus as they spoke again and again. (84)
Having spoken thus, those messengers of Viṣṇu, who were exceedingly fierce in battle, suddenly blew their conchs into the sky with joyful hearts. (85)
Then the three worlds were pervaded by our lion-roars, as it were by the thundering of clouds, and by the stretching of our bows. (86)
Then, by us with trees, stones, and likewise showers of mountain peaks,
those messengers of Viṣṇu were shattered by our arrows.
With spears, javelins, arrows, and iron clubs, as well as with axes, daggers, staffs, and tridents. ||88||
With swords and spears, with sharpened arrows, with maces, with the edges of discuses, and with most terrifying iron shafts. ||89||
With these and other various weapons, those servants of Viṣṇu, resembling thunderbolts, struck them in many ways out of anger in the great ocean. (90)
Then, shattered by his weapons, we all fled in terror;
some fell by the thousands in the battle, their lives departed.
Then, seeing us intent on flight, those powerful ones, servants of Viṣṇu, joyfully cried out, "Kaṃbūn! (Let us seize them! 92.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having severed that bond which was like unto Time itself,
they placed him upon this celestial chariot and departed for the city of the Blessed One.
O best of beings, by the mere power of being sprinkled with the spray of the Gaṅgā, even one who was like Death and a perpetrator of great sins attained the vision of Hari. 94.
Having remained there for a hundred kalpas and enjoyed captivating pleasures,
he attained knowledge right there and reached supreme liberation.
"O Lord, by the power of the Gaṅgā, this suffering of ours has vanished;
go now, O Brahmin, may it be well with you, and return to your own home well-pleased. (96)
Having spoken thus, O twice-born one, those messengers of Yama went to the city of Yama;
and that virtuous man, being delighted, returned once more to the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having performed his bath in the Gaṅgā, the mother of all the worlds, that brahmin, with palms joined in reverence, praised that supreme goddess. 98.
Dharmasva said:
O Gaṅgā, mother of the entire world, you whose moving waves are like a beautiful flower-garland upon the head of the enemy of Ananga!
O you who remove the dust from the two beautiful feet of the enemy of Kaṃsa, I bow to you with devotion, O you who cause the destruction of evil. 99.
O Mother, bestower of all happiness, most excellent among rivers,
whose virtues are sung by the multitude of sages such as Vyāsa, rich in qualities,
you are the boat in the midst of the terrifying great ocean of saṃsāra.
I bow to your pair of feet, which destroy all misfortune. ||100||
O Daughter of Jahnu, by obtaining even a single drop of your water,
the king named Saudāsa— a slayer of ten million brahmins—
attained liberation that is unobtainable even by the gods.
I bow my head to you, O Giver of Boons; be gracious. ||101||
O Goddess, O Mother, for me who am uttering the names Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta, Janārdana, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Gaṅgā—
the names that ward off the sins of saṃsāra— may there be the falling away of this body.
May there be water from you here through your grace. ||102||
O Sovereign of All, what need is there for austerities, or for recitations,
or for gifts, or for sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice,
once one has obtained a spray of your water, which is unattainable even by the gods?
Even sinful men attain liberation. ||103||
Svāhā, you alone are she who is Svadhā, O Supreme Goddess; you are the cause of complete satisfaction for the hosts of gods and the world of the ancestors;
you are the embodiment of the three qualities: sattva, rajas, and tamas.
I bow to you, O Goddess, the cause of creation, sustenance, and dissolution; he who always bears upon the surface of his forehead the sand-paste mark with the clay from your banks,
and who recites your name— the abode of all aesthetic flavors— with devotion.
May the dust of his feet rest upon my very head. ||105||
Having made her dwelling upon your banks, O triple-pathed river, having drunk your water which destroys all sins,
and having remembered your name and beheld the multitude of your waves—
May my birth be for the purpose of removing the bonds of saṃsāra. ||106||
O Mother, considering it a source of great fear and exceedingly difficult to traverse, men do not build even a very large and lofty palace in the sky;
for that [palace] is indeed merely for the sake of pleasure, whereas yours is the giver of immortality.
Water serves as a staircase for the journey to the third heaven. ||107||
O Sovereign of all, O Giver of liberation, sins and multitudes of diseases remain within the bodies of embodied beings only so long as they do not perform ablutions in your pure waters.
For there is no bathing in the Tripathagā, the foremost of rivers. ||108||
O Supreme One, bestower of the state of ultimate liberation, even the hosts of gods such as Acyuta, Viriñci, and Śiva are not able to reach the further shore of Your greatness.
Yet some, out of delusion, speak of you as if you were a river.
O Gaṅgā, bestower of all happiness, even the blessed Lord Paśupati knows but a small portion of your greatness,
since he, though the most excellent of those with well-disposed minds, [worships you] with devotion.
O Sovereign of the World, he always bears you upon his own head. ||110||
O Goddess Gaṅgā, Mother of the World, be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign!
Protect me; salutations to you, guard me, your own servant. (111)
O Giver of Liberation, how can I, whose mind is deluded, possibly praise you, who are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman and the sole mother of all the worlds? 112.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born one, having been thus praised by that wise brahmin, the Mother of the World suddenly manifested in personified form as Gaṅgā. 13.
He saw before him Gaṅgā, two-armed and seated upon a crocodile, white as a kunda flower, a moon, or a conch shell, and adorned with all ornaments. 14.
Seeing the Gaṅgā before him, proclaiming "Gaṅgā,
Gaṅgā," he prostrated with his head at her feet and embraced the earth.
O Jaimini, the Supreme Goddess, being well-pleased, deluded him with the light of her smiles and said to that best of brahmins, "Choose [a boon]."
Dharmasva said:
"O Mother, by the touch of your water, even a slayer of a Brahmin becomes a partaker of liberation;
you are seen by me in person—what else remains for me to accomplish? (117)
Nevertheless, O Supreme Goddess, I beg for one boon from you:
O Devi, let death come to me while I am remembering your name. (118)
O Goddess of all, whoever praises you with this hymn composed by me shall also enjoy all desires and, at the end, attain the supreme goal.
Gaṅgā said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am pleased by this devotion of yours;
all will quickly become well for you, without a doubt. (120)
If any person recites this hymn composed by you at the three junctions of the day,
I too, being well-pleased, shall grant him supreme liberation.
Vyāsa said: O best of brahmins, having thus granted that boon to him who was named Dharmasva, that goddess, who is affectionate toward her devotees, vanished right there.
Having obtained the boon from the best of Brahmins, she felt as though her purpose was already accomplished;
she remained there on the banks of the Gaṅgā, which were delightful to the sages.
Then, after a long time, having attained a peaceful death in the pure waters of the Jāhnavī, he went to the supreme state.
Even Kālakalpa, though evil-minded, attained supreme liberation when sprinkled with droplets of Ganges water; O twice-born one, what need is there to speak of others? (125)
Even by unintentionally touching the water of the Gaṅgā, one obtains its fruit; as for what would happen to those who touch it with a spirit of devotion, I truly do not know that. 126.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; this I declare again and again. By touching even a single drop of its water, supreme purity is attained. (127)
Those who here touch even a single drop of water from this best of rivers with a spirit of devotion surely go to the abode of the Imperishable, liberated from all most terrible sins. (128)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Droplets of the Gaṅgā," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
[Verse 7]
(8) The Eighth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O best of Brahmins, I shall speak again of the supreme majesty of Gaṅgā;
drink the nectar of the story of Gaṅgā if you desire liberation.
By him all gifts have been given, by him all sacrifices have been performed,
and by him Viṣṇu has been fully worshipped— namely, he who possesses devotion toward his mother, Bhīṣma.
O Jaimini, whatever religious acts are performed in the Gaṅgā,
all of them become inexhaustible for him.
He who, seeing that water, rises with devotion and drinks the waters of the Gaṅgā,
is as one who has performed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
O Jaimini, for one who stands with devotion when the waters of the Gaṅgā arrive,
their state as a beast persists eternally throughout birth after birth.
If one approaches the water of the Gaṅgā and does not accept it with devotion,
the merit accumulated over ten million lifetimes perishes in an instant.
O twice-born one, he who prevents another who desires to go to the bank of the Gaṅgā shall go to the Raurava hell together with ten million members of his lineage.
For one who voids urine or excrement on the bank of a limb [of the river], there is no atonement for him even in hundreds of millions of kalpas, provided he is not seen [to do so]. (8)
He who spits out phlegm, or discharges rheum from the eyes, tears, or impurity upon the bank of the Gaṅgā, will certainly become a denizen of hell. 9.
He who casts impure remnants or phlegm into the womb of the Gaṅgā shall go to a terrible hell and incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. ||10||
If a man of deluded intellect commits a sin on the banks of the Gaṅgā, that [sin] will surely become inexhaustible; it is not pacified at other holy fords.
Sin committed at another sacred site is destroyed in the Gaṅgā;
however, sin committed in the Gaṅgā is not pacified anywhere. 12.
Therefore, those learned in the scriptures should not commit evil at the Gaṅgā;
rather, they should gather merit through action, mind, and speech. (13)
Neither distant lands, nor mountains, nor forests,
nor trees exist where the celestial river, the destroyer of sins, does not flow.
O Jaimini, one must not remain even for a moment on the banks of the Gaṅgā, even if there are hundreds of tasks to be performed. 15.
Even after eating alms-food, one should remain on the bank of the Jāhnavī;
for there, even upon attaining the status of a king, one should not stay for even a moment.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated by casting off his body in the Gaṅgā;
elsewhere, one would not be freed even by performing a thousand horse-sacrifices. (17)
He who, dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā, becomes devoted to the worship of Hari,
is one by whom Hari has never been worshipped in any previous birth.
He has no devotion toward Gaṅgā, the mother of the world.
Listen, all you men; I tell you again and again. (19)
Having performed your ablutions in the Gaṅgā, go to the supreme state;
for that man who, at the time of death, invokes "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," [attains liberation]. ||20||
O twice-born one, he whose discourse on the Gaṅgā begins at the time of death shall be liberated from all sins and dwell in heaven for ten thousand divine yugas.
O best of the twice-born, that wise man who remembers Viṣṇu’s abode at the time of death has all his impurities dissolved and goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Hari becomes pleased with him who, at the time of death, possesses the excellent sectarian mark (puṇḍra) made from the clay of the Gaṅgā; indeed, "Gaṅgā" is a name that bestows liberation. (23)
O best of the twice-born, he who casts off his body even in a cremation ground upon seeing one bathing in the Gaṅgā attains the merit of dying in the Gaṅgā. (24)
The bones of the embodied being remain in the Ganges for as long as time endures.
For that many thousands of kalpas, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The wise man whose ashes, bones, nails, and even his hair are immersed in the Gaṅgā shall dwell in the realm of Viṣṇu. (26)
O twice-born one, listen with an undistracted mind as I describe all the fruit that a man obtains when his bones rest in the Gaṅgā. (27)
Once, the Lord Śakra, adorned with various ornaments and full of desire,
went to a pleasure-house with a young woman who was like a lotus-stalk.
Possessing a lotus-like gait and having attained fresh youth through the knowledge of medicinal herbs,
she brought delight to the gods by bestowing various flavors.
Delighted and infatuated by love, the victorious Arjuna rested his head at the soles of the feet of that fawn-eyed woman, who was the golden pinnacle of her co-wife.
Then Śakra, his mind drawn by the king's virtues, being supremely pleased, fashioned a golden betel-roll for him and gave it to him. (31)
And at that very time, Paulomī, the most beautiful of women,
adorned with all her ornaments, came personally to his house.
Seeing Śakra, the lord and sovereign of all the gods, in such a state,
Paulomī, Prāheti, and Sulakṣaṇā became exceedingly enraged.
Śacī said: O Lord of all the gods, why do you act like a lover toward Devakī?
You give a gold betel-roll to her who is merely the form of my maidservant.
All the gods touch your feet with their heads;
O lotus-scented one, how could you be at the soles of the feet of this Lord? (35)
And because you are fragrant when requested, you would be like a bee; yet that is not your fame, O Lord who possesses all aesthetic flavors and are the husband of millions of beautiful women.
"Why do you perform such an utterly contemptible deed? O you who possess the fragrance of a lotus, though devoid of virtue, depart from here and wander far away! (37)
"You are the sovereign mistress, and Keśava is at the soles of your feet.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was that virtuous lady addressed in many ways by Paulomī with words full of humility. 38.
The celestial maiden Padmagandhā spoke thus without anger:
"Padmagandhā said:
'Only the Lord himself truly knows both virtue and vice. (39)
O one devoid of qualities, by what authority have you come here to revile me?
Even with their two eyes, others perceive both virtues and faults.
Even with a thousand eyes, one could not perceive this evil intent;
for just as the faults of people prevail, so too does their virtue remain hidden. (41)
At first, some quality of the moon is perceived by people;
yet she speaks words of misfortune, is cruel, possesses an ugly form, and is devoid of virtue. 42.
"Since I am not virtuous, let my husband worship you instead.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that lotus-eyed woman, out of anger, [cast] the lotus-hued one [into the fire]. 43.
She rose from her golden couch, uttering a great cry of compassion.
Indra said:
"O beloved, O mistress of my life, O most excellent one, where are you going, leaving me behind?"
What offense have I committed against you? Tell me that, O beautiful one; surely I am your slave—indeed, I shall perform the work of a servant for you.
"You have not heard even a word from the wife of a slave, much less from a slave woman.
Then Śakra, his mind agitated by that delusion, rose up.
She placed that most beautiful woman within her womb.
Śacī said:
"O Krauñcī, your life is blessed; mine is surely in vain. (47)
"You are always fortunate through your husband, whereas I am unfortunate, O excellent woman;
as long as my merit lasts, O Krauñcī, that merit of yours shall go to its exhaustion. (48)
"O Krauñca, you shall experience even more suffering arising from this act;
meanwhile, enjoy yourself at your pleasure, sporting like the Lord of the Gods. (49)
After a few days, she would become devoid of her qualities, like a *krauñcī* bird;
having heard those most wonderful words of hers, Padmagandhā [was struck with wonder]. (50)

Having abandoned the state of duality and bowed down, he spoke to that virtuous lady. She who dwells in the lotus said: "O daughter of Puloman, O lady of noble form, what you have spoken is wonderful. (51)
"O Krauñcī, tell me, how shall I speak? I desire to hear this with great effort:
who am I, where was I situated, and how did I come to be here? (52)
"After how many kalpas will my merit come to an end?
Śacī said:
"O you who have the fragrance of a lotus, you were indeed born from the Krauñcī bird in the past. (53)
Eating impure food, meat, and insects, she remained upon the earth;
however, there was a single nyagrodha tree on the delightful bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having constructed a nest there, she made that her dwelling;
once, upon that banyan tree, a black cobra appeared. (55)
Having entered the nest and bitten you, she suddenly met her death;
then the serpent, filled with rage, devoured all the flesh-eating birds.
O lady of excellent countenance, bones remained there as if fleshless;
at times, O auspicious one, they were struck down by great winds. (57)
O beautiful woman, it fell broken into the Gaṅgā along with its very roots;
when that banyan tree had fallen into the Gaṅgā, [the world was shaken].
Those bones of yours have been washed by the waters of the Gaṅgā;
as long as those bones remain in the Gaṅgā, so long do they endure. (59)
"For so long you shall indeed always be the beloved of your husband;
thus has everything regarding the lotus-born one been told to you by me just now. (60)
By the power of whose merit even Śakra is brought under your control;
blessed indeed is the goddess Jāhnavī, by whose grace Krauñcī [attained her state]. (61)
"You are untouchable even by Cāṇḍālas; you have slept upon the very couch of Indra.
Therefore, O virtuous lady, you were insulted even by Śakra, the son of Pulomā. (62)
With her face withered, she returned to the Bhojas exactly as she had come;
who indeed could have stayed near Śakrāṅgī, that woman of excellent lotus-like fragrance?
That speech remained in his heart as if ever-watchful.
Then once, O twice-born one, the lord of the asuras was well-pleased with his virtues.
"Choose a boon yourself, O lady of beautiful hips," he said to her. She replied to the Lotus-Gone One:
"You are the sovereign lord of all deities, the master of ten million women. (65)
Nevertheless, O Lord, I am dependent on this samādhi; what need have I for other boons?
Yet, since you, O Supreme among Gods, desire to grant a boon, [I shall accept one]. (66)
"Make a vow before me by deed, mind, and speech.
Indra said:
"My life, my wealth, my kingdom, and even my retinue—" [67]
"Command me, O beautiful one; what shall I give to you?
Truly, truly, and again truly—there is no doubt in this. (68)
"If you desire it, O deer-eyed one, I shall certainly give it to you.
Padmagandha said:
"Surely you are pleased, O Lord of the Thirty-three, if you [speak thus]. (69)
"May I have birth as a woman, a cow, and a mare; let me obtain this very boon again and again.
Indra said:
"O fair-hipped one, having made this vow, I shall indeed grant you this boon."
But what are these many sorrows that have entered my heart? O lady of beautiful hips, not seeing you, not even for a moment can I find any joy. (71)
How can I endure this unbearable long separation, when there exists upon me that very same breast of yours which was once so full? 72.
Then, O lady of excellent limbs, she remained for several days without food;
thereafter, she spoke to the king of gods concerning his great prosperity.
That virtuous woman remained in that divine abode for ten thousand years.
Padmagandhā said: "O Lord of the Gods, grant me your command so that I may fulfill my noble desire. (74)
"I am going to the land of action; I bow at your two feet.
Indra said:
"O moon-faced one, I have been made to yearn by the splendor of your love."
After staying for some days, you shall afterwards depart as you please;
meanwhile, you should spend day and night with him in the chamber of curiosities.
While playing there, she approached the Lord of the Gods, who was seated upon a lotus and had lived for a full year; then, filled with joy, she spoke to him.
"Give me your command; I shall now go throughout the earth.
Indra said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, abandon your dullness; stay right here with me."
"I am indeed unable to abandon you, who are dearer to me than my own life.
Padmagandhā said:
"O Lord of the Gods, when my merit is exhausted, I shall come to the earth. (79)
Then your separation from me will soon come to pass;
O protectorless one, once that separation occurs, I shall return once more to the earth. (80)
"O Vāsava, I desire to go once more to the land of action for the sake of acquiring merit; tell me by what means I may do so. (81)
"Therefore, I shall do it; perhaps there might be a separation from you.
Indra said:
"O blessed lady, since you truly desire to perform this deed," (82)
Therefore, come back quickly, O beautiful one;
for then your body will be drenched by tears flowing profusely from your eyes. (83)

Having deliberated upon all your scriptures, I declare this:
a human being who bathes even once in the waters of the Gaṅgā attains liberation.
He who performs his bath even in the water of a well while contemplating the Gaṅgā— the sovereign who destroys the flood of all afflictions, sorrows, sins, and fears— [attains the same merit].

O twice-born one, by the grace of the Gaṅgā, he too shall be liberated from the entire accumulation of sins, such as the killing of cows and Brahmins, and go to the city of Viṣṇu, which bestows all happiness.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gaṅgā," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||9||
(10) The Tenth Chapter. Jaimini said:
Through your grace, O Guru, I have heard this majesty of the Gaṅgā;
now I desire to hear the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O child, to the supreme fruit of the service rendered to the Lord of Lakṣmī, hearing which all human beings shall obtain the highest knowledge. 2.
The eternal Lord is to be worshipped according to the prescribed rites during the twelve months beginning with Māgha; listen, and I shall describe those rites to you. (3)
When the month of Māgha has arrived— the most auspicious of all months—
an excellent Vaiṣṇava should indeed renounce both meat and sexual intercourse.
One should always bathe in the morning and avoid oils;
one should renounce eating twice a day and food from others during the month of Māgha. (5)
In the morning, wearing white garments and having performed the five great sacrifices, the Himalayan man, with a steady mind, began the worship of Viṣṇu.
One should bathe the immutable Viṣṇu with pure water that is slightly warm,
and one should anoint the limbs of Viṣṇu with very soft sandalwood paste.
One should worship the Lord of the World, the God of gods, the wielder of the discus;
one should have the vessels washed and then rendered free of water.
Having bathed the Lord of the World with slightly warm water,
his body should be diligently wiped with a divine cloth.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the fruit obtained by one who bathes Keśava with slightly warm water during the month of Māgha.
Liberated from all sins accumulated throughout various births and lives,
he enjoys every happiness here in this world and, at the end, goes to the abode of Hari.
Listen to the merit of him who, having diligently washed the vessels with water until they are pure, worships the Lord of the World. 12.
Having enjoyed all desires here on earth, free from all diseases,
he shall dwell in the abode of Keśava for thousands of ages until the end of time.
At dawn and at both twilights, the Vaiṣṇava person should place a smokeless, blazing fire in front of the Discus-wielder (Viṣṇu). 14.
For the purpose of warding off that cold, one who is devoted to Viṣṇu should kindle a fire before Viṣṇu every morning and evening during the month of Māgha; hear now the fruit of that act.
Having enjoyed all desires here in this world, accompanied by sons and grandsons, he shall go at the end to the city of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. 16.
As is the self, so is Viṣṇu; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should lie down upon one's back beside Keśava, the Lord of the gods of gods, as he sleeps. (17)
Just as a mortal provides for himself protection against the cold,
so too he who bathes Janārdana with milk during the month of Māgha—
to him Viṣṇu, the supreme deity, being fully satisfied, what will he not grant? (18)
Likewise, one should effect the destruction of the cold of the Wielder of the Discus with a divine garment. ||19||
I shall now declare the fruit for him who, having bathed the four-armed Lord in the month of Māgha, worships Him even once with coconut water and milk. (20)
Having rescued ten million persons who were sinking in the ocean of hell due to their own insurmountable karma, he goes to the abode of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu).
O best of the twice-born, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
and especially on the eleventh and fifth days, one should perform the worship of Hari.
Milk-rice accompanied by incense should be offered day after day during the month of Māgha to the God of gods, the enemy of Mura, who holds a lotus. (23)
O Jaimini, listen as I describe the fruit of merit for that Vaiṣṇava who offers milk-rice mixed with ghee to the Wielder of the Discus on the full moon day of Māgha. ||24||
Oṃ! Having gone to the city of Viṣṇu, may you enjoy delightful pleasures for four Manvantaras through the grace of the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi). 25.
Returning again to the earth, he shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin);
having enjoyed prosperity for a very long time, upon death, he goes to the abode of Hari.
O Jaimini, on the fifth, the seventh, or the eleventh lunar day,
a Vaiṣṇava who is unable [to perform other rites] should indeed offer *paramānna* (milk-rice) to Murāri.
O best of the twice-born, especially during the bright fortnight rather than the dark fortnight,
one should offer food to the Enemy of Mura on these lunar days of the bright fortnight.
Even for a single day in the month of Māgha, he who offers milk-rice with cakes to Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the Daityas—for him, Hari is not difficult to attain. (29)
Whatever is given in the month of Māgha for the sake of pleasing the twice-born becomes inexhaustible for that man; there is no doubt whatsoever in this matter. (30)
O Brahmin, whether the deed performed during the month of Māgha be auspicious or indeed inauspicious,
there is no destruction of it even in hundreds of manvantaras.
He who worships the Lord of Kamalā with a *māghī* flower during the month of Māgha shall go to the supreme abode, liberated from all sins. (32)
For as many golden flowers as one offers to the Discus-wielder (Cakrapāṇi),
for that many thousands of eons does one dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving gold equal in weight to Mount Meru,
that same fruit is obtained by worshipping Hari with a single golden flower.
O best of Brahmins, the golden flower is always dear to Keśava;
it is especially pure and beloved by Keśava during the month of Māgha.
He by whom Hari has not been propitiated with divine golden flowers shall be destitute of jewels, gold, and the like, in birth after birth. (36)
O best of the twice-born, listen with special attention to the fruit of the full-blown flower that I shall describe, together with its unsurpassed history.
There was a powerful king named Suvarṇa, a knower of all scriptures, who possessed the splendor of a Brahmin throughout the entire land of Āryāvarta. (38)
O brahmin-sage, that king, due to royal splendor, ignorance, and youth, was excessively intoxicated and was always devoted to sinful deeds.
O twice-born one, because of the words of heretical ministers, that king, out of greed for wealth, punished those virtuous people even though they were without fault. (40)
Surrounded by singing, instrumental music, and other such entertainments, he squandered all the wealth acquired through unjust means, devoid of sacrifice and charity. ||41||
He did not provide nourishment for his kinsmen, nor did he feed the gods or the twice-born;
being always intent on evil, he gave no satisfaction to beggars. 42.
Constantly devoted to sin,
that king, whose abode was evil, never performed worship for his guest and daily departed from his palace.
Even in hundreds of years, would one be able to enumerate all the various sins committed by the undiscriminating through this [birth], as well as those produced in other [lives]? (44)
Once, O protector of the earth, that king, utterly deluded by desire and possessed of an evil intent, went to the abode of a courtesan at nightfall.
Then, seeing that king approaching, she whose name was Ujjvalā rose suddenly from her couch and performed a prostration at his feet.
Having washed his pair of feet with water from the *bhṛṅgāra* vessel,
she placed that king upon her lap, embracing him with both arms.
Sprinkled by those streams of the nectar of love, that lord of the earth dwelt with her upon that couch,
filled with curiosity.
Then that courtesan, smiling with affection and in the full bloom of her youth, personally offered him a handful of ripe flowers. (49)
From that, a single flower from the garland fell from the king's hand onto the surface of the earth, its fragrance pervading the quarters of space. (50)
Seeing that fallen flower, the king, out of extreme agitation, uttered "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*. (51)
O King, by the utterance of the words "Nārāyaṇāya" and by the offering of a golden flower, all his sins were destroyed.
Then all the villagers, having assembled together, struck him— who was staying in the courtesan's house— as that very night drew to a close, for he was exceedingly difficult to overcome.
Then, as if enraged, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, dispatched his messengers to bring that king, the foremost of all sinners.
Then, commanded by him, messengers with nooses and mallets in their hands arrived with great speed, their eyes bloodshot with rage.
Then the messengers of Yama exerted themselves to lead him to their own abode;
thereupon, the servants of Nārāyaṇa appeared, bearing conchs, discs, and maces.
Having seen that king bound by a noose, the messengers of Viṣṇu, with nooses in their hands, arrived mounted on Garuḍas to lead away that lord of the earth.
The mighty ones struck the messengers of Yama with discuses and maces;
having mounted the Lord upon a divine chariot, they blew their unsurpassed conchs.
Likewise, mounted upon the king’s chariot, adorned with a garland of *tulasī*, wearing yellow silken garments, and decorated with golden ornaments; ||59||
Being praised by hosts of sages who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and surrounded by the messengers of Viṣṇu, he attained the same world as Hari.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Viṣṇu himself rose up and embraced that king with his four long arms, and spoke to him.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O King, best among all virtuous souls, speak of your welfare. What is there to be accomplished for you? Command me now."
To whoever recites even once daily, "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," I am always to be protected—just like a brother and just like a father. (63)
Whenever a man utters my name "Nārāyaṇa" with a smile,
I fulfill all his desires, just as a son fulfills the wishes of his father.
"O best of kings, you are my devotee; therefore, reveal your wonderful desire, O father, and I shall grant it to you now."
The king said:
"O ocean of compassion, everything has undoubtedly been granted by you;
even by me, a sinner, this station so difficult to attain has been reached. (66)
Pleased by these words of his, the Lord of Kamalā, out of affection, established the king [in that state]; listen to that.
Then, out of compassion, she herself fashioned for him a pavilion adorned with golden ornaments crafted by Viśvakarman.
