whoever utters the sound "kala" at the time of worship of the Teacher of the World [attains this]. (36)
O best of Brahmins, I shall now describe the merit of one who plays a wind instrument;
accompanied by ten million times ten million of his kinsmen, he goes to the abode of Hari.
Having attained knowledge there, one shall obtain this imperishable liberation;
for he who, endowed with devotion, dances in the abode of Viṣṇu.
O best of Brahmins, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu belongs to him who sings the songs of the Gāyatrī with devotion before Nārāyaṇa. (39)
A Vaiṣṇava person, with devotion, praises the Lord of the World with hymns of praise and attains the status of a king among the cities of the Gandharvas. (40)
The Blessed One, being pleased with him, grants all desires to whoever worships Hari month after month according to this rite.
O brahmin-sage, that Acyuta grants his grace very quickly indeed.

Those mortals who desire to cross this ocean of the world—so exceedingly deep and bestowing all manner of suffering—should indeed worship that pair of beautiful lotus feet of the Supreme Person, which are served by the hosts of the gods. 43.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Worship of the Blessed Lord," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(15) The Fifteenth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born one, listen as I speak again of the majesty of Nārāyaṇa, by hearing which a human being becomes liberated from all sins. (1)
O best of the twice-born, this entire world has Viṣṇu as its soul;
therefore, the wise who seek the supreme truth perceive it as consisting of Viṣṇu. ||2||
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Rudra, and ending with Viṣṇu, are complete within him;
therefore, one takes refuge in the one Viṣṇu as the worship of all the deities. ||3||
For those who remember the names of Viṣṇu, which remove all sins,
no inauspiciousness exists anywhere by whatever means it may be.
O best of the twice-born, every action whatsoever is said to be sinful;
yet this constant remembrance of Viṣṇu is the destroyer of sin. (5)
Whether sleeping, eating, speaking, standing,
rising, or walking, a Vaiṣṇava person seeking liberation should indeed remember Viṣṇu without ceasing.
All the eminent sages have declared that there is no restriction regarding time for the remembrance of the Lord of Kamalā,
which destroys all suffering.
I shall speak in brief of the power of the name of the high-souled Keśava, the brahminical seer; listen to this account together with its history.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a pure Vaiśya named Sapaśu, the best of the Vaiśya lineage, who had reached the further shore of all virtues. (9)
O twice-born one, by the turn of fate, that Vaiśya, afflicted by the diseases of cough and asthma, fell into the power of death during his first stage of life.
His wife, named Jīvantī, who was slender-waisted and in the prime of her youth, went to his abode when her husband had died. (11)
O best of the twice-born, that Ajīvantī, proud of her fresh youth,
moved about even while being pursued by her kinsmen as if she were afflicted by the arrows of a lover.
She disregarded his religious observances as well as his domestic affairs, for her heart was constantly devoted to her lover and she had not yet lost her youth.
O best of the twice-born, that woman with beautiful hips and full breasts, who had been made wise by her longing [for him], never once beheld the path of dharma. (14)
Seeing her indeed to be of immoral conduct, her father—who was devoted to righteousness and fearful of ill repute—spoke thus, being exceedingly wrathful: (15)
O wicked and sinful woman, having obtained birth in this body which is free from all defects, why do you commit such a sin? (16)
If your mind is indeed set upon this sin, do not come here at all; O inauspicious one, go from this place and abandon my home! 17.
Addressed thus as "Father," she, her eyes reddened with anger, abandoned her father's house and departed at her pleasure.
Then, wandering about at her own will, that woman, having exhausted her paramours,
abandoned all shame and took up the profession of a courtesan.
Whether it be a tiger, a Śabara, or even a Cāṇḍāla who comes to her house,
that unchaste woman joyfully sports with him.
That woman of the frontier did not, even for a moment, contemplate in her mind the fear of the next world, as she proceeded in due order.
Once, a certain excellent brahmin, who was actually a hunter, arrived at his house bringing a young parrot for the purpose of selling it. ||22||
That courtesan also, having honored the hunter with wealth, took that excellent young parrot with the greatest affection. (23)
By providing him with suitable food,
that courtesan, her curiosity having been aroused, constantly nourished Śuka.
Considering the young parrot, who was most distressed by the loss of its mother,
as his own son, he took charge of its protection.
O best of the twice-born, by his command that bird also acted daily toward him with a heart of affection and conduct like that of a kinsman.
Then, having attained that state, Śuka was constantly made to recite the name "Rāma" in beautiful syllables by the courtesan. (27)
The name of Rāma is the supreme Brahman, greater than all the gods and most exalted;
Śuka constantly recited it, for it destroys all sins. (28)
By the mere utterance of the name "Rāma," all the most terrible sins of both that parrot and the courtesan were utterly destroyed. (29)
O best of the twice-born, at one time both the courtesan and the parrot also passed away simultaneously.
Thus, they both reached the state of death at the same moment. (30)
Then,
in order to bring him back, Dharmarāja dispatched his servants, Caṇḍa and others, who had been assigned to carry out all manner of punishments.
Then all those fierce servants, Caṇḍa and the others, possessing great speed and holding nooses and mallets in their hands, arrived there by the command of Yama. ||32||
All those of Viṣṇu’s prowess arrived to bring them back;
but seeing the two bound with nooses and fallen, they stood motionless like Viṣṇu’s attendants.
They spoke these words to the messengers of Yama, who were like the foremost of gods: ||34||
The messengers of Viṣṇu said: "Oh, how wonderful is this speech heard from the mouth of the messengers of Yama! (35)
Even while they were devotees of Hari, these two were punished by the son of Bhāskara;
alas, the conduct of the wicked is never at its best! 36.
Even with great effort, the wicked who have committed sins constantly inflict injury upon the virtuous; this is a truly marvelous conduct.

Those whose souls are virtuous perceive the entire world as free from sin; however, the sinful do not see it so, but rather perceive the whole world as if it were filled with their own committed sins.

Virtuous people find great satisfaction upon hearing of the merit of those whose souls are meritorious; likewise, sinful people find satisfaction upon hearing of the transgressions of those who are wicked. (39)
Just as sinners find satisfaction upon hearing talk of evil,
they do not find such satisfaction even upon obtaining hundreds of loads of gold.
O twice-born one, those who perform even a sin that causes them personal suffering do so through the great illusion of the high-souled Mahāviṣṇu, which is like the power of Ahobala.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, those messengers of Viṣṇu, who were solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu,
severed the bonds of those two brahmins with the edge of their discus.
Then the messengers of Yama, enraged and resembling fire itself,
suddenly rained down heaps of blazing coals upon that spot.
Daṇḍa said:
"It was ordained by me as well that you should come here to take away Śuka and the sinful prostitute; this has become like a marvel. (44)
"O most excellent ones, surely when you wish to take these two away, then engage in battle with us this very moment. (45)
Having spoken thus, those powerful messengers of the garden, brandishing their weapons and full of arrogance, filled all the directions with lion-like roars. ||46||
Likewise, the high-souled messengers of Viṣṇu, headed by Supratīka, made the entire world resound with the most melodious blasts of their conchs. 47.
Then, in that exceedingly terrible battle, those messengers of Viṣṇu were covered by the messengers of Yama with arrows released from bows. 48.
Some hurled spears, some [hurled] pikes into the great ocean; others, in their fury, [hurled] thousands of arrows and discuses.
The great gods, the messengers of Viṣṇu, pulverized those great weapons discharged by them with arrows, maces, strikes, and other means. ||50||
Then, by the followers of the Lord, some were covered by the edge of the discus, while the arms of others were likewise covered by their feet. (51)
Some with severed heads, some with pierced chests,
and others with most extraordinary wounds, fell down lifeless, their limbs cast wide apart.
Some with one foot severed, others with one hand cut off,
those belonging to Yama suddenly abandoned the battle and fled.
Then, beholding those messengers intent on flight,
he, fierce with rage and grasping a mallet, entered the battle.
And Caṇḍa, the most excellent among the hosts of Yama’s messengers and possessed of extreme majesty, struck Viṣṇu’s servants by the hundreds with mallets. (55)
Then the messengers of Bhagavān, enraged, swiftly rained down showers of sharp weapons upon him who possessed fierce valor. 56.
Then Caṇḍa, his body drenched with flowing blood, struck the messengers of Viṣṇu one by one with a mallet.
Struck by Caṇḍena in battle, those messengers of the Blessed One, having lost their strength, fled toward the back of Suprakāśa. (58)
Then Suprakash, enraged, his eyes resembling the Japā flower,
entered the battle with mace in hand, possessing great strength.
Enraged, he whose prowess was equal to Viṣṇu struck with a mallet from his formidable hand,
which inspired fear in people upon being seen.
Greatly terrifying, smoky, and foul-smelling, he rose up when struck by his [the opponent's] forceful and violent *samudgara* blow. (61)
Then, that enraged Caṇḍa immediately discharged a shower of sparks that caused extreme terror,
using that very same mallet.
He struck the great-souled Brahmin seer Suprakash. Then, O Brahmin, Suprakash, having forgotten his vow of anger, became enraged. 63.
And he struck Caṇḍa, the servant of Śamana, with a mace;
struck by him, Caṇḍa was drenched there in blood.
O Jaimini, he fell unconscious upon the ground like the morning sun;
then those messengers of Yama took up the swooning Caṇḍa.
Uttering cries of "Alas! Alas!", they fled from the battle in fear;
meanwhile, O Brahmin, all the messengers of Viṣṇu were exceedingly delighted.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the messengers of Yama presented their accounts to Jaimini;
they were drenched in a flood of blood.
Terrified and overwhelmed by fear, they went into the presence of Yama. ||68||
The messengers of Yama said:
"O mighty-armed son of the Sun, we are the executors of your commands;
nevertheless, such a miserable plight has been inflicted upon us by the messengers of Viṣṇu. (69)
O Lord, although these two were indeed the foremost among those who have committed great sins,
by the power of the name of Rāma, they have gone to the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
If even those wicked souls who have committed sins and deserve to be punished by you go to the city of Viṣṇu, what then is your sovereignty? (71)
This humiliation has not been inflicted upon us by the messengers of Viṣṇu;
it is yours alone, O Lord. What then can we do? (72)
Yama said:
"O messengers, remember those two syllables of the name of the Immortal Lord (A-ra).
Then Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, shall be the one to punish them."
In this saṃsāra, there is no such sin that does not go to complete destruction through the remembrance of Rāma;
listen now, what can those with firm hands do? (74)

Those humans who daily remember with devotion the names of Madhusūdana—which destroy the flood of terrible evils—of him who is worshipped by the foremost of the gods, are not to be punished by me at all, even if they are sinners. (75)

Those men on earth who constantly address Him with devotion as Govinda, Keśava, Hara, Jagadīśa, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the one compassionate toward those who bow to Him, and Mādhava—even if they are great sinners, my soldiers shall not punish them. (76)
O Destroyer of the distress of devotees, Lord of the gods, Friend of the lowly, Consort of Lakṣmī, You who cause the destruction of all sins!
Those men on earth who constantly recite this [mantra] at its conclusion—even if they are sinners, they shall not be punished by me with my army. (77)
I bow daily to those in whose mouths the words "Dāmodareśvara," "the one served by hosts of immortals," "Śrī-Vāsudeva," "Puruṣottama," and "Mādhava" always reside. 78.

I am always under the command of those excellent warriors whose minds are fixed upon the discourse of Nārāyaṇa, the sole Lord of the world and enemy of Mura; they possess the form of the lotus-eyed one. (79)
Those who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, who are devotees of the devotees of Hari, who are intent upon the vow of Ekādaśī, and who are free from deceit;
those who carry the water from the feet of Viṣṇu upon their heads—even if they are sinners, they are not to be punished by me, O Bhaṭa. (80)

I bow down to those soldiers who eat the remnants of the food offering (naivedya) of the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana, which destroys the entire multitude of sins, and who constantly wear tulasī upon their ears and heads. (81)

Those who are solely intent upon worshipping the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, those devoted to honoring brāhmaṇas and serving virtuous qualities, and those who bestow supreme happiness upon the hearts of the distressed—for them I am forever a servant, subject to their will. (82)

Those who are always devoted to speaking the truth, who are beloved by the world, who protect those who have come for refuge, and who constantly regard the wealth of others as poison—they are my soldiers, O Mānava, and they are certainly not to be punished. (83)

Those who are devoted to the gift of food, those who provide water, those who grant land, and those who desire the welfare of the entire world; those who satisfy people deprived of their livelihoods, and those who are peaceful messengers—these indeed shall never be punished. (84)

Those who are devoted to sacrifice and nourishing others, who speak kindly, whose minds are free from pride, anger, and envy, and who are devoid of evil views and have conquered their senses—I shall never engage in debate with them. (85)
Vyāsa said:
Thus enlightened by Yama,
those servants of Yama came to know the incomparable power of Hari, the sustainer of the world.
O best of Brahmins, the names of Viṣṇu indeed surpass all other deities;
among them, however, the name Rāma is remembered by those who know the truth as the most excellent.
O twice-born one, this pair of syllables "Rā-ma" is indeed superior to all mantras;
by its mere utterance, even a sinner attains the supreme goal. (88)
O Jaimini, Maheśa alone knows the power of the name of Rāma, which is the worship of all the gods; no one else knows it.
A mortal obtains that same fruit which is gained from reciting the thousand names of Viṣṇu simply by remembering the name of Rāma. (90)
How strange is this conduct of human beings that has been described:
those of evil intent do not remember the name "Rāma," which bestows liberation. (91)
To speak it is not even a slight labor, yet to hear it is exceedingly beautiful;
nevertheless, those of evil intent cry out, "Rāma! Rāma! //92//
Even liberation, which is extremely difficult for the humans of this world to attain, is obtained through the name of Rāma alone; what further action could there be beyond this? (93)
O best of embodied beings, those evils remain within the bodies of living beings only so long as they do not remember "Rāma, Rāma," which bestows happiness. 94.

In the ancestral rites (śrāddha), in the libation (tarpaṇa), in the offering of oblations (balidāna), as well as in festivals, in sacrifice, in giving, in vows, and also in the propitiation of deities; ||95||
A wise person who desires the fruit of other Vedic rites as well should remember "Rāma, Rāma" with devotion. (96)
He who recites the six-syllabled mantra "Oṃ namo rāmāya," preceded by the syllable Oṃ, attains union with Hari. (97)
A person who performs the worship of Hari with the six-syllabled mantra attains all desires through the grace of the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrapāṇi). 98.
O best of the twice-born, at the time of death, whatever man remembers "Rāma, Rāma," even if he be the most sinful, he attains supreme liberation. (99)
For those wise ones who remember the name "Rāma" during this pilgrimage, all success shall be theirs on that journey; of this there is no doubt. (100)
O twice-born one, whether in a forest, a wilderness, or even in a terrifying cremation ground, no calamities shall befall him who remembers the name of Rāma. 101.
O Jaimini, likewise at the king’s gate, in a fortress, in a foreign land, in the presence of bandits,
upon seeing an evil dream, or during the afflictions of the planets.
In times of sudden calamity and likewise in fear of wind-related diseases, a mortal who remembers the name of Rāma never encounters anything inauspicious anywhere. (103)
O best of the twice-born, the name of Rāma wards off all inauspiciousness;
it grants both desires and liberation, and should therefore be constantly remembered by the wise. (104)
O brahmin-sage, that very moment in which the name of Rāma is not remembered becomes useless; this is indeed the truth as I speak it. (105)
Remembering the names of Hari, human beings do not perish. ||106||

A mortal on earth who desires the destruction of the evils of ten million births and seeks prosperity, should constantly and with devotion remember the name of Viṣṇu, which is exceedingly sweet and bestows liberation. (107)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||15||
(16) Chapter Sixteen. Vyāsa said:
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, listen as I speak again of the majesty of Mahāviṣṇu, the Supreme Self, which destroys all suffering. (1)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise others who are outcasts—those who have taken refuge in devotion to Hari have achieved their life's purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Even a Brahmin who is not a devotee of Hari should be known as worse than a dog-eater;
even a dog-eater who is a devotee of Hari should be known as superior to a Brahmin. (3)
How can he be a brāhmaṇa who is devoid of devotion to Hari?
And how can he be a dog-eater (outcaste) whose mind is possessed of devotion to the Blessed Lord? (4)
When Viṣṇu is worshipped even by an outcaste with sincerity, then one should regard him as superior even to a twice-born who knows the four Vedas. ||5||
In former times, during the age known as Dvāpara, there was a Śabara named Cakrika who caused distress to the world; he was devoid of noble birth and righteous conduct.
One who speaks truthfully, has conquered anger, is free from harming others, is compassionate, devoid of hypocrisy, and devoted to his father and mother. (7)
Neither was conversation with Vaiṣṇavas held, nor was the scripture of liberation heard;
nevertheless, unwavering devotion to Hari arose in his heart. (8)
Constantly remembering these and other names of the Wielder of the Discus, such as "Hare," "Keśava," "Govinda," "Vāsudeva," and "Janārdana. (9)
O best of the twice-born, whatever forest fruit he obtains, that descendant of the Śabara clan first places it into his own mouth. (10)
Having realized its sweetness from that, he would take it out of his mouth and,
being well-pleased, would daily give it back to Hari with devotion.
He does not distinguish between what is defiled by remnants and what is not;
for his own innate nature, O destroyer of Mura, always remains so.
Once, O best of the twice-born, while wandering within the forest, he obtained a single ripe fruit from a priyāla tree. (13)
Then that Cakrika, filled with joy yet failing to obtain the fruit from him, recognized [the truth] with great agitation and placed it inside the mouth of the merchant. (14)
O twice-born Jaimini, listen: as soon as he placed that fruit within his own mouth, it entered his throat. (15)
O twice-born one, he then bound the opening of his throat with his left hand, holding it firmly with his entire left palm. 16.
Cakrika, who was solely devoted to devotion for Hari, reflected:
"This is the result [of my sin] because I did not offer it to that enemy of Mura. (17)
"Has no one else been born in this world as sinful as I am?
Having thus reflected repeatedly upon Hari, he then formed a resolution. (18)
Nevertheless, O twice-born one, that fruit did not emerge from his throat;
for he was an exclusive devotee of Hari, who cut his own throat with an axe.
Having brought that ripe fruit, he gave it to Lord Viṣṇu;
he had come into His presence while meditating upon Him alone in his heart.
With all his limbs drenched in blood, he fell upon the surface of the earth;
seeing him lifeless, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu was deeply distressed.
There is not even one among my own people who is his equal in devotion, since he has brought me satisfaction by cutting off his own throat. (22)
What object do I possess that, by giving it away, I might attain freedom from debt, as this devoted man has performed a truly virtuous deed? (23)
Blessed is he, most blessed is he; blessed indeed is he, there is no doubt about this.
Even by sacrificing his own life, he has brought me complete satisfaction. (24)
Whether the state of Brahmā, or the state of Śiva, or even the state of a Cakrin is bestowed,
even then, the debt of this devotee is certainly not discharged.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, whose banner is Garuḍa, being exceedingly well-pleased,
then touched his head with his own lotus-like hand.
From the touch of his lotus-like hand, that Śabara, a great being devoted to Nārāyaṇa, rose up with his pain gone. (27)
Vyāsa said:
Then, O twice-born one, Keśava wiped the dust from the body of that best of devotees with his own garment,
just as a father would for his son.
Beholding that Janārdana in embodied form, Cakrika, with his head bowed and palms joined in reverence, praised him with sweet words. (29)
Cakrika said: O Govinda, Keśava, Hare, Lord of the Universe, Viṣṇu! Although I do not know the words appropriate for praising You, [I shall speak].
Nevertheless, O Lord, my tongue desires to praise you; be gracious and remove this burgeoning fault. (30)
Having abandoned that state of existence, O Lord of all, wielder of the discus, men here on earth indeed worship another.
They alone are fools, the sole abode of a multitude of evils; yet You, O God, are one who bestows grace even upon me.
Although the Lord knows that for men, devotion to You alone—the sole Lord of all states of existence—removes the bonds of worldly existence;
nevertheless, the Blessed One is well-pleased with me, even though I was born into a lineage of Śabaras who are exclusively devoted to sin.
O Lord, even the hosts of gods, headed by the four-faced Brahmā, do not obtain the touch of Your beautiful lotus-hand,
which is now known to me and has been attained by me today.
Among your servants born of noble wombs, there is no one superior to him. ||33||

Salutations to You, the supreme source of auspiciousness, by whom the son of Nimi—accompanied by the Asuras and hostile toward the Thirty-three gods and others—was previously rendered free from all sin for the benefit of mortals and the hosts of gods led by Indra; salutations to You, the Blessed One. (34)

Salutations to you, who resemble a dark cloud—the most powerful one by whom this Alāruṇa was slain, as well as the wicked Kālayavana and Dhenuka in battle, by that son of Vasudeva, the supreme among gods. 35.

Obeisance to You, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Dāmodara-Bhojana, by whom the immovable opulence of the Lord of the Gods was formerly established by the Supreme Lord; obeisance to You, the ultimate refuge of the Yadu dynasty. (36)
Salutations again and again to you, by whom the Pārijāta tree was carried away and Indra was conquered; salutations to you who have effortlessly defeated even Maheśa.
Having made Vṛkodara the instrument, Jarāsaṃdha was struck down;
and those arms of Bāṇāsura which were not slain by you have now been destroyed by him.
Śiśupāla offered him water for his feet, saying: "Constant salutations, constant salutations to You, by whom, the Great-Souled One, the burden of the earth has been removed. (39)
"Salutations again and again to him who has slain the Kṣatriyas through his illusory power.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was Viṣṇu praised by that high-souled wielder of the discus.
He said: "O Jaimini, being supremely pleased, choose a boon.
Cakrika said: "O Supreme Brahman, O Supreme Abode, O Supreme Self, O Compassionate One! (41)
O twice-born one, I see you directly before me; what need is there for other boons? Your form has not been meditated upon, nor have you performed worship unto me. (42)
With food offerings, divine flowers, divine incenses, and lamps, your names have never been remembered by me. 43.
O Lord, I have indeed not borne the water from your feet upon my head;
I have not consumed your food offering, nor have I performed your vow. (44)
Nevertheless, I beheld you; what can I do with other boons?
I am born among the Śabaras and am excluded from all religious duties. (45)
Nevertheless, even that lotus-foot, which is difficult to obtain even for the gods, has been attained by me today;
what need have I for other boons? (46)
Nevertheless, since you, the beloved of Kamalā, desire to grant a boon, may my mind remain fixed on you and sink into you through your grace. 47.
The Blessed Lord said:
O noble-minded one, by the rain of nectar from your words, I, a sinful servant, have attained great satisfaction. (48)
"O Vatsa Medātta, because of this supreme lotus offered by you, I am exceedingly pleased; filled with joy, I accept your devotion. (49)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu, who accepts devotion and whose nature is compassion,
embraced that devotee with his four long arms.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am pleased with your devotion, O best of the Cakrikas; whatever is given by you, my child, shall certainly be realized quickly. (51)
Furthermore, the Supreme Lord,
the soul of the universe and protector of the world, embraced that great devotee and vanished right there.
Sacakrika, being exceedingly satisfied and solely devoted to the worship of Hari,
abandoned his sons, wife, and other attachments, and went to the city of Dvārakā.
And there, having thus attained [the state] through the compassion of the Lord of Kamalā,
he reached liberation at the end of his life— a state difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Therefore, the God who is subject to devotion is pleased by devotion alone;
not by hymns, nor by wealth, nor by austerities, nor by recitations.
O best of the twice-born, although the fruit given by him was leftover, Viṣṇu was nevertheless pleased, having recognized his unwavering devotion. (56)
Therefore, the god Nārāyaṇa [is to be worshipped] in this saṃsāra by those seeking liberation. ||57||
Those who worship with firm devotion the pair of lotus feet of Vāsudeva,
which are worthy of adoration by the foremost of the gods, such as Indra;
Those men indeed go to liberation. ||58||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||16||
(17) Chapter Seventeen. Jaimini said:
O Guru, speak once more of the majesty of the Lord of Kamalā;
for who could ever feel satiety after drinking the nectar of Hari’s stories? (1)
Śrī Vyāsa said:
Indeed, there is no one else in this world as meritorious as you, since you desire to hear the greatness of Keśava with devotion. (2)
The delightful narrative of Nārāyaṇa thus purifies the three worlds—the listener, the questioner, and the speaker alike, O best of the twice-born. (3)
Listen, my child, to the greatness of the Lord of Lakṣmī’s son, which destroys sin;
I shall relate it in brief, as it bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. (4)
If one should worship Viṣṇu with supreme devotion for even a single day, Hari shall instantly remove the sins committed throughout ten million lifetimes. (5)
How can he be a virtuous soul who has not worshipped Hari?
And how can he be a sinner who possesses devotion for the Lord Nārāyaṇa? (6)
There is a city named Puruṣottama, the most excellent of all cities, endowed with every virtue and the refuge of all the hosts of gods. ||7||
It is declared to be the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas), because in that delightful city Keśava himself dwells in person. (8)
In that place, there was formerly a certain twice-born man named Bhadranu;
he was handsome, pleasant of speech, and born of a pure lineage. (9)
Having reached the prime of youth, the handsome brahmin, deluded by passion, abandoned all fear of the next world and became devoted to courtesans. ||10||
He did not engage in the study of the Vedas nor of the Purāṇas in any way; and he abandoned his status as an "Uttama" due to association with heretical people. (11)
He was one who accepted gifts from those unfit to offer sacrifices, a stealer of others' property,
a reviler of dharma, and that brahmin was wholly devoted to sin.
That lowest of Brahmins abandoned the conduct of a Brahmin as well as the cultivation of truthfulness, and likewise the honoring of gurus and guests. (13)
Whatever action is more sinful, that very one is prescribed;
never, O Jaimini, is a most meritorious action [so ordained] by him.
Once, having committed a sin and filled with shame and fear of the world, that brahmin indeed performed a śrāddha ceremony, though it was devoid of faith and devotion. (15)
"Go to the house of a courtesan," he said, and at night he went there.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O lady of broad hips, today is the day of my ancestral śrāddha ceremony. (16)
Though bound by your virtues, I have nevertheless come to your abode;
behold this night of yours, which brings fear to all the worlds. (17)
My mind, drawn by your virtues, has left the ground and pervaded the sky, which is filled with masses of raining clouds and where the paths have been obscured by fresh raindrops. (18)
Even during this night, I have come to your house, driven by a desire that is like lightning amidst clouds and that instructs me in my purpose. (19)
O beloved of the night, having come here through faith in meditation upon your virtues, not even for a single moment does joy arise within me when I do not behold you. (20)
Moreover, since I am free from suffering and have no cause [for it], I have come here to see you;
what need have I for bathing in the waters of sacred fords? (21)
Sprinkled with the water of the sacred ford of your love, I have attained this state in heaven;
yet what fruit is there for me in performing service that grants happiness only in the hereafter? (22)
"By living alone through your grace, heaven is attained by me;
what ill-repute could there be for you from the performance of the *śrāddha* rite in my home out of fear? (23)
In this act of faith, even my own faith does not appear to be very slight;
you are my recitation, you are my austerity, and you are my moral conduct, O beautiful one. (24)
O beautiful one, I have taken refuge in you alone with my whole being throughout this cycle of existence;
command me always, what shall I do? (25)
Sumadhyamā said:
"O father, because of you as a son, he has become as if sonless;
even on the day of the ancestral śrāddha rite, you desire to engage in sexual intercourse. (26)
O evil-minded one, he who engages in sexual intercourse on the anniversary of an ancestor's death—his ancestors as well as he himself shall become consumers of semen. 27.
If a fool, out of delusion, engages in sexual intercourse on the day of the ancestors, that śrāddha will be seized by rākṣasas; there is no doubt about this. ||28||
If your heart were truly filled with such affection for Viṣṇu as it is for me when you speak to me, then what indeed would you not attain? (29)
The life of embodied beings stands between the staffs of Yama;
yet, O fool, you always commit sin without fear. (30)
O fool, why do you always smear yourself with the notion of permanence regarding this life, which is as fragile as a water bubble and perishes in an instant? (31)
How can he who has the two syllables "Death" inscribed upon his forehead commit a sin that bestows all manner of suffering? (32)
Oh, how great is the Māyā of Mahāviṣṇu on this earth!
For even while constantly committing sin, O twice-born one, he remains ever joyful. (33)
Grant me a place for my sin within your own body, that wretched abode;
for the fire of asceticism burns like a blazing sacrificial flame.
Vyāsa said:
Thus it was spoken by that beautiful courtesan due to the impulse of fate;
the Brahmin, having committed the sin, reflected within his mind. (35)
"Fie, fie upon me, a great sinner, a fool, the foremost among the wicked! That very knowledge belongs only to the courtesan; how has it come to such a wretched soul as mine? (36)
Having indeed obtained birth in a pure brahmin family, I have constantly committed great sins that lead to self-destruction. (37)
Since death is certain once born, and since Yama is the master when one has died, how indeed can I commit sin through a lack of discernment? (38)
Recitation, austerity, as well as burnt offerings, the study of the Vedas, the conduct of a Brahmin, the honoring of guests, devotion to the guru, and the worship of the twice-born; ||39||
I have not performed rites such as the ancestral sacrifices (śrāddha), nor have I offered worship to the Lord of Kamalā; how then can there be a supreme destination for me? (40)
Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, that twice-born man praised the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, the best among those who know all dharmas, with these words. (41)
The brāhmaṇa said:
Obest be to you, O best of the twice-born; O long-lived one, salutations unto you!
Salutations to you, the great soul whose very nature is Nārāyaṇa. (42)
Homage to the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, who desires the welfare of all the worlds;
homage indeed to you, the ocean of knowledge, who are truly changeless. ||43||
Having been praised by that brahmin, Mārkaṇḍeya, of great austerity and one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures, spoke with supreme delight: 44.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O highly fortunate one, I am exceedingly pleased by your devotion; choose a boon.
I shall immediately fulfill your desire; it shall not be otherwise. (45)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"I am the foremost among the sinful, devoid of the conduct of the twice-born;
I am constantly intent on harming others and always devoted to the wives of others. (46)
O best of Brahmins, by me, a fool, great sin has always been committed;
never at any time have I performed meritorious deeds with devotion for the sake of the next world. (47)
In this terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which bestows suffering and is exceedingly fearsome, how may I, a great sinner, achieve deliverance? (48)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

O best of Brahmins, even though you have committed sins, you are indeed the foremost among the meritorious, since this wisdom, so difficult to attain in the cycle of existence, has arisen within you. (49)
The virtuous vision of those whose souls are meritorious increases day by day;
however, the sinful vision of those whose souls are wicked increases day after day. (50)
Even by you, who possess a sinful nature, the sinful view is being warded off;
therefore, the Lord of the World appears as if pleased with you. (51)
Even after committing a sin, that mortal who turns away from evil further is called a superior man, by whom Acyuta was worshipped in a previous birth. (52)
Seeing his own devotee engaged in sinful acts, the Lord Mahāviṣṇu bestows upon him vast intelligence so that he may attain a virtuous state.
Therefore, O best of brahmins, you who have worshipped Acyuta in every birth, prosperity shall be yours before long; of this there is no doubt. (54)
O Brahmin, whatever you have asked, you shall not hear it from me, for the time for my daily rites has now arrived. (55)
"There is a certain twice-born man named Dānta who knows the true nature of all things;
he will explain it all to you, so go to his hermitage. (56)
Instructed thus by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya,
that Brahmin quickly went to the exceedingly beautiful and holy Dānta hermitage.
It was adorned with *aśvattha*, *campaka*, *bakula*, and *priyaka* trees,
as well as other flowering trees, making it exceedingly beautiful and enchanting.
The fragrance of fully blossomed flowers pervaded the quarters of the sky;
it was filled with swarms of humming bees and resounded with the great noise of falling fruit. ||59||
The water was cool with a breeze blowing very gently;
it was crowded with hundreds of wild beasts and thronged with disciples and their pupils.
Then, having entered that most enchanting hermitage, the brahmin beheld one who was self-controlled and a knower of reality, surrounded by a multitude of all his disciples.
Having praised him, the best of Brahmins—who was self-controlled and whose nature is Nārāyaṇa—that most excellent of the twice-born prostrated his head at his feet. (62)
Dānta said:
"Who are you, O blessed one, who have arrived here? What is your purpose?
Tell me that; for what reason do you now praise me? (63)
Bhadratanu said:
"O highly fortunate one, I am a brāhmaṇa who has abandoned the conduct of a brāhmaṇa;
I am known by the name Bhadratanu, having committed every kind of sin. (64)
"How may the destruction of the evils of saṃsāra come about for me, a sinner?
Tell me this, O Brahmin, since you are a knower of all truths. (65)
Dānta said:
Listen, O Brahmin, to this supreme secret which I shall speak out of affection for you;
by means of it, the severance of the bonds of worldly existence occurs for men. (66)
Abandon association with heretics; always cultivate the company of the virtuous. [Renounce] desire, anger, delusion, greed, pride, and envy.
O twice-born one, even with great effort, abandon untruth and violence while constantly remembering the names of the high-souled Mahāviṣṇu. (68)
O best of the twice-born, perform the sweeping and likewise the smearing [with cow dung], as well as the beautification of the path and the lighting of lamps in the temple of Keśava. (69)
Always perform service to brahmins and service to your kin; by doing so, you will never lack water for offerings and will constantly perform the five great sacrifices. (70)
Listen to the story of Hari and chant the twelve-syllable mantra;
O best of beings, perform all these actions for yourself.
Supreme knowledge will arise; through that knowledge, you shall attain liberation.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O Brāhmaṇa, regarding those auspicious things which have been mentioned by you, please explain their detailed description; what are delusion, pride, and envy? (73)
What was not practiced? Non-violence, compassion, hope, self-restraint, and equanimity were practiced; and what was proclaimed? The worship of the Lord of Kamalā (Viṣṇu) without hypocrisy. (74)
What is declared to be one day and night? Likewise, what is the remembrance of Viṣṇu? What are the five great sacrifices? And what is the twelve-syllable mantra? (75)
O best of Brahmins, tell me the full explanation of these;
through your grace, I shall attain the supreme state. (76)
Dānta said: Those who abandon the duties sanctioned by the Vedas and perform other actions, being devoid of their own traditional conduct, are proclaimed to be heretics (pākhaṇḍas). ||77||
Those who adhere to their own proper conduct, act in accordance with what is sanctioned by the Vedas, and are free from sinful desires, are proclaimed as virtuous people (sajjana). ||78||
O best of Brahmins, that longing which always exists toward women, the acquisition of wealth, and so forth, is called desire (kāma).
That burning which arises in the heart upon hearing one's own censure should be known as anger; it is the destroyer of all dharma. (80)
O best of the twice-born, that longing which arises in the heart upon seeing the wealth and other possessions of others, with the desire to acquire them, is proclaimed as greed (lobha). ||81||
"This house, my wife, my mother, my maternal grandfather, and my paternal grandfather—all this is 'mine-ness'; indeed, this is proclaimed as delusion. (82)
"I am a great soul, wealthy, and peerless on this earth"—whatever arises thus in the mind is called pride by the wise. (83)
"Always the world reviles me; my life is contemptible"—he who speaks thus to himself is possessed by self-contempt and envy. (84)
That which expresses things as they truly are and bestows happiness upon the entire world should be known as truth; untruth is the absolute opposite of that. (85)
When the thought arises in the mind, "May I attain sovereignty, wives, sons, and so forth, which are imperishable in the next world," that indeed is proclaimed as non-violence (ahiṃsā). 86.
O best of the twice-born, that state of mind which arises in the heart even with effort to remove the suffering of others is proclaimed as the ground of desire (icchā-bhūmi). 87.
That satisfaction which arises in the mind is called peace by the wise;
it is the non-restraint of the mind from despicable actions. (88)
O best of Brahmins, you who are praised by the wise and esteemed by those who perceive the truth, always remain content in both suffering and happiness. (89)
Likewise, viewing enemy and friend with equal vision is indeed declared to be non-violence (ahiṃsā).
A person [should worship] Hari with faith using offerings of food, incense, flowers, and so forth. (90)
O Brahmin, that worship which one performs at midday and at night is proclaimed as the "Sāpūjā"; it is characterized by being both mobile and substantial. 91.
O best of beings, that which is to be known as day and night is the destruction of both the preceding and succeeding days for both Ātman and Keśava.
That unification is called the remembrance of Viṣṇu;
it is the sacrifice to Brahman, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to the gods, O best of beings. (93)
The sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛ-yajña) and the sacrifice to the beings (bhūta-yajña)—these are proclaimed as the five sacrifices.
[One should perform them] preceded by the syllable Oṃ and the salutation "namo bhagavate vāsudevāya. (94)
Those who know reality call this great mantra the twelve-syllabled one.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, everything you asked has been told to you. 95.
Having known which, all the Āmānavas obtained that supreme knowledge;
thereafter, every day, [he performed] one hundred and eight [recitations] by the name of the Brahmins. 96.
"By reciting this, you shall attain liberation, which is difficult even for the Lord of Kamalā to obtain.
Bhadratanu said:
"Tell me the one hundred and eight names of Viṣṇu, the Lord of Lakṣmī. (97)
Dānta said:
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall proclaim the one hundred and eight names, having extracted the essence of the thousand names of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self. (98)
This hymn of one hundred and eight names destroys even the greatest sins;
it should be recited while meditating as follows—listen, for the meditation is now described by me. (99)
Having the appearance of an *atasī* flower, with eyes like blossoming lotuses, his entire body adorned by the dust from the hooves of cows. 100.
The Lord’s head was adorned with a noose made of cow-tail hair,
and his beautiful lips were set against the sound of the flute.
One should meditate upon the supreme face of Kṛṣṇa—his countenance like that of Cupid, clad in yellow garments, and surrounded by affectionate children living in the cow-pen. 102.

Oṃ, obeisances. For these one hundred and eight names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Veda-vyāsa is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), and Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the deity (devatā). This is the application (viniyoga) for recitation (japa) for the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||103||
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, the enemy of Keśin, the eternal one; the foe of Kaṃsa, the slayer of Dhenuka, the adversary of Śiśupāla, and the Lord. 104.
The son of Devakī, Śauri, whose eyes resemble lotuses, Dāmodara, the Lord of the World, the Creator of the World, who is identical with the World. 105.
Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of Bali, Vāmana, the son of Aditi;
Viṣṇu, the best of the Yadu clan, Vāsudeva, the bestower of wealth. 106.
Ananta, Kaiṭabhāri, Mallajit, Narakāntaka, Acyuta, Śrīdhara, Śrīmān, Śrīpati, and Puruṣottama. ||107||
Govinda, the wearer of the forest garland, Hṛṣīkeśa, the remover of all suffering, Nṛsiṃha, the enemy of the Daityas, Matsyadeva, and the one who pervades the universe. 108.
The upholder of the earth, the great tortoise, the boar, the lord of the earth;
Vaikuṇṭha, clad in yellow garments, the wielder of the discus, and the bearer of the mace. ||109||
Śaṅkhabhṛt, Padmapāṇi, Nandakī, Garuḍadhvaja, Caturbhuja, Mahāsattva, Mahābuddhi, and Mahābhuja. (110)
The Lord of great splendor, dear to Mahābāhu, Viṣvaksena, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Padmanābha, and Janārdana; ||111||
The beloved of Tulasī is the boundless Supreme Lord, the Highest Sovereign; he is the remover of supreme suffering and the ultimate bestower of happiness in the hereafter. (112)
He who dwells in the heart and dwells in the lotus, who destroys delusion through delusion, who is the destroyer of all sins, and the ender of even the most powerful among the mighty. ||113||
The lover of Rukmiṇī, the great shatterer of Rukmin’s vow, Hari—who was bound with a rope, the remover of suffering, and the upholder of Govardhana. 114.
The enemy of Pūtanā, the enemy of Muṣṭika, the destroyer of the Yamalārjuna trees;
Upendra, the universal form, whose feet are the sky, the eternal one. 115.
The Supreme Self, the Aparabrahman, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him;
Trivikrama, the Great Illusion, the knower of Yoga, and Viṣṇu (the one whose feet are a seat for the gods). 116.
The treasure of fortune, the abode of fortune, the enjoyer of sacrifice, the bestower of happiness;
the Lord of sacrifice, the enemy of Rāvaṇa, the slayer of Pralamba, the inexhaustible, the immutable. ||117||
And this [list] of one hundred and eight names from among the Thousand Names is entirely pleasing to Viṣṇu and destructive of all sins. (118)
It destroys bad dreams and eliminates the afflictions caused by planetary influences;
it brings about the destruction of all diseases and likewise bestows supreme sovereignty. ||119||
O best of the twice-born, I have proclaimed this—which destroys all calamities and bestows the fruits of all actions—for the sake of pleasing the Vaiṣṇavas. 120.
He who constantly recites these one hundred and eight names with devotion before Hari at the three junctions of the day—Hari is always pleased with him. (121)
If a devoted Vaiṣṇava person recites this during a Śrāddha ceremony, his ancestors, being fully satisfied, proceed to the supreme abode. 122.
Whoever recites this at the time of sacrifice, likewise during the worship of deities, at the time of giving gifts, or on a pilgrimage, shall obtain all these fruits. ||123||
One who is childless obtains a son, one seeking wealth obtains wealth, and one seeking knowledge obtains knowledge, through the recitation of this hymn. (124)
Those who recite the one hundred and eight names of Hari with devotion—no inauspiciousness shall ever be found for them upon this earth. (125)
Dānta said: "Go, O Brahmin; may it be well with you. By propitiating Hari with devotion according to the method prescribed by me, you shall attain supreme welfare."
Thus enlightened by that self-controlled seeker of the ultimate truth,
he became devoted to the worship of Hari in that most meritorious and excellent field.
O Jaimini, that brahmin, with constant devotion,
performed the worship of Hari every day according to the rules prescribed by Dānta.
Having perceived his exceedingly firm devotion, Hari, who is composed of compassion,
suddenly manifested, resplendent like ten million suns.
Having seen that Lord of the worlds, the beloved of Kamalā, the Infallible One,
the Brahmin bowed his head at His two lotus feet.
Then that best of Brahmins, his mind overflowing with joy,
joined his palms in reverence and praised the Lord of the World, the Consort of Kamalā.
O Lord, You have drawn away my vision that was directed toward evil, yet You have brought me to Your own compassionate devotion which bestows auspiciousness;
therefore, although I am burdened with extensive sins committed, [I am saved].
Today, however, you have been made rustic, like a common man.
When you, whose pair of feet are worshipped by the gods, are angry,
the very glance [cast at a person] surely leads that human being toward evil;
yet when you are pleased, that same glance leads him toward merit.
O Supreme Lord, this has been understood by me alone and exclusively.
I tell you this, O Lord: because of the power of remembering you,
even one who has accumulated every possible sin attains that supreme state which is obtainable only through a single lifetime as a minister of Indra.
Having ascended a celestial chariot adorned with pure gold. ||134||
O sole Lord of the universe, even that hunter Kanika— who has committed every sin— knows the virtues of the water from your lotus feet,
for he constantly reaps the fruit of sweeping your abode.
The lord of the earth was a banner of sacrifice and was honored by the gods. ||135||

O Murāri, the Lord who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, he who wears the garland of sacrifices and whose banner bears the enemy of serpents, knows the fruit of smearing the walls of your dwelling.
And his brother Sumāli was afraid of the sin he had committed. ||316||
Only Dharma knows what fruit would arise from circumambulating you, Hari; no one else in the three worlds does.
O Lord, who on earth is capable of describing the compassion of your heart?
Even the hunter, having pierced you with his arrows, attained the supreme state. (138)
Even after reviling you, the Lord of the World and Sovereign of the Thirty-three Gods, Śiśupāla attained liberation; what then need be said of your devotee? (139)
My mind has attained the state of immortality within you—that Mahāviṣṇu by whom this world was created in the form of Brahmā. ||140||
By you, as Viṣṇu, the destruction of the entire world is brought about;
by you, in the form of Rudra, [it is sustained] within saṃsāra—salutations be to you, O Lord! ||141||
Since there is nothing more minute than you, and since there is nothing greater than you, and since the entire world is pervaded by you—to you, therefore, be homage! 142.
Salutations to you, that deity from whose two eyes the sun, the maker of day, was born, and from whose mouth fire was produced. 143.
O Keśava, from whose ears even the winds were born as his vital breaths—to you, the best of gods, let there be salutation from me at all times. (144)
Salutations to you, for whom Lakṣmī always dwells with perfect contentment upon your dark-limbed chest, just as lightning rests upon a dark cloud. 145.
Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are unable to reach the limit of your greatness; therefore, let there be salutation to you. (146)
Salutations be to you, who manifest in every age for the sake of establishing the Dharma and for the destruction of the wicked. (147)

Salutations to that Great-Souled One by whom this world is deluded through his illusory power (māyā), and who, through that same power, destroys the vast multitude of worldly desires; may there be salutation to him from me. 148.
Salutations to you, who are satisfied by mere devotion, and not by wealth, nor by offerings, nor likewise by gifts or austerities. ||149||
Salutations to you, who bestows compassion and likewise brings about the welfare of cows, brahmins, and virtuous people. 150.
O God, who removes the suffering of the protectorless, of kinsmen, of yogis, and likewise of those in pain—to you, I offer my salutation. (151)
Salutations to you, who abide with equanimity toward humans, gods, and all elephants alike. 152.
Salutations to you, by whose satisfaction even a mountain instantly becomes like a blade of grass, yet by whose anger even a blade of grass becomes like a mountain! 153.
May my merit be toward you just as it is toward merit itself, as it is a father’s toward his own son, and as it is for virtuous women toward their husband. (154)
Just as the minds of youths are toward women, as those who are greedy are toward wealth, and as those who are hungry are toward food, so indeed let my mind be toward you. (155)
Just as those afflicted by heat find relief in the moon, those afflicted by cold in the sun, and those afflicted by thirst in water, so do we offer praise to you. 156.
Whatever sin of approaching the wife of my guru I have committed through my lack of wisdom, may that transgression come to an end as I behold you. (157)
May that sin of killing those who should not be killed, committed by one possessed by deceit and delusion, come to an end as I behold you. (158)
O Supreme Lord, may that sin of drinking what is unfit to be drunk, which was committed by me, come to destruction as I behold you. (159)
Likewise, whatever emission of semen was committed in a watery womb or within water—may that sin go to destruction as I behold you. (160)
May the sin committed by the emission of semen upon the ground through the killing of an embryo go to destruction as I behold you. (611)
May that sin of betraying trust, committed through ignorance and by means of deceit, go to destruction as I behold you. (162)
May whatever false speech has been uttered by me at every moment go to destruction upon my beholding you. (163)
May that sin of mine, committed by harming others even unintentionally at all times, go to destruction as I behold you. 164.
May that sin which was committed by me in my mouth through phlegm and mucus go to destruction as I behold you. (165)
May that sin of destroying a grove of trees committed by Someya come to an end for me, who beholds you. (166)
Whatever root-mantra has been recited at a roadside shrine or in a cow-pen, may that sin go to destruction as I behold you. (167)
O Keśava, may that sin of lack of devotion toward my father and mother, who are as vast [as the earth], go to destruction as I behold you. (168)
May that sin of whoever was prevented from going for the sake of bathing or eating perish as I behold you. (169)
O best of gods, on the eleventh day I have observed a fast;
may that sin perish as I behold you. (170)
O Lord, an guest came to my house and was not honored by me;
may that sin perish for me as I behold you. (171)
Whatever double meal was consumed on the twelfth or the tenth day—may that sin come to destruction as I behold you. (172)
May that sin which was committed by obstructing cows as they ran for water perish while I behold you. (173)
May that sin—the vow which I undertook but have not yet completed or renounced—go to destruction as I behold you. (174)
May that sin of false testimony which was uttered by me out of affection for my friend perish as I behold you. (175)
May that sin incurred by approaching one's own wife during her fertile season be destroyed for me as I behold you. (176)
May that sin which was committed by me while eating in the house of one who has not yet entered the religious life perish as I behold you. (177)
May that sin of practicing the livelihood of a village beggar, which was committed by me against You, O Hari, the slayer of Mura, perish as I behold You. (178)
O Lord, whatever sovereignty was exercised by me while punishing the king, may that sin perish as I behold you. (179)
Whatever obstacle has been created by me in the midst of this ancient narrative, may that sin perish as I behold you. (180)
With great care, I have listened to the discourse on the ripening of karma for others;
may that sin perish as I behold you. (181)
May that sin which was committed by cutting down the Aśvattha tree and the Dhātrī tree go to destruction upon my beholding you. (182)
May the sin committed by me through the sale of curd, milk, and ghee perish as I behold you. (183)
May that sin of mine, incurred by having given hope to others and then rendered it fruitless, go to destruction as I behold you. (184)
May that sin of those twice-born ones and beggars who have been looked upon by me with a gaze of anger perish as I behold you. (185)
May that sin of those who, out of anger, have reviled me—the giver of the means of livelihood—come to an end as I behold you. (186)
What is the use of saying more? All the sins accumulated over many lifetimes have gone to destruction as I behold you. (187)
I have achieved my purpose, I have achieved my purpose, I have achieved my purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Homage to you, homage to you, homage to you, O Lord of the World! (188)
Having spoken thus, O Jaimini, that twice-born man, his body covered with horripilation out of devotion,
fell at the two beautiful lotus-feet of Viṣṇu.
The Blessed Lord said: Arise, arise, O brāhmaṇa! I am pleased with your devotion.
Tell me what you desire; I shall certainly grant it to you. (190)
Bhadratanu said:
O Supreme Lord Govinda, O Compassionate One, O Supreme Acyuta!
What has been obtained by me through my present state—who on earth could obtain such a thing? (191)
Nevertheless, O Enemy of Mura, I would beg for one boon in Your presence:
that I may possess firm devotion unto You in birth after birth, O Lord. (192)
O you who are pleased, you shall grant all the desires of that man who recites this hymn composed by me with devotion. (193)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O brāhmaṇa, this boon has been granted to you; there is no doubt about this.
However, O wise one, I desire to form a friendship with you. (194)
"O twice-born one, they are not fit to be my servants; rather, I am your servant here.
Therefore, a friendship has now been established between you and me. (195)
Vyāsa said:
Then, O Jaimini, the compassionate Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, formed a friendship with that virtuous soul. 196.
Hari joyfully gave him the garland that was upon his own neck;
that brahmin also, with devotion, gave a garland of tulasī to Hari.
Stretching out his four arms, Hari embraced him;
the lordly brahmin also joyfully embraced Viṣṇu. (198)
Having thus established friendship with that brahmin, Hari,
who is compassionate and accepts devotion, vanished right there as it were.
Thereafter, Hari began playing with the ball every day in that field at Puruṣottama along with his elder brother.
Once, seeing that brahmin weakened, the compassionate Hari spoke these words out of affection for his friend: "O brahmin-sage! [201]
The Blessed Lord said:
"O friend, why are you so weak? By whom has your wealth been taken? What anxiety dwells in your heart? O friend, you ought to tell me that. (202)
Bhadratanu said:
"O Lord of the World, for the sake of pleasing you, I constantly perform penance; O Master, my body is becoming weak. (203)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O friend, O best of the twice-born, I am as pleased with you as I am with anyone else; why then do you again subject yourself to such bodily austerity?"
Beholding you so weak, a thought arises in my heart;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, abandon all bodily affliction. (205)

With his own upper garments, his own clothes and ornaments, with two very beautiful golden buds, and with the rings shining on his own hands, that brahmin was personally honored by the Lord of the Gods. (206)
Bringing his crown from his own forehead and his two sandals from his feet,
and a golden necklace from his own neck, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, gave them to that best of Brahmins.
Adorned with those ornaments bestowed by the illustrious Hari, this virtuous twice-born man shall always sport with Kṛṣṇa—the knower of divine pastimes—who is as beautiful as a dark lotus. (208)

Once, there within that place, he beheld one whose limbs were adorned with ornaments, whose pair of lips was beautiful with the tint of betel-juice, who wore a divine and most excellent upper garment, and whose face was smiling. (209)
Dānta said:
"O Bhadratanu, even now you do not abandon your sinful vision;
for even upon seeing it, your deed is censured by all people. (210)
Since you have been made my disciple, everything is indeed an ornament for me;
whereas I am ill-behaved, merciless, and devoted to evil. (211)
These five are the most wicked of disciples: one who destroys the teacher's reputation, one who is devoid of devotion, one who speaks excessively, and likewise one whose mind is fickle. (212)
Those who speak ill of the guru behind his back are declared to be the lowest of disciples; having ascertained their excellent conduct, they should be accepted as disciples by the wise. (213)
For even the ignorance of wicked people and teachers causes suffering; yet that very ignorance has been described as bestowing fame by those seers of reality. (214)
Those who frequent the company of the wicked instantly destroy the tree of their spiritual teacher’s fame; moreover, those of virtuous deeds never take pleasure in sinful acts. (215)
Just as flies do not relish fragrant sandalwood paste,
nor indeed are donkeys ever satisfied by sweet food and drink.
The wicked are never satisfied, even with the contemplation of Dharma; yet, out of fear of ill-repute, they abandon both Fortune and Dharma, which grants all desires. (217)
Sometimes one may not serve the wicked, or having served them, one suffers decline;
yet through the power of fortune, in every birth, one eventually attains the supreme knowledge.
Sometimes, indeed, the rule applies even within the interval between the present and the future. ||219||
Bhadratanu said:
"O brahmin-sage, you speak the truth; you are an expert in the scriptures. As your disciple, no ill repute shall ever come to me. (220)
O best of the twice-born, by your grace all that I have desired has attained fulfillment, for you alone are difficult to find on this earth. (221)
Dānta said: "O Brahmin, tell me what you desire; you have attained perfection. How was the conclusion of your austerities accomplished so swiftly?"
Bhadratanu said:
"Even with very little effort, I have obtained the vision of Hari, by whose command, O Guru, I have abandoned my daily rites and other such duties. (223)
His own upper garment and cloth, two golden jars,
a ring for his own hand, and also the crown upon his own forehead.
O best of the twice-born, the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, being well-pleased, gave me the tip of his own foot and his own pearl necklace.
Having performed this a thousand times, he remains my friend, the destroyer of the suffering of his servants;
O Guru, I play with him day and night. (226)
Having heard this very thing, I am coming; for although it was not spoken by me out of consideration, nevertheless, it was said in your presence. (227)
Dānta said:
"Even though I have worshipped Viṣṇu with supreme devotion for seven thousand years, that all-pervading Lord has not granted me his vision."
"O best of beings, having propitiated Viṣṇu for five days, you have obtained a vision that is difficult even for the gods to attain! (229)
You are blessed, you have achieved your purpose; you are said to be a god in person, since the Lord himself has formed a friendship with you out of love. (230)
O best of the twice-born, since there exists within you a love that is not false, how is it, O brahmin, that you speak of the vision of Viṣṇu as being difficult to attain? (231)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by his guru,
the wise brahmin, devoted solely to devotion to Viṣṇu, went to his own hermitage in the forest, filled with wonder.
Then, on that day when he had gone and performed his play, he spoke thus to the compassionate Lord of the World with humility: ||233||
Bhadratanu said:
"O Lord of the gods, my preceptor indeed desires to see you. Tell me, O Lord whose speech is pure with compassion, what is the reason for your remaining here?"
O lotus-eyed one, this brahmin is your exclusive devotee;
therefore, O best of gods, you ought to grant him a vision of yourself. (235)
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of Brahmins, because you have worshipped me with supreme devotion throughout many births, I have now granted you my vision."
After honoring me for some days, that wise brahmin wishes to see Māndhātṛ, who is invisible even to the gods.
"Even though he is my great devotee and solely intent upon my worship, O twice-born one, he shall nevertheless obtain a vision of me only at some future time. (238)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, that brāhmaṇa again spoke with devotion to Keśava, the Lord of Kamalā and destroyer of afflictions. 239.
Bhadratanu said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master of the World, since you have shown me favor, then grant me the vision of your face, O you who are compassionate toward your devotees. (240)
The Guru entreated the deity for the fee of the vision:
"O Lord, having not given the vision as a fee to my Guru, protect me! (241)
The Blessed Lord said:
"Since you have already offered the sacrificial fee for the sight of Me,
now bring your preceptor here and cause him to behold Me."
Having been thus commanded by him, Bhadratanu then went with joy to the excellent hermitage of his guru; thereafter, his guru returned.
When that best of givers, the Brahmin, had arrived, Hari revealed himself to him,
endowed with all auspicious marks.
Then, beholding Hari, that brahmin, a devotee of Hari, with palms joined in reverence and eyes filled with tears of joy, praised him. ||245||
Dānta said:
O you who are beautiful with a compassionate gaze, O protector of those who have come for refuge!
Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again! ||246||
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic toil has become fruitful;
today everything of mine has become fruitful, for I have obtained the sight of you.
O Lord, Master of Śrī, whatever words were previously contemplated have now been set forth before you, who are as deep as ten million oceans. (248)
There is no such hymn in this world for Vāgīśa, the Lord of the universe, by which I might produce delight in your heart. (249)
"Protect, protect me, O Lord! Protect me, O Master of the World! Be gracious!
Accept me even as a servant of the servants of Your servants.
Vyāsa said:
Then, O Jaimini, the Lord of Gods— who accepts devotion and is composed of compassion— smiled, placed his lotus-hand upon his head, and spoke thus.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of the twice-born, you are my devotee; you have obtained a vision of me.
By my grace, O auspicious one, all that shall surely come to pass."
Vyāsa said:
Then, having affectionately embraced that self-controlled Bhadratanu, the Supreme Lord suddenly vanished right there before the eyes of the brahmin. 252.

In that most excellent field, difficult to attain even for the meritorious, the best of men beheld Hari through the practice of ritual yoga; with his senses subdued, he went to the supreme abode. (253)
That brahmin Apibhadra-tanu, being solely devoted to devotion for Hari, attained liberation at the end of his life—a state difficult even for the gods to obtain. ||254||
Whoever worships the Supreme Lord with devotion for even a single day, the sins committed over many lifetimes are destroyed and love for Hari increases. (255)
Even today, O Jaimini, all the gods, including Brahmā and the others, do not know the power of that devotee of Hari on this earth. (256)
This land of action is even more difficult to attain than heaven;
here, by worshipping Viṣṇu, mortals become honored by the gods. (257)
O best of the twice-born, all the thirty gods, beginning with Śakra, fearing the exhaustion of their great merit, were constantly conversing with one another. (258)
"When shall we go once again to the land of action?
When shall we perform worship there to the Lord of Śrī-Kamalā? (259)
These people are exceedingly blessed and even greater than we;
for in the rare land of Bhārata-varṣa, they worship the Lord. (260)
Ah! Who is capable of describing the virtues of Bhāratavarṣa, wherein we formerly attained divinity by worshipping Hari? (261)
In this manner, O best of the twice-born, all the hosts of gods, headed by Vāsava,
constantly praise the region of Bhārata as the bestower of auspiciousness.
In this world, there has never been seen or heard of anyone equal to him who did not propitiate Hari by means of the attainment of birth. (263)
Truth, truth, and yet again it is said: this alone is the truth—that human beings worship the Soul of the Universe even once. (264)
Even those who, with unwearied and very firm devotion, perform their duties in this land of action,
are freed from sins easily committed and quickly attain liberation.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of the Excellent Body of Bhadra" at the Puruṣottama-kṣetra, in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(18) The Eighteenth Chapter. Jaimini said:
O Guru, if you have favor toward me, please tell me the majesty of that Puruṣottama which was described by you as the best of sacred fords (tīrtha).
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born one, listen briefly to the majesty of Puruṣottama;
who in this world, other than Viṣṇu, is capable of describing it correctly? (2)
O best of brahmins, that city named Puruṣottama on the shore of the salt ocean is even more difficult to attain than heaven itself. (3)
Since Śrī Puruṣottama himself resides in that city, it has therefore been called "Puruṣottama" by those learned in its name. ||4||
O Brahmin, that sacred field is difficult to find for ten yojanas in every direction;
the embodied beings residing there are seen by the gods as four-armed.
Indeed, upon entering that sacred field, all shall become embodiments of Viṣṇu;
therefore, no deliberation on this matter should be made by the wise.
O best of the twice-born, even food touched by a Cāṇḍāla should be accepted there by the elder brothers,
because the Cāṇḍāla is Viṣṇu himself present there.
There, Lakṣmī herself is the cook of the food and Janārdana is the eater;
therefore, O Brahmin, even for the gods, rice is difficult to obtain there. (8)
For those people who eat the food that remains after Hari has eaten—which is pure and difficult to obtain on earth—liberation is not hard to attain. 9.
All the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, come regularly and eat that food which is exceedingly difficult to obtain; what then need be said of human beings? 10.
If one’s mind does not take delight in that food which is so difficult to obtain, all the great seers declare him to be a hater of Viṣṇu. 11.
O twice-born one, just as the water of the Gaṅgā is pure everywhere on earth, so too is his food pure everywhere and a destroyer of sin. 12.
O best of the twice-born, although that food was soft and divine, it was as if made of saws to the stomach; nevertheless, it served to tear away all sins.
Indeed, for one in whom devotion toward that most difficult food arises, the sins accumulated in the past shall surely go to destruction. (14)
O best of the twice-born, he whose merit accumulated over many births is being exhausted—that person’s devotion does not arise toward that food. (15)
Likewise, in the lake of Indradyumna, in the pool of Mārkaṇḍeya, in Rohiṇī, in the ocean, and in the waters of the Śveta-Gaṅgā. ||16||
Those mortals who perform their ablutions endowed with a spirit of devotion, for them there is no further birth upon this earth. ||17||
O twice-born one, when the ancestors are satiated with the waters of the salt ocean,
they are liberated from all suffering and go to the abode of Hari.
This ocean is proclaimed by the seers of reality as the king of holy fords (tīrtha-rāja);
therefore, every action performed there becomes entirely inexhaustible. (19)

In that delightful sacred field, one should perform the worship of the ancestors, as well as acts of charity, the worship of the Lord’s feet, the chanting of prayers, sacrifices, and other such rites. (20)
Whatever action a mortal performs for the purpose of pleasing Viṣṇu, all of that shall indeed become inexhaustible; there is no doubt in this matter. ||21||
For those men who behold Balabhadra, Subhadrā, and the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain.
Without seeing Śrī Jagannātha, as well as Subhadrā and Balarāma, a mortal does not attain liberation, even while performing hundreds of meritorious deeds. (23)
O best of the twice-born, all the gods, headed by Śakra, pay homage to him whose body has become red from being struck there with a cane. (24)
O twice-born one, standing in the sky in their celestial chariots, all the hosts of gods, headed by Śakra, spoke to one another in great joy:
"When will the Lord of Kamalā grant us human birth?"
Let us go as human beings to see the Lord Hari then.
"When will our bodies become red with blood upon being struck by a cane in the field of Śrī Puruṣottama? (27)
O best of the twice-born, all the gods, headed by Vāsava, always desire blows from canes at that non-field which bestows boons. (28)
Those men who behold the Akshaya-vata there with devotion are liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births and attain the supreme goal. ||29||
[He visited] Subhadrā and Balabhadra, the Lord of the World who is free from ailment;
likewise Śveta, Mādhava the Lord of Gods, and the Mārkaṇḍeya lake. ||30||
O twice-born one, those mortals who behold Jyāmeśvara, Hanumān, and the Akṣayya-vaṭa there with devotion, indeed attain eternal liberation.
Listen to the merit of those men who, with devotion, behold Govinda swinging there in the month of Phālguna. (32)
Freed from all sins, they go at the end to the abode of Hari;
having attained knowledge there, they reach liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
O Jaimini, he who beholds the Lord of the World on the day of Varuṇa in the month of Caitra shall, upon death, enter the body of the Lord of the World.
Furthermore, that man who beholds the Lord of the World on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in Vaiśākha, and also on the third day, is indeed liberated. (35)
O brahmin sage, all the heart's desires of that man who enters upon the great ablution of the Lord of the World shall be fulfilled. (36)
All the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, standing in the sky, behold the great ablution of the Lord of the Universe, filled with a spirit of devotion. (37)
And on the day of Mahājyeṣṭhī, O brahmin-sage, by beholding the Lord of the World who is free from all ailment, a mortal attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (38)
He who beholds the Lord of Kamalā and Balabhadra as they proceed to the Guṇḍicā pavilion in the month of Āṣāḍha is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (39)
He who beholds the Lord of the World, the lotus-eyed one, seated upon his chariot, shall have no further birth in this saṃsāra which gives rise to all suffering. (40)
And those men who behold Subhadrā with devotion as she is mounted upon the chariot—the Blessed One cuts through their bonds of suffering, pride, and delusion. (41)
O twice-born one, that woman who beholds Subhadrā—whether she be childless or whose children have died—becomes possessed of many offspring and lives with her children still living. 42.
Whether she be unfortunate or barren as a crow, the woman who beholds Subhadrā shall indeed become blessed with a good husband and many children. (43)
The man who beholds Kṛṣṇa, along with Balabhadra and Subhadrā, situated within the Guṇḍicā pavilion, goes to the supreme abode. (44)
O Jaimini, he who is diseased or suffering who beholds Hari in the pavilion of Guṇḍikā is instantly liberated from both disease and sorrow.
O best of the twice-born, he who, being childless, beholds the Lord of the World situated within the Guṇḍikā pavilion, indeed obtains a Vaiṣṇava son. (46)
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking a wife obtains a wife; and one seeking liberation shall attain liberation. ||47||
O brāhmaṇa, that king who has been deprived of his kingdom but beholds Hari with devotion in the Guṇḍikā pavilion shall regain his own kingdom. (48)
O brahmin sage, he who beholds Hari with devotion at the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa, being freed from his enemies, finds that those enemies perish. (49)
Whoever, being severely oppressed by a king, beholds [the deity] in the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa, shall immediately bring that very king under his own control. (50)
Among all forms of travel, the *guṇḍikā* (palanquin) is considered the best;
therefore, it should be employed by men even while setting aside hundreds of other tasks. (51)
That mortal who beholds Hari while lying down or likewise upon rising—even in that place which is not a sacred field, yet is delightful—is worshipped even by the gods. (52)
Who on earth is able to describe the greatness of Puruṣottama, by the mere entrance into whom a man becomes Nārāyaṇa? (53)
What is the use of saying much here? I shall speak in brief:
Puruṣottama is the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
He who desires to cross this exceedingly deep ocean of saṃsāra— which bestows affliction and is the refuge for a multitude of treacherous evils—
[should do so] in the field named Puruṣottama, which grants all happiness.
One should behold that best of gods and the Supreme Person.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Puruṣottama," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(19) The nineteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, for those men who have taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa and are endowed with devotion, no inauspiciousness ever exists. (1)
I shall once again proclaim the majesty of the Lord of Kamalā, hearing which all human beings attain the supreme state. (2)
Having heard the majesty of Vāsudeva, the Vaiṣṇavas are indeed satisfied;
the heretics, however, who partake in the sufferings of hell, are not satisfied at all. ||3||
O best of the twice-born, the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu should not be spoken of in the presence of heretics; it should indeed be spoken of before the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas. ||4||
Formerly, O Jaimini, in the Tretā-yuga, there was a brahmin named Aurvīśu who was constantly devoted to sin and intent upon reviling righteousness. ||5||

O best of Brahmins, one who seizes the property of a Brahmin, one intent on approaching another's wife, one who eats beef, one who drinks liquor, and one who is greedy for the amorous dalliances of a prostitute— [these are the ones who fall]. (6)
One who kills those who have come for refuge, one who constantly reviles others, one who betrays trust, one who slays friends, and likewise one who causes suffering to kinsmen; ||7||
One who speaks untruths, one who is cruel, one who associates with heretics, one who cuts off the livelihood of the twice-born, and likewise one who misappropriates a deposit; ||8||
Beholding him to be such—a wicked man devoted to sin—all his kinsmen returned to their own homes in anger. (9)
The kinsmen said:
"The established reputation acquired by our ancestors in this stainless lineage—O fool, you are leading that very reputation toward destruction. (10)
Abandoning the path of Dharma, you constantly commit sinful acts;
you have been born as a destroyer of the fame of my lineage and a bringer of sorrow to your kin. (11)
