The creation of the Creator is considered to cause extreme wonder in you, since from that very ocean the moon was born, and from it also the poison was produced. 12.
Oh, the power of wicked sons cannot be fully reckoned;
in an instant, they destroy the fame accumulated by many men. (13)
Thus, even a lowly person becomes excellent upon the birth of a most noble son; yet even an excellent person falls into inferiority when the son is lowly. 14.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus,
O twice-born one, all those kinsmen, enraged by the fear of infamy, suddenly abandoned that foremost of sinners.
Abandoned by his kinsmen and despised by all people, he, having lost all his prosperity, became miserable and fell into the state of a *dāsa*. (16)
All the people of the countryside, having seized him as he was committing acts of banditry and mercilessly harming others, reported it to the king. (17)
O best of the twice-born, out of affection for his father, that ruler of the earth did not kill that man of evil conduct, but rather banished him from his own country. (18)
Then that merciless man, having taken refuge in the forest together with bandits, stood there with many arrogant men for the purpose of plundering the property of travelers. (19)
O Jābāli, once, weary from wandering through the forest, he went to the riverbank together with his companions in order to bathe. (20)
On the bank of that river, that evil-minded one beheld many who were devoted to the service of the Blessed One, appearing in the form of brahmins.
Then all those brāhmaṇas, having propitiated Janārdana,
spoke to one another out of great curiosity.
Today, these ripe flowers have indeed been offered by me;
someone says, "I have given betel-leaf to the Enemy of Mura. (23)
Betel should never be consumed throughout one's life;
today, this excellent plantain fruit has been offered by me. (24)
Throughout birth after birth, I have never eaten a plantain fruit;
yet someone says that I gave a pomegranate fruit to Hari. (25)
"One person said, 'I gave the excellent mango fruit'; another said, 'It was given by me. Having heard these words as they were speaking to one another, [the sage] smiled. (26)
Urvīśu reflected: "What shall I give to Viṣṇu?
Whatever edible things exist in this world, those I [possess]. (27)
Indeed, I am unable to give this up; what shall I offer to the enemy of Mura?
Dwelling constantly within the forest, I am terrified by the fear of thieves and kings. (28)
"O best of the twice-born, there will never be for me the opportunity to mount a cart.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus repeatedly to that hunter, O best of the twice-born... (29)
The cart was given to Hari, the bestower of the fourfold aims of life;
then, O Brahmin, all those brāhmaṇas departed just as they had come.
That Asura also went to his own abode along with the robbers;
once, he indeed [took] a vessel of molasses by that very same path.
Having taken [the food], a certain traveler came alone to the village; then, that thief—fearless and intent on harming others—suddenly [attacked him]. (32)
Just as they had carried away the ball and the swing of that traveler,
so too did those enemies carry off the ball and the swinger of this man.
O best of the twice-born, having reached a cart made of molasses belonging to Urvīśu, Urvīśu’s cart fell apart. (34)
He reflected in his mind upon the words preceded by remembrance:
"In this manner, Anomā herself bestowed [the gift] upon the enemy of Mura."
Therefore, one should never think of taking what is not given in this life;
having reflected thus, one should take only that which has been fashioned as a ball of molasses. (36)
O twice-born one, having learned of that devotion of his— who had given [the gift] to some brahmin for the sake of pleasing Mādhava— even though he was a great sinner— 37.
On that very day, Janārdana, being pleased, instantly took away all his sin;
then, O Brahmin, he entered the great forest.
Then, as he was being struck by all the enraged citizens,
the Lord sent forth a celestial chariot made of gold to take him away.
Then they dispatched messengers adorned with various ornaments;
those messengers of the Blessed One then approached that king, whose sins had been removed.
Having ascended this celestial chariot, they immediately went to the city of Hari;
then, that best among the virtuous attained the presence of Hari.
Having remained for another hundred manvantaras in the presence of Keśava,
and having attained supreme knowledge, he entered the body of Hari.
Vyāsa said:
By whatever means possible, a person should practice devotion to Hari;
thus, O King, like a swan, he shall go to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence. 43.
He in whose heart devotion to Hari exists for even a single moment attains that supreme state; even one who is a sinner goes there.
Having given even a single excellent object to the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), one should consume it oneself afterwards for the sake of pacifying sin. 45.
Whatever object has been given to Viṣṇu, that very thing one should give to a twice-born;
the wise must certainly not consume even a small remnant of it themselves. (46)
O best of Brahmins, those desirable things and whatever else there may be, without first offering them to Viṣṇu, they must certainly not be consumed by Vaiṣṇavas. (47)
O Brahmin, listen with a concentrated mind as I recount once more, along with its history, the greatness of the food offered to Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins. (48)
There was a brahmin named Sarvajani, born of a pure lineage, who was endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, and compassion, and who honored his gurus and brahmins. (49)
He was devoted to the worship of Hari and intent upon the constant remembrance of Hari.
He is the destroyer of the afflictions of those who have sought refuge, a speaker of truth, and one whose senses are conquered. ||50||
Bathing every morning, adhering to his own traditional conduct, avoiding all violence, devoted to the vow of Ekādaśī, and intent upon the worship of the Lord. ||51||
Once, O best of the twice-born, he saw Keśava in a dream—
dark-complexioned, with stainless lotus-like eyes, a smiling face, and clad in yellow garments.
His form was radiant with golden earrings, necklaces, and a crown;
his chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and he was adorned with a forest garland.
The Lord has four arms, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
he is endowed with all the auspicious marks and wears a golden sacrificial thread.
Having obtained a vision of the Lord of the World in a dream, that brahmin,
with palms joined in reverence and his body covered in horripilation, praised him with joy.
Salutations be to you, the sustainer of the entire world; to the destroyer of the sorrow, fear, and disease of these living beings;
to Nārāyaṇa, whose heart is dear to Kamalā; to you, the giver of the supreme nectar of dharma, artha, and kāma. (56)
O Enemy of Mura, all these sins have been committed by me while under the constant influence of intoxication and delusion;
therefore, I am afraid of this deep ocean of worldly existence—please rescue me by providing the boat of your own devotion. (57)
O Enemy of Kaiṭabha, although I know that a human being may take away his sin, yet I still constantly experience delusion with impurity;
nevertheless, I always commit evil with joy—therefore, there is no person as utterly deluded as I am. (58)
The tree of merit suddenly bears the fruit of happiness; "What can I do? I think, O Nṛhari, for I am a sinner.
I have no wealth for the rite of offering a flowering tree; O Lord, be gracious, O Blessed One, what shall I do? (59)

This bee of my mind, abandoning your pair of lotus feet—the abode of supreme nectar—is flying toward the face of a woman, which bestows death; for it constantly mistakes that face, from which phlegm is ever oozing, for a lotus. (60)
My hand is devoid of giving, my mouth speaks falsehoods, and my ears are ever intent on hearing evil;
yet, O Lord, since You destroy these very faults of Your servant who has come to You for refuge, You are indeed the destroyer of faults. (61)
O Nṛhari, the boat of devotion to you has at last been obtained by me here, firm and unshakeable, to cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra;
yet, being subject to fate and possessed of a wicked soul even therein, I shall surely continue to revolve, and thus my time of suffering persists forever. (62)
Is there a path that leads to the further shore of saṃsāra—one that is free from all suffering, compassionate, and serene?
Alas, O Viṣṇu, because my mind has been made dull by the great darkness of delusion, my vision has never at any time turned toward You here.

O Murāri, destroyer of the suffering of those whose parents have perished, this mind of mine, though evil by nature, has been destroyed [of its wickedness] by You—O Lord, O crusher of Keśin—who I behold even in a dream with Your lotus feet worshipped by all the gods. (64)
Vyāsa said:
Thus praised by him, the Lord, the Blessed One, the husband of Kamalā—who is skilled in speech and the savior from the ocean of worldly existence—spoke these words. (65)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of Brahmins, I am eternally pleased by your devotional praises;
therefore, all that is auspicious shall soon come to pass for you. (66)
O twice-born one, I have previously liberated even sinners;
now that you are my devotee, no calamity shall befall you.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Who was I that stood there before Viṣṇu, or what sin was committed by me? How was my rescue from being a sinner previously accomplished by you? (68)
How was I born in this saṃsāra, and how was I brought forth by you?
O All-pervading Lord, tell me all of this, for you are always compassionate. (69)
The Blessed Lord said:
O best of the twice-born, although this secret is not to be disclosed, nevertheless, out of affection for you, I shall speak it; listen.
O best of Brahmins, in the past you were born as a bird, and by the ripening of your own karma, you have become what you are in these regions of the earth. (71)
Constantly distressed by hunger and thirst, you wandered about eating insects as well as the water from mountain springs and hot springs. (72)
Always experiencing manifold suffering, born from the ocean of the boat of worldly existence,
you remained on this earth for four thousand years in the past.
Once, a Brahmin named Kulabhadraka, who knew all the truths, worshipped me with devotion on the bank of a river with food offerings and other gifts. (74)
Having worshipped the Lord along with the best of Brahmins and having offered that difficult-to-obtain food-offering (*naivedya*) to me,
he returned to his own home after depositing it there.
Then, having come from that tree, you, a hungry bird, devoured all the *dūlaka* fruit belonging to my offering. (76)
Having eaten [the fruit], you were immediately liberated from most terrible sins;
O twice-born one, when your time had come, you passed away according to the law of time.
My own messengers have been sent by me in every way to bring you here;
then, having placed you—whose impurities have vanished—upon a chariot, [they shall lead you].
All the hosts of immediate messengers arrived at the supreme state;
for thousands of millions of yugas, you have remained in my presence.
All worldly pleasures are difficult to obtain even for the gods;
therefore, O best of Brahmins, you have come from a pure lineage of Brāhmaṇas. (80)
Even there, O best of the twice-born, you have developed this exceedingly firm devotion toward me; by means of the yoga of action, you have constantly propitiated me.
"By the grace of this very [act], O long-lived one, you shall attain my own state;
for when I am pleased, O Brahmin, even one whose soul is full of sin becomes a partaker of liberation. (82)
Sometimes even one who is meritorious may become angry, or even a virtuous person may incur sin;
therefore, O observer of noble vows, you are my devotee—may you have the welfare of a brahmin.
"I shall grant you the supreme station, which is unattainable even by the gods.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Lord, through your grace, I have heard the account of my own former history. (84)
Now I wish to hear this; please speak something, O Lord:
with whom are you pleased, O Lord of Gods, or with whom are you angry, O Lord? (85)
"Out of great compassion, you ought to tell me all of this.
The Blessed One said: "O best of Brahmins, by what action does satisfaction arise in my heart? (86)
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe all that anger is, which always exists in all beings, briefly. 87.
I am devoid of the sense of "I," and I am always pleased with him who performs actions for my sake, endowed with righteousness and devotion. (88)
"I am always pleased with him who speaks for my sake;
having obtained a sweet thing, that immeasurable man gives it away. (89)
I am always pleased with that man who remains the same in honor and dishonor, and who knows me as dwelling within the bodies of all beings. 90.
I am always pleased with him who is free from harming others, and who performs his actions after reflecting well again and again. (91)
I am always pleased with him who desires the welfare of cows and Brahmins, and who diligently observes the words he has spoken himself. (92)
O best of the twice-born, I am always pleased with him who makes an effort to assist one who has sought refuge; he gives gifts even to those who have done him no service.
I am always pleased with him whose mind is ever fixed on me; that by which I am pleased through action has been briefly explained. 94.
I am angry because of this action; O Brahmin, listen to what I say:
he who is devoted to harming others is merciless toward all living beings. (95)
He who is always angry brings me into enmity with him;
he who speaks untruths, who is cruel, and who is intent on reviling others—[such a person is my enemy]. (96)
One who destroys the livelihood of poets is equal to an enemy;
likewise, parents, a wife, brothers, and sisters are enemies when their faults remain unseen. (97)
The deluded man who, out of ignorance, abandons his father and treats him as an enemy, that man of foolish intellect incurs the reproach of his ancestors. (98)
Those who destroy the teacher’s Vedic knowledge bring about enmity equal to that toward a Brahmin;
so too do those who cut down groves and those who fill up reservoirs. (99)
Those people who, upon seeing another's wife, fall into despondency, bring about the ruin of their own village and lead themselves into enmity with their enemies. (100)
I am always angry with those who listen to talk of evil;
those fools who hate the Protector and who steal from the protectorless. (101)
I am forever enraged at those who betray trust, as well as those who steal the strength of cows, and those who are the husbands of low-caste women.
I am always enraged with those who strike down the Aśvattha tree, and with those who create divisions among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. (103)
I am always enraged at those who are excessively attached to the wives of others, and at those men of sinful intent who, out of greed, eat on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight]. (104)
I am always angry with those who are intent on causing pain, who delight in evil thoughts, and likewise those who take pleasure in betraying their friends. (105)
I am always angry with those who destroy the *dhātrī* tree, and with those who, deluded by passion, engage in sexual intercourse during the day. (106)
I am always enraged at those who approach a menstruating woman,
and especially, O best of beings, those who out of delusion approach a woman who has not yet reached puberty.
Those base wretches who, while she was established in her vow, brought her into enmity with their enemies and ate at night on the day of the new moon—[may they suffer]. 108.
O twice-born ones, I am always angry with these two foods:
meat, sexual intercourse, and oil on the day of the new moon. (109)
O best of Brahmins, I am always angry with those who do not abandon [this path];
what is the use of saying more here? I shall tell you in brief. (110)
"I am always angry with those Vaiṣṇavas who indeed censure them.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu suddenly became invisible.
Having abandoned sleep at the words spoken by Keśava, that brāhmaṇa, a devotee of Hari, rose up from his seat. (112)
Having completely renounced all worldly duties, he became devoted to the yoga of action;
even while consuming the food offerings (naivedya) of Nārāyaṇa, this indeed was the fruit [of his practice]. (113)
I do not know what might happen to those men who perform the worship of Hari;
O Jaimini, best among the virtuous, listen as I tell you in brief. 114.
By performing the worship of Hari even once, the supreme state is attained;
human birth is difficult to obtain in this world, and within that, [the opportunity] to worship the Wielder of the Discus is even more so. 115.
Even there, O best of Brahmins, devotion is proclaimed to be difficult to attain.
For that man who has the desire in his heart to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with all suffering,
[he should perform] the worship of Vāsudeva constantly with devotion.
The noble one should perform all these actions. ||117||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra. ||19||
(20) The Twentieth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O Brahmin, the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu has been briefly described by me;
now I shall speak of gifts—listen with a concentrated mind. (1)
Between the two, charity and austerity, charity alone is remembered as supreme. It is said that through austerity one is freed from evil, but there is no evil in the act of giving charity.
Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age, and meditation alone is supreme in the Tretā; worship is supreme in the Dvāpara age, and charity is supreme in the Kali age.
Therefore, in the Kali age, the wise who desire the supreme state should constantly perform acts of charity for the pleasure of the Lord of Kamalā.
Just as the digit of the moon increases by each successive fraction, so too has the inexhaustible nature of giving and austerity been proclaimed by the wise. (5)
O best of the twice-born, even from a king, one should collect wealth;
that accumulated wealth, O wise one, one should employ in the act of giving.
That mortal who, though having wealth situated in the house of Dhanus (Sagittarius), neither eats nor gives, should be known as poor, being devoid of both giving and enjoyment. ||7||
O twice-born one, with what does wealth come?
It comes with that person who has departed; it comes from that city when he has been given away and has subsequently met his death here.
Those who give gifts, whether they have given much or little, do not become poor;
they are to be known as great lords in the world beyond.
Out of miserliness, these people guard their wealth; they should be known as deeply miserable.
In the end, O Jaimini, having abandoned all of that, they depart devoid of hope.
O best of the twice-born, in the next world, for one who is devoid of merit and virtue, destitute of wealth, and abandoned by kinsmen, that which was not given does not follow after him. (11)
O best of Brahmins, endowed with devotion and faith, Vaiṣṇavas should daily give gifts, even if they are small, according to their own capacity. (12)
O best of the twice-born, among all gifts, the giving of food and the giving of water have been proclaimed by the knowers of reality to be the most excellent. (13)

Without food, the vital breaths do not remain within the bodies of embodied beings; therefore, the giver of food should be known as the giver of life, and the giver of life is the giver of everything. (14)
Therefore, O Jaimini, among all gifts, the giver of food obtains the fruit; the gift of water is equal to the gift of food. (15)
Without water, there can be no food; therefore, water is given.
For, O best of Brahmins, hunger and thirst are proclaimed to be equal. (16)
Therefore, the wise have declared that the gift of water is the most excellent; for water is the life of men, whereas mere life itself is not truly life. ||17||
Therefore, for the sake of preserving his life, a wise man should even renounce his life, O best of Brahmins, by whom food and water have been given upon this earth. (18)
By him all forms of giving have been performed; of this there is no doubt.
Now hear the majesty of the gift of food and indeed the gift of water. (19)
In Hastināpura, there was a man as wealthy as Kubera;
in that very city, there lived a courtesan who was like a celestial nymph. (20)
She was renowned for her proficiency in the arts, endowed with all auspicious marks, a bringer of welfare, a non-Brahmin woman (or a non-Brāhmī), and born of a noble lineage. 21.
O best of the twice-born, that Brahmin woman was endowed with all virtues and was not widowed; yet her mind was infatuated with a paramour. (22)
She who performs forbidden actions and abandons discernment falls into a state of lack of discrimination; she is like a prostitute, even though she is a Brahmin woman. (23)
Out of affection, she entered the profession of a courtesan and formed a friendship with her;
both that courtesan and the Brahmin woman remained together in one place day after day.
Out of affection, O Jaimini, they performed innumerable sinful acts;
thereafter, having become exceedingly clever, she reached the state of old age.
O best of Brahmins, that Brāhmaṇī was also of very bad character and an extreme sinner;
once, while she was growing old, she [approached] her own friend, who was a chief courtesan. (26)
Filled with great astonishment, she spoke these words with humility; the one skilled in the arts of love replied:
"Friend, you have committed a single, terrible sin together with me. (27)
Even today, a great vision of sin remains before my eyes; both my beauty and my strength—indeed, everything of mine—has been snatched away by old age. (28)
Thus, this constant state of ill-health makes it impossible for me to abandon hope; I, a sinner, have encountered this vast and immovable calamity. (29)
Death, as it were, has now arrived before my very eyes; indeed, I have been brought low by the evil I have accumulated. (30)
"I shall protect [the property] when Matānikā has died childless;
therefore, all the riches, even those acquired by unjust means," [31]
"If you think it right, O friend, I wish to give [these] to the Brahmins.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"Whatever wealth has been seen and accumulated by me—" (32)
All those things given constantly to unworthy recipients—therefore, being destitute of wealth, what shall I give to the twice-born? (33)
"If you have any wealth, then give it away quickly.
Hearing these words of hers, that courtesan was exceedingly delighted. (34)
The eminent brahmin Hariśarman, being wealthy, gave a gift of food with his entire fortune and with great devotion. (35)
He constantly worshipped that Blessed One, Janārdana, having conquered his senses, subdued his anger, and being free from violence and hypocrisy. ||36||
For the sake of pleasing the Lord of Kamalā, they performed great penance with perfumes, flowers, offerings, incense of ghee, and lamps. (37)
He constantly worshipped Janārdana, the Lord of Gods;
although he was a wealthy Brahmin, his wealth was never subject to depletion.
O best of the twice-born, ants, mice, and likewise other small creatures were constantly hungry in the house of that miser. (39)
O best of Brahmins, he himself consumed all the wealth he had acquired day after day, completely devoid of the act of giving.
He never engaged in conversation with his friends, brahmins, or kinsmen that even hinted at a request for wealth. (41)
Having counted his own vast wealth in his own home and considering himself as if he were the most excellent man, that best of the twice-born rejoices. (42)
Once, O twice-born one, when his time had come, that Brāhmaṇa, who possessed immense wealth,
died along with both the courtesan and the Brāhmaṇī at the same time.
Then, extremely terrifying messengers arrived to lead them away,
holding nooses and mallets in their hands, belonging to the divine Dharmarāja.
O Jaimini, taking those messengers, such as Tecacaṇḍa and others, they immediately departed from there along a difficult path toward the city of Dharma.
Caṇḍa said:
"O Lord of Life, by your command Hariśarman has been brought here, along with the prostitute and that Brāhmaṇī woman; behold them standing before you. (46)
O best of the twice-born, having beheld them, the Lord of Jīva smiled and spoke thus to Citragupta, who was expert in all affairs: ||47||
Yama said:
O wise and high-minded Citragupta, examine from their very root all these deeds, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious. 48.
Then, by the command of Yama, the discerning Citragupta investigated all of their deeds, both auspicious and inauspicious.
Citragupta said: O gods, listen as I shall describe both merit and likewise sin;
this prostitute and Brāhmaṇī caused Hariśarman to perform [these deeds]. (50)
This courtesan named Aratidagdhā, possessed of exceedingly evil intent, has committed such sins that they cannot even be described. (51)
O son of the Sun, this courtesan, having reached the prime of her youth, gave gifts of food with all the wealth she had acquired through unjust means. (52)
By the power of the gift of food, she has been abandoned by all her sins—even those accumulated over ten million lifetimes—which otherwise cause one to dwell in the houses of torment. (53)
O Great King, those people on earth who perform the gift of food—
even if they are sinners— go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
As many meals as men consume upon the circle of the earth, so many sins of Brahmin-slaughter belonging to him perish; of this there is no doubt. (55)
While they were casting off their bodies as sins and receiving the vessels of food,
the son of the Sun arrived there suddenly.
Therefore, the wise do not accept food from sinners;
those fools who accept it out of delusion are themselves partakers of that sin. ||57||
O Lord, the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of a prostitute have been described;
now hear of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of a Brāhmaṇī.
This Brāhmaṇī Śuddhavaṃśajā, the beloved of Bhadrakīrti, who brings security to those who perform meritorious deeds, has destroyed all evil, O Lord. (59)
Abandoning the conduct of her own stage of life, she, proud of her youth,
became exceedingly sinful and lustful for union with a paramour.
Once, O King, while playing with other children in her childhood, she dug a square-shaped pit in the street. (61)
On that very day, O Lord, it rained like the water from the clouds of the dissolution;
the trench constructed by her was filled with those waters.
Then, O King, at the time of midday, a certain bull, tormented by the heat of the sun, drank water there out of thirst. (63)
By that very [act], all great evils were indeed destroyed through the power of the gift of water by that wise daughter of the Sun (Yama). ||64||
Freed from all sins, she shall go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa;
whereas this Brahmin woman, having committed sins against the Lord of Gods, possesses an evil disposition. (65)
Freed from all sins through the power of giving water,
this brahmin is a great devotee of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods.
Then, above him, the Lord Acyuta alone is remembered as the master of living beings.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, Citragupta, the bearer of the staff, [acted accordingly].
He paid homage to that courtesan, the brahmin woman, and that brahmin as well,
with divine golden ornaments and various kinds of garments.
O Jaimini, having heard of their worship and that of his family, Yama, being well-pleased, spoke these words with a smile and gentle syllables: 89.
Yama said:
"All of you are great souls whose sins have been entirely destroyed; go to the abode of the Lord, the Master of Śrī, which bestows all happiness. (70)
Then,
having placed them upon a divine golden seat adorned with royal swans, Yama dispatched them to the abode of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu).
Then, mounted upon divine chariots and adorned with all ornaments, they all,
their sins having been destroyed, went to the city of the Blessed One.
Having attained the presence of the God, that courtesan, who was formerly a Brāhmaṇī and whose every stain had been destroyed, remained there for a long time in happiness. (73)
Beholding Hariśarman approaching,
Janārdana affectionately offered him an excellent seat made of gold.
Having honored that best of the twice-born with water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping, Hari, as he sat upon an excellent seat, joyfully addressed him thus: 75.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O twice-born one, speak of your welfare; since you are the foremost among My devotees, you have long remained in My abode, which is free from all calamities."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Lord, even by merely remembering you, one obtains well-being;
I have attained your presence—what could be more auspicious than this? (77)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words spoken out of affection, the Blessed One,
being pleased, granted his own form to that twice-born man.
The Lord, the Master of Kamalā, would grant him every happiness that is difficult to obtain;
he did not give merely food, mindful of his own state of poverty.
After two days had passed, the Brahmin, fasting and distressed by hunger,
stood bowed in humility and spoke to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods.
The brahmin said:
"O Lord, this station of yours has been attained through the fruits of manifold austerities.
Yet even here, O Lord, I am constantly hungry; how is it that I am so fruitless? (81)
He was fanned even on his couch by celestial maidens of fresh youth, accompanied by divine hosts,
with the breeze of white chowries.
Adorned with great garlands of fragrant grains and flowers, and his entire body anointed with sandalwood, O Lord, he was like the most excellent of bull-kings. 83.
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, by your command, beautiful-limbed amorous women constantly dance and sing before me. (84)
All the gods, headed by Vāsava, indeed constantly carry Ajā on their heads, which are adorned with crowns, at his feet. 85.
O Lord of the World, the gods, celestial sages, and even the ṛṣis constantly praise me with hymns; what, then, can those like us ever do? (86)
I am four-armed, dark-complexioned, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; my eyes are like full-blown white lotuses, I wear yellow garments, and I possess beautiful earrings. ||87||
Wearing a golden sacrificial thread, a crown, and earrings,
you shall be seen by the gods and others like a second Garuḍa-bannered Lord.
"O Lord, these pleasures granted by you are difficult to obtain; O Supreme Lord, how is it that you do not give me food? (89)
My great body is being consumed by the fire of hunger, just as a tree is burned by a fire situated within its hollow. 90.
"O Keśava, this happiness has been granted by you; however, it does not please me, for my bodily limbs are distressed and the fire of my stomach is blazing. (91)
O Lord of the Universe, worshipped by the hosts of gods, there is no one who has been honored by me through action, mind, or speech without you being present. (92)
O Lord of the World, he has not offered you devotion even in his dreams;
for what fault, O Master, do you not grant me food? (93)
Vyāsa said:
Then the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, full of curiosity, spoke to him: "Go quickly, O Brāhmaṇa, may it be well with you, to Brahmā. (94)
Having heard these words, the Brahmin went quickly to Brahmā;
Brahmā spoke to him in return, demonstrating his own meanness.
Brahmā said:
O gods, that which is given away by one who has acquired it through hardship, yet does not enjoy it himself, is surely lost;
of this there is no doubt. (96)
Thus has the entire cause of that suffering been explained.
Go, O Brahmin; may it be well with you, for he has arrived here beyond all doubt. (97)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"By your grace, I have heard in its entirety this ripening of my own karma;
now, tell me which gifts should be given by men. (98)
Brahmā said: There are many gifts; it is not possible to describe them all. O Brahmin, listen with a concentrated mind as they are told in brief. 99.
O best of the twice-born, the gift of land is the most excellent of all gifts;
he by whom it is performed with a virtuous mind should be known as one who has bestowed every possible gift. (100)
O best of the twice-born, he who gives even a piece of land the size of a cow’s hide shall go to the supreme abode, liberated from all sins. (101)
O best of Brahmins, listen to the merit of him who gives land abounding in crops to a poor member of the twice-born. (102)
Completely liberated from all evil, he shall go to the city of Nārāyaṇa;
there he shall enjoy every happiness for as long as the fourteen Indras endure. (103)
Having attained the stage of Bhūyo, he becomes a sovereign emperor;
after enjoying the entire earth for a long time, that man becomes Nārāyaṇa. (104)
Since land should be accepted by the twice-born even after abandoning hundreds of other gifts, both the giver of land and the one who leads it away go to heaven. 105.
But that twice-born man of dull intellect who abandons the gift of land, O best of Brahmins, shall become exceedingly miserable in every birth. (106)
Viṣṇu is exceedingly pleased with whoever practices the gift of land by receiving it from others as well; he bestows upon him the supreme abode. (107)
Listen now to the merit of that person who bestows a village upon a poor brahmin of the twice-born caste, or even causes it to be given. (108)
As many as are the particles of dust upon the earth, and as many as are the drops of rain,
for so many intermediate eons (manvantaras) shall the wise one dwell in the world of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, I shall describe the merit of that high-souled person who bestows a milch cow together with her calf; listen to it. (110)
Whatever fruit one might obtain by giving away the earth consisting of seven islands and abounding in crops,
that same fruit a mortal obtains by giving a cow to a twice-born man.
He who gives a bull to a Brahmin who maintains a household is liberated from terrible sins and goes to the world of Udra. ||112||
For as many hairs as there are on the body of that bull,
for that many thousands of kalpas he rejoices together with Rudra.
But he who, being a knower of the Vedas, gives a cow with both faces,
for him there is never again a return from the world of Rudra.
He who bestows black sesame seeds joined with *lasa* shall reside in the abode of Rudra for as many years as there are grains of those excellent sesame seeds. (115)
If one gives even a sesame-seed’s measure of gold to a twice-born man,
he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
He who, with devotion, offers silver to a poor member of the twice-born reaches the world of the Moon and partakes of the nectar of immortality. (117)
O best of the twice-born, he who gives diamonds, pearls, coral, and likewise gems, goes to the world of Śakra.
O best of the twice-born, that noble-minded person who performs the gift of a horse attains the sovereignty of the king of the Gandharvas; of this there is no doubt. (119)
O twice-born one, he who gives away a young elephant free from defects shall become a sharer in the kingdom of the gods, like Indra himself.
Whoever should give a palanquin to a Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he too, having attained the station of Indra, shall dwell there for four kalpas.
O twice-born one, listen as I describe in brief the merit of that person who gives a Śāligrāma stone as a gift to a member of the twice-born class. (122)
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving away the earth with its seven islands, along with its mountains, forests, and groves, that same fruit the giver of a Śālagrāma stone attains. (123)
Whatever fruit is obtained by men through the gift of the tulā-puruṣa, one who gives a śālagrāma stone obtains ten million times that much. 124.
O best of the twice-born, by him who has given a Śālagrāma stone, the fourteen worlds have indeed been given. (125)
O best of men, he who performs the gift of the *tulā-puruṣa* becomes for a long time a lord of the earth, wearing divine garments and possessing celestial splendor. (126)
For that best of men who gives away his daughter adorned with ornaments, there is no further birth from a mother’s womb. (127)
That foolish man who, out of delusion, sells his daughter shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which there is no return. (128)
O twice-born one, the son born of a maiden who has been sold shall fall into the terrible hell known as Purīṣahrada.
One who sells his daughter should be known as a Śvapāka, excluded from all religious duties; a man learned in the scriptures should not even look upon the face of such a person. 130.
Even if one sees [the sun] out of ignorance, one should perform the rite of beholding the Sun;
whatever action is performed in the presence of a seller of a daughter [is rendered fruitless]. (131)
O twice-born one, all that auspicious karma shall go to fruitlessness for the seller of a daughter; there is no further atonement from hell for such a man.
For one who has performed the giving away of a daughter in marriage, there is no returning again from heaven; what is the use of saying more here? I shall tell you in brief. (133)
The merit for one who gives shoes and an umbrella on this earth shall be more than a hundredfold that of giving diamonds and the daughter of the Earth (the goddess Lakṣmī). 134.
Listen, I shall tell you its great merit in brief:
one shall live here for a hundred years, endowed with all prosperity.
Having died and reached the city of Śakra, he shall enjoy new garments for four hundred kalpas and attain the supreme goal.
He who gives away an old garment, or likewise a cow that has recently calved, or a menstruating maiden, shall go to hell forever. (137)
By the gift of fruit, a man goes to the abode of the thirty gods;
there he enjoys for thousands of kalpas a fruit that is like nectar.
O Brahmin, by giving vegetables as a gift, one attains the state of the Lord Śambhu;
there he enjoys for two kalpas a bliss difficult even for the gods to attain.
One who gives milk, curd, ghee, and likewise sugarcane juice,
attains the drinking of the waters of the celestial river before the Blessed Lord Hari.
A man who offers flowers to a Brahmin shall go to the abode of the gods and,
adorned with the fragrance of flowers, shall dwell there for thousands of yugas.
O best of the twice-born, O most excellent of brahmins, he who makes a gift of a bed comes to the world of Brahmā and remains there for a long time on a couch with a fine mattress. (142)
The giver of lamps and the giver of seats is indeed freed from all sins;
he sits upon a divine lion-throne, surrounded by rows of lamps. ||143||
O King, by giving betel-leaves as a gift, all auspiciousness is attained on earth;
intoxicated by betel, one sleeps in the lap of celestial nymphs in heaven. (144)
O best of the twice-born, that supreme among men who bestows the gift of knowledge shall remain for two hundred yugas having attained the presence of Viṣṇu. (145)
Then, O best of the twice-born, having attained knowledge there, one obtains liberation—which is difficult to attain—through the grace of the Lord of Kamalā. (146)
He who teaches a destitute and deeply distressed Brāhmaṇa goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which a return [to this world] is difficult to obtain. (147)
Even one of noble birth, though the best among the twice-born, does not shine without knowledge;
therefore, those who teach the twice-born attain the supreme state. (148)
Even a Brahmin who is a deity manifest on earth and a refuge for the gods, being the teacher of all castes, does not shine if he is devoid of knowledge. 149.
Whatever gifts there are in the cycle of existence, such as gold and other riches, they have all been given by him to the brahmin who was made to recite [the text]. (150)
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe in brief the merit of that man or woman who, endowed with devotion, makes a gift of a book. (151)
In that regard, for as many syllables as there are on each leaf and in each book,
one shall obtain for every single syllable the merit born from the gift of ten million tawny cows.
For as many days as the twice-born recite that book, for that many Manvantaras shall the giver of the book abide in Vaikuṇṭha. (153)
O Bhūsura, there are many such gifts as these;
who in this world, even with two hundred years, would have the power to describe them all correctly? (154)
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and other misdeeds committed by men are destroyed by these [acts];
therefore, one should practice giving.
Whatever gift is given by three people through their own merit, the fruit of that gift is obtained in proportion to the substance [of the gift]. (156)
Whatever gift is given by people out of affection for the Lord of Kamalā, one obtains ten million times that merit; of this there is no doubt. (157)
Therefore, a wise person, endowed with devotion to the Brahmins and the performance of their duties, should practice charity as a means to please Nārāyaṇa. (158)
"Even higher than austerity, charity has been declared by the seers of reality;
therefore, a wise person should perform the act of giving with great effort. (159)
O Brahmin, that best of men performed both charity and austerity;
indeed, there exists no one equal to him in this world.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of All Gifts," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||20||
(21) Chapter Twenty-One.
Vyāsa said:
O Jaimini, having heard the words of Brahmā, Hariśarman, the best of the twice-born, bowed to him once more with devotion and spoke as follows.
Hariśarman said: "O Lord, those gifts which bestow happiness have been described by you; it behooves you to tell me, for whom are those gifts intended? (2)
Brahmā said: Among all the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the supreme preceptor;
gifts should be given to him by those endowed with devotion and faith. (3)
The Brahmin is the refuge of all gods; he is the visible deity upon earth.
He delivers his donor across the difficult-to-cross ocean of worldly existence.
The Brāhmaṇa said: O best of gods, you have stated that the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor of all castes;
among them, who is the most excellent, and to whom should a gift be given? (5)
Brahmā said: "O best of Brāhmaṇas, all Brāhmaṇas are indeed always worthy of worship;
even those Brāhmaṇas who are afflicted by such faults as theft."
They are our enemies and never for others;
the twice-born who are ill-behaved are not to be honored, nor are Śūdras who have not conquered their senses.
Those who eat what should not be eaten are remembered as the mothers of the worlds. (7)
The greatness of the gods of the earth is being described by me in particular; out of affection for you, O best of the twice-born, listen with a concentrated mind.
For Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, the twice-born are their gurus;
likewise, Brāhmaṇas are gurus to one another, and these earth-dwellers are worthy of worship.
O best of men, he who honors a Brāhmaṇa with the thought that he is Viṣṇu, his lifespan, sons, fame, and prosperity increase. 10.
When a foolish man on earth accumulates sin by killing a twice-born,
Keśava desires to strike off that head with his Sudarśana discus.
O Jaimini, a wise man should not bow to a Brahmin who holds flowers in his hand, milk in his hand, or a sacrificial offering in his hand, nor to one whose body is smeared with oil.
A wise person should bow down to that Brāhmaṇa who is standing in water, or staying in a temple, whose mind is immersed in meditation, and who is performing worship of the deity. 13.

O best of the twice-born, a wise man, knowing him to be such, should not eat his food even if he performs the *bahīṣkraya* rite, nor should he bow to that Brāhmaṇa while he is chanting the *Sāmaveda*. (14)
O best of the twice-born, wherever many Brahmins reside, an intelligent person should offer a salutation to each one of them. (15)
If one does not respectfully greet with devotion a Brahmin who has already offered a salutation, he should be known as equal to a Cāṇḍāla and must never be greeted. 16.
The two parents should not bow to their son who has already offered his salutation;
likewise, all twice-born men who have already offered salutations must not be bowed to by other twice-born men. 17.
Wise men do not harbor hatred toward twice-born Brahmins or cows even when they have committed offenses;
nor do they hate them out of delusion—for Hari is always angry with those who do so. 18.
Yama inflicts the piercing of needles into the eyes of that person who looks upon begging brahmins with an angry gaze. (19)
Into that very mouth with which the fool utters insults against a Brahmin,
she indeed places this heated iron rod.
In whichever house a Brāhmaṇa eats, Keśava himself is present in that house, as are all the deities, the ancestors, and the celestial sages. ||21||
If a wise person carries even a single drop of water from the feet of a Brahmin,
every sin residing within his body perishes instantly.
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist within the midst of millions of cosmic eggs, all those sacred fords reside at the right foot of the Brahmin. 23.
He whose head is constantly sprinkled with the water from the feet of a brāhmaṇa has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.
All terrible sins, including even the killing of a Brahmin, are instantly destroyed for him by the wise through the honoring of the feet of a Brahmin. (25)
All diseases, beginning with consumption, which cause supreme affliction, go to their dissolution immediately by meditating upon the feet of a Brahmin. (26)
Whatever water is offered at the feet of the Brahmins for the sake of the ancestors, by that the ancestors remain satisfied in heaven as long as the moon and stars endure. (27)
The wise man who, having washed his feet, worships with *dūrvā* grass—by him is Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World and the best of all gods, truly worshipped. (28)
O Brahmins, that mortal who bears upon his head the floral remains from the feet of the wise—truly, truly, I declare to you—that his liberation shall indeed be eternal. (29)
The best of men who circumambulates and bows to a brahmin has, by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven continents. (30)
Whoever should offer fruit and betel-leaves to Brahmins after washing their feet shall be freed from disease if sick, and the sinner shall be freed from sin. (31)
One who is bound is released from bondage by washing the feet of Brahmins;
likewise, those noble women who are childless or whose children have died [are purified].

O best of Brahmins, listen to the greatness of Mahāmātya, which destroys all sins, resulting from sprinkling water upon the feet of a Brāhmaṇa who has many offspring and whose life is as dear as a calf. 33.
I shall now speak to you in brief regarding the sprinkling of the twice-born.
Formerly, there was one named Bhadrakriya, born of a pure lineage. (34)
There was a brāhmaṇa who was devoted to the service of Viṣṇu;
he was a knower of the Vedas, compassionate, peaceful, and dedicated to devotion toward his ancestors. ||35||
He was one who performed worship for guests and likewise honored his kinsmen;
once, O best of the twice-born, his body was anointed with oil. (36)
Having taken his bathing garments, he went to the lake to bathe;
and having performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rite, that best of Brahmins offered libations and other ceremonies.
The knower of all scriptures, devoted to the welfare of all the world, having completed his ritual ablutions, chanted the names of Hari. (38)
He returned to his own home and became intent upon the worship of Hari;
he washed [the Lord's] feet with exceedingly cool waters. (39)
Having washed his hands and feet, that Brāhmaṇa, a worshipper of Brāhmaṇas,
set out all the requisites for the ritual bath.
O best of the twice-born, at the gateway, a certain snake, scorched by the heat of the midday sun which was like fire, arrived. (41)
While he was fast asleep in that extremely cool water from the Brahmins' feet, that great sinner became purified by the touch of the Brahmins' foot-water. (42)
He was liberated from all sins, even those committed over ten million lifetimes;
yet, at the door of the temple, he lay fast asleep, agitated by thirst like a barking dog.
When they asked for water, the twice-born man was struck by the hands of those twice-born ones;
right there, the brahmin met his death instantly, like a dog.
From the touch of the water sprinkling the feet of the twice-born, the dog was cleansed of its impurities;
beholding that high-souled one, he saw him as if the Lord himself were incarnate. (45)
Bowing down in humility, that brahmin, rich in asceticism, spoke.
The brahmin said:
"Who are you? Tell me, O highly fortunate one; by what deed have you become so sorrowful?"
Born into the family of a dog, which is filled with various miseries. ||46||
Brahmā said:
Having heard the words of that brahmin-sage,
the highly illustrious one related his entire account from the very beginning.
I was a sovereign ruler of the entire earth named Śaṅkha, possessed of great strength; for four thousand years, I protected the whole world.
By my command, all enemies have been conquered in battle;
all gifts have been bestowed, and kinsmen have been protected. (49)
Once, O illustrious one, pierced by the arrows of Love, I forcibly carried off a certain exceedingly beautiful woman from among the wives of men. (50)
By the power of that sin, my glory has vanished;
consequently, even though I possess great strength, I have been rejected by all the worlds. (51)
Then, having been deprived of my kingdom and dwelling within the depths of the forest, exhausted by hunger and thirst, I eventually met my death. (52)
"O best of Brahmins, having gone to the city of Aṅgāraka, I have for a long time experienced suffering;
hear that, which causes pain to the hearts of those who listen. (53)
He took delight in a world made of glowing red-hot iron weapons and molten copper,
which was utterly terrifying with its blazing crests of fire.
Then, at the command of Śamana, I stood embracing that most terrifying iron pillar, which was heated by a blazing fire.
I was sprinkled with streams of cold sugar-water by the servants of Yama, and there in the abode of Yama, I experienced other very great sufferings as well. (56)
Then, having attained birth again and again in the remainder of hell, I experienced for a long time great suffering in a sinful womb. (57)
Through contact with the water of your feet, I am liberated from the rope of sin;
I go now to that supreme abode which is difficult even for yogis to attain.
O Meguru, best of the twice-born, salutations to you, the Great-Souled One!
By your grace, I am liberated from sins and shall go to the city of Hari. (59)
Bhadrakriya said:
"O King, in the human realm there is never a story of a previous birth; therefore, one should always practice righteousness, even by abandoning one's own son. (60)
For that king who grasps political wisdom, there is indeed no calamity;
he enjoys the earth for a long time, free from all thorns.
That evil-minded king to whom policy is not pleasing shall, before long, be deprived of his fortune; of this there is no doubt. (62)
By one who desires long life, strength, fame, friends, victory, and happiness, ministers and learned men should always indeed be appointed by the king. (63)
O wise ones, you should abandon this disregard for the king;
for in an assembly devoid of the wise, political wisdom holds no power.
Therefore, when the royal fortune of a lord of the earth has suddenly perished, his treasury, army, and vehicles also perish along with it. (65)
Brahmins, astrologers, physicians, and likewise kinsmen—
kings desire their welfare and never harbor enmity toward them.

One who hates astrologers is bereft of fortune; one who hates physicians is devoid of long life; one who hates kinsmen becomes familyless; and one who hates Brahmins suffers from all manner of afflictions. (67)
Kings are declared to be fathers, and likewise, the subjects are their sons;
therefore, the rulers protect their subjects like their own biological children. He should act toward the citizens with the same affection as he would for his own son.
And those kings who cause suffering to their subjects are exceedingly wicked. ||69||
The heads of those [offenders] who have fallen from their station should be recognized as such by the far-sighted; for it is through discernment that rulers protect their subjects. (70)
Likewise, Hari, the Lord of the gods, protects them as well incessantly;
for both the protection of subjects and the administration of punishment bring auspiciousness to a king.
Those kings who are devoid of these two should be known as the lowest of monarchs;
[the other two being] the punishment of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous. (72)
Ruling thus, the protectors of the earth shall endure for a long time upon this world;
therefore, a lord of the earth should diligently protect wealth acquired through righteous means.
For a king of evil conduct does not expand when facing calamity;
kings who desire their own welfare must consider whether their kingdom is auspicious or inauspicious. (74)
The best of Brahmins, acting with haste, constantly observe with the eye of a spy as long as the fear of an enemy army has not arrived; one should contemplate such danger.
O King, even though he may be fearless, he should act with caution when both [risks] have arrived; likewise, even when he knows [the truth], he should behave as toward a friend, a son, or a minister.
One should show fear with the mouth, but only pure love with the mind;
for ministers, kinsmen, friends, subjects, and likewise brothers [are to be treated thus]. (77)
O King, I consider you a cow devoid of fear; indeed, they do not treat you like a king.
They stay far away at first, yet likewise remain right in front of you.
The ministers did not desire a king who had abandoned the earth, for they feared the wrath of the world;
and the sole minister long desired the king to rule over the realm.
O Brahmin, this must be done for the prosperity of the entire kingdom; for one should not deprive servants of their wealth when they possess exceptional intelligence and capability. (80)
Therefore, a king should appoint another minister who is wise, truthful, and free from greed;
for a king who is defeated by fools and women, and who is always addicted to song and instrumental music, [is ruined]. 81.
One who is deprived of swift means of transport may suddenly fall into calamity;
therefore, the adoption of proper conduct and the fulfillment of one's own word are essential. (82)
O best of the twice-born, [you have described] the characteristics of cows, women, and kings;
but how can he be a king who is devoid of majesty? (83)
How can he be a king by whom the supreme earth has not been conquered? For as long as the king has not conquered the supreme earth, how far can he go on foot? (84)
By reciting this at every step, one obtains the inexhaustible fruit of the horse sacrifice;
and for one who desires victory over enemy lands, there shall be no defeat by kings in battle. 85.
Then, liberated from all sins, he shall go to the supreme abode;
the king who has attained victory in battle reaches the highest state. (86)
One who meets death in battle shall obtain the prosperity of a lord of disputants;
whereas one who has cast aside his weapons, abandoned his courage, and is intent on flight [shall not]. ||87||
O best of the twice-born, if a warrior kills one who is fleeing from battle, he, along with the king, goes to a downward state. Therefore, one should not flee in combat. 88.
Both of them shall remain in a hell of extreme suffering;
O best of the twice-born, a warrior who fights with such recklessness shall stay there for that duration.
May they both remain in heaven as long as the moon and sun endure; what is the use of saying more here? I shall speak in brief. (90)
"A king who performs the protection of his subjects never comes to grief.
Brahmā said:
"While that king, whose impurities had been washed away, was speaking thus," (91)
O twice-born one, a great rain of flowers fell from the sky upon him;
then, the messengers of the high-souled Keśava arrived.
Taking a beautiful, divine chariot yoked with royal swans, he ascended that celestial vehicle fashioned from gold. ||93||
The king, his sins having been removed, went to the abode of Viṣṇu. Thus has the majesty of the water from the feet of a brāhmaṇa been proclaimed to you. 94.
Having heard that with a spirit of devotion, a person shall attain liberation.
Thus, everything that you desired to hear has been told to you. 95.
"Go, O Brahmin, may it be well with you, toward the abode of the potter.
Hariśarman said: "My body is being consumed by a great fire of hunger. (96)
"O Blessed One, by what means may my hunger be appeased?
O Lord of Gods, you who are devoted to your devotees and affectionate toward them, please tell me this. (97)
"I constantly experience great suffering, being perpetually consumed by the fires of hunger.
Brahmā said:
"That body which was nourished by you with food at all times—" (98)
O best of the twice-born, eat the flesh of that body;
for those who satisfy themselves with the food of another shall indeed eat the flesh of their own bodies in the next world. (99)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those harsh words of Brahmā, that best of the twice-born again praised the Lord with words of gentle syllables. (100)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods, protector of those who have sought refuge! Forgive every fault, O best of deities; salutations unto you! (101)
For those men who carry heaps of impurities scattered at their very roots, all defects are present and there are no virtues whatsoever. (102)
I have committed this offense out of delusion; you ought to forgive it.
For the virtuous do not look for faults in those who have sought refuge. 103.
O Brahmin, it is impossible for embodied beings to eat the flesh of their own bodies;
therefore, satisfaction arises from whatever is appropriate for them. 104.
When these words had been spoken with devotion by that twice-born one, the compassionate, omniscient Brahmā, who is fond of brāhmaṇas, spoke: 105.
Brahmā said: "O best of Brahmins, do not grieve; listen to my auspicious words regarding the manner by which he may now obtain food in this world. (106)
A son is born from one's own self; as is the self, so is the son.
Therefore, it is indeed through the actions performed by the son that the ancestors receive their reward. 107.
"You have stayed for a long time in the exceedingly beautiful palace of the god.
Thus addressed by him, that brahmin was then overcome with hunger. (108)
Having appeared in a dream, he spoke these words to his son.
The Brahmin said:
"O best of sons, you have been initiated; likewise, you shall attain supreme auspiciousness."
O gentle son, listen to this account of your progenitor, who has attained the supreme light through the power of his asceticism and is now free from suffering. (110)
Tormented by the fire of hunger, I am constantly perishing there;
therefore, O son, you must now have affection for me as for a father. (111)
"O twice-born one, let food and water also be given for my sake;
whatever is offered on this earth by sons for the sake of their ancestors [should be done]. (112)
Your ancestors have gained that [merit], O sons born from the bodies of your fathers, because in former times the Blessed One was worshipped by me with supreme devotion. (113)
With songs, instrumental music, dances, and beautiful recitations of hymns;
with perfumes, incense, food offerings, and lamps filled with ghee. ||114||

"O son, because I am wretched, I have not offered water for the feet, the respectful oblation, and water for sipping, nor have I performed meditations, invocations, and other rites for the Lord of the Universe."
Even a mere morsel of cooked food offered as an oblation never removes the sins of one who has never performed worship for a guest, even with water or other offerings. (116)
Because I did not satisfy my kinsmen and those who came as supplicants,
by that very deed, O son, [this state] has come upon me even in the house of Nārāyaṇa.
Tormented by the fire of hunger, I am perishing day after day;
therefore, one should give gifts of food and water to a poor member of the twice-born.
"O best of gods, having given [this], quickly grant protection for my life, O Lord;
otherwise, if you do not do so because of your cruelty," (119)
"Then, in the temple of Viṣṇu, I shall eat only my own flesh. Then that brahmin was hungry, his palate, lips, and mouth parched.
Having spoken thus, he suddenly became invisible to his initiated son;
then, at dawn, when the sun had appeared in its stainless radiance.
Having been told this by his father in a dream, the consecrated one reflected:
"Even in the next world, my father [suffers] due to the fault of his own actions."
With all my limbs consumed by hunger, I waste away day after day;
shame on me, the dull-witted one, the foremost among the wretched! 123.
"By my own merit from [my father's] funeral rites, nothing at all needs to be given," he thought;
thus, O best of the twice-born, though he had been initiated in many ways, [he remained firm]. (124)
Endowed with faith and devotion, he gave food to the Brahmins;
by the power of that merit, he became free from thirst and hunger. 125.
Listen to this: He remained in the abode of Nārāyaṇa for as long as the day of Brahmā is proclaimed to last—namely, a thousand cycles of four yugas. (126)
On that very day, fourteen Manus come into being;
fourteen Indras are likewise said to appear on that same day.
The excellent Brāhmaṇa enjoys his own respective sense-objects individually; having enjoyed his own auspicious objects on a single day of Brahmā. (128)
When Hariśarman was established in that exceedingly radiant world of Viṣṇu, fourteen Indras and Manus perished.
When a day of Brahmā, consisting of all manner of happiness and other qualities, has passed, he, having enjoyed delightful pleasures there for that length of time, [falls]. (130)
Having attained supreme knowledge, he entered the body of Hari.
Vyāsa said:
"O Jaimini, there is no equal to food and water in this world. (131)
The fruits of all forms of giving are indeed obtained through the gift of food and water; there is no examination of the recipient, nor any restriction regarding the time. (232)
Regarding the giving of food and water, it has been declared by the seers of reality that the giving of food and water must indeed always be performed. 133.
Those men who recite with supreme reverence this majesty of food, water, and likewise of the twice-born,
shall obtain the fruit of giving food and water, and thereafter go to the blissful abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gift of Food and the Gift of Water," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||21||
(22) The Twenty-second Chapter. Jaimini said:
The auspicious majesty of the Gaṅgā, as well as the fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu, the majesty of the gift of food, and the supreme merit of the gift of water. (1)
Through your grace, O Guru, I have heard in its entirety the greatness of even the water from the feet of a Brahmin, which destroys all sins, along with its historical accounts.
Now, O tiger among sages, I desire to hear with reverence the entire fruit of Ekādaśī, which destroys all sins. (3)
Why is Ekādaśī the most excellent? What is its prescribed ritual? When is it observed, and what is its fruit? Please tell me this. (4)
Who is the most worthy of worship there, O ocean of the virtues of the virtuous? What fault would there be for one who does not perform such worship? You ought to tell me that here. (5)
Vyāsa said:
"O brahmin-sage, no one other than Nārāyaṇa is able to describe the entire fruit of Ekādaśī; therefore, I shall speak of it in brief."
Having first created the world with its moving and non-moving beings, that best of persons,
for the sake of subduing them all, created the Person of Sin (Pāpapūruṣa).
The murder of a twice-born man is its head; the drinking of intoxicants is its eyes;
the theft of gold is its mouth; and violating the Guru’s bed is its ears. (8)
The murder of a woman constitutes its nose, the sin of killing a cow its two arms, the misappropriation of a deposit its neck, and likewise, the destruction of an embryo its throat. (9)

The tip of his tongue was directed toward the wives of others; his belly was filled with the slaughter of friends and people; and his waist, down to the navel-cavity, was stained by the murder of those who had sought refuge.
The thigh-bone portion belongs to the Guru; the sale of a daughter and the penis belong to him as well.
Speaking words of betrayal belongs to the anus; killing a friend belongs to the heart. (11)
With hair like minor offenses (upapātaka), possessing a massive body that inspires fear,
black in color with tawny eyes, he causes extreme suffering to his own abode.
Having seen that most formidable person of sin, the Lord, the Supreme Person who removes the suffering of his subjects, thought with compassion: (13)
This wicked and cruel person has been created as one who inflicts suffering upon his own refuge;
for the sake of restraining the subjects, I shall create a means to deal with him.
Then that Blessed Lord Viṣṇu himself became Antaka (the God of Death) and created the hells, beginning with Raurava, which inflict suffering upon the wicked.
The fool who cultivates evil does not attain the supreme state;
by the command of Yama, he goes there to the Raurava and other hells. 16.
Once, the Lord Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the suffering of living beings,
mounted upon Vainateya and went to the abode of Yama.
Having seen that Lord of the worlds, the flawless Nārāyaṇa,
Bhāskari, with a gratified mind, worshipped him with incense and other offerings.
Having been worshipped by Yama, Viṣṇu, the sole leader of all the worlds,
dwelt upon a golden throne fashioned for the tiger among the twice-born.
Seated there with Yama, the Lord, the slayer of Daityas,
heard from the southern direction the sound of the *kṛndana* [of the bowstring] and the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of the Lord.
Then, his mind filled with great wonder, he spoke thus to Yama: "From where does this sound of wailing come from? (21)
Yama said:
Mortals who have committed offenses against the gods suffer in the hell that causes extreme misery,
and they languish in my abode due to the faults earned by their own hands.
The fruit of the tree of evil is to be consumed by Viṣṇu; it bestows extreme suffering.
Therefore, the sinners weep, and this is the great sound of them. 23.
Thus addressed by the son of the Sun, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa went there suddenly; those sinful ones were weeping.
Seeing those sinful mortals stationed in the Raurava and other hells,
the Lord, the Sovereign, felt compassion arise in his heart and reflected.
All these creatures created by me suffer due to the fault of their own actions;
even though I am present, they do not abandon this hell that bestows nothing but misery.
O best of Brahmins, reflecting upon this and other matters, the Compassionate One suddenly became present there in person on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī).
Then he caused all those sinners to perform that [penance] as it was heard;
they all, their impurities dissolved, went to the supreme abode. 28.

Therefore, know the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) to be the form of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self; it is the best among all vows and the most excellent of religious observances for the destruction of all evil deeds. 29.
Having made the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) purify the three worlds,
the personified form of sin, filled with fear, approached Viṣṇu to offer praise.
Then, O twice-born one, that man of sin, with palms joined in devotion,
praised the Lord Janārdana, the beloved of Kamalā.
Having heard his hymn of praise, the Supreme Lord was pleased and said:
"I am gratified; tell me what you desire."
The Sinful Person said:
"Created by Lord Viṣṇu as a giver of suffering through his own grace,
I am now reaching my end by the power of Ekādaśī."
In that [state] where the world shall become composed of nectar, all embodied beings shall be completely liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
And when all these best of embodied beings have been liberated, with whom, O Lord, will you play in this theater of the curiosities of saṃsāra? (35)
O Keśava, as if for the sake of sport in this temple of the world's curiosity, protect me today from the fear of the Ekādaśī lunar day! 36.
Indeed, it is not possible for me to be overcome by thousands of other merits;
only the merit of Ekādaśī is able to do so—O Giver of Boons, be such [a merit]. (37)
Among humans, cattle, insects, and likewise other living beings; on mountains, in trees, in various places, and in the waters. ||38||
In rivers and oceans, in forests and wildernesses, in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, among gods, gandharvas, and birds; (39)
Out of fear of the Ekādaśī lunar day, Viṣṇu fled far away;
yet he found no place anywhere that was free from fear, nor did he find such a place anywhere at all.
O eternal God of gods, in the midst of millions of universes, I have found no place to stand on this Ekādaśī day. (41)
"O Lord, where shall I dwell on the eleventh day free from fear?
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods; I have been created by you without cause. (42)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to Acyuta, the destroyer of afflictions, the personification of sin fell upon the ground, his eyes shedding tears like those of a cakravāka bird.
Then, laughing, the Blessed One, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, spoke to the personification of sin, who was terrified by the fear of Ekādaśī: 44.
The Blessed Lord said: Arise, O personification of sin! Abandon your grief and take joy;
I shall tell you where your place shall be on the day of Ekādaśī.
When this Ekādaśī has arrived, which purifies the three worlds,
you, O personification of sin, must remain subsisting upon food.
"Resorting to food, this personification of mine—the eleventh lunar day—will slay you, that sinful man. (47)
O brahmin-sage, having vanished right there like that, even the god departed;
and the personified sin, its purpose accomplished, went away just as it had come.
Therefore, those who desire their own welfare should never consume food on the day of Hari, even when it has arrived. 49.
By the command of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, whatever sins exist in saṃsāra abide on the day of Ekādaśī, taking refuge in food. (50)
For those committing all manner of sins, there may be atonement from hell;
but those who eat food here [in this world] should be known as the worst of sinners. (51)
Again and again I speak firmly: listen, listen, O people!
It must never be eaten, it must never be eaten, it must never be eaten at any time. (52)
O best of the twice-born, the Ekādaśī, which bestows the fruits of the four goals of human existence, should be observed by all—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others as well. (53)
Eighteen *nimeṣas* are declared by the wise to be one *kāṣṭhā*; thirty *kāṣṭhās* are said by those who perceive all objects to be one *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute one *kṣaṇa*, and twelve *kṣaṇas* make one *muhūrta*.
Thirty *muhūrtas* are proclaimed to be a day and night for human beings. (55)
O best of the twice-born, a fortnight (pakṣa) is to be understood by those fifteen [days];
a month is constituted by the two fortnights, the bright and the dark. ||56||
O best of the twice-born, if in that month—whether during the bright or the dark fortnight—one observes Ekādaśī, even if one is burdened with great sins, [one is purified]. (57)
Completely liberated from all sins, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu;
the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) is indeed called "Mātā" (Mother), for she is the sole mother. ||58||
In this very world, the mother-like Ekādaśī protects everywhere;
yet he who abandons the vow of Ekādaśī and performs another vow [is lost]. (59)
The fool, having abandoned the jewel situated in his own hand, grasps a clod of earth;
so it is with those who, endowed with devotion, have observed the Ekādaśī vow.
By them all sacrifices and every single vow have been rendered fruitless—
those sinful men who, out of delusion, eat on the Ekādaśī day.
Whether on a bright or a dark lunar day, Hari is always angry with them;
by him all dharmas have been transgressed, by whom a guest has been disregarded.
Just as Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be the best among all the gods, so too is the Ekādaśī vow the best among all vows. 63.
Just as the sun is among the Ādityas, and just as the moon is among the stars, so too has the Ekādaśī vow been declared the best of all vows. (64)
Just as the Śvattha tree is celebrated among trees, and the Sāman among the Vedas, so too the Ekādaśī vow is declared to be the best of all vows. 65.
Just as Uśanas is the best among poets and the Brāhmaṇa is the best among the social classes, so too has the Ekādaśī vow been declared the best among all vows. ||66||
Vyāsa is the best among sages, and Nārada is the best among divine seers;
likewise, the vow of Ekādaśī is the most excellent of all vows.
Just as the gift of food is remembered as the best among all gifts, so too the vow of Ekādaśī is declared the most excellent of all vows. (68)
Just as there is no friend equal to merit and no teacher equal to the scriptures, even so, there is no vow equal to Ekādaśī in the three worlds. 69.
Just as the mind is declared by the wise to be the foremost of the senses, and as Arjuna is the best among the Pāṇḍavas, so is Kārttika the most excellent of months. (70)
Just as the Vedas are proclaimed to be the most excellent among all scriptures,
so too is the Ekādaśī vow remembered as the foremost among all vows.
O twice-born one, among the Vedas, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and other scriptures, no vow equal to Ekādaśī has been proclaimed anywhere by the learned. (72)
All human beings on the circle of the earth remain fearless;
having performed the Ekādaśī vow, what can the son of the Sun (Yama) do? ||73||
Yama becomes a servant to those who properly observe even a single Ekādaśī;
therefore, the Ekādaśī vow should indeed be performed, for it bestows auspiciousness. (74)
I shall describe the procedure for the Ekādaśī vow in brief;
listen with a concentrated mind, O best of beings, Jaimini. (75)
On the tenth day, having risen in the morning, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth;
thereafter, one should bathe with water—excluding oil—and abstain from food. (76)
Then, having worshipped Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, with water for the feet and other offerings, one should take a single meal while remaining intent on meditation upon Hari. (77)
On the tenth day, one should avoid meat, salt, as well as *masūraka* lentils, large beans (*bṛhanmāṣa*), and leafy vegetables.
On the tenth day, one should avoid eating twice, consuming food from others, honey, sexual intercourse, and eating from vessels made of bell-metal. //79//
On the tenth day, one should avoid neem leaves, eggplant, burnt food, and even the fruit of the citron; likewise, one should avoid cow's products that are devoid of ghee.
One should completely avoid excessive eating, eating while still extremely hungry, and the consumption of betel-leaf on the tenth lunar day. ||81||
O best of the twice-born, those very things that are prohibited on the tenth day are likewise prohibited on the twelfth day; of this there is no doubt.
O tiger among Brahmins, on the tenth and also on the twelfth lunar day, a Vaiṣṇava who truly desires the fruit of his vow should not eat at night. (83)
Therefore, having prepared the sacrificial food on the tenth day, the observer of the vow,
acting with haste, should again perform the cleansing of the teeth according to the prescribed rule during the afternoon.
Having gone to the temple in the evening and having taken handfuls of flowers, while mentally meditating upon Keśava, one should utter this mantra: ||85||
"O Govinda, this vow has been undertaken by me in your presence;
may it reach fulfillment without obstacle through the compassion of your feet. (86)
I am exceedingly fickle-minded, a man consisting of greed and delusion;
how could I be able to observe this vow without your grace? (87)
Having recited this mantra and offered that very handful of flowers to Nārāyaṇa, one should then prostrate on the ground like a staff.
In that very temple of Viṣṇu, intent upon the remembrance of Viṣṇu, one should spread a bed of *kuśa* grass on the ground and perform one's sleep there. (89)
Then at dawn, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with vimala;
the wise man should effect the purification of the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water. 90.
One should perform the daily rites, such as the worship of Viṣṇu and other rituals;
thereafter, at night, O best of Brahmins, together with all the people observing the vow.
In one place, he should keep a vigil before the Lord of the World, together with his mother, his wife, his brother, and likewise his father. (92)
Likewise, O twice-born one, he who performs the vow and keeps a vigil for Hari along with his sons and friends shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu for a long time. 93.
Janārdana removes the sins committed over many lifetimes by whoever draws variegated designs, such as the conch and the discus, in the temple of Viṣṇu. (94)
One should draw various wonderful designs with rice-flour paste or with other forest products in the temples of Viṣṇu; hear now the fruit thereof. ||95||
Together with his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, he enjoys all auspiciousness;
and at the end, having gone to the city of Viṣṇu, he shall attain liberation there. ||96||
A person who raises a banner for the Lord of the Day-lotus (the Sun) on a single day shall uplift ten million people and go to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
O protector of the earth, a person who adorns the temple of Viṣṇu with rows of banners shall obtain [merit] in every birth. 98.
As long as the banner continues to flutter in the wind, all the sin of its maker is destroyed for that same duration. ||99||
On the day of Hari, those who desire the supreme abode should have wise men place garlands of multicolored banners at the temple of Hari. (100)
O brahmin sage, that person who holds a most beautiful umbrella over the head of Viṣṇu becomes a kṣatriya on earth in every birth.
A person who creates a flower mandala for Vāsudeva on his birthday shall obtain,
for every flower, merit exceeding that of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
On the day of Vāsudeva, the wise man, adorning [the deity] with fragrant flowers, should strive with effort to perform this rite for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life. 103.
O brahmin sage, he who constructs a house for clothing on the day of Hari becomes an inhabitant of a celestial mansion in the abode of the gods.
Having fashioned garments and a dwelling there, the man who is dear to Acyuta puts on clothing that is white, red, or black. (105)
There, the observer of the vow, with devotion, should bathe a Śāligrāma stone or an image of the Lord of Lakṣmī with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then install it. 106.
