At the beginning, the wise one should perform an auspicious rite (svastyayana) as well as the ritual preparation (saṃkalpa);
this must be performed with effort for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
O Brahmin, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the ritual procedure prescribed in the scriptures,
one should then become single-minded and take up an excellent flower.
Meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within the heart of the Bhojas, seated upon a golden throne as well as one made of jewels. (109)
Seated upon a golden throne adorned with blazing jewels, wearing playful attire,
his body beautiful with the luster of a cloud bright with lightning, possessing four long arms,
and eternally resplendent with all his weapons held in his lotus-like hands—
I worship Him who, with a sidelong glance, gazes incessantly at His glorious face, thereby dispelling all fatigue.
"Come, O Blessed One, accompanied by the gods, O beloved of Śrīpati! This worship of yours must be performed by me with devotion during this vow. (111)
O Teacher of the World, endowed with the splendor of all auspicious marks, remain upon this excellent seat for as long as I perform this worship. (112)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose fame is renowned throughout all the worlds, is all well with you? Tell me everything, O you who are worshipped by the gods.
O Lord of Gods, O Nārāyaṇa, accept this fragrant water for washing the feet—pure, exceedingly cool, and capable of removing the dust from both your feet. 114.
"O Viṣṇu, whose eyes resemble the white lotus, I offer this *arghya* accompanied by dūrvā sprouts and unbroken grains of rice. (115)
I give you this purifying water for sipping; accept it, which is supreme bliss, supreme bliss, and the source of prosperity. (116)
O destroyer of Jarāsaṃdha, O lord of Lakṣmī, may your body, adorned by me with the elephant Nāga, be made fragrant by the scent of the cow Dhenu.
I offer this water for sipping (ācamana), O Lord of Asuras, which is the primordial cause of the worlds; accept it, O God, for the sake of purification. 118.
This unprecedented incense has been created by Brahmā for the increase of the gods' satisfaction;
therefore, O best of deities, this incense is offered to you by me. (119)
O Janārdana, destroyer of people, may this lamp, filled with ghee and the remover of the darkness of ignorance, serve for Your pleasure alone. 120.
"O Lord of Gods, O Teacher of the World, I give you this upper garment, which beautifully adorns the hips and loins, along with a sacred thread. (121)
O Supreme Lord, please accept this fourfold food, endowed with the six delicious tastes, which has been offered by me with devotion. (122)
O high-minded Viṣṇu, accept this betel leaf, which removes foul odors from the mouth, is infused with camphor and khadira, and bestows absolute liberation. 123.
Surrounded by his retinue, he should worship Govinda with unsurpassed offerings according to this rite,
with devotion during all four watches of the day.
One should offer various kinds of oblations on the day of Hari;
one who desires the fruit of these rites must not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
Then, all those observant of vows, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, should perform a night vigil with dancing, singing, hymns of praise, and other such acts. ||126||
O best of the twice-born, those devoted to their vows should remember the names of the Lord of Kamalā, which destroy all sins, while performing circumambulation. (127)
Those people who hear the sound of the name of Hari vibrating from every one of his mouths shall be liberated from great accumulations of sin.
One should not engage in conversation with heretics on the day of Hari;
by the mere act of conversing with heretics, all dharma is destroyed. (129)
Having heard each verse of the song of Nārāyaṇa’s glory issuing forth [from the mouth],
the deluded are not satiated, just as dogs are never sated by the sound of a lute.
The virtuous experience great joy upon hearing the song of the Lord of the World, just as deer are moved by the sound of a lute that destroys all sins. 131.
Singing that song of Hari, they perform a supreme dance;
seeing this, those observing vows are satisfied, for they are satisfied by the Lord of Kamalā.
O twice-born one, those who do not find satisfaction in the abode of Viṣṇu while observing their vows shall remain in a state of animalhood perpetually throughout every birth.
Those who do not sing the Gītās on the day of Hari while observing their vows wander from birth to birth, deprived of sacred speech. 134.
One should play clay drums and other instruments before Hari, for by such musical instruments the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana becomes pleased. 135.
Devotees of Viṣṇu should perform a vigil for Viṣṇu, engaging in the excellent study of the Vedas or the recitation of the Purāṇas. (136)
The Rāmāyaṇa, the Bhāgavata, the Mahābhārata spoken by Vyāsa, and other Purāṇas should be recited on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī). 137.
Those who recite [the name] before Viṣṇu and those who hear it on the day of Hari obtain for every syllable the fruit born from the gift of a tawny cow.
A devotee of Viṣṇu should remain awake during the night, having bathed;
having fully conquered sleep, he should meditate properly on Keśava within his heart. (139)
Every day, performing circumambulations again and again,
one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground before Janārdana, the Lord Hari.
Then, at the clear dawn, having performed the five great sacrifices,
the devout observer of the vow should bathe Hari with milk and worship Him.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a twice-born man according to one's own capacity;
thereafter, while still within that twelfth day, the observer of the vow should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa).
Whoever performs the breaking of the fast on the day of Vilambī-Dvādaśī, his merit accumulated over ten million births is utterly destroyed. (143)
Those wise ones who desire the fruit of their vow must perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) during the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), and never on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*). (144)
On the day of fasting, even during the night, a Vaiṣṇava who desires the fruit of the fast should diligently avoid sleep. (145)
Without the vigil, fasting is surely fruitless;
therefore, the vigil must be performed on both lunar fortnights.
O best of the twice-born, those who perform the Ekādaśī vow according to this prescribed method—truly, truly, all of them go to liberation. (147)

O Jaimini, you should constantly and with great effort perform the essence of the Vāsudeva-day vow, which is the sole means for removing birth and death, and which must be observed even by the hosts of gods led by Indra. 148.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||22||
(23) Chapter Twenty-Three.
Vyāsa said:
Formerly, there was a king named Kocaraśa on this earth;
he was peaceful, a supreme knower of dharma, and the best among those who understand the science of royal policy. ||1||
He was a speaker of truth, one who had conquered anger and subdued enmity;
he was devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa and supremely intent on the service of Hari.
His chief queen was named Suprajñā; she spoke kindly, was endowed with all auspicious marks, and was devoted to the service of her husband. ||3||
Devoted to the vow of Ekādaśī, desiring the welfare of all living beings, she was a noble lady of excellent character and beautiful complexion who remembered her past lives. (4)
Having observed the Daśamī with the king, the knower of the supreme truth, together with his wife, prepared to perform the vigil on the night of Ekādaśī. ||5||
In the meantime, a certain Brahmin of great splendor named Śauri arrived at the king's pavilion for the vigil.
As he approached, the king, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa,
together with his wife, being exceedingly joyful, honored him with water for the feet and other offerings.
Seated in their midst, that brahmin, the knower of all truths,
saw there many ascetics devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Some worship Hari with various beautiful flowers, with perfumes, incense, lamps, and unsurpassed offerings. ||9||
Some, adorned with the mud of the Gaṅgā and garlanded with tulasī leaves,
being consecrated before Hari, dance with joy as observers of their vows.
Furthermore, some who have taken vows and are dear to the Blessed One sing charming songs of Hari while holding cymbals in their hands. 11.
Some praise Nārāyaṇa, the flawless Lord of the worlds, with unsurpassed hymns consisting of divine meanings and tender syllables. (12)
Some likewise fanned the Lord of the World, Hari, with the cool breeze of white yak-tail whisks, thereby causing him great delight.
Some high-souled ones play charming and pure-sounding musical instruments such as the vīṇā, while others sing of Keśava.
Both the king and the queen-mother were exceedingly joyful;
they sang a charming song and performed an excellent dance. ||15||
Śauri, the best of brāhmaṇas, laughed at the two high-souled lords of Tauda, who were performing dances, songs, and other such acts, with sweet words.
Śauri said:
"O protector of the earth, you are blessed; blessed is your queen.
This conduct of yours both is auspicious and rare upon this earth. (17)
I shall speak to you, for no one has ever been seen who is a superior devotee of Viṣṇu;
by you, O protector of the earth, this world has been blessed—of this there is no doubt. (18)
O King, this Ekādaśī vow is pure and dear to the Blessed Lord; since you observe it together with your wife, you are indeed the foremost among Vaiṣṇavas. (19)
O best of kings, you are the sole lord of the seven islands together with your wife;
out of devotion, you have come before Nārāyaṇa and are dancing and singing. (20)
This wondrous conduct of you two, husband and wife, has been seen; from what cause has this exceedingly pure intellect arisen in you both? (21)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the twice-born man named Śauri, she,
with a slight smile upon her face, spoke to that wise brahmin.
Suprājña said: "O best of the twice-born, by the power of Ekādaśī, we two, though formerly great sinners, were liberated by the high-souled son of the Sun. (23)
By the power of our recollection of past births, O best of Brahmins, we now perform this divine Ekādaśī vow with the desire for the supreme state.
Śauri said:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, if you indeed know your own previous birth, tell me of it; curiosity has arisen in my heart to hear it."
Previously, your husband Vāka remained in the form of a pillar;
how is it that you two have been abandoned by Bhāskariṇa, even though you are both sinners? 26.
Suprājñā said:
"O best of the twice-born, although this speech is not to be disclosed, I am a chief courtesan established here, well-versed in the science of love. (27)
O best of Brahmins, in that birth, indeed many terrible sins were committed by me, which truly grant the torments of hell. (28)
This man named Nityodaya was a Śūdra who had abandoned his own proper conduct;
he was cruel, a stealer of others' wives, and a plunderer of others' property. ||29||
A drinker of liquor, a betrayer of friends, a killer of embryos, one who harms others, one who is excessively angry, and one who always reviles the Dharma; ||30||
Once, abandoned by all his kinsmen who were devoted to virtuous vows, he came to my house, lusting after the amorous charms of courtesans. (31)
O best of the twice-born, upon seeing this youth so handsome, I too attained pleasure and was satisfied even by amorous dalliances with him. (32)
Then, O ascetic, after I had experienced amorous pleasure with him, he, bowing low out of modesty, spoke these words to me with affection: (33)
"I am an expert in the science of sexual pleasure, yet I have been abandoned by my own kinsmen;
if you so desire, I shall remain here together with you. (34)
O twice-born one, she heard these words spoken with humility:
"Having attained the state of being his wife, I remain here together with him. (35)
Once, O tiger among the twice-born, on the eleventh day of Hari’s festival, I was tormented by great beings who were intent on striking my body. (36)
O best of the twice-born, while she was thus with her body shattered by fever,
neither water was drunk nor food was eaten by that other woman out of intense fear.
On that very day, as affection for me arose in Hari toward him,
he abandoned his food and water, becoming despondent because of his birth.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having lit a lamp with ghee at night, I performed a vigil while my mind was overcome by fever. (39)
Muttering "Nārāyaṇa, Hare, Kṛṣṇa, protect me," he too kept vigil throughout the night, repeating this again and again. (40)
O twice-born one, by the power of our fast and by the utterance of the name Keśava, all of our sins were utterly destroyed.
Then, at the clear dawn when the blessed sun had risen,
O best of Brahmins, I, afflicted by fever, passed away.
Seeing me thus afflicted by disease and having reached the state of death, he, being pure, endured his own approaching death with a joyful heart, honored by all people. (43)
Then, bound with a firm noose by the servants of Sūryya, whose eyes resembled blazing fire, he was led along a difficult path.
By his command, this wise Citragupta thoroughly investigated everything— whether good or evil deeds— from their very roots.
Citragupta said: "O mighty-armed one, although these two are the foremost among great sinners,
nevertheless they have been liberated from their sins by fasting on the Ekādaśī."
Even one who might perform the meritorious vow of Ekādaśī without desire shall go to the supreme abode, freed from all sins. ||47||
Having been addressed thus by Citragupta, the highly illustrious Dharmarāja rose suddenly from his seat and paid obeisance to him.
They honored them with fragrant divine unguents, incenses, flowers, and nectar, as well as with golden ornaments; thus they were adorned and freed from all evil. (49)
There, with various kinds of sweet fruits comparable to nectar, Bhāskari affectionately provided a meal for the two of us. (50)
Then, having praised us with divine hymns, the lord Yama himself placed us upon his celestial chariot and spoke thus with palms joined in reverence.
Yama said:
"You two are the best among the meritorious and are free from all sins;
go now to that place where the Lord Viṣṇu resides."
Thus spoke the King of Dharma, truly bowed down by discipline;
then, having prostrated at his lotus feet, this was said by us two.
O God, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu must not be approached otherwise;
rather, we two desire to see the sun-like Indra residing in your house. (54)
Then, at Yama's command, O Brahmin, having ascended a splendid chariot,
we beheld there the various hells in their full extent, which are difficult to look upon.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O devoted wife, you ought to describe in detail all those various states of those who have fallen into sin, as they were seen by you. (56)
O lady of beautiful hips, tell me in detail by which path the meritorious souls go to the abode of Yama, and likewise the sinful souls.
What kind of Lord Vaivasvata would the meritorious soul see there?
[He sees] the place that bestows happiness upon the meritorious and suffering upon the sinners. (58)
Suprājña said:
"I have already described that place for meritorious men;
listen, O tiger among the twice-born, as it increases the joy of those who hear it. (59)
Covered with divine carpets and mats spread out wide, the path of the meritorious shines forth, entirely free from all calamities. (60)
In some places, wonderful songs were sung by the daughters of the Gandharvas;
in other places, Apsarases with exquisite bodies performed dances.
In some places they played the lute and various musical instruments that were enchanting to the mind;
in some places there was a rain of flowers, and in others a cool breeze.
In some places there were water-stalls with cool water, and in others, houses for eating;
in some places gods and gandharvas were chanting an excellent hymn of praise.
In various places there were beautiful oblong ponds with blooming lotuses, and in some spots there were trees providing excellent shade, such as *vañjula* and others in full flower.
Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, those meritorious men proceed along the path endowed with happiness, having attained a death in bliss.
Some, mounted on horses and adorned with various ornaments,
proceeded with white umbrellas held aloft, shading their heads.
Some go mounted on elephants, some mounted on chariots, and some people mounted on vehicles; thus they proceed happily to the abode of Yama.
Some go fanned by the breezes from chowries held in the hands of celestial nymphs,
while being praised by divine sages.
Some virtuous souls, bearing divine weapons and adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste, go to the abode of Yama while chewing betel leaf. (69)
Some, dwelling in the waters and eclipsing the ten directions with the radiance of their own bodies, proceed to the abode of Yama.
Some, O best of beings, eat divine food free from impurity;
performing excellent eating, they proceed along the path with ease. (71)
Some go to the abode of Yama while drinking milk, some likewise while drinking sugarcane juice, and others while drinking buttermilk.
Some, eating curds, some various fruits,
and some drinking honey— those meritorious ones indeed proceed.
Then, seeing those many people devoted to dharma who had arrived there,
Nārāyaṇa himself would experience solar joy.
He has four arms, a dark complexion, and eyes like full-blown lotuses;
he holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, and has Garuḍa as his vehicle. ||75||
Wearing a golden sacred thread, with a great face as beautiful as the god of love, he was adorned with a crown, earrings, and a forest garland. ||76||
The highly wise Citragupta and the servants of Yama, headed by Caṇḍa,
all assumed the form of Nārāyaṇa and became sweet-spoken.
Then, O twice-born one, Dharmarāja himself, having attained supreme joy, should honor all those best of men like a friend.
Then the son of the Sun spoke to them, saying, "Let him cause those meritorious men to eat with divine jewels and fruits."
Yama said:
"All of you are high-souled ones who fear the sufferings of hell;
by virtue of the absence of [further] personal karma, may you go to the supreme state."
Having obtained birth in this cycle of existence, that man who performs meritorious deeds is equal to his father, equal to his brother, equal to his kinsman, and equal to his friend. (81)
O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus by Dharmarāja,
they all ascended a divine chariot and went to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
O best of the twice-born, the destiny of those with meritorious souls has been declared in brief;
now listen as I describe in detail the destiny of those with sinful souls. (83)
The width of the path of those evil-minded ones is said to be eighty-six thousand yojanas, and it is filled with every kind of suffering. (84)
In some places there was fire and rain, and in others a shower of stones;
in various spots, O best of the twice-born, there was scorching hot sand.
In some places there are sharp rocks, and likewise in some places heated rocks;
in some places there is a rain of weapons, and in some places a rain of glowing coals.
In some places, O twice-born one, the winds blew with excessive heat like fire; in other places, there were terrifying whirlpools of foam and spray.
In some places there was a rain of *kaṇṭaka* thorns and *nārāca* arrows; in other places there were rows of stones, difficult to climb and infested with serpents. ||88||
The sinners go there with their lips and palates parched, amidst such manifold sufferings that are devoid of shade and water. (89)
O best of the twice-born, upon that path the suffering sinners go, known by the name Avimuktakeśa, having the appearance of pretas and causing fear. (90)
Some sinners go along the path drenched in streams of blood, some are smeared with mud, and others pull black cows. 91.
Some, their teeth chattering with agony and their moments clouded by flowing tears, go along lamenting their own deeds; others, being sinful, likewise depart. (92)
At some time, the binding of a leather noose was placed around the necks of some sinners; at another time, some were bound with their feet, while others were bound by both feet. (93)
Having cast a noose carved from a whetstone with great fury,
she was dragged forward by those who, though not servants, had committed some offense.
Carrying heavy stones upon their eyelashes through the openings of their ears,
and bearing loads of iron upon the tops of their heads, the sinners on the path proceed along.
The servants of Yama lead some sinners away by means of nooses and arrows that pierce their consciousness; others they lead away with firm blows from their hands upon their necks. (96)
The Yama-kiṃkaras hurl them down, cast them up, and drive them forward;
some they carry with their heads downward, while others carry them with their feet upward. (97)
Some go on their arms, and some on one leg;
thus they are of deformed appearance, uttering cries of distress and lamentation. (98)
Being beaten by the messengers of Yama, the sinners travel along that path;
when they have all arrived there, the sinful-souled Yama appears in person.
Having cast off his divine form, he became exceedingly terrifying, thirty *yojanas* in height, with eyes resembling those of a cow. (100)
Smoke-colored and possessed of great luster, with long, hanging ears and a gurgling voice,
he had a row of very long teeth and a line of nails resembling winnowing baskets.
Mounted upon a fierce buffalo, with his lips bitten, staff in hand, and holding a leather noose, his face is contorted with a frown. (102)
Citragupta, the master of great illusion, his eyes reddened with wrath,
shines resplendent as Samavartin while letting out a loud, boisterous laugh.
Then Caṇḍa and all the others, holding nooses and mallets in their hands, became Bhairavas;
enraged, they roared like thunderclouds. (104)
"Kill, kill the most wicked! Pierce and cut them to pieces!
Thus shouting as they run together, the henchmen of Yama leap about. (105)
The Lord Dharmarāja, uttering a roar of "hum," threatened all those sinners as they fell upon him with his staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa).
Yama said:
"O you sinners of wicked conduct, you who lack discernment! Alas, what sins have been committed by you, which bring such torment even to yourselves! (107)
"You did not perceive me standing above your heads, moving about right here;
even though you knew me to be the Lord of Life, you committed this sin. (108)
"I am the kinsman of the virtuous and the enemy of the sinful"—have you not heard this anywhere with your own ears? (109)
The hells exist as unbearable, filled with various sufferings; it is well known that sinners must experience them, and they cannot be avoided by you. (110)
"O you of evil intent, having falsely engaged in this deliberation, you who have committed a sin—behold yourselves with your own eyes this very day! (111)
"O you who are intoxicated by wealth and by the speech of women, you must all always act in such a way that you constantly weave webs of sin. (112)
Likewise, what was said by Danda regarding the wicked who experience the fruit of evil?
The wise one replied:
Having spoken thus, the son of Bhaskara, Deva, said to Citragupta: "Ha! (113)
"O illustrious one, deliberate upon these evil deeds.
Having heard the words of Dharmarāja, Citragupta then reflected deeply.
O best of the twice-born, as many sins as they had committed, so many [strokes] did he, being impelled by Prahlāda, inflict upon all those sinners. 115.
Thus spoke the terrified sinners, bound by the noose of leather,
to Yama, the Son of the Sun: "O Son of Bhāskara, whatever sins have been committed by us— " (116)
Who are the witnesses present there, and who are you that have been informed [of this], regarding whatever inauspicious or auspicious deed was previously performed by us? (117)
"Tell us then, who has seen this before us?
Thereupon, O twice-born one, the Blessed One laughed with great wrath. (118)
Having summoned all the witnesses, he spoke these words. Yama said: "All of you, as witnesses, must testify exactly as it occurred. (119)
The sky, the earth, the water, as well as the days, the night, both twilights, and Dharma—these are the witnesses. (120)
They recounted all the good and evil deeds of those wicked souls,
and at whatever time each individual had performed whatever action.
Yama declared that very person's witness in the absence of that person;
hearing this, the minds of all the sinners were drawn by terror. (122)
They stood with their hearts seized by fear like deer upon seeing a cloud;
then he, making a clattering sound with his arms, struck them. (123)
The King of Dharma struck each of those who had committed sins individually with his staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa). Thus beaten by the King of Dharma, all of them were tormented. ||124||
Then, crying out and lamenting their own deeds, filled with trepidation,
all those sinners were addressed by the messengers headed by Caṇḍa and others.
By the command of Yama, they cast those who had committed sins into the Raurava and other hells;
some they cast into Tapana, and others into Avīci.
In Saṅghāta, Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahāraurava;
in Saṃtapta, Vālukākuṇḍa, and likewise Kumbhīpāka—there they torment others.
In the breathless Mahāghora and Pramardana hells,
and in the terrible Asipatravana hell, they cast the sinners into various places where they are devoured.
Likewise, some threw [the deceased] into the Vaitaraṇī river; others, with their hands, cast them into the terrible pit of excrement, or into heaps of charcoal, bones, and gravel. (129)
The servants of Yama cast those who were excessively heated by their full [karma] into the application of excrement and likewise into the eating of excrement. (130)
And at their own meat-feast, this [food] was set out by those who could do nothing;
some ate phlegm, while others ate semen. (131)
Some sinners drink urine, while others drink blood; in the mouths of some there are leeches resembling serpents. (132)
O best of the twice-born, the serpents shall fill you with fear through the terrifying messengers of Yama, who will cause them to arise and torment you intensely. 133.
For certain evildoers, the cruel servants of Yama fill their ears, noses,
and mouths with boiling oil.
Some of those evil-minded ones have their arms,
feet, ears, and even their noses cut off with the edges of swords.
Some made their beds upon heaps of glowing charcoal,
while others lay upon thorns that were like iron arrows.
O best of the twice-born, some sinful beings, acting as tormentors of the deceased, drag them by the hair and throw them into heated mud and glowing iron spikes. (137)
And in certain vomitings, they repeatedly thrust thousands of red-hot needles into the nail-joints of some sinners. (138)
They indeed force some onto the points of heated iron spikes;
they bite the heads of others with sharp saws.
Seizing them by their hands and feet with iron pincers, they violently flay them while they cry out in agony with piteous screams. (140)
Having tied stones to their necks, some who perform acts of self-mortification repeatedly cast themselves into pits of blood and pits of water. (141)
The messengers of Yama, with extreme fury, repeatedly crush the heads of sinful men with stones as they tear them apart.
And upon the chests of some wicked-souled people who cause the world to cry out, they drive in heaps of iron spikes. (143)
O twice-born one, the eyes of which sinners must be torn out with hooks, and the noses of some must be filled with scorpions? (144)
Having bound the feet of some with nooses to the branches of trees, the servants of Yama set fire to the ground beneath them, accompanied by smoke. 145.
Having committed their misdeeds there, they practice the inhalation of smoke;
with their heads downward and feet upward, they remain thus as long as the moon and stars exist.
Some, being struck again and again with pestles and mallets by the messengers of Yama,
vomit forth blood like elephants.
O twice-born one, in houses filled with darkness and foul odors, certain sinners suffer from gadflies and mosquitoes. (148)
Some eat ashes, and some eat worms;
some eat foul-smelling flesh, and some eat putrid earth. (149)
Some, being devoured by dogs, tigers, and jackals with vajra-like teeth and claws, as well as by bears, cry out while drenched in the blood of elephants. (150)
Others were being devoured by snakes with extremely fierce venom, while still others,
O twice-born one, had their chests pierced by the tips of buffalo horns.
Fainting as they fell to the earth, they drenched the ground with blood from the terrible arrows resembling venomous serpents released from the bows of Yama’s messengers.
With their entire bodies shattered, others wallow upon the ground, [clinging to] glowing iron balls and even heated stones. (153)
Then, with weapons, some they tear apart in their mouths, some in the nostrils, and others in the mouths of the messengers of Yama. ||154||
Indeed, for the purpose of obstructing the wind of the breath, they pierce the nostrils of some with the uplifted, sharp-edged spears of Yama. 155.
Then those Yama-messengers of great strength will tear off your skin;
some, seizing you by the hair, will cast you down upon the surface of the earth. (156)
Those who have committed sins are always struck with blows from their feet and other limbs using stakes; some, being tormented, are drenched with showers of caustic acid. 157.
O twice-born one, some sinful people drink alkaline water, while others, O highly fortunate one, drink bile in various ways. (158)
Some of the worst among sinners drink the milk of the Snuhī plant; others, while sleeping on the ground, have their chests pressed by the hands of beautiful women. (159)
He gave him heavy stones, heated like mountains,
and likewise two pieces of wood, one for the neck and one for the throat.
They bind some with firm nooses by their faces turned upward, and having hoisted others onto the branches of trees, they hurl them to the ground. (161)
They lift them up and throw them back down again and again;
thus all those sinners remain hungry and thirsty. (162)
Crying out "Save us! Save us!", they weep in the house of torment, having experienced the agonies of hell until the end of the eon.
By not eating too much, the remnants of one's sins are exhausted; otherwise, they are born in sinful wombs.
Having been born in sinful wombs, they become afflicted by diseases. (164)

Those who serve evil, those who cause suffering to inferior or superior cows, those who are childless, those who are extremely foolish, and those devoted to harming others—[these are the ones reborn as such]. (165)
They will have short lifespans and small intellects, and likewise be husbands of wicked wives;
they will constantly perform sinful deeds through action, thought, and speech. (166)
Furthermore, by the power of their evil deeds, they go to hell as before;
therefore, the virtuous should never commit sin at any time. (167)
For men who have committed sins, there is no escape from hell;
in brief, O best of the twice-born, such is the suffering described for sinners. 168.
Who is capable of describing correctly, even in hundreds of tens of thousands of years, the miserable destinies of those men who have committed sins? (169)
Having ascended a celestial chariot, we two went to the city of Nārāyaṇa;
for thousands of millions of kalpas, we enjoyed pleasures in the abode of Hari. (170)
O best of the twice-born, when this birth-cycle has ended in purity, having enjoyed all pleasures endowed with every prosperity in this world, [one attains liberation]. (171)
Having attained a peaceful death, one goes to the supreme state;
there is no vow equal to the Ekādaśī vow in the three worlds. (172)
Even though we have come to such a state as this through no desire of our own,
those who observe the Ekādaśī vow with a spirit of devotion— ||173||
I do not know what will become of them through the compassion of Vāsudeva;
thus, O best of Brahmins, everything you asked has been told to you. (174)
"What else do you wish to hear regarding the greatness of Viṣṇu’s day?
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of his, that brāhmaṇa, who knew the supreme truth... [175]
Having enjoyed the earth for a long time together with the king and the queen, he made his own mind very firm in the vow of Ekādaśī. (176)
Even they, having gone to the city of Viṣṇu, have attained that supreme state—those who hear and read the majesty of this king of vows. ||177||
Freed from the fear of evil, may you obtain [this] in the presence of Hari. 178.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||23||
(24) Chapter Twenty-Four.
Sūta said:
Having heard the fruit of Ekādaśī, Jaimini was then greatly pleased;
with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to the lord Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
Jaimini said:
By your grace, I have heard the majesty of the divine Viṣṇu;
now tell me the majesty of Tulasī, which destroys the sins of those who hear it. (2)
Vyāsa said:
This Blessed Tulasī should always be served by all the deities, beginning with Indra; she bestows the fruits of the four goals of human life (caturvarga) upon those who are free from sin. 3.
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld (pātāla), the tulasī plant is difficult for the wicked to obtain;
yet devotion toward it truly brings about the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life (caturvarga). ||4||
O best of beings, wherever even a single *tulasī* tree stands,
there all the thirty gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the rest, are present.
Keśava resides in the middle of the leaf, Prajāpati at the tip of the leaf,
and Śiva always dwells upon the stem of the Tulasī plant.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, Caṇḍikā,
and all the other wives of the gods likewise resided upon its petals.
Indra, Agni, Śamana, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Pavana, and Cakrapāṇi—these dwell upon that branch. (8)
All the planets beginning with the Sun, the Viśvedevas at all times, the Vasus, the sages, and likewise all the divine seers; ||9||
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the surface of the earth within the midst of millions of universes,
they indeed all reside by taking refuge in a single leaf of Tulasī.
Whoever serves the Tulasī plant endowed with a spirit of devotion has thereby served all sacred pilgrimage sites as well as the gods, beginning with Brahmā. (11)
Just as those who cut away the masses of grass growing at the roots of the *tulasī* plant,
Hari instantly destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin residing within that person's body.
O best of the twice-born, by sprinkling water that is fragrant and cool upon the *tulasī* during the summer season, a person shall attain liberation. 13.
Whoever offers him a moonbeam or a parasol—especially during the summer heat—is declared to be liberated from all sins. (14)
That person who constantly sprinkles the Linga with streams of unbroken rice grains and water during the month of Vaiśākha obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. ||15||
Whoever sprinkles Tulasī with even a mere handful of water shall attain heaven, freed from all sins. ||16||
O brahmin sage, if that best of men should ever sprinkle the tulasī with milk, the goddess Lakṣmī remains steadfast in his house.
O brahmin sage, listen to the meritorious fruit of him who performs the smearing of the root of the *tulasī* plant with cow dung and its subsequent sweeping. (18)
O Jaimini, for as many particles of dust as there are that have been removed from that place,
for so many thousands of kalpas does one rejoice together with Viṣṇu.
He who places a lamp upon a tulasī leaf at twilight goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
Keśava always protects those who guard cattle, dogs, donkeys, humans, and children from the *lasī* disease. ||21||
The man who plants the tulasī with devotion attains supreme liberation upon death; of this there is no doubt. ||22||
The best of men who, endowed with devotion, beholds Tulasī at dawn, obtains the inexhaustible fruit that is indeed equal to the vision of Viṣṇu himself. ||23||
That man who, endowed with devotion, bows down to Tulasī, his lifespan, strength, fame, wealth, and progeny increase. (24)
By the mere remembrance of Tulasī, all sin is destroyed;
by the mere touch of Tulasī, the diseases of men perish. (25)
Whoever eats an auspicious tulasī leaf, which removes all sins, the sin residing within that person's body perishes at that very moment. (26)
The man who wears a garland produced from Tulasī wood—there is no sin in his body; this which I speak is the truth. (27)
Whoever carries on his head the water dripping from a Tulasī leaf obtains the merit born of bathing in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.
By worshipping the auspicious Tulasī with devotion using dūrvā grass, unbroken grains, flowers, and food offerings,
a person obtains the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu.

If one has at any time worshipped the Blessed Tulasī with food offerings, flowers, excellent incense, and lamps of ghee—she who bestows the supreme nectar of dharma, artha, and kāma—is there any need for that person to employ the practice of worshipping the feet of Viṣṇu? (30)

O Brahmin, in places free from defects, people plant the *tulasī*, which is served by hosts of gods and brings satisfaction to Hari; pleased, Hari, the Lord of the three worlds and enemy of the demons, swiftly grants them the supreme state.

Whatever vow, observance, worship of the ancestors, worship of Acyuta, charity, or any other auspicious deed men perform upon the ground of the faultless Tulasī, all those indeed become inexhaustible. (32)

Whatever righteous deed a person performs on this earth without the Tulasī, which is most dear to Nārāyaṇa, all of that becomes entirely fruitless; for even the lotus-eyed Lord of the twice-born, the God of gods, does not become pleased. (33)

That man who, endowed with a spirit of devotion, certainly beholds the sacred and auspicious Tulasī during his pilgrimage—by the grace of Hari, the entire fruit of that pilgrimage shall quickly be accomplished for him; this word of mine is most firm. (34)

Having abandoned fragrant flowers such as the mandāra, kunda, and lotus, even though he is infinite, the sole Lord of the universe joyfully accepts the tulasī plant, which is composed of excellent qualities and provides protection by destroying abundant sins—even when it is withered. (35)

Having uprooted the *tulasī*, which is like the very source of the creeper of immortality, those of sinful intent cast it upon the ground; though Nṛhari is fond of *tulasī* even when [the plant] is taken unknowingly, it is true that he constantly robs them of their prosperity.

Even those people who constantly discharge urine and feces upon the leaves of the *tulasī* plant—Hari swiftly seizes away the wealth of those whose sins have accumulated by taking refuge in the deity. (37)
I gather you for the sake of worshipping Nārāyaṇa; homage be to you! With flowers such as the pārijāta and with perfumes and other offerings, Keśava [is worshipped]. (38)
"O auspicious one, without you I do not find satisfaction;
therefore, O highly fortunate lady, without you every action is fruitless. (39)
Therefore, O Goddess Tulasī, grant me boons;
whatever pain arises in your heart, O Goddess, from being gathered [and plucked], let it be removed. (40)
Therefore, O Lord of the World, forgive me; I bow down to you with devotion.
Having recited these mantras with palms joined in reverence, the Vaiṣṇava person [attains his goal]. 41.
O best of the twice-born, having clapped his hands twice, he plucked a tulasī leaf from the branch of the tulasī tree just as a bird might pluck one. 42.
When a branch of the Tulasi tree belonging to the Lord is broken during the piling of the altar, then it arises in the heart of Viṣṇu, the Lord of Tulasī, just as if it were within His own chest. 43.
Even by an old leaf fallen from the tip of a branch onto the ground, Govinda, the crusher of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, is to be worshipped. 44.
He who worships the Lord Acyuta with tender tulasī leaves quickly obtains everything that he desires in his heart. 45.
Jaimini said:
O bull among the twice-born, what tree is equal to the tulasī tree?
O son of Satyavatī, I desire to know it; please tell me.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born one, just as Tulasī is eternally dear to Viṣṇu, so too is the Dhātrī tree, which destroys all sins, ever beloved by Him. 47.
O best of the twice-born, all the deities reside at the foot of the tulasī tree, and they dwell beneath the āmalakī tree as well. 48.
O best of the twice-born, all the sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā and others reside there,
where the Dhātrī tree, most dear to Viṣṇu and purifying, stands.
Whether it be impure or pure, whatever karma is performed by human beings upon the surface of the Amalaka stone,
that will truly arise as inexhaustible.
One should worship Hari with pure, fresh leaves of the dhātrī tree;
thus liberated from the web of sins, one attains sāyujya with Hari. (51)
O Jaimini, wherever the goddesses Dhātrī and Tulasī do not stand,
that place shall be impure, and one shall not obtain the fruit of ritual action.
If the auspicious Dhātrī and Tulasī do not remain in one's hermitage,
then all the ritual acts performed by that person will surely go to waste.
O Brahmin, he whose abode is never devoid of the *dhātrī* and *tulasī* plants—misfortune, all sin, and even the Kali age flee from him once he has propitiated them. (54)
O best of the twice-born, that place where there is neither the *dhātrī* nor the *tulasī* plant should be known by the seers of truth as being equal to a cremation ground. (55)
Where the Dhātrī and Tulasī reside, there all the gods dwell;
yet where the leaf of the Dhātrī or Tulasī is not present, there all sins reside. (56)
If a wise person wears a garland of *dhātrī* fruits, which destroys sin,
Viṣṇu shall always abide within his body together with Śrī.
A wise man should wear a rosary made of dhātrī wood;
all the deities reside within his body, taking refuge there. (58)
Whatever action a man performs while holding a garland of dhātrī fruits, all of that—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is declared to be inexhaustible. (59)
But that man who, knowing all the principles (tattvas), eats the fruit of the dhātrī tree, all the sin residing within his body is destroyed. (60)
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the supreme majesty of whoever wears a rosary made of *dhātrī* fruit, which removes all sins. (61)
Even if his death should occur in a cremation ground by the turn of fate, he obtains the merit born of dying in the Ganges; of this there is no doubt.
Upon seeing him, all sinners are instantly liberated from their most dreadful webs of sin, even those accumulated over hundreds of millions of births.
He who daily takes up the mud from the Dhātrī tree obtains merit day after day; he attains it, there is no doubt.
Whoever destroys the Dhātrī tree, which is the refuge of all the hosts of gods, commits a sin equal to that of killing Hari; there is no doubt in this matter. (65)
Because she is the sustainer composed of all the gods and is especially dear to Keśava,
even Brahmā is not able to fully describe her qualities.
That man who, having understood all principles, practices devotion to the nurse Tulasī, enjoys all pleasures and thereafter attains liberation through the grace of Hari. (67)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Tulasī," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||24||
(25) Chapter Twenty-Five. Jaimini said:
O highly fortunate one, please speak again in detail regarding the greatness of tulasī, which destroys sin,
as well as the greatness of honoring a guest.
Sūta said:
Thereupon, O best of the twice-born, the greatly effulgent Vyāsa began to recount the majesty of Tulasī, which destroys the sins of those who hear it. 2.
Vyāsa said:
"O Jaimini, this Tulasī is Mahālakṣmī herself, the beloved of Bhava;
therefore, those who know trees do not look upon her as a mere plant."
Just as a mortal serves the divine Tulasī on earth,
so too do the gods, including Indra, serve him in the abode of the immortals.
Wherever this Tulasī, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman, resides, there all is well; this I declare with firm conviction. (5)
Even one who is a sinner, if he obtains at the time of death water dripping from a *tulasī* leaf, goes to the presence of Hari.
He who applies the sectarian mark (puṇḍra) made from Tulasī clay at the time of death is liberated from all sins and goes to the city of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu).
O best of the twice-born, for him who has a tulasī leaf in his mouth, on his head, or in his ears at the time of death, Lord Bhāskari shall be his master.
Pavitra was his name; he possessed a virtuous mind and was a knower of the supreme truth. His wife was a Brāhmaṇī named Bahulā. (9)
There lived an excellent brahmin named Anapatyapati, who was devoted to the service of his virtuous wife and whose lineage originated from a noble family.
O best of beings, he formed a friendship with that impure performer of unholy rites who served the twice-born; thus, through greed for conversation, he became childless and lost his lordship.
Seated out of affection on the same excellent seat, he was purified;
at that moment, a virtuous twice-born man named Lomaśa, possessed of great splendor, arrived.
As they were telling various wonderful stories, they arrived and saw him; then those two brahmins rose from their seats to see the brahmin Lomaśa.
They both worshipped him with water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and other rites;
Lomaśa, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa, was well-pleased with them.
The best of Brahmins sat down, chanting the praises of Hari, as the high-souled Lomaśa remained seated with his hands joined in reverence. 15.
With devotion toward the sage who was like a purifier, they both spoke to Lomaśa:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, by the pair of your feet, men [attain their goals]. (16)

"Surely this hermitage has been purified by us two through the company of these virtuous ones who are worthy of being accepted; for whatever sins were previously committed by us out of delusion [have been cleansed]. (17)
All those have been destroyed by the sight of your pair of feet;
you are Nārāyaṇa himself, worthy of worship even by the immortals.
"Are we two humans capable of performing worship for these holy ones?
Nevertheless, we have offered worship to this guest according to our own ability. (19)
"Delighted by this, O Bhava, forgive our fault.
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, those two high-souled householders fell at the two feet of that guest.
Vyāsa said: Then Lomaśa, the best among the wise, was well-pleased by their devotion:
"O foremost of the twice-born, you two are the best among the humble, devoted to righteousness. (21)
I have been exceedingly gratified by the words of courtesy from you both;
for the wise declare that a guest is none other than Brahmā, Śiva, or Viṣṇu in person. (22)
"May there be auspiciousness for you both, who possess such great devotion toward him;
I have been properly honored as a guest with abundant food. (23)
Vyāsa said: Then, having risen and bowed again at the two lotus-feet of that brāhmaṇa, they both spoke to the sage Lomaśa.
The two Brahmins said:
"O Brahmin, you ought to speak of the greatness of honoring guests—that practice by performing which liberation is attained by human beings, even though it is difficult to obtain. (25)
Who is said to be a guest in this world, and what kind of worship is due to him? What are the two destinies that the host and the guest may attain? (26)
Lomaśa said:
"Because of the honoring of these— the forest-dweller, the student, and the mendicant—
the householder's stage is declared to be the best among all four stages of life."
Among the four stages of life, householders are considered the most important;
they, endowed with devotion, must perform the worship of guests.
The honoring of guests is declared to be the supreme duty of householders;
therefore, those who do not fall away from the conduct prescribed for their stage of life are considered true householders. (29)
If householders possess skill in honoring guests with the syllable *vaṃ*, then what need have they for other meritorious deeds? (30)
He whose name, lineage, and residence are not known, and who arrives at the house unexpectedly—he is called a guest by the wise. (31)
Whether they be Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or even Śūdras,
those who perceive the ultimate truth honor them when they have come to their homes, treating them like Viṣṇu himself.
Others born of low castes, headed by the Cāṇḍālas, should be honored like Viṣṇu with water for the feet, respectful offerings (arghya), and abundant food. ||33||
When guests have arrived, the householder should set out on his journey;
even if he is in a hurry, the twice-born man should nevertheless offer them water for the feet, the respectful oblation, and other honors.
One should ask auspicious questions with words of gentle syllables, or one should joyfully cause [the deity] to accept divine jewels as food. (35)
The wise man should cause a bed to be prepared for him in that palace of pleasure;
seeing him wishing to depart in the morning, he should avoid following after him as he leaves.
If, as a result of the ripening of karma, one becomes a wealthy householder, then a guest must be honored with hospitality; this I shall say, O most excellent ones. (37)
When guests have arrived, one should offer grass and such with devotion;
in the absence of grass, one should say with devotion, "O Earth, please stand [here]. (38)
One should offer excellent water for the purpose of washing the feet; then, with sweet and gentle speech, one should inquire after his welfare and other such matters. (39)
Then, one should devotedly offer fruit and other items for the purpose of food;
in their absence, one should manifest the [inner] deity within the mind. (40)
And he should say: "O guest, I am a great sinner and the foremost among the poor; I desire to offer devotion to you, who are the supreme deity, though you appear as an adversary. (41)
By this method, that indigent person, having abandoned the worship of lunar days, shall obtain the aforementioned fruit, provided he does not fall away from his own proper conduct. 42.
If a guest departs unhonored from the house of a householder,
the merit accumulated by that person over ten million lifetimes goes to ruin.
If even a single guest is honored with a spirit of devotion,
Hari shall instantly remove that person's sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes.
I speak the truth; I speak what is beneficial; I speak firmly with great effort.
For a householder, there is no other path than the hospitable reception of guests. 45.
Truth, truth, and again truth: without honoring guests, there is truly no higher goal, truly no higher goal, truly no higher goal for those who follow the dharma of householders. (46)
In the Dvāpara age, there was one known as Jñātidharma, who was beloved and a knower of all dharmas; his wife was named Śrīvallabhā. (47)
Thus, having performed all his duties as a devoted servant,
he made his residence in Saurāṣṭra together with that wife of his.
O twice-born ones, because of the movement of the planets in difficult positions, there was a great famine lasting twelve years, and for nine years it was caused by drought.
During that great famine, all the people living in that region became miserable and even abandoned the bounds of propriety.
In the age known as Dvāpara, the great yogi Jñānabhadra,
his wealth having been carried off by famine, became exceedingly distressed.
Seeing her sons and husband distressed by hunger, she, who was highly esteemed by the twice-born,
went to the mountain peak for the purpose of gathering fruits and roots.
At the edge of the mountain's foothills, the long-lived one, though hungry, obtained a single kūṣmāṇḍa fruit, O best of brahmins. (53)
Having taken that fruit of his undertaking, the illustrious Viprendra Jñānabhadra, filled with joy, returned swiftly to his own abode. 54.
In that interval, as the sky was covered by clouds of arrows like dark blue lotuses,
there fell a rain of great torrents.
His entire body drenched by that sudden downpour of rain, a certain forest-dweller, afflicted by the cold, came from the forest to his house. (56)
Seeing the guest afflicted by the cold, he then bowed his head in salutation;
thereafter, with devotion, he offered him a seat of grass, water for washing the feet, and other hospitality.
Then, with sweet speech, he stood together with that very guest,
his mind at ease, engaging in conversation.
Then, with her husband Gopa, she who was highly skilled in serving her master [prepared] a fresh pumpkin that had been thoroughly cooked with great effort. (59)
Having attained this, the virtuous woman was delighted; having performed the ritual division of the portion, that weak cowherd then fell under her control within ten days due to his fasting.
With joy, he gave that highly fortunate guest a meal worthy of hospitality;
then his virtuous wife, who was entirely devoted to her husband, [did the same].
With joy, she gave that fallen portion to him as a guest;
then, between those two high-souled lords, there arose a dispute regarding that guest.
O best of the twice-born, having eaten both portions, he was well-pleased;
that guest was honored by them with firm devotion like Viṣṇu himself. (63)
Having rested there during the night, he bathed in the morning and departed after a long time;
thus, twenty-one days passed while he remained fasting.

Then, by the power of that merit, those two high-souled ones attained the state of being lords of the earth. By the influence of that virtue, those two noble-minded ones became sovereigns of the world.
Through the power of their merit, consisting of the hospitality they offered to their guests, the two attained union with Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for yogins to achieve. (66)
In that kingdom, famine was then destroyed; consequently, the people became exceedingly happy, free from grief and disease. (67)
They became endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches, and were devoted to the Dharma;
there, thieves were destroyed, and the king was a protector of the world. (68)
Their ancestors, ten million men, were devoted to their own conduct and were like clouds raining down all desires; likewise were their descendants. (69)
By that very act, those who were like heaps of sin attained liberation;
they became endowed with faultless wealth and were uniquely honored by the entire world.
Free from grief and disease, their satisfaction increased.
Lomaśa said:
"I have related to you the greatness of honoring guests, along with its ancient history."
O Brahmin, since you two are pleased, what else do you wish to hear?
Vyāsa said:
While Lomaśa, that treasure of asceticism, was speaking thus—
Seized by death, a black rat emerged from its own hole there;
seeing that black mouse risen from the burrow, he was overwhelmed with rage.
And there the sacred grass arose, saying repeatedly:
"This wicked mouse of sinful intent has come to the hermitage at night. (74)
One who digs with sharp teeth and claws destroys household property;
yet, compassion is proclaimed as the highest virtue for all social classes alike. (75)
"And she must be performed for all [beings], but not for wicked creatures.
Having said this to that mouse, O best of the twice-born, who had committed a sin—
At the opportune moment, he struck him with an exceedingly sharp iron arrow;
Samūṣaka’s limbs were drenched by streams of flowing blood. ||77||
The brahmin seer fell to the ground, his consciousness struck by agony;
when he had fallen like a porcupine, that best of the twice-born was filled with compassion.
Then, letting out a cry of "Hā Hā!", he rose up with speed,
having brought from his own ear an excellent tulasī leaf.
He placed it upon the mouth, head, and ears of that bull;
"O Mother, O Goddess Tulasī, O delighter of Govinda! (80)
"O best of the twice-born, grant the highest state of rebirth to this dog that has committed sin," having spoken thus, he who benefits all the worlds— [81]
Due to the touch of a *tulasī* leaf, the mouse was freed from its sins and cried out loudly, "Hare! Nārāyaṇa! Ananta! (82)
By hearing the name of Hari, he was liberated from the bonds of worldly existence;
thereafter, messengers of Mahāviṣṇu, endowed with all auspicious marks, arrived.
Surrounded by hosts of Viṣṇu’s messengers, they ascended a divine chariot and arrived swiftly on their excellent vehicles to lead that sinless one away.
O best of the twice-born, that mouse went to the supreme abode after remaining in the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa for thousands of crores of yugas.
Having attained knowledge there, that mouse went to liberation.
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, the majesty of the goddess Tulasī has been recounted to you. (86)
Now tell me, O noble one, what do you wish to hear? ||87||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||25||
(26) The twenty-sixth chapter. Jaimini said:
When this most terrible Kali Yuga arrives, O illustrious one, tell me:
what will all people be like? (1)
Vyāsa said: They say that the first age was Satyayuga; therein, people such as the Brahmins were devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa and were free from sorrow and disease. (2)
They all speak truthful words, are compassionate, long-lived, endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches, and are free from pride and hypocrisy. (3)
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, in the Satya Yuga all people were devoted to helping others and were likewise learned in all the scriptures. (4)
And these kings, who uphold the duties of sovereignty and protect the people—oh, how difficult it is to describe the virtue and glory of the Satya Yuga! (5)
In that [age], no people at all uttered unrighteousness;
when the Tretā Yuga arrived, Dharma had become three-quarters diminished.
Some people were possessed of little sorrow, while others were the refuge of sin; some were devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, and others were intent upon sacrifice and charity.
Devoted to the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life, happy and composed in mind,
all the Śūdras served the Brāhmaṇas, making their lands into sacred fields.
And there were high-souled Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, who abstained from accepting gifts, who were true to their word, and who had conquered their senses.
Constantly devoted to austerities and vows, they were givers and worshippers of Viṣṇu;
at the end of the Tretā Yuga, when the Dvāpara Yuga had arrived.
The Dharma would be deficient by two feet; there would be men endowed with pleasure and pain—some devoted to evil, and some righteous. (11)
Some are deficient in various virtues, while others possess great virtues;
some are extremely miserable, and likewise, some are happy.
A Brahmin sometimes feels a longing for receiving gifts;
at other times, the subjects are oppressed by kings out of greed for wealth. (13)

O twice-born one, when in age after age Dharma has reached the state of being diminished by one quarter, the Brahmins become devoted solely to the worship of Viṣṇu, and the Śūdras become servants of the twice-born.
Then, O best of Brahmins, Vyāsa, who is the very form of Viṣṇu,
divided the Veda in the Kali age, that sole abode of all sins.
Dharma would remain as only a single foot, while all people—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike—would be intent upon sin. ||16||
In the Kali age, those who are excessively lustful will become cruel;
they will be revilers of the Vedas, as well as gamblers and thieves. (17)
In the Kali age, some will be immersed in union with widows,
and certain Brahmins, for the sake of a livelihood, will possess the character of great hypocrites.
All women will become users of intoxicants; they will always be devoted to the female womb and will steal the property of others. (19)
In the Kali Yuga, people will be constantly greedy for the food of others, averse to austerity and vows, and bound by association with heretics.
In the Kali age, Brahmins will wear red garments and follow the customs of Shudras; having lost their proper conduct, the highest castes will sink to the state of the very lowest.
All people will bestow gifts upon those who have helped them, and they will offer their faces toward high positions, even while descending from wealth and prosperity. (22)
In the Kali age, people will strive even with great effort to prevent the advancement of the Śūdras and the Brahmins; out of friendship, they will give false testimony.
They possess a mind that delights in unrighteousness and a disposition that revels in unrighteous views; they are cruel backbiters who speak pleasant words to one's face. ||24||
Unchaste women will call their husbands "virtuous," and twice-born men will speak ill of others' wives and sell their own lineages. (25)
In the Kali age, there will even be those who sell their daughters;
all men will be conquered by women, and women themselves will be exceedingly fickle. (26)
In the Kali age, mortals will be of evil intent;
the earth will yield little grain, and likewise the clouds will contain but scant water.
Furthermore, O Jaimini, in the Kali age cows will not give milk at the proper time;
they will eat dung and yield very little milk.
That milk will undoubtedly become devoid of ghee;
people will be intent on praising themselves and devoted to censuring others. (29)
In the Kali age, Brahmins will have short limbs, be like children, and eat much food; they will perform ancestral sacrifices (pitṛ-yajña) merely for the sake of hypocrisy.
Everyone speaks affectionately only as long as their purpose has not been accomplished;
indeed, seeing men devoted to righteousness, everyone mocks them.
Because of this increase in unrighteousness, people become devoted to sin;
consequently, within ten or twelve years, even the very root of the world goes to its destruction.
Just as increases of water occur during the rainy seasons,
so too will people come to have their youth drained away by the Kali age.
In the fifth or even the sixth year, women shall conceive;
men shall have many offspring and become exceedingly miserable. (34)
In the Kali age, all kings will be intent on seizing and none at all on giving; they will be barbarians devoted to sinful deeds.
In the Kali age, people will become of a single caste for the sake of sense-objects;
at the first twilight of the Kali age, human beings will revile Hari.
In the midst of the Kali age, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras do not perceive the exclusive name of Hari in the Kali Yuga.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, whenever there is a decline among those of meritorious deeds, even the four castes will come to have but a single color. (38)
O best of the twice-born, although this Kali age has been described by me as terrible, it should be understood that in that Kali age there is an increase for sinful men. 39.
Nevertheless, O best among the virtuous, for those possessed of merit, even a great fire-house may become a means of attaining merit through twelve years of truthfulness. (40)
Half of that occurs here in the Tretā age; it happens in a month during the Dvāpara age; and for the Brahmin, O Sage, it occurs in a single day and night during the Kali Yuga.
Therefore, in the Kali age, the supreme goal for men is attained through mortification alone;
for the fruit that is obtained by worshipping Hari in another yuga over twelve years is attained here [in the Kali age] in a much shorter time.
A mortal obtains that fruit by uttering the name of Hari in the Kali age;
for even if a man utters but a single name of Hari there in the Kali age, [he attains it].
"Kali will not afflict that person who possesses truth; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Jaimini said: "Because it is devoid of purity of mind, all action is fruitless. (44)
Thus was it previously spoken by you, which has caused wonder in my mind:
that in the Kali age, all will be devoid of purity of mind. (45)
"O Guru, tell me how all their karma comes to be.
Vyāsa said:
In the Kali age, a mortal performs some kind of meritorious action (dharma) as a renunciant (yati)."
One should offer that to Mahāviṣṇu, endowed with a state of devotion;
every action offered to Viṣṇu becomes entirely inexhaustible. ||47||
Vyāsa said:
Thus, O best of brahmins, everything that occurred has been told;
by hearing this with a spirit of devotion, a person shall attain liberation. 48.
Sūta said:
Thus enlightened by that Supreme Self, Jaimini became devoted to the yoga of action and attained the supreme state. 49.
Those seekers of liberation who read or listen with devotion to this *Kriyā-yoga-sāra* spoken by the high-souled Vyāsa, [attain their goal]. (50)
They are liberated even from all those terrible sins accumulated over many lifetimes; they shall attain supreme liberation—of this there is no doubt. (51)
Whatever desired object those seeking liberation hear while reciting this, they shall quickly obtain that very thing through the grace of the Lord of Kamalā. (52)
By reciting or hearing even half a verse, a single verse, or even a quarter-verse, a person obtains the desired fruit. (53)
Having written or caused this scripture to be written, a person who worships it obtains the very same fruit as the worship of Viṣṇu himself. ||54||

May this most excellent secret, this exceedingly beautiful Purāṇa issued from the mouth of Vyāsa, which brings joy to the Vaiṣṇavas, long bring delight to the Discus-wielder, Murāri, the sustainer of all worlds, who is ever saluted with reverence by the foremost of the immortals and others. (55)

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Purāṇas, preceded by the Exposition of the Duties of the Ages," in the Kriyā-yoga-sāra section of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini.
